profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2026-03-28T20:16:41.696+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Heaven First
The "Hétú" Kūodìxiàng states:
"The Yì has the Supreme Ultimate,
which gives birth to the Two Modes.
Before the Two Modes separated,
their energy was chaotic and undifferentiated;
once the clear and turbid separated,
that which lay prostrate became Heaven,
that which lay supine became Earth."
The "Shìmíng" states:
"Heaven,
is level (tǎn),
level, high, and distant."
The "Wùlǐlùn" states:
"The energy of water and earth rises to become Heaven."
The "Ěryǎ" states:
"Spring is called the Azure Heaven (Cāngtiān),
summer is called the Vast Heaven (Hàotiān),
autumn is called the Compassionate Heaven (Míntiān),
winter is called the Upper Heaven (Shàngtiān)."
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
"The south is called the Blazing Heaven (Yántiān),
the southwest is called the Vermilion Heaven (Zhūtiān),
the west is called the Complete Heaven (Chéngtiān),
the northwest is called the Dark Heaven (Yōutiān),
the north is called the Mysterious Heaven (Xuántiān),
the northeast is called the Changing Heaven (Biàntiān).
The Nine Heavens are also called the Nine Fields.
The boundaries of the Nine Heavens are called the Nine Margins (jiǔyín; yín pronounced like yúqín, meaning 'bank').
Beyond the Nine Heavens, the next layer is called the Nine Terraces (jiǔgāi; gāi pronounced like jūhé, meaning 'terrace'), indicating there are nine successive terraces.
In general, Heaven is 201,678.5 lǐ and degrees distant from Earth.
The thickness of Earth is equal to the height of Heaven.
Heaven's north-south span is 203,057 lǐ and 25 paces,
the east-west span is shorter,
by four paces."
The "Zuǎnyào" states:
"East, west, south, and north are called the Four Directions,
the corners between the directions are called the Four Dimensions,
Heaven, Earth, and the Four Directions are called the Six Harmonies,
Heaven and Earth are called the Two Modes,
with humanity added, they are called the Three Powers,
the four directions and up/down are called Space,
past and present coming and going is called Time.
Some call Heaven and Earth the Cosmos,
for all things are born from the primordial energy of Heaven and Earth.
Heaven is called Qián,
Earth is called Kūn.
Heaven is round and its color is dark,
Earth is square and its color is yellow.
The sun and moon are called the Two Luminaries.

The five planets are called the Five Weft Stars (the five planets are: the eastern Suì [Jupiter], the southern Yínghuò [Mars], the western Dàbái [Venus], the northern Chén [Mercury], and the central Zhèn [Saturn]).
The sun, moon, and stars are called the Three Luminaries,
also called the Three Lights.
The sun, moon, and five planets are called the Seven Luminaries.
The Heavenly River is called the Heavenly Han (also called Yúnhàn, Xīnghàn, Héhàn, Qīnghàn, Yínhàn, Tiānjīn, Hànjīn, Qiǎnhé, Yínhé, Jiànghé).
The "Wǔjīng Tōngyì" states:
"The greatest of the heavenly spirits is called the Vast Heaven God-on-High (i.e., Yàopòbǎo), also called the Heavenly August Great Emperor, also called Tàiyī.

His assistants are the Five Emperors (the eastern Green Emperor Língwēiyǎng, the southern Red Emperor Chìpiǎonù, the western White Emperor Báizhāojù, the northern Black Emperor Yèguāngjì, the central Yellow Emperor Hánshūniǔ).
Rotating Canopy Leaning Pestle
Huán Tán's "Xīnlùn":
"Heaven is like a rotating canopy,
turning leftward,
the sun, moon, and stars follow it east and west."
The "Hétú" Tǐngzuǒfǔ states:
"A hundred generations later,
Earth will be higher than Heaven.
After a thousand years like this,
Heaven can lean on a pestle,
turbulent, none know its beginning or end."
Overturned Bowl Rotating Hub
Wáng Chōng's "Lùnhéng" states:
"Heaven is level and no different from Earth,
like the shape of an overturned bowl."
The "Húntiānyí" states:
"The Twenty-Eight Lodges,
half hidden, half visible,
Heaven rotates like the movement of a chariot hub."
Resembling a Canopy Like a Bamboo Hat
Liú Shì's "Zhènglìwèn" states:
"Zhuānxū created the armillary sphere,
Huángdì made the canopy-heaven,
taking Heaven to resemble a canopy."
Yú Bǐng's "Qióngtiānlùn" states:
"The shape of Heaven is like a bamboo hat,
covering the surface of Earth."
Jade Instrument Bronze Armillary
The "Shàngshūkǎo" Língyào states:
"Observing the rotation of the jade instrument,
dusk and dawn mark the times."
Zhèng's commentary states:
"Using jade to make the armillary sphere,
thus it is called the jade instrument."
Hàn Famous Ministers Memorial states:
"The bronze instrument currently used by the history officials at the observation platform,
is the method of the spherical heaven."
The "Shùzhēngjì" states:
"South of Cháng'ān is the Spirit Terrace,
upon which is a bronze armillary sphere."
Establishing Positions Displaying Images
The "Yì" states:
"Heaven and Earth establish their positions,
and change moves within them."
It also states:
"Heaven displays images,
revealing good and bad fortune,
and the sage takes them as models."
Lofty and Bright Constant Observation
The "Lǐjì" states:
"The way of Heaven and Earth,
is vast,
thick,
lofty,
bright,
far-reaching,
and enduring."
Zhèng's commentary states:
"This speaks of their goodness manifesting in accomplished merit."
The "Yì" states:
"The way of Heaven and Earth,
is constant observation;
the way of the sun and moon,
is constant brightness."
Three Bodies Six Energies
Cài Yōng's "Tiānwénzhì" speaks of three theories of the celestial body:
first, the Gāubǐ (gnomon shadow),
second, Xuānyè (expansive night),
third, Húntiān (spherical heaven).
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Heaven has six energies,
which descend to produce the five flavors."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"The six energies are:
yin,
yang,
wind,
rain,
darkness,
brightness."
Four Pillars Nine Fields
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"In ancient times, Nǚwā,
smelted five-colored stones to patch the azure heaven,
and severed the legs of the Ao to set up the four pillars."
Gāo Yòu's commentary states:
"Ao,
is a great turtle.
Heaven collapsed and tilted,
so the legs of the Ao were used to prop it up.
The Nine Fields, see above."
Nine Layers Eight Pillars
The "Chǔcí" states:
"Round, then nine-layered,
who measured and planned it?"
Wáng Yì's commentary states:
"It says Heaven is round and has nine layers,
who measured and planned it and knew this?"
Also:
"Where are the eight pillars placed?
Why is the southeast deficient?"
The commentary states:
"It says Heaven has eight mountains as pillars."
Broken Pillars Severed Cords
The "Lièzǐ" states:
"Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū to become emperor,
angrily struck Mount Bùzhōu,
broke the pillar of Heaven,
severed the cords of Earth.
Heaven tilted to the northwest,
and the sun, moon, and stars moved there;
Earth was deficient in the southeast,
and all rivers and waters flowed there."
Sòng Yù's "Dàyánfù" states:
"A mighty warrior, suddenly severing the cords of Heaven,
the Northern Dipper wrenched, Mount Tài leveled."
Raining Grain Descending Black Millet
The "Zhōushū" states:
"In the time of Shénnóng, Heaven rained grain,
and farmers plowed and planted it."
Sūn Shì's "Ruìyìngtú" states:
"In Shùn's time, Hòujì sowed and planted,
and Heaven descended black millet and double-grained millet.
Therefore the Odes say:
'Heaven sent down the fine seeds,
the black millet and the double-grained millet.'"
Descending Barley — Lowering Grain
The Book of Han says:
"Láimóu
is barley.
It first descended from Heaven,
to bring harmony,
and restore Heaven's aid."
The Kong Congzi says:
"King Wèi asked Zǐ Shùn:
'I have heard
that in ancient times, Heaven, in its divine wonder, favored Hòujì
and sent down for him fine grain,
and thus Zhōu rose to prosperity.'"
Qǐ State's Worry — Qín Mì's Reply
The Liezi says:
"In the state of Qǐ, there was once a man who worried that the sky would collapse,
leaving him with nowhere to dwell,
and he neglected sleep and food.
Another man worried about his worry,
and enlightened him, saying:
'The sky is merely accumulated qi;
how could it collapse?'
The man said:
'If the sky is indeed accumulated qi,
then the sun, moon, and stars should not fall.'
The enlightener said:
'The sun and moon are luminous bodies within the qi;
even if they were to fall,
they could cause no harm.'"
The Records of Shu says:
"Wú sent Zhāng Wēn on a diplomatic mission.
Wēn asked Qín Mì:
'Does Heaven have a head?'
Mì said:
'It does.'
Wēn said:
'In which direction?'
Mì said:
'The Book of Songs says:
"He turns His gaze to look westward."
From this we infer
its head is in the west.'
Wēn said:
'Does Heaven have ears?'
Mì said:
'Heaven resides on high yet hears the lowly.
The Book of Songs says:
"The crane cries in the ninefold marsh,
its voice is heard by Heaven."
If it had no ears,
how could it hear?'
Wēn said:
'Does Heaven have feet?'
Mì said:
'The Book of Songs says:
"Heaven's steps are difficult."
If it had no feet,
how could it step?'
Wēn said:
'Does Heaven have a surname?'
Mì said:
'Its surname is Liú.'
Wēn said:
'How do you know?'
Mì said:
'Its son's surname is Liú;
from this I know.'"
Naming Yú — Opening Wèi
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Shū Yú's mother dreamed that Heaven said to King Wǔ:
'I command you to bear a son named Yú,
and I will grant him Yú.'
When the child was born,
there was the character 'Yú' on his palm,
so he was thus named."
The Zuo Tradition says:
"The Marquis of Jìn granted Bì Wàn the land of Wèi.
The diviner Yǎn said:
'Bì Wàn's descendants are sure to become great.
Wàn (ten thousand)
is a number of fullness;
Wèi
is a great name.
To begin the reward with this
is Heaven opening the way.'"
Granting Chǔ — Bestowing Qín
The Zuo Tradition says:
"Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the ruler of Chǔ in Sòng.
The people of Sòng reported their crisis to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to rescue them.
Bó Zōng said:
'It cannot be done.
Heaven is currently granting favor to Chǔ;
we cannot contend with it.
Though Jìn is strong,
can it defy Heaven?'"
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
"In ancient times, the Heavenly Emperor was pleased with Duke Mù of Qín and received him in audience.
He then made a golden register
and bestowed this land for his use,
cutting it from the region of Chúnshǒu,
so that its position aligned directly with Heaven's carriage."
Oily Clouds — Fattening Rain
Mencius says:
"Clouds gather thickly,
and rain falls abundantly."
The Zuo Tradition says:
"A small state looking up to a great state
is like the hundred grains looking up to the fattening rain."
Elm Stars — Cassia Moon
An ancient Music Bureau poem says:
"What is there in Heaven?
Clearly planted are white elms."
Yú Xǐ's "Discourse on Stabilizing Heaven" says:
"Common legend says there is an immortal's cassia tree in the moon.
Now, observing its first growth,
one sees the immortal's feet;
gradually they take form,
and the cassia tree grows later."
Jade-Disc Moon — Pearl Dew
The "Central Prognostication" chapter of the Book of Documents says:
"When Heaven and Earth first opened,
on the jiǎzǐ winter solstice,
the sun and moon were like suspended jade discs,
and the five planets were like strung pearls."
Lǐ Yóng's "Rhapsody on Stirred Emotions" says:
"Wind touches the waves, forming patterned ripples;
dew moistens the cinnabar, congealing into pearls."
Purple Lightning — Patterned Rainbow
Cáo Pī's "Poem on Continuous Rain" says:
"Great rain persists for ten days,
gloom shrouds the four regions in darkness.
Purple lightning flashes at the window,
swift thunder rumbles across the sky."
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on Sunny Spring" says:
"The gentle valley breeze blows,
the green spring flows abundantly.
Crimson clouds cast their light,
a patterned rainbow arches across the sky."
Silken Clouds — Threadlike Rain
The "Comprehensive Hexagram Divination" chapter of the Book of Changes says:
"At the beginning of autumn, as yin is kindled,
clouds emerge like red silk."
Zhāng Xié's poem says:
"The autumn wind fans the scene's season,
crimson clouds herald the yin period.
Soaring clouds resemble a leaky net,
dense rain is like scattered threads."
Wind Steeds — Cloud Chariot
Zhòngcháng Tǒng's poem says:
"Spring clouds are the horses,
autumn wind is the team.
Reining them does not slow them,
driving them does not weary them."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's ancient Music Bureau poem says:
"I wish to obtain a divine person,
to ride a cloud chariot drawn by white deer,
ascending to the gate of Heaven,
to come bestow the divine medicine."
Brocade Clouds — Gauze Mist
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on Clouds" says:
"Some are embroidered with brocade patterns,
subtle and exquisite."
Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Goddess" says:
"She stirs the gauze mist, pacing slowly,
brushing her jade pendants with a tinkling sound."
Patterned Dew — Luminous Wind
The "Assisting Period" chapter of the Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"Martial dew spreads openly;
civil dew sinks deep."
Sòng Jūn's commentary says:
"When sweet dew appears in a state,
if it spreads openly,
the people esteem martial prowess;
if it is patterned and splendid,
then the sweet dew is thick and heavy."
The Songs of Chǔ says:
"Rivers and valleys wind and flow murmuringly;
the luminous wind turns the huì orchid, rippling over the lofty lán."
Wáng Yì's commentary says:
"It means after the rain, the sun emerges and wind blows,
so the plants and trees have a sheen."
Auspicious Wind — Sweet Rain
The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents says:
Green Clouds and Purple Rainbows
Féng Yǎn's "Fu on Expressing My Aspirations" says:
"Driving a team of white hornless dragons I gallop,
With trailing green clouds forming a canopy."
Yáng Xióng's "Canon of Supreme Mystery" says:
"A purple rainbow encircles the sun,
Its swiftness cannot be severed."
Cháng'é's Moon and the Maiden's Wind
"Huáinánzǐ" says:
"Yì requested the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West.
Yì's wife Cháng'é stole it and fled to the moon,
Taking refuge there,
She became the toad,
And is the essence of the moon."
"Biography of Guǎn Gōngmíng" says:
"Gōngmíng was in Qīnghé.
At that time there was a great drought,
He was asked when it would rain.
He said that tonight there would be heavy rain.
As the day approached dusk,
There was not a trace of cloud in the sky.
Everyone clamored and mocked Gōngmíng.
Gōngmíng said that on the trees there was already a maiden's gentle breeze,
And dark birds were singing in harmony among the branches.
If the maiden's wind reverses,
And the dark birds scatter in flight,
Then the response will arrive.
In a moment, dark clouds gathered from all directions,
And a torrential downpour poured forth."
White Crane Clouds and Yellow Sparrow Wind
"Changes: Comprehensive Hexagram Divinations" says:
"At the Beginning of Spring, the Clear Yang,
Clouds emerge from the Fang constellation like accumulated water.
At the Spring Equinox, the True Yang,
Clouds emerge from the Zhāng constellation like white cranes."
Zhōu Chù's "Records of Local Conditions" says:
"The heavy rain in the fifth month,
Is called the Branch-Washing rain.
The wind that arises in the fifth month,
Lasts for six days before ceasing.
The Yellow Sparrow Wind:
At this time, sea fish transform into yellow sparrows,
Hence it is named thus.
The above generally records Heaven."
Jìn Chéng Gōngsuí's "Fu on Heaven and Earth"
Heaven and Earth are supremely divine,
Difficult to define with a single term.
Thus, speaking of their substance,
They are called the Two Modes;
Speaking of their nature,
They are called the Soft and the Hard;
Speaking of their colors,
They are called the Dark and the Yellow;
Speaking of their names,
They are called Heaven and Earth.
As for the dark signs forming patterns,
The arrayed lodgings having order,
The Three Luminaries shining like torches,
The Five Planets radiating doubly bright,
The multitude of stars shifting and encircling the pole,
The Dipper moving and pointing the direction,
The White Tiger sometimes stationed at Shēn and Mǎo,
The Azure Dragon trailing its tail at Xīn and Fáng,
The Dark Turtle hiding its head at Nǚ and Xū,
The Vermilion Bird spreading its wings at Zhěn and Zhāng,
The walls and screens linked like strung pearls,
The Three Steps uneven like geese in flight,
Xuānyuán spread out in a curved array,
Shètí standing like tripods facing each other.
Jìn Fù Xuán's "Poem on the Two Modes"
When the Two Modes first parted, the Primordial Breath was clear,
The arrayed lodgings hung their images, the Six Positions formed.
Sun and moon flow west, their light journeys east,
The myriad things, vast and varied, each with its distinct name.
The sage, concerned for the age, thinks of all living beings.
Also, "Poem in Praise of Heaven"
How vigorously Heaven moves!
Sun and moon leave no lofty trace.
All rivers rush to the sea,
The Three Luminaries revolve through Tài and Méng.
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Chapter on the Three Lights"
The Three Lights hang down their manifest signs,
Heaven and Earth have their measures of the gnomon's shadow.
When the sound is harmonious, good echoes respond;
When the form is established, the shadow naturally clings.
The plain sun embraces the dark bird,
The bright moon cradles the divine hare.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem: Obtaining the Theme 'The Autumn River at Dawn, Gleaming'"
Gleaming, the long river at dawn,
Vast, the night clouds float.
The celestial road spans the autumn waters,
The starry Dipper turns through the night's flow.
The moon sets where Cháng'é descended,
The wind startles the Weaver Girl of autumn.
The Virtuous Star can still be seen,
But the immortal raft remains no longer.
Sòng Zhīwèn's "Song of the Bright River"
In the eighth month, cool breeze, the weather crystalline,
For ten thousand li, no clouds, the River of Stars bright.
At dusk seen from the south tower, clear and shallow,
At dawn setting over western hills, now lengthwise, now across.
Luòyáng's city towers rise at heaven's center,
The long river night after night within its thousand gates.
Covered walkways linking roof-ridges together obscure its view,
Painted halls and jade doors are especially fitting.
Before the mica screen, it first spreads wide,
Beyond the crystal curtain, it turns winding.
Vast, that shining circuit, like unbleached silk white,
Emerges again east of the city, meeting the southern path.
On the southern path, the traveler has gone, not to return.
Who knows tonight who pounds the winter clothes?
On mandarin-duck-patterned silk, sparse fireflies pass;
By the Magpie Bridge, a single wild goose flies.
The goose flies, fireflies pass, sorrow hard to cease,
I sit and watch the river tilt, gradually fading faint.
Already it can stretch and roll, yielding to floating clouds,
Not grudging its radiance, conceding to the bright moon.
The bright river can be gazed at, not approached,
I wish to board a raft and inquire of the ford.
Moreover, take the Weaver Girl's stone from the loom,
And again visit the fortune-teller of Chéngdū.
Guō Pú's "Eulogy on Explaining the Diagram of Heaven and Earth"
Sacrificing to Earth, burying the offering extensively;
Offering to Heaven in the suburbs, sending up smoke.
The breath ascends to the Supreme Unity,
The essence sinks to the Nine Springs.
The utmost reverence needs no ornament,
Illustrious virtue alone is fresh.
Sòng Hé Chéngtiān's "In Praise of Heaven"
Xuānyuán altered things,
To order Heaven and humankind.
Róng Chéng created the calendar,
Dà Náo initiated the time-markers.
The Dragon's assembly has its sequence,
The Star Chronogram thus divides.
Sun, Part Two
The *Shuōwén* states:
"The sun is
substantial,
the essence of the great yang.
The character is composed of ○ and one,
it is pictographic,
and also symbolizes the ruler."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The sun emerges from Yánggǔ,
bathes in Xiánchí,
brushes against Fúsāng,
this is called dawn's light.
Ascending above Fúsāng
(Fúsāng,
the wilds of the east),
then it begins to travel,
this is called fěimíng
fěi
míng
(fěimíng,
approaching brightness).
Reaching Qū'ē
(Qū'ē,
a mountain name),
this is called morning light.
Arriving at Zēngquán
(Zēng,
meaning layered,
at breakfast time in the east, a place with abundant water,
hence called Zēngquán),
this is called early meal.
Stopping at Sāngyě,
this is called late meal.
Reaching Héngyáng,
this is called mid-morning.
Facing Kūnwú
(Kūnwú Hill is in the south),
this is called high noon.
Resting at Niǎocì
(Niǎocì,
a mountain name in the southwest),
this is called minor shift.
Reaching Bēigǔ
(Bēigǔ,
a great ravine in the southwest),
this is called afternoon.
Turning at Nǚjì
(Nǚjì,
the yin of the west),
this is called major shift.
Passing by Quányú,
this is called high pestle
(meaning not yet dark,
still receiving the earlier pestling,
called high pestle).
Halting at Lián
làn
shí,
this is called low pestle
(Liánshí,
a mountain name in the northwest.
Meaning about to become dark,
receiving the final pestling below,
hence called low pestle).
Here stops Xīhé,
here rest the six chī-dragons,
this is called suspended chariot
(the sun rides a chariot drawn by six dragons,
with Xīhé driving it.
The sun reaching here approaches Yúquán,
Xīhé here turns back the six chī-dragons).
Approaching Yúquán,
this is called dusk.
Sinking into Ménggǔ,
this is called settled dusk.
The sun enters Yān
yān
zī
(pronounced zī,
also called Luòtáng Mountain).
Passes through Xìliǔ
(Xìliǔ,
the wilds of the west),
enters the pool of Yúquán,
and dawns at the shore of Ménggǔ
(Ménggǔ,
the waters of Méngsì).
The sun in the west casts its light upon the treetops,
this is called sāngyú."
Meaning its light is upon the sāng and yú trees,
the above is all text from the *Huáinánzǐ*.
Also, the *Ěryǎ* states:
"East to where the sun emerges is Tàipíng,
west to where the sun enters is Tàiméng."
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Names for the sun include Yàolíng,
also called Zhūmíng,
also called Dōngjūn,
also called Dàmíng,
also called Yángwū.
The sun's charioteer is called Xīhé."
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"In the waters southeast of the sea,
within Gānquán,
there is the country of Xīhé.
There is a woman named Xīhé,
wife of Dìjùn.
She gave birth to ten suns,
and often bathed the suns in Gānquán."
Guō Pú's annotation:
"Xīhé could give birth to suns,
hence the sun is the child of Xīhé.
Yáo therefore established the office of Xīhé,
to oversee the four seasons."
The *Zuǎnyào* states:
"Sunlight is called jǐng
(the light of stars and the moon
is also generally called jǐng).
The sun's shadow is called guǐ,
the sun's vapor is called xiàn
(pronounced nǎi jiàn fǎn).
The *Shī* says:
'Seeing the xiàn means melting.'"
The *Máo Zhuàn* states:
"Xiàn,
is the vapor of the sun."
The sun just risen is called xù,
the sun at daybreak is called xī
(great brightness is called xīn).
The *Shī* says:
'Without the sun, it does not dry.'"
Xī,
means dry,
meaning the sun at daybreak dries damp things.
The sun's warmth is called xù,
at noon it is called tíngwǔ,
in the wèi hour it is called dié,
late in the day is called gàn,
the sun about to set is called bómù,
the sun setting in the west, its light reflecting back to the east,
is called fǎnjǐng,
when the reflection is above it is called fǎnjǐng,
when below it is called dàojǐng.
There is the beloved sun,
the feared sun
(beloved,
is the winter sun;
feared,
is the summer sun).
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
'The winter sun is lovable,
the summer sun is fearsome.'"
The lingering sun
(lingering,
is the spring sun).
The *Shī* says:
'The spring day lingers.'"
Adorning Heaven / Emerging from Earth
The *Yì* says:
"The sun and moon adorn heaven,
the hundred grains, grasses, and trees adorn earth."
The *Wénzǐ* says:
"The sun emerges from the earth,
and the myriad things multiply and thrive."
Joined Jade Discs / Linked Pearls
The *Hànshū* says:
"The Tàichū calendar,
its new moon, first quarter, full moon, and last quarter are all most precise,
the sun and moon are like joined jade discs."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"Ruòmù is west of Jiànmù,
at its tip are ten suns,
their splendor illuminates the earth."
Gāo Yòu's annotation says:
"Tip,
means end.
At the tip of Ruòmù are ten suns,
shaped like linked pearls,
their radiant light shines upon the land below."
Double Earrings and Overlapping Halos The *Miscellaneous Military Texts* states:
"A solar crown is like a half-halo;
by principle, there should be a crown above the sun.
If there are two earrings in the pattern, it is especially auspicious."
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
"When the full moon has overlapping halos,
illuminating all six directions,
is this not the power of the sun and moon?"
Fire Essence, Yang Virtue Fàn Zǐ Jìrán states:
"The sun
is the essence of fire.
Fire manifests its light outwardly,
governing the day.
It resides in the day and brings brightness,
dwelling in illumination and possessing radiance."
The *Chūnqiū Nèishì* states:
"The sun
is the mother of yang virtue."
Sun at Noon Twice, Sun Retreats Three Shelters The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Emperor Chéng asked Liú Xiàng:
'Popular legend says that when Emperor Wén was summoned to the throne,
he arrived late,
and could not be established immediately,
so the sun stood at noon twice.'
Liú Xiàng replied:
'Emperor Wén ascended the throne young;
it is impossible for the sun to be at noon twice.'" The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"Lord Lǔyáng was engaged in conflict with Hán.
The battle was intense as the sun set.
He raised his spear and brandished it,
and the sun retreated three shelters for him."
Split Moments, Inch Shadows Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Táo Kǎn was diligent and orderly from youth to adulthood,
striving tirelessly.
He often told people:
'The great sage Yǔ
cherished every inch of shadow.
As for ordinary people,
they should cherish every split moment.'" Pān Ní's poem says:
"A foot-long jade is easily lost,
an inch of shadow is hard to surpass.
Achieving fame is not my concern;
what I enjoy is the qin and books."
Qilin Fighting, Deer Shedding Antlers The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"When a tiger roars, the valley wind arrives;
when qilin fight, the sun and moon are eclipsed."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary states:
"The qilin,
a beast with large horns,
thus interacts with the sun."
It also says:
"The sun
is the ultimate yang,
so in spring and summer, all beasts shed their horns."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"On the winter solstice, elk antlers shed;
on the summer solstice, deer antlers shed."
Jūlíng, Ménggǔ The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"In the great wilderness, there is a mountain
named Jūlíng.
At the extreme east, Límào,
where the sun and moon rise.
Ménggǔ is mentioned above."
High Pestle, Lower Branches High Pestle is mentioned above.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"In the great wilderness lies Tānggǔ.
Above it grows the Fúsāng tree,
where the ten suns bathe.
Nine suns reside on the lower branches,
one sun resides on the upper branch,
and all are crowned with crows."
Measuring Shadows, Gauging Sun-dials The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"The Grand Minister of Education uses the method of the earth gnomon to measure the depth of the land,
correcting the sun's shadow to find the center of the earth.
If the sun is to the south, the shadow is short and there is much heat;
if the sun is to the north, the shadow is long and there is much cold."
Lù Shìhéng's *Imitated Linked Pearls* states:
"Emotion manifests in things;
though distant, it remains sparse.
Spirit is hidden within form;
though near, it is dense.
Thus, by measuring the heavens and gauging the sun-dial,
length and shortness can be measured;
by facing the river and gauging the water,
depth and shallowness are hard to fathom."
Jiànmù, Jùsōng The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
"South of the Báirén,
beneath the Jiànmù tree,
at noon there is no shadow,
for it is the center of heaven and earth."
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"In the great wilderness, there is a square mountain,
upon which grows a green pine,
named the Jùgé pine,
where the sun and moon rise and set."
White Rainbow Pierces, Red Birds Flank The *Hànshū* states:
"Zōu Yáng submitted a memorial to King Xiào of Liáng, saying:
'In the past, Jīng Kē admired the righteousness of Yān Dān,
and a white rainbow pierced the sun,
causing the crown prince to fear him.'" The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"In the first year of Duke Āi,
in Chǔ, there were clouds resembling many red birds,
flanking the sun and flying for three days.
The King of Chǔ sent someone to ask the Grand Historian of Zhōu,
and the Grand Historian said:
'This concerns the king's person.
If you perform a yíng sacrifice,
it can be transferred to the Prime Minister or the Minister of War.'
The king said:
'Transferring a disease of the heart and abdomen to the limbs—
what good would that do?'
The king did not perform the sacrifice and died.
Confucius said:
'King Zhāo did not lose his state;
how fitting!'"
Kuāfù Abandons His Staff, Lǔyáng Brandishes His Spear The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"Kuāfù chased the sun,
and when thirsty, drank from the Hé and Wèi rivers.
It was not enough,
so he went north to drink from the great marsh.
Before reaching it,
he died of thirst on the road,
and his abandoned staff transformed into the Dèng Forest."
Guō Pú's commentary states:
"Kuāfù
was a divine being,
said to be able to reverse the sun's shadow."
The story of Lǔyáng is already mentioned above in the note on 'three shelters.'
Like a Steed's Pace, Resembling a Duck's Flight Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* states:
"The sun travels a thousand lǐ by day
and a thousand lǐ by night.
A steed also travels a thousand lǐ in a day.
Thus, the sun's speed is similar to a steed's pace."
It also says:
"The sun and moon travel twenty-six thousand lǐ in one day and night,
resembling the flight of a crested duck."
Cháng'ān is near, the sun's wheel is far.
Liú Shào's "Biographies of Young Children" states:
"Emperor Míng of Jìn, personal name Shào,
was the crown prince of Emperor Yuán.
Initially, when Emperor Yuán was the Governor of Jiāngdōng stationed in Yángzhōu,
the Central Plains were in chaos and turmoil.
Someone came from Cháng'ān.
Emperor Yuán inquired about news from Luòyáng,
and secretly shed tears.
The Emperor was several years old at the time,
and asked the reason for the weeping.
He was fully informed of the intention to cross east.
Thereupon, he asked the Emperor:
'In your opinion, how does Cháng'ān compare to the sun in terms of distance?'
He replied:
'I have not heard of anyone coming from beside the sun,
only of people coming from Cháng'ān,
so it is clearly evident.'
Emperor Yuán was impressed.
The next day, he assembled his ministers for a banquet,
and posed this question again.
Emperor Míng then considered the sun to be nearer,
and Emperor Yuán, moved,
asked why his words differed from the previous day's.
He replied:
'Raising my head, I do not see Cháng'ān,
I only see the sun,
therefore I know it is near.'
The Emperor was greatly pleased."
The "Lièzǐ" states:
"Confucius was traveling east,
and saw two children arguing.
He asked them the reason.
One child said:
'I consider the sun to be nearer when it first rises,
and farther at midday;
when the sun first rises it is as large as a carriage wheel,
but at midday it is like a plate or bowl.
Is this not because what is far appears small and what is near appears large?'
The other child said:
'When the sun first rises it is cool and refreshing,
but at midday it is like dipping into hot water.
Is this not because what is near is hot and what is far is cool?'
Confucius could not decide.
The two children laughed and said:
'Who said you were knowledgeable!'"
Emperor Tàizōng Wénhuángdì's "Poem on the Clear Light of the Autumn Sun, Bestowed upon Fáng Xuánlíng"
Autumn dew condenses on the high palm,
morning light ascends the verdant peaks.
Unevenly beautiful are the twin towers,
shining full upon the layered gates.
The immortal chariot follows the wheel's turn,
the divine crow carries the light in flight.
Facing the waves, its colors are unfixed,
entering crevices, it has a round glow.
Still, it should be like the sunflower's heart,
its leaning leaves naturally depend on each other.
Also, "Poem on the White Sun Half Over the Western Mountains"
The crimson wheel does not linger,
birds in flight, how could they pause?
Peak clouds gradually descend,
stream shadows inch by inch grow.
Huo leaves turn with the light,
sunflower hearts follow the shine, leaning.
Evening mist holds the tree's hue,
roosting birds mingle with flowing sounds.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on the Morning Sun"
Round and round, it emerges beyond the sky,
brilliantly rising over layered peaks.
Its light follows the waves, high and low,
its shadow chases the trees, light and dense.
Liáng Lǐ Jìng's "Poem on the Distant Sun"
First overlooking from Dōngyuè's view,
soon ascending Ruòmù's branches.
How could duckweed fruit match its color?
Even a folded fan feels ashamed of its roundness.
Northern woods first gleam with its light,
round windows mirror the early dawn.
Illuminating the courtyard, the last snow melts,
reflecting on eaves, drips hang down.
Lingering around flowering trees,
shimmering full in spring ponds.
Willow shade just begins to sway,
curtain shadows again appear scattered.
Could Zēngquán ever halt its course?
Sāngyú suddenly arrives here.
Turning the spear, how can it be aimed?
Long ropes cannot tether it.
My soaring heart loves the setting scene,
clear feasts regret the fleeing light.
Warm radiance is but received in vain,
deep in my heart, I secretly know.
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Poem on the Sun, in Response to the Command"
Halting the carriage, galloping to Yánggǔ,
shining past the railings, emerging from Fúsāng.
How fortunate is the garden sunflower,
its leaning leaves offer to the parting light.
Chén Xú Líng's "Poem on Sunlight"
Morning glow sparkles on the winding pond,
evening shine fills the western slope.
Again there is midday scenery,
on the river, gleaming light appears.
Sometimes it rests with high waves,
suddenly it follows fine ripples, shifting.
Once upon a carved beam,
how can it compare to Fúsāng's branches?
Suí Kāng Mèng's "Poem on the Sun, in Response to Prince Zhào's Instruction"
The golden crow rises with dawn's breath,
jade railings ripple with morning light.
First sailing the seas of Fúsāng,
reflecting back on Ruòhuá's pond.
Luòpǔ fully opens its mirror,
Héngshān half hides its round shape.
Sharing joy, receiving the beloved light,
together cherishing each moment's passing.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem in Response on the Noon Sun"
High sky, pure autumn colors,
long Milky Way turns the sun's chariot.
Jade trees' shade first stands upright,
tóng guī's shadow not yet slanting.
Green canopies fly in round reflections,
bright mirrors emit light blossoms.
Reaching zenith truly shows auspiciousness,
all look up to distant jade radiance.
Chǔ Liàng's "Poem in Response on the Noon Sun"
The sun's chariot pauses at noon,
floating water clock not yet shifting its light.
Sunlight without setting glow,
tree shadows precisely centered.
Withered grass appears slightly drooping,
dry leaves look sparse, as if in doubt.
Ashamed of napping with the classics box,
temporarily loosening court attire.
Dǒng Sīgōng's "Poem on the Sun"
Vast sea, ten branches of light,
Xuānpǔ, double wheels of celebration.
Hibiscus blooms at morning pillars,
water chestnut colors flip in the morning mirror.
Suddenly met by startling wind's drift,
naturally there are floating clouds reflecting.
Moreover, all people look up to it,
no need to wield a spear to set it right.
Moon, Third
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The moon is
the essence of the great yīn."
The Shìmíng states:
"Yuè (moon)
means quē (deficiency),
meaning that when full, it returns to deficiency."
The Hànshū states:
"The moon,
at the beginning of summer and the summer solstice, travels along the southern red path,
called the Southern Land;
at the beginning of autumn and the autumn equinox, it travels along the western white path,
called the Western Land;
at the beginning of winter and the winter solstice, it travels along the northern black path,
called the Northern Land.
At the equinoxes, their paths are the same;
at the solstices, they pass each other.
When it is seen in the west at the end of the month, it is called tiǎo;
when it is seen in the east at the beginning of the month, it is called nǜ,
also called cènì.
Tiǎo is pronounced with the fanqie spelling 'tā liǎo fǎn',
nǜ is pronounced with the fanqie spelling 'nǚ liù fǎn'.
Tiǎo
describes a vigorous and swift appearance.
Nǜ,
describes a shrinking and delayed appearance.
Cènì is like shrinking and timidity,
also a delayed appearance.
The Shìmíng states:
"Fěi,
is when the moon has not yet become bright.
Pò,
is when the moon first begins to have a faint glow.
Following a long month,
the moon on the third day is called pò.
Following a short month,
the moon on the third day is called fěi.
Fěi is pronounced fěi.
Shuò,
is the name for the beginning of the month.
Shuò,
means sū (revival),
the moon dies and then revives to life.
Huì,
is the name for the end of the month.
Huì,
means huī (ashes).
Death becomes ashes,
the moonlight exhausted resembles it.
Xián,
is the name for the half-moon,
its shape is curved on one side,
straight on the other,
like a drawn bowstring.
Wàng,
is the name for the full moon,
the sun and moon gaze at each other from afar."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The moon has another name, Yèguāng (Night Light).
The moon's charioteer is called Wàngshū,
also called Xiān'ā."
Water Vapor Metal Essence
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"The sun and moon,
are the emissaries of heaven.
The cold qi of accumulated yīn,
over time becomes water,
the essence of water vapor is the moon."
The Hétú Dì Lǎn Xī says:
"The moon is
the essence of metal."
Observing the Míngjiá Viewing the Cassia
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"In ancient times, Emperor Xuān listened to the phoenix's cry to tune the pitch pipes,
and Emperor Táng Yáo observed the míngjiá plant to know the moon's phases."
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"During Yáo's time, there was a grass that grew flanking the steps,
on the first day of each month, it would produce one pod,
by the middle of the month, it would have produced fifteen pods.
After the sixteenth day,
one pod would fall each day,
until by the end of the month, they were all gone,
and if the month was short, one pod would remain.
The ruler used this to observe the calendar,
it responded in harmony and grew,
considered an auspicious sign for Yáo,
named it míngjiá,
also called lìjiá,
also called xiānmáo."
Yú Xǐ's Āntiān Lùn says:
"Common legend says there is a cassia tree and an immortal in the moon,
now observe its early growth,
one sees the immortal's feet,
gradually taking shape,
the cassia tree grows later."
Joined Discs Broken Ring
Joined discs has been mentioned above.
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Wáng Shēng said the moon is not round when first born,
and after it has waned,
looking at it should be like a three-inch mirror.
Slowly it turns larger,
it should not be like a broken ring,
gradually becoming full."
Golden Hare Jade Toad
The Hétú Dì Lǎn Xī says:
"The moon is
the essence of metal."
Also, Zhāng Héng's Língxiàn says:
"The moon is
formed from yīn essence into a beast,
resembling a hare or toad."
Also, Liú Xiàochuò's poem says:
"Bright, bright the moon of the fifteenth,
its shadow falls upon the tall trees.
Clustered branches half hide the jade toad,
dense leaves reflect the golden hare."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì says:
"South of the Yíng Sea there is the Jīnluán Observatory,
adorned with many treasures.
On the left hangs fire crystal as the sun,
carved from black jade into a crow.
On the right, water crystal serves as the moon,
carved from green jade into a toad and hare.
There are also divine dragons and phoenixes,
lingering by its side."
Round Disc Broken Mirror
Yǔ Sùzhī's Yù Zàn says:
"Round disc like the moon-mirror,
fine jades scattered like stars.
They bloom in beauty at Lántián,
their truth extracted from Jīng Hé."
An ancient poem says:
"Where is the executioner's block now?
Upon the mountain, there is another mountain.
When will the broadsword's head return?
A broken mirror flies in the sky."
Three Earrings Double Halo
Jūnguó Zhānhòu says:
"If the moon has three earrings,
high ministers will have joy.
If the moon is crowned and then haloed again,
the world will have joy."
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù says:
"When Hàn Míngdì was crown prince,
musicians sang four stanzas,
to praise the crown prince's virtue.
The first was called 'The Sun's Double Radiance',
the second 'The Moon's Double Halo',
the third 'The Stars' Double Brilliance',
the fourth 'The Sea's Double Moisture'."
Like a Hook Like a Disc
Méi Chéng's Yuè Fù says:
"Ah, splendid bright moon,
emerging at the heart of the sky.
Hidden behind round cliffs, it resembles a hook,
veiled by long battlements, it appears like a mirror."
Hé Yǎn's Yuè Fù says:
"The distant sun is like a mirror,
the full moon is like a disc."
Square Pearl Broken Halo
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"When Fāngzhū sees the moon,
it moistens and produces water."
Gāo Yòu's commentary says:
"Fāngzhū,
is a yīn suì, a large clam.
Rub it until hot and point it towards the moon,
then water will be produced."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary says:
"Zhū,
means pearl.
Fāng,
is its name."
The Huáinánzǐ also says:
"Draw with ashes and the moon's halo will break."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary says:
"When there is military encirclement and defense, the moon will have a halo.
Using reed ashes to form a ring,
break it on one side,
then the moon's halo will also break above."
Golden Waves and Jade Radiance
The Book of Hàn states:
"The moon shifts its splendor with golden waves,
the sun's brilliance shines with radiant clarity."
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
"On the winter solstice of the jiǎzǐ year,
the moon is like a suspended jade disc."
Hé Yǎn's "Rhapsody on the Moon" states:
"Though the sun and moon are like jade discs,
they take light as their form."
Northern Hall and Western Garden
Lù Jī's poem states:
"Peacefully resting in the northern hall,
the bright moon enters my window.
Its shining leaves lingering radiance,
yet grasping it does not fill my hand."
Cáo Zhí's poem states:
"On a clear night, I roam the western garden,
flying canopies follow one another.
The bright moon clarifies its pure reflection,
the constellations are scattered and uneven."
Residing Toad and Gazing Hare
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"The word 'moon' (yuè) means 'defect' (quē),
and it is furnished with a toad and a hare because
yin and yang dwell together as a pair,
illuminating how yang controls yin,
and how yin relies on yang."
The Chǔcí states:
"What virtue does the night light possess,
that it dies and is born again?
What benefit does it seek,
that a gazing hare resides in its belly?"
Like a Silk Fan and Like a Jade Hook
Bān Jiéyú's "Song of Resentment" states:
"Freshly cut Qí plain silk,
bright and pure as frost and snow.
Tailored into a 'joined joy' fan,
perfectly round like the bright moon."
Bào Zhào's poem states:
"First appearing at the southwest tower,
slender like a jade hook.
Finally shining on the northwest steps,
lovely like moth eyebrows."
Illuminating Ruǎn's Curtain and Shining on Pān's Chamber
Ruǎn Jí's poem states:
"In the night, unable to sleep,
I rise and sit, strumming my singing lute.
The thin curtain is illuminated by the bright moon,
a clear breeze blows upon my lapel."
Pān Yuè's "Poem Mourning the Deceased" states:
"Bright, bright, the moon in the window,
shines upon the southern end of my chamber.
The clear shāng melody responds to autumn's arrival,
the humid heat fades with the season's end."
Wú Ox Pants and Wèi Magpie Flies
Liú Yìqìng's Shì Shuō states:
"Mǎn Fèn feared the wind.
While seated with Emperor Wǔ,
the north window had a glass screen,
actually solid yet appearing porous.
Fèn showed a troubled expression,
the emperor laughed at him.
Fèn replied:
'Your subject is like a Wú ox,
seeing the moon and panting.'"
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's "Short Song" states:
"The moon is bright, the stars are sparse,
crows and magpies fly south.
Circling the tree three times,
on which branch can they perch?"
Toad and Hare Together, Kylin and Dragon Fight
The Wǔjīng Tōngyì states:
"Why are there a hare and a toad in the moon?
The hare
represents yin;
the toad,
represents yang.
And being together with the hare
illustrates how yin is tied to yang."
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"When kylin and dragon fight,
the sun and moon undergo eclipses."
Sòng Dynasty Xiè Língyùn's "Rhapsody on Resenting the Dawn Moon"
Lying in the secluded chamber, what joy is there?
Extinguishing the splendid candle, I play with the dawn moon.
Yesterday, on the fifteenth, it was full,
today, on the sixteenth, it will wane.
Floating clouds part, gathering shimmering ripples,
brightly spreading its shine, exceptionally pure and clear.
The courtyard steps are like a mirror's reflection,
the corridor eaves are clear and transparent.
Sòng Dynasty Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Moon"
Prince Chén, having newly lost Yīng and Liú,
was solemnly grieving with much leisure.
Silently pained in heart,
unhappy in the middle of the night.
At that time, the slanting Milky Way marked the left boundary,
the Northern Dipper coursed southward.
White dew veiled the sky,
the pure moon flowed across the heavens.
Pondering deeply the Qí odes,
earnestly recalling the Chén verses.
Taking up brush and advancing tablets,
he commanded Zhòngxuān.
Zhòngxuān knelt and declared:
"Your servant has heard that the sun possesses yang virtue,
the moon possesses yin essence.
It monopolizes the supporting light from the eastern pool,
succeeds the radiant blossoms in the western sea.
It leads the dark hare to the emperor's terrace,
gathers the plain maiden in the rear courtyard.
As for when the air clears over the earth's surface,
clouds withdraw at heaven's edge.
The Dòngtíng Lake begins to ripple,
tree leaves lightly fall.
The pure essence rises, serene and far,
descending with clear radiance, gentle and mild.
The arrayed stars are obscured in their splendor,
the long river hides its gleam.
The soft earth congeals like snow,
the round void mirrors like water.
Connected galleries are frosted white,
surrounding steps are water-clear."
The song says:
"The beautiful one is distant, her sound and trace far removed,
separated by a thousand lǐ, yet we share this bright moon."
Emperor Tàizōng Wénhuángdì's "Poem on Viewing the Moon from Liáochéng"
The dark hare, the moon first brightens,
its clear radiance shines upon the slow night.
Reflecting clouds, its light temporarily hidden,
shining through trees, its light seems strung together.
Its full spirit rounds the cassia branches,
its waning orb lacks the mirror's colorful flaw.
Facing the city walls, its shadows scatter,
encircled by halos, heavy siege formations knit.
Halting the imperial carriage, overlooking the nine capitals,
standing to observe, the baleful aura is extinguished.
Liáng Dynasty Emperor Yuán's "Poem on Viewing the Moon in the River"
The clear river holds the bright moon,
the water's reflection seems to float in the sky.
If the wind came, one could sail upon it,
the current swift, it cannot form a perfect circle.
A Qín hook severed, then rejoined,
a Hé jade disc shattered, yet still connected.
Split silk follows the bank's grass,
slanting cassia pursues the moving boat.
Right here on this clear river,
there's no need for a hundred torches to blaze.
Liáng Dynasty Shěn Yuē's "Poem Chanting the Moon"
Moonlight descends upon the pure night,
the night pure, extinguishing dusty haze.
Square radiance finally enters the door,
round shadows come through the cracks.
High towers stir the thoughts of longing wives,
the western garden is roamed by superior talents.
Latticed windows reflect beaded tassels,
the main gate illuminates the green moss.
The secluded chamber is not yet dawn,
the clear light truly lingers far and wide.
Liáng Dynasty Zhū Chāo's "Poem on Viewing the Moon from a Boat"
The great river stretches a thousand lǐ wide,
the lone boat has no neighbors on four sides.
Only the moon from my former tower remains,
whether near or far, it surely follows me.
A faint light circles the halo,
thin fog swiftly shifts the orb.
If only it could always be like a fan,
it could brush away the dust of amorous songs."
Liáng Dynasty Yǔ Jiānwú's "Matching Poem on Viewing the Moon"
The cassia hall, the moon comes especially,
retaining its light, it attracts superior talents.
Round, following the eastern pearl from Hàn,
haloed, pursuing the Huáinán ashes.
Crossing the river, its light does not get wet,
moving its wheel, how could ruts be opened?
This night, facing the clear scene,
I still raise the final banquet cup.
Also, "Poem on Gazing at the Moon, Harmonizing with Assistant Editor Xú"
The moon lingers on the tower,
A sorrowful person at the window.
Its light on snow seems especially cold,
Facing flowers, its hue turns to spring.
Stars flow, sometimes entering the halo,
The cassia grows, about to encroach upon the wheel.
I wish to offer the tune 'Double Radiance',
To bear the dust on your singing fan.
Liáng Dynasty Dài Sōng's "Poem on the Moon's Double Wheel"
The crown prince belongs to the bright pair,
His deputy virtue manifests the double wheel.
The double wheel is not a halo,
The cassia full, the moon forever spring.
Sea pearls wax and wane completely,
Steps' míng grass obscured yet new.
The palace lady compares to a round fan,
Prince Cáo likens to the Luò River goddess.
Floating on the river, it seems like yielding jade,
Entering the door, it resembles molten silver.
Since ancient times, we've seen the jade rabbit,
But never heard of battling unicorns.
The northern hall—how could it fill the hand?
The western garden especially shines upon people.
Chén Dynasty Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on the Bright Moon Shining Through Thin Curtains"
The moon's cassia on the long river,
Its clear brilliance shines on the high tower.
Parting the curtain, it seems like shattered jade,
Beyond the screen, like a double hook.
Outside the window, its light is always full,
Within the curtains, its shadow briefly flows.
How could it compare to nights in the western garden,
Forever following the flying carriage canopy in wanderings?
Zhōu Dynasty Wáng Bāo's "Poem on the Moon over the Frontier Pass"
The moon is bright over the frontier pass at night,
Its sorrowful hue shines on the lonely city.
Half its shape resembles the Hàn battle array,
Its full shadow pursues the Hú soldiers.
Ashes cold, its color turns white,
Wind strong, a halo about to form.
Send word to the officer at the post station:
The traveler understands the rooster's crow.
Suí Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Poem on Gazing at the Moon from a Boat"
The boatman leaves home at night,
Sets sail and gazes at the moon's splendor.
Mountains bright, as if bearing snow,
Banks white, not due to sand.
Look at the Milky Way for the pearl oyster,
At the Star Bridge for the cassia blossom.
Ashes fly, the double halo breaks,
Míng grass falls, the lone wheel slants.
Dǒng Sīgōng's "Poem in Praise of the Moon"
The northern hall not yet settled for sleep,
The western garden, let us gaze afar.
Jade doors illuminate silk bed-curtains,
Pearl-framed windows brighten patterned screens.
Parting guests on the road to Cháng'ān,
Longing wives in the high tower.
My wish is that you not break your promise,
So the clear breeze may be visited in time.
Stars, Fourth
The Shìmíng says:
"Xīng (star) means
sàn (to scatter),
meaning they are arranged in positions and scattered about."
The Hànshū states:
"Stars are
the scattered qi of metal,
and correspond to humans.
All the essence of the myriad things
ascends to become the arrayed stars.
Chánggēng
is the Tàibái star."
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící says:
"Xīng (star) means jīng (essence),
the glory of yáng.
Yáng is the sun,
the sun divides to become stars,
hence the character is formed by 'sun' and 'born' to make 'star'."
Yùyáng
is the Láng star.
Jīnjī
is the Zhì star.
The Zhōuguān states:
"All celestial stars have corresponding terrestrial divisions among the provinces and states.
Jiǎo, Kàng, Dī correspond to Yǎnzhōu,
Fáng, Xīn to Yùzhōu,
Wěi, Jī to Yōuzhōu,
Dǒu, Qiānniú, Wùnǚ to Yángzhōu,
Xū, Wēi to Qīngzhōu,
Yíngshì, Dōngbì to Bìngzhōu,
Kuí
(pronounced kuí)
Lóu, Wèi to Xúzhōu,
Mǎo, Bì to Jìzhōu,
Zī, Shēn
(pronounced yǐ mí)
to Yìzhōu,
Dōngjǐng, Guǐ to Yōngzhōu,
Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng to Sānhé,
Yì, Zhěn to Jīngzhōu."
Kānyú practitioners say:
"Xuánxiāo corresponds to the division of Qí,
Xīngjì to Wú-Yuè,
Xīmù zhī jīn to Yān,
Dàhuǒ to Sòng,
Shòuxīng to Zhèng,
Chúnwěi to Chǔ,
Chúnhuǒ to Zhōu,
Chúnshǒu to Qín,
Shíchén to Wèi,
Dàliáng to Zhào,
Jiànglóu to Lǔ,
Zī
(pronounced jí yí)
Jū
(pronounced zǐ yú)
to Wèi.
The Grand Historian oversees this
to observe portents of calamity and auspice."
The Gǔliáng states:
"The arrayed stars are called héngxīng (constant stars),
also called jīngxīng (regular stars)."
Héng (constant)
and jīng (regular)
both mean 'constant'.
The Hànshū Yīnyì states:
"Auspicious stars are called jǐngxīng (brilliant stars),
also called déxīng (virtue stars).
Baleful stars are called bèixīng (bursting stars),
huìxīng (broom stars),
chángxīng (long stars),
also called chānchēng (comets).
Those that vanish from sight are called fēixīng (flying stars).
Those whose light trails connect are called liúxīng (flowing stars),
also called bēnxīng (racing stars).
The light of a star is called máng (rays)."
The Ěryǎ states:
"To sacrifice to stars is called bù (spreading)."
Bù means
to scatter food upon the ground.
Purple Culmen Literary Brilliance
The Jīngzhōu Xīngzhàn states:
"Běichén is also called Tiānguān,
also called Běijí.
Běijí is
the celestial seat of the Purple Palace."
The Shǐjì states:
"The Dipper's bowl bears a frame of six stars,
called the Wénchāng Palace.
The first is the Supreme General,
the second is the Second General,
the third is the Noble Minister,
the fourth is the Director of Destinies,
the fifth is the Director of the Center,
the sixth is the Director of Emoluments."
Celestial Street Imperial Seat
The Hànshū, third year of Emperor Gāozǔ:
The moon was haloed,
encircling Shēn and Bì sevenfold.
The prognostication said:
"Between Bì and Mǎo is the Tiānjiē (Celestial Street),
north of the street is the Hú,
south of the street is Zhōngguó."
The Shǐjì states:
"In the center is the Duānmén gate,
to its left and right are the Yèmén gates.
Inside the gates are six stars,
the feudal lords;
inside them are five stars,
the seats of the Five Emperors."
Strung Pearls Linked Shells
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
"When heaven and earth were opened up,
on the jiǎzǐ winter solstice,
the sun and moon were like suspended jade discs,
the five planets like strung pearls."
The Shàngshū Kǎo Língyào states:
"The sun, moon, and five planets,
begin from Qiānniú at the winter solstice.
The sun and moon are like suspended jade discs,
looking up, the shape of heaven is like a carriage canopy,
the multitude of stars piled up like linked shells."
String of Pearls Meteorites
The "Kun Ling Tu" of the Book of Changes states:
"In the court of utmost virtue,
the five planets align like a string of pearls."
The Zuo Zhuan records: In the spring of the sixteenth year of Duke Xi,
five meteorites fell in Sòng.
These were falling stars.
Mars Eclipsing the Pleiades Mars Assailing the Moon
The Book of Han records a memorial submitted by Zōu Yáng:
"When Master Wèi devised the plan for the Battle of Chángpíng for Qín,
Mars eclipsed the Pleiades,
causing King Zhāo to doubt him."
Liú Xiàng's Garden of Persuasions states:
"When Húhài of Qín ascended the throne,
the sun and moon were obscured and eclipsed,
mountains and forests sank and vanished,
crooked arrows shone at night,
and Mars assailed the moon."
Essence of Metal Substance of Stone
The Celestial Officials' Astrological Prognostications states:
"The planet Venus
is the essence of metal,
the son of the White Emperor,
and symbolizes the great general."
The Records of Huáng Shígōng states:
"Huáng Shí
is the essence of the planet Saturn.
'Huáng' (yellow)
refers to the color of Saturn.
'Shí' (stone)
refers to the substance of the star."
Five Colors Double Radiance
The "Dou Wei Yi" chapter of the Book of Rites states:
"Carefully observe the five colors."
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
"The seven stars of the Northern Dipper possess five colors,
corresponding to the notes gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ,
each matching its respective star."
Cuī Bào's Notes on Past and Present states:
"When Emperor Míng of Hàn was Crown Prince,
musicians composed a song called 'The Stars Shine Doubly Bright,'
comparing the Crown Prince's virtue to this,
hence the term 'double'."
Rainbow Flow Lightning Encircling
The River Chart states:
"A great star like a rainbow
flowed down to Huá Zhǔ.
Nǚ Jié was moved by its intent,
and gave birth to the White Emperor Zhū Xuān."
The Annals of Emperors and Kings states:
"At the end of Shénnóng's reign,
Shǎo Diǎn married Fù Bǎo.
She saw a great lightning flash encircle the Northern Dipper,
with the Pivot Star illuminating the suburbs.
Moved by this, Fù Bǎo
conceived and after twenty months
gave birth to the Yellow Emperor at Shòu Qiū."
Heavenly Granddaughter Wù Woman
The Book of Han states:
"The great star Hé Gǔ is the Supreme General.
To its north is the Weaving Maiden.
The Weaving Maiden
is the heavenly granddaughter."
The Guangya states:
"Xūzhī is the Wù Woman.
The Wù Woman is also called Shíchén."
Scattered Brocade Dragging Silk
Yǔ Chǎn's poem states:
"The dark night sky is like a reflecting jade disc,
the scattered stars are like strewn brocade."
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng states:
"In the second year of the Yǒng'ān era of Sūn Xiū's reign, as the general was about to assume his post,
the sons of the hostages were gathered playing.
A strange child suddenly appeared and said:
'I am not human,
I am the planet Mars.'
Having spoken, he flew upwards.
Looking up at him,
it was as if a bolt of silk was being dragged across the sky,
and after a moment he vanished."
Five Assistants Two Envoys
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Water, Fire, Metal, Wood, and Earth —
these five planets
are Heaven's assistants,
forming the warp and weft [of the cosmos],
appearing and hiding according to their times."
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Han states:
"Emperor Hé separately dispatched two envoys,
each to the provinces and commanderies,
to observe and collect folk songs and rumors.
When the two first arrived in the Yì region,
they lodged at the post station official Lǐ Hé's residence.
Hé asked them:
'When you two gentlemen departed from the capital,
did you know the court was sending two envoys to the commandery?'
They asked how he knew.
Hé pointed to the stars and said:
'Earlier, there were two stars
moving towards the field of division corresponding to Yìzhōu.'"
Essence of the Year Star The Pleiades Constellation
The Esoteric Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
"When the envoy of the Queen Mother of the West arrived,
Dōngfāng Shuò had died.
The Emperor asked the envoy about him.
The envoy replied:
'Shuò is the essence of the Wood Emperor,
the Year Star (Jupiter),
who descended among men
to observe the world.
He is not Your Majesty's subject.'" The "Spring and Autumn" Supportive Prognostications states:
"The Hàn Chancellor Xiāo Hé
was seven chi and eight cun tall.
He was the essence of the Pleiades star,
born with triple-pierced ears
and prominent moon-horn features."
The Erya states:
"The 'Western March' refers to the Pleiades star."
Guō Pú's commentary states:
"The Pleiades
is a western constellation,
also named 'Máotóu' (Banner-tassel Head).
This refers to it."
The Recluse's Worry The Gathering of Worthies
Tán Dàoluán's Sequel to the Annals of Jìnyáng states:
"Xiè Fū (courtesy name Qìngxù) of Kuàijī
lived in seclusion on Mount Ruòyē.
Suddenly, the moon encroached upon the Shàowēi star.
The Shàowēi star is also called the Recluse Star.
At that time, Dài Kuí's fame rivaled Xiè Fū's,
and people worried for him.
Soon after, Xiè Fū died.
Therefore, the gentlemen of Kuàijī mocked the people of Wú, saying:
'The eminent scholar of Wú
could not even obtain death.'" When Chén Zhònggōng visited Xún Jìhé and his sons with his own sons and nephews,
at that time the Virtuous Stars gathered.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"Within five hundred lǐ, worthy men are gathering."
The Qílín is Born The Whale Dies
The "Spring and Autumn" Pivotal Chart of the Dipper states:
"When the Celestial Pivot is attained, the Auspicious Star appears;
when the Balance Star is attained, the qílín is born,
and the people enjoy longevity."
The Huainanzi states:
"When a whale dies, a comet appears."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary states:
"The comet
signifies removing the old and establishing the new."
Three Lodgings Four Guardians
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars was in the Heart constellation.
The Duke summoned Zǐ Wéi to ask about it.
Zǐ Wéi said:
"The calamity concerns you, my lord.
It can be transferred to the chancellor."
The Duke said:
"The chancellor is there to govern the state with me."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the common people."
The Duke said:
"If the people die,
for whom would I, the solitary one, be lord?"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The Duke said:
"If the harvest fails, people will surely die.
For a ruler to kill his people in this way,
who would regard me as lord?"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"My lord, you have spoken three supremely virtuous statements.
Heaven is sure to reward you.
Mars is sure to retreat three lodgings."
It indeed retreated three times.
The Huainanzi states:
"The Four Guardians
are in charge of rewards and punishments."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary states:
"The Four Guardians
are the Purple Palace, Xuānyuán, the Pool of Harmony, and the Heavenly River."
Following the Seven Regulations, Operating the Four Seasons
The "Chūnqiū Yùn Dǒu Shū" states:
"The Five Emperors shared the same Way but held different positions,
all following the divisions of the Dipper's pivot and balance,
adhering to the regulations of the Seven Governors and the methods of the Nine Stars."
The "Guān Lìng Nèi Zhuàn" states:
"Each star of the Northern Dipper covers a hundred miles,
separated by ninety thousand miles,
and establishes the twenty-four solar terms.
The Four Lodges operate the four seasons.
The Five Directions establish the Five Planets,
which govern the Five Sacred Mountains."
Sòng Zhāng Jìng's "Guān Xiàng Fù"
Ascending the beautiful peak to gaze afar,
I behold the spiritual images in the nine heavens.
Observing the Purple Palace encircling,
I admire the solitary prominence of the Imperial Seat.
Gazing upon the lush canopy of the Huágài,
how distant and empty it is within.
Then I let my eyes roam far and wide,
reaching to the four corners,
looking north to monitor the Celestial Pole,
and south to behold Tàiwēi.
To the left are Tiānjì, Qiāng, and Bàng,
Shètí and Dàjiǎo,
Èrxián guarding against extravagance,
Qīgōng adjudicating legal cases.
To the right are Shàowēi and Xuānyuán,
where hierarchy and order prevail,
Yùgōng managing garments,
Nǚshǐ holding the brush.
Nèilǜ upholds rituals to watch for evil,
while Tiānláo restrains transgressions and examines faults.
Searching far into ancient times,
I leisurely chant alone.
Admiring the Auspicious Star that outshines the day,
and the great virtue of Táng Yáo flourishing.
Praising the Yellow Star's blunted edge,
highlighting Yú Shùn's lack of contention.
Sighing at Yínghuò dwelling in the heart,
and praising Sòng Jǐng's steadfast governance.
Jié executed remonstrators, leading to a comet's appearance,
Zhòu indulged in excess, causing a broom star.
When the fixed stars disappeared, Zhōu declined,
and when the Wǎngshǐ slithered like a snake, Qín perished.
Truly, human affairs have their causes,
how can disasters be mere illusions?
Indeed, foolish rulers are hard to enlighten,
thus wise monarchs remain vigilant.
Strive to act through non-action and observe the signs,
especially if one's virtue falls short of wisdom.
Liáng Lù Yúngōng's "Xīng Fù"
Emperor Hàn Wǔ traveled by night to the Kūnmíng Pond,
and turning to Sīmǎ Qiān and Xiàngrú, said:
"The stars are bright and beautiful,
yet when examined in odes or sought in classics and histories,
the Dragon's Tail is mentioned in Guó's children's songs,
the Milky Way is noted in Zhōu's scholars' works.
Their forms in folk songs are crude,
and their expressions of grievance are rustic.
Often, I feel stifled and unexpressed,
and wish to commission a piece from you two."
Then Sīmǎ Qiān replied:
"I, your servant, have inherited the office of celestial official,
with lineage tracing to the Nánzhèng,
and have examined charts and records,
passing down what is seen and heard.
I have heard that the alignment of pearls and jades
marks the rise of the shining luminaries;
the spring birds and autumn emptiness
are what the calendar records.
They align with Huángzhōng to assume correct positions,
and establish Yùhéng to distinguish directions.
The Five Planets adorn and encircle the Way,
the four fields divide and demarcate boundaries.
When those below lack virtue,
the heavens above signal changes.
Sometimes positions are held but shift places,
sometimes brilliance is encroached upon and dimmed.
Thus, responses turn like a ring,
as reliable as matching tallies.
Let the clear mirror and the sacred tortoise
serve to admonish and enlighten."
Chángqīng took up brush and paper,
his thoughts overflowing, emotions stirred,
delaying as he held the brush,
then continued with these words:
"The sun hides in the west,
the moon rises in the east.
Double halos dim and wane at times,
upper branches perch but do not merge.
How can they compare to the Imperial Chariot's solitary course,
following the round canopy endlessly?"
The Emperor then sang:
"The white sun sets, the bright moon shifts,
the myriad stars dawn, yet my spirit does not tire."
Běi Qí Xíng Zǐcái's "Hè Lǎorén Xīng Shī"
Auspicious movements, starlight shines,
transforming harmony, the moon's wheel grows heavy.
Common signs align with blessings' records,
soon to praise this era of peace.
Suí Yángdì's "Yuè Yè Guān Xīng Shī"
Round, pure white moon bright,
serene, the evening scene clear.
Valley springs startle dark stones,
wind in pines stirs night's sounds.
Clad, I leave the rustic door,
in sandals, tread mountain steps.
Glad to see the bright hall's light,
joyed to find Tàijiē level.
Zī and Shēn still discernible,
Niú and Nǚ yet distinct.
Further, the Dipper's handle turns,
late at night, the Milky Way spans.
Pacing, unable to sleep,
mingled feelings, several kinds.
Zhūgě Yǐng's "Fèng Hé Yuè Yè Guān Xīng Shī"
Deep and distant, divine abodes far,
desolate, the night's water-clock deep.
Thin mist clears distant hues,
tall trees stand, cool shade serene.
Stars and moon fill this night,
brilliant, shining upon each other.
Linked pearls wish to rise east,
round fan slowly sinks west.
Clear waters hold the slanting Han,
tall trees hide the horizontal Shēn.
At times, I hear the watchman's clapper,
often see birds circling branches.
The sage's thoughts record lingering matters,
jade chimes ring, golden bells sound.
Yuán Qìng's "Fèng Hé Yuè Yè Guān Xīng Shī"
Six dragons first hide their light,
the gazing hare begins to race its glow.
Border wells relay the night's water-clock,
mountain courtyards bid evening cool farewell.
The imperial abode, a place of noble retreat,
leisurely steps lead from the jade hall.
Dazzling, starlight shimmers,
bright and clear, the long Milky Way.
Qīngdào shifts the Celestial Steeds,
the Northern Pole turns Wénchāng.
Tall branches still hide Bì,
steep ridges half encroach on Zhāng.
Looking up, I behold the jade legacy,
wise works stir golden images.
In vain, I embrace solitude,
how to continue linked verses?
Xiāo Cóng's "Fèng Hé Yuè Yè Guān Xīng Shī"
The sun's essence leaves the southern land,
the great light begins to flow west.
Evening winds mourn the fading heat,
night air welcomes the new autumn.
Layered gates already bathed in moonlight,
the strict city's water-clock slowly marks time.
Facing the wind, I emerge from layered trees,
passing the moon, I shelter in tiered towers.
The divine river separates the goddess,
immortal reins stir the starry ox.
Yùhéng points to the roof's descent,
Yáoguāng faces the curtain's stay.
Only knowing to gaze at the heavenly gate,
no means yet to ride the raft.
Yú Shìnán's "Fèng Hé Yuè Yè Guān Xīng Yìng Lìng Shī"
Early autumn's fiery scenes at dusk,
the first crescent moon's colors fresh.
Clear breeze washes away summer's heat,
gentle dew cleanses clamorous dust.
Dispersing mist dissolves light silk,
fresh clouds roll like evening scales.
Radiant light burns with prior glow,
auspicious hues join layered halos.
Following emotion, I compose sage's verses,
together tasked with Xú and Chén.
Old grass truly overflows,
praise occasionally reaches the gentry.
Celestial patterns are hard to describe,
only knowing to gaze at the Northern Star.
Dǒng Sīgōng's "Yǒng Xīng Shī"
Distinctly, the Dōngjǐng Lodge,
brightly, the Right Wall's enclosure.
Dragon patterns emerge beyond the clouds,
bird colors flip within the pond.
Flowing light descends on moonlit dew,
falling shadows enter the river's source.
Only then I know the Yǐngchuān collection,
holds another Tàiqiū's gate.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Star Names: A Poem on Joining the Army"
The general pacifies the northern frontier,
The night-watch clapper sounds from Qílián.
Tall willows stretch across the distant fortress,
Long elms reach to the far-off sky.
Wellsprings, frozen, run dry,
Beacon fires blaze toward Yānrán.
If you wish to know the traveler's heartbreak,
See the perilous banner hung ten thousand miles away.
Clouds, Section Five
The *Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* says:
"Yīn and yang gather to form clouds."
The *Shuōwén* says:
"Clouds
are the vapor of mountains and rivers.
The character is formed from 'rain' and 'cloud' (云),
depicting a swirling, turning shape.
霠
(pronounced yīn)
means clouds covering the sun.
沉
means prolonged overcast skies.
淒,
means rain clouds gathering.
渰
(pronounced yǎn)
describes the appearance of cloudy skies before rain.
The *Shī* says:
"Gathering clouds, dark and dense,
Bring down rain, gentle and steady."
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"The Bǎozhāng official uses the appearances of the five-colored clouds to discern good and ill fortune."
Zhèng Sīnóng comments:
"Observe the cloud colors at the two solstices and two equinoxes.
Green signifies insect plagues,
white signifies mourning,
red signifies warfare and famine,
black signifies floods,
yellow signifies abundance."
'Solstice' refers to winter and summer solstices,
'equinox' refers to spring and autumn equinoxes.
Also, the "Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò" says:
"In general divination,
when a senior official first arrives at his post, he should observe the heavens.
If yellow clouds come resembling an overturned cart,
the five grains will have a great harvest.
Green clouds bring troops,
white clouds bring thieves,
dark black clouds bring much water,
red clouds bring fire."
The *Gōngyáng* says:
"They rise touching the rocks,
and join together within a hand's breadth.
Only the clouds of Mount Tài can bring rain
before the morning is over."
Jīng Fáng's *Yì Fēihòu Zhān* says:
"If one sees constant large clouds of five colors in the four directions,
it means a worthy man is in hiding below.
If green clouds, moist and glossy, are in the northwest,
it signifies the recommendation of worthy and excellent men.
If yellow clouds resemble an overturned cart,
it signifies great abundance."
The *Xījīng Zájì* says:
"Auspicious clouds are called qìngyún,
or jǐngyún.
Clouds of five colors are called qìng
Qìngyún is also called qīngyún.
Clouds red on the outside and green inside are called yùnyún
(clouds of two colors are called yùn,
also auspicious clouds.
Pronounced yù).
Rain clouds are called yóuyún
Mèngzǐ said:
"Clouds gather thickly."
Snow clouds are called tóngyún
The *Shī* says:
"The heavens are uniformly clouded,
snow falls thick and fast."
Tóngyún means the sky is entirely overcast with clouds,
all of the same color.
The master of clouds is called Píngyì
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says.
Yúnjiāng is also a master of clouds
Sīmǎ Biāo, commenting on the *Zhuāngzǐ*, says:
"Yúnjiāng
is the chief master of clouds."
Yáo's Disc Hàn Dynasty Tripod
The *Shàngshū Zhōnghòu* says:
"When Yáo cast a jade disc into the river,
white clouds arose,
and a whirlwind shook down leaves."
The *Hànshū* says:
"A precious tripod was obtained at Fényīn,
and the Son of Heaven performed rites to sacrifice to it.
When the tripod reached Zhōngshān,
yellow clouds covered it like a canopy."
Also, the "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
"The precious tripod appears, its color misty and dense,
emitting golden light and exhaling floating clouds."
Peì Song Fén River Lyric
The *Shǐjì*: When Gāozǔ of Hàn passed through Peì,
he struck the zhù (a stringed instrument)
and composed a song himself:
"A great wind rises, oh! clouds fly and scatter,
Majesty over the four seas, oh! I return to my old home."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Autumn Wind Lyric" says:
"The autumn wind rises, oh! white clouds fly,
Plants and trees turn yellow and fall, oh! wild geese return south."
Red Birds Crimson Serpent
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"In the first year of Duke Āi,
there were clouds like a flock of red birds,
flying on either side of the sun for three days."
A *Bīngshū* (Military Treatise) says:
"If there are clouds like a crimson serpent following behind a star,
a great battle will occur and generals will be slain."
Following the Dragon Aiding the Phoenix
The *Yì* says:
"Clouds follow the dragon,
wind follows the tiger."
Lù Shìhéng's "Rhapsody on Clouds" says:
"They aid the divine phoenix at Cāngwú,
and rouse the stagnant dragon from the marsh."
Roc's Wings Fish Scales
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"The great roc beats the whirlwind and rises ninety thousand li,
its wings like clouds hanging from the heavens."
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"Mountain clouds resemble grass and thickets,
water clouds resemble fish scales,
drought clouds resemble smoke and fire,
rain clouds resemble water ripples."
Supporting the Sun Reaching the Pitch-pipes
The *Luòshū* says:
"When the Green Emperor arises,
green clouds support the sun.
When the Red Emperor arises,
red clouds support the sun.
When the Yellow Emperor arises,
yellow clouds support the sun."
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shízhōu Jì* says:
"In the third year of the Tiānhàn era,
the Yuèzhī state presented divine incense.
The envoy said:
'Our state has constant divinations.
When the east wind enters the pitch-pipes,
it does not cease for a hundred days.
When green clouds reach the pitch-pipes,
they do not disperse for months on end.
We understood that the Middle Kingdom would have a ruler of wondrous virtue,
so we sought out rare treasures to present this divine incense.'"
Golden Branches Jade Leaves
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
"When the Yellow Emperor battled Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
there were always five-colored clouds and vapors,
with golden branches and jade leaves,
halting above the Emperor.
They had the appearance of flowers and blossoms,
so based on this, the huágài (canopy) was made."
Touching the Rocks Moistening the Plinth
The *Chūnqiū Shuōtící* says:
"The word for cloud (yún) means 'to move'.
When moving yin paths touch rocks and rise, it is called cloud;
containing yang and rising, it moves by essence."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"When mountain clouds steam,
the pillar plinths grow moist."
Cap Tassels Carriage Canopy
The *Yì Tōngguà Yàn* says:
"At Hánlù, when yin is dominant,
clouds emerge like cap tassels.
At Shuāngjiàng, when great yin prevails,
clouds emerge, above like sheep,
below like millstones."
Wáng Chén's *Wèishū* says:
"When Emperor Wén was born,
there was a bluish cloud vapor,
round like a carriage wheel,
remaining above him all day.
Those who observed vapors considered it an omen of supreme nobility,
not the vapor of a subject."
Skin Joining, Inches Merging
The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says:
"Emerging upon touching the stone,
joining skin by inch,
raining across the world before the morning is over—
this is only the clouds of Tài Shān."
Yuán Bào's "Ode to Autumn Rain" says:
"Dark clouds gather from all four directions,
skin joins and inches merge.
Their light curtains the six directions,
dense and deep, obscure and dark."
Like Silk, Resembling Cloth
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* says:
"At the start of autumn, turbid yin [appears],
clouds emerge like crimson silk.
At the end of heat, clouds also emerge,
yellow to the south, blue-green to the north."
The Military Manual of Divination says:
"If on a Rénzǐ day there are black clouds resembling a bolt of cloth,
then that state will raise troops."
Like Smoke, Not Mist
The *Shǐjì* says:
"Like smoke yet not smoke,
like clouds yet not clouds,
luxuriant and profuse,
serene and coiling round,
this is called 'ministerial clouds'.
Ministerial clouds
are auspicious vapor."
Cáo Cāo's *Essentials of Military Texts* says:
"Sūnzǐ speaks of observing cloud-qi:
It is not cloud, not smoke,
not dust, not mist.
Its form resembles birds and beasts.
It is auspicious for the guest,
a taboo for the host."
Encircling Zhěn, Obscuring the Sun
The *Chūnqiū Wényào Gōu* says:
"In Chǔ there were blue-green clouds like a rainbow,
encircling Zhěn, coiling sevenfold.
Within them was a man holding an axe,
squatting facing Zhěn."
Jīng Fáng's *Essential Decisions on Wind and Rain* for divination says:
"The method for morning rain:
If there are black clouds like a bolt of black silk obscuring the sun,
then there will be heavy rain for one day;
two bolts,
rain for two days;
three bolts,
rain for ten days."
Emerge from Cāngwú, Reach the Emperor's Land
The *Guīcáng* says:
"There were white clouds emerging from Cāngwú,
entering into Dàliáng."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"As for the sage,
when the world has the Way,
he prospers together with all things;
when the world is without the Way,
then, weary of the vulgar, he ascends to immortality,
riding upon those white clouds,
reaching the Emperor's Land."
Jìn Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Floating Clouds"
They possess the beautiful semblance of lightness and insubstantiality,
lacking the true form of solid substance.
Tracing back to their origin,
they float and sink, mingled and merged.
The six pitch-pipes harmonize in response,
the eight winds move in season.
Dark yin touches the stone,
sweet moisture pours down abundantly.
Their force does not last a full morning,
yet they cover and envelop without exception.
Like layered terraces and lofty towers,
multi-storied buildings and stacked pavilions.
Sometimes like the dense massing of bell-mountains,
suddenly resembling the vast emptiness of frontier passes.
Golden branches part,
jade leaves scatter.
Green tips gleam,
dense blossoms blaze.
Like phoenixes soaring and dancing,
wild swans startled, cranes rousing.
Whales and giant fish breasting the waves,
shark-crocodiles charging and fleeing.
Vermilion silk threads, order in disarray,
gauze skirts losing their collars.
Flying transcendents ascend the void,
roaming and galloping with the wind.
As if clusters of lotus flowers spreading out,
hibiscus blossoms gathered together,
chariot-wheel jade with winding grain,
agate with intricate patterns.
Jìn Chéng Gōng Suí's "Rhapsody on Clouds"
Then the dark wind scatters upward,
returning clouds swirl on four sides,
ice melts, tiles crumble,
graceful and fluttering.
Departing, they erase their tracks leaving no trace;
coming, they are obscure and dark, profound and dim.
Stretched out, they extend and envelop the four seas;
rolled up, they dissolve and vanish into formlessness.
Sometimes close-packed like fish scales in rows,
uneven and interlocking.
