The Dòngmíngjì states:
"In the second year of Yuánfēng,
Shù'èguó presented a talking turtle,
with a neck two chǐ long."
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"Only by receiving cassia dew can it drink."
Crane Alert Cicada Sings
Zhōu Chǔ's Fēngtǔjì states:
"White cranes are alert by nature.
When the eighth month arrives and white dew descends,
flowing on grass and leaves,
dripping with sound,
they then call."
Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn states:
"The King of Wú wished to attack Jīng,
and told his attendants:
'Whoever dares to remonstrate shall die.'
Among the retainers was a young lad who wished to remonstrate.
Carrying pellets and a slingshot in the rear garden,
dew moistened his clothes,
thus for three mornings.
The King of Wú said:
'You, come here.
Why is dew moistening your clothes like this?'
He replied:
'In the garden there is a tree,
on it there is a cicada.
The cicada, perched high, sings mournfully and drinks dew,
unaware of the mantis behind it.
The mantis, bending its legs, takes the cicada,
unaware of the oriole stretching its neck to peck.
The oriole, in turn, is unaware of the pellet beneath it.
I wished to shoot the oriole,
and was unaware of the pit beside me, so I fell.'"
Golden Palm Bronze Plate
See above, Hàn Wǔdì Gùshì.
Bān Gù's Xīdū Fù states:
"Caress the immortal's palm to receive dew,
raise the twin-standing golden stems."
Cáo Zhí's Chénglùpán Míng states:
"Among visible forms, nothing is greater than height;
among things imperishable, nothing surpasses metal;
among clear qi, nothing surpasses dew;
for secure containment, nothing surpasses a plate.
Thus he ordered the officials
to cast bronze and erect a dew-receiving plate in the Fānglín Garden."
Hàn Palace, Wèi Hall
The Book of Hàn records an edict of Emperor Xuān:
"Recently, phoenixes gathered on Tàishān and in Chénliú,
and sweet dew descended upon the Wèiyāng Palace.
Therefore, a general amnesty is granted throughout the land."
Emperor Míng of Wèi, in an edict to the Prince of Dōng'ē, said:
"In the time of the late emperor,
sweet dew repeatedly descended before the Rénshòu Hall,
and numinous mushrooms grew in the Fānglín Garden.
Since I erected the Dew-Receiving Plate,
sweet dew has again descended in the Fānglín Garden and before the Rénshòu Hall."
Aiding the Sea, Deepening the River
Zhāng Héng memorialized, saying:
"Flying dust adds to mountains,
mist and dew aid the sea."
Fù Xián's poem says:
"Scattered dew deepens rivers and seas,
flying dust elevates mountains and peaks.
If my flawed efforts can assist the high ministers,
how could I presume to prepare the cauldron's stew?"
Resting on the Paulownia, Drying on the Allium
Master Sū said:
"A human life lasts but a generation,
like morning dew resting on a paulownia leaf—
how long can it endure?"
The Gǔjīn Zhù states:
"Xièlù (Allium Dew)
is a song of lament,
meaning human life is like dew on an allium leaf, easily dried.
Dew dries, yet returns with the next dawn's fall;
when a person dies and departs, when will they return?"
Purple Color, Cinnabar Color; Descending on Mounds, Descending on Commanderies
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū records Yī Yǐn advising Tāng:
"Among the finest waters
is the dew of Sānwēi.
Among the finest harmonizing agents
is the dew of Jiéyú,
its color is purple."
The Shíyí Jì says:
"On Kūnlún Mountain there is sweet dew.
Viewed from afar, its color is like cinnabar;
adhering to wood or stone, it appears bright as frost and snow.
When received in a precious vessel, it is like malt sugar.
It descends when the ruler possesses sagely virtue."
Fàn Yè's Hòu Hàn Shū records:
"In the seventeenth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng,
sweet dew descended upon Yuánlíng."
It also says:
"In autumn, the eighth month of the first year of the Yǒngkāng era of Emperor Huán,
Wèi Commandery reported auspicious grain growing
and sweet dew descending."
Liú Dànjīng of Liáng, "Poem on Morning Dew"
Nine orchid-plots congeal fragrant leaves,
a hundred grasses gleam with new pearls.
Though filling lotuses, it does not moisten deeply,
brushing bamboo, it ultimately struggles to wither them.
Gù Xuān of Liáng, "Poem on Dew"
Flying in the void, it still holds its form;
gathering on things, it first displays splendor.
It wilts the yellow, ailing autumn bamboo shoots,
dampens and fosters the spring buds.
Not only does it spread over creeping plants,
it also transforms the reeds and rushes.
Still it increases the river and sea's waves,
and casually dots the magnolia flowers.
Jiāng Zǒng of Suí, "Poem on Gathering Sweet Dew in Response to an Imperial Edict"
Auspicious dew at dawn, misty and dense,
the Shànglín Garden in morning's clear light.
A thousand rows of pearl trees emerge,
ten thousand leaves on jade branches grow long.
Slow wheels move the immortal carriage,
a serene feast invites divine appreciation.
Dān River's waves surge,
Huáng Mountain's mists rise.
Wind pavilions open with emerald pennants,
cloud halls resound with vermilion strings.
Only knowing favor and ritual are abundant,
I pity myself for failing in name and reality.
Yǔ Bào, "Poem on Dew at Xū Terrace"
Since Xū Terrace's structure has fallen,
thorns and brambles gradually encroach upon its gates.
Beams broken, they connect with cloud shadows;
rafters shattered, they reflect the sun's radiance.
Soaring kūn-birds chase, never catching up;
nesting swallows return to find no home.
Only the dew on the round steps remains,
gathering on lashes, together dampening our clothes.
Luò Bīnwáng, "Poem on Autumn Dew"
At Yù Pass, the cold air comes early;
to the golden pond, autumn hues return.
Spreading on palms, its light grows purer;
adding to the river, its drops remain faint.
Changing to frost, it congeals as morning liquid;
receiving the moon, it bestows round brilliance.
There is another on the Wú Terrace,
sure to dampen the robes of Chǔ's minister.
Dǒng Sīgōng, "Poem on Dew"
Night's hues condense on the immortal's palm,
morning's sweetness descends the imperial court.
Unaware, the deep autumn arrives;
from afar, it falls toward Sānwēi.
On reed islets, flowers though white;
in mallow gardens, leaves still green.
Once the sun dries it, its moisture bestowed,
I then wish it would increase the vast sea.
Liáng Shéntì's "Eulogy on the Sweet Dew of the Fānglín Garden"
Blessings are made manifest through virtue,
auspiciousness follows deeds, bright and clear.
How much more this fine dew,
an omen of fortune specially revealed!
Turning moist under starry nights,
flowing sweet in the moonlit dawn.
More wondrous than carved mists,
more precious than plain birds.
The ultimate Way here blends,
the great transformation awaits its dawn.
Only through this great transformation
is heaven's favor truly felt.
Descending liquid on vermilion steps,
flying essence in ornate halls.
The nine domains follow its influence,
the eight wilds change their visage.
I dare present these obscure words,
to display our dancing joy.
Lú Sīdào of Suí, "Memorial of Congratulations from the Hundred Officials on the Sweet Dew [Written] in Qí"
I humbly consider: the Hé River flourishing, the Luò River changing—
these bestowed blessings upon Yáo and Shùn;
the dark jade, the white scale—
these descended as numinous signs upon Tāng and Wǔ.
In between, tiny birds and frail grasses
altered their forms and appearances;
lodging at night, clouds at dawn,
starlight stirred its hues—
all to shine upon the lands below,
and glorify the imperial enterprise.
Once in a thousand sacrifices it arrives,
across eras the same portents align.
I reverently consider Your Majesty,
above holding the cords of heaven,
beside grasping the order of the rivers.
Maintaining a reverent and cautious mindfulness,
continuing the great task of prosperous peace.
Myriad spirits crane their necks,
responding as the Three Terraces journey west;
the Two Modes are correctly observed,
riding the Six Breaths to point east.
Since the auspicious clouds have emerged,
we again hear the songs of all the lords;
the river's clarity can be awaited,
truly gaining the praise of ten thousand people.
And now the High Heaven deigns to regard,
divine objects repeatedly bestow:
flying sweetness sprinkles moisture,
jade scattered, pearls linked.
In the past, the immortal's palm of Wèi Míngdì
ultimately held no numinous liquid;
the golden plate of Hàn Wǔdì
gazed emptily toward the cloud's surface.
How could they compare to divine nectar that can be ladled,
flowing pearls before the nine gates;
celestial wine naturally falling,
condensing its light beneath the three steps?
This is truly an auspicious token rare across ages,
seldom encountered by former kings.
Splendid! Excellent! Imperial! Vast! We, your servants, together encounter this prosperous fate,
all bathed in the profound creation,
suddenly hearing of this secret blessing,
repeatedly witnessing this dark boon.
Shaking scales, stroking wings—
vainly gallop the hearts of fish and birds;
burying jade, inscribing gold—
we shall await the rites at Yún and Tíng.
Shěn Yuē's "Thanks for Bestowing Sweet Dew"
Yuē states to the left and right,
Xú Yǎn conveyed the imperial decree,
bestowing sweet dew from the pine leaves of Fǎyīn Temple.
In past years, I have witnessed it,
merely moistening the branches,
sometimes condensing,
only like a light mist;
never before has it gathered like jade or strung like pearls,
shining so brilliantly.
Truly, it is due to accumulated benevolence ascending to the heavens,
and hidden virtue descending,
that it can bestow its splendor upon the night's zenith,
and spread over the enduring pines.
The gracious decree is deeply felt,
bestowing this auspicious gift.
I cannot contain my joy and gratitude,
and respectfully submit this memorial to express my thanks.
Later Liáng Xiāo Xīn's "Thanks for Bestowing Sweet Dew"
Your subject Xīn memorializes,
I received the imperial decree bestowing sweet dew from the peach leaves of the side hall,
and upon receiving it, I leapt for joy like a sparrow,
my heart dancing like a bird.
I humbly believe that the sage virtue is supremely great,
and harmonious energy flourishes far and wide.
Thus, divine nectar flows sweetly,
and spiritual moisture spreads richly.
Searching through previous eras,
and examining the middle ages,
sometimes it descended upon cities and capitals.
Even then, rulers and ministers were moved,
and near and far rushed to celebrate.
Never before has it manifested as an auspicious sign in the palace courtyard,
presenting its wonder for admiration,
rarely heard or seen,
an auspicious event unparalleled through the ages.
I, participating in this glorious brightness,
am specially favored with this gift.
My joy and dance are profound,
though my station is ordinary.
I cannot fully express my humble feelings,
and respectfully submit this memorial to make them known.
Mist, Part Six
The "Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo" states:
"Mist
is the energy of yīn and yáng.
When yīn and yáng are agitated, it becomes wind;
when they are disordered, it becomes mist."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"When rising water overflows, it becomes mist."
The "Shìmíng" states:
"Mist
means to cover,
as energy obscures and covers things on the ground."
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"If winter follows summer's ordinances,
then dense mist will be dark and obscure."
The "Xījīng Jì" states:
"In an era of great peace,
mist does not block the view,
but only spreads gently and moistens."
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Whenever there is heavy mist,
within three days, heavy rain will surely fall.
Before the rain falls,
one should not venture out into the mist."
The "Bówùzhì" states:
"Wáng Sù, Zhāng Héng, and Mǎ Jūn
all ventured out in heavy mist.
One was unharmed,
one fell ill,
and one died.
When asked the reason,
the unharmed one said:
'I drank wine,'
the sick one had eaten his fill,
and the dead one had an empty stomach.'"
Mist varies, including red mist, blue mist, white mist, and yellow mist.
The "Wàngqì Jīng" states:
"If mist appears on the guǐsì day of the tenth month,
red indicates warfare,
blue indicates calamity."
The "Bàopǔzǐ" states:
"If white mist surrounds a city on all sides,
within a hundred days,
a great army will surely arrive.
When Hàn Chéngdì's five maternal uncles were enfeoffed as marquises on the same day,
that summer, yellow mist filled the four directions."
Three Days, Five Lǐ
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"In the eighth year of Emperor Wòdīng's reign,
Yī Yǐn passed away,
over a hundred years old.
Heavy mist lasted for three days.
Wòdīng buried him with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
sacrificed with the Great Tàiláo offering,
and personally attended the mourning for three years,
to repay his great virtue."
Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Zhāng Kǎi, styled Gōngchāo,
had a fondness for Daoist arts,
and could create mist spanning five lǐ.
At that time, Péi Yōu from Guānxī could also create mist spanning three lǐ."
Serpent Gliding, Leopard Hiding
The "Hánzǐ" states:
"The flying dragon rides the clouds,
the soaring serpent glides through the mist.
When the clouds clear and the mist disperses,
they are the same as earthworms and ants."
Liú Xiàng's "Liènǚ Zhuàn" states:
"The wife of Táo Dázǐ
was the wife of Minister Táo Dázǐ.
After Dázǐ governed Táo for three years,
his reputation did not flourish,
but his family wealth tripled.
His wife repeatedly admonished him, saying:
'Your ability is meager, yet your office is high;
this is called inviting harm.
Having no merit, yet your household prospers;
this is called accumulating calamity.
In the past, under the transformation of Chǔ's Prime Minister Zǐwén,
his household was poor, but the state was rich;
blessings were secured for his descendants,
and his name was passed down to later generations.
Now, you greedily seek wealth and greatness,
heedless of future harm.
I have heard that on the southern mountain, there is a dark leopard
that does not come down to eat for seven days during misty rain.
Why is that?
It wishes to moisten its fur,
and perfect its patterned coat,
thus hiding to avoid harm.
Now, if you continue like this,
you will not escape future troubles.'" Note: hiding
means to conceal.
Thus, Xiè Tiǎo's poem states:
"Though lacking the dark leopard's grace,
I shall hide in the southern mountain's mist."
Surrounding a City, Encircling an Army
See above.
The "Bàopǔzǐ" also states:
"When heavy mist encircles an army,
wherever the mist is,
below it, there is a general's order being obstructed."
Smoke Swirling, Water Overflowing
The "Yídū Shānchuān Jì" states:
"Thirty lǐ northwest of the commandery by land,
there is Dānkǒu.
When the sky clears and one emerges from the ridge,
suddenly mist rises,
swirling like smoke.
Within two mornings,
rain is sure to fall."
See above, the "Zhuāngzǐ."
Spraying Water, Blowing Sand
Shěn Yuē's "Sòngshū" states:
"In the Later Hàn, on the first morning of the first month,
the Son of Heaven attended Déyáng Hall to receive court congratulations.
A shèlì came from the south,
performing in front of the hall.
It stirred water, transforming it into flatfish,
which leapt and sprayed water,
creating mist that obscured the sun."
The "Shíyí Jì" states:
"Flat sands stretch for a thousand lǐ,
their color like gold,
fine as powder.
When wind raises the sand, it becomes like mist,
also called golden mist."
Zhuōyě, Mèngzé
The "Gǔjīn Zhù" states:
"Huángdì battled Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
and Chīyóu created heavy mist."
Wáng Càn's "Yīngxióng Jì" states:
"After Lord Cáo's defeat at Chìbì,
he traveled through the great marsh of Yúnmèng,
encountered heavy mist,
and lost his way."
Summer Well, Hàn Tomb
See above, Quān Chēng's "Fēngsú Tōng" from Chénliú.
The "Hàn Wǔdì Gùshì" states:
"Emperor Wǔ was buried at Màolíng.
An extraordinary fragrant energy
accumulated around the tomb mound,
like heavy mist."
Silver Mountain, Cinnabar Ridge
The "Xiāngzhōu Jì" states:
"In Qūjiāng County, there is a silver mountain,
often shrouded in white mist."
See above, the "Yídū Shānchuān Jì."
Riding the Turtle, Riding the Deer
Wáng Lièzhī in "Ānchéng Jì" said:
"In the county, there was someone named Xiè Lǐn,
who, while returning on the path from plowing the fields,
suddenly encountered clouds and mist.
In the mist, there was a person
riding a turtle.
Lǐn, knowing it was a divine being,
bowed and requested to follow.
The elder said:
'You lack the immortal bones,
you cannot go.' " "Chǔ Cí" said:
"Send Xiāo Yáng to lead the way,
the white tiger as guard before and after,
riding the clouds and mist to enter the underworld,
ride on a white deer at ease."
Dèng Gōng Breathing, Ferocious Beasts Coughing
Sūzǐ said:
"Shǔ's Dèng Gōng's breathing turns into mist."
Dōngfāng Shuò in "Shí Zhōu Jì" said:
"During Emperor Hànwǔ's Tiānhàn era,
the Huíhú nation presented ferocious beasts.
The envoy said:
'The emergence of ferocious beasts
is born from Kūnlún,
or emerges from Xuánpǔ,
they consume breath and drink mist,
and understand human speech.
When their divine nature is realized,
they swiftly raise wind and clouds,
emitting and coughing out mist and dew,
all wickedness flees in haste,
hence they are named ferocious beasts.'"
Blue Mountains and Sky, Four Corners Rise
Xú Gàn in "Zhong Lùn" said:
"King Wén encountered Jiāng Gōng at Wèiyáng,
holding a fishing rod.
King Wén obtained him,
as if seeing the sun break through clouds,
like seeing green mountains unveiled by mist."
Wáng Yǐn in "Jìn Shū" said:
"Lè Guǎng served as Shàngshū Lìng,
Wèi Wàn found him remarkable,
ordering his sons to visit him,
saying:
'This man is like a water mirror,
whenever seen,
it is clear as mist opening to see the blue sky.'" "Hàn Shū" said:
"The five marquises of the Wáng clan were enfeoffed simultaneously,
on that day yellow mist filled all directions for the whole day."
"Jīngfáng Yāo Zhàn" said:
"A great fog,
the ruler is confused.
Clouds and mists rise in four directions,
then there will be many hermits."
Emperor Tàizōng "On the Mist in the Flower Court"
The fragrance of orchids has already perfumed the palace,
new buds half adorn the clusters.
The colors contain light and heavy mist,
the fragrance attracts the wind coming and going.
Brushing leaves thickly, deepening the green,
entwining flowers thinly, veiling the red.
Returning to mingle with the scattered rain,
faintly distant in the sky.
Again "An Evening Mist Clears the Distant Green Peaks"
The remaining clouds withdraw from the green peaks,
the evening mist fills the long sky.
The mountains wear full green, solid,
the mists obscure half-red sunsets.
Subtly the first moon emerges,
drifting across with dawn winds.
Then through the three-mile place,
carriages and caps connect from afar.
Emperor Liáng Xiàoyuán "Poem on Mist"
Three luminaries give rise to distant mist,
five miles darkening the city walls.
With the wind resembling fine rain,
reflecting the sun like floating dust.
Suddenly like light smoke dispersing,
at times like fresh good air.
Without hindering the birds in the trees,
at times veiling those picking flowers.
Again:
The morning mist darkens the front steps,
strands of pearls hang at the edge of leaves.
Five miles float over the long marsh,
three luminaries darken the distant sky.
Enjoying it is like good air,
viewed from afar like flying smoke.
Sparse curtains become dense again,
a new beam seems connected in suspicion.
Recall meeting Lè Guǎng,
able to make the mist and dew vanish.
Liáng Fútǐng's "Poem on Sailing Amidst Morning Mist"
Water mist mingles with mountain smoke,
dimly no sky is seen.
Hearing the gibbons one considers the mountain,
hearing the rapids one knows the river.
Fishermen confuse the coves and shores,
boats lose their way, struggling up and down the stream.
At noon, the air and mist entirely clear,
empty waters join in clarity and freshness.
Liáng Shěnqū "On Mist"
Dense and leafy, obscuring gardens,
mist lightly covers windows and rooms.
Gazing at the mist, it seems to be void,
looking into the void, it seems to exist.
Wandering snakes hidden in the distant Milky Way,
patterned leopards resting on the southern hill.
Already different from the three or five splendors,
looking afar, one only turns the head.
Dǒng Sīgōng "Poem on Mist"
The azure mountains have already entered the night,
the emerald view darkens, about to sink.
Chóngnán conceals the leopard in the morning,
Wūxiá echoes with the night gibbons' call.
The cold skies, the air does not cease,
the dim scene deepens in color.
Await to visit Gōngcháo's market,
preparing to proceed to Huáyin.
Sū Wèidào "Poem on Mist"
Mist rises in dense layers from the caves,
subtly surrounding the level fields.
It briefly resembles a dragon sword unsheathed,
and is thought to reflect the mirage towers.
Brushing the forest closely like the rains,
drifting over the distance, the mist floats with smoke.
Appropriately thanking Gōng for the great steps,
finally to accompany Yànfǔ on a journey.
Rainbow and Mist, Chapter Seven
"Chūnqiū Yuán Mìng Bāo" says:
"A rainbow is the essence of yin and yang.
The male is called hóng,
the female is called ní."
"Shìmíng" says:
"The rainbow,
is the movement of yang energy.
A rainbow,
is an attack,
pure yang attacks the energy of yin."
"Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" says:
"When yin and yang are not harmonized,
marriage is disordered,
this energy is born.
When a rainbow appears, it has blue and red colors,
often depending on the dark clouds to appear by day,
it does not appear without clouds during the sun,
nor does it appear under the moon.
When seen, it corresponds with the sun,
moving with it to the west,
appearing in the east.
Hence the poem says,
'Dì is frozen there in the east.'
Dì is a rainbow,"
says "Erya."
"Ní,
the female rainbow,
also known as qiè (with a reverse reflection of the mouth)."
"Erya" says.
"In general, if two rainbows appear together,
the more vivid and bright one is male,
the male is called hóng,
the darker one is female,
the female is called ní."
"Jīngfáng Yìzhùan" says:
"Ní,
the surrounding air."
Its divination states:
"When a wife overrides her husband, it appears,
a sign of yin overcoming yang,
occurring in all seasons.
Only the male rainbow appears hidden with the moon,
there are these two interpretations."
Spitting Gold, Transforming into Jade
Liú Jìngshū's "Garden of Marvels" states:
"In Jìnlíng, Xuē Yuàn,
during the Yìxī era, a rainbow drank from his cauldron,
and in a moment, with a sucking sound, it was emptied.
Yuàn carted wine to pour into it,
and as it dried up,
it spat out gold filling the vessel.
Thereafter, calamities and hardships daily receded,
and abundance arrived year after year."
Gān Bǎo's "In Search of the Supernatural" states:
"After Confucius composed the 'Spring and Autumn Annals' and established the 'Classic of Filial Piety,'
he fasted and purified himself, bowed toward the North Star,
and reported the completion to Heaven.
Then, dense white mist rose, skimming the ground,
and a red rainbow descended from above,
transforming into a piece of yellow jade,
three chǐ long,
with carved characters on it.
Confucius knelt, received it, and read it."
Beautiful Woman, Gentleman
Guō's commentary on the "Ěryǎ" states:
"Commonly called a beautiful woman."
"The Continued In Search of the Supernatural" states:
"There was a man named Chén Jì from Bāqiū in Lúlíng,
who served as a provincial clerk.
His wife was alone at home.
Often, a gentleman,
tall and handsome in appearance,
wearing a crimson-green robe,
with dazzling colors,
would meet her by a mountain stream.
When it came to sleeping together,
she was unaware of any human interaction.
Neighbors observed that whenever he arrived,
a rainbow would appear."
Trailing Over Balconies, Winding Around Mansions
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" states:
"Pulling fragrant sand yet seeing nothing,
climbing high to touch the sky.
Shooting stars pass through inner chambers,
curving rainbows trail over balustraded balconies."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" states:
"Modeling the Purple Palace to construct chambers,
expanding the vastness of the temple courtyard.
Cold and heat are separated by deep halls,
rainbows wind around cloud-reaching mansions."
Two Qì, Five Colors
"Wénzǐ" states:
"When heaven's two qì combine, a rainbow forms;
when earth's two qì combine, they seep and hide;
when human two qì combine, illness arises."
"Chūnqiū Qiántánbā" states:
"When a rainbow appears,
the consorts and concubines oppress the ruler from the shadows."
It also states:
"When five colors arrive in succession,
shining upon the palace halls,
there will be matters of war and arms."
Piercing the Sun, Emerging from the Halo
"Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Jīng Kē admired Yān Dān's righteousness,
a white rainbow pierced the sun,
and the Crown Prince feared it."
Yìng Shào states:
"Crown Prince Yān nurtured Jīng Kē,
ordering him to assassinate the King of Qín.
His utmost sincerity moved Heaven,
and a white rainbow pierced the sun."
"Miscellaneous Military Texts" states:
"When a solar halo has a white rainbow piercing its inner part,
and it is outside,
victory in battle will come from where it stops."
Descending Upon the Palace, Piercing the City
"Book of Hàn" states:
"Shàngguān Jié plotted to depose Emperor Zhāo,
and welcome Yān King to the throne,
ordering all officials to prepare.
At that time, it rained,
and a rainbow descended upon the palace to drink from a well,
emptying the well water."
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" states:
"When Liú Yìqìng was in Guǎnglíng,
at night, a white rainbow pierced the city,
and a wild deer entered the government office.
He felt deeply troubled by this,
and thus requested to return."
Appearing by Day, Emerging at Night
Xuē Yíng's "Book of Later Hàn" states:
"In the first year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng,
a rainbow appeared by day at the imperial residence,
in the front courtyard of the Chóngdé Rear Hall,
its colors blue and red."
Wáng Sháozhī's "Annals of Jìn'ān" states:
"On a night in the seventh month of the second year of Yìxī,
a rainbow emerged in the west, obscuring the moon."
Crown Prince's Fear, Omen for Petty People
See above in "Records of the Grand Historian."
Yìng Shào's commentary states:
"Rú Chún's commentary states:
'The rainbow is the qì of ministers,
the sun is the sovereign.'"
"Biographies of Resolute Men" states:
"After Jīng Kē set out,
the Crown Prince saw a rainbow piercing the sun,
but it did not fully penetrate.
He said,
Zhāng Fán's "Annals of Hàn" states:
"During Emperor Líng's time,
a rainbow appeared by day in the courtyard.
He summoned Court Gentleman Cài Yōng to the Jīnshāng Gate to inquire,
and he replied:
'Rainbows
Yīn and Yáng Intertwine, Pivot and Guardian Stars Scatter
"Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo" states:
"When yīn and yáng intertwine, rainbows form."
"Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū" states:
"When the Pivot Star scatters, it becomes rainbows."
"Hétú Jīyàogōu" states:
"When the Guardian Star scatters, it becomes rainbows."
Like a Bird Flying, Resembling a Dragon Descending
"Book of Hàn" states:
"Emperor Wǔ traveled east to Dōnglái,
facing the great sea.
That year, something like rainbow qì,
blue-yellow like a flying bird,
gathered atop the Chéngyáng Palace."
The renowned Hàn minister Cài Yōng memorialized:
"I have received the edict stating:
'On the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month, a black vapor fell in the eastern courtyard of the Wēn Hall,
black like a carriage canopy.
It soared up vigorously,
with five colors and a head,
a body over ten zhàng long,
its shape resembling a dragon.
Diviners identified it as a rainbow.
Rainbows appear in the sky but descend into courtyards.
From what I have heard,
this is a rainbow cast down by Heaven.'"
Piercing the Moon Gives Birth to Zhuānxū, Ascending to Heaven Foretells Xióng's Rise
"Shī Hánshénwù" states:
"Yáoguāng, like a rainbow piercing the moon,
pure white,
inspired Nǚshū,
giving birth to Zhuānxū."
Cháng Qú's "Records of Huáyáng" states:
"Lǐ Tè's eldest son was Dàng,
courtesy name Zhòngpíng;
his youngest son was Xióng,
courtesy name Zhòngjùn.
Initially, when Lǐ Tè's wife Luó was pregnant with Xióng,
she dreamed of twin rainbows rising from the earth to the sky.
One rainbow broke in the middle.
Luó said:
'My two sons,
if one dies first,
the other will surely achieve nobility.'
Later, Xióng indeed became king of Shǔ."
"Rhapsody on the Crimson Rainbow" by Liáng Jiāng Yān
Beyond the southeastern mountains,
There lies the Mountain of Nine Stones,
With crimson cliffs stretching a thousand miles,
And verdant peaks towering hundreds of fathoms.
Moss grows slippery by the water's edge,
And perilous rocks are girded by streams.
Unless one were Wū Xián gathering herbs,
Or the celestial emperors ascending and descending,
All would restrain their thoughts here.
At that time, summer lotuses had just begun to bloom,
While spring sweet flags had not yet faded.
I solemnly moored my boat at the islet,
And slowly drifted along the river's pools.
Just then, the cliffs and precipices mirrored each other,
As rainclouds blazed with color.
Suddenly, a majestic rainbow appeared resplendent,
Its haloed light shimmering upon the water,
Arching proudly over the mountain's peak,
And stretching magnificently along the riverbank.
Drawing near to observe it,
I realized it was truly the qi of yin and yang,
Truly a wondrous sight to behold.
I also recalled how in the past, upon ascending Lú Peak,
I reached out to touch the white clouds;
Now, beneath the Nine Stones,
I personally admire this crimson rainbow.
These two marvels are rarely encountered together,
Moved, I composed this rhapsody:
"Winding and rugged,
These endless connected mountains.
With horned dragons, tigers, and leopards,
And jade serpents soaring aloft.
In the hazy early summer,
Lotus leaves cradle the blossoms.
Melancholy, what thoughts bring me solace?
I hope to briefly ease these sorrowful years.
Having lost the extraordinary men of the world,
I linger for the empty traces in the mountains.
Plucking immortal herbs from perilous peaks,
Carving divine elixirs upon crumbling rocks.
Watching the sturgeon cave spew forth giant fish,
Nurturing the intertwined gathering of giant turtles upon the bridge.
Then, purple mists rise to the River of Heaven,
Crimson vapors descend to the Milky Way.
The boundless white sun,
Half-veiled by azure clouds.
The passing rain is desolate,
While light and mist blaze brilliantly.
The water learns to shimmer like golden waves,
The stones resemble jade banks.
The towering forms of tortoises and scales stand majestic,
Wreathed in the boundless colors of flood dragons.
Suddenly, a crimson rainbow flashes forth like lightning,
Coiling and divine, it soars,
Dimly transforming,
Vague and inconstant.
Neither void nor solid,
Now vanishing, now glowing,
Blazing crimson upon the mountain peak,
Illuminating the waterside.
Though charts and weft texts have recorded it,
For generations, none have truly recognized or encountered it.
Sighing and pacing in hesitation,
I wander at leisure, composed.
Gazing upon the vast marshes of Pānyú,
Remembering the lofty peaks of Dān Mountain.
Riding upon the single star of Fù Yuè,
Ascending upon the two dragons of Xià Hòu.
How long will such numinous beings remain?
Silently, the fire extinguishes upon the crimson mountain.
Its lingering form can still be seen,
Its fading colors have not yet departed.
Shining luxuriantly upon the grass,
Reflecting verdantly among the trees.
Dimming the green moss upon the crimson isle,
Warming the vermilion herbs upon the stony path.
Rosy clouds shimmer and descend flying,
The sun, radiant, ascends on high.
Looking down upon the plight and solitude of my mortal fate,
I lament the impermanence of worldly customs.
Determining that crimson shoes are easily lost,
I yearn instead for Dǐng Hú.
Having already considered the steed with four crimson manes,
And the man with square pupils and a single horn.
At the borders of Dì Tái in the northern wilderness,
By the shores of Yǎn Mountain and the Western Sea.
In the wilds of the flowing sands,
At the ford of Xī Mù.
Clouds sometimes display strange hues,
Mists sometimes form unusual scales.
They must be mingled with the qi of rainbows,
The spirits of yin and yang."
"Poem on the Rainbow" by Dǒng Sīgōng
In late spring, duckweed sprouts early,
After sunset, rain flies lingeringly.
A transverse splendor divides the long River of Heaven,
Its inverted colors grace the clear canal.
Before the beam, its morning shadow emerges,
Upon the bridge, its evening light expands.
I wish to follow the turning of banners and flags,
Fluttering, to serve in the duty chamber.
"Poem on the Rainbow" by Sū Wèidào
Winding and lingering, it belts the Starry Islet,
Graceful and deep, it reaches the celestial shore.
In vain, seen by the stalwart man,
Yet it sinks together with the beauty.
Its transcendent form contains fine jade,
Its divine light adorns auspicious gold.
Alone, it leaves behind the splendor of a long sword,
Ultimately betraying the heart of sages past.
Eighth: Clear Skies After Rain
The *Shuōwén* states:
"Jì
means rain has stopped.
Qī
means the sky has cleared after rain.
Kuò
(pronounced huǒ guō fǎn),
describes the appearance after rain has ceased and clouds have dispersed.
The *Shū* mentions: 'When governance is proper, then sunshine is timely.'
Sunshine dries things.
Jì
means clear weather.
Yì
means to govern well.
Ruò
means compliant.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
'When the ruler's governance is proper, then timely sunshine follows.'
This is the response of auspicious signs.
'When there is transgression, constant sunshine occurs.'
Héng
means constant.
The commentary states:
'If the ruler's actions are transgressive,
then constant, adverse sunshine occurs.'
This is the response of inauspicious signs."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* says:
"In times of peace,
there is timely rain and timely clearing.
Not constant sunshine,
but timely sunshine,
for the qi of heaven and earth is harmonious.
Yìng Yáng of the Later Hàn, Wèi Wéndì, Miào Xí, Fù Xuán of Jìn, Lù Yún,
all composed 'Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky';
Zhàn Fāngshēng of Jìn composed 'Poem on Clear Weather',
Jī Hán composed 'Poem on Rejoicing in Sunshine'.
Among recent literary men,
authors are very numerous,
for they suffered from gloomy, continuous rain and thus rejoiced in clear, sunny skies."
Rain Ceasing, Clouds Dispersing
See the *Shuōwén* above.
Sacrificing at the Gate, Fasting at the Altar
The *Lǐjì* says:
"Yú and yòng
are sacrifices for flood and drought."
The *Sān Shè Yì Zōng* states:
"Yú
is a sacrifice to pray for rain;
yòng
is a sacrifice to stop rain,
performed each time at the city gate."
The *Chángshā Qíjiù Zhuàn* records:
"Wén Quán, styled Zhòngrú,
served as the Commandery Merit Clerk.
At that time, continuous rain disrupted people's livelihoods,
and the Grand Administrator was worried and distressed.
He summoned Quán to supplement the Household Clerk position.
Quán reverently received the instruction and fasted,
remaining at the altar for three days.
At night, he dreamed of a white-haired old man who said to him:
'Why have you come so late!' Quán fully reported his dream,
and the Grand Administrator said:
'In the past, Yǔ dreamed of a man in green embroidered robes,
who called himself the Messenger of Cāngshuǐ,
and Yǔ knew the water veins would then flow freely.
If this dream of yours, Assistant,
can be compared to that.'
The next day, the sky indeed cleared completely."
Collecting Rainbows – Shài Yáng
Above, see the "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" (Monthly Ordinances Chapter Commentary).
Also, Pān Ní's rhapsody says:
"Gather crimson rainbows at the Hàn's northern bank."
Lú Chén's "Cháohuá Fù" (Morning Blossoms Rhapsody) says:
"Just as the deep gloom begins to disperse,
With light rain newly clearing,
Moistened by muddy liquid,
Dried by the sun's essence."
Shài is pronounced with the fanqie spelling huǒ guāng fǎn.
The "Yùpiān" says:

Jī's Poem – Lù's Rhapsody
Jī Hán's "Yuè Qíng Shī" (Delighting in Clear Weather Poem) says:
"A strong wind returns to the Xùn forest,
Dark clouds rise from heavy foundations.
Morning sunbeams bake the jade trees,
Evening shadows reflect on jade fungus.
The singing phoenix dries its light wings,
The responding dragon suns its fine fins.
All grains, once flattened, now stand erect,
Great trees, toppled, are restored and held."
． Lù Yún's "Xǐ Jì Fù Xù" (Preface to the Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky) says:
"In the second year of Yǒngníng,
Yèdū had great continuous rains,
So I composed the 'Qiū Lín Fù' (Autumn Rains Rhapsody).
When the rhapsody was finished,
The sky's rain had already cleared,
Therefore I composed the 'Xǐ Jì Fù' (Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky)."
Opening the Yang Gate – Whipping the Yin Stone
The "Hànshū" says:
"Dǒng Zhòngshū served as Chancellor of Jiāngdū,
Governing the state according to the 'Chūnqiū',
When calamitous anomalies occurred,
He deduced the misalignment of yin and yang.
Therefore, to pray for rain,
He closed all yang [gates],
And opened all yin [gates];
To stop rain, he did the opposite."
The "Yīnyì" says:
"To pray for rain, close the south gate;
To stop rain, close the north gate."
The Sòng dynasty "Yǒngchū Shānchuān Jì" says:
"In Yídū commandery there are two large stones,
One is yang,
One is yin.
Whipping the yin stone brings rain,
Whipping the yang stone brings clear weather."

Both seen above.

The matter is seen above.
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
"Shēn Mountain encircles several hundred lǐ,
Its towering shape resembles an incense burner.
When clouds clear,
The sky brightens and scenery becomes transparent,

Wèi Miào Xí's "Xǐ Jì Fù" (Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky)
Alas, the four seasons are evenly divided,
Yet why are yin and yang not balanced! At the summer solstice when sprouts emerge,
There may be drought and aridity lasting ten days.
Just as the barley is about to be harvested,
Torrential downpours turn into rivers.
How can I bear the people's drowning distress,
And abandon the fine grain in the central fields.
I grieve for that vast Heaven,
And the encompassing Earth.
You nurture our black-haired people,
And bestow upon them this blessing.
Having already shown radiance with the Horn star,
You further urge with the Nine Bird Officers.
Why are disasters and pestilences so inconstant,
That they disregard even the sacrificial grain! I recall the great flood of the Táng clan,
And brood with melancholy and long contemplation.
The sun grows dusk and I cannot sleep,
Thinking until dawn in solitary sorrow.
The white sun at times hides its morning glow,
Clouds billow and churn, intertwining.
Thunder rumbles faintly, shaking with its sound,
Rain pours down continuously and collapses again.
Observing the long eaves' gushing flow,
It is like the Dragon Gate not yet opened.
Relying on our sovereign's brilliance and sageliness,
He alone examines himself and blames himself.
Uttering one word that moves the spirits,
What can the people rely on if they have no food.
I inquire of Heaven's mirror, so swift,
Yet like shadow and echo, not yet manifest.
Massing dark clouds to travel eastward,
Fanning the auspicious wind to soar south.
The vault of heaven gleams, displaying its colors,
Xīhé shines brightly, raising her light.
Farmers rejoice as rivers recede,
Field overseers plow along the border ridges.
Fù Xuán's "Xǐ Jì Fù" (Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky)
Delighted that the gloomy rains have cleared,
I praise this fine hour that begins the clear sky.
Rejoicing that the ominous lightning has hidden away,
Happy that Heaven's mirror is so bright.
Flowing puddles return to the hundred streams,
The seven ethers penetrate the cloudy court.
The east wind is gentle, fanning the road,
The double yang rises, stretching its spirit.
Away from the worry of inundation and ruin,
Approaching the open path's broad levelness.
Shedding the ignorance of drowning distress,
Beholding the glorious light of sun and moon.
Like a hidden dragon emerging from a spring,
Leaping and soaring beyond the Great Purity.
In the past, the Táng Emperor, reverent and bright,
Encountered the great harm of flooding waters.
In the prosperous era of Yīn Tāng,
Severe drought and blazing heat lasted for years.
But our sovereign, so divine and sagely,
Spreads the imperial way, residing as emperor.
Though wind and rain lose their proper measure,
Yet the fine grain does not fail.
All are harmonized and flourish here,
Heaven and humanity solemnly in mutual prosperity.
Commanding joy and pleasure to exhale harmony,
Spreading benevolent winds without limit.
Jìn Lù Yún's "Xǐ Jì Fù" (Rhapsody on Delighting in the Clear Sky)
Resenting the lingering season of poisonous rain,
My heart harbors indignation without joy.
Solemnly seeking through human plans,
Reversing extreme yin by Heaven's act.
Clearing Píngyì's great tunnel,
Suddenly Tài Shān strikes the rocks.
Changing Wàngshū's departure from the Bì constellation,
The six dragons leap in the purple pavilion.
Then the vermilion sun is bright,
The auspicious wind comes from the south.
Restoring Huǒzhèng to his former office,
Dismissing Hòutǔ from the heavy gloom.
Leveling the central plain's many floods,
Returning high banks to the lofty peaks.
Lodged grain stands tall and shakes its heads,
Fallen trees rise and become a forest.
Revering the great fields not yet lost,
Fortunate that the spirits enjoy the offerings.
Thereupon, I bow and follow the familiar坎坷,
Look up and ignite the double lí.
Clarity spreads and heaven and earth are refreshed,
All living beings rejoice and the myriad things are aligned.
Halting flowing waves in the Cassia River,
Raising fragrant dust from the sinking mud.
Disaster did not reach harm,
Harmony thus has auspicious signs.
Lush and abundant millet and grain,
Glossy and rich rice and fine grain.
Hoping for a bountiful year since ancient times,
Longing for the poet's ten thousand cartloads.
Tàizōng Huángdì's "Chū Qíng Luò Jǐng Shī" (Poem on Clearing Sky at Dusk)
Evening clouds I casually admire,
The newly clear sky is all the more delightful.
Sunlight on a hundred flowers' hues,
Wind's force on a thousand forests' verdure.
Pond fish leap, each differently,
Garden birds sing, each with distinct voice.
I send word to the broadly learned,
Know my mind beyond worldly things.
Jìn Zhàn Fāngshēng's "Tiān Qíng Shī" (Clear Sky Poem)
Píngyì rests his divine reins,
Fēi Lián furls his spirit fan.
The blue sky glistens like a mirror,
Condensed essence gleaming like an inkstone.
Lowering sail by the Jiāng's bank,
Leisurely gazing to the farthest reach.
Clear air brightens mountain valleys,
A thousand lǐ distant, we see each other.
Liang Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on Clearing Skies"
The sun sets, autumn winds cease,
Mists disperse, the four wilds grow still.
Arching high, the evening mountain rainbow,
Sinking low, the sun descends the peak.
Water ripples stir atop the city walls,
The city tower emerges from the water's midst.
In vain I strive for shared governance merit,
Idly I rest in Huáiyáng's official rank.
Another
Scattered threads and mountain vapors,
Suddenly clear, then cling again to brightness.
Thunder's sound slowly enters the ridges,
Lightning's glow still connects the city walls.
After rain, clouds grow slightly thin,
Winds gather, heat returns to life.
Liáng Wángyún's "Poem on Evening Clearing"
Rolling mountains coil with chaotic clouds,
Tall forests quiet the many sounds.
Dense trees hold moist green,
Distant peaks congeal in emerald haze.
Stone streams rush and gurgle,
Mountain springs begin to clear and purify.
Nature's splendor just enters appreciation,
On tiptoe, my heart awaits the meeting.
Zhōu Yǔxìn's "Poem on Joyful Clearing"
These days longing for light and scene,
This morning at last briefly met.
Rain halts, heat promptly arises,
Clouds clear, instantly forming peaks.
Water white, clear and still shallow,
Flowers red, sun-drenched yet more intense.
Already glad there are no stone swallows,
Even more wish to discard clay dragons.
Another "Poem on First Clearing"
Damp flowers fly not far,
Dark clouds withdraw, still hanging low.
Swallows dry, return to stone,
Dragons broken, become mere mud.
Suí Wángzhòu's "Poem on Rain Clearing"
First clearing, nature's signs turn cool,
Evening light shines on the mountain villa.
Fading rainbow drinks low from the stream,
Fresh runoff climbs to invade the pond.
Wind carries cicada sounds afar,
Clouds part, wild geese's path grows long.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem in Response to Command After Rain on Secluded Mountain"
Sùchéng neighbors the imperial park,
Huángshān lies near Cassia Palace.
Rain ceases, linked peaks emerald,
Mists disperse, the whole wild opens wide.
Soaring through emptiness, playful birds,
Spanning water, a long rainbow descends.
Sun sets, woods wholly darken,
Clouds gather, ridges half empty.
Mountain springs sing in stone ravines,
Earth's pipes sound, wind arises.
"Poem in Response to Command on First Clearing"
First sun brightens Swallow Lodge,
Fresh runoff fills Liáng's pool.
Returning clouds half enter the ridges,
Remaining droplets still hang from branches.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem After Rain"
Evening brings scenery lovely,
Just cleared, nature's hues splendid.
Thin clouds toward sky vanish,
Light rainbows follow gaze, slanting.
Rear window faces shore bamboo,
Front step rests on shore sand.
Lonely, none to speak with,
Wine cup faces wind and flowers.
Sòng Xiàowǔdì's "Prayer for Clear Skies"
Dark and bright lose order,
Leaning to shade brings stagnation.
Continuous rain, soaking and drenching,
Pours unceasing.
Moisture already untimely,
Beneficence not a boon.
Fortunate to halt downpour and emit light,
Temporarily stop clouds and withdraw gloom.
Shine phoenix carriage in the great outskirts,
Illuminate dragon banners at field's edge.
Plows and hoes may be employed,
Millet and grain gain cultivation.
Raise high granaries in auspicious years,
Reach ten thousand in this very season.
Spring First
. The "Monthly Ordinances of the Lǐjì" states:
"In the first month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Xū,
at dusk the constellation Mǎo culminates,
at dawn the constellation Xīn culminates.
Mèng means eldest.
The movements of the sun and moon
result in twelve conjunctions in one year;
by observing the direction the Dipper points to,
the four seasons are named.
In the first month of spring,
the sun and moon conjoin in the constellation Jūzī,
and the Dipper points to Yín.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ,
its sovereign is Tàihào,
its spirit is Gōumáng.
Zhèng Xuán said:
'This is the sovereign of the azure essence,
the minister of the wood office.
Since ancient times,
among those who manifested virtue and established merit,
Tàihào
is Fúxī.
Gōumáng,
the son of Shàohào,
named Zhòng,
served as the wood official.'
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Tàicù
(pronounced cāng dòu fǎn).
The pitch-pipes
are tubes for observing the ethers,
made of bronze;
'corresponds to' means resonates with.
Gāo Yòu's commentary states:
'All things stir into life,
emerging clustered from the earth,
hence it is called Tàicù.'
The east wind thaws the ice,
hibernating insects begin to stir;
'stir' means to move.
Fish rise to the ice,
otters offer fish in sacrifice,
wild geese arrive.
These all record the seasonal signs.
The heavenly ether descends,
the earthly ether ascends,
heaven and earth harmonize and unite,
grasses and trees sprout and stir.
This is when the yang ether steams and moves,
the time suitable for plowing.'
The "Xiǎo Zhèng of Xià" states:

pheasants shake and call
(call,
the ancient character for gòu,
pronounced gǔ dòu fǎn).
'Call' means to cry;
'shake' means to beat their wings.
At times there is the jùn wind
(jùn means
great wind,
south wind).
The frozen ground thaws and softens
(thaw means
to change,
to change and become warm).
Field mice emerge
(field mice are qiǎn mice.
Qiǎn,
pronounced jiǎn diàn fǎn).
Farmers attend to the snow,
in the marshes they gather yún
(pronounced hún).
Yún resembles xiéhāo and is edible.
Willow tí

tí means
to sprout buds).
Plum and apricot,
yí
sī
and peach then blossom

The "Monthly Ordinances" states:
"In the second month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Yíngshì,
at dusk the constellation Dōngjǐng culminates,

Zhòng means middle.
In the second month of spring,
the sun and moon conjoin in the constellation Jiànglóu,
and the Dipper points to Mǎo.
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Jiázhōng
(Gāo Yòu said:
'In this month,
all things leave yin and are born,

Rainwater begins,

cānggēng sing

Eagles transform into doves,

The "Xiǎo Zhèng of Xià" states:
"In the second month, offer wěi in sacrifice
(the arrival of wěi,
its season is excellent).
Gather qǐ
(qǐ pronounced qǐ,
is qú).
Descending swallows then dì

The "Huáinánzǐ" states:

Nǚyí drums and sings,

Nǚyí is the name of a spirit.
The "Monthly Ordinances" states:
"In the third month of spring,
the sun is in the constellation Lóu,
at dusk the constellation Liǔ culminates,

In the third month of spring,
the sun and moon conjoin in the constellation Dàliáng,
and the Dipper points to Chén.
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Gūxiǎn
(Gāo Yòu's commentary on the "Monthly Ordinances" states:

xiǎn means new.
In this month the yang ether stirs,
therefore it leaves the old and approaches the new').
Paulownia begins to blossom,
field mice transform into rú,
rainbows begin to appear,
píng begin to grow
(dìdōng is called a rainbow.
Píng are duckweed).
The vital ether is just flourishing,
the yang ether spreads and vents,
the curved ones all emerge,
the sprouting ones all reach forth

The "Xiǎo Zhèng of Xià" states:
"In the third month, Shēn then hides

Hú
hú
then sing

The commentary to the "Ěryǎ" states:

Distributing Ice
Dividing ice to bestow upon senior officials.
Brushing the Paulownia Buds
The appearance of the paulownia buds just beginning to grow,
gently brushing.
． 《The Zhou Shu Shi Xun》 says:
"In the third month, the turtledove brushes its wings,
the hoopoe descends upon the mulberry tree.
Brushing its wings,
means striking with its wings.
Hoopoe,
a bird that urges weaving,
also called Dài Rén.
Rén is pronounced like 'ér zhèn fǎn'.
" Emperor Yuán of Liáng's 《Zuǎn Yào》 says:
"Spring is called Qīngyáng
the air is clear and warm with yang.
also called Fāshēng, Fāngchūn, Qīngchūn, Yángchūn, Sānchūn, Jiǔchūn.
Heaven is called Cāngtiān
all things grow lush and green.
Wind is called Yángfēng, Chūnfēng, Xuānfēng, Róufēng, Huìfēng.
Scenery is called Mèijǐng, Héjǐng, Sháojǐng.
Time is called Liángshí, Jiāshí, Fāngshí.
Moment is called Liángchén, Jiāchén, Fāngchén.
Season is called Huájié, Fāngjié, Liángjié, Jiājié, Sháojié, Shūjié.
Grass is called Ruòcǎo, Fāngcǎo, Fānghuì.
Trees are called Huámù, Huáshù, Fānglín, Fāngshù.
Forest is called Màolín.
Birds are called Yángniǎo, Shíniǎo, Yángqín, Hòuniǎo, Shíqín, Hǎoniǎo, Hǎoqín.
The first month, Mèngchūn,
also called Mèngyáng, Mèngzōu
pronounced Zōu
, Shàngchūn, Chūchūn, Kāichūn, Fāchūn, Xiànchūn, Shǒuchūn, Shǒusuì, Chūsuì, Kāisuì, Fāsuì, Xiànsuì, Zhàosuì, Fāngsuì, Huásuì.
The second month, Zhòngchūn,
also called Zhòngyáng.
The third month, Jìchūn,
also called Mùchūn, Mòchūn, Wǎnchūn. 」
Cāngjīng Qīngzhī
Zhāng Xié's 《Zá Shī》 says:
"Tàihào opens the eastern season,
at the spring suburban altar, rites are performed for Qīngzhī. "
Cāngjīng is seen in the annotation of "Narrative".
Shēnfú Xiángzhèng
《The Dà Dài Lǐ》 says:
"In the third month, Shēn (constellation) then hides and is not seen. "
《The Guóyǔ》 says:
"The agricultural auspice is upright at dawn. "
Táng Gù's annotation says:
"Agricultural auspice,
refers to the Fáng star.
Upright at dawn,
means appearing upright in the south at dawn,
referring to the day of Lìchūn. "
Gǔyǔ Tiáofēng
《The Xiàojīng Wěi》 says:
"Within the seven circuits and six intervals of the celestial sphere, it is called Lìchūn,
after fifteen days, the Dipper points to Yín for Yǔshuǐ,
fifteen days later pointing to Jiǎ for Jīngzhé,
after fifteen days pointing to Yǐ for Qīngmíng,
after fifteen days pointing to Chén for Gǔyǔ. "
． 《The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn》 says:
"At Lìchūn, the Tiáofēng arrives. "
Sòng Jūn's annotation says:
"Tiáofēng is
the wind that facilitates the growth of all things. "
Chírì Héfēng
《The Máo Shī》 says:
"The spring days are long and drawn out,
gathering the white southernwood in abundance. "
Zhèng's annotation says:
"Chíchí,
means slow and gentle. "
Lù Shìhéng's Yuèfǔ poem says:
"A traveler in the fragrant spring forest,
the spring fragrance wounds the traveler's heart.
The gentle wind flies with a clear sound,
fresh clouds hang with a light shade. "
Shūjǐng Xiānyún
Lǐ Yóng's 《Bēi Sì Shí Shī》 says:
"Unfolding the beauty and freshness of the bright scenery. "
The matter of Xiānyún is already seen in the annotation of "Héfēng".
Jiǔyáng Sānjié
Fù Xuán's 《Yángchūn Fù》 :
"Vital energy is at its peak,
the nine yangs vigorously arise. "
Again, a Yuèfǔ poem says:
"Majestic is the three-spring season,
the weather is warm and harmonious. "
Cānggēng Xuányǐ
《The Máo Shī》 says:
"In spring, the sun grows warm,
there sings the cānggēng. "
Annotation says:
"Cānggēng,
is the huánglí (oriole). "
Cài Yōng's 《Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù》 says:
"In Zhòngchūn, the xuánniǎo arrives.
Xuánniǎo,
is the swallow. "
《The Ěryǎ》 says:
"Swallow,
is yǐ. "
Fúyǔ Huīlín
《The Lǐjì》 says:
"In the month of Jìchūn,
the turtledove brushes its wings. "
Lǐ Yóng's 《Bēi Sì Shí》 says:
"Spring days are sorrowful,
fish wave their scales in the great river. "
Míngjuān Gòuzhì
《The Línhǎi Yìwù Zhì》 says:
"Tíjiū,
also called tiánjuān,
sings in the third month,
day and night without cease.
Until the wheat ripens,
its singing then stops. "
《The Dà Dài》 says:
"In the first month, the pheasant drums and calls. "
Gòu,
means to call;
zhèn,
means to beat its wings.
Xuánniǎo Cānglóng
《The Lǚshì Chūnqiū》 says:
"In the month of Zhòngchūn,
the xuánniǎo arrives. "
《The Lǐjì》 says:
"In the month of Mèngchūn,
the Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of Qīngyáng,
rides in a green carriage,
drawn by cānglóng (azure dragons). "
Jiàngyàn Láihóng
《The Dà Dài Lǐ》 :
"In the second month, the swallow descends. "
Jiàng,
means to descend.
《The Lǐjì》 :
"In the month of Mèngchūn,
the wild geese come. "
Sāngrén Màizhì
Cài Yōng's 《Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù》 says:
"In Jìchūn,
the dàirén descends upon the mulberry tree. "
Cáo Zhí's 《Shèzhì Fù》 says:
"In the month of Mùchūn,
the overwintered wheat fills the fields,
wild pheasants call in flocks. "
Huàjiū Guīyàn
《The Zhōulǐ》 :
"In Zhòngchūn, the official of nets presents doves,
to nourish the state's elders. "
Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
"In spring, the hawk transforms into a dove,
changing the old into the new,
fitting to nourish the elderly and assist vital energy. "
《The Lǐjì》 says:
"In the first month, the wild geese come. "
Lái,
means to return.
To the north is the Yànmén (Wild Goose Gate),
hence they are called returning geese.
Xuányàn Huánglí
Both seen in the above annotation for "Xuányǐ Cānggēng".
Bīnghuàn Yúnzī
Wáng Yì's 《Chūn Kělè》 says:
"In the month of Mèngchūn,
the ice melts and disperses into tiny streams. "
Lǐ Yóng's 《Bēi Sì Shí》 says:
"Sorrowful that the sunny marsh is just spreading,
clouds rise and multiply over beautiful rocks,
gales whistle through the branches on lofty mountains. "
Apricot Blossoms Calamus Leaves
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"On the Qingmíng Festival,
have the silkworm maids tidy the silkworm rooms.
In this month,
apricot blossoms flourish."
"The Annals of Lü Buwei" states:
"Fifty-seven days after the winter solstice,
the calamus is the first among all plants to sprout,
and then plowing begins."
Gāo Yòu's annotation states:
"Calamus,
an aquatic plant."
Blossoming Cassia Tender Mulberry
"The Writings of Shīzi" states:
"Its spring flowers and autumn splendor,
its name is cassia."
"The Book of Songs" states:
"The spring days grow warm,
and we seek the tender mulberry leaves."
Orchid Path Willow Avenue
"The Songs of Chu" states:
"As the new year begins and spring arrives, I journey southward;
orchids cover the path by the marsh, this road grows lush."
Xiè Huìlián's "Third Day Poem" states:
"Slender willows shade the long avenue."
Green Duckweed Green Water Caltrop
Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli" states:
"Linger among the green duckweed,
roam with the clear breeze,
revel in the yang energy,
and stir the heart of spring."
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Spring's Delights" states:
"Pluck the flowing green water caltrops."
Supple Willow Luxuriant Peach
Wǔ Jízhī's "Spring Fragrance Poem" states:
"Peach and willow burst forth in supple glory,
crimson and green brighten the suburbs and towns."
"The Book of Songs" states:
"The peach tree is lush and tender,
its blossoms glow radiantly."
Proclaim Virtue Assess Merits
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the month of Lìchūn,
the Son of Heaven welcomes spring in the eastern suburbs,
proclaims virtue and harmonizes ordinances,
distributes blessings and bestows favors,
reaching down to the myriad people."
"The Elder Dai's Book of Rites" states:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven, in the first month of spring, assessed the virtue, conduct, and achievements of his officials."
Evaluate Achievements Deliberate Rewards
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the last month of spring,
when the silkworm work is completed,
cocoons are divided and silk weighed,
to evaluate achievements and provide garments for the ancestral temples."
"The Guanzi" states:
"At the court assembly in the first month of spring,
the ruler personally hears governance and deliberates on ranks and rewards."
Imperial Field Divine Matchmaker
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the first month of spring,
the Son of Heaven personally plows the imperial field."
Cài Yōng states:
"The Son of Heaven's field for borrowing labor is one thousand acres,
used to provide grain offerings for the Supreme Deity.
It borrows human labor to accomplish its purpose,
hence it is called the imperial field."
"The Annals of Lü Buwei" states:
"In the second month of spring,
on the day the dark birds arrive,
a grand sacrifice of beef, mutton, and pork is offered to the High Matchmaker."
Cài Yōng states:
"The High Matchmaker,
is the name of a deity."
Present Lambs Sacrifice Sturgeon
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the second month of spring,
the Son of Heaven presents lambs and opens the ice,
first offering them in the ancestral temple."
"The Elder Dai's Book of Rites" states:
"In the second month, sacrifice sturgeon."
The sturgeon,
is the first among fish to arrive.
Pray for Wheat Offer Leeks
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the last month of spring,
the Son of Heaven prays for the grain of the wheat."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states:
"He seeks its maturation while it is still in the ear."
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"On the day of sacrificing to the Great Earth Altar in the second month,
offer leeks and eggs to the ancestors."
Proclaim with Bells Carry the Plow
"The Book of Documents" states:
"Every year in the first month of spring,
the herald proclaims with a wooden bell along the roads."
The annotation states:
"The herald,
is an officer who announces decrees.
The wooden bell,
has a metal clapper with a wooden tongue,
used to promote civilizing teachings."
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the first month of spring,
an auspicious day is chosen,
the Son of Heaven personally carries the plow and share,
leading the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials to personally plow the field for borrowing labor."
Fire Prohibition Ice Opening
"The Rites of Zhou" states:
"The Director of Fire is responsible for using a wooden bell in the second month of spring to enforce fire prohibitions."
Cài Yōng's "Exegesis on the Monthly Ordinances" states:
"In the second month of spring,
the Son of Heaven presents lambs and opens the ice."
Prune Mulberries Gather Mugwort
"The Book of Songs" states:
"In the silkworm month, prune the mulberries."
Zhèng Xuán states:
"Pruning mulberries means removing their leaves."
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"In the third month, one may gather mugwort."
Flower Canopy Leaf Pavilion
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Spring's Delights" states:
"Spring is delightful!
Adorn a canopy with assorted flowers,
gather lush petals to decorate one's robe."
Leaf Pavilion appears below in Xiè Wàn's "Rhapsody on Spring".
Green Fields Azure Thoroughfare
Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on Entering the Mouth of Pénglí Lake" states:
"In late spring, the green fields are splendid,
high cliffs gather white clouds."
The wife of Liú Zhēn's "Ode to Presenting Spring" states:
"The dark path descends to the north,
the azure thoroughfare ascends to the east;
the dark spirits send off winter,
the bright spirits welcome spring."
Bathe in the Yí Purify at the Luò
"The Analects" states:
"In late spring,
when spring garments are ready.
Five or six capped youths,
six or seven boys,
bathe in the Yí River,
enjoy the breeze at the Wǔyú altar,
and return home singing."
Cài Yōng's "Purification Text" states:
"Vast is late spring,
its month clears on the sì day.
High and low bustle about,
only women and men.
Each seeks a hundred blessings,
on the banks of the Luò."
Elm Seed Rain Peach Blossom Flood
Fàn Shèngzhī's Book states:
"In the third month, the elm seed rain falls,
and on high, firm ground, grain can be planted."
"The Hán School's Exegesis on the Book of Songs" states:
"The Zhēn and the Wěi flow full and broad,
meaning the peach blossom flood in the third month.
It was the custom in the state of Zhèng
that on the third day of the third month,
they used this water to summon and restore souls,
to cleanse away inauspiciousness."
Fù Xuán of the Jìn Dynasty, "Rhapsody on Sunny Spring"
Heaven and Earth intermingle,
their vital breath harmonious and pure.
Dormant creatures stir,
all things delight in life.
Graceful are the willows,
drifting the duckweed.
The peach tree is lush and tender,
its blossoms glow radiantly.
Luxuriant flowers blaze, illuminating the fields,
splendid petals part, displaying their glory.
Magpies build nests in tall trees,
swallows carry mud to broad courtyards.
Observe the hoopoe alighting on mulberries,
listen to the cuckoo's morning call.
I delight in the universal feast of benevolent transformation,
and marvel at the hawk and falcon changing their forms.
Jìn Dynasty Xiè Wàn's "Rhapsody on Spring Outing"
The Azure Yang governs the season,
Gōumáng drives the chariot of time.
Displaying cleansing and irrigation to wither the dry,
Fresh shoots flourish, gleaming with new life.
Lush leaves form a canopy like a tent,
Green grasses spread out like a mat.
Thus, from afar I summon fine companions,
Nearby I invite honored guests.
Raise feathered cups and offer toasts in turn,
Arrange silk and bamboo instruments to play together.
Chant of new garments' dazzling splendor,
Recall the lingering dust of the Rain Dance Altar.
Strum the singing zither, cherishing antiquity,
Ascend the tall terrace to delight in spring.
Then, blue cliffs grow more profound,
Thick shrubs weave shade.
Light clouds, dim and hazy, veil the peaks,
Gentle winds, clear and cool, open the lapels.
Jìn Dynasty Zhàn Fāngshēng's "Rhapsody on Longing for Spring"
Wild geese soar on wings in the returning wind,
Swallows carry mud in their beaks, arriving on their journey.
Birds of prey, moved by benevolence, change their nature,
The cuckoo, riding transformation, alters its song.
Wheat grows lush, bearing elegance,
Mulberry trees flourish, spreading glory.
Blossoms shine brightly, setting the grove ablaze,
Leaves sway gracefully, charming the stems.
Sòng Dynasty Liú Yìgōng's "Rhapsody on Feeling Spring"
Listen to the songs of seasonal birds,
Truly, they warble and chirp.
Grieve for the sunward geese heading north,
Pity the spring swallows entering the eaves.
The sky dims as clouds drift,
The sun hides, its light obscured.
Winds, mild and gentle, blow over orchids,
Rain, drizzling and misty, washes the stems.
Grass, blessed by moisture, rises in beauty,
Flowers, following the ether, scatter fragrance.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwén Emperor's "Rhapsody on Late Spring"
Await the lingering spring at the northern pavilion,
Recline at a lofty feast upon the southern slope.
Water, sifted through emptiness, reflects the bottom,
Wind enters the trees, fragrant among the branches.
Alas, the turning of seasons,
Sigh at the shifting of natural signs.
Gaze upon young bamboos by the ridge,
Admire new lotuses budding in the pond.
Rocks, leaning on waves, stand inverted,
Forests, veiled by sun, hang sideways.
See playing fish among the algae,
Hear startled birds, the female calling.
Trees by the flowing stream, their shadows quiver,
Cliffs at dusk, cloaked in parting clouds.
Waves churn, sand drifts,
Moss grows, paths grow perilous.
Liáng Dynasty Xiàoyuán Emperor's "Rhapsody on Spring"
West of the small garden in Luòyáng,
East of the broad avenue in Cháng'ān,
Moss stains the pond entirely green,
Peach blossoms fill the hills, all red.
Dew moistens branches, weighing down leaves,
Nets entwine flowers, tugged by the wind.
Suí Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Rhapsody on Spring"
In Yíchūn Garden, spring has returned,
In Pīxiāng Hall, spring clothes are made.
New year, birdsongs of a thousand warbles,
Second month, willow catkins fill the road, flying.
Héyáng county is entirely flowers,
Jīngǔ has always been gardens full of trees.
A clump of fragrant grass enough to hinder passersby,
Several feet of drifting silk threads already block the path.
Open Shànglín Park, all rush to enter,
Crowd the river bridge, vying to cross.
Emerge from Lìhuá's golden chamber,
Descend from Fēiyàn's orchid palace.
Hairpins numerous, surprisingly heavy,
High coiled hair buns, fearing the wind.
Eyebrows vie with willows for green,
Faces compete with peaches for red.
Reflections come upon the pond,
Petals fall upon the gown.
The terrace where Xiāo was played for Nòngyù,
The waters where girdle jades chimed over ripples.
Move to Qīlǐ, households wealthy,
Enter Xīnfēng, wine exquisite.
Moss just turns green, hiding fish,
Wheat barely greens, covering pheasants.
Suí Dynasty Xiāo Què's "Rhapsody on Spring"
Fallen flowers, countless in number,
Flying birds row through blossoms, passing.
The forbidden garden, exceedingly rich in wind,
Blows blossoms, spring fills the road.
Before the cliff, a flat rock like a tower,
In the water, linked sand gathers into islets.
Second month, oriole songs just about to cease,
Third month, spring breezes already flow again.
Divided streams wind around small fords,
Moat waters still intermingle.
Mountain top, gaze upon water and clouds,
Water's depth, view mountain and trees.
After the dance, fragrance still lingers,
After the song ends, sound yet remains.
Wheat fields, one startled pheasant,
Water chestnut pond, two flying egrets.
Táng Dynasty Tàizōng's "Poem on Early Spring"
Cold follows the waning pitch-pipes, changing,
Spring pursues birdsongs, unfolding.
First winds waft through willow strands,
Dawn snow intersperses plum blossoms.
Jade forests, green with old bamboos,
Emerald ponds, verdant with new moss.
Fairy fields, first wild geese depart,
Ornamental trees, no orioles yet come.
Southern Qí Dynasty Yú Xī's "Poem on Spring Countryside"
Wind gentle, butterflies play with flowers,
Scenery lovely, birds harmonize with spring.
Woodcutter songs clamor on ridges at dusk,
Fisher oars disturb the river at dawn.
In the mountains, fragrant asarum,
Lingers alone, thinking of someone.
Southern Qí Dynasty Wáng Jiǎn's "Poem on Spring Evening"
Dew's splendor just illuminates the year,
Cloud hues again pass through spring.
Empty chamber, gradually grass piles up,
Secluded curtains, daily dust gathers.
Also "Spring Poem"
Orchids have grown, filling the garden,
Duckweed spreads, about to half-cover the pond.
Light breeze sways mixed blossoms,
Fine rain tangles clustered branches.
Also says
Scenery bathed in dew's glow,
Mist colors dot orchid's radiance.
Green shoots knot with emerald algae,
Yellow birds sport, flying in spring.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwén Emperor's "Poem on Thinking of Shànglín in Spring"
Spring breeze is inherently wondrous,
Willows and poplars are most fitting.
Willow branches always touch the ground,
Poplar catkins love to rise, blown upward.
Everywhere, spring hearts stir,
Often lament the passing of time.
Also "Late Spring Poem"
Purple orchids, leaves first full,
Yellow orioles, warbling not sparse.
Rocks crouching, still like beasts,
Vines lengthening, further like garments.
Water bends, patterned fish gather,
Forest dims, crows and birds fly.
Island reeds change to new joints,
Cliff paulownias grow with old girth.
Wind-blown flowers fall, not yet ceased,
Mountain window opens, night's door.
Liáng Dynasty Xiàoyuán Emperor's "Spring Poem"
New orioles hidden among leaves, warbling,
New swallows toward windows, flying.
Willow catkins sometimes cling to wine sprinkles,
Plum blossoms suddenly enter garments.
Jade bridle ornaments follow the wind's pace,
Golden saddles shine in sunlight's glow.
Do not let spring hues grow late,
Alone gazing for the traveler's return.
Also "Gazing on Spring Poem"
Leaves dense, know willows are thick,
Flowers spent, feel plums are sparse.
Orchids sprout, not yet graspable,
Reeds small, unfit for writing.
Liáng Dynasty Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Grieving Spring"
Tender grass half-drawn yellow,
Slender twigs not fully green.
Year's blossoms enclosed within forbidden gardens,
Mist blossoms wind around layered paths.
Cold moss curls, then stretches,
Winter springs break, then resume.
Early flowers scatter,凝结成金,
First dew drips, forming jade.
Also "Early Spring Poem"
Supporting the path, seek the sunny spring,
Together hand in hand we go.
Grass colors still seem not so,
In the woods, none yet to show.
With nothing to do, chase plum blossoms,
Vainly trust in willow's promise.
Better to return again,
Bearing feelings, entrust to cup and wine.
Liáng Bàoquán's "Poem in Response to the Prince of Xiāngdōng on Spring Days"
New orioles begin their new return,
New butterflies again newly fly.
New blossoms fill the new trees,
The new moon adorns the new light.
New radiance, new air arrive early,
New vistas, new fullness embrace.
New waters bear new green afloat,
New birdsongs are newly pleasant to hear.
New scenes naturally renew themselves,
New leaves once more newly climb.
Though new branches can be knotted,
New sorrows—how can they ease my face?
New thoughts alone swirl thickly,
New understanding cannot be heard.
New fans are like the new moon,
New canopies mimic new clouds.
Newly fallen are linked pearl tears,
Newly dotted is the pomegranate-red skirt.
Liáng Wénrénqiàn's "Spring Day Poem"
High terraces stir with spring hues,
Clear pools reflect the sun's splendor.
Green sunflowers turn toward the light,
Jade willows slant with the chasing wind.
In the woods are birds singing from the heart,
The garden abounds with dazzling flowers.
All together know the season's change,
I sigh that I alone am far from home.
Zhōu Yǔxìn's "Chanting on Spring Poem"
Last night, birdsong heralded spring,
Startled cries stirred the four neighborhoods.
This morning beneath the plum trees,
Surely there will be people breaking blossoms.
Zhōu Zōnglǐn's "Spring Gaze Poem"
At dusk by the spring terrace,
I linger, fond of the lingering light.
The Commandant has newly transplanted date trees,
The Minister of Works begins planting poplars.
One branch still holds the cassia's fragrance,
Within ten steps there is orchid scent.
Gazing and gazing, no day-lilies are seen,
To forget sorrow—in the end, I do not forget.
Also, "Early Spring Poem"
Last evening the spring wind arose,
This morning the spring air arrives.
Orioles warble once or twice,
Flower trees open in several layers.
Scattered powder becomes first butterflies,
Cut silk makes new plum blossoms.
The wandering traveler grieves over a thousand miles,
With no leisure to ascend the high terrace.
Chén Zhāngzhèngjiàn's "Poem on the Pond in Early Spring, Composed by Imperial Command"
The distant sky clears the dense rain,
The high pavilion reflects the rushing sunlight.
Snow is gone from the green mountain paths,
Ice melts in the clear green pond.
Spring light falls on cloud-like leaves,
Flower shadows emerge from sunlit branches.
Lute and wine cup offered for the final feast,
How could one tire of breeze and moon?
Suí Emperor Yáng's "Late Spring Poem"
Luòyáng's spring is somewhat late,
Gazing all around, spring radiance fills the view.
Poplar leaves will soon grow dark,
Peach blossoms fall, not yet sparse.
Peeking under eaves, swallows vie to enter,
Piercing the woods, birds fly in chaos.
Only those at the frontier passes,
Are just now soaked by thick dew on their clothes.
Suí Yángxiūzhī's "Spring Day Poem"
Slowly, slowly, the late spring day,
Lush and abundant, spring light ascends.
Gentle dew washes the golden plate,
Fine threads adorn the pearl-like web.
Gradually I see the steps' fragrant vines creep,
Slightly I sense the pond's lotus lengthen.
Butterflies flit mirrored among flowers,
Chǔ sparrows chirp along the twigs.
Suí Xiāoquè's "Gazing from the Garden on a Spring Evening Poem"
In the spring courtyard, idly I gaze far,
Towers and terraces naturally hide each other.
Fragrant plums shed their late blossoms,
Bamboo by the pond sprouts its first shoots.
The spring's murmur tells the water's haste,
Clouds drawing near make the mountain feel close.
I do not worry that flowers won't fly away,
But fear only that flowers will fly away entirely.
Suí Jiāngzǒng's "Spring Poem"
Water moss suits the flowing hues,
Mountain cherries aid the setting glow.
Bathing birds dive and play again,
Drifting blossoms pass, not to return.
Chén Shūdá's "Poem on the Beginning of Spring"
Snowflakes link jade trees,
Icy colors scatter on the jade pool.
Soaring birds appear and vanish in the distance,
Accumulated greenery stretches far, uneven.
Also, "Poem Composed by Imperial Command at the Guìlín Palace in Early Spring"
Golden knockers reflect spring hues,
Jade pitch-pipes move the year's flow.
Vermilion towers—clouds resemble canopies,
Cinnabar cassia—snow is like flowers.
The water's edge curves with the steps,
Wind-swept twigs emerge slanting from willows.
A light carriage approaches the Tàiyè Pond,
Deep dew is sipped like flowing rosy clouds.
Yú Shìnán's "Spring Night Poem"
In the spring garden, the moon lingers,
The bamboo hall opens as night encroaches.
Startled birds push through the woods to pass,
Wind-borne blossoms come across the water.
Yáng Shīdào's "Leisurely Stroll on a Spring Morning Poem"
On holiday rest, seizing idle delight,
At clear dawn I stroll to the northern woods.
Ponds and banks are matted with fragrant grass,
Orchids and angelica assail my secluded lapel.
Through mist, the dawn sun parts,
Amid flowers, I play with spring birds.
Wild paths are ever full of scent,
Mountain steps see bamboo shoots encroach again and again.
Why need I order a light carriage canopy?
Peach and plum trees naturally form their shade.
Shàngguān Yí's "Poem in Response to Early Spring"
The imperial palanquin departs from Pīxiāng Hall,
Clear songs rise by the Tàiyè Pond.
Dawn trees are full of flowing orioles,
Spring banks accumulate fragrant grass.
Wind hues turn dew patterns over,
Snow blossoms ascend the empty azure.
Flower-seeking butterflies arrive unceasingly,
Mountain light grows dim, nearing dusk.
Yuán Wànqǐng's "Poem in Response on the Spring Day Pond and Terrace"
Sunlight shadows flit in the Flowery Palace,
Wind patterns gather on the Grassy Pond.
Phoenix towers open wide through the night,
Dragon-carriages gaze toward spring's shift.
Also, "Poem in Response to Spring Days"
Light flowers, chaotic butterflies—the immortal's apricot;
Dense leaves, clamorous orioles—the imperial maiden's mulberry.
On the Flying Cloud Pavilion, spring should arrive,
In the Bright Moon Tower, night is not yet half gone.
Also said:
The phoenix carriage meets the wind, riding to the Purple Pavilion,
The simurgh carriage avoids the sun, turning at the Vermilion Gates.
Within the pond, urgent pipes prolong the spring gaze,
In the rear palace, clear songs open the night's doors.
Summer, Part Two
The "Monthly Ordinances" of the Book of Rites states:
"In the first month of summer,
the sun is in the constellation Mǎo,
at dusk the constellation Yì is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Qiānniú is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán comments:
'The first month of summer
is when the sun and moon meet in the constellation Shíchén,
and the Dipper points to the hour of Sì.'
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Bǐng means 'bright,'
all things are brightly visible and strong.
Its emperor is Yándì,
its deity is Zhùróng,
this is the sovereign of red essence, the minister of fire.
Yándì
is Dàtíngshì.
Zhùróng,
the son of Zhuānxūshì,
named Lí,
is the official in charge of fire.
The pitch standard is Zhònglǚ.
Gāo Yòu comments:
'Yang disperses outward,
yin is solid within,
thus it assists yang to achieve success,
therefore it is called Zhònglǚ.'
Frogs chirp,
earthworms emerge,
wángguā grows,
bitter vegetables bloom.
Frogs
are toads;
wángguā
is bìqiè.
Gāo Yòu says:
'Frogs
are toads.
Bì,
pronounced as pújié.'
Fragile grasses die,
wheat harvest arrives,
light punishments are decided,
minor crimes are judged.
Fragile grasses
are such as jì and tínglì.
" The "Xiǎo Zhèng" of the Xià calendar states:
"In the fourth month, Mǎo becomes visible."
Mǎo
is the name of a star.
The "Tōng Guà Yàn" of the Book of Changes states:
"At the beginning of summer,
the clear and bright wind arrives,
the summer magpie sings,
the bógǔ flies,
lightning appears,
the dragon ascends to heaven."
Dragon,
is the name of the star Xīn.
The "Monthly Ordinances" states:
"In the middle month of summer, the sun is in the constellation Shēn,
at dusk the constellation Jiǎo is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Wēi is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán comments:
'The middle month of summer
is when the sun and moon meet in the constellation Chúnshǒu,
and the Dipper points to the hour of Wǔ.'
The pitch standard is Ruíbīn.
Gāo Yòu says:
'In this month, yin qi withers below,
resembling the host;
yang qi is above,
resembling the guest.'
Minor heat arrives,
mantises are born,
jú begins to sing,
the fǎnshé becomes silent.
Mantises
are the mother of piāoxiāo.
Jú,
is the bóláo.
Fǎnshé,
is the bǎishé bird.
Gāo Yòu says:
'Mantises are called tiānmǎ in some places,
also known as héyóu,
in Yǎn and Yù they are called jùfǔ.
In this month, yin acts below,
yang disperses above.
Bóláo,
after the summer solstice, responds to yin and kills snakes,
then impales them on thorns and begins to sing.
Fǎnshé,
is bǎishé,
it changes its voice,
imitating the calls of a hundred birds,
therefore it is called bǎishé.'
Deer shed their antlers,
cicadas begin to sing,
bànxià grows,
mùjǐn blooms."
Mùjǐn,
is yùzhēng,
also called shùn,
also known as chèn.
The "Xiǎo Zhèng" of the Xià calendar:
"In the fifth month, when Shēn appears, lángtiáo sings,
lángtiáo has five colors.
At early dusk, Dàhuǒ is at the zenith."
Dàhuǒ,
is the star Xīn.
The Book of Documents states:
"The day is long and the star Huǒ
is used to determine the middle of summer.
Yǒng,
means long,
referring to the day of the summer solstice.
Huǒ,
is the middle star of the Azure Dragon,
by raising the middle star, the appearance of the seven stars can be known.
Birds and beasts shed their fur."
At this time, feathers and fur become sparse and change.
Gé,
means change.
The "Monthly Ordinances" states:
"In the last month of summer,
the sun is in the constellation Dōngjǐng,
at dusk the constellation Dī is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Dōngbì is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán says:
'The last month of summer
is when the sun and moon meet in the constellation Chúnhuǒ,
and the Dipper points to the hour of Wèi.'
The pitch standard is Línzhōng.
Warm winds arrive,
crickets dwell in walls.
According to the Ěryǎ:
'Crickets are qióng.'
Liú Shào comments:
'That is lièqīng.'
Sūn Yán says:
'In the state of Liáng, it is called qióng.'
Guō Pú says:
'Now it is called cùzhī.
Qióng's pronunciation and meaning,
sometimes written as qióng.'
The "Fāngyán":
'Qīngliè,
in Chǔ is called xīshuài,
resembling a locust but smaller,
pure black,
glossy like lacquer,
with horned wings,
also called qióng,
also called qīngliè.
People in Yōuzhōu call it cùzhī.'
Hawks then practice learning,
