rotten grass transforms into fireflies."
Hawks practicing learning refers to seizing and grappling.
Fireflies,
are flying insects,
fireflies.
Liáng Yuándì's "Zuǎnyào" states:
"Summer is called Zhūmíng,
the qi is red and bright.
Also called Chángyíng,
pronounced yǐ zhēng fǎn.
Zhūxià,
Yánxià,
Sānxià,
Jiǔxià.
Heaven is called Hàotiān,
meaning the qi is vast.
Wind is called Yánfēng,
season is called Yánjié,
grass is called Màocǎo, Zácǎo,
trees are called Wèilín, Màolín, Mìshù, Màoshù.
The first month of summer is also called Wéixià, Shǒuxià;
the last month of summer is also called Cúshǔ."
Cú,
means to go,
meaning the heat begins to go.
Dragon appears, Quail perches.
The Book of Documents states:
"The day is long and the star Huǒ,
is used to determine the middle of summer."
The commentary says:
"Huǒ,
is the middle star of the Azure Dragon."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"When the dragon appears, the rain sacrifice is performed."
The commentary says:
"The dragon appears in the month of Jiànsì,
the body of the seven mansions of the Azure Dragon,
appears in the east at dusk."
Zhāng Héng's "Yìngwèn" states:
"When the humid heat arrives, the quail fire perches,
when the cold ice freezes, the yuántuó hibernates."
Wheat Autumn, Plum Rain
The Book of Rites says:
"In the first month of summer, the wheat autumn arrives,
and light punishments are carried out."
Cài Yōng's "Monthly Ordinances Commentary" says:
"Each of the hundred grains takes its sprouting as spring,
and its ripening as autumn.
Therefore, wheat regards the first month of summer as its autumn."
Zhōu Chù's "Records of Local Conditions" says:
"The rain that falls when plums ripen
is called plum rain."
Soaring Shrike, Chirping Cicada
The Book of Rites says:
"In the middle month of summer, the shrike begins to cry."
Lǐ Yóng's "Admiring Summer" says:
"The forest cicadas chirp ceaselessly,
and the crying shrikes soar gracefully."
The "Changes: Comprehensive Divination Verification" says:
"When the summer solstice arrives, the seasonal wind comes,
cicadas begin to chirp,
and praying mantises are born."
Flowering Hibiscus, Blooming Yāo
The Book of Rites says:
"In the middle month of summer, the hibiscus flowers."
The Mao Commentary on the Book of Songs says:
"In the fourth month, the yāo blooms."
The annotation states:
"To bear fruit without flowering is called 'blooming.'
Yāo
is a type of grass."
Grasses Flourish, Trees Grow Lush
Cáo Zhí's ancient Yuefu "Song of Beauty" says:
"The summer season is pure and harmonious, the sky clear and cool,
a hundred grasses thrive and spread, orchids release their fragrance."
Fù Xuán's "Describing Summer Rhapsody" says:
"The fourth month belongs to summer,
the season reaches its peak of yang,
deer shed their antlers in the wilds,
grasses and trees grow lush and their branches lengthen."
White Plums, Red Plums
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" says:
"Red cherries ripen in spring,
white plums mature in summer."
Emperor Wén of Wèi, in his "Letter to Wú Zhì," says:
"Float sweet melons in clear springs,
sink red plums into cold ice."
Scorching Wind, Blazing Sun
Chén Lín's "Rhapsody on Great Heat" says:
"The soil is moist and steamy, damp and oppressive,
the times are murky and turbid.
Warm winds gather thick and red,
like a blazing fire in a kiln."
Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on Great Heat" says:
"Yán Dì controls the seasons,
Zhù Róng governs the direction.
Like the high flames of the Fusang tree,
blazing with the multiplied light of nine suns."
Vermilion Carriage, Red Banner
The Book of Rites says:
"In the first month of summer,
the Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Bright Hall,
riding in a vermilion carriage."
The Art of War says:
"When deploying troops in summer,
a red banner leads the front,
holding halberds and advancing forward."
Virtue Symbolized, Merit Rewarded
Fàn Zǐ's Strategies says:
"Virtue takes its symbol from spring and summer,
punishment takes its symbol from autumn and winter."
Jīng Fáng's Changes Divination says:
"At the summer solstice, the Li trigram reigns,
the seasonal wind prevails.
The ruler should ennoble the virtuous
and reward the meritorious."
Wind-Viewing Tower, Ice Terrace
Pān Yuè's "Records of Guānzhōng" says:
"The Cassia Palace is also called Sweet Springs Palace.
They also built a Wind-Viewing Tower and a Cold Dew Terrace to escape the heat."
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng" says:
"Shí Jìlóng stored ice at the Ice Well Terrace.
On the three fu days,
he bestowed ice upon his ministers."
Offering Millet, Presenting Peaches
The Imperial Reader: Lost Rites says:
"In summer, one rides a vermilion carriage, drives red horses, carries a red banner,
to welcome summer in the southern suburbs.
The offerings are first millet and chicken."
The Book of Rites says:
"In the middle month of summer,
the Son of Heaven presents cherries
as offerings first to the ancestral temple."
Tuning Pipes, Distributing Ice
The Book of Rites says:
"In the middle month of summer,
command the musicians to repair drums and tambourines,
and tune the qin, se, pipes, and xiao."
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"The Ice Officer is in charge of distributing ice in summer."
The annotation states:
"When the summer heat is intense, ice is distributed as a gift."
Encircling Stoves, Waving Fans
Huán Tán's New Treatise says:
"When sending off Wáng Zhòngdū in Hànzhōng,
on a day of great summer heat,
they made him sit exposed to the sun,
and also encircled him with ten stoves.
He did not speak of the heat, and his body did not sweat."
Liú Yìqìng's A New Account of the Tales of the World says:
"Què Jiābīn visited Xiè Ān during the three fu months.
The scorching heat was blazing and oppressive.
Even though fans were waved facing the wind,
he was still drenched in dripping sweat."
Whistling in the Wind, Inhaling the Dew
Wáng Càn's "Rhapsody on Great Heat" says:
"Looking up at the blazing courtyard, I whistle in the wind.
The wind arrives, hot as boiling water.
Breathing in and out to dispel the heat,
sweat falls like rain, soaking my clothes."
Wáng Dù's "Inscription on a Fan" says:
"The bright red sun blazes with light,
opening the window invites a cool breeze.
Wearing coarse cloth, I inhale the cloud-like dew;
my body soothed, my spirit naturally harmonizes."
Branch-Washing Rain, Flying Awn Dew
Zhōu Chù's "Records of Local Conditions" says:
"In the middle month of summer, branches are washed and rivers swell."
The annotation states:
"During this season, there is often heavy rain,
called 'branch-washing rain.'"
Fù Xuán's "Summer Rhapsody" says:
"A gentle breeze blows softly, fanning all things.
Wheat contains dew, and its awns fly in the wind."
Yellow Sparrow Wind, Red Fish Water
Zhōu Chù's "Records of Local Conditions" says:
"In the middle month of summer, long winds fan the heat."
The annotation states:
"During this season, there is often a wind from the southeast,
commonly called the 'yellow sparrow long wind.'"
Lì Dàoyuán's commentary on the Water Classic says:
"The Dān River produces red fish.
Ten nights before the summer solstice, watch for them.
When the fish surface, red light shines upward like fire."
Heat-Avoiding Drink, Coolness-Feasting Gathering
Emperor Wén of Wèi's Discourses on Literature says:
"When the imperial carriage arrived at Xǔ,
the Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, Liú Sōng, was sent north to oversee Yuán Shào's army.
He feasted daily with Yuán Shào's sons and brothers.
Often during the three fu period,
they drank day and night,
getting extremely drunk
to the point of unconsciousness,
saying it was to avoid the summer heat for a time.
Thus, in Héshuò, there was the 'heat-avoiding drink.'"
Fù Xián's "Rhapsody on Feeling Cool: Preface" says:
"In the height of summer, oppressed by the scorching heat,
the intense heat lasts no more than ten days
before it turns cool again.
Taking advantage of the timely coolness,
I gathered close friends for a feast and composed this rhapsody."
Later Hàn Fán Qīn's "Rhapsody on Heat"
The blazing heat is just arriving,
the time is the sixth month.
Línzhōng marks the pitch,
Zhù Róng governs the season.
The Great Fire star radiates light,
scorching winds are fierce and intense.
The sinking sun shoots its rays,
stagnant heat spreads everywhere.
The world is choked with smoke,
things are scorched, people are parched.
Brilliant wild fires
spread across the central plains;
blazing, intense heat
steams my layered pavilion.
Jìn Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Rhapsody on Great Heat"
As the season of spring passes away,
It connects with the final month of summer.
How the sun blazes fiercely,
Gathering oppressive heat and stirring warmth.
Then the Dàlǚ pitch governs the tones,
Zhùróng marks the season.
Steam rises and spreads outward,
While the moon remains hidden within.
If the three periods of intense heat follow one another,
The scorching summer advances relentlessly.
Above, not a wisp of cloud;
Below, not a trace of breeze.
Suí Lú Sīdào's "Rhapsody on Enjoying the Cool"
Zhùróng presides over the direction,
The bright summer arrives in its order.
The air signals the beginning of the hot season,
The time is the advancing summer heat.
Accumulated sultriness steams behind curtains and windows,
Restless dampness flows through garden fences.
The warm wind feebly waves its long fan,
Fiery clouds blaze and rise on all sides.
Then alert the six carriages,
Follow the three routes,
Beat the alligator-skin drums,
Play the phoenix flutes.
Cloud-like chariots interlock their wheels,
Unicorn-like horses align their bits.
Enter the towering heights of the cloud palace,
Ascend the lofty peaks of the immortal observatory.
Draw the mighty wind from caverns,
Receive the clear dew from the crimson sky.
Stir rustling breezes in emerald tents,
Scatter fine mists within ornate towers.
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on Early Summer"
Suddenly spring turns to summer,
Overnight, birds and flowers shift.
Yīn and yáng deepen in the leaves' hues,
Morning and evening vary in light and heavy mists.
Orioles still sing within the halls,
Spider threads just weave across the sky.
High pendants meet orchid shadows,
Thin ribbons link with grass patterns.
Green scales startle beside the oars,
Dark swallows dance before the eaves.
Why must one be at Fényáng
To again find mountain springs?
"Poem on the Beginning of Summer's Season"
At the northern gate, three springs wane,
In southern camps, the nine summers begin.
Yellow orioles sport with dawn's changes,
Emerald forests hold lingering fallen blossoms.
Waterfalls still echo through valleys,
Gibbons' cries naturally answer the emptiness.
Early lotuses curl toward their centers,
Tall poplars stretch with their shadows.
At this moment, joy knows no bounds,
Tuning the zither, we sit and amuse ourselves.
Qí Xiè Tiǎo's "Summer Poem"
The wheat season brings clarity and harmony,
Cool rain dispels scorching heat.
Red lotuses sway with tender water chestnuts,
Vermilion vines twine around new bamboos.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Matching Prince Xiāngdōng's Poem on Early Summer"
Chilly winds mingle with fine rain,
Hanging clouds aid the wheat's coolness.
Bamboos and trees both lush and green,
Flowers and butterflies both take flight.
Swallows' mud nests are carried and fall again,
Cuckoos' songs fade then rise anew.
Reclining stones have vines as cables,
Mountain bridges use trees as beams.
I long to wait by the splendid pond,
Where the bright moon exhales clear light.
Liáng Xiāo Zǐfàn's "Poem on Sitting Alone on a Summer Night"
The season meets the advancing heat,
This night falls within the three periods of intense heat.
Leaning on the balcony, I await cool air,
Amid the banquet, weary of oppressive warmth.
Lonely, I face the empty window,
Clear window overlooking night bamboos.
Insect sounds disrupt the steps' grass,
Firefly lights circle the courtyard trees.
The slender moon passes slanting rays,
Wind-blown blossoms stir lingering fragrance.
Liáng Xú Pēng's "Summer Poem"
Fiery light rests within the eaves,
Clear air enters the rooms.
Evening lotuses still curl green,
Sparse lotus flowers long shed their red.
Liáng Xú Chī's "Summer Poem"
Summer scenes weary the rooms,
Drawing near the mat to enjoy clusters of flowers.
Lotus shadows slant, merging in green,
Lotus reflections face, dividing the red.
Now avoiding the scorching heat,
The clear wine cup alone remains not empty.
Suí Yǔ Xìn's "Poem in Response to the Summer Command"
Vermilion blinds roll up the splendid sun,
Emerald curtains shield the double sunlight.
Fifth month's fiery air steams,
Three periods make the water-clock long.
Wheat ripens with the wind,
Plums turn yellow in the rain.
Open ice comes with well water,
Mixed with powder, it carries raw fragrance.
Robes hold plantain leaf scent,
Fans stir bamboo flower coolness.
Early water chestnuts grow soft horns,
First lotus blossoms open fine chambers.
I wish to accompany immortal cranes in flight,
At Luòpǔ, listen to reed organ music.
Suí Lǐ Délín's "Summer Poem"
Summer scenes bring much oppressive steam,
Temporarily seek cool by mountains and waters.
Paulownia branches cover jade railings,
Lotus leaves fill silver ponds.
Light fans sway the bright moon,
Precious mats brush against yellow dye.
Pots hold immortal guest wine,
Jars store imperial terrace nectar.
Talented ladies descend from the Bronze Sparrow Tower,
Attendant maidens come from Bright Light Palace.
Songs surpass the markets of Qí,
Dance tunes crown Píngyáng.
Gentle breezes stir silk sashes,
Light sweat stains rosy makeup.
Together we delight in accompanying the feast,
Endless joy for a thousand autumns.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem in Response to Teaching on Plum-Rain Summer"
Long corridors connect purple halls,
Fine rain answers the yellow plums.
Floating clouds half ascend the sky,
Clear sounds come from across the pond.
Phoenixes gather, paulownia blossoms scatter,
Turtles emerge, lotus leaves unfold.
Fortunate to encounter the joy of doing good,
Repeatedly bestowed are talents that aid the times.
Also, "Poem on Summer Evening"
The flowing fire star slightly inclines west,
Evening shadows cover layered walls.
High sky clears to distant hues,
Autumn air enters cicada songs.
Suí Wèi Yànchēn's "Poem in Response to the Command on Early Summer"
Though the fragrant spring festival has passed,
Scenery still retains lingering splendor.
Beyond the blinds, small swallows fly,
Against the door, fading blossoms fall.
Dance robes flutter with fine gauze,
Song fans conceal light silk.
Orchid chambers are best by night,
Unafraid of the sun's slanting rays.
Yáng Shīdào's "Poem Matching the Command on Summer Evening Scene"
Imperial paths flanked by drooping willows,
Traveling palaces connect to Jiànzhāng Palace.
Sunset casts horizontal peak shadows,
Clouds return, stirring evening cool.
Carved balconies move with flowing music,
Feathered canopies rest by winding ponds.
Cut grass grows green again,
Fading blossoms sparse yet fragrant.
Green cliffs resemble Gūyè,
Jade streams resemble Fényáng.
Fortunate to belong to a time of inaction,
Joy and amusement are just beginning.
Wèi Wéndì's "Letter to Wú Zhì" states:
The matter has already been seen in the annotation on "vermilion plums" above.
Autumn, Part Three
The "Monthly Ordinances" chapter of the *Book of Rites* states:
"In the first month of autumn,
the sun is in the constellation Zhāng,
at dusk the Tail constellation is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Lóu is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán said:
'The first month of autumn
is when the sun and moon meet at the Chúnwěi constellation,
and the Dipper's handle points to the Shēn direction.'
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Gēng means 'to change',
Xīn means 'new'.
The sun travels in autumn,
following the white path in the west,
ripening the myriad things.
The moon assists it.
The myriad things all solemnly change and renew,
their blossoms and fruits newly formed.
Its emperor is Shàohào,
its deity is Rùshōu.
This is the lord of the white essence,
the minister of the metal office.
Shàohào is
the Jīntiān clan.
Rùshōu,
the son of the Shàohào clan,
named Gāi,
served as the metal official.
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Yízé.
Gāo Yòu said:
'The sun's force declines,
the moon's qi arises,
the myriad things wither and suffer,
responding to the law and completing their nature.'
Cool winds arrive,
white dew descends,
cold cicadas sing,
and hawks then sacrifice birds.
'Hawks sacrifice birds' means
before eating them, they show precedence.
In the second month of autumn,
the sun is in the constellation Jiǎo,
at dusk the Southern Dipper is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Bì is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán said:
'The second month of autumn
is when the sun and moon meet at the Shòuxīng constellation,
and the Dipper's handle points to the Yǒu direction.'
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Nánlǚ.
Gāo Yòu, annotating the *Monthly Ordinances*, said:
'Yang qi is stored within,
the yin pitch assists the yang,
allowing it to achieve completion.'
Blinding winds arrive,
wild geese come,
the dark birds return,
flocks of birds store up food.
'Blinding winds'
means swift winds.
'Dark birds'
are swallows.
'Return' means they go to hibernate.
All birds that follow the yang
do not dwell in the central states.
'Store up' refers to what they gather.
Day and night are equal,
thunder then begins to cease,
hibernating insects reinforce
their burrows.
Doors [are closed],
yang qi daily declines,
water begins to dry up.
'Reinforce'
means to increase.
In the last month of autumn,
the sun is in the constellation Jiǎo,
at dusk the constellation Qiānniú is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Dōngjǐng is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán said:
'The last month of autumn is when the sun and moon meet at the Dàhuǒ constellation,
and the Dipper's handle points to the Xū direction.'
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Wúyì.
When the qi of the last month of autumn arises,
then the Wúyì pitch-pipe responds.
Gāo Yòu said:
'Yin qi ascends,
yang qi descends,
the myriad things follow the yang and flourish,
and there is nothing that emerges and appears.'
Wild geese come as guests,
sparrows enter the great water and become clams,
chrysanthemums have yellow blossoms,
jackals then sacrifice beasts and kill birds.
'Come as guests'
means they lodge as guests and have not yet left.
'Great water'
is the sea.
'Kill'
means to slaughter.
Frost begins to descend,
plants and trees turn yellow and fall.'
The *Book of Documents* says:
'At night the middle star is Xū,
thereby determining the mid-autumn.
'Xiāo'
means night.
'Xū'
is the middle star of the Black Tortoise,
appearing on the autumn equinox day.
Birds and beasts [grow] fine fur.'
'Xiǎn'
means to order,
fur regrows and is put in order.
Pronounced sū qí fǎn,
also xīng tiǎn fǎn.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
'In the seventh month,
the hundred insects hibernate,
Qīngnǚ then emerges.'
Gāo Yòu said:
'Qīngnǚ is the Jade Maiden of Qīngyào,
she who oversees frost and snow.'
To send down frost and snow.'
The *Xiǎozhèng Calendar of Xià* says:
'In the eighth month,
the red bird offers
'offers'
means to present.
White birds,
white birds,
are mosquitoes and gnats.
Chén then hides.
'Chén'
is the constellation Fáng.
Rú becomes a rat.
In the ninth month,
the fire enters.'
'Fire'
is the great fire,
the Heart star.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's *Compiled Essentials* says:
'Autumn is called Báicáng (White Storehouse),
its qi is white and it stores the myriad things.
Also called Shōuchéng (Harvest Completion),
the myriad things mature and are gathered in.
Also called Sānqiū (Third Autumn), Jiǔqiū (Ninth Autumn), Sùqiū (Plain Autumn), Sùshāng (Plain Shang), Gāoshāng (High Shang).
Heaven is called Míntiān (Compassionate Heaven),
'Mín'
means to pity,
pitying the withering and falling of the myriad things.
Wind is called Shāngfēng (Shang Wind), Sùfēng (Plain Wind), Qīfēng (Chilly Wind), Gāofēng (High Wind), Liángfēng (Cool Wind), Jīfēng (Stirring Wind), Bēifēng (Sad Wind).
Scenery is called Lǎngjǐng (Bright Scenery), Chéngjǐng (Clear Scenery), Qīngjǐng (Pure Scenery).
Time is called Qīchén (Chilly Time), Shuāngchén (Frosty Time).
'Frosty Time' can be applied to the ninth month.
Season is called Sùjié (Plain Season), Shāngjié (Shang Season).
Grass is called Shuāicǎo (Withered Grass).
Trees are called Shūmù (Sparse Trees), Shuāilín (Withered Woods), Shuāngkē (Frosty Branches), Shuāngtiáo (Frosty Twigs).
Seventh month: first autumn, beginning autumn, early autumn, commencing autumn, orchid autumn.
Eighth month: mid-autumn,
also called Zhòngshāng.
Ninth month: last autumn,
also called mùqiū (late autumn), mòqiū (end autumn), mùshāng (late Shang), jìshāng (last Shang), miǎoqiū (tip of autumn).
Also called Shòuyī (Bestow Clothes),
at this time women's work is finished,
and clothes begin to be bestowed.
Also called Xuányuè (Dark Month).'
Fire Flows, Earth Rules
The *Máo Odes* says:
'In the seventh month the Fire star flows,
in the ninth month clothes are bestowed.'
The *Explanations of the Changes* says:
'Kūn in the southwest governs the beginning of autumn.'
Jīng Fáng's *Divinations from the Changes* says:
'At the beginning of autumn, Kūn rules,
and cool winds are in operation.'
The *Forest of Collected Studies on the Zhou Changes* says:
'Kūn
is earth.'
Dew Descends, Wind Rises High
The *Comprehensive Hexagram Verification* of the *Changes* says:
'At the beginning of autumn, cool winds arrive,
white dew descends.'
Jiāng Yóu's poem says:
'High winds hasten the season's change,
congealing frost urges things to transform.'
Knotweed Wind, Reed Dew
Cài Yōng's *Exegesis on the Monthly Ordinances* says:
'In the mid-autumn White Dew season,
blinding winds arrive.
The people of Qín call knotweed wind blinding wind.'
The *Máo Odes* says:
'The reeds are green and luxuriant,
white dew becomes frost.'
Condensed Mist, Cool Mist
Yuán Shù's "Ode to Autumn Sentiments" states:
"Dragging the condensed mist of the sorrowful spring,
Turning the stern clouds of the farthest border."
Bào Zhāoyuǎn's "Ode to Autumn Thoughts" states:
"Autumn trees spanning the riverbank,
Cool mist covering the river."
Fierce Wind, Bright Moon
Pān Yuè's "Ode to Autumn Stirrings" states:
"Courtyard trees rustle and shed leaves,
Fierce winds sweep and blow the curtains."
Zhàn Fāngshēng's "Ode to Autumn Night" states:
"The night is long and endless,
The moon is bright and halts its light."
Receding Floodwaters, Cleansed Air
The "Chǔcí" states:
"How sorrowful is the autumn air! Vast and empty, the sky is high and the air clear,
Desolate and bleak, the floodwaters recede and the water clears."
Yuán Shù's "Ode to Autumn Sentiments" states:
"The fiery capital lifts the dust,
The autumn sky cleanses the air."
Cool Wind, Chilly Sun
The "Lǐjì" states:
"The cool wind arrives."
The "Máo Shī" states:
"The autumn sun is chilly,
All plants wither."
Long Night, Short Daylight
Lú Chén's poem states:
"Chilly, pure autumn,
Days shorten, nights lengthen."
Pān Yuè's "Ode to Autumn Stirrings" states:
"How brief the faint sunlight,
I feel the long night is just beginning."
Metal Emperor, Jade Maiden
The "Lǐjì" states:
"In early autumn,
Its emperor is Shàohào."
The note states:
"Shàohào,
is Jīntiānshì."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"When the three autumn months arrive,
Qīngnǚ then appears,
Descending frost and snow."
Gāo Yòu's note states:
"Qīngnǚ is the heavenly deity Qīngyāo Jade Maiden,
Who presides over frost and snow."
Condensed Dew, Flying Frost
Cáo Zhí's "Ode to Autumn Thoughts" states:
"The four seasons alternate in dominance, autumn's breath is sorrowful,
High clouds are still, dew condenses on clothes."
Xú Guǎng's "Ode to Autumn" states:
"At this time, Zhāoyáo points west,
The sky is high, the air clear.
Flying frost condenses and sprinkles,
Withered leaves drift and fall."
Gathering Warmth, Cleansing Heat
Zhàn Fāngshēng's "Autumn Night Song" states:
"The autumn night is pure and bright,
Spreading the shāng breath to gather warmth,
Fanning the chilly wind to change the coolness."
Lǐ Yóng's "Lament for the Four Seasons" states:
"Autumn days: fire flows in the sky to cleanse the heat,
Wind enters the forest and thins the branches."
Pearl-like Dew, Golden Wind
Lǐ Yóng's "Ode to Stirred Emotions" states:
"Wind touches waves, creating ripples,
Dew moistens plants, pearls condense."
Zhāng Xié's poem states:
"The golden wind fans the pure season,
Crimson dew opens the yīn period."
White Emperor, Qīngnǚ
The "Lǐjì" states:
"In the month of the beginning of autumn,
The Son of Heaven leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials to welcome autumn in the western suburbs."
Zhèng Xuán's note states:
"In this month, sacrifice to the White Emperor in the western suburbs to welcome autumn."
Qīngnǚ is found in the note for "Jade Maiden" above.
Returning Swallows, Chirping Cicadas
The "Zhōushū" states:
"Five days after White Dew,
The dark birds return."
Also:
"After the beginning of autumn,
Cold cicadas chirp."
Striking Falcons, Transforming Fireflies
The "Hànshū" states:
"Sūn Bǎo served as Governor of the Capital.
On the day of the beginning of autumn, he appointed Hóu Wén as the Eastern District Commandant.
When Hóu Wén entered for an audience,
Sūn Bǎo instructed him:
'Now falcons begin to strike,
We should follow the heavenly breath,
To capture the treacherous and evil, executing them like severe frost.'" The "Yì‧Tōng Guà Yàn" states:
"At the beginning of autumn, rotting grass transforms into fireflies."
Insect Chirps, Bird Strikes
Sū Yàn's "Long Autumn Night" states:
"Seasonal birds sing in the courtyard willows,
Seasonal insects chirp by the door and hall."
The "Yì‧Tōng Guà Yàn" states:
"At the autumn equinox, birds of prey strike."
Leaves Fall, Grass Withers
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Yāngē Xíng" states:
"The autumn wind soughs, the weather turns cool,
Grass and trees wither and fall, dew becomes frost."
Lǐ Líng's "Reply to Sū Wǔ's Letter" states:
"In the cool ninth month of autumn,
Beyond the frontier, the grass withers."
Dewy Leaves, Frosty Branches
Xiè Huìlián's poem states:
"Round and round, leaves full of dew,
Rustling, branches stirred by wind."
Hé Jǐn's "Lament for Autumn" states:
"Frost condenses on branches, sparkling,
Dew drips from leaves, clear and cold."
Falling Blossoms, Shedding Leaves
Sū Yàn's "Long Autumn Night" states:
"Withered leaves scatter, their blossoms intermingle,
Falling petals drift, scattering fragrance."
Pān Yuè's "Ode to Autumn Stirrings" states:
"Wandering mists rise in the morning,
Withered leaves fall in the evening."
Nine Laws, Five Policies
The "Zhōulǐ" states:
"The duty of the Grand Minister of War
Is to uphold the nine laws for establishing the feudal states,
To assist the king in pacifying the feudal states,
In mid-autumn, instruct in military administration."
The "Guǎnzǐ" states:
"In the three autumn months, on the gēng and xīn days, issue the five policies.
The first policy: prohibit gambling.
The second policy: do not display the blades of the five weapons.
The third policy: encourage the traveling farmers to hasten gathering the harvest.
The fourth policy: repair deficiencies, fill cracks, mend walls, and secure gates and alleys.
The fifth policy: respect the season,
For all the five grains are to be gathered in."
Welcoming Cold, Welcoming the Breath
The "Zhōulǐ" states:
"The Yuèzhāng official is in charge of striking the earth drum in mid-autumn,
Playing the Bīn poems,
To welcome the cold breath."
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Continued Hànshū" states:
"On the day of the beginning of autumn,
Before the fifth mark of the night water-clock,
All officials in the capital wear white silk robes with black collars and trim, and inner garments,
To welcome the breath in the western suburbs."
Presenting Fur Garments, Bestowing Armrests
The "Zhōulǐ" states:
"The Sīqiú official is in charge of making the great fur garment,
For the king's clothing when sacrificing to heaven.
In mid-autumn, present fine fur garments,
In late autumn, present serviceable fur garments."
The "Lǐjì" states:
"In the month of mid-autumn,
The Son of Heaven resides in the Zǒngzhāng Grand Temple.
In this month,
Care for the aged and decrepit,
Bestow armrests and staffs."
Moonlit Canopy, Windy Curtains
Tāng Huìxiū's "White Ramie Poem" states:
"The autumn wind soughs into the winding chamber,
The gauze canopy holds the moonlight, sorrowful thoughts."
Windy curtains are already mentioned in the note for "Fierce Wind" above.
Frosty Steps, Windy Cracks
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Ode to Autumn Sorrow" states:
"Autumn evenings are long and distant,
Sorrowful heart forever wounded.
Trees rustle, covered by wind,
Steps turn white, receiving frost."
Xiè Língyùn's "Seventh Night Poem" states:
"The crescent moon's light enters the door,
Early autumn wind winds through cracks."
Chilly Sun, Piercing Wind
The "Máo Shī" states:
"The autumn sun is chilly."
Zuǒ Sī's "Miscellaneous Poem" states:
"The autumn wind is piercing,
White dew becomes frost."
Illuminating the curtains, the moon fills the tent with light and the wind blows through.
Xiàhóu Zhàn in "Autumn's Sorrow" said:
"The moon obscurely hides in clouds,
while the stars faintly lose their light.
Reflecting on the sparse windows of the front balcony,
illuminating the tranquil rooms behind the curtains."
Sòng Xiàowǔ in "Autumn Poem" said:
"The soughing wind fills the tent."
Branches sway in the wind, dewdrops hang on branches.
"Chǔ Cí" says:
"The autumn wind is sighing,
caressing the branches with fragrant ease."
Xiàowǔ's poem says:
"Dewdrops glisten on bent branches."
The vigil of cranes against the dew, the cicadas cherishing the wind.
Zhōu Chǔ in "Records of Secluded Lands" says:
"The singing cranes warn of the dew,
they are white cranes.
This bird is naturally cautious,
when the white dew descends in August,
they cry and alert one another."
Xiè Huìlián in "Longing for Autumn Poem" says:
"Desolate and withstanding the wind cicadas,
geese croon through clouds."
Hàn Fánqīn in "Autumn Reflections"
Why is Hé Yàn saddened by autumn?
He dwells in the quiet night and harbors sorrow.
The wind's coolness invigorates the spirit,
trees stir, leaves rustle, and branches echo.
Clouds rise in the east towards western streams,
then advance fiercely towards Dān Qiū.
Concealing the sun's dark shadows by day,
shrouding the bright moon in layered gloom.
The rain falls swiftly and scattered,
yellow floods gush and swirl across.
Jìn Pān Yuè in "Autumn's Exaltation"
Suddenly the cycles of the seasons shift,
all things turn in whirling flux.
Observing the flowering and planting,
discerning where prosperity and decline lodge.
Feeling the winter's chill and spring's bloom,
lamenting the summer's flourish and autumn's fall.
How true Sǒng Yù's words are:
"Mournful is the essence of autumn,
rustling as grasses and trees shake and wither.
Tremulous and restless like being far-traveled,
climbing mountains, gazing at waters, sending off the returning ones.
The affection in parting with longing companions,
the unrest of distant travel burdens the heart.
On the riverbank stirred by emotion, lamenting departure,
atop mountains yearning afar, grieving what’s near.
The multitude of feelings burdens the heart,
encountering one path too trying to endure.
Alas, how mournful is the autumn sun,
no sorrow remains unfulfilled.
Wild geese return to the fields,
hawks fly in the marshes.
Morning mists rise,
withered leaves fall by evening.
At this time, one's light fan is put away,
the thin silk garment set aside,
the seat covered with rush matting,
wearing lined clothes.
Trees in the courtyard rustle and shed their leaves,
the strong wind bends and billows the curtains.
Cicadas sadly murmur in their cool song,
geese float southwards drifting.
The sky bright and high,
the sun lingers and gradually fades.
Knowing the short days of autumn's sunlight,
feeling the long nights ahead.
The moon faintly illuminates with hazy light,
the dew chills and congeals in cool coldness.
Sparks brilliantly shine on steps and doors,
crickets chirp by the house screens.
Hear the early cries of departing geese,
gaze at remnant embers of the fading sun."
So forth.
Jìn Cáo Pí in "Autumn's Exaltation"
Pure autumn begins anew,
the cool breeze dispels the heat.
Leaves fall upon the jade steps,
branches pressed low by sturdy trees.
Distant birds chirp with morning cries,
light curtains flutter gently and rise slightly.
Evening dew saturates the orchid courtyard,
autumn insects sound along the halls.
Qí Chǔ Yànhuí in "Autumn's Sorrow"
Clouds whirl and gather thickly,
trees smoke golden and their leaves fall.
Beholding the lonely wandering geese,
observing the soaring cranes amidst clouds.
The scene dimly fades towards decline,
as time gradually nears its end.
Alone in sorrow and grief-stricken,
I gather my light garments to return to the tent.
Yú Shìnán in "Autumn Poem"
Observing the chronology of four seasons,
beholding the clarity of autumn's salubrious festival.
Clouds cleared, the sky is high,
floods will withdraw, waters become pure.
The dew of pearl condenses coldly,
the green mountains bright as mirrors.
Swallows pack tents, their nests empty,
startled flocks of geese finish their flight.
At this time,
ascending the patterned pavilion,
facing the flying view.
Pull back the fine gauze of thin curtains,
lift the light silk of the green canopy.
Reflecting the white waves of bright moonlight,
observing the resplendence of clear skies.
Watching the night magpies circle branches,
gazing across the Milky Way at the Loom Weaver.
Lotus still fragrant on riverbanks,
grass yet green by the river banks.
Táng Tàizōng in "Poem of Passing Through Autumn"
Summer's intensity left ash yesterday,
Autumn's arrows now shift time forward.
The twin peaks of Emei Mountain emerge first,
as waves rise gradually on Dòngtíng Lake.
Osmanthus blossoms in the secluded cliffs,
Chrysanthemums bloom golden by the side of Bà River.
The rotation of seasons worthy of lament,
subtle principles comprehended with brush in hand.
Also, "Sitting at Night in Early Autumn Poem"
Corridors that meander to painted pavilion,
early moonlight illuminates evening curtains.
Cold in border regions hastens the flying geese,
in the autumn garden cicadas chirp slowly.
Dew forms on sparse forest leaves,
cool light on chrysanthemums revealing their splendor.
The sorrowful heart meets this season,
with long sighs, containing deep sadness.
Also, "Autumn Day Poem"
The refreshing air clears the blue pond,
autumn wind stirs the forest of osmanthus.
Dew congeals like a thousand jade fragments,
chrysanthemums disperse like clusters of gold.
The sun's height varies with mountain shadows,
clouds embellish the sky with patterns.
The Isles of Immortals are out of sight,
springs and rocks entertain the heart.
Also,
Chrysanthemums disperse, as autumn's wind arises,
lotuses sparse, the pure dew full.
Geese flock with the arrival of autumn,
cicadas fade with the departure of summer forests.
Clouds accumulate in half mountain sorrow,
dew shattered high in the sky.
Seems like gazing from Chéngdū,
straight to the front of Emei peak.
Also, "Imperial Palace of Cùiwēi in Autumn Poem"
Autumn light condenses on Cùiwēi peaks,
cool breezes the imperial palace in solemnity receive.
Lotuses sparse as the canopy is incomplete,
trees cold leaving parts of the curtain empty.
Nearby ranks move, casting geese shadows,
round flowers nail the chrysanthemum clumps.
Expressing feelings beyond worldly dust,
gazing high among the white clouds.
Also, "Facing Autumn by Night in Liáodōng Mountains Poem"
Smoke arises, banks distant concealed,
the moon sets, casting shadows over half the cliff.
Mountains in series, startled birds abound,
distant peaks, severed calls of gibbons echo.
Also, "Autumn Late at Mountain Pavilion Poem"
The mountain pavilion fills with autumn,
cool wind passes through rocky windows.
Sparse orchids still retain mist,
fading chrysanthemums still bear dew.
Ancient stones covered with fresh moss,
new nests sealed in old trees.
Surveying the scene, feelings limitless,
shadows of the sun diminish by the hour.
Jìn Zuǒ Sī in "Miscellaneous Poems"
How the autumn wind chillingly blows,
white dew turns into morning frost.
Tender branches morning and evening firm,
green leaves daily and nightly yellow.
Bright moon emerges from clouded cliffs,
shining softly flowing pure light.
Open the windows to face the front courtyard,
morning geese soar and cry aloud.
Xiè Huìlián’s “Autumn Poem”
Bright, bright shines the heavenly moon,
Splendid, splendid gleam the river stars.
Desolate, the wind-bearing cicadas,
Lonely, the cloud-crossing geese cry.
Cold autumn stirs the quiet chamber,
A lone lamp dims the secluded curtain.
Upright thoughts, myriad worries gather,
Tossing and turning through half the long night.
Sòng Nánpíng Wáng Liú Shuò’s song says:
The autumn sky clear and high,
Autumn air brings the first chill.
White dew descends in fine droplets,
The bright moon flows with pure light.
Condensed mist floats over city gates,
A mournful wind enters the chamber.
Sòng Bào Zhào’s “Autumn Day Poem”
Withered mulberry leaves fall easily,
The weary traveler’s heart startles easily.
Why so early this year too?
Already I hear the weaver’s chirping.
Chilly, chilly cold on the mat,
Desolate, desolate clear within the tent.
Scenery prolongs evening thoughts,
Frost and dew press upon morning glory.
White poplars now bleak and soughing,
Long sighs arise from this.
Sòng Tāng Huìxiū’s song says:
Autumn wind soughing enters the winding room,
Silken curtains hold moonlight, grieving the heart.
Crickets cry at night, breaking one’s heart,
Through the long night thinking of you, my heart flies afar.
Others yearn for you, but you forget me,
Brocade quilts and jade mats are fragrant in vain.
Liáng Wéndì’s “Early Autumn Poem”
Autumn wind suddenly soughs,
Toward evening brings coolness home.
Rolling up the curtain reveals river hues,
Opening the window gazes upon moon’s glow.
Evening flowers shine beneath the railing,
Sparse fireflies fly over the mat.
Even staying still is like this,
How much more bidding farewell to one departing?
Also:
Blind wind crosses Hángǔ Pass,
Falling dew descends upon fragrant branches.
Green pools reflect cloud vapors,
Blue hills hold the moon’s circle.
Flower hearts turn in the wind,
Leaf shadows shift among trees.
Traveling afar alone a thousand miles,
Evening sighs—who knows them with me?
Liáng Fàn Yún’s “Poem for Dàorén Jùngōng”
Autumn tumbleweed drifts over autumn fields,
Cold algae float in cold ponds.
Wind-tossed branches shake with wind’s sound,
Frosty leaves break from frosty twigs.
Luckily when the clear river is full,
Do not let the bright moon wane.
If the moon wanes and you do not come,
When shall we meet as promised?
Liáng Shěn Yuē’s “Autumn Night Poem”
The moon sets, night approaches midnight,
Purple mist thickly gathers.
Dimly, fireflies enter the fog,
Scattered, geese emerge from clouds.
Bā lads secretly tune the se,
Hàn girls sew skirts at night.
New friends find joy like this,
Long-standing bonds—how can they be heard?
Liáng Bào Quán’s “Autumn Poem” says:
Dew’s color has turned to frost,
Parasol trees and catalpas half yellow.
Swallows gone, eaves ever quiet,
Lotus chilled, pond no fragrance.
Traveler’s feelings often bitter,
Autumn nights gradually grow longer.
Zhōu Hóngràng’s “Beginning of Autumn Poem” says:
This morning warns of fading fire-star,
Autumn winds have long stirred.
Cloudy skies change summer’s hue,
Tree leaves stir with autumn’s sound.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn’s “Harmonizing with Héngyáng Wáng’s Autumn Night Poem”
Cool breeze rises at Suī Garden,
Cloud vapors gather at Zhāngtái.
Firefly glow joins flickering candles,
Moon’s shadow accompanies the river’s flow.
Green silk, vermilion strings ripple,
Yellow flowers, pale ale float.
High carriage displays splendid verse,
This is to compose of new autumn.
Suí Yángdì’s “Mourning Autumn Poem” says:
Last year’s autumn just departed,
This year’s autumn comes again.
Dew thick, mountain air cold,
Wind urgent, cicada cries mournful.
Birds strike, first shifting trees,
Fish chill, about to hide in moss.
Broken fog sometimes lets sun through,
Remnant clouds still make thunder.
Suí Yáng Xiūzhī’s “Autumn Poem” says:
Sunshine on bamboo before the window,
Dew moistens violets in the back garden.
Night insects chirp by the steps,
Light moths circle the candle flying.
Suí Yǔ Xìn’s “Late Autumn Poem”
Desolate and clear, facing twilight scene,
Sparse and lonely, gazing at cold steps.
Damp courtyard congeals falling dew,
Whirling wind rolls fallen locust leaves.
Sun’s warmth slanting, still cold,
Cloud peaks evening, more gloomy.
Pitiful several lines of geese,
Dot by dot line up in distant sky.
Also “Harmonizing with Early Autumn Poem”
Falling stars, first hidden fire,
Autumn frost just stirs the bell.
Northern tower connects across the Milky Way,
Southern sky mirrors carved dragons.
Auspicious phoenix perches on bamboo fruit,
Divine tortoise climbs upon lotus.
Naturally there is the south wind tune,
Coming again to blow through the ninefold heavens.
Suí Xiāo Què’s “Harmonizing with Early Autumn West Garden Poem at Imperial Command”
After the third heat by pond pavilion,
Before the ninth autumn in forest lodge.
Clear and cool, ravine spring rocks,
Scattered and mixed, mingled wind and mist.
Lotus blooms, a thousand leaf shadows,
Pomegranates bright, a hundred branches blaze.
Resting banners on the ridge,
Rippling painted boats on the waves.
Also “Harmonizing with Sītú’s Assistant Yáng Pìqiáng’s Late Autumn Poem”
Leaves sparse, know the tree sheds,
Fragrance gone, feel the lotus fade.
Mountains and marshes hold many thoughts,
Fields and gardens—let me return again.
Also “Autumn Day Poem”
Autumn skies emulate literary elegance,
Autumn waters excel in Zhuāngzǐ’s wisdom.
Grass wet with reed dew,
Waves rolling Dòngtíng wind.
Sitting idly, turning over fallen leaves,
Long slope rests orchid clusters.
Eaves still noisy with swallows,
Pond quiet, geese not yet come.
Cicada songs heard, seemingly broken,
Pond clear as if reflecting the sky.
Yuán Lǎng’s “Autumn Day Poem in Response to Imperial Command”
Jade trees, cool breeze rises,
Golden pond, fine grass wilts.
Leaves fall at Shāngbiāo Tower,
Geese return to Bright Moon Pond.
Welcoming cold, osmanthus wine ripens,
Holding mist, chrysanthemums droop.
Once attending Zhāngtái feast,
A thousand autumns long wish thus.
Yáng Shīdào’s “Early Autumn Night Sitting in Response to Imperial Command”
Jade pipes, coolness first responds,
Golden pot, night gradually wanes.
Cāngchí flows somewhat clear,
Immortal’s palm dew just forms beads.
Goose sounds break in the wind,
Tree shadows chill in the moonlight.
Crisp air, vast sky pure,
Chanting aloud, thoughts feel broad.
Shàngguān Yí’s “Poem Harmonizing with Mountain Night Facing Autumn”
Palace tents clear summer heat,
Imperial path holds autumn shade.
Mournful wind shifts Hàn’s zither,
Flowing water enters Yú’s qin.
Clouds fly, sending off stray geese,
Moon rises, cleansing sparse woods.
Dripping, dew-laden branches sound,
Vast and misty, smoky valleys deep.
Also, "Matching Lord Yǐngchuān's Poem on Autumn Night"
Vast and empty, distant the hue of the sky,
Yellow leaves, mournful as the season changes.
Over the cave-fringed shore descend the following geese,
The long gale sends off the nesting swallows.
A thousand autumns flow with the evening scene,
A hundred sounds hold the night's call.
Steep battlements listen to the golden watch,
Layered terraces cut the silver arrow.
Liú Yīzhī's "Poem on the Early Autumn at the Jiǔchéng Palace, Composed by Imperial Command"
The imperial park spreads from the golden palace gates,
The immortal terrace halts the jade carriage.
The wilds divide at the singing phoenix peaks,
The road connects to the Precious Chicken Altar.
Forest trees accumulate a thousand frosts,
Mountain palaces are cold through the four seasons.
Cicadas urgent, know autumn comes early,
Orioles sparse, feel summer draws to a close.
Pleasing the spirit beyond the purple ether,
Gazing intently toward the white cloud's edge.
From Shùn's sea, waves of verse arise,
Vainly startled by the difficulty of roaming with sages.
Winter, Fourth
The "Monthly Ordinances" of the Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,
the sun is in Fáng,
at dusk Xū is at the zenith,
at dawn Zhāng is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán says:
'The first month of winter
is when the sun and moon meet at the ford of Xīmù,
and the Dipper establishes the hour of Hài.'"
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Rén means 'to bear',
Guǐ means 'to measure'.
The sun's northward path follows the black way,
closing and storing the myriad things.
The moon acts as its assistant.
The myriad things conceive within Rén and Guǐ,
then sprout buds.
Its Thearch is Zhuānxū,
its spirit is Xuánmíng.
This is the lord of black essence, the minister of water.
Zhuānxū
is of the Gāoyáng clan.
Xuánmíng
is the son of Shàohào,
named Xiū
and Xī,
and is the minister of water.
The pitch-pipe matches Yìngzhōng.
Gāo Yòu says:
'Yīn responds to Yáng,
transforming to complete its work.'"
Water begins to freeze,
earth begins to harden,
pheasants enter the great waters and transform into clams,
rainbows hide and are not seen.
Great waters
means the Huái River.
Large clams are called shèn.
In the second month of winter,
the sun is in Jī,
at dusk Yíngshì is at the zenith,
at dawn Zhěn is at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán says:
'The second month of winter is when the sun and moon meet at Xīngjì,
and the Dipper establishes the hour of Zǐ.'"
The pitch-pipe matches Huángzhōng.
Huángzhōng
is the beginning of the pitch-pipes.
Gāo Yòu says:
'Yáng qi gathers below,
Yīn qi flourishes above,
sprouting beneath the Yellow Springs,
therefore it is called Huángzhōng.'"
Ice grows thicker,
earth begins to split,
the day is at its shortest,
Yīn and Yáng contend,
all living things stir.
'Contend' means
Yīn is at its peak,
and Yáng desires to arise.
'Stir' means things that are about to sprout buds.
Rue begins to grow,
iris shoots emerge,
earthworms coil,
elk shed their antlers,
spring waters move.
Rue
is a fragrant herb.
Iris shoots
are horse chives.
'Spring waters move'
means moisture ascends.
In the last month of winter,
the sun is in the Southern Dipper,
at dusk Kuí is at the zenith,
at dawn Dǐ and Kàng are at the zenith.
Zhèng Xuán notes:
'The last month of winter is when the sun and moon meet at Xuánxiāo,
and the Dipper establishes the hour of Chǒu.'"
The pitch-pipe matches Dàlǚ.
Wild geese face north,
magpies begin to nest,
pheasants call and hens brood,
gòu
means a pheasant's cry.
Earthen oxen are brought forth to send off the cold qi.
'Bring forth' means to make.
Earthen oxen:
Chǒu corresponds to the ox,
the ox can be led and halted.
'Send off' means to conclude.
The sun reaches the end of its lodge,
the moon reaches the end of its conjunction,
the stars revolve through the heavens,
the count is nearly finished."
This means the sun, moon, and stars,
having run their course to this point,
have all circled back to their former places.
Lodge
means resting place.
Conjunction means meeting.
The Shàngshū states:
"The day is short and the star is Mǎo,
thereby rectifying the midwinter.
'Day is short'
means the day of the winter solstice.
Mǎo
is the central star of the White Tiger.
Birds and beasts grow soft
(pronounced rùn).
fur."
Birds and beasts all grow moist, fine down to warm themselves.
Cài Yōng's "Explanations of the Monthly Ordinances" states:
"Winter
means 'end'."
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's "Compiled Essentials" states:
"Winter is called Xuányīng (Mysterious Essence),
its qi is black yet greenish essence.
Also called Ānníng (Peaceful Tranquility),
also called Xuándōng (Mysterious Winter), Sāndōng (Three Winters), Jiǔdōng (Nine Winters).
Heaven is called Shàngtiān (Upper Heaven).
Meaning the season is without affairs,
being above and overseeing below.
Winds are called Hánfēng (Cold Wind), Jìnfēng (Forceful Wind), Yánfēng (Severe Wind), Lìfēng (Harsh Wind), Āifēng (Sorrowful Wind), Yīnfēng (Overcast Wind).
Scenery is called Dōngjǐng (Winter Scene), Hánjǐng (Cold Scene).
Time is called Hánchén (Cold Hour).
Season is called Yánjié (Severe Season).
Birds are called Hánniǎo (Cold Birds), Hánqín (Cold Fowl).
Grasses are called Hánhuì (Cold Plants), Huángcǎo (Yellow Grasses).
Trees are called Hánmù (Cold Trees), Hánkē (Cold Boughs), Sùmù (Plain Trees), Hántiáo (Cold Branches).
The tenth month, first winter,
also called Shàngdōng (Upper Winter),
also called Yángyuè (Yang Month).
At this time pure Yīn holds sway,
but disliking its lack of Yáng,
it is therefore called Yang Month.
The twelfth month, last winter,
also called Mùdōng (Late Winter), Miǎodōng (Tip of Winter), Chúyuè (Expelling Month), Mùjié (Late Season), Mùsuì (Late Year), Qióngrěn (End of Ripening), Qióngjì (End of Cycle)."
Huángzhōng Xuánpèi
The Lǐjì states:
"In the second month of winter, the pitch-pipe matches Huángzhōng."
Lǐ Yóng's "Stirred by Winter" says:
"Gāoyáng grasps the dark reins,
Tàihào drives the start of winter.
Wàngshū roams the celestial chart,
Yàolíng harmonizes with Yàn's chronicle."
Běilù Nánjiāo
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Continuation of the Hàn History" states:
"When the sun is in Běilù, it is called winter."
Shěn Yuē's "History of the Sòng" states:
"On the gēngyín day of the tenth month, the winter solstice,
the emperor personally sacrificed at the circular mound in the southern suburbs."
Jade Snow Pearl Ice
Liú Yìgōng's "Poem on Night Snow" says:
"Massed clouds shut out stars and moon,
flying jade gathers on courtyard trees."
Xiè Huìlián's "Rhapsody on Snow":
"Dripping streams hang as ice,
along the eaves, catching the corners.
Brilliant! Like Féngyí
cutting a clam to bring forth bright pearls."
Springs Stir, Waters Freeze
The Zhōu Shū states:
"Fifteen days after the winter solstice,
the springs in the water stir.
If they do not stir,
the yīn does not receive the yáng."
Liú Zhēn's "Ode to the Capital of Lǔ" says:
"In the winter of this year,
the clouds and air are clear and bright,
the waters freeze and dew congeals,
ice and snow gleam white."
Beloved Sun, Severe Frost
Dù Yù's commentary on the Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The winter sun is lovable,
the summer sun is fearsome."
An ancient poem says:
"In the harsh winter's eleventh month,
at dawn I rise and tread on severe frost."
Snapping Ice, Splitting Earth
The Wénzǐ states:
"Winter ice can be snapped,
summer branches can be tied."
The Lǐjì states:
"In the midwinter month, the earth begins to split."
Piercing Wind, Grim Clouds
Xiè Huìlián's "Poem Chanting Winter" says:
"Treading on frost, the ice grows ever harder;
accumulated cold, the wind becomes more piercing."
Bào Zhāo's "Winter Poem" says:
"Grim clouds rise chaotically over the mountains,
the white sun wishes to return to its place."
Dark Clouds, White Snow
Ruǎn Jí's "Poems Expressing My Feelings" says:
"Where is the fine hour?
Congealed frost soaks my clothes.
A cold wind shakes the mountain ridge,
dark clouds gather, bringing heavy shade."
Poetry by Zhōng Fūrén says:
"Bitterly cold late winter,
white snow falls thickly."
Ice Fish, Frost Crane
The "Yì‧Tōng Guà Yàn" states:
"During Heavy Snow, fish bear ice on their backs."
Zhèng Xuán says:
"Fish bear ice,
meaning they approach the ice above."
Bào Zhāo's "Winter Poem" says:
"Lonely, the frost-bearing crane;
bright and white, the cloud-accompanying wild goose."
Dragon's Blowing, Crane's Speech
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The Torch Dragon dwells north of Yànmén,
hidden by Wěiyǔ Mountain,
where the sun is not seen.
Its spirit has a human face, dragon body, and no feet."
Xǔ Shèn's commentary says:
"As the sun is not seen,
the dragon illuminates it with its eyes.
It is perhaps a thousand lǐ long.
When it opens its eyes, it is day;
when it closes them, it is night.
When it blows, it is winter;
when it exhales, it is summer."
Liú Jìngshū's Yì Yuàn states:
"In the second year of Tàikāng, during winter,
it was extremely cold.
People in Nánzhōu saw two white cranes under a bridge.
They said:
'This year's cold is no less than the year Yáo died.'
Then they flew away."
Hibernating Birds, Hidden Scales
Wèi Wǔdì's "Chū Xiàmén Xíng" says:
"In the first month of winter, the tenth month,
the north wind lingers and circles.
Hibernating birds lie hidden,
bears and brown bears dwell in caves."
Wáng Càn's poem says:
"Bitterly cold winter days,
stern and severe great cold.
Hidden scales are in the rivers,
returning geese soar aloft."
Cassia Blooms, Pine Flourishes
The Chǔcí states:
"Praise the fiery virtue of the southern land,
admire the cassia tree's winter blooms."
Hé Shào's "Yóuxiān Shī" says:
"Lush green are the pines on the mound,
tall and straight the cypresses on Southern Mountain.
Their splendor flourishes in winter and summer,
their roots never wither and fall."
Drilling in Arms, Deliberating Punishments
The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,
the Son of Heaven commands his generals and marshals to drill in arms and practice archery."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"This is to prepare for the grand review in midwinter."
The Dàdài Lǐ states:
"In the last month of winter, hearing cases and deliberating punishments
is the means to rectify the law."
Gathering Harvest, Storing Grain
The Máo Shī says:
"In the tenth month, gather in the grain harvest:
millet, both early and late sown,
grain, hemp, beans, and wheat."
Cuī Shí's Sì Mín Yuè Lìng states:
"In the tenth month, farm work concludes.
The five grains are already harvested.
Every household stores and preserves,
thus following the seasonal ordinances."
Praying for the Year, Divining the Year
The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,
the Son of Heaven prays to the Celestial Ancestors for the coming year."
The commentary states:
"Celestial Ancestors
are the sun, moon, and stars."
The Zhōu Lǐ states:
"The Tiānfǔ official oversees the display of jade in the last month of winter,
to divine the quality of the coming year."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"To inquire about the correctness of affairs is called 'divination'.
To inquire about the year's quality,
means to consult the turtle shell."
Guarding Gates, Sealing Doors
The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,
command the officials to inspect the stores and accumulations,
repair the city walls,
and guard the gates and wards."
The Máo Shī says:
"Stop up holes and smoke out rats,
block the north window and seal the door."
The commentary states:
"The window facing north.
'Seal'
means to plaster."
Cutting Ice, Lighting Fires
The Lǐjì states:
"In the last month of winter,
ice is at its peak,
waters and marshes are solid through to the center.
Command to gather ice from where it is thickest.
In this month, the sun is in the northern constellation,
the time when ice is hardest and thickest."
The Máo Shī says:
"On the second day, cut ice with a chōng chōng sound."
The commentary states:
"When ice fills the waters to their depths,
command to gather ice from the mountain forests.
'Chōng chōng'
is the sound of cutting ice.
The second day
refers to the twelfth month of the Xià calendar."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"In the first month of winter,
when the Dipper points to Hài,
light fires with pine kindling."
Bear Mat, Fox Fur
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"Duke Líng of Wèi dug a pond in cold weather,
saying he was not cold.
Yuǎn Chūn said:
'Your Majesty wears fox fur,
sits on a bear mat,
with fires at the four corners,
therefore you are not cold.'"
Icy Ravines, Frozen Sea
Lù Shìhéng's Yuèfǔ "Kǔhán Xíng" says:
"Traveling north to the city of Yōu Shuò,
the plains and wilds hold many dangers and hardships.
Bending down, I enter the depths of a deep valley;
looking up, I cross the winding high mountains.
Congealed ice forms in layered ravines,
accumulated snow covers the long ridges."
Ruǎn Jí's "Song of the Great Man" says:
"The yang harmony is faint, the yīn energy exhausted,
the sea freezes and does not flow, cotton wadding snaps.
Breathing is blocked, bitterly, piercingly cold."
Withered Pines and Damaged Bamboo
The Analects states:
"Only when the year grows cold do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to fade."
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Han states:
"Dòu Wǔ submitted a memorial saying:
'This winter, the great cold has exceeded the season,
poisoning and harming birds and beasts,
even extending to the fish in the ponds.
The pines and bamboo by the city walls
have all been damaged and destroyed.'"
Clad in Silk Wadding and Bestowed a Silk Robe
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Xiāo.
Shēn Gōng Wūchén said:
'The troops are suffering greatly from the cold.
If the king tours the three armies,
comforting and encouraging them,
the soldiers will feel as if clad in silk wadding.'"
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"When Fàn Suī served as Prime Minister of Qín,
Wèi Xū Jiǎ was sent as an envoy to Qín.
Suī, in plain clothes and worn garments,
went out privately to meet him.
Jiǎ said:
'How could Fàn Shū be in such dire straits!'
He then took a silk robe and bestowed it upon him."
Warming the Mat and Breaking the Ice
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural states:
"Luó Wēi, styled Déxíng,
lost his father at a young age
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
When his mother was seventy years old,
the weather was extremely cold.
He would often warm the mat with his own body
before letting her lie down."
Shī Jué's Biographies of Filial Sons states:
"Wáng Xiáng was virtuous and upright from a young age.
After losing his mother,
his stepmother despised him and slandered him,
yet Xiáng remained even more filial and respectful.
During the severe cold, the river was frozen,
and fishing nets could not be cast.
His mother desired fresh fish,
so Xiáng removed his coarse garment and broke the ice to seek them.
Suddenly, the ice parted slightly,
and a pair of carp swam out.
Xiáng cast his line and caught them.
At that time, people said it was due to his utmost filial piety."
Singing of the Red Phoenix and Sacrificing the White Dog
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural states:
"During the Hàn dynasty, on the fifteenth day of the tenth month,
people would bring pork and wine into the Temple of the Divine Maiden,
strike the zhù and play the shàngxián melody,
linking arms and stamping the ground while singing 'The Red Phoenix Comes.'
This was a shamanistic custom."
Cuī Shí's Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes states:
"Five days before and after the winter solstice,
buy a white dog and raise it
to offer to the ancestors."
Tree Bark Three Inches Thick and Ground Frozen Ten Feet Deep
The Shīzǐ states:
"In the north, the cold ice
is six feet thick,
and tree bark is three inches thick."
The Book of Hàn records Cháo Cuò's memorial:
"In the lands of the Hú and Mò,
where yin accumulates,
tree bark is three inches thick,
and ice is six feet thick."
Wén Yǐng's commentary states:
"This is due to the cold ground."
Guō Yìgōng's Extensive Records states:
"In the north, the ground is thick,
the cold ice is three feet thick,
and the ground freezes ten feet deep."
Layered Ice a Hundred Zhang Thick and Flying Snow a Thousand Li Distant
Dōngfāng Shuò's Classic of Divine Wonders states:
"In the north, there is layered ice spanning ten thousand li,
a hundred zhàng thick."
The Shīzǐ states:
"In the cold of the north,
the ground freezes six feet thick,
and to the left and right of the North Pole, there is ice that never melts."
The Chǔcí states:
"The soul returns, but the north cannot be halted.
Layered ice towers high,
and flying snow stretches a thousand li."
Wáng Yì's commentary:
"The North Pole is perpetually cold."
Fù Xuán of Jìn, "Rhapsody on the Great Cold"
The five phases swiftly gallop away,
the four seasons end as lightning departs.
Truly, heat goes and cold comes,
the twelfth month completes the year.
The sun and moon meet at Xīmù,
layered yin grows bleak and more severe.
In the midst of winter's great cold,
the final ten days hasten and press urgently.
Rainbows hide in the empty vastness,
scaled and shelled creatures lie hidden and long dormant.
Then heaven and earth turn bitter cold,
all vital energy stifled and blocked.
Harsh frost congeals at night,
sorrowful winds rise by day.
Flying snow piles mountain-high,
desolation stretches ten thousand li.
All rivers choke and cease to flow,
ice freezes solid across the four seas.
The Fúmù tree withers in Yáng Valley,
the Ruòhuā flowers scatter in Méngsì.
Lù Jī of Jìn, "Rhapsody on Moved by the Season"
Alas, the qi of winter—
how bleak and desolate, how severe!
The sky stretches endlessly, ever higher,
mist thickens, shrouding the four directions.
Night, drawn-out and endless, struggles to conclude,
day, lingering and dim, easily fades.
Layered clouds spread luxuriantly,
scattered snowflakes fall swiftly.
The cold, piercing and severe, gradually intensifies,
the wind, rustling and mournful, wildly arises.
Withered branches whistle, clear and cold,
falling leaves flutter, vast and silent.
Mountains, lofty and towering, bear exhaustion,
rivers, winding and twisting, embrace dryness.
Gazing to the eight extremes, all is vast and boundless,
throughout the cosmos, empty and expansive.
Now, as the season turns harsh,
how can the myriad things rejoice?
Fish stir slightly, seeking mates,
beasts gather boldly, crowding together.
Gibbons cry long in the forest peaks,
birds soar high above the clouds.
Lù Yún of Jìn, "Rhapsody on the Year's End"
Zhuānxū governs the season,
Xuánmíng commands the office.
The double yang sinks into hidden gates,
severe accumulated yin lies with the Cold Controller.
Solid ice hardens at the river's bottom,
white snow falls from the clouds' edge.
The season, bitter and cruel, is truly lamentable,
the qi, bleak and desolate, wounds the heart.
A mournful wind grieves, whistling through branches,
fallen leaves tumble and scatter in the woods.
Beasts hide in hills, leaving no trace,
birds cling to trees, resting their calls.
Mountains shake with withered trees on layered ridges,
people harbor sorrow within doubled lapels.
Xiāo Zǐyún of Liáng, "Rhapsody on Year's End Duty at the Lodge"
The sun treads the Maid's degree,
the year's splendor says it ends.
The light scale, charcoal dry,
the heavy weight, springs dried up.
The Dark Warrior hides in the great yin,
the soaring serpent lies dormant in high mist.
The sun approaches the gnomon and easily sets,
the shadow at the central post turns southward.
Condensed cold air gathers in the broad courtyard,
penetrating layered shadows in the straight corridors.
The wind, biting and sharp, rises at dusk,
clouds, deep and vast, darken the light.
Hailstones glisten in the vermilion court,
snowflakes flutter luxuriantly against the crimson screen.
The flying rafters of the pierced screen are veiled,
the tall shadow of the Túsū hall is obscured.
First, dancing flakes swirl over the round pool,
finally, settling blossoms rest on the square well.
Zhāng Huá of Jìn, "Poem on a Minor Gathering at Winter's Beginning"
Sun and moon do not linger,
the four qi cycle and revolve.
Festivals and celebrations alternate in sequence,
all states share the same repose.
All officials harmonize together,
holding goblets, ascending to court.
We have fine rites,
feasting all the hundred officials.
Also, "Miscellaneous Poem" states:
The sundial's measure follows heaven's course,
the four seasons mutually ride each other.
The Eastern Wall is precisely dim at midnight,
stagnant yin, the cold season ascends.
Heavy frost descends that very night,
sorrowful winds rise at midnight.
Vermilion flames, blue without light,
orchid oil sits and congeals by itself.
Jìn Cáo Pí's "Ode to Winter"
Far-reaching winter nights grow long,
Severe cold air ascends strong.
Leaves part from trees at dawn's descent,
Long winds stir branches, rising bent.
Night quiet, faint sounds arise,
Sky clear, moonlight pure and wise.
Cold ice fills channels, frozen tight,
White frost congeals on rails in sight.
This year now suddenly draws to its end,
The coming year returns, time's blend.
Sòng Xiè Língyùn's "Year's End Poem"
Deep sorrow keeps me from sleep,
Bitter this night, slow to retreat.
Bright moon shines on accumulated snow,
Northern wind fierce and mournful in blow.
Time passes, nothing lingers long,
Years fade, feeling urged along.
Also "Poem on Year's End in Péngchéng Palace"
Hastily, I cherish things that wane,
Anxiously, I grieve the year's last grain.
Chǔ songs bring sorrow once again,
Wú dances feel joy's severed chain.
Wide belts loosen old robes worn,
White temples change the face once adorned.
Late dusk, sad sitting alone,
Cuckoos cease, spring orchids gone.
Sòng Bào Zhāo's "Winter Poem"
Dark clouds rise over chaotic hills,
White sun wishes to return, stills.
Hazy fog veils the sky's far end,
Evening gloom obscures cold land.
Vast seas have returning tides,
Aging faces, youth no longer abides.
Now, sir, sing peacefully for a while,
Forget not old age's coming trial.
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì's "Poem on the Tenth Month, Wùyín Day"
Noisy dust now settles down,
Sitting quietly facing layered mound.
Deep winter, willow twigs fall,
After snow, cassia branches small.
Stars bright, mist colors fade,
Sky pale, wild geese in single parade.
Clouds fly, suddenly thinking of towers,
Ice forms, distant as fine silk flowers.
Late tangerines hide behind double screen,
Withered vines wrap around returning beam.
Mountain shade joins water's breath,
Peaks add chill to moonlight's depth.
Also "Cold Night in Xuánpǔ Poem"
Dòngtíng's gate not yet closed,
Golden pot's water-clock has imposed.
Dusk smoke rises from stream bends,
Dark hues emerge where forest ends.
Snowflakes have no stems to hold,
Ice mirrors rest not on stands of old.
Steps' poplars begin to droop,
Shore cassia half newly planted troop.
Old roots wither, fallen orchids lie,
Tiny leaves bloom, fragrant plum nearby.
Wild geese depart, reeds in beak stay,
Monkeys play, around branches sway.
Also "Winter Poem"
This garden's planted arts accrue,
Mountain valleys long winding through.
Joyful moods hold many threads,
True matters also find their beds.
This season, stern winter's scene,
Cold clouds veil the setting sun's sheen.
From afar, wind whispers sough,
Chaotic sight, snow flurries now.
Waves rise, rivers hard to cross,
Forests deep, people sparse and lost.
Mountain birds flee the path's way,
Wild birds fly over ponds in play.
Běi Qí Xíng Zǐcái's "Winter Poem Mourning Aspirations"
In past times, idle wandering men,
Self-indulgent, little restraint then.
Morning drove horses with agate bits,
Evening held bear-ear cups in fits.
Plucking flowers to gift Qí's stream,
Strumming zithers toward Cóng Tower's dream.
Splendors of old now changed and gone,
Decay and illness suddenly come along.
Added by the three winter months' reign,
Sorrowful clouds gather and part again.
Sky high, sunlight pale and thin,
Forests stark, birds' cries begin.
Final winds beat against eaves,
Remaining snow clings to twigs and leaves.
Far travels once to Wǎn and Luò,
Now hesitating in grassy plot.
Current affairs now slip away,
Reflecting on self, alone I stay.
Suí Yángdì's "Winter Night Poem"
Unaware the year will soon conclude,
Already back in Cháng'ān's solitude.
Moon shadows hold frozen ice,
Wind sounds mournful, night's cold price.
Rivers and seas, waves grand and vast,
Xiáo and Tóng passes, dangers amassed.
No way to send wings in flight,
Only wishing to move carriage's light.
Běi Qí Xíng Zǐcái's "Poem in Response to Wèi Shōu's Winter Night at the Historiography Institute"
Year and illness arrive in turn,
Rest and action, peace I cannot earn.
Even beans cannot fill my hunger,
Heavy furs hardly ease winter's anger.
Especially on winter's night,
Frost's breath holds lingering bite.
Wind sounds echo by north window,
Moon shadows pass south sill's narrow.
Lamp light bright then dims away,
Splendid candles new then decay.
Faded face changes with season's call,
Strong will fades as time takes all.
Body frail, belt not fully tied,
Hair fallen, forced to hold crown with pride.
Night scene soon to end its stay,
Evening rest thus finds no wide way.
Suddenly, a clear breeze's gift,
Words graceful as orchid's lift.
First speaking of three friends with sigh,
Last speaking, ashamed of official tie.
Elegant phrases surpass Zhèng and Wèi,
Focused learning beautifies Qí and Hán's decree.
Though careful metaphors have their place,
Few can edit with brush's grace.
High achievements know no bound,
Accumulated winds can be wound.
Vainly think of blue clouds' ease,
Hard to see Red Pine's release.
Send word to Dōngshān's way,
Noble carriage, linger and stay.
First Day of the Year
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"The first day of the first month is called the 'Correct Day'.
On this day, one purifies oneself and offers sacrifices to the ancestors and father,
presenting wine to invoke the spirits."
The "Precious Canon of the Jade Candle" states:
"The first month is called the 'Inaugural Month'.
The 'Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary' says:
'To tread the beginning is to start.'
Its first day is called Yuánrì (the Primary Day).
Yuán means
the greatest of goodness.
The former kings embodied Yuán to reside in correctness.
Furthermore, Yuán means
origin,
beginning.
It is the One,
the head.
It is also called Shàngrì (the Superior Day),
also called Zhèngcháo (the Correct Court),
also called Sānyuán (the Three Primaries):
the primary of the year,
the primary of the season,
the primary of the month.
It is also called Sānshuò (the Three Firsts).
The 'Great Commentary of the Book of Documents' says:
'The Xià dynasty took dawn as Shuò (the first of the month),
the Yīn dynasty took cockcrow as Shuò,
the Zhōu dynasty took midnight as Shuò.'
Setting off bamboo firecrackers in the courtyard.
The "Record of the Seasons of Jīng and Chǔ" states:
"This is to ward off the mountain goblins and evil spirits."
Mountain goblins.
According to the "Classic of Divine Marvels":
"They dwell in the deep mountains of the west,
are over a foot tall,
cause illness to those they encounter,
and fear the sound of bamboo firecrackers."
Also, the custom of burning bamboo and grass as firecrackers originated from the courtyard torches.
Presenting pepper and cypress wine.
The "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"Pepper is the essence of the Jade Balance star.
Consuming it makes one's body light and able to run.
Cypress is an immortal's medicine."
It also says:
"The order of presenting wine
should start from the young,
beginning with the youngest."
Drink peach soup,
and present Fūyú powder.
The "Record of the Seasons of Jīng and Chǔ" states:
"The peach is
the essence of the Five Phases,
suppressing evil qi,
and controlling all ghosts.
Nowadays, people also present Túsū wine
and sticky malt candy."
Prepare the plate of five pungents.
Zhōu Chù's "Record of Local Conditions" says:
"On the Yuánrì of the first month,
the five aromas refine the body."
A note states:
"The five pungents are used to stimulate the qi of the five viscera."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"In spring, drink wine and eat onions
to open the passages of the five viscera."
Make peach boards and attach them to the doors,
calling them 'immortal wood'."
The "Precious Canon of the Jade Candle" states:
"They resemble the mountain peach trees of Yùlǜ;
all ghosts fear them."
Shàngrì (Superior Day) - Shǒuzuò (Inaugural Blessing)
The "Book of Documents" says:
"On the Shàngrì of the first month,
he received the mandate from the Cultured Ancestor."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Shàngrì
is Shuòrì (the first day of the month)."
Wáng Xīzhī's "Monthly Ceremonial Letter" says:
"As days go and months come,
Yuánzhèng brings the inaugural blessing.
Tàicòu announces the time,
and faint yang begins to spread.
May all be well,
nourishing the spirit and cultivating simplicity."
Sìshǐ (Four Beginnings) - Sānyuán (Three Primaries)
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"The first day of the first month is the beginning of the year, and Lìchūn (Start of Spring) is the beginning of the four seasons."
It also says:
"The calendar orders the beginnings of the four seasons,
correcting the nodes of the equinoxes and solstices.
Therefore, the sages examined the calendrical numbers to rectify the Three Primaries.
This is the method by which the sages understood fate."
Lǚduān (Treading the Beginning) - Zhèngshǐ (Correct Beginning)
Zāng Róngxù's "History of Jìn" records:
"Xióng Yuǎn proposed:
'On Lǚduān Yuánrì,
at the moment of correct beginning,
men of understanding
observe the rites and music,
delighting in the sights and sounds,
and exalting the pleasures of refined play.'"
Kāiyuán (Opening the Primacy) - Zhàozuò (Initiating the Blessing)
Shěn Yuē's "History of Sòng" records:
"The 'Southern Suburb Music: Ascension Song' says:
'Opening the primacy, initiating the correct,
rites are complete and music is raised.
The six statutes work in concert,
the nine offices stand in order.'
Hé Chōng's 'Congratulatory Memorial for the New Year' says:
'The jade balance completes its cycle,
Yuánzhèng initiates the blessing.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty responds to Heaven and receives blessings,
sharing in Heaven's endless grace.'"
Jiàngzhǐ (Descending Blessings) - Nàhù (Receiving Blessings)
Wáng Shěn's "Congratulatory Memorial for the New Year" says:
"As the three luminaries change their course,
Yuánzhèng initiates the blessing.
From Heaven descend blessings,
like the rising sun."
Nàhù (Receiving Blessings) - see the note on Zhàozuò.
Bǎifú (Hundredfold Blessings) - Wànshòu (Myriad Longevity)
Féng Yǎn's inscription says:
"On Yuánzhèng Shàngrì,
hundredfold blessings are most efficacious."
Wáng Sù's "Congratulatory Ceremony for the New Year" says:
"Yuánzhèng brings the inaugural blessing,
the jade sphere changes its measure.
I bow and proclaim 'myriad longevity'."
Zhé Sōng (Breaking Pine) - Suǒ Wěi (Reed Ropes)
Dǒng Xūn's "Answers to Questions" states:
"At the beginning of the year, one toasts with pepper wine and drinks it,
because pepper is fragrant by nature,
and also can serve as medicine.
Also, breaking pine branches:
seven for men, fourteen for women,
has the same meaning."
Zōng Lǐn's "Record of the Seasons of Jīng and Chǔ" states:
"On the first day of the first month,
which is the day of the Three Primaries,
paste a painted chicken on the door,
hang reed ropes above it,
and insert talismans beside it.
All ghosts fear this."
Zhé Jī (Slaughtering Chickens) - Fàng Què (Releasing Sparrows)
Shěn Yuē's "History of Sòng" records:
"In former times, at the year's beginning,
they often set reed charms, peachwood figures, and slaughtered chickens at the gates of the palace and all government offices,
to exorcise evil qi."
Péi Xuán's "New Discourses" says:
"On Zhèngcháo,
the county magistrate kills a sheep,
hangs its head on the gate,
and also slaughters a chicken to accompany it."
The "Kǒng Cóngzǐ" records:
"A man from Hándān presented a sparrow to the King of Zhào on Zhèngcháo,
decorated with five colors.
The king was greatly pleased.
Shēn Shū reported this to Zǐshùn.
Zǐshùn said:
'Release it on Zhèngcháo,
to show respect for life.'"
Táogěng (Peachwood Figures) - Jiāo Shāng (Pepper Goblets)
Táogěng (Peachwood Figures) - see the note above on Zhé Jī.
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
"The first day of the first month
is called the Correct Day.
Personally leading one's wife and children,
one purifies oneself and offers sacrifices to the ancestors and father.
On the day of sacrifice,
after presenting wine and invoking the spirits,
then the family, high and low,
great and small,
line up in order before the ancestors.
Sons, wives, and grandchildren
each present pepper wine to the family head,
raise their goblets and wish him longevity,
full of joy."
Běn Sāntǒng (Based on the Three Sequences) - Chóng Bǎilǐ (Exalting the Hundred Rites)
The "White Tiger Discussions" states:
"Why are there three systems for the first month?
They are based on Heaven's Three Sequences,
called the Three Subtle Months.
What are the Three Subtle Months?
When yang qi begins to be dispensed,
and the myriad things in the Yellow Springs begin to stir,
subtle and not yet manifest."
Zhōu Chù's "Record of Local Conditions" says:
"On Yuánrì of the first month,
all rites are doubly exalted."
Jìn King Shěn's "Rhapsody on the Grand Assembly"
Ah, the first auspicious day of the month,
Responding to the central numen of the Three Systems.
Following Heaven and Earth in harmonious prosperity,
Aligned with the profound essence of the Grand Cluster.
Receiving great blessings from the Supreme God,
May the sage emperor's fortune be eternally steadfast.
Embroidered canopies reflect against flying clouds,
Vermilion curtains spread in the front courtyard.
Five banners gleam in the eastern wing,
Displaying the mighty rainbow as pennants.
Preparing the dance forms of six dynasties,
Refining the Sháo music through nine movements.
Awaiting dawn after the dark night,
Gazing at the high blaze of courtyard torches.
Mighty armored warriors arrayed like stars,
Splendid shields and axes fluttering.
Heralds stand solemn in orderly rows,
Nine guests dignified in formation.
Unifying the eight wilds as vassal states,
All bow in homage, coming to honor the king.
Wèi Prince Sī of Chén, Cáo Zhí's "Poem on the First Assembly"
The year's beginning, the first fortune,
This day is truly auspicious.
Thus we hold this fine assembly,
Feasting in this lofty hall.
Garments fresh and clean,
Embroidered patterns black and yellow.
Rare delicacies diverse and abundant,
Filling round and square vessels.
Looking down at carved carriages,
Gazing up at ornate beams.
May we preserve this goodness,
For a thousand years as constant.
Laughter and joy reach full delight,
Happy indeed, without end.
The royal house glorious and noble,
Longevity boundless and endless.
Suí Emperor Yáng's "Poem on Feasting Palace Officials at the Year's Start"
The Three Origins established in the capital,
Six rows of dancers feast in Lìchéng.
Vermilion courtyard, guards solemn,
Azure sky, spring air bright.
Morning light glints on sword hues,
Long steps part the sound of pendants.
Wine ends, bells and chimes cease,
Joyful to see rites and music accomplished.
Suí Xiāo Què's "Poem in Response to New Year's Day"
The imperial palace torches burn all night,
Heaven's Gate opens at dawn's light.
Auspicious clouds rise from the precious tripod,
Glorious light ascends the dew terrace.
Huàshān's leaves never wither,
Yíchéng offers ten-thousand-year cups.
From afar see the flying ducks descend,
Surely knowing they come from Yè County.
Chén Shūdá's "Poem on the Year's Beginning"
Gentle winds rise on the celestial road,
Severe cold melts in the ice well.
Rustling branches not yet soft,
Weary, the water clock still long.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem in Response to Feasting Palace Officials at the Year's Start"
Treading the beginning, the festival commences,
The long garden commands high feasts.
The Xià music resounds with metal instruments,
Heavy dew echoes on icy strings.
Silken light urges willow colors,
Sun's glow floats amid locust mist.
This humble minister joins the indiscriminate piping,
Erroneously gaining audience with the heavenly music.
Jìn Liú Zhēn's Wife's "Eulogy on Presenting Pepper Flowers on New Year's Day" says:
The jade firmament revolves,
The Three Beginnings commence.
Youthful sunlight scatters radiance,
Clear scenes unfold in brilliance.
Beautiful, numinous flowers,
We gather and present them.
The sage countenance reflects them,
Eternal longevity for ten thousand years.
Renrì, the Second
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
"The seventh day of the first month is Renrì (Human Day)."
Dǒng Xūn's "Inquiry into Ritual Customs" says:
"The first day of the first month is for chickens,
The second day for dogs,
The third day for pigs,
The fourth day for sheep,
The fifth day for oxen,
The sixth day for horses,
The seventh day for humans."
Make a soup with seven kinds of vegetables,
Cut colored silk into human shapes.
Or carve gold foil into human shapes,
To paste on screens,
Also wear them in hair.
Dǒng Xūn's "Inquiry into Ritual Customs" says:
"People enter the new year,
Their appearance changes anew."
Also make huāshèng ornaments to give each other,
Originating in the Jìn dynasty.
Seen in Jiǎ Chōng's Lady Lǐ's "Diǎnjiè",
