It says:
"Resembling the patterns of auspicious diagrams and golden shèng ornaments,"
Also modeled after Xīwángmǔ wearing shèng.
Dǒng's Custom Chén's Ceremony
Dǒng Xūn's reply says:
"On Renrì in the first month,
Customarily cut colored silk into human shapes."
Liú Zhēn's wife, Lady Chén's "Jìnjiàn Yí" says:
"On the seventh day of the first month,
Present rénshèng ornaments to others."
Cutting Colored Silk Carving Gold
Both seen in the narrative.
Ascending Western Mountain Climbing Ānrén
Lǐ Chōng's "Poem on Climbing Shàn Western Temple on the Seventh Day of the First Month" says:
"Order the carriage to ascend Western Mountain,
Lodge my gaze overlooking the plains."
The "Ānrén Peak Inscription" says:
"The seventh day of the first month,
That day is for humans.
Whip my fine team of four,
Climb that Ānrén."
Suí Yáng Xiūzhī's "Poem on Climbing Heights and Attending a Feast on the Seventh Day of the First Month"
Vast halls splendid with New Year's radiance,
Shànglín Park stirs with spring hues.
Wind rises, brushing carved chariots,
Clouds swirl, floating over brocade mats.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem on Homesickness on Renrì"
Entering spring just seven days,
Away from home already two years.
My return falls behind the wild geese's,
My longing arises before the flowers.
The Fifteenth Day of the First Month, the Third
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"On the fifteenth day of the first month,
Make a fatty porridge to sacrifice to the doors."
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
"Now the customs of the prefectures and villages,
On the full moon day sacrifice to the doors,
First insert willow branches on the doors.
Following the direction the willow branches point,
Then use wine, dried meat, food and drink, and bean porridge, inserting chopsticks to sacrifice.
That evening welcome the Zǐgū spirit for divination."
Liú Jìngshū's "Yìyuàn" says:
"Zǐgū was originally a concubine in a household,
Driven out by the principal wife,
On the fifteenth day of the first month, she died of grief and resentment,
Therefore people make her image in the toilet,
To welcome her for divination."
The "Records of the Grand Historian: Treatise on Music" says:
"The Hàn dynasty sacrifices to Tàiyī,
From dusk until dawn."
Now people on the full moon night of the first month go out to view lanterns,
Which is a legacy of this.
Lighting Lanterns Gazing at the Moon
The "Nirvana Sutra" says:
"After the Tathagata's cremation,
Collect the relics in urns placed on golden beds,
Celestial beings scatter flowers and play music,
Circling the city, lighting lanterns every step for twelve miles."
Also the "Xīyù Jì" says:
"In the country of Móhètuó,
On the fifteenth day of the first month,
Monks and lay people gather like clouds,
To see the Buddha's relics emit light and rain flowers."
An ancient poem says:
"At this time the Quail Fire is at its center,
The sun and moon are precisely at the full moon."
The Quail Fire at its center is precisely the full moon of the first month.
Floating Porridge Sacrificing Fat
The "Xù Qíxié Jì" says:
"Zhāng Chéng of Wú County,
At night saw a woman standing at the southeast corner of his house,
Who said to him:
'This place is your silkworm room,
I am the earth god.
Tomorrow is the fifteenth of the first month,
You should make white porridge,
Float fat on it to sacrifice to me,
I will certainly make your silkworms multiply a hundredfold.'
Finished speaking,
She disappeared.
Chéng did as she said,
Made the fatty porridge,
And every year gained great silkworm harvests."
Sacrificing fat seen in the narrative.
Sū Wèidào's "Poem on the Fifteenth Day of the First Month"
Fiery trees and silver blossoms converge,
Star bridges with iron locks open.
Hidden dust follows the horses away,
Bright moonlight chases people hither.
Roaming riders all resemble lush plum blossoms,
Strolling singers exhaust the tunes of falling plum flowers.
The Golden Guards impose no night curfew,
Jade water-clocks, do not hasten to urge us on.
Cuī Yè's "Poem on Night Excursion"
Jade water-clocks and silver pots, do not hasten yet,
Iron passes and golden locks open until dawn.
Which household, seeing the moon, can sit idly?
What place, hearing of lanterns, does not come to look?
Another
Divine lanterns and Buddha's flames, a hundred wheels unfurled,
Carved images and painted forms adorned with seven treasures.
In the shadows, as if hearing the golden mouth speak,
In the air, seemingly scattering jade-hair radiance.
Another
Golden bridles and silver saddles control purple steeds,
Jade wheels and crimson canopies drive blue oxen.
Carriages first disperse at the eastern city's bend,
Suddenly, they meet again at the southern road's head.
Fourth: Last Day of the Month
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
"From New Year's Day until the last day of the month,
people gather for feasting and drinking.
Every month has its first quarter, full moon, last day, and new moon,
but with the first month marking the year's start,
customs particularly emphasize it as a festival.
Gentlemen and ladies float in boats,
or feast and make merry by the waterside."
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"From New Year's Day until the last day of the month,
people all feast and cross waters.
Gentlemen and ladies all rinse their skirts and pour libations of wine by the water's edge,
believing it dispels calamity."
Nowadays, people only perform the cleansing ritual by the river on the last day of the month,
and women may rinse their skirts.
Tíyuè (Last Month) / Last Day of the Month
The "Gōngyáng Zhuàn" says:
"In the last month, six yi birds flew backward past the capital of Sòng."
What is meant by "last month"?
It merely indicates the last day of that month.
Hé Xiū's commentary says:
"Tíyuè
means 'border,'
the language of the Lǔ people,
referring to the very end of that month."
Withering Míngjiá / Concealing Cassia
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" says:
"Yáo had a grass
that grew flanking the steps.
On the first day of each month, one pod sprouted;
by mid-month, fifteen pods had grown.
From the sixteenth day, one pod fell daily,
until by month's end, all were gone.
If the month was short, one pod remained,
suppressed and not falling.
Only under rulers of great virtue,
responding to harmonious energy, did it grow,
considered an auspicious grass,
named míngjiá,
also called calendar pods."
Yú Xǐ's "Āntiān Lùn" says:
"Folklore says there is a cassia tree and an immortal in the moon,
which grows at the beginning of the month."
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on the Last Day of the Month"
The waning moon shifts mid-season's measure,
Gathered warmth rises in the splendid city.
Hazy clouds form a canopy in the morning,
Dewdrops pierce through, gleaming at dawn.
Laughing trees, flowers share their hues,
Birds on branches sing in harmony.
Opening my lapels, I joyfully gaze afar,
Scanning the horizon, I express spring's sentiments.
Later Wèi Lú Yuánmíng's "Poem on Boating on the Last Day of the Month, in Response to Imperial Command"
Light ash blown into the pipe,
Falling míngjiá pods drift from their stems.
Slowly, spring's colors blossom,
Gently, the year's light shines bright.
Northern Qí Wèi Shōu's "Poem on Boating on the Last Day of the Month, in Response to Imperial Command"
Slender, tender spring branches sway,
Chirping, calling, new birds cry.
Suddenly, the oar's song winds afar,
Water chestnut gatherers' songs occasionally turn to gaze.
The wise ruler appreciates the fragrant moonlight,
Feasting words make us forget the dusk.
Roaming and leisure comfort people's hearts,
His radiance and governance bring peace to the nation's course.
Fifth: Cold Food Festival
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
"One hundred and five days after the winter solstice,
there is swift wind and heavy rain,
called the Cold Food Festival.
According to the calendar, it should be two days before Qingmíng,
though some say one hundred and six days after the winter solstice.
Fire is prohibited for three days.
The "Qíncāo" says:
"Duke Wén of Jìn fled with Jiè Zǐtuī.
Zǐtuī cut flesh from his thigh to feed Duke Wén.
When Duke Wén regained his state,
Zǐtuī alone received no reward.
Zǐtuī composed the 'Song of the Dragon and Snake' and went into hiding.
Duke Wén sought him.
He refused to come out,
so Duke Wén ordered the trees around him set ablaze.
Zǐtuī embraced a tree and died.
Duke Wén grieved for him
and ordered that on the fifth day of the fifth month, no fire be lit."
Also, "Zhōu Jǔ's Transferred Document",
and Cáo Cāo's "Míngfá Lìng", Lù Huì's "Yèzhōng Jì",
all say the fire prohibition during Cold Food originated with Zǐtuī.
The "Qíncāo" mentions Zǐtuī;
Tuī is the same person.
It also says:
"The fifth day of the fifth month
differs from the present custom,
all due to popular transmission."
According to the "Zuǒzhuàn" and "Shǐjì",
there is no record of Jiè Zǐtuī being burned to death.
Consulting the "Zhōushū · Sīxuǎn Shì":
"In mid-spring, wooden clappers are used to enforce fire prohibition in the state."
The commentary says:
"This is because late spring is when fire will be issued."
Now, Cold Food, according to the solar terms, is at the end of mid-spring,
and Qingmíng is at the beginning of the third month.
Thus, the fire prohibition is likely an old regulation from the Zhōu dynasty.
Making malt sugar and barley porridge.
Lù Huì's "Yèzhōng Jì" says:
"During the three days of Cold Food, sweet wine and fermented milk are consumed.
Also, glutinous rice and wheat are boiled to make fermented milk,
and almonds are pounded and boiled into porridge."
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"Nowadays, people all make barley porridge,
grind almonds into fermented milk,
and pour malt sugar over it."
Sūn Chǔ's "Sacrificial Text for Zǐtuī" says:
"A plate of millet rice,
two bowls of sweet wine and fermented milk."
This refers to the practice.
Cockfighting,
carving eggs,
egg fighting.
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"During this festival, cockfighting and egg fighting games are especially common in cities.
The 'Zuǒzhuàn' mentions Jì and Hòu cockfighting,
so its origins are ancient.
In ancient times, wealthy families
ate what were called painted eggs.
Today, people still dye them with indigo and madder in various colors,
and additionally carve them,
exchanging them as gifts,
or placing them on plates and stands."
The "Guǎnzǐ" says:
"Carve eggs and cook them thoroughly,
to stimulate accumulated stores,
and disperse all things."
Zhāng Héng's "Nándū Fù" says:
"Spring eggs and summer bamboo shoots,
autumn leeks and winter greens,
these supplement and enhance flavors.
As for egg fighting, its origin is unknown."
Dǒng Zhòngshū's writings say:
"The heart is like a lodged egg,
a hidden store within the body,
relying on its firmness,
somewhat analogous to the principle of fighting."
Ball kicking,
the "Liú Xiàng Biélù" says:
"Cùjū (kickball)
was created by the Yellow Emperor,
originally a military exercise.
Some say it began in the Warring States period."
Note: Jū is the same as qiú (ball),
ancient people kicked it as a game.
Swinging."
The "Gǔrén Yìshù Tú" says:
"Swinging
is a game of the Shānróng people in the north,
to practice lightness and agility."
Order of Wèi Wǔ, Letter of Zhōu Jǔ
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi, in his "Order to Clarify Punishments," stated:
"I have heard that in Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, and Yànmén,
for one hundred and five days after the winter solstice,
all fires are extinguished and cold food is eaten,
said to be for Jièzǐtuī.
Moreover, in the bitterly cold northern regions,
the elderly and young, frail and weak,
will suffer unbearable hardships.
Upon receipt of this order,
people are not permitted to eat cold food.
If anyone violates this,
the head of the household shall be sentenced to six months of penal servitude,
the chief official to one hundred days of penal servitude,
and the magistrate shall forfeit one month's salary."
Fàn Yè's *History of the Later Hàn* states:
"Zhōu Jǔ was transferred to be Governor of Bīngzhōu.
In the entire commandery of Tàiyuán,
the old custom, due to Jièzǐtuī being burned to death,
included a prohibition against fire, called 'dragon's taboo.'
During that month,
it was commonly said that the spirits did not approve of lighting fires.
Zhōu Jǔ sent a letter to the temple of Jièzǐtuī, stating:
'In mid-spring, eating cold food for a full month
is unbearable for the old and young;
now let it be only three days.'"
One Month of Cold Food, Three Days Without Fire
Zhōu Fěi's *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* states:
"The old custom in Tàiyuán,
due to Jièzǐtuī being burned to death,
was one month of eating cold food,
with no one daring to light a cooking fire."
Lù Huì's *Records of Yèzhōng* states:
"The custom in Bīngzhōu
is that one hundred and five days after the winter solstice,
fire is extinguished for Jièzǐtuī,
eating cold food for three days,
making dry porridge,
which is what is now called qiǔ."
Lǐ Chóngsì's "Poem on Cold Food Festival"
Throughout the land, all flames are extinguished;
Everywhere, smoke is hidden away.
I know not from where a fire comes,
To kindle the heart of this traveler.
Sòng Zhīwèn's "Poem on Cold Food Festival While Traveling"
On horseback, I encounter the Cold Food Festival;
On the road, it is late spring.
How pitiful, gazing by the riverbank—
I see no one from the Luòqiáo.
Shěn Quánqī's "Poem on Encountering Cold Food Festival South of the Ranges"
South of the ranges, I encounter the Cold Food Festival;
Spring has come, yet I see no malt sugar.
In Luòyáng, a new cycle begins;
On which day will be the Clear and Bright Festival?
Third Month, Third Day, Part Six
The *Hánshī Zhāngjù* states:
"The custom in Zhèng:
On the first Sì day of the third month, on the banks of the Zhēn and Wěi rivers,
they hold orchids and perform ablutions to dispel evil."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Continued Hànshū: Treatise on Rituals* states:
"On the first Sì day of the third month,
officials and commoners alike perform purification rites and drink by flowing eastern waters."
Shěn Yuē's *History of the Sòng* states:
"After the Wèi dynasty, only the third day was used,
and the Sì day was no longer employed."
The *Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì* states:
"On the third day of the third month,
local people all go out to islets in the water,
to drink from winding streams with floating cups."
A note states:
"The *Continued Qíxié Jì*: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn asked the Secretary Zhì Yú:
'The winding stream on the third day—
what is its meaning?'
He replied:
'During the Hàn dynasty,
in Píngyuán, Xú Zhào had three daughters born at the beginning of the third month,
and all three died on the third day.
A village considered this ominous,
so they went together to wash by the water's edge,
and thus used the flowing water to float wine cups;
the winding stream originated from this.'
The Emperor said:
'If that is the case,
it is not an auspicious matter.'
The Gentleman of the Masters of Writing Shù Xī said:
'Zhì Yú is a young scholar,
and cannot know of this.
Your servant requests to explain its origin.
Formerly, the Duke of Zhōu divined to establish the city of Luòyì,
and used flowing water to float wine;
thus a lost ode states:
"Feathered cups follow the flowing waves."
Also, King Zhāo of Qín, on the first Sì day of the third month, set out wine by the bend of the river.
A golden man emerged from the east,
presenting a water-heart sword,
saying:
"I order you to rule over Western Xià."
When Qín became hegemon over the feudal lords,
they established a Winding Stream Shrine at that place.
The two Hàn dynasties carried this on,
and it became a grand gathering.'
The Emperor said:
'Excellent.'
He bestowed fifteen catties of gold,
and demoted Zhì Yú to be Magistrate of Yángchéng."
Yuánsì, Shàngchú
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Southern Capital" states:
"The purification rite of late spring,
the hour of Yuánsì,
carriages side by side, wheels aligned,
purifying by the sunny bank."
Zhāng Huá's "Poem on the First Sì Day" states:
"The Gūxiǎn month responds to the season;
Yuánsì opens an auspicious hour."
Xú Gàn's "Rhapsody on the Qí Capital":
"In the late month of clear spring,
the auspicious time of Shàngchú,
neither great nor small excluded,
purifying by the water's sunny side."
Zhōu Purification, Zhèng Ablution
Yìng Shào's *Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"According to the *Zhōulǐ*,
female shamans oversee annual ablutions to dispel diseases.
Xì means purification;
thus, by the water, one is cleansed."
The Hánshī states:
"When peach blossoms bloom in the third month,
and the waters flow down,
the custom in the state of Zhèng
on the first Sì day of the third month,
on the banks of the Zhēn and Wěi rivers,
is to hold orchids to summon and restore souls,
and dispel inauspiciousness."
Winding Stream, Winding Flow
The matter of the winding stream is fully detailed in the narrative notes.
Xú Guǎng's "Poem on the Third Day by the Water" states:
"Warm is this fine day,
for pleasure and wandering.
Rising to speak, I order the carriage;
entrusting joy to the winding flow."
Purifying at Bà, Purification at Luò
The *Hànshū* states:
"Several years after Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he had no sons.
Princess Píngyáng sought over ten fine maidens from good families,
adorned and kept them at her residence.
The Emperor purified himself at Bà and passed by there."
Dài Kuí's *Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* states:
"Wáng Jì once performed purification rites at the Luò River."
Golden Dike, Stone Altar
Lù Huì's *Records of Yèzhōng*:
"In the Huálín Garden, the Thousand-Gold Dike
has two bronze dragons made,
facing each other, spouting water
to fill the Tiānquán Pond,
connecting to the imperial moat.
On the third day of the third month,
Shí Jìlóng, the empress, and all officials gather by the pond."
Dài Yánzhī's *Record of a Western Campaign* states:
"South of Tiānquán,
there are east and west channels,
receiving water from the imperial moat.
North of the water is a piled-stone altar,
said to be the place where, on the third day of the third month, the imperial seat floated cups."
Southern Ravine, Eastern Hall
Sūn Chuò's preface to a poem states:
"At the beginning of late spring,
we performed purification rites by the southern ravine's bank.
High peaks a thousand fathoms tall,
vast lakes ten thousand qǐng wide."
The Jìn *Records of Daily Activities* states:
"On the first day, Gēngwǔ, of the third month in the sixth year of the Tàihé era of Hǎixī,
an edict stated:
'On the third day, we will go to the floating cup pool,
following the small gathering at the Eastern Hall.'"
Huálín, Sparse Garden
Xún Xù's "Poem on the Third Day of the Third Month from Huálín Garden" states:
"Clear season in mid-spring,
Gūxiǎn unblocks stagnation.
Jade carriage by the green pool,
facing the stream to wash away harsh evils."
Pān Ní's "Poem on the Sì Day" states:
"Lush is the sparse garden,
so luxuriant, so flourishing.
Tranquil is the heavenly spring,
so green, so clear."
Southern Floating Bridge, Eastern Flowing Water
The "Biography of Xià Zhòngyù" states:
"Zhòngyù arrived in Luòyáng.
When the third day of the third month arrived,
all the nobles and officials in Luòyáng and below
could not help but line up their carriages side by side,
and all proceeded to the side of the Southern Floating Bridge for the purification ritual.
The men wore vermilion robes that illuminated the road,
while the women were resplendent in brocade and silk."
Also, the "Book of Sòng" states:
"In the Later Hàn, there was a man named Guō Yú.
On the first chén day of the third month, he fathered two daughters,
and within two days, he fathered three daughters in total.
None of them survived,
and it became a widespread taboo.
On that day, to avoid the inauspicious,
every household would perform prayers and exorcisms by the eastern flowing water."
Jìn Chénggōng's "Rhapsody on the Luòyáng Purification Festival"
Select an auspicious day,
choose a fine hour.
Perform the ablution, the purification ritual,
gather together by the banks of the Luò River.
Handsome youths and lovely maidens
play and wander along the river's bends.
Some wave their delicate hands,
others wash their fair feet.
By the clear stream,
they sit on the sandy shore.
Arrange the wine vessels and jars,
pass the winged cups in flight.
Jìn Zhāng Xié's "Rhapsody on the Luòyáng Purification Festival"
Ah, what a fine month in late spring,
admiring the harmonious, misty weather.
The gentle breeze spreads softly and freely,
a hundred blossoms bloom brightly, exuding fragrance.
Fish swim and dart in the clear waves,
dark swallows flap their wings in the high clouds.
Marvel at how the festive season stirs all creatures,
delight in the joy and happiness of all living beings.
Seeing that new garments are already made,
they will perform the purification by the water's edge.
Then the gentlemen and scholars,
whistling to call companions, summoning friends,
bringing along comrades, gathering in groups,
youths and capped elders, eight or nine in number,
their hosts aspire to be like Confucius and Mòzǐ,
their guests admire Yán Huí and Liǔ Xiàhuì,
by the cliffs they chant and wander,
washing feet and waving hands.
As for the capital's men and women,
graceful and numerous,
carriages and horses crowd together,
filling the main thoroughfares,
fragrant and lush,
lining the banks and covering the shores,
sleeves fluttering, creating breezes,
lapels connecting, forming canopies.
As for the families of powerful relatives,
the clans of the wealthy and extravagant,
colorful steeds halt with bits stilled,
ornate wheels with square hubs,
green canopies floating like clouds,
unevenly following one another.
They gather at the shores of the long islets,
shining at the bends of the Luò River.
Then they stop their carriages at the orchid islet,
rest their teams in the orchid fields,
vermilion curtains spread like rainbows,
emerald screens connect like halos.
They scatter pepper-infused wine,
offer tender delicacies,
pray for good fortune and auspiciousness,
ward off all ailments.
Rinse in the clear source to wash away impurities,
gather the slender stems of green algae.
Float plain eggs to cover the water,
sprinkle dark wine into the midstream.
Jìn Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Rhapsody on the Purification Festival"
Admiring the fine day in late spring,
praising the gentle harmony of the vital ether.
Form carriages side by side on the great road,
spread the joyous festival for a pleasant excursion.
Then they raise emerald banners,
hang down tasseled ornaments.
Light clouds ride the carriages,
clear breezes guide the flags.
Flying wheels whirl up like gusts,
fine horses startle like lightning.
Brilliant and dazzling,
blending and radiantly overflowing.
Just as morning blossoms burst forth in spring,
evening glow embraces the moon.
Jìn Ruǎn Zhān's "Rhapsody on the Shangsi Festival Gathering"
By the clear stream, a fine banquet,
taking leisure time for amusement and travel.
Shaded by morning clouds as a canopy,
relying on dense trees to form a shelter.
Delighting in the lushness of the fine woods,
enjoying the spreading growth of the grassy wilderness.
Arrange mats and set out seats,
pray for good fortune on this path.
Pour from winged cups and exchange toasts,
offer wishes for longevity without end.
Sharing joyful feelings and delight,
rejoicing in this happiness, spirited and bold.
Express heartfelt emotions with strings and song,
entrust pure aspirations to the musical notes.
Liáng Xiāo Zǐfàn's "Rhapsody on the Third Day of the Third Month at the Family Garden"
Spring is also nearing its end,
the farming family's Shangsi Festival.
The time for the ritual slaughter at the nine gates,
the festival for suburban rites at seven li.
Fan the gentle, soothing breeze,
shine the lingering, glorious sunlight.
Cleanse the new and wash the old for now,
following the precedent of the eastern flowing stream.
Dwellings avoid leaking from above,
trees are not hazelnut or chestnut.
Since there is no choice for high, dry ground,
nor any consultation on ill or good omens.
Looking right, one sees the green stream a thousand ren deep,
gazing north, the coiled dragon rises in elegance.
With the passing years, it grows wild and vast,
like the woods and marshes, overgrown and dense.
Rejoice in this fine month,
delight in this excellent time.
Courtyards scatter flower stamens,
beside them, bamboo shoots are planted.
Sprinkle dark wine in the ponds and islets,
float red dates upon the vast waters.
Watch the green fishing lines appear and disappear,
play with the blue boats rising and falling.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Rhapsody on the Horse Archery at Huálín Garden on the Third Day of the Third Month"
The year falls under Zhāoyáng,
the moon is in Dàliáng.
The day is Shangsi,
the time is Shàoyáng.
Spring officials perform their duties,
the green spirit manifests auspicious signs.
Summon ten thousand riders to Pínglè,
open a thousand gates at Jiànzhāng.
The emperor reviews the four regiments in the immortal garden,
turns the six dragons in the celestial park.
The imperial canopy flies level,
the wind bird turns finely.
Tent palaces are set up overnight,
canopied halls open for feasts.
Adjacent to the slender willows,
bordering obliquely on Yínián.
By the riverbanks, weeds are cleared,
at the Wèi River mouth, springs are poured.
Target clouds in five colors,
the bright halo double-layered.
The yang pipes are already tuned,
the spring strings are indeed played.
Jade pitch-pipes harmonize the bells,
gold chun-bells rhythm the drums.
Then, biting bridles and pulling irons,
chasing the sun and pursuing the wind.
Together they test on the long qiū track,
all descend to the Lánchí Palace.
Cracking whips, sweat turns reddish,
entering the track, dust rises red.
Change three drives to painted deer,
climb a hundred feet to hang the bear.
Ritual corrects the six pairs,
poetry sings of the nine sections.
Bows like full moons facing the target,
horses like floating clouds toward the track.
Geese, separated from the flock, break formation,
apes, seeking the forest, find the path cut off.
Then there are the heroic talents from six commanderies,
the elite selections from five mausoleums.
Newly returned from the soldiers of Mǎyì,
just ceased the battles of Lóngchéng.
Belts still like shooting stars,
mounts still like galloping lightning.
First, hearing the drum, they call the tally,
then moving the pole, they mark the arrow.
Xíong'ěr engraved cups,
Fēiyún painted jars.
Water衡's coins pile up like mountains,
Weaving Room's brocades spread like rosy clouds.
The feast overseer bestows rewards,
the wine steward brings cups.
Then, as the sun sets over the marsh palace,
the feast ends at the archery range.
Regret lingers for the joy of following the imperial procession,
longing remains for the lingering majesty of the returning carriage.
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Huà's "Poem on the Garden Gathering on the Third Day of the Third Month"
On the first day of late spring,
The yang energy is clear and bright.
Abundant sweet rain,
Nourishes and flows in abundance.
Gentle auspicious winds,
Awaken stagnation and guide life.
Birds and fowl are at ease,
Mulberries and hemp flourish and thrive.
Slender branches clad in green,
Jade-like blossoms hold their splendor.
Oh, majestic is our sovereign,
Reverently aligned with Heaven's will.
Observing the season and inspecting things,
He speaks of viewing the central garden.
Feasting with all the lords,
He issues commands and sets the banquet.
Harmonious music in the flowery pond,
Purifying ablutions in the clear stream.
Floating upon those dragon boats,
Rowing upstream to the great source.
Also, "Poem on the Shangsi Festival"
Benevolent winds guide harmonious qi,
Gōumáng drives the vast clear sky.
Gūxiǎn responds to the timely moon,
Yuánsì heralds this fine morn.
Dense clouds shade the morning sun,
Drizzling rain sprinkles fine dust.
Flying carriages roam the nine wilds,
Setting wine to feast the many guests.
Jìn Dynasty Pān Ní's "Poem on the Third Day at the Luòshuǐ"
In late spring, spring garments are complete,
A hundred grasses spread their blooming glory.
Let us wander for three days,
With aligned chariots and dragon banners.
The court halls hold many heroes,
The capital city boasts beauties fair.
Vermilion canopies shade orchid banks,
Emerald curtains reflect by Luò's shores.
Sinking hooks bring forth paired fish,
Raising arrows bring down flying pairs.
Feather cups ride the waves forward,
Plain eggs drift along the stream homeward.
Jìn Dynasty Lǘqiū Chōng's "Poem in Response to the Edict on the Third Day of the Third Month"
In the month of late spring,
Spring garments are already complete.
Rising sun moistens the earth,
Ice melts and rivers brim.
Remaining sprouts reach the soil,
Fine trees spread their glory.
The sovereign proclaims an outing,
Both feasting and at peace.
Glorious imperial carriage,
Numerous attending ministers.
Above shaded by crimson canopies,
Below resting on patterned mats.
By the pond, ladling for washing,
Cleansing the old, purifying the new.
Looking down at the clear stream's reflection,
Gazing up at the Celestial Ford.
Lush and splendid Huálín,
Majestic and lofty Jǐngyáng.
Towering grand halls,
Elegant soaring bridges.
Drooping shade and inverted reflections,
As if soaring, as if gliding.
Vast white waters,
Floating dragon boats.
The emperor at the spiritual pond,
All lords journey together.
Beating oars with clear songs,
Drumming paddles while chanting.
Hearing music, all harmonize,
Fully drunk, thus softened.
In ancient times, Emperor Yú,
Virtue reached distant wilds.
Shield and axe in court,
The Miáo people came to pay homage.
Now our wise sovereign,
Matches ancient sages in glory.
Blessing this central realm,
To pacify the four directions.
The sovereign's head is bright,
His ministers are truly good.
Joyful are the noble men,
Today is but peace.
Jìn Dynasty Ruǎn Xiū's "Poem on the Shangsi Festival"
The beauty of the third spring month,
A fine time of the year.
Drizzling rain already misty,
Wind scatters it away.
Blossoms shine and gleam,
Flying birds frolic in flocks.
Clear, clear green waters,
Gentle, gentle its ripples.
Long cliffs winding afar,
Great rivers passing by.
Let us wander freely,
How joyful it is.
Sòng Dynasty Yán Yánzhī's "Poem on the Banquet by Imperial Edict at the Winding Stream"
Only the king creates things,
Eternally bestowing great fortune.
Benevolence founded Zhōu,
Righteousness exalted Hàn.
Opening glory, sprinkling grace,
Unfurling rainbows, flashing lightning.
Thinking of feasts at Hào,
Often recalling banquets at Luò.
Suburban farewells have altars,
The lord's actions follow ritual.
Evening tents in orchid fields,
Daytime flow at high steps.
Divided courts present music,
Parted waves float sweet wine.
Joy as in Xià's proverbs,
Events combined with crossing streams.
Sòng Dynasty Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on Serving at the Banquet at West Pond on the Third Day of the Third Month"
Especially in late spring,
Seasonal things flourish fragrantly.
Winding streams for floating cups,
Circling through orchid halls.
Rituals complete the court's demeanor,
Music ends the evening feast.
Xiè Huìlián's "Poem on the Shangsi Festival"
The four seasons show equal division,
The three spring months hold melting brilliance.
Slow, slow, mild and gentle scenes,
Lush, lush, garden peaches ablaze.
Taking friends to the wilds,
At dawn leaving the city walls.
Bright clouds rise over emerald ridges,
Fragrant breezes stir from flowery groves.
Unhitching reins by lofty hills,
Resting on grass around winding valleys.
By islets gathering seasonal greens,
Upon waves floating light cups.
Qí Dynasty Xiè Tiǎo's "Poem on Serving at the Winding Stream Banquet at Huáguāng Hall for the Crown Prince"
The first auspicious day is here,
A fragrant feast at this place.
Long lingering, divine gaze,
Beholding heaven's grace.
Dragon essence already shines,
Wēiyǎng not yet moved.
Leaves follow the yellow birds,
Flowers fall in spring ponds.
Grand feast, vast and open,
Forbidden forest dense and thick.
Green ridges rise abruptly,
Vermilion towers appear between.
Jade-like canopies follow the wind,
Golden spears stir the sun.
Melancholy clear pipes,
Wandering light dancers.
Bà and Chǎn enter the feast,
Hé and Qí flow by the steps.
Hǎiruò comes and goes,
Cups and dishes drift up and down.
Joyful drinking all day long,
Clear light nearing dusk.
Light carriages echo softly,
Ornate sashes stroll slowly.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwén Emperor's "Poem on Serving at the Winding Stream Banquet at Línguāng Hall on the Third Day"
Fragrant years retain imperial favor,
Responding to things stirs heaven's heart.
Hunting grounds link golden formations,
Divided roads pass through feather forests.
Tent-palace facing broad wings,
Layered halls near high peaks.
Wind-blown banners vie in swaying shadows,
At noon together casting shade.
Forest flowers first drop their stems,
Pond lotuses about to reveal hearts.
Also, "Casually Composed Poem on the Third Day"
Gorgeous flowers not of one kind,
Wind-threads tangle a hundred strands.
Clouds rise over the相思觀,
Sun shines on the flying rainbow bridge.
Also, "Poem on Attending the Crown Prince's Banquet at the Winding Stream on the Third Day"
The virtue of thunder harmonizes with the spirits,
The year's fragrance and the season's grace.
Washing in the Yī, approaching the Bà,
Cleansing the heart, delighting the eyes.
Swift steeds gallop through morning fields,
Golden bells ring at dawn on land.
Orchid-scented air rolls the banners,
Divine gusts alert the carriage wheels.
Layered peaks rise steeply,
Lofty towers stand tall.
Mist rises from emerald bamboos,
Sunlight shines on ornate pavilions.
Silver blossoms scatter at dawn,
Golden fungi sway at dusk.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Attending the Banquet at the Winding Stream of the Phoenix Light Hall on the Third Day"
Light lingers over orchid fields,
The air is mild in pepper-scented terraces.
The emperor's heart is fond,
The sovereign says, "Let us roam!"
Jade carriage bells slowly chime,
Green phoenixes gently circle back.
Separate halls broadly overlook,
Detached palaces open wide.
River deities offer longevity,
The River Lord assists in rites.
The clear Luò flows by the mats,
The long Yī streams past the steps.
Fine delicacies swirl around,
Fragrant wines ripple and sway.
Light songs easily encircle,
Gentle dances hard to sustain.
White clouds linger in pipes,
Black cranes pause the strings.
Drawing thoughts to mark the year,
The year too reaches its sunny peak.
Unworthily adorned in this body,
This body too flourishes.
Vainly toil with cinnabar and lacquer,
In the end, ashamed before patterned catalpa.
Also, "Poem on the Banquet at the Winding Stream of the Forest Light Hall"
Feasting at Hào, jade bells ring,
Roaming at Fén, immortal carriages rise.
Glory sinks into colored banners,
Long winds stir mushroom-shaped canopies.
Auspicious air ascends at dawn,
Heaven's procession raises cloud pennants.
Tent halls face spring hunting grounds,
Curtained palaces encircle fragrant thickets.
Mats spread, feathered cups circulate,
Steps divide, drawing back the rapids.
Solemn, dark transformation ascends,
Grand, the imperial steps are peaceful.
About to ride the lingering wind's carriage,
To serve afar at the Jasper Terrace gathering.
Also, "Casually Composed on the Third Day"
A splendid day belongs to the third of the third month,
The year's fragrance all gathered here.
Blossoms already cover the trees,
Flowing orioles again fill the branches.
The dashing youths of Luòyáng,
The frivolous lads of Cháng'ān.
Eastward they exit the Thousand-Gold Weir,
Westward they approach the Wild Goose and Duck Marsh.
Gossamer threads shimmer, turning in the air,
Tall willows brush the pond, hanging low.
Green duckweed patterns gleam and shine,
Purple swallows glimmer, dazzling bright.
At dawn they sport by the Yī River,
At dusk they lodge at the Orchid Pond.
Ivory mats resound with precious zithers,
Golden bottles float jade wine cups.
Who would recall the spring silkworms stirring,
As dusk falls, the mulberries about to wither.
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Poem on Attending the Banquet at the Winding Stream of the Splendid Light Hall on the Third Day"
Fumigation and cleansing on the eve of the third month,
Washing and purification at the start of the third day.
The emperor's heart delights in joyful drinking,
The tent hall overlooks the spring channel.
Pleasure outings surpass Xià's proverbs,
Victorious music rivals Zhōu's dwellings.
Again on the day of burning the fields,
Luxuriant flowers and trees spread out.
Feathered cups circle the steps, passing round,
Clear ripples flow beside the mats, spaced apart.
Beautiful songs already clear and loud,
Exquisite dances again lingering and graceful.
Nine-fold variations of strings and pipes,
Hundred entertainments arise—dragons and fish.
Also, "Poem on Attending Prince Ānchéng's Banquet at the Winding Stream on the Third Day"
Converging waters truly abundant,
Divided regions screen the central counties.
Striding across, blending flowing colors,
At the strategic throat, near the fief's outskirts.
Five kings encompass Fēng and Bì,
Receiving jade tablets, inheriting feathered dispatches.
Not relying on Lǔ's customs shifting,
How could Qí's manners change?
Dōngshān abounds with roaming scholars,
The northern lands lack no outstanding talent.
A single word lighter than white jade,
A sliver of goodness cheaper than gold.
The remaining hours belong to the third day,
Pure purification follows ancient proverbs.
Holding this, frequently joining pleasure outings,
Must unfold the feast at the city's corner.
Fragrant isles stretch for a thousand lǐ,
Far and near, gentle breezes fan.
Just as we rejoice in the weight of great virtue,
Who speaks of weariness from light excursions?
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Poem on Attending the Banquet at the Winding Stream of the Orchid Pavilion on the Third Day"
The guiding star moves with the night,
The imperial carriage suddenly journeys at dawn.
Bannered gates face garden trees,
Wind vanes emerge from the phoenix tower.
Spring born, dew thick and abundant,
Heaven covering, clouds lush and dense.
Peach blossoms grow by jade streams,
Willow leaves darken golden ditches.
Purification streams branch from the winding Luò,
Tent halls shelter fragrant isles.
Leaping, crimson fish drunk,
Uneven, scarlet dates float.
Hundred entertainments all approach the water,
A thousand bells together chase the flow.
Northern Qí Xíng Zǐcái's "Poem on the Official Banquet at the Huálín Garden on the Third Day"
The imperial carriage returns from the joyful wilds,
Halting canopies belong to the Jasper Pond.
Five ministers connect light and scenery,
Seven friends establish graceful demeanor.
Fragrant spring soon to hasten away,
Viewing things, regret their passing.
New duckweed already covers the ponds,
Remaining flowers still fill the branches.
Grass grows, paths overgrown and lost,
Forests lengthen, mountains obscured and hidden.
Square mats array jade stands,
Churning water ripples golden cups.
Song voices break and then continue,
Dance sleeves join and then part.
Suí Lú Sīdào's "Poem on the Purification Feast on the Third Day"
Mountain springs, fine wind and sun,
The city wearies of clamorous dust.
Casually holding a cup of wine,
Together seeking spring for a thousand lǐ.
Remaining light falls on secluded cassia,
Evening breeze dances over green duckweed.
When will we exit the pass again,
To have once more those who enter the woods?
Suí Jiāng Zǒng's "Poem on Attending the Banquet at the Xuānyóu Hall Winding Stream on the Third Day"
The third day entertains the spring purification,
The fine hour delights in the moon's parting.
The northern palace commands pipes and drums,
The southern lodge arrays banners and flags.
Embroidered pillars support flying pavilions,
Carved galleries adjoin winding ponds.
Drunken fish sink in distant peaks,
Floating dates ripple on clear waters.
Falling flowers dangle, casting shadows,
Flying threads do not hinder branches.
Trees stir, vermilion towers emerge,
Mountains slant, green steps precarious.
Rites complete, feathered cups passed around,
Music ends, time and light shift.
Shěn Quánqī's "Poem on Attending the Banquet at the Pear Garden Pavilion on the Third Day of the Third Month"
Nine gates, the imperial road emerges,
The third day, the purification hall opens.
Painted waterbirds move mid-stream,
Blue dragons come from the upper park.
Wild flowers drift over the imperial seat,
River willows brush heaven's cups.
As dusk falls at the place welcoming auspiciousness,
Sheng and yong bells descend the emperor's terrace.
Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Gathering on the Third Day of the Third Month by Wáng Xīzhī of the Jìn Dynasty
In the ninth year of the Yǒnghé era,
the cyclical year being guǐ-chǒu,
at the beginning of late spring,
we gathered at the Orchid Pavilion in Shànyīn of Kuàijī,
for the purification ritual.
All the worthies were present,
young and old alike assembled.
This place boasts lofty mountains and towering ridges,
dense forests and tall bamboos;
there are also clear streams and rushing rapids,
shining and winding around us,
which we used for the floating wine cups along the winding water,
and we sat in rows along its banks.
Though lacking the grandeur of strings and pipes,
with each cup of wine and each poem sung,
it was enough to express our deep feelings freely.
On this day,
the sky was clear and the air fresh,
a gentle breeze blew softly.
Looking up, we observed the vastness of the universe;
looking down, we examined the abundance of all things.
Thus, letting our eyes wander and our hearts roam,
we could fully enjoy the pleasures of sight and sound,
truly a joyful occasion.
Preface to the Poem on the Winding Water on the Third Day of the Third Month by Wáng Róng of the Qí Dynasty
The Blue Bird governs the time,
the east wind heralds the year.
On this Shangsi day,
in the late spring season,
the day for the purification feast is here,
and the spirit of phoenix dances fills all hearts.
With thoughts of the level garden,
we turn our gaze to the fragrant woods.
Flying towers seem to move as if by spirits,
empty eaves are constructed like clouds.
Separate chambers are newly set up,
layered pavilions rise intermittently.
Facing the morning sun, they oppose the palace halls;
spanning the divine pond, they float with splendor.
Rainbow patterns are mirrored on ornate lattice windows,
orchid-scented springs soak the jade steps.
Lush and dense are the thickets,
orderly and neat are these banks.
New duckweeds float on the islets,
blossoming paulownias emerge from the peaks.
Brilliant colors mingle among tender shoots,
chirping sounds interweave with feathered brocades.
The imperial carriage receives the royal favor,
the clear palace awaits the feast.
Orange curtains are set overnight,
canopies are hung by evening.
Then, as the night stars fade and dawn breaks,
clear light distinguishes the colors.
Slow bells mark the rhythm,
ringing chimes spread harmonious sounds.
Seven elite troops ride side by side,
nine banners move in aligned tracks.
Then the carriages turn and halt their wheels,
like mountains standing firm and deep waters still.
The emperor’s bright countenance is solemn,
the guests’ etiquette follows proper order.
Benches are arranged and mats spread out,
aligned according to the flowing waves;
fragrant dishes and sweet wine,
are carried along by the rushing water.
Feather dancers line the steps,
golden and gourd instruments are placed on the mats.
Martial dances are performed with vigor,
flutes accompany the Bīn odes.
Summoning the singing birds from Yǎn Mountain,
recalling Líng Lún from Xiè Valley.
Clear songs come to an end,
feathered cups are countless.
Above, the blessings of prosperity are bestowed;
below, longevity like the Southern Mountains is offered.
Truly, a joyous feast among the water plants,
knowing harmony and pleasure while eating duckweed.
Preface to the Poem on the Winding Water on the Third Day by Emperor Jiǎnwén of the Liáng Dynasty
I consider that when King Chéng of Zhōu built Luòyì,
he performed purification by the flowing water.
When the Jìn gathered at Huálín Garden,
they held a grand feast with shared culture and standards.
In all cases, rituals were complete and righteousness upheld,
repeating the established rules and norms.
They moved the spirits with clarity,
harmony filled the bells and stones.
On this festival,
the Shangsi day falls at its proper time,
remaining sprouts reach the soil,
the oriole responds to the pitch pipes,
the goddess Nǚyí governs the season.
Then, feathers are arranged along the steps,
springs are channeled for floating cups.
Orchid wine cups drift up and down,
fragrant dishes come and go.
Guests’ etiquette follows proper order,
great virtue is displayed with grace.
Dances dazzle on seven plates,
songs renew with six variations.
Wandering clouds halt their colors,
divine cranes arrive in auspicious manner.
City dwellers and country elders,
gather like clouds and mist.
Carriages converge at the square crossroads,
flying eaves shine under the sun.
The Seventh Day of the Fifth Month
Zhōu Chù's "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"On the Duānwǔ of midsummer,
ducks are cooked and jiǎoshǔ are prepared."
A note explains:
"Duān
means 'beginning,'
referring to the fifth day of the fifth month."
Tube-shaped zòng are offered.
"Xù Qíxié Jì" states:
"Qū Yuán threw himself into the Mìluó River and died on the fifth day of the fifth month.
The people of Chǔ mourned him.
Every year on this day,
they would store rice in bamboo tubes
and cast them into the water as an offering to him.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn dynasty,
Ōu Huí of Chángshā saw a man who called himself the Sānlǘ Dàfū.
He said to Huí:
'Your offerings are very good,
but I am often troubled by their theft by flood dragons.
You can stuff them with gū leaves
and bind them with colored silk threads.
These two things are what flood dragons fear.'"
Another name is jiǎoshǔ.
"Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"Sticky rice is wrapped in gū leaves,
symbolizing yīn and yáng wrapped together before they disperse."
Another name is zòng.
Pronounced zòng,
also written as 粽.
Making multicolored cords to tie on the arm.
"Fēngsú Tōng" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
tying multicolored silk threads on the arm wards off weapons and ghosts,
and prevents people from contracting warm diseases."
It also says:
"This is also because of Qū Yuán."
Another name is chángmìng lǚ,
another is xùmìng lǚ,
another is bìbīng zēng,
another is wǔsè lǚ,
another is wǔsè sī,
another is zhū suǒ.
There are also items like tiáodá and other woven ornaments,
which are given as gifts.
"Xiàojīng Yuán Shénqì" states:
"In midsummer, silkworm cocoons first appear,
women dye and process fabrics,
all having their tasks."
"Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"Many preparations are made for this festival,
a tradition with a long history.
There are also shapes of sun, moon, stars, birds, and beasts,
embroidered, gold-threaded, and appliquéd,
presented as offerings to the respected."
An ancient poem says:
"Twined around the arm, a pair of tiáodá."
Gathering ài and hanging it above the door.
"Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" says:
"To ward off poisonous vapors."
"Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" states:
"Zōng Zé, styled Wéndù,
often gathered ài before the rooster crowed on the fifth day of the fifth month.
When he saw something resembling a human form, he would seize and take it.
Using it for moxibustion proved effective.
On this day, people compete to gather various herbs."
"Xià Xiǎozhèng" states:
"In this month, store medicine
to eliminate poisonous vapors."
Treading on a hundred herbs.
"Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" states:
"Four people together tread on a hundred herbs;
nowadays people also have the game of competing with herbs."
Dragon boat races.
"Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" states:
"Custom says this is the day Qū Yuán died in the Mìluó River.
Grieving his place of death,
they raced boats to save him,
which remains a custom to this day."
Also, "Yuè Dì Zhuàn" says:
"It originated with King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè."
This month, customs have many taboos against building houses and sunning mats."
"Fēngsú Tōng" says:
"Building a house in the fifth month
causes people to go bald."
Also, "Yì Yuàn" says:
"In the household of Yǔ Shí of Xīnyě,
they once sunned a mat in the fifth month.
Suddenly, a small child died under the mat,
and then disappeared.
Afterwards, Shí's daughter died,
and it was passed down as a strong taboo."
These two matters pertain to the fifth month,
so they are appended here.
Dǒng Xūn's "Wèn Lǐsú" says:
"The fifth month is commonly called the evil month,
customs often include six days of fasting and releasing life."
According to "Yuè Lìng":
"In midsummer, yīn and yáng interact,
life and death are divided.
The noble person fasts and abstains,
rectifies sounds and sights,
restrains desires."
Offering to Qū Yuán; Offering to Chén
The offering to Qū Yuán has already been mentioned in the narrative above.
"Xiè Chéng Hòuhànshū" states:
"Chén Lín served as the Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.
He governed with sincerity,
guiding people with filial piety and fraternal duty.
When Chén Lín was summoned away,
later, the commandery offered sacrifices to Lín at the east city gate on the fifth day of the fifth month,
having young boys in clean clothes dance."
Vermilion Cords; Red Talismans
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hànshū" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
vermilion cords and five-colored decorations adorn doorways,
to stop evil vapors."
"Bàopǔzǐ" states:
"Someone asked about the method to ward off the five weapons.
The reply: On the fifth day of the fifth month, make a red spirit talisman and wear it in front of the heart."
Gathering Atractylodes; Jiǎoshǔ
"Yǎngshēng Yào Jí" states:
"Atractylodes,
tastes bitter, slightly warm,
grows in the valleys of Hànzhōng Nánzhèng,
gathered on the fifth day of the fifth month."
Zhōu Chù's "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"On the Duānwǔ of midsummer,
ducks are cooked and jiǎoshǔ are prepared."
Fàn Wāng's "Cí Zhì" says:
"In midsummer, offer jiǎoshǔ."
Bathing with Orchids; Hanging Ài
"Dàdài Lǐ" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
gather orchids for bathing."
"Chǔ Cí" states:
"Bathe in orchid-scented water and wash with fragrant huì."
Zōng Lǐn's "Jīngchǔ Jì" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
people of Jīngchǔ together tread on a hundred herbs,
gather ài to make human figures,
hang them on doorways,
to ward off poisonous vapors.
Therefore, Shī Kuàng's divination says:
'In years with much illness, the ài grass grows first.'"
Warding-off-weapons Silk; Life-prolonging Cords
Péi Xuán's "Xīn Yǔ" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month,
gather five-colored silks,
called 'warding-off-weapons.'"
Yìng Shào's "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month, life-prolonging cords,
custom says they increase a person's lifespan."
Liáng Wáng Yún's "Poem: Looking Out on the Fifth Day While Gathering"
Tailoring meets the early summer,
Dotting and painting guard the dawn.
Silk gauze is already lovely and charming,
Rouge and powder also fragrant and fresh.
Long ribbons mark the fine festival,
Life cords respond to the auspicious day.
Tying mugwort like a Chǔ visitor,
Gathering ài differs from the poet.
Plucking flowers, competing in fresh colors,
Wiping dew, staining fragrant banks.
Holding a charming glance, rising askew,
Restraining a smile, stirring a slight frown.
Offering earrings by the Luò's shore,
Holding pendants as by the riverbank.
Must await the grace-light's touch,
At midnight, presenting clothes and towel.
Běi Qí Wèi Shōu's "Poem for the Fifth Day"
Wheat coolness not yet ended,
Cicada song early wishes heard.
Noisy woods still hold yellow birds,
Floating sky already white clouds.
Warding-weapons writing ghost characters,
Spirit seals inscribing mystic texts.
Thus thinking of Cāngwú commandery,
This day sacrificing to Lord Chén.
The Eighth: Fù Rì
"Lì Jì Shì" states:
"The four seasons succeed one another,
all born from each other.
At the beginning of spring, wood succeeds water,
water gives birth to wood;
at the beginning of summer, fire succeeds wood,
wood gives birth to fire;
at the beginning of winter, water succeeds metal,
metal gives birth to water;
as for the beginning of autumn,
metal succeeds fire.
Metal fears fire,
hence by the Geng day it must be concealed.
Geng,
is metal."
"Yīn Yáng Shū" states:
"The third Geng after the solstice marks the initial concealment,
the fourth Geng marks the middle concealment,
the first Geng after the beginning of autumn marks the final concealment,
termed the three concealments."
Cáo Zhí refers to them as three ten-day periods.
"Shǐ Jì" states:
"Duke Dé of Qin first established the concealment sacrifices."
"Jīng Chǔ Suì Shí Jì" states:
"On concealment day, soup and cakes are offered,
named as warding off evil."
Metal hidden, fire ascends
"Lì Jì Shì" states:
"What is concealment?
The day when the metal energy is concealed and hidden."
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Great Heat Fu" states:
"The three concealments succeed one another,
the intense heat glows red.
Above, no wispy clouds,
below, no slight breeze.
The sun ascends fiercely,
the great fire rises in the south."
Qin sacrifices, Han choices
"Shǐ Jì":
"Duke Dé of Qin first established the concealment sacrifices."
According to "Hàn Shū":
"Gāo Dì divided troops in the four prefectures,
using Liáng Píng's strategy,
to pacify the three Qins,
and sweep across the world.
This reflects the foundation that a nobleman utilizes,
determining rewards and assigning honors,
adding gold and silk,
repeatedly granting exceptional favors,
allowing freedom to choose the day of concealment,
differing from the ordinary."
Intense sunshine, extinguishing heat
Wáng Piáo's "Well Fu" states:
"The three concealments of scorching heat,
intense sunshine gives again.
A light breeze fails to fan,
wispy clouds fail to cover."
The extinguishing heat is already mentioned above in the fire's ascent note.
Labor wine, presenting melons
"Hàn Shū" states:
"Yáng Yùn's 'Letter to Sūn Huìzōng' states:
'The peasant families work hard,
during the concealment and winter solstice.
Roasting lambs and calves,
toasting oneself with wine.'" Cuī Shí's "Four People’s Monthly Instructions" states:
"Initially present wheat melons to the ancestors on the first concealment day."
Rewarding the East, sacrificial altar to the Yellow Stone
"Hàn Shū" states:
"Dōngfāng Shuò served as a lieutenant,
and received meat on concealment day by imperial edict.
Shuò alone drew his sword to cut the meat,
saying to his colleagues:
'On concealment day, one should return early,
to receive the reward.'
Then he took the meat and left.
The emperor asked Shuò:
'Why did you leave without waiting for an edict for the meat?'
The emperor ordered him to self-reproach,
Shuò replied:
'Receiving the reward without waiting for an edict,
how disrespectful! Drawing a sword to cut the meat,
how bold! Taking not much,
yet how honest! Bringing it back to share with my wife,
how kind!'
The emperor laughed and said:
'Ordered to self-reproach,
but instead praised oneself.'
Again granted a goblet of wine,
a hundred jin of meat,
and sent to his wife."
"Shǐ Jì" states:
"Zhang Zifang first met the old man at the bridge of Xiàpí, who held a book from the Grand Duke,
thirteen years later,
accompanying Gāo Zǔ across Jìbĕi,
he indeed saw the Yellow Stone below Gǔchéng Mountain,
took it and treasured, worshipped it.
After Liú Hòu's death,
together with the Yellow Stone, it was buried,
worshipped every concealment and winter solstice at the grave."
Chéng Xiǎo's "Concealment Day Poem"
In all my life during the three concealments,
there are no carriages on the roads.
Doors are closed to avoid the heat while lying down,
comings and goings do not cross paths.
Nowadays the foolish,
brave the heat to visit homes.
The hosts hear of guests arriving,
frown, wondering what to do.
Waving fans makes the arm ache,
sweat flows in torrents.
To admonish the wise and high,
walking in the heat should be censured."
Pān Yuè's "Huáixiàn Poem"
The southern land welcomes the long days,
red brightness sends off the end’s droop.
Early autumn swallows the new season,
the blazing scene reaches peak brightness.
In the morning, hoping for auspicious clouds,
late, wishing for the sun to move.
Sweat is wiped as I bid farewell to the inner chamber,
climb the city and look onto the clear pool.
The cool wind gathers from afar,
light sleeves sway with the breeze.
Spiritual garden dazzles with blooming fruit,
broad streets line with high chairs."
Seventh day of the seventh month – Number nine
Zhōu Chǔ's "Fēngtǔjì" states:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
clean and sweep the courtyard at night,
put out a mat and low table,
set out wine, dried meat, and seasonal fruits.
Scatter fragrant powders over Hé Gǔ and,
"Ěr Yǎ" states:
'Hé Gǔ refers to Qiān Niú.'
the Weaving Maid,
these two stars meet.
Those who keep vigil all hold secret wishes,
some claim that in the celestial river one sees startlingly white ether,
shimmers with five colors,
taking this as an omen.
Those who witness it bow and pray for wealth or longevity,
without children they pray for children.
Can only request one,
not multiple,
and three years pass before bringing it up,
some indeed receive blessings by it."
Wú Jūn's "Continuations to Qíxiá Jì" states:
"Below Gǔlǐng City in Guìyáng there's an immortal path,
he suddenly told his younger brother:
'On the seventh day of the seventh month the Weaving Maid crosses the river,
I have been summoned.'
His brother asked why the Weaving Maid crosses the river,
he replied:
'To briefly visit the Herd Boy.' Since then, people claim the Weaving Maid married the Herd Boy."
Also, Fù Xuán's "Imitation of Heavenly Questions" states:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
the Herd Boy and the Weaving Maid meet at the Celestial River."
"Jīng Chǔ Suì Shí Jì" states:
"On the seventh night, women weave colorful threads,
pierce needles with seven holes,
using gold, silver, or stone needles.
Song Emperor Xiàowǔ's 'Seventh Night Poem' says:
'Facing the wind, displaying colorful threads,
facing the moon, threading through the black needles.'
Offer melons and fruits in the courtyard to beg for skill,
if spider web appears on them,
consider it successful."
"Five Kings' Traditions" states:
"Empress Dòu was young and bald,
not regarded by family.
On the night of the seventh month,
everyone viewing the Weaving Maid,
she alone was not allowed out.
A light filled her room,
an omen for the empress."
Cuī Shí's "Four People’s Monthly Instructions" states:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month, make leaven,
combine indigo and Sichuan lacquer pills,
air books and clothes."
"Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn" states:
"Ruǎn Xián styled as Zhòngróng.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
all the Ruǎn family gathered in the courtyard,
all dressed in brocades,
Xián at the time was a child.
They raised a long pole,
mark with large cloth at the crotch in the courtyard,
saying:
'Unable to escape the ordinary,
just amuse oneself like this.'"
Sailing Among Stars Flying to the Moon
Xiè Zhuāng's "Ode to the Cowherd on the Seventh Night" says:
"Gracefully sailing along the starry path,
Winding, I cross the misty shore."
Yán Yánzhī's "Poem from the Weaving Maid to the Cowherd" says:
"The Weaving Maid adorns the constellations,
Cháng'é dwells on the flying moon."
Riding a Crane Galloping Dragons
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"Wáng Zǐqiáo said to Huán Liáng:
'Tell my family,
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Wait for me atop Mount Gōushì.'
Indeed, he rode a white crane to the mountaintop,
But looking from afar, one could not reach him.
Raising his hand, he bade farewell to the people of his time,
And after several days, he departed."
Xiè Huìlián's "Poem on the Cowherd and Weaving Maid for the Seventh Night" says:
"Lingering affection gazes upon the splendid chamber,
A distant heart pursues the galloping dragons."
Heavenly Road Starry River
Xú Yuán's "Poem on the Cowherd and Weaving Maid" says:
"Adorned colors blaze on the heavenly road,
Fading fragrance graces the divine terrace."
Wáng Jiàn's "Poem on Viewing the Weaving Maid on the Seventh Night" says:
"Faintly driving a thousand chariots,
Resoundingly crossing the starry river."
Cloudy River Han River's Islet
Wáng Wēi's "Poem of Lament on the Seventh Night" says:
"Algae-covered curtains surpass the starry waves,
Jade ornaments cross the cloudy river."
Yán Cè's "Linked Verse Poem for the Seventh Night" says:
"Cloudy gates cease their wandering colors,
On the Han River's islet, distant light arises."
Phoenix Slippers Crane Canopy
The Private Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Queen Mother of the West descended to Emperor Wǔ,
Wearing the crown of Tàizhēn's morning tassels,
Treading on dark jade slippers with phoenix patterns."
Liú Zhēn's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Lǔ" says:
"In the plain autumn, on the fourteenth,
The Milky Way points to the corner.
As dusk falls and the feast ends,
Carriages and riders fill the thoroughfare.
The canopies are like flying cranes,
The horses like swimming fish."
Feathered Chariot Cloudy Carriage
The Biographies of Divine Immortals says:
"Wú Cài Jīng left home when already old,
But upon returning, became youthful and strong again,
His hair all black.
He told his family:
'On the seventh day of the seventh month, Lord Wáng will come.'
When the day arrived,
Wáng Fāngpíng indeed came,
Riding a feathered chariot,
Driving five dragons."
The Private Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
"The Emperor ascended the fasting terrace for seeking truth,
And on the night of the seventh day of the seventh month,
Suddenly saw from the southwest sky something like white clouds rising,
Lush and dense, heading straight for the palace rear.
Soon, Queen Mother of the West arrived,
Riding a carriage of purple clouds."
Nine-Light Lamps Hundred Sons Pond
The Private Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
They swept and cleaned the inner palace chambers,
Hung curtains of cloud-patterned brocade,
And lit nine-light subtle lamps.
After the second watch of the night,
Queen Mother of the West, riding a five-colored striped dragon, ascended the hall."
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital says:
"Lady Qī attended upon Emperor Gāozǔ,
And on the seventh day of the seventh month,
They visited the Hundred Sons Pond."
Blue Bird Arrives Red Dragon Comes
The Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn says:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
The Emperor was fasting in the center of Chénghuá Hall.
Suddenly, a blue bird came from the west,
And alighted before the hall.
The Emperor asked Dōngfāng Shuò,
Who said:
'This means Queen Mother of the West is coming.
There is a blue bird, like a crow,
That attends beside the Queen Mother.'" The Biographies of Immortals says:
"There was one Táo Āngōng,
A master smelter from Liù'ān.
One morning, flames scattered upward,
Purple aura rushed to the sky,
And Āngōng prostrated beneath the furnace, pleading for mercy.
In a moment,
A scarlet bird alighted on the furnace,
Saying:
'Āngōng's smelting connects with Heaven.
On the seventh day of the seventh month, a red dragon will come to welcome you.'
When it arrived,
Āngōng mounted it and ascended to the southeast."
Southern Qí Xiè Tiǎo's "Rhapsody on the Seventh Night"
The Metal Spirit governs the compass,
The Fire Star just begins to flow.
The plain bell ascends to rule,
Yízé heralds autumn.
The red light has already faded,
Cool clouds begin to float.
Abundant with the evening dew's luxuriance,
Rising is the night moon's endlessness.
Strolling the broad courtyard, I extend my gaze,
Awaiting the Heavenly Maiden, I linger.
Alas, this spirit's beautiful scene,
Summons the beloved to shoulder the box.
Dimpled with white jade as adornment,
Misted with cinnabar clouds as robes.
Turning the dragon carriage, graceful and slow,
Mingling the phoenix pipes, mournful and clanging.
Leaning on the Imperial Chariot, I discard my pendant,
Soaring above the Heavenly Ford, I ascend.
Melancholy at the Han River's islet, the evening tide swells,
Joyful that the broad river already has a bridge.
Alas, the barred night is hard to prolong,
Weeping, the meeting brief, resentment long.
Resenting Xiān'ā for just harnessing her carriage,
Regretting Chánggēng's light not yet shining.
Stroking the singing zither, I cultivate vastness,
Rinsing with peaceful songs, I wound myself.
The song says:
"The moon palace clear, oh, cassia wine is pledged,
Cloudy curtains still, oh, fragrant winds float.
Dragon bits prance, oh, jade bells adjust,
Gazing at the starry river, oh, cannot stay."
Suí Yǔ Xìn's "Rhapsody on the Seventh Night"
The rabbit moon rises first,
The sheep lanterns are next arranged.
Beholding the Cowherd Star's shining light,
Viewing the Weaving Maid's railing.
Then, the beautiful consorts of Qín,
The gorgeous ladies of Zhào.
Graceful, famous as Yàn,
Elegant, surnamed Qín.
Disliking morning attire half old,
Cherishing evening freshening, wholly new.
At this time, together leaving their chambers,
They go together to the courtyard.
Threads tight, strung through the square,
Needle eyes fine, piercing the void.
An Ancient Poem Says
Far, far away, the Cowherd Star,
Bright, bright, the River Han Maiden.
Slender, slender, she lifts her pale hands,
Click, clack, she plays with loom and shuttle.
All day she weaves, yet completes no pattern,
Her tears fall like rain.
The River Han clear and shallow,
How far apart are they, after all?
Full, full, the water between them,
Gazing, gazing, unable to speak.
Jìn Pān Ní's "Poem on Attending the Crown Prince's Feast at Xuánpǔ Garden on the Seventh Day of the Seventh Month"
The autumn wind first bestows,
The morning fire faintly flows.
The crimson brightness sends off summer,
Shǎohào welcomes autumn.
Fine trees flourish in the garden,
Fragrant grass covers the fields.
At this time, our sovereign,
Takes leisure, takes a stroll.
Sòng, Prince of Nánpíng, Liú Shuò's "Poem on the Cowherd and Weaving Maid for the Seventh Night"
Autumn stirs, the clear breeze fans,
Fire moves, the blazing heat rests.
Broad eaves hold the night's shade,
High pavilions connect with the evening moon.
Walking peacefully, I roam the fragrant woods,
Gazing intently, I reach the cloud-girt towers.
Brocade curtains wind along the Han's array,
The dragon carriage soars, departing at dawn.
Deep feelings not yet expressed,
The flying light already drifts away.
The coming encounter, distant and hard to expect,
Today's joy from this moment fades.
Xiè Huìlián of the Sòng Dynasty, "Poem on the Cowherd and Weaver Girl for the Seventh Night"
The setting sun hides behind eaves and pillars,
The rising moon shines through blinds and lattice.
Round and full, dew fills the leaves,
Soughing and sighing, the wind shakes the branches.
Treading lightly along the broad steps,
Blinking eyes, I gaze at the layered heavens.
In the Milky Way, there is a divine pair,
Year after year, they are kept apart and cannot follow each other.
Distant streams hinder intimate love,
Long islets leave their pure faces desolate.
Throwing down the shuttle, no pattern is woven,
Raising the reins, they gallop after former traces.
Once parted, autumn has seen two,
Now reunited, this night is without equal.
Pouring rivers may easily turn and swirl,
But deep affection finds it hard to long endure joy.
Lush and glossy, the divine carriage turns back,
Lonely and still, the cloud canopy lies empty.
Lingering feelings glance at the splendid resting place,
A distant heart pursues the galloping dragon.
Wáng Sēngdá of the Sòng Dynasty, "Poem Under the Moon on the Seventh Night"
Distant mountains gather ominous vapors,
The broad courtyard ripples with moonlight waves.
Breath gone, wind gathers in crevices,
Autumn returns, dew drips from branches.
Since the seasonal festival is already waning,
At midnight, silken robes are shaken out.
How can the coming joy last the whole night?
Tears are wiped away, weeping at the parting river.
Xiè Língyùn, "Poem on the Cowherd and Weaver Girl for the Seventh Night"
Fire fades, the first autumn festival,
Newly bright, the crescent moon night.
Crescent moonlight shines upon the door,
First autumn wind enters through cracks.
Treading over peaks, pacing layered cliffs,
Relying on clouds, stretching distant veins.
Wandering to the northwest courtyard,
Rising eagerly to gaze southeast.
Silks and damasks bear no woven reply,
The Milky Way has a swift yoke.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Threading the Needle on the Seventh Night"
Pity emerges from within the bed-curtain,
Longing to see the night window open.
The needle tilts, suspecting the moon is dim,
Threads scatter, resenting the wind's arrival.
Liǔ Yùn of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Threading the Needle on the Seventh Night"
The northern horses in autumn do not return,
Black and white silks no longer have order.
Welcoming the cold, arranging night sewing,
Reflecting the moon, drawing out fine threads.
Clear dew falls on silk garments,
Autumn wind blows past jade pillars.
Flowing light faces the autumn night,
Remaining rays suddenly hard to stay.
Liú Zūn of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Threading the Needle on the Seventh Night"
Strolling under the moon as if with intent,
Emotions arise, unable to restrain oneself.
Facing the light, drawing out a single thread,
Raising sleeves, playing with twin needles.
Liú Xiàowēi of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Threading the Needle on the Seventh Night"
Threads in disorder, fearing the wind's arrival,
Light gown, shy to let fingers show.
Thus threading a double-eyed needle,
Specially sewing a 'union-of-joy' fan.
Shěn Yuē of the Liáng Dynasty, "Weaver Girl's Poem to the Cowherd"
Rouge and bright mirror,
These two things are naturally close.
Used to apply dots and strokes,
They do not shine upon those living apart.
Last autumn, though once they shone,
Once shone, then returned to dust.
Dust gathers, never again wiped away,
Disheveled hair facing the river ford.
Winter nights are cold like this,
How could they suddenly speak of spring warmth?
Early autumn suddenly arrives,
Briefly able to serve with clothes and towel.
Bestowing the lapel has already become past,
Each meeting always feels like new.
Wáng Yún of the Liáng Dynasty, "Cowherd's Reply to Weaver Girl"
Newly known, yet parted in life,
From the start, perhaps destined to meet.
How could it be that within an inch of the heart,
One night holds two matters?
Joy and pleasure not yet deeply entwined,
Suddenly, swiftly, become separation.
All day long, gazing from afar,
Only increases sorrowful thoughts.
Still recalling this spring's sadness,
There remain tears from years past.
Suddenly encountering the long river's turn,
Alone rejoicing in the cool breeze's arrival.
Rushing feelings assist the phoenix carriage,
Xiān'ē alerts the dragon reins.
Liú Xiàowēi of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on the Weaver Girl"
Golden hairpins already glitter,
The white sun has not yet idled away.
Waiting for dusk to arrive,
Bearing tender charm, crossing the shallow river.
Hé Xùn of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
Immortal chariots halt at the seven shifts,
Phoenix carriage emerges from the celestial river.
Moonlight reflects the nine delicate fires,
Wind carries the scent of hundred harmonies incense.
Meeting joy, briefly a clever smile,
Returning tears, already a weeping makeup.
Parting, unable to speak,
The Milky Way gradually flows vast.
Yǔ Jiānwú of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
Jade casket, rolled-up hanging clothes,
Needle and thread open the night door.
Cháng'é follows the moon's setting,
Weaver Girl chases the stars' movement.
Before parting, resentful of grasping the night,
After parting, facing the empty loom.
Entreating words to the Diāolíng magpie,
Filling the river, not yet able to fly.
Jiāng Zǒng of the Suí Dynasty, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
Hàn melody, heavenly elm cold,
Riverside, osmanthus in autumn.
Lovely and charming, hoping for tonight,
Fluttering and swaying, crossing the shallow stream.
Wheels follow the moving constellations,
Road pursues the floating colored clouds.
Rippling waves churn, pouring tears,
Bound plain silk, instead sealing sorrow.
At this time, loom and shuttle rest,
Alone facing the rouge, ashamed.
Wáng Shèn of the Suí Dynasty, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
The heavenly river stretches, about to dawn,
Phoenix carriage solemnly should fly.
Setting moon moves the dressing mirror,
Floating clouds stir the parting clothes.
Joy chased away, tonight ends,
Sorrow follows the return journey home.
Still carrying tears from past nights,
Again mounting last year's loom.
Zhāng Wéngōng, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
Phoenix pitch-pipes startle autumn's breath,
Dragon shuttle quiets the night loom.
Star bridge, a hundred branches move,
Cloud road, seven fragrances fly.
Reflecting the moon, turning the carved fan,
Riding the mist, trailing brocade clothes.
Bearing emotion toward the splendid canopy,
Flowing demeanor enters layered gates.
Joy remaining, night water-clock exhausts,
Resentment knotted, dawn steeds return.
Who remembers parting at the Milky Way?
Still recalling two hearts at odds.
Dù Shěnyán, "Poem for the Seventh Night"
White dew holds the bright moon,
Blue clouds sever the crimson river.
Celestial street, seven shifts turn,
Pass road, two deities pass.
Festive robes clink with rings and pendants,
Fragrant mats brush against silks and damasks.
Year after year, this night ends,
Loom and shuttle, parting emotions many.
The Fifteenth Day of the Seventh Month, Tenth
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" says:
"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
Monks, nuns, Daoists, and layfolk all prepare basin offerings to various temples."
According to the "Yúlánpén Jīng," it states:
"There are seven-leaf merits,
Along with banners, flowers, songs, drums, fruits, and food, they are presented."
This probably originates from this.
Hundred flavors, five fruits, offered to the Buddha, presented to the monks.
The *Ullambana Sutra* states:
"Mùlián saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts,
so he filled his alms bowl with rice and went to feed her.
Before the food could enter her mouth,
it turned into burning coals,
and thus she could not eat.
Mùlián cried out loudly,
hurried back, and reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
'Your mother's sins are heavy;
they are not something you alone can manage.
It requires the majestic spiritual power of the monastic community from the ten directions.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
for the sake of parents and ancestors of seven generations suffering in hardship,
prepare a hundred flavors and five fruits,
place them in a basin,
and make offerings to the great virtuous ones of the ten directions.
The Buddha instructed all monks to dedicate blessings for the donors' parents of seven generations,
enter meditative concentration,
and then receive the food.
At that time, Mùlián's mother was freed from all the sufferings of the hungry ghosts.'
Mùlián said to the Buddha:
'For future Buddhas,
disciples who practice filial piety
should also present the Ullambana basin as an offering.'
The Buddha said:
'Excellent.'
Therefore, later people widely embellished it,
even carving wood and cutting bamboo,
making sweets from wax and cutting colored silks,
imitating the shapes of flowers and leaves,
with the utmost exquisite craftsmanship.'"
Zhongyuan, Grand Offering, Banners, Flowers and Fruits
The *Daoist Scriptures* state:
"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the day of Zhōngyuán,
the Earth Official examines and selects all people,
distinguishing good and evil.
All celestial sages and beings
gather at the palace,
determining the kalpas and numbers,
recording humans and ghosts.
Hungry ghosts and imprisoned souls
assemble together at once.
On that day, a grand Xuán Dū offering is made at the Yùjīng Mountain,
gathering various flowers and fruits.
All rare and wondrous things of the world,
playthings and ornaments,
banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies,
vessels for solemn offerings,
pure delicacies and food and drink,
a hundred flavors and fragrant aromas,
are presented to all the sages.
Together with Daoist priests,
on that day and night, they recite this scripture;
the great sages of the ten directions
chant the sacred texts in unison.
Imprisoned souls and hungry ghosts
are then liberated,
all are fully satisfied,
spared from all sufferings,
and able to return among humans.
If not done thus,
it is difficult to redeem them.'"
Yáng Jiǒng's "Rhapsody on the Ullambana Basin"
Primordial chaos announces autumn,
Xīhé heralds dawn.
The full moon shines bright as the Great Yin ascends,
the gates of heaven open as cool breezes waft.
The four seas clear, all rivers gleam,
Yīn and Yáng solemn, heaven and earth profound.
Sweep the detached palaces,
cleanse the layered pavilions,
set up the imperial screens,
spread the emerald curtains.
Phoenixes soar, simurghs glide,
flames blaze and shimmer.
Clouds stretch, mists spread,
brilliant and dazzling, swift and sudden.
Arrange the Dharma offerings,
adorn the Ullambana.
Marvel at the wondrous objects of divine workmanship,
how varied are the creations of nature!
Blue lotuses bloom, yet it is not summer;
red fruits sway, yet there is no chill.
Copper, iron, lead, tin,
fine jades and precious stones,
reflected by the jade trees of sweet springs,
crowned by golden plates that catch the dew.
Modeled on the Three Ultimates,
shaped to represent all things.
Above, vast and boundless, emulating heaven;
below, peaceful and steadfast, symbolizing earth.
Exhausting strange powers,
exploring divine wonders.
Young lords and princes,
pulled along as if arriving;
jade maidens and fairy damsels,
gracefully dancing, surely coming.
Cry of the sùshuāng and yuèzhuó birds,
dance of the kūnjī and kingfishers.
Venomous dragons rage, blazing fiercely;
wild elephants charge, as if intoxicated.
Terrify the forest demons,
drive away the mountain spirits.
Even Lílóu with his keen eyes
could not perceive its subtleties;
even the artisan Shí with purified mind
could not fathom its mysteries.
Multicolored and profuse,
misty and dense,
five hues form patterns,
like auspicious glows and radiant vapors,
emitting brilliance through layered clouds;
vivid and splendid,
resplendent and dazzling,
a magnificent spectacle of the three lights,
like joined jades and linked pearls,
shining brightly across the vast Milky Way.
As for its distance,
Tiāntāi Peak rises steeply,
encircled by crimson clouds.
As for its proximity,
sheer and solitary it stands,
covered with lotus flowers.
Glimmering like the imperial chambers of jade terraces,
crimson like the immortal abodes of golden gates.
Its height
reaches the heavens of the great Brahmā.
Its breadth
spreads throughout the Dharma-realm as numerous as Ganges' sands.
Above, it can present auspicious signs to the seven temples;
below, it can gather all beings into the three vehicles."
Ninth Day of the Ninth Month, Eleventh
The *Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì* says:
"On the ninth day of the ninth month,
local people together spread mats in the wilds for feasting."
The *Xù Qíxié Jì* says:
"Huán Jǐng of Rǔnán
followed Fèi Chángfáng in study.
Chángfáng said to him:
'On the ninth day of the ninth month,
Rǔnán will suffer a great disaster.
Quickly have your family sew pouches, fill them with cornus berries, tie them on your arms,
climb a mountain, drink chrysanthemum wine,
and this calamity can be avoided.'
Jǐng did as told,
and his whole family sat on the mountain.
Returning in the evening,
they saw their chickens and dogs suddenly dead.
Chángfáng said:
'They took your place.'
This is why people today climb heights on the ninth day."
The *Xījīng Zájì* says:
"Jiǎ Pèilán, a palace lady of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
on the ninth day of the ninth month, wore cornus berries,
ate pastries,
drank chrysanthemum wine,
saying it makes one live long.
This has been passed down since antiquity,
but none know its origin."
The *Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn* says:
"As for eating pastries,
at that time both millet and sorghum are harvested.
Because of the delicious taste of glutinous rice,
people try new things of similar kind,
and it gradually became a custom."
