The *Zhōu Guān· Biān Rén Zhí* says:
"The delicacies in the bamboo baskets
are qiǔěr and fěncí."
Gān Bǎo's commentary says:
"Qiǔěr is
bean powder and rice flour steamed with the flavor of dates and beans,
which is today's ěrzhuī."
The *Fāngyán* says:
"Ěr is called gāo,
or sometimes cí."
Wáng's Wine, Jiǎ's Pastries
Tán Dàoluán's *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Táo Qián had no wine on the ninth day of the ninth month,
so by the chrysanthemum bushes near his house,
he picked a full handful,
and sat beside them.
After a long while,
he saw a man in white,
who was Wáng Hóng bringing wine.
He then drank it and afterwards returned home."
Jiǎ's pastries are mentioned in the narrative above.
Climbing Mountains, Sitting by the Lake
Climbing mountains is mentioned in the narrative above.
Yán Cè's "Linked Verse Poem on Sitting at North Lake on the Ninth Day" says:
"The pavilion mat gathers fading orchids,
clear wine floats with early thoroughwort."
Wearing Yellow Chrysanthemums, Adorning with Red Fruits
The "Various Herbal Formulas of the Great Clarity" states:
"On the ninth day of the ninth month, gather chrysanthemums along with poria and pine resin;
taking them over a long period prevents aging."
The "Book of Rites" states:
"Chrysanthemums have yellow blossoms."
The "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" states:
"On the ninth day of the ninth month, wear cornelian cherries;
it grants longevity."
The "Erya" states:
"Pepper trees and the shā have clustered fruits."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"In the Materia Medica, the cornelian cherry
is also called shā,
and its fruits are small and red."
Roaming Dragon Mountain, Sporting at the Horse Terrace
The "Separate Biography of Mèng Jiā" states:
"Jiā served as Huán Wēn's military advisor.
Once Huán understood his governance,
he greatly valued him.
On the ninth day of the ninth month,
Huán roamed Dragon Mountain,
with all his staff assembled.
The wind blew off Jiā's hat,
but he did not notice,
and went to the restroom.
Sūn Shèng was present at the time;
Huán gave him paper and brush, ordering him to mock Jiā,
and placed it at Jiā's seat.
When Jiā returned and saw it,
he laughed, requested paper, and immediately replied,
without needing to ponder."
The "Book of Southern Qí" states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Sòng, when he was Duke of Sòng,
was in Péngchéng.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, he ascended Xiàng Yǔ's Horse Terrace for sport;
to this day, it is continued
as a customary event."
Fù Liàng of Sòng, "Rhapsody on Ascending the Língxiāo Lodge on the Ninth Day of the Ninth Month"
In the late month of the ninth autumn,
solemnly, at dawn, I drive my carriage and depart.
Crossing winding valleys, I halt my shafts;
ascending the solitary lodge, I rest afar.
What is bleak, making the season mournful?
Again, clouds stretch and winds grow fierce.
Withered green duckweed on clear islets,
fallen lush shrubs by desolate shores.
Enjoying the fragrant chrysanthemums of the central plains,
lamenting the withering orchids in the orchid garden.
Praising the steadfast heart of bamboo and cypress,
bidding farewell to the falling fragility of parasol trees and catalpas.
Xiè Zhān of Sòng, "On the Ninth Day, Following the Duke of Sòng to the Horse Terrace"
The wind arrives, bestowing cold garments;
frost descends, halting all labors.
No swallows remain in the nest on the curtain;
along the islets, wild geese return.
Light clouds crown the autumn sun,
swift autumn winds brush the clear sky.
The sage's heart cherishes this fine festival;
bells jingle as he arrives at the traveling palace.
At the four banquets, fragrant wine is shared;
in the central hall, silk and paulownia music rises.
The setting sun hastens to the western shores;
remaining joys of the feast have their end.
Xiè Língyùn of Sòng, "Poem on Seeing Off Magistrate Kǒng from the Horse Terrace on the Ninth Day, Following the Duke of Sòng"
Late autumn, the northern border harsh,
migrating geese flee frost and snow.
Chill, chill, the sunny plants wither;
bright, bright, the cold pond's clarity.
This fine day moves the sage's heart;
cloud-like banners rise in the late season.
Reeds sound as he reaches the vermilion palace;
orchid wine cups offered to the wise of the time.
The returning guest heads to the sea's corner,
removing his cap, bidding farewell to the court ranks.
The river's flow has urgent waves;
floating steeds have no slow tracks.
Wáng Jiǎn of Qí, "Four-Character Poem on Attending the Crown Prince's Ninth Day Feast at the Mysterious Garden"
Autumn sun in the chamber,
wild geese come soaring.
Vast, vast, the clear scene;
thick, thick, the light frost.
Plants and trees sway and fall,
solitary orchids alone fragrant.
With fond thoughts of the Zī garden,
still longing for the Háo bridge.
Having fully enjoyed fine wine,
also sated with fine counsel.
Those who come find joy here,
no distance remains unsoftened.
Liú Bāo of Liáng, "Poem on Attending the Ninth Day Feast at the Joyful Wandering Garden's Zhèngyáng Hall"
Fine sons from the upper commanderies,
wandering knights from Yōu and Jìng.
Standing in chariots vie in hitting targets,
mounted sideways compete in galloping.
Jade ornaments adorn splendid plumes,
golden robes reflect jade bridles.
Delicacies exhaust sea and land,
harmony and balance suit the autumn.
Clouds fly as elegant zithers play,
wind rises as panpipes blow.
The melody ends, the grand feast concludes;
shadows fall as tree shade shifts.
Humble, I receive this gracious favor,
drinking virtue, truly priceless.
Achieving merit leaves no record,
gratitude in the heart, only I know.
Wáng Xiūjǐ of Liáng, "Ninth Day Poem"
Frost's might begins to fade the green,
cold air first enters the hall.
Suì pearls gleam like candles,
hanging pears seem like night-shining gems.
Liú Xiàowēi of Liáng, "Poem on Drinking Chrysanthemum Wine on the Ninth Day"
Frosty blossoms, as if just picked;
silken robes, as if freshly scented.
The remaining cup I will not take,
wishing to offer it to my charming lord.
Hé Xùn of Liáng, "Poem on Attending the Ninth Day Feast at the Joyful Wandering Garden"
The emperor's virtue leaves no room for yielding,
repeating the pattern, inheriting imperial merit.
Soaring flight delights in the Way;
plants and trees share in balanced grace.
The imperial heart stirs with seasonal joy,
the year's sequence belongs to cool air.
City's morning glow shines bright;
scholar trees' mist at dawn hangs thick.
Feathered cups sing of heavy dew;
row dances play 'Receiving Clouds.'
The forbidden grove ends its evening feast;
splendid pond's hues grow dim.
Sparse trees turn their high leaves;
cold streams gather fine patterns.
Sunny balconies join auspicious air;
flying eaves hold imperial fragrance.
Yǔ Jiānwú of Liáng, "Poem on Attending the Ninth Day Feast"
Track marks glorify the Zhōu odes;
tours and journeys, summer's great deeds.
The Hooked Array, ten thousand riders turn;
the Chānghé gate, nine passes open.
Autumn light follows the moving clepsydra;
northern air winds around the wind vane.
Offering longevity on the Double Ninth Festival;
returning the carriage to the upper garden.
Clearing mountains opens the imperial path;
spaced trees reveal the detached palace.
Jade wine blows over cliff chrysanthemums;
silver well-frames catch falling paulownia leaves.
Arrows hit their mark in western hills;
floating clouds, the Jìbei steed.
Dust flies, the golden track fills;
leaves pierced, willow branches bare.
Wáng Bāo of Zhōu, "Poem on Following the Imperial Carriage on the Ninth Day"
Huángshān hunting grounds vast;
Qīngmén official road long.
Season changes to the third autumn festival;
air responds to nine-bell frost.
Shot horses hang double straps;
luxurious sable furs adorned with twin jades.
Garden cold, pear trees purple;
mountain autumn, chrysanthemum leaves yellow.
Flower dew drifts, chill and dense;
light gusts rustle, rising swift.
In the end, ashamed to face the auxiliary carriage;
vainly borrowing the title of Palace Attendant.
Jiāng Zǒng of Suí, "Héngzhōu Ninth Day Poem"
Autumn day, truly bleak and chill;
thatched roof, again desolate.
Consort offers newly brewed wine;
young son asks of lingering ailment.
Garden chrysanthemums hold yellow blossoms;
courtyard pomegranates split pearl-like fruits.
Thus to express my book-writing sentiment;
momentarily dispelling this sojourner's day.
Also, "Poem on Reaching Wēishān Pavilion on the Ninth Day of the Ninth Month"
Heart chases southern clouds, departing;
form follows northern geese, coming.
Chrysanthemums by the fence in my homeland;
today, how many blossoms open?
Hè Kǎi's "Poem Harmonizing with the Ninth Day of the Ninth Month"
The autumn wind congeals on the white flute,
The profound gaze adorns the yellow chart.
Morning frost startles the parting geese,
Dawn winds knot the roosting crows.
Cold flowers bow the chrysanthemums by the shore,
Cool leaves descend from courtyard parasol trees.
The marsh palace renews old rites,
The archery field follows former models.
Jade steps divide carved halberds,
Golden moats turn through engraved avenues.
Arrows fly with stars, swift as summer,
Bows reflect the moon above the railings.
Celebrations spread through caps and robes in harmony,
Grace blends like rain and dew, soaking all.
Celestial patterns emit crimson seals,
Precious thoughts conceal dark pearls.
Receiving joy, I merely tremble with applause,
Bearing slackness, I secretly forget my body.
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Letter to Zhōng Yáo"
Years pass, months come,
Suddenly it is again the ninth day of the ninth month.
Nine is a yang number,
And sun and moon correspond together,
Custom esteems its name,
Considering it suitable for long endurance,
Hence feasts and grand gatherings are held.
This month's pitch corresponds to Wúyì,
Meaning that among the many trees and common grasses,
None shoot forth and grow.
Yet the fragrant chrysanthemum,
Blooms profusely and alone.
If not for containing heaven and earth's pure harmony,
Embracing the fragrant, gentle qi,
Who could achieve this?
Thus Qū Yuán lamented the gradual approach of old age,
Longing to eat the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums.
To nourish the body and prolong life,
Nothing is more precious than this.
Respectfully presenting one bundle,
To aid the art of Péngzǔ.
Winter Solstice, Twelfth Month
The "Precious Canon of the Jade Candle" states:
"The eleventh month establishes Zǐ,
Zhōu's first month.
On the winter solstice, the sun reaches the southern extreme,
Shadows are extremely long.
It is the beginning of yin, yang, sun, moon, and all things.
The pitch corresponds to Huángzhōng,
Its pipe is the longest,
Hence there are congratulations for 'treading on length.'"
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" states:
"For the winter solstice, court congratulations and sacrificial offerings
All follow the same rituals as New Year's Day.
Additionally, shoes and socks are presented.
Cuī Yīn's 'Inscription on Socks' mentions 'the month that establishes Zǐ,
Aiding the nourishment of primordial qi.'"
Cuī Hào of Northern Wèi, Minister of Education, states in "Women's Rituals":
"In recent antiquity, women often presented shoes and socks to their parents-in-law on the winter solstice."
These are all related matters.
'Sock' is also written as '袜',
Both pronounced as 'fá'.
Cook red bean congee."
The "Records of Seasons" states:
"Gònghóngshì had an unworthy son,
Who died on the winter solstice,
Becoming a malevolent ghost.
He feared red beans,
Hence congee is made to ward him off."
The "Rites of Zhōu" states:
"On the winter solstice, the sun is in Qiānniú,
The shadow length is one zhàng three chǐ.
On the summer solstice, the sun is in Dōngjǐng,
The shadow length is five cùn."
Mǎo Star Flourishes, Ascending Chen
The "Book of Documents" states:
"The day is short, the star is Mǎo,
To rectify midwinter."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"'Day is short'
Refers to the winter solstice day.
Mǎo
Is the central star of the Black Tortoise,
Also using the seven stars to rectify the three nodes of winter."
Fù Liàng's "Winter Solstice Poem" states:
"The Mǎo star flourishes in midwinter,
Short shadows exhaust the southern path."
The "Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yǒu" states:
"When the sun reaches winter solstice,
The Chén star ascends."
Like New Year's Day, Second to the Year
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes" states:
"On the winter solstice day,
Offer millet and lamb,
First to Xuánmíng and then to ancestral temples.
Presenting wine and delicacies, and paying respects to rulers, teachers, and elders,
Is like on New Year's Day."
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" states:
"During Wèi and Jìn, on the winter solstice day,
The emperor received congratulations from all states and officials,
Holding a minor gathering,
Its ceremony second only to the New Year's court assembly."
Yin Transforms, Yang Ascends
The "Book of Rites" states:
"In the midwinter month,
The day is shortest,
Yin and yang contend,
All living things stir."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"'Contend' means
Yang wishes to bestow,
Yin wishes to transform,
Struggling to achieve completion."
Cuī Yīn's "Winter Solstice Sock Inscription" states:
"Yang ascends from below,
The sun endures in heaven,
Long treading on abundant blessings,
Reaching thousands of millions of years."
Yang Returns, Yin Declines
The "Essentials of Nourishing Life" states:
"Zhāng Héng of Nányáng said:
'On the winter solstice, yang qi returns to the inner abdomen,
Hot foods entering the stomach are easily digested.'"
Wáng Zàn's "Poem on the Imperial Crown Prince's Gathering" states:
"The dark yin receives decline,
The green yang initiates its name.
Qi ascends anew,
Light shines perpetually."
Pearl Stars, Jade Moon
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"Eunuch Chúnyú Língqú reviewed the Tàichū calendar,
Finding new moons, first quarters, and full moons most accurate,
The five planets like a string of pearls."
Yìng Shào's commentary states:
"This refers to the time of the Tàichū calendar's first epoch, Jiǎzǐ, midnight, new moon, and winter solstice,
When the seven luminaries all converged in Qiānniú."
Huán Tán's "New Discourses" states:
"Since the celestial origin,
Up to the new moon and winter solstice of the eleventh month,
The sun and moon are like joined jade discs."
Observing the New Moon, Calculating the Origin
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"In the fifth year of Duke Xī, first month, Xīnmǎo day, the sun reached the south,
The duke, having observed the new moon,
Then ascended the observation platform to gaze and record,
Which was according to ritual."
Huán Tán's "New Discourses" states:
"Combining the calculations of various calendrical schools,
Investigating and calculating their epochs,
From the ancient celestial origin,
Up to the Jiǎzǐ day, midnight, new moon, and winter solstice of the eleventh month."
Cease Arms, Practice Music
The "General Meanings of the Five Classics" states:
"On the winter solstice, arms and drums are stilled,
Merchants and travelers do not journey,
The ruler does not attend to governmental affairs."
The "Yì Tōng Guà Yàn" states:
"Beginning from the winter solstice,
The ruler and his ministers, left and right, engage in music for five days.
All under heaven,
Also every household engages in music for five days,
As a ritual to welcome the sun's arrival."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"'Engage' means
To approach.
On the winter solstice,
Ruler and ministers all approach the office of the Grand Director of Music,
Overseeing the practice of music for the circular mound sacrifice to heaven,
Considering no sacrificial matter greater than this."
Record Phenomena, Observe Winds
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"At all equinoxes, solstices, openings, and closings,
Clouds and phenomena must be recorded,
For preparedness."
The "Yellow Emperor's Acupuncture Classic" states:
"On the winter solstice day,
If the wind comes from the south,
It is called 'empty',
Harmonizing the Pitch Pipes and Calendar, Measuring the Gnomon's Shadow
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn states:
"From the winter solstice onward,
the ruler summons men of eight abilities:
some to tune the huángzhōng pitch,
some to tune the six pitch pipes,
some to harmonize the five phases,
some to harmonize the pitch pipes and calendar,
some to harmonize yīn and yáng,
and some to harmonize correct virtue."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Summoning men of eight abilities means
selecting from among the multitude
those who are skilled and knowledgeable, and having them perform the tuning.
Xié (harmonizing)
means to bring them into accord."
Sīmǎ Biāo's Xù Hàn Shū states:
"The Son of Heaven, on the winter and summer solstices,
presides in the front hall,
assembles the men of eight abilities,
arranges the eight sounds to listen to the music,
measures and standardizes the gnomon's shadow,
observes the bell pitches,
weighs the earth and charcoal,
and verifies the yīn and yáng."
Perfecting the Three Luminaries, Circling the Four Extremities
The Yì Tōng Guà Yàn states:
"The winter solstice perfects the celestial patterns."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"The celestial patterns are called the Three Luminaries (sun, moon, stars);
their movements illuminate all under heaven,
and their cycles are completed at the winter solstice.
At this time,
sacrifices are offered to perfect them,
as a means of requital."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"On the winter solstice, the sun travels far,
its path circling the four extremities;
this day is named Xuánmíng Tiān (Day of Profound Brightness)."
Winter Solstice Poem by Fù Liàng of the Sòng
The constellation Mǎo marks midwinter's height,
The shortest shadow reaches the southern land's limit.
Tender lichee greets the season, lush and bright,
Fragrant rue responds to the node, its scent exquisite.
Winter Solstice Poem by Yuán Shū of the Sòng
Linked stars thread the newly begun calendar's line,
The auspicious month arrives at the year's head.
Music is offered, yīn governance to refine,
Ascending metal praises yáng's stagnation shed.
Coolness gathered, Heaven's virtue descends,
Buds sprout, Earth's bounty extends.
The Director of Auspices records the night's fading gleam,
The Cloud-Scribe in morning court takes the vow's theme.
Winter Solstice Poem by Bào Zhāo of the Sòng
Light shifts, the wind's manner changes its way,
The sun arrives, the shadow's turn holds sway.
Dimly seen, a crane bearing frost's hue,
Gleaming bright, wild geese through clouds pursue.
Poem in Response to 'Winter Solstice' by Xiāo Què of the Suí
In celestial halls, the chime stone first stirs its sound,
In the crimson chamber, flying ash is found.
Evening wind rises, stirring bamboo with its breath,
Sunlit clouds come, covering the stone beneath.
Cracking ice reveals the lichee's colored face,
Clearing snow uncovers orchid seedlings in their place.
Ashamed I lack Sòng Yù's discerning grace,
I rashly blow my flute in Chǔ King's terrace space.
Memorial Presenting 'Eulogy on Winter Solstice Socks' by Cáo Zhí of the Wèi
I have observed the old rites:
the state presents shoes and offers socks on the winter solstice,
to welcome blessings and tread upon the lengthening [days].
Former officials have composed eulogies for this.
Having enjoyed their fine compositions,
I wish to relate the court's celebration.
A thousand-year era of prosperity,
the auspicious festival of the First Yáng.
The four directions communicate in peace,
the myriad things are vividly revived.
Welcoming auspices at the Secondary Year,
treading upon the long [days] and receiving felicity.
Unable to contain my feelings for the season,
my heart is tied within the curtains,
I bow and present this memorial to offer congratulations,
and also present seven pairs of patterned shoes
and several pairs of socks.
I present these upwards for your attention,
respectfully offered.
Section Thirteen: The Là Sacrifice
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
"In the Xià it was called Qīngsì (Pure Sacrifice),
in the Yīn it was called Jiāpíng (Excellent Peace),
in the Zhōu it was called Dàzhà (Great Zhà),
and in the Hàn it was called Là.
Là
means liè (hunting),
for it involves hunting animals to offer in sacrifice."
The Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn states:
"Là is the sacrifice to the ancestors,
while Zhà is the requital to the hundred spirits;
they are different sacrifices performed on the same day."
Also, the Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven's Great Zhà has eight [objects of worship].
Yīqí Shì first instituted the Zhà.
Zhà
means suǒ (seeking out),
for in the twelfth month of the year,
all things are gathered and sought out to be feasted.
The eight Zhà are:
first, the First Husbandman;
second, the Overseer of Husbandry;
third, the Farmers;
fourth, the Field Altars and Paths;
fifth, Cats and Tigers;
sixth, Dikes;
seventh, Ditches and Waterways;
eighth, Insects.
The Hàn took the xū day as the Là.
The Wèi Tái Fǎng Yì states:
"A king takes the day corresponding to his dynasty's flourishing phase as the Zǔ (ancestral) day,
and the day of its decline as the Là day.
The Hàn had the virtue of Fire;
fire declines on the xū day,
therefore they took the xū day as the Là."
The Wèi took the chén day;
the Wèi had the virtue of Earth ruling,
earth declines on chén,
therefore they took chén as the Là.
The Jìn took the chǒu day.
The Jìn had the virtue of Metal;
metal declines on chǒu,
therefore they took chǒu as the Là.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The state of Yú will not have another Là."
Jiāpíng (Excellent Peace) Míngsì (Bright Sacrifice)
The Shǐjì states:
"In the twelfth year of Duke Huìwén of Qín, the Là was first instituted.
In the thirty-first year of the First Emperor, the name Là was changed to Jiāpíng."
Zhōu Chù's Fēngtǔ Jì states:
"Present clear, mellow [wine] to announce the Zhà;
exhaust reverence in the bright sacrifice."
Wèi (chǒu) Hàn (xū)
The Jìn Sòng Jiù Shì states:
"When the Wèi emperor abdicated,
the Zǔ sacrifice was on the yǒu day,
and the Là on the chǒu day.
The Wèi Míngchén Zòu states:
'The Grand Minister of Agriculture Dǒng Yù proposed:
"A ruler of the Earth phase
should properly take the wèi day for the Zǔ,
and the chǒu day for the Là,
to obtain the node of flourishing's end;
he should not take xū for Zǔ and chén for Là."
'"Yìng Shào's Fēngsú Tōng states:
"Some say Là
means jiē (to connect),
the交接 (handover) of the old and new,
involving a grand sacrificial hunt
to requite merits.
The Hàn's fire phase declines on xū,
therefore they took xū as the Là."
Sacrificing with Pigs Dismembering Chickens
The Hàn Shū states:
"In the spring of the tenth year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
officials proposed that districts and circuits should regularly in the second month of spring and at the Là sacrifice to the gods of soil and grain with sheep and pigs."
Wáng Sù's Yílǐ states:
"In the last month of winter, the Great Exorcism is performed;
chickens are dismembered on all sides,
and an earthen ox is brought out to expel the cold qi.
This is the present-day Là,
which expels and drives away pestilence, involving dismembering chickens, reed ropes, peachwood figures, and the like."
Wèi Chén Jìn Chǒu
The "Wèitái Fǎngyì" states:
"The imperial edict inquired why the Wèi dynasty uses the Wèi day for the ancestral sacrifice and the Chǒu day for the Là sacrifice.
Minister Chóng replied:
'According to the Monthly Ordinances,
in the first month of winter, the tenth month, the Là sacrifice is offered to the ancestors and the five household deities,
referring to the offering of wild animals obtained from hunting,
which is called Là.'"
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"The state of Yú no longer performs the Là sacrifice,
only these two instances are seen,
and neither records the day.
I have heard the explanation of my late teacher:
'Each king uses the day corresponding to the peak of his dynasty's element for the ancestral sacrifice,
and uses the day corresponding to the end of that element for the Là sacrifice.
Water first arises on Shēn,
peaks on Zǐ,
and ends on Chén.
Thus, a ruler whose dynasty follows the water element uses Zǐ for the ancestral sacrifice and Chén for the Là sacrifice.
Fire first arises on Yín,
peaks on Wǔ,
and ends on Xū.
A ruler whose dynasty follows the fire element uses Wǔ for the ancestral sacrifice and Xū for the Là sacrifice.
Wood first arises on Hài,
peaks on Mǎo,
and ends on Wèi.
Thus, a ruler whose dynasty follows the wood element uses Mǎo for the ancestral sacrifice and Wèi for the Là sacrifice.
Metal first arises on Sì,
peaks on Yǒu,
and ends on Chǒu.
Thus, a ruler whose dynasty follows the metal element uses Yǒu for the ancestral sacrifice and Chǒu for the Là sacrifice.
Earth first arises on Wèi,
peaks on Xū,
and ends on Chén.
Thus, a ruler whose dynasty follows the earth element uses Xū for the ancestral sacrifice and Chén for the Là sacrifice.'
Now, the Wèi dynasty is based on the virtue of earth,
so it should use Xū for the ancestral sacrifice and Chén for the Là sacrifice.'"
The "Jìn Qǐjū Zhù" states:
"In the fourth year of Āndì Ānchóng's reign, on the Xīnchǒu day of the twelfth month, music was performed at the Là sacrifice ceremony."
Láo Nóng Zòng Lì
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hànshū" states:
"In the last month of winter,
the stars complete their cycle and the year ends,
yin and yang have already intersected,
so the farmers are rewarded and the Là sacrifice is held to send off the old year."
Cài Yōng's "Dú Duàn" states:
"The Là sacrifice is the great sacrifice at the end of the year,
during which officials are allowed to feast and drink freely."
Jiàn Qín Jì Shòu
Offering the wild birds obtained from hunting,
as seen above.
Yìng Shào's "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
"In the Zhōu dynasty it was called Dà Zhà,
the Hàn dynasty changed it to Là,
hunting for animals to sacrifice to the ancestors."
Chén Chuī Dōng Niàng
Gān Bǎo's "Sōushén Jì" states:
"During the reign of Xuāndì,
there was a man named Yīn Zǐfáng,
who was extremely filial and benevolent.
Once, on the morning of the Là day while cooking,
the Kitchen God appeared in form,
and Zǐfáng bowed repeatedly to receive the blessing.
His family had a yellow sheep,
which he slaughtered to sacrifice to the god."
Cuī Shí's "Sì Mín Yuèlìng" states:
"On the first Xīn day of the tenth month,
order the kitchen steward to prepare clear yeast,
and brew winter wine
for use in the Là sacrifice."
Qí Wǔ Sì Jì Bǎi Shén
The "Lǐjì" states:
"The Son of Heaven then prays for the year to the heavenly deities,
greatly slaughters animals,
sacrifices at the public altars and the gates of the city and villages,
and performs the Là sacrifice to the ancestors and the five household deities."
Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén" states:
"Là is the sacrifice to the hundred deities
on the Rénxū day after the winter solstice."
Jìn Péi Xiù's "Dà Zhà Shī"
The sun treads the constellation Jì,
Dàlǚ governs the hour.
The celestial signs change their order,
and all things are renewed.
The year's affairs are declared complete,
the eight Zhà sacrifices repay diligence.
What is declared complete?
The year's abundance and prosperity of goods.
Rich offerings and filial sacrifices,
bring forth these myriad blessings.
What repays diligence?
The achievements of farming are acknowledged.
Solemn is our sovereign,
who pities these multitudes of people.
Feasting in the pure sacrifice,
from all directions they come in peace.
Filling the suburbs and outskirts,
gathering like scales in the capital.
Intermingling and trading,
in colorful crowds they pursue each other.
Rolling up sleeves forms curtains,
connecting lapels forms canopies.
There is meat like hills,
there is wine like springs.
There are dishes like forests,
there are goods like mountains.
Throughout the land there is shared joy,
harmonious energy arrives.
Auspicious winds follow smoothly,
blessings descend from heaven.
The borders are peaceful and tranquil,
good fortune extends daily.
With the people at leisure,
may they enjoy longevity for ten thousand years.
Sòng Zhāng Wàng's "Zhà Chú Shī"
Fresh ice forms against the flowing water,
condensed drips hang like falling curtain beads.
People delight in the eight Zhà's exuberance,
who knows the year's splendor is ending?
Běi Qí Wèi Shōu's "Zhà Jié Shī"
The凝固 cold presses upon the pure sacrifice,
there is wine for the feast of Jiāpíng.
What can express my longstanding heart?
I rely on this to console my inner feelings.
Suì Chú Dì Shí Sì
The annotation to "Lǚshì Chūnqiū ‧ Jì Dōng Jì" states:
"On the day before the year ends,
drums are beaten to drive away the ghosts of pestilence,
this is called Zhú Chú,
also known as Nuó."
The "Lúnyǔ" states:
"When the villagers performed the Nuó,
Confucius stood in court robes on the eastern steps."
Zhāng Héng's "Dōngjīng Fù" states:
"At the end of the year, the great Nuó is performed."
The "Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" states:
"Before the year ends, there is also the game of hiding the hook."
Xīn Shì's "Sān Qín Jì" says:
"Emperor Zhāodì's mother, Lady Gōuyì, had clenched fists and was a beauty of the state,
now people learning to hide the hook also imitate this."
Hook,
also written as 彄.
Sù Suì Yíng Nián
The "Jīngchǔ Jì" states:
"At year's end, every household prepares dishes and vegetables,
goes to the position for staying up for the year,
to welcome the new year,
gathering together to drink heartily."
Qù Gù Nà Xīn
The "Jīngchǔ Jì" states:
"Keep the meal from staying up for the year,
until the twelfth month of the new year,
then discard it in the streets,
as a way of discarding the old and taking in the new."
Táng Tàizōng's "Shǒu Suì Shī"
Evening light slants on the fragrant hall,
the year's splendor adorns the brocade palace.
Cold hooks remove winter snow,
warm sashes bring in spring breeze.
Steps fragrant with spreading plum purity,
plate flowers curl with candle red.
Together we rejoice in the new and old year,
welcoming and sending off within a single night.
Another Poem
The year's shadow ends in the twilight of the season,
offering the festival opens new fragrance.
Winter ends tonight, brief,
the year opens tomorrow, long.
Ice melts into mirror-like water,
plums scatter into the wind's fragrance.
Facing this, we joyfully end the feast,
tipping the pot, awaiting the dawn light.
"Poem on Summoning Attendant Ministers for a Feast in Tàiyuán to Stay Up for the Year"
The four seasons move the ash pipes,
in one night, winter turns to spring.
Sending off cold, the remaining snow ends,
welcoming the year, early plums renew.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Suì Jìn Yīng Lìng Shī"
The year's sequence is already exhausted,
the heart of spring cannot be at ease.
Casually opening the cypress leaf wine,
trying to set out the plate of five pungents.
Gold leaf pictures the divine swallow,
vermilion mud stamps the ghost pills.
Plum blossoms should be pluckable,
pity they are seen amidst the snow.
Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem in Response to Instruction at Year's End"
The old year ends with the night,
Early spring arrives with the dawn.
Now I experience the joy of joining the army,
Drinking to victory upon entering Xījīng.
General Record, Earth, Part One
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"When the Supreme Ultimate first took form,
The clear and turbid began to separate,
Therefore heaven was completed first and earth was established later."
The Báihǔtōng states:
"Earth is what is born from the primordial qi,
It is the ancestor of the myriad things."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Heaven has nine sections and eight guidelines,
Earth has nine regions and eight pillars.
The Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng says:
"Mount Kūnlún serves as the pillar of heaven,
Its qi ascends and connects to heaven.
Kūnlún is the center of the earth.
Below the earth there are eight pillars,
Each pillar is 100,000 lǐ in breadth,
There are three thousand six hundred axles,
Mutually restraining one another.
Famous mountains and great rivers,
Have interconnecting cavities and caves."
Beyond the nine regions there are eight expanses.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The east is called Shā Hǎi (Sandy Sea),
The southeast is called Yuán Zé (Distant Marsh),
The south is called Dān Zé (Cinnabar Marsh),
The west is called Quán Zé (Spring Marsh).
The northwest is called Hǎi Zé (Sea Marsh),
The north is called Sāi Zé (Frontier Marsh),
The northeast is called Wútōng Zé (Impassable Marsh)."
The Hétú says:
"In all, the world has nine divisions,
Separately called the nine regions.
The nine regions within China are named Chìxiàn (Red District),
Which are the nine regions of Yǔ.
The aforementioned 'nine regions and eight pillars',
Refers to the great nine regions,
Not the small nine regions of Chìxiàn from the Tribute of Yǔ."
Beyond the eight expanses there are eight cords.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The cord of the northeast,
Is called Hé Qiū (Harmonious Hill),
Also called Huāng Tǔ (Wild Land);
The cord of the east,
Is called Jílín Yě (Bramble Forest Wilds),
Also called Sāng Yě (Mulberry Wilds);
The cord of the southeast,
Is called Dà Qióng (Great Exhaustion),
Also called Zhòng'ān (Multitude's Peace);
The cord of the south,
Is called Dū Guǎng (Capital Expanse),
Also called Fǎn Hù (Reverse Door);
The cord of the southwest,
Is called Jiāoyáo (Burning Heights),
Also called Huǒ Tǔ (Fire Land);
The cord of the west,
Is called Jīn Qiū (Metal Hill),
Also called Wò Yě (Fertile Wilds);
The cord of the northwest,
Is called Yī Mù (One Eye),
Also called Shǎo Suǒ (Few Dwellings);
The cord of the north,
Is called Jī Bīng (Accumulated Ice),
Also called Wěi Yǔ (Drooping Feathers)."
Beyond the eight cords there are eight extremes.
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The northeast is called Fāngtǔ Zhī Shān (Square Earth Mountain),
Also called Cāng Mén (Azure Gate);
The east is called Dōngjí Zhī Shān (Eastern Extreme Mountain),
Also called Kāimíng Mén (Gate of Opening Brightness);
The southeast is called Bōmǔ Zhī Shān (Wave Mother Mountain),
Also called Yáng Mén (Sun Gate);
The south is called Nánjí Zhī Shān (Southern Extreme Mountain),
Also called Shǔ Mén (Heat Gate);
The southwest is called Biānjū Zhī Shān (Woven Colt Mountain),
Also called Bái Mén (White Gate);
The west is called Xījí Zhī Shān (Western Extreme Mountain),
Also called Chānghé Zhī Mén (Gate of Changhe);
The northwest is called Bùzhōu Zhī Shān (Mount Bùzhōu),
Also called Yōudū Mén (Gate of the Dark Capital);
The north is called Běijí Zhī Shān (Northern Extreme Mountain),
Also called Hán Mén (Cold Gate)."
The breadth of the eight extremes,
East to west is 233,000 lǐ,
North to south is 231,500 lǐ.
The land within the four seas governed by Xià Yǔ,
East to west is 28,000 lǐ,
North to south is 26,000 lǐ.
On earth, east-west is the weft,
North-south is the warp."
The Zhōulǐ also states:
"East-west is called breadth,
North-south is called circumference."
The Ěryǎ states:
"East reaching Tàiyuǎn,
West reaching Bīn Guó,
South reaching Pǔqiān,
North reaching Zhùlì,
These are called the four extremes.
The nine Yí, eight Dí, seven Róng, and six Mán are called the four seas."
Meaning their dwellings are near the sea.
The Zuǎnyào states:
"Sōng, Tài, Héng, Huá, Héng,
Are called the Five Peaks;
Jiāng, Hé, Huái, Jì,
Are called the Four Watercourses;
Upper, middle, and lower are called the three soils;
Mountain forests, river marshes, hills, raised plains, plateaus, and lowlands are the five types of land."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The Grand Minister of Education distinguishes the products of the five lands.
The first is mountain forests,
Their appropriate animals are furred creatures,
Their appropriate plants are dark-hued plants;
The second is river marshes,
Their appropriate animals are scaly creatures,
Their appropriate plants are oily plants;
The third is hills,
Their appropriate animals are feathered creatures,
Their appropriate plants are hollow-stemmed plants;
The fourth is raised plains,
Their appropriate animals are shelled creatures,
Their appropriate plants are pod-bearing plants;
The fifth is plateaus and lowlands,
Their appropriate animals are naked creatures,
Their appropriate plants are clustered plants."
The Wùlǐlùn states:
"Earth,
Its hexagram is Kūn,
Its virtue is that of a mother,
Its spirit is called Zhǐ,
Also called Ǎo.
In its grand aspect it is named Huáng Dìzhǐ (Yellow Earth Spirit),
In its smaller aspect it is named Shénzhōu (Divine Land),
Also named Hòutǔ (Queen Earth)."
Huáng Dìzhǐ,
Refers to the land within the eight extremes.
Shénzhōu,
Is the spirit of the land within the thousand-lǐ square royal domain.
Hòutǔ,
Is the Shè (altar of the soil).
Shè,
Is the lord of the land,
And can be spoken of wherever it exists.
Kūn's Primacy; Zhǐ's Position
The Yì states:
"How supreme is Kūn's primacy!
The myriad things draw their life from it.
It contains and magnifies, is bright and great,

is the earth spirit."

Xījìn Péi Xiù's "Discussion on the Regional Maps of the Nine Provinces in the Yǔ Gòng"
The establishment of maps and records
has a long history.
Since ancient times, celestial phenomena were observed and systems established,
relying on their utility. The Three Dynasties appointed historians
to oversee these duties.
By the time of Hàn Gāozǔ's sacking of Xiányáng,
Chancellor Xiāo Hé collected all of Qín's maps and records.
Now, the imperial archives lack both ancient and modern maps,
as well as the Qín maps obtained by Xiāo Hé.
Only the geographical maps and various miscellaneous maps from the Hàn dynasty remain,
none of which include scales,
nor are they calibrated for orientation.
They do not fully record famous mountains and great rivers,
and though they list places,
their outlines are crude,
lacking precision,
and thus unreliable.
Some contain exaggerated or fantastical claims about remote regions,
inconsistent with facts,
and of no substantive value.
Today, the principles for making maps consist of six elements:
First, scale, to distinguish breadth and width;
second, orientation, to correct relative positions;
third, distance, to determine routes;
fourth, elevation;
fifth, slope;
sixth, curvature.
These three—elevation, slope, and curvature—are each adapted to the terrain,
accounting for differences in difficulty and ease of travel.
A map with imagery but no scale
cannot accurately gauge distances;
with scale but no orientation,
even if accurate in one area,
it will be erroneous elsewhere;
with orientation but no distance measurement,
it cannot connect places separated by mountains or seas;
with distance but no adjustment for elevation, slope, or curvature,
the calculated path lengths
will deviate from actual distances.
These six elements,
when cross-referenced and examined,
allow true distances to be determined by scale,
true relative positions by orientation,
true path lengths by distance measurement,
and true measurements by elevation.
Thus, even with barriers like towering mountains or vast seas,
or the remoteness of distant lands,
or the complexities of ascents, descents, and winding paths,
all can be accurately represented and determined."

cannot compare to this.
The square maps of the Jìn dynasty
are less exquisite than this.
Compared to Chánglè Palace,

General Overview of Mountains, Part Two
The Guóyǔ states:
"A mountain is the accumulation of earth."
The Ěryǎ states:
"Where the earth is high and there are stones, it is called a mountain."
The Shìmíng states:
"Shān (mountain),
means chǎn (to produce),
meaning it produces the myriad things."
The Shuōwén states:
"Shān (mountain),
means xuān (to diffuse),
it diffuses the vital breath, scattering and giving birth to the myriad things;
having stones and being high,
it is a pictographic character."
The Hánshī Wàizhuàn states:
"Now, a mountain,
is what the multitudes gaze upon and look up to.
Timber and materials are born there,
treasures and stores are planted there,
flying birds gather there,
running beasts crouch there.
It nurtures the multitude of creatures without weariness,
resembling the benevolent person and the person of purpose.
This is why the benevolent take delight in mountains."
The Shìmíng states:
"The summit of a mountain is called zhǒng."
Also called diān,
also called jiāo.
The ridge of a mountain is called gāng.
A mountain that is large and high is called sōng.
Sōng,
means high and lofty.
Now, the central peak Sōng Shān is probably named according to this,
also written as sōng.
Small and high is called cén.
Sharp and high is called jiào.
Low and large is called hù.
Small and numerous is called kuī.
Large on top and small below is called yǎn.
A mountain with grass and trees is called hù,
pronounced hù.
Without grass and trees is called gāi,
pronounced gǔ líng fǎn.
Stones bearing earth is called jū.
Earth bearing stones is called cuīwéi.
These are named according to their form.
The eastern side of a mountain is called cháoyáng.
The western side of a mountain is called xīyáng.
Named according to the sun's illumination.
The foot of a mountain is called lù.
A mountain cave is called xiù.
The edge of a mountain is called yá.
A high yá is called yán.
The elegant part on top is called fēng.
The steep, rugged, and high part is called jié.
A mountain slope is called bǎn.
A mountain with three successive rises is called zhì.
A mountain formed in two layers is called pī.
A break in the middle of a mountain is called xíng.
Not yet reaching the top is called cuìwēi.
Another explanation,
the bluish-green misty color of a mountain's atmosphere is called cuìwēi.
A connected range of mountains is called yì,
meaning linked in continuous succession.
Now, in the state of Lǔ there is a Yì,
a mountain purely of stones piled and constructed,
connected to form a mountain,
this probably refers to it.
Narrow and high is called luán.
A luán mountain is called duò.
Pronounced tā guǒ fǎn,
refers to a mountain shape that is long and narrow.
In Jīngzhōu it is also called luán.
The Shī says:
"The duò mountain and the lofty peak."
An earthen hill is called fù.
Fù,
means thick,
referring to its height and thickness.
A curved fù is called ē.
A large fù is called líng.
A small líng is called qiū.
The mountain spirit is called kuí,
also called qí,
also called yúnyáng.
Sacrificing to a mountain is called guǐ xuán.
From "the summit of a mountain is called zhǒng" onward,
all come from the three books: Shuōwén,
Shìmíng,
and Ěryǎ.
Enveloped in peril, containing marshes
