Táng Tàizōng's "Rhapsody on a Small Hill"
Why do the four seasons alternate in their course,
turning to the dusk of the three yang?
The wind leaves warmth and enters summer heat,
trees shed brocade and form canopies.
Longing for Pénglái and Yíngzhōu, yet they are unseen;
gazing toward Kūnlún and Làngyuàn, they are hard to reach.
Raise a tiny hill beside the patterned steps,
lay a narrow ridge across the crimson courtyard.
Open a small plot to establish its base,
pile a few feet high to form its mound.
It lacks majestic towering peaks,
and has no endowment of clouds and mist.
It catches the lingering drips from falling eaves,
and hangs broken threads in the low sky.
Then, jagged and steep cliffs,
winding and narrow short paths.
The wind, pausing briefly, is about to drift away;
the mist, just rising high, does not yet darken.
Within inches, solitary ridges connect and break again;
within a foot, layered peaks tilt and then stand upright.
Gullies with willows join like paired eyebrows;
stones clear the flow, dividing into twin mirrors.
Then, transplant fragrant plants, cultivate beauty,
raise trunks and sprout stems.
Pines newly green and sparse,
osmanthus small, cinnabar light.
Slender shadows mingled, all in disarray;
delicate forms clustered, intertwined together.
Just strong enough to outlast butterflies,
unintentionally attracting orioles.
Half a leaf unfurls, and the cliff darkens;
a single flower scatters, and the peak brightens.
How can such minute things share the same scene,
yet, humble and small, they complete each other?
Thus, exchange fleeting power for deep contemplation,
appreciate gentle benevolence in this fine place.
Looking down at ant hills, I feel content;
looking up at Zhōngnán Mountain, I feel much shame.
Not to be steadfast through nine twists,
but hoping not to fail for lack of one basket of earth.
I leisurely admire it at dusk and approach at dawn,
enough to express my feelings and uplift my spirit.
Liáng Jiāng Yān's "Rhapsody on the Mountains by the River"
Vast and boundless, the waters of Chǔ and the rivers of Wú;
sharply carved, towering and steep, the mountain clouds and azure peaks.
Hanging green vines for ten thousand ren,
erecting cinnabar rocks in a hundred layers.
A hundred layers of cliffs and crags,
as if hewn, as if carved.
Lofty and precipitous, sharply protruding;
craggy and towering, with caverns dug.
Waves and tides inhale and exhale,
cliffs and banks accumulate and pile.
I see red grasses growing intertwined,
gaze upon green trees enclosing from all sides.
Grasses grow naturally with a thousand blossoms;
trees, though heartless, display a hundred hues.
Alas, human life differs from this;
worries and ailments press upon me.
In a fleeting moment, I harbor burning coals;
in a single breath, I clutch at silken threads.
Customs chase after affairs and change;
the heart responds to things and turns about.
Already startled and not yet awakened,
also entangled and already shifted.
How long is a human lifespan?
Like a shooting star across the night sky.
Melancholy, as dusk falls, I have thoughts;
facing the broken mountains by the river.
Though not keen and without steadfastness,
I wish to follow the orchid's fragrance and be as firm as jade.
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on a Small Hill"
Near the valley, intertwining stamens;
distant peaks, paired lotuses emerging.
The path narrow, without complete steps;
pines small, not yet holding mist.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Poem on Mountains"
Layered clouds shroud the steep ridges,
deep streams reflect the perilous peaks.
Carved and hewn, facing a thousand ren;
towering and lofty, rising a hundred layers.
The traveling sunlight ascends into obscurity,
condensed mist descends, vast and merging.
A benevolent heart remains in this company,
ashamed to serve among the multitude of dragons.
Zhōu Xiāo Huī's "Poem on Ascending Lián Mountain"
Alone I stride over Qīnglián Ridge,
transcending the wonder of Zǐgài Peak.
Hanging streams afar resemble cranes;
inserted stones nearby are like dragons.
Sand slides sound like rhythmic drums;
frost falling resembles ringing bells.
Flying blossoms fill the clustered cassia;
gentle breezes stir the tall bamboo.
Stone calamus still remains now,
gathering and plucking, we may meet again.
Poem "Often the Lonely Mountain Shines" by Chén Xiāo Quán of the Chén Dynasty
Green mountains reflect the setting sun's glow,
Shining far, gazing at the continuous flight.
Immortal peaks view the Jade Bamboo Box,
Mountain passes gaze upon Jīnwēi.
The sound of drums and pipes seems to fade away,
Incense burner smoke feels sparse and thin.
With you, I part by the waterside,
Toiling here to send you on your return.
Poem "Ode to the Mountain" by Monk Huì Biāo of the Chén Dynasty
The spiritual mountain holds a beautiful name,
Elegantly emerging, depicting Péng and Yíng.
The incense burner rises with smoke,
Purple canopies emerge amidst the clouds.
Mist rolls back, lotus peaks appear,
Cliffs open, the stone mirror gleams bright.
Surely within these hills and valleys,
Together lingers the sentiment of white clouds.
Another
Éméi truly is steep and perilous,
Tiānmù originally an immortal's abode.
Jīnhuá embraces the cinnabar furnace,
The Jade Bamboo Box contains divine texts.
The recluse dons the creeping fig,
The resentful concubine gathers the miwú herb.
No evening rain at the purple furnace,
When will she send off her former husband?
Another
Cinnabar clouds brush against layered pavilions,
Jade-green waters drift toward Pénglái.
Turtle peaks shrouded in mist rise high,
Lotus cliffs open to the sun's light.
Pine gates flanked by slender leaves,
Stone steps stained with fresh moss.
It could make Píngzǐ come to see,
Yet he lingers, unwilling to return.
Poem "In Response to Instruction: Gazing at the Mountain" by Xiāo Què
Immortal journeys are inherently full of delight,
And now again, early autumn ascends.
Low cliffs, rocks perilously inverted,
High ridges, pines even more sparse.
Peak shapes resemble birds' wings,
Mountain paths seem like wolves' dens.
Gazing afar, feelings know no end,
Words exhausted, meaning still remains.
Poem "Ode to the Mountain" by Lǐ Délín of the Suí Dynasty
Ascending the ridge, I gaze at the layered passes,
Jade pendants at my waist gently chime.
The Milky Way seems near enough to drink,
The moon's cassia almost within grasp to climb.
The Queen Mother arrives at the immortal mountain,
Lady Wèi returns from Nányuè's peak.
Why must one beneath the Yángtái terrace wait,
To await a dreamt visage to seek?
Poem "Ode to the Mountain" by Liú Bīn of the Suí Dynasty
Snowy peaks stand a thousand rèn high,
Blocking the sun, towering and steep.
Purple canopies, clouds and shadows far,
Incense burners, smoke and mist deep.
Stone bridges, paths for high-flying birds,
Waterfalls near the Heavenly River flow.
If you wish to know the way's distance told,
Separately, there are immortal songs to know.
Preface to "Records of Traveling Famous Mountains" by Xiè Língyùn of the Sòng Dynasty
Clothing and food are the means for sustaining life,
Mountains and waters are where nature finds its ease.
Now, hindered by the burdens of these means,
One clings to the nature that brings such ease.
Common opinion often says joy lies in splendid halls,
That those who pillow on cliffs and rinse in streams lack great ambition,
Thus preserving their withered state.
I say this is not so.
The noble person has affection for all things,
And the ability to save them.
The flaws of rampant currents
Cannot be governed without talent.
Thus, some humble themselves to aid others.
How could the arena of fame and profit
Be superior to the realm of clarity and openness?
Speaking of the myriad-chariot lord, then at Dǐnghú there was loosening of the reins;
Discussing the heir apparent, then at Sōngshān there was severing of control.
Again, Táozhū highly bowed out as Yuè's minister,
Liúhóu wished to resign as Hàn's tutor.
Inferring from this,
It can be made clear!
Mount Tài, Third
Regarding Mount Tài,
It is the Eastern Peak of the Five Sacred Mountains.
The "Records of Diverse Matters" states:
"Mount Tài is also called Tiānsūn,
Meaning it is the grandson of the Celestial Emperor.
It governs the summoning of souls.
In the east, all things begin to form,
Thus it knows the length of human life."
The "General Meanings of the Five Classics" states:
"One name is Dàizōng,
Meaning when a king receives the mandate and changes the dynasty,
To report achievements and announce completion,
It must be at Dàizōng.
It is the place in the east where all things begin their succession.
Zōng
Means elder,
Meaning it is the foremost among all peaks."
The "Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall" states:
"When a king receives the mandate,
He must perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Fēng means to increase height.
Shàn means to broaden and deepen.
Shàn
Is clearing the ground to make an altar.
The character originally was shàn,
Because it sacrifices to spirits,
Thus it uses the shì radical.
All carve stone to record the title,
Displaying one's own merits and achievements to prove oneself.
Heaven regards height as honorable,
Earth regards thickness as virtuous.
Therefore, increase Mount Tài's height
To show repaying Heaven.
Perform the shàn sacrifice at the base of Liángfǔ
To repay Earth."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Wúhuáishì performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Fúxī performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Shénnóng performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Yándì performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Huángdì performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Zhuānxū performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Dìkù performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Yáo performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Shùndì performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài and the shàn sacrifice at Yúnyún.
Yǔ performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
And the shàn sacrifice at Kuàijī.
King Chéng of Zhōu performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
And the shàn sacrifice at Shèshǒu.
Qín Shǐhuáng performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
And the shàn sacrifice at Liángfǔ.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
And the shàn sacrifice at Liángfǔ.
At Sùrán and Hāolǐ Shílǘ,
Later, he performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài a total of five times."
The "Book of the Later Hàn" states:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
And the shàn sacrifice at Liángfǔ a total of three times,
At Yúntíng.
Sùrán, Hāolǐ, Shèshǒu, Liángfǔ
Are all small hills below Mount Tài.
Shílǘ is below the western cliff."
The "Hàn Official Ceremonials" and "Records of Mount Tài" state:
"The winding path ascends in twists and turns,
Totaling over fifty bends,
Passing through the Small Heavenly Gate and the Great Heavenly Gate.
Looking up at the Heavenly Gate,
It is like viewing a skylight from within a cave.
From the bottom to the ancient fēng and shàn site,
It is forty lǐ in total.
The western cliff at the mountaintop is the Immortal's Stone Gate,
The eastern cliff is Jièqiū,
The southeastern cliff is named Rìguān.
Rìguān
Is where, at the first crow of the rooster,
One sees the sun just beginning to rise,
About three zhàng long.
Further southeast is named Qínguān.
Qínguān
Is where one gazes and sees Cháng'ān.
Wúguān
Is where one gazes and sees Kuàijī.
Zhōuguān
Is where one gazes and sees Qí.
The Yellow River is over two hundred lǐ from Mount Tài,
From the sacrificial site, gazing at the Yellow River, it is like a ribbon.
As if at the mountain's base.
South of the mountain is a temple,
All planted with a thousand cypress trees,
The largest fifteen or sixteen arm-spans around,
Traditionally said to have been planted by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
At the Small Heavenly Gate are the Five Grandee Pines from the Qín era,
Still existing."
The "Inner Biography of Máo Jūn" states:
"Among immortal abodes, there are thirty-six grottoes.
The grotto at Dàizōng
Has a circumference of three thousand lǐ,
Named the Heaven of the Three Palaces and Empty Cavern."
Immortal Gate Divine Mansion
The *Book of Han* states:
"Emperor Wu of Han performed the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
and performed the Shàn sacrifice at Shílǘ."
Yīng Shào's commentary states:
"Shílǘ is located to the south at the foot of Mount Tài.
The local people say it is the gate of immortals."
The *Blessed Lands Record of Daoist Texts* states:
"Mount Tài has many spirit fungi and jade stones.
Below it is a grotto-heaven,
with a circumference of three thousand *lǐ*,
which is the mansion of ghosts and spirits."
Cloudy Palaces Heavenly Gate
Yuán Shānsōng's *Book of the Later Han* states:
"When Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
clouds and vapors formed into palaces and towers."
The *Han Official Ceremonial* states:
"Ascending seventy *lǐ* east of Mount Tài leads to the Heavenly Gate."
Five Sacrifices Three Temples
The *Book of Han* states:
"For the Five Sacred Peaks and the Four Great Rivers,
there are regular sacrifices.
For the Hé River at Línjìn,
for the Jiāng River at Jiāngdū,
for the Huái River at Píngshì,
and for the Jì River within the boundaries of Línyì,
all are performed by envoys holding tallies for special sacrifices.
Only Mount Tài and the Hé River receive five sacrifices annually,
the Jiāng River receives four,
and the rest receive one prayer and three sacrifices."
Wǔ Jīzhī's *Record of Following Campaigns* states:
"Mount Tài has upper, middle, and lower temples.
In front of the temples is a large well.
Its water is extremely fragrant and cold,
different from ordinary water.
It is not known from which era it was dug."
Sun-Viewing Peak Celestial Grandson
"Sun-Viewing Peak" is mentioned in the narrative section.
Zhāng Huá's *Records of Diverse Matters* states:
"Mount Tài
is the grandson of the Celestial Emperor,
and is in charge of summoning human souls."
Stone Gate Jade Table
The *Book of Han* states:
"Emperor Wu performed the Shàn sacrifice at Shílǘ."
Liú Xiàng's *Biographies of Exemplary Immortals* states:
"Within the stone chamber of Dàizōng, the heights are sheer and precipitous.
Inside are a golden bed and a jade table."
Golden Casket Jade Slips
The *Comprehensive Meaning of Customs* states:
"In ancient times, when performing the Fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài
and the Shàn sacrifice at Liángfǔ,
it was said that upon Dàizōng there is a golden casket containing jade tallies,
which can tell the length of a person's lifespan.
Emperor Wu of Han drew a tally and got 'eighteen'.
He then read it aloud as 'eighty'.
Later, he indeed lived to the age of eighty."
Liú Yìgōng's poem states:
"The Great Brilliance [Emperor] commands divine martial prowess,
riding the times to rule heaven.
The golden document sealed Liángfǔ,
the jade slips performed Shàn at Dàishān."
Lǔ's Gaze Qín's View
The *Máo Odes* states:
"Lofty is Mount Tài,
gazed upon by the state of Lǔ."
"Qín's View" is mentioned in the narrative section.
Zhèng's Sacrifice Wú's View
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"The Earl of Zhèng requested to be released from the sacrifice to Mount Tài,
and instead sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"Zhèng had a bathing-town for assisting in the sacrifice to Mount Tài located at Bēng."
"Wú's View" is mentioned above.
Yú's Burnt Offering Yǎn's Guardian Mountain
The *Book of Yú* states:
"In the second month of the year,
he made an eastern tour of inspection,
and reaching Dàizōng, performed the burnt offering."
The *Offices of Zhōu* states:
"For Yǎnzhōu,
its guardian mountain is called Dàishān."
Cloud-Sealed Rainy Slope
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"When Emperor Wu of Han performed the Fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
white clouds arose from the sealed mound."
It also states:
"When the First Emperor of Qín ascended Mount Tài,
he encountered wind and rain on the middle slope."
Old Man with Hoe Fungus-Bearing Youths
Gě Hóng's *Biographies of Divine Immortals* states:
"There was an old man at the foot of Mount Tài
whose name was lost.
When Emperor Wu of Han traveled east,
he saw the old man hoeing by the roadside,
with white light emanating from his head."
Cáo Zhí's "Flying Dragon" poem states:
"Traveling at dawn on Mount Tài,
the clouds and mist are deep and secluded.
Suddenly I met two youths,
their countenances fresh and fair.
Riding upon white deer,
their hands shading with spirit fungi."
Thousand Trees Three Palaces
The *Records of Mount Tài* states:
"The Temple of Mount Tài is on the southern side of the mountain,
all planted with a thousand cypress trees."
The *Inner Biography of Master Máo* states:
"The cavern of Dàizōng Mountain
has a circumference of over three thousand *lǐ*.
It is named the Heaven of the Three Palaces and the Hollow Cavern."
Divine Chamber Fragrant Well
The *Book of Master Shī* states:
"Within Mount Tài,
there are divine chambers and lofty pavilions."
"Fragrant Well" is mentioned above in the note for "Three Temples."
Lord Jìqiū Cuī Wénzǐ
Liú Xiàng's *Biographies of Exemplary Immortals* states:
"Lord Jìqiū
was a Daoist priest at the foot of Mount Tài.
When Emperor Wu of Han made his eastern tour to Mount Tài,
he came holding his *qín* to pay respects."
It also states:
"Cuī Wénzǐ
was a mountain recluse of Mount Tài.
He was fond of the arts of Huáng-Lǎo,
lived in seclusion at the foot of the mountain,
and made yellow pills to sell as medicine.
Those afflicted by epidemic qi,
upon drinking the medicine, would be cured immediately."
Chiseled Stone Cauldron Drawing the Jade Tally
Cuī Hóng's *Records of the Former Qín* states:
"The retired scholar Zhāng Zhōng lived in seclusion on Mount Tài.
He dwelled among cliffs and drank from valleys,
cultivating methods of guiding and nourishing [life],
and chiseled stone to make cauldrons.
The people of Mount Tài still follow his method today."
"Drawing the Jade Tally" is mentioned above in the note for "Golden Casket."
Lǐ Yìfǔ's "Poem from Afar in Xīzhōu Recalling the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
Tiānqí marks the great guardian peak,
Rìguān opens the lofty shrine.
Towering, it overlooks the Bóxiè Sea,
lofty and rugged, it controls the Hé and Yí Rivers.
Establishing this peak is truly paramount,
the merit of ascent surely lies here.
The emperor's plan accords with vast fortune,
profound words express literary thought.
Fame spreads throughout the earth's network,
transforming influence soothes heaven's cords.
Auspicious tallies reveal the precious phoenix,
propitious charts present the treasure turtle.
The eastern queen then came to audience,
the western capital led the six armies.
The imperial carriage moved to the starry park,
hunters drove the wind-chariots.
Boiling drums clamored on the level plain,
halted carriages quieted the great roads.
Wènyáng sped moon-feathered arrows,
Méngyīn alerted lightning-chariots.
Hunting pennants fluttered at dawn carriages,
mountain leaves waved on spring flags.
Shílǘ encircled by patterned guards,
golden altars reflecting embroidered canopies.
Immortal steps overflow with secret millet,
spiritual omens shine with auspicious fungus.
Three beginnings bestow distant favor,
ten thousand years receive double blessings.
Though unworthy, molded by grace and reward,
I hasten to serve at the palace steps.
Touching the net, I sink to the remote border,
riding the frontier, limited by enlightened times.
Zhōunán's lament was in the past,
Qiōngxī's sorrow is now renewed.
Xiè Língyùn of the Sòng Dynasty, "Chant of Mount Tài"
Dàizōng, splendid among the sacred peaks,
towering, pierces the cloudy heavens.
Its cliffs are steep and perilous,
touching the stone, it stretches far and winding.
Ascending for Fēng, burying in the lofty mound,
descending for Shàn, concealing at Sùrán.
How dim and luxuriant is Shílǘ,
the Bright Hall holds secret spiritual texts.
Emperor Xiàowén of Later Wèi "Ceremonial Address to Mount Dàiyuè"
In the nineteenth year of Tàihé,
I respectfully announce to the spirit of Tàishān, the Eastern Peak,
that the essence of creation,
gave birth to the dual forces.
The dark and yellow have spread,
mountains and rivers have formed.
The four streams contain spirits,
the Five Sacred Mountains embrace the earth.
They encompass all things,
fulfilling hopes like Xi Yǐ.
The majestic Dàizōng,
towering Liángfǔ.
The verdant hills are steep,
the spring paths are lush.
All living things emerged,
illuminating all creatures.
Above, the divine works unfold,
below, harmonizing the spiritual order.
In harmony with creation,
the four elements overflow.
Every king has achieved completion,
none are without this shrine.
Gāo Yǔn of Later Wèi "Ceremonial Address to Mount Dàizōng"
In the second year of Huángxīng,
I respectfully announce to the spirit of Dàizōng,
that the earth’s foundation is correct,
acting as the eastern bastion.
The dual forces are harmonized for eternity,
noble virtues match heaven,
harnessing primal energy to create,
harmonizing yīn and yáng to transform.
As for the cliffs standing sharply,
the valleys are profound,
miracles are strange and extraordinary,
swift like spirits.
Breathing in the wind and clouds,
nurturing myriad life forms.
It is the source of life,
the gathering of fortune.
Therefore, revered by successive emperors,
receiving enshrinement and merit,
proclaiming their achievements.
Seventy-two rulers,
all are here,
unless their achievements rival creation,
and resonate with nature,
who can accomplish this?
Since the founding of our state,
reverently observing sacrifices,
kindly accommodating all spirits,
within the territory,
all is orderly.
Previously, as the heavenly path was not prolonged,
although offering ceremonies were wished for,
now that great harmony prevails,
we possess Huáidài,
I carefully offer to the spirit of the mountain,
still may you receive this.
Mount Héng, the Fourth
"Zhōu Official Records":
"Jīngzhōu,
its mountain guardian is called Mount Héng."
Xú Língqī’s "Record of the Southern Peak" and Shèng Hóngzhī’s "Record of Jīngzhōu" state:
"Mount Héng,
is the Southern Peak of the Five Sacred Mountains,
its origin is ancient!
Up to Xuānyuán,
it was made
sound Qián.
Huò's mountain was its counterpart.
Thus the 'Erya' states:
'Huò Mountain as the Southern Peak,
it was regarded as its counterpart.'
Some say Mount Héng was also named Huò Mountain.
In the southward tour of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
seeing Mount Héng is far to the south,
the path obstructed by Jiānghàn,
he moved the Southern Peak’s rites to Lújiāng Qián Mountain,
this also maintained Xuānyuán's deputy status,
Gān Bǎo's 'Search for the Spirits' says:
'Emperor Wǔ moved the Southern Peak's rites to Huò Mountain in Qianyán County, Lújiāng.'
Guō Pú's 'Erya' commentary states:
'Huò Mountain is in Lújiāng County Qián County,
also known as Heaven's Pillar Mountain.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, seeing Mount Héng was distant,
prophesied and used Huò Mountain as the peak,
thus offering sacrifices.'
Thus, the Southern Peak is Mount Héng.
Zhūlíng's spiritual terrace,
Tàixū's treasure cave,
above receiving the stars,
fusing virtues and balancing objects,
therefore named Mount Héng.
Below anchoring the detached palace,
occupying the searing township,
the Red Emperor governs its ridge,
Zhùróng entrusted its sunward side,
therefore called the Southern Peak.
Spans several hundred lǐ in circumference,
rises four thousand and ten zhàng high,
overlooks Xiāng River to the southeast,
from Xiāng River to Chángshā is seven hundred lǐ,
nine approaches, nine retreats,
then it disappears.
Yǔ controlled the waters,
ascended and offered sacrifices,
in a dream met the envoy of Xuányí,
thus obtaining a jade-inscribed book,
gaining the key to water management.
The mountain has three peaks,
one named Zǐgài,
with clear heavenly scenes,
with a pair of white cranes,
circling above.
One peak named Shíqún,
below has a stone chamber,
often echoes with chanting.
One peak named Fúróng,
above a spring cascades,
like unfurling a white silk.
The 'Classic of Mountains and Seas' says:
'Mount Héng is also called Gǒulóu Mountain,
it has much green ochre,
many birds of the Qúyù type.'
Gǒu is pronounced jǔ,
Lóu is pronounced lǚ.
Zǐgài and Zhūlíng
Both "Zǐgài" and "Zhūlíng" appear in the narrative.
Nine Approaches, Three Peaks
Luó Hán's 'Record of Central Xiāng' says:
'Mount Héng viewed from afar like an array of clouds,
stretching a thousand lǐ along Xiāng,
nine approaches, nine retreats.'
'Three Peaks' mentioned in the narrative.
The Song of Shùn, The Whistle of Yǔ
Luó Hán's 'Record of Central Xiāng' says:
'Mount Héng's nine doubts,
each has a temple for Shùn.
When the governor arrives in office,
often sends tribute to respectfully repair the rites,
it seems there is sound of string music.'
Zhào Yè's 'Spring and Autumn Annals of Wú and Yuè' says:
'Yǔ mourned the incomplete works of his father,
thus consulting the Central Scripture of the Huángdì,
where he noted the Saint's record saying:
'At the nine doubts mountain to the southeast of Heaven's Pillar,
named Wănwěi Mountain.
The Red Emperor's left chamber,
atop the crag,
supported by jade script,
covered by a giant rock.
The text of gold book with jade characters,
interlinked by silver,
all inscribed with its writings.
Yǔ thus toured east ascending Mount Héng,
sacrificing a white horse,
whistled at the heavens,
suddenly reclining still.
In a dream he saw a man in red embroidered robes,
called the envoy of Xuányí from the dark waters,
who told Yǔ:
'To obtain the divine book of my mountain,
purify yourself below the peak of Huángdì.'
Yǔ thus retreated, purified for three months,
on the day of the jié cycle,
ascended Wănwěi Mountain,
unearthing the stone to acquire the book.'
Shíqún and Treasure Cave
Zāng Róngxù's 'Book of Jìn' says:
'Liú Línzhī enjoyed wandering mountains and wetlands,
collecting herbs reaching Mount Héng,
venturing deep into forgetting to return.
He saw a ravine of water,
south of which had two stone chambers,
one open, one closed,
the water being too deep to pass.'
'Treasure Cave' in the narrative.
Jade Script, Stone Book
'Jade Script' in the narrative.
Xú Língqī's 'Record of the Southern Peak' says:
'Xià Yǔ guided water through channels,
engraved a stone to record the height of sacred mountains,
with Southern Peak text stating,
a height of four thousand and ten zhàng.'
Spiritual Terrace, Immortal Abode
'Spiritual Terrace' in the narrative.
Mount Héng houses the Red Emperor at its ridge,
Zhùróng resides at its sunny side,
its powerful and grand spirit,
casting a towering shade,
thus it is the abode of gods and spirits,
a celestial dwelling of immortals.
Steep Slope Elegant Cliff
Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Qin" states:
"Where the phoenix tree grows,
On the steep slope of Mount Héng."
Huán Xuán's "Preface to Traveling South to Mount Héng" states:
"Lofty peaks towering, wrapped in clouds,
Elegant cliffs rising into the azure sky."
Holding Books Left Behind Characters
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu" states:
"Once, a herb gatherer on Mount Héng
saw an old man
with four or five youths,
sitting opposite each other, holding books."
Liú Jìngshū's "Garden of Marvels" states:
"Yáo Zǔ of Xiāngdōng,
during the Tàiyuán era, served as a commandery clerk.
Passing by Mount Héng,
he saw several youths at the foot of a cliff, all holding brushes and writing.
Zǔ thought they were travelers resting,
so he approached them.
Before he was within a hundred paces,
the youths flew away together,
leaving behind a sheet of paper with writing at their sitting place.
The first few lines were in ancient characters,
while those following were all in bird script."
Building a Dwelling Resting the Carriage
Sūn Yán's "History of the Sòng" states:
"Zōng Bǐng sought out famous mountains,
ascending Jīng and Wū in the west,
and climbing Mount Héng in the south.
Thus, he built a dwelling on Mount Héng,
wishing to embrace the aspirations of Shàng Píng."
Huán Xuán's "Preface to the Poem on Traveling South to the Mountains" states:
"In the middle month of spring,
I first reached Mount Héng.
Resting the carriage on plain stones,
reflected in the washing waters by the shore."
Divine Abode Immortal Cliff
"Divine Abode" see the note for "Immortal Dwelling" above.
"Immortal Cliff" see Xiè Língyùn's poem below.
Bird Script Crane Dance
"Bird Script" see the note for "Left Behind Characters" above.
Luó Hán's "Records of Xiāngzhōng" states:
"On Mount Héng, there is a hanging spring,
dripping between the cliffs,
its sound clear and cold like strings being plucked.
Cranes circle and soar above it as if dancing."
Poem "Traveling to Mount Héng" by Yǔ Chǎn of the Eastern Jìn
Gazing north at the path to Mount Héng,
Looking south to the ends of the Five Ridges.
Sitting in silence, embracing emptiness and tranquility,
Sweeping my gaze, emotions expand in all directions.
Soaring dragons ascend the nine heavens,
Land-dwelling fish struggle in shallow puddles.
Never having experienced wandering rivers and lakes,
How can one know the vastness of the Southern Sea?
Poem "Mount Héng" by Xiè Língyùn of the Sòng
An old man at the foot of the cliff,
Four or five youths.
A herb gatherer on Mount Héng,
Lost his way, provisions also exhausted.
Stopping to rest, sitting at the cliff's base,
He saw them facing each other, speaking.
One old, four or five young,
Immortal or recluse, indistinguishable.
Their writings not of worldly teaching,
These men must be sages and worthies.
Preface to "Poem on Traveling South to Mount Héng" by Huán Xuán of the Eastern Jìn
In the year of Jiàng Lóu,
At the beginning of Jiá Zhōng,
I prepared the oars to journey to Mount Héng,
Crossing the Xiāng River for a thousand miles,
Forests and hills stretching continuously.
Clear streams, their flow pure and reflective to the end,
Banks and shores without a speck of dust or filth.
The long road stretches ever onward,
Its end not yet in sight.
All I passed through each day,
Was nothing but wondrous delight.
In the middle month of spring,
I first reached Mount Héng.
Thereupon, I entrusted my steps to a light carriage,
Speaking by night, driving swiftly on.
Three hundred li of level road,
Mountain paths completely open.
Sometimes drooping branches span the valleys,
Narrow gorges intertwined in shade.
Sometimes winding streams seem blocked,
Already cut off, then opening again.
Sometimes walking along long ridges,
Gazing afar into the distant expanse.
Sometimes resting the carriage on plain stones,
Reflected in the washing waters by the shore.
The reason for my joyful haste and delight,
Forgetting fatigue while seeking the path,
Is that such moments arise with every encounter.
Looking up at the green peaks,
Far off at the sky's edge.
My body ascends to the great clarity,
Alone communing with the rosy clouds.
Having just completed my circuitous view,
I suddenly reined in at the cliff's recess.
Pipes and strings played together,
Clear melodies sounded once more.
Thoughts of antiquity forever departed,
My spirit and energy left unspoken.
Huàshān, the Fifth
Regarding Huàshān,
it is the Western Peak of the Five Sacred Mountains.
"The Rites of Zhōu" states:
"For Yùzhōu,
its guardian mountain is called Huàshān."
"Records of Huàshān" states:
"On the mountain's summit, there is
a pond that grows thousand-petaled lotuses.
Consuming them leads to ascension as an immortal,
hence it is called Huàshān."
Also, "Báihǔ Tōng" states:
"The western Huàshān,
where lesser yin holds sway,
and all things bloom,
thus it is called Huàshān."
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"Also named Tàihuà.
The mountain of Tàihuà,
hewn square on all sides,
five thousand ren high,
and ten li broad."
Xuē Zōng's commentary on "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"Huàshān faces Shǒuyáng Mountain east of the river.
The Yellow River flows between these two mountains.
An ancient saying holds that originally this was one mountain blocking the river.
The river water, passing it, curved its course.
The river god, the Giant Spirit,
with his hands split the mountain above,
and with his feet kicked apart the mountain below,
cleaving it in two,
to allow the river to flow through.
Now, the handprint can be seen on Huàyuè,
the shape of fingers and palm fully present.
The footprint is below Shǒuyáng Mountain,
and also remains there."
Guō Yuánshēng's "Record of a Campaign" and "Records of Huàshān" state:
"From the foot of the mountain, starting from the Huàyuè Temple, cypresses line the way.
Heading south for eleven li,
then turning east for three li,
one reaches the Middle Shrine.
Then southwest for five li to the Southern Shrine.
Entering the valley mouth southward for seven li,
one reaches another shrine.
All who wish to ascend the mountain pray here.
Another li south to Tiānjǐng (Heavenly Well),
the well barely allows a person to climb up.
It is about six zhang or more in length.
Emerging from the well is like looking at the open sky, seeing brightness,
as if peering through a window from inside a room.
Exiting the well, southeast for two li,
one reaches a steep slope ascending sharply.
Then eastward up the Bǎizhàng Cliff,
all requiring grasping ropes and clinging to vines to proceed.
Then southwest for six li,
one reaches another shrine,
named the Temple Deity of Húyuè.
Walking another two li,
one then arrives at the mountain summit.
Above, spanning seven li,
there are two numinous springs.
One named Pú Chí,
the other named Tàishàng Quán.
North of the pond is a stone drum,
its sound has been heard before.
Above it are three peaks rising straight up,
visible on clear, rainless days."
Two Huà Square on All Sides
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"Adorned with the Two Huà,
referring to Tàihuà and Shàohuà.
Shàohuà lies west of Huàshān."
"Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"The mountain of Tàihuà,
hewn square on all sides."
The Earth Bears, the Spirit Cleaves
The Book of Rites says:
"The way of Heaven and Earth
is vast
and deep.
It bears Mount Huàyuè without feeling heavy,
and contains the rivers and seas without letting them leak."
Guō Yuánshēng's Record of a Campaign says:
"Mount Huàyuè and Mount Shǒuyáng were originally one mountain.
The river god Jùlíng
split them into two."
The details are given in the narrative section.
Yùzhèn, Qínchéng
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"For Yù Province,
its guardian mountain is called Mount Huà."
The Book of Hàn says:
Jiǎ Yì's "Discourse on the Faults of Qín" states:
"The King of Qín inherited the remaining might of six generations,
brandished his long whip to rule the world,
then trod upon Mount Huà to make his walls,
and used the Yellow River as his moat."
Fourfold Enclosure, Two Peaks
The Record of Mount Huà says:
"Mount Huà has high cliffs enclosing it on four sides,
with layered ridges rising in beauty."
Guō Yuánshēng's Record of a Campaign says:
"Mount Huà has two peaks,
soaring straight up for thousands of ren.
From below, the smaller peak rises in layered splendor,
reaching to the top of the ridge,
as if carved by a knife."
Lotus Peak, Cypress Arrow
The Record of Mount Huà says:
"On the summit of Mount Huà grows a thousand-petaled lotus."
The Hánzǐ says:
"King Zhāo of Qín ordered craftsmen to use hooked ladders to ascend Mount Huà.
He had arrows made from the heartwood of pine and cypress,
eight chi long,
with arrowheads eight cun long,
and inscribed them, saying:
'King Zhāo once gambled here with a celestial god.'
The text has 'qí' for arrowhead,
which is incorrect."
Jade Slip, Golden Elixir
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Yān says:
"Shí Jìlóng sent men to gather herbs.
They ascended Mount Huà
and obtained a jade slip."
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"Mǎ Míngshēng received the formula for the Golden Elixir Divine Pill from Master Ānqī.
He then entered Mount Huàyīn,
combined the ingredients for the Golden Elixir,
but, not wishing to ascend to heaven,
took only half a dose to become an earthbound immortal."
Riding a Dragon, Driving a Deer
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"There was one Hū Zǐxiān,
a diviner at the Hánguān Pass in Hànzhōng,
over a hundred years old.
When about to depart,
he urgently told an old tavern woman to prepare.
An immortal arrived holding two straw dogs.
Upon arrival,
he first gave one to the tavern woman.
They both mounted them,
and they turned out to be dragons.
They ascended Mount Huà,
and he often called out loudly on the mountain,
saying, 'Zǐxiān and the tavern mother are here.'"
The Biographies of Divine Immortals says:
"Wèi Shūqīng often rode on clouds,
driving a white deer.
He appeared before Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
who wanted to make him a minister.
Shūqīng left without a word.
The emperor regretted it
and found his son, Dù Shì,
ordering him to pursue his father.
Dù Shì climbed Mount Huà
and saw his father gambling with several men on a rock.
Shūqīng commanded Dù Shì to return."
Stone Drum, Jade Nectar
The Record of Mount Huà says:
"On the summit of Mount Huà there is a stone drum."
The Elders' Tradition says:
"There have been those who heard it sound."
Guō Pú's Eulogy says:
"Divine Mount Huà, lofty and steep,
carved square on all sides.
Here there is a goddess,
who draws forth jade nectar."
Returning Horses, Leaving a Disc
The Book of Documents says:
"Return the horses to the southern side of Mount Huà,
release the oxen in the wilderness of Táolín,
to show the world they will no longer be used."
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"In the thirty-sixth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Zhèng Róng came from east of the pass.
Arriving at Huàyīn,
he saw a plain carriage with white horses
descending from the mountain.
Knowing they were not human,
he stopped and waited.
They arrived
and, holding a disc, said to Zhèng Róng:
'Deliver this for me to the Lord of Hàochí.'
The next year, the First Dragon died."
Heavenly Well, Stone Couch
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"The middle path of Mount Huà is called the Heavenly Well.
It barely allows a person to pass.
Winding and twisting upward,
it is over six zhang high.
On the mountain there is a trickle of fine water
that flows into the well,
yet does not wet people.
Emerging from the well and looking at the sky,
it is like peering through a window from inside a room."
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"There was one Xiū Yánggōng,
a man of Wèi,
who dwelled in a stone chamber on Mount Huàyīn.
Inside hung a stone couch.
He lay upon it,
and the stone wore completely through."
Catching Lice, Holding Dogs
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Yān says:
"Wáng Měng lived in seclusion on Mount Huà.
When Huán Wēn entered the pass,
Měng, wearing coarse cloth, went to see him.
Speaking of contemporary affairs,
he caught lice while talking,
as if no one else were around."
"Holding dogs" is already mentioned in the note for "Riding a Dragon."
Hairy Maiden, Jùlíng
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"There is a Hairy Maiden
on Mount Huàyīn.
Mountain travelers and hunters
have seen her through the ages.
Her body is covered in hair.
She says she was a palace lady of Qín Shǐ Huáng."
"Jùlíng" is mentioned in the narrative section.
Five-Li Fog, Thousand-Petaled Lotus
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn says:
"Zhāng Kǎi, styled Gōngchāo,
lived in seclusion on Mount Hóngnóng.
Scholars followed him.
Where he lived became a market.
He could create a five-li fog.
Later, south of Mount Huà, there was Gōngchāo's Fog Market."
"Thousand-petaled lotus" is mentioned in the narrative.
Palace of Gathered Spirits, Gate of Gazing at Immortals
Huán Tán's Preface to the "Rhapsody on Immortals" says:
"Below Mount Huà is the Palace of Gathered Spirits.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn wished to gather and cherish immortals,
so he named the hall 'Preserving Immortals'
and the gate 'Gazing at Immortals.'"
Suí Dynasty Kǒng Déshào's "Poem on Passing by Mount Tàihuà"
Entangled in worldly nets, yet finding leisure,
I seek the hidden depths of the divine peak.
Vast and far from the dusty world,
deep and dim the river valleys.
The mountain dimmed by five-li fog,
the sun setting on the two Huà's shade.
Scattered peaks rise like lotus leaves,
perilous passes hide the peach grove.
Why must one go beyond the eastern commandery?
Here one may withdraw the hairpin.
Shěn Quánqī's "Poem on the Western Peak"
How lofty and grand is this western guardian peak,
Truly magnificent, a creation of the divine.
All its ridges are steep and elegant,
But the central peak is especially fine.
Beside it, the giant palm print remains,
Its posture like propping up the east, yet leaning to fall.
I have heard that from Shǒuyáng it departed,
Cleaving open this river's course.
Vast and mighty, it presses upon the great source,
Towering high, it bears the clear sky.
Clouds and springs cascade in chaotic waterfalls,
Heavenly stone steps jut out, firmly embracing.
Zǐ Xiān called out from its summit,
Palace maidens there never grow old.
Below there is the temple of the Prefect Lord,
Through the ages, offerings have been swept and cleaned.
The Emperor's brilliance responds to Heaven's journey,
In the tenth month, he prepares at Fēnghào.
Humbly, I am privileged to leisurely accompany,
And also able to tend to the duckweed and algae.
Long have I loved this mountain in my heart,
Wishing to gather its spiritual herbs.
The shadowy ravines are forever closed,
The cloud-filled caves, beyond exploration.
I vow to return when fragrant months come again,
Turning my horse, my thoughts vast and boundless.
Posterity Hàn Zhāng Xù's "Inscription on Huà Mountain Stele Preface"
The "Yì" says:
"Heaven and Earth take their positions,
Mountains and marshes communicate their breath."
Thus, among mountains, none are more revered than the peaks,
Among marshes, none are loftier than the rivers.
There are five peaks, and Huà occupies one of them,
There are four rivers, and the Hé is among their number,
Their spiritual power is supreme.
The rise and fall of rulers
Must have their correspondences.
Thus, when stones stood on Dài Mountain,
Zhōngzōng succeeded to the throne.
When Tàihuà bestowed the jade disc,
The Qín Hú lineage was cut off.
Arranged among the five directions, it receives the west,
Placed among the three ridges, it resides in the center.
As for the broad beasts and strange creatures,
The "Classic of Mountains" has records.
The classics have rituals of gazing and ranking,
The canons have sacrifices for growth and reproduction,
All to revere the mountains and rivers and repay their merits.
When the four seas are unified,
The Son of Heaven conducts the sacrifices;
When the feudal lords contend by force,
The powerful states oversee the offerings.
Its fief has long been called Huàyīn.
Western Jìn Fù Xuán's "Inscription on Huà Mountain Stele Preface"
The "Yì" says that among models and images, none are greater than Heaven and Earth.
Heaven is named for its height and brightness,
And the peaks match it.
Earth is based on its breadth and thickness,
And the peaks embody it.
As for Tàihuà being a guardian peak,
Among the five peaks arrayed in position, it stands at their head;
Among the three ridges dividing the directions, it resides in the center.
It partakes of the two primal forces to compare its virtue,
Harmonizes with the blending of peaceful energies,
Aids the clouds' movement and rain's bestowal,
Arouses thunder and wind to stir creatures.
Therefore, sage emperors and enlightened kings
All without exception burn offerings, add sacrificial animals,
Revere it, and make sacrifices.
Eastern Jìn Guō Pú's "In Praise of Tàihuà"
Huà Mountain, spiritually lofty,
Hewn square on all sides.
Here there is a divine maiden,
Who draws forth jade nectar.
Who roams there?
Dragon-drawn chariots and cloud garments.
Héng Mountain, the Sixth
Note: Héng Mountain
is the Northern Peak of the Five Peaks.
The "Zhōu Guān" says:
"Bīng Province
has its guardian mountain called Héng Mountain."
The "Fēngsú Tōng" says:
"Héng
means constant.
All things submit to the north, which has constancy,
thus it is also called Cháng Mountain."
The "Báihǔ Tōng" says:
"Why is the north called Cháng Mountain?
Because yin ends and yang begins there,
its way is constant and enduring,
thus it is called Cháng Mountain."
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Cháng Mountain is called Héng Mountain."
The "Chart of the Five Peaks" says:
"Héng Mountain is 3,900 zhàng and 7 chǐ high,
its summit plateau is 30 lǐ across,
its circumference is 3,000 lǐ.
There is the Tàixuán Spring,
and nineteen kinds of divine herbs;
consuming them enables one to transcend the world."
The "Guǎnzǐ" says:
"Héng Mountain faces Dài to the north,
looks down upon Zhào to the south,
and connects to the region between the river and the sea to the east.
Crops sprout early and are harvested late,
the five grains flourish and ripen there,
yielding four plantings and five harvests."
The "History of the Later Wèi" says:
"Dàowǔ established a temple upon it,
and appointed ninety attendants for sacrifices.
They prayed seasonally for rain or clear weather.
When Emperor Wénchéng toured east,
he personally paid respects to its deity."
Zhào's Talisman Yān's Jade
The "Records of the Grand Historian" says:
"Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào said to his sons:
'I have hidden a precious talisman in Cháng Mountain.
Whoever goes and obtains it shall be established as heir.'
All his sons rushed to go,
but found nothing.
Wúxù said:
'Cháng Mountain overlooks Dài;
Dài can be taken.'
Jiǎnzǐ said:
'He understands the talisman!'
Thus he was established as heir."
Cuī Hóng's "Records of the Former Yān" says:
"In the second year of the Shòuguāng era of Mùróng Jùn,
seventy jade discs and
seventy-three jade tablets were found beneath the roots of a great tree at the Cháng Mountain temple.
Their luster and color were exquisite and extraordinary,
unlike common jade.
Jùn considered it a mandate from the divine peak
and sacrificed to it with the Great Tribute."
Shuàirán Divine Guardian
The "Art of War by Sūnzǐ" says:
"The snake of Cháng Mountain
is named Shuàirán.
It has one body but two heads.
Strike one head, and the other head comes;
strike its middle, and both heads come together."
The "Shénnóng's Materia Medica" says:
"On Cháng Mountain there is a herb named Divine Guardian.
Place it on the door,
and each night it scolds people."
Jade Tablets and Discs Péngléi
"Jade tablets and discs" already appeared in the note on "Yān's Jade" above.
The "Biographies of Exemplary Immortals" says:
"There was Chāng Róng,
a Daoist of Cháng Mountain,
who called herself a daughter of the Yīn.
She ate the roots of péngléi
and came and went below the mountain.
She was seen for over two hundred years,
her appearance like that of a twenty-year-old."
Overlooking Dài Looking Down on Zhào
Both matters are seen in the narrative section.
Yú's Inspection Bīng's Guardian
The "Book of Yú" says:
"In the eleventh month, he inspected the north, reaching the Northern Peak,
performing the rites as for the west."
"Bīng's guardian" is seen in the narrative.
Two-Headed Snake Five-Harvest Grain
"Two-headed snake" is seen in the note on "Shuàirán."
"Five-harvest grain" is seen in the narrative section.
Essence of Bì and Mǎo Territory of Zhào and Dài
The "Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo" says:
"Bì disperses to become Jì Province,
divides to form the state of Zhào,
and establishes Cháng Mountain."
Sòng Jūn's commentary says:
"Cháng Mountain is Héng Mountain,
the essence of Bì and Mǎo."
It also says:
"The state of Zhào has Cháng Mountain,
overlooking Dài."
Wúxù Obtains the Talisman Chāng Róng Attains the Way
"Obtaining the talisman" is already seen in the note on "Zhào's Talisman."
"Chāng Róng" is already seen in the note on "Péngléi."
Western Jìn Fù Xián's Poem
Majestic Héng Mountain,
Guardian of Jì's region.
Behold, Zhào established its state
On the southern side of the peak.
Zhōu Wángbāo's "Crossing the River North Poem"
The autumn wind blows through the leaves of trees,
Just like the waves on Dòngtíng Lake.
Chángshān overlooks the Dàijùn commandery,
Watchtowers and barriers encircle the Yellow River.
My heart grieves at the music of a foreign land,
My innards break at the song from Lǒngtóu.
At dusk I face my warhorse,
Having lost my way in the northern mountain's curve.
Táng Tàizōng's "Sacrificial Text to the Northern Peak, Héng Shān"
In the nineteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era of the Great Táng,
With offerings of the great sacrifice,
I reverently sacrifice at the spirit altar of Héng Peak.
The vast primordial ether,
Records the three luminaries to form images;
The boundless earth,
Anchors the Five Peaks to take shape.
Héng and Dài open the southeastern foothills,
Sōng and Huá manifest the solidity of the west and center.
Only this numinous mountain stands in splendid majesty,
Stretching across the northern wilds, marking its uniqueness.
Beasts roar and dragons soar,
Where wind and clouds are inhaled and exhaled;
Rainbow garments and crane canopies:
Where immortals come and go.
Layered peaks rise unevenly,
Gathering mist, holding emerald hues.
Heavy ridges twist and tangle,
Reflecting sunlight, parting crimson.
Sheer cliffs a thousand fathoms high,
Solitary peaks ten thousand ren tall.
Cassia blossoms invade the moonlight,
Pine vines hang upon the clouds.
Deep streams are warm in winter,
Flying springs are cool in summer.
The precious tally approaches the beauty of the Dài region,
The numinous serpent reveals the wonder of battle formations.
Even smelting stone for seven years,
Could not diminish its greatness;
Even containing waves for nine years,
Could not damage its height.
Towering, eternally firm with heaven and earth;
Vast, spanning past and present without end.
Now, as I receive the banner in Zhào's outskirts,
And pledge the army in Jì's soil,
I dare to present the sacrificial animals and jades:
May the spirit enjoy them.
Later Wèi Xiàowéndì's "Sacrificial Text to Héng Peak"
In the eighteenth year of the Tàihé era,
I reverently and clearly announce to the spirit of Héng Peak.
The celestial pole constructs the heights,
Human brilliance begins to dawn,
The hidden and manifest join in joy,
All spirits share the delight.
Now, with dragon banners and chiming bells,
I return to the Yī chamber.
Traversing the Héng ridges,
The road nears the shadowy peak.
Only the spirit serves as guardian,
Issuing forth heat and ice.
The emperor's way relies on its merit,
The earth's pattern depends on its virtue.
Therefore, I dispatch an official to present sacrificial animals and jades to the spirit of Héng Peak:
May it enjoy them.
Sōnggāo Shān, Section Seven
According to this, Sōnggāo Shān is the Central Peak among the Five Peaks.
The "Shìmíng" says:
"The character Sōng may also be written as Sōng;
a mountain that is large and high is called Sōng."
The "Báihǔ Tōng" says:
"Why is the character for 'high' uniquely added to the Central Peak?
Because the center resides within the four directions and is high,
hence it is called Sōnggāo Shān."
The "Xù Hànshū" says:
"Hàn Wǔdì performed rites and ascended the Central Peak,
hearing the exclamation 'Wànsuì' three times.
Thereupon, he enfeoffed three hundred households to maintain the sacrifices,
naming it Chónggāo.
By the time of Later Hàn Língdì,
he again changed Chónggāo to Sōnggāo."
Dài Yánzhī's "Xīzhēng Jì" says:
"Its eastern part is called Tàishì,
its western part is called Shàoshì,
seventeen lǐ apart,
Sōng being their collective name.
They are called 'shì' (chamber)
because below each there are stone chambers.
Shàoshì is eight hundred and sixty zhàng high,
its summit measures ten lǐ across,
comparable to Tàishì,
only smaller."
The "Zá Dàoshū" says:
"Twenty lǐ northeast from the peak spirit temple is a mountain named Dōnglóngmén.
East of it are Sāntái Shān.
Long ago, Hàn Wǔdì passed this mountain during his eastern tour,
saw a maiden studying immortality.
The emperor observed her,
and subsequently named it.
To the south is Xǔyóu Shān,
high, large, and secluded on all sides.
North of it flows the Yǐng River.
Yáo summoned Xǔ Yóu;
the site still has an altar platform.
Long ago, Crown Prince Jìn of Zhōu Língwáng loved playing the shēng,
creating phoenix cries.
He roamed between the Yī and Luò Rivers.
The Daoist Fú Qiūgōng escorted him up Sōng Shān,
where he remained for over thirty years,
coming and going to Gōushì Shān.
Gōushì Shān lies near the west of Sōng Shān.
During the Hàn dynasty, a Daoist priest
brought Bodhi seeds from a foreign land
and planted them on the western foothills of Sōnggāo.
There were four trees,
different from other trees,
blooming three times a year,
with white, fragrant, and beautiful flowers."

Liú Yù respectfully offers tribute to the spirit of Zhōngyuè,

Jade and jade disc,

connecting the various mountains east and west,

The *Xīn Shì's Records of Sānqín* states:
"This mountain stretches westward from Cháng'ān,

and one can only see him after purifying oneself through fasting.

which can protect from floods.
It is traditionally said that there is a water deity on the mountain;
when people travel by boat,
they cannot catch up to it,
yet they still see those who used to lacquer boats.

Han Dynasty Bān Gù's *Rhapsody on Zhōngnán Mountain*
Oh, that Zhōngnán,
majestic, rugged, and towering.
It rivals the Green Palace,
and touches the Purple Star.
Lofty and densely wooded,
it gathers amidst the misty clouds.
Dim and shadowy,
like ghosts or spirits.
From its sides gush flying rapids,
upon its heights rise tall forests.
Dark springs drip steadily,
dense shade lies deep and heavy.
Róng Qī and Qǐ Jì,
found peace of mind here.
In the season of late spring,
at the beginning of early summer.
The weather is clear and crisp,
I gaze all around the eight directions.
Imperial simurghs and yuèzhuó birds,
sound warnings as they lead the way.
As for its rare wonders,
green jade stands upon its slopes,
dense dwellings nestle on its peaks.
Soaring phoenixes, crying mournfully, gather upon it,
clear waters, gushing forth, flow before it.
Péng Zǔ dwelled here and shed his mortal coil,
Ānqī feasted here to prolong his years.
Only perfect virtue is considered beautiful,
my emperor, responding to blessings, has come to this.
Sweeping the divine altar to declare sincerity,
offering precious incense to pray to the immortals.
Alas, this great blessing,
shall forever be bestowed for a hundred million years.
Táng Dynasty Emperor Tàizōng's *Poem on Gazing at Zhōngnán Mountain*
Layered peaks overlook the Wèi River,
green barriers pierce the distant sky.
Emerging red supports the sun over the ridges,
entering green stores mist within the cliffs.
Layered pines make morning seem like night,
doubled ravines, incomplete, appear whole.
Facing this, a thousand cares are calmed,
no need to trouble visiting the Nine Immortals.
Zhōu Dynasty Yǔwén Chǎng's *Poem on Accompaining the Imperial Carriage to Zhōngnán Mountain*
Yáo's canopy approached the Hé and Yǐng rivers,
Hàn's imperial steps trod upon Huà and Sōng peaks.
Sun banners turn back the northern phoenix,
star streamers shift the southern swan.
Past Xuānqū beneath azure clouds,
the vanguard turns its back on Shèxióng.
Golden drumsticks brush the spring's depths,
jade pipes blow amidst the clouds.
Ancient tracks are said hard to reach the end,
new paths may sometimes lead to exhaustion.
Mist rises as the mountains seem to end,
pools clear, the water ever empty.
Intertwined pines above connect to the fog,
tall bamboos below welcome the wind.
Immortal talent and the Way are not separate,
numinous energy and Dharma can be the same.
Eastern dates are offered at the morning court,
western peaches presented at the night palace.
By decree, Prince Jìn is summoned,
to come forth and face Fúqiū Gōng.
Sui Dynasty Hú Shīdān's "Imitating an Ancient Poem on Mount Zhōngnán"
I built my hut on Mount Zhōngnán,
Gazing northwest toward the imperial capital.
Mist and rosy clouds obscure the birds' path,
Looking down, I see the city of Cháng'ān.
Palace walls reflect each other,
Twin towers rise amidst the clouds.
Bells and drums boil at the palace gates,
Flutes and pipes sob in the Chéngmíng Hall.
Vermilion pavilions overlook locust-lined roads,
Purple canopies fly crisscross.
Gazing and gazing, not yet reaching the end,
Autumn wind startles at my jar-window.
Cliffs and peaks, grass and trees turn yellow,
Migrating geese leave their cold cries behind.
Fallen leaves pile on secluded paths,
Heavy dew hangs in the desolate courtyard.
New wine matures in the jar,
Cold insects chirp in the ravine.
Let me face a pot of wine,
Why care for worldly fame?
A message to those bustling in market and court:
Join me in delighting in this peace.
Yáng Shīdào's "Rhapsody on Mount Zhōngnán, Matching the 'Wind' Rhyme in Response to Imperial Command"

Halts his carriage to tread the deep thicket.
White clouds fly with summer rain,
Jade-green ridges arch with spring rainbows.
Grass greens the long poplar road,
Flowers brighten the Wǔzuò Palace.
Ascending, the day grows late,
Orchids and osmanthus stir fragrant winds.
Zhōu Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Inscription on the Righteous Valley of Mount Zhōngnán"
In the second year of the Bǎodìng era of the Zhōu,
The Grand Steward, Duke of Jìn, ordered the quarrying of stone and opening of the valley,
To bring down timber from the southern mountains.
The Duke aids in ordering human relations,
Broadly spreads numerous achievements.
In leisure from harmonizing governance,
He peruses mountain classics.
Considering Mount Zhōngnán's abundant resources,
Blocked by sun and moon.
Cypress, juniper, cedar trunks,
Catalpa, paulownia, Chinese cedar, lacquer trees.
Accumulated over ages,
What is not here?
Thus he consulted mountain and marsh officials,
And assembled foresters and craftsmen.
Eastward exiting Lántián,
It controls the Bà and rides the Chǎn;
Westward linking Zǐwǔ,
It holds the Jīng and floats the Wèi.
Tributaries branch into eight streams,
Dividing flow through nine valleys.
Bronze beams pour from four sides,
Stone towers twin and soar.
Azure splendor of spring gates,

Green locusts of autumn markets,
Boats and oars connect.
Transporting to the dark palace,

How unlike moving stone from Dānquán,

State rich, people prosperous,

"Vast emptiness floats above,
Lofty peaks anchor below.
Sheer cliffs a thousand zhang high,

Pines and osmanthus hang perilously,

Carriages climb ridge slopes,

Eight streams divide and flow,

North holds the copper well,

Crosswise pouring the great river,

Intricate ninefold layers,

Osmanthus rafters surmount waves,

Dredging streams, settling ridges,
