You will see a large catalpa tree.
Take a patterned stone and knock on the catalpa tree.
Someone will respond.
Then give them the letter.'
Zhèng Róng did as he was told.
He used the stone to knock on the catalpa tree,
and indeed someone came to take the letter."
Liú Jìngshū's *Yì Yuàn* says:
"During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the bank of Línpíng in Wújùn commandery collapsed,
revealing a stone drum.
When struck, it made no sound.
They asked Zhāng Huá about it.
Huá said:
'You can take paulownia wood from Shǔ,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it—then it will sound.'
They followed his advice,
and the sound could be heard for tens of *lǐ*."
Sòng Meteorite, Jìn Speaking Stone
*Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Five meteorites fell in Sòng—
they were falling stars."
Dù Yù's commentary says:
"If one only says 'stars,' it might imply the stars caused the stones to fall,
so 'falling stars' is repeated for clarity."
It also says:
"A stone spoke in Wèiyú of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng:
'Why did the stone speak?'
He replied:
'I have heard that when actions are untimely,
and resentment and slander stir among the people,
then even non-speaking things may speak.'"
Transformed Woman, Gazing Husband Stone
Liú Yìqìng's *Yōumíng Lù* says:
"Wú Kān, a minor clerk in Yángxiàn County,
had his master south of the stream.
One day, while poling a boat across the water,
he suddenly saw a five-colored floating stone in the stream.
He took it and placed it by his bed.
By night, it transformed into a woman."
It also says:
"On Běishān in Wǔchāng, there is a Gazing Husband Stone,
standing like a person.
Ancient legend says that in the past, there was a chaste wife
whose husband went off to service,
traveling far for the nation's crisis.
She brought her young child to bid him farewell at this mountain,
stood gazing at her husband, and turned into a standing stone.
Hence, it was named accordingly."
Paper Mortar, Writing Inkstone
Yǔ Zhòngyōng's *Xiāngzhōu Jì* says:
"South of Càizi Pond in Yìngyáng County, there is a stone mortar.
It is said to be Cài Lún's paper-pounding mortar."
Liú Chéngzhī's *Jiāngzhōu Jì* says:
"South of Càizi Pond in Xīngpíng County, there is a stone cave,
about two hundred *zhàng* deep.
The stone is green in color
and suitable for making writing inkstones."
Immortal's Game Board, Emperor's Chess Pieces
"Immortal's Game Board" appears in the "Huàshān" entry under "Matching Antitheses," note for "Driving Deer."
Zhāng Huá's *Bówù Zhì* says:
"Táolín is at Xiūmǎzhīshān in Húchéng County, Hóngnóng.
There is a stone there
named the Emperor's Terrace Chess Pieces.
They are five-colored and patterned,
shaped like chicken eggs."
Well Turtle, Seal Magpie
Guō Bān's *Wèi Jìn Shìyǔ* says:
"Prince Sīmǎ Yì of Chángshā was enfeoffed as Prince of Chángshān.
Upon arriving at his fief,
he dug a well four *zhàng* into the ground
and found white jade.
Beneath the jade was a large stone,
on which was a spiritual turtle
over two *chǐ* long."
Gān Bǎo's *Sōushén Jì* says:
"Zhāng Hào of Chángshān was Chancellor of Liáng.
After a fresh rain,
a bird resembling a mountain magpie
flew into the marketplace.
Someone threw something at it, and it fell to the ground.
People rushed to grab it,
and it turned into a round stone.
Hào broke it open with a hammer and found a gold seal inside,
inscribed 'Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety.'"
Floating Chime Stone, Arrayed Coins
*Shàngshū* says:
"Floating chime stones from the banks of the Sì River."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"The banks of the Sìshuǐ River.
Stones seen in the water
can be used to make chimes."
*Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"If the floating chime stone falls silent,
it is no different from ordinary stones."
*Dòngmíng Jì* says:
"When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was born,
flocks of sparrows soared over Bàchéng Gate.
It was renamed Qīngquè Gate,
and decorated with brocade-patterned stones
in the shape of arrayed coins."
Qín Bridge, Hàn Pillars
Guō Yuánshēng's *Shùzhēng Jì* says:
"Qínliáng is a place name.
Some say that when Qín Shǐhuáng toured east,
he did not take the old road
but crossed this water.
He ordered all officials and below
to each carry a stone to fill it,
and soon a bridge was formed.
Now, looking at the piled stones,
there are no signs of artificial construction."
*Sānfǔ Gùshì* says:
"The Qín built Héngqiáo Bridge.
The Hàn inherited it and established an office to oversee it.
Stone pillars marked the boundary:
south of them belonged to Jīngzhào,
north to Right Fúfēng,
each divided in half."
Divine Whip, Immortal Traces
*Sānqí Lüèjì* says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge,
wanting to cross the sea to see the sunrise.
A divine being could drive stones into the sea.
If the stones moved too slowly,
the deity would whip them,
and they would bleed."
Lì Yuán's commentary on *Shuǐjīng* says:
"East of Sīyángchuān water is Dúshān Mountain.
To the north is a cliff.
On the cliff are traces of someone sitting.
On the mountainside stone are two handprints,
and at the foot of the mountain on the stone are two footprints.
Commonly called the Immortal's Stone."
Arrowhead Buried in Stone, Book Hidden Under Rock
The Han Shi Wai Zhuàn states:
"Chǔ Xióng Qúzǐ was traveling by night when he saw a sleeping stone,
mistaking it for a crouching beast.
He bent his bow and shot at it,
the metal arrowhead sank in, buried in the feather fletching."
The Wú Yuè Chūnqiū states:
"Yǔ consulted the Huángdì Zhōng Jīng,
and saw recorded by the sages:
'Located southeast of the Jiǔyí Mountains,
it is called Yuǎnwěi.
It is supported by patterned jade,
and covered with a massive rock.
The book within has characters on golden slips and jade tablets.'
Yǔ then retreated to fast for three days,
then opened the rock and retrieved the book.'"
Kūnmíng Fish, Línglíng Swallow
The Xī Jīng Jì states:
"In the Kūnmíng Pond,
a stone was carved into a whale.
Whenever thunder and rain came,
the fish would often roar and bellow."
Gù Kǎizhī's Qǐ Méng Jì states:
"In Línglíng Commandery there are stone swallows.
When wind and rain come, they fly,
just like real swallows."
Sùshèn Arrowheads, Línhǎi Arrows
The Dì Wáng Jì states:
"During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the Sùshèn people came to present arrowheads of stone and arrows of hù wood,
measuring one chǐ and eight cùn in length."
The Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The land of Yízhōu has no copper or iron.
They take and sharpen blue stones to make bows and arrows.
These are of the same kind as the stone arrowheads and hù wood arrows."
Stone Rhapsody by Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn
Linked mountains obscure and block the view,
Giant rocks stand lofty and precipitous.
Above, they give rise to clouds, lush and dense;
Below, they churn the waters, pushing them onward.
They unfurl crimson clouds across the nine bends,
Mingle with white dew upon the Sānwēi Mountains.
They guard Fāngchéng by the Hàn River,
And fortify the heavenly pass with its boiling moat.
They stretch afar, clinging to islands,
And dwell within the perilous ravines and gullies.
Then they harbor marvels and contain spirits,
Embrace the strange and store transformations.
Beast-shaped and bird-imaged,
With animal bodies and human faces.
Already transformed into the rooster of Chéncāng,
Again dancing as the swallows of Línglíng.
Welcoming a child from the waters of Luòyáng,
Sending off five women in the district of Chéngdū.
An emperor rests here and plays pitch-pot,
An immortal sits aloft at a lofty feast.
They span the divine embankment of the vast sea,
Majestically stand as the auspicious ground of Yílíng.
They reveal the secret slips of yellow gold,
Conceal white jade upon an immortal's bed.
Twin peaks stand as the commandery of the Heavenly Gate,
Uniquely rise as the hall of Jìnyún.
Lǐ Guǎng shot at one, thinking it a beast,
Chū Píng shouted at them, turning them into sheep.
They chart Kǒngmíng's Eight Formations,
Spanning the three bridges of Wú's orange trees.
They startle the divine man at Wǔluò,
And terrify the traveling merchants at Qútáng.
Poem on a Solitary Rock by Liáng Zhū Chāo
Invading the rosy clouds, near to the setting sun,
Calming the waters, dividing the rushing flow.
Facing its shadow, like a pair of watchtowers it seems,
Solitary birth, like a severed cloud.
Halting the wind, it stills the patterned waves,
Rising mist stirs the faint evening glow.
Though said to be near the Seven Peaks,
Alone it towers, unmatched by the crowd.
Poem on Receiving the Topic 'Kingfisher Stone' by Liáng Xiāo Tuī
Following the peak, shaped like a mirror,
Constructing the ridge, poised like a lotus.
Reflecting in the woods, akin to green willows,
Facing the pool, it disrupts a hundred streams.
The blue moss never falls away,
The cinnabar characters, hard to transmit.
Some journey to the heights of Dōngmíng,
All who come here roam as practiced immortals.
Poem on Stone by Chén Yīn Kēng
The Heavenly River's Weaving Shuttle laid aside,
The Immortal Peak's chess game remnants remain.
Línglíng's former swallows were of stone,
Kūnmíng's fish originally learned from rock.
Clouds shift, the lotus form emerges,
Moss mottles, brocade patterns scatter.
It should also lie beneath Gǔchéng,
There, of itself, explaining the art of war.
Poem on a Solitary Rock by Master Chén Biāo
In the central plains, a solitary rock,
Its place in the earth, its age unknown.
Its roots contain the waves of Péngzé,
Its summit enters the smoke of Incense Burner Peak.
The cliff forms two birds' wings,
The peak becomes a single pond's lotus.
When did it depart from Dōngwǔ?
Now it comes to guard the Lǐ River.
Poem on a Solitary Rock by Master Gāolí Dìng of Chén
A lofty rock rises straight into the void,
The placid lake stretches open on all sides.
Constant waves wash its winding coves,
The treetops steadily sway in the wind.
Reclining currents still soak its reflection,
Invading the rosy clouds, it reddens further.
Alone, it rises beyond the clustered peaks,
Solitary and elegant amidst the white clouds.
Poem in Response to Prince Zhào of Zhōu on Stone by Suí Cuī Zhòngfāng
The Jade Rope follows the moon's descent,
The golden tablet gleams fresh in the sun.
Entering the river, like brocade being rinsed,
Emerging from the gorge, like a lotus unfurling.
A patterned steed, auspicious sign from Héxī,
A tally of troops, a text from Jìběi.
It will join the divine raft ascending,
And return to the edge of the Heavenly River.
Poem on Receiving the Topic 'Precarious Rock by the Steps' by Suí Cén Déruìn
By the steps towers a precarious rock,
Its strange form, vast and hard to name.
Ridged like a mountain, it seems a beast,
Invading the waves, perhaps akin to a whale.
Cloud-capped peaks rise before the ridgepole,
Lotus shadows enter beneath the eaves.
The people of Chǔ would never recognize it,
Vainly itself containing worth of linked cities.
Poem on Receiving the Topic 'Chanting on Stone' by Suí Yú Mào
The Shǔ gateway, gloomy and remote, obstructed,
The Yān boundary stones, far and uneven.
Alone it marks a thousand zhàng of steepness,
Together they rise, a hundred layers of peril.
Mirror-peaks hold the moon's essence,
Canopy-ridges press close to cloud-branches.
Futilely embracing steadfast integrity,
Filling the sea—who, in the end, will know?
Poem on Stone by Sū Wèidào
Jìběi revealed the divine boon,
Héxī rinsed the auspicious patterns.
Its sound answers the rain of the Heavenly Pond,
Its shadow touches the clouds of Mount Dàizōng.
Wild geese returning still may be awaited,
Sheep rising up spontaneously form a flock.
When might one unearth its numinous marrow,
And rest high upon it, severed from clamorous airs?
General Record, Water, Part One
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The accumulated yīn energy forms water."
The Wénzǐ states:
"The way of water is such that,
ascending to heaven it becomes rain and dew,
descending to earth it becomes rivers and streams."
The Hànshū states:
"The Book of Documents refers to water as 'moistening and descending'.
Kǎn represents water,
its position is in the north,
it is that which ultimately stores the myriad things.
When governance and decrees accord with the seasons,
yīn and yáng are harmoniously regulated,
and beginning and end complete each other.
When all twelve months obtain their proper qi,
then water obtains its nature.
This is what is called 'moistening and descending'.
If governance and decrees go against the seasons,
fog and water burst forth,
all rivers overflow,
destroying villages and towns,
drowning the inhabitants.
And when excessive rain damages the crops,
this is water not moistening and descending."
The Ěryǎ says:
"A place in water that can be inhabited is called a zhōu."
Also called a tǎn.
Pronunciation: dá hàn fǎn.
A small zhōu is called a zhǔ,
a small zhǔ is called a zhǐ.
Also called a small zhǐ,
called a zhǐ.
Again, a small zhǐ is called a qì.
Generally, the edge of water is called chuí, yá, pàn, gān, zì, bīn.
A flat, level bank is called a chún,
also called a yǎn.
A layered bank is called an àn.
The land above the bank is called a hǔ,
a curved bank is called an ào.
Also called a wēi.
Where water and plants meet is called a méi,
an earthen embankment added to the water's edge,
where people stop is called a shì.
A bend in the water is called a ruì,
north of the water is called yáng,
south of the water is called yīn.
Water emerging from between mountain rocks is called a lín,
pronunciation: lín.
A mountain gorge with water is called a jiàn.
Water flowing into a river is called a xī,
water flowing into a xī is called a gǔ,
water passing through a valley is called a hè,
rocks blocking water is called a liáng,
earth built to dam water is called a táng.
Also called a dī,
also called a fáng.
A large fáng is called a fén,
where water gathers is called a zé,
a broad zé is called a yǎn,
a curved part of a zé is called a gāo,
a barrier is called a bēi.
A marsh without water but with plants and trees is called a sǒu,
water flowing freely is called a chuān.
The origin of water is called a yuán,
a yuán is called a quán,
a spring flowing straight out is called a làn quán,
one flowing out from the side is called a guǐ
pronunciation: guǐ.
quán.
A spring whose source is the same but whose destination differs is called a féi quán,
different sources flowing together is called a fèn.
Pronunciation: fū wèn fǎn.
Deep water is called a tán,
fast-flowing water is called a liú.
Water over sand and stones is called a lài,
also called tuān, tān, qì.
A branch of water is called a pài.
A large body of water with a small opening leading elsewhere is called a pǔ,
wind blowing causing water to surge is called a bō.
Also called a làng.
A large wave is called a tāo,
a small wave is called a lún,
a gentle wave is called a lán,
a straight wave is called a jīng.
Water arriving morning and evening is called a cháo,
wind blowing on water creating patterns is called a lián,
water ripples like brocade patterns are called yī.
Traveling through water is called shè,
going upstream against the current is called sù huí,
going downstream with the current is called sù yóu,
also called yán liú.
Crossing a stream by cutting through the current is called luàn.
Crossing water with clothes on is called lì,
from below the knee is called jiē,
from above the knee is called shè.
A place to cross water is called a jīn,
also called a jì.
Moving underwater is called yǒng.
From "a place in water that can be inhabited" onward,
all are from the three books Ěryǎ, Shìmíng, and Shuōwén.
The water spirit is called Tiānwú,
the Shānhǎijīng states:
"Tiānwú has eight heads and eighteen tails,
also called the Water Earl."
The god of great waves is called Yánghóu,
the Bówùzhì states:
"Formerly, the Marquis of Yáng drowned,
and thus became the god of the great sea."
The god of tides is called Língxū.
The Bówùzhì states:
"Formerly, the Wú minister Wǔ Zǐxū
was killed by King Fūchāi of Wú,
his body was floated on the river,
his spirit became the tides."
Flowing Moisture Moistening and Descending
The Yì states:
"Water flows to the moist,
fire goes to the dry."
The Shàngshū:
"Of the Five Elements, the first is water.
Water is said to moisten and descend,
moistening and descending produces saltiness."
Enveloping Heaven Girdling Earth
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"Water is the enveloping curtain of heaven and earth,
the beginning of the Five Elements,
that from which the trust of the myriad things is born."
Wáng Biāozhī's "Shuǐ Fù" states:
"Water girdles the earth and moistens the soil,
the moon flows across the sky and the night is bright."
Lù Shìhéng's poem states:
"Gone are the days passing through heaven,
sad is the river girdling the earth."
Practicing Kǎn Filling the Hollows
The Yì states:
"Water arrives repeatedly,
practicing Kǎn.
The nobleman thereby constantly cultivates virtue and conduct,
and practices the affairs of teaching."
The Mèngzǐ states:
"Water as a thing
does not move unless it fills the hollows.
The nobleman in regard to the Way
does not reach it unless he achieves full expression."
Zhào Qí states:
"Yíng
means to fill;
kē
means a hollow."
Eight Rivers Three Rivers
Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēng Jì states:
"The eight rivers within the Pass:
first, the Jīng;
second, the Wèi;
third, the Bà;
fourth, the Chǎn;
fifth, the Láo;
sixth, the Jué;
seventh, the Lǐ;
eighth, the Hào."
The Hànshū states:
"Hénán was formerly the Qín commandery of Sānchuān."
Wéi Zhāo's commentary states:
"It had the Hé, Luò, and Yī,
hence called Sānchuān."
Autumn Drying Up Winter Freezing
The Lǐjì states:
"In the month of midwinter,
water begins to dry up."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Now water, facing winter, congeals and becomes ice;
facing spring, it melts and becomes water."
Nine Rivers Eight Seas
The Shàngshū states:
"The nine rivers were already channeled."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"The Yellow River divided into nine courses,
those north of the plain are them."
The Guānlìng Nèizhuàn states:
"To the southeast of Mount Sumeru is a mountain called Kūnlún,
located within the eight seas."
Three Rivers Five Lakes
The Shàngshū states:
"When the three rivers had entered,
Zhènzé was settled and stable."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"The three rivers having entered,
caused Zhènzé to be settled."
The Zhōulǐ:
"The marshes of Yángzhōu are called the Five Lakes."
Róng Hé and Wēn Luò
The "Shàngshū‧Zhōng Hòu" says:
"Yáo governed for seventy years,
establishing altars at Hé and Luò.
On the Xīn day of the second month,
rituals were complete at dawn,
radiant light emerged from the Hé,
serene energy filled all around."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Radiant light of five colors,
emerged from the Hé River."
"Yì Qián Záo Dù" says:
"Empirical manifestation of great virtue,
the Luò River was first warm,
nine days later it turned cold,
and in five days transformed into five colors of dark and yellow."
Bì Hǎi and Jiàng Hé
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Shí Zhōu Jì" says:
"In the east is the Bì Hǎi,
vast and expansive,
comparable to the Eastern Sea,
its water is not salty or bitter,
indeed pure blue in color."
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shí Yí Jì" says:
"Jiàng Hé is one hundred thousand lǐ south of the sun,
its waves are crimson.
There are many red dragons and red-colored fish,
which are plump and delicious to eat,
consumed by the immortals,
allowing them to live past natural death."
Qīng Jì Zhuó Hé and Xuán Bà Sù Chǎn
Yuán Hóng's "Běi Zhēng Fù" says:
"Then, turning back from Liáng Mountain,
cutting across the Wèn waves,
sailing on the pure Jì,
beside offering sacrifices at Ā."
Liú Shào's "Zhào Dū Fù" says:
"To its south are grand torrents and vast rivers,
the yellow waters of Zhuó Hé originate from piled stones,
passing by Tài Huá."
Pān Yuè's "Xī Zhēng Fù" says:
"To the north are the clear Wèi and turbid Jīng,
winding through Lánchí;
to the west are Xuán Bà and Sù Chǎn,
with hot springs and warm valleys."
Fěn Shuǐ and Jǐn Liú
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
"West of Zhùyáng County is Fěn Shuǐ,
sourced from Fánglíng County,
its water is used for making powder,
pure and distinct from Jǐn Shuǐ,
thus named Fěn Shuǐ.
In Bā Commandery, Lín Jiāng County also has this water,
used for making powder,
traditionally presented in tribute."
"Huáyáng Guó Zhì" says:
"Chéngdū lies west of Xīchéng,
where the former Jǐn office is.
Brocade craftsmen weave,
rinsed in the central stream appears bright and clear,
less so in other rivers,
hence named Jǐn Lǐ Chéng."
Benefit All Things and Accomplish All Tasks
"Lǎozǐ" says:
"The highest good is like water,
benefiting all things without contention,
dwelling where everyone dislikes,
thus close to the Dao."
"Wénzǐ" says:
"The way of water is,
immensely vast,
and unfathomably deep.
All things must be born,
all tasks must be accomplished."
The Noble View and The Small One Drowns
"Sūn Qīngzǐ" says:
"Kǒngzǐ observed the east-flowing water,
Zǐgòng asked:
'Why does a noble person always observe great waters?'
Kǒngzǐ replied:
'Water,
widespread and life-giving without action,
resembles virtue,
its flow is lowly and follows its course;
resembles righteousness,
vast and unceasing,
resembles the Dao,
extending through valleys,
fearless like courage,
holding balance like law,
full but without caprice;
resembles uprightness,
agile and subtly responsive;
resembles discernment,
exiting and entering preserving purity;
resembles goodness,
always flows eastwards;
resembles resolve,
therefore, the noble always observes great waters.' "
"Lǐjì" says:
"The small one drowns in water,
the noble drowns in words.
Water is close and easily drowns people."
Embrace Mountains and Flood Lands – Float On and Support the Earth
"Shàngshū" states:
"The emperor addressed the four leaders,
mighty and surging floods,
sweeping over mountains and flooding lands,
surging to the heavens."
"Guōshì Xuán Zhōng Jì" says:
"Of all under heaven, water is the most abundant,
floating to the skies and supporting the earth,
reaching high and low,
nourishing all things."
Accumulate to Form Rivers and Seas – Above as Rain and Dew
Huán Kuān's "Yán Tiě Lùn" says:
"Water accumulates to form rivers and seas,
deeds accumulate to form a noble person."
"Wénzǐ" says:
"The way of water is,
immensely vast,
and unfathomably deep.
Above it manifests as rain and dew,
below it nurtures growth."
Steal Soil to Stanch – Pile Ash to Stop
"Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"The flood surged to the heavens,
Gǔn stole the emperor's soil to stanch the flood."
Also "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"In ancient times,
the four extremities failed,
nine provinces split,
water flowed tirelessly,
then Nǚwā piled reed ash to stop the flood."
Close but Not Respected – Familiar but Not Played With
"Lǐjì" says:
"Water to people,
is close but not respected,
heaven is respected but not close."
"Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
"Zhèng Zǐchǎn told Zǐ Tàishū:
'Only the virtuous can soften people through tolerance,
otherwise, severity is best.
Fire is fierce,
people watch and fear it,
thus few die in it.
Water is weak,
people become familiar and play with it,
thus many perish,
tolerance is hard.'"
Eastern Jìn: Wáng Biāo Zhī's "Water Rhapsody"
Dwelling in solitude and chanting from afar,
recording the highest good to convey meaning.
Truly encompassing vastness,
discerning subtlety in clear springs.
Springs remain clear, calm, and placid,
embodied but utilizes the mysteries.
Moves without intent through stillness,
not constrained by shape or form.
Deep and secluded yet able to accept impurities,
dissolve the void and gentle to prevail over strength.
Sometimes forming great waves beyond bounds,
sometimes delicately threading through gaps.
Thus able to pour into the four seas,
guide and flow through the hundred rivers.
Bear liquid to form clouds and rain,
surge and solidify as sweet springs."
Liáng Xiàoyuán Dì's "Poem of Ascending the Dyke to View Waters"
Driving the horse along the river dyke,
not intending a leisurely stroll by the city edge.
Embracing mountains unresolved,
exerting futilely the nine sorrows.
Lodging by the village trees,
river boats obstructed by guard towers.
High banks flipped into bays,
winding ports now connect boats.
The Zǎo grove surely sings praise,
the Hù River can now be compared.
Wishing to borrow the teachings of Xuān Ní,
turning the Sì River's cross flow.
Liu Xiaochuo of Liang, "Poem on Viewing the Water at Sunset from the Crown Prince’s Ferry"
The river stretches level as the sun sets far away,
The evening glow spreads full across the stream.
Here again at the rippling water’s edge,
Branching currents draw from the Jǔ and Zhāng.
Bright and clear flows the enduring pulse,
Glimmering, shimmering, stirs a gentle light.
Cold birds follow rafts afloat,
Startled cormorants skim the waves in flight.
By the flowing stream beauty abounds of itself,
How much more so, returning to my homeland.
Boatmen by night ready their oars,
Rowing maids in darkness finish their attire.
Waiting for dawn on the spring river,
They vie for the way toward Luòyáng.
Shěn Jūnyōu of Later Liang, "Poem on Facing the Water"
Spread the feast by the Cassia River,
Hand in hand gaze toward Peach Blossom Spring.
Falling blossoms trace circles on the water,
Swift winds churn the slender streams.
Light shimmers, rippling the bank’s reflection,
Waves subside, layering sandy traces.
The deep blue waves bring joy enough,
Why speak of rinsing one’s hat strings?
Chán Master Huìbiāo of Chen, "Poem in Praise of Water"
Once it filled the sparse wells of Shūlè,
And surged through the camps of Èrshī.
Jade fords bright with floral hues,
Silver streams gleam on brocade shoals.
Boats seem to float in empty air,
People walk as if in a mirror.
Holding fast to the virtue of supreme goodness,
Its benefit stirs lofty sentiments.
Zǔ Sūndēng, "Poem in Praise of Water"
Líquán’s purple palace mirrored,
Zhūpǔ’s green sands sink deep.
Broad banks carry lotus fragrance far,
Clear currents hold clouds’ shadows deep.
Wind-swept pools like polished mirrors,
Mountain streams like tuned lutes.
I ask you to behold this purity,
And know the heart of tranquil calm.
Also, "Poem on Lotus Tune"
Long river, sunset glow,
Deep inlet, clear breeze rippling.
Tender willows droop, river emerald,
Fresh lotuses flank the banks in red.
Boats move as if floating into distance,
Moon’s reflection seems to sink in sky.
I long to follow Qín Gāo’s play,
Riding fish into the waves.
Lǐ Jùrén of Sui, "Poem on the Square Pond Holding White Water"
White water overflows the square pond,
Vast and boundless, pure waves rising.
Layered ripples sway ducks’ shadows,
Ripples trace wild geese in flight.
Long dikes with willows’ emerald hue,
Banks lined with yellow duckweed blooms.
Watching fish brings joy enough,
Why need the Háo River bridge?
Kǒng Déshào, "Poem on Encountering Floodwaters at Wángzé Ridge"
Earth’s pipes, wind’s voice urgent,
Heaven’s ford, clouds’ hue sorrowful.
Slowly, a hundred streams fill,
Suddenly, ten thousand acres float.
Like golden dikes overflowing,
Or turning into azure sea’s flow.
Startling waves afar stir herons,
Swirling banks obscure the oxen.
Vainly longing for Zhào Jǐng’s refuge,
At last weary of Yáng Hóu’s might.
Great logs truly find no mooring,
Reed ashes—who has time to seek?
Wishing for a raft’s convenience,
Carefree, to roam the Milky Way.
Zhāng Wéncóng, "Poem in Praise of Water"
Its name marks supreme goodness,
Its flow reveals divine endurance.
Maps chart the Four Great Rivers,
Heaven’s records hold the Five Celestial Pools.
Square currents hold jade’s moisture,
Round bends stir pearls’ light.
Only the gardener of Méng,
Lingers at play on the Háo bridge.
Guō Pú of Jin, "In Praise of Explaining Water"
Rivers and streams embroider the land,
Spreading waves flow like ribbons.
Seeping moisture connects all sides,
Weaving patterns beyond splendor.
Different sources, same return,
Merging eastward to the sea.
Dài Kuí, "In Praise of Water"
Water’s virtue lies in mild neutrality,
Springs profound, an inner mirror.
Utmost softness, fond of low places,
Harmonizing with the Way’s nature.
Stillness reflects precious clarity,
Supreme goodness inspires song.
Thus there are recluses,
Who come with wheels to gaze.
Yǔ Sùzhī, "In Praise of Water"
Deep and clear, embracing green,
Pure waves, limpid and profound.
Marvelous substance, soft and bright,
Clouds deep, liquid moist.
Second of the seas
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Hǎi (sea) means huì (dark).
It governs the attraction of filth and turbidity,
its water being black and obscure."
The *Bówùzhì* states:
"Between heaven, earth, and the four directions,
all seas connect and communicate.
The land is within them,
and there is very little of it.
The Seven Róng, Six Mán, Nine Yí, and Eight Dí,
their forms and kinds are different.
Speaking of them collectively,
they are called the Four Seas,
meaning they are all near the sea.
Beyond the Four Seas,
there are, it is said, seas again."
Note: The Eastern Sea has a separate part called Bóxiè,
as found in the *Shuōwén*.
Therefore, the Eastern Sea is collectively called Bóhǎi,
and is also commonly called Cānghǎi.
The *Bówùzhì* states:
"Within the Cāng Sea,
there are Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu, the three divine mountains.
Their palaces and towers are made of gold and silver,
where immortals gather."
The *Lièzǐ* mentions that east of the Bó Sea there is a great chasm,
named Guītáng.
This is what the *Zhuāngzǐ* calls the Wěilǘ.
Within it are the five mountains: Dàiyú, Yuánqiáo, Fānghú, Yíngzhōu, and Pénglái.
The *Shízhōu Jì* says:
"Separate from the Eastern Sea,
there are also the Míng Sea and the Yuán Sea."
The *Shízhōu Jì* says:
"Fúsāng is within the Bì Sea.
There is the palace of the Great Emperor,
where the Great Perfected Dōngwáng resides.
There is Pénglái Mountain,
with a circumference of five thousand *lǐ*.
Outside the mountain, the Yuán Sea encircles it.
The seawater is truly black in color,
and is called the Míng Sea."
Note: The *Zhuāngzǐ* mentions a Northern Míng,
thus all four seas can be called Míng.
The *Shānhǎijīng* mentions the Qí Sea, the Yòu Sea, and the Shào Sea.
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"Ōu and Mǐn are both within the Qí Sea."
It also states:
"From Wúgāo Mountain,
one looks south to the Yòu Sea."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"The Yòu Sea is the Shào Sea."
Note: The Southern Sea, separate from the great sea, has the Zhàng Sea.
The *Xiè Chéng Hòuhànshū* says:
"The tribute from the seven commanderies of Jiāozhǐ
all passes through the Zhàng Sea for entry and exit."
Also, the *Wàiguó Zá Zhuàn* says:
"Southwest of Dàqín, in the Zhàng Sea,
after about seven or eight hundred *lǐ*,
one reaches Coral Island.
At the bottom of the island is a large flat rock,
where coral grows upon it.
People use iron nets to gather it."
Note: East of the Western Sea's great sea,
small bodies of water named 'sea' include: Púchāng Sea, Púlèi Sea, Qīnghǎi, Lùhún Sea, Tánmí Sea, and Yángchí Sea.
The *Hànshū* says:
"The Púchāng Sea is also called the Salt Marsh.
It is three hundred *lǐ* in breadth and length.
Its water is still,
not decreasing in winter or summer.
It all flows underground,
emerging south at Jīshí."
Also, Guō Yìgōng's *Guǎngzhì* says:
"The Púlèi Sea is in the northeast of the Western Regions.
Dòu Gù attacked Yījìn,
and fought at the Púlèi Sea."
The *Shísānzhōu Jì* says:
"West of Yǔnyá County,
there is the Bēihé Qiāng Sea,
which later generations call Qīnghǎi."
The *Hòu Wèi Shū* says:
"Tàizǔ campaigned west and halted at the Lùhún Sea."
Guō Yìgōng's *Guǎngzhì* says:
"West of the Qiāng territory,
there are the Tánmí Sea and the Yángchí Sea."
Note: The Northern Sea,
separate from the great sea, has the Hàn Sea.
South of the Hàn Sea, small bodies of water named 'sea' include: Bódī Sea, Yīlián Sea, and Sīqú Sea.
The *Hànshū*:
"Huò Qùbìng attacked the Xiōngnú,
reaching north to the Hàn Sea.
Later, Dòu Xiàn of the Hàn attacked the Xiōngnú,
reaching the Bódī Sea."
Guō Yìgōng's *Guǎngzhì* says:
"North of the Xiōngnú territory is the Yīlián Sea.
Later, Liáng Fèng of the Hàn persuaded the Northern Chányú.
The Chányú was pleased,
and immediately led his people to return with Fèng to the Sīqú Sea."
All seas are commonly called Pí Seas,
the opposite of Pí.
Beyond the Pí Seas, there is the great Yíng Sea encircling them.
The *Zōuzǐ* says:
"What is called Zhōngguó (the Central States)
is merely one part in eighty-one of the world.
Zhōngguó is named Chìxiàn (Red Region).
Within it are the Nine Provinces,
which are Yǔ's Nine Provinces.
These cannot be counted as the number of provinces.
Outside Zhōngguó, there are regions like Chìxiàn provinces,
also called the Nine Provinces,
encircled by Pí Seas.
Each such area constitutes one continent.
There are nine such [continents],
all encircled by the great Yíng Sea beyond them.
This is called the Eight Extremities,
and here the world reaches its bounds."
The sea is called the King of a Hundred Valleys.
The sea god is called Hǎiruò.
The sea is also called the Tide Pool,
also called the Heavenly Pool,
and also called the Great Chasm or Giant Chasm.
From the *Lǎozǐ* and the *Fēngsútōng*.
Mountains in the sea are called dǎo (islands).
Islets in the sea are called yǔ (islets).
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shízhōu Jì* says:
"There are Zǔzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Xuánzhōu, Yánzhōu, Chángzhōu, Yuánzhōu, Fènglínzhōu, Jùkūzhōu, Liúzhōu, and Shēngzhōu.
Among them, Shēngzhōu and Yíngzhōu are in the Eastern Sea,
Yánzhōu is in the Southern Sea,
Fènglínzhōu and Jùkūzhōu are both in the Western Sea,
Yuánzhōu and Xuánzhōu are in the Northern Sea.
The above are the ten isles in total."
Conveyance and Tributary Flow
Mù Xuánxū's *Hǎi Fù* says:
"Oh vast and numinous sea,
forever the place of conveyance."
The *Shàngshū* says:
"The Jiāng and Hàn rivers flow tributary to the sea."
The commentary states:
"Zōng means 'to honor,'
resembling a court audience."
Gathering Waters and Accumulated Flow
The *Lǐjì* says:
"When the Three Kings sacrificed to rivers,
they all gave precedence to the Hé River and afterwards to the sea,
some being the source,
some being the gathering place.
This is called attending to the root."
It also says:
"The washbasin is on the eastern steps;
its water is east of the basin,
honoring heaven and earth's leftward sea."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states:
"It is where the sea water gathers."
The *Sūnqīngzǐ* says:
"Without accumulating half-steps,
one cannot reach a thousand *lǐ*;
without accumulating small streams,
one cannot form rivers and seas."
Clustered Cassia and Fúsāng
Wáng Càn's *Yóuhǎi Fù* says:
"As for the long shores and separate isles,
spread out like banners, standing like stars,
cassia and orchids cluster upon them,
coral surrounds their bases."
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shízhōu Jì* says:
"Fúsāng is in the Bì Sea.
The tree is several thousand *zhàng* tall,
over a thousand arm-spans in girth.
Two trunks share one root,
mutually leaning on each other,
hence it is named Fúsāng."
Earth's Veins and Heavenly Pool
The *Guānlìng Nèi Zhuàn* says:
"Heaven is five hundred and five million, fifty-five thousand, five hundred and fifty *lǐ*;
earth is also like this,
each taking the four seas as its veins."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"North of the land of sparse hair, there is the Míng Sea,
which is the Heavenly Pool."
Reaching Heaven, Moving Earth
Zhāng Huà's "Treatise on the Investigation of Things" says:
"According to an old tale, the Heavenly River is connected to the sea.
Recently, there was a man living on an island in the sea.
Every year in the eighth month, a floating raft would arrive,
very large,
coming and going without missing its schedule.
This man then stood upon the raft,
took ample provisions and rode the raft away,
suddenly unaware of day and night.
Abruptly, he arrived at a place,
where there were city walls and houses.
Looking into the rooms, he saw many weaving women.
He saw a man leading an ox to the water's edge to drink.
Startled, they asked this man how he had come here.
This man then asked what place this was.
They replied:
'You may go to Shǔ and ask Yán Jūnpíng.'
This man returned and asked Jūnpíng.
Jūnpíng said:
'On such-and-such a day and month, a guest star trespassed upon the Dipper and Ox constellations,
which was precisely when this man reached the Heavenly River.'"
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Seawater flows and clashes in a cycle every three years,
which causes the earth to move."
Azure Isles, Verdant Shore
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "Records of Nányuè" says:
"South of Hǎi'ān County there is a small stream,
which flows south into the sea.
Gazing into the distance, one sees azure isles;
looking afar, one beholds boundless waves."
The "Record of the Ten Continents" says:
"Placing the Mysterious Wind in the northwest,
seating the Queen Mother in the divine land.
Kūnwú is set amidst flowing marshes,
Fúsāng is anchored at the verdant shore.
Separating and combining the essence of water, luminous beasts dwell in the fiery wilds;
Kǎn gathers all the yīn forces,
thus the immortal capital is situated on a sea island."
Golden Palace, Jade Towers
"Golden Palace" is discussed in the narrative section.
Cuī Yǎn's "Rhapsody on Fulfilling My Original Intent" says:
"Pénglái luxuriantly rises hidden,
Yínghú densely arrays itself in rows.
Arranging the towering golden terraces,
facing the lofty jade towers."
Tí Abyss, Péng Ocean
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Beyond the sea from Kuàijī there is the Eastern Tí Abyss,
divided into over twenty states,
which come to offer tribute according to the seasons."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Qí Capital" says:
"To its east lies the vast ocean, a great abyss,
immense and boundless."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"In the Northern Ocean there is a fish,
its name is Kūn.
It transforms into a bird,
its name is Péng.
When it prepares to migrate to the Southern Ocean,
it strikes the water for three thousand lǐ."
Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Red Parrot":
"Auspiciousness flows through the Lǒng region,
good fortune emanates from the Péng Ocean."
Barren Land, Niè'ěr
"Barren Land" is found under the "Heavenly Pool" entry.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"The Niè'ěr State lies east of the Wúcháng State.
With both hands holding their ears,
they dwell suspended within the Red Waters."
Non-Action, Skilled at Staying Low
The "Wénzǐ" says:
"The ancient rulers skilled at lordship
modeled themselves on the sea to emulate its greatness,
pouring downwards to achieve its vastness."
The "Lǎozǐ" says:
"The reason rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys
is because they are skilled at staying low."
Carrying Stones, Riding a Raft
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Zōu Yáng submitted a memorial:
Shēntú Dí drowned himself in the Yōng River,
Xú Yǎn carried stones and entered the sea.
Not tolerated by the world,
they would not improperly grasp for gain."
Yìng Shào's "Comprehensive Meaning of Customs" says:
"Jiāng Gōng, styled Bówéi.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
he summoned Gōng to serve as Grand Administrator.
Gōng told others:
'I gain substance through emptiness,
accumulating reputation and status.
In an era of brilliant clarity,
I still did not offer my allegiance.
Now governance lies with private factions;
what is there to do?'
Thereupon, he rode a raft and floated upon the sea,
none knowing his ultimate destination.'
People of the time considered him extraordinary."
Mirage Tower, Jiāo People's Abode
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"By the sea, there are mirage vapors that form towers and terraces."
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
"In the deep heavens and watery strange creatures,
lies the abode of the Jiāo people."
Péng Isle, Mulberry Fields
Lǐ Yóng's "Rhapsody on Soaring Immortals" says:
"Gazing upon the beautiful isle of Pénglái,
hoping the Eastern Sage might be found.
About to arrive, yet turning back to fall,
fearing the great waves drawing near."
Gě Hóng's "Biographies of Immortals" says:
"Mágū said to Wáng Fāngpíng:
'Since I began receiving you,
I have seen the Eastern Sea become mulberry fields three times.
Just now, arriving at Pénglái,
the water is shallower than before by about half.
Will it become hills and land again?'
Fāngpíng then said:
'The Eastern Sea will once more stir up dust.'"
Qín Bridge, Hàn Pillar
The "Record of Sān Qí" says:
"On Qīngchéng Mountain,
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended this mountain,
built a wall and constructed a stone bridge,
extending thirty lǐ into the sea."
Zhāng Bó's "Wú Record" says:
"In the Xiànglín Sea there is a small islet,
where soft gold grows.
Traveling thirty lǐ south from the north, there is the Western Dependent State.
Its people call themselves descendants of Hàn.
There is a bronze pillar,
said to mark the border of Hàn."
Water Lord, Wave Subject
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"In Cháoyáng Valley,
the spirit is called Tiān Wú,
who is the Water Lord.
As a beast,
he has eighteen tails, eight heads, a human face, and eight feet."
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
"Tiān Wú appears fleetingly, as if glimpsed."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Zhuāng Zhōu looked back at the rut and saw a crucian carp there.
It said, 'I am a subject of the waves of the Eastern Sea.
Would you, sir, have a dou or sheng of water to keep me alive?'"
Golden Palace, Purple Stone Chamber
The "Records of the Grand Historian" says:
"The King of Yān sent men to Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu.
These three spirit mountains are in the sea,
not far from people.
Those who reached them saw them like clouds.
But upon arrival,
the three mountains were instead beneath the water.
There, immortals and the elixir of immortality were found,
with palaces and towers made of gold and silver."
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Record of the Ten Continents" says:
"On the Cānghǎi Island,
there are purple stone palaces and chambers,
the immortal capital of the Nine Elders."
Immortality Grass, Soul-Returning Tree
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Record of the Ten Continents" says:
"Zǔzhōu lies in the Eastern Sea,
a land five hundred lǐ square.
Upon it grows the immortality grass,
born in jade fields.
The grass resembles wild rice,
its shoots about three chǐ long.
For people already dead,
if covered with this grass,
they all revive."
It also says:
"Jùkūzhōu lies in the Western Sea.
There is a great tree,
similar to a maple.
When the tree is in bloom,
its fragrance can be smelled for hundreds of lǐ.
Its name is the Soul-Returning Tree."
Pouring Out a Hundred Rivers, Whirling Back for Ten Thousand Lǐ
Liú Zhēn's "Rhapsody on the Lǔ Capital" says:
"The great sea divides them,
pouring out a hundred rivers."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Wú Capital" says:
"A hundred streams branch off,
converging as they return to the sea.
Tides and waves surge up,
Later Han Dynasty, Wáng Càn's "Rhapsody on Roaming the Sea"
Embracing the ultimate Way of pure essence,
I shall rise lightly and soar high.
Let my heart roam for a broad view,
And wander about the western border.
Riding a light boat of orchids and cassia,
I float upon the great river and drift far away.
Winged by startling winds, I drive long,
And gather at Kuàijī for a single gaze.
Climbing the shady corner to gaze eastward,
I behold the form and momentum of the vast sea.
It spews forth stars and brings out the sun,
Where sky meets water's edge.
Its depth is unfathomable,
Its breadth has no shore.
Seeking it in the dark earth,
No boundary or outlet is seen.
Where neither Zhānghài reached the limit,
Nor Lú Áo arrived.
Vast and expansive,
Truly it cannot be measured.
Dwelling in the proper position of Yúyí,
It shares the same color and name as the vault of heaven.
Encompassing the grand capacity to contain filth,
It rectifies the principles of the ancestral temple.
Gathering all streams as its subjects below,
It is the sovereign lord of all valleys.
Jìn Dynasty, Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea"
In ancient times, during the great era of Emperor Guī and the mighty Táng,
The celestial web surged and swelled.
It brought withering and calamity,
With vast waves, boundless and sprawling.
For ten thousand lǐ, no horizon in sight,
Rivers and waterways were then channeled.
All myriad caverns flowed together,
Towering and lofty, how precipitous!
It uprooted the five peaks,
Drained dry the nine regions.
As for its breadth,
And its wondrousness.
Then it is shimmering and glistening,
Floating under the sky with no shore.
Waves like connecting mountains,
Now merging, now scattering.
Inhaling and exhaling all rivers,
Washing and cleansing the Huái and Hàn.
If then haze and gloom secretly vanish,
With no stirring, no trembling.
Light dust does not fly,
Fine gossamer does not move.
Yet still there is gulping and swallowing,
Surplus waves overflowing and surging.
If then remote borders swiftly report,
And the king's command urgently proclaimed.
Swiftly flying, drumming the oars,
Crossing the sea, ascending the rivers.
Thereupon awaiting the strong wind,
Hoisting the hundred-foot,
Securing the long silk,
Hanging the sail mat.
Gazing at the waves, far and decisive,
Brightly like a bird vanishing.
Leaping three thousand at once,
Not a full morning to reach the destination.
Liáng Dynasty, Emperor Jiǎnwén's "Rhapsody on the Sea"
In ancient times, Yǔ opened the Dragon Gate,
The mountain ranges were then carved.
The lofty and bright clarified the ether and floated pure,
The thick and substantial, broad in momentum, stood majestic.
The virtue of the abyss repeatedly arrived,
The water's source deep and extensive.
Pouring into a hundred rivers,
Controlling the clear, drawing the turbid.
Beginning from a floating wine cup,
Conveying and transporting to the great chasm.
Measuring it, vast and without boundary,
Gazing at it, distant and endlessly faint.
Lush and brushing, dark and boundless,
The sun and moon come and go.
The crescent dim and faint,
Now bright, now vanishing.
As for the long wind drumming fury,
Swelling waves crashing and booming.
Whipping waves across ten thousand lǐ,
Drifting foam beyond Fúsāng.
Táng Dynasty, Emperor Tàizōng's "Poem: Gazing at the Sea on a Spring Day"
Opening my lapel, I gaze at the vast sea,
Leaning on the chariot rail, I enjoy the spring blossoms.
Accumulated flows cross the earthly order,
Divided branches draw from the celestial pool.
Immortal ether congeals on three peaks,
Harmonious breeze fans the eight wilds.
Brushing the tide, clouds spread color,
Piercing the waves, the sun stretches light.
Shining on the shore, flowers share their hues,
Lost in clouds, geese break their flight lines.
Humble in heart, it conveys depth and breadth,
Holding fullness, guarding spiritual endurance.
Having form, yet not easily gauged,
Without source, how could it be measured?
Great billows pass through transformed wilds,
Jade-green islands often become mulberry fields.
At Zhīfú, I think of Hàn Emperor,
At Jiéshí, I recall Qín Shǐhuáng.
Rainbow garments were not my original intent,
Sitting upright in dignity is to plan for kingship.
Sòng Dynasty, Xiè Língyùn's "Poem: Sailing on the Sea After Visiting Chìshí"
Early summer is still clear and mild,
Fragrant grasses have not yet ceased.
Lodging on water, lingering through dawn and dusk,
Shadowy clouds repeatedly rise and vanish.
Circling and viewing, weary of ocean shores,
How much more crossing to the barren lands.
The River Lord sometimes calms the flow,
Tiānwú remains still, not stirring.
Hoisting sail to gather stone blossoms,
Hanging mat to collect the bright moon.
The vast swell has no bounds or edges,
The empty boat has transcendence.
Zhònglián disdained Qí's official regalia,
Zǐmóu yearned for Wèi's palace gates.
Boasting of fame, the Way is insufficient,
Suited to oneself, things may be overlooked.
I beg to append Master Rén's words,
Finally, I decline Heaven's chastisement.
Northern Qí Dynasty, Zǔ Xiàozhēng's "Poem: Gazing at the Sea"
Climbing high, facing the great chasm,
I know not how many thousand lǐ.
Cloudy islands connect continuously,
Wind and tide have no end.
At times watching distant geese pass,
Only see startled gulls rise.
No need to send the departing off,
Naturally, it wounds the wanderer.
Suí Dynasty, Emperor Yáng's "Poem: Gazing at the Sea"
Though I delight in viewing the blue sea,
The golden terrace is but an empty tale.
Distant waters appear flipped like shores,
Remote mountains inverted like clouds.
Broken billows still join together,
Connected waves sometimes divide.
Tame gulls, once approachable,
Plants and trees suffice to form a crowd.
Now I know little Gūshè,
Who again speaks of Línfén?
Also, "Poem: Viewing the Sea in Late Autumn"
Mèng Kē narrated roaming sages,
Méi Chéng spoke of curing illness.
Listening afar to ancient accounts,
Facing the depths, I verify this day.
Floating under the sky, remote without shore,
Containing spirits, truly not one alone.
Conveying and transporting, all valleys return,
Paying homage, myriad streams overflow.
Dividing walls, blue mist clears,
Connecting isles, colored clouds dense.
Glad to share the Master's view,
Deeply ashamed before Xuánxū's brush.
Suí Dynasty, Yú Mào's "Poem: In Response to Gazing at the Sea"
The clear imperial path reaches the swelling sea,
Gazing at the great ocean, vast and surging.
Ten isles, clouds and mist far,
Three mountains, waves high.
Long billows seem to bathe the sun,
Connected islands resemble rushing tides.
Spirit roaming to distant Gūshè,
Your wise verses crown the winds of poetry.
Mere gazing upon the sea in vain,
How could I offer a tiny hair's worth?
Yáng Shīdào's "Poem: In Response to Gazing at the Sea on a Spring Day"
Spring mountains overlook Bóhǎi Sea,
The journeying troop halts morning attire.
Looking back at Lúlóng Pass,
Glancing sideways at Sùshèn land.
Great waves turn the earth's axis,
Lone isle reflects cloud light.
Setting sun startles on the billows,
Floating sky, dreadful waves long.
Immortal terrace hides the dragon carriage,
Water palace floats the giant turtle bridge.
Jiéshí's morning smoke vanishes,
Zhīfú's returning geese soar.
Northward patrol is not the Hàn empress,
Eastward venture differs from Qín Shǐhuáng.
Seizing banners, Yǔlín guests,
Uprooting stakes, youthful arena.
Lightning strike drives Liáo River,
Roc flight emerges from Dàifāng.
About to raise the Qīngqiū arrow,
Why seek the white rainbow garments?
The "Ode to the Four Seas" by Xiè Huìlián of the Sòng dynasty:
The nine Yí and six Mán,
the eight Dí and seven Róng.
Carved and engraved with diverse forms,
their garments and caps differ in customs.
To guide them with virtue,
then chariot tracks become the same.
River, third
The Shuōwén states:
"The river is what descends,
following the land's downward flow and thus connecting."
The Yuánshénqì says:
"The river is the chief of waters,
above it corresponds to the Milky Way."
The Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn states:
"The river, together with the Jiāng, Huái, and Jǐ rivers, are the four great rivers;
the river is called the river's ancestor,
the one revered by the four great rivers."
According to the annotations in the Shuǐjīng Zhù and the Shānhǎijīng,
the source of the river emerges from the ruins of Kūnlún,
the Shānhǎijīng says:
"Mount Kūnlún stretches ten thousand lǐ in length and breadth,
eleven thousand lǐ in height,
fifty thousand lǐ from Mount Sōng.
There are green, white, red, and black rivers encircling its ruins,
the white water emerges from its northeastern corner,
bends and flows southeast,
becoming the river of the Middle Kingdom.
The river makes a small bend every hundred lǐ,
a large bend every thousand lǐ,
from its source until it enters the Middle Kingdom,
this is generally always the case."
Flowing east, it travels underground,
reaching Mount Guīqī,
then flows north and divides into two sources,
one emerging from the Cōnglíng mountains,
one from Yútián.
The river then reunites,
flows east into Lake Púchāng,
and again travels underground.
Emerging south at Mount Jīshí,
flowing southwest,
then turning east, it enters the frontier passes,
passing through the commanderies of Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Zhāngyè,
merging with the Táo River in the south,
passing through the commanderies of Āndìng and Běidì.
Flowing north past the west of Shuòfāng commandery.
Then flowing south past the south of Wǔyuán commandery,
then flowing east past the east of Yúnzhōng and Xīhé commanderies,
then flowing south past the west of Shàngdū and Hédōng commanderies,
and emerging at Lóngmén.
The Fén River enters the river here from the east,
Hédōng is where Lóngmén is located.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"Before Lóngmén was opened,
the river emerged east of Mèngmén in a great overflow,
this was called the great flood,
Yǔ excavated Lóngmén and it began to flow south."
Reaching Huáyīn and Tóngguān,
it merges with the Wèi River.
Then turning east, it passes Dǐzhù
Dǐzhù,
is the name of a mountain.
The river water divides,
flows around the mountain and passes,
the mountain appears in the water like a pillar.
Now within the boundaries of the three counties of Shǎnzhōu, Héběi, and Shǎnxiàn.
Reaching Luòyáng,
where Mèngjīn is located.
Reaching Gǒng County, it merges with the Luò River,
Chénggāo merges with the Jǐ River.
The Jǐ River emerges north of the river,
reaches Mount Wángwū and turns south,
cuts across the river crossing,
directly opposite Chénggāo.
Then flowing northeast past Wǔdé,
it merges with the Qìn River,
reaching Líyáng and Xìndū,
Xìndū is now Jìzhōu,
where the Jiàng River is located.
The Jiàng River is also called the Zì River,
also called the Zhāng River.
North of Jùlù,
it then divides into nine rivers,
Jùlù,
now Xíngzhōu,
where Dàlù is located.
Dàlù,
is the name of a marsh.
The nine rivers,
first is Túhài,
second Tàishǐ,
third Mǎjiá,
fourth Fùfǔ,
fifth Húsū,
sixth Jiǎn,
seventh Jié,
eighth Gōupán,
ninth Géjīn.
Then they merge into one river and enter the sea.
Duke Huán of Qí blocked the nine rivers to expand fields and settlements,
therefore in Guǎntáo, Bèiqiū, Guǎngchuān, Xìndū, Dōngguāng, Héjiān, and eastward cities and ponds,
old traces of the nine rivers remain.
During the Hàn dynasty, the river breached the Jīndī,
north and south suffered greatly from its harm,
discussants often sought to find the old courses of the nine rivers and dredge them,
but did not know their locations,
therefore Bān Gù said:
"From then until the Hàn, eight branches had already been lost.
The old course of the river,
divided from the Shāqiū weir,
from which the Túnshì River emerged."
Therefore the Shàngshū states: guiding the river from Jīshí,
reaching Lóngmén,
now within the boundaries of Lóngmén County in Jiàngzhōu.
South reaching Huáyīn,
north reaching Dǐzhù.
East reaching Mèngjīn,
north of Luò,
where all roads converge,
since ancient times considered a ford.
East passing Luòruì,
reaching Dàpī,
Luòruì,
now Gǒng County,
is where the Hé and Luò rivers merge.
Mount Dàpī,
now Sìshuǐ County,
that is, old Chénggāo,
a mountain with two layers is called pī.
North passing the Jiàng River,
reaching Dàlù,
the Jiàng River is now Xìndū in Jìzhōu,
Dàlù,
marsh name,
now Jùlù in Xíngzhōu.
Then north it spreads into nine rivers,
together as the Nì River entering the sea,
this is correct.
Tóng,
means to merge.
The nine rivers again merge into one,
named the Nì River.
Nì,
means to welcome,
meaning at the river mouth there are morning and evening tides,
to welcome the river water.
Initially, Yǔ from the northeastern border of Líyáng,
divided the river into two channels to guide the water,
one emerging south to meet the Xíchuān,
which is the current river's course.
The river now east of Huázhōu,
is the old Xí River.
One emerging from Bèiqiū,
that is, the upper river of the nine rivers,
during Wáng Mǎng's time it was blocked and abandoned,
therefore commonly called Wáng Mǎng's River.
The Shǐjì, "Treatise on Rivers and Canals":
"Also states the river's disasters,
were especially severe in the Middle Kingdom.
Yǔ guided the river from Jīshí,
passed Lóngmén,
then divided two channels to guide the river,
as noted by Rú Chún.
One channel emerged from Bèiqiū,
the other was the Xíchuān,
during Wáng Mǎng's time the river was then blocked,
only the Xí was used."
Emperor Yáng of Suí at Wèi County,
now Wèi County in Wèizhōu.
Because the Qí River enters the river,
the Qí River is also called the Qīng River.
Established Qímén to connect to the river,
traveling northeast,
obtained Yǔ's old course of the nine rivers,
the Suí people called it the Imperial River.
Emerges from Kūnlún, guided from Jīshí
both seen in the narrative.
Encloses Dǐzhù, covers Shímén
"Encloses Dǐzhù" seen in the narrative.
The Shānhǎijīng says:

below it there is a stone gate,

Guō Pú's annotation says:

Fish Breaks the Current, Dragon Treads the Water
The River Chart states:
"The Yellow Emperor said:
'I dreamed of two dragons
holding up a white chart,
which they then bestowed upon me at the capital of the river.
Tiān Lǎo said:
"Could Heaven be bestowing the chart upon the Emperor?
Let us fast and go observe it."
The Yellow Emperor then fasted between the Yellow River and the Luo River,
seeking a manifestation.
Arriving at Cuì Guī Spring,
a large black fish broke the current and arrived.
He then asked Tiān Lǎo:
"Do you see that which breaks the current in the middle of the river?"
Seeing it,
he and Tiān Lǎo knelt and received it.
The fish floated a white chart,
with orchid-like patterns in vermilion script,
and bestowed it upon the Yellow Emperor.
Unfurling it to look,
it was named the Record Chart.'"
The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Pivot of Heavenly Movements states:

he viewed the scene with the Three Dukes and the feudal lords.

Sòng Jūn stated:

Sinking a White Horse, Sacrificing a Black Fox
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"During the Yuánguāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,

he hunted at Shènzé,

Entering the Cōng Mountains, Sinking into the Pú Sea
Both are seen in the preceding narrative.
Scale-roofed Halls and Dragon Halls, Spring Chambers and Water Palaces

Dragon Palace, Shell Watchtower
The Book of Hàn states:

Holding Earth, Turning Stones

Floating Cypress, Sailing on a Reed

The River Chart states:

Horse Chart, Turtle Prophecy
The Book of Rites states:

Zhèng Xuán's commentary notes:

Three Gates, Nine Bends
Lì Dàoyuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:

looking at it like a pillar,

After the three rivers were opened,

Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Great River" states:

The River Chart states:

turns west and travels,

It flows south for a thousand lǐ,
reaching the northern side of Huà Mountain.
It flows east for a thousand lǐ,
reaching Zhíyōng.
It flows north for a thousand lǐ,

the longest entering the Bó Sea."
Dark Blue Canopy, White Jade Disc
Wèi Hóng's Old Rituals of Hàn states:

"White jade disc" is seen in the commentary for "jade slips" above.
Lamenting Shēntú, Seeking Fāng Shū
The *Han Shi Wai Zhuan* says:

Cuī Jiā heard of this and stopped him,
saying:

is it permissible not to save a drowning man?'
Dí said:
'In the past, Jié killed Lóng Páng,
Zhòu killed Bǐ Gān,
and lost the world;
Wú killed Zǐ Xū,

The *Chǔ Cí* says:

The *Lún Yǔ* says:

Chéng Gōng Suí's "Great River Rhapsody" says:

and extol the great undertaking of launching boats."
Three Days of Transformation, A Millennium of Clarity
The *Yì Qián Záo Dù* says:

Wáng Zǐnián's *Shí Yí Jì* says:

Glory Light, Auspicious Aura

Later Hàn Yìng Yáng's "Spirit River Rhapsody"
I inquire of the distant source of the spirit river,
at the divine hill of Kūnlún.
I ascend the shady corner of Zēngchéng,
relying on the hidden flow of Hòutǔ.
Traversing the layered perils of Jīshí,
parting the overflowing floats of the mountain's foot.
Stumbling over Lónghuáng and heading south,
winding the great body and flowing in four directions.
Crossing the slopes and springs of Jīnluò,
spreading nine courses through the Central Provinces.
Fén surges and gallops forth,
ever diligent and marching on.
Beginning to ride the heights and swiftly depart,
Yáng Hóu is terrified and trembles in fear.
Jìn Chéng Gōng Suí's "Great River Rhapsody"
Beholding the vast grandeur of the hundred rivers,
none compare to the beauty of the Yellow River.
It hides beneath the lofty peaks of Kūnlún,
emerges from the towering heights of Jīshí.
Ascending Lóngmén and journeying south,
brushing Huáyīn and Qū'ē.
Surmounting Dǐzhù and stirring rapids,
crossing Luòruì and raising waves.
Its body winds across the earth,
matching the spirit Han in the vault of heaven.
Piercing the central plains and royal domains,
passing through the distant wilds of the northern Dí.
Traversing the northern borders of the two Zhōu,
flowing through the southern lands of the three Jìn.
Qín opened territory from the west,
Qí drew borders based in the east.
Yīn moved across to seek stability,
Wèi relocated to Jì and thus grew strong.
Zhào diverted the flow and repelled Wèi,
Yíng channeled the ditch and destroyed Liáng.
Thinking of the sighs of ancient sages,
how immeasurable is the virtue of water!
Suí Xiāo Què's "Poem in Response to an Imperial Command on Crossing the Yellow River"
The great vassal connects to the imperial house,
carriage teams uphold the imperial plans.
Before dawn, driving the cavalry,
at daybreak, just painting the boats.
The ferry city spans brocade-like,
riverbank willows flank crimson-oiled.
Bell sounds waft to separate isles,
banner shadows reflect on the azure flow.
Early light gleams on sword robes,
morning wind rises at the signal tower.
Billowing, fine waves stir,
swiftly, light gunwales float.
Turning oars to avoid nearby shoals,
releasing the stern down to the isle ahead.
All seems like ascending the Milky Way,
no different from visiting Péngqiū.
Gazing, I know the clouds converge,
hearing, I recognize the autumn water's sound.
What joy to follow you, my lord,
glad to roam with immortals!
Chén Jiāng Zǒng's "Poem on Crossing the Yellow River"
Cōng Shān sinks in outer realms,
Yán Zé hides in distant lands.
Two sources part, boundaries far,
nine courses branch, streams long.
Not exhausting what I've heard and seen,
no need to verify with words and chapters.
Lingering, I sigh for the Grand Historian,
melancholy, I tread Líyáng.
Guiding waves coil around earth's nodes,
dispersing aura brightens the celestial pool.
Pity Zhōu, sinking its precious vessel,
praise Jìn, first building its bridge.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem on Crossing the Northern River"
Linked banners shine on the creek banks,
layered drums boil on sandy isles.
Peach blossoms swell the new waves,
bamboo arrows rush down the flowing stream.
Frontier clouds approach distant warships,
northern winds enter the battle tower.
Swords drawn, flood dragons about to emerge,
carriage teams startled, giant turtles about to surface.
Goose letters will finally prove merit,
Yān's minister indeed was enfeoffed as marquis.
Do not resent the distance of passes and rivers,
and ease the sorrows of the borderlands.
Liú Xiàosūn's "Poem on Viewing the River at Dawn Departing from Chénggāo"
At dawn I depart the cliff-bound city,
driving my horse along Huányuán.
Looking back at the Yellow River above,
dazed, my soul repeatedly takes flight.
The great flow guides from Jīshí,
startling waves descend from Lóngmén.
The immortal raft's place indistinguishable,
the sunken jade disk, I imagine, still remains.
Distant and near, islets emerge,
rushing and gurgling, ducks and geese clamor.
Cherishing antiquity, I stand idle in vain,
sighing at what has passed, what is there to say?
Liáng Liú Xiàowēi's "Poem: Sir, Do Not Cross the River"
I beg you, sir, do not cross the river,
the river is vast, the wind's might fierce.
The mast falls, the golden crow sinks,
the boat capsizes, the rhinoceros oar is submerged.
Dark canopies, empty solemn sacrifices,
white horses, vain living offerings.
Holding stones wounds my widowed heart,
collapsing walls shroud my frosty sleeves.
The sword flies, still sharing the water,
the jade disk sinks, souls both depart.
You are a minister of the River Lord,
I shall be a sister of the River Consort.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem: Sir, Do Not Cross the River"
The golden embankment divides brocade cables,
a white horse crosses a lotus boat.
Wind severe, song echoes cut off,
waves surging, the boatman grieves.
Oars break in the peach blossom water,
sails sweep across the bamboo arrow stream.
What need to speak of the sunken jade disk's place?
For a thousand years, by chance, Yáng Hóu.
Eastern Jìn Guō Pú's "Illustrated Eulogies for the *Ěr Yǎ*"
Kūnlún has three layers,
named the Pillar of Heaven.
Truly it is the source of the river,
the spirit mansion of water.
Sòng Bào Zhāo's "Ode to the River's Clarity"
Defiling those four waterways,
adorning these twin rivers.
Hidden spirits, distant records,
concealed blessings, extended years.
Clear source from Kūnlún's peak,
mirroring flow from Cōng Shān.
Spring chambers congeal sediment,
water mansions clear and pure.
Sòng Zhāng Chàng's "Hé Qīng Sòng"
The vast and mighty river,
by the shores of home and country.
Embracing Jìn and Wèi,
leading Qí and Qín.
Its rapids born at Lóngmén,
its waters known at Jīshí.
Riding the fortunes, it is able,
communing with heaven and man.
Transforming flows of the supreme deity,
marking the initial stars of time.
Joyful writings reveal auspiciousness,
illuminated by the divine draconic map.
Cooperating with illustrious spirits,
it connects breaths and carries honor.
Later Wèi Emperor Xiàowén's "Essay on Sacrificing to the River"
In the nineteenth year of Great Peace,
the Emperor addressed the spirit of the river deity,
as Earth's energies surge and overflow,
the Yellow River as a treasure.
Vast and mighty currents,
truly aid the shade.
Flowing and connecting, guiding all things,
containing shells and hiding scales,
initiating moisture to all creations,
nurturing under the great heavens.
Only the sage sets the example,
only Yǔ can bear to follow.
Floating vessels and flying sails,
piercing the hundred rivers.
I inherit the precious mandate,
capably continuing the heavenly text.
Luqī doves fly over Huái,
royal egrets turn on river banks.
Dragon vessels command the river,
phoenix banners ride the clouds.
Gliding leisurely with oars,
gracefully over Yígī passage.
My imperial excursion in banquet,
glories over peaceful shores.
Initiating water conservancy,
the transport provisions renewed.
A thousand grand ships,
ten thousand majestic vessels.
Protect our great ceremonies,
only you become the spirit.
Yán Shīgǔ's "Prayer to the Four Great Rivers"
The spirit connects illustriously to the heavenly river,
enlightening writings and history,
dividing into nine branches,
moistening thousands of miles beside.
The pure autumn aligns with order,
following the usual standards.
Sòng Gǒulún's "Letter to the River Deity"
Humbly thinking of the River Deity Lord,
Your lordship gleams in the sacred spring.
Soaring above divine islets,
releasing great currents from Kūnlún.
Raising high waves at Dǐzhù,
encompassing the four streams to claim kingship,
mastering all rivers as sovereign.
Fourth Jiang
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Jiāng (river)
means gōng (public).
All waters flow into it,
it is what all share in common."
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Jiāng (river)
means gòng (tribute).
The precious things it produces can be offered as tribute."
The *Zhōuguān* states:
"In Yángzhōu, its rivers are the Three Jiāng."
Regarding the Three Jiāng,
the commentary on the *Hànshū‧Dìlǐzhì* states:
"The Mín Jiāng is the Great Jiāng,
reaching Jiǔjiāng it becomes the Middle Jiāng,
reaching Xúlíng it becomes the Northern Jiāng,
thus it is one source with three names."
Zhèng Xuán and Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"To the left, joining the Hàn, it becomes the Northern Jiāng;
meeting Pénglí, it becomes the Southern Jiāng;
the Mín Jiāng lies between them,
thus it is the Middle Jiāng.
Therefore, the text refers to the east as the Middle Jiāng,
clarifying that the Mín Jiāng reaches Pénglí and joins with the north and south,
only then can it be called 'middle'."
Also, the *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"The Three Jiāng are:
the Great Jiāng,
the Middle Jiāng,
and the Northern Jiāng.
In Wénshān Commandery there is Mínshān,
from which the Great Jiāng emerges;
from Xiáshān the Middle Jiāng emerges,
flowing east to join the Great Jiāng;
from Mínshān the Northern Jiāng emerges,
flowing east to join the Great Jiāng,
their sources are all in Shǔ."
Also, Wéi Zhāo's theory states:
"The Mín Jiāng, Sōng Jiāng, and Zhè Jiāng,
are also all in Wú."
Also, Shěn Huáiyuǎn's *Nányuèzhì* states:
"Guǎngxìn Jiāng, Shǐ'ān Jiāng, and Yùlín Jiāng,
are also considered the Three Jiāng,
in Yuè."
According to the *Shuǐjīng* and the *Jīngzhōujì*, it states:
"The Jiāng emerges from Mínshān,
its source is like the mouth of a jar,
one can float a wine cup on it.
In Yìzhōu, Jiànníng Commandery, Mǎnjiāng County,
it flows hidden underground,
for several *li* until reaching the capital of Chǔ,
then it widens to ten *li*,
and is named the Southern Jiāng.
Initially in Qiánwéi,
it joins with the Qīngyī Shuǐ
and the Wén Shuǐ,
reaching Luò County,
it joins with the Luò Shuǐ.
Northeast to Bā Commandery,
it joins with the Fú Shuǐ, Hàn Shuǐ, and Bái Shuǐ.
East to Chángshā,
it joins with the Lǐ Shuǐ, Yuán Shuǐ, and Xiāng Shuǐ.
Reaching Jiāngxià,
it joins with the Miǎn Shuǐ.
Reaching Xúnyáng,
it divides into nine channels.
The *Xúnyángjì* describes the Jiǔjiāng as:
first, Báiwū Jiāng;
second, Bàng Jiāng;
third, Wūtǔ Jiāng;
fourth, Jiāmí Jiāng;
fifth, Quǎn Jiāng;
sixth, Fú Jiāng;
seventh, Bǐng Jiāng;
eighth, Tí Jiāng;
ninth, Jūn Jiāng.
East, they converge at Péngzé,
pass Wúhú,
and are named the Middle Jiāng.
Northeast to Nánxúzhōu,
they are named the Northern Jiāng and enter the sea."
Note: Nánxúzhōu is present-day Rùnzhōu.
The *Shàngshū* states that from Mínshān the Jiāng is guided,
east it diverges to become Tuó.
The Jiāng diverges to become the Tuó Shuǐ.
Further east it reaches Lǐ,
Lǐ,
is a water name,
in Jīngzhōu.
Passing Jiǔjiāng,
it reaches Dōnglíng.
Dōnglíng,
is a place name.
East it extends
(pronounced yǐ).
North it converges at Huì,
(pronounced huì),
Huìzé is Pénglí.
East it becomes the Middle Jiāng,
entering the sea, this is it.
All branches of the Cháng Jiāng include:
Pí Jiāng.
Rén Yù's *Yìzhōujì* states:
"Pí Jiāng
is a branch of the Great Jiāng.
It is also called Fú Jiāng,
also called Jiān Shuǐ.
In Shǔ it joins with the Luò Shuǐ,
Pí is pronounced pī."
Wèn Jiāng.
The *Yìzhōujì* states:
"Wèn Jiāng's source emerges from beneath Sānlúnbǎn."
Dié Jiāng.
Cuī Hóng's *Xījīngjì* states:
"Tǔyùhún observed the source of Dié Jiāng and asked Lǔ Hé:
'This water passes through Qiúchí and then Jìnshòushān Tuóqú,
only then is it called Dié Jiāng,
reaching Bā Commandery it enters the Great Jiāng.'" Dié is pronounced dié.
Ruòliǔ Jiāng.
The *Yuánjiāngjì* states:
"A branch of the Xī Jiāng is Ruòliǔ Jiāng."
Zhè Jiāng.
The *Shuōwén* states:
"A branch stream of the Jiāng is Sì,
reaching Kuàijī, Shānyīn, it becomes Zhè Jiāng."
Also, Gù Yěwáng states:
"Zhè Jiāng originates between Dōngyáng and Xīn'ān,
it is not connected to the Jiāng from Mínshān,
reaching Qiántáng it enters the sea."
Sōng Jiāng.
Liú Chéngzhī's *Yángzhōujì* states:
"In Wú County there is Sōng Jiāng,
from Wú it enters the sea,
present-day Sūzhōu."
All alternative names for the Cháng Jiāng include:
Jīng Jiāng,
in Nánxúzhōu,
it is the Northern Jiāng referred to in the *Yǔgòng*.
Present-day Dāntú County in Rùnzhōu.
Guābù Jiāng,
present-day within the boundaries of Liùhé County in Yángzhōu,
southwest facing Jiāngníng County in Rùnzhōu,
this is the place where Emperor Wén of Wèi and Emperor Tàiwǔ of Later Wèi visited.
Wū Jiāng,
this is where Xiàng Yǔ died,
present-day Wūjiāng County in Hézhōu.
Qǔ Jiāng.
Méi Chéng's *Qīfā* states:
"Observing the Qǔ Jiāng in Guǎnglíng."
Qǔ Jiāng,
is present-day Yángzhōu.
Also, Shǐxīng Commandery has a Qǔ Jiāng,
present-day Sháozhōu.
Also, Hàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's *Diào Qín Èrshì Fù* states:
"Facing the Qízhōu of Qǔ Jiāng,
this is Cháng'ān.
Because its waters are winding,
very similar to the Jiāng of Guǎnglíng,
present-day Lèyóuyuán."
All Jiāng that pass through commanderies and counties take their names from them,
these include: Dāntú Jiāng, Qiántáng Jiāng, Kuàijī Jiāng, Shānyīn Jiāng, Shàngyú Jiāng, Guǎnglíng Jiāng, Yùlín Jiāng, Guǎngxìn Jiāng, Shǐ'ān Jiāng, Zāngkē Jiāng, Chéngdū Jiāng."
Guiding the Jiāng / Cutting through the Hàn
The *Shàngshū* states:
"From Mínshān guide the Jiāng,
east it diverges to become Tuó."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The Jiāng emerges from Mínshān,
flows east, cuts through the Hàn, and enters the sea."
Jīngchí / Chǔwàng
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"In the lands of former Jīng Chǔ,
the Rǔ and Yǐng served as moats,
the Jiāng and Hàn served as pools."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"The Jiāng, Hàn, Jǔ, and Zhāng,
are the objects of worship for Chǔ."
Sìdú / Liùchuān
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Yīn Tāng made a proclamation about the Jiāng, saying:
'In ancient times, Yǔ and Gāoyáo long labored abroad,
and the people were then at peace.
To the east was the Jiāng,
to the north was the Hé,
to the south was the Huái,
to the west was the Jǐ.
The Four Great Rivers were regulated,
and the myriad people could then dwell.'"
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
"What are the Six Great Rivers?
The Hé Shuǐ, Chì Shuǐ, Liáo Shuǐ, Hēi Shuǐ, Jiāng Shuǐ, and Huái Shuǐ,
these are the Six Great Rivers."
Spitting Shells / Receiving Turtles
The *Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū* states:
"When Yáoguāng is attained, the Jiāng spits out great shells."
The *Shàngshū* states:
Origins of a River River Like a Girdle
The Family Sayings states:
"The River's waters first emerge from Mínshān;
at its source, one can fill a wine cup from it.
But when it reaches the river crossing,
even double boats cannot cross to avoid the wind."
Yuán Shānsōng's Records of Yídū says:
"Facing the western bank of Xīlíng, there is a mountain.
Its peak stands solitary and elegant.
If one climbs from the southern side of the mountain to the summit,
looking down upon the great river, it appears like a coiled girdle,
and the boats and ships seem like ducks and geese."
Duckweed Fruit Water Caltrop Blossoms
The Family Sayings states:
"King Zhāo of Chǔ was crossing the river.
There was an object in the river,
as large as a dou measure,
round and red,
which struck the king's boat directly.
The boatman retrieved it.
The king found it exceedingly strange
and sent someone to Lǔ to inquire of Confucius.
Confucius said:
'This is a duckweed fruit.
It can be cut open and eaten.
It is an auspicious sign;
only a hegemon can obtain it.'
When the envoy returned,
the king promptly ate it,
and it was very delicious."
Fù Xuán's song says:
"There was a woman, peerless in her generation,
who crossed the river to gather water caltrop blossoms.
Above, they shade the scenery of azure clouds;
below, they mirror the waves of green water."
Parrot Isle Magpie Bank
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The river waters reach the northwest of Shāyí County in Jiāngxià,
then flow east past Tànfù Mountain.
On the right bank of the river lies Parrot Isle."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"In the winter of the sixteenth year of Duke Zhāo,
the ruler of Chǔ attacked Wú.
The people of Wú defeated him at Magpie Bank."
The Records of Xījīng states:
"Now, on the southern waters of Jūcháo, there is a place called Magpie Tail Islet,
which is this very spot."
Sacrificing to Zǐxū Mourning Qū Yuán
Dǒng Lǎn's Records of Wú Lands states:
"When Fūchāi ascended the throne,
Wǔ Zǐxū, due to his loyal and outspoken nature, was condemned to death.
He was thus ordered to commit suicide,
and his corpse was cast into the river.
Fūchāi later regretted this
and, with his ministers, performed sacrifices by the river, erecting an altar.
The people of the state subsequently built a temple for him."
Yáng Xióng of the Hàn dynasty's "Elegy for Qū Yuán" states:
"Passing Xiāng and Yuán, yet not tolerated by the ruler,
he threw himself into the river and died.
In writing, he often drew upon the verses of the Lí Sāo and responded to them,
casting [his writings] from Mínshān into the river's flow,
to mourn Qū Yuán."
Discarding the Jue Losing the Pendant
The Chǔcí states:
"I discard my jade jué in the river's midst,
and leave my jade pendant on the shores of Lǐ."
Liú Xiàng's Biographies of Immortals states:
"The two river goddesses,
strolling by the riverbank,
encountered Jiāo Fǔ.
They then removed their pendants and gave them to him.
Jiāo Fǔ accepted the pendants and departed.
After several tens of steps,
the pendants were no longer in his bosom,
and the maidens had also vanished."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" states:
"Moved by Jiāo Fǔ's loss of the pendant,
and saddened by the divine maiden's entanglement in the net—
this is it."
Sinking Letters Tossing the Gaming Board
Xiāo Fāngděng's Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States states:
"When Yīn Xiànzhī, the Minister of the Imperial Stud, returned to Yùzhāng,
many nobles entrusted him with letters.
Upon reaching Bǎnqiáo,
Yīn Xiànzhī cast the letters into the river, saying:
'Let those that sink, sink;
let those that float, float.
Yīn Hóngqiáo will not act as a letter carrier.'" Zāng Róngxù's History of the Jìn states:
"Táo Kǎn said to others:
'The Great Yǔ was a sage,
yet he cherished every inch of time.
As for ordinary people,
they should cherish every fraction of time.
If any of my aides or subordinates neglected their duties due to games,
I would take their gambling boards and gaming implements
and cast them all into the river.'"
Laughing at the Lord of Wú Sighing at the Wèi Emperor
Huán Jì's Records of Wú states:
"Sūn Quán issued an edict stating:
'Lǚ Dài and Zhūgě Kè reported according to Bù Zhì's account
that the northerners wished to use cloth sacks filled with earth to dam the river.
Every time I read this memorial,
it makes me laugh for days on end.
Since the creation of heaven and earth,
has this river ever been something that could be dammed?'" Yú Pǔ's Chronicles of Jiāngbiǎo states:
"Emperor Wén of Wèi marched to Guǎnglíng intending to attack Wú.
Gazing upon the great river, he sighed and said:
'Wú relies on this vast flow,
and moreover has abundant grain stores.
Even with a thousand teams of cavalry,
there is nothing to be done.'
Thus, he withdrew."
Prefect's Rapids Zhōngláng's Shore
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The river flows east to the south of Yúfù County,
then passes Yángcháng and Hǔbì Rapids.
When Yáng Liàng served as Governor of Yìzhōu,
his boat capsized here.
Awed by its turbulent waves,
the people of Shǔ to this day still call it 'Prefect's Rapids.'"
It also states:
"The river again flows east to the west of Huáróng County.
To the left, it branches off to form the Zhōngxià River;
to the right, Zhōngláng's Shore emerges."
Emerging from Huángcén Striking the Red Bank
Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīngzhōu states:
"The commandery of Shǐ'ān has two rivers, eastern and northern.
The northern river originates from Huángcén Mountain in Línwǔ, Guìyáng.
The eastern river originates from below the Dàyǔ Ridge in Nánkāng.
It flows through the boundaries of Shǐxīng County,
turning southward and then westward,
merging with the northern river east of the commandery,
and empties into the South Sea."
Shān Qiānzhī's Records of Nán Xúzhōu states:
"The Jīng River
is the northern river mentioned in the Tribute of Yǔ.
It broadens to thirty lǐ,
opening to a vast expanse.
Often, on the first and fifteenth days of spring and autumn,
great tides arise,
their sound and force terrifyingly majestic,
forming an extremely wondrous spectacle.
When the tide reaches the north bank, it strikes the Red Bank,
becoming even more swift and fierce."
Golden Sands Shore Purple Shell Tower
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The river flows east to Xiàguī County in Chángshā,
then east again to the right bank where Chénglíng Mountain stands.
On the mountain, there is an ancient city,
connecting east to Zhēngluò Mountain.
The southern bank of the river is named Golden Sands Shore,
and east of the shore lies Golden Sands Inlet."
The Chǔcí states:
"Lotus leaves form the canopy, water caltrop blossoms the carriage;
purple shells the tower, white jade the hall."
Wáng Yì's commentary states:
"Purple shells
are aquatic creatures."
The Aid to the Spirit and Destiny states:
"Great floods produce large shells."
Not Disdaining Small Valleys Not Rejecting Tributary Streams
The Mòzǐ states:
"Rivers do not disdain small valleys that fill them;
thus they can become great.
Therefore, the waters of rivers
do not flow from a single source."
The Lǎozǐ states:
"The reason rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys
