is that they accept all without refusal.
If there were rejection,
many tributary streams would not reach them."
Eastern Jin Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River"
Consider the five materials all in use,
Yet the virtue of water is most divine and enduring.
Only the Mín Mountains guide the River,
Its source begins from a cup's overflow.
It starts its course at Luò and Mò,
Gathering myriad streams from Bā and Liáng.
It charges through Wū Gorge with swift urgency,
Crosses Jiāngjīn and swells to rise.
Reaching vast capacity, it moves like the sea,
Appearing boundless, flooding to the heavens.
It encompasses the Hàn and Sì,
Embracing both the Huái and Xiāng.
It swallows up the Yuán and Lǐ,
Draws in the Jū and Zhāng.
Its source divides at Jū and Lái,
Its flow forms nine branches at Xúnyáng.
It drums with great waves at Chì'àn,
Its lingering ripples sink at Cháisāng.
It networks all streams,
Weighs every rivulet and ditch.
It reveals divine abundance at Jiāngdū,
Mingles flowing tributaries to meet in the east.
It pours into five lakes, vast and boundless,
Irrigates three rivers with roaring force.
Its expanse covers the lands of six provinces,
Its reach operates beyond the fiery realm.
Thus it forms a boundary for Huá and Yì,
Strengthening Heaven and Earth's perilous frontier.
It breathes across ten thousand miles,
Exhaling and inhaling divine tides.
Naturally ebbing and flowing,
Sometimes at dusk, sometimes at dawn.
Stirring latent force to charge ahead,
It then drums with fury to create great waves.
Southern Qí Xiè Tiǎo's "Rhapsody on the Chǔ River"
From south of the mountains I come,
At dusk by the river pool.
Torrential accumulated waters,
Mist-like frosty haze.
Worry with the river—boundless as ever,
The traveler's journey—the year already severe.
Then clouds sink over western peaks,
Winds sweep the central stream.
Galloping waves churn white,
Terrifying billows float to the sky.
Bright sands and enduring thickets,
Stone paths hang suspended.
Then fog hides traveling geese,
Frost glows in empty woods.
Far, far the setting light falls,
For ten thousand miles shade is born.
Rows of gathered reed-pipes at the distant shore,
Mooring orchid-prowed boats by the riverbank.
I long for the autumn moon's radiant light,
To receive its last gleam upon a forgotten hairpin.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Poem in Response to 'Sailing on the River'"
The spring river flows down from Báidì,
Painted boats head toward Huángniú.
Brocade cables turn on sandy shoals,
Orchid oars avoid reed islets.
Damp blossoms float with the water,
Empty nests drift along the trees.
From Jiànpíng, boat masts descend,
At Jīngmén, warships float.
Riverbanks thick with many clusters of trees,
The mountain city is the mast tower.
Sunset, river winds grow still,
Dragon chants echo upstream.
Suí Emperor Yáng's "Poem: Facing the River on a Summer Day"
Summer pool shaded by tall bamboos,
High bank seated beneath long maples.
Sunset, the dark river grows calm,
Clouds scatter, distant mountains empty.
Egrets fly white beyond the woods,
Lotuses bloom red upon the water.
Carefree, with lingering delight,
Yet gazing wistfully, my feelings do not end.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem: Entering Chēn River"
Holding my tally, I follow the solemn assembly,
Raising the sail, I ascend the rushing current.
The journey is not like the White Horse,
But the water's force resembles Huángniú.
Leaping waves clamor on stone shoals,
Splashing foam hugs sandy islets.
Banks curve, rafts turn backward,
Long rapids make boats float in reverse.
Along the shore, towlines frequently snap,
Hanging on cliffs, hooks are shifted again and again.
I still recall the rider with black silk reins,
Coming from the east up above.
Suí Liǔ Gùyán's "Poem in Response to 'Teaching on the Evening Sun over Yángzǐ River'"
The great river, a metropolis of convergence,
The long isle bears an ancient name.
Controlling Mín and Shǔ to the west,
Sailing east, nearing Péng and Yíng.
Before seeing fine silk flutter,
First hearing distant wave sounds.
Vast and hazy, cloud colors darken,
Layered and piled, wave blossoms arise.
To know the evening rain has ceased,
One should watch the light fluttering of banners.
Sū Wèidào's "Poem: Jiǔjiāngkǒu, South Ferry, North Connecting Qíchūn, South with Xúnyáng Bank"
The river road stretches far and leisurely,
Torrential, the nine branches come.
Distant pools dusky like fog,
Frontal shores boiling into thunder.
Scaly and shelled creatures mostly breed hidden,
How many fishermen and merchants sail upriver?
Wind shakes the Shǔ pepper below,
Sunshine opens the Chǔ duckweed.
Near rinsing the bends of Yìchéng,
Slanting breeze at the corner of Lí Marsh.
Tribute turtles still enter as offerings,
Floating musical stones cease new cutting.
Ferry officials swiftly ply their oars,
Posthouse lads hasten to prepare relays.
How can one ask of my homesick heart?
I gaze at the turning ebb tide.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Text for Sacrificing to the River"
In the first year of the Kāihuáng era,
The Field Marshal, Prince of Jìn,
Reverently with the offering of the Great Sacrifice,
Respectfully sacrifices to the Great River Spirit of the Southern Watercourse.
We look up to your divine nature, encompassing peace and wisdom,
Your virtue excelling in divine endurance.
Above you correspond to the Eastern Well,
Below you mark the southern lands.
Drawing twin currents and dividing nine branches,
Longest of the Four Watercourses, receiving a hundred streams.
Since the Jìn's Yǒngjiā era,
Heaven's order fell into disarray,
Petty Wú and Yuè,
Usurpers falsely succeeded one another.
The Chén traitor Shūbǎo,
Generations compounding his wickedness,
Officers and commoners plunged into misery,
Thus gods and men harbor resentment and fury.
I, unworthily commanding the nine punitive campaigns,
To cleanse that region,
Dispatch generals and soldiers,
To cross the stream southward,
Relying upward on your divine aid,
All received safe passage.
Now I again command the gray rhinoceros,
Personally leading elite troops,
Directly charging toward Jīnlíng,
Soon ascending Shíshǒu.
May flood-dragons flee to islets and shores,
And canopies grow still upon the waves.
The region south of the River shall be conquered and pacified,
Within the seas, all clear and tranquil.
Reverently I present this ritual offering,
O Spirit, may you accept and enjoy.
End of Fascicle Five
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Huái means
to encircle.
It encircles the northern boundary of Yángzhōu,
extending east to the sea."
The *Zhōuguān* states:
"The rivers of Qīngzhōu are the Huái and the Sì."
According to the *Shuǐjīng Zhù* and the *Shānhǎijīng*:
"The Huái River originates from Tóngbǎi Mountain in Píngshì County, Nányáng.
Its source initially gushes forth,
then flows underground for thirty *lǐ*,
after which it emerges and flows freely.
It passes northeast by Dàfù Mountain,
goes north of Yìyáng Commandery,
passes east by Jiāngxià,
north of Píngchūn County.
It then passes east south of Xīnxī County,
north of Qīsī County,
reaching south of Hòulù County,
where it joins the Rǔ River.
It then passes east by Ānfēng County, Lújiāng,
where it joins the Jué River,
reaches northeast to east of Shòuchūn County, Jiǔjiāng,
where it joins the Yǐng River,
and north of Shòuchūn County it joins the Féi River.
It then goes east to north of Dāngtú County,
where it joins the Guō River,
reaches northeast to Huáiyīn County, Xiàpī,
where it joins the Sì River.
It goes east to Huáipǔ County, Guǎnglíng, and enters the sea.
For several hundred *lǐ* near the sea,
it experiences the morning and evening tides."
The *Shàngshū* says that [Yǔ] channeled the Huái from Tóngbǎi,
eastward met with the Sì and the Yí,
and entered the sea.
This is it.
Sūn Shèng's *Jìnyángqiū* says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng traveled east.
Those who observed the vapors said
that five hundred years later,
there would be the vapor of a Son of Heaven in Jīnlíng.
Thereupon, Shǐhuáng dug a channel at Fāng Mountain,
directing the flow west into the Jiāng River,
which is also called the Huái.
It is now in Jiāngníng County, Rùnzhōu.
Locally it is also called the Qínhuái."
Two Mountains, Three Islets
Lì Yuán's annotation of the *Shuǐjīng* says:
"Píng'ē County has Dāngtú Mountain.
The Huái emerges to the left of Jīng Mountain,
to the right of Dāngtú.
It rushes between these two mountains, raising waves and flowing northward."
The *Máoshī* says:
"Strike the bells and beat the great drum;
on the Huái are three islets."
Máo's annotation:
"The three islets are on the Huái."
Treasure-House, Market of Heaven
Jiāo Gàn's *Yìlín* says:
"The Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Hǎi
are Heaven's treasure-house.
All benefits gather there;
one can become wealthy."
Jiāo Gàn's *Yìlín Biànzhān* says:
"The Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Hǎi
are Heaven's market.
Merchants receive blessings;
the state becomes rich."
Channeled into the Jiāng, Enters the Sea
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
"Yǔ channeled the Huái and Sì and directed them into the Jiāng."
The *Shānhǎijīng* says:
"The Huái River originates from Yú Mountain.
Yú Mountain is east of Cháoyáng in Yìxiāng,
flowing west into the sea."
Guō Pú's annotation says:
"Now the Huái River originates from Tóngbǎi Mountain in Píngshì County, Yìyáng.
It flows northeast through Rǔnán, Huáinán, Qiáoguó, Pèiguó, and Xiàpī,
passes through Huáiyīn County and enters the sea."
Yǔ Regulated It, Jìn Dried Up
The *Shàngshū·Yǔgòng* says:
"The Huái and the Yí were regulated."
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation says:
"The two rivers were already regulated."
Zāng Róngxù's *Jìnshū* says:
"In the third year of Yǒngjiā,
the Huái and Pú rivers dried up."
Transformed into Trifoliate Orange, Changed into Birds
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
"When an orange tree crosses the Huái and goes north, it transforms into a trifoliate orange.
This is due to the local climate."
Guō Pú's *Yóuxiān Shī* says:
"How can the six dragons be halted?
The flow of fortune has its succession.
The Huái and Hǎi transform small birds,
yet my life alone does not transform."
Irrigate the Crucian Carp, Transform into a Pheasant
Liú Xiàng's *Shuōyuàn* says:
"Zhuāng Zhōu was poor
and went to borrow grain from Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Marquis Wén said:
'Wait until the grain from my fief arrives, then I will give it to you.'
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
'On my way here today,
I saw a crucian carp in a cow's hoofprint on the road.'
It sighed and said to me:
'Can I still be saved?'
I said:
'Wait for me to go south for you to see the King of Chǔ,
to have him channel the Jiāng and Huái to irrigate you.'
The crucian carp said:
'My life now is in this basin or jar.
If you go see the King of Chǔ for me
to channel the Jiāng and Huái to irrigate me,
you will then seek me in the dried fish market.'" The *Guóyǔ* says:
"Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào sighed:
'A sparrow entering the Huái becomes a clam.
Turtles and alligators—none cannot transform.
Only man cannot.
Alas!'" Lǐ Yóng's *Gǎndōng Piān* says:
"The coiled rainbow hides in the great shade;
the patterned pheasant transforms by the Huái's banks."
Hán Fished, Wáng Floated
Annotation of the *Shuǐjīng* says:
"The Huái River flows east through Huáiyīn County.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Hán Xìn as Marquis there.
Formerly, Hán Xìn left Xiàxiāng and fished at this place."
"Wáng Fú" appears below in Wáng Càn's rhapsody.
Meets the Sì and Yí, Passes through Qiáo and Pèi
"Meets the Sì and Yí" see the narrative section.
"Passes through Qiáo and Pèi" see the annotation above under "enters the sea."
Submerged Zhōu Tripod, Sunk Wèi Jade Disc
The *Chǔcí* says:
"Submerge the Zhōu tripods in the Jiāng and Huái,
and cook in an earthen pot in the central hall."
Wáng Yì's annotation says:
"It means to hide the Nine Tripods in the Jiāng and Huái."
Yú Huàn's *Wèilüè* says:
"In the sixth year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the emperor entered the Huái with his naval forces
and sent an envoy to sink a jade disc in the Huái's waters."
Pearl Oysters, Jade Seal
The *Shàngshū* says:
"The *Yǔgòng* states:
'Floating musical stones from the banks of the Sì;
pearl oysters and fish from the Huái Yí.'" Kǒng Ānguó's annotation says:
"The two rivers of the Huái Yí produce pearl oysters and fine fish."
Zāng Róngxù's *Jìnshū* says:
"In the twelfth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
soldier Chén Yáng of the Left Guard found a jade seal in the Huái waters in front of the Eastern Administration.
This refers to the Qínhuái of Jīnlíng,
not the Huái of the Four Great Rivers.
Because material on the Huái is scarce,
this is borrowed to form a parallel couplet."
Rhapsody on Floating on the Huái by Wáng Càn of the Later Hàn
Following the royal army on the southern campaign,
I float on the Huái waters, journeying far.
Turning from the winding flow at Guōpǔ,
I gaze at the high shore of Mǎqiū.
Great oars sweep through the midstream waves,
light boats fly along the banks and crossings.
Forests of masts are raised,
like trees planted on a treeless mountain.
Then swift winds raise the waves,
gongs and drums thunder.
Banners and standards blot out the sun,
flying clouds swirl in the sky.
Grey hawks soar gracefully,
vying with each other in succession.
They mount the startling waves in high flight,
racing across the terrifying billows to reach their goal.
Add to this the utmost skill of the boatmen,
praise the ease and speed of the oarsmen.
Before the sun has shifted,
the vanguard has already arrived.
All commanders keep to their formations,
left and right fall into their ranks.
Ships stretch for a thousand *lǐ*,
famed troops number in the hundreds of millions.
Wielding this might in majestic wrath,
they clear the remotest corners of the sea of all obstructions.
Achieving the highest merit in a single action,
they bequeath glorious achievements to future generations.
Wèi Wén Dì's "Fú Huái Fù"
In the fourteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
the royal army set forth from Qiáo for the eastern expedition.
They vigorously employed water transport,
launching boats in the thousands.
At that time I accompanied the expedition,
beginning the journey at Huái's mouth.
Our journey paused at Dōngshān,
where I beheld the troops,
observing the standards and sails,
magnificent and splendid indeed.
Although the grand hunt of Xiàowǔ of the flourishing Táng,
with boats stretching for a thousand li,
might not surpass this.
Thus I composed this rhapsody saying:
"The Huái flows southward,
casting its mighty waves upon the expanse.
I gaze upon the towering hills,
passing by the bends of the eastern mountains.
Floating are the myriad boats,
with the constructed Kānjiāng's sharp spears.
The cloud-like banners flutter in profusion,
the shouts of the oarsmen resound.
Then the golden bell tolls,
followed by the drumming of thunderous drums.
The white pennants pierce the sky,
the yellow axes shine brightly.
Martial generals are spurred on,
the gallant riders fiercely furious."
Suí Dù Táiqīng's "Introduction to Huái Fù"
The ancients would compose upon ascending heights,
or observe by the waterside.
Chanting and composing, they could readily express their feelings!
In the "Zhōu Nán" section of the "Shījīng" it is said:
"The Hàn is so wide,
it cannot be swum.
The Jiāng is so long,
it cannot be waded."
"The Zhēng Fēng" section says:
"The Jīng muddles the Wèi,
clear and still are its shoals."
The "Wèi Fēng" says:
"The Hé River flows smoothly,
flowing northward in a gentle current."
The "Xiǎo Yǎ" mentions:
"The rushing Jiāng and Hàn,
are the markers of the southern lands."
"Dà Yǎ" states:
"The Fēng Waters flow east,
the achievements of Yǔ are evident."
"Zhōu Sòng" says:
"Oh the Qī and Jù Waters,
teeming with many fish.
There are zhān, wěi,
tiáo, shāng, yán, and lǐ."
"Lǔ Sòng" states:
"Reflecting on the pleasures of the Pàn Waters,
we pluck its reeds."
All these are origins of water-themed compositions.
Later Hàn Bān Biāo composed "Lǎn Hǎi Fù",
Wèi Wén Dì authored "Cāng Hǎi Fù",
Wáng Càn wrote "Yóu Hǎi Fù",
Jìn Chénggōng Suī authored "Dà Hǎi Fù",
Pān Yuè composed "Cāng Hǎi Fù",
Mù Xuánxū and Sūn Chuò both wrote "Hǎi Fù",
Yáng Quán composed "Wǔ Hú Fù", and
Guō Pú authored "Jiāng Fù".
Only the Huái had no dedicated rhapsody:
though Wèi Wén Dì's "Fú Huái Fù" exists,
it merely describes martial valor,
but does not wholly encompass transformation and prosperity,
with little mention.
At the beginning of Qí Tiāntǒng,
working in the department of literature,
appointed chief historian of Guǎngzhōu,
traveled via Huáiyáng to his post,
often encountering favorable crossings.
He was impressed by the vast, churning Huái,
which pours into the great ocean,
connecting south to Qǔjiāng.
With its water monsters and divine beings,
where are they not found?
Thus, he compiled his hearings and sightings,
pursuing and composing a rhapsody.
He says:
"Praise the virtue of the great river,
truly inherent, not borrowed.
Originating from Yuánshì's domain,
flowing broadly beneath Tóngbǎi.
Initially traversing the red lands,
finally dispersing into fiery plains."
Suí Yáng Dì's "Early Crossing of the Huái Poem"
The calm Huái stretches wide,
morning mists rise densely.
The Huái lands are not yet distinguished,
waters merge with the morning's light.
A lone island turns in the clear haze,
colorful sails emerge from long banks.
Fish leap in the waves,
birds call and wish to fly.
Waiting until late autumn,
my sorrow shall be carried home by these waters.
Suí Zhūgě Yǐng's "Responding to the Order, upon Arrival from Yǐng to Huái Poem"
Weary of the winding paths of Yǐng,
delighted by the straight course of the Huái.
Distant villages bear water's mist,
remote inlets reflect the sky’s colors.
Spiritual waves beckon close,
immortal journey recognized.
Profound insight aligns with sagacious words,
the wind and clouds have additional strength.
Cài Yǔngōng's "Responding to the Order, upon Arrival from Yǐng to Huái Poem"
Long weary of the winding river paths,
suddenly overlooking Huái and Yí.
Waves spread wide and vast,
gazing upon the wide expanse, fond feelings linger.
Gradually perceiving the golden crow's movement,
seeing colorful sails sparsely appear.
To know when benevolence infuses peace,
songs of praise fill the returning path.
Hóng Zhígōng's "Responding to the Order, upon Arrival from Yǐng to Huái Poem"
Delighting in exquisite enjoyment of profound sentiments,
arriving at Huái and Féi's confluence.
Noise of oars resounds along the shores,
spanned sails rise through the clouds.
Clear currents hold the sun's hues,
turbulent waves dash against rosy skies.
Like the winding Zhāng Waters,
the sound of horns opens the return path.
Also Yú Shìnán's "Responding to the Order, upon Arrival from Yǐng to Huái Poem"
On a fine morning delighted with favorable crossings,
casting off into the Huái grounds.
Cold currents flow beneath prow-shaped rocks,
frost-laden winds echo somberly.
Hidden scales leap within the waves,
water birds sink before the tides.
The Hán Canal is not far off,
gazing fills one's heart and mind with joy.
Xú Yànbó's "Huái Pavilion Chant"
Solemn contemplation amid Huái's secluded mountains,
admiring fragrant blossoms on Niúzhōu Isle.
Torrents rush day and night,
a lone traveler sits worriedly.
As cranes cry out amidst morning winds,
and gibbons echo in frosty autumn.
Crickets sing with flickering light,
leaning against a clear stringed instrument, playing a cool qín.
Gathering jade-like flowers, mourning the Chǔ Waters,
playing with the beauties of the Yuè peaks.
Mountainous slopes curve along the shore,
streams wind around serene pools.
Golden rays rise and fall swiftly,
green moss fades and duckweed wanes.
Duckweed wanes as red hues wither,
lonely beauty remains, when will peace come?
Do you not see the lovely Tóngbǎi heights,
hands repair cassia trees, their blossoms fill the mountain?
The "Sacrificial Ode to the Huái" by Xuē Dàohéng of the Suí Dynasty
The Commander-in-Chief, Prince of Jìn,
reverently presents offerings of clear libations, ritual silks, and the grand sacrifice of a bull,
to solemnly sacrifice to the spirit of the Great Eastern Tributary, the Huái River.
For the sage's virtue responds to the times,
and his divine achievements govern all things.
Above, he aligns with the seven celestial bodies;
below, he encompasses the four seas.
Since the people of Jìn lost the Way,
the constant principles of human relations were corrupted.
Heaven divided the inner from the outer;
earth was shattered in the southeast.
Sān Wú became a land of peril and chaos;
Bǎi Yuè became a den for fugitives.
The Emperor initiated the founding of the dynasty,
gloriously possessing the sacred vessel of rule.
Divine charts emerged from tortoises and dragons;
mirrors of gold and jade were suspended.
He toiled diligently over all affairs of state,
never forgetting them even in sleep.
His thoughts dwelled on the common people,
with deep compassion and care.
From the source of the Yellow River to lands beyond the seas,
none failed to come and pay homage.
Mòdú and Hūhán,
annually came to bow in audience.
But the false Chén, insignificant as it was,
still obstructed the spread of imperial influence and teachings.
The treacherous rebel Shūbǎo,
usurped the remaining legacy.
His poison flowed through Jiāngzuǒ,
accumulating grievances among humans and spirits alike.
The Emperor, deeply grieved,
righteously launched a punitive campaign.
I, unworthy, have received the court's commission,
to pacify and bring peace to the Huái region.
I look up to you, whose source flows from Tóngbǎi,
stretching far to Pénglái.
You mark the four great rivers and guide the hundred streams,
commanding the five forests and embodying the seven virtues.
May I rely on your spirit that washes away evil,
to accomplish the task of eradicating tyranny.
So that the banners on water and land,
may advance unhindered wherever they go.
And the rulers of Wú and Kuài,
may surrender and submit without resistance.
Reverently, I present these offerings;
may the spirit deign to accept them.
Jì, the Sixth
The "Shìmíng" states:
"Jì means 'to aid,'
for it is said its source lies north of the river,
and it aids the river by flowing south."
The "Zhōuguān" says:
"In Yǎnzhōu, its rivers are the Hé and Jì."
According to the "Shuǐjīng Zhù" and the "Shānhǎijīng":
"The Jì River originates from the Wángwū Mountain in Yuán County, Hédōng.
Initially named Yǎnshuǐ,
the "Fēngsútōng" states:
"The Jì River originates from the Zànhuáng Mountain in Fángzǐ County, Chángshān.
This is actually another river altogether.
Yìng Shì's claim that it flows into the Jì in Hénán
is incorrect."
Flowing east from northwest of Wēn County,
it is then called the Jì River.
Kǒng Ānguó, in his commentary on the "Shàngshū," notes:
"The spring source is called Yǎn;
when it flows away, it becomes Jì,
located on the flatlands northwest of Wēn."
It then flows southeast,
passing north of Gǒng County,
and enters the river from the south,
flowing alongside it.
Passing Chénggāo,
Chénggāo
is present-day Sìshuǐ County.
The "Jìnshū ‧ Dìdàozhì" states:
"The Jì enters the river from Dàpī,
and contends with the river's waters.
Dàpī,
Chénggāo,
ancient Chénggāo also encompassed the boundaries of Gǒng County."
Overflowing, it becomes the Xíng River,
flowing east past Yángwǔ and north of Fēngqiū County.
Continuing east past south of Yuāngǒu County,
it reaches south of Dìngtáo County.
Then flowing northeast,
it converges with the Hé River,
and east to west of Chéngshì County, it divides into two branches.
One branch flows northeast into the Jùyě Marsh,
passing west of Shòuzhāng,
where it merges with the Wèn River.
It then flows north past west of Gǔchéng County.
Continuing northeast past north of Lú County,
it passes through Qí Commandery and Dōnglái Commandery before entering the sea."
The "Shàngshū" mentions guiding the Yǎn River eastward to become the Jì,
entering the river,
overflowing to form the Xíng,
and emerging east from north of Táoqiū.
This is where the Hé River is located.
Further northeast, it meets the Wèn River,
and then flows northeast into the sea,
as described.
Additionally, the "Shuǐjīng Zhù" states:
"Initially, when the Jì River reaches west of Chéngshì County,
it splits into two branches.
One flows northeast.
The one that now enters the sea
is the branch that flows southeast,
passing north of Chāngyì County and south of Jīnxiāng County,
reaching Fāngyú,
where it becomes the Pèi River.
Passing northeast of Pèi County,
it reaches Xiàpī and enters the Huái River."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"The Jì River is suitable for wheat."
The "Zhōuguān" states:
"Magpies do not cross the Jì."
Guiding Yǎn, Jì River
Both are mentioned in the narrative.
Dual Sources, Different Banks
Lì Yuán, in his commentary on the "Shuǐjīng," said:
"The Jì River has dual sources,
emerging from the flatlands northwest of Hénèi County.
The water arises from two sources,
hence it is again called Jìyuán.
The western source converges and emerges west of Yuánchéng,
flowing east to irrigate south of the city,
then merging with the northern waters."
Guō Yuánshēng's "Shùzhēngjì" states:
"In Wēn County, Hénèi, there is also a Jì,
which enters the Yellow River,
and is considered the source of the Jì."
According to this, the two Jì rivers have different northern and southern banks,
and are separated by over a thousand lǐ.
Wú Ditch, Qí Barrier
Zhào Yè's "Wúyuèchūnqiū" states:
"King Fūchāi of Wú raised an army to attack Qí,
digging a deep ditch,
connecting between Shāng and Lǔ,
and linking it north to the Jì River."
The "Zhànguócè" states:
"Zhāng Yí advised the King of Qín,
'Qí relies on the Hé and Jì rivers,
which suffice to form a barrier.'"
Contending Waters, Cutting Across the Flow
Dài Yánzhī's "Xīzhēngjì" states:
"The Jì River enters the river from Dàpī,
contending with the river's waters as it flows east."
The "Shàngshū" states:
"Guide the Yǎn River eastward to become the Jì,
enter the river,
and overflow to form the Xíng."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"The Jì River enters the river,
flows alongside it for several thousand lǐ, cutting across the river.
Then, alongside the river for several lǐ,
it overflows to form the Xíng Marsh."
Virtuous Beauty, Harmonious Flow
Liú Xiàng's "Shuōyuàn" states:
"Why are the four great rivers—Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jì—regarded as equivalent to feudal lords?
Because they can wash away filth and impurity,
channel all streams into the sea,
and generate clouds and rain.
Their virtue is exceedingly beautiful,
hence they are regarded as feudal lords."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"The Huái and Jì rivers flow harmoniously and are suitable for wheat."
Féng's Journey, Yuán's Voyage
Féng Yǎn's "Míngzhìfù" states:
"Flowing past mountains and peaks, I gaze all around,
following Jiéshí and Dòngtíng.
Floating on the Jiāng and Hé rivers into the sea,
I journey upstream along the Huái and Jì rivers."
Yuán Hóng's "Běizhēngfù" states:
"Thus, leaving Liáng Mountain behind,
crossing the Wèn River's waves,
sailing upon the clear Jì,
and passing by Zhù'ā."
Equalizing Measures, Washing Away Filth
The "Fēngsútōng" states:
"Jì means 'to equalize,'
equalizing its measures."
"Washing away filth and impurity" is explained above under "Virtuous Beauty."
Overflowing Xíng Marsh, Flowing into Bó Sea
"Overflowing Xíng Marsh" is mentioned in the narrative.
The "Shānhǎijīng" states:
"The Jì River emerges from south of Gòng Mountain, east of Qiūjué, passes through the Jùyě Marsh,
and flows into the sea."
Xiāo Chǔcái's "Poem on Following the Ritual Journey to Mount Dàizōng, Passing Through Pú and Jì"
Brushing the Milky Way, star banners turn,
Parting the dawn, sun-feathered wings gleam.
We shall trace the traces of Lǔ's peak,
And again engrave Mount Dàizōng's stele.
Forest spears choke the Jì River's shore,
Beast-skin drums shake the Hé's courtyard floor.
Leaf-arrows soar fierce against the cold,
Crow-bows gaze at dawn, startled and bold.
Already the Fén water ode descends,
Still deepens the feeling for welcoming Wèi.
Xuē Kègòu's "Poem on Following the Ritual Journey to Mount Dàizōng, Passing Through Pú and Jì"
The Dragon Chart crowns Xūlù,
The Phoenix Carriage points to Yúntíng.
Not mist, but it drifts on Jì's banks,
Green canopies open on Hé's sandbanks.
Painted robes at dawn answer the moon,
Patterned halberds at daybreak part the stars.
Four fields patrol with bowing rites,
Three drives follow the way of covenant scriptures.
The journey delights in offering ten thousand years,
I secretly clap, matching a thousand ages.
Later Wei Emperor Wén's "Sacrificial Text to the Jì River"
In the nineteenth year of the Tàihé era,
The Emperor dispatches the Grand Chamberlain's Court Attendant, the Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant Jǐng,
To solemnly announce to the spirit of the Jì River.
Heaven's light aids its radiance,
Earth's foundation spreads its moisture.
Only the river flows with numinous power,
Harmonizing brilliance, opening the shades.
All images rely on harmony,
Rising and falling, fragrant drips.
It harbors spirits, embraces transformations,
Compared to soil, it proclaims achievements.
Warm regions surge with auspiciousness,
The Yǎn source guides the Jì.
Drawing currents, connecting to the vast sea,
Truly matching the four limbs.
It creates moisture for Mount Dàizōng,
Holding clouds, spitting sweet dew.
Moist waves deep and still,
River winds gently rippling.
Gazing at the great ford, we cherish its virtue,
Riding the long waves, we revere its wisdom.
Floating with the dragon's solemn majesty,
Adorning the jade carriage, floating and covering.
Sinking the bright objects of jade tablets and discs,
Hoping the pure sacrificial animals return entrusted.
The Luò River, Seventh
The "Chūnqiū Shuōtící" states:
"Luò means 'to unfold,'
meaning the water unfolds with shimmering light."
Yú Huàn's "Diǎn Lüè" states:
"The character Luò is sometimes written as Luò (with a bird radical).
Initially, the Hàn dynasty's element was fire, which feared water,
so Luò removed the water radical and added the bird radical.
The Wèi dynasty's element was earth,
earth being the mother of water.
Water gains earth to flow,
earth gains water to soften,
so the bird radical was removed and the water radical added."
The "Zhōu Guān" states:
"In Yùzhōu, its rivers are Xíng and Luò,
forming the Three Rivers with the Yī and Chán rivers."
The Qín dynasty established the Sānchuān Commandery south of the river.
According to the "Shuǐ Jīng":
"The Luò River originates from Zhǒnglǐng Mountain in Shàngluò County, Jīngzhào,
passing through the commanderies of Shàngluò, Hóngnóng, Hénán, and the counties of Lúshì, Líchéng, Yángshì, Yíyáng, Luòyáng, converging with the waters of the Yī, Chán, Gǔ, and Jiàn rivers,
reaching Gǒng County and entering the Hé River."
The "Shàngshū" states:
"Channeling the Luò from Xióng'ěr,
northeast meeting with the Jiàn and Chán,
further east meeting with the Yī,
and further northeast entering the Hé River, this is it."
Also, the "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"In Yōngzhōu,
its river is Luò Ruì,
this Luò is also called Qī Jǔ,
originating from Féngyì,
this is the water of Guānfǔ,
not the Luò River of Hénán."
Also, the "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"The Luò River originates from Zhāng Mountain,
flowing east through Luò County and Xīndū,
merging with the Jiān River,
this is again in the land of Shǔ."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"The Luò River's light and swift water is suitable for grain."
The "Shùzhēng Jì" states:
"The bottom of the Luò River has alum stones,
therefore there is no ice on its surface.
The spirit of the Luò is called Fú Fēi."
During the time of King Líng of Zhōu,
the Gǔ and Luò rivers clashed.
Meeting the Jiàn, according to the Hé
"Meeting the Jiàn" see narrative.
The "Hé Tú" states:
"The Luò River's geography,
is the palace of yin essence.
When the emperor is wise and sagely,
the turtle script emerges with writing.
Heaven bestows the mandate,
earth confers the auspicious sign.
According to the Hé, meeting at the border,
centered, protecting the multitude.
The kingly way harmonious and well-governed,
spits forth charts to aid the spirits.
Rebellious names confuse the teachings,
plucking the perishing, lamenting the surviving.
Therefore, the sage observes the Hé and Luò."
Fish Leaping, Phoenix Soaring
Yú Huàn's "Diǎn Lüè" states:
"Tāng gazed east at the Luò,
sank jade discs,
and pairs of yellow fish leaped,
emerging from the altar."
Cáo Zhí's "Liǎngyí Piān" states:
"The emperor transforms the eight extremes,
nurtures the myriad things,
harmonizes yin and yang,
yin and yang harmonized, phoenixes arrive, Hé and Luò soar."
Phoenix Gathering, Dragon Appearing
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shū" states:
"Huángdì fasted in the central palace,
sat above the Xuán Hù Luò River,
phoenixes gathered,
not eating living insects,
not treading on living grass.
The males sang by themselves,
the females danced by themselves."
The "Yì Qián Záo Dù" states:
"When the emperor first rises and is about to emerge,
dragons appear in the Hé and Luò,
all observe their heads.
Black ones signify human rectification,
white ones signify earth rectification,
red ones signify heaven rectification."
Black Jade, Red Script
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"During Tāng's time,
a spirit led a white wolf holding a hook into the Yīn court,
then he gazed east and sank jade discs into the Luò.
Obtained the auspicious signs of yellow fish and black jade,
thereupon he first received the mandate and claimed kingship."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"In ancient times, during the operation of utmost virtue,
pearls and jades were moist and glossy,
the Luò produced red script,
the Hé produced green charts."
Mysterious Turtle, Blue Carp
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shū" states:
"The mysterious turtle and Luò script,
are heavenly tallies.
When the king's virtue reaches the rivers and springs,
then the Luò produces turtle script."
The "Hé Tú" states:
"Huángdì traveled to the Luò,
saw a carp three zhàng long,
blue body without scales,
red patterns forming characters."
Turtle Categories, Phoenix Casket
The "Shàngshū" states:
"Heaven then bestowed upon Yǔ the Great Plan with nine categories,
the constant principles were thus set in order."
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation:
"Chóu,
means category.
Heaven gave Yǔ the Luò-produced book,
a divine turtle carried the writing and emerged,
arranged on its back,
with numbers up to nine.
Yǔ then accordingly ordered them,
to complete the nine categories."
The "Huáng Lù" states:
"The emperor sat above the Xuán Hù Luò River,
with the Grand Marshal Róng Guāng, Left and Right Assistants Zhōu Chāng, and one hundred twenty others.
They approached to observe,
a phoenix held a chart in its beak and placed it before the emperor,
the chart had a casket made of yellow jade."
Phoenix Flute and Jade Chicken
Liú Xiàng's "Biographies" states:
"Prince Jìn loved to play the flute,
producing phoenix cries between the Yī and Luò rivers.
There was a Daoist priest, Fú Qiū Bó,
who escorted him up to Mount Sōnggāo."
"The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
Zhāolíng Empress, named Hán Shǐ,
was wandering by the Luò Pool,
when a jade chicken appeared, holding a red pearl in its beak,
inscribed 'Jade Essence.'
It was said that whoever swallowed this would become king.
Hán Shǐ swallowed it,
and gave birth to Liú Jì, the founding ancestor of the Hàn dynasty."
Yáo's Altar and Zhōu's Terrace
"The Book of Documents: Central Portents" states:
"Yáo cast jade discs into the Luò River,
and a black turtle emerged bearing a chart on its back.
The red markings on its carapace formed characters and stopped at the altar."
"The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he established his capital at Luòyì and set up the tripods there.
The present-day Dǐngzhōng Terrace north of the Luò River southwest of Luòyáng is precisely that place."
Xuānyuán's Journey and the Zhōu Divination
"The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
"During the time of the Yellow Emperor, a great fog covered the sky for three days.
The Emperor journeyed to the banks of the Luò River,
where he saw a giant fish.
He sacrificed five kinds of livestock to make offerings to it,
whereupon the heavens poured down heavy rain
for seven days and seven nights.
The fish drifted away, and only then did he obtain the charts and writings,
which are the present-day 'River Chart: Observing Sprouts' chapter."
"The Book of Documents" states:
"After Duke Shào had inspected the site for the capital,
Duke Zhōu went to oversee the construction of Chéngzhōu.
He sent a messenger to report the divination results,
composing the 'Announcement Concerning Luò.'
It says:
'I also divined about the area east of the Chán River,
and the omens were likewise favorable.'"
The Xià's Drying Up and the Zhōu's Clashing Waters
"The Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"In the second year of King Yōu of Zhōu,
earthquakes occurred in all three rivers of the Western Zhōu region.
Bó Yángfǔ said:
'In the past, the Yī and Luò rivers dried up, and the Xià dynasty perished.
Now the virtue of Zhōu resembles that of the last rulers of those two dynasties.
With mountains collapsing and rivers drying up,
these are signs of its impending demise.'" "The Discourses of the States" states:
"In the twenty-second year of King Líng of Zhōu,
the Gǔ and Luò rivers clashed,
threatening to destroy the royal palace.
The king wished to dam them,
but Crown Prince Jìn said:
'Mountains
are the gathering of earth;
marshes,
the home of creatures;
rivers,
the passage of energy;
lakes,
the accumulation of water.
Now Heaven and Earth gather what is high
and return it to what is low.
If we, in our governance,
are perhaps truly acting with bias, we bring calamity upon the spirits of these two rivers.'
The king proceeded to dam them nonetheless,
and great disorder befell the royal house."
Jiǎ Kuí's commentary states:
"When two waters converge,
it resembles a clash."
Zhāng's Purification and Pān's Dwelling
Zhāng Xié's "Rhapsody on the Luò River Purification" states:
"Ah, what a fine day in this third month of spring,
I delight in the harmonious, misty weather.
The gentle breeze blows softly and spreads freely,
a hundred plants shine brightly, spreading their fragrance.
Seeing that my spring garments are already made,
I shall go to cleanse myself by the water's edge."
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Living in Idleness" states:
"Retiring, I lived in idleness on the banks of the Luò."
Luminous Pearls and Ornamental Jade
"Luminous pearls" appear below in Cáo Zhí's rhapsody.
"The Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"From Qín Mào Mountain,
the Luò River flows forth.
It runs eastward and empties into the Yellow River.
Within it, there is ornamental jade."
Sinking Discs and Falling Bells
"The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
"Tāng sank jade discs into the Luò River
and obtained the auspicious signs of a yellow fish and black jade."
Sūn Yán's "History of the Sòng" states:
"When Emperor Gāozǔ pacified Guān and Luò,
he had the old bells and their stands sent south.
One large bell fell into the Luò River."
Azure Clouds Float and Crimson Light Rises
"The Book of Documents: Central Portents" states:
"King Wǔ observed the River,
and after completing the ritual of sinking the discs,
he was about to withdraw
when the sun grew dim.
Glory-light filled the River where the discs sank,
azure clouds floated over the Luò,
a crimson dragon approached the altar,
and holding a chart of dark armor in its mouth, it spat it out and departed."
Jiāng Yān, in his "Letter Presented to Prince Jiànpíng," states:
"Now the sacred calendar is revered and bright,
all under heaven find joy in their labors,
azure clouds float over the Luò,
glory-light fills the River."
"The Book of Documents: Central Portents" states:
"Yáo led his assembled ministers
and cast discs eastward into the Luò River.
He withdrew and waited until the time of Xiàjì.
Crimson light arose,
a black turtle emerged bearing writings,
and crimson markings formed characters."
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
"The character 'jì' here is read as 'cè'."
Nine Days Warm and Seven Nights Rain
"The Qian Zao Du of the Book of Changes" states:
"In response to the Emperor's abundant virtue,
the Luò River first grew warm.
After nine days it turned cold,
and within five days it changed to the five colors of dark and yellow."
"Seven nights rain" is seen in the note above for "Xuānyuán's Journey."
Cáo Zǐjiàn of Wèi, "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River"
I, leaving the capital,
returned to my eastern fief.
Northward I passed Yīquè,
crossed Huányuán.
I traversed Tōnggǔ,
ascended Jǐngshān.
At ease in Yánglín,
my gaze wandered over the Luò River.
I beheld a beautiful woman
upon the riverbank.
Taking hold of my charioteer, I asked him:
"Who is that person there,
so radiantly beautiful?"
The charioteer replied:
"I have heard that the goddess of the Hé and Luò rivers
is named Fú Fēi.
Could it be, my lord, that what you see
is none other than she?"
I told him:
"Her form, soaring like a startled swan,
graceful like a swimming dragon.
Vaguely, like light clouds veiling the moon;
floating, like swirling snow in the flowing wind.
Then suddenly she moved her body freely,
to wander and to play.
On her left, she leaned on colored pennants;
on her right, shaded by cassia banners.
She bared her fair wrist at the divine shore,
to pluck the dark lingzhi from the rushing rapids.
I composed my gentle expression and calmed my heart,
reaffirming ritual bounds to restrain myself.
Then a host of spirits gathered in throngs,
calling to companions, summoning friends.
Some sported in the clear stream,
some soared over the divine islets,
some gathered luminous pearls,
some collected kingfisher feathers.
Following the two consorts of Southern Xiāng,
accompanied by the roaming maiden of the Hàn River's shore.
Her body swift as a flying duck,
floating and fleeting as a spirit.
Treading lightly over rippling waves,
her silken stockings seemed to stir the dust.
Then Píngyì stilled the wind,
and the River Lord calmed the waves.
Féng Yí beat the drums,
Nǚwā sang a clear song.
Literary fish leapt to alert the carriage,
jade bells chimed as they departed together.
Six dragons drew up solemnly, heads aligned,
pulling the cloud-chariot in majestic procession.
Whales and giant fish surged, flanking the wheels;
waterfowl soared, forming her guard.
Then she passed the northern islet,
crossed the southern ridge.
Moving her vermilion lips, she slowly spoke,
setting forth the great principles of our meeting.
She lamented the gulf between human and divine ways,
regretted that in the prime of youth we could not be joined.
Entrusting subtle feelings to express love,
she offered the bright earrings of Jiāngnán.
Though she dwells hidden in the Great Darkness,
forever she entrusts her heart to her lord."
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on the Luo River"
Spring hunt, galloping steeds' bones,
Grasping reins, gazing down upon the long river.
Where clouds flow, brocade-like ripples entwine,
Before the wind, silk-like waves curl and roll.
Water blossoms shimmer, reflecting the trees,
Bank-side orchids dip inverted into the waves.
Must one seek the melody of Fényīn?
Autumn clouds inspire the boatman's song.
Sū Wèidào's "Poem on Receiving the Chart at the Warm Luo River"
The green chart received by the river's inspection,
The blue altar overlooks the Luo's banks.
Heaven's turn, the imperial halt is decreed,
Filial offerings belong to solemn sacrifice.
Ascending to match the glory of three ancestors,
Pacifying and embracing all the hundred spirits.
Mist parts, the sun on the central path,
Snow clears, dust from the attendant carriages.
In anticipation, the harmonious and elegant music is played,
Long songs for a hundred million springs.
Lǐ Qiáo's "Poem on Paying Homage to the Luo"
The seven elite guards, the imperial carriage moves,
The thousand-year auspicious chart is opened.
Its script like borne by a turtle emerges,
Its diagram like carried by a phoenix arrives.
Solemnly presented, the three spirits partake,
Brightly worshipped, ten thousand states attend.
Zhou banners where yellow birds gather,
Han tents where purple clouds return.
Dusk falls, the Hooked Array turns,
Clear songs rise to the Emperor's terrace.
Niú Fèngjí's "Poem on Receiving the Chart at the Warm Luo River"
Eight spirits support the jade carriage,
Six feathered guards alert by the jade stream.
The guarded path north of the Yī River,
Banners extend west of the Jiàn River.
The imperial chart opened from the Luo casket,
The carved stone rivals Heaven's height.
Auspicious sun rises from the waves,
Divine birds dip low within the mist.
This humble minister, with feeble wings,
Claps and dances to greet the phoenix and simurgh.
Xuē Shèn's "Poem on Boats Advancing on the Luo River"
The forbidden garden grants the sage's view,
The immortal boat sails in timely excursion.
North of Luo, wind-blossom trees,
South of the river, painted pleasure boats.
Fragrance grows from orchid and iris grass,
Spring enters the phoenix tower.
Joy ends, parting thoughts at dusk,
Mist-light rises on the evening flow.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Luo"
The Luo emerges from Xióng'ěr,
Flowing eastward to gather and meet.
Xià Yǔ channeled and dredged it,
Passing through the city of Luòyì.
The dark turtle with crimson script,
The Hàn mandate was thereby established.
The imperial capital's thoroughfare,
Establishing the state southward.
Ten thousand chariots finally cross,
Building boats to form a bridge.
Three capitals, five provinces,
Tribute baskets from ten thousand directions.
Broadening vision, extending hearing,
Carefully appointing the worthy and good.
The sovereign bright and illustrious,
All creatures thereby thrive.
The Wèi River, Eighth
The "Chūnqiū Shuōtící" states:
"Wèi means 'to spread',
describing its flowing, rippling appearance."
The "Zhōuguān":
"Yōng Province,
its waterways are the Wèi and Luò."
The "Guānzhōng Jì" says:
"The Wèi, along with the Jīng and Luò,
one name is the Qījǔ River,
one name is the Luò River,
emerges from Féngyì."
They are the three rivers of Guānzhōng,
referring to the earthquake of the three rivers during King Yōu of Zhōu.
Together with the Jīng, Wèi, Bà, Chǎn, Láo, Jué, Fēng, and Hào, they form the Eight Rivers."
According to the "Shuǐjīng Zhù" and the "Shānhǎijīng" commentary,
the Wèi River emerges from the Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué Mountain in Shǒuyáng County, Lǒngxī,
flows northeast past the south of Dídào County,
and north of Shàngguī County.
South of Chéncāng County,
north of Wǔgōng County,
south of Huáilǐ County,
it merges with the Láo and Fēng rivers.
East to Gāolíng,
it merges with the Jīng River.
It also merges with the Qījǔ River,
passes through the capitals of Qín and Hàn,
and reaches Tóngjīn before entering the Yellow River.
The "Shàngshū" states:
"Channeled the Wèi from Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué,
eastward met with the Fēng,
eastward met with the Jīng.
Further east past the Qījǔ,
entered the Yellow River."
The "Sānfǔ Jiùshì" states:
"Initially, Qín's capital was north of the Wèi,
south of the Wèi, the Chánglè Palace was built.
A bridge connected the two palaces.
Marking the Hé as Qín's eastern gate,
marking the Qiān as Qín's western gate,
the two gates were eight hundred lǐ apart.
The Wèi River pierced through the capital,
to mirror the Heavenly River;
the bridge crossed southward,
to mirror the Herdboy Star.
Hàn's capital was south of the Wèi,
opening the northern gate-tower facing the Wèi.
North of the Wèi were the imperial tombs and ancestral temples."
Piercing the Capital Waterway of Yōng
The "Sānfǔ Huángtú" states:
"The First Emperor's capital was Xiányáng,
building palaces upon the northern hills.
The main gate extended in four directions,
modeled after the Purple Palace,
mirroring the dwelling of the Emperor.
The Wèi River pierced through the capital,
to mirror the Heavenly River."
The "Zhōuguān":
"Yōng Province,
its waterways are the Wèi and Luò."
Knowing Stars Observing Auras
Chén Shòu's "Yìbù Qíjiù Zhuàn" states:
"During the reign of Hàn Wǔdì,
Shǔ's Zhāng Kuān served as Palace Attendant,
accompanying the sacrifice at Gānquán.
Arriving at the Wèi Bridge,
there was a woman bathing in the Wèi River,
her breasts seven chǐ long.
The Emperor, finding this strange,
sent someone to question her.
The woman said:
'The person in the seventh carriage behind the Emperor knows whence I come.'
At that time, Kuān was in the seventh carriage.
He replied:
'The celestial star governs sacrifices.
If purification and fasting are not pure, then a woman appears.'"
Gě Hóng's "Shénxiān Zhuàn" states:
"Commandant-escort of Běihǎi, Wū Yán, styled Zǐdū.
When Hàn Wǔdì went out,
Zǐdū was seen at the Wèi Bridge.
The Emperor saw above his head a dense purple aura over a zhàng high.
The Emperor summoned Dōngfāng Shuò,
bidding him observe this gentleman,
asking what arts he possessed.
He said:
'This gentleman possesses the arts of the Yin way.'"
Dangling a Hook Tossing Coins
Xú Gàn's "Zhōng Lùn" states:
"King Wén encountered Tàigōng on the banks of the Wèi,
white-haired and hoary,
holding a pole, dangling a hook.
King Wén obtained him,
bright as dispelling clouds to see the sun,
sudden as opening mist to view mountains."
Zhào Qí's "Sānfǔ Juélù" states:
"Among the pure of Ānlíng,
there was Xiàng Zhòngxiān watering his horse in the Wèi River,
each time tossing three coins."
Jìn Encampment Fú Altar
Zāng Róngxù's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Zhūgě Liàng led troops out through Xiégǔ.
Gāozǔ [of Jìn] resisted Liàng,
then crossed the Wèi River,
building an encampment with the river at his back."
Péi Jǐngrén's "Fú Shū" states:
"When Fú Jiàn reached Cháng'ān,
Jiǎ Xuán and others presented the imperial title.
Following the old rites, they established the hundred officials,
Building Boats and Presenting Carriages
The Mao Odes states:
"In the early years of King Wén,
Heaven made the match for him.
On the sunny side of the Jiā River,
On the banks of the Wèi River.
He fixed the auspicious date,
And personally went to meet her at the Wèi.
He built boats to form a bridge."
It also says:
"I escorted my uncle,
All the way to the north of the Wèi.
What did I present to him?
A great carriage with a team of yellow steeds."
Responsive Virtue and Lost Order
The Book of Hàn states:
"In ancient times, the Three Dynasties resided within the Three Rivers region,
and the Hé and Luò Rivers produced charts and writings.
The Qín resided north of the Wèi River,
and the frequent red auspicious signs on the water were the manifestation of responsive virtue."
Jiāo Gòng's Forest of Changes states:
"Mountains collapse, valleys are severed,
Heaven's blessings are utterly exhausted.
The Jīng and Wèi lose their order,
The jade calendar is already broken."
Connecting Bridges and Elevated Walkways
Old Affairs of the Three Capital Regions states:
"When the First Emperor ascended the throne,
he built the Chánglè Palace south of the Wèi River.
A bridge connected the two palaces.
The Hé River was designated as the eastern gate of Qín,
and the Qiān River was designated as the western gate of Qín."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The First Emperor of Qín built an elevated walkway towards the Ēpáng Palace,
crossing the Wèi River to connect it to Xiányáng,
in order to represent the Celestial Pole's Gallery Path crossing the Milky Way to reach the Encampment constellation."
Qín Sacrifices and Hàn Worship
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng states:
"When Qín and Hàn had their capital at the Western Capital,
although the Jīng and Wèi Rivers were not in the canon of sacrifices,
because they were near Xiányáng,
they still received sacrifices as major rivers."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wén personally worshipped at the confluence of the Bà and Wèi Rivers to perform the suburban sacrifice to the Five Emperors north of the Wèi."
Rú Chún's commentary states:
"It refers to the confluence of the two rivers."
Dragon Drinking and Pheasant Soaring
Mr. Xīn's Records of the Three Qín states:
"Lóngshǒu Mountain is sixty lǐ long.
Its head enters the Wèi River,
its tail reaches Fánchuān,
and it is twenty zhàng high.
It is said that in the past, a black dragon emerged from the Southern Mountains,
drank from the Wèi River,
and the path it traveled formed this earthen mountain."
Péi Jǐngrén's Book of Fú states:
"In the fourth year of the Huángshǐ era of Fú Jiàn,
mountain pheasants came into people's homes.
They roosted, raised their young, and then left,
gathering in flocks to swim and soar along the Wèi River,
no different from domestic fowl."
Unearthing the Zhōu Tripod and Obtaining the Yān Seal
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"In the fifteenth year of Emperor Wén,
a man from Zhào named Xīnyuán Píng, skilled in observing vapors, had an audience.
He advised the emperor to establish a temple to the Five Emperors north of the Wèi,
hoping to unearth the Zhōu tripod,
and that jade blossoms would often appear."
Wáng Jǐnghuī's Book of Southern Yān states:
"In the third year of the Huángchū era of Yáo Qín,
the year being Dīngyǒu,
a red seal was obtained on the banks of the Wèi River at Cháng'ān.
On it were the words: 'Heaven Mandates Virtue to Yān.'"
Lǚ Fishing on the South Bank and Féng Farming on the North Bank
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Tàigōng was fishing in the Wèi River.
The Western Earl of Zhōu was about to go hunting.
A divination said:
'What you will catch is not a dragon, not a serpent,
not a bear, not a brown bear.
What you will catch is an assistant to a hegemon king.'
Thereupon, the Western Earl went hunting,
and indeed met Tàigōng on the south bank of the Wèi.
Speaking with him, he was greatly pleased."
Féng Yǎn's Preface to the "Ode to Integrity" states:
"Master Féng farmed in the valley of Líshān,
on the north bank of the Wèi River.
He abandoned the rituals of condolence and inquiry,
and severed the path of traveling for office.
Aloof, he had a mind that transcended worldly things,
and no ambition to conform to vulgar customs."
Originating from the Bird-and-Rat Cave and Entering Lóng Mountain
The Book of Documents states:
"The Wèi River is guided from where the birds and rats share the same cave."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Birds and rats become mates,
sharing the same cave dwelling in this mountain.
Thus the mountain is named Bird-and-Rat,
and the Wèi River emerges from it."
"Entering Lóng Mountain" see the note under "Dragon Drinking."
Bridge Modeling the Ox and Vapor Like a Clam
The Yellow Charts of the Three Capital Regions states:
"The First Emperor unified all under heaven,
and made Xiányáng his capital.
Following the hills and mounds, he constructed palaces.
The main gate extended in four directions,
modeling the Purple Palace to represent the dwelling of the emperor.
The Wèi River flowed through the capital,
to represent the Heavenly River;
A bridge spanned it for crossing south,
modeling the Herd-boy star."
The Miscellaneous Book of Military Strategy states:
"The Eastern Sea emits vapor like a turtle,
the Wèi River emits vapor like a clam."
Emerging from the Earth's Stem and Representing the Heavenly River
The River Chart states:
"Bird-and-Rat Same Cave Mountain
is the stem of the earth.
The Wèi River emerges from within it."
"Representing the Heavenly River" see the note under "Bridge Modeling the Ox."
Frightening the Carriage and Horses and Boarding the Tower Ship
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"When Zhāng Shìzhī was Commandant of Justice,
Emperor Wén of Hàn was leaving via the Middle Wèi Bridge.
A man came out from under the bridge.
The emperor's carriage horses were startled.
He sent horsemen to arrest him and hand him over to the Commandant of Justice.
The Commandant of Justice memorialized:
'This man violated the imperial path and should be fined.'" The Book of Hàn states:
"When Xuē Guǎngdé was Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
he remonstrated directly and frankly.
Emperor Yuán was performing the Zhòu sacrifice at the ancestral temple,
and exited by the Biànmén Gate.
He wished to board a tower ship.
Guǎngdé stood before the imperial carriage, removed his cap, and said:
'You should take the bridge.'
The emperor then took the bridge."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Wèi Bridge is a Qín institution.
It is also called the Biànmén Bridge."
Poem by Yǔwén Yōu of the Later Zhōu Dynasty, "Reaching the Source of the Wèi"
The Wèi's source rushes from the bird-and-rat cave,
Light ripples rise by the traveler's lodge.
Shallow waters fill the ravine with sound,
Vast and surging, the whole river sings.
Pān Yuè praised moving stones,
Master Féng listened to the sound of waves.
Diagonally departing, it reaches the sky's midpoint,
Horizontally arriving, it faces Shǐpíng.
Confluent flows should not be mixed,
Only then is its nature's purity known.
Zhōu Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Gazing at the Wèi River Poem"
The trees resemble the banks at Xīntíng,
The sand is like a dragon's tail, curved.
Still saying, at this evening's shore,
There should be returning boats with lowered sails.
Sui Dynasty Emperor Yáng's "Poem at the Source of the Wèi"
Westward campaign has brought me to this place,
The mountain road stretches long and far.
The earth's stem records spiritual wonders,
The shared cave spews forth a mighty flow.
A floating cup is not fit for comparison,
A raft of driftwood can hardly match.
Startling waves sound against ravine stones,
Clear banks pour past cliffside towers.
Torrential, it flows down to Dí County,
Boundless, it spreads across the Divine Land.
In deep forests, white beasts howl,
On cloudy paths, a blue ox is imagined.
The wind returns, scattering flowers and leaves,
The sun rises, gathering mist and smoke.
Truly, I seek a recluse's retreat,
Not a journey tracing old wheel ruts.
Suí Dynasty Xuē Dàohéng's "Fèng Hé Lín Wèi Yuán Yìng Zhào Shī" (Poem in Response to the Imperial Edict on Visiting the Source of the Wei River)
Mysterious merit restored Yǔ's traces,
Supreme virtue surpassed Tāng's net.
Jade Pass's watchtowers stretch afar,
Golden region's waters and stones abound.
Eight rivers here share one form,
Ten thousand lǐ guide the long waves.
Startling currents pour into the land-sea,
Churning waves resemble the Milky Way.
Imperial banners pass through cliffs and valleys,
Dragon's lair briefly traversed.
Western elders accompany the tour's feast,
Southern breeze stirs songs of praise.
All things receive benevolent grace,
Living beings harmonize in great peace.
This humble minister laments the evening scene,
Wishing to halt Lǔ Yáng's spear.
Suí Dynasty Liǔ Gùyán's "Fèng Hé Chūn Rì Lín Wèi Shuǐ Yìng Lìng Shī" (Poem in Response to the Command on Visiting the Wei River in Spring)
Watering horses at the bank where coins were cast,
Unhooking fish, splitting jade at the ford.
Wind threads tug fragrant bait,
Overturned cup recalls men of old.
Wéi Sìlì's "Fèng Hé Sān Rì Fú Xì Wèi Bīn Shī" (Poem in Response to the Third Day Purification by the Wei River)
Riding spring's purification, chasing the scenery,
Escorting the imperial carriage by the Wei's isle.
Still recognizing the old man by the water then,
At feeble eighty, awaiting King Wén.
Lǐ Yì's "Fèng Hé Sān Rì Fú Xì Wèi Bīn Shī" (Poem in Response to the Third Day Purification by the Wei River)
Mid-garden flowers and willows in late springtime,
Third day of the third month, accompanying the tour's joy here.
This day delights in the Wei River viewing,
Past years vainly spoke of crossing the Fén's verse.
Xú Yànbó's "Fèng Hé Sān Rì Fú Xì Wèi Bīn Shī" (Poem in Response to the Third Day Purification by the Wei River)
Clear breeze, bright sun fill the fragrant isle,
Imperial spring feast purifies the brocade stream.
All speak of attending the feast by Huáng Stream,
Briefly like riding a raft to the Heavenly River.
Jīng River, Ninth
The "Zhōu Guān" states:
"Yōng Province,
its rivers are Jīng and Ruì."
The "Guānzhōng Jì" says:
"Jīng, Wèi, and Luò
are the three rivers of Guānzhōng,
with Wèi, Bà, Chǎn, Láo, Jué, Fēng, Hào,
forming the eight waters of Guānzhōng."
According to the "Xīnshì Sānqín Jì" and the "Shānhǎi Jīng" commentary,
the Jīng River originates from the Western Jiāntóu Mountain in Cháo Commandery County, Āndìng.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"The Jīng River originates from Bóluò Mountain."
Gāo Yòu's commentary states:
"Bóluò Mountain is also called Jiāntóu Mountain."
Flowing southeast through Xīnpíng and Fúfēng,
it enters the Wèi at Gāolíng County, Jīngzhào,
merging with the Wèi River for three hundred lǐ,
clear and turbid not mixing.
Eastward it joins the Qījǔ River,
reaching Tóng Ford to enter the Yellow River.
The "Shàngshū" mentions guiding the Wèi from Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué,
then eastward meeting the Jīng.
It also states:
"Jīng connects to Wèi Ruì."
Both refer to this.
屬 is pronounced zhú.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the "Shàngshū" states:
"屬
means to reach.
North of the water is called ruì,
meaning to manage the Jīng River into the Wèi."
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Hán, hearing of Qín's fondness for profitable ventures,
wished to exhaust
pronounced pí.
it,
to prevent its eastern campaigns.
Thus, they sent the hydraulic engineer Zhèng Guó to persuade Qín,
to dig the Jīng River from Zhōngshān,
west to Hùkǒu,
creating a canal to irrigate fields,
hence named the Zhèng Canal.
During Hàn Wǔdì's reign, the Grand Master of the Palace Zhào Bái Gōng petitioned to dig a canal diverting the Jīng River,
starting from Gǔkǒu,
ending at Yuèyáng,
flowing into the Wèi for two hundred lǐ,
irrigating four thousand five hundred qǐng of fields,
hence named the Bái Canal.
People benefited from its abundance,
singing:
'Where to farm?
Yuèyáng, Gǔkǒu.
Zhèng Guó before,
Bái Canal after.
Raise shovels like clouds,
open channels like rain.
One shí of Jīng water,
holds several dǒu of silt.
Irrigating and fertilizing,
nourishing our millet and grain.
Clothing and feeding the capital,
millions of mouths.'"
Liú Chéngzhī's "Jiāozhōu Jì" states:
"Lóngbiān County has a high mountain,
source of the Jīng River,
now Jiāozhōu."
The "Hànshū‧Dìlǐ Zhì" states:
"Dānyáng Commandery has Jīng County."
Wéi Zhāo's commentary states:
"The Jīng River originates from Wúhú,
north of Jīng, now Xuān Prefecture's Jīng County."
Joins Wèi Passes Through Gorge
The "Xīnshì Sānqín Jì" states:
"The Jīng and Wèi merge for three hundred lǐ,
clear and turbid not mixing."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
"The Jīng River flows east through a gorge,
called the Jīng Gorge."
Qín Divination Hàn Sacrifice
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Qín Èrshì dreamed a white tiger bit his left lead horse,
killing it.
Divination blamed the Jīng River as the cause,
Èrshì then fasted at Wàngyí Palace,
intending to sacrifice to the Jīng."
The "Hànshū" states:
"The waters of Bà, Chǎn, Fēng, Láo, Jīng, and Wèi,
are not among the great rivers,
but being near Xiányáng,
all receive sacrifices comparable to mountains and rivers."
Zhōu Earthquake Hàn Blockage
The "Shǐjì" states:
"In the second year of King Yōu,
the three rivers of the western region all quaked."
Bóyáng Fǔ said:
"Zhōu will perish!"
Xú Guǎng's commentary states:
"Jīng, Wèi, and Luò.
In the fourth year of Hàn Chéngdì's Hépíng era,
Chánglíng's bank by the Jīng,
collapsed, blocking the Jīng River."
Poisoned by Jìn Haunted Qín
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"The Marquis of Jìn attacked Qín,
leading the feudal lords' armies forward,
crossed the Jīng and encamped.
The Qín people poisoned the Jīng upstream,
many soldiers died."
"Haunted Qín" see note under "Qín Divination."
Building Boats Sinking Horses
Xuē Yíng's "Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Emperor Zhāng toured north,
descended to Chángpíng, visited Chíyáng Palace,
east to Gāolíng,
built boats reaching the Jīng before returning."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
"The Jīng River passes north of Wàngyí Palace,
facing the Jīng River to watch the northern barbarians.
Qín Èrshì, about to sacrifice to the Jīng,
sank four white horses in the Jīng,
and fasted within this palace."
Zhèng Guó Dug Bái Gōng Pierced
Both already mentioned in the narrative.
Mountain Collapse Dries Up Bank Collapse Blocks
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"Yáo Mountain collapsed, and the Bóluò waters dried up."
Gāo Yòu's commentary states:
"Yáo Mountain is in Yōng,
Bóluò is the Jīng River."
"Bank collapse blocks" see under "Hàn Blockage."
Emerges from Jīng Valley Connects to Wèi Ruì
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
"Fifty lǐ west of Jīng is Jīng Valley Mountain,
the Jīng River emerges there,
flowing east into the Wèi."
"Connects to Wèi Ruì" event mentioned in the narrative.
Wàngyí Palace Chángpíng Observatory
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
"The Jīng River passes Wàngyí Palace,
north facing the Jīng River."
Also states:
"The Jīng River passes north of Chángpíng Observatory,
in the third year of Gānlù, Hūhányé Chányú came to court.
The emperor ascended Chángpíng Observatory,
decreed the Chányú need not bow,
this is that observatory."
Xú Héng's "Poem on Gazing at the Jīng River at Dusk"
Its source flows through Lǒng's slopes,
Its bends pierce Yíng's capital.
Down the rapids waves ever swift,
Round the bends the current also winds.
Its poison stream slew Qín's soldiers,
Its silt enriched Hàn's fields.
Only the traveler who has lost the ford,
Yearns for home as dusk slowly falls on the road.
Wěi Tǐng's "In Praise of the Jīng River"
It breaches channels with turbid flow,
Joining Wèi's clear ford.
Its flow also poisoned Jìn,
Its spirits once plagued Qín.
Lakes, Part One
The "Guǎngyǎ" states:
"A hú (lake)
is a chí (pond)."
The "Shuōwén" states:
"A hú (lake)
is a large bēi (reservoir)."
The "Fēngsútōng" states:
"Hú (lake)
means dū (to gather).
It is where flowing waterways gather from all four sides."
The "Zhōuguān" says:
"For Yángzhōu,
its marsh is the Wǔ Hú (Five Lakes)."
According to Zhāng Bó's "Wúlù",
the Wǔ Hú is another name for Tài Hú (Lake Tai),
because its circumference is over five hundred lǐ,
hence it is named the Five Lakes.
Yú Fān also said:
"Lake Tai has five channels,
separately called the Five Lakes."
Another theory takes Tài Hú, Shèguì Hú, Shàng Hú, Táo Hú,
Táo Hú is also called Chángtáng Hú,
located in Yìxīng.
Gé
Pronunciation: hè bó fǎn.
Hú as the Five Lakes.
According to the "Guóyǔ",
when Wú and Yuè battled at the Five Lakes,
they fought right within the single lake of Lì Zé,
thus we know the other theory is incorrect.
The "Yángzhōu Jì" says:
"Tài Hú is also called Zhèn Zé,
also called Lì Zé,
also called Dòngtíng."
The "Shǐjì" says:

had Dòngtíng on the left,
and Pénglí on the right."

"Now within Tài Hú there is Bāo Shān,
which has a stone cavern,
its depth is cavernous, none know its limit,
named Dòngtíng.

thus we know the name of this cavern
is commonly called Dòngtíng,

The "Yuèjuéshū" says:
"Tài Hú's circumference is thirty-six thousand qǐng,
located in Wúxīng."
The "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:

called Péngzé Hú,
also called Huì

Zé,
located in Yùzhāng Commandery.
Qīngcǎo Hú is also called Dòngtíng Hú.

Dòngtíng is also called Tài Hú,

Yúnmèng Zé is also called Bāqiū Hú.
