Qīngcǎo (Green Grass) and Chìshā (Red Sand)
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
"South of Bālíng is Qīngcǎo Hú,
its circumference spans several hundred lǐ,
the sun and moon rise and set within it.
South of the lake is Qīngcǎo Shān,
hence it is named after it."
Lì Yuán's annotation of the "Shuǐjīng" says:
"Lǐ Shuǐ passes through Nán'ān County,
then eastward converges with Chìshā Hú.
The lake's water connects to the south of the river and flows into Lǐ Shuǐ."
Jīng's Marsh and Yáng's Marsh
Liú Chéngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
"Southeast of Huáróng County is Yúnmèng Zé,
also called Bāqiū Hú,
it is the marsh of Jīng."
The "Zhōulǐ" says:
"For Yángzhōu, its marsh is called the Five Lakes."
Quèbēi and Lì Zé
Liú Chéngzhī's "Yùzhōu Jì" says:
"North of Líng County is Quèbēi Hú,
where Wèi general Wáng Líng and Wú general Zhāng Xiū engaged in battle."
Zhāng Bó's "Wúlù" says:
"The Five Lakes is another name for Tài Hú,
its circumference is over five hundred lǐ,
hence it is named so."
The "Guóyǔ" says:
"They battled at the Five Lakes,
this was a battle within this one lake.
Lì Zé is another name for Tài Hú."
County Sinking and City Submerging
Zhào Yè's "Wúyuè Chūnqiū":
"Hǎiyán County sank and became Zhāo Hú,
the people moved to Wǔyuán Township,
which was ancient Yuè territory."
Gān Bǎo's "Sōushén Jì" says:
"Yóuquán County was Chángshuǐ County in Qín times.
During the First Emperor's time, a children's rhyme said:
'When the city gate has blood,
the city will sink and become a lake.
An old woman heard this,
and went to peek every morning.
The gate captain wanted to bind her,
the old woman told him the reason.
Later, the gate captain smeared dog blood on the gate.
The old woman saw the blood and fled.
Suddenly, a great flood came to submerge it.
The county registrar ordered a clerk to report to the magistrate.
The magistrate said:
"Why have you suddenly become a fish?"
The clerk said:
"Your Honor has also become a fish."
Thus it sank and became a lake.'"
Fish Descends, Dragon Ascends
Zhèng Jìzhī's "Records of Yǒngjiā" states:
"In Huàihuà County, there is Jiǎnggōng Lake."
The elders pass down the story:
"In former times, those who offered sacrifices and prayed,
the lake would always send down a large fish to them."
"Records of Qínzhōu" states:
"Before Wǔdū Commandery, there is a lake.
In the early Yìxī era, a white dragon ascended to heaven from this lake."
Bronze Boat, Golden Ox
Liú Xīnqī's "Records of Jiāozhōu" states:
"There is a lake,
forty lǐ north of Héliú.
On overcast days,
when the common people gather firewood or fish,
they see a bronze boat emerge on the water,
and there is also a water buffalo in the middle of the lake."
Liú Dàozhēn's "Records of Qiántáng" states:
"Míngshèng Lake is south of the county.
The elders pass down the story:
In the lake, there is a golden ox.
In ancient times, some saw it reflecting the jewel-like clouds and springs,
its radiance illuminating the flowing essence.
Its divine transformations are unfathomable,
hence it was named Míngshèng (Bright and Sagely)."
Dividing the Wind, Stirring the Rain
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu" states:
"The deity of the Gōngtíng Lake temple is very efficacious.
Travelers passing through
all pray to it.
It can make the wind divide on the lake,
so sails go north and south.
On Rénkōng Mountain in Nánkāng, there is a flat lake.
The bottom of a boat in the lake
floats and sways in the lake,
and then wind and rain arise."
Qín Rests, Fàn Roams
"Records of Qiántáng" states:
"Ten lǐ from the town is Zhàoxī Lake.
The ancients pass down the story:
In the past, when Qín Shǐhuáng was on an inspection tour,
he rested briefly along the way,
hence it was named Zhàoxī (Imperial Rest)."
"Discourses of the States" states:
"Wǔ Zǐxū admonished the King of Wú: 'To contend with me over the profits of the Five Lakes—
is it not Yuè?'
After Yuè destroyed Wú,
Fàn Lǐ then took a small boat and roamed the Five Lakes."
Three Mountains, Five Islets
Liú Chéngzhī's "Records of Yùzhōu" states:
"In Chéngfù County, there is Cháo Lake.
The lake is five lǐ in circumference.
In the lake, there are three mountains.
South of the lake is Sìdǐng Mountain."
"Strategies of the Warring States" states:
"Qín fought with Jīng,
routed them greatly,
and captured the Dòngtíng and Five Islets."
"Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Qín rode the current down the Hàn River,
and in four days reached the Five Islets."
Péi Yīn's annotation:
"The Five Islets are in Dòngtíng Lake."
Stone Casket, Bronze Dou
"Records of Wú" states:
"During Sūn Hào's time,
Wú Commandery reported that by Línpíng Lake, a stone casket was found.
Inside was a small stone,
greenish-white in color,
carved with the characters for 'emperor' on it.
The era name was changed to Tiānxǐ."
Xiè Chuò's "Supplemental Records of Sòng" states:
"Zhāng Yǒng, while excavating an ancient tomb mound at Xuánwǔ Lake, obtained a bronze dǒu,
which had a handle.
Tàizǔ inquired among the court officials.
Hé Chéngtiān said:
'This is a new wēidǒu (authority measure).
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
when dukes and princes died, they were all bestowed with one.
One is placed inside the tomb,
one outside the tomb.'
At that time, in Jiāngzuǒ, only Zhēn Hán held the position of Grand Minister over the Masses.
Soon after, another dǒu was found,
and also a stone inscription,
identifying it as the tomb of Zhēn Hán."
White Goose, Red Carp
Liú Chéngzhī's "Records of Yángzhōu" states:
"East of Xīnchéng County is Jù Mountain.
On the mountain, there is a lake.
In the lake, there is a white goose.
It occasionally flies here,
but cannot often be seen."
Zhōu Jǐngshì's "Records of Lú Mountain" states:
"On the mountain peak, there is a remote lake.
The lake is abundant with red carp,
their dorsal fins all scarred and worn.
There is also an old plank trough.
The lofty mountains are steep and distant,
not a place for boats to roam.
Could it be that deep valleys became hills,
and these things did not migrate with them?"
Dragon's Eye, Horse Bone
Liú Zhēn's "Records of Jīngkǒu" states:
"Lóngmù (Dragon's Eye) Lake.
The King of Qín journeyed east to observe it,
personally saw its topography,
and said:
'Here lies the aura of a Son of Heaven.'
He sent convicts in reddish-brown garments to dig through the long ridge in the lake to sever it.
Consequently, the place was renamed Dāntú,
and now the water flows north into the river."
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu" states:
"Around Yúndù County, there are large lakes such as Chǎn and Mǎgǔ (Horse Bone).
When summer floods come, they become vast and boundless like the sea.
When they dry up in winter, they become flat woods and open marshes,
with views of mist and sun in all directions."
Selling Medicine, Floating Boat
Liú Xiàng's "Biographies of Immortals" states:
"Dōngfāng Shuò
was a man of Chǔ.
During the reign of Hàn Wǔdì, he served as a court gentleman.
Later, he was seen in Kuàijī,
selling medicine by the Five Lakes."
Xúzhōu "Biographies of Former Worthies" states:
"After Gōu Jiàn destroyed Wú,
he said to Fàn Lǐ:
'I will share the state with you and we shall possess it together.'
Fàn Lǐ said:
'You, my lord, issue the commands;
I, your servant, follow my own will.'
He then took a small boat and floated on the Five Lakes,
never to return."
Gold and Silver Pond, Pearl and Jade Spring
Fú Tāo's "Preface to the Poem on Climbing the Ancient Terrace" states:
"Fūchāi's Gūsū Terrace,
to the east has a crimson lake of ten thousand qǐng,
within which is the Gold and Silver Pond."
Lù Jiǎ's "New Discourses" states:
"Shùn hid gold in the steep cliffs of the mountains,
and cast away pearls and jade into the springs of the Five Lakes,
to block the path of depravity and excess."
"Rhapsody on the Five Lakes" by Yáng Quán of the Western Jìn
I observe the lord of the Five Lakes and examine its clouds and phenomena—
how magnificent and vast it is!
I consider that famous mountains and great marshes
must have records and hymns in their praise.
Thus, Liáng Mountain has the splendid ode,
and Yúnmèng has the "Rhapsody of Sir Vacuous."
Now, Jùqū
is the great marsh of Yángzhōu.
It bears the traces of the Great Yǔ,
his achievements in dredging rivers and guiding the stagnant.
Yet it alone lacks the beauty of literary compositions.
I secretly feel indignant about this.
Presuming on my lack of talent,
I shall describe it in a rhapsody.
The words are as follows:
"How deep and great!
Behold these Five Lakes,
they are the mysterious source of heaven and earth,
where yīn and yang converge.
Above, they belong to the essence of the Dipper and Ox,
sharing the same pattern as the Milky Way.
Receiving irrigation from three directions,
they are the great metropolis of all rivers.
Situated in the great marsh of Yángzhōu,
they encompass Jùqū of Wú and Yuè.
To the south, they share a body with the Long River;
to the east, they join their flow with the vast sea.
They are the retreat of Tàiyīn,
where mysterious spirits roam.
Chasing the tides, they come and go,
connecting to Pénglái and Yíngzhōu."
And so on.
Lǐ Yóng, "Crossing the Lake"
Soon passing through Yìxīng's borders,
I pause my oars at Shílán's isle.
Where is Zhènzé now?
Only Tài Lake's shore remains.
Its rounded span winds five hundred li,
Gazing afar, nothing meets the eye.
The high sky vast as banks,
Long streams tangled like threads.
Seeking secluded bends and ripples,
Gazing at distant peaks and isles.
Startled, I see flying rapids surge,
Skimming the sky, brushing sheer cliffs.
Light birds soar through the Milky Way,
Swimming fish rest in midstream shoals.
Gloomy and dim, the sky turns overcast,
Lofty and steep, boats dance on waves.
How can one risk crossing the river?
Calmly observe, warn the traveling troops.
Liú Shān, "Sailing on Gōngtíng Lake"
Turning the prow to meet branching waters,
Hoisting sails to chase divided winds.
Vast and boundless, seeming without limit,
Fluttering and drifting as if crossing the void.
Mast crows line the birds' path,
The boat's shadow vanishes in the river's palace.
A lone rock in the blue waves,
Mount Kuāng amid mist.
I send word to the noble son:
How can you know the wanderer's far journey?
Chén Yīnkēng, "Crossing Qīngcǎo Lake"
Dòngtíng's spring waters brim full,
The calm lake's brocade sails unfurl.
Source waters hold peach blossom hues,
Xiāng River flows with dùruò fragrance.
Near to Máo Mountain's caves,
The river links to Wū Gorge's length.
Banded sky clears to distant blue,
Reflecting sunlight, shimmering light shifts.
Traveling boats pause by distant trees,
Crossing birds rest on high masts.
Torrential and unfathomable,
How could a mere reed vessel sail?
Suí Dynasty Lú Sīdào, "Prayer to Cháo Lake"
On the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Kāihuáng era, jiǎzǐ day,
The official of rank and name,
Dispatching a certain officer,
With pure wine and various delicacies as offerings,
Reverently prays to the spirit of Cháo Lake,
Saying:
"Vast and clear lake,
Boundary of the southern region.
Slantingly connecting to coastal lands,
Flanking the river's branches.
Depth exceeding a hundred fathoms,
Moisture spanning nine li.
Pénglí cannot compare,
Jùqū is no match.
Yángyuè rebels,
For many years and seasons.
The royal army campaigns,
The six armies arrive.
Setting the date, pointing to the day,
The horses' heads turn east.
Constant gloom brings disaster,
Drizzling rain falls thick.
Mist gathers at dawn,
Sky clouds merge at night.
Extended by bitter fog,
Followed by harsh winds.
Mud on the roads severe,
Wheel tracks impassable.
Heaven's punishment delayed,
Thus halting the great army.
Only the hundred spirits hold office,
Among them, the water spirit is greatest.
The emperor rules the realm,
All lands are within.
It should make sun and moon steadfastly bright,
Heaven and earth in harmony.
The rain master halts his downpour,
The cloud general rolls up his dense masses.
Eastern crossing of warships,
Southern raising of embroidered banners.
Receiving Wèi Tuó's yellow canopy,
Accepting Sūn Hào's green carriage cover.
Then armored chariots turn their wheels,
Soldiers sing victory songs.
Chǔ captives gather like mist,
Jì horses scatter like stars.
No virtue goes unrewarded,
Wine flows like rivers.
Spirits, hear this,
These words are not false."
Hàn River, Part Two
The Hàn is a river of Chǔ,
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Jīngzhōu's rivers are the Jiāng and Hàn."
According to annotations in the Water Classic and Classic of Mountains and Seas:
"The Hàn River originates from Mount Bōzhǒng in Lǒngdǐ Dào County,
Initially named the Yàng River,
Flowing east to Jù County in Wǔdū,
It becomes the Hàn River.
Southeast to Jiāméng,
It merges with the Qiāng River,
To Ānlù County in Jiāngxià,
Named the Miǎn River.
Hence the name Hàn-Miǎn.
This is where King Zhāo of Zhōu drowned.
Further east to Yīnlíng,
It joins the Cānglàng waters.
This is where Qū Yuán encountered the fisherman.
Further east passing Sānshì,
The waters touch the Dàbié Mountains,
Flow south and enter the Jiāng.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng's Records of the Hàn River states:
"The Hàn River emerges from Guǎnghàn,
The Yàng River emerges from Bōzhǒng,
Flowing east to Wǔdū, it merges with the Hàn River,
The Miǎn River emerges from Jù County in Wǔdū,
Also merging with the Hàn River."
The Book of Documents says Bōzhǒng guides the Yàng,
Flowing east to become the Hàn.
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation states:
"Springs emerging from the mountain form the Yàng River,
Flowing southeast to become the Miǎn River,
To Hànzhōng, flowing east to become the Hàn River."
Further east becoming the Cānglàng waters,
Passing Sānshì to Dàbié,
Entering the Jiāng to the south.
East converging into Pénglí Marsh,
East becoming the Northern River,
Entering the sea, thus."
Huì means to converge,
Pronounced hú huì fǎn.
Meaning the Hàn River joins the great Jiāng,
Converging flow enters Pénglí Marsh,
Northeast to Nán Xúzhōu,
Named the Northern River and enters the sea.
Southern Boundary Eastward Flow
The Book of Songs states:
"Torrential Jiāng and Hàn,
Boundaries of the southern states."
"Eastward flow" see narrative.
Sunk Stele Hidden Seal
Lì Yuán annotates the Water Classic:
"The Miǎn River flows east past north of Wàn Mountain,
Below the mountain is a deep pool,
In it, Dù Yuánkǎi, fond of posthumous fame, made two steles,
Both recounting his own achievements.
One stele is at Xiàn Mountain,
One stele sunk in this pool,
Saying:
'A thousand years hence,
Who knows if deep valleys may become hills?'"
Also, Records of the Three Kingdoms, Shǔ:
"Junior Tutor Wáng Móu and others memorialized:
Previously, men of Xiāngyáng, Zhāng Jiā and Wáng Xiū, presented a jade seal.
The seal hidden in the Hàn River's deep abyss,
Its brilliance shining bright,
The seal's light piercing the sky."
Encounter Rhinoceros Slay Flood Dragon
The Bamboo Annals states:
"In the sixteenth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu, he attacked Chǔ Jīng,
Crossed the Hàn,
Encountered a great rhinoceros."
Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīngzhōu states:
"The Miǎn River's bend pool is extremely deep,
First a flood dragon caused harm.
Dèng Xiá served as Governor of Xiāngyáng,
Drew his sword and entered the water,
The flood dragon coiled around his legs,
Xiá himself swung his sword,
Cut the flood dragon into several pieces,
Blood dyed the water red,
His courage unmatched at the time.
Henceforth, there were no more flood dragon troubles."
Near Two Bié Pass Three Shì
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The Wú army attacked Yǐng,
The Chǔ ruler faced crossing the Hàn to array troops,
From Xiǎobié to Dàbié.
Dù's explanation of geography states:
Unfastening Pendants and Playing with Pearls
The Han Poetry states:
"Zhèng Jiāofǔ passed by Hàngāo,
where he encountered two maidens,
dressed in enchanting attire and wearing two pearls as pendants.
Jiāofǔ spoke to them, saying:
'I wish to request your pendants.'
The two maidens unfastened their pendants and gave them to Jiāofǔ, who tucked them away.
After walking ten paces away,
he reached for them, but they were gone.
Turning back to look, the two maidens had also vanished."
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Southern Capital" states:
"Gēngfù raises light in the clear, cold springs,
while wandering maidens play with pearls at the bends of Hàngāo."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hàn River flows east past the north of Wànshān.
At the foot of the mountain, by the water's bend,
it is said the Hàn River maidens once roamed and lingered."
Zhān Rapids and Dragon Spring
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hàn River flows east past the old city of Xīchéng County, forming the Zhān Rapids.
Vast waves surge and swell,
crashing billows like tumbling clouds.
Ancient elders recount
that a sturgeon once raised its fins and rode the waves straight upstream,
reaching here to bask its gills,
hence the rapids were named accordingly."
It also states:
"The Hàn River flows past the old city of Xīchéng County to the south.
Further east, it becomes the Dragon Spring.
Above the spring lies Húbí Mountain,
so named because its rocks resemble the noses of foreign peoples.
Below, it overlooks the Dragon Well Islet,
where the spring is several fathoms deep."
Stele Pool and Bell Bank
"Stele Pool" — see the annotation for "Sinking Stele."
Sūn Yán's History of the Sòng Dynasty states:
"On the banks of the Hàn River in Chénggù County, Hànzhōng, there was a strange sound like thunder.
Soon after, the bank collapsed,
and twelve bronze bells emerged from the hidden earth.
Their craftsmanship was exquisite,
and when struck, they produced clear, resonant tones."
Chǔ's Sacrifice and Jīng's Rivers
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"The Jiāng, Hàn, Jǔ, and Zhāng rivers
are the objects of sacrifice for Chǔ."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"Directly south is Jīngzhōu,
its rivers are the Jiāng and Hàn,
and its marshes are Yǐng and Qí."
Whale Shoal and Shark Pool
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hàn River passes Xīchéng County
and flows east past Biēchí to become Whale Shoal."
"Shark Pool" — see the annotation for "Slaying Sharks" above.
Dreaming of a Goddess and Wandering Maiden
Xú Gàn's "Rhapsody on a Joyful Dream" states:
"Long ago, Yíngzǐ roamed with his companions on the Hàn River,
and that night dreamed of a goddess."
The Máo Poetry states:
"In the south are tall trees,
but one cannot rest beneath them.
On the Hàn River is a wandering maiden,
but one cannot seek her."
Sinking Jade and Lost Sword
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Marquis Zhāo of Cài brought two pendants and two fur robes to Chǔ,
presenting one pendant and one robe to King Zhāo.
Zǐcháng desired them,
but the Marquis refused to give them,
and was detained for three years.
When the Marquis of Cài returned,
upon reaching the Hàn River,
he held the jade and prayed:
'May the one who aids me cross the Hàn and go south
be like this great river.'" Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The old city of Xiāngyáng
rests north against the Miǎn River.
Long ago, when Lord Zhāng met his demise,
he lost his sword here."
Paying Homage to the Sea and Contending with the Jiāng
The Shàngshū states:
"The Jiāng and Hàn pay homage to the sea.
The Water Classic states that from where the Miǎn joins the Jiāng,
they flow east past Pénglí Marsh."
Lì Yuán quotes Zhèng Xuán, saying:
"The Hàn contends with the Jiāng,
turning east to form the marsh."
Containing Pearls and Concealing Jade
Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīngzhōu states:
"Jīng contains jade to moisten its region,
the Hàn holds pearls to purify its domain."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital" states:
"The flowing Hàn surges mightily,
startling waves thunder forth.
Gazing afar, the sky seems to curve;
drawing near, clouds darken.
Aquatic creatures of varied kinds,
scaled and shelled beings of different clans.
Some hide flood dragons and serpents,
others conceal jade discs and gems."
Matching the Celestial River and Facing Moon Valley
"Matching the Celestial River" — see below in Cài Yōng's rhapsody.
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hàn River faces Moon Valley Mountain to the right,
where there is a Moon Slope
and a Moon Stream,
within which lies fertile yellow soil."
Golden Water and White Stone Shoal
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hàn River flows past the Great and Small Golden South Mountains.
There is a Golden Precipice,
and north of the water faces Golden Valley,
where there is a Golden Garrison."
It also states:
"The Hàn River flows east past the old city of Xī County in Wèixīng Commandery.
To the north is White Stone Shoal.
This county was originally the land of Xīxué in the Spring and Autumn period."
Seven Armies Submerged and Six Divisions Lost
The Records of Wèi states:
"General Cháo Rén, Conqueror of the South, defended Fán.
Shǔ's Guān Yǔ attacked Fán,
and at that time, the Hàn River overflowed,
submerging the seven armies of Yú Jìn and others."
The Bamboo Annals states:
"In the nineteenth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
the sky grew greatly overcast,
pheasants and hares were all shaken,
and six divisions were lost at the Hàn River."
Rhapsody on the Hàn Ford by Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn
How vast is this great river!
Its mighty flow, boundless and darkly clear.
It matches the Celestial River in name and station,
piercing the thick earth to take form.
It originates from Bōzhǒng,
drawing from Lǐ and flowing eastward.
It receives what Tānggǔ spews forth,
and bears the distinct names Hàn and Miǎn.
It gathers all streams and rivulets,
spreading the essence of the western lands.
It passes Mànshān, turning left,
circles Xiāngyáng, winding south.
It cuts past the eastern hills of Dàbié,
connecting with the Jiāng and Xiāng, sharing their spirit.
I praise the clear source's form and force,
serene and tranquil, flowing peacefully.
Scales and shells nurture its myriad kinds,
flood dragons and serpents gather to play.
Bright pearls gestate in spiritual clams,
nocturnal luminescence hides in dark isles.
Divine treasures fill it to abundance—
how could mere fish and turtles exhaust its store?
Liáng's Yǔ Jiānyú: "Composed in Response to an Imperial Command on Boating the Hàn River to Wànshān"
Cassia oars propel the pearwood boat,
drifting and swaying across the great river.
Reflections sink into the water beneath the cliffs,
waves churn, rising to the edge of clouds.
On winding banks, tall flowers bloom;
spring ponds hang with slender grasses.
I accompany songs, receiving wise appreciation,
join the feast, attending the gracious banquet.
Who says only Lǐ and Guō
could resemble gods and immortals?
Lǐ Bǎiyào: "Crossing the Hàn River"
Eastward flow, vast and deep,
southern bounds, truly surging.
Waters churn against the sunken stele bank,
waves startle the pearl-playing heights.
Stars reflect in shallow stones,
floating canopies descend on rushing waves.
Broad currents, sunset glow draws near;
long river, dawn's breath rises high.
Masthead birds turn light wings,
playful birds shed feathers in the wind.
The traveler's heart, laden with many thoughts,
sings a long song to ease the toil.
Wáng Shī's "Crossing the Hàn River, Passing Xiāngyáng"
The Dǎo Yàng's source, dredged and distant,
Flows long to join the sea's confluence.
Its waves extend to connect Jīngmèng,
The view opens near Jǔ Zhāng.
High banks sink stele shadows,
Curved shores gleam with pearl light.
Clouds darken, emerald isles vanish,
Waters vast, white waves surge.
Gazing at the river, already many sighs,
Looking afar, sorrows multiply.
By the stream, still halting my horse,
Facing Xiàn Mountain, tears would wet my robe.
Tall trees shed cold leaves,
Pavilion groves scatter dawn frost.
Shān Gōng cannot be met,
With whom to visit Gāoyáng?
Sòng Zhīwèn's "Feast on the Hàn River"
The Hàn's breadth blurs with the sky,
Boats drift, remote as immortals.
Forest rainbows reflect the evening sun,
River cranes sport in clear mist.
Accumulated waters float caps and canopies,
Swaying winds carry pipes and strings.
Joyful wanderings know no limit,
Leaving regret in these mountains and rivers.
Líshān Hot Springs, Third
The Bówùzhì states:
"Wherever a water source has flowing sulfur stones,
its spring is warm.
Some say immortals warmed it,
it primarily heals human ailments."
The Xīnshì Sānqínjì states:
"Líshān Hot Springs;
old accounts say one must sacrifice three livestock to enter,
it can dispel ailments and cure diseases.
Common lore says Qín Shǐhuáng traveled with a goddess and offended her will,
the goddess spat at him, and sores grew.
The emperor, terrified, apologized;
the goddess produced hot springs to wash them away,
later generations thus regard it as proof."
The Hàn Wǔdì Gùshì states:
"Líshān Hot Springs;
first, the Qín emperor laid stones and raised structures,
by Hàn Wǔdì, they were further adorned."
The Shuǐjīng commentary states:
"North of Yúyáng Commandery are hot springs."
The Wúlù states:
"Shǐxīng Mountain produces hot springs,
Línglíng County produces hot springs."
The Dānyángjì states:
"Tāng Mountain produces three hot springs."
The Shùzhēngjì states:
"Dōnglái Commandery produces hot springs."
The Línchuānjì states:
"Línchuān County produces hot springs."
The Lúshānjì states:
"Below Zhǔbù Mountain emerge hot springs."
The Ānchéngjì states:
"South of Yíyáng's southern district emerge hot springs."
The Liángzhōujì states:
"South of the Hàn River emerge hot springs."
The Jīngzhōujì states:
"Xīnyáng County produces hot springs,
Yínshān County produces hot springs,
Lěiyáng County produces hot springs."
The Xúnyángjì states:
"Below Jīlóng Mountain emerge hot springs."
The Shǐxīngjì states:
"Língquán's source produces hot springs."
The Yōumínglù states:
"Ài County's Fǔ Mountain produces both hot and cold springs."
The Bówùzhì states:
"The waters of Bùzhōu Cloud River are warm as soup;
all such hot springs
can heal ailments,
people from near and far resort to them."
Like Boiling, As If Soup
Zhōu Jǐngshì's Lúshānjì says:
"Zhǔbù Mountain is several lǐ south of Húláng Temple,
below the mountain are hot springs.
The mouth of the cavern is about one zhàng around,
gushing forth like boiling soup,
constantly hot in winter and summer."
The Liángzhōujì states:
"South of the Hàn River are hot springs,
several thousand paces around,
constantly boiling and surging like soup in winter and summer.
Their heat can cook eggs;
from twenty lǐ away,
one can see white steam rushing skyward."
Scorching Birds, Swimming Fish
Guō Yuánshēng's Xùshùzhēngjì says:
"Dōnglái Commandery has hot springs,
constantly boiling;
birds falling in are immediately scorched."
The Shǐxīngjì says:
"Língshuǐ's source has hot springs,
gushing and flowing like boiling;
sometimes small red fish swim out,
none have ever been caught."
Warm Valley, Soup Mountain
"Warm Valley" appears below in Liú Yìgōng's poem.
Zhāng Bó's Wúlù says:
"Dānyáng's Jiāngshèng County has Tāng Mountain,
producing three hot springs."
Curing Illness, Flowing Filth
Yuán Shānsōng's Yídū Shānchuānjì says:
"Yínshān County has hot springs,
flowing into a great stream;
in summer merely warm,
in winter extremely hot.
Above often has misty vapor;
for all illnesses and chronic diseases,
entering this water often brings cure."
"Flowing filth" appears below in Zhāng Héng's rhapsody.
Tidal Spring, Divine Well
Zhāng Sēngjiān's Xúnyángjì says:
"Below Jīlóng Mountain, in the stream are several dozen places with piled stones,
as if by human effort,
water constantly over a chǐ deep.
Morning and evening, springs gush forth like tidal water,
timing never errs,
especially large on new and full moons,
called tidal springs,
constantly like boiling soup."
"Divine well" appears below in Zhāng Héng's rhapsody preface.
Expelling Evil, Warding Off Cold
"Expelling evil" appears below in Zhāng Héng's rhapsody.
The Jiāngshèng Dìjì says:
"Forty lǐ southeast of the county is Bàntāng Spring,
half warm, half cold,
sharing the same ravine,
called Bàntāng Spring."
Zhāng Bó says:
"Cold water in summer washes
can clear summer heat;
warm water in winter baths
can ward off cold."
Soup Chicken, Boiling Eggs
Cháng Qú's Huáyángzhì says:
"Sīyú entered the southern mountain cave's warm water cavern,
constantly hot in winter and summer;
its source can make soup of chickens and pigs.
Bathing in the lower spring
heals chronic illnesses."
Wáng Yì's Luòdū Fù says:
"Jītóu warm water,
Lǔyáng divine spring,
boils without fire.
Hot as if scorching;
scorching feathers, boiling eggs,
boiling silk, washing fresh.
Yuè pronounced yào."
Curing Illness, Preserving Nature
Wáng Yì's Luòdū Fù says:
"Withered ailments, paralysis, sickness;
soaking in it brings cure.
Merit surpasses medicine and stones,
achievement renowned without words."
"Preserving nature" appears below in Zhāng Héng's rhapsody.
Warm Waves, Scorching Water
"Warm waves" appears below in Liú Yìgōng's poem.
Lì Yuán's Shuǐjīng commentary says:
"Hot spring water emerges from the warm stream north of Yúyáng Commandery's mountain,
that is the warm source.
Those with chronic illness cannot bathe,
because it is excessively scorching."
Warm Billows, Fiery Liquid
Cáo Zhí's Shùxíng Fù says:
"I bathe my body in the divine well,
marveling at the warm billows as if aflame."
"Fiery liquid" appears below in Liú Yìgōng's poem.
Dividing Cold Water, Meeting Icy Spring
The Línlíng Xiànjì states:
"The county has hot springs;
within the spring are submerged stones dividing the flow,
its shady side clear water constantly cold,
its sunny side hot springs boiling.
Flying mist like smoke;
snow and frost cannot diminish its heat."
Liú Yìqìng's Yōumínglù says:
"Ài County's Fǔ Mountain has hot and cold springs,
their sources several chǐ apart.
The hot spring can cook chickens and pigs;
the cold spring constantly like ice.
Twin streams flow several zhàng and merge,
both meeting in one stream."
Bathing the sun and moon, flying through mist and fog
"Bathing the sun and moon" appears in the following rhapsody by Zhāng Héng.
"Flying through mist and fog" refers to the annotation above for "separating cold water."
Gathering scholars and women, surpassing medicinal stones
"Gathering scholars and women" appears in the following rhapsody by Zhāng Héng.
"Surpassing medicinal stones" refers to the annotation above for "curing illnesses."
Rhapsody on the Hot Springs by Zhāng Héng of the Later Hàn
I journeyed to Líshān,
beheld the hot springs,
bathed in the divine well,
admired the vast beneficence bestowed upon all,
and thus composed this rhapsody.
Surveying the rare wonders within the central realm,
none compare to the divine essence of these waters.
Drawing from the Tānggǔ valley on Yíngzhōu,
they bathe the sun and moon within their midst.
Sheltered by the northern extension of the lofty mountains,
they dwell in secluded tranquility, serene and pure.
Thus, from distant lands they trek,
swiftly hastening to arrive.
Scholars and women gleam like scales gathered,
mingling and swirling like mist.
The epilogue states:
"The virtue of heaven and earth,
is none greater than giving life.
The emperor nurtures the multitudes,
admirable is his achievement.
When the six qì become excessive and disordered,
diseases and plagues arise.
The hot springs gush forth,
to wash away filth.
Eliminating harshness and wickedness,
they embody balance and correctness.
Glorious are the emperor's deeds,
preserving life and fate."
Rhapsody on a Journey by Cáo Zhí of the Wèi
Following the winding path to the southern corner,
I beheld the tomb of Qín Shǐhuáng at Líshān.
Lamenting the suffering of the common people,
I deplored the First Emperor's cruelty as ruler.
Bathing my body in the divine well,
I marveled at the hot waves as if ablaze.
Passing by the Hot Springs by Emperor Gāozōng of Táng
At the warm isle, the imperial carriage halts,
by the lush outskirts, morning banners are stationed.
The winding road reflects the turning wheels,
from hollow cliffs, the sound of water clocks echoes.
Warm currents startle swift rapids,
cold skies traverse azure mists.
In the woods, yellow leaves scatter sparsely,
the fields gleam white with dawn frost.
Gazing and listening endlessly,
mist and clouds intermittently arise.
Hot Springs by Liú Yìgōng of Sòng
The Qín capital gloried in the warm valley,
the Hàn capital beautified the hot springs.
The fiery virtue conceals deep fluids,
warm waves arise from this source.
Bathing in the Hot Springs by Liú Tì of Northern Qí
Lí Mountain still cherishes its soil,
Xīnfēng yet retains its homes.
The divine well can dispel plagues,
the hot springs suffice to cleanse evils.
Purple moss grows on stone banks,
yellow froth embraces golden sands.
Shaking my robes, not yet finished,
I turn to halt the envoy's carriage.
In Response to Passing by the Hot Springs by Yuèwáng Zhēn
The phoenix carriage ascends the imperial journey,
the Lí imperial park follows celestial travels.
The virtue of water disperses warm fluids,
mountain bends channel warm streams.
Cold air gathers beyond the void,
steam floats upon the marsh.
Forests wither, curtain shadows scatter.
Clouds withdraw, canopy shade recedes.
Frosty outskirts expand profound vistas,
unevenly, the setting scene grows vigorous.
In Response to Passing by the Hot Springs by Wáng Dézhēn
Holding the charts, opening myriad parks,
attending the sage, inaugurating a thousand years.
Lí Hill arranges crimson riders,
startled swans reflect on colored banners.
Jade frost brightens phoenix fields,
golden formations adorn dragon rivers.
Auspicious mists gather on perilous peaks,
swirling waters overflow from flying springs.
Halting the carriage, inspiring sagely views,
returning to chant the "Great Wind" ode.
In Response to Passing by the Hot Springs by Yáng Sīxuán
At Fēngchéng, observe Hàn traces,
at the warm valley, delight in Qín remnants.
The land connects to King Yōu's ramparts,
the stream divides from the Zhèng State Canal.
Wind's might solemnizes literary guards,
sunlight mirrors carved chariots.
Distant peaks condense heavy atmospheres,
cold thickets cast sparse shadows.
Looking back at Hàn's majestic towers,
fine qì fills the imperial abode.
In Response to Passing by the Hot Springs by Zhèng Yìzhēn
At Luò River, the imperial halt awaits,
at lush fields, the imperial carriage briefly rests.
Hot springs ever surge alone,
warm valleys know no cold.
Water-clock drums rely on cliff sides,
wind vanes emerge from treetops.
Ridge mists gather afar on grasses,
mountain moons shine distantly on saddles.
Daily blessings truly abound,
thus I gaze up at celestial patterns.
Inscription on the Hot Springs by Yǔ Xìn of Zhōu
Xiánchí bathes the sun,
first receiving the green armor chart;
Dǐzhù floats in heaven,
beginning to bear the Xuányí mandate.
In benevolence, it washes away dust and haze;
in righteousness, it stirs clarity and turbidity;
in courage, it bears mountains with remaining strength;
in weakness, it cannot support a goose feather.
In mid-spring, it flows with elm seeds;
in the third month, it descends with peach blossoms.
Its changing colors flow as five-cloud nectar;
its delicious taste congeals as Sānwēi dew.
Greener than copper streams,
whiter than lead creeks.
Not a divine cauldron, yet perpetually boiling;
unlike dragon ponds, yet uniquely surging.
Cleansing stomachs and rinsing intestines,
reviving the weak and raising the frail.
Remaining stones from Qín Shǐhuáng,
still form goose-tooth steps.
Old pottery from Hàn Wǔdì,
immediately used as fish-scale tiles.
How could sweet springs alone cure diseases,
heard of in the Jiànwǔ era?
Divine water dispels ailments,
present in the Xiánkāng age.
Inscription on the Hot Springs by Wáng Bāo of Zhōu
Rising in this warm valley,
the northern shade of Lí Hill.
White alum penetrates upward,
cinnabar sinks downward.
Huáqīng preserves old age,
flying streams brighten the heart.
The valley spirit never dies,
the river's virtue grows ever deeper.
Kūnmíng Pool, Fourth
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Zhǎo means
chí (pool)."
The *Shuōwén* states:
"Chí refers to a banked pond,
the character is formed from the water radical with 'tuó' (它) indicating its sound."
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Sūnzǐ had the saying 'a city of metal walls and a moat of boiling water',
later people based on this excavated land to make pools,
for raising fish and turtles."
According to the *Hànshū* and the *Xījīng Zájì*,
the Kūnmíng Chí
was excavated in the third year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Initially, the Hàn wished to reach the Shēndú country,
but were blocked by the Kūnmíng barbarians.
The Kūnmíng region had a Diān Chí,
three hundred lǐ square,
named the Diān Hé.
The Hàn planned to attack Kūnmíng to open a route to Shēndú,
so they sent convict soldiers to clear brambles in the Shànglín Park,
and modeled the Diān Hé to create the Kūnmíng Chí,
to practice naval warfare.
The pool's circumference was forty lǐ.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn pacified the Kūnmíng barbarians,
and made their territory the Yìzhōu commandery.
The source of the Diān River was deep and broad,
but its end was instead shallow and narrow,
seeming to flow backwards,
hence it was called Diān Hé (Upside-down River).
Pān Yuè's *Guānzhōng Jì* says:
"The Kūnmíng
was where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn practiced naval warfare.
Within it were the Língzhǎo and Shénchí,
it is said that when Yáo had finished regulating the waters,
he moored his boat in this pool.
Thus, pools already existed in Yáo's time,
the Hàn dynasty merely deepened and widened it."
Cáo Pí's *Zhìguài* states:
"When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn excavated the Kūnmíng Chí to an extreme depth,
it was all ash and soot,
with no soil.
The entire court did not understand,
and asked Dōngfāng Shuò about it.
Shuò said:
'Your subject is foolish and insufficient to know this,
you might try asking a Hú person from the Western Regions.'
The Emperor, because Shuò did not know,
found it difficult to redirect the question.
Later, during the time of Emperor Míng of the Later Hàn,
a foreign monk came to Luòyáng.
Someone then remembered Dōngfāng Shuò's words,
and tried asking him about the ash and soot from Emperor Wǔ's time.
The Hú person said:
'The scriptures say:
"When the great kalpa of heaven and earth is about to end,
then there is a kalpa fire."
This is the remnant of that kalpa fire.'
Then they knew Shuò's words had meaning."
In the pool there were gē-chuán (spear boats) and lóu-chuán (tower ships),
several hundred of each.
On the tower ships were built watchtowers,
on the spear boats were erected spears and halberds.
From the four corners all hung banners and pennants,
with streamers, canopies, and command flags,
illuminating the banks.
They also made two stone figures,
facing each other east and west,
to represent the Herdboy and Weaving Maid stars.
They also carved a stone whale.
Whenever there was thunder and rain,
the fish would often roar,
its fins and tail all moving.
In the Hàn dynasty, sacrifices were made to it to pray for rain, which proved effective.
By the time of the young Emperor Zhāo,
they no longer practiced warfare.
They raised fish in it,
to supply the various imperial tombs for sacrifices,
the surplus was given to the Cháng'ān market,
and fish then became cheap.
The *Sānqín Jì*:
"Qín Shǐhuáng made a long pool,
extending the Wèi River east and west for two hundred lǐ,
north and south for twenty lǐ.
He built up earth to make Pénglái Mountain and carved stone into a whale,
two hundred zhàng long.
The Qín also had the Lán Chí, Gǎo Chí, and Lǐyǒu,
which was the Bì Chí of the Son of Heaven of the Míng dynasty.
When King Mù of Zhōu campaigned westwards,
there were the Xuán Chí, Yáo Chí, and Lè Chí,
where he feasted with the Queen Mother of the West.
The Hàn had the Tàiyè Chí in the Jiànzhāng Palace,
within which were built Fāngzhàng and Yíngzhōu,
resembling the divine mountains in the sea.
In the second month of spring, yellow swans descended into the pool.
The Wèiyāng Palace had the Cāng Chí,
within which was built the Jiàn Tái,
where Wáng Mǎng died.
The Hàn Shànglín Park had fifteen pools:
Chénglù Chí, Kūnlíng Chí,
in the pool were upside-down hanging lotuses,
interlocking coin-shaped water chestnuts,
and floating-rooted water caltrops.
Tiānquán Chí,
above which were connecting towers and elevated walkways,
within which was the Zǐgōng.
Jǐzǐ Chí, Lóng Chí, Yú Chí, Móushǒu Chí, Kuǎi Chí, Jūnhè Chí, Xībēi Chí, Dānglù Chí, Dōngbēi Chí, Tàiyī Chí, Niúshǒu Chí, Jīcǎo Chí,
in the pool was coral,
twelve chǐ high,
one trunk with three branches,
and four hundred and sixty strips.
It was presented by Wèi Tuó,
and called the Beacon Fire Tree.
Mí Chí,
Hánlì Chí.
Bǎizǐ Chí,
on the seventh day of the seventh month, they would go to the Bǎizǐ Chí,
and perform Yútián music.
When the music finished,
they would entangle each other with five-colored threads,
calling it 'linked love'.
The Eastern Hàn had the Jiǔlóng Chí, Yùlóng Chí, Língzhī Chí, Báishí Chí, Zhuólóng Chí, Tiānquán Chí.
The Wèi, in Yè, had the Lǜshuǐ Chí, Qiónghuá Chí, Shūpǔ Chí, Xuánwǔ Chí, Língzhī Chí.
In Luòyáng, there was the Tiānquán Chí,
within which was built the Jiǔhuá Tái.
Liúbēi Chí, Yōuquán Chí, Yīnliú Chí, Mínghè Chí.
The Wú had the Tàizǐ Chí,
built by Sūn Quán's son Hé,
by the time of Emperor Míng of Jìn it was called the Tàizǐ Chí.
The Western Jìn had the Hánlì Chí, Dūtíng Chí, Língzhī Chí, Méngsì Chí.
Zhāng Zǎi wrote a rhapsody on
the Qiánlíng Chí and Lǜ Chí.
The Eastern Jìn had the Qīngyóu Chí and Liúbēi Chí.
The Sòng had the Tiānquán Chí and Huálín Chí,
in the pool were twin lotuses sharing one stem,
and hibiscus flowers with different blossoms on one stalk.
Zhòu of Shāng had a wine pool.
Duke Jǐng of Qí had the Zhāohuá Chí.
The Later Liáng had the Língquán Chí.
The Later Wèi had the Hóngyàn Chí and Liúhuà Chí.
The Later Yān had the Qīngliáng Chí.
The Former Liáng had the Xiányù Chí,
in the pool was a dragon's shadow of five colors,
so they cast a bronze dragon and placed it above.
The Southern Yān had the Shēn Chí.
Hèlián Bóbó had the Lǜlián Chí.
The Great Liáng had the Péng Chí.
In Xiāngyáng was the Xí family fish pond,
where Shān Jiǎn used to roam.
In Jīngzhōu was the Càizǐ Chí.
In Línyuán county was the Míngyuè Chí.
In Yìzhōu were the Wànsuì Chí, Tiānjǐng Chí, Qiānqiū Chí, Shuānglóng Chí, and Qióng Chí.
In Míngzhōu were the Gānjiàng Chí and Huáqǔ Chí.
In Yúqián was the Jiāolóng Chí."

Pearl Bank Golden Dike

A man was fishing and his line broke, the fish left.

The next day the Emperor was amusing himself by the pool,
saw a fish holding the line in its mouth,
the Emperor took the hook and released it.
After three days he went to roam again,
and by the pool's bank found a pair of pearls.

Emperor Táng Tàizōng's "Visiting Kūnmíng Pond in Winter"
Stone whales divide the jade-like flow,
kalpa ashes lie hidden in the flat sands.
Willow shadows, ice without leaves,
plum hearts, frozen yet bearing blossoms.
Cold wilderness congeals morning mist,
frosty sky scatters evening glow.
Joyful feelings still not at their peak,
the setting sun swiftly slants westward.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Harmonizing with Venerable Fǎshī's Excursion to Kūnmíng Pond"
Autumn light beautifies the dawn sky,
yì boats drift on the midstream.
Dense water chestnuts screen bathing birds,
tall lotus leaves hide fishing boats.
Scattered pearls encircle broken chrysanthemums,
lingering threads wind around snapped lotus stems.
Falling petals urge a bout of drinking,
roosting crows accompany a single melody.
Suí Jiāng Zǒng's "Autumn Day at Kūnmíng Pond"
Gazing at the desolate divine marsh,
travelers' thoughts are many.
Zhōngnán's cloud shadows descend,
north of the Wèi, the sound of rain passes.
Cicadas drone in the willows of Jīn Dī,
egrets drink from the waves of the stone whale.
Pearls come, shining like the moon,
woven patterns form a river.
At this moment, sighing by the water,
it is no longer the song of gathering lotus.
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Autumn Excursion to Kūnmíng Pond"
Due to quiet retirement at Bàlíng,
I linger awhile at the divine marsh.
New boats with magnolia oars,
old halls built of Yùzhāng timber.
Lotus hearts suited to dew-drops trembling,
bamboo paths revisited by the wind.
Fish lurking, as if carved from stone,
sand dark, resembling sunken ashes.
The zither meets cranes about to dance,
wine encounters chrysanthemums just blooming.
A traveler's heart and autumn's inspiration,
contentedly entrusted to a single cup.
Suí Yú Mào's "Composing on One Thing from Kūnmíng Pond: The Weaving Maid Stone"
Across the river, the charted constellations,
the clear Milky Way resembling its radiant course.
The loom's shuttle rests on the whale stone,
the mirror wiped sinks into the pond's ashes.
Boats seem like rafts crossing the sea,
pearls like the guest star arriving.
What regrets the twin moth-eyebrows' frown,
meeting autumn, they never open.
Suí Yuán Xínggōng's "Autumn Excursion to Kūnmíng Pond"
A traveler grieves the distant journey,
a cup of wine consoles the ascent.
Pond whales hide by the old stones,
riverbank chrysanthemums gather fresh gold.
Formations low, cloud colors near,
lines high, wild goose shadows deep.
Leaning lotuses spill round dew,
reclining willows cast clear shade.
Robes share the autumn wind's chill,
hearts learn from ancient ashes' stillness.
Still as if in a place devoid of people,
elegant zithers welcome secluded orchids.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Harmonizing with Vice-Minister Xǔ's Excursion to Kūnmíng Pond"
The divine pond's vista knows no bounds,
dark waves connect to distant skies.
The patterned stars resemble the Milky Way,
the setting scene is like Yú Quán.
Years have smoothed the halls and lodges,
peace prevails, oared ships rest.
Unevenly descend the ducks and geese,
intermittently arise clouds and mist.
Wave patterns open then close,
wind lines straight and also linked.
Horses rested outside Jīn Dī,
boats moored before the stone shore.
Feathered cups pour green-ant wine,
flying sun sets on crimson freshness.
Accumulated waters float profound wisdom,
bright pearls illuminate elegant verses.
The great whale still roams far tethered,
sunken ashes alone not yet kindled.
I know you summon your companions,
my short wings merely flutter in vain.
Rèn Xīgǔ's "Harmonizing with an Excursion to Kūnmíng Pond on the Seventh Day of the Seventh Month"
Autumn wind begins to shake and shed,
autumn waters now clear and bright.
Gaze flies to the Herdboy's isle,
excitement appreciates the carved whale's stream.
Shore pearls drown the dawn's waning moon,
pond ashes gather the dawn's mist.
Rafts divide, pouring into the Han,
patterned stars separately frame the sky.
Cloud light moves where waves are,
sun shadows hang within the billows.
Startled swans meet full hunting lines,
swimming fish enter stout bamboo traps.
Duckweed leaves seem on the river's surface,
water chestnut flowers resemble before a mirror.
Tall woods replace light canopies,
fine grasses become fragrant mats.
Literary splendor opens on emerald peaks,
the sea of writing controls clear ripples.
Not dipping into the sage's orchid cup,
in vain I gaze upon the immortal's cassia boat.
Shěn Quánqī, "Fèng Hé Huì Rì Xìng Kūnmíng Chí"
The imperial carriage turns with the spring,
The divine pool mirrors the Han River's bend.
Twin stars leave traces on ancient stones,
A lone moon hides in lingering ash.
War-herons depart with the season,
Grateful fish await the royal visit.
Shore flowers encircle the imperial guard,
Dyke willows part the curtained city's gate.
Thoughts wander to the Hèng Fén song,
Songs flow with feasting cups at Hào.
This humble servant, a decayed and rotten form,
Shames to gaze upon Yùzhāng's timber.
Ice, Fifth
The Shuōwén states:
"Ice is water hardened."
The Hán Shī Shuō states:
"Ice is
the accumulated yin energy of deep valleys;
if not released, it congeals and becomes hidden yin."
The Yì states:
"Treading on frost, solid ice;
yin begins to congeal."
The Shī states:
"In the second month, chisel ice chōngchōng;
in the third month, store it in the icehouse."
The second month
refers to the twelfth month of the Xià calendar.
The third month
refers to the first month of the Xià calendar.
The Zhōu dynasty took the eleventh month as the first month,
so their second month corresponds to the twelfth month of the Xià calendar.
Their third month corresponds to the first month of the Xià calendar.
Chōngchōng
is the sound.
Líng yīn
is the icehouse.
In the twelfth month,
heaven and earth are bitterly cold,
water transforms into ice,
and solid ice is chiseled and collected.
By the first month, it is stored within the icehouse.
The ruler uses it for spring and summer sacrifices
and for regular consumption.
Should sudden misfortune occur, it can be used for burial preparations.
Ministers have no icehouses;
at their death,
the ruler grants them ice.
Thus, the Zuǒzhuàn states:
"When the sun is in the northern constellation, ice is stored; when in the western constellation,
it is taken out at dawn.
For storing ice,
deep mountains and remote valleys,
where yin is entrenched and cold congeals,
are where it is gathered.
For taking it out,
it is used for court officials' salaries, guests, funerals, and sacrifices;
thus it is employed.
For storing it,
a black bull and black millet
are offered to Sī Hán.
For taking it out,
peachwood bows and thornwood arrows
are used to dispel calamity.
Sacrifice to Sī Hán and store it;
present a lamb and open it.
When the Fire Star appears, distribution is completed.
From titled officials and their wives
to the elderly and infirm,
none fail to receive ice.
Ice is strengthened by wind and brought out by wind.
Its storage is thorough,
its use is universal.
Thus, winter has no unseasonable warmth,
summer no hidden chill,
and people do not die prematurely—
this is so."
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
"Accumulated ice is called líng;
ice grown thick is called dòng;
ice flowing is called sī;
ice melting is called pàn."
Resembling Jade, Compared to Pearl
Cáo Zhí's "Qī Fèn" states:
"Plain ice resembles jade,
its texture can be polished.
Earth molded into a dragon
is damaged by rain."
"Compared to pearl" appears below in Gù Kǎizhī's fu.

The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,

In the second month of winter,

The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Water faces winter and congeals into ice;
it welcomes spring and melts into water.
Ice and water transform before and after."
