If fish do not ascend to the ice, weapons and armor will not be stored away."
River Ice Melts, Sea Freezes Solid
The *Later Han Records of Xuē Yíng* states:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ arrived at Jìshàng.
Wáng Láng sent troops there,
so the Emperor departed from Jì,
traveling day and night.
When he reached the Hūtuó River at Xiàqūyáng,
the guide returned and reported that the river ice was melting,
and there were no boats to cross.
He sent Wáng Bà to go and verify this.
Wáng Bà, fearing it would alarm the troops,
returned and said:
'The ice is firm enough to cross;
by the time we reach it, the ice will be passable.'
Thus, the Emperor was able to cross the Hūtuó River."
The *Jìn Records of Wáng Yǐn* states:
"Mùróng Huàng memorialized:
'On the twelfth day of the first month,
I personally led the expedition to Píngguō.
Relying on the majestic power of Your Majesty, akin to heaven and earth,
the officers and soldiers exhausted their efforts,
and their utmost sincerity moved the spirits.
The sea froze solid with ice,
allowing us to travel over three hundred lǐ upon it.
I inquired of the elders,
and they said there had never been a year when the sea froze.'"
Hélǘ's Icehouse, Lángyé's Well
The *Yuèjuéshū* states:
"Outside the Chāng Gate of Wú, within the outer wall, there is a tomb; it is Hélǘ's icehouse."
The *Later Han Records of Xuē Yíng* states:
"In the winter of the sixth year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng,
the wells in Běihǎi, Dōnglái, and Lángyé had ice over a zhàng thick."
Hòujì's Birds, Wáng Xiáng's Fish
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Jiāng Yuán was the principal consort of Emperor Kù.
She went into the wilderness and saw the footprint of a giant.
She was delighted and pleased,
and wished to step on it.
Upon stepping on it, her body felt a movement.
After a full pregnancy term, she gave birth to a child.
Considering it inauspicious,
she abandoned the child on the ice of a ditch.
Flying birds covered and protected it with their wings."
The *Jìn Records of Zāng Róngxù* states:
"Wáng Xiáng, styled Xiūzhēng.
His stepmother, Madame Zhū, craved fresh fish.
At that time, the river water was frozen solid.
Wáng Xiáng braved the harsh wind each morning,
waiting by the bank for fish.
One morning, suddenly a small hole opened in the ice,
and a pair of carp jumped out."
Summer Distribution, Autumn Cleaning; Stored Meticulously, Used Widely
The *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"For sacrifices, ice vessels are provided;
for guests, ice is provided;
for grand funerals, ice is provided for the cooling plate.
In summer, ice is distributed;
in autumn, the officials clean [the icehouses]."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"When summer heat is intense,
the king distributes ice as a gift.
Then the king has [the icehouses] cleaned thoroughly.
In the cool of autumn,
ice is no longer usable,
so they clear and clean the chambers."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Ice is strengthened by the wind and brought forth by the wind.
Its storage is meticulous,
its use is widespread."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"'Meticulous' means thorough and careful;
'widespread' means it reaches even the elderly and infirm."
"Rhapsody on the Ice Well" by Yǔ Shū of the Western Jìn Dynasty
I praise the broad bestowal of yīn and yáng,
and admire the vast diffusion of the heavenly way.
The myriad things are diverse yet do not overstep,
not changing their kind to interfere with others.
Some are solely yang, bearing summer's heat;
some are firmly yīn, congealing in cold.
Though their paths differ, they share the same return,
truly harmonizing in virtue and enduring together.
Thus, in the month of early winter,
all yīn forces fully ascend.
Frost and snow mingle and fall together,
flowing waves congeal and form ice.
Opening the deep recesses of the southern wall,
to ward off heat and store ice.
Mountain men gather it,
county officials receive it.
They house it in the secluded halls of deep chambers,
quiet, serene, pure, and subtle.
Embracing the profound essence of solid purity,
emanating from the river spirit and long congealed.
Thus, as cold departs and heat arrives,
the four seasons alternate in sequence.
The emperor will ward off calamity,
to guard against fiery disasters.
Then he orders the officials
to open those hidden doors.
The bleak, mournful winter wind
brings cool relief from summer heat.
It checks the blazing glare of fiery spirits,
and curbs the fierce rage of intense yang.
It halts the chilly winds of mild spring,
and stops the bitter rains of warm summer.
It preserves the people from hardship,
and enables all living beings to dwell in peace.
And when limbs or support are lacking,
or ministers and scholars perish,
it soothes spirits and fans away heat,
imposing sternness, cool and clear.
Used in handling funeral rites,
never neglecting the constant norms.
I admire the profound virtue of universal love,
which bestows kindness upon both the living and the dead.
"Rhapsody on Ice" by Gù Kǎizhī of the Eastern Jìn Dynasty
Continuous, interconnected, veiled like curtains,
now forming, now disappearing.
Suddenly, by spiritual transformation,
it gradually becomes coarse and solid.
Pale white, following the rivers,
square or round, following the channels.
Righteous and firm, it can be broken;
reflected in a pot, it appears empty.
Assuming form beyond image,
comparable in brightness to the dark pearl.
One principle governs it, ever complete;
through a hundred transformations, it grows more distinct.
Turning like startling lightning,
shining like the clear moon.
Accumulating like piling emptiness,
melting like dropping joints.
Facing hardness, it yields lightly;
responding to change, it splits into threads.
Jade shatters, stars flow;
refined essence, clear and transcendent.
"Chanting on Ice, in Response to Instruction" by Shěn Jūnyōu of the Later Liáng Dynasty
Sunlight shines on the ice's hues,
glittering, illuminating each other.
The shady pool begins to half-thaw,
the sunny bank already entirely light.
Moss patterns not yet revealed,
grass scent about to arise.
Gradually, one can watch fish surface,
not only see foxes startled.
If I met the technique of the Queen of Wèi,
it would prove ice could form a wall.
"Ode on Ice" by Fù Jiāmó of the Táng Dynasty
The northern continent vast, rivers and seas congeal;
the southern mountains crisscrossed, ice day and night.
Splendid white radiance, the bright moon rises;
deep mountains, remote valleys, unseen by themselves.
How would one know it's gathered and cut for fine offerings?
The dark chamber firmly frozen, hiding the cold fan.
The sunny spring of the second month, dawn just breaks;
spring light ripples, passing through a thousand gates.
Bright ice timely presented to serve the supreme;
the crimson court majestic, nine rituals prepared.
Jade pendants gleaming, affairs of a thousand officials;
bright ice fully bestowed, all in their positions.
Recalling yesterday, northern sands, cold winds swelled;
the Kūnlún mountains, long river, ice first grew strong.
Vast, towering, accumulating like border fortresses;
harmoniously crying, wild geese come from the river.
The forbidden garden's ponds and terraces, ice first opens;
swaying spring, containing green, reflecting towers and pavilions.
The Bīn song of the seventh month, the royal air begins;
bright ice stored for use, illuminating the tracks of things.
The four seasons never err, for ten thousand sacrifices.
Well, Part Six
The Shìmíng states:
"Jǐng (well) means qīng (clear),
for it is the clear and clean source of a spring."
The Yìzhuàn states:
"Jǐng (well) means tōng (through),
for it is something universally used by all things."
The Lǐjì states:
"The well, along with the door, gate, stove, and central drain, constitutes the five sacrifices."
The Shìběn states:
"Bó Yì created the well."
It also states:
"Huángdì, upon observing all things,
first dug a well."
The Zhōushū states:
"Huángdì dug a well."
The Shuōwén states:
"Eight households constitute a jǐng (well),
its form resembling a constructed frame."
Furthermore, the Mòzǐ states:
"Two dwellings share one well."
The Fēngsútōng states:
"A well is a standard and a restraint.
It means establishing rules for the residents,
enjoining them to regulate their drinking and eating,
so that they are not exhausted.
Long uncleaned, it becomes well mud.
The Yì states:
'Well mud is not to be drunk.'
Mud is read in the departing tone."
Unceasing filth is called well seepage,
pronounced xiè.
The Yì states:
"Well seepage is not to be drunk."
Cleaning a well is called dredging a well.
Clear water is called a cold well.
The Yì states:
"The well is cold, a chilly spring."
Zhòu,
pronounced zéjiù fǎn.
It means lining a well with bricks.
The Yì states:
"Lining the well brings no blame."
Wells include celestial wells, pit wells.
The Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ states:
"Ground depressions are called celestial wells."
It also states:
"A frog in a pit well does not know the vastness of rivers and seas."
Fire wells, cloud wells.
The Yìshuō states:
"Línqióng County has fire wells.
When the Hàn dynasty was prosperous, they blazed fiercely.
During the reigns of Huán and Líng,
the fire gradually diminished.
Zhūgě Kǒngmíng glanced at them, and they blazed more fiercely again.
In the first year of Jǐngyào,
people threw a torch in, and it immediately extinguished.
That year, Shǔ was annexed by Wèi."
The Dòngmíngjì states:
"Seventy thousand lǐ east of Cháng'ān is Yún Mountain.
On the mountain peak, there is a well
from which clouds emerge.
If earth virtue reigns, yellow clouds emerge;
if fire virtue reigns, red clouds emerge;
if water virtue reigns, black clouds emerge;
if metal virtue reigns, white clouds emerge;
if wood virtue reigns, blue clouds emerge."
Wind wells, gold wells, salt wells, ice wells.
The Jīngzhōujì states:
"Wind wells: in summer, wind emerges; in winter, wind enters."
It also states:
"Yìyáng County has several hundred gold wells.
Ancient tradition says a golden man measured the ground with a staff,
and wells immediately formed.
Some suspect they were dug by people mining gold in the past,
hence called gold wells."
The Hànshū states:
"Shǔ has many salt wells.
Luó Bāo became wealthy through salt wells."
The Hòuhànshū states:
"Lángyá has ice wells,
over a zhàng thick."
Wave wells, powder wells, mica wells.
The Ruìyìngtú states:
"When the king is pure and tranquil, wave wells appear."
The Guǎngzhì states:
"Línqióng has powder wells.
Obtaining water to wash powder makes it more lustrous."
The Sōnggāojì states:
"Shǎoshì Mountain has mica wells,
which produce mica."
Coffered wells,
also called square wells.
The Fēngsútōng states:
"Made in halls and palaces,
to resemble the Eastern Well constellation.
Zǎo means water plants,
used to suppress fire."
Lǔ Líng's "Guāngdiàn Fù" states:
"Round springs and square wells,
with lotus plants planted upside down."
Rotten wells, sweet wells, boiling wells, army wells, household wells.
The Chǔcí states:
"Submerging fragrant zhǐ orchids in a rotten well."
A well that is rotten and foul.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"Straight trees are felled first;
sweet springs dry up first."
The Dānyángjì states:
"Jùróng County has boiling wells,
also called boiling pools."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The Qièhú official orders army wells."
Golden Vase, Jade Jar
An ancient dance song poem states:
"The King of Huáinán,
proclaims his own majesty,
a hundred-foot tower reaching the heavens.
In the rear garden, a well is dug with a silver frame,
a golden vase with a plain rope draws cold water."
"Jade jar" appears below in Guō Pú's fu.
Jade Railings, Jeweled Balustrades
The Shānhǎijīng states:
"Within the seas lies the Kūnlún ruins,
in the northwest.
The lower capital of the Emperor,
ten thousand rèn high,
above are nine wells,
with jade as railings."
Guō Pú's commentary states:
"Jiàn means balustrade."
Wáng Yì's "Luòdū Fù" states:
"Jade wells with jeweled balustrades,
towering like accumulated frost.
The main hall has twin wings,
this is called the Rain Hall."
Jade Sheep, Golden Bird
The Hánshī Wàizhuàn states:
"Duke Āi of Lǔ sent people to dig a well.
For two months, no spring was found,
but a jade sheep was obtained.
Duke Āi was very afraid.
Confucius said:
'I have heard the essence of water becomes jade,
the essence of earth becomes a sheep.
This sheep's liver is actually earth!'
Duke Āi had someone kill the sheep,
and its liver was indeed earth."
Liú Jìngshū's Yìyuàn states:
"In Lánlíng, Chānglǜ County, Yǐng City has Huà Mountain.
On the mountain is a well,
with a bird nesting inside it,
golden-beaked, black, with rounded wings.
When this bird appears, there is great flooding.
Moreover, the well cannot be peered into;
those who peer in do not live a full year before dying."
Ornate Balustrades, Jade Lining
Yú Huàn's Wèilüè states:
"Before the Jiǔlóng Hall of Emperor Míng,
there were jade wells with ornate balustrades."
"Jade lining" appears below in Jiāng Yōu's fu.
Pit Toad, Valley Minnow
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"A toad in a pit well said to a turtle of the Eastern Sea:
'How happy I am!
I leap about on the well frame,
rest on the edge of the broken lining.
The joy of this pit well is also supreme!
Why not come and see?'
The turtle of the Eastern Sea had not yet inserted its left foot
when its right knee was already stuck."
The Yì states:
"In the well valley, one shoots minnows; the jar is broken and leaks."
No Birds, There Are Fish
The Yì states:
"Well mud is not to be drunk;
an old well has no birds—
it is temporarily abandoned."
The Yì‧Zāihòu states:
"There are fish in the well,
resembling insects emerging and flowing out,
or as if the well boils with five-colored mysterious pearls."
Eight Families, Two Dwellings
The Shuōwén states:
"Eight families share one well,
resembling the structure of a frame,
it is an image of a jar."
The Mòzǐ states:
"In preparing a city, place a well every fifty paces,
surround it with a screen wall,
eight chǐ high."
It also states:
"Two dwellings share one well."
Tóng Trees Grow, Peach Blossoms Fall
Emperor Míng of Wèi's "Song of the Fierce Tiger" states:
"A pair of tóng trees grows by the empty well,
their branches and leaves intertwine themselves.
The flowing spring soaks their roots,
the dark clouds moisten their boughs."
Shī Kuàng asked Tiān Lǎo:
"People's households avoid killing living creatures on the Là day;
if there is a bloody glow in the hall,
that is the first inauspicious sign.
Planting a peach tree by the well,
with blossoms falling into the well,
that is the second inauspicious sign."
Throwing Linchpins, Submerged Tripod
The Hànshū states:
"Whenever Chén Zūn held a grand feast with guests filling the hall,
he would close the gates,
take the guests' carriage linchpins and throw them into the well.
Kǒng Róng's instruction to Chāng'ān County stated:
'A local named Gāo Yòu claimed to have found a tripod in a well.
This tripod had long been submerged in the well,
its discovery is auspicious and bright,
though small, it is weighty!
With yellow ears and golden hooks,
it is an image of favorable divination.
When the state suffers famine and disaster,
such ritual vessels emerge,
perhaps clearly to be offered to people.'"
Throwing the Seal, Obtaining a Bell
Zhāng Bó's Wú Lù states:
"Initially, the Hàn eunuch Zhāng Ràng and others abducted the Son of Heaven,
heading north to the riverbank.
The keeper of the seal threw it into a well.
When peace was restored and the court settled in Luòyáng,
there was a well south of the city at Zhēn Palace,
from which five-colored vapor emerged.
Sūn Jiān ordered the well to be dredged,
and the Hàn dynasty's imperial seal was obtained."
Zāng Róngxù's Jìn Shū states:
"When the Prince of Jìn was about to ascend the throne,
Guō Pú divined about the state's omens.
He obtained the hexagram Yù changing to Kuí.
According to the hexagram, a bell should emerge from Kuàijī Commandery,
and it should be obtained from a household's well.
Later, a man named Chén Qīng from Shàn County in Kuàijī
found a bell in a well.
Its shape and craftsmanship were exceptionally fine."
Carrying Jars, Holding Pots
Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn states:
"In Wèi, there were five men
carrying jars into a well
to water leeks, managing only one plot all day.
Dèng Xī passed by,
alighted from his carriage, and instructed them:
'Make a machine,
heavy at the back and light at the front,
called a jiégāo (well sweep),
it can irrigate a hundred plots in a day.'
The five men said:
'We have heard from our teacher,
where there is the cleverness of machinery,
there must be a mind of cunning.
We will not do it.'" The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"Zǐgòng passed by the south bank of the Hàn River,
where a man was tending his garden plots.
He dug a tunnel to enter the well,
and came out holding a pot.
Zǐgòng said:
'There is a machine here
that can irrigate a hundred plots in a day.'
The gardener laughed and said:
'Where there are mechanical devices,
there must be a mechanical mind.
I would be ashamed to do such a thing.'"
Lǎozǐ's Temple, Shénnóng's Altar
Liú Yìqìng's Yōumíng Lù states:
"South of Xiāngyì County is Lài Village,
the old hometown of Lǎozǐ.
There is a temple to Lǎozǐ,
within the temple are nine wells.
Those who can enter the temple with pure fasting
will find the water warm or cool,
according to their thoughts."
The Lài Xiāng Jì states:
"In Lǎozǐ's temple are nine wells.
If one draws from one well,
the water in the other wells all stirs."
Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"North of Suí Commandery is Lì Village.
South of the village are layered mountains.
Below the mountains is a cave.
The elders pass down a story:
'The forest where Shénnóng was born;
to the west are two layered moats.
Within is an area of one qǐng and twenty mǔ of land,
in which are nine wells.
After Shénnóng was born,
the nine wells opened by themselves.'" It also states:
"Drawing from one well causes the water in all the wells to stir.
This was therefore made Shénnóng's altar.
Every year they regularly offer sacrifices here.
Fúxī was born in Chén,
Shénnóng was nurtured in Chǔ.
Examining the records and matching the charts,
it is indeed here."
Chónghuá in Distress, Hàn Ancestor in Peril
The Shǐjì states:
"Gǔsǒu made Shùn dig a well.
He and Xiàng together threw stones down to fill the well.
Shùn had hidden a side tunnel to escape."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the Well" states:
"Strange that Jì Huán dug in Fèi,
and obtained a sheep from an earthen jar.
Chónghuá was distressed and transformed into a dragon;
Zǐ Qiú used it as a mirror to forget his ugliness."
Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēng Jì states:
"At the Bǎnzhǔ Ford,
south of the ford on the plain is the Peril Well.
The elders say:
'The Hàn Ancestor fought with Chǔ,
was defeated and fled to this well.
When the pursuing army arrived,
they saw two doves fly out from the well.
Thus he escaped peril,
hence the name Peril Well.'"
Mud Undrinkable, Sweet Springs First Dried
The Yì states:
"Well mud cannot be drunk;
an old well has no creatures.
It is abandoned for the time."
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"When Confucius was besieged in Chén and Cài,
Tàigōng went to console him, saying:
'You are almost like a straight tree being felled first,
a sweet spring drying up first.'"
Rhapsody by Sūn Chǔ of the Western Jìn
Leaning against the high mound to dig a well,
facing the vast marsh's overflowing mire.
Bitter over the turbid runoff's filth,
having no clear stream for my own delight.
Then I sighed deeply and was moved,
leading a few men from the neighboring left.
Probing the earth to bring forth a spring,
raising sweet liquor from the dark void.
Its form mirrors the round river,
descending through five rèn.
Hidden springs surge upward,
moisture spreads all around.
Holding a pot to draw water,
no mechanical device is used.
Rejecting that excessive ornamentation,
I rest secure in this simple caution.
Custom favors its splendor,
I hold fast to my sincerity.
Already placed in black yet not stained,
again ground yet not worn thin.
Though shot at yet without falsehood,
truly my mind wanders in great harmony.
Rhapsody by Guō Pú of the Eastern Jìn
Yì made the well,
the dragon ascended to heaven.
He excavated the earth below,
pierced through the Yellow Springs.
Hidden sources successively arrive,
gushing and trickling.
Dark, deep, round, and still,
swirling, penetrating, profound, and mysterious.
Then crown it with jade railings,
line it with鳞错tiles like fish scales.
Turn the windlass,
pluck the sturdy rope.
Light robes fly in profusion,
hands vie and grasp in turn.
Long coils twist and rise in layers,
jade jars like dragons leap and spray fiercely.
Mist gathers, dense and dark,
thunderous sounds crash and roar.
Eastern Jin Dynasty, Jiāng Yóu's "Rhapsody on the Well"
When the Great Simplicity was first divided,
The sage responded to needs and manifested his spirit.
He elaborated the Eight Trigrams to exhaust their use,
And employed the Five Materials to assist life.
He drilled the red glow into metal and stone,
Drawing the Yellow Springs from the deep and dark.
With wind below and fire above, the cauldron stands;
With wood above and water below, the well is formed.
Thus, the great system being established,
All things follow its subtle principles.
Paths and roads divide like melon sections,
Houses and dwellings spread like stars.
To secure lasting use for every household,
They dig through courtyard steps to create wells.
Piercing through ten fathoms of layered earth,
They construct a hundred sections of jade-like bricks.
Built not in a single day,
It draws water, it is dredged.
Hidden streams gleam brightly,
Cold springs run clear and chill.
Embracing the seven virtues, it nears the Way;
Gathering all goodness, none can surpass it.
Eastern Jin Dynasty, Wáng Biāozhī's "Rhapsody"
Examining the transformations of the Five Materials,
Silent and profound, they rely on stillness.
Water encircles the earth, moistening the soil;
The moon flows across the sky, brightening the night.
Drilling wood to produce fire with a drill,
Yì pierced the earth to construct a well.
Imitating Xuánxī's divine hexagrams,
I gaze upon the flying light of the eastern lodgings.
Treading the earth’s veins,
Testing the water springs.
Square railings are joined,
The windlass is suspended.
Lowering jars to draw water in turn,
Flying thin ropes pull from the depths.
Thus, in the profound darkness of the yellow furnace,
Fresh and moist, descending in purity.
Clear waves rest in tranquil stillness,
Deep and cold, bright and vast.
In harmony with the Great Yin, it transforms into liquid,
Embracing supreme goodness, it flows with grace.
Liang Dynasty, Fàn Yún's "Lament for an Abandoned Well"
Because it was old, it was never changed;
Because it was sweet, it dried up first.
For years, no birds came to drink;
One morning, it was opened and dredged.
Since the spring now gushes forth,
How shall the short rope be set?
Already gaining the benefit of the Dīng family,
Now seeing the dredging of Lord Guǎn.
Also, "Poem on the Well"
Behold the long autumn winding path,
Dug deep before the broad courtyard.
From its source, waves already form;
By its square shape, a circle is made.
In winter, it stores warm water;
In summer’s heat, cold springs seep.
If not sweet, it should not yet be exhausted;
Once dried, no birds will soar above.
Liang Dynasty, Tāng Sēngjì's "Finding a Golden Hairpin While Dredging a Well"
Once a singing girl of old,
Plucked flowers by the dew-covered well.
Plucking flowers to adorn herself,
Gazing into the well, she pitied herself.
Peering endlessly, never tiring,
Smiling, she became lovely on her own.
Her precious hairpin fell here,
Not just a year ago.
Kingfisher feathers turned to mud and vanished,
But the golden color remains fresh.
That person is no longer here,
This object now passes empty tales.
Later Zhou Dynasty, Zōng Lǐn's "Chanting the New Well at Línzhǐ Hall"
It should be a sweet spring emerging,
First causing the wave well to open.
Copper adorns the Nine Dragon Hall,
Stone surpasses the Língyún Tower.
Zhèng Yì's "Passing by Yán Jūnpíng’s Ancient Well"
Yán Píng was originally noble and lofty,
Following afar the ways of ancient sages.
He told fortunes in the city market,
His name flowed through the great Hàn.
The old well changed with the human world,
Cold springs long ceased to flow.
After many years, dredging stopped;
No birds came, so it became empty.
How, in the autumn air,
Only falling twin paulownias are seen.
Sū Wèidào's "Chanting the Well"
Exquisite, reflecting jade balustrades,
Clear and pure, pouring over the silver bed.
Flowing sounds gather like peacocks,
Shadows emerge with the fén sheep.
Paulownia leaves fall, autumn frogs scatter;
Peach blossoms unfold, spring brocade fragrant.
What, after all, are the emperor’s powers?
Scheming hearts may here be forgotten.
Song Dynasty, Kǒng Níngzǐ's "Ode to the Well"
Heaven is high yet hears the lowly,
The earth is thick, flowing with humility.
When the blade is swung and strikes,
Even kneeling and bowing are moistened.
Only Yì’s work remains,
Virtue far-reaching, deeds manifold.
The enlightened king draws from it,
All people gaze upon you.
Bridge, Seventh
The *Shìmíng* states:
"A bridge,
is a water beam."
The *Ěryǎ* states:
"No beam is greater than the Xù
(pronounced 'zǐyì')
Beam."
Guō Pú's annotation says:
"A beam is a bridge,
some say a beam is a stone bridge.
A stone pole
(pronounced 'jiāng')
is called a jì,
(pronounced 'jì').
This is also a stone bridge."
The *Guǎngzhì* states:
"A bridge of a single log is called a què,
(pronounced 'jué').
It is also called a zhuó."
(pronounced 'zhuó').
A què
is a single log laid horizontally across water for crossing.
A zhuó,
is now called a lüèzhuó.
The *Shuōwén* says:
"People of Chǔ call a bridge a yí.
(pronounced 'yí').
All bridges have wooden beams or stone beams.
A boat beam is called a floating bridge,
which is what the *Shī* refers to as 'making boats to form a beam'.
Zào,
means 'to reach'.
(pronounced 'qīdào').
It means from boat to boat,
linked together to form a bridge."
King Wén of Zhōu made a boat bridge on the Wèi River,
the Qín prince Zhēn fled to Jìn,
and made a boat bridge on the [Yellow] River.
It was at the Xiàyáng Ford in Púbǎn,
the present-day Pújīn Floating Bridge is at that location.
Qín's capital was Xiányáng,
the Wèi River flowed through the capital,
they built the Wèi Bridge and the Héng Bridge,
crossing south to the Chánglè Palace.
The Hàn built the Biàn Bridge,
to go towards Màolíng,
they built a bridge opposite the Biànmén,
so it was also called the Biànmén Bridge.
Both spanned the Wèi,
using wood for beams.
The Hàn also built the Bà Bridge,
using stone for beams.
Cháng'ān also had the Yìnmǎ Bridge.
In Luòyáng, before the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there was a floating bridge spanning the Luò River.
North of the Luò at the Fùpíng Ford,
there was a floating bridge spanning the [Yellow] River,
which was built by Dù Yù.
There was also the Chēmǎ Bridge.
Èbǎn had the Huáng Bridge.
Wú had the Zhūquè Bridge,
through the Jìn dynasty until after Wáng Dūn's rebellion,
it was renamed the Chéngquè Bridge.
There were also the Zhī Bridge, Luóluò Bridge, and Zhānghóu Bridge,
built by Zhāng Zhāo,
hence the name.

There were also the Chìlán Bridge, Báihǔ Bridge, Jīmíng Bridge. Shǔ had seven bridges: first, the Chōnglǐ Bridge; second, the Shì Bridge; third, the Jiāng Bridge; fourth, the Wànlǐ Bridge; fifth, the Yílǐ Bridge; sixth, the Suàn Bridge; seventh, the Chángshēng Bridge.
It is said Lǐ Bīng built them,
corresponding to the seven stars.
There were also the Yàn Bridge and the Hàn'ān Bridge,
one and a half *lǐ* wide.
There were also the Yīnpíng Bridge and the Shēngxiān Bridge,
where Xiàngrú inscribed a poem.
Xiāngyáng had the Mùlán Bridge,
also called the Zhūlán Bridge.
Quèshǔ Valley had the Lǔbān Bridge.
Shàngfāng had the Guǐ Bridge.
Shǎnchéng had the Yā Bridge.
Qīnghé had the Lǚmǔ Bridge.
Zhāng'ān had the Chìlán Bridge.
Shàngyú had the Bǎiguān Bridge.
Qiúchí had the Bóshān Bridge, Fùjīn Bridge, and Lùjiǎo Bridge.
The Sì River had a stone bridge,
where Zhāng Liáng met the Yellow Stone Lord.
The Eastern Sea had a stone bridge,
who wished to cross the sea.
Later Liáng had the Tōngshùn Bridge,
in Dūnhuáng.
Later Yān had the Wǔzhàng Bridge.
These are all particularly notable from before the Jìn and Wèi dynasties.
Making Boat Bridges; Whipping Stones
The "making boat bridges" matter is already seen in the narrative above.
The *Qídì Jì* says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge,
wishing to cross the sea to view the place of sunrise.
An old story says the First Emperor used magic to summon stones,
the stones moved by themselves.
To this day they all face east,
their rugged surfaces resembling whip scars,
their posture seeming to gallop in pursuit."
Flying over the Luò; Floating on the [Yellow] River
Chéng Gōngsuí's *Luòxì Fù* says:
"A flying bridge spans the river,
boats are made to form a beam."
The *Chūnqiū Hòuzhuàn* says:
"In the thirty-eighth year of King Nǎn,
Qín first made a floating bridge on the [Yellow] River."
Raising a Cup; Receiving a Shoe
The *Wángyǐn Jìnshū* says:
"Dù Yù proposed building a bridge over the [Yellow] River at the Fùpíng Ford.
Public opinion held that as this was the location of the capitals of Yīn and Zhōu,
and sages and worthies had passed through without building one,
it must be impossible to do so.
Dù Yù said:
'Making boats to form a beam,
is that not what a river bridge is?'
He then built the bridge and completed it.
The Emperor went with all the officials to the gathering,
raised his cup to encourage Dù Yù, saying:
'Without you, sir, this bridge would not stand.'
Dù Yù said:
'Without Your Majesty's wisdom,
I would not have been able to complete this holy project.'" The *Shǐjì* says:
"Zhāng Liáng was once strolling on a bridge in Xiàpī,
when an old man in coarse clothes came to where Liáng was,
and deliberately dropped his shoe under the bridge.
He looked at Liáng and said:
'Young man, go down and fetch my shoe.'
Liáng therefore knelt and handed it to him.
The father put his foot out for the shoe.
He laughed and left,
setting a date to return,
saying the young man could be taught."
Xú Guǎng's annotation says:
"Yí,
means bridge."
Submerged Rhinoceros; Trapping a Horse
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guózhì* says:
"Pújiāng in Shǔ commandery has seven bridges.
Directly west of the city gate, over the Pí River, is the Chōnglǐ Bridge.
Southwest at the Shíniú Gate is the Shì [Bridge],
below is the spring where the stone rhinoceros is submerged."
The *Wèizhì* says:
"In the fourth year of Jǐngyuán, they attacked Shǔ.
Zhōng Huì first ordered the Yámén General Xǔ Yí to go ahead and repair the road.
Huì followed behind.
But the bridge gave way and trapped his horse's hoof,
so he beheaded Yí."
Azure Dragon; White Otter
Zǔ Táizhī's *Zhìguài* says:
"Under the long bridge at the stream islet in Yìxīng commandery was an azure dragon,
which devoured people.
Zhōu Chù waited by the bridge with a sword in hand.
After a long time, it emerged.
He then leaped from the bridge onto the dragon's back,
and stabbed the dragon several times.
Blood filled the stream,
and it died only when it reached Jùpǔ in Lake Tàihú from the commandery islet."
Zhōu Chù's *Fēngtǔ Jì* says:
"In front of Yángxiàn county was a large bridge,
under which lived an otter.
When military action was imminent,
the otter would emerge from its burrow entrance,
and howl facing west."
Hélì; Xùliáng
Duàn Guó's *Shāzhōu Jì* says:
"The Tǔyùhún built a bridge on the [Yellow] River,
called the Hélì,
one hundred and fifty paces long.
On both banks of the bridge, they piled stones to make foundation steps,
section by section in succession.
Large timbers were laid lengthwise and crosswise,
pressing down on each other in turn."
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"No beam is greater than the Xùliáng."
Guō Pú's annotation says:
"A beam is a bridge."
Wànlǐ; Wǔzhàng
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guózhì* says:
"The south gate of the great city of Shǔ commandery is called the Jiāng Bridge.
Crossing south from the Jiāng Bridge is the Wànlǐ Bridge.
Going up west is the Yí Bridge.
Going northwest from the Chōnglǐ Bridge is the Chángshēng Bridge."
Cuī Hóng's *Hòuyàn Lù* says:
"Mùróng Chuí fought Liú Láozhī at Wǔqiáo Marsh.
Jìn was badly defeated.
Chariot and Cavalry General Mùróng Dé and others led troops to intercept Láozhī at the Wǔzhàng Bridge.
Láozhī spurred his horse and leaped across the five-*zhàng* ravine.
Fú Pī's rescue arrived and he escaped."
Yìngxīng (Corresponding to Stars) Sì Hóng (Resembling a Rainbow)
Cháng Qú's Huáyáng Guózhì states:
"Lǐ Bīng built seven bridges,
corresponding to the seven stars above,
thus Emperor Guāngwǔ said to Wú Hàn:
'The army should be stationed between the Seven Stars Bridges.'"
Zhōu Chù's Fēngtǔ Jì states:
"In front of Yángxiàn County, there is a large bridge,
seventy-two zhàng from north to south.
The center of the bridge rises high,
resembling the shape of a rainbow,
erected by Yuán Jūn."
Qiānniú (Leading the Ox) Yǐnmǎ (Watering Horses)
Sānfǔ Huángtú states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng unified the world,
established the capital at Xiányáng,
and constructed palaces.
The main gate extended in four directions,
modeled after the Purple Palace;
the Wèi River flowed through the capital,
symbolizing the Milky Way;
the horizontal bridge crossed southward,
modeled after the constellation Qiānniú (Leading the Ox)."
Sānfǔ Gùshì states:
"The tomb of Hàn Chancellor Xiàhóu Yīng is located east of the Yǐnmǎ Bridge, south of the road,
now commonly called the Horse Mound."
Zhānghóu Lǚ Mǔ
Shān Qiānzhī's Dānyáng Jì states:
"The Zhānghóu Bridge west of the Great Cháng'ān Road
was originally the residence of Zhāng Zǐbù."
Guō Yuánshēng's Shùzhēng Jì states:
"Shòuzhāng County's Liáng Mountain borders the Qīng River,
Lǚ Mǔ's residence is north of the mountain.
Northeast across the water,
the stone embankment of Lǚ Mǔ's Liáng still remains."
Chēmǎ (Carriages and Horses) Chīlóng (Hornless Dragons)
Huá Yánjùn's Luòyáng Jì states:
"The Chēmǎ Bridge west of the city
is thirteen lǐ from the city."
Zhāng Héng's Sī Xuán Fù states:
"Clad in a spiritual turtle to bear the foundation,
spanning with flying beams of hornless dragons."
Jī Yíng (Striking Pillars) Zhé Zhù (Breaking Columns)
Huán Jì's Wú Jì states:
"In the summer of the eighth year of Chìwū under Sūn Quán,
thunder struck the palace gate columns,
and also struck the pillars of the Shāngjīn Great Bridge."
Yú Huàn's Wèi Lüè states:
"During the Jīngchū era,
the columns of the Luòyáng East City Bridge, West City Bridge, and Luò River pontoon bridge
broke three times.
The three columns
symbolized the Three Dukes,
and at that time, corvée labor was heavily imposed,
causing the Three Dukes to bow their heads and hide."
Bǐ Yuántuó (Like Giant Turtles) Fú Yúbiē (Floating Fish and Turtles)
Jìnián states:
"In the thirty-seventh year of King Mù of Zhōu,
he traveled east to the Jiǔjiāng River,
using giant turtles as a bridge."
Wáng Chōng Lùn states:
"A servant girl from Gāolí Kingdom
had an aura like an egg come to her,
she swallowed it and became pregnant,
giving birth to a son named Dōngmíng.
Dōngmíng was skilled in archery,
and the king feared he would harm the state,
so he sought to kill him.
Dōngmíng fled to the Yān River,
struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles floated to form a bridge.
After he crossed,
the fish and turtles dispersed."
Zhāng Fēi Duàn (Zhāng Fēi Breaks the Bridge) Wú Hàn Jù (Wú Hàn Saws the Bridge)
Shǔ Zhì states:
"When the First Ruler was pursued by Lord Cáo,
Zhāng Fēi guarded the rear,
holding the river and breaking the bridge,
so no one dared approach."
Dōngguān Hàn Jì states:
"Gōngsūn Shù's Grand Marshal Tián Róng
led troops down the Jiāng River,
reaching Nánjùn,
and occupied a pontoon bridge on the river.
Wú Hàn sawed through the horizontal bridge,
and defeated him decisively."
Hàn Xuān Dēng (Emperor Xuān of Hàn Ascends) Jìn Huì Shè (Emperor Huì of Jīn Stays)
Hànshū states:
"Emperor Xuān stayed at the Chíyáng Palace from Gānquán,
with tens of thousands of tribal chieftains and marquises welcoming him,
lined up along the road.
The emperor ascended the Wèi Bridge,
and all hailed 'Long live!'"
Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū states:
"On the ninth month, day Dīngchǒu, of the second year of Tài'ān under Emperor Huì,
he stayed at the Hé Bridge."
Wěishēng Qī (Wěishēng's Appointment) Yù Ràng Qǐn (Yù Ràng Lies in Wait)
Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Wěishēng made an appointment with a woman under a bridge,
and when the water rose, he did not leave,
drowning as a result.
Though he had integrity, it would have been better not to."
Lè Zī's Chūnqiū Hòuzhuàn states:
"Zhào Xiāngzǐ was touring the garden,
and when he reached the bridge,
his horse retreated and refused to advance.
Qīng Jī was the attendant.
Xiāngzǐ said:
'Go and look under the bridge;
it seems like someone is there.'
Qīng Jī went to look under the bridge,
and Yù Ràng was lying there,
pretending to be dead.
Qīng Jī said:
'An elder is about to undertake a great task.'"
Táng Tàizōng's "Fúqiáo"
The winding bank is not a thousand lǐ,
the slanting bridge differs from the seven stars.
Temporarily low when the carriage passes,
rising high again when startled by waves.
The water ripples, stirring patterned egrets,
the cables twist, entwining brocade flowers.
Near and far follow the wheel's shadow,
light and heavy respond to people's steps.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānyú's "Shíqiáo"
The Qín king used gold for pillars,
the Hàn emperor used jade for beams.
Immortals fly by with ease,
Taoists depart but return with difficulty.
Later Zhōu Wáng Bāo's "Hé Yǔ Sīshuǐ Xiū Wèiqiáo"
Flowing eastward, gazing at the Milky Way,
crossing southward, resembling Qiānniú.
Long embankments lead to paved paths,
flying beams span crafted boats.
The envoy opens the golden dam,
the governor commands the river's flow.
Guǎnglíng awaits the tidal waters,
Jīngxiá looks to Yánghóu.
Waves arise from old vessels,
sand swells surge into new isles.
Heavenly stars recognize the dialogue,
inspecting jade, one should sink the hook.
In vain, I delight in the "Floating Clouds" ode,
no longer singing the "Gathering Lotus" song.
Later Zhōu Zōngjī's "Jī Dēng Wèiqiáo"
Zhòngshān watered his horse at dawn,
then sat again on the Wèi Bridge.
Gazing south at the detached palace,
looking north at the scattered lodges.
On all sides, robes and skirts converge,
along three roads, officials and nobles pass.
Orchid fragrance recalls Héjì,
clouds rising bring Chénggōng to mind.
On the bridge, we knew each other early,
at cockcrow, fortunate to share the moment.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Zài Sīshuǐ Kàn Xiū Wèiqiáo"
The grand councilor holds a lower post,
overseeing duties north of the Wèi.
Fùpíng moves the lock pillars,
Gānquán transports stone beams.
Spanning the rainbow, connecting distant banks,
floating giant turtles, mending broken voyages.
Spring boats gleam with parrot colors,
flowing water carries peach blossom scent.
Star spirits meet the Hàn emperor,
the fishing old man encounters the Zhōu king.
Level embankments, stone banks straight,
high dams, willow branches long.
Admiring Dù Yuánkǎi's words,
alone raising a cup on the Hé Bridge.
Zhāng Wéngōng's "Fù Qiáo"
Building boats to float on the Wèi River days,
whipping stones to mark Qín's beginnings.
Star patterns pour distantly into the Milky Way,
rainbow shapes still soar into the void.
Already bestowed the literary success shoes,
vainly inscribed the martial rider's letter.
Elsewhere by the Láoháo River,
reclining alone, watching the fish.
Zhèng Xuán annotated the "Lǐjì" saying:
"A guān
is a gate on the border."
"Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" states:
"The guān is at the border,
used to observe what goes out and defend against what comes in."
"Hàn Shū" states:
"In the astronomy between the two rivers, there is the Tiānguān star."
"Zhōulǐ":
"The Sīguān administers the state's goods for the purpose of the guān market,
thus there is taxation for the guān market,
but during national calamities, there is no levy for the gates."
A levy is also a tax.
According to the time of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
each border had guān gates
to inspect travelers.
Lǔ had six guān,
which were abolished by Zāng Wénzhòng.
Chǔ had the Zhāoguān.
Wǔ Zǐxū fled from Chǔ,
and the guān official detained him,
threatening with the matter of swallowing jewels.
In the land of Qín, in the west, there was Lǒngguān;
in the east, there were Hángǔguān and Línjìnguān.
Now they are at Pújīnguān location.
In the south, there was Yáoguān;
Wǔguān was in Guānzhōng.
Wǔguān was the place Qín deceived Chǔ.
"Hàn Shū" states:
"When Hàn rose, it established Guānzhōng,
and stationed Guāndūwèi
to inspect unlawful travelers,
using documents for entry and exit.
These documents are today's exit papers.
Pronunciation is zhāngliànfǎn,
and equally for the following.
Emperor Wén of Hàn abolished the guān without using documents,
but Emperor Jǐng reinstated their use.
During Wǔ of Hàn, Yáng Pú was successful in conquering Nányuè,
and was ashamed to be an outsider of the guān,
thus he relocated Hángǔguān to Xīn'ān."
"Luòyáng Jì" states:
"Hàn Luòyáng had four guān,
East Chénggāoguān,
South Yīquèguān,
West Hángǔguān,
North Mèngjīnguān."
Qín had Yŭzhōngguān,
located in the border county.
Hàn had Yùménguān, Yángguān, Wǔyuánguān, Xiāoguān,
located in the border county.
Tiānjǐngguān was in Tàiháng Mountains,
Jūyōngguān was in Shàng Gù,
Jiāngguān was in Wú,
Húguān was in Shàngdǎng,
Héngpǔguān, Huángxīguān were in Yuè.
The later Hàn had Sǎnguān.
Xié Gǔguān was southwest of Qín,
Lántiánguān was south of Qín.
Guǎngchéngguān, Huányuánguān, Xuánménguān, Èbǎnguān were in Luòyáng.
Báishuǐguān was in Nánzhèng.
Juélíguān was in Héxī.
Wèi had Tóngguān west of Hángǔ,
Jīnmén Guān east of Hángǔ.
Shǔ had Yáng'ānguān.
Jìn had Mǎnìguān in Wàngdū County,
Jǐngxínguān, Gāoliángguān were in Zhào land,
Yánshòuguān was in Xīnchéng,
Qīngníguān was southwest of Qín,
Tàihángguān was in Shàngdǎng,
Hóngshàngguān was in Zhōngshān,
Báimǎguān was in Shāzhōu,
Tóngguān, Tiěguān were in Wú,
Jìguān was in Lúshì County,
Chōngguān was south of Púbǎn,
Mǎ'ěrguān, Huánglánguān were in border counties.
Northern Guard, Eastern Seal
"Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Wáng Liáng was a middle-ranking general,
and with Jǐng Dān and Cài Zūn joined forces to strike at the barbarians,
defeating them,
and Liáng was ordered to specially guard Tiānzhōngguān to the north."
Also stated:
"Kuaǐ Xiāo sent general Wáng Yuán to Xiāo, saying:
'Please use a lump of clay
to seal Hángǔguān for the great king.
This is a once-in-ten-thousand-generations moment.'"
Guests Knock, Travelers Rejoice
"Zhōulǐ" states:
"All guests from the four directions knock at the guān,
are criticized but not barred,
so travelers from all over the world are pleased,
and willing to travel on these roads."
Abandoned Six, Occupied Two
"Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"Zāng Wénzhòng was unkind in three ways,
lowered Zhǎn Qín,
abandoned six guān,
and his concubine wove pu."
"Hàn Shū" states:
"During Emperor Xiào Wǔ's time,
Huò Qùbìng defeated the Xiongnu in both regions,
dividing them into four prefectures including Wǔwēi,
holding two guān."
Qín's Deceit, Hàn's Relocation
Qiáo Zhōu's "Old History Examination" states:
"The Qín ruler sent a letter to the Chǔ ruler saying:
'Wish to meet at Wǔguān and make an alliance.'
The Chǔ ruler went,
but the Qín ruler deceitfully ordered a general to ambush at Wǔguān,
claiming to be the Qín king,
and when the Chǔ ruler arrived, the gate was shut."
"Hàn Shū" states:
"In the winter of the third year of Yuándǐng under Emperor Wǔ,
Hángǔguān was relocated to Xīn'ān,
with the old guān becoming Hóngnóng County."
Flying Bolt, Fleeing Pearl
"Hàn Shū" states:
"In the first year of Yuán Yān of Emperor Chéng,
the bolt of the Hángǔguān gate flew away.
Gǔ Yǒng responded:
'Hángǔ is as perilous as Shāndōng,
guarding the state's stability.
To leave is why the bolt flew.'" "The Biography of Wú and Yuè" states:
"Wǔ Zǐxū fled to Wú,
arrived at Zhāoguān,
and the guān officials wanted to seize him.
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
'What the superiors seek
is my beautiful pearl,
but I have now lost it,
intending to tell you to take it and swallow it.'" Thus the guān officials let him go.
Chu Border, Shu Gate
"Zhànguó Cè" states:
"Chǔ had the barrier of Fénxīng."
Huáng Kuān's "Salt and Iron Discussions" states:
"Chǔ set up guān at Xíng Mountain to resist Qín."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody of Shu Metropolis" states:
"Expand Língguān as a gateway."
Observe Defense, Why Delay
"Observe Defense" is seen in historical accounts.
"Hàn Shū" states:
"The kitchen's delivery should not stop;
why delay at the guān river crossing?"
"Why" implies asking who and stopping them.
"Why"
means questioning.
Stone Platform, Copper Ridge
Li Yuán's "Commentary on the Water Classic" states:
"On the mountain of Jūyōngguān are three stone platforms,
probably the old guān's watchtowers."
Dǒng Lǎn's "Records of Wú" states:
"On the east of Qióngchóng Mountain, two ridges meet,
named Copper Ridge."
White Horse, Green Ox
Liú Xiàng's "Seven Summaries" states:
"Gōngsūn Lóng used the argument of the white horse to pass through the guān."
"Guān Officials' Inner Records" states:
"In the first year of Zhōu's Yuan Extreme,
with the year being Guǐchǒu,
on the 25th day of the twelfth lunar month,
Lǎozǐ passed through Hángǔguān.
The guān official Yǐn Xǐ had instructed the gate officials earlier:
'If an old man from the east rides a green ox in a humble cart,
do not allow him to pass through the guān.'
That day, indeed, an old man riding a green ox cart sought to pass.
Presented Yǐn Xǐ with "Tao Te Ching" of five thousand words."
Abandoning Reed, Removing Seal
"Hàn Shū" states:
"Initially, Zhōngjūn, from Jinan, was to visit a Bóshì;
upon entering the guān on foot,
the guān official offered a reed,
which he discarded and left."
Fàn Yè's "Later Hàn Shū" states:
"Lǐ Gù was an official of Guǎnghàn, Luò County,
upon reaching Bàishuǐguān,
removed his seal and returned to Hànzhōng."
Wrapped Transmission Sealed Pass
Zhāng Yíng's *Hànnán Jì* states:
"Guō Dān abandoned his army and went into seclusion,
wrapped his insignia,
and went out through Wǔguān to pay respects to Gēngshǐ."
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Guō Dān, styled Shǎoqīng,
first went to Cháng'ān,
and bought a pass to enter the frontier.
After entering,
he sealed the pass and gave it to a beggar,
sighing:
'I will not leave the frontier unless I ride in an envoy's carriage.'"
White Water Blue Mud
Liú Chéngzhī's *Liángzhōu Jì* states:
"One hundred and eighty lǐ southwest of the frontier region,
there is Báishuǐ Guān,
where Lǐ Gù once surrendered his seal and ribbon."
Sūn Yán's *Sòng Shū* states:
"When Gāozǔ launched the northern expedition,
Shěn Tiánzǐ entered Wǔguān,
and stationed at Qīngní.
Yáo Hóng personally led a large force of tens of thousands and suddenly arrived at Qīngní Guān."
Spring Dipper Winter Legs
*Tàigōng Jīnguì* states:
"In the third month of spring, the Dipper Star is the Celestial Pass.
If you fight with your back to the Celestial Pass,
facing the Celestial Beam,
the enemy cannot be withstood."
It also states:
"In winter, the Legs Star is the Celestial Pass."
Rooster Crows Horse Enters
*Shǐjì* states:
"The King of Qín imprisoned Lord Mèngcháng,
who then changed his name and surname,
and arrived at Hángǔ Guān at midnight.
According to the frontier law,
travelers were allowed to depart at the rooster's crow.
Lord Mèngcháng feared pursuit would catch up,
and among his followers was one of lowly status
who could imitate a rooster's crow.
Thus, they issued the travel permit and departed,
and shortly after, the pursuers indeed arrived."
Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòngmíng Jì* states:
"Dōngfāng Shuò obtained a divine horse,
nine chǐ tall.
Emperor Wǔ asked Shuò what kind of beast it was,
and Shuò replied:
'This horse was ridden by the Queen Mother in her carriage of divine light,
when she went to visit the dwelling of the Lord of the East.
She left this horse to graze in the fields of magical mushrooms,
and I, at the Lord of the East's altar,
rode it around the sun three times,
and this horse entered the Hàn frontier gate before it was even closed.'"
Golden City Jade Gate
Kàn Yīn's *Shàngdì Shísānzhōu Jì* states:
"Jīnchéng Commandery has Jīnchéng Guān."
*Hàn Shū* states:
"Shàngdǎng has Jǐng Guān,
and Dūnhuáng Lónglè has Yùmén Guān and Yáng Guān."
Recognize Strange Speech Prohibit Wandering Officials
*Lǐjì* states:
"The frontier enforces prohibitions to inspect,
prohibiting strange clothing,
and recognizing strange speech."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Inspect,
means to question and examine."
*Jiǎzǐ* states:
"The frontier is used to prohibit wandering officials from the feudal lords,
so they cannot leave."
Lapel and Belt, Throat Strike the Watchman's Clapper, Reverse Resistance
Lǐ Yóu's *Hángǔ Guān Míng* states:
"Hángǔ is strategically important,
like a lapel and belt, a throat."
Zhāng Héng's *Xījīng Fù* states:
"The frontier gates resist in reverse,
and Hàn can endure for a long time."
Also, his *Dōngjīng Fù* states:
"When Hángǔ strikes the watchman's clapper from east to west,
the court is overturned and cannot be upheld."
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's *Hángǔ Guān Fù*
Oh, the splendid achievements of the Imperial Hàn,
encompassing the eight extremes and occupying the center.
Blending the boundless vastness,
only the Táng Code reaches the highest honor.
All nations rejoice and are thoroughly harmonious,
flowing toward the heavenly thoroughfare.
The strategic and secure lapel and belt,
control the key points to capture and restrain.
To the south, there are Cāngwú and Lìpǔ,
Líshuǐ and Xièmù,
Huáipǔ and Língzhōng,
reaching the ends of sea and land.
To the north, there are Xiāojū and Tiānjǐng,
Húkǒu and Shíxíng,
crossing Yuè, Dài, and Shuò,
to face the Hú court.
Along the border, slanting and pointing,
meeting at Yáng and Yùmén.
Ascending and measuring, pushing like dragons,
some are placed to the west.
To the west, there are Suílǒng and Wǔyí,
Báishuǐ and Jiānglíng.
Miǎn and Hàn are winding and obstructed,
the roads, fields, mountains, and springs.
The surging waters overflow widely,
connecting settlements along the way.
Thus, I gaze all around and observe broadly,
passing through many frontiers to let my eyes wander.
Only the magnificent splendor of the expansive and broad,
alas, none is greater than Hángǔ.
Jìn Jiāng Tǒng's *Hángǔ Guān Fù*
I ascend that Hángǔ,
and gaze upon the hills and mounds.
The terrain is perilous and winding,
mountain ridges connecting one after another.
Deep ravines descend layer upon layer,
long peaks rise again and again.
Below, dark and dim, obscure and shadowy,
above, lofty and high, elevated and grand.
Girded by the Hé and Luò rivers,
doubly fortified by the Xiáo obstacles.
Managing and planning the capital region,
relying on natural strongholds to set up defenses.
Strange clothing is questioned,
odd speech is inspected.
Stop wickedness before it sprouts,
suppress evil and falsehood at its budding stage.
And when Wénzhòng neglected this,
he violated benevolence and received condemnation.
The sage kings established laws,
to guard against excess.
Ten thousand lǐ follow the proper course,
and the borders are not invaded.
Pacify the four barbarians and guard the frontiers,
how can one rely solely on high mountains and steep cliffs?
Those like Jié and Zhòu who fell,
did not lack deep mountains and rivers.
Consider Jìn Píng's love of strategic terrain,
and obtain Rǔ Shū's loyal admonition.
Despise Wèi Wǔ's loss of will,
praise Wú Qǐ's broad-mindedness.
In the declining age, decay sets in,
detesting the Yíng clan's rebellion and dispersion,
they thus increased their own defenses because of this.
Below, encroachment; above, neglect,
mountains crumble and peaks collapse.
Observing Lord Mèngcháng's escape,
relying on broad love and many favors.
Only the seven states' western expedition,
looked up at this obstacle and trembled with fear.
Was it that the hidden peril was difficult to assault,
or that the many commanders lacked courage?
Alas, Hàn Gāozǔ's cutting off the frontier,
was again defeated by the powerful Xiàng.
Yǐn Xǐ dwelled here,
observing the subtle and studying emotions.
Lǎozi journeyed west,
leaving behind the five thousand words.
After Zhāng Lù entered,
Ránghóu then fell.
When Yínglíng departed,
the foundation for building arose.
Wèi Yāng and Shāng,
lost their clan and ruined their names.
Zhōng Jūn discarded his pass,
holding his insignia, flying to glory.
Seeing the superficial falsity of the vulgar end-times,
I long for the profound truth of the great hall.
Táng Tàizōng's *Entering Tóng Guān*
Xiáo and Hán are famed for perilous terrain,
like a lapel and belt, they fortify the two capitals.
Frosty peaks directly overlook the road,
icy rivers curve around the city.
Ancient trees cast uneven shadows,
cold gibbons utter intermittent cries.
Officials and nobles come and go, meeting here,
wind and dust startle morning and evening.
Lofty talks precede the horse crossing,
false dawn anticipates the rooster's crow.
Discarding the pass, I cherish distant ambitions,
sealing the mud, I bear heroic sentiments.
If there had been the aura of a true man,
why care about fame or anonymity?
Chén Zhōu Hóngzhèng, "Entering Wǔguān"
Wǔguān established as a strategic terrain,
Travelers delight in its winding paths.
Generals descend as if from heaven,
Young boys discard their passes to enter.
Sweat waved off forms clouds and rain,
Carriages and horses stir up dust and dirt.
Do not trust the crowing of the rooster,
At dawn, do not open the gates too soon.
Suí Yú Mào, "Quatrain on Entering the Pass"
Lǒng's clouds hang low, never dispersing,
The Yellow River, choked, flows on again.
Passes and mountains stretch for many miles,
Connecting layers upon layers of sorrow.
Xú Xiánfēi, "Autumn Wind at Hángǔ, in Response to an Imperial Decree"
Autumn winds rise at Hángǔ,
Northern chill stirs rivers and mountains.
Reclining pines crown a thousand peaks,
Mingled rain falls between the two imperial tombs.
Weeping clouds grieve over vast marshes,
The setting sun casts gloom upon the heavy gates.
At this moment, purple aura drifts forth,
In response to the decree, the true man returns.
Lái Jì, "Quatrain on Departing from Yùguān"
Reining in, I follow the path of the Dragon's River,
Bridle in mouth, I cross Yùguān.
Today, beyond the flowing sands,
I shed tears, yearning to return alive.
Lǐ Xíngyán, "Crossing a Ruined Pass on an Autumn Evening"
The Qín outskirts level the old dangers,
The virtue of Zhōu cherishes the remaining people.
First hearing the night watch's clapper in the clear night,
Soon seeing the fallen sealed mud.
Scenes and sights come without limit,
The ferry and road depart without confusion.
In the empty pavilion, who asks about the horse?
At the frontier garrison, only the rooster crows.
The mountain moon grows colder, clearer still,
The river wind at dawn turns even more desolate.
I offer these words to Yáng Bóqǐ,
No longer is this the land west of the pass.
Sòng Zhīwèn, "Passing Hángǔ Pass"
For two hundred and forty years,
The seas and rivers grew turbulent.
The six states united their armies,
The seven powers' strength remained undivided.
Following plans to resist the Qín emperor,
Strategies were decided by asking Lord Sū.
With roosters crowing and dogs stealing,
They judged virtue, not merit.
Yáng Qízhé, "Passing Hángǔ Pass"
The perilous terrain lies north of Xiáolíng,
The route passes east of Fēnshǎn.
Winding springs and stones come to an end,
Desolate and empty, the ancient fortress stands.
River light flows with the dawn sun,
Tree shadows scatter in the morning wind.
Today, the sage's virtue knows no bounds,
Where, then, is the land within the passes?
Later Hàn Cuī Yuàn, "Admonition for the Frontier Commandant"
Vast and boundless are the nine provinces,
Guarded by passes and fords.
Táng Yáo accumulated virtue,
The three dynasties cultivated benevolence.
But when the last rulers strayed from the proper path,
They lost their people.
Sages and worthies went unused,
Stubborn and deceitful men were held dear.
Hàn breached Wǔguān,
Xiàng Yǔ shattered Hángǔ.
The Qín prince Zǐyīng,
Was strangled, made a captive slave.
You, commandant, guard the pass,
I dare to warn those who come and go.
General Preface: Provinces and Commanderies, First
The *Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng* states:
"Heaven has nine paths,
earth has nine provinces.
Heaven has nine divisions and eight guiding principles,
earth has nine provinces and eight pillars.
The ruins of Kūnlún,
below are caverns containing the right,
the province of Chìxiàn,
this is the central standard.
The southeast is called Shénzhōu,
due south is called Yíngzhōu,
also called Cìzhōu.
The southwest is called Róngzhōu,
due west is called Shízhōu.
The center is called Jìzhōu,
the northwest is called Zhùzhōu,
also written as Kuòzhōu.
Due north is called Xuánzhōu,
also called Gōngzhōu,
and also called Qízhōu.
The northeast is called Xiánzhōu,
also written as Bózhōu.
Due east is called Yángzhōu.
Under heaven are nine provinces,
internally conforming to the central region,
to fully manifest the transformations of the earth."
The *Zōuzǐ* states:
"Zhōngguó within the world,
occupies only one part out of eighty-one!
Zhōngguó is named Chìxiàn,
within Chìxiàn there are nine provinces,
these are the nine provinces ordered by Yǔ.
They cannot be counted as the number of provinces,
outside Zhōngguó there are nine regions like the Chìxiàn province,
called the nine continents.
There are marginal seas encircling them,
like one area within,
then constitutes one continent,
there are nine such.
Then there is a great encircling ocean surrounding their exterior,
at the edge of heaven and earth."
The *Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng* states:
"Southeast of Kūnlún, a land five thousand lǐ square,
is named Shénzhōu.
Within it are five mountains,
where emperors and kings reside."
The *Shàngshū* states:
"Yǔ distinguished the nine provinces,
the nine provinces were thus harmonized."
Yáo encountered the great flood,
and had Yǔ control it.
When Shùn ascended the throne,
he divided Jìzhōu into Yōuzhōu and Bìngzhōu,
divided Qīngzhōu into Yíngzhōu,
initially establishing twelve provinces.
Yǔ received the mandate,
and restored them to nine provinces.
Yīn Tāng received the mandate,
and followed the nine provinces of Xià.
The *Hétú* states:
"The nine provinces have distinct characteristics,
their waters and springs, hardness and softness, each differ.
Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu: jiǎo and yǔ gather,
broad, relaxed, and slow,
people's voices are gentle,
their springs are sour and salty;
Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu: jiǎo and zhǐ meet,
their qi is floating and light,
people's voices are urgent,
their springs are sour and bitter;
Liángzhōu: shāng and zhǐ connect,
firm, brave, and floating,
people's voices are hoarse,
their springs are bitter and acrid;
Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu: gōng and zhǐ combine,
peaceful, calm, and thoughtful,
people's voices are upright,
their springs are sweet and bitter;
Yōngzhōu and Jìzhōu: combine shāng and yǔ,
upright, swift, and intense,
people's voices are sharp,
their springs are acrid and salty."
The *Yúdìzhì* states:
"By the time of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the Duke of Zhōu served as regent,
fixed the offices and divided the duties,
altered Yǔ's nine provinces,
merging Xúzhōu and Liángzhōu into Qīngzhōu and Yōngzhōu,
and dividing the domain of Jìzhōu into the two provinces of Yōu and Bìng.
According to the laws of the Grand Minister over the Masses,
five dǎng constitute a zhōu.
The Director of Territorial Affairs was in charge of the lands under heaven,
distinguishing the states of the nine provinces.
The Guardian Astrologer was in charge of astronomy,
using star territories to distinguish the lands of the nine provinces.
The states that were enfeoffed,
all had allocated stars,
to observe good and ill fortune.
Qín Shǐhuáng unified the world,
divided and established thirty-six commanderies,
these thirty-six being:

Sānchuān, Hédōng, Nányáng, Nánjùn, Jiǔjiāng, Zhāngjùn, Kuàijī, Yǐngchuān, Dàngjùn, Sìshuǐ, Xuējùn, Dōngjùn, Lángyé, Qíjùn, Shànggǔ, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, Liáoxī, Liáodōng, Dàijùn, Jùlù, Hándān, Shàngdǎng, Tàiyuán, Yúnzhōng, Jiǔyuán, Yànmén, Shàngjùn, Lǒngxī, Běidì, Hànzhōng, Bājùn, Shǔjùn, Qiánzhōng, Chángshā.
Altogether thirty-five,
with Nèishǐ making thirty-six.
Each commandery governed counties.
A county with ten thousand households or more had a magistrate (lìng),
less than ten thousand households had a chief (zhǎng).
Having pacified the Bǎiyuè,
he further established four commanderies,
Mǐnzhōng, Nánhǎi, Guìlín, Xiàngjùn.
Totaling forty commanderies.
Each commandery established one governor (shǒu), one assistant (chéng), and two commandants (wèi) to administer it,
the Inspectorate Attendant Censor was in charge of supervising the various commanderies.
The Hàn possessed the world,
establishing both kingdoms and commanderies for kings and marquises,
reaching the time of Emperor Píng,
households and population had multiplied.
Altogether, sixty-seven new kingdoms and commanderies were established,
combined with the thirty-six of Qín, making one hundred and three.
They changed the Zhōu's Yōngzhōu to Liángzhōu,
restored the Xià's two provinces of Xú and Liáng,
and changed Liáng to Yì.

in the south they had Jiāozhǐ,

altogether thirteen regions."

Yá Province this is.
There were a total of one thousand five hundred and fifty-one counties.
By the fourteenth year,
the West conquered Gāochāng,
and also established the Xī Province Duòhù Prefecture and Tíng Province,
adding six counties,
making a total of three hundred and sixty provinces before.
They are organized into ten circuits as.
Nine Surroundings Hundred Commanderies
"Mao Poetry" states:
"The Emperor commands within the nine surroundings."
"Book of Han" states:
"In total, there are one hundred and three commanderies and kingdoms."
Eight Assists Nine Provinces
Zhāng Héng, "Língxiàn" states:
"Central Province contains spirits,
externally governs eight assists."
"Shang Shu" states:
"Yǔ divided the nine provinces."
Nine Territories Ten Capitals
"Shang Shu" states:
"With the army of the nine territories,
thereby correct the Xia's calendar."
The commentary says:
"The nine territories,
refer to the nine provinces."
"Great Commentary on Shang Shu" states:
"Five lis make a city,
ten lis make a capital,
ten capitals make a division,
each province has eleven divisions."
Divine Province Auxiliary Counties
"The River Diagram" states:
"Five thousand li southeast of Kunlun is Divine Province."
"Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Zhōngguó, the red county,
is surrounded by the auxiliary sea."
Three Assists Six Commanderies
"Book of Han" states:
"Jīngzhào Commandant,
Zuǒ Fèngyì,
Yòu Fúfēng are the three assists.
Jīnchéng, Lǒngxī, Tiānshuǐ, Āndìng, Běidì, Shàngdū are the six commanderies."
Six Assists Three Rivers
"Book of Han":
"Wéi Zhāo considers Hé Dōng, Hé Nán, and Hé Nèi as the three rivers,
encompassing the three assists to become six assists."
Distinct Headings Encompassing Types
"The River Diagram" states:
"The nine provinces have distinct headings,
waters and springs differ in hardness and softness."
"Chunqiu's Explanations" states:
"Province's name means distinction,
means distinction encompassing similar types,
different boundaries."
Liáng Bīn Xú Lǔ
"Book of Han":
"The name of Yōng Province was changed to Liáng Province."
"Shang Shu" states:
"Sea Dài and Huái are Xú Province."
"Han Official Explanation" states:
"Liáng Bīn is the black water,
Xú Lǔ is only the Yí."
"Qi Annals and Nations Annals Appraisal" by Xiāo Zǐxiǎn
The commanderies and nations were established,
thereby dividing provinces into parts.
Exceeding thirteen in division,
combining not exceeding nine.
Segmenting cities and listing townships,
names and titles flourish.
The merging and relocating of regions,
generations of kings and replacing generations.
The Second Henan Circuit
The Hénán Circuit comprises the territories of the four ancient provinces of Yù, Xú, Qīng, and Yǎn from the Tribute of Yǔ.
The *Shàngshū* states:
"Between the Jīng and Hé rivers is Yùzhōu;
between the Jì and Hé rivers is Yǎnzhōu;
from the sea and Dài mountains to the Huái river is Xúzhōu;
the sea and Dài mountains are Qīngzhōu."
According to the *Shàngshū*, Yǎnzhōu's northwest boundary reached the Hé river,
referring to the ancient Nine Rivers.
The Nine Rivers silted up,
and today's Bódé in Héběi,
Cānglì and other prefectures,
which were originally the territory of ancient Yǎnzhōu,
now belong to the Héběi Circuit.
The *Treatise on Astronomy* in the *Hànshū* states:
"Fáng and Xīn correspond to Yùzhōu;
Xū corresponds to Qīngzhōu;
Kuí, Lóu, and Wèi correspond to Xúzhōu;
Jiǎo, Kàng, and Dī correspond to the celestial division of Yǎnzhōu."
Its northern boundary reaches the Hé river,
east to the sea,
south to the Huái river,
west to the Jīng mountains,
encompassing all this land.
Hénán Prefecture is the land of Zhōu,
where wind and rain converge,
and yīn and yáng harmonize.
When the sun reaches its zenith, the gnomon's shadow measures one foot five inches;
this is called the center of the earth.
Long ago, Duke Zhōu established the city of Luòyì,
and King Píng resided there.
Sòng Prefecture is the land of Sòng,
within the ancient territory of Yùzhōu.
It is the ancient Shāngqiū,
the ruins of Èbó.
The Zhōu enfeoffed Wēizǐ there,
establishing the state of Sòng.
The *Treatise on Geography* in the *Hànshū* states:
"Fáng and Xīn correspond to Yùzhōu,
the celestial division of Sòng."
During the Hàn dynasty, Prince Xiào of Liáng made it his capital.
Qīngzhōu is the land of Qí,
the ancient ruins of Shuǎngjiūshì.
The Zhōu enfeoffed Tàigōng at Yíngqiū, establishing Qí.
Today it is Línzī County.
Yǎnzhōu is the land of Lǔ,
Lǔ being today's Qūfù County.
According to the *Treatise on Geography* in the *Hànshū*:
"Kuí and Lóu correspond to Lǔ,
belonging to ancient Xúzhōu."
It is the ancient ruins of Shàohàoshì.
The Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of Duke Zhōu as Marquis of Lǔ.
Chén Prefecture is the land of Chén,
within the ancient territory of Yùzhōu.
When King Píng moved east,
Duke Wǔ of Zhèng resided there.
Today it is Xīnzhèng.
Later, Marquis Āi of Hán destroyed Zhèng and occupied its territory.
Hán Zhēnzǐ initially had his capital at Píngyáng north of the Hé river;
Marquis Āi moved it here.
From Yù and Xǔ in the east,
passing through Rǔ and Dèng and westwards, he obtained Yángzhái of Hénán Prefecture,
Fúchāng,
Xīn'ān,
all Hán territory.
According to the *Treatise on Geography* in the *Hànshū*,
Chén, Hán, and Zhèng all share the celestial division of Jiǎo, Kàng, and Dī.
Biàn Prefecture is the land of Wèi.
Wèi initially resided north of the Hé river;
Wèi Jiàng moved to Ānyì.
King Huì, because Ānyì was close to Qín,
then moved the capital here,
which is today's Dàliáng city in Biàn Prefecture.
It obtained the territory of Huá Prefecture in Hénán,
and the eastern borders of several prefectures like Zhèng and Yù that were part of Hán were annexed to Wèi.
The *Treatise on Geography* states:
"Wèi
corresponds to the celestial division of Zīxī and Shēn."
Imperial Terrace Celestial Chamber
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"At Gǔzhōng mountain,
the Imperial Terrace is where the hundred spirits are feasted with wine."
Guō Pú's commentary states:
"Raising cups for feasts and gatherings
takes place at this mountain.
Now, according to examination, this mountain lies southwest of Yīquē."
The *Shǐjì* states:
"King Wǔ of Zhōu said:
'I gaze south towards the foothills of the sacred mountain,
look afar upon the Yī and Luò rivers,
not far from the Celestial Chamber.
I established Zhōu's dwelling at Luòyì and then departed.'"
Horse Slope Dragon Gate
Dài Yánzhī's *Record of a Western Campaign* states:
"Proceeding forward, one reaches Huángmǎ Slope, ten lǐ from Jìsùxù."
The *Appended Judgments of the Yìjīng* states:
"Yǔ cut through the Dragon Gate,
opened up Yīquē."
Máng Heights Luò River
The *Record of the Western Mountains* states:
"The Máng mountains connect west to the eastern wall,
with slopes and heights linked together."
Cáo Zhí's *Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò* states:
"Leisurely in the sunny woods,
gazing over the Luò river."
Eight Passes Four Impregnable Points
Lì Yuán's commentary on the *Water Classic* states:
"Emperor Líng of Hàn appointed Hé Jìn as Grand General,
stationing soldiers of the five barracks at Dūtíng,
and established eight pass commandants at Yīquē, Hángǔ, Guǎngchéng, Dàgǔ, Huányuán, Xuánmén, Píngjīn, and Mèngjīn."
The *Records of Luòyáng* states:
"With Chénggāo to the left,
Hángǔ to the right,
Yīquē in front,
and Mèngjīn at the back,
these form the four impregnable strongholds."
Huányuán Jiárǔ
Kǎn Yǐn's *Records of the Thirteen Provinces* states:
"The Huányuán road has twelve bends in total;
now, according to examination, it lies southeast of Gōushì County."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"King Chéng placed the tripods at Jiárǔ."
Nine Slopes Three Rivers
The *Account of King Mù of Zhōu* states:
"The Son of Heaven ascended westwards the nine slopes."
Guō Pú's commentary:
"Now, ten lǐ from Xīn'ān County there are nine slopes."
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Duke Xiāng of Qín initially established the Sānchuān commandery in Zhōu territory."
Golden Valley Bronze Camels
Guō Yuánshēng's *Record of a Campaign* states:
"Jīngǔ is a valley.
The land has a Golden River,
which flows south from the Tàibái source through this valley,
emptying into the Gǔ river."
Huá Yánjùn's *Records of Luòyáng* states:
"Two bronze camels stand on the southern street of the palace,
facing each other east and west,
nine feet tall.
The *Records of Luòyáng* calls it Bronze Camel Street."
Three Paths Nine Valleys
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"The four sacred mountains, three paths, are the strategic points of the nine provinces."
Dù Yù's *Explanatory Examples* states:
"The Three Paths
are the name of the Lùhún mountain."
Zhāng Héng's *Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital* states:
"Zhuólóng and Fānglín,
nine valleys and eight streams."
Square Lake Winding Luò
Lì Yuán's commentary on the *Water Classic* states:
"North of Jǐngyáng mountain in Huálín garden flows past Square Lake.
In the lake stands the imperial seat rock,
with Pénglái mountain erected in front."
The *Account of King Mù of Zhōu* states:
"Traveling east to Huáng Marsh,
lodging at Winding Luò."
Zǐ Marsh Zhī Fields
Liú Chéngzhī's *Records of Mountains and Rivers from the Sòng Dynasty's Yǒngchū Era* states:
"Zǐzé is a place name,
twenty-four lǐ from the royal city."
Cáo Zhí's *Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò* states:
"Resting the carriage at Hénggāo,
feeding the horses at the Zhī fields."
The above pertains to Hénán Prefecture.
Niúlán Hújù
Lì Yuán's commentary on the *Water Classic* states:
"Niúlán river originates from Niúlán mountain north of Lǔyáng County."
The *Hànshū* states:
"Liáng County has the settlement of Dànhú."
Huáng Marsh White River
The *Commentary on the Water Classic* states:
"Huáng water accumulates to form Huáng Marsh,
entering the city of Báishuǐtíng to the southwest."
The above pertains to Rǔ Prefecture.
State of Guó City of Yú
The *Hànshū* states:
"Shǎn Prefecture
is the state of Guó."
It also states:
"The Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of Tàibó,
who became the Duke of Yú,

Máojīn, Bǎigǔ
Dù Yù states:
"Máojīn is west of Tàiyáng County."
The "Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn" says:
"The Emperor traveled incognito to Bǎigǔ."
The above are in Shǎnzhōu.
Shídī, Jīnguì
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" says:
"At the foot of Shídī Mountain there is a shrine,

Jiūlǐ, Hóngguān

The "Commentary on the Water Classic" states:
"East of the Hànquè Pavilion is Hóngguān."
The above are in Guózhōu.
Běilì, Xīpíng
The "Records of the Thirteen Provinces" says:

Cuī Hóng's "Records of the Later Yān":

Lóngquán, Yángjiàn

Xītáng, Nánguō
The "Book of the Later Hàn" says:

The "Zhōu Map Records" says:

Liǎoguó, Xièchéng
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Húyáng County

The "Jīngzhōu Records" says:
"Jí County has Xiè City."
The above are in Tángzhōu.
Húguó, Táoqiū
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"Rǔyīn County was the ancient state of Hú."
The "Book of Jìn" says:
"Rǔyīn County has the Táoqiū district."
Rǔfén, Yǐngjìn
The "Máo Poetry" says:
"The Way's transformation spread along the Rǔfén."
The "Rites of Zhōu" says:
"Directly south is Jīngzhōu,
its marshes are Yǐng and Qí."
The above are in Yǐngzhōu.
Yándū, Chǔxǐ
"The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings":
"Shénnóng first established his capital at Chén."
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ moved east to Chén."
Jīshuǐ, Húqiū
The "Commentary on the Water Classic":
"The Wěishuǐ flows south,

The "Zuǒzhuàn":
"Chǔ invaded Chén,
and captured Húqiū."
The above are in Chénzhōu.
Èryǐng, Wǔdū
Chéng Gōngsuí's rhapsody says:
"Looking down upon the two Yǐng [rivers]."
The "Wèilüè" says:
"Taking Cháng'ān, Qiáo, Xǔchāng, Yè, and Luòyáng as the five capitals."
Fāngchéng, Qūwěi
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The state of Chǔ used Fāngchéng as its wall."
It also says:
"The feudal lords attacked Zhèng,
reaching Qūwěi."
The above are in Xǔzhōu.
Dàngqú, Yuánpǔ
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" says:
"Yīngōu emerges from Dàngqú in Yángwǔ County."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"Zhèng had Yuánpǔ,

Jiàntǔ, Hónggōu
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Duke Wén of Jìn built a royal palace at Jiàntǔ."
The commentary says:
"Land of Zhèng."
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Below Xíngyáng,

Féngzé, Biànqú
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"Féngzé is northeast of Kāifēng."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" says:
"Duke Xiào of Qín sent a prince to meet the feudal lords at Féngzé."
The "Record of a Western Campaign" says:
"South of Cāngyuán City borders the Biànqú."
Yánghú, Shāhǎi
The "Record of a Campaign" says:
"Dǒng Shēng south of Biàn,

The "Strategies of the Warring States" says:
"The ruler of Liáng wished to obtain the Nine Tripods,
and plotted at Shāhǎi,

Jīndī, Shíjì
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"The Yellow River breached at Dōng Commandery,

The "Record of a Campaign" says:
"There is an accumulation of stones in the river,
called Shíjì."
Púyì, Táochéng
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi made a verbal agreement at Pú."
The commentary says:
"Pú was the fief of Níng Zhí."
The "Continued Book of Hàn" states:
"Táochéng is south of Yàn County."
The above are in Huázhōu.
Qiáoguó, Làixiāng
The "Book of Jìn" says:
"Qiáoguó was established by partition by Emperor Míng of Wèi."
The "Làixiāng Records" states:
"The shrine of Lǎozi is in Làixiāng."
Màiqiū, Sāngyì
Huán Tán's "New Treatise" says:
"Duke Huán of Qí, while traveling, met a man from Màiqiū."
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" says:
"Shānsāngyì is commonly called Běipíng City."
The above are in Bózhōu.
Shāngqiū, Jǐngbó
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"È Bó resided at Shāngqiū."
It also says:
"Tāng had the covenant of Jǐngbó."
Jíbì, Tóngmén
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"When the seven states of Wú and Chǔ rebelled,

The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"Chǔ besieged Sòng,
and attacked at Tóngmén."
The above are in Sòngzhōu.
Qīngshuǐ, Liángshān
The "Record of a Campaign" says:
"Jùyě County has Qīngshuǐ,
and Liángshān connects Qīngshuǐ further to Dàizōng."
Wúyán, Yánggǔ
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"Wúyán County is near the state of Dōngpíng."
The "Zuǒzhuàn":
"The Marquis of Qí met at Yánggǔ."
The above are in Yùnzhōu.
Hézé, Kuíqiū
The "Book of Documents" says:
"Channeled Hézé,
reaching Méngzhū."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"Duke Huán of Qí met the feudal lords at Kuíqiū."
Wǔzhàng, Sānzōng
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" says:
"Héshuǐ,
commonly called the Wǔzhàng Ditch."
The "Book of Documents" says:
"Tāng then attacked Sānzōng."
The above are in Cáozhōu.
Gǔlín, Hùzǐ
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"Yáo was buried at Gǔlín."
The "Book of Hàn" says:
"The Yellow River breached the Hùzǐ dike."
The above are in Púzhōu.
Qíntíng, Lúyì
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"Lǔ built a pavilion at Qín."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"Northwest of Fàn County is Qíntíng."
It also says:
"Gāo Ruò rebelled with Lú."
Dù Yù's commentary says:
"Lú,
was a fief of the Gāo clan of Qí."
Láng Shuǐ Yú Shān
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"Láng Shuǐ originates from Láng Xī of Dàjiàn Shān,
flowing northwest,
passing west of Gǔchéng."
The Book of Han states:
"The Emperor Wǔ's 'Song of Hùzǐ' says:
'My mountain is leveled, the Jùyě overflows.'" Annotation:
"My mountain refers to Yú Shān."
The Record of a Western Campaign states:
"Yú Shān faces the river to the north."
The above concludes Jìzhōu.
Lái Yì Pú Tái
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"Láiwú County,
formerly, when Duke Jǐng of Qí destroyed Lái,
the people of Lái scattered to the northern valleys.
The settlements became desolate and overgrown,
hence it was called Láiwú."
The Brief Records of Sān Qí states:
"By the sea there is a terrace,
eight zhàng high.
Qín Shǐhuáng tethered his horse with rushes below this terrace,
hence it was named Pú Tái."
Jiǎ Shān Lóng Shuǐ
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"Méng Shuǐ originates from Jiǎ Shān."
The Record of a Campaign states:
"West of Liángzōu city is Lóng Shuǐ.
Some say it concerns a filial daughter-in-law of Qí.
A spring welled up within her residence.
She covered the water with a basket,
hence it was named Lóng Shuǐ (Basket Water)."
The above concludes Zīzhōu.
Jì Hé Zhū Sì
The Book of Documents states:
"Between the Jì and Hé lies Yǎnzhōu."
The Book of Rites states:
"Zēngzǐ said to Zǐxià:
'I served our Master with you between the Zhū and Sì rivers.'"
Fú Yì Guī Méng
The Book of Songs states:
"Establish your eldest son,
Make him lord over Lǔ.
He shall possess Fú and Yì,
And extend his domain to Xú."
It also states:
"He possesses Guī and Méng,
And extends his domain to the far east."
The above concludes Yǎnzhōu.
Shí Yàn Jīn Yú
Yàn Mó's Records of Qí states:
"The Shísāi Dam,
was built during Emperor Wǔ's time."
The Record of a Campaign states:
"Lǎnggōng's Jīn Yú Shān,
a solitary peak surrounded by beauty,
is truly a divine ridge."
Huá Quán Lì Jǐng
The Zuo Commentary states:
"Féng Chǒufù made Duke Qǐng of Qí descend to Huá Quán to fetch water."
The Continued Record of a Campaign states:
"Lì Shān has a bottomless well,
connected to the gushing spring southwest of the city."
The above concludes Qízhōu.
Ní Chéng Fèi Yì
The Zuo Commentary states:
"Ní Lílái came to court."
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"Northeast of Chānglú County in Dōnghǎi is Ní Chéng."
It also states:
"Fèi Bó led troops to fortify Láng.
This is Fèi County in Lángyá.
Later it became the fief of the Jì family."
Dà Xiàn Sǒu Gāng
Wǔ Jízhī's Record of Following a Campaign states:
"Dà Xiàn is a direct mountain pass of twenty-five lǐ.
Its ravines and gullies pierce the earth,
its cliffs and slopes are steep and winding.
Not even the Four Sacred Mountains or the Three Passes surpass it."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"Xiǎo Sǒu Gāng has two water sources,
which converge and flow eastward as one stream."
The above concludes Yízhōu.
Biǎo Hǎi Yíng Qiū
The Zuo Commentary states:
"Wú Jìzhá heard the music of Qí being performed,
and said:
'He who manifests virtue to the Eastern Sea must be Tàigōng!'" The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"King Wǔ enfeoffed his teacher, Shī Shàngfǔ, at Yíng Qiū in Qí."
Tiān Qí Dì Jìng
The Book of Han states:
"The reason Qí is called Qí (齐, level/equal)
is because of the Tiān Qí (Heavenly Level)."
Sū Lín's annotation:
"It is the center of Heaven."
Gù Yěwáng's Treatise on Geography states:
"During the time of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
the land south of Qīngzhōu city,
when viewed from afar, appeared reflected like water,
and was called Dì Jìng (Earth Mirror)."
The above concludes Qīngzhōu.
Lóng Gōu Hú Lǒng
The Continued Record of a Campaign states:
"From Péngchéng's Wǔ Gōu waterway to Lóng Gōu is five lǐ."
Zhāng Huá's Records of Diverse Matters states:
"A palace woman of Lord Xú laid an egg.
Deeming it inauspicious,
she abandoned it by the water's edge.
There was a dog named Hú Cāng,
who carried the egg back in its mouth.
A child was then born from it,
who became King Yǎn of Xú.
Later, when Hú Cāng was dying, it grew horns and nine tails,
revealing it was actually a yellow dragon.
It was buried within Xú territory.
A dog mound can still be seen there."
Xī Chǔ Běi Líng
The Book of Han states:
"Xiàng Yǔ proclaimed himself Hegemon King of Western Chǔ,
with his capital at Péngchéng."
