The Tàikāng Geographical Treatise of the Book of Jin records Běilíng County,
belonging to Xiàpī.
The above concludes Xúzhōu.
Dǐ Gé Háo Liáng
The Record of a Western Campaign states:
"Sùyù city was an old storehouse on the central route from Xiàpī."
The Record of a Campaign states:
"Háo Sì is a public waterway.
Its waters flow into the Sì River.
There is an old fishing weir there.
This is the place where Zhuāngzǐ strolled on the bridge over the Háo."
Bái Lóu Zhū Shǐ
Hóu Tāo's Record of a Northern Campaign states:
"Xiàpī city,
was where Hán Xìn established his capital.
The central city was defended by Lǚ Bù,
facing south towards the Bái Lóu Gate."
The Records of Diverse Matters states:
"King Yǎn of Xú, wishing to exercise hegemony over the states,
dredged a canal between Chén and Cài,
and obtained a vermilion bow and red arrows."
The above concludes Mìzhōu.
Lóng Tái Mǎ Ěr
The Brief Records of Sān Qí states:
"Inside the Píngchāng Gate there is a terrace,
six zhàng high.
Divine dragons emerged and entered there,
hence it was named Lóng Tái Chéng (Dragon Terrace City)."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"Mǎ Ěr Shān is a hundred zhàng high.
On top are rocks standing side by side, twin peaks rising like horse's ears."
Chái Fù Jiāo Yuán
The Records of Qí Lands states:
"Chái Fù is densely overgrown with thorns and brambles,
hence it is called Chái Fù (Firewood Mound).
Bǐng Yuán was buried east of it."
The Book of Shīzǐ states:
"In Jǔ there is a place called Jiāo Yuán.
It is fifty paces wide,
and overlooks a chasm a hundred rèn deep.
No one in the state of Jǔ dared approach it.
A Daoist adept appeared before the Lord of Jǔ,
and alone walked backwards with his heels aligned."
The above concludes Dēngzhōu.
Shèng Shí Xiān Cí
The Records of Qí states:
"In the shade of Lái Shān there is a great rock.
There is a place where a person emerged from it.
It is said an ancient sage came forth from here."
The Book of Han states:
"Bùjī County has nine temples dedicated to the Great One Immortal."
Sān Shān Jiǔ Xué
The Book of Han states:
"Qǔchéng County has three mountains."
The Records of Qí states:
"Jiǔmù Shān has nine caves."
The above concludes Láizhōu.
Lǚ Mǔ Fort and Tián Héng Island
In the late Hàn dynasty, during Wáng Mǎng's reign,
there was a woman named Lǚ Mǔ
whose son was killed by the county magistrate.
She distributed her wealth to recruit young men,
and together they killed the magistrate and fled into the sea.
Now, according to records, her fort still exists
north of Dōnghǎi County.
The Book of Hàn states:
"After Gāozǔ pacified the realm,
Tián Héng, fearing execution,
went to sea with five hundred followers
and settled on an island."
Immortal's Stone and the First Emperor's Stele
Cuī Yǎn's "Rhapsody on a Military Expedition" says:
"On Yùfēi Mountain there is an immortal's stone chamber,
so I went to see it
and encountered a Daoist."
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn states:
"In the sea, one hundred and fifty paces from the shore, there is a stele of Qín Shǐhuáng,
five chǐ wide,
and three chǐ eight cùn thick."
The above concerns Hǎi Prefecture.
Yáng Xióng's "Admonition for Yùzhōu"
Lush and verdant are the Jīng and Hé rivers,
where the Yī and Luò flow through.
Flourishing are the hemp and lacquer trees,
put to use and perfected.
Fields upon fields intertwined,
villages and villages adjoining.
Xià and Yīn did not make it their capital,
but Chéngzhōu was established there.
The land where Yùzhōu resides,
lies in the constellation of Chúnxū.
All four corners find dwelling,
none in the world can compare.
Vassals seize command,
with no thought or plan.
Do not say, "I am great,"
lest someone bring my downfall.
Do not say, "I am strong,"
lest I be vanquished.
King Nǎn reached the extreme,
truly ending the Zhōu lineage.
I, the shepherd-official overseeing Yù,
dare to inform the pillar historian.
Also, "Admonition for Qīngzhōu"
Vast and boundless Qīngzhōu,
bounded by the sea and Tài mountain.
Land of salt and iron,
lead, pine, and strange stones.
Where many waters converge,
the Láiyí tribes tend their herds.
Tribute and baskets offered in season,
do not neglect or defy.
In the past, under Wén and Wǔ,
Lǚ was enfeoffed in Qí.
Its soil is muddy,
on the hills of Yíngqiū.
Five marquises and nine earls,
all were governed and levied.
Horses weary of their bits,
drivers lose their measure.
The Zhōu house fell into chaos,
Xiǎo Bái brought peace.
All the lords submitted,
and revered the capital anew.
After Xiǎo Bái passed,
Zhōu eventually declined.
Alas, the Son of Heaven,
entrusted his mandate to the lower lands.
I, the shepherd-official overseeing Qīng,
dare to inform the holder of the square.
Also, "Admonition for Xúzhōu"
Between the sea, Tài, and the Huái,
Dōnghǎi forms its islets.
The lands of Yùzhōu,
settle in its borders.
The great marsh now a lake,
with Yǔ and Méng mountains.
Lone paulownia and pearl mussels,
the Sì and Yí rivers share.
Descended from Zhōu, entrusted to Jiāng,
guarding Lángyé.
The Jiāng lineage cut off,
the Tián clan made it their capital.
Events arise from subtlety,
with no thought or plan.
Disaster looms like mountains,
rooted in the sprout.
I, the shepherd-official overseeing Xú,
dare to inform the servant.
Also, "Admonition for Yǎnzhōu"
Flowing Jì and Hé rivers,
the domain of Yǎnzhōu.
Nine rivers channeled,
Léixià settled.
Grass lush, trees slender,
lacquer, silk, hemp, and ramie.
Jì and Tà rivers now connected,
descending hills to dwell on land.
Chéng Tāng moved five times,
finally settling in Bó.
Pán Gēng crossed north,
Mùyě became his home.
Jīzǐ sighed with grief,
his old dwelling now ruins.
I, the shepherd-official overseeing Yǎn,
dare to inform the keeper of records.
Guānnèi Circuit, Third
Guānnèi Circuit
is the domain of Yōngzhōu according to the Tribute of Yǔ.
The Book of Documents states:
"From the Black River to the Western River is Yōngzhōu."
According to records, Yōngzhōu from Lǒng westward
is divided into the Lǒngyòu Circuit.
The "Treatise on Astronomy" in the Book of Hàn states:
"The constellations Jǐng and Guǐ correspond to Yōngzhōu's division."
East from Tóng and Huà,
crossing the river northward,
west from Qí and Lǒng,
the plains converge at the northern frontier,
encompassing the entire region.
Jīngzhào Prefecture embraces the Fēng and Bà rivers,
and rests upon Hán and Xiáo.
Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
"To the left, it holds the perilous Hángǔ and the two Xiáo passes."
It also states:
"Embracing the Fēng and Bà rivers,
and resting upon Lǒngshǒu."
It gains the strategic advantage of 'one hundred and two' over a thousand lǐ.
The Book of Hàn states:
"Qín gained the advantage of 'one hundred and two.'"
Sū Lín explains:
"This means the terrain of Qín is perilously firm,
so that twenty thousand men are sufficient to withstand a million from the other lords."
The River Chart states:
"The land of Qín spans a thousand lǐ."
Zhōu's capital was Fēnghào,
Qín's capital was Xiányáng,
Hàn's capital was Cháng'ān,
now Wǔgōng County,
was the fief of Hòu Jì.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Hòu Jì was enfeoffed at Càn, which is this place."
Bīn Prefecture
was where Gōng Liú once resided;
Huà Prefecture
was the ancient state of Zhèng;
the "Preface to the Odes" states:
"King Xuān of Zhōu enfeoffed his younger brother at Xiánlín,
which became the state of Zhèng."
Qí Prefecture
was where Duke Dé of Qín first resided;
Xià Prefecture
was the capital of the Hèlián clan.
Four Impregnable Passes and Eight Rivers
The Book of Hàn states:
"Lóu Jìng said:
'Guānzhōng is surrounded by mountains and girded by rivers,
forming an impregnable stronghold.'"
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" says:
"Vast and mighty are the eight rivers,
Fēng, Hào, Láo, Jué,
Jīng, Wèi, Bà, and Chǎn."
Divine Plain and Blessed Land
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" says:
"Truly a profound region, a divine plain."
The Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú states:
"West of Lí Mountain lies a mound called Fēngliáng Plain,
a blessed land of Yōngzhōu."
Golden City and Stone Pillar
The Book of Hàn states:
"Guānzhōng is a golden city spanning a thousand lǐ."
The Old Affairs of the Three Adjuncts states:
"South of the stone pillar belongs to Jīngzhào,
north belongs to Fúfēng."
Xìliǔ and Chángyáng
The Book of Hàn states:
"Zhōu Yàfū garrisoned at Xìliǔ."
A Hàn palace was named Chángyáng.
Warm Water and Cāng Pool
The Records of the Three Qín states:
"West of the Wèi River bridge lies warm water."
Also, the Records of Cháng'ān states:
"Jiànzhāng Palace has the Tàiyè Cāng Pool."
Jītóu and Chúnshǒu
The Records of Yōngzhōu states:
"Jītóu Mountain lies in Hù County."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Heaven bestowed the land of Chúnshǒu upon Duke Mù of Qín."
Hànjīng, Qínlǐ...
The "Xīdū Fù" states:
"Expansive as Hànjīng."
Also, the "Xījīng Fù" states:
"Qínlǐ in the north."
Dānshuǐ, Huángshān...
The "Shān Hǎi Jīng" states:
"The southern mountains are rich with yellow, and Dānshuǐ emerges from them."
The "Xījīng Fù" states:
"Encircling Huángshān and reaching Niúshǒu."
Above mentioned are the territories of Jīngzhào Prefecture.
Táo Sài, Bǎiyuán...
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"The ruler of Jìn ordered Jiān Jiā to defend the fortification of Táolín."
Dù Yù notes:
"This is now Tóngguān."
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Guànshuǐ flows west from the lonely Bǎiyuán."
Pú Chí, Xué Shì...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"On Huàshān, there is a sacred spring named Pú Chí."
The "Gāo Shì Zhuàn" states:
"Zhāng Kāi secluded himself on Huàshān,
drawing scholars to form a market."
Above mentioned are the territories of Huàzhōu.
Hán Yuán, Yáo Gǔ...
The "Gǔjīn Dìmíng" states:
"Lord Hán Wǔzi received fief at Hán Yuán."
The "Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Yáo Gǔ belongs to Bái Shuǐ."
Qiàn Luò, Fēn Huà...
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Duke Jiǎn of Qín dug the Qiànluò,
which is now the eastern Great Wall of Pú Chéng County."
The "Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Emperor Xiàomíng divided Huàshān Dū and established Wǔxiāng Prefecture."
Above mentioned are the territories of Tóngzhōu.
Pú Gǔ, Bǎichéng...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Pú Gǔ’s water source comes from Zhōngbù County."
It also states:
"Zhūshuǐ flows through Bǎichéng."
Above mentioned are the territories of Tóngzhōu.
Dān Chuān, Wū Shuǐ...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Púshuǐ flows south from Luòchuān County into Dānyáng Chuān."
It also states:
"The source of Wūchuān waters emerges northwest of Fénchuān County."
Above mentioned are the territories of Dānzhōu.
Qīng Niú, Bái Dì...
The "Lù Yì Zhuàn" states:
"Duke Wén of Qín cut down trees in the southern mountains of Yōngzhōu,
and a green ox emerged in Fèngshuǐ."
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Duke Wén of Qín established Fū Zhì,
to worship the White Emperor."
Qī Shuǐ, Tóng Chí...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Qī Shuǐ emerges from Qīxī."
It also states:
"Tóng Chí waters flow northeast into Sānjiāo Shuǐ."
Above mentioned are the territories of Qízhōu.
Qíxià, Liángqiū...
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Ancient Lord Tǎnfǔ settled at Qíxià."
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Liángqiū Gǔ’s waters,
flow southwest into Zǐjīng."
Qínchuān, Ruìshuǐ...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"North of Yílù County is Qínchuān."
It also states:
"Ruìshǔ flows into the Jīng."
Above mentioned are the territories of Bīnzhōu.
Wūtíng, Kūn Rǎng...
Wūshì County during the Hàn,
renamed to Wūtíng by Wang Mang.
The "Sòngchū Shānchuān Jì" states:
"This was the old domain of Kūnróng in Āndìng."
Above mentioned are the territories of Jīngzhōu.
Lǒng Shuǐ, Wú Shān...
The "Sānqín Jì" states:
"It is sung locally about the waters of Lǒngtóu."
The "Dìdào Jì" states:
"Qiānyáng County belongs to the Qín State,
and Wú Shān is in its west."
Above mentioned are the territories of Lǒngzhōu.
Qín Gǔ, Zhà Tíng...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Qín Gǔ’s waters emerge eastward from Luóchūn County in the Zǐwǔ Mountains."
The "Xù Hànshū" states:
"There is a Wǔ Zhà Tíng in Fényáng County."
Above mentioned are the territories of Níngzhōu.
Tùchuān, Jī Shuǐ...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Tùchuān flows southwest into the Luòshuǐ."
It also states:
"Wǔjīshuǐ emerges and flows west into the Luò."
Above mentioned are the territories of Qìngzhōu.
Lán Shān, Nà Yì...
The "Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū" states:
"Hèlian Dìng scaled Kělán Shān."
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Nà,
is a Yíng territory."
Above mentioned are the territories of Yuánzhōu.
Báis Shuǐ, Púchuān...
The "Shuǐ Jīng" commentary states:
"The source of Báis Shuǐ emerges west of Fénshuǐ Ridge."
It also states:
"The waters of Xiǎo Púchuān flow southeast into Fāngzhōu."
Above mentioned are the territories of Fūzhōu.
Shénquán Zhàng, Lóngwěi Xī...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Lóngwěishuǐ emerges from Shénquán Zhàng,
and there is also Lóngwěi Xī."
Above mentioned are the territories of Yánzhōu.
Lù Liánchí, Qīng Yánzé...
The "Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū" states:
"Hèlian Bóbó hunted at Sānjiāo,
and returned at Lù Liánchí."
The "Hànshū" states:
"Qīng Yánzé of Shuòfāng Commandery is to the south."
Diǎnnóng Chéng, Huáihún Zhàng...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"The waters pass through Diǎnnóng Chéng,
and then flow northeast through Huáihún Zhàng."
Above mentioned are the territories of Língzhōu.
Méng Shuǐ, Jī Shān...
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" states:
"Méng Shuǐ Zǐhé is in Shuòfāng County."
The "Xù Hànshū" states:
"General Dòu Xiàn went out to Jī Lù Shān."
Above mentioned are the territories of Shèngzhōu.
Jìn Zhì Yú's "Yōngzhōu Poetry"
Oh Grand Ancestors,
traversing through the Nine Provinces.
Of all the states, only Yōng remains,
seated to the right of the capital.
The earth bears its depth,
the mountains embraced by spirit and sacred groves.
Flourishing with worthy growth,
a multitude thriving abundantly.
Vast is the dominion,
having both Huá and Róng.
Externally, touching foreign lands,
internally, encompassing Qí and Fēng.
Though the legacy of Zhōu has ceased,
the virtue of Yí is yet enduring.
All admire righteousness,
transforming customs and evolving winds.
Yáng Xióng's "Admonition of Yōngzhōu"
Black Water and Western River,
extending once to Kūnlún.
Following the deceitful gate of Heaven,
delineating the border of Yōng.
At the top, it invades the mass of stones,
at the bottom, blocked by the Dragon Gate.
In peace, never forget danger,
in prosperity, never deny decline.
The governor oversees Yōng,
daring to report while wearing humble attire.
Hédōng Route Number Four
The Hé Dōng Circuit,
a region in the Jìzhōu of the Yǔgòng.
The "Erya" states:
"The land between the two rivers is Jìzhōu."
Shùn established twelve provinces,
dividing Jìzhōu into Yōuzhōu and Bìngzhōu.
The present Hé Dōng Circuit comprises the lands of Bìng and Jì two provinces,
the "Hanshu‧Astronomy" states:
"Píxiù constellation belongs to Jìzhōu,
the Yíngshì constellation and the eastern wall belong to Bìngzhōu."
Southwest borders the river,
north reaches Shǔchuí,
encompassing its entire territory,
Hé Dōng was originally the capital of Yáo.
Zhōu Chéng Wáng enfeoffed his younger brother Shūyú,
his son Xiè,
thus became Marquis of Jìn.
When the three families divided Jìn,
from Púzhōu across Hé Dōng to Huái Zhōu belonged to Wèi,
Huái Zhōu belongs to Héběi Circuit now.
From Zé and Lù south to Wèi Zhōu,
to the north of Tàiyuán Prefecture, it belonged to Zhào.
Tàiyuán Prefecture,
formerly the residence of Gāoxīnshì's son Shí Chén and Jīntiānshì's son Tái Tái,
also became the state of Táng,
Yáo ruled as Táng Marquess there.
Zhèng Xuán's "Shī Pǔ" states:
"Táng,
the former capital land of Yáo,
later moved to Píngyáng."
Púzhōu,
Shùn's capital.
"Tàikāng Dìjì" states:
"Shùn's capital was Anyì."
Jiàng, Zhōu,
the place where Jìn Xiàn Gōng moved the capital.
Yáo's Ruins, Yǔ's Traces
Zhèng Xuán's "Shī Pǔ" states:
"Chéng Wáng enfeoffed his mother's younger brother Shūyú in Yáo's old ruins."
Huángfǔ Mì's "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Yu moved from Anyì to Jìnyáng,
his great-grandson Emperor Xiàng moved to Dìqiū.
Son Shàokāng revived,
returned to the old capital,
restoring Yǔ's traces."
Tài Xià, Zhōng Dōu
"Chūnqiū Dìmíng" states:
"Jìn Tàikāng is also called Tài Xià."
"Hòu Wèi Shū" states:
"Zhōng Dōu belongs to Tàiyuán County."
Six Names, Five Commanders
"Chūnqiū Dìmíng" states:
"Six names in Jìn: Tàilǔ, Tàiyuán, Tài Xià, Tài Xū, Jìnyáng, Tàikāng,
actually the same place."
"Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì":
"Bìngzhōu governs six counties in Tàiyuán,
also has five Dūwèi: Guards of the Xiōngnú, Left Division, Right Division, Central Division, Southern Division, and Northern Division."
Hāoyuán, Wěizé
"Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ" states:
"Zhāng Mèngtán told Zhào Xiāngzǐ:
'I have heard that when Dǒng Ānyú was in Jìnyáng,
the walls of the duke's palace were all covered with reeds.' " "Hòu Wèi Shū" states:
"Shí'ài County had Wěizé."
Qiánqiū, Wōshuǐ
"Erya" states:
"Jìn has Qiánqiū."
Guō Pú’s commentary states:
"Located in Jìnyáng County, Tàiyuán."
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Wōshuǐ flows out northwest from Pínglè County."
Qímù, Jiècǐ
"Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
"Jìnyáng has the tomb of Qíxiā."
It also states:
"Jìnyáng has the shrine of Jiè Zǐtuī."
Above is Bìng Zhōu.
Sùshuǐ, Dízǎi
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Sùchuan River is within the domain of Sāngquán County."
"Jìn Dìdào Jì" states:
"Léishǒu Mountain is also named Dízǎi."
Jiùtíng, Yúsǎn
"Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr took Jiùtíng."
Dù Yù’s commentary states:
"Jiùtíng is in Hé Dōng District of Jiě County."
"Zhànguó Cè" states:
"Steed driven to climb Yú Slope.
It is now located within Anyì County's boundaries."
Above is Púzhōu.
Yùbì, Tiānjǐng
In the fourth year of the Eastern Wèi Dàtǒng,
East Dao Executive Wáng Sīzhèng petitioned to build Yùbì City,
now checked to be west of Hòu Shān County.
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Tiānjǐng Water,
flows through the west of Yáo City,
into Fénshuǐ."
Zǎojiàn, Tóngxiāng
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Qiánzǎo Stream water emerges northward,
flows under Shírén Ridge and southward,
commonly called Fúsūshuǐ."
"Hàn Shū":
"Emperor Wǔ planned to visit Gōushì,
arrived at Zuǒ Yī Tóngxiāng,
within the domain of Wénxǐ County."
Above is Jiàng Zhōu.
Qiānmǔ, Wǔchéng
"Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Jìn Mùhóu begat the Crown Prince during the campaign at Tiáo,
named him Qiú.
His brother was born from the battle of Qiānmǔ,
named Shèngshī."
"Hòu Wèi Shū" states:
"Jìn Zhōu governs Wǔchéng County."
Xiānglíng, Húgǔ
During the Later Hàn, Xiānglíng was assigned to Hé Dōng County.
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"The Pínghé River emerges from Xī Húkǒu Mountain in Jìnyáng County,
flows east through Húgǔ Pavilion."
Above is Jìn Zhōu.
Zhāngchuān, Jìjìn
"Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"In Jìzhōu, its river is called Zhāng."
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary states:
"Emerges from Cháng'ān."
"Shísānzhōu Zhì" states:
"Lù River flows from Lù County,
immersion of Jìzhōu."
Chìrǎng, Huángshān
"Shàngdǎng Jì" states:
"Gāopíng Chìrǎng,
its terrain is perilous,
people do not settle there."
"Hòu Wèi Yútú Fēngtǔjì" states:
"Huángshān is east of Húguān County."
Above is Lù Zhōu.
Shùnzé, Jìnshān
"Mòzǐ" states:
"Shùn fished in Léi Marsh,
west of Hù Zé County."
"Hòu Wèi Yútú Fēngtǔjì" states:
"Sīmǎshān is north of Jìnchéng County,
during the Jìn dynasty, there was a temple for this mountain,
thus named."
Mèngmén, Wǔtái
"Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Qí Hóu attacked Jìn,
entered Mèngmén,
and ascended Tàiháng."
"Shísānzhōu Zhì" states:
"Tàiháng Mountain is also called Mèngmén,
due to its perilous pass."
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Wǔtái Pavilion is within the domain of Jìnchéng County."
Above is Zé Zhōu.
Shíshì, Tiěqí
"Hòu Wèi Yútú Fēngtǔjì" states:
"The mountain range of Tàiyuán County has Shíshì, square shaped,
with carvings in seal script on four walls,
people cannot decipher."
"Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū" states:
"At the time of birth of Shí Lè,
the grass and trees on the northern mountain,
transformed into the shape of armored cavalry."
Qīnggǔ, Huángyán
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Qīngshuǐ source emerges west of Wǔxiāng County,
called Qīnggǔ Water."
It also states:
"Huángyán Water source emerges west of Liáoshān County,
above is Yí Zhōu."
Ōuzé, Fén Guān
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"Dàshāo is also named Ōuzé."
"Shuǐjīngzhù" states:
"Hèrquè Ferry,
is the name of Fén Guān.
Southwest of Jiāxiū,
colloquially known as Quèshǔ Valley."
Eight Gates and Six Walls
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms states:
"Liú Yuānhǎi sent a general to attack Xīhé City,
who built a camp to fortify himself.
It had eight gates,
and the walls were nine feet high."
The Book of Later Wei says:
"Emperor Tàiwǔ campaigned against the Hú rebels at Liùbì.
The walls had six sides,
hence the name."
The above are in Fénzhōu.
Zǐ Chuān and Huáng Gǔ
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"The source of the Zǐ Chuān water is east of Xíchuān County,
in Zǐ Gǔ.
Huánglú water emerges from Huánglú Gǔ northeast of Xíchuān County."
The above are in Xízhōu.
Xiàwū and Xiāndū
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Zhào Xiāngzǐ ascended Xiàwū in the north,
to lure the King of Dài."
Xú Guǎng's annotation states:
"Xiàwū
is a mountain name."
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn,
the people of Yànmén fled the chaos and entered Wǔtái Mountain.
They saw an immortal leading the way,
and thus did not return.
Searching for them, no one knew their whereabouts.
Common people therefore call this mountain Xiāndū (Immortal Capital)."
The above are in Dàizhōu.
Sānhuì and Jiǔyuán
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"The Sānhuì water flows east into the Hūtuó water,
within the boundaries of Dìngxiāng County."
It also says:
"The Sānhuì water emerges west of Jiǔyuán County,
and its mountain passes through Jiǔyuán City."
Língqiū and Shèngfù
The Book of Later Wei says:
"In the second year of Tiānpíng, Héngzhōu was established,
temporarily residing in Xiùróng County city,
administering eight counties including Língqiū."
The Water Commentary says:
"The Hūtuó water flows east north of Shèngrén Fù.
Below the mound there is water.
Beside the spring, on a rock, there are handprints,
and further west are two footprints."
The above are in Xīnzhōu.
Wěizhōu and Méilǐng
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces says:
"Regarding the old city of Dài Commandery,
Lú Zhí said that when it was first built,
the framework was just being set up.
It was moved fifty *li* southwest into a great marsh, where reeds were woven to form nine gates.
Thus, it was made into a city,
with a circumference of seven *li*.
Now, it is verified to be within the boundaries of Fēihú County."
The Record of Lands says:
"Forty-eight *li* east of Lǔdì Zhōu is Méilǐng."
Lái Shuǐ and Jī Shān
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"Láizhōu has Lái Shuǐ."
Zhèng Xuán annotates:
"Lái Shuǐ emerges from Guǎngchāng."
The Records of the Grand Historian:
"Zhào Xiāngzǐ's elder sister was the wife of the King of Dài.
Xiāngzǐ killed the King of Dài,
then raised an army to pacify the land of Dài.
His sister heard of this,
wept and cried out to heaven,
sharpened a hairpin and killed herself.
The people of Dài pitied her,
and named the mountain where she died Mójī Shān (Grinding Hairpin Mountain).
Now, it is verified to be within the boundaries of Fēihú County."
The above are in Yùzhōu.
Rúhún Shuǐ and Hézhēn Shān
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"Rúhún Shuǐ,
the water course,
Fāng Shān is also called Hézhēn Shān.
In summer, snow accumulates,
and thousands of birds die daily."
Yíng Tái and Huǒ Jǐng
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"The volcanic mountain seems to have fire emerging from the ground,
hence it is called Yíng Tái (Glimmering Terrace)."
It also says:
"On the volcanic mountain, there is a fire well."
The above are in Lánzhōu.
Hú Shān and Fēng Xuè
The Book of Hàn says:
"Húkǒu Shān is southeast of Běiwū."
The Commentary on the Water Classic says:
"Ten *li* west of the old city of Běiwū County is Fēng Shān.
On this mountain is a cave like a wheel.
The wind is bleak,
and never ceases."
The above are in Shuòzhōu.
Yǒngshí and Chányú
The Geographical Records of the Tàikāng Era of Jìn says:
"Xīhé State,
by the end of Emperor Huì's reign, fell to Liú Yuānhǎi.
By the time of Shí Lè,
Yǒngshí Commandery was established.
Later, the Northern Wèi changed it to Líshí Commandery."
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms says:
"Líshí
was the court to which the Chányú moved."
The above are in Shízhōu.
Rhapsody on Jìzhōu by Bān Shūpí of the Later Hàn
Why concern myself with Jìzhōu?
I merely lodge here to wander and dwell.
Traversing the nine regions to observe customs,
is also the pleasure of a wise man.
Gazing at the towering Chángshān,
ascending the Northern Peak for a lofty journey.
Establishing the fēng altar on Dàizōng,
burying dark jade on this mound.
Visiting all five sacred peaks and four great rivers,
viewing the vast sea while roaming all around.
Yáng Xióng's Admonition for Bìngzhōu
Separated from Yōng is Shuòfāng,
the Hé River flows long and far.
To the north, it repels the Xūnyù,
to the south, it borders the Jīngliú.
Thus delineating this northern land,
rightly the Yōu region.
Since ancient times, for what reason?
None have failed to come and pay homage.
Tranquil and solemn, campaigning afar,
the Quǎnróng did not submit.
Then, slighting this virtue,
they invaded Ruǎn, a superior state.
King Xuān commanded his generals,
to repel them north of the Jīng.
The Zōng and Yōu, ignorant,
daily actions flawed and mistaken.
They neither upheld rites
nor wielded shield and spear.
The Quǎnróng rose in rebellion,
bringing ruin at Lí'ē.
The supreme ruler radiates virtue,
the next radiates military might.
When both virtue and arms are toppled,
none escape decline and desolation.
I, the shepherd-official in charge of Bìng,
dare to admonish those who hold the reins.
Admonition for Jìzhōu
Vast and magnificent Jìzhōu,
the great plain, the broad continent.
The southern side of the mountain is its capital,
the island barbarians wear fur garments.
Gently flowing rivers,
flanked by Jiéshí.
Three sovereigns descended here,
established as marquises and earls.
Descending from Zhōu to become Qín,
Zhào and Wèi made it their home.
Jì's order churned and boiled,
swirling and bubbling like hot water.
Now flourishing, now declining,
now following, now contending.
The Hàn arose, establishing order,
changing the ranks to feudal kings.
Governing, do not forget chaos,
in peace, do not neglect danger.
I, the shepherd-official in charge of Jì,
dare to admonish on this matter.
The "Discourse on Jìzhōu" by Wèi Lú Yù states:
Jìzhōu
is the foremost state in the world.
In the Shàngshū, Hé Píngshū and Dèng Xuánmào said its land produces no treasures,
its people are simple and unadorned,
and since ancient times,
it has not produced examples of benevolent worthies.
Jìzhōu, Xúzhōu, Yōngzhōu, and Yùzhōu are such states.
Lú Yù explained:
"Except for before the time of Huángdì,
which cannot be fully recounted,
speaking broadly from the time of Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn onward,
Jìzhōu has been a gathering place for sages and worthies,
a precious land for emperors and kings.
East of the Hé River and above,
west of the Hé River and onward,
north of the Nán Hé River,
south of the Yì Shuǐ River,
lies a thousand lǐ of fertile soil,
where heaven and earth converge,
and yīn and yáng intersect—
this is what is called the Divine Land."
Fifth: The Héběi Circuit
The Héběi Circuit
is the territory of Jìzhōu as recorded in the Yǔ Gòng.
Shùn established twelve provinces,
dividing Jìzhōu into Yōuzhōu and Bìngzhōu,
and dividing Qīngzhōu into Yíngzhōu.
The three provinces of Yōu, Jì, and Yíng,
along with the northern border of Yǎnzhōu,
now constitute the Héběi Circuit.
The "Treatise on Astronomy" in the Hànshū states:
"Bì and Mǎo correspond to Jìzhōu,
Wěi and Jī correspond to Yōuzhōu."
To the south, it reaches the Hé River;
to the east, it extends to the sea;
to the north, it encompasses all of Yōu and Yíng,
covering this entire territory.
Héběi was originally the old capital of the Yīn dynasty,
located in Wèizhōu.
When Zhōu destroyed Yīn,
it divided the inner territories into three states:
Bèi, Yōng, and Wèi.
By the time of Duke Yì of Wèi, who was destroyed by the Dí,
the land belonged to Jìn.
When the three families of Zhào, Hán, and Wèi partitioned Jìn,
Huái belonged to Wèi.
The "Treatise on Geography" in the Hànshū states:
"Wèi, upon partitioning Jìn, obtained Hénèi,
which is present-day Huáizhōu."
From Wèi, Xiàng, Luò, Zhào, Bèi, and Jì,
north to the Héng Shān mountains,
and east to the sea,
the land belonged to Zhào.
North of Yōupíng and east to the sea belonged to Yān.
Míngzhōu and Hándān were the state of Zhào.
The Shǐjì records:
"This was the capital of Lord Jìng of Zhào."
Xiàngzhōu was Yè.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi, Shí Jìlóng of the Later Zhào,
and Mùróng Jùn of the Former Yān, who moved from Jì,
all made it their capital, as did Emperor Wénxuān of the Northern Qí.
Yōuzhōu was called Yān,
the fief of Shào Gōng.
Yíngzhōu
was the capital of Mùróng Huàng of the Former Yān.
Partitioning Jìn, Bordering Yān
The Hànshū states:
"Zhào, upon partitioning Jìn, obtained Xìndū, Jùlù, and Qīnghé."
Lú Yù's "Discourse on Jìzhōu" states:
"Jìzhōu borders Yān and Dài to the north."
Nángōng, Northern Region
The Hànshū states:
"Nángōng County belonged to the state of Xìndū."
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
"In the northern region of Jìzhōu,
food is prepared at the beginning of the month for the Lóu sacrifice."
The above pertains to Jìzhōu.
Three Terraces, Nine Halls
Lù Huì's Yèzhōng Jì states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Wèi erected three terraces northwest of Yè City:
the central terrace named the Copper Sparrow Terrace,
the southern named the Golden Beast Terrace,
and the northern named the Water Well Terrace."
It also states:
"Shí Jìlóng, from Xiāngguó to Yè,
erected a palace every two hundred lǐ.
Each palace had one lady
and several tens of serving maids.
In total, Shí Jìlóng built nine large and small inner and outer halls,
and forty-four terraces, observatories, and traveling palaces."
Zǐmò, Chìqiáo
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Fǔyáng County has Zǐmò,
where a stupa was built ten lǐ away, and a living tomb was constructed here."
The Yèzhōng Jì states:
"Seven lǐ east of Yè City is the palace of Chìqiáo."
The above pertains to Xiàngzhōu.
Zhǐ County, Yuànxiāng
The Shǐjì states:
"King Zhāoxiāng of Qín attacked Wèi
and captured Zhǐ County."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Dān Shuǐ flows through the city of Yuànxiāng."
Píngjīn, Lùfù
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"A bridge was built over the river at Fùpíngjīn,
which is the Héyángjīn."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"South of Lùzhēnfù are the Huángmǔ
and Mǎmíng springs,
which converge southeast and flow into the Wúbēi."
The above pertains to Huáizhōu.
Shāng Ruins, Yú Defile
The Shǐjì states:
"King Chéng attacked Guǎn Shū
and enfeoffed Kāng Shū as the lord of Wèi with the remaining people of Yīn,
residing in the old Shāng ruins."
The Běizhēng Dàolǐ Bù states:
"Lóngtóu City
was the defile of the old state of Yú.
The Zhàn Shuǐ flows behind it,
and the Qīng Shuǐ flows in front."
Sū Ridge, Tángpén
The Shídào Zhì states:
"Sūmén Shān, also called Sū Ridge,
is where Sūn Dēng lived in seclusion."
It also states:
"The Tángpén Shuǐ, also called Pénquán,
originates thirty lǐ northwest of the county.
It curves like a basin,
and its taste is like sweet wine,
hence the name."
The above pertains to Wèizhōu.
Jīzé, Gǒushān
The Zuǒzhuàn records:
"In the sixth month of the third year of Duke Xiāng,
he met with Duke Qīng of Shàn and the other lords,
forming an alliance at Jīzé."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"On the summit of Gǒushān, there are dog footprints,
now located west of Línmíng County."
Tángquán, Yànzhǒng
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Míng Shuǐ flows northeast,
passing east of the old city of Guǎngpíng County.
The water accumulates in a large marsh,
forming Dēngquán.
It is forty lǐ from north to south,
twenty lǐ from east to west,
and is also called Huángtángquán."
The Yèzhōng Jì states:
"Ten lǐ southwest of Hándān City, on Zǐgāng, there is a tomb shaped like an inkstone,
commonly called the Inkstone Tomb."
The above pertains to Míngzhōu.
Chìqiū, Píngyì
The Xù Hànshū states:
"Chìqiū County belonged to Wèi Commandery."
The Zhúshū states:
"In the fourth year of Lord Liè of Jìn,
Zhào built the city of Píngyì,
now located northeast of Chānglè County."
Shālù, Shítái
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Shālù collapsed."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"It is in Jìn territory.
Southeast of Yuánchéng is Shālù Shān."
Lì Shàncháng's Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"In Wǔyáng County city, there is a stone terrace.
Outside the main city gate, there is also an old terrace,
called the Wǔyáng Terrace."
The above pertains to Wèizhōu.
Liǎo Shuǐ, Sūtíng
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Liǎo Shuǐ originates from Xiāngguó."
The Hànshū states:
"Xiāngguó has the Sūrén Pavilion."
Bǎiyán, Qiānbù
The Míngzhōu Jì states:
"Northwest of Lónggāng County is Bǎiyán Shān."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Míng Shuǐ is also called the Zhāng Shuǐ,
commonly known as Qiānbù."
Bótíng Huáishuǐ
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Míng River flows east past the Bóchàng Pavilion.
Now, upon investigation, the old city of Bóchàng Pavilion
lies west of Fángzǐ County."
It also states:
"The Huái River originates from Huángshí Mountain,
now within the boundaries of Yuánshì County."
Shízhù Guībēi
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"South of Píngfáng City's southern gate,
flanking the road are two stone pillars,
guarding the path like watchtowers."
It also states:
"When Emperor Míng of Hàn returned north,
he issued an edict to Gāoyì to erect a Guī-head stele
at the stone altar marking the site where Emperor Guāngwǔ ascended the throne."
The above pertains to Zhàozhōu.
Shànlù Qīnghé
The Book of Hàn states:
"Shū County,
the Hàn dynasty's Qīnghé Commandery,
was renamed Shànlù by Wáng Mǎng."
The Jìn Dìdào Jì states:
"The Qīnghé Kingdom
administered six counties including Qīnghé."
Xūlíng Gānquán
The Book of Hàn states:
"Dōngyáng County belonged to Qīnghé Commandery,
renamed Xūlíng by Wáng Mǎng."
The Shísānzhōu Zhì states:
"Lìchéng was originally the western territory of Zhōu's Gānquán."
The above pertains to Zhēnzhōu.
Chóngqiū Fúshuǐ
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The feudal lords formed an alliance at Chóngqiū,
now located southeast of Liáochéng County."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Fú River originates northeast of Liáochéng.
When it floods, it flows and connects;
when it diminishes, the flow ceases."
Tángyì Língchéng
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Chén Yīng as Marquis of Tángyì.
It also states:
"Língchéng belonged to Qīnghé Commandery."
The above pertains to Bózhōu.
Xūguó Wǎnxiāng
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Ràng, son of the Prince of Héjiān Xiàn, as Marquis of Xū.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Fú River flows northeast past the Wǎnxiāng City of Gāochéng County,
now within the boundaries of Yánchéng County."
Qiāntóng Bǎibó
Yìng Shào's annotation to the Book of Hàn states:
"Qiāntóng County
was renamed Ráo'ān by Emperor Líng."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hào River flows northeast past the north of the old city of Fùpíng,
where it divides into two streams.
The southern stream is the Chángjù Ditch,
flowing east into the sea;
the northern stream is called the Bǎibó Ditch,
flowing northeast into the sea."
The above pertains to Cāngzhōu.
Mǎjiá Hé Lóng'é Xiàn
The Ěryǎ states:
"Among the names of the Nine Rivers is Mǎjiá,
wide at the top and narrow at the bottom,
shaped like a horse's cheek.
The Hàn dynasty's Píngyuán Commandery administered Lóng'é County."
Guǎn Lù Zhǒng Mànqiàn Cí
The Wèi Zhì states:
"In Píngyuán County is the tomb of Guǎn Lù. The Hàn
Shū states: In Āndé County is a temple to Dōngfāng Shuò."
The above pertains to Dézhōu.
Xīnguǎn Yútíng
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed Wèiyāng, son of the Prince of Zhōngshān Jìng, as Marquis of Xīnguǎn.
The Continued Book of Hàn states:
"Twenty lǐ east of Běixīn County is the Fányú Pavilion."
Fánchéng Bóguó
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wǔ enfeoffed a son of the Prince of Zhōngshān Jìng as Marquis of Fányú.
The old city lies southeast of Qīngwǎn County."
It also states:
"During Emperor Wǔ's time,
Ránjí, son of Prince Zhào Jìngsù, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bólíng.
Now, south of Qīngkè County is the old city of his marquisate."
The above pertains to Yíngzhōu.
Xiānyán Tiānjǐng
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìjì states:
"Northwest of Xíngtáng County is the Xiānrén Cliff."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Pài River passes south of the Tiānjǐng Marsh."
Mǎguān Hóngguān
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"Northeast of the Hēi River is the site of the old palace of the Hàn dynasty Prince of Zhōngshān,
where Jiǎnwén constructed a viewing platform for horse games and angling."
It also states:
"The Dìng River flows east past the mountains.
Commonly, this place is called Xìtóu,
which is the Hóngshàng Pass mentioned in the Book of Jìn."
The above pertains to Dìngzhōu.
Lúnjǐng Héshān
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"In Xíngtáng City is a large well like a wheel,
its water boiling and unfathomable."
It also states:
"The Pài River flows north,
passing by Dàhé Mountain."
Fūchéng Nǚmiào
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìjì states:
"Twenty lǐ north of Xíngtáng County is the Rúfū City."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"Inside Xíngtáng City, on the east side of the northern gate, is a temple to the Jade Maiden Goddess.
The stele in front of the temple states:
'King Wǔlíng of Zhào built this city,
but for years it could not be completed.
A holy maiden sighed in lament.
Then all the walls rose up,
and it was finished in no time.'" The above pertains to Héngzhōu.
Níngtái Lìshì
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"King Zhāo of Yān attacked Qí,
obtained precious vessels,
and held a sacrifice at Níngtái."
The Strategies of the Warring States states:
"In a letter to King Huì of Yān, Yuè Yì wrote:
'The Dàlǜ bell was displayed at Yuándōng,
and the old tripods were returned to the Lìshì.'
Both are now within the boundaries of Jìzhōu."
Zhònglǐ Jīn Bóyōng Bì
The Biographies of Divine Immortals states:
"Zhònglǐ lived in the Wúzhōng Mountains.
He held a divine elixir in his mouth
and produced five thousand catties of gold
to save the common people."
The In Search of the Supernatural states:
"Yáng Bóyōng drew water to make charitable porridge.
A man came to drink it
and gave him a stone in return.
Bóyōng planted it,
and it grew into white jade discs.
The land there covered about one qǐng,
and was named the Jade Field."
The above pertains to Yōuzhōu.
Sānggǔ Chúxī
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Sānchéng River
flows south of Fúlíng Mountain
and joins the Shímén River.
It bears the name Sānggǔ,
likely because it flows out from the Sāng Stream."
It also states:
"The Bàoqiū River flows southeast,
and the Lóngchú Stream flows into it."
Sānchéng Qīdù
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Bàoqiū River flows south
and joins the Sānchéng River."
It also states:
"The river passes the old city of Yúyáng
and joins the Qīdù River."
The above pertains to Chánzhōu.
Bǎnquán Pèiyě
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Xuānyuán fought with the Yán Emperor on the plains of Bǎnquán."
The Book of Zhōu states:
"Chīyóu pursued the two emperors,
contending for the plains of Zhuōlù.
The Red Emperor was greatly afraid,
so he persuaded the Yellow Emperor.
They captured Chīyóu and killed him in Zhōngjì,
naming the place Juépèi Yě (the Field of Severed Reins)."
Fùfǔ Liègōu
The Hòu Wèi Yútú Fēngtǔ Jì states:
"Three lǐ northwest of Pānchéng is Lì Mountain,
shaped like an overturned cauldron,
hence the name."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"Legend says that in ancient times the earth split open,
forming a ravine.
There is water in it,
commonly called the Fēnjiā River."
Now, northeast of Huáiróng County, there is a place where the earth split.
The above pertains to Guīzhōu.
Sword Rock and Blade Cliff
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Xú River flows northeast past the west of Lángshān Mountain.
Numerous cliffs rise in competition like the wings of birds,
and the standing rocks, jagged and sheer, resemble swords."
It also states:
"The Qī River flows south past Cángdāoshān Mountain.
Its layered cliffs stand like walls,
rising straight up to pierce the clouds."
Qíongyú Hill and Jùmǎ River
The Bamboo Annals state:
"Xún Yáo of Jìn attacked Zhōngshān at Qíongyú Hill."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Jùmǎ River is the Qī River."
The above pertain to Yìzhōu.
Sù River and Huángluò River
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Sù River originates from Lánshān Mountain in present-day Pí County,
and flows south to join the Xīn River."
It also states:
"The Huángluò River originates from Lúlóngshān Mountain."
Xuán River and Lánshān Mountain
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Xuán River originates from the Xuán Stream north of Féirú County."
The Later Wei Gazetteer of Geography and Customs states:
"Thirty-nine lǐ west of Lú County is Lánshān Mountain."
The above pertain to Píngzhōu.
Cháng Valley and Píng River
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms states:
"Féng Bá's younger brother, Féng Hóng, rebelled.
Féng Bá died from the shock,
and Féng Hóng buried him at the Cháng Valley Mausoleum."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Gāopíng River originates from the Píng River in the northwest."
Láng River and Lóng Garden
The Wei Clan's Record of Lands states:
"The Láng River
descends northeast, near Huánglóng City."
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms states:
"In the third year of the Guāngshǐ era of Mùróng Xī of the Later Yān,
he constructed the Lóngténg Garden
and raised the Jǐngyún Terrace."
The above pertain to Yíngzhōu.
Yáng Xióng's "Admonition for Yōuzhōu"
Vast and boundless are the level plains,
A region distinct within Jìzhōu.
In ancient times, under Táng and Yú,
It was truly a land of peace.
By the Zhou's end, troubles gathered thick,
Pressed hard by the Xūnyù tribes.
When the Six States wielded power alone,
Yān and Zhào made it their capital ground.
To the east, bounded by the Huìmò,
And reaching to the Eastern Hú.
Mighty Qín pushed northward,
Lord Méng built walls to guard the frontier.
When the great Hàn was first established,
It bordered the wilds of northern tribes.
Our mighty armies campaigned often,
Sweeping like the wind in its soaring.
Righteous troops crossed the desert sands,
To pacify our border folk.
Once settled and made secure,
It returned to the peace of Yú and Táng.
Prosperity cannot be taken for granted,
Decline must never be forgotten.
A dike breaks from an ant's nest,
A vessel leaks, its contents lost.
I, a shepherd-official governing Yōu,
Dare to offer this warning to those by the throne.
The Sixth Route: Lǒngyòu
The Lǒngyòu Route
corresponds to the territory of Yōngzhōu in the Tribute of Yǔ.
The area of Yōngzhōu north of Qí and Lǒng
constitutes the Guānnèi Route.
The area south of Lǒng,
together with the northern lands of Liángzhōu from the Tribute of Yǔ,
constitutes the Lǒngyòu Route.
West of Lǒng
encompasses the entirety of its territory.
Qínzhōu contains the Qín Settlement.
Fēizǐ, an ancestor of Qín,
raised horses for King Xiào of Zhōu between the Qiān and Wèi Rivers.
King Xiào enfeoffed him as an attached lord with a settlement at Qín.
Liángzhōu
was the Hàn dynasty's Wūwēi Commandery,
formerly the land of the Xiūchú King of the Xiōngnú.
Zhāng Guǐ of the Former Liáng,
Lǚ Guāng of the Later Liáng,
and Jǔqú Méngxùn of the Northern Liáng all made it their capital.
Gānzhōu
was the Hàn dynasty's Zhāngyè Commandery,
formerly the land of the Húnyé King of the Xiōngnú.
Qǐfú Gānguī of the Western Qín made it his capital.
His son, Qǐfú Chìpán, moved the capital to Hézhōu. Sùzhōu was the Hàn dynasty's Jiǔquán Commandery.
Zhāng Guǐ of the Former Liáng,
Lǐ Gǎo of the Western Liáng,
and Jǔqú Méngxùn of the Northern Liáng all made it their capital.
Xīzhōu
was the Gāochāng Fortress of the Chēshī Kingdom in Hàn times.
Formerly, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn dispatched troops on a western campaign.
The army, exhausted and worn,
and those among them who were most fatigued
settled there.
The terrain was lofty,
and the population flourished,
hence it was named Gāochāng ("Lofty and Prosperous").
Tiānshuǐ and Shénquán
The Book of Hàn states:
"Tiānshuǐ Commandery
was established during Emperor Wǔ's reign."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"In Wèizhōu, [the river] joins the Shénquán in the southeast."
Hēichéng and Zhūyǔ
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Hēi River originates north of Hēichéng,
flows southwest past Hēichéng,
and reaches the Wèi River in the west."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"From the Shūjīng: 'West from Qīng, Zhūyǔ, and Niǎoshǔ,
to the great Huàshān.'"
The above pertain to Qínzhōu.
Àitíng and Jīnggǔ
The Book of Hàn states:
"The Commandant of Cavalry resided at Mì'àitíng."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The waters of Jīngtóu River
flow north through Jīng Valley and pour into the Wèi River."
Jījù and Mǎ Stream
The Book of Hàn states:
"Xiāngwǔ County has the Five-Chicken Settlement (Wǔjījù)."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Wèi River flows southeast,
passing south of Shǒuyáng County.
On the left is the Tiānmǎ Stream,
which joins it unevenly from the flank."
The above pertain to Wèizhōu.
Bǎiqǐng and Sìshān
The Records of Sān Qín states:
"Qiúchíshān Mountain is called Bǎiqǐng ('Hundred Acres').
On its summit is a hundred-acre pool,
with cliffs standing a hundred ren high.
If one man guards the path,
ten thousand cannot approach."
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng states:
"When Yáng Shèng succeeded to the position,
he divided the Dí and Qiāng peoples of the Sìshān ('Four Mountains') into twenty divisions."
The above pertain to Chéngzhōu.
Mǎ Dí and Cāngláng Zhǒng
Yìng Shào's annotation to the Book of Hàn states:
"Wǔdū Commandery
was formerly the land of the White Horse Qiāng Dí."
The Book of Hàn states:
"The Cāngláng Zhǒng
are the Wǔdū Qiāng."
The above pertain to Wǔzhōu.
Líntáo and Wàngqū
The Book of Hàn states:
"Líntáo County belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Táo River flows east,
passes Gāngēn Pavilion,
and goes through Wàngqū."
The above pertain to Mínzhōu.
Táo River and Diàn River
The Record of Shāzhōu states:
"The Táo River originates from Qiángtáishān Mountain."
It also states:
"East of the mountain is the source of the Táo River,
south of the mountain is the source of the Diàn River."
The above pertain to Táozhōu.
Jīshí and Xiāotóng
The Shūjīng states:
"He guided the [Yellow] River past Jīshí."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Lí River flows north past the west of Xiāotóng City."
Yúchéng and Má Lěi
The Commentary on the Water Classic states:
"The Lí River flows northeast past Yúchéng,
and a stream pours into it."
The Records of Qínzhōu states:
"West of Fúhǎn City is the Má Lěi ('Hemp Rampart'),
which can hold ten thousand men."
The above pertain to Hézhōu.
Swallow Cliff, Deer Pass
The Records of Chóuchí states:
"Below Wǔxīng City lies Swallow Cliff."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"Deer Pass is located ten lǐ south of Cāngsōng County."
These are the places.
Turtle Observatory, Bird City
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms states:
"During the time of Zhāng Xuánjìng of Former Liáng,
General of the Right Sòng Xī requested to take the soil from the Turtle Observatory to build his residence."
The Records of Xīhé states:
"Gūzāng was originally a Xiongnu city,
thus it was called Gàizàng City.
The city is not square in shape;
it has a head, tail, and two wings,
and is named Bird City."
The above pertains to Liáng Prefecture.
Willow Valley, Orchid Pond
Xí Zuòchǐ's Spring and Autumn Annals of Hàn and Jìn states:
"At night, the waves in Great Willow Valley surge and overflow,
their sound like thunder."
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn states:
"Lánchí County belongs to Lǒngxī Commandery."
Héli, Línzé
The Book of Documents states:
"The Weak Water is guided to Héli."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"Zhāowǔ County has Línzé Pavilion to its east."
The above pertains to Gān Prefecture.
Dídào, Yízhèn
The Book of Hàn states:
"Dídào County belongs to Lǒngxī Commandery."
The Geographical Records of Zhōu states:
"The city of Líntáo Commandery,
built during the Tàihé era of Later Wèi,
established Yízhèn Town to guard the strategic route against the Qiāng."
The above pertains to Lán Prefecture.
Lacquer Water, Golden Spring
Zhāng Huá's Records of Diverse Matters states:
"In Yánshòu County, a mountain stone spring flows into a ditch,
and its water contains grease.
When scooped and placed in a vessel, it appears pitch black,
like uncoagulated ointment.
When lit, it burns extremely brightly,
but it is inedible.
The locals call it stone lacquer."
Yìng Shào's Ceremonials of Hàn Officials states:
"Below Jiǔquán City lies the Golden Spring,
whose taste resembles wine."
Jiǔquán, Féishuǐ
The Book of Hàn states:
"Jiǔquán Commandery
was established in the first year of the Tàichū era of Emperor Wǔ."
The Records of Diverse Matters states:
"South of Yánshòu County in Jiǔquán, there is a mountain spring,
whose water contains grease,
like boiled meat broth."
The above pertains to Sù Prefecture.
Báitǔ River, Bēihé Sea
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The Báitǔ River flows from the northwest of Báitǔ City."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"West of Línqiāng County lies the Bēihé Sea,
also called the Azure Sea."
Jīgǔ, Lóngchéng
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The Huángshuǐ flows eastward,
and the Jīgǔ River flows northward to join it."
It also states:
"The Huángshuǐ originates beyond the frontier,
passing north of Lánchí.
It then flows southeast past Lóngyí City."
The above pertains to Shàn Prefecture.
Xiàogǔ, Yíhé
The Book of Hàn states:
"Xiàogǔ County belongs to Dūnhuáng Commandery."
The Geographical Records of the Tàikāng Era of Jìn states:
"Yíhé County belongs to Dūnhuáng Commandery."
Lóngduī, Yúzé
The Book of Hàn states:
"West of Dūnhuáng, outside the frontier pass, lies the White Dragon Mounds."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"Xiàogǔ County
was formerly the Yúzé Barrier."
The above pertains to Shā Prefecture.
Fertile Land, Rich Fields
The Book of Later Hàn states:
"During the reign of Emperor Shùn,
due to the fertile lands of the old Yīwú region,
which bordered the Western Regions,
orders were given to reopen the military farms,
and a Yīwú Commandant was appointed."
The Old Affairs of Xīhé states:
"Around the Pú Sea lie fertile and excellent fields,
with abundant water and lush vegetation."
Tiānshān, Dìjiāng
The Book of Hàn states:
"He sent the General of Èrshī to set out from Jiǔquán
to attack the Left Worthy Prince at Tiānshān."
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"Tiānshān is rich in gold and jade.
There is a divine bird shaped like a yellow sack,
red as cinnabar fire,
with six feet and four wings.
It is completely featureless,
yet understands song and dance,
and is truly Dìjiāng."
The above pertains to Yī Prefecture.
Chēshī Kingdom, Tiándì County
The Book of Hàn states:
"The Former Kingdom of Chēshī
resided in Jiāohé City."
The Geographical Records states:
"In the second year of the Xiánhé era of Jìn, Gāochāng Commandery was established,
and Tiándì County was founded."
Jiāohé City, Gāochāng Fort
The Book of Hàn states:
"Jiāohé City has the Jiāohé River,
which splits and flows around the city walls."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"Gāochāng Fort
originally belonged to Dūnhuáng.
To the east lies the Long Valley,
where the Commandant resides."
The above pertains to Xī Prefecture.
A Song of Liáng Prefecture by Wēn Zǐshēng of Later Wèi
Traveling afar to Wǔwēi Commandery,
Gazing distantly at Gūzāng City.
Carriages and horses crisscross,
Songs and music resound day and night.
Another song says:
The road leads out of Yùmén Pass,
The city connects to Lóngchéng Slope.
Only engaged in string music and song,
Who speaks of the distant mountains and rivers?
Yáng Xióng's Admonition for Liáng Prefecture
The Black Water and Western River,
Stretch horizontally to the Kūnlún Mountains.
Submitting to the Heavenly Gate,
Marked as the Yōng frontier.
Often in the reigns of later kings,
Their legacy was frequently lost.
The Lord on High was displeased,
Commanding Hàn to establish Liáng.
Beyond the Lǒng Mountains,
It stands as the western wilderness.
Repelling the fierce Yuè to the south,
Opening to the strong Hú in the north.
Wells and territories interconnected,
United in guarding that capital.
The Seventh: Shānnán Circuit
The Shānnán Circuit
corresponds to the regions of Jīng and Liáng Provinces as described in the Tribute of Yǔ.
The Book of Documents states:
"From Jīng Mountain to Héngyáng is Jīng Province,
from Huáyáng to the Black Water is Liáng Province."
Now note: the southern boundary of Jīng Province belongs to the Jiāngnán Circuit,
and its eastern boundary extends into the Huáinán Circuit.
Liáng Province, from Jiàngé southward, forms the Jiànnán Circuit,
while its northern periphery extends into the Lǒngyòu Circuit.
The Book of Hàn, Treatise on Astronomy states:
"The constellations Yì and Zhěn correspond to Jīng Province."
It borders north to the southern slopes of Jīng and Huá Mountains,
crosses the Hànshuǐ south to the Jiāng,
and borders west to Jiàngé,
encompassing all this territory.
Jīng Province
was first made the capital by King Wén of Chǔ.
Bāo Prefecture
is the ancient State of Bāo,
which is the site of Guīxū.
The Records of Jiānglíng states:
"King Wén of Chǔ first moved the capital from Dānyáng to Yǐng,
which is present-day Nánchéng north of the prefecture."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The Hànshuǐ flows east past Guīxū,
located within the boundaries of Jīnniú County."
Huángfǔ Mì's Records of State Capitals states:
"The old city of the State of Bāo lies two hundred paces east of the county seat."
Xiāng Prefecture
lies on the boundary between Jīng and Yù Provinces as described in the Tribute of Yǔ.
Dèng Prefecture
was the Southern Capital of Later Hàn,
from which Emperor Guāngwǔ arose.
Southern Jīng, Western Chǔ
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Directly south is called Jīngzhōu."
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"From north of the Huái River, Pèi, Chén, Rǔnán,
and Nánjùn constitute Western Chǔ."
Yúnzé, Jǐngzhōu
Chūnqiū Wényào Gōu states:
"East of Dàbié to Yúnzé, Jiǔjiāng, Héngshān, and Jīngzhōu.
Now note: this is Yúnmèngzé."
Records of Wú states:
"Wèi general Xiàhóu Shàng besieged Nánjùn,
constructing a pontoon bridge to measure Jǐngzhōu,
now within the boundaries of Jiānglíng County."
The above pertains to Jīngzhōu.
Southern Xiàn, Northern Jīn
Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"Xiāngyáng was originally a minor town of Chǔ,
with Huánxī flowing by its west,
and Xiàn Mountain stretching across its south."
Xí Zàochǐ's Xiāngyáng Jì states:
"Xiāngchéng was originally the northern ferry of the state of Chǔ."
Xí Pond, Gě Well
Xiāngyáng Jì states:
"Eight hundred paces south of Xiàn Mountain,
descending west along the path one hundred paces,
there is the Xí family fish pond."
Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"At the residence of Zhūgě Liàng there is a well,
over four zhàng deep,
with an opening one chǐ five cùn wide,
the brickwork remains as it was originally."
The above pertains to Xiāngzhōu.
Lìxiāng, Chōngyì
Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Chǔ attacked Xú,
and the Qí army attacked Lì to rescue them."
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"North of Suí County there is Lìxiāng."
Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Yuán, because Chōnglíng was low and damp,
carved out two townships, Báishuǐ of Càijì, to form the estate of the Marquis of Chōnglíng."
State of Suí, Tángxiāng
Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Dòu Bóbǐ said to the Lord of Chǔ:
'Among the states east of the Hàn River, Suí is the largest.'"
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"The state of Suí
is now Suí County of Yìyáng."
It also states:
"Jìn and Chǔ fought at Bì,
with the Marquis of Táng forming the left flank."
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"Táng belonged to Chǔ,
a small state,
located at present-day Shàngtángxiāng southeast of Ānchāng County in Yìyáng."
The above pertains to Suízhōu.
Mǎshuǐ, Tuó Lake
Nán Yōngzhōu Jì states:
"South of Lóngjū County there is Mǎshuǐ."
Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"Twenty lǐ east of Miǎnyáng County there is Tuó Lake."
The above pertains to Fùzhōu.
Shòuyá, Lángwěi
Yídū Shānchuān Jì states:
"On Shòuyá Mountain there is a stone cliff,
with patterns of yellow and red,
shaped like teeth."
Gōujiāng Shān Jì states:
"The county is forty lǐ from the mountain,
and from Lángwěi Beach one descends to the southern cliff."
The above pertains to Xiázhōu.
Huánglóng, Báidì
Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"At the head of the gorge, the north bank is called Báiyán Peak,
in the middle is Huánglóng Beach waters,
feared by those traveling upstream or downstream."
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Báidì Mountain,
connects to Yuánmǎ Ridge in the north,
and connects to Chìjiǎ Mountain in the south."
Jiǔbǎn, Sānxī
Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"Hánshān's Jiǔbǎn,
is the most steep and perilous."
It also states:
"Sānxī waters flow south for several lǐ,
then empty south into the great river."
The above pertains to Kuízhōu.
Míngyuè Gorge, Jìnyún Mountain
Huáyáng Guózhì states:
"Bājùn's Jiāngzhōu has Míngyuè Gorge,
at the head of the gorge, the southern peak's stone cliff has a round hole,
shaped like the bright moon,
hence the name."
Jìnyún Shān Zhuàn states:
"Huángdì compounded divine elixirs upon it,
thus the mountain gained its name."
Fúlíng, Yángquē
Book of Hàn states:
"Bājùn, called Bājùn, administered Fúlíng County."
Jìn Tàikāng Dìjì states:
"During Lǐ Xióng's rebellion,
Diànjiāng County was re-established at Yángquē,
also belonging to Bājùn."
Note: the present prefecture is the ancient Bājùn.
The above pertains to Yúzhōu.
Lóngxī, Niúdào
Dàojiā Zá Jì states:
"Zhāng Lǔ's daughter once washed clothes at the foot of the mountain,
white mist enveloped her body,
and she became pregnant,
ashamed, she took her own life.
Before dying, she told her maid:
'After I die, cut open my abdomen.'
The maid followed her words,
and upon cutting, obtained a pair of dragon offspring,
which then entered the Hàn River.
The girl was buried atop the mountain,
and later the dragon offspring repeatedly visited their mother's grave,
forming a path."
Shísānzhōu Zhì states:
"The King of Qín, not knowing the road to Shǔ,
had five stone oxen carved,
placed gold beneath their tails,
claiming these heavenly oxen could excrete gold.
The people of Shǔ believed it,
and had five strong men together pull the oxen, forming a road."
Now within the boundaries of Bāochéng County.
Ràngshuǐ, Liánchuān
Liángchuān Jì states:
"Ten lǐ southwest of Liáng there is Ràngshuǐ."
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Liánshuǐ emerges from Bálǐng Mountain,
flowing north into Liánchuān."
Now within the boundaries of Nánzhèng County.
The above pertains to Liángzhōu.
Luògǔ, Lóngtíng
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Luògǔ waters originate from Luògǔ,
flowing south."
Liángzhōu Jì states:
"Lóngtíng County belongs to Tǎngchéng Commandery."
The above pertains to Yángzhōu.
Huánghuāchuān, Zǐbǎi Bǎn
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Dàsàn waters flow west into Huánghuāchuān."
Huáyáng Guózhì states:
"Eighty lǐ east of Liángquán County there is Zǐbǎi Bǎn."
The above pertains to Fèngzhōu.
Wǔguān, Wényì
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"King Zhāo of Qín sent a letter to King Huái of Chǔ saying:
'I wish to meet with you at Wǔguān,
to personally conclude an alliance.'
Now located east of Shāngluò County."
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Luòshuǐ passes northeast by Wényì,
in Luònán County."
The above pertains to Shāngzhōu.
Jīnshuǐ, Xīchéng
Hànshuǐ Jì states:
"Jīnshuǐ Commandery administered Jīngāng County,
originally Jīnchéng Commandery,
later changed by the Northern Wèi."
Liángzhōu Jì states:
"The Northern Wèi combined Huáyáng and Jīnchéng commanderies to form Zhōngchéng Commandery,
administering Xiāngtíng, Xīchéng, and Jīnchuān counties."
Yú Shùn Shrine, Hàn Gāo Temple
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Within the old city walls of Xīchéng County there is a shrine to Yú Shùn."
Liángzhōu Jì states:
"At the foot of the southern mountain of Xúnyáng County there is a temple to Emperor Gāo of Hàn."
The above pertains to Jīnzhōu.
Méixī, Jíshuǐ
Nán Yōngzhōu Jì states:
"Seven lǐ from Nányáng County there is Méixī."
Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Jíshuǐ passes through Xīnyě County,
and by Huángyǒu settlement."
Wǔlǒng, Liùmén
Zhōu Dìtú Jì states:
"Wǔlǒng Mountain has five ridges,
connected in a continuous line,
called the Liùmén Weir.
Three lǐ west, damming the Tuān,
constructed by Shào Xìnchén."
The above pertains to Dèngzhōu.
Xióngchuān Lóngjǐng
The Nánjīngzhōu Jì states:
"Fēnglì Commandery administers the three counties of Fēnglì, Xióngchuān, and Yángchuān."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Hàn River flows east further to become Lóngtán,
below which lies the islet of Lóngjǐng."
The above are in Jūnzhōu.
Jǐngshān Fěnshuǐ
The Shānhǎijīng states:
"The first peak of the Jīng Mountains is called Jǐngshān,
upon which there is much metal and jade."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Fěnshuǐ,
originates and flows east past Shàngfěn County."
Yànsài Lángshān
The Jīngzhōu Túfùjì states:
"Yànfú Mountain
is Yànsài."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Yí River originates from Lángshān."
The above are in Fángzhōu.
Míngshuǐ Quánjiē
The Hòuwèishū states:
"Luòcóng Commandery,
with the two counties of Wǔdū and Míngshuǐ,
belongs to Dōngyìzhōu."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Quánjiēshuǐ emerges from Héchí,
flowing southeast into Jù County."
The above are in Xīngzhōu.
Jīnxī Tóngshuǐ
The Liángzhōu Jì states:
"To the northwest of the eastern mountain of Yìchāng County is Jīntóngxī,
a stream that yields gold,
hence the name."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Ten lǐ south of Jiāmēng County is Dāohuán Mountain,
from which Chìtóngshuǐ emerges."
The above are in Lìzhōu.
Tóngliáng Shíhù
Zuǒ Sī's Shǔdū Fù states:
"Outside, it bears Tóngliáng and Dàngqú."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"South of Lóngpán Mountain there is a stone,
thirty zhàng in length,
five zhàng in height.
In its midst are a door and door leaves,
as if shut by someone,
the ancients considered it the Jade Maiden's chamber."
The above are in Hézhōu.
Liáng Sòngshǐ's "Jīngzhōu Yuègē"
To Zhānghuá he went for hunting play,
past Yǐng he returned with captured game.
Billowing, purple mists converge,
dense and thick, red dust flies.
Another song
At dawn setting out on the Jiāngjīn road,
at dusk lodging on the Língxī path.
The level thoroughfare broad and straight,
the tall poplars lush and swaying.
Yáng Xióng's "Jīngzhōu Zhēn"
Remote and deep are the Wū Mountains,
south of Jīng.
Jiāng and Hàn flow to pay homage,
their currents vast and surging.
Lord Xià encountered the great flood,
Jīng and Héng were regulated.
Yúnmèng's muddy lands,
produced bundles of choice màoháo grass.
Gold and jade for whetstones,
ivory and dark tortoise shell.
Tribute baskets of a hundred goods,
generation after generation enriched thereby.
Trembling with fear and caution,
until Jié's wild excess.
Saying, 'In the imperial position,
it is as if I possess heaven's sun.'
Not submitting to the various states,
who dares to seize from me?
There was also Chéng Tāng,
who indeed grasped his battle-axe.
He banished him to Náncháo,
branding him with the name Jié.
Náncháo vast and boundless,
abounding in Chǔ and Jīng.
Their winds fierce and violent,
their spirit sharp and strong.
When the Way prevails, they submit later;
when the Way is lost, they are first to be strong.
Though the age be peaceful and stable,
none dare be idle or indulgent.
Your servant, the shepherd, oversees Jīng,
dare I inform the charioteer.
The Eighth: Jiànnán Circuit
Jiànnán Circuit
is the region of Liángzhōu according to the Tribute of Yǔ.
Liángzhōu, from Jiàngé southward,
was divided to form Yìzhōu,
hence it is called Jiànnán Circuit.
East of Jiàngé in Liángzhōu
was divided to belong to the two circuits of Shānnán and Lǒngyòu.
The Hànshū‧Tiānwénzhì states:
"Zī and Shēn correspond to the field division of Yìzhōu."
Its earliest kings were then Cáncóng and Dùyǔ.
Yáng Xióng's Shǔběnjì states:
"The first king of Shǔ was called Cáncóng,
next was Bóyōng,
next was Yúfú."
The Shísānzhōuzhì states:
"Shǔ King Dùyǔ
styled himself Wàngdì."
Later, the territory belonged to Qín.
At the end of the Former Hàn, Gōngsūn Shù occupied it;
at the end of the Later Hàn, Liú Bèi occupied it.
Cáncóng Dùyǔ
Both are seen in the narrative.
Shíjìng Tóngliáng
The Shǔběnjì states:
"A man of Wǔdū had a daughter,
whom the Shǔ king took as his consort.
She fell ill and died,
was buried in Chéngdū,
and a stone mirror was made
to mark her tomb."
Zuǒ Sī's Shǔdū Fù states:
"Outside, it bears Tóngliáng and Dàngqú,
within, it contains strategic points and fertile lands."
The above are in Yìzhōu.
Yínshuǐ Jīnshān
The Huáyángguózhì states:
"Fúlíng has Chánshānshuǐ,
whose source contains a gold mine."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Jīnshān faces east over a stream,
its light shining upon the river."
The above are in Miánzhōu.
Fēiliáng Juéjiàn
The Huáyángguózhì states:
"When Zhūgě Liàng governed Shǔ,
he cut through rock and spanned the air to build elevated gallery roads,
which are the ancient Jiàngé roads."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"When Jiāng Wéi resisted Zhōng Huì,
he fortified this mountain with ramparts.
Sheer cliffs of a thousand zhàng,
below which lie bottomless ravines."
The above are in Jiànzhōu.
Nánchí Xīshuǐ
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Nánchí is eight lǐ southeast of Lángzhōng County,
also, Xīshuǐ County was originally territory of the Qín-era Lángzhōng County."
The above are in Lángzhōu.
Qīdào Shèhóng
The Shǔzhì states:
"When Jiāng Wéi and others heard that Zhūgě Zhān had been defeated,
they led the army via the Qīdào of Guǎnghàn,
to ascertain the true situation."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Fújiāngshuǐ flows further southeast to Shèhóng."
It is now within the boundaries of Shèhóng County.
The above are in Zǐzhōu.
Lónghèshān Yúshéshuǐ
The Huáyángguózhì states:
"Fifteen lǐ northwest of Dānyáng County is Lónghèshān."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Yúshéshuǐ,
enters the boundaries of Qīngshén County from the northeast, from the boundaries of Língzhōu."
The above are in Méizhōu.
Yúshān Língjǐng
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Dōngyú, Xīyú, and Nányú, three mountains face each other."
It also says:
"The Sānyú Mountains are one lǐ from Língjǐng."
The above are in Língzhōu.
Jīntángmù Tónggōngshān
The Huáyángguózhì states:
"Xīndū County has Jīntángshān,
its waters connect to Bā and Hàn."
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Sixty lǐ southwest of Wǔchéng County is Tónggōngshān,
towering above the multitude of peaks."
The above are in Jiǎnzhōu.
Kǔnjǐng Jīyóuxī
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Sixty lǐ southwest of Nánchōng County lies Kǔnjǐng."
The Yánjǐng further states:
"The Jīyóu Shén is east of Xiàngrú County.
To the north, a short distance downstream, is Jīyóu Creek,
from which it derives its name."
The above pertains to Guǒzhōu.
Jǐnshān Miánshuǐ
The Huáyáng Guózhi states:
"North of Héjiāng lies Língjǐn Mountain."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Mián River flows to the foot of Fāng Mountain in Jiāngyáng County and enters the river,
where it is called Miánkǒu."
The above pertains to Lúzhōu.
Qióngshuǐ Dèngshān
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"From Xiá Mountain flows the Qióng River,
whose southern side is rich in gold."
The Hànshū states:
"Emperor Wén bestowed upon Dèng Tōng the copper mountain at Qióngdào,
granting him exclusive rights to mint coins."
The above pertains to Yǎzhōu.
Wēnxué Qǔchí
The Huáyáng Guózhi states:
"The Wēnshuǐ cave is warm in both winter and summer."
Yìng Shào, annotating the Hànshū, states:
"Northwest of Sūchū County lies a muddy pool."
According to current records, this is Qǔchí.
The above pertains to Xīzhōu.
Fúxītān Ténglóngshuǐ
The Yìzhōu Jì states:
"Sixty lǐ southeast of Fúxītān,
there is a yellow fish resembling the riverbank."
It is now within the boundaries of Bódào County.
It further states:
"The source of Lóngténg Creek is in Nánxī County."
The above pertains to Róngzhōu.
Yáng Xióng's "Yìzhōu Zhēn"
Lofty, towering Mín Mountain,
In antiquity called Liángzhōu.
Huáyáng to the western extreme,
The Black River flows southward.
Qín acted without the Way,
Three regions crumbled and rebelled.
Righteous armies quelled the violence,
Thus establishing the state of Hàn.
Expanding the borders and territory,
Restoring the wilds of Liáng.
Divided into twelve,
Its glory rivaled Yú and Xià.
The minister overseeing Liáng,
Attends to his duties and plans.
Managing prosperity and decline,
I dare inform the gentlemen.
Huáinán Dào, the Ninth
Huáinán Dào
is the region of Yángzhōu according to the Yǔ Gòng,
and also includes the eastern border of Jīngzhōu.
The Shàngshū states:
"Huái and the sea are Yángzhōu."
Now, according to records, the eastern part of Yángzhōu is Jiāngnán Dào,
and the southern part is Lǐngnán Dào.
Furthermore, the "Tiānwén Zhì" of the Hànshū states:
"The constellations Qiānniú and Wùnǚ correspond to the celestial division of Yángzhōu."
South of the Huái River,
skirting the river westward,
encompasses its entire territory.
Present-day Yángzhōu
was the Hàn dynasty's Guǎnglíng Commandery,
later renamed Jiāngdū.
King Bì of Wú resided there,
as did Guǎnglíng King Lì
and Jiāngdū King Yì.
Lúzhōu
was the ancient state of Lúzi,
where King Liè established his capital,
in the region of Náncháo.
The Shàngshū states:
"Chéng Tāng banished Jié to Náncháo."
Shòuzhōu
was where King Kǎoliè of Chǔ established his capital.
Nányǎn Dōngyáng
The Yǔdì Zhì states:
"Nányǎnzhōu
was first established by Emperor Wén of Sòng in the eighth year of Yuánjiá by carving out territory between the Jiāng and Huái,
with its seat at Guǎnglíng."
It further states:
"Guǎnglíng Commandery
was Dōngyáng Commandery during the conflict between Chǔ and Hàn."
Diàotái Yúpǔ
The Xīzhēng Jì states:
"At Léibēi there is a terrace,
twenty zhàng high."
The Nányǎnzhōu Jì states:
"It is considered the fishing terrace of King Bì of Wú."
The Nányǎnzhōu Jì states:
"Yúpǔ was perpetually turbid morning and evening,
but one day it became clear and pure.
Governor Fàn Miǎo reported this as an auspicious sign."
The above pertains to Yángzhōu.
Shèbēi Yándú
The Hànshū states:
"The Chancellor of Guǎnglíng, Shèng Zhī, memorialized,
requesting to seize the grassy fields of the king's Shèbēi,
and distribute them to the poor."
It further states:
"Yándú belonged to Línhuái Commandery."
The above pertains to Chǔzhōu.
Fēngpǔ Bāohú
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The river joins Fēngpǔ of Wūjiāng County to the north,
which connects upstream to the lake pools."
It further states:
"Next is the Yīntáng water,
which also receives water from Huánghòu Lake.
Huánghòu Lake connects to Bāo Lake,
which borders Tán Lake to the west."
Héngjīn Dòngpǔ
The Wú Zhì states:
"When Sūn Jiān was campaigning east of the river,
the Governor of Yángzhōu, Liú Yáo, sent his general Fán Xióng Yú Mí to garrison Héngjīn,
where he was defeated by Zhù."
The Wèi Zhì states:
"Wèi sent Cáo Xiū and Zhāng Liáo to attack Wú,
emerging from Dòngkǒu."
Lì Yuán, annotating the Shuǐjīng, states:
"On the river, to the left facing Dòngkǒu, is the riverbank of Dòngkǒu."
The above pertains to Hézhōu.
Quèfǔtíng Mǎqiūjù
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Quèfǔ Creek flows northwest,
passing south of Quèfǔ Pavilion."
The Xù Hànshū states:
"At Dāngtú there is Mǎqiūjù,
where Xú Fèng rebelled."
Yǔjù Qínxū
The Dìwáng Jì states:
"Yǔ convened the lords at Túshān,
in the region of Yángzhōu.
Dāngtú County has Yǔjù."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Luòjiàn flows north past Qínxū,
and empties into the Huái."
The above pertains to Háozhōu.
Lúguó Shūchéng
Yìng Shào, annotating the Hànshū, states:
"Lújiāng Commandery was the former state of Lúzi."
It further states:
"East of the six counties of Lújiāng lies Shūchéng."
Tóngxiāng Cháoyì
The Hànshū states:
"Zhū Yì served as the village head of Tóngxiāng.
He was honest, fair, and benevolent.
When he fell ill and was near death,
he instructed his son:
'The people of Tóngxiāng loved me;
you must bury me in Tóngxiāng.'" The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Chǔ fortified the city of Cháo."
The Yǔdì Zhì states:
"Chǔ named it Cháoyì."
The above pertains to Lúzhōu.
Zhàotúnchéng Zhōu Yú Miào
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"East of Pòlǔjī lies Zhàotúnchéng,
which contains a granary."
It further states:
"North of Léizhōu, facing the river, stands the temple of Zhōu Yú."
The above pertains to Shūzhōu.
Yángtóujiàn Lóngquánbēi
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Féi River joins Yángtóu Creek on the left,
receiving water from Sháobēi,
and is called Yángtóujiàn."
Fú Tāo's "Zhèng Huái Lùn" states:
"That Shòuyáng
looks upon the fine fields of Lóngquán, spanning ten thousand qǐng."
Huòlǐ Gǔchuān
The Wú Zhì states:
"Wú sent Sūn Chěn to mobilize a large force,
and garrison them at Huòlǐ."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Cǐ River joins Jígǔchuān water from the northeast on the right."
Dòngtái Yǐnshì
The Commentary on the Huángtíng Scripture states:
"Beneath Mount Huò there is a Dòngtái,
measuring two hundred *li* square.
It has two gates,
and within it are the fruits of the Five Fragrant Ganoderma and Flying Blossoms."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"On Mount Bāgōng there is a Yǐnshì (Hermitage) and a stone well."
The above pertains to Shòu Prefecture.
Fānchē Jībù
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Yīng Bù, King of Jiǔjiāng, built Fānchē City
north of the Fānchē River."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The river flows east again past the south of Mount Jībù,
commonly called Jībù Jī."
Huángshí Qīnglín
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"On the right bank of the river is Mount Huángshí.
The river flows past its north,
which is Huángshí Jī."
It also states:
"To the left of the river is the Qīnglín Estuary.
The water accumulates to form a lake,
called Qīnglín Lake."
The above pertains to Qí Prefecture.
Liǎo County Jiǎng City
The Zuǒ Commentary states:
"Chǔ's Prince Xiè destroyed Liǎo."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"Ānfēng has Liǎo County."
It also states:
"As for Jiǎng, Xíng, Máo, Zuò, and Zhài,
they are the descendants of the Duke of Zhōu."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"This refers to the Jiǎng Township City in Qīsī County of Yìyáng."
Xiánzidū Yúqiūguō
The Zuǒ Commentary states:
"The people of Chǔ attacked Xián.
The Viscount of Xián fled to Huáng."
The Records of the Thirteen Provinces states:
"The city
was the former capital of the Viscount of Xián."
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"East of Yìyáng Commandery is Yúqiūguō.
To its south is a temple to Wǔ Zǐxū.
Both are in Guāng Prefecture."
Shíchéng Tiānjǐng
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The Shī River flows past Mount Shíchéng,
which is extremely high and steep."
It also states:
"Fifteen paces south of Yìyáng Commandery,
facing the gate, is a Tiānjǐng (Heavenly Well),
over a hundred paces in circumference."
Jiǔsài Sānguān
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"What are the Nine Passes?
They are Dàfén, Míng'è, Jīngyuàn, Fāngchéng, Háobǎn, Jǐngxíng, Jīncī, Gōuzhù, and Jūyōng."
The Qí Annals states:
"The Later Wèi established the Píngjìng Pass at Yìyáng.
Thus it is said Yìyáng has the barrier of the Three Passes.
This is one of them."
The above pertains to Shēn Prefecture.
Chǔ Settlement Xīnchéng
The Record of the Hàn River states:
"Traveling two hundred *li* from the mouth of the Hàn River,
one reaches Juānkǒu.
There is a village.
Traveling three hundred *li* further, one reaches Zhèng City,
a settlement of Chǔ."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"East of Ānlù County is Xīnchéng,
built by Huán Wēn during his campaign against Shí Jìlóng.
It faces the Juān River to the south."
The above pertains to Ān Prefecture.
Guītóu Mountain Lóngxiāng River
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"The Jǔ River originates from Guītóu Mountain.
Also, on the left bank of the river,
it meets the mouth of the Lóngxiāng River."
Dùnyáng Garrison Xiàngshān City
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states:
"In the sixth year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
Wáng Dūn appointed Táo Kǎn as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
stationing him at Dùnyáng."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"Several tens of *li* along the river,
on Mount Xiàng there is a city,
which was the residence of the Wú-era Administrator of Jiāngxià."
The above pertains to Miǎn Prefecture.
Yáng Xióng's "Admonition for Yángzhōu"
Vast and lofty is Yángzhōu,
By the shores of Jiāng and Hàn.
Pénglí is its great lake,
Where the sun-birds dwell.
Oranges, pomelos, feathers, and shells,
Jade, gems, fine and coarse bamboo.
Mǐnyuè marks its northern border,
Yuán and Xiāng pour their waters here.
Tàibó yielded his rightful place,
His line in Wú continued.
Fūchāi's single grave error,
Cost Tàibó his posterity's throne.
The Zhōu house failed to uphold order,
So Gōujiàn entered their court.
When Zhōu's fortunes were rising,
Yuèshāng sent tribute through interpreters.
By the end of the Spring and Autumn era,
Lords of the domain rebelled.
The head cannot afford not to reflect,
The limbs cannot afford not to cherish.
Yáo esteemed frequent self-examination,
Shùn valued reverent counsel.
I, your shepherd-minister, oversee Yáng,
Dare to admonish those who hold the tallies.
Tenth Fascicle: The Jiāngnán Circuit
The Jiāngnán Circuit
corresponds to the domain of Yángzhōu in the Tribute of Yǔ,
and also includes the southern border of Jīngzhōu.
Yángzhōu:
the area north of the river constitutes the Huáinán Circuit,
the area south of the ranges constitutes the Lǐngnán Circuit.
It is bounded by the river to the north and reaches the sea to the east,
extending to the ranges in the south,
encompassing all this land.
Sū Prefecture is the site of Wú Tàibó's settlement.
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The land of Wú corresponds to the Dǒu lunar mansion."
When Tàibó died,
Zhòngyōng succeeded him.
The state was transmitted to his great-grandson Zhōu Zhāng.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he accordingly enfeoffed him there.
Yuè Prefecture corresponds to Yuè.
Xià's Shǎokāng enfeoffed his youngest son Wúyú there,
to maintain the sacrifices to Yǔ.
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The land of Yuè
corresponds to the Niú and Wùnǚ lunar mansions."
Rùn Prefecture
was Zhūfāng in the Spring and Autumn period.
Jiāngníng County
was the Jīnlíng settlement of Chǔ.
It served as the capital for six dynasties: Wú, Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén.
Dōngfǔ Xīzhōu
Shān Qiānzhī's Records of Dānyáng states:
"The land of Dōngfǔ City
was the residence of Jìn's Emperor Jiǎnwén when he was Prince of Kuàijī.
To the east was the residence of the Chancellor, Prince of Kuàijī Dàozi.
As Dàozi governed Yángzhōu,
it was commonly called Dōngfǔ (Eastern Prefecture)."
It also states:
"The Yángzhōu administrative compound,
founded by Wáng Dūn,
had three gates opened to the east, south, and west.
It was commonly called Xīzhōu (Western Prefecture)."
Sūn Tomb Jiǎng Temple
The Records of Dānyáng states:
"Jiǎng Tomb,
named after the mountain,
is the tomb of the Great Emperor of Wú."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The terrace is beside the winding slope of the Sūn Tomb,
hence the Jiǎng Tomb Pavilion is also called Sūn Tomb Pavilion."
The Records of Dānyáng states:
"Jiǎng Zǐwén was Commandant of Mòlíng.
He declared before his death
that he would become a god.
Later, he was killed by bandits.
His former subordinate suddenly saw Zǐwén riding a white horse,
just as in life.
Sūn Quán sent an envoy to enfeoff Zǐwén as Marquis of the Capital
and erected a temple for him on Mount Zhōng,
which was consequently renamed Mount Jiǎng."
The above pertains to Rùn Prefecture.
Hùdú Salt Fields
The "Wúdū Jì" states:
"The Sōng River flows east to the sea mouth,
which is named Hùdú."
The "Yǔdì Zhì" states:
"Hùyè refers to
a method of coastal fishing,
involving bamboo stakes inserted in rows into the sea,
bound together with ropes.
Two wings are spread towards the shore;
when the tide rises, they are submerged,
and when the tide recedes, they emerge.
Fish are trapped by the bamboo as the tide goes out and cannot escape;
this is called a 'hù'."
It also says:
"The coastal area is vast and saline,
with salt fields stretching as far as the eye can see.
Wú boils seawater to make salt,
which is within the territory of Yánguān County."
Bāo Shān Gānsuì
The "Xuánzhōng Jì" states:
"In the Jùqū Marsh west of Wú lies Bāo Shān,
