which contains the Dòngtíng Chamber."
The "Zhànguó Cè" states:
"The King of Yuè dispersed three thousand troops,
capturing Fūchāi at Gānsuì.
Northwest of Wú County, there is a place named Gānsuì, which is this location."
The above pertains to Sūzhōu.
Héng Shān Chángdú
The "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Chǔ's Zǐzhòng attacked Wú,
captured Jiūzī,
and advanced as far as Héng Shān."
The annotation states:
"It is located south of Wúchéng.
Héng is the ancient form of the character héng (衡),
used interchangeably."
The "Wúxīng Jì" states:
"The Hé Kǒu Shān borders a large stream to the east,
and is girded by the Chángdú to the west."
Ruòxià Yúzhōng
The "Wú Lù" states:
"The Ruòxià wine from Chángchéng is famous.
South of the stream is called Shàngruò,
north is called Xiàruò,
both are villages.
The villagers take water from Ruòxià to brew wine,
which is rich and exquisite, surpassing that of Yúnyáng."
The "Wúxīng Jì" states:
"Thirty lǐ south of Fēngzhǔ lies Yúzhōng,
which is Yú Shān."
The above pertains to Húzhōu.
Xībù Dōng'ān
The "Hànshū" states:
"Qiántáng
was where the Commandant of the Western Division resided."
The "Wú Zhì" states:
"In the fifth year of Huángwǔ,
mountain bandits from Dānyáng, Kuàijī, and Wúdū attacked and overran various counties.
Therefore, the strategic locations of three commanaderies were divided,
and the Dōng'ān Commandery was established,
based in Fùchūn."
Tree Calling Turtle Person Transforming into Crane
The "Yì Yuàn" states:
"During Sūn Quán's time,
a large turtle was captured
and presented to the Lord of Wú.
At night, they rested at Yuèlǐ,
tying the boat to a large mulberry tree.
The tree called out to the turtle:
'Yuánxù, what brings you here?'
The turtle replied:
'I traveled without choosing an auspicious day,
and now I am about to be cooked.
Nevertheless,
even if all the firewood from the southern mountains were used, it could not boil me.'" The "Yōumíng Lù" states:
"Sūn Zhōng made his living growing melons.
Two youths visited Zhōng to beg for melons,
saying:
'This spot at the foot of the mountain is excellent
and can serve as a burial mound;
we shall determine the tomb site for you.'
Zhōng followed them thirty paces down the mountain,
where the two transformed into white cranes,
flying into the sky.
This is the burial site of Sūn Jiān."
The above pertains to Hángzhōu.
Cāngjiāo Stream Báitǎ Den
The "Kǒngshì Zhìguài" states:
"Yìxīng had a white-browed beast, and at Chángqiáo in the stream islets there was a cāngjiāo; together with Zhōu Chǔ, they were known as the Three Scourges."
Zhōu Chǔ's "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"Beneath Chángqiáo there is a báitǎ.
If troops are about to move,
the tǎ emerges from its den,
gazes in all four directions, and howls.
It was traditionally said to be divine."
Héngxiàn Chángtáng
The "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"The mountains have many vertical rocks,
and there is a large Héngxiàn,
which channels the flow of numerous streams."
The "Yǔdì Zhì" states:
"Táo Lake is also known as Chángtáng Lake."
The above pertains to Chángzhōu.
Címǔ Shūgū
The "Dānyáng Jì" states:
"South of Jiāngníng lies Címǔ Shān,
a rocky mass overlooking the river,
where bamboo for making xiāo and guǎn grows.
Commonly called Gǔchuī Shān.
Jiāngníng refers to it as Címǔ Shān,
located north of Dāngtú County."
The "Xuānchéng Jì" states:
"A hundred paces up Gàishān, there is a spring.
In the past, a woman of the Shū family
was gathering firewood with her father on this mountain.
Suddenly, she sat down at the spring,
and could not be moved.
Her father hurriedly informed the family,
but by the time they arrived,
they only saw a clear, deep spring.
Thus, it was named Shūgū Spring."
Biēzhōu Niúzhǔ
The "Jiāng Jì" states:
"In the river lies Biēzhōu,
three lǐ in length,
connected to Wúhúzhōu."
The "Xù Hànshū" states:
"South of Mòlíng lies Niúzhǔ.
The above pertains to Xuānzhōu."
Yù Shān Shígài
Guō Pú's annotation to the "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
"Yù Shān,
from whose side the Zhèjiāng River flows."
The "Yǔdì Zhì" states:
"Líng Shān in Shè County is extremely lofty and steep.
There is a round rock,
tens of zhàng high,
with a stone cover on top."
Èrlì Sāngū
The "Yǔdì Zhì" states:
"South of Yī County, there are Wǔkēng
and Èrlì.
Both sides are earthen rocks,
with a channel in the center.
It is only about five chǐ wide,
and the water flows very swiftly.
Lì is pronounced lì.
Kēng,
pronounced xiàgēn fǎn."
It also says:
"East of Yī County lies Líng Shān.
The mountain has three peaks,
named the Sāngū Shān.
Every three years, a wildfire spontaneously ignites,
but when the common people set fires,
rain always falls and they do not burn."
The above pertains to Shèzhōu.
Hè Qí City Yánlíng Lài
The "Wú Zhì" states:
"The Great Emperor of Wú sent Hè Qí to attack the mountain bandits of Yī and Shè,
establishing the Xīndū Commandery."
The "Yǔdì Zhì" states:
"The commandery city
was founded by Hè Qí."
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Yán Guāng, styled Zǐlíng,
farmed in Fùchūn.
Later generations named the place where he fished Yánlíng Lài."
The above pertains to Mùzhōu.
Copper Cauldron Stone Steamer
The "Yì Yuàn" states:
"During the Wú period,
five hundred soldiers breached a lake
and obtained a copper cauldron.
When they opened it,
water violently gushed out,
creating the Five Hundred Men Lake."
The "Dōngyáng Jì" states:
"On the summit of Kūnlún Shān, there is a solitary rock,
about thirty zhàng high.
Its shape resembles a steamer,
and people call it the Stone Steamer."
The above pertains to Wùzhōu.
Lotus Cauldron Plum Pond
The Póyáng Chronicle states:
"On the Yìyáng Ridge, there are many dense cliffs.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Liu Song dynasty,
someone saw three iron cauldrons inside a cliff there.
Each cauldron could hold a hundred hú.
Lotus flowers grew inside them.
On another day, when they went to search for them,
they did not know where they had gone."
The Early Song Mountains and Rivers Record states:
"East of Guǎnglíng County, there is a Plum Pond."
Gazing Husband Ridge Nine-Son Stones
The Póyáng Chronicle states:
"West of Póyáng, there is the Wàngfū Gāng (Gazing Husband Ridge).
In the past, a county man named Chén Míng was betrothed to a woman of the Méi family.
Before the marriage was completed,
a demonic spirit deceitfully took the bride away.
Míng consulted a diviner for a decision.
The diviner said: 'Go fifty lǐ northwest and seek her.'
Míng did as told.
He saw a large cave,
deep and bottomless.
He was lowered in by rope,
and thus recovered his bride.
He then had his bride go out first.
But Qín Wén, a neighbor whom Míng had brought along, did not pull Míng up.
His wife then vowed to maintain her resolve.
She climbed to the top of this ridge to gaze into the distance for her husband.
Hence, it was named after this."
It also says:
"The Jiǔzǐ Shí (Nine-Son Stones) are on the left bank of the Yìyáng River,
several tens of paces apart from each other.
Their shape resembles seals."
The above pertains to Ráo Prefecture.
Stone Sail Jade Casket
The Kuàijī Gazetteer states:
"North of Shèdì, there is a Stone Sail standing like a wall,
facing the water, with rocks submerged.
Looking from Yíshān from afar,
it appears lush, somewhat like a spread sail.
It is also called the Yùsì Shān (Jade Casket Mountain),
and also called the Shíkuì Shān (Stone Basket Mountain)."
Mirror Water Copper Stream
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The Nánhú (South Lake) of Shānyīn
winds around the suburbs and city walls.
White waters and emerald cliffs
reflect and enhance each other,
like a mirror, like a painting.
Therefore, Wáng Yìshǎo (Wang Xizhi) said:
'Walking on the mountain paths of Shānyīn,
is like traveling within a mirror.'" The Kuàijī Gazetteer states:
"In the past, Ōu Yězǐ drained the Ruòyē Stream and obtained copper,
and broke open the Chìjǐn Mountain and obtained tin."
The above pertains to Yuè Prefecture.
Cinnabar Cave Red Wall
The Secret Instructions for Ascent to Perfection states:
"Below Chìchéng Shān (Red Wall Mountain) there is a Dāndòng (Cinnabar Cave),
counted among the Thirty-Six Grotto-Heavens.
The foot of that mountain is cinnabar-red."
The Brief Record of Famous Mountains states:
"Chìchéng Shān is also called Shāo Shān (Burning Mountain),
the residence of Lord Dōngqīng Simìng.
The grotto circumference is three hundred lǐ.
Above it is the Yùqīng Píngtiān (Jade Clarity Level Heaven)."
Golden Court Jade Chamber
The Taoist Texts state:
"Tiāntāi Shān has eight layers above,
yet looking at it, it appears as one.
Within it lies the Golden Court, the land of immortality."
Xǔ Mài, in his Letter to Wáng Yìshǎo (Wang Xizhi), said:
"From the mountains to Línhǎi,
there are many golden halls and jade chambers,
and immortal's magic mushrooms."
The above pertains to Tāi Prefecture.
Eastern Ōu Western Wěi
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Huì established the Mǐn lord Yáo as King of the Eastern Sea,
with his capital at Ōu."
The Yǒngjiā Chronicle states:
"The Xīwěi Shān (Western Wěi Mountain)
connects to Āngù in the east,
and to Sōngyáng in the west."
Máo Xiàn Sword Peak
The Yǒngjiā Chronicle states:
"Chén Yǔ has a Lú Wēi,
and also a Máo Xiàn,
twenty-five lǐ from Lú Wēi."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"The Lóushí Shān has three rocks,
each a hundred zhàng high.
Their tops are like sword peaks."
The above pertains to Kuò Prefecture.
Péngzé Fūqiǎnyuán
The Book of Hàn states:
"Péngzé County belonged to the Yùzhāng Commandery.
The Pénglí Marsh is to its west."
The Book of Documents states:
"Passing the Jiǔjiāng, one reaches Fūqiǎnyuán."
Lú Shān Pén Shuǐ
The Lú Shān Chronicle states:
"Kuāng Sú lived during the time of King Wēi of Zhōu.
He was born with divine intelligence.
He concealed his traces and hid his light,
building a hut on this mountain.
Commoners called him Lord Lú.
Therefore, the mountain took its name from this."
The Xúnyáng Chronicle states:
"The Pén Shuǐ (Basin Water) flows from Qīngpén Shān,
hence its name.
It winds through the mountains with twin streams,
irrigating Xúnyáng on the right,
and flows northeast into the river."
The above pertains to Jiāng Prefecture.
Copper Essence Sword Cavern
The Yùzhāng Chronicle states:
"Xī Shān has a circumference of three hundred lǐ.
At times, this mountain has a nocturnal glow,
seen from afar like fiery vapor."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"This is the radiant essence of copper."
The Yùzhāng Chronicle also states:
"Behind the prison of Fēngchéng County, Léi Kǒngzhāng excavated a cavern for divine swords,
about seven or eight zhàng square."
Burning Stone Hot Spring
The Sòng Yǒngchū Mountains and Rivers Record states:
"West of Jiànchéng County is Yáng Shān.
There is a burning stone,
yellow-white in color with a coarse grain.
When water is poured on it, it becomes hot,
and can be used to cook things.
Therefore, it is called a burning stone."
It also says:
"Pí County has a hot spring,
like boiling water.
If living creatures are thrown into it,
they become thoroughly cooked in a short while."
The above pertains to Hóng Prefecture.
Thistle Field Luòtíng
The Ānchéng Chronicle states:
"In the past, Yùzhāng Grand Administrator Jiǎ Méng and Marquis Ānchéng Zhāng Pǔ disputed over the border.
They fought in the field of Xīncì (New Thistles),
which is this very place."
Also, the Ānchéng Chronicle states:
"The commandery's rivers and streams,
having the same source, converge.
At Luòtíng Rock,
above there are magic mushrooms,
and below there is purple-polished gold."
Shāndū Mùkè
The Record of Strange Things states:
"In the great mountains of Lúlíng,
there are Shāndū, resembling humans, naked.
They run away upon seeing people.
They have their own males and females,
about four or five chǐ tall.
They can call to each other.
They often dwell in dark, obscure places,
like chīmèi ghosts and spirits."
It also says:
"In Lúlíng, there is the Mùkè bird,
as large as a magpie.
They gather in flocks of hundreds and thousands,
not mixing with other birds.
It is said they are transformed from Mùkè."
The above pertains to Jí Prefecture.
Golden Rooster Stone Goose
The Nánkāng Chronicle states:
"Yúndū County has a Jīnjī Shí (Golden Rooster Rock),
with a cave beside it.
During the Yǒngchū era of the Liu Song dynasty,
a golden rooster was seen perching and flying at this cave,
often flying and calling."
It also says:
"On Fùsì Shān, in the calm lake, there is a stone goose.
It floats on the water.
Whenever the seasons change to hot weather, it flies about,
as if aware of the climatic changes."
Sōng Quē and Zǐ Tán
The Yùdì Zhì states:
"On Guīměi Mountain there is a stone fortress,
several zhang high.
Two stones flank it on the left and right,
their shapes resembling pine trees,
solemnly like a pair of watchtowers."
The Nánkāng Jì says:
"In the past, there was a catalpa tree at Zǐ Tán,
of immense girth.
Its leaves were over a zhang wide,
and its drooping branches covered several mǔ.
The King of Wú felled the tree to make a boat.
He had boys and girls pull it,
but the boat flew into the water by itself,
and all the boys and girls drowned.
To this day, the sound of singing can sometimes be heard from the pool."
The above is from Qiánzhōu.
Gān Zhǔ and Mì Yán
The Línchuān Jì states:
"A household in Dōngxīng
once sank a wooden steamer into a well,
and it flowed out, reaching Fán Xī.
It was retrieved at Gān Zhǔ,
demonstrating that these water sources are connected."
It also says:
"The cliffs of Wǔzhāng Mountain are extremely steep and precipitous.
Bees rely on them to build their hives,
which are shaped like bamboo hats.
Those who wish to view them must first descend a hanging stone staircase for several zhang,
before they can reach the spot."
Shí Rén and Fēng Guǐ
The Línchuān Jì states:
"Inside the cliff of the great Yīngjù Mountain in Xūgǔ,
there is a stone man sitting on a flat rock.
When dust and filth cover his body, it stirs up wind;
when it becomes damp, it brings rain.
On clear days, his entire body becomes fresh and clean,
bright and pure like jade."
It also says:
"When people climb Mágū Mountain,
there is a creature with a human form,
having eyes, nose, mouth, and face, but no arms or legs.
Commonly, it is called the Maple Child Ghost."
The above is from Fǔzhōu.
Mǐ Shā and Xuě Bì
The Ānchéng Jì states:
"Zhōng Mountain overlooks the water, creating a gorge barrier.
In spring and summer, the currents swirl and churn.
On the banks, the white sand is like rice grains,
with over ten hú on each side.
It is called Mǐ Shā (Rice Sand).
It is used to predict the harvest.
If one bank has an abundance,
then that region will have a bountiful harvest."
Yīn Bīn's Shíshì Jì states:
"The third chamber is ten zhang high.
The others are roughly similar.
All have plain walls white as snow,
upon which myriad phenomena are arrayed."
Yíchūn Shuǐ and Luóxiāo Shān
The Wú Lù mentions:
"The spring water of Yíchūn."
The Dìdào Jì states:
"Yíchūn County produces fine wine,
which is presented as tribute annually."
The Ānchéng Jì states:
"On Luóxiāo Mountain there is a stone well.
During droughts, people make offerings to it.
If wood is thrown into the well,
rain immediately falls.
When the well overflows and the wood floats out,
the rain stops."
The above is from Yuánzhōu.
Yīng Zhōu and Fèng Què
The Yùdì Zhì states:
"In the river at Xiàkǒu, there is Yīngwǔ Zhōu (Parrot Islet)."
The Wǔchāng Jì states:
"At the southeastern corner of the city, there is a ridge
named Fèng Què (Phoenix Watchtower).
During the time of Wú, a phoenix alighted there,
hence the name."
È Zhǔ and Fán Shān
The Lísāo says:
"Mounting È Zhǔ, I look back."
The Wǔchāng Jì states:
"East of Fánkǒu lies Fán Mountain."
The above is from Èzhōu.
Xiāng Shān and Yuán Shuǐ
The Shǐjì states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng sailed down the river and reached Xiāng Mountain."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"The Yuán River flows into Dòngtíng Lake,
where it converges with the [Yangtze] River."
Dìdào and Jiāng Mén
The Xiāngzhōng Jì states:
"Jūn Mountain has an underground passageway."
Guō Pú's Jiāng Fù says:
"Here are the Bāo Mountain caverns of Dòngtíng,
and the underground passageway of Bālíng."
The Shānhǎijīng states:
"Dòngtíng Mountain,
where the Emperor's daughter dwells.
Upon it are the confluence of the Yuán and Fēng rivers,
the sources of the Xiāo and Xiāng rivers,
which are at the gateway of the Nine Rivers."
The above is from Yuèzhōu.
Chá Zhǔ and Jú Zhōu
The Xiāngzhōng Jì states:
"Opposite Chá Zhǔ lies an ancient city,
established by Sūn Quán's envoy Chéng Pǔ."
The Yùdì Zhì states:
"Jú Zhōu (Tangerine Islet) lies south of the commandery,
opposite Nánjīn, often appearing low from afar.
When the summer floods come,
and hills and islets are submerged,
Jú Zhōu alone remains above water."
Zhāo Tán and Yǔ Lài
The Xiāngzhōu Jì states:
"In Yuèyáng there is Zhāo Tán,
which has no bottom,
the deepest part of the Xiāng River."
It also says:
"West of Shízǐ Mountain there is a small stream,
where the water and stones reflect with crystalline clarity.
It is named Yǔ Lài (Feather Rapids).
In the past, when Guān Yǔ campaigned south,
he encamped at the foot of this mountain,
hence the name."
The above is from Tánzhōu.
Qīng Tán and Zǐ Gài
The Xiāngzhōu Jì states:
"On Zhùróng Peak there is a Qīngyù Tán (Green Jade Altar),
five zhang square,
a place for burning incense and practicing the Way on the peak."
The Yì Yuàn states:
"Héng Mountain has a peak named Huá Gài,
also called Zǐ Gài (Purple Canopy)."
Bǎo Dòng and Xiān Gōng
The Nányuè Jì states:
"Héng Mountain is
the treasure cavern of the Great Void."
It also says:
"Five lǐ south of Liúdān Cliff,
one finds the Xiānrén Gōng (Immortal's Palace).
If a Daoist abstains from grains and food,
making his body light and ethereal,
he may then enter this palace."
The above is from Héngzhōu.
Jīng Kǒu and Lán Yán
The Xiāngzhōu Jì states:
"Dū Xī flows northwest again into Yíng Shuǐ,
which is called Jīng Kǒu."
Wáng Shāozhī's Shénjìng Jì states:
"Lán Yán Mountain
has a perilous and obstructed path.
The cliffs are devoid of human traces.
Upon ascending the mountain,
there are stone paths and pine forests.
Vast and distant, it is like a lodge amidst the clouds and mist."
Jiǔyí Shān Yán and Wǔhuì Shuǐ
The Shānhǎijīng states:
"On the hills of Cāngwú,
at Jiǔyí Mountain,
Shùn was buried."
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
"Dū Xī water emerges left of Chōnglíng County,
and converges with the five streams.
The county has five mountains,
each with one stream.
The five waters converge at the county gate,
hence it is called Dū Xī (Converging Stream)."
The above is from Yǒngzhōu.
Rú Xī and Lǐ Pǔ
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"Rú Xī
originates from Rúlóng Mountain,
its water extremely clear and pure."
The Lísāo says:
"I left my pendant at Lǐ Pǔ."
Heavenly Broom · Pine Beam Mountain
The *Jīngzhōu Túfù Jì* states:
"On the corner of Tiānmén, a stone grows with a bamboo whisk hanging down from it,
called the Heavenly Broom."
The *Wú Lù* states:
"Pine Beam Mountain,
where the mountain rocks part,
can accommodate several tens of *zhàng*.
Its height is such that
even shooting arrows with a crossbow
cannot reach its summit."
The above are from Lǐzhōu.
Hot Stone · Hot Spring
The *Yǔdì Zhì* states:
"Línwǔ County has a mountain with a hot stone;
placing objects on it causes them to scorch instantly."
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* states:
"Chēn County has a hot spring,
whose downstream flow irrigates fields,
providing water for cultivation.
Seeds are often sown in the twelfth month,
and by the third month of the following year,
new grain is already harvested."
Immortal Shrine · Yìdì Temple
The *Yǔdì Zhì* states:
"Mǎlǐng Mountain has an altar for the immortal Sū Dān.
Dān was extremely filial.
One morning, he suddenly bid farewell to his mother, saying:
'I am destined to become an immortal;
I must leave your care.'
He wept and sobbed.
The common people erected an altar to worship him."
The *Xiāngzhōu Jì* states:
"South of Chēn County is the Yìdì Temple,
where the common people offer sacrifices."
The *Hànshū* states:
"Xiàng Yǔ honored King Huái of Chǔ as Yìdì."
The above are from Chēnzhōu.
Dragon Pool · Crane Marsh
The *Wǔlíng Jì* states:
"When Xiè Chéng served as the governor of Wǔlíng Commandery,
a yellow dragon appeared in the waters east of the commandery.
He submitted a memorial to congratulate the emperor,
and thus it was named Dragon Pool."
Liú Yìqìng's *Shìshuō* states:
"When Jìn's Yáng Hù garrisoned Jīngzhōu,
he obtained a crane from the marshes of Jiānglíng.
He taught it to dance
to entertain guests and friends."
Dīngkǒu · Wind Gate
The *Yuánchuān Jì* states:
"The Yuánchuān River is named Dīngkǒu,
as a divine tripod once emerged there in ancient times."
The *Wǔlíng Jì* states:
"Wind Gate Mountain has a stone gate,
over a hundred *zhàng* above the ground.
When wind is about to rise,
this gate faintly emits black vapor upward,
and soon a black wind fiercely arises."
The above are from Lǎngzhōu.
Scallion Ridge · Tea Mountain
The *Yuánchuān Jì* states:
"Yuánchuān has a solitary mountain,
with towering scallion-like rocks and scallions growing on top as if planted by humans.
When people go to pick them,
the stems break off.
If they pray to the gods before picking,
the scallions come loose on their own without pulling.
The *Wǔlíng Jì* calls it Scallion Ridge."
The *Jīngzhōu Túfù* states:
"Tea Mountain has nine perilous and steep ridges,
with many fir and pine trees,
and numerous bears and leopards among its beasts."
Dragon Gate · Deer Cave
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states:
"There is the Dúmǔ River,
which flows south from Dragon Gate."
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* states:
"In the early Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
a man of the Wǔxī tribe shot a deer,
which fled into a stone cave
barely large enough for a person.
The tribesman entered the cave
and saw a ladder beside it.
Climbing the ladder,
he suddenly found himself in an open, bright world,
with lush mulberry trees and fruit,
and people strolling leisurely,
unperturbed by his presence.
This tribesman marked trees along the way as signs,
but afterward, the path became vast and indistinct,
with no further traces to follow."
The above are from Chénzhōu.
Stone Bed · Cloud Water
The *Xiāngzhōu Jì* states:
"Wénjīn Mountain has a stone bed,
square and one *zhàng* high,
surrounded by lush green bamboo
that often sways and brushes with the wind."
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states:
"The Shàolíng River flows east to meet Yúnquán."
The above are from Shàozhōu.
Làng River · Wǔ Stream
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states:
"The Làng River originates from the northern border valley of Wǔlíng Tánchéng;
the *Jīngzhōu Jì* calls it Làng Stream."
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* states:
"The Wǔ Stream flows east into the Yuán River
and connects to Zāngkē in the west."
The above are from Wūzhōu.
Bronze Pillar · Stone Gate
The *Zhōu Dìtú Jì* states:
"There is a Bronze Pillar Shoal in the river."
It also states:
"Thirteen *lǐ* east of Jūntí,
east of Stone Gate,
there is a stone drum."
Qīng Terrace · Divine Grotto
The *Shǐjì* states:
"The widow Qīng of Língyì
had ancestors who obtained a cinnabar mine,
making the family immeasurably wealthy.
Qīng was able to preserve their estate.
The Qín emperor considered her a chaste woman
and built the Nǚhuáiqīng Terrace for her."
The *Yìzhōu Jì* states:
"Huánggé Gorge has the Xiāngsī Cliff,
surrounded by fragrant springs,
commonly called the Divine Grotto."
The above are from Fúzhōu.
Zāngkē · Guìpǔ
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn pacified the southern barbarians
and established Zāngkē Commandery.
It is also said:
"Zāngkē Commandery has the Guìpǔ Pass."
Heavenly Well · Stone Pass
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
"Zāngkē Commandery
lies directly under the Heavenly Well,
hence it experiences frequent heavy rains and floods."
It also states:
"Southwest of Qiělán County is a place named Shítóng Pass."
The above are from Zāngzhōu.
□□ *Rùnzhōu Zhēn*
Vast and magnificent Rùnzhōu,
with rivers and streams of outstanding beauty.
Jiǎng Temple and Zhōng Mountain,
Sūn's tomb on winding shores.
The city of Jiāngníng,
called Jīnlíng in Chǔ times.
Wú, Jìn, Liáng, and Sòng—
six dynasties made it their capital.
The Eleventh: Lǐngnán Circuit
The Lǐngnán Circuit
comprises the southern territories of Yángzhōu from the *Yǔ Gòng*,
all lands belonging to the Yuè division.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states:
present-day Cāngwú,
Yùlín,
Hépǔ,
Jiāozhǐ,
Jiǔzhēn,
Rìběn,
and Nánhǎi all belong to the Yuè division.
From south of the mountains to the sea,
encompasses the entire region.
Guǎngzhōu was formerly Nánhǎi Commandery;
at the end of the Qín dynasty, the Nánhǎi Commandant Zhào Tuó became king over this land.
Rush Stream · Orchid Lake
The *Nányuè Zhì* states:
"Northeast of Xī'ān County is the Rush Stream.
During the Xián'ān era, Yáo Chéngfǔ once met a gentleman by the stream,
who said:
'This rush
was consumed by Master Ānqī
to forget old age.'
He also said:
'North of Pānyú is the Orchid Lake,
both flowing into the Western Sea.'"
Greed Spring Zhēn River
The Book of the Jin Dynasty's Restoration states:
"It was traditionally said that if one went to Guǎngzhōu and drank from the Greed Spring,
one would lose one's integrity.
Wú Yǐnzhī, when he became the Regional Inspector,
personally drew and drank from the Greed Spring,
and inscribed a poem on the Stone Gate, saying:
'At Stone Gate lies the Greed Spring,
a single drink makes one covet a thousand gold.
But if you made Bóyí and Shūqí drink it,
their hearts would never change.'
The Book of Han states:
'The Towered Ship General Yáng Pǔ set out from Yùzhāng,
and descended the Zhēn River.'"
Two Mountains Eight Cassias
The Records of Nányuè states:
"In Pānyú County there are the Pānyú and Yú mountains,
and it was named after them."
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"In Guìlín there are eight trees,
located east of Pānyú."
The above pertains to Guǎngzhōu.
Tidal Cave Quán Mountain
The Records of Cháozhōu states:
"This stream flows west to the Huái River.
Its cave is like a well.
Sometimes it dries up for a full year,
sometimes it fills and empties ten times in a single day,
like the tide."
It also states:
"Quán Mountain has steep cliffs rising high,
connected ridges stretching continuously.
Stone springs pour down suspended,
waterfalls fly and flow."
The above pertains to Liánzhōu.
Coin Stone Jade Mountain
The Records of Xiāngzhōu states:
"East of Qūjiāng County is Quánshí Mountain.
Its shape is square like a terrace or pavilion.
To its south is a stone,
with three sides forming sheer cliffs.
On its top are coins,
hence it is called Coin Stone."
It also states:
"East of Qūjiāng County is Yù Mountain.
Plants and trees flourish abundantly,
springs and stones are clear and moist.
Tradition says:
'It is where someone once gathered jade.'"
Stone Terrace Silver Jars
The Records of Shǐxīng states:
"On the eastern bank of Láokǒu,
there is a square stone, high,
about a hundred ren or more.
Its shape is like a terrace."
It also states:
"The water of Línshuǐ springs from atop a boulder.
Ten jars are arranged in a row,
all covered with green basins.
Inside are all silver ingots.
If someone encounters them,
they can open and look but cannot take them.
If they try to take them, they immediately lose their way,
become confused and distressed, almost to death."
The above pertains to Sháozhōu.
Lóngchuān Ox Ridge
The Book of Han states:
"Lóngchuān County belonged to Nánhǎi Commandery."
The Records of Nányuè states:
"Luófú Mountain has a stone tower.
To its right it adjoins Niúlíng Mountain,
to its left it rests upon Dragon's Tail."
The above pertains to Xúnzhōu.
Patterned Shell Brocade Snake
The Records of Nányuè states:
"South of Cháoyáng is a small stream,
which empties into the seashore,
bordered by layered mountains.
Within it are many patterned shells,
which can counteract poison."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"Lóngxī is called Coiled Dragon.
The snake is greenish-black,
with red bands of brocade pattern.
It follows the watercourse and gushing water into the sea.
It is poisonous,
and if it injures someone, they die immediately."
The above pertains to Cháozhōu.
Plain Maiden Green Ox
The Records of Enlightenment states:
"Xiè Duān of Hóuguān
once obtained a large conch from the sea.
Inside was a beautiful woman,
who said:
'I am the Plain Maiden of the White River from the Heavenly Han.
Heaven pities your poverty,
and commands me to be your wife.'"
The Records of Nányuè states:
Long ago, King Jiàndé of Yuè felled trees to make a ship,
its capacity a thousand shi.
Three thousand boys and girls pulled it.
Later, both the ship and they fell into a deep pool.
At times, voices urging and driving them on were heard clinging to the ship.
Often a green ox galloped around together with the ship.
This was indeed the arrival of a spirit."
Spirit River Divine Herbs
The Treatise on Geography states:
"From Yúyáo to the sea is thirty lǐ.
Crossing the Wēnmá River,
there is a river named Língjiāng."
The Taoist Texts state:
"On Huò Mountain there are thirty-four kinds of divine herbs."
The above pertains to Quánzhōu.
Jiàn'ān Jiànglè
The Records of Wú states:
"In the third year of the Yǒng'ān era,
the southern commandery of Kuàijī was made Jiàn'ān Commandery."
The Records of Wú states:
"Jiànglè County belonged to Jiàn'ān Commandery."
The above pertains to Jiànzhōu.
Stone Chamber Sōng Terrace
The Records of Nányuè states:
"The stone chamber of Gāo'ān
naturally produces wind and caves.
It has north and south gates.
Their appearance seems man-made.
It is thought to be an immortal capital."
It also states:
"Gāoyào has towering rocks,
over sixty zhang wide,
and about two hundred ren high.
The local people call them Sōng Terrace."
The above pertains to Duānzhōu.
Duān Stone Cén's Pearl
The Records of Wú states:
"Duānxī has Duān Mountain.
The mountain has five-colored stones,
and the stones have much fragrant water."
The Records of Nányuè states:
"Cén Bān, a man of the Lǐ people of Duānxī,
entered the mountains
and encountered a precious pearl,
five inches in diameter.
He took it back.
At night it shone brightly, illuminating everything.
The Lǐ people were very frightened.
They tried to burn it with fire.
Although it was slightly damaged,
it still illuminated an entire room."
The above pertains to Kāngzhōu.
Fragrant Forest Lún Tree
The Records of Nányuè states:
"On Lì Mountain in Pényuán County,
there are many fragrant forests."
It also states:
"In Wēiníng County there is Chuānzhōu.
On it grow many lún trees.
Their bark resembles that of the paper mulberry,
and can be used to make silk wadding."
The above pertains to Gāngzhōu.
Cāngwú Variegated Stone
The Book of Han states:
"Cāngwú Commandery
was established in the sixth year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ."
The Treatise on Geography states:
"In the Shòu Township of Guǎngxìn County there is a solitary cliff.
On the cliff are variegated stones,
all of which are five-colored."
The above pertains to Wúzhōu.
Wéizhōu Hépǔ
The Records of Jiāozhōu states:
"Eighty lǐ from Hépǔ is Wéizhōu,
with a circumference of a hundred lǐ."
The Book of Han states:
"Hépǔ Commandery
was established in the sixth year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ."
The above pertains to Liánzhōu.
Hè River Fùchuān
The Records of Xiāngzhōu states:
"The Lín River passes east of Línhè County,
then south to the left of the commandery seat,
where it joins the Hè River."
The Book of Han states:
"Fùchuān County belonged to Cāngwú Commandery."
The above pertains to Hèzhōu.
Two Drums, Three Harvests
The Yǔdìzhì states:
"In the Later Hàn, Zhōu Chǎng served as the Governor of Jiāozhǐ.
He cut wood from Lóngshān to make drums.
The lower portion of the drum was given to Guìlín Commandery,
and the upper portion to Jiāozhǐ Commandery.
When one drum was struck, both drums would resonate."
The Guǎngzhì states:
"The climate in the southern regions is hot and humid,
allowing for three harvests of rice in a year.
Winter planting yields a spring harvest,
spring planting yields a summer harvest,
and autumn planting yields a winter harvest."
The above pertains to Jiāozhōu.
Sūqiáo, Málǐng
The Nányuèzhì states:
"To the southeast of Níngpǔ Commandery lies Sūmóqiáo."
Qū Qiú's Dàolǐjì states:
"Shāmálǐng is located south of Níngpǔ Commandery,
and the commandery lies at the northern foot of the ridge."
The above pertains to Héngzhōu.
Tree Dwellings, Bamboo Beams
The Línyìjì states:
"The Lángyě people live without houses,
resting and sleeping in trees."
The Nánzhēng Bājùnzhì states:
"In Mílíng County, there are large bamboos several arm-spans in circumference, solid in the center.
They are used as roof beams and pillars,
and when laid over, they serve as tiles."
The above pertains to Fēngzhōu.
Ant Lacquer, Tide Rooster
The Wúlù states:
"In Jūfēng County, there is an ant lacquer vine.
When people observe the soil and know ants are present,
they dig it up.
They insert tree bark into it,
and the ants emerge,
climbing along it to produce lacquer."
The Yǔdìzhì states:
"In Yífēng County, there is a tide rooster.
Its crow at dawn is clear, like the sound of a horn.
It crows whenever the tide comes in,
and it is also known as a forest rooster."
Stone Embankment, Golden Clogs
The Nányuèzhì states:
"Mǎ Yuán excavated a passage through the Jiǔzhēn Mountains,
and also piled stones to form an embankment,
to block the sea waves.
From then on, the sea no longer flooded."
It also states:
"A woman named Zhào Yù from Jūn'ān County
once gathered in the mountains,
assembling a band of followers,
and attacked and plundered commanderies and counties.
She wore golden-toothed clogs
and often fought from atop an elephant."
The above pertains to Àizhōu.
Xiánhuān, Dūwò
The Hànshū states:
"Xiánhuān County belonged to Jiǔzhēn Commandery."
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì states:
"Dūwò County belonged to Jiǔdé Commandery."
The above pertains to Huānzhōu.
Beyond the Extremity, In the Sea
The Jiāoguǎng Èrzhōu Jì states:
"Zhūyá is located in the great sea,
beyond the southern extremity.
During the Wú period, a Grand Administrator was reinstated,
stationed in Xúwén County to govern it remotely."
The Hànshū states:
"Emperor Wǔ established Zhūyá Commandery,
located in the great sea to the south,
spanning a thousand lǐ in breadth."
Nest Dwellings, Topknots
The Guǎngzhì states:
"The people of Zhūyá all live in nests."
The Zhūyá Zhuàn states:
"Both men and women wear their hair in topknots,
or go barefoot with disheveled hair.
'Jì' is pronounced like 'jì' (髻)."
The above pertains to Yázhōu.
Dān'ěr, Tattooed Cheeks
The Hànshū states:
"In the sixth year of Yuándǐng under Emperor Wǔ,
Yuè was pacified and established as Dān'ěr Commandery."
Zhāng Yàn's annotation states:
"Dān'ěr
involves tattooing the cheeks and connecting them to the upper ear rim,
divided into several branches,
resembling chicken intestines,
hanging down in clusters."
The above pertains to Dānzhōu.
Patterned Pí, Vermilion Pí
The Nányuèzhì states:
"In the sea, there is a patterned pí fish,
with a bird's head and tail,
whose call resembles a chime stone and produces jade."
It also states:
"The sea is abundant with vermilion pí fish,
shaped like a lung,
with four eyes and six legs, capable of spitting pearls."
Péng Horse, Water Rhinoceros
The Nányuèzhì states:
"In the vast sea east of Píngdìng County, there is a péng horse,
resembling a horse,
with an ox's tail and a single horn."
It also states:
"In the vast sea of Píngdìng County, there is a water rhinoceros,
resembling an ox.
When it emerges or submerges, it emits light,
parting the water as it moves."
The above pertains to Gāozhōu.
Yáng Xióng's "Inscription for Jiāozhōu"
Jiāozhōu, a remote borderland,
where water meets the sky's edge.
Yuècháng lies to the south,
beyond the wild lands.
Since the dawn of creation,
it has remained unbound and unfettered.
When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
a white pheasant was presented as tribute.
When King Zhāo declined,
the Zhōu court fell into chaos.
Yuècháng ceased its tribute,
and Jīngchǔ rebelled in defiance.
The great Hàn received the Mandate,
unifying the Central Realm.
The lands of the Southern Sea
were restored by the Sage-Martial Emperor.
Gradually brought under rein,
they reached as far as Huángzhī.
Rhinoceroses were led forth,
sailing thirty thousand lǐ across the seas.
When springs run dry, the center empties;
when ponds dry up, the shallows parch.
Your servant, the Shepherd of Jiāo,
dares to inform the upholders of the law.
General Account of Emperors and Kings
The term "Huáng" (皇) refers to
the supreme unity of Heaven and humanity,
a title of magnificent greatness.
The "Yì Wěi" states:
"The term 'Dì' (帝) is a designation of Heaven.
One whose virtue matches Heaven and Earth,
who does not treat the public position as private,
is called 'Dì'.
The 'Tiānzǐ' (天子)
succeeds Heaven in governing all things,
reforms governance to unify all,
ensuring each finds its proper place.
Heaven as father and Earth as mother nurture the people,
making it the most exalted title.
The 'Dà Jūn' (大君)
is the pinnacle of rulership over people."
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"The 'Dì' is where all under Heaven turns to,
the 'Wáng' is where all under Heaven goes."
The "Shàngshū Wěi" states:
"'Dì' is a title of Heaven,
'Wáng' is a designation of humanity.
Heaven has the Five Dì to establish names,
humanity has the Three Wáng to rectify measures.
'Tiānzǐ' is a title of nobility,
'Huáng' signifies brilliance."
The "Luò Shū" states:
"When the Way of Huáng is deficient, the Dì arises."
The "Hán Shī Wàizhuàn" states:
"The 'Jūn' (君) means 'to assemble',
one who dares to assemble all things under Heaven and eliminate their harms
is called 'Jūn'.
Tiān Huáng (天皇)."
Yán Jùn's "Shǐxué Piān" states:
"When Heaven and Earth were established,
there was Tiān Huáng with thirteen heads,
named Tiān Líng,
who ruled for eighteen thousand years."
The "Dòng Míng Jì" states:
"They were thirteen people of one surname."
Xú Zhěng's "Sānwǔ Lìjì" states:
"When the year began with Shètí, the Primordial Qi,
there first appeared a divine spirit, one person,
with thirteen heads,
named Tiān Huáng."
The "Chūnqiū Wěi" states:
"Tiān Huáng, Dì Huáng, Rén Huáng,
nine brothers,
divided the nine provinces,
and ruled over all under Heaven."
The "Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú" states:
"Tiān Huáng left his traces at the foot of Mount Kūnlún in Guìzhōu,
Dì Huáng."
The "Shǐxué Piān" states:
"Dì Huáng arose at Mount Xióng'ěr Lóngmén,
Rén Huáng."
The "Shǐxué Piān" states:
"Rén Huáng had nine heads,
each brother lived three hundred years.
Based on the configurations of mountains, rivers, and lands,
they measured and divided into nine provinces,
each residing in one direction,
thus distinguishing them."
Róng Shì states:
"Rén Huáng had nine brothers,
born at Mount Jīngmǎ,
their bodies of nine colors."
Yǒu Cháo Shì (有巢氏):
The "Shǐxué Piān" states:
"In high antiquity, all lived in caves;
a sage taught them to dwell in nests,
named Dà Cháo Shì."
Huángfǔ Mì believed Yǒu Cháo came after Nǚ Wā.
The "Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú" states:
"Mount Shílóu is in Lángyá;
in the past, Yǒu Cháo Shì governed south of this mountain."
Suì Rén Shì,
the "Shàngshū Dà Zhuàn" states:
"Suì Rén was Suì Huáng,
using fire to record offices."
The "Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā" states:
"Suì Rén first drilled wood to obtain fire,
cooked the raw to make it ripe,
so people had no abdominal illnesses.
Following Heaven's will,
thus called Suì Rén,
Tài Hào Páo Xī Shì."
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Páo Xī Shì,
surname Fēng,
with a snake's body and human head,
possessed sagely virtue.
After Suì Rén Shì passed away,
Páo Xī succeeded him,
continuing Heaven's mandate to rule.
His primary virtue corresponded to Wood,
making him the first of the hundred kings.
The Dì emerges from Zhèn,
with nothing prior to rely on,
thus his position is in the East.
He presides over Spring,
symbolizing the brightness of the sun,
hence called Tài Hào.
He established his capital at Chén,
instituted the rituals of marriage,
took sacrificial animals to fill the kitchens,
thus named Páo Xī Shì, also called Xī Huáng.
Later generations corrupted the pronunciation,
thus calling him Fú Xī,
or sometimes Mì Xī."
One explanation states:
"Fú (虙),
is the ancient character for Fú (伏).
Later, Fú was mistakenly taken as Mì,
thus called Mì Xī."
The preface to the "Shàngshū" states:
"When Fú Xī Shì ruled all under Heaven,
he first drew the Eight Trigrams,
created writing and tallies,
to replace the governance by knotted cords,
from which written records arose."
The "Shī Hán Shén Wù" states:
"Huá Xū trod in a giant's footprint and gave birth to Fú Xī."
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"Fú Xī Shì used the dragon to record offices,
Dì Nǚ Wā Shì."
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Nǚ Wā Shì was also of the Fēng surname,
inheriting Páo Xī's institutions,
also with a snake's body and human head.
Also named Nǚ Xī,
she was the Nǚ Huáng."
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"In ancient times,
the four pillars were broken,
the nine provinces split,
Heaven did not fully cover,
Earth did not completely support.
Nǚ Wā smelted five-colored stones to mend the azure sky,
cut off the turtle's legs to set up the four pillars,
slayed the black dragon to aid Jìchuān,
piled reed ashes to stop the flooding waters."
At the end, there was the feudal lord Gòng Gōng Shì,
who relied on wisdom and punishments to become strong,
ruling as a Bó but not as a Wáng.
Using Water to succeed Wood,
was not in the proper sequence,
thus the "Yì" does not record it.
After Nǚ Wā Shì passed away,
successively came Dà Tíng Shì, Bó Huáng Shì, Zhōng Yāng Shì, Lì Lù Shì, Lí Lián Shì, Hè Xū Shì, Zūn Lú Shì, Hùn Dùn Shì, Yǒu Cháo Shì, Zhū Xiāng Shì, Gě Tiān Shì, Yīn Kāng Shì, Wú Huái Shì.
Fifteen generations in total,
all inheriting the title of Páo Xī.
Yán Dì Shén Nóng Shì:
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Shén Nóng Shì,
surname Jiāng.
His mother was named Rèn Sì,
daughter of the Yǒu Qiáo clan,
named Nǚ Dēng.
Traveling in Huáyáng,
a divine dragon's head moved Nǚ Dēng at Shàngyáng,
giving birth to Yán Dì,
with a human body and ox head,
raised by the Jiāng River.
He possessed sagely virtue,
using Fire to succeed Wood.
His position was in the South,
presiding over Summer,
thus called Yán Dì.
He established his capital at Chén,
ruled for one hundred and twenty years before passing away,
down to Yú Gāng,
eight generations in total,
altogether five hundred and thirty years."
The "Zhōu Shū" states:
"In Shén Nóng's time,
Heaven rained millet,
Shén Nóng plowed and planted it,
making pottery, forging axes."
The "Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo":
"Yán Dì had a fire response,
thus all official titles were named after fire."
Lù Jǐng's "Diǎn Yǔ" states:
"Shén Nóng tasted herbs and distinguished grains,
the people then ate grain food,
Huáng Dì Yǒu Xióng Shì."
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states:
"Huáng Dì,
son of Shào Diǎn,
surname Jī.
His mother was named Fù Bǎo,
who saw great lightning light encircling the Northern Dipper's pivot star, illuminating the wilds,
moved Fù Bǎo, giving birth to Huáng Dì at Shòu Qiū.
He had a dragon's countenance,
possessed sagely virtue,
received the state of Yǒu Xióng,
dwelt at Xuānyuán Hill,
thus taking that as his name.
He obtained the precious tripod,
initiated the fēng and shān sacrifices,
There was an auspicious sign of auspicious clouds,
so he used clouds to designate official titles,
making them cloud masters.
He ruled by virtue of earth,
reigned for a hundred years and then passed away,
at the age of one hundred and ten years old,
some say he lived three hundred years.
Therefore, Zǎi Wǒ doubted and asked Confucius,
Confucius said:
'People relied on his benefits,
for a hundred years and then he passed away;
people feared his spirit,
for a hundred years and then he vanished;
people followed his teachings,
for a hundred years and then they changed.
Thus it is said three hundred years.'
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Huángdì's surname was Gōngsūn,
he was born with divine intelligence,
and could speak when still young.
He succeeded Shénnóngshì,
and when some feudal lords did not submit,
he followed by attacking them,
never resting peacefully.
He went east to the sea,
ascended Huánshān and Dàizōng,
went west to Kōngtóng,
ascended Jītóu.
He went south to the river,
ascended Xióngxiāng,
went north to drive away Xūnyù,
united tallies at Fǔshān,
and established a city in the valley of Zhuōlù.
He moved about without fixed abode,
traveling with his army as camp guards,
and all official titles were named after clouds.
He mined copper from Shǒushān,
and cast a tripod on top of Jīngshān.
When the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with hanging beard to welcome Huángdì.
Huángdì mounted it,
over seventy ministers and palace attendants followed him up,
and the dragon then ascended to heaven.
The remaining minor officials could not ascend,
so they all grabbed the dragon's beard,
pulling down Huángdì's bow,
and the common people looked up in awe.
After the emperor ascended to heaven,
they embraced his bow and the dragon's beard and wailed,
so later generations named that place Dǐnghú,
and his bow was called Wūhào."
Shàohào Jīntiānshì:
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Emperor Shàohào's name was Zhì,
styled Qīngyáng,
with the surname Jī.
His mother was called Nǚjié.
During Huángdì's time, there was a large star like a rainbow,
descending to Huázhǔ.
Nǚjié was inspired and gave birth to Shàohào,
who was also known as Xuánxiāo.
He descended to dwell by the Jiāngshuǐ,
established a city at Qióngsāng,
and ascended to the imperial throne.
He made Qūfù his capital,
reigned for a hundred years and then passed away."
The Ancient Historical Investigations says:
"Shàohào ruled by virtue of metal,
hence he was called Jīntiānshì.
Some say he inherited the way of Tàihào,
so he was called Shàohào."
The Zuo Commentary says:
"At his establishment, the phoenix happened to arrive,
so he designated official titles as bird masters.
Fèngniǎoshì,
was the calendar official."
Emperor Zhuānxū Gāoyángshì:
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Zhuānxū,
was the grandson of Huángdì,
son of Chāngyì,
with the surname Jī.
His mother was called Jǐngpú,
a woman of the Shǔshān clan,
the principal consort of Chāngyì,
also known as Nǚshū.
At the end of Jīntiānshì's reign,
the star Yáoguāng,
pierced the moon like a rainbow,
inspiring Nǚshū in her secluded palace,
and she gave birth to Zhuānxū at Ruòshuǐ.
He was born with a helmet and spear on his head,
possessing sagely virtue.
At age ten, he assisted Shàohào,
at twelve, he was capped,
and at twenty, he ascended to the imperial throne.
He succeeded metal with water,
his position was in the north,
governing winter.
He designated official titles based on water affairs.
He first made Qióngsāng his capital,
later moved to Shāngqiū.
He reigned for seventy-eight years,
and lived to be ninety-eight years old."
Emperor Kù Gāoxīnshì:
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Emperor Kù,
had the surname Jī.
His mother was unaware,
he was born with divine marvels,
and he himself said his name was Qūn,
with Qūn teeth.
He possessed sagely virtue,
at age fifteen, he assisted Zhuānxū,
at thirty, he ascended to the imperial throne,
and made Bó his capital.
He succeeded water with wood,
reigned for seventy years,
and passed away at the age of one hundred and five."
Táo Hóngjǐng says:
"He reigned for sixty-three years,
and lived to be ninety-two."
Emperor Yáo Táotángshì:
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Yáo had the surname Yīqí.
His mother was called Qìngdū,
she was pregnant for fourteen months and gave birth to Yáo at Dānlíng,
named Fàngxūn.
He had a bird-like forehead and lotus-shaped crown,
eyebrows with eight colors,
full below and sharp above.
Some say he took his mother's surname Yīqíshì.
At age fifteen, he assisted Emperor Zhì,
was enfeoffed in Táng,
and at twenty, he ascended to the imperial throne.
He succeeded wood with fire,
made Píngyáng his capital.
Auspicious stars shone in the sky,
sweet dew fell on the earth,
vermilion grass grew in the suburbs,
and phoenixes rested in the courtyard.
In the kitchen, dried meat strips appeared spontaneously,
thin as funeral fans,
shaking them produced wind,
keeping food cold and odorless.
There was also grass growing along the steps,
dying and reviving with the moon,
named Míngjiá.
Yáo had been on the throne for fifty years when he elevated Shùn,
after twenty years he began to age,
and had him act as regent.
Twenty-eight years later he passed away,
having been on the throne for ninety-eight years,
and lived to be one hundred and eighteen years old."
Emperor Shùn Yǒuyúshì:
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Shùn,
had the surname Yáo,
his ancestors came from Zhuānxū.
Zhuānxū had a son Qióngchán,
Qióngchán had a son named Jìngkāng,
Jìngkāng had a son Gōumáng,
Gōumáng had a son named Qiáoniú,
Qiáoniú had a son Gǔsǒu.
Gǔsǒu's wife was called Wòdēng,
she saw a great rainbow,
was inspired and gave birth to Shùn at Yáoxū,
hence the surname Yáo.
He styled himself Dūjūn,
his family was originally from Jìzhōu.
His mother died early,
Gǔsǒu remarried,
and had a son Xiàng, who was arrogant.
His father was stubborn and his stepmother was treacherous,
both wanting to kill Shùn,
but Shùn could harmonize,
avoiding heavy blows,
and enduring light ones.
At age twenty, he became known for filial piety.
Yáo gave him his two daughters, Éhuáng and Nǚyīng, as wives,
and he plowed at the southern side of Lìshān.
Plowers yielded boundaries,
he fished at Léizé,
fishers yielded deep pools,
he made pottery by the river,
potters' wares were not flawed.
Yáo then appointed Shùn as Minister of Education and Grand Commandant,
tested him with the five canons,
promoted the Eight Talents and Eight Virtues,
removed the four evils and all under heaven submitted.
Then he was sent into the great wilderness,
and fierce winds, thunder, and rain did not confuse him.
Yáo then ordered Shùn to act as regent in his place.
The following year, in the first month, Shùn began to receive the mandate at the ancestral temple,
acting as Grand Commandant.
Shùn acted as regent for twenty-eight years when Yáo passed away.
After three years of mourning ended,
Shùn was eighty-one years old.
In midwinter, on the jiǎzǐ day, the moon lodged in Bì,
and he began to truly reign.
Earth succeeded Fire,
and the color yellow was esteemed.
On the first day of the first month, he paid homage at the ancestral temple of Wénzǔ,
re-appointed the Nine Ministers and Twelve Pastors,
and appointed Yǔ as Minister of Education.
Shùn was eighty-one when he truly ascended the throne,
eighty-three when he recommended Yǔ,
ninety-five when he had Yǔ act as regent,
and died after five years of regency,
at the age of one hundred. 」
The *Shàngshū* says:
"Shùn was thirty when he was employed,
thirty when he was in position,
and died after fifty years of traveling to the regions."
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation states:
"Including the three years of mourning for Yáo,
this makes a total of thirty years,
giving a total lifespan of one hundred and eleven years. 」
Bó Yǔ was the emperor of the Xiàhòu clan. 」
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* says:
"Yǔ,
of the Sì surname,
his ancestors descended from Zhuānxū.
Zhuānxū begat Gǔn,
whom Yáo enfeoffed as the Earl of Chóng.
He married a woman of the Yǒushēn clan named Zhì,
who was Xiūjǐ.
She saw a shooting star pierce the Pleiades,
and also swallowed a divine pearl,
and through spiritual conception gave birth to Yǔ at Shíniǔ.
His given name was Wénmìng,
his courtesy name was Gāomì,
he grew up among the Western Qiāng,
being a man of the Western Barbarians.
Yáo appointed him as Minister of Works,
to succeed Gǔn in controlling the floods.
After thirteen years, the great waters were calmed.
Yáo praised his achievements,
and bestowed upon him the surname Sì,
enfeoffing him as Earl of Xià,
hence he was called Bó Yǔ.
When Yáo died,
Shùn again ordered him to remain in his former office.
When Yǔ was seventy-four,
Shùn first recommended him to Heaven.
Twelve years after the recommendation,
Shùn grew old,
and began to have Yǔ act as regent, performing the Son of Heaven's duties.
Five years later, Shùn died.
Yǔ concluded the mourning for Shùn,
and the following year truly ascended the throne.
Metal succeeded Earth,
he established his capital at Píngyáng,
or some say at Ānyì.
At the age of one hundred,
he died at Kuàijī.
He first married a woman of the Túshān clan,
who bore a son, Qǐ,
who succeeded to the throne. 」
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From Yǔ to Jié, including the Yǒuqióng,
there were nineteen kings in total,
altogether four hundred and thirty-two years.
Yǔ first,
Qǐ second,
Tàikāng third,
Zhòngkāng fourth,
Xiāng fifth,
Yì sixth,
Hánzhuó seventh,
Shàokāng eighth,
Zhù ninth,
Huái tenth,
Máng eleventh,
Xiè twelfth,
Jiàng thirteenth,
Jiōng fourteenth,
Jǐn fifteenth,
Kǒngjiǎ sixteenth,
Gāo seventeenth,
Fā eighteenth,
Jié nineteenth. 」
The Shāng Yīn clan:
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* says:
"The Yīn descended from Emperor Kù,
of the Zǐ surname.
The consort of Zhǔguǐ was named Fúdū,
who saw white vapor piercing the moon,
and through spiritual conception gave birth to Tāng on a yǐ day,
hence his given name was Lǚ.
His courtesy name was Tiānyǐ,
he was called Emperor Chéng Tāng.
He had a broad jaw and a pointed forehead,
was fair-skinned and bearded,
stood tall and had a resonant voice,
was nine chǐ tall,
with four elbows on his arms.
He possessed sagely virtue,
and when the feudal lords acted unrighteously,
Tāng followed and attacked them.
When about to attack Jié,
he first destroyed Wéi, Gù, and Kūnwú,
then fought in the wilderness of Míngtiáo.
Jié fled to the mountains of Náncháo,
and Tāng then ascended the position of Son of Heaven.
Water succeeded Metal,
he first resided at Bó,
was Son of Heaven for thirteen years,
and died at the age of one hundred.
Tāng married a woman of the Yǒushēn clan as his principal consort,
who bore Crown Prince Dīng, Wàibǐng, and Zhòngrén.
The Crown Prince died early,
and Wàibǐng succeeded. 」
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"The Shāng dynasty enjoyed the state for thirty-one kings,
but those who actually held the throne were thirty kings.
The reason for saying thirty-one
is that Crown Prince Dīng is included in the count.
From Tāng obtaining the throne to Zhòu,
it was altogether six hundred and twenty-nine years.
Chéng Tāng first,
Wàibǐng second,
Zhòngrén third,
Tàijiǎ fourth,
Wòdīng fifth,
Tàigēng sixth,
Xiǎojiǎ seventh,
Yōngsì eighth,
Tàiwù ninth,
Zhòngdīng tenth,
Wàirén eleventh,
Hédǎnjiǎ twelfth,
Zǔyǐ thirteenth,
Zǔxīn fourteenth,
Wòjiǎ fifteenth,
Zǔdīng sixteenth,
Nángēng seventeenth,
Yángjiǎ eighteenth,
Pángēng nineteenth,
Xiǎoxīn twentieth,
Xiǎoyǐ twenty-first,
Wǔdīng twenty-second,
Zǔgēng twenty-third,
Zǔjiǎ twenty-fourth,
Lǐnxīn twenty-fifth,
Gēngdīng twenty-sixth,
Wǔyǐ twenty-seventh,
Tàidīng twenty-eighth,
Dìyǐ twenty-ninth,
Zhòu thirtieth. 」
The *Shāngshū* says:
"After Chéng Tāng's death,
it was the first year of Tàijiǎ. 」
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation states:
"Tàijiǎ was the son of Tàidīng,
and grandson of Tāng.
Tàidīng died before he could be established.
When Tāng died, Tàijiǎ was established,
and the first year was proclaimed.
The posthumous naming rule:
'Destroying righteousness and harming goodness is called Zhòu.'
He was defeated at Mùyě,
and his head was hung on a white banner.
From the Yellow Emperor to Zhòu, there were thirty-six generations.
In the second year of Zhòu, he took Dájǐ.
In the twentieth year, he imprisoned King Wén.
In the thirtieth year, King Wǔ reviewed troops at Mèngjīn. 」
Zhōu:
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* says:
"The Zhōu,
of the Jī surname.
King Wén began to cultivate governance,
and after three years, two-thirds of the world submitted to him.
He entered and became one of Zhòu's Three Dukes.
At the age of fifteen, he begat Crown Prince Fā.
King Wén died at ninety-seven,
and Crown Prince Fā succeeded him,
this was King Wǔ.
In the second year of King Wǔ,
he reviewed troops as far as Mèngjīn.
In the fourth year, he began to attack Yīn,
and became Son of Heaven.
Wood succeeded Water,
he moved the capital from Fēng to Hào.
King Wǔ died at the age of ninety-three,
and Crown Prince Sòng succeeded him,
this was King Chéng. 」
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From the conquest of Yīn to the year Qín destroyed Zhōu,
there were thirty-seven kings in total,
for eight hundred and sixty-seven years.
King Wǔ first,
King Chéng second,
King Kāng third,
King Zhāo fourth,
King Mù fifth,
King Gōng sixth,
King Yì seventh,
King Xiào eighth,
King Yí ninth,
King Lì ten,
King Xuān eleven,
King Yōu twelve,
King Píng thirteen,
King Huán fourteen,
King Zhuāng fifteen,
King Xī sixteen,
King Huì seventeen,
King Xiāng eighteen,
King Qǐng nineteen,
King Kuāng twenty,
King Dìng twenty-one,
King Jiǎn twenty-two,
King Líng twenty-three,
King Jǐng twenty-four,
King Dào twenty-five,
King Jìng twenty-six,
King Zhēndìng twenty-seven,
King Yuán twenty-eight,
King Āi twenty-nine,
King Sī thirty,
King Kǎo thirty-one,
King Wēiliè thirty-two,
King Yuán'ān thirty-three,
King Yílìè thirty-four,
King Xiǎnshèng thirty-five,
King Shènjìng thirty-six,
King Nǎn thirty-seven.」
The Qín Family:
"Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"Qín,
of the Yíng clan.
In the past, Bó Yì managed many livestock for Shùn,
thus he was granted the surname Yíng.
Lord Xiàoxiāng began to cultivate hegemonic enterprises,
destroyed the well-field system,
opened the policy of fields and paths,
and was made lord by the Son of Heaven.
By the reign of King Zhāoxiāng, he proclaimed himself Western Emperor,
attacked Zhōu,
deposed King Nǎn,
took the Nine Tripods,
and by the time of King Zhuāngxiāng, he destroyed Eastern and Western Zhōu.
King Zhuāngxiāng died,
Zhèng ascended as the First Emperor,
unified the realm,
and established thirty-six commanderies.
Considering himself aligned with the virtue of water,
he made October the beginning of the year,
and preferred the color black.
He ordered Méng Tián to build the Great Wall,
burned the books of poetry and other schools' teachings,
and buried alive four hundred and sixty scholars.
In the thirty-seventh year, he died at Shāqiū Terrace,
at the age of fifty. "
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From King Zhāoxiāng's destruction of Zhōu to Zǐyīng,
there were four kings and two emperors,
totaling forty-nine years.
King Zhāoxiāng one,
King Xiàowén two,
King Zhuāngxiāng three,
the First Emperor four,
Húhài five,
Zǐyīng six. "
Also, "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"Qín changed Hào to Xiányáng,
where it was the capital.
Drove away by Hàn,
it did not seek the five phases,
but instead ruled by the virtue of water.
From the initial enfeoffment of Qín to its downfall,
a total of thirty-six generations,
lasting six hundred and fifty years.
Qín,
is the descendant of Zhuānxū.
In ancient times, Zàofù acted as Mùwáng's charioteer,
performed meritoriously,
and was enfeoffed at Zhào city,
thus the state became Zhào,
sharing ancestry with Jiǎnzi,
bearing the Yíng surname.
Qín was also situated between water and fire. "
The Hàn Family:
Fire Virtue.
"Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"Hàn descends from Emperor Yáo,
bearing the Liú surname.
Duke Fēng gave birth to Zhí Jiā,
who is the Supreme Ancestor Emperor.
The Supreme Ancestor's consort was named Ǒu,
known as Empress Zhāolíng,
who bore the son Bāng,
styled Jì,
who became the High Emperor of Hàn.
In the first year of Qín's second generation,
the vassals rebelled against Qín,
and the people of Pèi collectively established him as Lord Pèi.
In the second year, he entered Wǔ Pass,
reached across the Bà,
and the Qín King Zǐyīng surrendered.
Xiàng Yǔ established himself as the Overlord of Western Chu,
appointing Lord Pèi as King of Hàn,
ruling Bāshǔ.
In the first year of Hàn,
returned to attack Yōng,
thus pacifying the Three Qíns.
In the fifth year, he defeated King of Chǔ Xiàng Yǔ at Gāixià,
pursued and executed him at Dōngchéng,
and the world was at peace.
In the spring of the first month, King of Chǔ Hán Xìn and others requested to honor him as Emperor,
and in February, he ascended the throne at Dìngtáo Fànshuǐ to the north,
establishing the capital at Cháng.
In the twelfth year, he passed away in Chánglè Palace,
at the age of sixty-two.
Initially taking in Lǚ Gōng's daughter,
she was known as Empress High,
giving birth to Crown Prince Yíng,
who succeeded him. "
According to the twelve emperors of the Former Hàn:
Gāozǔ one,
Huì Emperor two,
Empress High three,
Wén Emperor four,
Jǐng Emperor five,
Wǔ Emperor six,
Zhāo Emperor seven,
Xuān Emperor eight,
Yuán Emperor nine,
Chéng Emperor ten,
Āi Emperor eleven,
Píng Emperor twelve.
Wáng Mǎng appointed Rúzǐ Yīng as Regent,
usurped the throne in the third year,
and lasted two years until Gèngshǐ was established.
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From Gāozǔ's first year to Gèngshǐ's second year,
altogether 230 years."
Later Hàn:
"Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"The Light Martial Emperor,
descends from Emperor Jǐng,
named Xiù,
styled Wénshū.
In the first year of Gèngshǐ, he served as a general,
defeated Wáng Yì,
killed Wáng Xùn,
executed Wáng Láng,
and in the second year of Gèngshǐ, he was established as King Xiāo.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ in April, Gèngshǐ surrendered to Chìméi,
and in June Light Martial ascended the emperor's throne at Chángshān Hào, Qiānqiū Pavilion to the north,
establishing the capital at Luòyáng.
Reigned for thirty-three years,
and in the second month of Zhōngyuán's second year, passed away in Southern Palace of Luòyáng,
at the age of sixty-three.
Crown Prince Zhuāng succeeded him,
becoming Emperor Xiàomíng."
According to the twelve emperors of the Later Hàn:
Light Martial one,
Míng Emperor two,
Zhāng Emperor three,
Hé Emperor four,
Shāng Emperor five,
Ān Emperor six,
Shùn Emperor seven,
Chōng Emperor eight,
Zhì Emperor nine,
Huán Emperor ten,
Líng Emperor eleven,
Xiàn Emperor twelve.
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From the first year of Hàn to Gèngshǐ's fifth year,
a total of 212 years;
from the first year of Regency to Gèngshǐ's second year,
a total of 18 years;
from the first year of Jiànwǔ to the first year of Yánkāng,
totaling 195 years.
Including the former and later Hàn, with abolished emperors and Wáng Mǎng,
there were a total of thirty-one emperors over 426 years."
The Wèi Family:
Earth Virtue.
"Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" says:
"Wèi,
of the Cáo surname.
The Martial Emperor's personal name was Cāo,
styled Méngdé,
raised to the title of King of Wèi in the twenty-fourth year of Jiàn'ān during the Hàn,
and changed the twenty-fifth year to the first year of Yánkāng.
He passed away in Luòyáng in spring January,
at the age of sixty-six,
and Crown Prince Pī succeeded him,
known as the Civil Emperor.
In the winter of that year, in October, he received the abdication from the Hàn,
changing Yánkāng's first year to Huángchū,
with the capital at Luòyáng.
He died in the seventh year of Huángchū,
at the age of forty."
Huángfǔ Mì says:
"From the first year of Huángchū to the year of surrender to Jìn,
there were five emperors in total.
Forty-five years.
Emperor Wén, one;
Emperor Míng, two;
Deposed Emperor Qí King, three;
Deposed Emperor Gāoguìxiāngōng, four;
Emperor Yuán, five.
According to the first establishment of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
it was called the first year of Huángchū.
In the second year of Huángchū, Liú Bèi declared himself emperor in Shǔ,
called it the first year of Zhāngwǔ,
reigned for three years and then died,
at the age of sixty-three,
his son Chán succeeded to the throne.
These two rulers together reigned for forty-three years,
and were extinguished by Wèi.
In the third year of Huángchū,
Sūn Quán declared himself King of Wú in Wǔchāng,
called it the first year of Huángwǔ,
later he declared himself emperor.
He reigned for twenty-one years and then died,
at the age of seventy,
his son Liàng succeeded to the throne.
From Quán to Hàochì there were four rulers,
together fifty-nine years in total,
and were extinguished by Jìn.
The Jìn dynasty:
The virtue of gold.
"The Book of Jìn" says:
"The esteemed name of Emperor Wǔ was Yán,
styled Ānshì,
from Wēn County in Hénèi,
of the Sīmǎ clan.
In the first year of Tàishǐ, he ascended the altar to accept the abdication,
and after the rites, he went immediately to the palace in Luòyáng,
posthumously honoring Prince Xuān as Emperor Xuān,
the ancestor of Emperor Wǔ.
Prince Jǐng was honored as Emperor Jǐng,
the uncle of Emperor Wǔ.
Prince Wén was honored as Emperor Wén.
The father of Emperor Wǔ.
In the first year of Dàxī, he died,
at the age of fifty-five."
He reigned for twenty-six years,
the Crown Prince Zhōng succeeded,
becoming Emperor Huì.
According to the "Book of Jìn", from Emperor Wǔ to Emperor Gōng,
there were altogether fifteen emperors,
for a total of one hundred sixty-five years,
and the abdication was to Sòng.
Emperor Wǔ, one;
Emperor Huì, two;
Emperor Huái, three;
Emperor Mǐn, four;
above were the Western court in Luòyáng.
Emperor Yuán, five;
Emperor Míng, six;
Emperor Chéng, seven;
Emperor Kāng, eight;
Emperor Mù, nine;
Emperor Āi, ten;
Deposed Emperor, eleven;
Emperor Jiǎnwén, twelve;
Emperor Xiàowǔ, thirteen;
Emperor Ān, fourteen;
Emperor Gōng, fifteen;
above were the Eastern court in Jiànyè.
The present Jiāngníng County in Rùnzhōu is this.
Xīxuān and Yánhào
both appear in narratives.
Nine Shùn and Ten Yáo
Huán Fàn’s “Essential Discussions” states:
“To criticize a duke is easy,
although one virtuous man may have few mistakes,
there are many who hold grudges,
even nine Shùn would still bring chaos.”
“Han Feizi” stated:
“If Yáo and Shùn were born in positions of power,
even ten Jié could not cause disorder,
and the situation would be stable.
If Jié and Zhòu were born in positions of power,
even ten Yáo and Shùn could not transform them,
and the situation would be chaotic.”
The White Emperor and Xuán King
"The River Chart" states:
"White Emperor, Zhūxuān."
Sòng Jūn says:
"The clan of Shào Hào."
"The National Language" states:
"Xuán King served diligently in Shāng,
flourishing for fourteen generations."
Jiǎ Kuí’s note states:
"Xuán King refers to Xiè,
the ancestor of Tāng Xiè,
referred to as Xuán King."
Cloud Names and Fire Records
"The Commentary of Zuǒ" states:
"The Yellow Emperor recorded with clouds,
thus he managed clouds and was named for clouds.
Also it is said the Flame Emperor,
recorded with fire,
thus he managed fire and was named for fire."
Great Court and Shào Hào
Qiáo Zhōu’s “Examination of Ancient History” states:
"The Great Court clan,
of the Jiāng surname,
ruled by the virtue of fire,
thus called the Flame Emperor."
Huángfǔ Mì's "Chronicles of Emperors" states:
"Emperor Shào Hào's name was Zhì,
styled Qīngyáng."
Six Wings and Nine Feathers
"The Spring and Autumn Annals of Orders" states:
"The Human Sovereign had nine heads,
harnessed six wings,
crossing cloud valleys and ridges."
"The River Diagram" states:
"The Heavenly Sovereign had nine feathers,
named as Revolving Return."
Ruòshuǐ and Tú Mountain
"Lǚ's Annals" states:
"Emperor Zhuān Xū was born from Ruòshuǐ,
settled in empty mulberry trees,
and ascended to the imperial throne."
"Chronicles of the Warlords of Shǔ" states:
"Yǔ's mother conceived him with pearls,
split and gave birth to him on Tú Mountain."
Born Under the Wing and In the Constellation
"The Spring and Autumn Diagram of Sincerity" states:
"The essence of the Red Emperor,
born under the wing."
"The Spring and Autumn Original Book of Orders" states:
"Jī Chāng, the essence of the Blue Emperor,
his position in the heart of the chamber."
Sòng Jūn’s note states:
"The Blue Emperor’s spiritual majesty is revered."
Xuán Bird and Red Dragon
"Biographies of Exemplary Women" states:
"Jiǎn Dí was a lesser consort of Emperor Kù,
a daughter of Yǒusōng,
bathed in the waters of the Xuan Hill,
a xuán bird held an egg and fell,
multicolored,
Jiǎn Dí received it and swallowed it,
thus giving birth to Xiè."
"The Poem Contains Divine Mist" states:
"Qìngdū joined with the red dragon,
creating a marriage to give birth to the Red Emperor,
also known as Yí Qí Yáo."
Dream of the Sun and Feeling the Star
"The Story of Emperor Hàn Wǔ" states:
"Empress Wang was inside the palace of the Crown Prince,
she received favor and conceived,
dreaming of the sun entering her bosom."
"The Book of Documents on Imperial Mandates" states:
"Yáo's successor was Huá sensing the axis,
the note states:
'Shùn's mother was moved by the essence of the axis star,
thus giving birth to Shùn Zhònghuá.'"
Stars Surround and Piercing the Moon
"The Poem Contains Divine Mist" states:
"Great flashes surrounded the Northern Bushel Axis star illuminating the fields,
influencing the attachment of a jewel to give birth to the Yellow Emperor."
"The River Chart" states:
"The star Yáoguāng,
like a rainbow piercing the moon,
moved the female axis essence in the secluded room of the palace,
giving birth to the Black Emperor Zhuān Xū."
Pearl Hall and Jade Principle
"The Luo Book" states:
"The Black Emperor's son Tāng,
was eight feet one inch tall,
with a pearl hall."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals of Orders" states:
"Shénnóng adorned with jade principles."
Sòng Jūn’s note states:
"The jade principle is akin to jade essence."
Four Breasts and Eight Eyebrows
"The Spring and Autumn Original Book of Orders" states:
"King Wén had four breasts,
it is called embracing goodness.
Implement the method of wine flags,
spreading benevolence and enlightenment."
Sòng Jūn’s note states:
"Wine refers to milk,
meaning the distribution of benevolence to the world."
"The Great Tradition of the Book of Documents" states:
"Yáo had eight eyebrows,
eight eyebrows like the character eight."
Double Pupils and Double Teeth
The *Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* states:
"Shùn had double pupils,
which are called 'zī liáng'."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"Zī liáng means having the moisture of abundant fluid,
and being clear, cool, bright, and seeing many things."
It also says:
"King Wǔ had double teeth,
which are called 'gāng qiáng'."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"Double teeth serve as an outward sign."
Dragon Forehead and Bird Beak
The *Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* states:
"Huángdì had a dragon-like forehead."
The *Shīzǐ* states:
"Yǔ had a long neck and a bird-like beak,
his appearance was also ugly!
Yet the world followed and esteemed him,
because he was fond of learning."
Broad Gaze and Full Gaze
The *Chūnqiū Hécéng Tú* states:
"The appearance of the Cāng Emperor,
when gazed upon, is broad;
when he looks, it is focused,
and he is nine chǐ and one cùn tall."
It also says:
"The appearance of the Chì Emperor,
when gazed upon, is full;
he is eight chǐ and seven cùn tall."
Scaly Body and Ox Head
Wáng Yánshòu's "Lǔ Língguāng Diàn Fù" says:
"Fúxī had a scaly body,
Nǚwā had a snake-like torso."
Huángfǔ Mì's *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
"There was a woman of the Yǒujiǎo clan named Nǚdēng,
who was a consort of Shǎodiǎn.
She traveled to Huáyáng.
There was a divine dragon's head,
which moved Nǚdēng, and she gave birth to Yándì,
who had a human body and an ox head."
Carrying a Shield and Embracing the Dipper
The *Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* states:
"Dì Kù carried a shield,
which is called 'qīng míng'."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"'Gān'
means shield."
The *Luò Shū* states:
"There was a man who emerged from Shíyí, dug the earth to replace, carried a chéng qián, and embraced the jade dipper."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Embracing the way of the Xuánjī and Yùhéng (the Dipper).
Yáo Shì believed that Yǔ had a black mole on his chest resembling the Big Dipper."
Zhāohuá and Yánxǐ
The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states:
"Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
Yáo gave him his two daughters in marriage,
entrusted him with his nine sons,
and presented him with the jade of Zhāohuá."
The *Shàngshū Xuánjī Qián* states:
"Yǔ bestowed upon Qǐ, who held the xuán guī as he emerged,
an inscription saying it was the jade of Yánxǐ,
receiving the virtue of Heaven's bestowed pendant."
Grasping the River and Sinking in the Luò
Huángfǔ Mì's *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
"Yáo led the feudal lords and ministers,
sank a jade disc into the Luò River,
and received charts and writings.
This is now the chapter 'Wò Hé Jì' in the *Shàngshū Zhōnghòu*."
The *Shàngshū Zhōnghòu* states:
"I led my ministers to sink a jade disc into the Luò River,
and waited well until Xiàjì.
A red light arose,
a black turtle emerged bearing writings,
with red characters forming words."
Golden Ox and Jade Horse
The *Sūnshì Ruìyìng Tú* states:
"The golden ox is an auspicious vessel.
When the king's land is opened up,
the golden ox arrives."
It also says:
"The jade horse
is an auspicious vessel.
When the king is clear-sighted and sincerely values worthies, it arrives."
Warm Luò and Glorious River
The *Yì Qiánzàodù* states:
"In response to the Emperor's abundant virtue,
the Luò River first becomes warm,
after nine days it turns cold,
and in five days it changes to five colors."
The *Shàngshū Zhōnghòu* states:
"When Emperor Yáo assumed governance,
glorious light emerged from the River."
Great Sovereign and Primal Lord
The *Zhōu Yì* states:
"The great sovereign has a mandate,
to found states and continue families."
The *Shàngshū* states:
"What is lovable if not the sovereign?
What is awe-inspiring if not the people?
Without the primal lord, whom would the multitude uphold?"
Emerging from Zhen and Opening the Steps
The *Zhōu Yì* states:
"The Emperor emerges from Zhèn,
and aligns with Xùn."
The *Chūnqiū Kǒngyǎn Tú* states:
"All Sons of Heaven are the essence and treasure of the Five Emperors,
each having their assigned sequence.
They rise in succession according to their turn,
and there must be spiritual signs and records,
causing the steps to open and the path to be established."
Facing the Gate and Placing the Charts
The *Lǐjì* states:
"The Son of Heaven stands facing the screen,
and the feudal lords face north to see the Son of Heaven; this is called an audience.
The Son of Heaven stands facing the gate,
and the dukes face east while the feudal lords face west; this is called a court assembly."
The *Chūnqiū Kǒngyǎn Tú* states:
"The king should place charts and records by his side,
to correct himself."
Holding the Reins and Dropping the Sleeves
The *Lùzǐ* states:
"The Three Sovereigns dropped their sleeves (ruled effortlessly),
the Five Emperors dropped their hands.
Táng and Yú held the reins,
Yǔ and Tāng raced the chariot.
Even if Duke Zhōu were to control the yoke,
and Confucius were to hasten the pace,
it would certainly not stop."
Yìng Shào's *Fēngsútōng* states:
"August Heaven does not speak,
yet the four seasons proceed,
and the hundred things are born.
The Three Sovereigns dropped their sleeves and acted through non-action,
resembling August Heaven,
therefore they are called 'Huáng' (Sovereign)."
Timely Riding and Sometimes Leaping
The *Zhōu Yì* states:
"Timely riding six dragons to驾驭 Heaven."
It also says:
"The fourth nine: sometimes leaping in the abyss."
Continuing Yáo and Bestowing upon Shùn
The *Hànshū*'s account of Gāozǔ states:
"August indeed was Hàn's ancestor,
continuing Yáo's legacy.
Truly Heaven-born virtue,
intelligent, divine, and martial."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Yáo bestowed it upon Shùn,
Shùn bestowed it upon Yǔ,
Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu."
Striking the Ground and Drumming the Belly
History says:
"In Yáo's time, there was an old man
who struck the ground and played by the roadside,
saying:
'I dig a well and drink,
plow the field and eat.
What has the Emperor's power to do with me?'"
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"In the time of Hèxūshì, people
dwelled without knowing what to do,
traveled without knowing where to go.
They held food in their mouths and played,
drummed their bellies and wandered."
Dropping the Garments and Rolling the Collar
The *Yì* states:
"Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn
dropped their garments and governed the world,
taking this from Qián and Kūn."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"In ancient times, there were those with móu tóu and rolled collars,
who ruled the world."
The commentary says:
"The ancients, probably before the Three Sovereigns,
wore móu tóu, which is a hood.
It means they did not yet know how to make caps.
Rolled collar
means leather garments were folded and layered.
Dwelling Like a Quail, Drinking from Cupped Hands
The Shīzǐ states:
"People say that those who rule the world
should have jade towers nine stories high,
yet Yáo lived in a simple thatched hut;
they should wear robes embroidered with nine patterns,
yet Yáo wore coarse cloth;
within the palace there should be three markets,
yet Yáo dwelt like a quail."
The Lǐjì states:
"They used clods of earth for drums and drumsticks,
and drank from hollows in the ground, scooping with their hands."
Zhèng's commentary says:
"Drinking from a hollow in the ground means
scooping it up with the hands."
Stitched Collars, Knotted Cords
The Yànzǐ states:
"In ancient times, there were those who ruled the world wearing garments with stitched collars!"
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"In the times of Róngchéngshì, Dàtíngshì, Bóhuángshì, and Zhōngyāngshì,
the people of that era
used knotted cords for administration."
Hanging Whips, Discarded Robes
The Lùzǐ states:
"The Three Sovereigns hung down their whips, and the Five Emperors gestured with their hands."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"Yáo's court was like discarded robes,
meaning there were few affairs."
Nests in Trees, Cave Dwellings
The Yànzǐ states:
"In ancient times, there were those who lived in nests in trees and ruled the world!"
The Lǐjì states:
"In former times, the ancient kings dwelt in cave dwellings in winter,
and in nests in trees in summer."
Emulating Earth, Measuring Heaven
Huáng Shígōng's Sān Lüè states:
"The Emperor embodies Heaven and emulates Earth;
when he speaks and issues commands,
the world is at peace."
The Wénzǐ states:
"When Fúxīshì ruled the world,
his achievements measured up to Heaven and Earth."
Drawing Near to the Sun, Gazing at the Rainbow
The Dàdài Lǐ states:
"Zǎi Wǒ respectfully inquired about Emperor Yáo."
Confucius said:
"Fàngxūn's benevolence was like Heaven,
his wisdom like the spirits;
drawing near to him was like drawing near to the sun,
gazing upon him was like gazing upon clouds."
The Mèngzǐ states:
"When Tāng launched his first campaign starting from Gé,
the world trusted him,
and the people looked to him as in a great drought they look to clouds and rainbows."
Uniting with the Spirits, Complying with Fate
The Qī Jīng Yì Gāng states:
Confucius said:
"The virtue of the Son of Heaven moves Heaven and Earth,
penetrates the eight directions;
one whose transformative power unites with the spirits is called Huáng.
One whose virtue unites with Heaven is called Dì;
one whose virtue unites with benevolence and righteousness is called Wáng."
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo states:
it is not the achievement of a single emperor.
The King is illustrious;
it is not the constant possession of a single house.
Those who comply with fate survive;
those who defy it perish."
Great Virtue, Vast Reputation
The Yìjīng states:
"The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life;
the great treasure of the sage is called position.
That by which one guards position is called benevolence;
that by which one gathers people is called wealth."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's Fēngshàn Shū states:
"This is how the former sages eternally preserved their vast reputation,
and were constantly praised as foremost."
Understanding the One, Penetrating the Three
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"One who understands the One is Huáng;
one who discerns the Way is Dì;
one who penetrates virtue is Wáng;
one who achieves his plans and is victorious in war is Bà."
The Dǒngzǐ states:
"The ancients who created the written character
made three strokes connected in the middle to signify 'Wáng' (king).
The three strokes
represent Heaven, Earth, and Man;
connecting them in the middle
means penetrating their Way.
To take the talents of Heaven, Earth, and Man and penetrate all three,
who but a king could be capable of this?"
Uniting with the Primordial, Complying with the Order
Hé Xiū's commentary on the Gōngyáng Zhuàn states:
"One whose virtue unites with the Primordial is called Huáng."
The Dàdài Lǐ states:
"Huángdì was one who complied with the order of Heaven and Earth."
Lofty, Reverent
The Lúnyǔ states:
"How lofty! Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world yet did not interfere with it!"
Hé Yàn's commentary says:
"Praising Shùn and Yǔ for not seeking the world yet obtaining it;
'lofty' describes an appearance of great height."
The Máo Shī states:
"This King Wén,
was reverent and cautious.
Clearly serving the Lord on High,
he thus secured abundant blessings."
Zhèng's annotation says:
"'Reverent'
describes an appearance of caution."
