Illustrious, Resplendent
The Máo Shī states:
"Brilliantly below,
illustriously above."
Máo Cháng's commentary says:
"King Wén's virtue shone brilliantly below,
thus appearing illustriously in Heaven."
The Hànshū states:
"Xiàochéng was resplendent,
presiding over court with radiance.
The majesty of his dignified bearing
was like jade tablets and scepters."
The Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven is solemn;
the feudal lords are majestic."
Solemn, Vigilant
The Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven is solemn;
the feudal lords are majestic."
The Yìjīng states:
"The third nine line: The nobleman is vigilant all day long;
at night he is cautious as if in danger, thus without blame."
Five Virtues, Three Sequences
The Yuèlìng states:
"On the day of the Beginning of Spring,
the flourishing virtue resides in Wood,
its Emperor is Tàihào;
in summer the flourishing virtue resides in Fire,
its Emperor is Yándì;
in late summer the flourishing virtue resides in Earth,
its Emperor is Huángdì;
in autumn the flourishing virtue resides in Metal,
its Emperor is Shàohào;
in winter the flourishing virtue resides in Water,
its Emperor is Zhuānxū."
The Hànshū states:
"The Three Sequences
are the guiding principles of Heaven's bestowal, Earth's transformation, and human affairs."
Pacing, Galloping; Substance, Refinement
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"The Three Sovereigns paced,
the Five Emperors trotted;
the Three Kings galloped,
the Five Hegemons raced."
The Dàdài Lǐ states:
"Substance and refinement alternate twice and change,
the calendar and first month change thrice."
Three Bonds, Unified Rule
The Lúnyǔ states:
"Zhōu based itself on the rituals of Yīn;
what was added or omitted can be known."
The commentary says:
"What was based upon refers to the Three Bonds and Five Constants;
what was added or omitted refers to substance/refinement and the Three Sequences."
The Yì Qián Záo Dù states:
"The Son of Heaven succeeds Heaven to order things,
establishes governance to unify rule,
so that each attains its proper place.
He regards Heaven as father and Earth as mother to nurture the people;
this is the title of utmost honor."
Qīngqiū, Dānpǔ
The Guīcáng Qǐ Shì states:
"Chīyóu came forth from Yángshuǐ,
with eight limbs and eight toes,
a sparsely-haired head.
He ascended the Nine Marshes to attack Kōngsāng.
Huángdì killed him at Qīngqiū."
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"The Yǒumiáo people, dwelling among the southern barbarians, did not submit.
Yáo campaigned against them and defeated them at the banks of the Dānshuǐ."
Mùyě Bǎnquán
The *Book of Documents* says:
"King Wǔ had three hundred war chariots,
three thousand tiger warriors,
and fought Zhòu at Mùyě."
The *Da Dai Liji* says:
"Xuānyuán fought the Red Emperor on the plains of Bǎnquán."
Xuānyuán's Encampment Zhōu's Battle Array
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"Xuānyuán established his city at the foot of Zhuōlù,
moving about without fixed abode,
using his troops to form encampments for defense while on the march."
The *Book of Documents* says:
"When King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
on the wùwǔ day of the first month, his army crossed the Mèngjīn,
on the guǐhài day, he arrayed his forces in the outskirts of Shāng,
awaiting Heaven's gracious command."
Huángfèngxū Wěishuǐ
The *Hánfēizǐ* says:
"King Wén attacked Chóng,
and upon reaching Huángfèngxū, the ties of his leggings came loose.
Looking around, there were no attendants to order to tie them,
so King Wén tied them himself."
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"In the fourth year, King Wǔ raised an army and marched east,
leading his war chariots to the Wěishuǐ,
and on the jiǎzǐ day, he reached the outskirts of Shāng."
Shùn's Battle-axe Xuānyuán's Bow
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"The Yǒumiáo clan, relying on their stronghold, refused to submit.
Shùn then cultivated civil virtue and education for three years,
and danced holding a shield and battle-axe,
whereupon the Yǒumiáo requested to submit."
The *Book of Changes* says:
"After Shénnóng passed away,
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn arose.
They bent wood to make bows,
and sharpened wood to make arrows.
The advantage of bows and arrows
was to awe all under Heaven,
likely derived from the hexagram Kuí."
Personally Plowed Personally Sowed
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"The teachings of Shénnóng said:
'If there are men of working age who do not plow,
then someone in the world may suffer hunger;
if there are women of working age who do not spin,
then someone in the world may suffer cold!'
Therefore, he personally plowed the fields,
and his wife personally spun."
The *Analects* says:
"Yǔ and Jì personally sowed and thus possessed the world."
Rejecting Jade Hiding Gold
Zhāng Héng's *Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital* says:
"Rejecting jade into the valleys."
Lù Jiǎ's *New Discourses* says:
"Shùn hid gold in the Zhǎnyán mountains,
to stop desires for wickedness and excess."
Yáo's Kitchen Shùn's Steamer
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"In Yáo's kitchen, dried meat strips grew of themselves,
thin as a fan's shape.
When shaken like a drum, they produced wind,
keeping food cool,
and not spoiling; they were called shà fǔ (fan-dried meat)."
The *Han Shi Waizhuan* says:
"In the past, Shùn's steamer and basin had no rank odor,
yet the craftsmen were not punished for their skill."
Unhewn Pillars Earthen Steps
The *Book of Zhou* says:
"King Wén was in Hào,
and summoned his heir, Fā, saying:
'I use unhewn pillars and thatched roofs,
to be sparing of the people's resources.'" *Mòzǐ* says:
"Yáo's hall was three chǐ high,
with earthen steps in three tiers.
The thatch was not trimmed,
the rafters were not planed."
Two Eights Four Sevens
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Shùn served as Yáo's minister,
recommended the Eight Kǎi,
putting them in charge of the land,
to manage all affairs.
Everything was timely and orderly,
the earth was level and Heaven's work accomplished.
He recommended the Eight Yuán to spread the five teachings throughout the four quarters:
fathers righteous, mothers kind,
elder brothers friendly, younger brothers respectful, sons filial.
Peace within, accomplishment without."
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"The Confucian scholar Qiáng Huá,
coming from Guānzhōng, presented the Red Talisman, saying:
'Liú Xiù raises troops to capture the unprincipled,
clouds gather from the four quarters, dragons battle in the wild,
at the time of four sevens, fire becomes lord.'" Also, Zhāng Héng's *Rhapsody on the Western Capital*:
"My Emperor Guāngwǔ, angered by this,
then like a dragon soared from Báishuǐ,
like a phoenix soared over Cānxū.
He received the mandate at four sevens,
and removed the Gònggōng.
Chánchēng and Xúnshǐ (comets),
all villains were wiped out."
Grasping Hair Spitting Out Food
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"Yǔ, while washing his hair, would grasp it three times (to attend to business),
during one meal, would rise three times."
Bān Shūpí's *Discourse on the Mandate of Kings* says:
"Emperor Gāozǔ was sincere and fond of strategy,
open to listening and accepting advice.
While eating, he would spit out his food,
to accept Zǐfáng's counsel."
Yú's Sháo Xià's Yuè
The *Analects* says:
"The Master heard the Sháo music in Qí,
and for three months did not notice the taste of meat."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"Sháo,
is the name of Shùn's music."
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"When Yǔ was established,
he ordered Gāoyáo to create the Xià Yuè in nine movements to make his achievements manifest."
Fúxī's Sè Nǚwā's Shēng
The *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"Fúxī made the sè,
with thirty-six strings,
eight chǐ and one cùn long."
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Nǚwā's shēng huáng (reed pipes)."
Hàn's Zhù Yú's Qín
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"Emperor Gāozǔ returned home,
passed by Pèi,
set out wine at the Pèi palace,
summoned all his old friends, elders, and younger generations,
drank freely.
He gathered over a hundred and twenty children from Pèi,
and taught them songs.
When the wine was at its height,
Emperor Gāozǔ struck the zhù,
and composed a song himself."
The *Book of Rites* says:
"In the past, Shùn made the five-stringed qín,
to sing the 'South Wind'."
Order and Manage Shelter and Moisturize
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Clouds and thunder: Zhūn.
The nobleman orders and manages."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"The Emperor embodies the Supreme Unity,
regulates the eight extremities,
orders the six directions,
shelters, moisturizes, enlightens, and guides,
bestowing universally and without selfishness."
Nurture and Perfect Regulate and Complete
The *Lǎozǐ* says:
"Nurture them, perfect them,
cover them, shelter them."
Wáng Bì's commentary says:
"Tíng means to give them form,
dú means to perfect their substance."
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Heaven and earth interact: Tài.
The ruler regulates and completes the ways of heaven and earth,
assists the fitting aspects of heaven and earth,
in order to aid the people."
Shade Under Trees Push into Ditches
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"King Wǔ gave shade to a sunstroke victim under a tree,
and the world turned to him,
moved by his kindness."
Huán Kuān's *Discourses on Salt and Iron* says:
"Yǔ and Jì, starting as commoners,
thought that if anyone in the world was not in their proper place,
it was as if they themselves had pushed them into a ditch."
Weep for Criminals Fan the Sunstruck
Liú Xiàng's *Garden of Stories* says:
"Yǔ went out and saw a criminal,
asked about him and wept for him."
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"King Wǔ returned from Mèngjīn and arrived in Zhōu,
saw a sunstroke victim,
and the King himself held him with his left arm and fanned him with his right."
Divine Support, Human Assistance
The Chunqiu Yuanming Bao states:
"The term 'king' (wáng) means 'to go forth' (wǎng),
that which the divine spirits support and turn towards,
that which the people return to and delight in."
Fàn Yè's "Hòu Hàn Shū · Guāngwǔ Zàn" says:
"Since the auspicious blessings were revealed,
human plans all proved successful.
Brilliant were the court's strategies,
resolute and heroic were the decisions."
Presenting Pheasants, Offering Mastiffs
The Shǐ Jì states:
"During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
Yuècháng presented white pheasants as tribute."
The Shàng Shū states:
"Xīlǚ offered mastiffs."
A commentary notes:
"Xīróng, a distant state, presented large dogs as tribute."
Displaying Righteousness, Observing Customs
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The Son of Heaven does not tour the domains except to display righteousness."
The Lǐ Jì states:
"He orders the Grand Music Master to present the odes,
in order to observe the customs of the people."
Zhōu's Wheel Ruts, Xià's Traces
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The Right Minister of Chǔ, Zǐ Gé, said:
'In the past, King Mù wished to indulge his heart's desires,
traveling throughout the world under heaven.
Surely there must have been the ruts of his chariot and the hoofprints of his horses.
Jì Gōng Móufǔ composed the poem "Qí Zhāo",
to halt the king's desires,
and thus he was able to die peacefully in the Qí Palace.'" It also states:
"Vast and boundless were Yǔ's traces,
he divided them into the Nine Provinces."
Shùn's Banner, Yáo's Drum
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"Shùn had a banner for reporting goodness,
and thus the ruler was not kept in the dark.
Yǔ set up a drum for remonstrance at court,
to prepare for litigation and appeals."
Dèngzǐ states:
"Yáo established a drum for those daring to remonstrate."
Xià's Stone Chimes, Zhōu's Hand-Drum
Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn states:
"When Yǔ transformed the world under heaven,
he listened through the five tones.
He hung bells, drums, hand-bells, and stone chimes at the gate and placed a hand-drum there,
to await scholars from the four seas."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"Shùn had the slander-post,
Tāng had officers to oversee faults,
King Wǔ had the warning hand-drum,
yet they still feared they might not know their own faults."
Presenting Cherries, Offering Millet
The Hàn Shū states:
"Emperor Huì once went on an excursion to a detached palace.
Shūsūn Tōng said:
'In ancient times, fruits were tasted in spring.
Now cherries are ripe,
they can be presented.
I wish Your Majesty would go forth,
and take the opportunity to present cherries to the ancestral temple.'
The emperor approved.
The presentation of various fruits originated from this."
The Lǐ Jì states:
"In the mid-summer month,
the farmers present the new millet.
Then they taste the millet with young fowl,
and offer cherries as delicacies,
first presenting them to the ancestral temple."
Feet Marked 'Jǐ', Hands Holding 'Bāo'
Huángfǔ Mì's Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"Xiūjǐ was walking in the mountains,
saw a shooting star traverse the Pleiades,
dreamt of an encounter and was moved by the thought,
and gave birth to Yǔ at Shíniǔ.
He had a tiger-like nose and a large mouth,
and the pattern on his feet formed the character 'jǐ'."
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
"Shùn had a dragon-like forehead and a large mouth,
and his hands held the character 'bāo'."
Sòng Jūn's commentary notes:
"Holding 'bāo',
means the character 'bāo' was in his hands.
It symbolizes receiving praise and honor after toil and hardship,
leading to great fortune."
Obtaining the Jade Calendar, Wearing the Precious Script
Gān Bǎo's Sōu Shén Jì states:
"Yú Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
and obtained a jade calendar from a cliff by the river.
Shùn knew the Mandate of Heaven was upon him,
and tirelessly embodied the Way."
The Hé Tú states:
"After Yǔ had regulated the waters,
his merit was great.
The Celestial Emperor bestowed upon Yǔ a pendant inscribed with precious script in large characters,
to help him cross the difficulties of the Běihǎi and the Ruòshuǐ."
Sweet Springs Emerge, Auspicious Phoenix Arrives
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
"When Emperor Yáo had been governing for seventy years,
sweet dew moistened and nourished,
sweet springs emerged from the mountains,
glorious light issued from the river,
and auspicious vapors filled the four quarters."
The Lǐ Dǒu Wēiyí states:
"When the ruler's governance and litigation are fair,
then the auspicious phoenix arrives."
Jade Turtle Prophecy, Stone Horse Diagram
The Ruìyìng Tú states:
"The jade turtle,
appeared in the time of Shī Kuàng at the banks of the Hé Dōng,
for the emergence of the sage's diagram from the river,
bearing the register and prophetic writings."
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
"In the first year of the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái,
a jade turtle emerged from the Bàshuǐ."
The Wèishì Chūnqiū states:
"In the third year of the Qīnglóng era of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
at Jīnshān Xuānchuān in Shāndān County, Zhāngyè Commandery, waters overflowed and surged.
A stone horse bore a diagram,
shaped like a numinous turtle.
It stood west of the river.
There were seven stone horses,
a qílín to the east,
and a phoenix to the south."
Recording the Phoenix, Dancing Divine Fish
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"When Shǎohào's clan was established,
the phoenix happened to arrive.
Therefore, they recorded affairs using birds."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the Shàng Shū states:
"The male is called fèng,
the female is called huáng,
they are numinous birds."
The Hàn Shū states:
"During Emperor Xuān's time, when he journeyed east upon the great river,
divine fish danced in the river."
Driving Two Dragons, Harnessing Six Phoenixes
The Kuòdì Tú states:
"Yǔ executed Fángfēng.
The virtue of Xià flourished,
and two dragons descended to him.
Yǔ had the Fàn clan drive them to travel."
The Chūnqiū Mìnglì Xù states:
"Chénfàng had six heads and four breasts,
and reigned for two hundred and fifty years.
Líguāng succeeded him,
and was called Huáng Tán.
He had a sharp head and a sun-like protuberance on his forehead.
He harnessed six phoenixes and emerged from Dìhéng,
reigning for five hundred and sixty years."
Creating Boats and Carts, Making Plows and Hoes
Bān Gù's "Dōngdū Fù" states:
"Creating boats and carts,
manufacturing tools and implements,
this is how Xuānyuánshì opened the work of emperors."
The Yì states:
"After Páoxīshì passed away,
Shénnóngshì arose.
He carved wood to make plowshares,
and bent wood to make plow handles.
The benefit of the plow and hoe,
he taught to the world under heaven."
Establishing the Royal Standard, Conforming to Heaven's Center
The Shàng Shū · Hóng Fàn states:
"Establish and employ the royal standard."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Huáng means
great.
Jí means
center.
In all affairs, one should employ the great and central Way."
The Chūnqiū Yùndǒu Shū states:
"Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng are the Three Sovereigns.
Huáng (sovereign) means center,
and vastness.
They conformed to Heaven and trod the center,
opened the yin and spread the guiding principles.
They stopped and conformed to the royal standard,
their influence was bright and luminous.
Resplendent and full of beauty,
it cannot be fully measured."
Embracing the Qian Origin, embodying the Great Unity
Huán Tán's "New Discourses" states:
"The sovereign who embodies the kingly way,
his virtue can bear and
encompass all, thereby unifying the Qian Origin."
"Wénzǐ" states:
"The Emperor embodies the Great Unity,
the King models himself on Yin and Yang."
Modeling on the Three Powers, all share one virtue
"Huáinánzǐ" states:
"Emperors and Kings embody the Great Unity to model themselves on the Three Powers."
"The Book of Documents" states:
"Only Yǐn Yī and Tāng
shared a single virtue."
The August One matches Heaven, the Emperor accords with Earth
"Chūnqiū Fánlù" states:
"One whose virtue matches Heaven and Earth is called August."
Huángfǔ Mì's "Chronicles of Emperors and Kings" states:
"One whose achievements accord with the divine is called August,
one whose virtue accords with Earth is called Emperor,
one whose virtue accords with humanity is called King."
Yǔ was diligent, Tāng was trembling
"The Book of Documents" states:
"Yǔ said:
'I think daily of being diligent.'" Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"He says he thinks daily of being diligent and not slackening,
merely to complete the achievements of his ministers."
It also states:
"After Tāng had ended the mandate of Xià,
he returned to Bó,
and composed the 'Announcement of Tāng', saying:
'Trembling with fearful caution,
as if about to fall into a deep abyss.'"
Applying the Five Conquests, changing the Three Standards
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"When Qín unified the world,
it had no time for leisure,
and also extensively applied the theory of the Five Conquests (the mutual conquest of the Five Phases).
Qín considered Zhōu to be Fire,
and Water conquers it."
"The Elder Dài's Record of Rites" states:
"The calendar standard changes thrice."
Yǔ ate coarse food, Tāng wore plain cloth
Confucius said:
"With Yǔ, I can find no fault!
He ate coarse food and drink, yet showed utmost filial piety to the spirits and gods."
"Shīzǐ" states:
"When Tāng sought to relieve the drought,
he rode in a plain carriage with white horses and wore plain cloth garments,
wearing white thatch around his neck,
offering himself as a sacrificial victim.
At that time, playing stringed instruments, singing, and dancing were prohibited."
Yáo's soup of wild greens, Shùn's parched grain
"Hánzǐ" states:
"When Yáo ruled the world,
he ate coarse grain
and soup of wild greens."
"Mèngzǐ" states:
"Shùn eating parched grain and wild herbs
seemed as if he would do so for his entire life."
Wèi's empty seat, Hàn's side-seat
"The Book of Wú" states:
"Yú Fān, styled Zhòngxiáng,
wrote a commentary on the 'Yì' of great significance.
Emperor Wén of Wèi heard of Fān's fame,
and set an empty seat awaiting him."
"The Book of the Later Hàn" states:
"I long for and think of upright scholars,
and set a side-seat for extraordinary views."
Singing of dragon scales, sighing at swan's wings
Fù Xuán's "Miscellaneous Songs from the Music Bureau" states:
"The phoenix has wings,
the dragon has scales.
A ruler does not rise alone,
he must have good ministers."
"Guǎnzǐ" states:
"When Duke Huán was at Bàn,
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng came to see him.
Suddenly two swans flew past.
The Duke sighed and said:
'I have my uncle Zhòng,
just as a flying swan has wings!'"
Obtaining six ministers, having five officials
"Guǎnzǐ" states:
"In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor obtained Chīyóu,
who understood the Way of Heaven;
he obtained Tàicháng,
who discerned the advantages of Earth;
he obtained Qīngdì,
who distinguished the East;
he obtained Zhùróng,
who distinguished the South;
he obtained Dàfēng,
who distinguished the West;
he obtained Hòutǔ,
who distinguished the North.
The Yellow Emperor obtained these six ministers and the world was transformed."
"The Analects" states:
"Shùn had five ministers and the world was well-governed."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary:
"Yǔ, Jì, Xiè, Gāo Yáo, and Bó Yì."
Having ten administrators, employing three heroes
King Wǔ said:
"I have ten administrative ministers.
'Administrative' means
to govern.
The ten governing officials are:
the Duke of Zhōu, the Duke of Shào, the Duke of ?, the Grand Duke, the Duke of Bì, the Duke of Róng, Dàdiān, Hóngyāo, Sǎnyíshēng, and Nángōng Kuò.
One of them refers to King Wén's mother."
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"Emperor Gāo said:
'For devising strategies within the command tent,
and determining victory a thousand miles away,
I am not equal to Zǐfáng;
for pacifying the state,
comforting the people,
and supplying provisions,
I am not equal to Xiāo Hé;
for commanding a million troops,
winning every battle fought,
and capturing every city attacked,
I am not equal to Hán Xìn.
These three are all heroes among men.
I was able to employ them;
this is how I gained the world.'"
Promoting from herdsmen, elevating from the ranks
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"The Emperor above desired to employ the civil and martial,
seeking them as if he could not get enough.
He began by sending a carriage with padded wheels to welcome Master Méi,
and sighed upon meeting Zhǔfù.
All scholars admired and turned towards him,
and extraordinary men emerged together.
Bǔ Shì was promoted from being a herdsman,
Sāng Hóngyáng was elevated from being a merchant."
Bān Biāo's "Discourse on the Mandate of Kings" states:
"He elevated Hán Xìn from the ranks,
and recruited Chén Píng from among the fugitives.
Heroes exerted their strength,
all strategies were fully employed.
This was Emperor Gāo's grand strategy,
by which he achieved imperial enterprise."
Creating 'Bearing Clouds', harmonizing 'Dew Regulation'
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"Emperor Zhuānxū ordered Fēilóng to compose music imitating the eight winds,
and named it 'Bearing Clouds'."
"Yuè Yè Tú Zhēng" states:
"The seasons and their nodes,
movement and stillness each have their proper duties,
and must not overstep.
They should proceed according to measure;
this is called the music of 'Dew Regulation'."
A commentary states:
"'Dew Regulation' harmonizes and brings about the music of sweet dew."
Phoenixes alight on paulownia, tortoise emerges from mushroom pond
"Hánshī Wàizhuàn" states:
"When the Yellow Emperor ascended the throne,
a phoenix came to rest in the emperor's eastern garden,
alighted on the emperor's paulownia tree,
ate the emperor's bamboo seeds,
and never left for the rest of its life."
"Wèi Lüè" states:
"During the reign of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
a divine tortoise emerged from the Língzhī Pond."
Wild geese line the road in Dōnghù; western neighbor's simple sacrifice
"Zǐsīzǐ" states:
"In the time of Dōnghù Jìzǐ,
wild geese walked in lines on the road and none picked up lost items;
after plowing and weeding, surplus grain was left overnight at the head of the fields."
"The Book of Changes" states:
"The eastern neighbor's sacrifice of an ox
is not as good as the western neighbor's simple sacrifice,
which truly receives its blessing."
Pursuit at Wūjiāng, Defeat at Chìbì
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"When King Xiàng reached Dōngchéng,
he had only twenty-eight horsemen left,
while his pursuers numbered in the thousands.
He intended to cross the Wū River to the east.
A village headman had a boat ready at the bank and waited,
saying to King Xiàng:
'Though the lands east of the river are small,
they extend a thousand *li*,
with a population of several hundred thousand,
sufficient for you to be king!
I urge Your Majesty to cross quickly.
Now, I alone have a boat.
When the Hàn army arrives,
there will be no means to cross.'
King Xiàng laughed and said:
'I, Jí, led eight thousand sons of the lands east of the river
across the river and marched west.
Now, not a single one returns.
Even if the elders east of the river took pity and made me their king,
what face would I have to see them?
Even if they said nothing,
would I, Jí, feel no shame in my heart?'"
The Records of the Three Kingdoms: Book of Shǔ states:
"Lord Cáo campaigned south against Liú Biǎo.
Leading five thousand elite cavalry,
he urgently pursued the Late Sovereign.
He caught up at Chángbǎn of Dāngyáng.
The Late Sovereign fled to Xiàkǒu
and sent Zhūgě Liàng to forge an alliance with Sūn Quán.
They fought Lord Cáo at Chìbì
and inflicted a great defeat upon him,
King Wǔ of Zhōu Wielded the Axe; Emperor Gāo of Hàn Raised the Sword
The Book of Documents states:
"King Wǔ fought with Shòu at Mùyě.
At daybreak on the jiǎzǐ day,
the king arrived at the outskirts of the Shāng capital.
In his left hand he wielded a yellow axe,
in his right he held a white yak-tail banner,
with which he gave the signal."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"When Emperor Gāo attacked Yīng Bù,
he was hit by a stray arrow
and fell ill.
Empress Lǚ summoned an excellent physician.
When the physician entered,
Emperor Gāo berated him, saying:
'I, a commoner,
raised a three-foot sword and won the empire.
Was this not the Mandate of Heaven?
Fate lies with Heaven.
What use would even a Biǎn Què be?'"
Apology at Hóngmén; Defeat at Chǐ River
The Book of Hàn states:
"When Xiàng Yǔ reached the Hángǔ Pass,
there were troops guarding it,
and he could not enter.
Hearing that the Lord of Pèi had already sacked Xiányáng,
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly enraged
and sent Dāngyáng Jūn, Yīng, to attack the pass.
Xiàng Yǔ then entered
and reached Hóngmén west of Xì.
The next day,
the Lord of Pèi, accompanied by over a hundred horsemen, came to Hóngmén to apologize to Xiàng Yǔ,
explaining himself:
'I sealed up the treasuries and storehouses of Qín
and withdrew the army to Bàshàng to await Your Majesty.
I closed the passes to guard against other bandits.
I dare not betray your virtue.'"
The Book of Later Hàn states:
"Wáng Mǎng sent Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì to lead a million troops to besiege Kūnyáng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ then led three thousand daring warriors to charge their central stronghold,
and succeeded in killing Wáng Xún.
Wáng Mǎng's troops were utterly defeated,
those fleeing trampling over each other.
They fled over a hundred *li*,
when suddenly a great storm with thunder arose.
Roof tiles flew everywhere,
rain poured down like a deluge,
and the Chǐ River swelled to overflowing.
The soldiers struggled to cross,
tens of thousands drowned,
The Zhōu Officials Were Like the Yù and Pò; The Shāng Minister Was Like Salt and Plum
The Máo Odes states:
"The 'Yù Pò'
is about King Wén's ability to appoint men to office.
Lush are the yù and pò trees,
gathered as firewood, piled for burning."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"Lush
means the trees are abundant.
Yù is the white ruǐ.
When the mountain trees are luxuriant,
the myriad people can gather them for firewood.
This metaphorically means when worthy men are numerous,
the state obtains and uses them to flourish and prosper."
The Book of Documents states:
"Emperor Gāozōng dreamed of Fù Yuè,
then established him as minister.
The king placed him at his left and right
and commanded him, saying:
'If I am metal, I use you as a whetstone;
if I cross a great river,
I use you as boat and oar;
if I make sweet wine,
you are the yeast and malt;
if I make a harmonious soup,
you are the salt and plum;
if the year sees great drought,
I use you as the soaking rain.'"
Eight Movements of Gětiān; Nine Completions of Emperor Yú
The Annals of Lǚ Buwei states:
"In ancient times, the music of Gětiān Shì
had three men holding ox tails,
stamping their feet and singing eight movements."
Gāo Yòu's commentary states:
"Gětiān Shì
is the name of an ancient sovereign.
Stamping feet means tapping the feet.
A movement is a finale."
The Book of Documents states:
"When the Sháo music with pipes reached its ninth completion,
the phoenixes came to posture."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Sháo
is the name of Shùn's music."
The Annals of Emperors and Kings states:
"Emperor Shùn was Yǒuyú Shì."
Xuānyuán's Kuí Drum; The Hàn Emperor's Luán Banner
Huángfǔ Mì's Annals of Emperors and Kings states:
"Huángdì, at Liúbō Mountain in the Eastern Sea,
obtained a strange beast,
shaped like an ox.
Blue-bodied and hornless, it could run.
When it entered or left the water, wind and rain arose.
Its light was like the sun and moon,
its voice like thunder.
Its name was Kuí.
Huángdì killed it
and made a drum from its skin,
whose sound could be heard for five hundred *li*."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Huángdì was called Xuānyuán Shì."
The Book of Hàn states:
"During Emperor Wén's time,
someone presented a thousand-*li* horse.
The emperor issued an edict, saying:
'With the luán banners ahead
and the accompanying carriages behind,
on auspicious days we travel fifty *li*.
Where would the horse go ahead alone?'
Thereupon, he returned the horse
and gave the travel expenses for the journey."
Cornered at Lánchí; Traveling Incognito to Bǎigǔ
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The First Emperor traveled incognito
with four warriors.
Going out at night, they encountered robbers at Lánchí
and were cornered.
The warriors struck and killed the robbers."
The Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
"The Emperor once dressed lightly and traveled incognito.
Reaching Bǎigǔ,
he sought lodging from the village headman at night but was not admitted,
so he stayed at an inn."
The Chariot Emerged; The Pearl Was Spat
The Imperial Mandate Prognostication of the Book of Documents states:
"Southeastern brilliance poured down, essence recorded,
the Chang light emerged from the Chariot, already mapped."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"This refers to the Liú clan.
It means the fire essence should arise in the region of the Wings and Chariot."
The Divine Revolution of the Book of Documents states:
"The Hé River Chart's son arose in time, the land remained,
the red was used and stored,
the dragon spat a pearl."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The Hé River Chart's son is the Liú clan, which arose.
The pearl
is a precious object,
metaphor for the Way.
The red Hàn should use Heaven's secret Way,
therefore the river dragon spat it out."
Insult People in Lèpèi
“Hànshū”:
“Wáng Líng said:
'Your Majesty is arrogant and insults people,
Xiàng Yǔ is benevolent and loves people.'” Also said:
“Gāozǔ said:
'Even though I later ruled Cháng’ān,
my soul still longs for Lèpèi.'”
Xiàng Zǐyīng Yields, Yōngchǐ is Enfeoffed
“Shǐjì” says:
“In the first year of Hàn, in October,
Lord of Pèi's forces reached Bàshàng before the other lords,
Qín King Xiàng Zǐyīng yielded at Zhǐdào.”
“Hànshū” states:
“Gāozǔ at the Wèiyāng Palace,
saw the generals whispering in the sand,
thus first enfeoffed Yōngchǐ.
Everyone rejoiced and said:
'Since Yōngchǐ is enfeoffed as marquis,
we have no worries!'”
Greedy for Wealth, Rises from Commoner
“Shǐjì” states:
“Fàn Zēng advised Xiàng Yǔ, saying:
'The Duke of Pèi living in Shāndōng,
is greedy for wealth.
Now entering Guānzhōng,
he takes nothing,
his ambitions are not small,
attack quickly, do not let him escape.'” “Xún Yuèjì” says:
“Gāozǔ rose from commoner status,
seized the world with his sword.”
Commands Ten Thousand Courts, Travels Five Stars
“Hétú” says:
“Gāo Huáng adjusts the alignment, commands ten thousand courts,
four seas return singing the logic of power and clarity,
the virtues of culture and the Dao accept the essence of heaven.”
“Xījīng Fù” says:
“When Gāozǔ first entered,
the five stars aligned,
to station at Dōngjǐng.”
Hides in Máng Zé, Works in Xiányáng
“Emperors' Centuries” says:
“When Gāozǔ was Magistrate of Sìshuǐ,
escorted sent prisoners to Líshān.
Many prisoners escaped along the way,
considering that they might all escape,
he stopped to drink in the marshes west of Fēng.
At night he released the prisoners,
Gāozǔ doubted himself and hid in the marshes and rocks of Mángzhàng.”
“Shǐjì” says:
“Gāozǔ often worked in Xiányáng,
observed the First Emperor of Qín,
sighed deeply and remarked:
'Alas!
A great man should be like this.'”
Red Geese, White Qilin
“Hànshū” says:
“Emperor Xiàowǔ on tour in the Eastern Sea,
caught a red goose,
composed the Song of the Red Goose.”
Also says:
“Wǔdì inspected Yōng,
sacrificed at the five shrines,
caught a white qilin,
and composed the Song of the White Qilin.”
Mushroom Hall, Gourd Song
“Hànshū” states:
“In the second year of the Yuánfēng era, the edict said:
'Inside the Palace of Gānquán,
nine stalks of mushrooms grew,
with connected leaves,
the Song of the Mushroom Hall was composed.'” Also states:
“During Wǔdì's eastern tour of the sea,
returned in April,
sacrificed at Mount Tāi.
At the Gourd Song Dam,
ordered all from generals down to carry firewood to block the river embankment,
composed the Song of the Gourd.”
Shèng Táng, Hāolǐ
“Hànshū” states:
“In the fifth year of Yuánfēng,
the emperor toured south to Shèng Táng.
Again in the fifth year of Yuánshòu,
sacrificed at Hāolǐ.”
A note says:
“Hāolǐ,
the name of a mountain.”
Jia Tent, Jiāo Gate
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn erected nine rooms in the shrine,
with glass beads and jade like the bright moon at night,
various precious treasures from across the land as Jia tents,
with the next as Yi tents.
Jia to house the gods,
Yi upwards to be personally used by him.
“Hànshū” says:
“In the fourth year of Yuánfēng,
fortunately at Buqí,
sacrificed to spirits at Jiāo gate palace,
like someone sat and worshipped there.
Composed the Song of the Jiāo Gate.”
Through Míngzé, Across the Fén River
“Hànshū” says:
“In the fourth year of Yuánfēng,
travelled north through Xiāoguān,
through Lùmíngzé.”
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's “Song of the Autumn Wind” says:
“Set sail with towers of boats across the Fén River.
In the middle of the stream, raise the white waves.
Flutes and drums sound as paddlers sing.
When joy is at its height, emotions of sadness abound.
How brief the time of youth, what to do about age.”
Exit Bamboo Palace, Born Orchid Hall
“Hàn Rituals” states:
“At Táizhì,
the emperor exits the Bamboo Palace at dawn,
bowing to the east towards the sun,
in the evening bows west towards the moon.”
“The Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn” states:
“In the year of Yǐyǒu on the seventh day of the seventh month, born at Yīlán Hall.”
Second to Saints in Mind, Mind Like God
Zhāng Yǎn's “Silent Record” says:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, of talents second only to saints,
possessing literary and military strategies,
intelligent and benevolent,
emerged at the appointed time.”
Xuē Yíng's “Hàn Record” says:
“Guāngwǔ was tolerant and accommodating,
his calculations were godlike.
Thus he appointed Rèn Guāng and Dòu Róng,
who followed with wind and joined like shadows.”
Serve at Golden Mirrors, Strike Bronze Horses
“Hòu Hànshū” says:
“Infinite Empress Yīn's name was Lìhuá,
from Xīnyè of Nányáng.
Guāngwǔ visited Xīnyè,
heard of her beauty,
and was pleased at heart.
Later in Cháng'ān,
saw the grand parade of the Gold and Silver guards,
and sighed:
'In office, one should be a Gold and Silver guard,
to marry one should wed Yīn Lìhuá.'” “Eastern Han Records” states:
“During the reign of Gèng Shǐ, when he stood for King Xiāo,
struck the Bronze Horse,
and greatly defeated it,
thus accepted the surrender.”
Killed Wáng Xún, Captured Zhāng Bù
“Hòu Hànshū” states:
“In the first year of Gèng Shǐ,
Wáng Mǎng sent Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì with an army of a million,
with banners and supply trains,
stretching a thousand li without end,
besieging Kūnyáng City tens of times over.
Guāngwǔ, leading three thousand death-defying soldiers from the west of the city by water,
charged the center.
Xún and Yì's formation fell into chaos,
thus Wáng Xún was killed,
Mǎng's forces were utterly routed.”
Zhāng Yǎn's “Silent Record” says:
“Hàn Guāngwǔ's restoration,
defeated the Red Eyebrows,
captured Zhāng Bù and the followers of Wèi Xiāo.
The group's villains were eradicated,
and Huáxià was thoroughly cleansed.”
Northern Division, Western Ling
“Wèi Zhì” says:
“Tàizǔ Wǔdì,
at twenty, was elected a filial and honest man as a court officer.
Appointed as the officer of the Northern Division of Luòyáng,
Wèi Wǔdì sent an order:
‘My concubines and entertainers,
all reside at Copper Sparrow Tower,
on the platform set up six-foot beds with gauze curtains,
provide dried meat and snacks morning and evening.
On the 15th of every month,
prepare to enjoy music towards the curtains.
At times ascend Copper Sparrow Tower,
observe my tomb and field at Xīlíng,
do not miss this duty.'”
Striking the Dragon, Shooting the Pheasants
"Biography of Young Heroes" states:
"Tàizǔ was wise and brave from a young age.
At the age of ten,
he once bathed in Qiáo River,
and a dragon approached.
He emerged from the water and struck,
so the dragon retreated.
He finished his bath and returned,
without speaking of it."
"Book of Wei" states:
"Tàizǔ shot pheasants in Nánpí one day,
capturing thirty-six."
The Plum Forest and Wild Kudzu
"Records of Liú Yìqìng" says:
"Wèi Wǔdì was leading troops and lost the way.
The entire army was thirsty.
The Emperor said,
'Ahead lies a great plum forest,
its fruits sweet and sour,
which can quench our thirst.'
Hearing this, the soldiers salivated,
and thus they were able to reach the source ahead."
Zhāng Huá's "Records of Diverse Matters" states:
"Tàizǔ was accustomed to eating wild kudzu.
When it reached one foot,
he also drank poison wine sparingly."
Repairing the River, Building Luo
"Records of Wei" states:
"In the sixth year of Huángchū,
the Emperor with the naval forces entered Huái from Qiáo repairing the river,
taking the overland route to reach Xuzhou,
and built the Eastern Patrol Tower.
At the old city of Guǎnglíng,
he inspected troops by the river."
It further says:
"In the first year of Huángchū, December,
the Emperor first built the palace at Luoyang.
On the day Wùwǔ, he visited Luoyang."
Reading with a Whip, Striking the Melon
Wèi Wéndì's "Preface to Línwōfu" states:
"In the year Jiàn'ān eighteen, he arrived at Qiáo,
my brothers and I followed,
where he paid respects at the graves.
We rode on horseback to view,
passed through the Eastern Garden,
and followed the Wo River.
Under a tall tree, we stopped, read with a whip,
and composed Línwōfu."
Wèi Wéndì in "Autobiographical Notes" says:
"In my youth, I learned swordplay,
drinking with General Liú Xūn, who calmed the rebels, and Fènwēi Liú Zhǎn among others.
I heard that Zhǎn could confront blades barehanded.
We discoursed on swordsmanship,
and I critiqued the general's methods.
Since I had an interest,
and possessed some skill,
I was challenged.
At that time, a bit tipsy,
while eating sugarcane,
I used it as a staff.
Descending from the hall,
we exchanged several blows,
thrice hitting his arm."
Golden Chariot, Sacred Cauldron
"Records of Wu" states:
"At the beginning of the Xīngpíng period,
there was a children's rhyme in Wú:
'Golden chariot,
decorated with patterns.
Open the Chāng Gate,
out goes the emperor.'"
The Chāng Gate,
is the western gate of Wú,
where Fūchāi was born."
"Records of Wu" says:
"In the twelfth year of Chìwū,
a jade cauldron appeared in Línpíng Lake."
Settling Wǔchāng, Moving to Jiànyè
"Records of Wu" states:
"In the second year of Huángchū,
Sūn Quán moved the capital from An Provincial to È,
renaming it Wǔchāng."
It also states:
"In the first year of Huángwǔ, April,
he performed sacrifices at the southern altar,
claimed the imperial title,
and moved the capital to Jiànyè."
Holding the Reins, Receiving Arrows, and Turning the Boat
Yú Pǔ's "Records of the Jiang Province" states:
"Sūn Quán attacked Héféi,
but was ambushed by Zhāng Liáo.
Riding a startled horse across the Jīn Bridge south,
he saw Chè Gúlì pursuing behind.
Quán held the bridle and loosened the reins wielding the whip,
and managed to leap across the water."
Yú Hùan's "Records of Wei" states:
"Sūn Quán, aboard a large ship to inspect the army,
was met with a barrage of arrows from Cáo's archers.
The ship became heavy and was about to capsize.
Quán turned the ship,
taking arrows on its lighter side.
The balance restored,
they sailed away."
Wide Mouth, Square Jaw, Upper Long, Lower Short
Yú Pǔ's "Records of the Jiang Province" states:
"When Sūn Jiān was the magistrate of Xiàpī,
Quán was born.
He had a square jaw and wide mouth,
with eyes that shone bright."
"Spring and Autumn Annals of the Han Emperor" states:
"Zhāng Liáo asked a surrendered man from Wú:
'The bearded general,
long upper body, short lower limbs,
who is that?'
He replied:
'That is Sūn Huìjī.' "
Alliance with Wu, Serving Han
"Records of Shǔ" states:
"The Former Lord sent Zhūgě Liàng to make an alliance with Sūn Quán."
"Huáyáng Countries Annals" states:
"At the end of the Han, many heroes rose,
the Former Lord was of humble beginnings,
started anew to serve the Han,
and stood alongside them."
Abandoning Family, Losing Utensils
"Records of Shǔ" states:
"Cáo Gōng dispatched elite cavalry to pursue the Former Lord at Chángbǎn of Dāngyáng.
The Former Lord abandoned his family,
and fled with a few dozen riders."
It also says:
"Cáo Gōng said to the Former Lord:
'In this world, only you and I are true heroes!
The likes of Yuán Běnchū,
are of no account!'
While the Former Lord was eating,
he dropped his utensils."
Pruning the Fine Orchid, Riding the Feathered Canopy
"Records of Shǔ" states:
"The Former Lord sought to execute Zhāng Yù,
Zhūgě Liàng pleaded guilty,
the Former Lord said:
'The fine orchid blocks the path,
it must be pruned.'
Further, it states:
"At the southeast corner of his dwelling,
there was a mulberry tree,
thick and lush like a small carriage cover.
In his youth,
the Former Lord played with his clan,
saying, 'I will ride in a carriage with this feathered canopy.'"
Possessing Extraordinary Character, Engaging in Great Plans
Gàn Bǎo's "Search for the Supernatural" states:
"The Gaozu Emperor Xuán had extraordinary character from a young age,
intelligent and full of grand strategies."
It also states:
"Xuán Emperor was promoted to middle scribe of the crown prince.
In great plans,
his counsel was often excellent,
and thus he was trusted and valued by the crown prince."
Conquering Gōngsūn, Welcoming the Wei Emperor
"Book of Jìn" by Zāng Róngxù states:
"Tàishǒu Gōngsūn Wényì in Liáodōng rebelled.
An imperial edict commanded Xuán Emperor to suppress him.
He mobilized from the eastern capital,
passing through Wèi Wēn,
ordering all prefects to gather at his encampment.
He feasted with elder statesmen and old friends for several days."
"Book of Jìn" by Wáng Yǐn states:
"The Emperor of Wèi paid homage at Gāopíng Mausoleum,
accompanied by Cáo Shuǎng and his brothers.
Gaozu, seeing the unfair governance by Shuǎng,
deposed him.
He reported matters at Yongning Palace,
mobilized the city troops and remaining forces.
He commanded the arsenal,
opened the four gates,
and went to welcome the Emperor of Wèi at Luòbīn,
bringing charges against Shuǎng."
Promoted to Palace Attendant, Enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔyáng
Gān Bǎo's "Jìn Jì" states:
"After the State of Wei was established,
Emperor Gāozǔ was promoted to Palace Attendant of the Heir Apparent,
and together with Chén Qún, Wú Zhì, and Zhū Shuò,
they were called the Four Friends."
It also states:
"When the Son of Heaven was critically ill,
the Emperor, along with Cáo Zhēn, Chén Qún, and others, met in the Southern Hall of the Chónghuá Palace,
and together received the final edict to assist in governance.
The edict to the Crown Prince stated:
'Should there be any slander against these three dukes,
take care not to doubt them.'
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔyáng."
His Grace Extended to the Southern Lands, Yet He Ultimately Remained a Subject
Zāng Róngxù's "Jìn Shū" states:
"As reports of victories from various generals in Liáodōng arrived one after another,
he reiterated the previous command, saying:
'Personally donning armor,
I reverently carry out Heaven's punishment.
Sweeping clean the region,
I display might in Wú and Kuàijī.
Assisting the imperial majesty,
his grace is extended to the southern lands.'"
Lù Shìhéng's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Emperor Wén's power was elevated above the threefold division,
yet he ultimately remained a subject.
Though it is said he had no leisure,
the royal enterprise was already secure."
Loyal and Forbearing Without Errant Words, Benevolent and Kind with Wisdom and Magnanimity
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Emperor Wǔ displayed noble conduct from a young age,
acting with loyalty and forbearance even in haste,
never uttering improper words or showing a change of countenance toward others."
It also states:
"Emperor Wǔ was generous, kind, benevolent, and tolerant,
profoundly reserved and possessing wisdom and magnanimity."
Reducing Meals, Burning a Fur Robe
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"In the third month of the seventh year of the Tàishǐ era of Emperor Wǔ,
an edict was issued for the imperial kitchen to reduce meals."
It also states:
"When someone presented a pheasant-head fur robe,
the Emperor said:
'Unusual garments and extraordinary furs
are prohibited by the statutes and regulations.'
He then burned the robe in the front hall,
and ordered that those wearing unusual garments be punished according to ritual."
Wei Abdication, Pacification of Wu
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"In the second year of Xiánxī,
Wei abdicated the throne to His Majesty."
Zāng Róngxù's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Emperor Wǔ asked Liú Yì:
'To which Han emperor would you compare me?'
He replied:
'You could be compared to Emperors Huán and Líng.'
The Emperor said:
'Though my virtue does not match that of the ancients,
I still restrain myself in governance.
Moreover, I have pacified Wú and Kuàijī,
unifying the realm under one rule.
To compare me to Huán and Líng,
is that not excessive?'"
Yán Shīgǔ's "Ode to Sagely Virtue"
Gazing back to distant ages,
Examining the records of the past in detail.
The alternation of the Five Phases between substance and refinement,
The evolution of the Three Correct Beginnings.
Chaos abundant, transformation scarce,
Clarity few, obscurity accumulated.
The fiery essence already fallen,
The great cycle thus broken.
Vast is all under heaven,
Darkened as if dusk had come.
Great is the sage emperor,
Who receives the heavenly mandate.
Like clouds soaring over the nine regions,
Like lightning striking the eight directions.
Gònggōng's wickedness perished,
The evil of Zhuōlù was eradicated.
The harmful branches thus cleared,
The baleful stars left no trace.
Establishing martial power, sheathing the blades,
Ceasing warfare, smearing the chariots.
Abolishing harsh laws, reducing severity,
Seeking out grievances, comforting the hidden.
The zither and lute restrung,
Bridles and whips all laid aside.
The hall full of joy,
Yet songs of praise still linger.
Fanning the heat-stricken, bestowing benevolence,
Weeping for the guilty, flowing with compassion.
Officials encouraged to be upright and pure,
The people return to honesty and diligence.
Reverent and respectful in sacrificial rites,
Devotedly serving Heaven above.
Forever filial in offerings,
Fully prepared with pure sacrifices.
Externally honoring the elderly,
Internally harmonizing with kin and in-laws.
Yearly gifts of silk and floss,
Seasonal offerings of sweet wine and thick gruel.
Widows and orphans are cared for,
The sick and ailing are healed.
Village gates left open,
Horses and cattle kept in inner stables.
Fields exchanged among farmers,
Broad roads shared with mutual deference.
No need for war drums,
No worry of border posts.
Tribute received from the Jiāo people,
Northern tribes submit at Lángwàng.
Utmost sincerity moves to celebration,
Auspicious energies bring forth blessings.
A tame one-horned beast,
Gatherings of five-colored phoenixes.
Huápíng trees stand tall,
Vermilion grass shines fragrant.
Fine plowshares work diligently,
Abundant rice grows lushly.
State reserves reach billions of measures,
Households fill ten thousand chests.
Those outstanding talents,
Entrusted with loyal service.
Their hearts and strengths illuminated,
They reside among the high ministers.
As level as a whetstone,
As straight as an arrow.
Careful in minor duties,
Keen in rules and standards.
Luxuriant is the artemisia,
Flourishing are those oak trees.
Cultivating demeanor in the ritual court,
Soaring in the garden of books.
Discussing the extremes of the Five Interactions,
Delighting in admiration of the Three Antiquity.
Profound and subtle are the caverns of meaning,
Vast and expansive the halls of learning.
Confucians and Mohists both presented,
Shēn and Hán alternately dismissed.
Why rely on Bó Liàng?
What need for Fēng Jù?
Virtuous words lofty and clear,
Silken edicts shining far and wide.
The "Yellow Bamboo" in beautiful verses,
The "Bǎiliáng" in pure strains.
Profound and serene, elegant and refined,
Fluid and penetrating, sharp and swift.
Drawing out and expanding incomplete texts,
Gathering and compiling lost rhymes.
Who can enter the inner chamber?
Few glimpse beyond the wall.
A wondrous mind thoroughly penetrating,
A divine brush truly compliant.
Majestic and rugged, new in force,
Vigorous and spirited, wondrous in edge.
Like jade tablets, graceful and delicate,
Like mist dispersing, smoke thickening.
Towering as a crane standing on tiptoe,
Lush as a dragon poised.
Not only surpassing Zhào,
Truly exceeding Zhōng.
The Way bestowed by Heaven,
Arts combined with human skill.
Used yet unknown,
Swift yet not hurried.
Supreme virtue has no form,
Subtle words rarely expressed.
Jade-like in the Cassia Palace,
Golden planted in the Orchid Chamber.
Ritual utmost in reverence and love,
Conduct returning to loyalty and unity.
All under heaven civilized and enlightened,
Sun and moon steadfastly observed.
Hundreds of spirits receive their duties,
The Three Potencies harmoniously assist.
The Three Steps already level,
Splendor constantly radiant.
Transcending Xuān, surpassing Hào,
Surpassing Zhōu, excelling Hàn.
Ten thousand years without bound,
Eternally extending the distant calculation.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Ode to Imperial Virtue"
I have heard that the sage aligns his virtue with heaven and earth,
and matches his brilliance with the sun and moon.
He contains and exhales the energies of yīn and yáng,
and subdues the essence of mountains and rivers.
He nurtures the myriad things with flourishing growth,
and unifies the One to achieve constancy.
Thus did our sovereign receive the bright mandate,
and greatly preserve his vast renown.
It also says:
"Only the great Táng rules alone,
surpassing the fame of all past ages.
It refines the five energies beneath the round canopy,
and extends the four poles across the square earth.
It settled the strife of contending heroes,
and rescued the drowning from widespread calamity.
During the decline of fiery virtue's rule,
when imperial virtue was corrupted and failing,
heaven sent down calamities from above,
and wanton roars filled the Middle Kingdom.
None, great or small,
but schemed to be emperor or king.
Common men and women alike
became pests and thieves.
All under heaven were abandoned,
even fellow travelers turned to evil.
That tyrant indulged his will,
how he muddied the classics and disrupted norms!
He truly opposed the Way and destroyed virtue,
indeed, heedless, he acted with madness.
First he incurred the people's hatred,
in the end he cut himself off from heaven.
All eight directions and nine regions,
mountains crumbled and rivers dried.
Heaven's axis was about to turn,
earth's cords were near to snapping.
Literature and refinement were swept away,
the Odes and Elegantiae were lost.
Loyal and good men were burned,
caps and coronets all shattered alike.
Some flooded heaven and shifted blame,
some struck mountains and wrought disaster.
The Yin realm sank into ruin,
the Han roads ran with blood.
Heaven bestowed divine martiality,
the auspicious charge fell to the Supreme Sovereign.
From Báishuǐ the dragon soared,
from Sānxū the phoenix took flight.
Midway he listened to petitions,
and would march again to cut down Shāng.
Only his divine foresight worked alone,
then he spread his wings and soared high.
He commanded the grey rhinoceros at the river bend,
slew the black dragon and aided Jìfāng.
Pointing to Mùyě he made the great oath,
at Míngtiáo he taught the arrogant their fall."
It also says:
"Only sagely virtue embraces the distant,
spreading constant principles to the farthest deserts.
Even the barren-haired were fully capped,
those left-lapped all had their collars trimmed.
Border posts stood empty of alarms,
guarding beyond the great wilderness.
All perilous terrain was leveled,
surpassing the central plains' ease.
They gathered for tribute at assembly points,
from the farthest reaches they offered treasures.
Presenting fur robes they pledged allegiance,
awaiting favorable winds across seas they turned their hearts.
Throughout the eight wilds all followed,
through ninefold translations they sought audience.
Mimicking suānní in the Valley of Darkness,
hanging divine shields in the Dèng Forest.
Dancing in step to Xiánchí's music,
wandering the upper park they cherished the sounds.
Exhausting precious goods they all vied,
emptying sincere hearts they fully offered.
At times ringing bells in viewing towers,
at times roaming forest preserves.
Writings manifest benevolence and righteousness,
sounds harmonize with pitch pipes.
Divine sparrows descend at the Emperor's Terrace,
sweet springs guided to divine islets.
Turtle texts and dragon caskets,
the Hé and Luò will be toured.
Eastern flounders and western jiān birds,
at Yúntíng they stand waiting.
Other treasures hidden in mountains and secret marshes,
companions who grasp substance and reject emptiness.
All accord with records on charts and registers,
hardly can they be fully named and ordered."
It also says:
"In past ages, Tiānlíng's eighty thousand years,
the thirty-six kings of Jī Zhōu,
their allotted spans were but trifling,
truly insufficient for praise.
Only our sacred dynasty's destined fortune,
matches the Lord-on-High's flourishing assembly.
Your servant bows and touches head to ground,
offering boundless fortune and longevity.
Aiding divined years and divined reigns,
sharing earth's endurance and heaven's length."
"Ode to Táng Tàizōng"
At creation's dawn,
human relations arose.
Then rulers were established,
to shepherd the black-haired masses.
Beginning from hexagram lines,
they replaced knotted cords.
Xuānyuán and Hàoxū having passed,
Táng and Yú rose in turn.
Later, Suí's virtue declined,
according with the times, the mandate changed.
At the end of the three decayed eras,
spears and shields were contested.
Resplendent, divine and martial,
he met the time and became sage.
Below encompassing the nine regions,
above aligning the seven regulators.
His achievements unite civil and martial,
his merit surpasses Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ.
What peril did he not cross?
What trouble did he not quell?
Men and women all rejoiced,
presenting dark and yellow silks in baskets.
These things arriving,
shone upon our king.
Our king nurtures and rears,
sustaining life, embracing creation.
Matching Yáo, ascending to Táng,
like Zhōu at Hào.
Receiving and spreading widely,
clear proof of settled security.
Truly practicing his virtue,
he purifies the imperial Way.
The imperial Way reverent and bright,
all under heaven peaceful.
The three seasons unharmed,
the hundred grains thus ripen.
Our granaries thus amassed,
like mounds, like hillocks.
Once enriched, then taught,
disputes cease, punishments clear.
Brilliant Son of Heaven,
his fair fame unceasing.
The common people as his heart,
all regions within himself.
Homes rely on lenient governance,
court praised for many talents.
Unifying Huá and Róng,
mixing script and axle-track.
Eastern pool the vast sea,
western park the Yúqiū heights.
Eight Mán bring tribute,
six Dí cherish kindness.
Supreme virtue silently permeates,
mysterious transformation spreads widely.
Each day more cautious,
though praised, not resting.
Not opposing heaven's prior will,
numinous creatures offer substance.
Red-feathered ones mark the Sháo music,
green-yellow ones bear the bridle.
Sweet dew falls on grass,
auspicious winds answer the pitch pipes.
Fine grain and sweet springs,
appear side by side.
Portents and signs appear, brightening charts and writings,
altars and grounds prepared, gazing for the imperial carriage.
The perfect man forgets self, embodying emptiness,
concentrating spirit at Gūshè, weary of the palace.
Weary of the palace,
in accord with dark union,
the dragon carriage ascends, far departing.
Leaving dark models to shine on future generations,
with dark images ever clearly visible.
His flying glorious fame surpasses the Three Dynasties,
eternally bestowing blessings for myriads of generations.
Táng Ruìzōng's "Eulogy for Hàn Gāozǔ"
Heaven creates in primal chaos,
heroic plans entangled.
Resplendent Hàn ancestor,
responding like rising clouds.
On Qín plains the deer was lost,
at Pèi marsh the snake divided.
Once the great wind arose,
facing south he called himself lord.
Also "Eulogy for Jìn Xuāndì"
Zhòngdá suspicious and jealous,
wolf-like in his glances as a man.
Feigning illness, deluded and mistaken,
form and spirit not intimate.
Xīn Pí held the tally,
Shǔ general bestowed a kerchief.
He pledged allegiance facing north,
in the end remained a Wèi minister.
Also, "In Praise of Emperor Wu of Liáng"
Reflecting on Emperor Wu of Liáng,
who held the supreme throne as the Son of Heaven.
Why did he humble himself
and immerse in the Buddhist faith?
Disasters arose from the Buddhist temples,
and troops besieged the imperial gates.
In the end, he met with violent misfortune—
how can one speak of the Way of Heaven?
Jìn Dynasty Zhì Yú's "In Praise of Páo Xī"
In ancient times of high antiquity,
only virtue determined one's position.
Páo Xī became king,
and the world esteemed purity and excellence.
He established the trigrams and divided the symbols,
opening up things and recording categories.
Setting out nets and traps,
people's needs were never lacking.
Jìn Dynasty Wáng Biāozhī's "In Praise of Fú Xī"
Vast and remote, the August Fú Xī,
his body tranquil, his spirit clear.
Through non-action, he transformed,
emerging from the coagulation of the Way.
Unaware of his own existence,
dark influences naturally arose.
Following the traces of response,
he drew images and knotted ropes.
Zhì Yú's "In Praise of Shénnóng"
Shénnóng lived in the world,
comprehending change and encompassing the ultimate.
When the people were many and beasts few,
he taught them farming and harvest.
Goods were gathered and exchanged in markets,
trees and grasses were sown and planted.
He focused on aiding their foundation,
not on adorning superficialities.
Jìn Dynasty Cáo Pí's "In Praise of Huángdì"
Xuānyuán responded to the dark epoch,
in youth able to command all spirits.
His body refined, the wonders of the five numina,
his breath imbued with the essence of cloud and dew.
He gathered stones from the layered city's peaks,
and cast the tripods by the shores of Jīng Lake.
Suddenly, the heavenly gates swung open,
and lightly he mounted, soaring on scaled steeds.
With reins and carriage, he swept through the long winds,
lifting his robes to tread the Purple Palace.
Zhì Yú's "In Praise of Huángdì"
Huángdì on the throne,
was truly named Xuānyuán.
Carts for traveling on land,
boats for crossing rivers.
The advantage of bow and arrow
quelled calamities and dissolved troubles.
Governing with robes hanging idle,
all states found peace and righteousness.
"In Praise of Táng Yáo"
The Táng Emperor Fàngxūn,
reverent, enlightened, cultured, and thoughtful.
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself upon it.
Lofty and vast,
all nations were harmonious and bright.
"In Praise of Xià Yǔ"
Breaching dikes and dredging rivers,
clearing mountains and spreading earth.
The four corners were settled,
and constant principles were set in order.
Humble palaces and simple fare
brought peace to the realm.
"In Praise of Yīn Tāng"
Wise indeed was the Shāng,
and truly so was Chéng Tāng.
The Three and Five rose in succession,
abandoning the title of "Thearch" to be called "King."
"In Praise of Zhōu Wénwáng"
Zhōu Wénwáng, reverent and cautious,
exemplified ritual and embodied teaching.
The Lord on High oversaw him,
and spirits and gods toiled for him.
The benighted neighbor to the east,
the shining neighbor to the west.
The nine regions once gathered,
he replaced tyranny with sageliness.
"In Praise of Zhōu Wǔwáng"
O august Wǔwáng,
Heaven's Mandate was concentrated in him.
The seven virtues now radiant,
none failed to follow and submit.
Swiftly he cleansed the cosmos,
sweeping away the traces of Shāng.
"In Praise of Zhōu Xuānwáng"
Xuānwáng inherited decline,
the state and house faced many obstacles.
Chastened by hardship, he pondered governance,
appointing officials in proper order.
Shānfǔ mended shortcomings,
Fāngshū repelled insults.
Thus was the Restoration achieved,
recovering the realm of Zhōu.
"In Praise of Hàn Gāozǔ"
Hàn Gāozǔ was wise and perceptive,
combining consultation with authority and might.
He commanded all the heroes,
cutting down and subduing the powerful Chǔ.
Swiftly he rectified Huáxià,
planning and managing the realm.
Thus he ascended the Heavenly throne,
continuing the legacy of Yáo.
"In Praise of Hàn Huìdì"
Xiàohuìdì cultivated kinship internally,
and externally honored the chancellor with ritual.
He generously favored Qí Dào and Zhào Yǐn,
his kindness and respect were profound.
Hearing Shūsūntōng's remonstrance,
his countenance became startled.
Accepting Chancellor Cáo's reply,
his heart was greatly pleased.
He may be called a broad-minded and benevolent ruler.
Meeting with Empress Dowager Lǚ,
his utmost virtue was impaired—
alas, how sorrowful!
"In Praise of Hàn Wéndì"
The flourishing greatness of Hàn
truly lay in Xiàowéndì.
Embracing benevolence and esteeming frugality,
he mastered himself to serve as ruler.
Reining in at Xìliǔ,
he humbled his dignity to complete the army.
He planned his tomb on the southern plain,
and his mound was not raised high.
Hànshū ‧ "Account of Gāozǔ"
August indeed was Hàn Gāozǔ,
continuing the legacy of Yáo.
Truly Heaven endowed him with virtue,
intelligent, divine, and mighty.
The Qín people lacked order,
their net let slip the Chǔ.
From this, he rose to prominence,
cutting the snake and rousing his troops.
The divine mother revealed the portent,
and the vermilion banner was raised.
He then trod upon Qín's suburbs,
and Yīng came bowing in submission.
Revolutionizing and establishing institutions,
the Three Articles were his rule.
"Account of Wéndì"
Great Ancestor, solemn and grave,
truly reverent, profound, and silent.
Transforming the people by his own person,
leading those below with virtue.
My teaching like the wind,
the people's response like grass.
The state grew rich, punishments clear,
thus elevating the Hàn way.
"Account of Jǐngdì"
Xiàojǐngdì oversaw governance,
the feudal lords defied commands.
He vanquished the Seven States,
and the royal house was thereby stabilized.
Neither negligent nor wasteful,
he focused on agriculture and sericulture.
Recorded in the statutory orders,
the people enjoyed peace and well-being.
Account of Yuándì
Xiàoyuándì, reverent and cautious,
lofty and bright, yielding yet mastering.
He honored and ritualized the aged,
and leisurely supported the upright and honest.
Externally, he reduced the imperial parks,
internally, he curtailed the royal attire.
Detached palaces went unguarded,
imperial tombs had no attached towns.
The slander of the eunuch steward
defiled his bright virtue.
Emperor Chéng reflects: Filial Emperor Chéng was anxious,
yet shone when facing court matters.
His manner was impressive,
like a jade tablet.
In the inner chamber he indulged Zhào,
while the affairs of the state remained with the Wáng.
The intense fire,
yet truly did not spread.
"Reflection on Emperor Píng":
Filial Emperor Píng did not achieve,
the new capital was established as the center.
Neither proper nor complete,
losing the whole realm.
Emperor Táng Tàizōng’s "Discussion on Emperor Jìn Wǔ's Records":
Emperor Wǔ inherited the foundation,
bestowed with the mandate of heaven.
He held the maps and governed,
spreading enlightenment and expanding the doctrine.
Thus, he replaced labor with leisure,
and made order from chaos.
He abolished the tribute of silk and damask,
discarded ornate decorations.
He curtailed extravagant customs to promote frugality,
led by example to revert to simplicity.
He appreciated honest discourse,
focused on selecting and promoting.
Liú Yì and Péi Kǎi,
were accepted for their integrity.
Jī Shào and Xǔ Qí,
though opponents, were not discarded.
He ruled with benevolence,
gained the support of the people through leniency.
With vast and generous strategy,
he had the measure of an emperor.
At that time, the people were harmonious and customs were peaceful,
households had enough,
martial disciplines were polished,
contemplating the expansion of the borders.
He made strategic decisions from deep within,
resolved grand plans through consultation.
Mǎ Lóng campaigned west,
Wáng Jùn campaigned south.
The army did not delay,
reducing the enemy’s traces.
The blades remained unstained with blood,
yet conquered the southern tribes.
He achieved what had not been achieved in previous ages,
subdued those whom former kings could not subdue.
Auspicious signs visibly appeared,
the culture and etiquette were rigorously purified.
Heaven and earth's achievements were completed,
the hegemony's enterprise was vast.
Though rituals of honor were ascended,
he refrained from undertaking them.
Pride and complacency,
thus arose.
Seeing the vast lands,
he believed in endless security.
Observing the peace in the realm,
he foresaw eternal governance.
He did not realize that valuing vastness should consider limitations,
so that the vastness may last.
Dwelling in peace but forgetting danger,
leads to instability.
Adding to this the establishment in the wrong place,
and appointing unworthy people.
Wishing for stability in prosperity,
actions led to disaster first.
It is like one intending to travel to Yuè,
but pointing to the desert as their path.
Desiring to ascend a mountain,
yet seeking routes by boat.
The direction pursued becomes more distant,
the path chosen more difficult.
The differences between north and south,
and the opposites of high and low,
do not ease the arrival;
is it not difficult indeed?
Furthermore, using easily swayed foundations,
without considering enduring stability.
Thus, Jiǎ Chōng, a treacherous villain,
harbored evil intentions and wielded power.
Yáng Jùn, a wolf in disguise,
concealed malicious desires while holding authority.
So it came to late departure of the palace carriage,
and incomplete mourning period,
the protective bonds turned to estrangement,
linked armies ultimately destroyed their origin.
The pillars of loyalty turned to deceit,
each supporter wielded their might,
not several years passed
before the system was in total disorder,
leading to turmoil throughout the seas,
the temples were scattered,
the emperor's way and king's rule
became that of tattooed barbarians,
the sacred land became a wasteland of unkempt hair.
Abandoning the significant to profit others,
hiding the minor to rely on oneself,
was mocked by the world.
Why was this so?
It was largely due to the previous lack of caution,
resulting in subsequent troubles.
Moreover, a son with insight is a wise father,
a minister with understanding is a sage ruler.
If a son is unworthy, the family perishes,
if a minister is disloyal, the state is in chaos.
An unstable country cannot bring peace,
a faltering family cannot be preserved.
Thus, a gentleman prevents the beginning,
a sage closes the root cause,
yet Shìzǔ was bewildered by Xún Xù's deceitful schemes,
and misled by Wáng Hún's false strategies.
His heart vacillated by the voices of the crowd,
his decisions unsettled by his planning.
Yuán Hǎi should have been removed but was not,
ultimately leading to disturbances in the realm.
Emperor Huì could be deposed but was not,
eventually causing the overturn of great foundations.
Preserving one individual’s virtue
pales against saving the world;
abandoning one son’s harshness
diminishes against securing the state.
Especially since relying on two generations' support
extends the undertaking but leads to its ruin.
So it's said: seeking light virtue while disregarding great merit,
fearing small cruelty while forgetting great filial piety;
how can this be the way of sages and worthies?
Even if the beginning was good,
rarely do ends align with ideals,
which is why historical records earnestly proclaim,
they cannot avoid heartfelt lament!
Furthermore, "On Suí Gāozǔ":
The mandate of emperors is not from the choice of many,
since different conditions of seizing the opportunity vary,
strengths and weaknesses of situations differ.
Some have internal determination with grand visions,
clear strategies with decisive actions outside,
encompassing as the sea, accommodating like a mountain.
Appearing as if bearing the sky, embracing the land, generous and open-minded—
truly an emperor.
Take Wén Huáng,
who rose from a commoner,
to rule the four seas.
Deceiving the orphan to accomplish the world,
taking from the widow to ascend to the throne,
yet still attending to the people,
promoting simplicity and thrift.
After conquering Jīnlíng,
extravagant tendencies grew daily,
constructing the Palace of Rénshòu at Wǔzhuò,
relocating the new capital to Bà [Banks].
Collected pearls from Hépǔ,
filled the treasury with them.
Southern beauties were brought
into the harem.
The project at Rénshòu drained the people's strength,
the carvings exhausted the populace.
From the Weì to Bà,
how could it not be laborious?
Why relocate from old to new,
when reasons for this abound?
Ambition expanded with land,
intent grew arrogant over time.
Mistrust arose without cause,
many taboos and prohibitions existed.
The mother of Wén was executed,
the emperor’s mother was also killed.
As the hen crowed in the morning,
the imperial lineage was thoroughly eradicated.
Removing the elder to establish the younger,
entrusted roles went to the unworthy.
Meritorious ministers and good generals
were completely exterminated.
His years were not long,
was it not heaven's will?
The Later Han Dynasty's Bān Shūpí's "Discourse on the Mandate of Kings"
In ancient times, when Emperor Yáo abdicated,
he said, "I consult you, Shùn,
the celestial succession rests upon your person."
Shùn likewise commanded Yǔ.
Reaching to Jì and Xiè,
all assisted Táng and Yú,
illuminating and aiding the Four Seas,
generations bearing virtue,
until Tāng and Wǔ possessed the realm.
Although their encounters differed in time,
and their abdications and successions were not the same,
in responding to Heaven and complying with humanity,
their measure was one.
Therefore, the Liú clan received Yáo's legacy.
The lineage of the clan,
recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Táng held the virtue of Fire,
and Hàn succeeded it.
Beginning his rise from the marshes of Pèi,
then a divine mother cried out at night,
to manifest the omen of the Red Emperor.
Thus it is said,
the legacy of emperors and kings,
must possess the virtue of brilliant sageliness and manifest excellence,
the accumulated deeds of abundant merit and profound benefit,
only then can sincerity and purity connect with the divine and luminous,
and flowing grace be bestowed upon the living people.
Thus they can be blessed and enjoyed by the ghosts and spirits,
and returned to by all under heaven.
Never has it been seen that a ruling age lacked foundation,
or merit and virtue went unrecorded,
yet one could arrogantly occupy this position.
Common custom sees Gāozǔ rising from common cloth,
not understanding the reason,
thinking he merely encountered violent chaos,
and was able to wield his sword.
Itinerant persuaders,
even compare the contending for the realm to chasing deer,
fortunately succeeding by swiftness and obtaining it,
not knowing the sacred vessel has its mandate,
cannot be sought by intellect or strength.
Alas!
This is why the world has many rebellious ministers and villainous sons.
If so,
are they merely ignorant of the Way of Heaven?
They also fail to observe human affairs!
Those starving refugees and wandering bondsmen,
suffering hunger and cold on the roads,
think only of having a short coarse garment to wear,
a store of a dan or shi of grain,
their wish no more than a single piece of gold.
Yet they end up dying, their bodies turning in ditches and gullies.
Why is this?
Poverty and destitution also have their fate.
How much more so the nobility of the Son of Heaven,
the wealth of the Four Seas,
the legacy of the divine and luminous—
can these be recklessly occupied?
Jìn Dynasty Gān Bǎo's "Discourse on the Jìn Martial Emperor's Revolution"
The Historian Official says:
"The rise of emperors and kings
must await the Mandate of Heaven.
If there is succession and replacement,
it is not a matter of human affairs.
Refinement and substance differ with the times,
their establishment and rise are not the same.
Therefore, the ancients who possessed the realm,
before Bóhuáng and Lìlù,
acted but did not possess,
responded but did not seek,
holding to the Great Image.
In the vast primordial age, hereditary succession,
was to unify the people.
Yáo and Shùn's internal abdication,
embodied cultured virtue.
Hàn and Wèi's external abdication,
Tāng and Wǔ's revolution,
responded to Heaven and humanity.
Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ's contention and conquest,
established merit and achievement.
Each according to their fortune obtained the realm.
How great indeed is the meaning of following the times!
The ancients, revering their affairs, then received the mandate to begin;
today's emperors and kings receive the mandate and use it to end.
Is this human affairs?
Is it the will of Heaven?"
Also, "General Discourse on the Jìn Annals"
The Historian Official says:
"In the past, the Xuān Emperor Gāozǔ,
with heroic talent and great capacity,
responded to fortune and entered service.
Encountering the founding beginnings of Wèi Tàizǔ,
he planned for the army and state,
his excellent strategies repeatedly hitting the mark.
Thus he served the carriage and chariot,
driving and galloping for three generations.
His nature was deep and hidden as if within walls and mansions,
yet he could be broad and expansive to accommodate.
In action, he employed stratagems to control things,
and knew men well, skillfully selecting and promoting.
Therefore, the worthy and foolish all cherished him,
the small and great exhausted their strength.
Then he took Dèng Ài from agricultural leisure,
drew Zhōu Tài from corvée service,
entrusting them with civil and military affairs,
each excelling in their tasks.
Thus he could capture Mèng Dá in the west,
raise Gōngsūn Yuān in the east,
pacify Cáo Shuǎng internally,
and attack Wáng Líng externally.
With divine strategy and independent decision,
he campaigned and conquered in all four directions,
reigning over the many lords,
great authority in himself.
He repeatedly repelled Zhūgě Liàng's disciplined troops,
and in the east supported the Wú people's interdependent situation.
Though armies were frequently mobilized,
the border regions suffered no loss.
Thereupon the common people supported the capable,
and the Great Image began to be constructed.
Shìzōng inherited the foundation,
Tàizǔ continued the enterprise.
Xuán and Fēng caused chaos internally,
Qīn and Dàn invaded externally.
Though their secret plots were covert,
the opportunity was destined to show signs.
Though Huáipǔ was disturbed again,
Xǔ and Luò did not tremble.
All rejected different schemes,
to glorify the former achievements.
Then they pushed the chariot of Zhōng and Dèng,
and drove long into Yōng and Shǔ.
The three passes were swept like lightning,
Liú Chán entered as a subject.
Heaven's signs and human affairs,
were thus believed.
At first, he received extraordinary rituals,
in the end, he received the full regalia's bestowal.
His name and vessels were exalted above Zhōu Gōng,
his authority and control stricter than Yī Yǐn.
Reaching to Shìzǔ,
he then enjoyed the imperial ultimate.
Correct in position and embodying his place,
he valued words and was cautious with laws.
Benevolent to generously treat those below,
frugal to sufficiently supply needs.
Harmonious yet not lax,
broad yet able to decide.
Therefore the people sang of renewal,
and the Four Seas were pleased and encouraged!"
Táng Tàizōng's "Sacrificial Text for Wèi Tàizǔ"
Now, great virtue is called life,
relying on the Two Modes to complete transformation.
The great treasure is called position,
responding to the Five Fortunes to successively prosper.
Nobility and baseness, abandonment and rise,
are none not the Mandate of Heaven.
Therefore, the dragon countenance and sun horns,
manifest the signs of emperors and kings.
Lightning shadows and rainbow lights,
display the auspicious omens of heaven and earth.
They cannot be contended for by wisdom,
nor striven for by strength.
In the past, the Hàn house split like beans,
the many heroes stood like mountains.
When the people were scattered and governance chaotic,
the one who pacified them was a wise man.
When virtue was lost and times perilous,
the one who stabilized them was a worthy assistant.
Yī Yǐn's service to the Yīn house,
the Kingly Way, dark, again became bright.
Huò Guāng's assistance to the Hàn court,
the Imperial Order, blocked, returned to peace.
Establishing loyalty and treading the path of integrity,
lay precisely in this.
The Emperor, with heroic and martial bearing,
faced a time of difficult fortune.
The responsibility of pillar and beam,
was the same as in former times;
the merit of rectification and correction,
differed from past generations.
He watched the drowning and did not rescue,
saw the overturning and did not support.
Deviating from the sentiment of sacrificing for the state,
he had traces of lacking a ruler.
Then, when the tripartite division began its celebration,
the response of the yellow star had long been clear.
Divination opened the period,
the fortune of the true man now belonged.
This was the will of Heaven!
Could it be human affairs?
Chén Shěn Jiǒng "Eulogy for the Tomb of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn"
The minister heard that though the towering mountains are concealed,

I humbly submit to Your Majesty,

Shooting at the fu among the sea shore,

How immensely joyful,

Emerald curtains and bead blinds,

The ancient foundation of the tomb,

Remnants of Fúfēng,

A traveler in bondage,

In the past, Chéngmíng was dismissed,

Carriages could be ridden,

Respectfully hearing past realities,

Millets and rice are not fragrant,

The heart of Júetái,
empty sorrow for Lord Wèi.
The shrine of Yǒng Qiū,
has yet to illuminate Xià Hòu.
Looking up to the noble virtues,

Empress Chapter One
"Bái Hǔ Tōng" states:
