Truly there were virtuous women,
who indeed became good matches.
Táng Yuán revived Guī,
and Wénmǔ flourished Zhōu.
Their virtue did not waver,
greatly aiding as if by Heaven's decree."
Daughter of the Great Emperor, Sister Matched with Heaven
The *Chūnqiū Hécéng Tú* states:
"Yáo's mother Qìngdū
was the daughter of the Great Emperor.
She was born in the wilds of Shíwéi,
often to the southeast of Sānhé.
Heaven sent great thunder and lightning,
and there was blood flowing to moisten within a great rock,
giving birth to Qìngdū."
The *Máo Shī*, *Dà Míng* chapter, states:
"The great state has a maiden,
a sister matched with Heaven."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"Qiàn
means 'to exhaust',
'to complete'.
King Wén considered Tàisì to be virtuous.
After inquiring her name and returning,
he divined about it.
It being auspicious,
he fully performed the rites and honored her,
as if Heaven had a younger sister.
Qiàn
is pronounced with the fanqie 'kǒu jiàn'."
Thoughtful and Reverent Tàirén, Loving and Gracious Zhōu Jiāng
The *Máo Shī*, *Sī Qí* chapter, states:
"Thoughtful and reverent was Tàirén,
mother of King Wén.
Loving and gracious was Zhōu Jiāng,
wife of the Jīng house."
The *Máo Cháng Zhuàn* states:
"Qí
means 'solemn', 'reverent'.
Mèi
means 'to love', 'to be gracious'.
Zhōu Jiāng
is Tàijiāng.
Constantly thinking of the solemn reverence of Tàirén, who became the mother of King Wén,
and also constantly thinking of the loving graciousness of Tàijiāng in matching King Tài,
thus she could become the wife of the Jīng house.
This speaks of her virtuous conduct being pure and complete,
thus giving birth to a sage son."
The above concerns worthy Empresses.
Weaving Chamber, Mulberry Altar
The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* states:
"The Míngdé Empress Mǎ established a weaving chamber and a silkworm palace within the Zhuólóng Garden,
and frequently went to observe them."
The Jìn Yuánkang ceremonial text states:
"The Empress's mulberry-picking altar is located southwest of the silkworm palace."
Dividing Silk, Presenting Cocoons
Cài Yōng's *Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù* states:
"In the last month of spring,
the Empress and consorts observe purification,
personally face east and engage in mulberry picking.
After the silkworm affairs are completed,
they divide the cocoons and weigh the silk."
The *Lǐ Jì* states:
"In the first month of summer,
after the silkworm affairs are completed,
the Empress and consorts present the cocoons to the Son of Heaven."
Domestic Duties, Inner Principles
The *Yì* states:
"She does not deviate; she attends to the domestic duties."
The *Nǚshǐ Zhēn* states:
"Fastening the lapel and tying the sash,
reverently attending to domestic duties,
refers to the affairs of sacrifices and food and drink." The *Lǐ Jì* has the *Nèi Zé* chapter. Yán Jùn's *Huánghòu Miào Dēng Gē* states:
"Our sagely King Wén,
encompassed all within the Four Seas.
He regulated the external state and family,
and internally bequeathed the female principles."
To Govern the Six Palaces and Lead the Eight Concubines
The Records of Wei states:
"When Empress Wéndé Guō was about to ascend to her position,
Commandant Péi Qián submitted a memorial stating:
'In the past, when emperors possessed the realm,
they relied not only on external assistance,
but also on internal support.
Therefore, wise rulers would establish their principal consort in advance,
invariably selecting her from a renowned clan of a previous dynasty,
choosing one who was virtuous and gentle,
to govern the Six Palaces.'"
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"In the third year of the Yǒngpíng era,
officials petitioned for Empress Mǎ Míngdé to be established in the Chángqiū Palace,
to lead the Eight Concubines.
The Emperor had not yet spoken.
The Empress Dowager said:
'Lady Mǎ's virtue is supreme among the rear palace.'
Thus she ascended to the highest honor."
As the Sun Has the Moon, As Heaven Has Earth
The Memorials of Wei Ministers states:
"Your servant has heard that the emperor having an empress
is like the sun having the moon."
Lú Zhí's memorial states:
"The empress and consorts
are those who sacrifice to Heaven and Earth,
and reverently serve the ancestors.
Externally, they solemnly honor the bright spirits;
internally, they lead and correct the Nine Ladies.
Those who order yin and yang
are like Heaven having Earth,
like yang having yin."
The above concerns the empress's internal duties.
Studying the Book of Songs and Book of Changes, Favoring Huang-Lao
The Continued Book of Han states:
"Empress Mǎ Míngdé
recited the Book of Changes, Book of Songs, and Analects,
grasping their essential meanings."
The Book of Han states:
"Empress Dòu,
mother of Emperor Jǐng,
favored the teachings of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ.
Emperor Jǐng and all the Dòu clan were compelled to read Lǎozǐ,
and all followed its methods."
Cultivating the Motherly Way, Heeding Women's Compliance
The Book of Rites states:
"The empress cultivates women's compliance,
which is the motherly way."
Zhèng Xuán states:
"The mother applies yin teachings to the women."
It also states:
"The Son of Heaven heeds the male teachings,
the empress heeds women's compliance;
the Son of Heaven governs the yang way,
the empress governs yin virtue;
the Son of Heaven attends to external governance,
the empress attends to internal duties."
Clothing Without Choosing Colors, Food Without Seeking Delicacies
The Continued Book of Han states:
"The Biography of Empress Dèng Héxī states:
'At palace banquets,
the various noble ladies vied to adorn themselves,
wearing the most extravagant garments.
Yet the empress alone was serene,
her clothing not chosen for color,
her attire not seeking ornamentation.'"
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"The Biography of Empress Mǎ Míngdé states:
'The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"I, the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
wear plain silk skirts myself,
and do not seek delicacies in food.
Those around me have no perfumed adornments."'"
Restraining the Clan Externally, Without Jealousy or Resentment Internally
The Continued Book of Han states:
"Empress Dèng Xiàohé was by nature humble and cautious.
Her brothers, both paternal and maternal,
were all favored by the late emperor.
After she assumed regency,
she restrained those around her internally
and restrained the clan externally."
It also states:
"When Empress Liáng Shùnliè was established,
Emperor Shùn passed away,
and Emperor Chōng was still in swaddling clothes.
The Empress Dowager assumed regency.
Initially,
Empress Dòu Zhāngdé, jealous that Empress Gōnghuái alone had borne the imperial heir,
framed her with false charges,
and her family was exiled to Jiǔzhēn.
A daughter of Empress Dòu Zhāngdé's paternal cousin, named Zhāng, became a noble lady,
and shared favor with the Empress Dowager.
Zhāng attained the high position of Grand Herald,
and when the Emperor passed away,
the Empress Dowager ascended to the highest honor.
Zhāng was terrified.
The Empress Dowager harbored no jealousy or resentment in her heart,
and thus did not hold past wrongs against her."
Not Fond of Sightseeing, Not Fond of Play
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"Empress Mǎ Míngdé
was not fond of going out for sightseeing,
and rarely looked out from the palace windows."
The Records of Wei states:
"Empress Zhēn Wénzhāo,
from childhood to adulthood,
was not fond of play.
At age eight,
when there were people outside performing equestrian stunts on standing horses,
all her family members and elder sisters went up to the pavilion to watch,
but she alone did not go.
When her elder sisters asked her,
she replied:
'How can such things be for women to watch!'"
Not Valuing Extravagance, Not Fond of Music
Wáng Chén's Book of Wei states:
"Empress Biàn Wǔxuān was frugal and modest by nature,
not valuing extravagance.
She had no embroidered silks, pearls, or jades."
It also states:
"Empress Guō Wéndé was frugal and modest by nature,
not fond of music,
and often admired the character of Empress Mǎ Míngdé."
The above concerns the empress's talents and abilities.
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Huá's "Palace Song Poem"
The Former Kings unified the great enterprise,
Their mysterious transformation spread to the eight directions.
Their rituals and laws won over the myriad states,
Internal instruction revered within the palace walls.
Huáng and Yīng upheld the imperial model,
The Great Odes sing of the three consorts.
Embodied grace, gentle and compliant,
Following ritual, treading with humble reverence.
The locusts spread broad kindness and grace,
The bending tree reaches the obscure and subtle.
Their virtuous sound harmonizes with the clear wind,
Their lofty righteousness, distant and beyond pursuit.
Noble glory partakes of sun and moon,
The whole world gazes upon their lingering radiance.
Jìn Dynasty Chéng Gōngsuí's "Palace Poem"
Heaven and Earth do not stand alone,
Creation arises from yin and yang.
Qián and Kūn bestow covering and bearing,
Sun and moon shine with double light.
Governing the state begins with the family way,
Establishing teaching starts within the women's chambers.
The two consorts aided Yǒuyú,
The three mothers assisted the Zhōu kings.
Túshān flourished with Great Yǔ,
Yǒushēn assisted Chéng Tāng.
Qí and Jìn hegemonized the feudal lords,
All relying on Jī and Jiāng.
The "Guān Jū" longs for a worthy consort,
These words, how can they be forgotten?
Wèi Dynasty Cáo Zhí's "Ode to Maternal Model"
The virtuous consort of Yīn Tāng,
Was a daughter of Yǒushēn.
Benevolent teachings cultivated within,
She dwelled according to righteousness.
She purified and tranquilized the rear palace,
The Nine Ladies were in order.
Yī was a accompanying minister,
And thus became the chief assistant.
Also "Ode to Worthy Enlightenment"
Oh, radiant Empress Jiāng,
Whose light matched Zhōu Xuān.
She did not act without righteousness,
She did not speak without ritual.
Rising late, missing court,
She reported her fault in the Eternal Lane.
The King thus diligently governed,
And the myriad states became reverent.
Cáo Zhí's "In Praise of Jiāng Yuán and Jiǎn Dí"
Kù had fourteen consorts,
Their sons all became sovereigns.
Emperor Zhì died early,
Yáo received the great mandate.
The mysterious bird, the great footprint,
Were the auspicious signs of Yīn and Zhōu.
Also, "In Praise of Yǔ's Wife"
Yǔ's wife was of Túshān,
Earthworks were urgent.
Only at Qǐ's birth,
Did he pass the gate without entering.
Exalting the clear principle,
He grasped merit and service.
Nurturing the sage heir,
Heaven's favor was inherited.
Jìn Dynasty, Zuǒ Guìpín's "In Praise of Shùn's Two Consorts"
Marvelous were the two consorts,
Embodiment responding to spiritual signs.
Serving as consorts to Guī,
They glorified this Yǒuyú,
Sinking into Xiāng to show instruction,
Their numinous virtue spread forever.
Such goodness and beauty,
Surely will not perish.
Liáng Dynasty, Jiāng Yān's "Memorial Congratulating the Empress on Her Enthronement for Prince Jiànpíng"
I respectfully acknowledge that in this auspicious month and favorable season,
You have received the brilliance of the stars and assumed the correct position,
With pheasant pendants displaying rank.
Ceremonial sashes serve as adornment,
Blessings pervade all Xià,
Renown resounds in the spiritual realm.
I humbly consider your radiant and tranquil virtue,
Embracing humility and compliance.
Rising and falling according to charts and traditions,
Attended by poetry and history.
Long acquainted with abundant talents,
Early spreading fragrant teachings.
Extending instruction in the Purple Palace,
Adorning the tracks of the splendid chambers.
Voice stirring embroidered sashes,
Influence pacifying family and state.
Later Wèi Dynasty, Wēn Zǐshēng's "Memorial from Ministers Congratulating the Wèi Emperor on Taking an Empress"
Your subjects have heard that Xuānyuán, being divine,
Was matched with Xīlíng.
Xiàhòu, being supremely sage,
Thus welcomed a bride from Túshān.
We humbly consider Your Majesty, dragon-soaring to continue the throne,
Greatly illuminating and ordering fate.
Since Chángqiū has been established,
The feminine teachings have a master,
The destined mandate is endless.
The imperial plan is long secured,
Under the entire heaven,
None do not rejoice and leap.
Sòng Dynasty, Fàn Yè's "Discussion on the Annals of Empresses"
Now, according to Zhōu rituals, the empress and consorts hold correct positions within the palace,
Sharing substance with the Heavenly King.
The Fūrén sit and discuss women's rites,
The Jiǔpín oversee instruction in the four virtues.
The Shìfù are in charge of knowledge of mourning, sacrifices, and guests,
The Nǚyù are ordered in the king's resting chambers.
Offices are established and duties divided,
Each has its canonical responsibility.
The female scribes with red-tube brushes,
Record merits and write down faults.
In residence, there are instructions of the Bǎo'ā;
In movement, there is the sound of jade pendants.
They advance worthy talents to assist the gentleman,
Lament the gentle and fair without indulging their beauty.
Thus they were able to proclaim and transmit the feminine transformation,
Cultivate and complete the inner rules.
When Qín annexed and took the world,
It mostly acted with arrogance and greatness.
Offices were equipped as in the Seven States,
Ranks were arranged in eight grades;
Hàn, upon rising, followed this,
And the system for women was not regulated.
Gāozǔ did not cultivate the bed-curtains,
Xiàowén made no distinction on the mat.
Yet selection and acceptance were still simple,
Adornments and playthings were few and unadorned.
From Wǔ and Yuán onward,
Each generation increased licentious expenditure,
To the extent that the rear palaces had three thousand,
With ranks increased to fourteen.
When Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty,
He returned ornamentation to simplicity,
The titles of the six palaces,
Were only Empress and Guìrén,
And additionally established three grades: Měirén, Gōngrén, and Cǎinǚ;
Emperor Míng diligently followed the former intent,
And palace instruction was quite cultivated.
In elevating and establishing consorts and empresses,
He always prioritized virtuous conduct.
Within, there were no words going beyond the women's quarters,
Power had no grants of private favoritism,
Which may be said to have corrected its abuses! From Xiàozhāng onward,
Gradually, beauty was used for granting,
Favor exalted harmonious union,
Thus forgetting the stains and worms.
Since ancient times, although there were times of young rulers and hardship,
And the royal house had many troubles,
Entrusting completion to the chief minister,
None had exclusively relied on women,
To decide and cut the heavy vessel.
Only the Qín Empress Dowager Mǐ,
Began to administer government affairs,
Hence the Marquis of Ráng held power heavier than King Zhāo,
And his household was richer than the Yíng state.
Hàn continued this error,
Knowing the trouble but not changing it,
The Eastern Capital's imperial line repeatedly broke.
Power returned to female rulers,
Four emperors were established from outside,
Six empresses presided over court,
None failed to decide policies within the curtains,
Entrusting affairs to fathers and brothers,
Coveting child rulers to prolong their rule,
Suppressing the wise and worthy to monopolize their authority.
The burden heavy, the road long,
Profit deep, disaster swift,
Their persons encountering dew and mist atop the Cloud Terrace,
Their families bound in fetters beneath prison bars.
Obliteration followed on heels,
Overturned carriages continued on the road,
Yet they rushed forward without cease.
With scorching and rotting as their end,
Ultimately, the great fortune declined,
And the divine treasure was lost and perished.
What the Odes and Documents lament,
Is roughly the same principle!
The "Elegiac Memorial for the Respectful Empress of Qi by Xiè Tiǎo" says:
"The green canopy spreads over the mound,
the dark hall opens its doors.
The sacrificial vessels are cleared after the triple offering,
the mats are rolled up with the six ceremonial robes.
Longing for the serpent-guarded carriage, I crane my neck,
yearning for the phoenix-adorned chariot, I press my hand to my heart.
Grieving that the pepper-scented path is now desolate first,
lamenting that the Eternal Trust Palace is no longer visited.
Her body lies separated, yet her spirit attends both realms,
in this time, there is no second display.
Swiftly came the imperial decree, spoken by the left-side officials,
gloriously proclaiming her sage virtue.
Its words say:
'Descended from the distant lineage of Emperor Táng,
continuing the remote ancestry of Yùlóng.
In Qín, they became the Liú clan,
in Hàn, they opened the state of Chǔ.
Beginning with this virtuous sage,
she was capable of gentleness and grace.
The clear Milky Way manifested her spirit,
the layered sands received her blessings.
Thus her auspicious signs were determined,
her virtuous reputation truly harmonious.
Her radiance illuminated the ponds and islets,
her splendor shone in the central valley.
Reverent from the start in managing the ceremonial cap strings,
teaching first the cultivation of early and late crops.
Her wise insights flowed like rivers,
her divine heart was fragrant as orchids.
Her former virtue concealed its light,
the way of rulership was just being spread.
In assisting, she sought the worthy,
in audiences, there was no bias.
Consulting the historians to broaden the models,
presenting poems to display righteousness.'
The thick lower part says:
'Benevolence,
storing the past—this is wisdom.
The ten capable ministers were thus present,
the four teachings were without error.
She endeared herself to all her aunts,
bequeathing to us the principles for consorts.
Transformation spread from the ducal palace,
far-reaching to the southern states.
The carriage's splendor cherished her light,
the plain moon awaited her virtue.
Alas, I am not blessed,
her kind instruction was lost early.
Just in tender, youthful years,
I had no one in whose bosom to rely.
The family reached the treasure of enterprise,
I myself inherited the flourishing brilliance.
The longevity palace is silent and distant,
the pure temple stands empty, awaiting her return.
The emperor moved the bright mandate,
humans and spirits all rejoiced.
The heavenly scene looked down from without,
the feminine presence was lacking within.
Vainly grieving for the old sword,
only sighing for the golden vault.
How to present the jade libation cup?
The ceremonial robes are not set out.
The astrologer announces the ominous sign,
the imperial carriage has gone forever.
She left behind far-reaching plans,
her final commands are to be honored.'
Cherishing the deep bonds of Fēng and Pèi,
turning away from the vast expanse of the divine capital.
Disdaining Cāngwú for not following suit,
following Fùyú to share the same soil.
Arranging the symbolic settings in the garden tomb,
reflecting the carriage ornaments among the pines and catalpas.
Gazing toward Chéngmíng but unable to enter,
crossing the clear Luò River to travel south.
Continuing the serpent-emblazoned ropes along the open track,
connecting the dragon-adorned curtains on the constructed boat.
The winding pond lies silent, already at dusk,
the eastern river flows calm and still.
Recording the distant achievements of the secluded palace,
hearing of the remote blessings of the continuing woman.
Longing still entangled in the bestowed robes,
grief growing daily while facing the mirror.
Thinking of the cold spring without limit,
entrusting to the red-tube brush these lingering chants.
Alas, how sorrowful!'"
Imperial Consorts and Concubines, Part Two
"Zhou Li":
"The Son of Heaven's empress establishes six palaces,
three ladies,
nine concubines,
twenty-seven deputies,
eighty-one attendant wives,
to oversee state domestic affairs,
to clearly illustrate the harmony among women.
Thus, the domestic peace leads to the proper governance of the family."
Zheng's commentary says:
"The six palaces are,
one palace in front,
and five behind.
The five are,
one palace for the empress;
one palace for the three ladies;
one palace for the nine concubines;
one palace for the twenty-seven deputies;
one palace for the eighty-one attendant wives,
totaling one hundred and twenty people.
The empress holds the central position in the palace,
embodying the likeness of the King of Heaven;
the ladies discuss the rites of women;
the nine concubines manage the teaching of the four virtues;
the deputies handle funerals, sacrifices, and guests;
the attendants arrange the king's private quarters."
Under the Han, following the Qin system,
the principal wife was called:
"Empress.
Other titles within the palace
included Lady, Beauty, Good Lady, Eighth-ranked Lady, Seventh-ranked Lady, Senior Assistant, and Junior Assistant.
Emperor Wu added titles such as Favorite Lady,
and others like Yu, Ronghua, Chuyi;
Emperor Yuan added Zhaoyi."
There were also five officials:
Shunchang, Wujuan, Gonghe, Yuling, Baolin, Liangshi, Night Attendant positions.
From "Han Shu Waiqi Zhuan"
During Emperor Guangwu's restoration,
previous positions were eliminated.
Besides the principal wife,
only titles like Noble Lady, Beauty, and Multicolored Lady remained.
From Fan Ye's "Hou Han Shu"
Under Emperor Wei Wudi, building on the Western Han system,
titles such as Lady, Zhaoyi, Favorite Lady, and Ronghua, Beauty were established;
Emperor Wen added Noble Concubine, Shuyuan, Xiurong, Shuncheng, Good Lady;
Emperor Ming added Shufei, Zhaohua, Xiuyi;
from "Wei Zhi"
Emperor Jin Wudi adopted the titles from Han and Wei,
emulating the Zhou's six palaces,
establishing Noble Concubine, Lady, Noble Lady,
as the three ladies.
Shufei, Shuyuan, Shuyi, Xiurong, Xiuhua, Xiuyi, Favorite Lady, Ronghua, Chuhua,
making up the nine concubines.
Beauties, Talented Ladies, Middle Talented Ladies,
served as honorary positions.
From "Zang Rongxu Jin Shu"
After the Song and Qi,
mostly followed the Jin system.
Increases and decreases were due to reforms,
or slight differences therein."
"Song Shu" states:
"Emperor Xiaowu eliminated the Jin titles of Lady, Xiuhua, Xiuyi,
and established Imperial Noble Consort,
grouped with Noble Concubine and Noble Lady as the three ladies.
Established Zhaoyi, Zhaorong, Zhaohua,
to replace Xiuhua, Xiurong,
as the nine concubines;
Emperor Ming further reduced Noble Lady,
and established Noble Consort,
to complement the three ladies.
Added Shurong,
grouped with ancient Shuyuan, Shuyi, Zhaohua, Zhaoyi, Zhaorong, Xiuhua, Xiurong, Xiuyi for the nine concubines.
Also introduced Chenghui, Lierong,
alongside ancient Favorite Ladies, Ronghua, Chuhua totaling five ranks,
just below the nine concubines.
Beauties, Talented Ladies, Good Ladies served as honorary positions."
"Qi Shu" states:
"Emperor Gao used Noble Concubine, Lady, Noble Lady for the three ladies.
Xiuhua, Xiuyi, Xiurong, Shufei, Shuyuan, Shuyi, Favorite Lady, Ronghua, Chuhua constitute the nine concubines."
"Liang Shu" states:
"The Liang followed the Qi system,
and at the start of the Chen,
they made no changes.
Until Emperor Wen used Noble Concubine, Noble Consort, Imperial Noble Consort for the three ladies.
The nine concubines were Shuyuan, Shuyi, Shurong, Zhaohua, Zhaorong, Zhaoyi, Xiuhua, Xiurong, Xiuyi.
Favorite Lady, Ronghua, Chuhua, Chenghui, Lierong were five titles below the nine concubines.
Beauties, Talented Ladies, Good Ladies were honorary titles."
"Hou Wei Shu" states:
"Emperor Taiwu first established the titles Zhaoyi, Noble Lady;
Emperor Xiaowen set up Left and Right Zhaoyi analogous to Da Situ,
three ladies analogous to the Three Dukes,
three concubines like the Three Advisors,
six concubines like the Six Ministers,
deputies ranked as Zhong Daifu,
attendants as Yuan Shi."
"Bei Qi Shu" states:
"Emperor Wenxuan, though having titles for Ladies and Concubines,
did not specify numbers;
Emperor Wucheng followed the ancient system,
having three ladies,
nine concubines,
twenty-seven deputies,
eighty-one attendant wives.
Established Left and Right Zhaoyi, like Chancellor,
set up Hongde, Zhengde, Chunde Ladies analogous to Three Dukes,
Guangyou, Zhaoxun, Chonghui Senior Concubines like the Three Advisors,
Xuanyou, Ninghui, Xuanming, Shunhua, Ninghua, Guangxun Junior Concubines like the Six Ministers,
deputies like Third Rank Officials,
female attendants like Fifth Rank Officials,
also chose elegant titles,
for their categories.
Besides, others were Talented Ladies, Multicolored Ladies,
as additional titles.
Later rulers also established titles like Eying, Shufei."
"Sui Shu" states:
"Emperor Gaozu reduced the number according to the 'Zhou Li',
appointing three concubines,
nine deputies,
thirty-eight attendant women.
Earlier, Empress Dugu was jealous,
and did not establish three ladies,
to prevent coercion from above.
Below the concubines,
only sixty positions were established.
After her death,
three Noble Lady positions were created,
increased concubines to nine,
deputies to twenty-seven,
attendant women to eighty-one;
Emperor Yang established Imperial Noble Consort, Shufei, Defei as the three ladies.
Shunyi, Shunrong, Shunhua, Xiuyi, Xiuhua, Xiurong, Chongyi, Chongrong, Chonghua formed the nine concubines.
Twelve Favorite Ladies, fifteen Beauties and Talented Ladies for the deputies.
Baolin twenty-four, female attendants twenty-four, Multicolored Ladies thirty-two as attendants,
totaling one hundred and twenty positions.
There were also officials called Chengyi, Daoren,
all serving beside the ruler,
with no fixed number."
On Rites: Clarifying Harmony
Zheng Xuan's commentary on "Zhou Li" states:
"In antiquity, the three ladies to the empress
were like the Three Dukes to the king.
Sitting and discussing women's rites,
without official positions,
to manifest the order of things."
Yu Di: Gong Duo
"Li Ji" states:
"The queen wears an ornamented robe,
ladies wear Yu Di.
'Yu' pronounced 'yu'."
Cai Yong's "Moon Ordinance Chapters" states:
"In mid-spring,
on the day the swallows arrive,
a grand sacrifice is made to the goddess Gaomei,
who is worshiped for fertility.
The empress and consorts all gather at Gaomei,
to pray for offspring.
Then, offering a libation to the Emperor,
adorned with 'gong duo'.
The Emperor's libation,
referred to the empress down to the consorts,
related to births with an inkling.
'Duo',
is a bow cover.
Drinking with a sweet wine,
with a bow and arrow,
before Gaomei.
Bow and arrow,
symbolizing men's affairs.
'Duo' pronounced 'du'."
Honoring with Great Vessels: Setting Baskets
"Zhou Li" states:
"For all sacrifices,
the nine concubines present jade vessels filled with grains.
The empress presents and removes the ceremonial dishes and baskets."
Zheng's commentary states:
"The jade vessels,
containers for millet and rice.
'Zi' pronounced 'zi',
'Dun' pronounced 'dui'."
"Han Wei Stories" states:
"The empress leads the silkworm ceremony,
the empress wearing twelve pins and hair ornaments,
rides in a cloud-mother carriage,

black and yellow,

The Remaining Three Stars: Regarding the Eighth Month

Sending officers and palace overseers

Choosing the Tall and Fair; Compatible Appearance

Viewing Dukes and Ranking Lords: Silver Seal and Emblems

Sparrow Hairpin; Ivory M at

"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" states:
"Emperor Wǔ made mats from ivory,

Gold Ring; Jade Hairpin
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" states:

Facing the Bear; Declining the Sedan
"Hàn Shū" states:
"Consort Féng during the Xiàoyuán era,

The emperor visited the tiger pen for beast fights,

climbed the barrier intending to rise.
Consort Féng stepped forward,
standing in front of the bear.
The emperor asked why,
Consort replied:
'A beast stops upon encountering people,
I feared the bear might reach the sovereign's seat,
thus I placed myself before it.'" It also says:
"Consort Bān during the Xiàochéng era,
when the emperor was newly enthroned,
was selected to enter the harem.
Emperor Chéng wandered the rear courtyard,
occasionally wishing to ride with Consort in the same sedan,
Consort declined, saying:
'Observing ancient paintings,
wise and sage rulers,
always had notable ministers by their side;
but in the late three dynasties,
there were favored concubines.
Now to ride together,
could it not resemble that?'
The emperor appreciated these words and ceased."
Feast at the Northern Garden; Welcoming the Western Palace
"Records of the Wèi Dynasty" states:
"Emperor Míng traveled to the rear garden,

"Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū" states:

Zhāoyáng Hall; Zēngchéng Palace

With the death of Emperor Chéng,

It also says:
"Consort Bān during the Xiàochéng era,
when the emperor was newly enthroned,
was selected into the harem,
soon becoming favored.
Became a consort,
resided in Zēngchéng Palace,
twice staying in a Zēngchéng Palace house.

both lost,
one perished at Yánglù,

Offering Wine with Blessings; Bowing Head Weeping at Xíng
"Hàn Shū" states:
"Consort Fù during the Xiàoyuán era,

Emperor Yuān favored her,

She was resourceful,

Palace women, during drinking rituals,

"Shǐjì" states:
"During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time,
Lady Yǐn and Lady Xíng were both favored,
with orders to prevent them from meeting each other.
Lady Yǐn personally requested Emperor Wǔ,
wishing to see Lady Xíng.
The emperor permitted it,
thus arranged for Lady Yǐn to dress as an attendant with dozens, to come before.
Lady Yǐn observed and said:
'This is not Lady Xíng.'
The emperor asked:
'How do you know?'
She replied:
'Based on her stature and demeanor,
she cannot compete with mine.'
Then there was an order for Lady Xíng to dress plainly, approaching alone,
Lady Yǐn upon seeing her said:
'It truly is her,
bowed down weeping,
lamenting her inferiority!'
A proverb says:
'When a beauty enters a room,
an ugly girl resents her.'"
The Picture of Gānquán: Burial at Yúnlíng
The Book of Hàn states:
"The younger brother of Empress Lǐ, Yánnián,
had a keen sense of music,
and excelled in singing and dancing.
Each time there was a new tune,
Yánnián would attend upon the Emperor, start dancing,
and sing:
'In the north, there is a beautiful lady,
surpassing the world and standing alone.
With one glance, she overthrows a city,
with another glance, she overthrows a country.
Though one knows the overthrow of a city and country,
beautiful women are hard to find again.'
The Emperor sighed and said:
'Excellent!
Is there truly such a person in the world?'
Princess Píngyáng then mentioned Yánnián had a younger sister,
and the Emperor summoned her.
She was indeed exquisite and skilled in dance,
and therefore favored by the Emperor.
She bore a son,
who became the Āiwáng of Chāngyì.
Lady Lǐ, young and dying early,
was lamented by the Emperor,
who had her portrait painted at Gānquán Palace. "
The Story of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn says:
"The lady accompanied the Emperor to Gānquán and passed away,
buried at Yúnlíng.
The Emperor mourned deeply,
and built the Spirit Communication Pavilion.
Often, a blue bird visited the pavilion,
until the time of Emperor Xuān when it stopped.
Lady Quán was the mother of Emperor Zhāo. "
Fu for Lady Lǐ of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn
Beautiful and graceful,
her life tragically short.
Adorning the new palace with elegance,
she perished, never to return home.
Gloomy and sorrowful,
dwelling in hidden seclusion, harboring grief.
Stopping the carriage and horses at the mountain peak,
suddenly swallowed by night and darkness.
The autumn air brings tears,
and laurel branches fall, withering away.
Self-lamenting Fu by Bān Jiéyú of Emperor Chéng of the Hàn
Inheriting the legacy of ancestors,
what virtue and destiny were so pure and spiritual.
Ascending the palace courtyard,
serving in the back halls.
Covered by the emperor's grace,
admired under the sun and moon's bright illumination.
Her brilliance was remarkable and radiant,
receiving unparalleled favor at Zēngchéng.
Having surpassed favor undeserved,
always longing for auspicious times.
Constantly sighing awake and asleep,
considering her adornments and reflecting.
Presenting female portraits as a mirror for introspection,
looking to female historians to inquire about poetry.
Mourning the morning wife's admonitions,
lamenting the post of Bāo Yán.
Admiring Huáng Yīng's daughter Yú,
and honoring Zhōu's mother Rèn Sì.
Though inferior and unworthy,
daring not to forget these by heart.
Enduring years with sorrow and fear,
grieving the lack of flourishing.
Pained by sunshine and hospitality,
in swaddling clothes departing calamity.
Is it the disaster of a mere person,
or Heaven's will unattainable.
Serving the Eastern Palace,
entrusted to the last stream of Chángxìn.
Together sweeping the tent and canopy,
committing to death as the end.
Repeatedly she said:
'The hidden profound palace, secluded and clear,
the gate tightly shut,
the magnificent hall dusty, jade steps covered in moss,
in the courtyard green grass grows.
The spacious room dim, curtains dark,
airy chambers cold and chilling.
Looking down, red stairs;
thinking of the Lord, worn shoes.
Looking up, clouded houses;
tears flow unrestrained.'
Cáo Zhí's Tribute to Bān Jiéyú
With virtue and words,
truly she was Bān Jié.
Overflowing with modesty,
enduring in her pleasures.
In adversity pure and steadfast,
in fortune proper and engaged.
Facing the wind, steadily upright,
against the frost, shaking leaves.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Edict on Establishing Inner Positions
Establishing conduct based on ancient teachings,
Zhōu Wén thus exemplified virtue,
the urn and towers disordered;
Hàn Wǔ thus lost the state,
all recorded on various policies,
serving as clear warnings.
From the Wèi and Jìn onwards,
although it was said to be simplistic,
the titles and positions within,
were not uniform.
During Sòng Tàishǐ's time,
the ranks were overly complex,
thus setting up nine ranks.
Appearing like the outer court,
crowding the pepper chamber,
the expenditures kept rising.
Since then, it continues,
following tradition.
With nine-flower banners in Zhāoyáng,
thousands of doors and myriad households.
I have received the mandate from Heaven,
expecting to extend for seven hundred years,
thinking of establishing defenses nearby,
to pass on to future generations.
Previous dynasties' ranks,
should be adapted and changed.
Matters to be discussed externally,
ensuring they are comprehensive and appropriate.
Shěn Yuè of Liáng's Memorial for the Six Palaces
With modest origins,
virtuous and pure without limit.
Ascending from obscurity,
reaching the royal realm.
Servingly adorned by the sun and moon's splendors,
attending at the edge of the screen.
How could I partake in the grandeur of the phoenixes and dragons,
while longing for the clear dust of carriages.
Jiāng Zǒng's Thanks for the Six Palaces of Chén
Receiving the court's order respectfully,
ashamed by the scarlet binding of status.
Serving with private humility,
troubled by the colors of emerald feathers.
The palace of Lǔ burning at night,
Duke Yuán was not alarmed.
With torrents rushing on Chǔ terraces,
Chaste Jiāng had no fear.
Who would have expected the sun and moon to ascend their shadows,
the wind and clouds to pour their essence.
Thus reinstated to the nine palaces of esteem,
with acclaim throughout the six departments.
Ceremonial robes become more splendid,
scarlet banners shine brightly.
How could one assist the flourishing of royal customs,
transforming the gentle influence.
Alert and apprehensive together,
reflecting on the poetry of flowing greenery.
Serving quickly together,
losing the rhythm of resonant jade rings.
Jìn Zhāng Huá's "Admonitions for the Female Historian"
The myriad transformations of the primal essence,
The two principles began to separate.
Scattered qi flowed into forms,
Both molded and refined.
In the time of Emperor Fúxī,
He first established the norms of Heaven and humanity.
Thus began the relationship of husband and wife,
Extending to sovereign and minister.
The way of the family is thereby rectified,
The kingly path has its proper order.
A woman's virtue esteems gentleness,
Embracing refinement, chaste and auspicious.
Gracious, gentle, virtuous, and cautious,
She maintains her proper position within the household.
Fán Jī moved Duke Zhuāng,
Refusing to eat fresh game.
The woman of Wèi admonished Duke Huán,
His ears forgetting the pleasure of music.
Their wills were stern, their righteousness lofty,
Causing the two lords to change their hearts.
The black bear climbed the railing,
Féng Yuán rushed forward.
Was it that she had no fear?
She knew death was certain, yet did not begrudge it.
Lady Bān had her words,
Renouncing pleasure, refusing to share the imperial carriage.
Was it that she had no affection?
She guarded against the subtle, considering the distant.
All people know to adorn their appearance,
But none know to adorn their nature.
If one's nature is not adorned,
One may transgress ritual and correctness.
If one's speech is good,
It finds response a thousand lǐ away.
If one violates this principle,
Even sharing a quilt breeds suspicion.
Joy must not be profaned,
Favor must not be monopolized.
Monopoly indeed breeds arrogance,
Love at its extreme then shifts.
Fullness inevitably leads to loss,
This principle is inherently so.
Sòng Xiè Zhuāng's "Posthumous Title Document for Noble Consort Yīn"
On such-and-such year, month, day, the Emperor says:
"Alas, the late Shūyí Yīn-shì,
You, who embraced excellence and stood out in splendor.
Thus bringing glory to your humble origins,
Companion to the qin, flowing like duckweed,
You truly blossomed in the Purple Apartments.
Serving the imperial presence with gentle brightness, you gained renown,
Dwelling in the Pepper Breeze Palace, with grace and charm your fame rose.
The model of quiet refinement,
Daily graced the layered chambers.
The felicity of abundant blessings,
Was just elevating your flourishing lineage,
When, amidst spring, the algae were covered,
Midstream, the source was extinguished.
We are thereby shaken with grief,
Wounded in Our heart.
The pine-clad region is already cleared,
The dark spring will soon become a tunnel,
It is fitting to honor virtue and rank conduct,
To propagate your fragrant reputation.
Now dispatch such-and-such official to assemble the document and announce the posthumous title:
'Xuān.
May your soul, if conscious,
Accept this gracious honor.
Alas, how sorrowful!'"
Crown Prince, Part Three
The "Hánshī Wàizhuàn" says:
"The Five Emperors treated the world as public office,
The Three Kings treated the world as a family possession.
The family passes it to sons,
The office passes it to the worthy.
Therefore, from Táng and Yú upwards,
Classics and commentaries contain no title of Crown Prince.
The kings of Xià and Yīn,
although they passed on succession,
the records are brief.
It was not until Zhōu that the institution of the King Wén's heir apparent is seen."
The "Báihǔ Tōng" says:
"How do we know the son of the Son of Heaven is called 'Shìzǐ' (heir)?
The 'Chūnqiū' commentary says:
'The King's Shìzǐ met at Shǒuzhǐ' — this is it.
How do we know the son of the Son of Heaven is called 'Tàizǐ' (crown prince)?
The 'Shàngshū' says:
'Tàizǐ Fā ascended the boat' — this is it.
Some say the sons of feudal lords are called Shìzǐ,
yet the 'Chūnqiū' commentary says Jìn had Tàizǐ Shēnshēng,
Zhèng had Tàizǐ Huá,
Qí had Tàizǐ Guāng.
From this we observe that
under the Zhōu system,
the terms Tàizǐ and Shìzǐ
were also not fixed.
Under the Hàn system,
the Son of Heaven is called Huángdì (Emperor),
his principal heir is called Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince),
the principal heirs of kings and princes are called Shìzǐ,
later generations have all followed this."
