Wèi Wén Dì's "Diǎnlùn" says:
"On the bǐngwǔ day of the second month of the 24th year of Jiàn'ān,
Wèi Crown Prince Pī crafted three knives.
Two were called Hánzhāng,
resembling the color of Dānxiá."
It also says:
"Crafted three treasured swords of Bai Bì,
of which two were called Liú Cǎihóng."
Above are the attire and accoutrements of the Crown Prince.
Xià Qǐ and Zhōu Sòng
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Xià Yǔ toured the east,
and passed away at Kuàijī,
passing the realm to Yì.
Yì yielded to Emperor Yǔ's son Qǐ,
and Qǐ was virtuous,
so the world supported him.
The feudal lords all left Yì to return to Qǐ.
They said:
'Our sovereign is the son of Emperor Yǔ.'" It also says:
"After Zhōu Wǔwáng passed,
the Crown Prince Sòng succeeded,
and became known as King Chéng."
Zhōu Fā and Hàn Zhuāng
The "Shàngshū‧Zhōnghòu" says:
"Emperor Wén replaced Bér Yìkǎo,
appointing Fā as Crown Prince.
The king said:
'Cultivate our norms,
and follow the virtuous paths,
and thereafter always refer to the Crown Prince.'" Fàn Yè's "Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Emperor Xiàomíng's taboo name was Zhuāng,
the fourth son of Guāngwǔ.
Born with a full form,
at ten, he understood the "Chūnqiū,"
and at nineteen, was made the Crown Prince.
He studied under Scholar Huán Róng,
and learned the "Shàngshū."
Wèi Pī, Jìn Shào
"Wèi Zhì" states:
"Wén Dì, whose given name was Pī,
was the crown prince of Wǔ Dì.
In the sixteenth year of Jiàn'ān, he was made General of the Central Guards,
and in the twenty-second year, he was established as the Crown Prince of Wèi.
Pī was upright, firm, intelligent, and perceptive,
capable of managing significant affairs."
Hé Fǎshèng's "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Míng Dì, whose given name was Shào,
styled Dào Jī.
When the Middle Emperor ascended the throne,
he was honored with the title of Crown Prince.
In the Eastern Palace, he honored and respected virtuous scholars,
and associated closely with men of evident virtue."
The titles of crown princes named above.
Four Arts, Three Virtues
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"The Music Master excelled in the Four Arts,
established the Four Teachings,
and followed the poetry, books, rituals, and music of former kings to cultivate scholars.
The king's crown prince and sons,
the crown princes of all the lords,
the hereditary sons of the high ministers and great families,
the exemplary talents of the nation,
all came to be educated there."
It also states:
"The heir apparent was ranked in learning,
so when a father was present it was as a son,
when a ruler was present it was as a minister,
maintaining the dignity of both son and minister,
thereby respecting the ruler and close kin.
Therefore, education treated them as father and son,
education treated them as ruler and minister,
education treated them as elder and younger,
achieving all three virtues by following a single measure,
this was only for the heir apparent."
Jade Richness, Golden Sound
Lù Shìhéng in "Poem on the Deeds of the Crown Prince in Xuānyóu Hall" states:
"Great virtue flows like a river,
heavenly talent is as abundant as jade."
Pān Ní in "Eulogy for the Offering of the Crown Prince" states:
"Honoring the Way, deferring by age,
humbling oneself to inquire.
Resounding with a golden sound,
glowing with jade-like grace."
Five Praises, Three Exhaustions
"Zhōu Shū" states:
"The Crown Prince of King Líng,
was bright and intelligent from a young age.
Duke Píng of Jìn sent Shūyù to Zhōu.
He met Crown Prince Jìn,
conversed with him,
and praised him five times while exhausting three topics."
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"When King Wén was the heir apparent,
he attended upon King Jìng three times a day,
arriving outside the sleeping quarters at the first crow of the rooster.
He asked the attendants on duty:
'How is his Majesty today?'
The attendants replied,
'He is well.'
Only then was King Wén pleased.
Again at midday, he did the same.
And again in the evening, he followed the same procedure."
Hàn Tent, Zhōu Bedroom
Fàn Yè's "Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
"At that time, the cultivated land throughout the realm
was mostly not reported accurately,
and an edict was issued for the states and commanderies to investigate the matter.
The emperor saw on a report from Chénliú official:
'Yǐngchuān and Hóngnóng can be investigated,
Hé'nán and Nányáng cannot.'
The emperor interrogated the official,
who admitted he had heard it at Chángshòu Street.
At that time, Míng Dì was the Duke of Dōnghǎi,
at the age of twelve.
From behind the curtain, he remarked:
'The official received the commandery's order,
intending merely to obstruct each other with their cultivated lands.'
The emperor asked:
'Why is it said that Hé'nán and Nányáng cannot be investigated?'
The reply was:
'Hé'nán, being the imperial city, has many close associates;
Nányáng, being the emperor's hometown, has many close relatives,
whose lands and residences exceed the regulations,
making them unsuitable as precedents.'
The interrogation confirmed Míng Dì's words."
"Zhōu Bedroom" refers to "Three Exhaustions" note.
Bedroom Gates, Racing Road
"Bedroom Gates" refers to "Three Exhaustions" note.
"Hàn Shū":
"Emperor Xiàochéng,
was the crown prince of Emperor Yuán.
Emperor Xuān loved him,
and gave him the name:
'Grandson Prince.'
Initially residing in Guì Palace,
he was once urgently summoned by the emperor.
Exiting from the Dragon Tower Gate,
he did not dare to cross the racing road,
and went west to the city gate,
and then crossed only when safe.
The emperor, upon asking why he was delayed,
was given the explanation.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and thus made a decree allowing the crown prince to cross the racing road."
Trying Medicine, Inspecting Meals
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"The crown prince visited outside the bedroom gates morning and evening,
asking the attendants:
'How is his Majesty today?'
If an attendant mentioned an illness,
the crown prince personally fasted and donned mourning attire to encourage meals.
When preparing food,
he was always respectful in overseeing it.
When handling medicine for the illness,
he personally tasted it."
"Hàn Yí" states:
"The crown prince visited the office once every five days,
and sat in the eastern wing,
inspecting the meals."
Tooth Order, Asking the Attendant
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"The heir apparent was ranked in learning,
and the people of the state observed this, saying:
'Why does he who will rule us defer to us by age?'
It was replied:
'When a father is present, the rites demand this.'
It also states:
'The king's crown prince and sons,
the crown princes of all the lords,
the hereditary sons of the high ministers and great families,
all entered the school in order of age.'"
"Asking the Attendant" refers to "Three Exhaustions" note.
Spring Recitation, Summer String; Commanding the Army, Overseeing the State
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"In all studies,
the scholar of the heir apparent recited in the spring and played the string in the summer,
as instructed by the Grand Master."
"Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"The Marquis of Jìn sent Crown Prince Shēnshēng to attack the Gāoluò clan of Dōngshān,
Lǐ Kè advised:
'The crown prince serves in the ancestral temples and the state sacrificial offerings,
and attends to the ruler’s meals at morning and evening,
hence he is called the heir to the ancestral temple.
When the ruler travels, he guards;
when there is a guardian, he accompanies;
accompanying is called commanding the army,
guarding is called overseeing the state,
this was the ancient practice.'" The above are all the talents and virtues of the crown prince.
Asking Dù, Respects for Xún
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Dù Yí, styled Xíngqí,
served as Chancellor of the Literary Forest.
The crown prince visited Dù's residence three times,
holding the classics and inquiring about their meanings."
"Wèi Zhì" states:
"While Wén Dì was in the Eastern Capital,
Tàizǔ said to him:
'Master Xún is a model and teacher of men,
you must treat him with utmost respect.'
Once when Xún was ill,
the crown prince inquired about his health,
bowing alone beneath the bed."
Zhèng's Book, Liú's Yì
"Hàn Shū" states:
"In the first year of the Yuán era, the crown prince was established,
and the Scholar Zhèng Kuān taught the crown prince the 'Shàngshū.'"
"Xù Hàn Shū" states:
"Liú Kūn, in his youth, studied Shī's 'Yì'.
While Míng Dì was the crown prince,
it was taught to him through 'Yì.'"
Biàn's Prose, Wēn's Counsel
Biàn Lán in "Praise of the Crown Prince" states:
"When composing ‘Diǎnlùn’ and various proses and eulogies,
his deep thoughts surged like springs,
and his ornate language floated like clouds.
Listening to it made one forget taste,
and reading it never tired."
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Wēn Jiào was appointed Middle Attendant of the Crown Prince,
frequently advising and admonishing him,
and also presented him with a ministerial counsel,
which was greatly beneficial."
The Two Shūs and the Four Hoary Elders
The Book of Hàn states:
"In the third year of Dìjié, the Crown Prince was established.
Shū Guǎng was appointed as Grand Tutor,
and his elder brother's son Shòu was appointed as Junior Tutor.
Father and son both served as tutors,
and the court considered it an honor.
After five years in office,
they submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to old age,
and the Emperor granted it.
Officials and old friends held a farewell feast outside the eastern capital gate,
and onlookers along the road said:
'How virtuous are these two great officers!'"
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Emperor Gāozǔ intended to change the Crown Prince,
but the Marquis of Liú's remonstrance went unheeded.
Later, at a banquet with wine set out,
the Crown Prince was in attendance,
and Dōngyuán Gōng, Lùlǐ Xiānshēng, Qǐlǐ Jì, and Xià Huáng Gōng accompanied the Crown Prince.
All were over eighty years old,
with hoary white beards and eyebrows.
The Emperor was surprised by them,
and the four men came forward to respond,
each stating their names.
The Emperor exclaimed in great astonishment:
'I have troubled you gentlemen to finally guide and protect the Crown Prince.'"
The Four Friends and the Six Tutors
The Records of Wú states:
"Sūn Dēng, styled Zǐgāo,
when Quán assumed the imperial title,
was made Crown Prince.
He selected outstanding scholars,
to serve as honored friends.
Zhūgě Kè served as Left Supporter, Zhāng Xiū as Right Assistant, Gù Tán as Auxiliary Rectifier, and Chén Biǎo as Wing Rectifier Commandant—
these were called the Four Friends."
The Jìn dynasty's "Rituals and Ranks of the Ministers" states:
"When Mǐnhuái was established in the Eastern Palace,
six tutors were appointed,
the duties of the Imperial Secretary were reduced,
and the position of Chamberlain for the Crown Prince's Household was first established.
Documents were transmitted through the six tutors for the prince to hear,
and they were called the Crown Prince's Six Friends at the time."
Teachers and Friends, Guests and Visitors
The Book of Hàn states:
"Shū Guǎng, styled Zhòngwēng,
served as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince's maternal grandfather, Marquis Píng'ēn Xǔ Bó,
because the Crown Prince was young,
had his younger brother Shùn oversee and protect the Crown Prince's household.
The Emperor asked Guǎng about this,
and Guǎng said:
'The Crown Prince is the state's reserve and deputy,
the deputy ruler's teachers and friends
must be chosen from the most talented in the realm;
it is not appropriate to exclusively favor the maternal family.'"
It also states:
"Empress Wèi gave birth to Crown Prince Jù of Lì,
and when he reached capping age, he took up residence.
The Emperor established the Bówàng Garden for him,
to enable him to receive guests."
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
"Emperor Wén established the Sīxián Garden for the Crown Prince,
to recruit guests."
Upright Scholars and Correct Men, Recording Faults and Reducing Meals
The Elder Dài's Record of Rites states:
"In the past, when King Chéng of Zhōu was young,
still in swaddling clothes,
he selected those in the realm who were filial and fraternal, broadly learned, and possessed of the Way and arts to assist and support him,
making them live with the Crown Prince and accompany him in his comings and goings.
Thus, what the Crown Prince saw with his eyes were correct affairs,
what he heard with his ears were correct words,
and to his left and right, before and behind,
all were correct men."
It also states:
"When the Crown Prince has been capped and become an adult,
and is freed from the strictness of his guardians and tutors,
then there are officials who record his faults,
and stewards who reduce his meals.
If the Crown Prince has faults,
the officials must record his faults,
and the stewards withdraw his meals."
The above concerns the assistance and support of the Crown Prince.
Wèi Biàn Lán's "Rhapsody in Praise and Description of the Crown Prince"
Brilliant is the Crown Prince,
both wise and intelligent.
Broadly learned and strong in memory,
his sagely thoughts are without peer.
Splendid are those to his left and right,
like tigers, like dragons.
Eight outstanding men are at his side,
beside him there is no flattery or evil.
Wealthy yet not forgetting to bestow,
honored yet increasingly reverent.
He delves deeply into books and records,
pondering similarities and differences.
Establishing plans and setting forth proposals,
vastly he dispels ignorance.
All under heaven crane their necks,
singing praises of his virtuous voice.
Heard of in antiquity,
seen now in the present.
Deep, unfathomable,
high, beyond seeking.
Creating laws for ten thousand generations,
handing down this fine tradition.
Liáng Liú Xiàowēi's "Poem in Response to the Crown Prince"
The Crown Prince is the foundation of the realm,
the primary good, the rectitude of all states.
The Zhōu dynasty exalted the superior heir,
the Hàn dynasty recorded the doubly bright.
The front star contains auspicious hues,
repeated thunder spreads distant sounds.
The three excellences are transmitted by the Music Rectifier,
the hundred conducts recorded by the Director of Instruction.
The nine streams are already distinguished,
the seven classics all mastered.
In broad learning, strong as Zǐzhèng,
in lofty talent, surpassing Chángqīng.
In ritual reverence, exceeding self-abasement,
in abundant virtue, increasing humble sentiment.
Immortal aura bequeathed to Zhòng Xiàng,
the Confucian Way promoted by Huán Róng.
Extending to worthies at the Bówàng Garden,
overseeing meals in Cháng'ān City.
Yuán and Qǐ follow the golden carriage,
Fúqiū attends the jade sheng.
The wise counselor before gathers his tablet,
the upright scholar behind lets his tassels hang.
The nine immortals are truly esteemed,
the four seas further incline eastward.
Bān and Shū together plan the carriage,
the Jia Hall equals Péng and Yíng.
Xú Líng's "Poem on Climbing the Southern Tower of the Palace City with Chamberlain Jiāng"
The primary good resides in superior virtue,
all within the realm are covered by inner sincerity.
The Hàn tent in morning, without negligence,
the Zhōu gate at dusk, again hastening.
Having received instruction in Huán's classics,
and paying respects, moreover honoring Confucians.
Lofty aspirations all are of the Odes and Elegance,
elevated writings meet the Dipper's pivot.
Clanging and clashing harmonize with dance and rhythm,
shining and brilliant equal Kūn and Yú.
The ditch water shames before the great hero,
the Zhāng River looks up to the great shaman.
How could a Bào fish enter the sacrificial stand?
Angling for a sea turtle is not to fill the kitchen.
Shū Yù's words were ever defeated,
could Fáng Nián have been wrongly executed?
Jiāng Zǒng's "Poem in Response to Command at a Banquet in the Xiū Hall"
The solemn city leads to the Jiǎ Observatory,
Chénghuá opens the painted hall.
The northern palace bestows gracious rewards,
the western garden passes the feathered cups.
Special favor offers the jade-like abundance,
the final feast is in the golden chamber.
Courtyard radiance joins with tree colors,
eave shadows connect with cloud light.
Immortal as the Yi River carriage,
joyous as the Dòngtíng display.
Plucking strings commands qin and se,
blowing bamboo moves sheng and huang.
Mediocre and lax, presuming to match Ruǎn,
declining and decaying, ashamed to link verses.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem on Following the Imperial Carriage at Dusk, Halting Beneath the Xì"
Double wheels rest by the Purple Pole,
before, brilliance serves the cinnabar sky.
The heavenly warp clings to the imperial screen,
the imperial command escorts the immortal bridle.
Riding the stars, opens the Crane Palace,
bearing the moon, descends the rainbow bridge.
Mist clears, the pavilion camp is near,
dust dims, the Dipper City is distant.
Lotus flowers part the beautiful calyxes,
bamboo arrows descend with startling tides.
Examining myself, ashamed of ability and talent,
receiving favor, gathering phoenix branches.
Shaking the mountains, abundant are the festive music,
drawing slips, presenting the accompanying ballads.
Chǔ Liàng presents "Poem in Response to the Imperial Command on Farewell in the Forbidden Garden"
The great vassal first receives auspicious signs,
Departing to govern near the imperial capital.
Temporarily honored with the green carriage,
Speaking of inheriting the glory of the crimson envoy.
Peach blossoms stretch toward distant riders,
Weeping willows reflect the military camp.
Benevolent influence spreads for a thousand miles,
Majestic aura moves a hundred cities.
The forbidden garden fragrant with a fine festival,
The divine heart bids farewell with emotion.
The golden carriage hastens the parting scene,
Jade pipes keenly sound the notes of separation.
Wild flowers bloom and fall again,
Mountain birds sing and startle once more.
Your humble servant has long been fortunate,
Holding a minor office, serving the enlightened heir.
Ashamed to compose rhapsodies at the fishing terrace,
Indulging in hearing pipes by the Yī River.
Cherishing virtue, long aware of its worth,
Repaying kindness, knowing life is light.
Hánwáng Lǐ Yuánjiā presents "Poem in Response to the Crown Prince's Sentiments on Separation While Overseeing the Capital"
Heavenly signs open layered structures,
The brightness of Li trigram reveals Shàoyáng.
Divining the journey follows auspicious reports,
Guarding the vessel belongs to the worthy heir.
Far surpassing the recitations of Zhōu,
Distant, overshadowing the Zhuāng of Hàn.
Esteeming scholars, leaning toward southern Luò,
Abundant talents flourish in the northern arena.
Land divided at Dānjiù Ridge,
Pathway passing White Cloud Country, storing sincerity.
Reverent from dawn to dusk,
Imperial affection accumulates through heat and cold.
Pearls and jade connect to the Milky Way,
All things gaze upon the doubled light.
Xuē Yuánchāo "Poem in Response to the Crown Prince's Sentiments on Separation While Overseeing the Capital"
The heir's forbidden bronze gates open,
Imperial journey, the jade departure distant.
Vainly missing the officials of Shòu Street,
Still separated from the court at the chamber door.
At the land's head, gazing at dragon halberds,
Beyond the dust, imagining phoenix bridles.
Flying words reflect the immortal roster,
Pouring thoughts match the divine whirlwind.
The emperor's thoughts extend to the green land,
Heavenly writings illuminate the purple sky.
Returning ponds span the sea of brushes,
Level gardens vibrate with lines of verse.
Wishing to respond to the double-wheel melody,
Resonant and vast, harmonizing with the Nine Sháo.
"Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Edict Establishing Crown Prince Zhāomíng"
We, in accord with the destined cycle,
Trace the footsteps of former kings,
Thus prolonging the flowing mandate,
Passing it down for ten thousand generations.
All officials agree that entrusting the heir,
Is foremost for any state.
Since wise rulers of old,
Down to recent times,
None have failed to establish a crown prince and designate an heir,
To guard the vessel and inherit the ancestral temple.
Having broadly gathered various opinions,
And deeply considered the seven-hundred-year legacy,
We establish this young and tender one,
To uphold and match the ancestral shrine.
Chénghuá Palace begins to open,
Chóngxián Hall can endure forever.
The boundless celebration,
Is not Ours alone.
Grace moistens with abundant favor,
Reaching far and wide.
Also "Edict Establishing Prince of Jìn'ān as Crown Prince"
Without utmost fairness, one cannot rule the world;
Without broad love, one cannot oversee all within the seas.
Thus Yáo yielded to Shùn,
Granting only to virtue.
King Wén passed over Bó Yìkǎo and established King Wǔ,
Reaching to heaven and earth,
Shining to the four corners.
Now Tàizōng stands desolate,
The steps of heaven are difficult,
Pure customs remain stifled,
The common people are not yet settled.
Unless one is discerning and wise,
Truly civil and martial,
How can one bear the weight of the divine vessel?
Succeed to the dignity of the dragon chart?
Prince of Jìn'ān, Gāng,
Virtuous in conduct, keen within,
Majesty and kindness proclaimed abroad.
All lords praise his excellence,
The whole land rests its heart upon him.
Let Gāng be established as crown prince.
May a century overcome remnants of evil,
Spreading lasting blessings.
A generation of benevolence thereafter,
Eternally securing the great enterprise.
Later Wèi Wēn Zǐshēng "Edict of Amnesty on Emperor Zhuāng's Birth of the Crown Prince"
For a state, the three excellences,
Belong to the worthy heir.
Main branch for a hundred generations,
Righteousness focuses on succession.
We, responding to heaven, continue the mandate,
Holding the chart, receiving the tally.
The auspicious legacy renewed,
Divined years to be long.
This fine month, auspicious day,
The imperial prince is born.
Colored clouds reflect the sun,
Divine light illuminates the hall.
Just opening Bówàng,
Soon to raise the dragon tower.
Far and near rejoice together,
Humans and spirits share delight.
Sòng Xiè Zhuāng "Memorial to the Supreme Emperor on the Crown Prince's Capping Ceremony"
Humbly considering His Highness the Crown Prince,
Brightness succeeding heaven,
Worthy heir serving as deputy.
Upholding law, refining self,
Splendor naturally far-reaching.
Music to cultivate the inner,
Ritual to govern the outer.
The three excellences flourish richly,
Virtue perfected, teaching revered.
Today, auspicious hour,
Clearly adding the capping ceremony.
Facing the spirits' expectations,
Sharing the joy of the upper school.
All under heaven, throughout the world,
None do not leap with joy.
Also "Memorial to the Empress Dowager on the Crown Prince's Capping Ceremony"
The Li trigram's light succeeds the Zhèn,
Pivot radiance accompanies the pole.
Nurturing fame at Dōnghuá,
Flying splendor in the upper sequence.
Music master sings of customs,
Director of Education praises virtue.
Clear and bright, a divine mirror,
Gentle and cultured in person.
Choosing the day, selecting the hour,
Clearly preparing the capping ceremony.
Enhancing the teachings of the three kings,
Entrusted with the weight of Shàohǎi.
Liáng Shěn Yuē "Memorial of Thanks for the Crown Prince's Initial Appointment"
Your subject is truly immature and ignorant,
Lacking in gentle culture.
Unfamiliar with the teachings of the three excellences,
Not yet learned in the rituals of the four studies.
Though inquiring after peace within the palace,
Arises from sincere heart,
Yet attending meals at the chamber door,
Cannot yet be done repeatedly.
Then descending imperial grace,
Early receiving the grand ceremony.
Deputy to the celestial pole,
Guardian of the vessel for the ancestral temple.
Reflecting on following childish will,
As if facing icy abyss.
Memorial by Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng on Presenting the Separate Biography and Literary Collection of Crown Prince Zhāomíng
As for occupying the position of Shàoyáng,
and presiding over the rules of succession to the ancestral temple,
verbal praise is considered beautiful,
with only Qǐ and Sòng being praised.
Since then,
it has rarely been heard of.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng,
endowed with the qualities of benevolence and sagacity,
possessed the capacity of innate knowledge.
Filial piety and respect were both perfected,
gentleness and reverence were embodied in his person.
Like the bright moon flowing westward,
he showed literary talent from a young age.
With ceremonial dances at the eastern school,
he cultivated the virtues of a worthy heir in his maturity.
He did not rely on the two Shū,
nor trouble the four Hào.
The Hǔbēn felt ashamed of their classical learning,
and the Zhìnáng were humbled by his care and protection.
Was it only that Bówàng extended hospitality to guests?
Shòuchūn could compose fu,
and asked questions to resolve doubts like Zǎo Jù.
He wrote admonitions against aggression, and that was all!
How can we recover the broken jade?
The fallen star cannot be continued,
the esteemed position of the Guó heir,
the arts of Wàiyáng left no trace.
His status compared to the Zhōu heir,
the carriage to Gōushān never returned.
Your subject, being unworthy,
presumptuously serves as the Míngliǎng.
Entering and exiting the Tónglóng Gate,
I gaze upon past precedents.
Thinking to extol his splendid example,
and proclaim the record of his virtuous words.
I have respectfully compiled the separate biography and literary collection of Crown Prince Zhāomíng,
and request that they be stored in the Yángé,
and kept within the ancestral temple.
May they forever illuminate his abundant achievements,
and serve to manifest his great glory.
Memorial by Wáng Bāo of Zhōu on Behalf of the Officials Requesting the Establishment of a Crown Prince
Your subjects have heard that repeated thunder resides in Zhèn,
spring corresponds to the rites of safeguarding the vessel.
Míngliǎng acts as Lí,
Shàoyáng continues the enterprise of double brilliance.
Thus, the three excellences illuminate virtue.
The fortune of the sacrifices can prosper.
Once there is a worthy heir,
the state's foundation is eternally secure.
As for Xuānyuán obtaining surnames,
Gāoyáng's talented sons,
the superior heir awaits the worthy,
the front star's position remains empty.
Duke Wén of Lǔ,
personally occupies the position of primary son,
and is suited to be the heir apparent.
All officials look up to him as a model,
and all lords regard him with reverence.
We, your subjects, have deliberated,
and request that he be established as Crown Prince.
His duties should honor supervision and governance,
his education should rely on careful instruction.
He should inquire after peace at the bedchamber door,
and oversee meals in the imperial tent.
Admonitions for the Crown Prince by Wáng Bāo of Zhōu
Heaven gives birth to the multitudes of people,
and establishes shepherds to rule them.
All achieve splendid accomplishments,
manifesting the kingly measure.
Thus, with reverence and clarity,
he grandly inherits the precious throne.
Re-knotting the cords of the earth,
and again rectifying the steps of heaven.
The benevolent ruler hands down the line,
and the worthy heir continues the body.
Adorning the correct, departing from brilliance,
promoting the subtle, heaven opens the way.
Renowned reputation and esteemed fame,
hearing the odes and hearing the rites.
In attendance, he is called the army supervisor,
in residence, he is called the state overseer.
In autumn, he communicates dreams,
in the spring palace, he cultivates virtue.
Huán Róng presented books,
Xún Yōu observed the rules.
The primary son becomes a scholar,
his rank matches that of a minister.
In ancient times, in Zhōu and Hàn,
kinsmen and worthies protected and assisted.
Court robes at the bedchamber door,
turning the carriage to build the chamber.
Zhèngyáng occupies the position,
the tall branches follow the father's way.
What subjects and sons revere,
is loyalty and filial piety as treasures.
Do not say that because one resides in honor,
fortune and calamity have no gate.
Do not rely on kinship and worth,
the kingly way has no partiality.
Act without action, yet have concerns,
begin by attending to affairs.
Diminish it yet again,
and preserving it also preserves it whole.
There is no going that does not return,
no level ground without a slope.
Beautiful illnesses and sweet words,
rarely do they not bring encumbrance.
To discern the wise is difficult,
to know people is not easy.
Dwelling in the chamber, do good,
do not waste a fraction of shade.
Preserve what is about to perish,
secure what is in danger.
If the spirits hear without confusion,
heavenly portents will then be忌惮.
Wénchāng is manifested in the front star,
the libationer arises from safeguarding the vessel.
All officials in charge of admonitions,
dare to inform the gatekeepers and attendants.
Crown Princess, Fourth
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"Fēi means mate.
What does 'mate' mean?
It means to pair together.
In ancient times, in the Son of Heaven's rear palace,
both principal and secondary wives were called fēi."
The Shǐjì states:
"Huángdì had four fēi,
Dì Kù had four fēi,
Yú Shùn had two fēi."
Zhōu referred to the principal wife of the Son of Heaven as Wánghòu.
Qín, calling the emperor Huángdì, thus called her Huánghòu,
and referred to the principal wife of the Crown Prince as fēi,
which Hàn followed.
The Hànshū‧Wàiqí Zhuàn states:
"The Crown Prince has a fēi,
has liángdì,
has rúzǐ.
Wives and concubines total three ranks.
After Wèi and Jìn,
all followed this."
Gold Seal Jade Pendant
Shěn Yuē's Sòngshū states:
"The Crown Princess,
gold seal with turtle knob,
dark red ribbon,
wears a jade pendant."
Also, Zhāng Chǎng's Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is a woven ceremonial belt and white jade pendant."
Dragon Pillow Duck Lamp
The Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is one lacquered dragon-head hairpin pillow,
with silver floral ring buttons included."
Also states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is one gold-coated linked tray duck lamp."
Patterned Shoes Flowered Basket
The Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is one pair of crimson ground patterned shoes."
Also states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there are two lacquered flowered baskets."
Turtle Knob Sparrow Inlay
"Turtle knob" matter seen above in the "gold seal" note.
The Dōnggōng Gùshì states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is one set of同心 sparrow inlay."
Ceremonial Belt Patterned Ribbon
"Ceremonial belt" seen in the "jade pendant" note.
Also states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
there is a crimson ground woven patterned ribbon."
Four-View Carriage Nine-Inlay Case
The Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì states:
"When the Crown Prince takes a fēi,
a four-view carriage,
with feather canopies and front and rear sections of鼓吹 music, one set each."
Also states:
"One set of bùyáo hair ornament,
contained in a nine-inlay case."
Investiture by Divination
The "Jìn Qǐ Jū Zhù" states:
"In the first year of Yuándì's Tàixīng,
the sovereign sat upon his throne and decreed that Yǔ, consort of the Jìn prince, be appointed Crown Princess."
Shěn Yuè's "Sòng Shū" states:
"Empress Jiāng, the Empress Dowager to be removed,
was named Jiǎnguī.
She was from Kǎochéng, Jìyáng,
granddaughter of Zhìshēn, long-serving historian of the Northern Central General.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
the Taizong sought out a crown princess,
but both her father and grandfather had passed away,
and her brother was still a child.
Their house had no strong shelter.
Yet by means of divination, the results were most auspicious,
and she was appointed Crown Princess. "
Jǐng Hall - Painted Hall
The "Hàn Shū" states:
"When Yuándì was the Crown Prince,
after Sīmǎ Liángdí's death,
the Crown Prince grieved to the point of illness.
Xuāndì ordered the Empress to select daughters of the inner palace attendants who could comfort and serve the Crown Prince.
Among them was Wáng Jìn's daughter Zhèngjūn,
who was among five chosen,
wearing only a crimson-edged garment,
an outer robe of the Ta-Ye sect.
She was sent to live in the Crown Prince’s palace,
and was seen in the Jǐng Hall.
She was favored, became pregnant,
and was established as the Crown Princess.
In the Jiǎ Observatory's Painted Hall, she gave birth to a son,
who became Chéngdì."
The Painted Hall,
was a hall within the Crown Prince's palace.
Cheers of Longevity - Five Merits
The "Hàn Shū" states:
"The daughter of Chēqí General Xǔ Jiā
was chosen as a match for the Crown Prince.
The sovereign ordered that she be personally escorted by a trusted court eunuch to the Crown Prince's residence,
and upon return, he reported the Crown Prince's delight.
Yuándì joyfully said to those around:
'Pour wine and congratulate me!'
The attendants all shouted 'Long live!'
The Crown Prince was enthroned as Emperor,
becoming Chéngdì.
The consort was made Empress."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Wǔdì married Yáng and bore Huìdì,
initially arranging a marriage for the Crown Prince,
which was long undecided.
The sovereign wished to marry a daughter of Wèi Guàn,
but Empress Yáng wanted a daughter of Jiǎ Chōng.
Chōng's wife Guō was a notorious jealous woman,
so the sovereign said:
'Wèi's daughter has five merits,
while Jiǎ's daughter has five demerits.
The daughter of the Wèi family
is of noble lineage and has many sons,
is upright and fair;
the daughter of the Jiǎ family
is born of jealousy and has few children,
is ugly and short with dark complexion.'
Lady Guō bribed Empress Yáng,
and thus the marriage with Jiǎ’s daughter was concluded,
leading to the later turmoil in Jìn."
The Daughter of the Minister of Works and the Birth of the Lord of Xīn'ān
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Liú Yáo and Wáng Mí raided Luò,
taking the imperial consorts.
The Crown Prince Mǐnhuái’s consort drew a blade against the enemy and said:
'I am the daughter of the Minister of Works,
the Crown Princess,
if I must die, then I die,
but I will never be the wife of bandits.'
The bandits then killed her."
It also states:
"Empress Ānxī, née Wáng, styled Shénshòu,
was the daughter of High Minister Wáng Xiàn,
whose birth gave rise to the Lord of Xīn'ān, hence being an aunt to Emperor Ān.
Since Empress Xiàowǔ was orphaned young,
with no brothers or sisters,
she was appointed Crown Princess for Emperor Ān.
Xiàowǔ arranged the engagement of Crown Princess Wáng,
during which the full court gathered at the residence of the Lord of Xīn'ān,
supervised by the Secretariat director Wáng Cāozhī."
Hú Yuánfàn's "Poem for the Ceremony of the Crown Prince's Consort"
The elegance of the imperial son is unparalleled,
the rites honoring the Crown Princess are grand.
The sound of drums accompanies the celestial observatory,
the sound of flutes encircles the adorned sedan.
The intense divine fragrance fills the air,
vibrant colors of clouds float above.
Decorated brocades line the heavens,
joy fills the imperial realm.
The gold chambers still glow with light,
the jade tree resonates with heaven’s love.
The moonlit path adorns return journeys,
starlit embankments stir returning gems.
The Emperor's grace flows from the purple pole,
noble traditions await kind instruction.
The benevolent waves benefit all ranks,
the glory surpasses a thousand years,
esteemed guests announced and close kin,
celebrate like immortal deities.
Sacred literature flies from holy pen,
heavenly music plays in divine harmony.
The canal reflects auspicious scenes,
literary structures birth lucky vapors.
Lesser officials unite with all creatures,
dance in joy for Yáo's age."
Péi Shŏuzhēn's "Poem for the Ceremony of the Crown Prince's Consort"
The jade ornaments ascend the blue palace,
abundant blossoms descend upon the purple microcosm.
Like peaches and plums blooming,
like phoenixes soaring.
The golden house symbolizes purity,
the jade tower rises to honor.
Colorful tassels flutter over the green seats,
works of feathers grace the grand robe.
The cloud path transports the crimson chariot,
the celestial mirror turns in the Heavenly Ford,
the immortal pearl reflects as the chariot rests.
The double moons cast their glow,
at the garden, a harmonious feast gathers,
the host's abode filled with joyous delight.
Music and dance bring imperial fragrance,
pins and robes pay tribute to the imperial celebration.
Cloudy masses soften morning light,
dew evaporates in the morning sun.
The celestial phenomena beautiful,
wise writings and words fragrant,
the jade courtyard scatters autumn hues,
silver palaces give rise to evening coolness.
The grand peace surpasses ancient times,
longevity and joy boundless."
Táng Tàizōng's "Edict for Appointing Sū Dǎn's Daughter as Crown Princess"
Pairing virtue with a worthy heir,
requires a nation's elite women.
To be the match for the heir apparent,
it is proper to choose from a crowned family.
Sū Dǎn, Vice Director of the Secretariat's eldest daughter,
comes from a line of eminent officials,
and their family inheritance is righteousness.
With natural gentleness and propriety,
innate calmness becomes her nature.
Her training was highlighted in national history,
her reputation spread across the nation.
Her rightful position is by the heir's side,
indeed fitting the courtly standards.
She is suitable to be Crown Princess,
let the respective officials prepare the ceremonies and appointment,
and the responsible parties execute."
Táng Tàizōng's "Documents on the Crown Princess Appointment"
You, Sū Dǎn's eldest daughter, Vice Director of the Secretariat,
your family is honored and crowned.
Your cultivation completes the ceremonial instruction,
chastity and submission come naturally.
Your words and presence are consistent and proper,
you are a fitting match for the Spring Palace.
You truly align with the three virtues,
and it is said:
"A consort is a keeper of virtue."
So you will bring flourishing to many generations,
and fulfill this exceptional ceremony.
Reverent of national models,
it is therefore commanded you are appointed Crown Princess.
Proceed with this honor!
May you carry this command with brightness,
and exercise due care."
Xiè Zhuāng of the Sòng dynasty, "Elegiac Memorial for the Crown Princess"
The pillars hold the cassia offerings,
The courtyard is solemn with the dragon-hearse.
The wind sinks along the state road,
Clouds rise over the suburban gates.
The emperor grieves that the gathered tassels veil the colors,
Mourns that the deputy veils extinguish splendor.
The journey’s light already dims,
The long river again slopes.
Looking back, he speaks:
"Even jade disks may shatter,
But fragrant virtue never fades."
He cuts plain silk, trims bamboo slips,
And entrusts them to the historian.
The words say:
"Huò peaks fall short of heaven,
Qián streams congeal the Milky Way.
Auspice sprouts from tóng jade tokens,
Blessings shine in golden tallies.
Nurturing radiance in the imperial precincts,
Flying fragrance among noble gates.
Secret grace bestowed in the valley,
Rising tones gathered in the grove.
The moon’s shadow nears fullness,
The younger sister’s sleeves, virtuous and fine.
She left the curtains of the spring palace,
To bear the basket in Shàoyáng.
Five generations spread elegance,
Four teachings drew forth light.
Luxuriant like fragrant sachets,
Graceful as jade companions.
Pure eminence now departs afar,
Baleful influences gather force.
Facing blossoms, the kingfisher hues cease,
At brilliance, the orchids are gathered.
Double halls echo with sound,
Long corridors knot with cold.
Ritual shifts to empty offerings,
The air changes, robes of mourning appear.
In the central courtyard, grasses grow lush,
On the steps, fireflies flit.
Grief winds through the mansion lanes,
Pain overflows the morning palace gates."
Wáng Dìwǔ
The Yìjīng states: "The former kings established ten thousand states and drew the feudal lords close."
The Shǐjì says:
"Huángdì established left and right grand overseers
to oversee the ten thousand states."
The Yáodiǎn states:
"Harmonizing the ten thousand regions."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Túshān,
those holding jade and silk numbered ten thousand states.
The number 'ten thousand states'
likely refers to enfeoffing both kin and worthies.
The Xià dynasty enumerated nine provinces,
instituted five zones,
established five ranks of nobility,
and divided land into three grades.
Dukes and marquises had domains of one hundred lǐ square,
earls seventy lǐ square,
viscounts and barons fifty lǐ square,
those under fifty lǐ were called attached territories.
The Yīn dynasty then had three ranks of nobility;
the Zhōu again enumerated five ranks,
where dukes had domains of five hundred lǐ square,
marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons each differed by one hundred lǐ,
those under one hundred lǐ were attached territories.
All sons and brothers of the king
were enfeoffed accordingly.
The Qín called themselves emperor,
abolished the five-rank system in favor of commanderies and counties,
and sons and brothers became commoners.
The Hàn arose,
establishing two ranks of nobility.
The greater were kings,
the lesser were marquises,
and the title 'king' was termed 'feudal lord king.'
Cài Yōng's Dúduàn states:
"Under the Hàn system,
imperial sons were enfeoffed as kings,
but in essence they were feudal lords.
At the end of the Zhōu, some feudal lords styled themselves kings,
while the Hàn themselves used the title emperor.
Therefore, they added the title 'king' to feudal lords,
collectively naming them feudal lord kings."
In the early Jiànwǔ era of Later Hàn,
Zhū Yù proposed that the land cannot have two kings,
and subjects' ranks should not exceed that of duke,
so all were enfeoffed as commandery dukes.
In the seventeenth year, they reverted to the old title of king.
The Wèi changed the enfeoffment to commandery king.
The Jìn again enfeoffed as state kings.
From the Sòng and Qí onward, all were enfeoffed as commanderies.
The Suí restored enfeoffment as state dukes."
The above all seen in the Qí Zhíyí and the Wǔdài Shǐzhì.
Línzhǐ Quǎnyá
The Máoshī states:
"The feet of the qílín,
the earnest, faithful prince.
Ah, the qílín!"
The annotation says:
"Zhǐ means foot.
The qílín is trustworthy and conforms to ritual,
coming on foot.
Zhēnzhēn means sincere and generous.
Yūjiē is an exclamation of sighing."
The Hànshū states:
"The sons and brothers of Emperor Gāo
were interlocked like dog's teeth,
forming what is called a rock-solid defense."
Pánshí Wéichéng
"Pánshí" see annotation under "Quǎnyá."
The Máoshī states:
"Upholding virtue brings peace,
the patriarchal sons are the walls."
Fānpíng Huángjiā Wéihàn Dìshì
The Wèizhì, Cáo Zhí zhuàn states:
"Upon Zhí's initial enfeoffment, the edict said:
'Herewith the green altar,
enfeoffed in the eastern lands,
to screen and protect the imperial house,
as a bulwark for Wèi.'"
The Jìn Bǎiguān Biǎo Zhù states:
"Enfeoffing imperial sons and royal kinsmen as kings
is to uphold and support the imperial house."
The Shī states:
"The great states are its pillars."
Dàotǔ Jūmáo Jīnxǐ Tuóniǔ
Cài Yōng's Dúduàn states:
"The Son of Heaven's Grand Altar of Soil
is a mound of five-colored earth.
Under the Hàn system,
when the crown prince was enfeoffed as a king,
he received earth from the Son of Heaven's Grand Altar of Soil
in the color corresponding to his enfeoffment's direction.
For the east, he received green earth;
for other directions, their respective colors,
wrapped with white cogon grass.
He took it back to his state to establish his altar,
hence it was called 'cogon-earth.'"
Kǒng Ānguó's annotation on the Shàngshū states:
"When the king enfeoffs with the five-colored earth for the altar,
he cuts the earth of the corresponding directional color and gives it,
so they may establish their altar.
Covered with yellow earth,
wrapped with white cogon grass.
The grass is for purity,
the yellow represents the king covering and sheltering the four directions."
The Hànshū Jiùyí states:
"Feudal lord kings have a gold seal
with a camel knob."
The above comprehensively records the feudal system.
Èr Nán Liǎng Dōng
The Máoshī Xù states:
"Zhōunán and Shàonán
are the way of correct beginnings,
the foundation of kingly transformation."
Pān Yuè's Xīzhēng Fù states:
"I went to Ānyáng,
speaking of ascending Shǎn’s walls.
How splendid and distant!
This land of old.
Truly it was where the duties of Zhōu and Shào were divided,
where the winds of the Èr Nán intermingled.
The Línzhǐ finds faith in the Guānjū,
the Zōuyú responds to the Quècháo."
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"Xiànpíng King Cāng of Dōngpíng,
in youth had the virtue of filial piety and brotherly love,
broad-minded, benevolent, and magnanimous.
In the second year of Zhōngyuán,
Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away.
Emperor Míng’s edict said:
'Dōngpíng King Cāng,
broad and resourceful,
can be entrusted with a six-foot orphan,
facing great trials without being swayed.'
Therefore, appoint Cāng as General of Agile Cavalry."
The Wèizhì states:
"The Marquis of Línzī excelled in literary composition,
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as King of Dōng'ē."
Lǔ and Wèi, Liáng and Chǔ.
The "Zǔo Zhuàn" states:
"Guǎn, Cài, Chéng, Huò,
Lǔ, Wèi, Máo, Dān.
Gào, Yōng, Cáo, Téng,
Bì, Yuán, Fēng, Xún.
These were the manifestations of civil virtue."
The "Hànshū" states:
"At the beginning of the establishment of Hàn,
the land within the seas was newly settled,
and there were few of the same surname,
so territories were divided,
and ranks of two classes were established.
The sons and brothers of the king were honored,
and nine states were greatly established.
They possessed Guī and Mèng,
which became Liáng and Chǔ."
Jìn's tóng yè and Wèi's zǐ cái.
The "Shǐjì" states:
"Táng Shūyú was
King Chéng's younger brother.
King Chéng was playing with Shūyú,
cutting a leaf from a phoenix tree into the shape of a jade tablet,
and used it to enfeoff Shūyú.
Historian Yì then said,
'Please choose a day to appoint Shūyú.'
King Chéng replied,
'It is just play.'
Historian Yì said,
'The Son of Heaven does not speak in jest.'
Thus, Shūyú was enfeoffed in Táng,
and later became Jìn.
Therefore, "The Mào Poetry" says,
'This is Jìn now called Táng.'" It is also stated:
"Wèi Kāngshū's given name Fēng,
was Zhoū Wǔ Wáng's half-brother.
Enfeoffed as Wèi's ruler,
residing between Hé and Qí.
Zhōu Gōng feared Kāngshū's youth,
thereby admonishing Kāngshū,
composing the Zǐ Cái chapter,
saying the way of governance is like a carpenter handling wood!'"
The above lists the enfeoffed states.
Sharing a Room, Riding Together in a Carriage.
Fàn Yè's "Hòu Hànshū" states:
In "The Biography of Prince Qìng of Qīnghé," it is stated:
"At first, the emperor decreed to the empress,
commanding that her clothing be on par with the crown prince.
The crown prince was affectionate,
they shared a room indoors,
and rode together in a carriage outdoors." "The Hànshū" states:
"Huáinán Prince Cháng,
was the youngest son of Gāo Dì.
When Emperor Xiàowén ascended the throne,
he considered himself the closest relation.
Arrogant and often disobeying the law,
yet the emperor forgave him leniently.
In the third year of service,
he acted most freely.
Accompanying the emperor into the park for hunting,
he rode together with the emperor in the same carriage."
Entering the Northern Palace for Lodging, Thus Staying in the National Residence.
"Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"In 'The Biography of Prince Qìng of Qīnghé,' it is stated:
'In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he moved to the Northern Palace, Zhāng Dé Hall,
to discuss at Bái Hǔguan,
and Qìng was permitted to enter and lodge.' " "The Han Shu: Xuān Yuán Six Kings Account" states:
"Emperor Chéng had no heir,
and his body was often unwell.
Dìngtáo's Prince Gòng came to court,
and the emperor said to Prince Gòng:
'I have no son,
life and death are not predictable.
If one day something happens,
we may not meet again,
you must remain and serve me!'
Thus, he stayed in the national residence,
attending to the emperor day and night,
gaining much intimacy and respect."
Treated as Family, Rank Equal to the Emperor's Sons.
"The Hànshū" states:
"Qí Dàohuì Prince Wáng,
paid a court visit in the second year of Xiàohuì.
The emperor and Prince Qí dined in front of the empress dowager,
with Xiàohuì regarding Prince Qí as a brother,
seating him above in observance of etiquette as if he were family.
Also, Chǔ Yuán Prince Jiāo,
was a younger brother of Gāo Dì.
From the reign of Emperor Wéndì,
Jiāo studied poetry,
attending to internal matters.
Emperor Wéndì honored and favored the sons of Yuán Prince,
ranking them on par with the emperor's sons."
Driving a Cloudy-Mica Carriage, Setting Up Bell Racks.
Fù Chàng's "Jìn Gōngqīng Ritual Order" states:
"Ānpíng Prince Fú borrowed the yellow axe,
with feathered cover front and back.
Raising nine banner streams,
driving a team of four horses,
employing a cloudy-mica carriage." "Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Dōnghǎi Prince Jiāng,
ruled over five commanderies and twenty-nine counties,
with tribute income surpassing the other princes.
He enjoyed favors and sponsorships,
unmatched in the realm,
possessing the tiger's bravery, hairstyle, palace bells, and racks."
The above demonstrates the favor and affection shown to the princes.
Loving Books and Delighting in Kindness.
"The Hànshū" states:
"Huáinán Prince Ān was fond of books,
skilled at playing the qin.
He did not like hunting." It also states:
"Héjiān Prince Dé,
pursued learning and cherished antiquity.
When obtaining good books from others,
he would gladly transcribe and share them.
Retaining the originals,
he rewarded them with gold to attract them." "Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Dōngpíng Prince Cāng,
possessed the virtues of filial piety and friendship from an early age,
being broad-hearted, benevolent, and elegant.
With beautiful beard and hair,
the Bright Emperor once leisurely asked the prince:
'When at home,
what brings the greatest joy?'
Cāng replied:
'Doing good brings the greatest joy.' "
Chǔ Poetry and Pèi's Yì.
"The Hànshū" states:
"Chǔ Yuán Prince Jiāo, courtesy name Xiàoyóu,
was the younger brother of Gāozǔ by the same father.
Fond of books,
skilled in many arts.
Yuán Prince excelled in reading poetry,
and all his sons studied poetry,
known as:
'Yuán Prince's Poetry. '" "The Xù Hànshū" states:
"Pèi Xiàn Prince Fǔ,
was serious and proud by nature,
possessing authority.
Fond of classic texts,
skillful in explaining 'Jīngshì Yì'."
Ants Sealing Holes, Elephant Boats.
"Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Pèi Xiàn Prince Fǔ excelled in 'Jīngshì Yì'.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng,
there was a drought,
the emperor performed divination at the sacred terrace,
using the 'Zhōu Yì Lín' for prediction.
The line read:
'Ants seal the entrance to their holes,
great rain is coming.'
The emperor asked Fǔ,
and Fǔ replied:
'Kǎn above Gèn below,
represents water;
mountains produce clouds and rain,
ants reside in hills,
knowing rain is imminent.'" "The Wèi Zhì" states:
"Dèng's lamenting King Cāngshū,
was perceptive and discerning from youth.
Sūn Quán once brought a giant elephant,
and Tàizǔ wanted to know its weight.
Cāngshū said:
'Place the elephant in a large boat,
and mark the waterline,
then weigh the cargo to load it,
thus knowing its weight.'"
Time for Eating, Seven Steps.
"The Hànshū" states:
"Upon entering to pay homage, Huáinán Prince Ān began writing commentary on 'Lí Sāo.'
He received the edict in the morning,
presenting his work by mealtime."
Liú Yìqìng's "World's Speech" states:
"Wèi's Emperor Wén ordered the Eastern Ē Prince to compose a poem in seven steps,
failing which harsh punishment would follow.
He composed the poem:
'Boiling beans with bean stalks,
the beans in the pot weep.
From the same root were they born,
why must they be cooked so hastily?'
Emperor Wén appeared greatly ashamed."
Responded to the Three Yong Palaces; Discussed the Five Classics
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"The King of Héjiān, Xiàn Wáng,
was a son of Emperor Jǐng.
He cultivated learning and revered antiquity.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ, Xiàn Wáng came to court,
presented refined music,
and responded to inquiries at the Three Yong Palaces.
Yìng Shào's annotation states:
'The Bìyōng, the Míngtáng,
and the Língtái.'" The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* states:
"Pèi Xiàn Wáng, Fǔ,
was by nature fond of the Classics.
He compiled and discussed the Classics, commentaries, charts, and apocrypha,
composing the *General Discussion of the Five Classics*.
From the time he received his fiefdom until his death,
he followed and upheld laws and regulations,
never once violating prohibitions,
and was praised as a worthy king."
Běihǎi Excelled at Calligraphy; Dōngpíng Was Skilled in Odes
Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Běihǎi Jìng Wáng, Mù,
excelled at large-character calligraphy.
It was considered a standard model in his time.
When he was bedridden with illness,
the Emperor, while on horseback, ordered him to compose ten pieces of cursive script on wooden slips."
It also states:
"Dōngpíng Wáng, Cāng,
once presented the 'Ode to the Restoration of Emperor Guāngwǔ',
which the Emperor greatly admired."
Coins and Silk to Aid the State; Rent and Salaries to Relieve the People
The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* states:
"The King of Dōnghǎi, Qiáng's grandson, the King of Qīng, Sù,
was by nature modest and frugal.
During the Yǒngchū era,
because the Western Qiāng were not yet pacified,
he presented twenty million coins;
during the Yuánchū era,
he presented ten thousand bolts of silk to aid the state."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Qí Wáng, Yōu,
within his state, for civil and military officials,
down to the common soldiers,
those who did not receive official provisions or rewards due to legal statutes,
he all used his own salary and taxes to provide for those who were ill or had died.
When there were floods or droughts,
he increased the land tax by twelve percent,
to relieve the people of his state.
He would only collect the original amount when a bountiful year arrived."
The above concerns the talents and abilities of kings.
Winding Tower; Level Terrace
Cáo Zhí's *Yú Bīn Fù* states:
"Moved by the blazing heat of the summer sun,
I wander in the coolness of the winding tower."
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"Liáng Xiào Wáng expanded the city of Suīyáng for seventy *lǐ*,
extensively built palaces and chambers,
and constructed elevated walkways.
From the palace, they connected continuously to the Level Terrace for over forty *lǐ*."
Orchid Slope; Cassia Mountain
Cáo Zhí's poem states:
"The bright moon purifies the clear scene,
the constellations are arrayed unevenly.
Autumn orchids cover the long slope,
vermilion blossoms emerge from the green pool."
Wáng Yì's *Preface to Liú Ān's 'Summoning the Recluse'* states:
"'Summoning the Recluse'
was composed by the King of Huáinán.
In the past, the King of Huáinán was erudite and fond of antiquity,
summoning and welcoming the talented and outstanding scholars of the world.
The group of the Eight Lords,
moved and admiring his virtue, submitted to his benevolence.
Each exhausted their wisdom and talent,
composing writings and chapters,
separately creating lyrics and rhapsodies,
grouped by category.
Therefore, some are called 'Lesser Mountain',
some 'Greater Mountain',
their meaning is similar to the *Shī* having the 'Lesser Odes' and 'Greater Odes'.
The lyrics say:
'Cassia trees grow thick in the mountain's depths,
towering and intertwined, their branches entwined.'"
Gibbon Cliff; Wild Goose Pond
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
"Liáng Xiào Wáng was fond of the pleasures of palaces, chambers, parks, and gardens.
He built the Yàohuá Palace.
He constructed the Rabbit Garden.
Within the garden was Bǎishì Mountain,
on the mountain were gibbons descending.
There was the Wild Goose Pond,
and within the pond were Crane Islet and Duck Shallows."
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Zhǎo
means pond."
Elegant Bamboo; Intertwined Cassia
Méi Chéng's *Rabbit Garden Rhapsody* states:
"Tall bamboos, elegant and graceful, flank the ground."
(The Rabbit Garden
was Liáng Xiào Wáng's garden.)
"'Intertwined cassia' see the annotation under 'Cassia Mountain'."
Tortoiseshell Mat; Glass Bowl
Liú Zhēn's *Preface to the 'Melon Rhapsody'* states:
"While at Cáo Zhí's seat,
the kitchen staff presented melons.
Zhí ordered a rhapsody to be composed,
urging immediate completion.
Its lines said:
'Spread the ivory mat,
perfume the tortoiseshell feast.
Lean on the crimson jade table,
pour from the pale green jade cup.'" Bào Zhào's *Song of the Huáinán King's Palace Envoy* states:
"The King of Huáinán,
fond of long life.
Ingesting elixirs, refining *qì*, reading immortal scriptures.
Glass medicine bowl, ivory tray,
golden tripod, jade spoon, compounding divine cinnabar."
Feast at Pínglè; Gaze at Gāotáng
Cáo Zhí's poem states:
"Cockfighting on the eastern suburb road,
racing horses among the tall catalpas.
All spectators praised it as excellent,
the many experts acknowledged my skill.
Returning, we feast at Pínglè,
fine wine, ten thousand coins per gallon."
Sòng Yù's *Gāotáng Rhapsody* states:
"In the past, King Xiāng of Chǔ was traveling at the Yúnmèng Terrace,
and gazed at the Gāotáng Tower."
The above concerns the residences of kings.
Forget-Worry Tower; Think-of-Immortals Terrace
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
"Liáng Xiào Wáng traveled to the Forget-Worry Tower,
gathered various wandering scholars,
and had each compose a rhapsody."
Gě Hóng's *Biographies of Immortals* states:
"Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán, was fond of matters concerning immortals and alchemy.
Thereupon, the Eight Lords went to welcome him,
and they ascended the Think-of-Immortals Terrace."
Establishing Lodges; Building Palaces
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
"The King of Héjiān, Dé,
built the Rìhuá Palace,
and established over twenty guest lodges to receive scholars."
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"King Zhāo of Yān ascended the throne.
He humbled himself and offered generous gifts to summon worthy men.
He said to Guō Kuí:
'If I truly obtain worthy scholars,
to together avenge the former ruler's disgrace,
that is my wish!'
Kuí said:
'If the King truly desires to seek scholars,
I request that you start with Kuí.
How much more for those worthier than Kuí,
would they consider a thousand *lǐ* far?'
Thereupon, King Zhāo built a palace for Kuí with earthen walls and treated him as a teacher.
Scholars then competed to go to Yān."
Broad Thoroughfare; Jiéshí Palace
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"Zōu Shì,
one of the various Zōus of Qí,
also extensively adopted Zōu Yǎn's techniques to compose writings.
Thereupon, the King of Qí praised him.
From Chúnyú Kūn downwards,
all were appointed,
called 'Arrayed Great Officers',
and a broad, level thoroughfare was opened for them.
The world said that Qí was able to attract the worthy scholars of the world!" It also states:
"When Zōu Yǎn went to Yān,
the King of Yān built the Jiéshí Palace,
and personally went to treat him as a teacher."
Granting Land and Setting Out Sweet Wine In Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Small," it is said:
"King Xiāng of Chǔ had ascended the Yángyún Terrace,
and ordered his senior officials Jǐng Chāi, Táng Lè, Sòng Yù, and others to compose rhapsodies on the grand.
In the end, Sòng Yù received the reward.
He then composed the 'Rhapsody on the Small.'
The King said:
'Excellent,
I grant you the fields of Yúnmèng.'" The *Book of Hàn* states:
"Initially,
King Yuán treated Shēn Gōng, Bái Gōng, Mù Shēng, and others with respect and courtesy.
Mù Shēng did not enjoy drinking wine,
so whenever King Yuán held a banquet,
he would always set out sweet wine for Mù Shēng.
When King Wù succeeded to the throne,
he also set out sweet wine.
Later, he forgot to set it out,
and Mù Shēng withdrew, saying:
'It is time to leave!'"
Entertaining Guests and Honoring Visitors "Entertaining guests" is explained in the note on "Qū Guān." Also, Cáo Zhí's poem says:
"The noble lord honors and loves his guests,
throughout the feast he knows no weariness.
In the clear night, we roam the Western Garden,
carriage canopies flying as we follow one another."
Táng and Sòng, Yìng and Liú Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Grand" says:
"King Xiāng of Chǔ traveled to the Yángyún Terrace with Táng Lè, Jǐng Chāi, and Sòng Yù.
The King said:
'Those who can speak of the grand shall take the highest seats.'" The *Records of Wèi* states:
"Yìng Yáng, Liú Zhēn, and others
all served as literary officials under the General of the Household for All Purposes.
They were all skilled in composing poetry and rhapsodies,
but later Yìng Yáng, Liú Zhēn, and others passed away."
Emperor Wén's "Letter to Wú Zhì" says:
"In past years, during the epidemic,
many relatives and old friends fell victim to the disaster.
Xú, Chén, Yìng, and Liú
all passed away at the same time."
Traveling to Liáng and Hastening to Yān The *Book of Hàn* states:
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
finding that Emperor Jǐng did not favor men of letters,
and with men like Zōu Yáng from Qí, Méi Chéng from Huáiyīn, and Yán Jì Fūzǐ from Wú,
met them and was pleased,
so he resigned due to illness.
He traveled as a guest to Liáng,
where he was able to reside with various wandering scholars from the feudal states.
After several years,
he composed the 'Rhapsody on Sir Vacuous.'" The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"When King Zhāo of Yān ascended the throne,
he humbled himself and offered generous gifts to attract worthy scholars,
and treated Guō Kuí as his teacher.
Thereupon, Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and so scholars competed to hasten to Yān."
First Holding the Broom and Not Having Time for Shoes The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"When Zōu Yǎn went to Yān,
King Zhāo held a broom and cleared the way ahead.
He requested to be seated among the disciples and receive instruction at the Jiéshí Palace,
personally going to study under him." Gě Hóng's *Biographies of Immortals* states:
"Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán, was fond of Confucian learning.
He also encompassed divination and occult arts,
composing an inner book
that spoke of matters of immortals and the art of alchemy,
titled *Hóngbǎo*.
Thereupon, the Eight Lords went to him.
When the Eight Lords first arrived at the gate,
their temples and eyebrows were white with age,
and the gatekeeper secretly reported this to Ān.
The gatekeeper, thinking to test them with his own ideas, questioned them.
When he finished speaking,
the Eight Lords all transformed into fifteen-year-old youths,
with cloud-like topknots and complexions like peach blossoms.
The gatekeeper was startled and awed,
and reported to the King.
Upon hearing this, the King did not even have time to put on his shoes,
but immediately went out to welcome them,
ascending with them to the Terrace of Longing for Immortals."
Trailing Long Robes and Fluttering Wide Sleeves Zōu Yáng's "Letter to the King of Wú" states:
"I have heard that when the flood dragon raises its head and spreads its wings,
then floating clouds emerge and flow,
and misty rains all gather.
When a sage cultivates his virtue and polishes his integrity,
then wandering scholars
return to righteousness and think of fame.
Now, if I exhaust my wisdom and fully present my counsel,
changing my essence and utmost thoughts,
then there is no state I cannot approach.
If I adorn my simple and crude heart,
then at what king's gate could I not trail my long robes?" The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
"King Xiào of Liáng traveled to the Forgetful Worries Pavilion,
gathered various wandering scholars,
and had each compose a rhapsody.
Zōu Yáng composed the 'Rhapsody on Wine,' saying:
'When a wise king rules the state,
how ample is his leisure!
He summons white-haired ministers,
gathers solemn guests.
With brocade and silk as mats,
rhinoceros horn and jade as weights.
Trailing long robes,
fluttering wide sleeves,
brandishing long tassels.'
The heroic and magnificent scholars
smiled gently and approached."
The above concerns the king's fondness for scholars.
Wèi,
Xiàhóu Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Heir"
Observing the superior form of the two principles,
rooted in the great order of human relations.
No way is more revered than that of the sovereign,
no lineage greater than continuing the sacrifices.
Behold the radiant splendor of the imperial path,
enjoying the primal blessings of heaven and earth.
In the fifth year of Tàihé,
began the flourishing start of the imperial heir.
It was the season of early autumn,
with harmonious and pure air.
As the auspicious hour commenced,
the imperial prince was born.
Then issued the enlightened decree of kindliness,
spreading the abundant grace of deep benevolence.
The final favor reached the common people,
lofty bestowals extended without bounds.
Ennobling the masses to spread virtue,
pardoning capital crimes to show humanity.
The black-haired people sang and rejoiced together,
praying the imperial fortune be renewed daily.
Sòng, Liú Xiàoyì's "Poem on Passing by the Former Garden of King Kāng"
Entering Liáng, I came upon the old garden,
crossing Xuē, I saw the remaining palace.
I still recognize the Pavilion for Summoning the Worthy,
and cherish the custom of loving scholars.
The glorious spirit once soared far,
the hall of balance now overgrown.
The cavern gate remains from the old city,
the sweet pear tree leaves its ancient grove.
Sending off birds, sorrow does not depart,
passing travelers, admiration hard to exhaust.
Pond bamboos merely seem as before,
forest halls dim, already empty.
Distant bridges emerge beyond trees,
far streams hidden, cliffs connecting.
Fragrant flows, the small hill's cassia,
dust rises, the great king's wind.
All things are thus,
this place stirs my heart.
Suí, Xuē Fǎng's "Poem Matching Rhymes at Prince Cháo's Seat, Obtaining the Rhyme 'Yú'"
The terrace platform loves guests and friends,
scholars in wide-sleeved robes, ranked by cap and sash.
Sitting on grass, yearning for late spring,
opening the lapel, nearing early summer.
Tender branches still reveal birds,
fine algae about to hide fish.
Dance sleeves at the flying pavilion,
singing voices from behind patterned lattices.
Do not worry the return road is late,
galloping wheels await the lingering delight.
Suí, Yú Zhòngwén's "Poem in Reply to Prince Qiáo"
The Wú Terrace opens a grand feast,
the Bamboo Garden arrays heroes and worthies.
Jǐng Chāi just entered Chǔ,
Yuè Yì first traveled to Yān.
Breaking corners, wielding the talking staff,
layered mats, words gushing like a spring.
Martial riders first capture writing brushes,
literary scholars rightfully brandish whips.
Jade pegs tune the green qín,
jade disks sink in the green fields.
Evening clouds pale over distant peaks,
setting sun adorns the long river.
Not yet accompanying the eastern pavilion's enjoyment,
alone I chant the Western Garden's verse.
Chǔ Liàng's "Poem Harmonizing with Gazing at the Moon, in Response to Prince Wèi's Instruction"
Tiered verandas ascend the bright moon,
flowing light fills the mid-heaven.
Its hue matches Liáng's pearls afar,
its glow follows Zhào's jade disk round.
Falling shadows by the autumn fan,
empty wheel enters the night feast.
What delights within the eastern lodge,
is preparing to offer the Western Garden's verse.
Lǐ Jìngxuán presents "Poem Harmonizing with Farewell to Prince Lǔ"
Green carriages circle in Chǔ attire,
Red imperial steps await at Qínchuān.
Pearl marshes turn the returning steeds,
Golden banks guide the traveling banners.
Once parted by plains and lowlands,
A thousand lǐ divide wind and mist.
Orioles clamor in Shànglín valley,
Ducks resound before the imperial moat.
Broken clouds shift the Lǔ canopy,
Parting songs stir Shùn’s strings.
Farewell thoughts congeal at the divine screen,
Lofty grace suffuses the tortoiseshell feast.
Looking back, ashamed to disturb the silence,
In vain I gaze up at the heavenly music.
Also presents "Poem Harmonizing with Farewell to Prince Yuè"
Flying canopies return with orchid carriages,
Imperial thoughts linger at Bǎiliáng.
Separate lodges divide Jīng and Wèi,
The homeward road points to Héng and Zhāng.
Border mountains meet the dawn’s hue,
Forest orioles harbor spring light.
The emperor’s concern extends a thousand lǐ,
Words ripple, illuminating the five marshes.
Yáng Sīxuán presents "Poem Harmonizing with Farewell to Prince Lǔ"
Prince Yuán’s poetry spreads broad,
Wénhòu’s favor shines bright.
Crane-canopies stir imperial regard,
Dragon-insignia send off distant travels.
Hánguān’s orioles part from the road,
Bà’s banks guide the moving boat.
Northern woods share garden trees,
Eastern streams overflow the imperial moat.
Birdsong carries feathery fragments,
Steeds’ shadows trail floating blossoms.
Imperial grace pervades the nine realms,
Celestial patterns circle the seven luminaries.
Just about to offer elegant music,
Hairpins and sashes present chiming jades.
Zhāng Dà’ān "Poem Harmonizing with Farewell to Prince Yuè"
A prosperous fief relies on imperial kin,
Linked blossoms deepen royal affection.
Parting hearts grieve at Suī Garden,
Separate paths point to Yèchéng.
Bright sun opens fragrant fields,
Auspicious air gathers in the divine capital.
When will the team of horses enter,
To again pay homage at Chéngmíng?
Liú Huīzhī "Poem Harmonizing with Farewell to Prince Yuè"
Zhōu screens leave the golden hall,
Liáng steeds adjust jade bridles.
Pipe sounds follow broken willows,
Lute rhythms stir flowing waves.
Crane-canopies part, shade hastens,
Dragon-carriages, farewell thoughts abound.
Extending thoughts on the small mountain road,
Still rising is the song of the great wind.
Wèi Chénwáng Cáo Zhí "Ode on the Birth of the Imperial Prince"
Oh, august our sovereign,
Virtuous model of former aims.
Able to continue the Three Sovereigns,
Royal spirit shines in service.
Reverent in suburban temples,
Bright virtue, mindful of caution.
Silently harmonizing, accumulating virtue,
Receiving heaven’s blessings.
Auspicious month, fine hour,
Solemnly born, the holy heir.
Joy from one person,
Ten thousand states rejoice.
Eagerly, ten thousand states,
Anxiously, all living beings.
Receiving fate from our sovereign,
Pacified, they flourish.
Long as subjects and servants,
Heaven’s constant way.
Benevolent sage through generations,
Forever bearing bright brilliance.
Equal year with God on High,
Auspicious, virtuous, and blessed.
Feudal ministers compose odes,
Light flows, virtuous fame.
Táng Tàizōng "Edict Appointing Hànwáng Yuánchāng as Governor of Liángzhōu"
Now, the Yì sets forth establishing benefit,
The Way penetrates the three talents.
The Zuǒzhuàn speaks of supporting assistance,
The enterprise prospers for a hundred generations.
Thus Zhōu’s Lǔ and Wèi,
Strengthened the defensive walls.
Hàn’s Liáng and Zhào,
Able to uphold the cornerstone.
You, from youth, heard teachings of righteousness,
Your talent and insight are intelligent and keen.
Early granted land,
Ritual honors elevated and esteemed.
Far-reaching Nánzhèng,
Girds the western Shǔ.
The gravity of overseeing the region,
Calls for a close relative.
Granted the fief with sacred soil,
Bestowed this canonical edict.
Thus pledge with mountains and rivers,
Forever serve as protective screen.
I have heard it said:
"Serving the ruler with full propriety,
Depends on filial reverence.
Governing with virtue,
Begins with benevolence and kindness.
Thus, whether noble or humble,
Those who follow this gain fame.
Whether past or present,
Those who turn from this sully their conduct.
Go forth, be reverent!
Reject extravagance, embrace frugality,
Distance flatterers, honor the worthy.
Be diligent without slack,
Establish a model for posterity.
Can you not be cautious!"
Also "Edict Appointing Jīngwáng Yuánjǐng as Governor of Jīngzhōu"
Now, the way of establishing offices,
Truly relies on bright virtue.
The principle of conferring ranks,
Must await close kin.
Thus Jìn and Zhèng aided Zhōu,
Their merit displayed in loyal assistance.
Jiān and Píng supported Hàn,
Their enterprise honored in protective screens.
You, whose conduct values loyalty and gravity,
Whose capacity embraces reverence and virtue.
From youth receiving family instruction,
Early receiving court favor.
Benevolence and forbearance known within the domain,
Integrity and fairness recorded in the annals.
Jīnghéng stands as bulwark,
Jiānghàn forms the bounds.
Encompassing the regions of Bā and Hàn,
Striding over the borders of Wú and Yuè.
Lifting the curtain, ever harmonious,
Dividing the jade tablet, all agree.
Therefore, preparing this fine canon,
Granting this auspicious mandate.
Possessing the Chǔ domain,
Generations as Táng’s support.
Can you not be cautious!
"Memorial from the Eight Ministers of the Chén Department of State Affairs Requesting Enfeoffment of Póyángwáng Bóshān"
Your ministers have heard: when the trunk and branches are luxuriant,
The Zhōu dynasty’s enterprise expands.
When the cornerstone is laid,
The Hàn dynasty’s plan extends far.
Thus able to harmonize and propagate the five phases,
And set a model for a hundred kings.
Strengthening the spiritual root,
Able to prosper the great lineage.
The third imperial prince, Bóshān,
Manifested wise virtue in childhood,
Displayed extraordinary bearing at this time.
Shining bright in the crimson palace,
Radiant, reflecting the blue chambers.
Yet the jade scepter not yet held,
The golden tally not yet driven.
How can this order the protective branches,
And establish the feudal relatives?
Your ministers, after deliberation,
Recommend he be enfeoffed as Prince of Póyáng.
Liáng Shěn Yuē "Memorial for Ceding the Command of the Central Army to the Nánjùn King"
I have heard that establishing marquises in thriving states,
is not done without virtue.
In distributing responsibilities in grand plans,
only the worthy are prioritized.
Yet I have not fully embraced the Way,
and have many deficiencies in observing righteousness.
I merely occupy a place of established customs,
and undeservingly receive imperial favor.
The glory of the jade seals and fine silks,
shines faintly over distant lands,
their legacy is illustrious and noble.
Yet solitude lies beyond the plains,
and in the morning, I extend the belt respectfully.
In the evening, I adjust my appearance,
as the royal highway begins to open.
The country's fortunes just begin,
with both Lǔ and Wèi initiated.
Righteousness extends far into the ages,
as both Qí and Chǔ stand established.
The customs exceed the days of Hàn,
I find myself in a lowly position.
Enjoying this brilliance from above,
to guide against adversity.
Embracing the seal in a grassy nook,
my ambitions thereby are stirred,
holding it like a pestle.
Liáng,
Liú Xiàochuò "First Memorial for Ceding Yōngzhōu to the Prince of Póyáng"
I have heard that great states are protective barriers,
I am ashamed when reciting the poem of the ancestral son,
thinking fondly of that stately palace.
There is a lack of odes for Duke Xī,
despite the magnificence of the Nine Lords of Zhōu,
bestowing lands and triple rewards.
Hàn established both rivers,
dividing the seal of ancient Chǔ.
Experiencing private family celebrations,
while humbly collecting my scarce merits.
The Yōng region has natural defenses,
spanning several states.
To the west, it holds Ngáo Pass,
to the north, it crosses Dèng Fortifications.
Even if Hán was summoned to court,
the dried streets retained their offerings.
The two usurpers pursued with weapons,
but the four suburbs remained undisturbed.
In this way, emulating the wise recognition of Wáng Róng,
and the noble integrity of Yáng Yòu.
I reflect on myself,
never seeking repose.
With endeavor to serve loyally,
almost exhausting private resources.
Liáng Shěn Yuē "Thanksgiving to Nán Yǎn Prefecture for the Prince of Jìn'ān"
I have always been weak,
and in youth lacked notable achievements.
Relying on heavenly habitation,
leaning on the sea for support.
Royal rank was granted early,
boundary commands were established in time.
Still unable to be proficient in Western Chǔ poetry,
or fond of Northern Hé rites.
No ability to renew the glory of the Six Canons,
proclaiming virtue over ten thousand miles.
Shame and fear arise in my heart,
covering my visage completely.
The imperial clarity illuminates brightly,
shining far and wide.
Thus relocating the banner to the Huái region,
transferring governance across the Jiè.
The red-harnessed horses exit the mansion,
blue-banded streams face the region.
Pondering such bestowed favor,
I forget my position amidst it all.
Also "Thanksgiving to Jīngzhōu for the Prince of Ānlù"
I entrusted to a celestial realm early,
enjoying the favor extended in advance.
Being among the imperial kin,
holding foremost the royal seals.
Fond of rituals, ashamed of Hé,
earnest in poetry, embarrassed by Chǔ.
Displaying the banner beyond the pass,
only to leave the crimson capital.
Intending to enter Jiè with gold,
understanding the righteousness of military standards.
Yet, the luminosity extends even wider,
again taking undeserved recognition.
With the beauty of Jìnán,
bearing overall rising duties.
Westward connecting with both Mín and Qióng,
northward continuing Huó and Xiǎn.
Holding the six reins in my hands,
yet still esteemed as difficult.
Flocks of herds rely on majestic power,
whose path is easy?
Thus spreading purity to the white plain,
sincerely conveying consultation.
The distant path of the sky is strict,
relations are drawn and clarified.
Honoring this appearance,
bearing this mistaken responsibility.
With reverence and trepidation,
not knowing where to place trust.
The Sixth Princess
In the past, Emperor Yáo's daughters were Éhuáng and Nǚyīng,
Shùn's sister was known as Kinghumer,
Kinghumer,
pronounced as "Qīhuō fan".
Shùn's daughters were Xiāo Míng Zhúguāng,
Tāng had the imperial younger sister Guīmèi
which refers to Emperor Tāng's sister.
Zhōu Wǔwáng's daughter married to Chén,
thus the princess did not have the title of fief.
By the middle of the Zhōu dynasty,
the emperor married his daughters to feudal lords.
The emperor, being supreme,
did not arrange marriages himself,
but made lords of the same surname oversee marriages,
thus calling them princesses.
The Qín dynasty followed this,
also calling them princesses.
As said in "Records of the Grand Historian":
"Lǐ Sī's sons all married Qín princesses,

Under Hàn law,
the emperor's daughters were called princesses;
the emperor's sisters were great princesses;
the emperor's aunts were grand princesses.
Later Hàn laws,
made all imperial daughters county princesses.
Their ceremonial attire matched that of princely peers,
those more highly respected received the title of great princess.
The daughters of various princes were called township or pavilion princesses.
Their ceremonial attire matched that of village or pavilion marquises.
Fàn Yè's "Book of Later Hàn" says:
"Emperor Zhāng named the daughters of Eastern Pingsuì King Cāng, and Láng Yáxiào King Jīng as county princesses.
Later, the sister of Emperor Ān had the title of great princess,
just like the imperial daughter who was a county princess.
Their sons inherited their mother's titles as marquises,
succession then continues in that manner.
The township and pavilion titles don’t pass on."
Since the Jìn period,
imperial daughters revert to being called princesses like in Western Hàn,
while aunts and sisters are called great princesses.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
they have a separate establishment for residences and officials.
Until the Suí period, administrative offices were suspended.
These are noted in the "Qiáo's Ceremonies" and "Jìn's Bureaucratic Records."
In the early Táng Shénlóng period,
official positions were set again.
They were removed by the end of Jǐnglóng.
