The seventh of the imperial sons-in-law.
According to the Han system,
the Son of Heaven would have marquises
marry imperial princesses.
Regional kings would have men from their own kingdoms receive their daughters.
Cuī Hào explained:
"The terms 'marry' (shàng) and 'receive' (chéng)
are both names implying inferior status.
Imperial princesses had separate residences established for them.
For the daughters of the Crown Prince,
marquises were ordered to go to their residences to serve them,
hence 'marrying the princess'.
For the daughters of the various kings,
then men from their kingdoms should come to receive and serve them.
In neither case could they pay formal visits to their parents-in-law,
only exchange inquiries.
The Son of Heaven was exalted,
so he ordered the various dukes to act as hosts for the marriage,
hence they were called 'gōngzhǔ' (duke-hosted).
The various kings were of lower status and hosted it themselves,
hence they were called:
'wēngzhǔ' (lord-hosted).
In Later Han, imperial daughters became county princesses,
and the daughters of kings became township and village princesses.
After the Jin dynasty,
kings' daughters became county mistresses."
After Wei and Jin,
those who married imperial princesses were all appointed Commandant of the Imperial Chariot.
Originally,
the Commandant of the Imperial Chariot,
was established by Emperor Wu of Han,
and was in charge of the imperial horses.
The Shuōwén says:
"The character for 'fù' (駙) in 'fùmǎ' is composed of 'horse' (馬) with 'fù' (付) indicating its sound.
One explanation says:
'Fù'
means 'near' or 'swift'."
Yìng Shào said:
'Bringing peace from above to below is called 'wèi' (尉, commandant),
and 'dū' (都) means overall command'."
Through the two Han dynasties,
it was mostly held by members of the imperial clan, maternal relatives, and descendants of various nobles.
By the time of Wei,
Hé Yàn,
grandson of the Grand General Hé Jìn,
was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Chariot as the emperor's son-in-law.
Later, Dù Yù married Gāolù Princess, daughter of Jin's Emperor Xuān,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Chariot.
Wáng Jì married Chángshān Princess, daughter of Jin's Emperor Wén,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Chariot.
Later generations followed Wei and Jin as the constant practice,
that whenever one married an imperial princess, he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Chariot.
From the Book of Han and the Qí Official Regulations.
Also the Book of Jin says:

"Fù Xuān married Hóngnóng Princess, daughter of Jin's Emperor Wǔ; Huán Wēn married Nánkāng Princess, daughter of Emperor Yuán; Xún Xiàn married Xúnyáng Princess, daughter of Emperor Yuán; Liú Shèn married Lúlíng Princess, daughter of Jin's Emperor Míng;
