with no prospect of peering through the gate.
Banquets are canceled and mats withdrawn,
cutting off all reason for reception and interaction.
Not only are friends and associates estranged,
but even brothers become distant and remote.
Nurses and governesses vie in flattery,
urging each other toward severity.
Flattering matrons compete to come forward,
fawning upon each other with urgency.
Among them, there are also those who respond to inquiries, diviners, and instructresses,
even to the leftover food and drink,
interrogating to whom it was given.
If clothing and bedding are old and worn,
they inevitably blame the head of the household.
Sometimes when advancing, one is not permitted to proceed,
sometimes when entering, one is not granted audience.
If one goes out and does not enter, they suspect estrangement from entering;
if one requests to go out, they suspect ulterior motives.
Summonses are invariably set for the third watch as the deadline,
dismissals are invariably limited to sunrise as the cutoff.
In the evening, one does not see the waning moon,
at dawn, one does not recognize the morning stars.
As for walking under the moon at night and playing the qin,
or folding sleeves by day and perusing scrolls,
within a single lifetime,
one is forever separated from these.
Moreover, as soon as one's voice or shadow is barely heard,
young maids come rushing forth.
When skirts and sleeves approach the mat,
ugly old women come clustering.
If attendants are neat and tidy,
they are suspected of currying favor and viewed with suspicion.
If guests are not yet capped,
they are reproached for their youthful appearance.
As for your servant's family standing,
generations have borne exceptional honor.
It is sufficient to establish the family's reputation,
and to anticipate promotion and advancement.
Prestigious posts in the Eastern Palace or fine offices,
may be attained through talent.
Once entangled in imperial marriage,
all becomes favor.
Therefore, presuming to venture into what is improper,
I lay bare my sincere heart.
It is not merely to state my own case,
and seek to preserve my person and wishes,
but truly to broadly explain the acute suffering endured by all such families.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty's compassionate wisdom will illuminate and consider this,
and specially grant its cessation and annulment.
If the gracious decree is suddenly issued,
and my earnest plea is not granted,
then I shall carve my skin and cut my hair,
and flee to the mountains or escape to the sea.
And so forth.
Grand Preceptor, Grand Mentor, Grand Guardian: First
The "Hàn Guānyí" states:
"The Grand Preceptor, Grand Mentor, and Grand Guardian
are all ancient offices.
During the time of King Tàijiǎ of the Shāng,
Yī Yǐn was Grand Guardian;
during the time of King Zhòu,
Xū Yú was Grand Preceptor;
King Wǔ of Zhōu, having conquered the Shāng, established the Zhōu offices,
and established the Grand Preceptor, Grand Mentor, and Grand Guardian as the Three Dukes."
Yìng Shào states:
"The Grand Preceptor
is whom the Son of Heaven takes as his model;
the Grand Mentor
means to mentor and assist the Son of Heaven in virtue and righteousness;
the Grand Guardian
means to protect and secure the Son of Heaven in virtue and righteousness.
The old theory considered the Minister of War, Minister of the Masses, and Minister of Works as the Three Dukes.
The Zhōu considered the Minister of War, Minister of the Masses, Minister of Works, Minister of Justice, Prime Minister, and Minister of Rites as the Six Ministers,
and thus considered the Preceptor, Mentor, and Guardian as the Three Dukes."
The "Shū" states:
"These Three Dukes
deliberate on the Way and govern the state, this is it.
The Grand Preceptor is above the Grand Mentor,
the Grand Guardian is next to the Grand Mentor.
They have no subordinate officials,
share duties with the King,
and oversee everything without exception."
The "Lǐjì" states:
"The Three Dukes have no fixed office,
meaning that when there is a suitable person, then it is filled,
when there is no such person, then it is left vacant."
During the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
the Grand Duke of Qí was Grand Preceptor;
during the time of King Chéng,
the Duke of Zhōu was Grand Mentor,
the Duke of Shào was Grand Guardian.
During the Qín and Hàn periods,
these offices did not exist,
until the reign of Empress Dowager Lǚ, only the Grand Mentor was established.
Wáng Líng served as Grand Mentor.
In the late Hàn, the Grand Minister of War, Grand Minister of the Masses, and Grand Minister of Works were considered the Three Dukes.
The offices of Preceptor, Mentor, and Guardian were established,
their positions above the Three Dukes,
honored with the title of Superior Dukes.
During the reign of Emperor Píng, Kǒng Guāng was made Grand Mentor,
and later promoted to Grand Preceptor.
Wáng Shùn served as Grand Guardian,
Mǎ Gōng served as Grand Preceptor.
After the Eastern Hàn,
the Grand Commandant, Minister of the Masses, and Minister of Works were all considered the Three Dukes.
The Grand Commandant and the Grand Minister of War were never established simultaneously,
through successive dynasties, either the Grand Commandant or the Grand Minister of War was considered one of the Three Dukes.
The Preceptor, Mentor, and Guardian were commonly called Superior Dukes.
The "Hòu Wèi Shū · Guānshì Zhì" states:
"The Later Wèi honored the Preceptor, Mentor, and Guardian as the Three Preceptors."
The "Wǔdài Shǐ · Bǎiguān Zhì" states:
"The Northern Qí, following the Later Wèi, also called them the Three Preceptors;
the Later Zhōu, following the Zhōu rituals,
again considered the Preceptor,
Mentor,
and Guardian as the Three Dukes;
the Suí dynasty initially reverted to Three Preceptors,
but Emperor Yáng abolished them.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
they all opened offices and established staff,
until the Suí dynasty, when the staff was abolished."
Three Legs · Six Tallies
Huán Jì's "Yàolüè" states:
"The Three Dukes
resemble the three legs of a tripod,
jointly supporting what is above."
The "Hàn Shū" states:
"Six Tallies.
Mèng Kāng's commentary states:
'The Tàijiē
are the three steps.
Initially three stars,
in total six stars.
The Six Tallies,
are the celestial verifications of the stars.'"
Yìng Shào states:
"The 'Huángdì Liù Fú Jīng' states:
'The Tàijiē
are the three steps of heaven.'"
Yellow Pavilion · Dark Green Ribbon
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shū" states:
"The Three Dukes' Yellow Pavilion has no precedent meaning in earlier histories,
your servant considers the 'Lǐjì' which states:
'The knee-cover of a scholar is the same as the Son of Heaven's,
those of dukes, marquises, and senior officials differ.'"
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The Three Dukes and the Son of Heaven
have ceremonial ranks that are secondary.
Therefore, their pavilion is yellow to show humility,
not daring to rival the Son of Heaven.
It is suspected to be a system of the late Hàn."
The "Jìn Guānpǐn Lìng" states:
"Dukes have dark green ribbon tassels,
the character '綟' is pronounced lì."
Sophora Position · Terrace Steps
The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"Three sophora trees,
The law of the Three Luminaries models after the Five Sacred Mountains.
Hán Fēi states:
"Shedding personal interests means:
'Public is the same as
the Three Dukes likened to tripod legs.
The number three is
modeled after the Three Luminaries.'" In "Chūnqiū Hàn Hánzī," it says:
"The Three Dukes are likened to the Five Sacred Mountains."
Regulate Yin and Yang, Moderate Wind and Rain
Fùzǐ says:
"The Three Dukes
assist the Son of Heaven in regulating Yin and Yang."
Liú Xiàng's "Shuōyuàn" says:
"The Three Dukes rectify the world,
harmonize Yin and Yang,
and moderate wind and rain."
Above are matters concerning the Three Dukes and the Three Teachers.
Manage State Affairs, Hold National Balance
"Shàngshū" states:
"Establish the Grand Tutor, Grand Mentor, Grand Protector."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"Shī,
is the model for the Son of Heaven.
Assist the king in discussing the Way,
to manage state affairs,
only those with virtue can be suitable."
"The Book of Poetry" says:
"The Yǐn Clan's Grand Tutor,
the foundation of Zhōu.
Holds the balance of the state,
maintains the four directions.
Assists the Son of Heaven,
so the people are not confused."
Zhèng's annotation says:
"Assists,
means support.
It says the Yǐn Clan occupies the office of Grand Tutor,
holds the balance of state governance,
and maintains the four directions."
Assist the Son of Heaven, Serve as National Teacher
"The Book of Poetry" says:
"Assist the Son of Heaven."
This is seen in the note on "Hold National Balance."
"Xù Hànshū" says:
"Zhào Diǎn, erudite learning and broad knowledge,
suitable as a National Teacher.
The National Teacher is the Grand Tutor."
Harmonize Yin and Yang, Manage Rites and Music
"Shàngshū" states:
"Establish the Grand Tutor, Grand Mentor, Grand Protector,
these are the Three Dukes.
Discuss the Way and manage the state,
harmonize and regulate Yin and Yang."
"Kǒng Ānguó's Commentary" says:
"Shī,
is the model for the Son of Heaven,
fulfills the duties of the Three Dukes.
Assists the king in discussing the Way,
managing state affairs,
harmonizing and regulating Yin and Yang."
"Dà Dài Lǐ" says:

"If the Son of Heaven does not discuss the virtues of past sage kings, does not understand the ways of military and civil affairs, does not see the correctness of rites and music, does not scrutinize the principles of handling affairs, does not have a broad understanding of ancient and modern classics, and is not well-versed in protocols of authority and restraint,
rites and music have no standards,
and studies are not in accordance with law.
On all these accounts,
the Grand Tutor instructs."
Instruct the Emperor's Conduct, Hold State Governance
Yìng Shào's "Hàn Guān Yí" says:
"In the first year of Yuánshǐ under Emperor Píng,
Kǒng Guāng was appointed as Grand Tutor.
The Empress Dowager said:
'The Grand Tutor is a descendant of sage men,
his way and skills are clear and bright.
Suitable for the position of four assistants,
to instruct and guide the emperor's conduct.'"
"Holding state governance" is seen in the note on "Hold National Balance."
Found at Pánxī, Bestowed with Spiritual Longevity
"Shǐjì" says:
"Zhōu Wénwáng found Lǚ Shàng at Pánxī,
made him a teacher,
called him Tàigōng;
Wǔwáng succeeded the throne,
and called him:
'Teacher and esteemed father;'
When Chéngwáng took power,
he honored him as Grand Tutor.'" "The Book of Poetry" says:
"It is the esteemed father as a teacher,
when eagles soar."
Yìng Shào's "Hàn Guān Yí" says:
"In the first year of Yuánshǐ under Emperor Xiàopíng,
the Empress Dowager decreed:
'Grand Tutor Guāng, now aged and ailing,
a respected and worthy minister,
a weight of the nation.' " "The Book" says:
"Do not abandon the accomplished aged,
when a country is about to rise.
Respect the Grand Tutor and valued mentors,
decree the Grand Tutor not to attend court.
Once in ten days, grant meal offerings,
bestow the staff of spiritual longevity.
The Yellow Gate Commissioner arranged the seating in the palace,
where the Grand Tutor leans the staff in the court."
Above are the matters concerning the Grand Tutor.
Veteran Statesmen, Neutral and Balanced
"Dōngguān Hàn Jì" says:
"A decree states:
'The acting Grand Commandant Zhào Xǐ,
in office for three generations,
is a veteran statesman for the nation.
Appoint Xǐ as Grand Mentor,
at the age of eighty,
yet his heart and vigor remain strong.
His stepmother is present,
he attends her morning and evening,
no staff at his side,
and his words do not reference old age.
He adeptly manages affairs,
and profoundly understands court protocol.
Although lacking straightforward frankness,
he repeatedly compensates for deficiencies.'"
Therefore, the capital's saying goes:
"When matters are unresolved, ask Bóshǐ;
mediocrity governs the world with Hú Gōng."
Assist the Son of Heaven, Record Shàngshū
"Shàngshū" states:
"Establish the Grand Tutor, Grand Mentor, Grand Protector,
these three are the Three Dukes.
Discuss the Way and manage the state."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"Fù,
assists and supports the Son of Heaven."
"Xù Hànshū" states:
"One Grand Mentor,
should be based on virtuous ways,
without fixed duties.
Shìzǔ appointed Zhuó Mào for this role.
Thereafter, whenever an emperor ascended,
a Grand Mentor was appointed to handle Shàngshū affairs,
and upon their passing, they were dismissed."
High in Three Surrenderals, All is Governed
Yìng Shào's "Hàn Guān" says:
"Emperor Hé's edict states:
'Former Grand Commandant Dèng Biāo,
of meritorious clan,
grew ever higher despite three renunciations.
Now appoint Biāo as Grand Mentor overseeing Shàngshū affairs,
and all officials heed him.'" "All is governed" is mentioned above.
Enlighten Court Protocol, Warn of Martial Matters
"Enlighten court protocol" is seen in the note under "Neutral and Balanced."
"Dà Dài Lǐ" states:
"If the Son of Heaven is not benevolent to the populace, does not trust the feudal lords, and does not warn of martial matters.
All such affairs,
are the responsibility of the Grand Mentor."
Three Generations in Office, All Officials Heed
"Three generations" is seen in the note under "Zhào Xǐ."
Moreover, "All officials heed" is seen in the note under "Three Surrenderals."
Above are matters concerning the Grand Mentor.
Supreme Duke, Veteran Statesmen
"Supreme Duke" is mentioned in the narrative.
"Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū" says:
"Wáng Xiáng, styled Xiūzhēng,
appointed as Grand Protector.
The decree states:
'Venerable aged elders,
of noble conduct and pure character.
They are whom I rely upon,
to enhance morals and broaden culture.'"
Secure the Son of Heaven, Admonish King's Wrongs
"Shàngshū" says:
"The Grand Tutor, Grand Mentor, Grand Protector,
these are the Three Dukes.
Discuss the Way and manage the state."
The annotations say:
"The Grand Protector
secures the Son of Heaven with virtue and justice."
"Zhōu Lǐ":
"The office of the Protector oversees advising the king's wrongs."
The annotation says:
"Advising means
to correct with rites and justice."
Appoint Yī Yǐn, Duties of Zhāo Gōng
"Qízhí Yí" states:
"During the time of Yīn Tàijiǎ,
Yī Yǐn was the Grand Protector;
during the time of Zhōu Chéngwáng,
Zhāo Gōng was the Grand Protector."
Brilliantly discerning and sincerely devoted, with lofty conduct pure and refined.
The Jin Qiju Zhu records:
"Grand Tutor Wèi Guàn,
brilliantly discerning and sincerely devoted.
He possesses the will to disregard personal safety for duty,
and is granted a thousand infantry and a hundred cavalry."
"Lofty conduct pure and refined" appears in the annotation for "Yuánlǎo."
The above concerns the Grand Tutor.
Chén Shěn Jiǒng's "Memorial Declining the Post of Grand Tutor"
Performing the music of the Six Dynasties
cannot beseech Heaven.
Presenting the songs of all deities
is powerless to move the Sage.
Lifting my head toward the imperial gate,
my anxiety and fear only increase.
All rivers boil and surge,
the royal house is as if aflame.
Relinquishing my position to join the plan,
the feudal lords all gather.
The covenant is recorded at the assembly hall,
I alone remain among the ministers.
If I were to don a simple headband and dwell in a humble lane,
my lips never speaking of conquering Wú,
roaming with Chìsōng in the morning,
passing by Jìběi in the evening,
emerging to don a marquis's robes,
entering to shed the dragon-adorned garments,
then with fortifications at the four outskirts,
who would guard the altars of state?
If, with halberds held before me,
and strong crossbows for self-defense,
bearing the map of the young ruler,
adorning the tripod with the egret pattern,
military prestige outweighing that of protecting generals,
state rituals valuing the sealing of gates,
the minister's way still being humble,
who can say it is not coercion?
This is why I emerge to decline the high officials,
enter to instruct my wife and children,
bow at the garden of Chánglíng,
pay respects at the temple of Tàizǔ.
Not allowing the nine clans to violate kindness and righteousness,
not allowing the common people to betray the state.
What I hope is that Your Majesty be as revered as the North Star,
the court as steadfast as the Southern Mountain.
Zhōu Wángbāo's "Stele for Grand Tutor Wú Wǔgōng Yùchí Gāng"
In ancient times, the royal house had protective screens;
those of the same clan were called kin.
Among the feudal states and lords,
those of different surnames were termed uncles.
For great merit and virtuous conduct,
Zhōu honored the enfeoffments of Qí and Lǔ.
Apportioning ranks and rewarding service,
Hàn valued the positions of Hán and Wú.
The Director of Merit recorded their grand achievements,
the canonical registers detailed their glorious insignia.
Shānfǔ exemplified the merits of the various lords,
recording deeds on vessels.
Zhuāngshū rectified the troubles of Chéng and Xiàn,
making virtue manifest on tripods and cauldrons.
Great fame and grand accomplishments,
the Duke indeed combined them all.
The Duke, born for his era, stood out,
responding to the occasion with his emergence.
Lofty as Sōng and Huà peaks,
he received the numinous essence of the great mountains.
Where frost and dew are evenly distributed,
he embodied the refined energy of central harmony.
The winter pine shoots forth,
showing its quality of enduring late withering.
The true cassia stands tall,
already bearing the splendor of winter blossoms.
Thus, with Chén and Mǎo stars receiving blessings,
wind and clouds interacted responsively.
The Duke, gentle and firm within,
radiant brilliance shining forth outwardly.
He adorned benevolence and righteousness,
a model of jade tablets and fine conduct.
His steadfast and vigorous integrity,
through the four seasons grew even more outstanding.
His firm and true character,
tempered a hundred times, remained unmelting.
Moreover, with Péng Méng's archery skill,
he could hit distant halberd branches.
With Yǎng Yóu's arrow way,
he pierced suspended leaves from afar.
His skill reached the pinnacle of a general's art,
his mastery exhausted the duties of a commandant.
When his years passed the age of service,
his responsibilities honored the highest ministerial ranks.
His mansion faced the thoroughfare,
announcements clearing the way.
Yet he never grew arrogant from favor and status,
always maintaining humility and self-restraint.
Words of changing dwellings,
he never forgot even in illness and rest.
The ambition to fortify Yǐng,
persisted until his closing eyes.
The inscription says:
"The pearl-horned one met his time,
the mountain-forehead revealed his virtue.
Loyal in service, filial at home,
from family he extended rule to state.
A crown among men,
a model of constant principles.
Entrusted with duties during alarms,
his office linked to the pivotal guard.
Inspecting the six regulations,
deliberating with the three officials.
Flowing waters—how can they pause?
Time and light do not linger.
Suddenly leaving the inn of life,
swiftly grieving the great change.
Banners spread like summer silk,
coffin placed within Wèi's curtain.
Sparse are the folk north of the walls,
the western mountain's light descends.
The three thousand unseen,
who in the nine plains will arise?
Inscribe this on the tripod and cauldron,
to eternally transmit Sōng and Huò."
Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, Minister of Works: Second
The Qí Zhíyí states:
"All are ancient offices."
Yìng Shào said:
"From above pacifying those below is called Wèi."
Huàn said:
"The Grand Commandant oversees military affairs.
In ancient times, officials of soldiers and prisons were all called Wèi.
Wèi
means wèi (net).
It means soldiers and prisons net and ensnare.
It means soldiers and prisons net and ensnare the wicked and unlawful."
Also, Yìng Shào said:
"Tú
means multitude.
The Minister over the Masses
is master of the multitude.
Kōng
means cavity.
The Minister of Works
presides over earth.
In ancient times, people lived in caves.
He oversaw digging earth to make cavities for people to dwell in."
In Yáo's time, Shùn was Grand Commandant;
in Shùn's time, Xiè was Minister over the Masses and Yǔ was Minister of Works.
These were also the three ducal offices in antiquity.
Thereafter, the Grand Commandant and the Grand Marshal were often set up alternately,
not coexisting.
When there was a Grand Marshal, the Grand Commandant was not established;
this was so through successive dynasties.
Zhōu took the Grand Preceptor, Grand Tutor,
and Grand Guardian as the Three Dukes;
the Grand Marshal, Grand Minister over the Masses, Grand Minister of Works, along with the Grand Minister of Justice, Grand Steward, and Grand Minister of Rites formed the Six Ministers.
By the end of Western Hàn,
the offices of Preceptor, Tutor, and Guardian
were elevated in title to Superior Dukes;
the Grand Marshal, Grand Minister over the Masses, and Grand Minister of Works became the Three Dukes.
In early Eastern Hàn, the Grand Marshal was abolished,
and the Grand Commandant established.
Together with the Minister over the Masses
and Minister of Works, they formed the Three Dukes.
All removed the "Grand" character.
This remained through Wèi, Jìn, Sòng, Qí, and thereafter.
By the Later Zhōu,
they again followed the Zhōu rituals,
taking Preceptor, Tutor, and Guardian as the Three Dukes.
The Wǔdài Shǐzhì states:
"Suí again took the Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works as the Three Dukes."
Through successive dynasties, they all established offices and set up official staff;
Táng abolished the office staff.
Superior Officer; Secondary Libation
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"Yáng Zhèn, styled Bóqǐ,
served as Grand Commandant.
He was by nature loyal and sincere.
Whenever he remonstrated and contended,
the Regular Palace Attendants like Fán Fēng and others slandered him.
His seal and ribbon were taken, and he returned to his commandery.
Zhèn reached the capital lodge at Luòyáng.
He said to his disciples:
'I received grace to occupy a superior office,
yet cunning treacherous ministers I could not punish;
favored ones causing disorder I could not restrain.
What face have I to see the sun and moon?'
Thereupon he drank poison and died."
The Xù Hànshū states:
"The Grand Commandant, at suburban and ancestral temple ceremonies, presides over the secondary libation;
at grand funerals, he announces the posthumous title at the southern suburb."
Commanding Troops and Overseeing Military Affairs
The *Xu Han Shu* states:
"There is one Grand Commandant,
who oversees military affairs of the four directions.
He assesses achievements and merits,
and at the end of the year, determines the best and worst to carry out rewards and punishments."
Also, the *Han Shu* says:
"The Grand Commandant
is an office from the Qin dynasty,
overseeing military affairs."
Not Like a Stone, Yet Cuts Metal
Yīng Shào's *Han Guan* says:
"In the edict of Emperor Chōng,
Grand Commandant Zhào Jùn,
who for two generations held the pivotal position,
had a heart not like a stone, unwavering and undivided."
It also says:
"The Three Dukes are the pillars of the state;
the court looks to them for rectitude,
to achieve the cutting of metal.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Lǐ Gù,
a scion of the ducal clan,
loyal and upright, unyielding,
shall be appointed as Grand Commandant."
Two Deer and Three Sturgeons
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"When Zhèng Hóng was Governor of Línhuái,
during the spring inspection tour,
two white deer followed his carriage,
running alongside the wheels.
Hóng, finding it strange, asked his Registrar Huáng what the deer portended, good or ill.
Huáng congratulated him, saying:
'I have heard that the carriage screens of the Three Dukes are painted with deer.
Your Excellency is destined to become Chancellor.'
Hóng later indeed became Grand Commandant."
Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"Yáng Zhèn, styled Bóqǐ,
once sojourned beyond the lakes,
and for decades did not accept invitations from the commanderies and prefectures.
People said his time was past,
yet Zhèn strengthened his resolve even more.
Later, a stork carried three sturgeon fish in its beak,
flew and alighted before the lecture hall.
The assistant lecturer picked up the fish and presented it, saying:
'Generally, the sturgeon
is a symbol of the attire of high ministers.
The number three
corresponds to the Three Terraces.
From this, Master, you shall rise!'
Later, he reached the position of Grand Commandant."
Painted Deer Screens and Flying Magpie Seal
"Painted deer screens" see above.
The *Bówù Zhì* says:
"When Zhāng Hào of Chángshān was Chancellor of Liáng,
just after a new rain,
a bird like a magpie
flew down gradually,
fell to the ground, and someone picked it up;
it transformed into a round stone.
Hào broke it open with a hammer,
and obtained a gold seal,
which said:
'Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety.'
Hào reported it to the throne,
and it was stored in the secret archives.
Hào
reached the position of Grand Commandant during the reign of Emperor Líng of Hàn."
Protect the Imperial House, Secure the Liú Clan
Zhì Yú's *Lǒngxī Wáng Tài Wèi Tàiwèi Cè* says:
"Your conduct is a model for the times,
by kinship you are a ministerial pillar of the clan;
discussing the Way and governing the state,
protecting and securing the Imperial House,
therefore you are advanced to the high office."
The *Han Shu* says:
"The Emperor said:
'Zhōu Bó is earnest and厚重, lacking refinement,
yet he who will secure the Liú clan must be Bó;
he may be made Grand Commandant.'"
Preside Over the Nine Punitive Expeditions, Harmonize the Seven Governors
Xiè Língyùn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"The Qin had the Grand Commandant,
overseeing the military.
The Hàn continued this practice,
sometimes establishing it, sometimes abolishing it.
Therefore, the office of the Marshal
presides over the duties of the Nine Punitive Expeditions."
The *Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn* says:
"When Chén Fān was appointed Grand Commandant,
he declined, saying:
'In harmonizing the Seven Governors,
and training the five arms of the military,
I am not equal to Court Counselor Wáng Chàng.'"
Sighing for Huáng Xiàn, Recommending Cài Mó
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"When Chén Fān was appointed Grand Commandant,
he sighed before the court, saying:
'If Huáng Xiàn were here,
I would not dare to receive the seal and绶 first.'" The *Jìn Shū*:
"Xī Jiàn, styled Dàohuī,
was promoted to the emolument of Grand Commandant.
When critically ill,
he recommended Cài Mó to succeed himself."
Setting Up a Screen, Bestowing a Brocade Quilt
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"Zhèng Hóng, styled Jùjūn,
served as Grand Commandant.
His former superior, Dìwǔ Lún, was Minister of Works,
and his rank was lower.
Every New Year's audience,
Hóng would humbly bow and demean himself.
The Emperor, learning of this,
then set up a mica screen to separate them,
and this became a precedent."
Also:
"Zhū Chǒng, styled Zhòngwēi,
served as Grand Commandant.
He ate unpolished rice,
and slept under a cloth quilt.
The court bestowed upon him a brocade quilt and fine grain and meat,
all of which he dared not accept."
The above concerns matters of the Grand Commandant.
Assisting Instruction, Land Taxes
The *Zhōu Lǐ*:
"The duties of the Grand Minister of Education:
then establish the Minister of Education of the Earth Office,
to lead his subordinates and oversee the instruction of the state,
to assist the king in pacifying and governing the states."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"This is how to be close to the hundred surnames,
and instruct them in the five relationships;
'rǎo' also means to pacify."
It also says:
"Using the method of equitable land allocation to distinguish the five products and nine grades,
and regulate the land taxes of the realm."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"'Jūn'
means to equalize.
The five products
are the things produced by the five types of land.
The nine grades
are: reddish firm soil, reddish-yellow soil, grave壤 soil, parched marsh soil, salty泻 soil, loose壤 soil, clayey壚 soil, strong㯺 soil, light爂 soil, and the like.
'Zhēng'
means tax."
Five Rites, Six Musics
The *Zhōu Lǐ*:
"The duties of the Grand Minister of Education:
use the Five Rites to guard against the falsity of the myriad people and teach them the mean."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary:
"Rites are used to restrain people's extravagance and falsity,
enabling them to attain the mean."
It also says:
"Use the Six Musics to guard against the emotions of the myriad people and teach them harmony."
The commentary says:
"Music is used to channel and correct people's emotions and thoughts,
making their hearts harmonious."
Measuring Land, Distinguishing Soils
The *Zhōu Lǐ*:
"The duties of the Minister of Education:
when establishing states,
use the gnomon to measure their land and define their territories."
The commentary says:
"'Tǔ qí dì' is like saying 'measure its land.'"
It also says:
"Using the method of soil suitability,
distinguish the names and characteristics of the twelve soils."
The commentary says:
"The twelve soils
correspond to the twelve feudal divisions.
The soils are linked to the twelve stations,
each having its own suitability."
Seven Administrations and Five Teachings
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
"Since the era of Jiànwǔ,
scholars cultivated their learning,
opening and examining charts and apocrypha.
It was said that the Han dynasty's prime minister
would emerge from the Kūn region.
Thereupon, Minister over the Masses Lǐ Gōng
repeatedly ascended to the Seven Administrations.
Grand Tutor Yú Jiān
discoursed on the Way for successive generations."
*The Book of Documents: Qì Dì* states:
"When the hundred clans are not affectionate,
and the five relationships are not harmonious,
you shall serve as Minister over the Masses,
reverently spreading the Five Teachings,
with leniency."
The annotation states:
"The teachings of the five constant virtues
must be carried out with leniency."
Dreaming of a Pine and Taking an Ear
Zhāng Bó's *Wú Lù* states:
"Dīng Gù served as Minister over the Masses.
Earlier, when he was a Secretary,
he dreamed a pine tree grew from his abdomen.
He told others:
'The character for pine (松) is "eighteen" and "duke" (十八公).
After eighteen years, shall I become a duke?'
It later happened as in his dream."
Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Cài Mào, styled Zǐlǐ,
in the twentieth year of Jiànwǔ,
succeeded Dài Shè as Minister over the Masses.
In office, he was pure, frugal, and never lax.
Earlier, while in Guǎnghàn,
Cài Mào dreamed he was at the ridgepole of a great hall.
Above, there were three ears of grain.
Mào jumped to take them,
obtaining the middle ear.
But then he lost it again.
The Registrar Guō Hè left his mat to congratulate him, saying:
'The great hall
is the image of the government office.
Having grain at the ridgepole
signifies the highest salary for a minister.
Taking the middle ear
means the position of the central ministry.
In terms of characters, "grain" (禾) and "lose" (失) combine to form "rank" (秩).
Although it is said
you lost it,
this actually means you will obtain official rank and salary.
When the duties of high office are lacking,
you, sir, shall supplement them.'
"Within a month, Mào was summoned to office
and appointed Hè as his assistant."
The Stench of Copper and Ivory Tallies
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū* states:
"Emperor Líng sold offices.
The Commandant of Justice Cuī Liè paid five million cash to buy the post of Minister over the Masses.
Liè's son, Jūn, styled Kǒngpíng,
also had a reputation for talent in his time.
Liè asked him:
'Now that I have become a duke,
what do people in the world say?'
He replied:
'My lord, you have long had a lofty reputation,
and no one says you are unfit to be a duke.
But now that you have ascended to this position,
all within the seas suspect it reeks of copper.'
Liè raised his staff to strike him,
and Jūn fled.
Liè said:
'A son flees when his father beats him;
can this be called filial?'
Jūn replied:
'When Shùn served his father,
he accepted minor beatings,
but fled from major ones,
so as not to entrap his father in unrighteousness.'
Liè said:
'Do you take me for Gǔsǒu?'
Also, Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
'Wáng Róng succeeded Wáng Hún as Minister over the Masses.
He often used ivory tallies to calculate his family wealth day and night,
extending even to fields and pastures.
His nature was also extremely frugal,
unable to provide well for himself.
He would not spend money on food and drink outside.
The world called it his fatal obsession.'"
Clarifying the Seven Teachings and Cultivating the Six Rites
*The Book of Rites* states:
"The Minister over the Masses clarifies the seven teachings to elevate the people's virtue."
It also states:
"The Minister over the Masses cultivates the six rites to regulate the people's nature."
Spreading the Five Canons and Harmonizing the Eight Administrations
*The Book of Documents* states:
"The Minister over the Masses is in charge of the state's instruction,
spreading the five canons,
and pacifying the myriad people."
The annotation says:
"To spread means to promulgate.
He presides over the state's instruction and transformation,
promulgating the teachings of the five constant virtues,
to pacify and harmonize the multitude of people under heaven."
*The Book of Rites* states:
"The Minister over the Masses harmonizes the eight administrations to prevent excess."
The above pertains to the Minister over the Masses.
Distinguishing the Five Soils and Delineating the Nine Provinces
*Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ* states:
"When Confucius served as Minister of Works,
he distinguished the nature of the five soils and determined what was suitable to produce in each."
Yú Huàn's *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"When Yǔ served as Minister of Works,
he cleared the nine mountains,
dredged the nine marshes,
arranged the nine provinces,
causing each to bring tribute according to its duty.
The land extended five thousand *lǐ*,
reaching the wild territories."
Creating Maps and Managing State Affairs
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Péi Xiù, styled Jìyàn,
served as Minister of Works.
He created the *Yǔ Gòng* Regional Maps.
When the work was completed, he presented it to the emperor.
It was stored in the secret archives,
and he was a renowned duke of his time."
*The Book of Rites* states:
"The Minister of Works holds the measures and measures the land."
Zhèng Xuán said:
"The Minister of Works is the minister of the Winter Office,
in charge of state affairs."
Dredging the Nine Marshes and Settling the Four Peoples
"Dredging the nine marshes" see the note under "Nine Provinces."
*The Book of Documents* states:
"The Minister of Works is in charge of the state's land,
settling the four peoples,
and timing the benefits of the land."
The annotation says:
"The minister of the Winter Office presides over the state's empty lands,
settling the four peoples—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—upon them,
causing them to follow the heavenly seasons and share the benefits of the land."
Building Palaces and Leveling Water and Earth
Zhèng Xuán's annotation on the *Kǎo Gōng Jì* states:
"The Minister of Works is in charge of constructing city walls,
building state capitals and towns.
Establishing the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temples,
building palaces, dwellings, vehicles, garments, and tools,
overseeing the hundred artisans.
Before the times of Táng and Yú, he was called the Director of Works."
*The Book of Documents* states:
"The Four Peaks all said:
'Let Bó Yǔ be the Minister of Works.'
The Emperor said:
'Yes!
I consult you, Yǔ.
You shall level the waters and the earth;
strive diligently!'" The annotation states:
"Mào
means to strive."
Lǐ Tōng's Prophecy and Wáng Liáng's Omen
Huá Qiáo's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Lǐ Tōng, styled Wényuán,
using prophecies and records, persuaded Emperor Guāngwǔ
and was made Grand Minister of Works."
It also states:
"Wáng Liáng, styled Jūnyán,
was appointed Grand Minister of Works."
*The Chìfú Fú* states:
"Wáng Liáng presides over Wèi and acts as Xuánwǔ.
The Emperor considered Yěwáng originally part of Wèi territory.
He moved,
and Xuánwǔ is the water deity.
The Minister of Works is the official of water and earth,
so he was promoted and appointed Liáng."
The Red Prophecy, the Pure Silk Integrity
Huá Qiào's History of the Later Hàn states:
"Wáng Liáng served as magistrate of Yěwáng."
The Red Prophecy said:
"Wáng Liáng governs Wèi and acts as Xuánwǔ,
Xuánwǔ is the water deity,
the Minister of Works is the official of water and earth,
thus he promoted Liáng and appointed him as Grand Minister of Works."
The Jìn Court Diaries state:
Emperor Wǔ's edict to Zhèng Mào said:
'Your conduct is pure and upright,
your practice of the Way is profound and refined.
In retirement, you possess a clear and harmonious demeanor,
in advancement, you uphold the integrity of pure silk.
You should align with the brilliance of the three celestial steps,
and mend the deficiencies of the imperial duties.'
Thus, Mào was appointed as Minister of Works."
Consulting on Governance and Transformation, Encouraging Virtuous Customs
The Family Biography of Xún Yù states:
"Yǐ served as Minister of Works.
When Emperor Wén pacified Shǔ,
discussions resumed on the five ranks of nobility.
He memorialized the Wèi court,
urging the Duke to establish rituals and ceremonies.
Central Protector of the Army Jiǎ Chōng rectified the laws,
while Imperial Secretary Péng Xiù deliberated on the official system.
The Duke then revised and finalized the old texts,
implemented proper forms,
establishing the standards for an era.
When the documents were completed and presented to the throne,
they were stored in the secret archives.

The regulations for ceremonial attire, banners, and imperial processions, the rituals for music, sacrifices, and burnt offerings, and the systems for ancestral temples, sacrifices, and posthumous honors,
as well as the ceremonies for the Bright Hall and the Pìyōng Academy,
were all deliberated and established by the Duke.
The court attributed the excellence to him.
As the Duke served as a high minister,
his virtue and reputation were clear and weighty,
and he paid close attention to ritual teachings.
Due to old age and frequent illness,
he seldom attended court audiences.
An edict ordered the Palace Attendant Rén Kǎi to consult him on whether governance and transformation measures should be implemented."
Also, Huá Qiào's History of the Later Hàn states:
"Although Dìwǔ Lún was stern and upright,
he often believed that since the restoration of the dynasty,
the two sovereigns favored frequent reforms,
and customs tended toward harshness.
The foundation of governance and transformation should prioritize leniency and harmony.
When he became one of the Three Dukes,
he encountered Emperor Zhāng, a benevolent ruler who often practiced forbearance,
and repeatedly implemented good governance.
Lún submitted a memorial praising these great achievements,
thereby encouraging the cultivation of virtuous customs."
Promoted in Months, Reaching in a Hundred Days
The Book of Hàn states:
"Zhū Bó, styled Zǐyuán,
was promoted from Governor of the Capital to Grand Minister of Works in a few months."
Fàn Yè's History of the Later Hàn states:
"Xún Shuǎng firmly declined the summons for appointment,
but eventually had no choice but to comply.
He rose from home and reached the position of Minister of Works in a hundred days."
The above pertains to matters of the Minister of Works.
Jìn Sūn Chuò's "In Praise of Minister of Works Xún's Portrait"
Thinking of the cultured Duke,
who preserved auspiciousness.
Pure as jade,
adorned with golden brilliance.
From youth, he harbored virtue,
concealing his light in humble attire.
Since the chaos of old,
war drums daily resounded.
Rituals and music lay hidden,
poetry and books were covered in dust.
The wise man sighed from afar,
leaving a model to clarify the spirit.
Gazing upon the rivers of Zhū and Sì,
waves rose, cutting off the ford.
Just as his brilliance shone like a golden pivot,
assisting in balancing the mechanisms of state.
Heaven showed no pity,
and did not spare him.
Officials lost their model,
the imperial virtue found no support.
With the Duke's passing,
all within and beyond the realm grieved together.
Later Hàn Cuī Yīn's "Admonition for the Grand Commandant"
The celestial official, the chief steward,
leader of the multitude of officers.
Heaven bestowed upon the emperor,
commanding Yú to serve as Commandant.
Harmonizing with the celestial pivot,
pacifying the nation's domains.
Regulating the military and enforcing prohibitions,
the royal army follows the model.
The nine provinces are thus pacified,
all dukes governed in order.
Weapons of war are stored away,
the constellations follow their courses.
Above, he is relied upon,
below, he is supported.
If not the right person,
he ruins the emperor's governance.
In the past, the Zhōu people thought of Duke Wén,
and the Shàonán ode sang of the sweet pear tree.
Kūnwú honored the Xià,
Yī Zhì praised the Shāng.
In the latter ages, deviation arose,
and rituals were not rectified.
Do not say I am strong,
that none dare defeat me.
Do not say I am great,
lightly waging war and fond of slaughter.
King Zhòu's army of a million,
ultimately met its end.
The minister in charge of the military,
dares to admonish those in power.
Also, "Admonition for the Minister over the Masses"
Heaven observes from above,
and benevolent virtue arises.
Thus, the Minister over the Masses is established,
to govern these multitudes.
Vast are the common domains,
all within the lands are numerous.
The people all look to you,
the four directions are upheld.
Diligent and cautious day and night,
neither negligent nor transgressing.
Reverently spread the five teachings,
the nine virtues are all practiced.
The diligent are recognized,
the common people are enriched.
Do not say you are perverse,
forgetting your duty to assist.
Do not say I am sage,
neglecting governance.
If not using the worthy,
then your mandate is abandoned.
If achievements are not harmonious,
shame falls upon your salary.
As the arm may break,
so the tripod may overturn its stew.
The Documents praise the limbs,
the Poetry criticizes the southern hill.
Minister Yǐn could not bear it,
the state's measures thus erred.
Your subject in charge of agriculture,
dares to admonish the guardian of the borders.
Also, "Admonition for the Minister of Works"
Praise that earthly spirit,
equal to heaven in setting rules.
Dividing into five domains,
delineating ten thousand states.
Thus, the earthly official is established,
with the duty of emptiness.
Vast are the nine provinces,
capitals and borders fill the regions.
Bound together by group overseers,
linked by regional lords.
Outstanding talents in rows,
reverent royal ministers.
Ministers fit their offices,
offices suit their persons.
The governance of nine to one,
seven taxes to equalize.
In the latter ages of old,
ranks and emoluments neglected the worthy.
Extortioners filled the court,
and outward reverence overflowed to heaven.
Not by such men's strength,
nor by such governance's order.
Goods flowed to buy favor,
and bribes were openly sold.
The king's way thus grew weeds,
who would not then fall?
Your subject in charge of the earth,
dares to admonish those by your side.
Sòng Xiè Zhuāng's "Memorial by Xiè, Northern Central General, Concurrently Minister over the Masses"
Your subject hears that harmonizing yīn and yáng,
reverently illuminating heaven and earth,
depends not only on the office,
but without the right person, it is lacking.
The Minister over the Masses is tasked with spreading the five canons,
his duty to pacify the myriad people.
How could I have expected the heavenly spirit to be without deficiency,
its radiant favor now revealed,
an extraordinary appointment beyond order,
surpassing even the feudal lords.
How could I temporarily occupy the three duties,
falsely prepared with the six tallies,
ashamed and trembling all around,
looking back and stepping with mutual fear.
Later Hàn,
Cài Yōng's "Inscription for the Stele of Grand Commandant Yáng" says:
Heaven oversaw the Hàn,
and gave birth to a great minister.
Generations served in the three highest offices,
their merit lay within the royal court.
Then came the Lord Yǐn,
who could glorify the former model.
With wholehearted devotion and exhaustive effort,
he continued the deeds of his ancestors.
His transformation harmonized with all living beings,
his grace soaked the entire realm.
Shěn Yuē's "Epitaph Inscription for Prince Wénxiàn, the Grand Commandant of Qí" says:
"His virtue encompassed the nine ministers,
his merit included the ten wise men.
The emperor's plans were always implemented,
the king's way shone brightly together.
This is called the nation's pillar,
this is indeed the people's support.
Soaring in the garden of rites,
leisurely strolling in the halls of literature.
Profound meanings like mist held within,
rare words like rain scattering.
On the path of governance he radiated brilliance,
the court's appearance was transformed.
Just as he was assisting in achieving peace,
harmonizing this heavenly order,
his fortune and position were often lacking,
the years granted him were many yet flawed.
Subtle words are forever silenced,
whom among the multitude of officials can look up to?"
Section Three: The Imperial Secretariat Director
The Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū),
was established in Qín.
The *Shàngshū* says:
"I command you to be the one who receives and conveys words."
The *Shī* says:
"Zhòngshān Fǔ issues and receives the king's commands,
he is the king's mouth and tongue,"
both refer to the duties of the Shàngshū.
The Zhōu official system had the Controller of Accounts."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation:
"This is like the present-day Shàngshū."
The *Treatise on Astronomy* says:
"The six stars of the Dipper's bowl are called the Wénchāng Palace."
Xún Chuò says:
"The Shàngshū is what is called the Wénchāng Heavenly Repository."
Xiāo Wàngzhī says:
"The Shàngshū is the foundation of all officials."
Later Hàn Lǐ Gù's memorial says:
"The state has the Shàngshū,
just as heaven has the Northern Dipper.
It serves as the mouth and tongue,
regulating the primal breath."
The *Hàn Official System* says:
"Initially, in the Qín dynasty, the Privy Treasurer (Shàofǔ)
dispatched four clerks to be in the palace halls,
in charge of issuing documents,
hence they were called Shàngshū.
Shàng means 'to be in charge of',
the Hàn followed Qín in establishing it."
In Hàn times it was still subordinate to the Shàofǔ.
After Wèi and Jìn,
administration returned to the central ministries,
so it was no longer subordinate.
Therefore, the Shàngshū was the Central Terrace (Zhōngtái),
the Receptionists (Yèzhě) were the Outer Terrace (Wàitái),
the Censor (Yùshǐ) was the Surveillance Terrace (Xiàntái),
these were called the Three Terraces (Sāntái).
The *Qí Official Regulations* says:
"Wèi, Jìn, Sòng, and Qí all called it the Shàngshū Terrace."
The *Five Dynasties History Monograph* says:
"Liáng, Chén, Later Wèi, Northern Qí, and Suí then called it the Shàngshū Department;
in the second year of Táng Lóngshuò reign,
it was renamed Central Terrace;
at the beginning of Xiánhēng reign, it reverted to Shàngshū Department;
at the beginning of Guāngzhái reign,
it was renamed Wénchāng Terrace;
at the beginning of Cháng'ān reign,
it again became Central Terrace;
at the beginning of Shénlóng reign,
it reverted to the old name Shàngshū Department."
Note: The Imperial Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Lìng) was a Qín office.
Hàn followed it.
The *Hàn Official System* says:
"In early Hàn, scholars were concurrently appointed as Shàngshū Lìng,
with a salary rank of 2,000 dàn."
By the time of Hàn Wǔdì,
a separate office of Receptionist Director (Yèzhě Lìng) was established,
using eunuchs,
and subsequently the Shàngshū office was abolished.
Emperor Chéng abolished the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū) office,
again appointing scholars as Shàngshū Lìng,
and it became the head of the Terrace.
It was in charge of presenting memorials,
overseeing laws and regulations.
Also:
"In Eastern Hàn, along with the Colonel Director of the Capital (Sīlì Xiàowèi) and the Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), they all had exclusive mats to sit on,
in the capital they were called the 'Three Sole Sitters'."
The *Jìn Official Ranks and Salaries* says:
"When a Shàngshū Lìng is appointed, an edict of appointment is issued;
when he dies, mourning is held in the court hall."
The *Five Dynasties History: Monograph on Officials* says:
"The Shàngshū Lìng,
by Liáng times had his salary rank increased to Fully 2,000 dàn."
The *Hàn Official System* says:
"The Shàngshū Lìng's salary rank was 1,000 dàn,
when a duke held it,
it was increased to 2,000 dàn.
Qín and Hàn salary ranks had Fully 2,000 dàn (Zhōng èrqiān dàn),
True 2,000 dàn (Zhēn èrqiān dàn).
There were four grades in all:
Equivalent to 2,000 dàn (Bǐ èrqiān dàn),
monthly receiving 100 dàn of grain;
2,000 dàn (Èrqiān dàn),
monthly receiving 120 dàn of grain;
True 2,000 dàn (Zhēn èrqiān dàn),
monthly receiving 150 dàn of grain.
The lower three grades, although called 2,000 dàn,
the actual amount did not reach that.
Only Fully 2,000 dàn (Zhōng èrqiān dàn),
monthly received 180 dàn of grain.
Averaging one year, one got 2,160 dàn.
Zhōng means 'full'.
It means it reaches the full 2,000 dàn.
However, in ancient times three dàn was only equivalent to one dàn today."
By Chén times,
its grade was raised to the first rank,
and thereafter it followed this without change.
Since Wèi times onward,
the Shàngshū Lìng's grade has been the third rank.
Central Terrace / Upper Department
"Central Terrace" is explained in the narrative.
The *Record of the Ten Continents* says:
"The Chónglǐ Gate is inside the Eastern Side Gate, west of the road,
that is the Upper Department of the Shàngshū.
East of the Chónglǐ Gate, inside the Jiànlǐ Gate,
that is the gate to the Shàngshū Lìng's lower residence."
Heavenly Repository / Immortal Terrace
Xún Chuò's *Annotations to the Jìn List of Officials* says:
"The Shàngshū is the Wénchāng Heavenly Repository."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Continuation of the Hàn Official System* says:
"The Shàngshū Department is inside the Shénxiān Gate."
Wáng Yún's *Poem Harmonizing with Minister Liú* says:
"The guest lodge stirs with autumn light,
the immortal terrace rises with cold mist."
Heavenly Pavilion / Rites Gate
The *Sòng Yuánjiā Reign Period Diaries* says:
"Shàngshū Left Assistant Yuán Pán reported:
Head Section Gentleman Xún Wànqiū.
Whenever he arranges matters, he uses them as a pretext for private excursions,
indulging wherever he goes.
How can he again be ranked among the scholars?
His name is listed in the Heavenly Pavilion;
I request that Wànqiū be dismissed from his post."
Lǐ Chōng's *Rhapsody on Harboring Sorrow* says:
"On a distant night in mid-autumn,
I stand straight in the forbidden gate of Chónglǐ."
Heavenly Terrace / Painted Department
Fù Xuán's *Preface to a Poem in Reply to Biǎn Kǔn* says:
"The Shàngshū Left Assistant,
impeaches officials of the eighth rank and below,
residing at the confluence of all affairs.
This is the rectifier of the imperial court,
the control of the Heavenly Terrace."
Cài Zhì's *Hàn Official Duties* says:
"The Shàngshū presented memorials in the Bright Light Hall (Míngguāng Diàn).
Within the Department, ancient martyrs were painted,
with inscriptions of praise written in successive lines."
Controller of Accounts / Wénchāng
The *Zhōu Rites* says:
"The duty of the Controller of Accounts (Sīkuài) of the Ministry of Heaven."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
"Kuài,
means great accounting.
The Sīkuài is in charge of the great accounting of the realm,
the head of the accounting officials,
like the present-day Shàngshū."
"The Wénchāng matter" is already seen in the annotation for "Heavenly Repository."
Issuing and Receiving Imperial Edicts / Comprehensively Managing Documents and Charts
The *Hàn Official System: Explanatory Notes* says:
"The Shàngshū issues and receives imperial edicts and commands,
coordinating the many mouths and tongues."
Mǎ Biāo's *Continuation of the Hàn History* says:
"In the fourth year of Emperor Chéng's Jiànshǐ reign,
the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū) office was abolished.
Initially, five Shàngshū personnel were established,
one as the Vice Director (Púyè),
divided into four Sections (Cáo),
comprehensively managing documents, secret records, memorials, and petitions,
each with their Section responsibilities."
The above comprehensively records the Shàngshū Central Department.
Eight Seats; Three Solitaries
The *Continued Book of Han* states:
"Emperor Guangwu divided and increased the Three Dukes Section into two sections.
One section was in charge of year-end reports and the evaluation of affairs in the various commanderies and prefectures.
He changed the Regular Attendants Section to the Officials Section,
in charge of selections for office and sacrificial rites.
The People Section was in charge of construction projects, salt ponds, parks, and enclosures.
The Guest Section was in charge of escorting the imperial carriage and the court congratulations of the Qiāng and Hú tribes.
The Two-Thousand-Bushel Section was in charge of litigation and the officials of the capital region in charge of water and fire, bandits, and thieves.
Together with the Three Dukes, these formed the Six Sections.
Combined with the two Directors of the Left and Right,
they are called the Eight Seats."
"Three Solitaries" is seen in the narrative.
Exclusive Mat; Turning the Carriage
Yìng Shào's *Han Officialdom* states:
"The Imperial Secretary, a Qin office,
had a bronze seal with a black silk ribbon.
The Colonel-Director of Retainers, the Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk, and the Imperial Secretary all sat on exclusive mats;
in the capital they were called the 'Three Solitary Seats',
indicating their high respect.
Emperor Wén of Wei once arrived at the gate of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Imperial Secretary Chén Jiǎo knelt and asked, 'Your Majesty, where do you wish to go?'
The Emperor said:
'I merely wish to inspect the documents!'
Jiǎo said:
'This is the duty of your servant;
it is not appropriate for Your Majesty to personally oversee.'
The Emperor listened and turned his carriage back."
The *Han Officialdom* states:
"When an official of the Imperial Secretariat goes out,
all the hundred officials turn their carriages aside to avoid him."
Black Carriage; Crimson Robes
Xú Guǎng's *Regulations for Carriages and Attire* states:
"The Imperial Secretary
rides in a yáo carriage with black ear-flaps and a rear door."
The *Qi Official Regulations* states:
"The Imperial Secretary is of the third rank,
with a salary of one thousand shi,
wears crimson court robes,
and carries a pale blue-green jade."
Upright and Stern; Broad and Brilliant
The *Continued Book of Han* states:
"Chén Fān's nature was upright and stern;
he was summoned to serve as Imperial Secretary."
The *Jìn Restoration History* states:
"Diāo Xié was promoted to Imperial Secretary.
An edict stated:
'Imperial Secretary Xié
holds his will high and bright.
His talent and discernment are broad and brilliant;
We greatly commend him.'"
Those in Office Were Awed; The Entire Court Feared
Zhāng Fán's *Han Records* states:
"Zuǒ Xióng served as Imperial Secretary.
He set an age limit of forty-nine for testing in the classics,
and only then could one be recommended as Filial and Incorrupt.
Thus, when Xióng was Secretary,
those in office were all awed."
The *Jìn Restoration History* states:
"Biǎn Kǔn served as Imperial Secretary.
The Minister of Education, Wáng Dǎo, claimed illness and did not attend court.
Kǔn memorialized that Dǎo, holding a special appointment, showed no respect.
The matter was shelved and not carried out,
and the entire court feared Kǔn."
Nàyán Headcloth; Jìnxián Cap
Xún Chuò's *Jìn Annotated Table of Officials* states:
"The Imperial Secretary has a bronze seal with a black silk ribbon,
and wears the five-season court robes with the Nàyán headcloth."
It also states:
"The Imperial Secretary wears the Jìnxián cap with two cross-beams,
and carries a pale blue-green jade."
Black-Earflap Carriage; Vermilion Tube at the Ear
Xú Guǎng's *Regulations for Carriages and Attire* states:
"The Imperial Secretary rides in a yáo carriage with black ear-flaps and a rear door."
Yìng Qú's new poem states:
"The vermilion tube is worn at the ear for receiving remonstrance;
the sable and golden ornaments mark the military cap."
Well-Versed in Past Affairs; Thoroughly Knowledgeable of Old Institutions
The *Dōngguān Records of the Han* states:
"Fán Huái, styled Yòuqīng,
served as Imperial Secretary."
The *Clarifying Han Family Past Affairs* states:
"Xióng Yuǎn submitted a memorial stating:
'I humbly observe that the Ministry of Personnel has appointed Grand Commandant Xún Zǔ as Imperial Secretary,
concurrently governing Yùzhōu.
Zǔ is a respected figure in the court,
thoroughly knowledgeable of old institutions;
he should not be placed outside.'"
*Text of the Appointment Edict by Emperor Hòuzhǔ of Chén Conferring the Title of Imperial Secretary upon Jiāng Zǒng*
Now, the Wénchāng Star is the foundation of governance,
and the Controller is the warp of transformation.
Wéi Biāo called it the pivot;
Lǐ Gù compared it to the Dipper and Pole Star.
How much more so when it synthesizes the five sections,
and harmonizes the myriad affairs.
It shares the duties of the Prime Minister,
and holds exclusive responsibility for the Secretariat.
You, whose moral conduct is stern and lofty,
and whose capacity is broad and profound.
Your exemplary conduct and pure regulations,
are taken as the standard by the refined.
A master of Confucianism and a treasury of learning,
you are regarded as the leader by the gentry.
Thus you are able to instruct and lead the six ministries,
and the gaze of all is truly fixed upon you.
To illuminate the government and the eight seats,
your exemplary form extends far.
To properly govern and wield authority,
is what We hope from you.
Go forth and be reverent!
Strive to establish your splendid plans.
Brightly assist our state;
can you not be cautious!
*Admonition for the Imperial Secretary* by Zhāng Huá of Jìn
Brilliant were the former kings,
who founded states and continued families.
They established institutions and handed down laws,
looking up to observe the arrayed stars.
Looking down, they commanded the hundred officials,
so governance was without error.
In ancient times, Shùn was received into the great mountains,
and the seven governments were thereby regulated.
Internal affairs were accomplished, external matters pacified,
and wind and rain were not misdirected.
Zhòng Shānfǔ assisted Zhōu,
neither overly harsh nor overly gentle.
He mended the flaws in our ruler's duties,
and elucidated our royal plans.
The royal plans were truly fulfilled,
and all within the four seas enjoyed peace.
Though one may be called sage and bright,
one must rely on excellent talent.
Do not say, 'I am wise,'
and fail to appoint capable officials.
Words spoken are like silk threads,
but when issued they become thick cords.
When the way of the kings declined,
heaven's net was loosened and neglected.
Since there were no seasoned elders,
the old laws and institutions were changed.
When laws and institutions are not cultivated,
one's descendants do not flourish.
I, your servant, oversee the Secretariat;
I dare to speak of guarding and protecting.
*Postscript to the Memorial Declining the Appointment as Imperial Secretary* by Jiāng Zǒng of Suí
The Controller is the root of transformation,
the Prime Minister is the pinnacle of the court.
It is what the gentry look up to,
and where exemplary forms reside.
Since the time of the imperial house,
if there is no suitable person, the post remains vacant.
Your Majesty intends to fill this position,
to harmonize your officials.
It is impermissible to begin with someone as mediocre and unworthy as I,
and thereby provoke public criticism.
At present, among the most trusted imperial relatives guarding the realm,
there are not none who are suitable.
Among the weighty ministers of the court,
there are also those with the capacity.
I humbly hope You will be cautious in following past precedents,
and elucidate the way of equitable governance.
With a public heart, I lay bare my sincerity;
there is reason in this.
Director of the Left and Right, Part Four
The position of Púshè in the Qín government,
was the director of the government.
In ancient times, military matters were highly valued,
so the head of government offices
led their subordinates and specialized in archery matters.
The "Book of Hàn - Table of Officials" states:
"From Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, Bóshì, Láng, military, and Tún officers, all had Púshè,
named according to the affairs overseen.
For example, the Shàngshū was called Shàngshū Púshè."
The Hàn, following the Qín, initially appointed one person,
until Emperor Xiàn made Zhíjīnwú Yíng Shào the Shàngshū Left Púshè,
thus establishing both left and right positions,
starting from this point.
Under Qín and Hàn, the rank was six hundred shí,
performed by dukes,
increased to two thousand shí.
By the Liáng,
the rank was raised to in-between two thousand shí.
From Wèi onward, it was ranked third.
By Chén,
it was raised to second rank.
From Wèi and Jìn to later,
the position's setup was inconsistent.
If two are established, they are left and right Púshè,
or sometimes only one is set,
called Shàngshū Púshè.
From the Eastern Jìn on,
the Praying Department Shàngshū was often not established,
with the Right Púshè taking charge.
If both Left and Right Púshè are vacant,
a Shàngshū Púshè is set,
responsible for the left duties;
a Praying Department Shàngshū is set,
responsible for right duties.
Therefore, Shàngshū Púshè and Praying Department Shàngshū
were not always established.
The above is from "Qí Zhíyí" and "Five Dynasties History - Official Records".
In the second year of Táng Lóngshuò, the left and right Púshè were changed to left and right Kuāngzhèng.
At the beginning of Xiánhēng, it reverted to the old.
At the start of Guāngzhài, it changed to left and right Prime Ministers.
At the start of Shénlóng, it reverted to the old.
At the beginning of Kāiyuán, it was again changed to left and right Chancellors.
Blue jade and black drape
"Jìn Hundred Officials' Table Annotation" states:
"There is one Púshè,
with copper seal and black ribbon.
In the morning court attire, Nàyán cap,
Jìnxián crown,
and wears water blue jade.
Office rank third,
monthly stipend of forty-five shí."
"Dongguan Hàn Jì" states:
"Bào Yǒng, styled Jūncháng,
was appointed Púshè.
He conducted general affairs,
leading troops to pacify Hé Dōng.
Yǒng excelled in literary virtue,
even as a general,
he often dressed in black drape,
and was known as General Bào Shàngshū among the soldiers."
Entering the gate, dragging shoes
Zhōng Lí "Biography of Yì" states:
"Yì, as Shàngshū Púshè,
in that year the Xiōngnú came to surrender,
granted three hundred bolts of silk by edict.
The Shàngshū Shìláng Jù Fēng received the edict,
mistakenly granted three thousand bolts to the Xiōngnú.
The emperor was greatly angered,
and had Fēng whipped nearly to death.
Yì alone entered the palace gate to remonstrate.
The Ming dynasty emperor recognized the righteousness of the action,
and his anger subsided.
The emperor said to Yì:
'Without Zhōng Lí Shàngshū,
a mistake would have degraded authority to that official.'" "Hàn Shū" states:
"Zhèng Chóng, styled Zǐyóu,
was Shàngshū Púshè.
He frequently requested audience to give remonstrance,
initially it was accepted by the emperor.
Whenever he was seen slipping in his leather shoes,
the emperor laughed and said:
'I recognize the sound of Zhèng Shàngshū's shoes.'"
Purely respectful, genuinely loyal
"Biography and Actions of Worthies" states:
"Máo Jiè, styled Xiàoxiān,
was Shàngshū Púshè,
performing with purity and respect in office."
"Jìn Qījūzhù" states:
"Shàngshū Gāoyáng Wáng Guī,
genuinely loyal and competent in governance,
and was appointed to the Right Púshè."
Managing a hundred agencies, subordinately pleasing
"Xiè Língyùn Jìn Shū" states:
"In antiquity, military affairs were valued,
with importance on archery and driving.
For its adaptation and swiftness as subordinates,
one was placed in each position,
six Shàngshū,
known as eight seats.
Participation in managing a hundred agencies,
issuing and receiving royal commands,
is the role of the ancient Yuánkǎi."
Hé Fǎshèng "Jìn Revival History" states:
"Gù Hé was Shàngshū Púshè,
but declined due to his mother's old age.
An edict authorized him to leave in the evening and return in the morning,
with such special treatment.
The court later discussed that for secondary supervisors of status,
it was inappropriate to be placed externally,
and he was additionally honored as Silver Blue Light Lù Grandee."
Coordinating and declaring various achievements, overall administering
"Jìn Qījūzhù" states:
"In the first year of Tàikāng, an edict said:
'The Shàngshū used to have left and right Púshè,
to expand and apply government codes,
coordinating and declaring various achievements.'" "Wèi Zhì" states:
"Huán Fàn recommended Xú Xuān as Púshè,
later added as Shìzhōng Light Lù Grandee,
when the imperial carriage visited Xǔchāng,
he was overall administering.
When the emperor returned,
the manager submitted the documents to the emperor,
the edict said:
'What is different from me and Púshè?'
He ultimately did not review them."
Chief justice of the state, master and head of officials
"Wèi Zhì" states:
"Máo Jiè, styled Xiàoxiān,
was Shàngshū Púshè.
At the time, the crown prince's position was undecided,
Línzī Wáng Zhí was favored,
and Jiè advised:
'Recently Yuán Shào's failure to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate led to the downfall of his line,
and the ruin of his state,
this is a significant matter of succession,
not to be treated lightly.'
As Jiè rose for a toilet break,
the Tàizǔ said:
'The chief justice of the state,
my own Zhōu Chāng.'" Again it says:
"During the time of Wén Emperor, considering Jiǎ Xù for Púshè,
he said:
'The Shàngshū Púshè,
is the master and head of officials,
on whom the world places hopes.
Xù's reputation has never been esteemed,
and cannot command respect.'"
Five advancements and four refusals, two dragons and twin steeds
Fàn Yè "Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
"Hú Guǎng, styled Bóshǐ,
advanced five times to Shàngshū Púshè."
"Wáng Yǐn Jìn Shū" states:
"Xún Yǐ succeeded Chén Tài as Púshè,
managed the Personnel Department,
refused four times before accepting."
Zhāng Quán "Nányàn Shū" states:
"Mùróng Dé made Right Púshè Fēng Sōng as Left Púshè,
and Shàngshū Hán as Right Púshè.
At the time, Sōng and the others were all thirty years old,
also appointing Sōng's brother Róng as Western General,
and his brother Guǐ as Eastern General.
Sōng and others all accepted appointments,
the emperor from the throne gave a command for all four to enter together,
Sōng and others ascended to the hall to give thanks.
The emperor said approvingly:
'Two dragons leaping on the long road,
racing twin steeds to a thousand.'
The court and the public honored them."
Liáng Rényìshēng's "Poem on Mourning Deputy Director Fàn at the County Relay Station"
In life, the rituals were utmost,
I looked up to him as a pillar of the state.
In a single day, all transformations ceased,
Yet my old friend's affection remains.
Awaiting the time of rising fortune,
A king's aide awaits a man of excellence.
Our friendship spanned thirty years,
A bond of life and death, a single friendship.
Hand in hand, we escaped decline and calamity,
Facing the light, we served in times of peace and brightness.
When fortune was blocked, words of balance were reformed,
When times were prosperous, the jade steps were level.
Jùn Chōng obtained the talented Yàn,
While you, sir, encountered a wild youth.
That man had the clarity of Jīng and Wèi,
It was not for me to stir up muddiness or purity.
On the verge of parting, I cannot bear to bid farewell,
Wishing to dispel the sorrow of separation.
Unable to bear the sentiment of a single moment,
A thousand ages, ten thousand regrets arise.
Alas, the affairs of a lifetime,
Songs and chants fill the boxes and baskets.
Moreover, we often teased and joked,
Often encountering an empty boat.
When will I see Lord Fàn again,
To recount the sentiments of a lifetime?
How many moments since parting from you,
The journey has not filled ten days.
Not seeing the rosy face changed,
Only imagining the person of a lifetime.
How could I know the day of peaceful song,
Was not the time you laid aside the zither?
Alas, what can be done but sigh,
Ceasing the spring plow, mourning the state's balance.
Rén Xīgǔ's "Poem Harmonizing with Deputy Director Yàn's Spring Day Quiet Dwelling, Recounting Sentiments"
The fertile fields shone with three heroes,
The Guī court praised five ministers.
Silk and hemp sang of fine reputations,
Strings and bamboo chanted fragrant dust.
The sage's calendar opened the cycle of phenomena,
Prosperous years brought forth Fǔ and Shēn.
The lofty gate was not built by common hands,
The splendid structure was not woven by hanging threads.
The phoenix mansion soared to the heavens,
The dragon pond leaped with sea scales.
The jade tripod ascended to the Yellow Pavilion,
The golden seal paid homage at the Purple Palace.
The ritual court connects to governance's root,
Wénchāng oversees the state's balance.
Adjusting the winds to shake shallow customs,
Purifying teachings to rectify constant principles.
Stars return in response to the pitch pipes,
The sun's charioteer alerts the welcoming of dawn.
Leaves on the once Huái tree change,
Flowers bloom in the small hall's spring.
Thinking of hanging the crown of the Eastern Capital,
Speaking of visiting the headscarf of the Northern Mountain.
Resplendent on the ceremonial terrace,
A thousand sacrifices shine on Píngjīn.
Zhào Yànzhāo's "Poem Presented in Harmony Mourning Deputy Director Yáng Zàisī"
Two measures illuminated heaven's order,
Three courts served the emperor's brightness.
How could one speak of gathering the great bird,
Suddenly here, the loss of the sacred turtle.
Sitting, sighing the public Huái tree's fall,
Walking, hearing the minister's tree's sorrow.
The ravine boat has now departed,
How can there be a time to cross the river?
Chén Xúlíng's "Memorial Declining the Position of Deputy Director"
Your subject has heard that at seventy years of age,
Yáng Xióng emulated the classics.
At sixty years of age,
Jīn answered the policy questions.
If such are considered robust,
Then certainly there are no elders.
Your subject Lì is of noble lineage, adorned with carriage and crown,
His talent befits a minister or chancellor.
In administration, his reputation flows,
Both court and countryside look up to him.
Your subject Hóngzhèng is a state elder, a Confucian patriarch,
His disposition favors emptiness and simplicity.
In profound style and surpassing achievements,
He alone reigns in his time.
Your subject Zhòngqì harbors deep secrecy,
Well-versed in literature and history.
A distinguished talent of the southeast,
Beloved and worthy in the court.
All exhibit grand strategies,
All are fit for the left hand's duty.
If Hàn Wǔ favored youth,
Then your humble subject is already old.
If Zhōu Wén cherished age,
Then there are these many talents.
I humbly hope Your Majesty's wisdom,
Will further seek master craftsmen.
Seeking their exquisite selection,
To match capable officials.
Suí Jiāngzǒng's "Memorial Declining the Position of Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat"
Examining official standards,
Assessing and judging individuals.
The gate startled like a marketplace,
Not ashamed even in the hidden corner.
The heart holds clear as water,
Deceiving not even in the dark room.
But repeatedly delayed by the star bird,
Often aware of the millet's plainness.
Bound by the world's net,
Affairs return to forced exertion.
Now this summons and meeting,
Especially increases anxiety and unease.
I privately consider the deputy position of chief minister,
An office called teacher and elder.
With leather shoes ascending and descending,
Heralds proclaiming favor and splendor.
Modeling the court's forefront,
Crowning the constant principles.
Moreover, participating in overseeing the flow of balance,
Assisting in rectifying the sage's governance.
Presumptuously bearing heavy responsibility,
Must tread on crisis.
Fifth Section: The Various Department Heads
The various department heads,
Are offices of the Qín dynasty.
The Hàn dynasty followed them,
And employed scholars.
Emperor Wǔ changed to using eunuchs.
Emperor Chéng again changed to using scholars.
The "Hàn Shū" states:
"Emperor Wǔ amused himself in the rear court,
Dukes and ministers could not enter,
Therefore he used eunuchs to oversee the Imperial Secretariat."
Four department heads were established,
Collectively managing documents, charts, memorials, and reports,
Each with their own duties.
The first was called the Constant Attendant Department,
The second the Two Thousand Piculs Department,
The third the People's Department,
The fourth the Guest Department.
Emperor Guāngwǔ divided them into six departments:
Dividing the Two Thousand Piculs Department into two,
Dividing the Guest Department into two.
Changing the Constant Attendant Department to the Personnel Department.
Together with one Director and one Deputy Director,
They were called the Eight Seats.
Wèi had five departments with two Deputy Directors and one Director,
Called the Eight Seats.
Wèi had the Personnel Department, Left People's Department, Guest Department, Five Military Departments, and Finance Department,
Totaling five department heads.
Jìn had six departments.
Jìn initially established the Personnel Department, Three Dukes Department, Guest Department, Carriage Department, Agricultural Colonies Department, and Finance Department, six department heads.
During Tàikāng, there were the Personnel Department, Palace Department, Five Military Departments, Fields Department, Finance Department, and Left People's Department, six department heads.
Eastern Jìn had the Sacrificial Department, Personnel Department, Left People's Department, Finance Department, and Five Military Departments, five department heads.
Sòng had six departments.
Sòng added the Eastern Capital Officials Department.
Liáng and Chén had six departments.
Qí department names were the same as the Sòng dynasty.
Later Wèi and Northern Qí had six departments.
Later Wèi and Northern Qí had the Personnel Department,
Palace Department, Sacrificial Department, Seven Military Departments, Capital Officials Department, and Finance Department.
Later Zhōu followed the Zhōu Rituals,
Establishing the six official department head positions.
Suí dynasty had six departments.
Suí had the Personnel Department, Rites Department, War Department, Capital Officials Department, Finance Department, and Works Department.
In the third year of Kāihuáng,
The Finance Department was changed to the Revenue Department,
The Capital Officials Department to the Justice Department,
This is so.
Táng had six departments.
Initially establishing the People's Department,
The rest were the same as the Suí dynasty.
At the end of Zhēnguàn, the People's Department was changed to the Finance Department,
Soon changed again to the Revenue Department.
In the second year of Lóngshuò, department heads were changed to Grand Regular Ministers,
Changing the Personnel Department, Rites Department, Revenue Department, War Department,
Justice Department, and Works Department to the Department of Ranks, Department of Rites, Department of Origins, Department of Military, Department of Justice, and Department of Peace.
Empress Zétiān again followed the six officials of the Zhōu Rituals.
Initially, the Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén dynasties also had a Construction Department Head.
When constructing ancestral temples, it was temporarily established,
Upon completion, it was abolished.
The above are all from the "Hàn Officialdom," "Qí Official Regulations," and the "Five Dynasties History: Treatise on Officials."
Repeated Ascension Circulating Through
The *Later Book of Han* by Xiè Chéng states:
"Wèi Lǎng, styled Zhòngyīng,
entered the court to serve as a Secretary.
He repeatedly ascended to the Purple Palace.
Outspoken and upright within the forbidden precincts,
he did not yield to powerful magnates,
and was respected by all officials.
He was dismissed due to factional affairs.
Lǎng's nature was stern and dignified.
He closed his doors and maintained discipline,
rarely seen by senior officials.
His actions were always according to ritual order.
His family treated each other like guests,
and his children and grandchildren served him as a stern lord."
It also states:
"Cài Yōng, styled Bójiē,
was promoted from Attendant Censor to Secretary.
Within three months,
he circulated through the three terraces,
and was promoted to Palace Attendant."
Discarding Pearls Bestowing Swords
The *Later Book of Han* by Xiè Chéng states:
"Zhōnglí Yì, styled Zǐ'ā,
was summoned by Emperor Míng to serve as a Secretary.
The Governor of Jiāozhǐ was executed for corruption.
His assets were recorded and entered into the Grand Minister of Agriculture's office.
An edict ordered them distributed and bestowed upon the assembled ministers.
Yì received pearls and jades,
but discarded them all on the ground and did not bow in gratitude.
The Emperor, surprised, asked the reason.
He replied:
'Your servant has heard that Confucius endured thirst rather than drink from the water of Dào Quán,
and Zēng Shēn turned his carriage around at the village of Shèngmǔ,
detesting their names.
Treasures tainted by corruption,
I dare not accept.'
The Emperor laughed and said:
'How pure is the Secretary!'
He bestowed upon him three hundred thousand cash."
The *Records of the Eastern Lodge* states:
"Emperor Zhāng bestowed upon each Secretary a sword,
personally inscribing their names.
Hán Léng received a Lóngquán sword from Chǔ,
Zhì Shòu received a patterned sword from Shǔ-Hàn,
Chén Chǒng received a forged sword from Jǐnán.
One chamber had two blades,
the rest were all straight swords.
Commentators of the time
believed Léng was profound and strategic,
hence he received the Lóngquán.
Shòu was intelligent and accomplished in literature,
hence he received the patterned sword.
Chǒng was sincere and simple, with goodness within,
not apparent outwardly,
hence he received the forged sword.
Each was matched according to their name to express their qualities."
White Robes Patterned Sword
The *Book of the Later Han* states:
"Zhèng Jūn, styled Zhòngyú,
served as a Secretary.
He was indifferent and without desires.
Due to illness, he requested retirement,
and ultimately refused to resume office.
Emperor Zhāng's carriage visited Jūn's residence,
and by decree bestowed upon him the salary of a Secretary for life."
People of the time called him
"the White-robed Secretary.
'Patterned Sword' is already mentioned above."
Circulating Through Three Terraces Serving for Seven Years

Bestowing a Forged Sword Enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎngwǔ

Responses and Consultations Excellent Plans and Good Strategies

Zhū Mù's Uprightness Huáng Wǎn's Resolute Integrity
The *Later Book of Han* by Xiè Chéng states:
