A Poem by Yán Yánnián of the Sòng Dynasty, "Answering Secretary Zhèng from the Eastern Palace"
The imperial abode embodies the celestial pole,
Its defenses established by heavenly craft.
Two gates hinder the thoroughfare,
Facing prohibitions, limiting clear winds.
I stand tiptoe at the eastern lodge, a traveler,
Singing alone by the southern wall.
Resting and rising, pent-up without end,
I rise to gaze at the stars in the Han River sky.
Flowing clouds shroud the azure towers,
The bright moon mirrors the crimson palace.
Hesitant, the clear guard is dense,
Pacing, the constant drip of the clepsydra runs dry.
The nobleman sends forth fragrant tidings,
Moved by things, he inclines to my inner heart.
Alas, I lack the grace of hill and garden,
To admire the conduct of those lofty peaks.

Liú Bīn's "Poem Mourning Secretary Niú, Harmonizing with Attendant Xǔ"

Minister of Personnel Chapter Six
The Minister of Personnel,
was first established by Hàn Chéngdì with four ministers.
One of them said:
"The Cabinet of Attendants,
oversees the affairs of the Chancellor, the Censor, and the Dukes and Ministers.
At the beginning of Later Hàn,
with Emperor Guāngwǔ's reform, the Cabinet of Attendants was renamed the Personnel Division,
in charge of selecting officials and sacrificial ceremonies,
later changed to the Selection Division in the end of Later Hàn.
During the Wèi dynasty, it again became the Personnel Division,
solely responsible for managing appointments,
superior to the other divisions.
By the Sòng, two Ministers of Personnel were established,
but later reduced to one. "
Shěn Yuè in "Book of Sòng" states:
"In the early Jìn, the expectation for Attending Gentleman was no different from that of Palace Attendant,
but later their duties dispersed,
with less weight placed on personnel selection.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng wished to emphasize the selection,
and relied heavily on the Minister of Personnel's role,
thereby dividing the Personnel Division among three people,
to lighten the burden."
Cài Xīngzōng said:
"The importance of the Selection Division,
Attendant Gentleman is known to hear,
with a change in name but not in essence.
Although the ruler’s intention is to weigh it heavily,
can human hearts change?"
From Hàn to Wèi,
those granted this position,
were sometimes called Minister of Personnel.
If appointed to the other divisions of ministers,
they were simply called 'minister.'
In Hàn, Wèi, and Jìn times,
if appointed as Minister of Personnel,
they were told to take role of Minister of Personnel.
For other divisions,
they were called just 'minister.'
After Jìn, Sòng, and Qí,
it began to specify the departments of Engineering, Justice, Military, and Finance ministers.
Therefore, through the historical records of various dynasties,
the Minister of Personnel’s position is separately recorded,
not listed with the various other officials.
This book is thus modeled after these mentions.
From "Officials of Hàn,"
"Ceremonial Regulations of Qí," and the "Records of the Officials of the Five Dynasties."

Left and Right Vice Directors, Seventh
The Vice Directors of the Imperial Secretariat
are offices from the Qín.
The Hàn continued them.
By Emperor Chéng's time, four Ministers for various bureaus were established,
and accordingly four Vice Directors were appointed.
By Emperor Guāngwǔ's time, two were reduced,
leaving only the Left and Right Vice Directors.
Chéng (Vice Director) means
to receive (chéng).
It means receiving and assisting the Directors and Vice Directors,
overseeing the affairs of the Secretariat.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat and the Left Vice Director jointly oversee discipline and regulations.
The Vice Directors and the Right Vice Director manage the receipt and disbursement of funds and grain.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the Left Vice Director gained the authority to impeach the eight high officials.
Therefore, Fù Xián said this is the 'Upholder of Justice' for the imperial court,
the 'pivot and linchpin' of the celestial platform (central administration).
The Sòng Shū, "Treatise on Officials," states:
"In the Jìn and Sòng eras,
the Left Vice Director was in charge of prohibitions and orders within the Secretariat,
ancestral temple sacrifices,
and court rituals and ceremonies.
He selected and appointed clerks,
and impeached unlawful conduct.
The Right Vice Director managed the treasuries, storehouses, and buildings within the Secretariat,
all implements and utensils, as well as legal cases and weapons."
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
their rank was always the sixth grade,
with a salary of 400 shí.
The Liáng raised the rank to the fourth grade,
with a salary of 600 shí.
From the Qí Zhí Yí and the Wǔ Dài Shǐ, "Treatise on Officials."
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng (662 CE),
they were renamed Left and Right 'Sùjī' (Rectifiers of Order).
In the early Xiánhēng era (670 CE), the old titles were restored.

Assistant Directors, Department Heads, and Vice Department Heads: The Eighth
Regarding Assistant Directors (Shìláng),
they were established by Emperor Yáng of Suí.
Department Heads (Lángzhōng),
are officials from the Qín dynasty.
Vice Department Heads (Yuánwàiláng),
were established by Emperor Wén of Suí.
Initially, the Western Hàn established four Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat.

One was in charge of the Xiongnu Chányú's camp and tribes; one in charge of Qiāng and Yí officials and people; one in charge of household registration and land reclamation; one in charge of money, silk, tribute, and transport.
Emperor Guāngwǔ divided the Imperial Secretariat into six Bureaus,
each Director of the Imperial Secretariat then led six Gentlemen,
making a total of thirty-six Gentlemen.
In early Qín, the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace was established.
He led the Gentlemen serving within the palace and acted as their commander.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn renamed it the Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
Its subordinate offices had three Divisions,
the Leader of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Five Offices, the Leader of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Left, and the Leader of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Right,
making three Divisions in total.
Within the Divisions were Gentlemen of the Palace (Lángzhōng) and Attendant Gentlemen (Shìláng), with no fixed number,
sometimes reaching over a thousand.
They were divided among the three Divisions,
primarily responsible for bearing halberds and guarding the palace halls,
and when traveling outside, they served as mounted escorts.
The Hàn dynasty followed this system.
The Gentleman of the Palace (Lángzhōng) had a rank equivalent to 300 shí,
the Attendant Gentleman (Láng) equivalent to 400 shí.
Because they served as Gentlemen within the palace,
they were called Lángzhōng (Gentleman of the Interior).
Because they served as Gentlemen in internal attendance,
they were called Shìláng (Attendant Gentleman).
"The Hàn Official System" states:
"Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat,
were initially selected from the Gentlemen of the three Divisions to be tested at the Imperial Secretariat.
For each Gentleman vacancy, five candidates were tested,
first testing their drafting of memorials.
Upon first entering the Secretariat, they were called Lángzhōng (Department Head),
after a full year, they were called Shìláng (Assistant Director).
Therefore, the titles Lángzhōng and Shìláng
still derived from the original designations of the three Divisions."
In Western Hàn records, many references to "Gentlemen"
are not to Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat.
Only Tián Fén serving as a Gentleman in various Bureaus in his youth is an example.
In Emperor Wén's time, Féng Táng served as Chief of the Gentlemen's Division.
Zhí Bùyí stole gold from a fellow Gentleman.
In Emperor Wǔ's time, Yán Sì served as a Gentleman for three generations without promotion.
In Emperor Chéng's time, Yáng Xióng served as an Attendant Gentleman.
And references to purchasing a Gentleman post,
or a father holding office as a Gentleman,
all refer to Gentlemen of the three Divisions.
Up to the Eastern Hàn, it is still difficult to distinguish;
if prefixed with "Imperial Secretariat" or a Bureau name, it refers to a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
Simply stated as "Gentleman" also refers to a Gentleman of the three Divisions.
After the Wèi dynasty, there were no longer Gentlemen of the three Divisions.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
the Department Heads (Lángzhōng) and Assistant Directors (Shìláng) of the various Bureaus of the Imperial Secretariat
were sometimes not both established.
Sometimes only Department Heads were established,
sometimes only Assistant Directors were established,
but both also generally served as Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat.
In the Hàn era, both were established,
there were Department Heads and Assistant Directors.
In Wèi, Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Later Wèi, and Northern Qí, only Department Heads were established.
In Liáng and Chén, both were established,
there were Department Heads and Assistant Directors.
"The Treatise on Officials of the Five Dynasties" states:
"In Liáng, Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat,
upon first entering the Secretariat, were called Department Heads.
Those with greater merit were transferred to become Assistant Directors.
The Chén dynasty followed the Liáng system.
According to previous dynasties where both Department Heads and Assistant Directors were established,
the Assistant Director held the responsibilities of the present-day Department Head,
and the Department Head held the responsibilities of the present-day Vice Department Head.
If only Department Heads were established,
they also held the responsibilities of the present-day Department Head."
In the early Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wén of Suí,
only Assistant Directors were established.
These were also Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat.
The Suí dynasty avoided the character "zhōng" (中),
so they did not establish Department Heads (Lángzhōng),
establishing only Assistant Directors (Shìláng) as Gentlemen of the Imperial Secretariat.
Soon after, each Bureau also established one Vice Department Head.
Emperor Yáng established six Assistant Directors under each of the six Ministers,
increasing their rank to the fourth grade,
to serve as deputies to the Ministers.
These are the present-day Vice Ministers of the Six Boards.
The Assistant Directors of the various Bureaus were simply called Gentlemen (Láng),
omitting the character "shì" (侍).
Each Bureau established two Gentlemen,
soon after, each Bureau reduced one Gentleman,
and added one Administrative Assistant (Chéngwùláng),
equivalent to the Vice Department Head position of the Kāihuáng era.
The Táng dynasty changed it back to Department Head (Lángzhōng),
and again, following the Kāihuáng system, established one Vice Department Head per Bureau.
The Suí dynasty avoided the character "zhōng" (中),
so they simply called them Gentlemen (Láng).
In the early Táng, they reverted to saying:
"Department Head (Lángzhōng).
The above is drawn from 'The Hàn Official Ceremonial', 'The Qí Official Regulations', and 'The Treatise on Officials of the Five Dynasties'."

In morning I roamed the layered walls,
At dusk I rested, returning to my duty lodge.
Sudden thunder roared at midnight,
Startling lightning flashed through the night.
Dark clouds draped the vermilion towers,

The lingering gloom congeals, unresolved,
The broad avenues transformed into channels.
Submerged crops drown in Liáng and Yǐng,

Zhōngshū Lìng, the Ninth
The Zhongshuling,
established by Hàn Wǔ.
Responsible for conveying the emperor's orders,
handled the memorial submissions to the Shàngshū,
similar to the role of the Zhōu officer Nèishǐ.
The Zhōu Nèishǐ oversaw the king's eight commands.
Initially, after Hàn Wǔ's banquets in the rear court,
officials were not allowed to enter,
leading to the eunuchs being appointed to handle the Shàngshū,
managing the archives and memorials.
During the Qín era, the Shaofǔ,
sent four officials to manage documents in the palace,
called Shàngshū.
"Shàng" means to manage.
Hàn continued this practice,
initially using scholars,
Wǔ Dì switched to using eunuchs.
Later, the Shàngshū was abolished,
replacing it with the Zhōngshū Yèzhělǐng,
entirely manned by eunuchs.
Therefore, Shěn Yuè's "Song Shu: Hundred Officials Record" states,
"Zhongshu originally referred to Shàngshū officials."
Xiè Língyùn's "Jin Shu" states,
"Because they managed the confidential records,
it was called Zhongshu.
After Sīmǎ Qiān suffered punishment during Hàn Wǔ's era,
he became the Zhongshuling,
this was his position."
"Hàn Shu" does not mention Yèzhě,
due to historical abbreviation.
The original title of the position was "Zhongshū Yèzhělǐng."
"Hàn Shu" directly refers to Qiān as "Zhongshuling,"
an abbreviation in historical records.
During Xuān Dì's era,
Hóng Gōng was punished and
promoted several times to the position of Lǐng,
familiar with the law,
wielding power inside and outside the court.
However, after Gōng's death,
Shí Jūnfáng, also punished, succeeded as Lǐng.
When Chéng Dì established the Shàngshū office,
the role of Zhōngshū Yèzhělǐng was changed,
its responsibilities no longer involved handling important documents.
It became the position of eunuchs in the inner court,
not involving significant state affairs.
Therefore, Xiè Língyùn's "Jin Shu" states,
"After Hàn Chéng Dì, there was no role of Zhongshu."
In the early Eastern Hàn, there was also no such position,
until the time of Xiàn Dì,
Wèi Wǔ became King of Wèi,
established the position of Mìshū Lǐng,
which was again the role of Zhongshu.
Since Zhongshu managed confidential records and archives,
it was named Mìshū.
Wèi Wén changed Mìshū Lǐng to Zhongshuling,
appointing Sūn Zī, the Mìshū Yòuchéng, as Zhongshuling.
Since Wèi and Jìn, one person was always appointed,
ranked third,
exceptionally selected scholars with literary knowledge served,
responsible for the king's words.
The Jiangzuo further emphasized this role,
often held concurrently by Dukes.
Originally, the Prime Minister was of the Three Dukes,
by Wèi and Jìn, the Zhongshuling managed the king's words,
with significant prestige,
often held concurrently by Dukes.
In recent generations,
if no suitable Three Dukes were found, the position was vacant,
with the Zhongshuling taking the role of advisor.
In recent times, specializing in this position began,
the Suí Wén Dì changed it to Nèishǐ Lǐng,
appointing two people.
The Suí house avoided using "Zhōng,"
following Zhōu officials and changing to Nèishǐ,
Hàn Wǔ established Zhongshu,
with a Lǐng,
and a Pùshè.
During Xuān Dì's time Hóng Gōng was Lǐng,
Shí Jūnfáng was Pùshè,
after Gōng's death,
Shí succeeded as Lǐng.
When Wèi Wǔ established the Mìshū Lǐng,
Wèi Wén changed Mìshū Lǐng Zuǒ Chéng to Zhongshuling,
also appointing one Jiān,
equivalent to the position of Pùshè.
Initially, Sūn Zī, Mìshū Yòuchéng, became Zhongshuling,
Liú Fàng, Zuǒ Chéng, became Zhongshūjiàn.
Throughout Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, Chén, Northern Qí, Later Wèi,
a Zhongshūjiàn was always appointed,
ranked above the Lǐng.
During the Suí period, it was abolished,
so two Lǐngs were appointed.
Yáng Dì changed it to Nèishū Lǐng.
The above is sourced from "Hàn Guān" and "Qí Zhí Yí,"
and "Wǔ Dài Shǐ: Hundred Officials Record."
In the early Táng, it once again became Nèishǐ.
In the 3rd year of Wǔdé, it was restored to Zhongshuling.
In the 2nd year of Longshuo it changed to Xītái Yòuxiàng.
At the beginning of Xiánhēng, it was restored.
In the beginning of Guāngzhài, it changed to Fènggé Nèishǐ.
At the beginning of Shénlóng, it was restored.
At the beginning of Kāiyuán, it changed to Zǐwēi Lǐng.
In the fifth year it was restored.

Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tenth
Zhōngshū Shìláng
is an office of the Wèi dynasty.
According to the *Huán Jì Yàolüè*:
"The Zhōngshū had Lìng, Púyè, Chéng, and Láng,
referring to the Western Hàn period."
Also, according to Wèi Hóng's *Hàn Jiù Yí*:
"The Hàn established the Zhōngshū,
overseeing the Shàngshū Xiōngnú camp section with one Láng, the People section with one Láng, and the Receptionist section with one Láng.
This shows that Zhōngshū Láng was already known in the Hàn dynasty.
Records and biographies lack clear text,
so the reasons for its abolition and establishment are unknown!"
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Zhì* states:
"During Emperor Wén of Wèi's Huángchū era, the Zhōngshū established the office of Tōngshì Láng,
ranking below Huángmén Láng.
After the Huángmén Láng had endorsed,
the Tōngshì would then add his signature,
and the Emperor would review and read it for approval.
The Jìn changed Tōngshì Láng to Zhōngshū Shìláng,
which likely began then."
According to the *Wèi Zhì*:
"Emperor Míng issued an edict to recommend candidates for Zhōngshū Láng.
He said to Lú Yù:
'In recommending, do not choose those with mere fame.
Fame is like drawing a cake on the ground;
it cannot be eaten.'
Yù recommended Hán Jì,
and the Emperor employed him."
Also, Sīmǎ Xuānwáng recruited Wáng Bóxīng,
promoting him to Zhōngshū Shìláng,
also during Emperor Míng's time.
Based on this,
Zhōngshū Shìláng originated in the Wèi dynasty.
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū* says the Jìn changed it,
which seems erroneous.
The Eastern Jìn changed it back to Tōngshì Láng,
and soon restored it to Zhōngshū Láng.
Later periods followed this.
According to records, at the beginning of the Suí dynasty, the Zhōngshū Shěng was changed to Nèishì Shěng.
At the end of the Suí, it was changed to Nèishū Jiān.
At the beginning of the Táng, it was changed again to Nèishǐ Shěng.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era, it was changed to Xī Tái.
In the Zāichū era, it was changed to Fèng Gé.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era, it was changed to Zǐwēi.
The Shìláng titles each changed according to the name of the Tái or Gé.
For example, for Fèng Gé it was called Fèng Gé Shìláng,
and the Shèrén and below all followed this pattern.

and each time they were treated as honored guests entering the inner chamber.
Huī, styled Zhēncháng,
was pure and lofty from a young age.
People of the time compared Méng to Yuán Yàogīng,
and Huī to Xún Fèngqiàn."
Solely in Charge, Without Equal
Hé Fǎshèng's *History of the Eastern Jin* says:
"Fàn Nìng, styled Wǔzǐ,
loved learning from a young age,
and was widely read.

solely in charge of the Western Bureau.

benefiting governance and policy."

it was considered difficult to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Méng."
Regulations and Institutions, Documents and Proclamations
Hé Fǎshèng's *History of the Eastern Jin* says:

after the Jin state was established,

Yǎn was broadly learned in the classics,
and also well-versed in ancient institutions.
Regarding court rituals, regulations, and institutions,
he provided much correction and guidance.
Thus, Emperors Yuán and Míng both cherished him."
Also, the *Genealogy of the Jī Family* says:
"Jī Hán served as a Secretariat Gentleman.

Utmost Conduct, Frank Speech

The *History of the Eastern Jin* says:
"Fàn Nìng was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat.

they would frequently consult him,

Guō Bān's *Anecdotes from Wei and Jin* says:
"Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng ordered the Secretariat Gentleman Yú Sōng to draft a memorial.
After presenting it twice, it was still unsatisfactory,
so he ordered Sōng to revise it.
After a long time of exhausting his thoughts, he could not make changes,
and his worry showed on his face.
The Secretariat Gentleman Zhōng Huì noticed his troubled expression,
asked Sōng about it,
and Sōng answered truthfully.
Huì took the draft to look at it,
fixed five characters,
and Sōng was pleased and convinced.
He presented it to Jǐngwáng,
and Jǐngwáng said:
'Isn't this much better?'
Sōng said:
'It was Zhōng Huì.'
The Prince said:
'Such a person can be greatly employed;
he truly has the talent to assist a king.'"

Five Characters, A Few Words
"Five characters" is seen in the note for "Zhōng's Memorial."
Lù Shìhéng was transferred to Vice Director of the Secretariat.
Prince Qí arrested Shìhéng and handed him over to the Commandant of Justice.

and I was originally known for my writing,

not a single word or character

"Difficult to stand shoulder-to-shoulder" is seen in the note for "Without Equal."

Táng Tàizōng's "Poem Farewelling Vice Director of the Secretariat Lái Jì"
Dimly, leaving dusty gloom by the Bà riverbank,
lightly flying canopies point toward the bridge over the river.
Cloud-peak garments knot a thousand layers of leaves,
snowy cliffs bloom with several trees of fragrance.
Deeply grieve the yellow crane, a lone boat far away,
alone sigh for the green mountains, the parting road long.
Let me compose parting tears that soak the lapel,
and still use them to fill the farewell banquet's cup.
Wèi Liú Gōnggàn's "Poem Presented to Xú Gàn"
Who says the distance between us is far,
separated by this Western Wall barrier?
Limited by the strict prohibitions of this pure, intimate place,
my inner feelings have no way to express.
Thinking of you sinks into the depths of my heart,
long sighs, unable to speak.
Rising and sitting, losing all order,
three or four times a day I move about.
Walking out the North Temple gate,
from afar I see the Western Park garden.
Slender willows line the path growing,
square ponds hold clear springs.
Light leaves turn with the wind,
flying birds, how they flutter and soar.
Qí Xiè Xuāntíng's "Poem While on Duty in the Secretariat"
The Purple Hall solemn, deep and shaded,
the vermilion courtyard vast and grandly open.
Wind stirs the ten-thousand-year branches,
sunlight shines on dew-holding palms.
Exquisite knots of patterned coins,
deeply reflecting pearl-like nets.
Red peonies by the steps flutter,
dark moss climbs along the base of the walls.
Here we speak of the soaring phoenix pool,
where girdle jades chime with many clear sounds.
Truly fine, but not my chamber;
in the central garden I long to recline and gaze.
Friendship's feelings, so deeply pent,
spring things now rippling and swaying.
How can I obtain wings to ride the wind,
and freely indulge in mountain and spring's delight?
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Poem Mourning the Late Vice Director of the Secretariat Wáng Róng"
Yuáncháng held a wondrous tone,
in his youth he admired former traces.
With affection he cherished his ancestors' footsteps,
one basket of earth hoping to form a peak.
The road hard, travel easily stumbles,
fate adverse, ambition rarely met.
Broken wind fells swift feathers,
flowing regret composes the green pine.
Wèi Zhīgǔ's "Poem on a Spring Night Lodging at the Phoenix Pavilion, Thinking of All My Colleagues"
At the gate receiving the night-watch, late the water-clock sounds,
lodging in the bureau, seeking solitude this time.
Once we valued Ānrén's rhapsody,
now we praise Bóyù's poem.
The mandarin-duck pool full but not overflowing,
the rooster-tree long, ever more flourishing.
Morning and night I cherish Shānfǔ,
Wéi Chéngqìng's "Poem Written While on Duty in the Central Secretariat"
Clear and secluded is the Phoenix Pool;
Luxuriant and spreading are the Rooster Trees' branches.
Here should only luan and egrets gather—
Why does a lone female bird lodge here?
The great creation opened heaven and earth;
Deep grace lets rain and dew descend.
The kunpeng is nurtured and sustained,
While nags and jades alike are driven forth.
A wooden puppet, turned to use;
Suddenly I peek at the seal-paste, unworthy.
Nine thoughts I ponder, striving in vain;
Five-word verses, truly of no avail.
Only glad to meet this thousand-year reign,
But by what step can I answer the Two Modes?
Firefly light fades before the sun;
An ant's strength wearied by bearing a mountain.
Within forbidden halls, the courtyard broad;
Leisurely night, the water-clock's arrow moves.
Dim flowers bloom by the door;
The waning moon tilts down past the curtain.
White temples change as years go by;
A loyal heart laid bare for my lord.
Fate and times together bring peace;
Words and actions both walk peril's edge.
I send word to the guest nesting on high:
Yáo's era is here once more.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Memorial Declining the Post of Central Secretariat Gentleman on Behalf of the Duke of Níngguó"
Your servant has heard: climbing that Tàiháng Mountain,
The lord's carriage often slackens.
Gazing at this Wú slope,
Shàoyóu's horse finds it hard to ascend.
Thus we know beauty is not flowing water,
That instantly breaks the axle.
A steed is not floating cloud,
That soon expects the reins to halt.
Rising to tread the Heavenly River,
How could I accompany the ninety-thousand-mile wind?
Sitting to cross the Star Bridge,
I lack the thousand-year wings.
How could one who in youth was called clever and discerning,
Be fit to face Yuánlǐ?
Who, tender in years yet marked by brilliance,
Could mock Zǐshū?
Jade is heavy, the sash long—
Vainly I see favor and honor.
Deep palaces, secluded halls—
Who knows the cares within?
Central Secretariat Attendant, Eleventh
The Huán Jì Yàolüè states:
"Attendant is an ancient office."
The Rites of Zhōu, Office of Earth, includes Attendants,
Two senior gentlemen.
Shè (attendant) is like gōng (palace).
They administer affairs within the palace,
Distributing provisions and dividing wealth.
The Biographies of Immortals says:
"Qín Gāo was a man of Zhào,
Skilled at playing the qin,
And served as an attendant to King Kāng of Sòng."
Records of the Grand Historian:
"Lǐ Sī served as a palace attendant for Qín."
Book of Hàn:
"Emperor Gāozǔ rose from Fēng and Pèi.
Zhōu Bó, Fù Liàng,
Fán Kuài all followed as attendants.
Lì Yìjī also, as an attendant, handled palace affairs."
Thus, the Central Secretariat Attendant is a Jìn dynasty office.
Since Hàn established the Central Secretariat,
Its duties were not well known.
In the Wèi period, the Central Secretariat
First established one Messaging Officer,
Responsible for presenting memorials.
In Emperor Míng of Wèi's time, there was Messaging Officer Liú Tài.
During Duke Gāoguìxiāng's reign, it was changed to Messaging Commandant,
Soon changed again to Messaging Gentleman.
At the start of Jìn, one Attendant was established,
And one Messaging Officer.
By Eastern Jìn,
The two posts of Attendant and Messaging Officer were combined, called Messaging Attendant.
From Jìn and Sòng onward,
They only handled presenting memorials
And proclaiming the king's words,
Holding significant authority.
By Liáng,
Appointments were especially weighty.
Often held concurrently by high-ranking officials,
Who entered the inner chambers
And began exclusively handling imperial edicts and proclamations for the Central Secretariat.
From Wèi and Jìn, edicts and proclamations
Were all managed by the Central Secretariat Director and Central Secretariat Vice Director.
By Liáng, Attendants began handling them.
Péi Zǐyě once served as Minister of Ceremonies concurrently holding the post of Messaging Attendant.
Later, the two characters "messaging" were removed,
Simply called "Central Secretariat Attendant."
Chén and the Northern Dynasties followed this,
Managing the drafting of edicts.
Chén and Later Wèi
Also separately established Messaging Attendants,
Responsible for announcing memorials.
Northern Qí only established Central Secretariat Attendants,
Concurrently handling announcement of memorials.
Suí again separately established Messaging Attendants,
Exclusively responsible for announcing memorials.
Suí and Táng both followed the names of the central departments;
With the Department of Internal History, it was called "Internal History Attendant."
All from Qí Official Ceremonial and the Five Dynasties History: Treatise on Officials.
Loyal and Prudent | Confucian Simplicity
Jìn Restoration History states:
"Liú Chāo, courtesy name Shìyú,
Was promoted to Central Secretariat Attendant.
At that time, the central departments were newly established,
With many affairs internal and external.
Chāo issued documents and commands,
And was praised as loyal and prudent.
He governed himself with purity and austerity,
Wearing no double layers of silk."
It also says:
"Xú Miǎo, courtesy name Jǐngshān,
As a Confucian scholar of simple virtue from the eastern provinces,
Was by nature fond of learning,
Especially skilled in classics and commentaries.
When Emperor Lièzōng began studying classical texts,
He summoned and welcomed scholars of ritual and learning.
General Xiè Ān recommended Miǎo for selection,
And he was appointed Central Secretariat Attendant,
Working exclusively in the Western Department,
Compiling and correcting the Pronunciation and Glosses of the Five Classics.
Scholars revered him.
Whenever he participated in consultations,
He would offer criticisms and suggestions,
Providing much benefit.
Emperor Lièzōng greatly cherished him."
Participate in Consultations | Much Benefit
"Participate in consultations" and "much benefit" both appear above in the "Confucian Simplicity" note.
Issue Documents and Commands | Skilled in Classics and Commentaries
"Issue documents and commands" appears in the "Loyal and Prudent" note;
"Skilled in classics and commentaries" appears in the "Confucian Simplicity" note.
Administer Legal Documents | Responsible for Presenting Memorials
The Collection of Xún Xù states:
"During Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's reign,
The Chancellery proposed that Clerks Yī Xiàn and Zhào Xián become Central Secretariat Attendants,
Jointly administering legal documents.
Xún Xù memorialized that this was not permissible."
The Treatise on Officials states:
"At the start of Wèi,
The Central Secretariat established one Messaging Officer,
Responsible for presenting memorials.
At the start of Jìn,
The Central Secretariat also established one Attendant.
By Eastern Jìn,
The two posts of Messaging Officer and Attendant were combined, called Messaging Attendant,
Concurrently responsible for presenting memorials."
Combine Two Posts | From Four Households
"Combine two posts" appears in the "Responsible for Presenting Memorials" note.
Xiāo Jǐngchàng's Qí History states:
"In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
A comet entered the Purple Forbidden Enclosure.
At that time, there were four Central Secretariat Messaging Attendants,
Each assigned to one household,
Called the Four Households.
They held concentrated, weighty power,
Their influence overshadowed the realm.
Then celestial phenomena became disordered.
The Grand Astrologer memorialized:
'We should cultivate blessings to avert this.'
Grand Commandant Wáng Jiǎn said to the emperor:
'The anomalies in the heavens
Are due to the Four Households.'
Subsequently, Attendants Wáng Wénmíng and others were each memorialized against.
By Liáng,
The two characters "messaging" were removed,
Simply called Attendant,
Managing literary documents,
Still concurrently presenting memorials."
Tang Dynasty, Shàngguān Yí's "Poem in Response to Secretary Xuē's Evening Scene at the Wànnián Palace, Composed While on Duty, Longing for Friends"
Majestic stands the nine-tiered terrace,
Secluded and free from worldly dust.
Lush and verdant, the ancient trees of ten thousand years,
Delicately veiled by the mist below.
The pond's hues shimmer in the evening sky,
The cliff's glow fades with the lingering twilight.
Pure and serene, the crimson palace lies in stillness,
Vast and boundless, the river of literature flows.
Lingering to exhaust the records of splendid sights,
The winds of time part from lighthearted banter.
Gazing eastward toward Ānrén's office,
Looking westward near Zǐyún's pavilion.
A long whistle parts the mist and clouds,
With lofty steps, I seek the orchid sanctuary.
Golden guardians conceal the thoroughfare gates,
Carved saddles return as riders clamor.
Swallows linger beneath the bright moon,
Crafted beauty hastens the fragrant cup.
There lies another path through verdant hills,
Leaning on a staff, I visit the noble scions.
Zhāng Wéncóng's "Poem Harmonizing with Secretary Yáng on the Flowering Trees in the Zhōngshū Department"
Blossoms and calyxes reflect among fragrant clusters,
Unevenly interspersed with early crimson hues.
Drifting with the wind, they sometimes fall upon the steps,
Mingling with rain, they suddenly float in the air.
Their shadows mirror in the waters of the Phoenix Pond,
Their fragrance wafts on the breeze of the Rooster Tree.
How could one not wish to pluck them?
I hope you will cherish them within your sleeves.
Xú Yànbó's "Poem in Ancient Style Presented to Secretary Liú"
Perched upon the bed, the mystical bird remains hidden,
Its literary brilliance rare in this world.
It nests in your jade-green parasol tree,
And dances within your azure-lattice gates.
Some speak of the joy at the Phoenix Pond,

The Phoenix Pond encircles the forbidden grove,

Jade-carved eaves stir the flowing waters,

Solemn and dignified, the emperor's words carry weight,

Singing loudly in the Western Department,

First in the Service of the Palace.
The position of Shìzhōng is an ancient official post.
In the time of Huángdì, Fēnghòu served as Shìzhōng.
During the Zhōu dynasty, it was called Chángbó.
In the "Lìzhèng" chapter by the Duke of Zhōu,
King Chéng was admonished to have Chángbó and Chángrèn as his left and right assistants, which refers to this.
The Qín dynasty adopted ancient official titles
and established the position of Shìzhōng.
Yìng Shào's "Hàn Guān" states:
"Shìzhōng is a Zhōu official title,
because in the Zhōu it was called Chángbó,
hence it is called a Zhōu official title."
Bān Gù's "Hàn Shū" states:
"Shìzhōng is a Qín official title,
because the Qín adopted the ancient official title and reinstated it,
hence it is called a Qín official title,
though in reality it is an ancient official post."
Initially, when Qín established Shìzhōng,
it was originally a secretary to the Chancellor.
The Chancellor sent five secretaries to move within the palace to report affairs,
hence they were called Shìzhōng (侍中, "serving within").
The Hàn dynasty followed this,
often using it as an additional title.
"Hàn Shū‧Gōng Qīng Biǎo" states:
"Shìzhōng,
Sǎnqí and Zhōngchángshì were added as titles,
or given to Lièhóu, generals, ministers, and senior officials.
This means these officials concurrently held the additional title of Shìzhōng.
Initially, the Hàn dynasty employed old Confucian scholars of high virtue,
prepared for close consultation and immediate responses,
but later, the children of noble families and favored ministers coveted the prestige of the position.
Some even received esteemed positions while still in swaddling clothes,
wearing silk jackets and fine trousers.
In the early Hàn, Jírú and Hóngrú
both wore quail-feather caps,
shell-decorated belts,
and applied powder and makeup.
Zhāng Pìqiáng at age fifteen,
and Huò Qùbìng at age eighteen,
both served as Shìzhōng."
"Hàn Guān" states:
"Shìzhōng wore a military-style cap, a large cap."
It is also said:
"Huìwén cap.
"Hàn Shū" states:
"King Chāngyì, Hè, wore a Huìwén cap."
"Yīnyì" states:
"Huìwén,
is what Shìzhōng wear today."
Adorned with a golden dang,
with a cicada design attached,
and a sable tail as decoration,
it is called Diāochán.
When worn by Shìzhōng, the sable tail is on the left;
when worn by Chángshì, it is on the right.
"Dǒng Bā Yúfú Zhì" states:
"Gold symbolizes firmness and strength,
refined a hundred times without loss;
the cicada symbolizes dwelling high and drinking pure dew;
the sable symbolizes inner strength and fierceness, outer warmth and smoothness.
This originated from King Wǔlíng of Zhào's adoption of Hú clothing.
Qín Shǐhuáng conquered Zhào,
obtained this cap,
and bestowed it upon Shìzhōng."
In the Western Hàn, there was no fixed number of Shìzhōng,
sometimes as many as ten.
"Qí Zhíyí" states:
"In the Hàn, Shìzhōng were in charge of the emperor's vehicles, clothing, and objects,
down to intimate utensils like the hǔzi.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Kǒng Ānguó served as Shìzhōng.
Because he was a Confucian scholar,
he was specially allowed to hold the imperial spittoon,
which was considered an honor in the court.
Initially, Hàn Shìzhōng personally attended to the emperor's daily life,
hence they were colloquially called 'hǔzi handlers.'
Hǔzi is an intimate utensil.
By the time of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
Sū Zé served as Shìzhōng.
Jí Mào, who once lived in seclusion with Zé,
was at that time serving as a county magistrate.
Seeing Zé, he teased him:
'Advancing in office never stops one from handling the hǔzi.'"
In the early Eastern Hàn, there was no fixed number of Shìzhōng.
"Qí Zhíyí" states:
"Eastern Hàn Shìzhōng
served closely by the emperor's side,
accompanying him in his movements.
When the imperial procession went out,
one knowledgeable person would ride in the accompanying carriage,
carrying the imperial seal,
and wielding the sword that cut the white snake."
By the time of Emperor Líng,
there were eight quarters for Shìzhōng,
leading commentators to say the number was originally eight.
"Xiàndì Qǐjū Zhù" states:
"Initially, six Shìzhōng were appointed,
who entered and exited the forbidden palace.
They served closely within the imperial tents,
reviewing memorials from the Shàngshū.
Based on this, the number was not reduced by the end of the Hàn."
In Wèi, four Shìzhōng were appointed.
"Qí Zhíyí" states:
"Wèi Shìzhōng were in charge of ceremonial reception.
When the grand procession went out, the deputy on duty Shìzhōng would guard the carriage.
The principal on duty Shìzhōng would carry the seal,
ride in the accompanying carriage,
not carry a sword,
and all would follow on horseback.
When the emperor ascended the hall,
they would stand opposite the Sǎnqí Shìláng, flanking the emperor.
Shìzhōng stood on the left,
Chángshì on the right,
prepared for close consultation and immediate responses,
to point out oversights and remedy deficiencies."
Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén each appointed four Shìzhōng.
"Qí Zhíyí" and "Wǔdài Shǐ Zhì" state:
"From Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, Wèi, to Chén,
Shìzhōng participated in state governance alongside the Three Dukes.
They served directly by the emperor's side,
responding to inquiries and offering advice.
When the imperial procession went out, the principal on duty would carry the seal."
Later, Northern Wèi and Northern Qí appointed six Shìzhōng.
"Wǔdài Shǐ‧Bǎiguān Zhì" states:
"Northern Qí Shìzhōng,
following Northern Wèi, appointed six.
They were in charge of presenting memorials, remonstrating, correcting, and attending to the emperor's needs,
participating with the various dukes in discussing state governance."
In the early Later Zhōu,
following the Zhōu rituals, the Tiānguān Fǔ established Yùbó and Zhōngdàfū.
Emperor Wǔ changed Yùbó to Nàyán,
which was also the responsibility of Shìzhōng.
By the end of Emperor Xuān's reign, Shìzhōng was separately established again
as an additional title.
Emperor Wén of Suí changed Shìzhōng to Nàyán,
appointing two.
Emperor Yáng changed it to Shìnèi.
The Sui court avoided the character 'zhōng' (中),
hence changed it to evade the taboo.
In the Táng dynasty, it was restored to Shìzhōng.
In the early Lóngshuò era, it was called Dōngtái Zuǒxiàng.
In the early Xiánhēng era, it was restored to the old name.
In the early Guāngzhái era, it was changed to Nàyán.
In the early Shénlóng era, it was restored to the old name.
In the early Kāiyuán era, it was changed to Huángmén Jiān,
and after five years, restored to the old name.
The Ménxià Shěng
has been named thus since the Jìn dynasty.
In the third year of the Táng dynasty, it was changed to Dōngtái.
In the early Guāngzhái era, it was changed to Luántái.
In the Kāiyuán era, it was changed to Huángmén Shěng.

Fù Xián of the Western Jìn Dynasty, "Poem Presented to Hé Shào and Wáng Jì with Preface"
Duke Lǎnglíng Hé Jìngzǔ,
is Xián’s maternal elder cousin.
The National University Chancellor Wáng Wǔzǐ,
is the grandson of Xián’s paternal aunt.
Both are esteemed in the world for their illustrious virtue.
Xián is close to them and holds them in high regard,
with affection akin to that for siblings.
In righteousness, they are like teachers and friends.
Since Lord Hé has already been appointed as Palace Attendant-in-Chief,
and Wǔzǐ soon also received appointment,
these two worthies find great joy in each other’s company,
and Xián too rejoices for them.
Yet I regret my own dullness and inferiority;
though I wish to be closely attached to them,
I have no means to follow them.
Repeated attempts have proven fruitless,
and moreover, I face family hardships.
My heart is set on daily decline,
so I compose this poem to express my feelings and present it to them:
"The sun and moon shine upon the great clarity,
the constellations gleam in the Purple Palace.
Resplendent is the great Jìn court,
brightly opening the imperial gates.
My elder brother has soared like a phoenix,
and the prince has also taken dragon flight.
A pair of luan birds roam the orchid isles,
two phoenixes spread their clear radiance.
Hand in hand they ascend the jade steps,
seated together they attend by the crimson curtains.
Golden ear ornaments adorn their ceremonial caps,
brilliantly displaying their noble grace.
Such glory is admired by the world,
and deep affection is what the heart desires.
How could I not aspire to such lofty traces?
But the unicorn’s hoofprints are distant and hard to follow.
By the river’s edge, there is no fragrant bait;
why then vainly guard the islet?
Withered, I await the wind’s drift,
soon to part from you.
Parting from you, how can I not feel longing?
Holding office idly, I should speak of returning.
Returning to my thatched hut,
I delight in the Way and forget hunger.
Advancing, I have nothing to supplement;
retreating, I care for my private concerns.
I only hope you will magnify your splendid virtues,
and the royal rule will grow ever more peaceful and harmonious."
Hú Guǎng of the Later Hàn Dynasty, "Admonition for the Palace Attendant-in-Chief"
Great is the sage sovereign,
dwelling in divine abode, residing in heaven.
Diligently seeking the talented and virtuous,
to assist and support him.
Never lax in his position,
all officials are in proper order.
In ancient times, King Wén of Zhōu,
cultivated virtue in the western neighbor.
He was praised by the Lord on High,
relying on these four ministers.
He consulted Xīn and Yǐn,
and inquired of the Eight Yú.
With many scholars gathered in dignity,
he thus achieved meritorious deeds.
Duke Wén revered and complied,
and so the Zhōu way flourished.
It was also due to the former worthies,
who could be prudent in their attendants.
The regular attendants and regular officers,
were truly the heads of governance.
Descending to King Lì,
he was neither reverent nor respectful.
He favored those rebellious kinsmen,
and thus unleashed his cruelty.
He only brought ruin to the Mandate of Heaven,
and rebels and barbarians arose together.
The ancestral lineage collapsed and fell,
the ancestral temples had no support.
Do not say, 'I am worthy,'
and fail to select the closest kin.
Do not say, 'I am benevolent,'
and recklessly employ favorites.
Jí Hóng adorned his countenance,
defiling our divine martiality.
Dèng Tōng presumptuously minted coins,
and did not end well thereafter.
The Palace Secretary usurped commands,
Shí Hóng wrought disaster.
Gāo'ān cut his sleeve,
and sorrow had no master.
Palace Attendant-in-Chief, overseer of the center,
I dare to inform the keeper of the square.
Wáng Yún of the Liáng Dynasty, "Memorial on Behalf of My Cousin Declining the Post of Palace Attendant-in-Chief"
As for the descendants of great meritorious officials and veteran Confucian scholars,
families that have accumulated virtue and benevolence for generations,
with the splendor of nine generations and seven leaves,
the nobility of serving Hán and attending to Hàn—
if not that, then possessing learning like Zǐ Jùn’s, penetrating past and present,
or thoughts like Píngzǐ’s, matching the Creator’s work,
or debate and insight like Zhòngxuān’s, without obstruction,
or interpretation of the classics like Cìzhòng’s, inexhaustible.
Only then can one convey intentions to the dukes and ministers,
respond to inquiries before the curtained throne.
Accompany the six-foot carriage,
and communicate the will of the four quarters.
Seeking among humble ministers like myself,
this path is utterly blocked.
Rèn Fǎng, "Memorial on Behalf of Wáng Sīyuǎn Declining the Post of Palace Attendant-in-Chief"
In action, within six feet,
one accompanies and receives the heavenly light.
Above, one bears the seal and proclaims commands,
sincerely trustworthy throughout the realm.
Recommending the acceptable and rejecting the improper,
issuing and receiving only what is fitting.
Presenting memorials above the Golden Flower Hall,
advancing and deferring below the Jade Hall.
Jīn Qiān, eminent among the seven nobles,
Wáng Càn, grandson of a Three Duke.
Even if again, I am but a solitary thread from a middle-rank family,
a last descendant of a chief minister.
None can ascend without relying on others’ praise,
or presumptuously receive crooked favor.
Assistant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Part Two
According to records, the Assistant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate
is an office of the Qín dynasty.
The Hàn dynasty followed it,
with no fixed number of personnel.
The "Hàn Book" by Dǒng Bā states:
"The forbidden gate is called the Yellow Gate;

hence it is called the Director of the Yellow Gate.
Thus, gentlemen of the Yellow Gate serve within the Yellow Gate,
enter to attend within the forbidden palace,
and are therefore called Assistant Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate."
Liú Xiàng’s "Letter Admonishing His Son Xīn" says:
"Now if a young man obtains the post of Assistant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
it is a crucial position.
Lǐ Xún and Dǒng Xián
both served as Assistant Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
Emperor Chéng sent Zhāng Yǔ back to his residence,
and at the foot of the bed appointed Yǔ’s young son also as Assistant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate."
Yìng Shào said:
"The gentlemen of the Yellow Gate each evening bow at the Green Lattice Gate,
and are called 'Evening Gentlemen.'"
"The Qí Official Regulations" states:
"Initially, Qín also had the duty of Attendant at the Yellow Gate,
and Hàn followed it."
"The Book of Hàn" says:
"Yáng Xióng and Liú Xiàng
both served as Attendants at the Yellow Gate."
By the beginning of the Eastern Hàn,
the two offices were combined as Assistant Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
later changed to Palace Attendant-in-Chief Assistant Gentleman.
Soon it reverted to the old title.
From Wèi to Jìn,
four Assistant Attendant Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate were established,
managing various affairs of the Chancellery together with the Palace Attendant-in-Chief,
and, along with the Cavalier Attendants-in-Ordinary, considered pure and illustrious,
called 'Huáng-Sàn' in their time.
Sòng and Qí established four.
"The Qí Official Regulations" says:
"In the Qí dynasty, the Palace Attendant-in-Chief was called 'Ménxià,'
and the Assistant Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate was called 'Xiǎo Ménxià.'"
"The Monographs of the Five Dynasties Histories" says:
"Liáng and Chén established four.
By Emperor Yáng’s time, two positions were reduced,
and the 'Attendant' title was removed,
simply called Assistant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
The Suí dynasty placed even greater importance on the personnel for this post;
Péi Jǔ and Péi Yùn held it,
and both participated in governance.
The Táng dynasty followed this."

Scattered Cavaliers and Attendants
According to the original two official posts of Scattered Cavaliers and Attendants,
both were established by the Qin.
The "Handbook of Han Officials" states:
"Qin established Scattered Cavaliers,
and also established Central Attendants."
Scattered Cavaliers would ride following the imperial vehicle,
accompanying closely behind,
suggesting recommendations and replacing objections.
Central Attendants had the privilege to enter and exit the inner palace,
serving beside the ruler.
The Han continued this,
using scholarly individuals concurrently,
with no fixed number,
often as an honorary title.
Those conferred sometimes included lords, generals, ministers, and high officials added to the role.
Originally, these two positions were established,
all were old scholars with integrity,
prepared for inquiry and consultation,
sharing the role with Attendants-on-Duty.
During Emperor Yuán's time, Liú Xiàng was repeatedly promoted to Scattered Cavalier,
serving alongside great scholar Xiāo Gù, this was the case.
Later, a mix of distinguished sons arose,
Bān Bó during Chéngdì's era served as Central Attendant,
mingling with the sons of Wáng and Xǔ,
among the luxuriously dressed and leisurely youths.
All adorned with silver ornaments,
decorated with cicada patterns,
adorned with mink tails,
called "mink ornaments."
When Attendants wore it, it was called "left mink,"
wearing Central attendants wore it on the right.
In the Eastern Han, the position of Scattered Cavaliers was abolished,
and Central Attendants were replaced by eunuchs,
with no fixed number.
During Emperor Shāng's reign, granted gold ornaments.
The "Ritual Code of Qi" states:
"Emperor Wén of Wei restored the Scattered Cavaliers' roles,

Removing the word 'central,'
directly referred to as Scattered Cavaliers,
appointed four individuals,
handling official documents and commands personally.
Jìn established four,
subordinate to the palace administration."
There were also assistant Scattered Cavaliers,
with no limit.
By the end of the Wei era, there were also four Direct Scattered Cavaliers,
in the tenth year of Jìn Wǔ's Tàishǐ era,
two were placed along with the four Scattered Cavaliers,
from Wei to Jìn,
Scattered Cavaliers and Attendant Lords with Attendants-on-Duty, Yellow Gate Attendants jointly deliberated on palace memorials,
in Jiang Zuo, these were abolished.
There also existed assistant Scattered Attendants,
with no fixed number.
Established by Jìn Wǔ,
there were also four Direct Scattered Attendants.
At the start of the Yuán's Tàihīng era,

Initially in Jìn,

Since the Sòng,
the responsibility became more relaxed,

During Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng's Dàmíng years, appointments to this Attendant-on-Duty position were carried out,

Separately established a Bureau of Collected Books to oversee it,

Regarding managing written and textual matters,
thus called the Bureau of Collected Books,

Later Wei, Northern Qí, the Bureau of Collected Books also established six individuals,
its management of the various Scattered Cavaliers,

Sui Wén abolished the Bureau of Collected Books,

At the start of the Táng, the six Scattered Cavaliers were abolished,

in the Central Secretariat called Right Attendant-in-Extremes,

Now, the importance of evaluating and selecting officials
relates to the rise and fall of the state.
Looking back distantly, even the wise rulers of antiquity
found it difficult.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
men of broad understanding have followed in their tracks,
and the odes of praise have been directed
solely at men like Xǔ Shào and Guō Tài.
In the declining years of the Qí,
official norms slackened and fell into disorder.
The work of reform and creation has only just begun.
The principle lies in altering and remaking.
Your Majesty respectfully faces south as sovereign.
The responsibility for achieving success rests here.
How can favor and private affection be rashly bestowed?
To the detriment of the royal enterprise,
the adornment of attached cicadas
would merely become an empty mark of favor.
Seeking it, whether for public or private reasons,
would result in mutual failure in both giving and receiving.
In recent times, achievements and merits have been uneven.
Some ensured ample provisions in Guānzhōng,
others formed armies in Hénèi,
some possessed abundant virtue like Zhuó Mào,
others upheld the teacher's way like Huán Róng.
The four clans serving at the sacrifices
are already not worth recording.
The five marquises of the imperial consort families
moreover do not follow old statutes.
Yet that to which your servant is attached
lies solely in imperial favor.
Your servant, at the beginning of last winter,
was merely an old Erudite of the National University.
Now, at the start of this summer,
I am to be second only to the highest ministers.
Though Qiānqiū was promoted nine times in a single day,
and Xún Shuǎng traveled from afar and arrived within a hundred days,
compared to your insignificant servant,
they were not swiftly advanced.
Your servant, though lacking in discernment,
sees only benefit.
As for damaging reputation and diminishing substance,
for the state and for myself,
I know it cannot be done.
I dare not act recklessly.
If Your Majesty does not discard the coarse grass,
but loves it as silk and hemp,
and if the words of a lifetime
are still heard and considered,
then my long-held heart and simple resolve
admit of no second argument.
Pitying your servant's plea,
specially revoke this gracious command.
Then canonical rules will be fully respected,
and your insignificant servant will know how to avoid [disgrace].
Remonstrance Counselor, the Fifth
Regarding the Remonstrance Counselor,
it is an office of the Qín.
The Qí Regulations for Offices states:
"Initially, the Qín established the Remonstrance Counselor,
subordinate to the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace.
There was no fixed quota;
it could be as many as several tens of men.
They oversaw discussion and deliberation."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn changed the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace to the Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
Early Hàn did not establish the post;
it was only under Emperor Wǔ that it was established following the Qín.
There was no fixed quota.
All were famous Confucian scholars and men of long-established virtue.
They were subordinate to the Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
Emperor Guāngwǔ added the character 'yì' (議),
making it Remonstrance Counselor.
Thirty men were appointed,
subordinate to the Superintendent of the Imperial Household,
following the Hàn system.
The Jìn, Sòng, and Qí dynasties all did not establish it.
The Monograph on Officials in the History of the Five Dynasties states:
"The Liáng and Chén also established it.
The Northern Qí, following the Later Wèi,
established seven Remonstrance Counselors in the Chancellery.
The Sui established seven in the Department of State Affairs.
The Táng followed this,
reducing it to four men.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era, it was changed to Chief Remonstrance Counselor.
In the early Shénlóng era, it reverted to the old name."
Pure and cautious; honest and upright.

Until the Xiàndì period,

the reestablishment of the position.
During the Huángchū period under Wèi Wén, restored and like before,

Established a Dàfū,

Head of Attendants; Clerk of the Knife and Brush

None Could Replace Yáo; None Dared Oppose Cuò

The Book of Han states:
