Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Seventh
According to the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
it was a position in the Qín administration.
It assisted the Dàfū,
and the Hàn dynasty continued this system.
The Yùshǐ Dàfū originally had two deputies,
one called Yùshǐ Chéng,
the other called Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
It was called "Zhōng" because
it was separately located in the palace,
overseeing the Lántái secret archives.
Externally, it supervised the Bùcìshǐ,
and internally, it managed the Shìyùshǐ.
It received the memorials of the ministers,
scrutinized the hundred officials,
and had a brilliant legacy.
During the reigns between Chéng and Āi,
the Dàfū was renamed Dàsīkōng.
The Zhōngchéng was then renamed Yùshǐ Zhǎngshǐ,
serving externally as the head of the Táizhǔ.
Guāngwǔ later restored the title of Zhōngchéng alongside Shàngshū Lìng,
with them and the Sīlì Jiào Wèi having exclusive seats,
in the capital known as the "Three Exclusive Seats."
Emperor Xiàn placed the Dàfū back in power,
but did not reinstitute the Zhōngchéng.
At the beginning of the Wèi, the Dàfū was abolished,
and the Zhōngchéng was renamed Guānzhèng,
again becoming the head of the Táizhǔ.
It was soon reverted to Zhōngchéng.
The Jìn and Sòng dynasties both followed this method.
All of the above is recorded in the "Hàn Official System" and "Qí Administrative Rituals."
The "Book of Later Wèi - Officials and Clans Records" states:
"During the Later Wei, Zhōngchéng was changed to Zhōngwèi."
The "Five Dynasties History - Hundred Officials" says:
"Northern Qí again changed it to Zhōngchéng.
The Suí avoided the term 'Zhōng,'
abolished Zhōngchéng,
and elevated the position of Chíshū Yùshǐ to replace it."
According to the Chíshū Shìyùshǐ,
it originally emerged during Emperor Xuān of Hàn when Lù Wēnshū presented a memorial.
Advocating for valuing virtue and reducing punishments,
the emperor deeply appreciated it.
After late autumn, during sentencing reviews,
the emperor would retreat to the Xuānshì for decisions,
ordering two Shìyùshǐ to carry documents.
Thus, they were called Chíshū Shìyùshǐ.
Thereafter, they were separately established,
wearing official caps,
and jointly adjudicating court cases with the Seals and Ranks Official.
Subsequent dynasties established it,
until the Suí elevated its rank,
replacing the role of Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
The early Táng dynasty adopted this.
It was abolished at the end of Zhēnguān.
The early Táng followed this,
but abolished the Chíshū Shìyùshǐ by the end of Zhēnguān,
and reinstated the Zhōngchéng.
In the second year of Lóngshuò, it was changed to Sīxiàn Dàfū.
It was restored to its original state at the beginning of Xiánhēng.
Exclusive Seats, Dividing the Road
The "Continuation of the Hàn Book" states:
"Fù Jùgōng was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
meeting with the Sīlì Jiào Wèi and Shàngshū together,
all having exclusive seats,
hence the capital calls them 'Three Exclusive Seats.'"
The "Spring and Autumn of the Wèi" records:
"By tradition,
if the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and the Magistrate of Luòyáng met,
they would divide the road to walk.
As the Zhōngchéng often pursued and captured,
they did not wish to be delayed."
Stone Chamber, Lántái
"Summary by Huán Jì" states:
"The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng has a Stone Chamber,
used for storing secret archives' diagrams and prophecies."
"The Rites of Hàn Officials" states:
"There are two Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
originally the deputies of Yùshǐ Dàfū.
One is separately positioned in the palace,
also managing the Lántái secret archives,
externally supervising the Bùcìshǐ,
internally leading the Shìyùshǐ.
It received the memorials from the ministers,
scrutinized the hundred officials,
and had an illustrious reputation."
Reporting and Investigation, Praiseworthy and Radiant
"Book of Hàn" states:
"There are two Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
originally deputies of Yùshǐ Dàfū.
One is separately positioned in the palace,
reporting and investigating cases,
hence called Zhōngchéng."
"Praiseworthy and radiant" is noted in the "Lántái" annotations.
Maintaining Order Inside and Out, Distinguishing Black and White
"Biographies of Fù Xuān" states:
"Xuān, as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
was upright and principled,
instilling awe internally and externally,
possessing great authority."
"Book of Hàn" records:
"Bào Xuān, styled Gòngjūn,
as Zhōngchéng,
upheld the law within the palace.
He externally oversaw the inspectors of commanderies and states,
dismissing or advancing them appropriately.
His discernment of right and wrong was clear,
thus gaining fame."
No Evasion, Not Swallowing Tenderness
"Continuation of the Hàn Book" states:
"Mǎ Yán, styled Wēiqīng,
was appointed as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
granted a crown, robes, carriage, and horses.
Yán handled cases without delay,
elucidating old standards.
He followed the law in inspections,
evading nothing,
making the hundred officials afraid of him."
"Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Annals" states:
"Xióng Yuǎn, styled Xiàowén,
was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Central King often praised his public loyalty,
saying to Yuǎn:
'You maintain proper demeanor at court,
not swallowing tenderness, speaking harshness.
Such loyalty and brightness can be called a royal minister.'"
Impeachment at Night, Disciplining the Imperial Tutor
"Annals of Jìn's Revival" states:
"Wáng Tián, styled Yuányú,
served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
during the deposition of the Hǎixī Gōng.
Tàizōng ascended the throne,
yet strict controls weren't lifted,
and Dàsīmǎ Huán Wēn camped in the central hall,
blowing horns at night.
Tián accused him of severe disrespect,
requesting judgment.
The next day Wēn saw the report,
sighed, saying:
'This child dares to impeach me,
truly fearsome.'" "Méi Táo's Autobiography" states:
"In my post as Zhōngchéng,
I once disciplined the Imperial Tutor with due law,
despite friends advising against it.
I laughed, responding:
'The hall stands tall with tributes,
thus the crown prince stands exalted.
I obey the king's law,
avoiding deforming paths with obsequiousness.
Later, when the crown prince invited me,
he presented a clear banquet,
thus respecting me like a teacher.'"
Zhōu Chù's Straightness, Chén Qiān's Law Abiding
"Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Annals" states:
"Zhōu Chù, styled Zǐyǐn,
served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He impeached General Shí Chóng,
along with General Liáng Wángtáng and others,
ensuring correctness with unbending records,
causing the powerful to be awed."
"Continuation of the Hàn Book" states:
"Chén Qiān, styled Bǒràng,
was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Upholding law and abiding by standards,
he corrected many errors,
gaining respect from the hundred officials."
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xián's "Admonition for the Imperial Censor"
The admonitions of the hundred officials
serve to admonish the king's faults.
I, inheriting the path of my late father,
have presumptuously occupied a position in the Censorate.
Fearing the responsibility of disgracing the legacy and failing in my duty,
I have composed this admonition.
To spur and encourage myself,
it is not called a self-admonition.
But rather "Admonition for the Imperial Censor,"
because for all who serve as Imperial Censor,
I wish to universally admonish them.
Resplendent are the celestial patterns,
encircled by multitudes of stars.
Thus was established the office of law enforcement,
its radiance shining brightly.
Upholding the principles of the law,
wielding the statutes of the state.
Like a soaring eagle, like a glaring tiger,
sternly purging transgressions and negligence.
Loyal and forthright, not for oneself,
this is called a royal minister.
Having upheld the right path,
then one may consider one's own person.
If one does not consider one's own person,
who would not be awed?
When the state faces adversity,
there is only Zhòng Shānfǔ.
Since Shānfǔ is discerning,
what need is there for that assistant?
None could support its collapse,
as in Huáinán's plotting rebellion.
They truly feared Jí Shēng.
A majestic and powerful state,
can it be without loyal integrity?
Where there is concern and responsibility,
the plumb line must also be straight.
A good farmer weeds out the vile,
not allowing them to take root.
Drive out those without propriety,
why spare their wings?
Alas, you numerous officials,
each revere your duties.
Do not be the first to incur punishment,
do not rely on your power.
If resentment reaches friends,
show no shame in your countenance.
If you offend the Son of Heaven,
introspection brings remorse.
Therefore I compose this admonition,
solely to discipline myself.
Palace Attendant Censor, the Eighth Rank
The Palace Attendant Censor
is an office from the Qín dynasty.
The Hàn dynasty records state:
"Lǎozi served as the Pillar Historian of the Zhōu,
Zhāng Cāng served as a Censor during the Qín era.
They were in charge of documents under the pillar,
which is the duty of the Palace Attendant Censor."
The Hàn dynasty followed this,
appointing fifteen persons.
The Wèi dynasty had eight persons.
The Jìn dynasty had nine persons.
The Sòng and Qí dynasties had ten persons.
The Liáng and Chén dynasties had nine persons.
The Later Wèi, Northern Qí, and Suí dynasties had eight persons.
From "Hàn Officialdom" and the "Treatise on Officials" in the *Histories of the Five Dynasties*.
The Palace Censor,
was established in the Wèi dynasty.
Initially, the Wèi dynasty's Orchid Terrace dispatched two censors to reside in the palace,
to observe and investigate unlawful activities,
hence called Palace Censors.
The Jìn, Sòng, and Qí dynasties appointed two persons.
The Liáng and Chén dynasties appointed four persons.
The Later Wèi dynasty appointed fourteen persons.
The Northern Qí dynasty appointed twelve persons.
The Suí dynasty initially renamed them Palace Censors,
Emperor Yáng abolished them.
From *Qí Official Regulations* and the "Treatise on Officials" in the *Histories of the Five Dynasties*.
The Investigating Censor,
was established in the Suí dynasty.
The Jìn dynasty established the Inspector Censor, responsible for affairs outside the palace gates,
the Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén dynasties all abolished it.
The Later Wèi and Northern Qí dynasties reinstated it with twelve persons.
The Suí dynasty renamed the Inspector Censor to Investigating Censor,
likely also drawing from the meaning of the Qín dynasty's Investigating Censor to name it.
From the "Treatise on Officials" in the *Histories of the Five Dynasties*.
Zhì Cap and Iron Pillar
*Hú Guǎng's Hàn Official Ceremonial* states:
"Four censors,
holding documents,
all wear the law cap.
Also called 'Pillar Rear,'
also called 'Xièzhì.'
The xièzhì is a mythical beast,
knowing right from wrong in people,
goring the wicked and deceitful."
*Hàn Officialdom* states:
"The Palace Attendant Censor, a Zhōu dynasty office,
served as the Pillar Historian,
wearing the law cap.
Also called 'Pillar Rear,'
with an iron pillar,
meaning firm and unyielding in judgment."
Embroidered Robe and White Brush
*The Book of Hàn* states:
"Wáng Jìn, styled Wēngshòu, served as Embroidered Robe Censor during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
pursuing and capturing bands of bandits."
*The Wèi Lüè* states:
"The Emperor once held a grand assembly,
the Palace Censor wore a white brush in his hair,
sitting by the side steps.
The Emperor asked his attendants,
'What office is this, and what is its duty?'
The attendants did not reply.
Xīn Pí said:
'This is called the Censor.
In former times, they wore a brush in their hair,
to memorialize against unlawful acts.
Now they merely fill the office,
and only have a decorative brush!'"
Avoiding the Horse and Burying the Chariot Wheel
*The Continuation of the Book of Hàn* states:
"Huán Diǎn, styled Gōngyǎ,
served as Palace Attendant Censor.
At that time, eunuchs disrupted governance,
Diǎn upheld his duty with integrity,
avoiding none.
He often rode a piebald horse,
and the capital feared him.
A saying circulated:
'Walk on, then stop,
avoid the Censor on the piebald horse.'" Also states:
"Zhāng Gāng, styled Wénjì,
was promoted to Palace Attendant Censor.
At the beginning of the Hàn, eight commissioners were selected to inspect customs,
the eight commissioners were appointed on the same day,
called the Eight Worthies.
All were venerable scholars in high positions,
only Gāng was young and of low rank. Upon receiving orders to proceed to their respective regions,
Gāng alone buried his chariot wheel at the capital lodge in Luòyáng,
saying:
'With wolves blocking the road,
why inquire about foxes?'
He then memorialized the crimes of Grand General Liáng Jì and his brothers,
shaking the capital with awe."
Drawing the Sword and Holding the Halberd
*The Continuation of the Book of Hàn* states:
"Zhòng Hào, styled Jǐngbó,
served as Palace Attendant Censor during Emperor Shùn's reign,
overseeing and protecting the Crown Prince at Chéngguāng Palace.
but carried no written decree,
and tried to take the Crown Prince out in a curtained carriage.
The Crown Prince's Grand Tutor Gāo Xiāng did not know what to do,
unable to stop him by force,
opened the gate as they were about to leave.
Hào arrived,
drew his sword and blocked the carriage, saying:
'The Censor has received an edict to oversee and protect the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince is the state's heir,
bound to the Mandate of Heaven.
The Palace Attendant has come
without a foot of written edict;
how do we know this is not a treacherous scheme?
In today's matter,
I would rather die.'
Fàn dared not argue."
*Chén Shòu's Traditions of the Elders* states:
"Yáng Rén, styled Wényì,
was summoned for an audience by Emperor Míng,
who asked about contemporary governance.
Rén replied,
and the Emperor greatly marveled at him,
appointing Rén as Palace Attendant Censor.
When Emperor Míng passed away,
at that time the various Mǎ clan members were powerful and influential,
each vying to enter the palace.
Rén donned armor and held a halberd,
blocking and ordering at the palace gate,
not allowing them to enter.
After Emperor Zhāng ascended the throne,
the various Mǎ clan members further slandered Rén as harsh and severe,
yet the Emperor thought well of him."
Accusation of Huò Guāng; Arrest of Liáng Jì
The "Book of Hàn" states:
“Yán Yánnián was promoted to Attendant Censor,
and accused Huò Guāng of monopolizing power to depose and establish emperors.”
The "Continued Book of Hàn" states:
“Chén Xiáng, styled Zǐlín,
was promoted to Attendant Censor.
On New Year’s Day, during the court ceremony,
Liáng Jì’s demeanor was unruly,
so he requested his arrest and trial for his crimes,
which people of the time marveled at.”
Zuǒ Yōng’s Promotion by Ability; Sūn Chēn’s Training for Appointment
The "Biographies of the Cáo Family" states:
“Zuǒ Yōng rose from the position of a summoned official,
and Emperor Wǔ deemed him capable,
thereby promoting him to Attendant Censor within the Imperial Guard.”
"Shāngōng's Memorandum" states:
"In the Central Secretariat was the document official Sūn Chēn,
who had long been trained in internal affairs beyond required limits.
His talent made him suitable for Attendant Censor within the Imperial Guard,
and he should be appointed when there is a vacancy.
Whether this can be done or not remains unknown,
the edict states:
‘It can be.’"
Sū Wèidào's "Poem Presented to the Censor Who Enters the Platform"
According to tradition, there are three independence tests,
and this morning they stand before two grand doors.
In the evening forest, there are resonant dances,
where bent grasses meet the fragrant beauty.
The grand office inscribes blue satchels,
distinct chapters move embroidered clothes.
The wind stirs up from the platform and building,
frost settles, writing flies.
Majesty fills the appearance before the court,
marching along the road with full authority.
With only determination to send the falcon away,
again witnessing the return of the fallen eagle.
Also "Starting to Leave Luò City, Viewing the Autumn Fields, Present Thoughts to Fellow Attendant Censors"
With short travels I partake with the frosty departments,
directing with a cautious heart like ice.
Lìpǔ is just to the south chronicle,
Hénggāo temporarily overlooks from the north.
With clear mountains the passes sever,
in the evening the plains become broadly shaded.
Field circles lead smoothly through jade farmlands,
ditches and ridges obstruct stone forests.
Wild children come to gather up,
old farmers leave with songs.
Crickets rise with the autumn wind,
reeds grow dense with evening dew.
The emperor's city remains lush and overgrown,
conveyances of departure race quickly.
Recalling the place where I read books,
my labor songs thank those I respect.
Yuán Xīshēng's "Poem Presented to Huángfǔ Attending the Capital"
From the beauty of the southeast,
born in Kuàijī.
The energy of the constellations,
gathered at Kūnxī.
With jade as precious as jade,
it matches a city of jewels.
With power like phoenixes,
they rest only on wutong trees.
♀Part One♂“Ah, such multitude of treasures,
comparable to a gentleman.
Descendants of dukes and marquesses,
beginning at the heart.
Sharp tools long endure,
talent warm and dignified.”
♀Part Two♂“The Taoist heart is subtle,
its use is truly sufficient.
The radiance of virtue never diminishes,
yet illuminates the nation.
Calmness possesses spirit,
movement sets examples.
The ponds across a thousand miles,
its sound never errs.”
♀Part Three♂“Long ago in ancient times,
when officials were first appointed.
Correcting wrongs and errors,
none but the worthy hold office.
Upright in conduct,
powerful in official writings.
Jade pendants ringing,
embroidered clothes ascend chariots.”
♀Part Four♂“Elegant and fine gentleman,
shoulder the burden under the pillar.
Guidelines looked upon with hope,
honored instruments without falsehood.
Favor covering Bóshān,
spirit strong as court elegance.
Standing upright in court,
awaiting capable men like me.”
♀Part Five♂“Carrying thoughts of friendship,
often joining leisurely feasts.
Harmony with brothers,
official ranks connected to provinces and counties.
Like those pines and bamboos,
glorious in spring and winter green.
Branches and leaves abundant,
unwavering amidst frost and sleet.”
♀Part Six♂“Meetings are not mine,
mountains and rivers separate us.
Departing swans call at dawn,
leaves of farewell fly in autumn.
Carriages move slowly,
banquets parting side by side.
Distant feelings transcend suddenly,
paths diverge in brilliance.”
♀Part Seven♂“Heart as steadfast as metal and stone,
home as fragrant as orchids.
While words are exchanged,
grace naturally overflows.
Solemn breeze and mighty demeanor,
severe as frost in character.
Words of farewell in late year,
to preserve integrity and fortune.”
♀Part Eight♂
Administrator of the Imperial Archives, The Ninth
According to records, the position of Administrator of the Imperial Archives
was established by Emperor Huán of Eastern Hàn.
In charge of secret documents and books,
thus called the Imperial Archives,
later simplified.
During the Jiàn'ān period of Emperor Xiàn,
Cáo Cāo, as King of Wèi,
established the position of Chancellor of the Archives,
overseeing memorials to the Emperor,
equal in duties to the central secretariat,
and also managing secret documents and books.
In the beginning of Huángchū, during Emperor Wén of Wèi,
the Archives were divided to create the Central Secretariat,
where the Central Secretariat had its own Chancellor,
handling memorials to the Emperor.
The Imperial Archives changed the title of Chancellor to Chief,
specifically managing literature and records.
According to "Hàn Officials" and "Qí Ceremonial Standards," Qín and Hàn established the Secretariat,
generally managing secret documents, books, petitions, and memorials.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn abolished the Secretariat office,
and established the Central Secretariat,
taking charge of such matters.
When the Central Secretariat was abolished during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the Secretariat was reestablished.
Emperor Xiàn of Hàn established the position of Chancellor of the Archives,
to manage memorials to the Emperor,
taking on the role of the Central Secretariat.
Thus, we know that the Central Secretariat originally belonged to the Secretariat's duties,
and the Archives originally belonged to the Central Secretariat's duties.
Initially, Hàn established the Secretariat within the Ministry of Revenue,
according to "Hàn Officials,"
during the early Qín dynasty replacing the Ministry of Revenue,
sending four officials to manage documents in the palace,
thus called the Secretariat,
where "Shàng" implies chief.
The Central Secretariat was originally a Secretariat office,
so it was generally subordinate to the Ministry of Revenue.
The Archives was originally a Central Secretariat office,
thus initially during Wèi it was still subordinate to the Ministry of Revenue.
When Wáng Sù became Chief,
he argued that the Wèi's Archives were equivalent to the Eastern bureau of Hàn.
It could not be under the Ministry of Revenue again,
from then on it was not again.
The "Later Hàn Book" states:
"At that time, scholars saw the Eastern bureau as the repository of Lǎozi’s works,
a Taoist refuge.”
During Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the Archives were merged into the Central Secretariat.
The Chief position was abolished,
restored later during Huì of Jìn with one separate Chief of the Archives,
a practice continued by later generations.
The position of Assistant Chief,
was established by Emperor Yáng of Suí,
all of the above are extracted from "Hàn Officials" and "Qí Ceremonial Standards."
The Tāng dynasty followed this,
during the Longshuo period, the Imperial Archives were renamed the Lántái,
and its Chief was renamed Grand Historian.
During the Xiànhéng period, it was restored to Chief of the Imperial Archives.
In the Tiānshòu period it was renamed the Líntái,
but its Chief was not changed.
In the Shénlóng period it was restored to the old.
Initially, the Deputy of the Inspectorate was within the palace,
managing the archives and secret documents in the Lántái.
In the Tāng dynasty, the Imperial Archives were made into the Lántái,
thus following that principle.
In the Western Jīng of Hàn's Wèiyáng palace, there was a Lín Pavilion,
also storing secret documents,
where Yáng Xióng collated books.
Renaming the Archives as Líntái,
also following that principle.
In the Spring and Autumn period, when Hán Xuānzǐ visited Lǔ,
he viewed books from the Grand Historian's office.
In ancient times, the Grand Historian was in charge of books,
renaming the Chief to Grand Historian,
also follows that principle.
Secretary's Office; Immortal Chamber
Yú Huàn's *Wèi Lüè* states:
"The Orchid Terrace
is a terrace.
Yet it is the Secretary's office."
Huà Qiáo's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Scholars refer to the Eastern Lodge as the repository of the Elder Master,
the Pénglái Mountain of Daoism."
Wáng Róng's "Preface to the Poem on the Winding River" states:
"Recording words and events in the Immortal Chamber,
refers to the repository."
Artemisia Terrace; Péng Lodge
Yú Huàn's *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"Artemisia fragrance repels paperworms and bookworms,
thus the book storage terrace is called Artemisia Terrace."
"Péng Lodge" is seen in the annotation for "Immortal Chamber."
Extended Pavilion; Secret Repository
Liú Xīn's *Qī Lüè* states:
"Emperor Wǔ expanded the paths for presenting books,
within a hundred years,
books accumulated like hills and mountains.
Therefore, externally there were the collections of the Grand Ceremonialist, the Historian, and the Erudites;
internally there were the repositories of the Extended Pavilion, the Vast Interior, and the Secret Chamber."
*Hàn Shū* states:
"All the literary records of the realm,
are in the chambers of the Vast Interior Secret Repository,
called the Secret Books."
Eastern Wall Eastern Lodge; Orchid Terrace Unicorn Terrace
*Shí Shì Xīng Jīng* states:
"The star of the Eastern Wall governs literary records."
"Matters of the Eastern Lodge" are seen in the annotation for "Immortal Chamber."
*Hàn Shū* states:
"The Palace Assistant Imperial Secretary is in charge of the secret books, maps, and records of the Orchid Terrace."
Also, Yú Huàn's *Wèi Lüè* states:
"Xuē Xià served as Secretary's Assistant.
At that time, the Secretary's office handled official documents transferred to the Orchid Terrace.
The Orchid Terrace, considering itself a terrace,
and the Secretary's Assistant at that time being merely an office,
said Xià could not transfer them,
and that someone should be held accountable.
Xià replied:
'The Orchid Terrace is the outer terrace,
the Secretary's office is the inner cabinet.
Whether terrace or cabinet,
why should they not transfer documents to each other?
The Orchid Terrace had no rebuttal.'"
*Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú* states:
"East of the Wèiyāng Palace was the Qílín Hall,
which stored secret books,
this was the place where Yáng Xióng collated texts."
The above records pertain to the Secretaries.
Administering Books and Charts; Overseeing Secrets and Profundities
*Dōng Guān Hàn Jì* states:
"In the second year of the Yánxī era of Emperor Huán,
the position of Secretary's Supervisor was first established,
to administer books and charts.
Ancient and modern writings,
were examined for differences and similarities."
Wēn Qiáo recommended Xún Sōng for the post of Secretary's Supervisor,
saying:
"The canon of the state's history,
serves to illuminate the traces of gains and losses,
this is called a true record.
It makes the canon of an era
brilliant and worthy of contemplation.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Sōng,
is refined in both substance and form,
his understanding of righteousness is broad and penetrating.
He has served in previous courts,
and handled affairs with reverence.
He is fit to oversee secrets and profundities,
and to elucidate historical texts.'"
Examining Similarities and Differences; Collating Ancient and Modern
"Examining similarities and differences" is seen in the annotation for "Administering Books and Charts."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"An edict from the first year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Huì states:
'The Secretary's Supervisor comprehensively manages the classics and texts,
examining and collating ancient and modern works.
Testing and appointing clerks,
he leads four hundred men,
and should devote himself to these duties.'"
Administering Literary Works; Synthesizing Classics and Texts
*Huá Qiáo Jí* states:
"An edict to the Imperial Secretary states:
'Marquis Tíng Qiáo,
is by nature broad-minded and simple,
his literary learning is comprehensive and penetrating,
he has perused ancient and modern works.
Well-informed and deeply knowledgeable,
he writes books that are true records.
Having the ambition of a good historian,
he is therefore transferred to be Secretary's Supervisor.
He is additionally appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
his rank equal to that of the Central Secretariat, making it an inner terrace,
causing the Secretariat's Cavalier Attendants and the Writers to manage rituals, music, astronomy, and numerology.
Literary works from the Southern Department,
and compilations from the Chancellery,
are all to be administered by him.'"
"Synthesizing classics and texts" is seen in the annotation for "Collating Ancient and Modern."
Compiling the Imperial Survey; Arranging the Bamboo Books
*Wèi Zhì* states:
"Wáng Xiàng, styled Xìbó,
Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary concurrently serving as Secretary's Supervisor,
compiled the *Imperial Survey*."
Fù Chàng's *Jìn Zhū Gōng Zàn* states:
"Xún Xù served as Secretary's Supervisor.
In the second year of the Tàikāng era, bamboo books were obtained from a tomb in Jíjùn.
Xù personally arranged, annotated, and transcribed them,
considering them part of the central canon,
and listed them among the secret books.
Missing passages in the classics and commentaries
were largely corroborated."
Writing the *Yáng Qiū*; Administering Written Works
Hé Fǎshèng's *Jìn Zhōng Xīng Shū* states:
"Sūn Shèng, from Ānguó, became Secretary's Supervisor,
and was additionally appointed Gentleman Attendant.
He was earnest and fond of learning,
from youth to adulthood,
he constantly kept books in hand without setting them aside.
Once he held the post of Historiographer,
he wrote the *Sān Guó Yáng Qiū*."

"Continuation of the Hàn Book" states:
"Below the Grand Minister those having consorts,
with scarlet fan and the horses' wings and tails darkly dyed."
It further indicates:
"All with mid-grade 2,000 stone rank have black canopies and vermilion carriages."
Assisting the Three Dukes, positioned at the Nine Thorns
The "Records of Emperors and Kings" states:
"The Nine Ministers
are those who assist the Three Dukes."
Also, the "Rites of Zhou" says:
"Facing the three locust trees,
are the positions of the Three Dukes."
It also says:
"The Court Officer is in charge of the laws of the outer court.
To the left are nine thorn trees,
where the positions of the solitary ministers, high officials, and grandees are located."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Planting thorn trees to mark positions
is to take their red heart and outward thorns,
symbolizing a red heart and three pricks."
Fèngcháng (Reverence of Ritual) Zōngbó (Minister of Rites)
The "Book of Han" states:
"In the Qín dynasty, it was called Fèngcháng,
in charge of ancestral temple rituals and ceremonies.
In the sixth year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Jǐng, it was renamed Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies)."
The "Rites of Zhou" says:
"The Spring Official Zōngbó is in charge of the heavenly gods and earthly deities."
In charge of ancestral temples, creating ritual music
"In charge of ancestral temples" is mentioned in the note for "Fèngcháng."
The "Continued Book of Han":
"Zhāng Fèn was appointed Tàicháng,
and stated that ritual music should be reformed and created.
The emperor approved of this."
Overseeing the three rites, foremost of the nine ministers
The "Book of Han" states:
"Tàicháng is an ancient office.
It is said that Bó Yí, as Zhìzōng, oversaw the three rites.
Wishing for the state to be grand and prosperous,
and for the altars of soil and grain to endure forever,
it was anciently called Tàicháng."
The "Explanations of Han Officials" states:
"Tàicháng is responsible for the altars of soil and grain and suburban sacrifices.
The matters are weighty and the duty is esteemed,
hence it is called the foremost of the nine ministers."
Specially bestowed upon visiting his hut, selling his house to support himself
The "Book of the Jin Restoration" states:
"Hè Xún, styled Yànxiān,
was appointed Tàicháng.
When Emperor Zhōngzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an order stating:
'Xún is pure as ice and flawless as jade,
his conduct is a model for customs.
Moreover, his position is among the high ministers.
His dwelling and clothing
are merely enough to cover his body.
His house barely shelters him from wind and rain.
I have often visited his hut,
and was especially moved.
I bestow upon him a six-foot bed, mat, cushion, and two hundred thousand cash,
to manifest his utmost virtue.'" The "Records of the Wei" states:
"Hé Qià, styled Yángshì,
served as Tàicháng.
He was poor and upright,
and sold his fields and house to support himself."
Huán Róng provided with a table, Sūntōng bestowed with gold
Huà Qiáo's "Later Book of Han" states:
"Huán Róng, styled Chūnqīng,
was promoted from Junior Tutor to Tàicháng.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he honored him with the etiquette due a teacher,
and he was greatly cherished and esteemed.
He was appointed.
The imperial carriage often visited the Tàicháng's office,
ordering Róng to sit facing east,
providing a table and staff,
and assembling all officials."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn destroyed Qín,
and had already assumed the imperial title,
his ministers drank and contended over merits.
Drunk, some shouted wildly,
drew swords and struck pillars.
Gāozǔ was troubled by this.
Thereupon, Shūsūntōng offered advice,
and then set up ceremonial markers in the wilderness.
They practiced for over a month.
Tōng said:
'You may now observe a trial.'
The emperor had them perform the rites to completion,
then again set out ceremonial wine.
None dared to be clamorous or breach etiquette.
Gāozǔ said:
'Only today do I realize the dignity of being emperor.'
He appointed Tōng as Tàicháng,
and bestowed five hundred catties of gold upon him."
Sīmǎ Ān reached four times, Duàn Róng ascended twice
The "Book of Han" states:
"Sīmǎ Ān was an artful official,
who reached the nine ministers four times."
It also states:
"Púyáng Duàn Róng initially served Gàihóu Xìn.
Xìn trusted Róng,
and his office also reached the nine ministers twice."
Returning home to handle affairs, angering his wife for disturbing his fast
The "Jin Court Diaries" state:
"In the second year of Emperor Ān's reign,
Tàicháng Línchuān Prince Bǎo petitioned,
stating that his office residence was narrow and cramped,
insufficient to move his family.
His mother Zhōng was advanced in years,
and being separated caused her no peace.
He begged to return home to handle affairs.
An edict permitted this."
Yìng Shào's "Han Officials" states:
"Běihǎi Zhōu Zé served as Tàicháng.
He constantly fasted.
His wife, pitying his old age, fatigue, and illness,
peeked inside to inquire about him.
Zé became greatly angry,
considering it a disturbance of his fast.
His subordinate officials kowtowed and pleaded for her.
He would not listen,
and so had her arrested and sent to the imperial prison,
and also impeached himself.
Commentators criticized his excessive fervor.
A proverb says:
'If you marry, do not marry
the wife of a Tàicháng.
In one year of three hundred sixty days,
three hundred fifty-nine are fast days.
On the one day not fasting, drunk as mud,
once he starts his duties,
he is again dazed and confused.'"
Liáng dynasty Lù Chuí's "Memorial Declining the Promotion of Wáng, the Minister of the Imperial Stud, to Tàicháng"
In ancient times, when the virtue of Chǔ was flourishing,
Shū'áo washed his clothes.
When the Hàn way thrived,
Wáng Yáng tied his official sash.
Thus they accepted appointments without declining,
and received ranks without yielding.
How much more so for the esteemed and pure Minister of Rites,
a selection difficult through the ages.
From Hàn and Jìn onward,
none were not models of simplicity.
Those who declined rank include Huán Yù and Zhāng Fèn,
those who yielded fiefs include Dīng Hóng and Liú Kǎi.
Pān Ní's literary elegance was pure and profound,
Huà Biǎo's composure in retiring and silence.
From them until now,
their refined manner has been followed.
Comparing me to them,
I am not of their rank at all.
Chén dynasty Shěn Jiǒng's "Memorial on behalf of Zhōu Hóng Declining the Position of Tàicháng"
I have heard that jade shoes and carved pillars
are not made from gnarled wood.
Vermilion pearls and embroidered axe-patterns
are surely not taken from ivy and vines.
Why is this?
Each is suitable for its own purpose,
court and countryside cannot be judged by one standard.
Shūsūntōng's establishing rites in the wilderness,
doubly relied on canonical substance;
Diāo Xié personally leading the chanting,
could his ceremony be easily changed?
If the nine ushers lack a master of ceremonies,
or the fēng and shàn sacrifices lose their proper form,
and responsibility is placed on the office in charge,
whose fault would it be?
Moreover, the Historian of the South holding his tablets
would further reveal misplaced talent.
The ruler's actions must be recorded,
making it especially difficult to presumptuously assume.
Later Hàn Cuī Yuān's "Admonition"
Reverent and careful Tàicháng,
truly the Minister of Rites.
Solemn and majestic numinous deities,
ancestral temples grand and lofty.
Orderly arranging the great sacrifices,
ranking among the multitude of spirits.
Our sacrifices are reverent,
our grain offerings most pure.
Without error, without fault,
fitting for the impersonator of the dead.
Not praying, not seeking,
only virtue's recompense.
Not feigning, not falsifying,
hopefully without blame or regret.
Do not say, "I have talent,"
and lightly rely on divination.
The sacrificial ox of the eastern neighbor
is not as good as the wheat and fish of the western neighbor.
Qín perished at Wàngyí,
Yǐn was slain at Zhōngwū.
Your constant minister in charge of the ancestral temple,
dares to inform those in office.
Fourteenth: Minister of Agriculture
The Minister of Agriculture
is an official position from the Han Dynasty.
The "Han Officials" states:
"Initially, the Qin Dynasty established the Chancellor of the Treasury,
responsible for grains and currency.
The Han Dynasty followed this,
with Emperor Jing changing the title to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and Emperor Wu changing it to Grand Minister of Agriculture."
According to records, Yao appointed the four sons of Xi and He to respectfully teach the people the seasons,
and among Shun's twenty-two officials,
Qi served as Minister of Agriculture,
sowing the various grains,
which aligns with this responsibility.
Under the Zhou Dynasty's Minister of State, there was the Grand Steward, a lower grand master.
Zheng Xuán's annotation states:
"The Grand Steward
was the chief in charge of storage, similar to today's Minister of Agriculture,
and also held the duties of the Minister of Agriculture."
Wáng Mǎng changed the title of Grand Minister of Agriculture to Xi Hé,
and later changed it again to Nà Yán.
The Eastern Han Dynasty restored it to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
The "History of the Five Dynasties: Treatise on Officials" states:
"The Liang Dynasty added the character 'Qīng' (Minister), calling it Minister of Agriculture,
and omitted the character 'Dà' (Grand).
The Later Wei Dynasty added the character 'Dà' again.
The Northern Qí Dynasty removed the character 'Dà' again.
The Suí Dynasty followed this.
The Táng Dynasty initially followed this,
but in the second year of the Lóngshuò era, it was changed to Minister of Crops.
In the first year of the Xiánhēng era, it was restored to its former title."
Six Treasuries; Ten Thousand Shi
Cuī Yuàn's "Eulogy for Bào Dé" states:
"He then managed the great affairs,
overseeing these six treasuries,
with the three tasks being particularly urgent,
so he cultivated and gathered."
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Bóliáng Poem: Grand Minister of Agriculture" states:
"Ten thousand shi of old grain, winnowed and tossed."
Celestial Granary; Nation's Spring
Hán Yáng's "Essential Collection of Astronomy" states:
"The Celestial Granary refers to the Grand Minister of Agriculture."
Shǐ Yóu's "Quick Mastery Primer" states:
"The Minister of Agriculture and the Privy Treasurer
are the nation's springs."
Overseer of Metals; Keeper of Silk
Yáng Xióng's "Admonition for the Grand Minister of Agriculture" states:
"At that time, the Grand Minister of Agriculture
competed to oversee metals and grains."
The "Continued Book of Hàn" states:
"The Grand Minister of Agriculture is one person,
with a salary of two thousand shi,
responsible for various currencies, grains, metals, and silks."
Zhōu Called It Grand Steward; Mǎng Changed It to Xi Hé
"Zhōu called it Grand Steward" is seen in the narrative annotation.
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"In the first year of the Yuánshǐ era of Emperor Píng,
the Grand Minister of Agriculture was changed to Xi Hé,
with Liú Xīn appointed to the position."
Gāo Xǔ Upright and Righteous; Móu Róng Clear and Perceptive
The "Records of the Eastern Pavilion":
"Gāo Xǔ, styled Jì Huí,
was summoned for his Confucian learning.
He was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and in court, he was praised for his integrity, uprightness, and righteousness."
It also states:
"Móu Róng, styled Zǐ Yōu,
served as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
He was clear and perceptive by nature,
and was called a renowned minister."
Carriage Summoned Zhèng; Emperor Valued Gěng
The "Continued Book of Hàn" states:
"Zhèng Xuán was summoned by imperial carriage to serve as Grand Minister of Agriculture,
provided with a single comfortable carriage,
with local officials along the way sending him off and welcoming him."
It also states:
"Gěng Guó, styled Shū Lǜ,
served as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
He understood border affairs,
was skilled in debate,
and frequently submitted appropriate proposals,
earning the emperor's esteem."
Yánnián Embezzled Money; Zhào Diǎn Associated with Virtue
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"Tián Yánnián served as Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and was implicated in embezzling three hundred thousand coins from the capital treasury, leading to his suicide."
The "Continued Book of Hàn" states:
"Zhào Diǎn, styled Zhòng Jīng,
served as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
He closed his doors and ceased social interactions,
refusing to associate with those lacking virtue."
Hàn Dynasty Yáng Xióng's "Admonition for the Grand Minister of Agriculture"
At that time, the Grand Minister of Agriculture
oversaw metals and grains.
From the capital to the remote lands,
he measured grain for the people.
From the very beginning,
the true practice lies in food.
His colleague, the Minister of Agriculture,
ensured exchange and circulation.
Balancing surplus and deficit,
he set standards for the capital.
Extending clothing and food,
he governed the people.
Looking up to the two emperors,
and reviewing the three kings below.
The tithe tax
became the people's constant.
Tributes from near and far,
a hundredfold, never forgotten.
The prosperity of emperors and kings
truly lies in agriculture.
In the late Zhōu's decadence,
eastern cultivation was not ordered.
Fertile lands yielded no harvest,
and all things fell into ruin.
Treasuries were exhausted and empty,
with no accumulation in granaries or chests.
Decline and decay set in,
and Zhōu ultimately perished.
Qín collected more than half,
and the second generation brought no relief.
Pleading with tears of blood,
the land was left without solace.
The agricultural minister oversees fairness,
daring to inform those in power.
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Huá's "Admonition for the Grand Minister of Agriculture"
Families have their homes and wells,
the king has his granaries and registers.
Prosperity enriches all things,
harmonizing measures and weights.
In the late Zhōu era,
they were not reverent in governance.
Abandoning agriculture, neglecting duties,
not cultivating the thousand acres.
Depleting spirits, lacking sacrifices,
defeated by barbarian foes.
The agricultural minister oversees farming,
daring to inform those on the left and right.
Fifteenth: Minister of the Grand Steward
The Minister of the Grand Steward
is an official position from the Zhōu Dynasty.
Under the Ministry of Heaven in the Zhōu Rites, there was the Grand Steward, a lower grand master,
responsible for tributes and taxes,
receiving the income from goods and valuables.
He oversaw the storage of goods and valuables.
From the Qín and Hàn Dynasties onward, this position was not established,
and its duties were divided between the Minister of Agriculture and the Privy Treasurer.
It was not until the Liáng Dynasty that the Minister of the Grand Steward was established.
The Chén, Later Wèi, Northern Qí, and Suí Dynasties all followed the Liáng Dynasty in establishing it.
All are seen in the "History of the Five Dynasties: Treatise" and the "Later Wèi Treatise on Officials and Clans."
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng Dynasty, it was changed to Minister of the Outer Treasury.
At the beginning of the Xiánhēng era, it was restored to its former title.
At the beginning of the Guāngzhái era, it was changed to Minister of the Treasury.
At the beginning of the Shénlóng era, it was restored to its former title.
Before the Liáng Dynasty, there was no Grand Steward,
so its paired allusions and literary works are lacking.
Now that it is listed among the Nine Ministers,
it is specially preserved in the narrative.
If literary works are needed,
one may also refer to and adopt matters related to the Minister of Agriculture.
Sixteenth: Minister of the Imperial Household
Guānglùqīng,
an official position in the Hàn dynasty.
The Qí Zhí Yí states:
"The post of Lángzhōnglìng was originally established during the Qín dynasty,
in charge of palace gates and doors.
Responsible for the guards within the palace,
thus named Lángzhōnglìng.
The Hàn Guān states:
'The subordinate officials under the Lángzhōnglìng
include the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng,
the Left and Right Zhōnglángjiāng,
collectively called the Three Bureaus.
Each bureau has Zhōngláng, Yìláng, Shìláng, and Lángzhōng officers,
but without external staff,
numbering up to a thousand people,
in charge of guarding the gates of the palace.
The Hǔbēn and Yǔlín troops were also under their control.
They were termed Lángzhōnglìng
because they led all the guards and acted as their chief.'
The Hàn dynasty continued this practice,
until Emperor Wǔ changed the name to Guānglùxūn.
Yìng Shào said:
'Guāng
means brightness,
Lù
refers to rank,
and Xūn
represents meritorious deeds.
It signifies that the Guānglù officials, yèyì zhěs, Hǔbēn, and Yǔlín
select without losing virtue,
and reward without missing effort,
hence named Guānglùxūn.'
Yìng Shào and Zhèng Xuán together stated:
'Xūn is similar to the position of gatekeeper.'
Today, the office of Guānglùxūn corresponds to the ancient position of doorkeeper.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Xiàn of the Eastern Hàn, it was restored to Lángzhōnglìng.
The Wèi Emperor Wén also restored the title Guānglùxūn,
continuing through later generations."
The Wǔdài Shǐ, in the section on Official Ranks, states:
"During Liáng, the character Qīng was added to Guānglù,
removing the character Xūn,
with later generations following this change.
During Běi Qí, it oversaw meals,
and in Suí, it fully managed the meals
without being responsible for the palace gates.
The early Táng followed this,
until the second year of Lóngshuò, when it was renamed Sīzàiqīng.
In Xiánhēng, it was reverted to the original title.
In the beginning of Guāngzhái, it was changed to Sīshànqīng.
In Shénlóng, it returned to the old title."
First among the Nine Columns, overseeing the Three Bureaus
In the Yǔ Bīng Jí, Yòng Yuèmó Zhào Cǎo states:
"Guānglù is first among the Nine Columns,
also managing the clerical bureaus."
The Xù Hànshū states:
"Dù Lín, courtesy name Báishān,
served as Guānglùxūn.
He attended the guards within,
and oversaw the Three Bureaus outside.
His governance was meticulous and careful,
earning a reputation for fairness in selections."
Marking the palace rooms, overseeing the Yèmén
"Marking the palace rooms" is seen in the following Yáng Xióng Jiàn.
The Hànshū states:
"Reportedly:
'The Lángzhōnglìng is in charge of the palace's inner gates,
with support officers.
In the first year of Tàichū of Emperor Wǔ, it was renamed Guānglùxūn.'"
Admiring supreme virtue, recommending scholars
The biography of Mèng Zōng states:
"Zōng, as Guānglùxūn,
held a grand banquet,
rarely consuming alcohol,
coincidentally was forced to drink a cup and vomited,
and this was reported by inspectors to the emperor.
Zōng vomited rice,
which was reported by the inspectors.
The emperor sighed and said:
'Such purity and supreme virtue.'" The Xù Hànshū states:
"Dù Lín, courtesy name Báishān,
was just in selections,
frequently recommending notable scholars."
Entering the inner chambers, overseeing subordinate officials
The Hànshū states:
"Zhōu Rén,
during the reign of Emperor Jǐng, served as Lángzhōnglìng.
He was reserved and did not divulge secrets.
Because of this, he gained favor,
entering the inner chambers,
and privy to the secrets of the harem,
Rén was always by their side,
but never spoke of it." The Baílíngfú Shī Guānglùxūn states:
"He managed subordinate officials on the Baílíng Terrace."
Exposing the discarding of armor, inquiring about the rainbow
The Wèizhì states:
"Wáng Sù, courtesy name Zǐyōng,
served as Guānglùxūn.
At that time, a fish, one foot long,
appeared on the roof of the military arsenal,
regarded by officials as auspicious.
Sù explained:
'Fish are born in springs but appear on roofs,
a creature of scales out of its place.
Could it indicate a military disaster where armor is discarded?'
Later, indeed, there was a defeat at the Eastern Gate."
The Later Hànshū by Xiè Chéng states:
"Yáng Cì, courtesy name Bókín,
was appointed as Guānglùxūn,
with the rank of Tèjìn.
A blue-red aura was present in front of Jiàdé Hall,
and the emperor dispatched imperial messengers to inquire about the omen of fortune or disaster,
consulting Cì due to his erudition and reputation as a great scholar.
Hence, he was asked in confidence,
and was expected to express his true opinions,
and had previously submitted a memorial stating that,
according to the prophecies in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
'When the rainbow appears,
chaos is within the land.
This is caused by the eunuchs and powerful ministers monopolizing the court.'"
King Xuān's bowing to Lín, Emperor Jǐng's inquiry about Mào
The Wèizhì states:
"Cháng Lín transferred from Guānglùxūn to Tàicháng.
Emperor Xūan of Jìn treated Lín as an elder of his hometown.
He would bow to him,
and someone advised Lín,
'Sīmǎ Gōng is of high status,
you should advise him to refrain.'
Lín replied,
'Sīmǎ Gōng wishes to maintain the sequence of seniority and youth,
to establish a model for the younger generation;
distinction is not something I can control.'
The advisor was embarrassed and withdrew." It also states:
"Zhèng Mào served as Guānglùxūn,
when Wú Qi in rebellion.
Emperor Jǐng personally led the campaign,
and officials saw him off.
At that time, Mào was ill and absent from the gathering,
and the emperor remarked to Wáng Sù,
'I regret not seeing Zhèng Guānglù.'
Upon hearing this,
Mào rushed on a stretcher to follow the emperor,
and upon arrival, the emperor laughed and said,
'I knew you would come.'
He was then allowed to ride with him,
consulting on strategies,
which the emperor greatly valued."
Ānshì punishing a slave, Yào Qīng receiving grain
The Hànshū states:
"Zhāng Ānshì, courtesy name Rúzǐ,
served as Guānglùxūn.
When a lèng behaved indecently within the palace,
the official in charge appealed to follow legal procedures,
but Ānshì said,
'How do you know it wasn't just covering with water?'
Another lèng was involved with an official maid,
and the maid's brother reported it himself,
and Ānshì said,
'The servant, out of indignation and anger, sullies the reputation of officials;
reporting to the official to punish the slave,
everything hidden about people's transgressions is of this type.'" The Wèizhì states:
"Yuán Huàn, courtesy name Yào Qīng,
served as Lángzhōnglìng.
At that time, word came of Liú Bèi's death,
and ministers all celebrated,
but Huàn, due to having served under Bèi,
did not join in celebration,
eventually dying in office,
causing extreme distress to the Taìzǔ.
He was bestowed two thousand shík of grain, one thousand of grain from the imperial granary, and another thousand from the walls below,
given to Yào Qīng's family.
Mentioning official statutes,
and in private discussions with relatives."
Hàn Yáng Xióng's "Inscription for the Palace Guard Commander"
The palaces are laid out with measured care,
Divided into inner and outer spheres.
Corridors, halls, gates, and doors
Are bounded by forbidden lines.
The state has its perimeter guards,
Men have their fences and walls.
Each has its proper protection,
Held fast without deviation.
In ancient times during the Xià and Yīn,
Jié and Zhòu were dissolute and drunk.
Holding feasts with oxen for drinking,
Their households fell into chaos and ruin.
Though guardsmen held halberds in hand,
The ushers were in disarray.
The palace halls turned into markets,
Some beat drums within chambers,
Forgetting their ancestral temples.
They gathered fugitives and runaways,
From the four quarters came many crimes,
With shouts and clamor rising loud.
The inner court must be examined,
The outer realm must be kept clear.
Virtuous men stand at court,
Righteous scholars fill the halls.
The officer of emolument oversees the light,
I dare to warn those who uphold the classics.
The Minister of Ceremonies, Number Seventeen
The Minister of Ceremonies
is a Hàn dynasty official.
The "Hàn Officialdom" states:
"In ancient times, during the reigns of Táng and Yú, guests were received at the four gates.
This was the system for hosting guests with ritual,
which is also the same duty as that of the Minister of Ceremonies."
The "Zhōu Rituals" states:
"The Messenger was in charge of guests and the affairs of feudal lords attending court audiences,
which was his duty."
The "Hàn Officialdom" states:
"The Qín established the Office of Guest Reception,
in charge of feudal lords and surrendered barbarians who submitted to righteousness.
The Hàn followed this.
Emperor Jǐng changed its name to the Grand Herald.
Emperor Wǔ changed it to Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Hú Guǎng said:
'Hóng
means sound.
Lú
means to transmit.
It is used to transmit sounds,
to guide and assist the Nine Guests.'"
Liú Xī said:
"Hóng
means great."
Fù Qián said:
"Lú
here means considering the capital as the heart and abdomen,
and the feudal lords and vassal states as the four limbs."
Wéi Zhāo said:
"Hóng
means great.
Lú
refers to arranging in order.
It desires to arrange guests in order with great ritual."
Initially, Qín also had the Office of Dependent States,
which also managed surrendered barbarians.
The Hàn also followed this,
and Emperor Chéng merged it into the Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Wáng Mǎng changed the Minister of Ceremonies to Director of Music.
The Eastern Hàn again called it Minister of Ceremonies,
and thereafter it was followed accordingly."
The "Treatise on Officials" in the "History of the Five Dynasties" states:
"By the Liáng dynasty, the character 'Qīng' (Minister) was added, making it Minister of Ceremonies,
and the character 'Dà' (Grand) was removed.
The Later Wèi again added the character 'Dà'.
The Northern Qí again removed it.
The Suí dynasty followed this.
The early Táng followed it.
In the second year of Lóngshuò, it was changed to Minister of Unified Culture.
At the beginning of Xiánhēng, it was restored to the old name.
At the beginning of Guāngzhái, it was changed to Minister of Guest Reception.
At the beginning of Shénlóng, it was restored to the old name."
In Charge of Barbarians / In Charge of Precedents
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"The Office of Guest Reception
was a Qín official post,
with a rank of fully two thousand shi.
It was in charge of feudal lords and surrendered barbarians from the four quarters who submitted to righteousness,
and the bestowal of seals and ribbons upon imperial princes."

duty was already severed.
To consider them wives and have them executed
was not correct in name,
and they should not be held culpable.
An edict was issued settling the matter according to Guāng's deliberation. "
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Hàn says:
"Fàn Yánshòu
served as Chief Justice during Emperor Xuān's time.
At that time, in the region between Yān and Zhào,
three men together married one wife,
and had four sons.
When they grew up, each sought separation,
disputing over property and dividing the sons.
The matter reached the county,
but the county could not decide it,
and referred it to the Chief Justice.
Thereupon, Yánshòu decided it,
considering it a violation of human relations,
comparable to beasts.
The sons born belonged to their mother.
He gave all the sons to the mother,
executed the three men in the marketplace,
and memorialized to dismiss the commandery governor, county magistrate, and others
for lacking the way to lead and transform.
The Son of Heaven then approved his proposal. "
The three generations of the Wú family and the seven members of the Guō family
as stated in the "Huá Qiáo Hòu Hàn Shū":
"Wú Xióng from Hénán, styled Jìgāo,
was known for his understanding of the laws.
During the time of Emperor Huán, he rose from the post of Court Justice to the position of Minister over the Masses.
When Xióng was young, his family was poor.
When his mother passed away, she was buried in unmarked land,
and the funeral was conducted swiftly,
without choosing an auspicious day.
Witches predicted that his lineage would be extinct.
However, Xióng's son Qí and grandson Gōng served as Court Justice for three generations,
making the family renowned for their legal expertise."
It also states:
"Guō Gōng, styled Zhòngsūn,
served as a Court Justice officer.
He was later promoted to Court Justice,
with his family being entrusted with legal matters for generations.
Zhèn rose from Left Supervisor of the Court Justice to Court Justice,
and altogether seven members of the Guō family served as Court Justice."
Hàn Yáng Xióng's "Encomium of the Court Justice":
Heaven bestowed the five punishments,
it was the achievement of the Xià dynasty.
Bringing chaos to the common people,
neither deviating nor excessive.
In former times, in the era of Chīyóu,
cruel punishments were established.
These spread to the Miáo people,
causing unrest for the Xià clan.
King Mù in his senility and negligence,
with the counsel of Fǔ Hóu and Yī.
Eventually, things decayed and declined,
yet Heaven did not forsake them.
The Zhōu lightened their regulations,
while the Qín exacerbated their punishments.
The five punishments were in disarray,
ceaseless, unstoppable.
Bandits filled the mountains,
and criminals filled the markets.
In ancient times, in the eras of Yáo and Shùn,
the people of Heaven were safe.
Yet Zhòu created the bronze flame torture,
casting people into an abyss.
Thus, those with a state,
how could they speak of anything?
Whether amputating a foot or nose,
what harm does it cause to say anything?
Whether stripping or cutting,
only cruelty or killing.
People have no one to rely on,
Yīn overturned due to punishments.
Qín perished due to brutality,
the law servant manages the trials,
daring to report and offer up an audience.
Later Hàn Cuī Dézhèng’s “Admonition of Dá Lǐ”
Far off were Gāo Yáo,
assisting Táng to set up offices.
Thus were built the prisons and dungeons,
the nine provinces were thus governed.
As even as a stone,
as clear as a deep spring.
Distinguished by three cypresses and nine thorny plants,
by virtue and merit.
Criminals were executed,
evil tribes scattered.
Splendid peace under Heaven,
widely bestowing brightness.
In former times, with Zhòngní,
sympathetic was the sage.
Zǐ Hǎn revered laws,
the people of Wèi cleared of difficulties.
His loyalty pardoned,
honored by Emperor Xiàowén.
Duke Yú lamented the widowed,
broadening the doors of the kingdom.
Far and distant,
yet not following former teachings.
The ruler negligent, ministers arrogant,
oppressively employing the people.
Rewarding to indulge desires,
punishing to vent anger.
Zhòu created the bronze flame torture,
the Zhōu people extinguished the Yīn.
The Shāng used cruel punishments,
Tāng declared war.
Wèi Yāng was ruthless,

Bù Yí understood the harm,

Wú’s Chén and Wǔ Xū,

Heaven's perception evident,

The official of reason overseeing laws,

The Guǎnzǐ says:
"Rites,
are based on human feelings,
follow principles of righteousness,
and establish regulated patterns for them."
The Qū Lǐ says:
"Now rites,
are what determine closeness and distance,
resolve doubts and suspicions,
distinguish sameness and difference,
clarify right and wrong.
Virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness,
cannot be accomplished without rites;
teaching, instruction, governance, and customs,
cannot be complete without rites;
disputes and litigation,
cannot be decided without rites.
Ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
father and son, elder and younger brother,
cannot be fixed without rites;
official studies and serving teachers,
cannot be intimate without rites;
ordering the court and governing the army,
assuming office and executing laws,
cannot be carried out with authority and dignity without rites;
prayers and sacrifices,
supplying ghosts and spirits,
cannot be sincere and solemn without rites."
The Lǐ Jì also says:
"Thus, rites for people,
are like yeast for wine.
Like bamboo arrows having their smooth outer skin,
like pine and cypress having their heartwood."
The Hàn Shū:
"Shūsūn Tōng established twelve chapters of ritual regulations for Gāozǔ."
The Hòu Hàn Shū:
"In the first year of Zhānghé, an edict ordered Cáo Pú to examine and correct old rites at the Eastern Tower of the Southern Palace.
From the Son of Heaven above,
to the common people below,
the systems for marriage, capping, auspicious and inauspicious events, from beginning to end,
amounted to one hundred and fifty chapters."
Clarify Substance Distinguish Position
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící says:
"Rites,
are what establish appearances and clarify the substance of heaven and earth."
The Jiāyǔ says:
"Confucius said to Duke Āi of Lǔ:
'Of the reasons why humans live,
rites are the greatest.
Without rites, there is no way to serve the spirits of heaven and earth,
or distinguish the positions of ruler and minister, elder and younger.'"
Receive Heaven Model Earth
The Lǐ Jì says:
"Now rites,
the former kings used to receive the way of heaven,
and order human feelings.
Therefore, those who lose it die,
those who obtain it live."
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
"The reason for creating rites and music,
music is to emulate heaven,
rites are to model earth."
Establish Appearances Distinguish Ranks
See above in the "Clarify Substance note."
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"Using humans to distinguish ranks ensures people do not overstep."
Observe Yīn Go to Lǔ
The Lǐ Jì says:
"Yán Yǎn asked again:
'Master, you speak of rites to the utmost,
may I hear about it?'
Confucius said:
'I wished to observe the way of Xià,
therefore I went to Qǐ, but it was insufficient for evidence.
I obtained the Xià calendar there.
I wished to observe the way of Yīn,
therefore I went to Sòng, but it was insufficient for evidence.
I obtained the Kūn Qián there.'" The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Hán Xuānzǐ went to Lǔ,
and said:
'The rites of Zhōu are all in Lǔ.'"
Harmonize the People Secure the Ruler
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"The third is the canon of rites,
to harmonize the states,
to govern the hundred officials,
to harmonize the myriad people."
The Xiào Jīng says:
"For securing the ruler and governing the people,
nothing is better than rites."
Teach Reverence Cultivate Harmony
The Zhōu Lǐ "Twelve Teachings,
first is to teach reverence through sacrificial rites,
second is to teach deference through yang rites, third is to teach intimacy through yin rites."
The Lǐ Jì says:
"Formerly, Zhòngní participated as a guest at the Zhà sacrifice,
when the affair was finished,
he went out and wandered atop the tower gate,
sighed deeply and said:
'When the Great Way prevailed,
all under heaven was for the public good,
selecting the worthy and capable,
discussing trust and cultivating harmony.
Therefore, people did not only treat their own parents as parents,
nor only treat their own children as children.'"
Regulate the Center Cultivate the Exterior
The Lǐ Jì says:
"Zǐgòng stepped over the mat and replied:
'May I ask what will be used to achieve this center?'
The Master said:
'Rites!
Rites are what regulate the center.'" The Hàn Shū says:
"The way of the Six Classics leads to the same end,
but the use of rites and music is urgent.
Therefore, music is used to govern the interior and create unity,
rites are used to cultivate the exterior and create distinction.
Unity leads to harmony and intimacy,
distinction leads to awe and reverence.
Harmony and intimacy lead to no resentment,
awe and reverence lead to no contention."
Follow the Times, Conform to Customs
The Book of Han states:
"A ruler must base his rituals on those of previous kings,
adapting them appropriately according to the times.
He makes additions and subtractions,
regulates people's hearts and minds,
and gradually establishes new institutions."
The Shenzi states:
"Rituals follow customs,
governance follows superiors,
and envoys follow the ruler of the state.
There are rituals for the noble and the humble,
but not for the worthy and the unworthy."
Social Intercourse, Rules and Standards
The Zuo Zhuan states:
"When Duke Yin of Zhū came for an audience,
Zǐgòng observed the proceedings.
The Viscount of Zhū held the jade tablet high,
his countenance looking upward;
the Duke received the jade low,
his countenance looking downward.
Zǐgòng said:
'Judging by ritual,
both rulers are heading toward death or downfall!
For ritual
is the substance of life and death, survival and ruin.
From the movements to left and right, the social intercourse,
the advances and retreats, the bowing and looking up,
it is taken as the standard.
Now in the first month they hold a court audience,
yet both fail to observe the proper measure:
holding high and looking upward
indicates arrogance;
receiving low and looking downward
indicates decline.
Arrogance is close to disorder,
decline is close to sickness.
Since our ruler is the host,
will he not perish first?'" The Book of Rites states:
"Ritual in governing a state
is like scales for determining weight, the marking line for straightness, or compass and square for circles and squares.
Thus, if the scales are truly hung,
one cannot be deceived about weight;
if the marking line is truly laid out,
one cannot be deceived about straightness;
if compass and square are truly set,
one cannot be deceived about circles and squares;
if a gentleman examines ritual carefully,
he cannot be misled by deceit and fraud."
Serving Teachers, Respecting Elders
See above in the narrative section.
Yuán Huái's Correct Writings states:
"What is ritual?
It is the patterned restraint based on human feelings,
the sentiment of honoring fathers and loving kin,
the duty of respecting parents and honoring elders."
Heaven's Constant Principle, Earth's Righteousness
The Zuo Zhuan states:
"Zǐ Tàishū visited Zhào Jiǎnzǐ,
and Jiǎnzǐ asked about the rituals of bowing, yielding, and social intercourse.
He replied:
'That is ceremonial form,
not ritual.'
Jiǎnzǐ said:
'May I ask what ritual is?'
He replied:
'I, Jí, have heard from the late senior official Zǐchǎn:
"Ritual
is the constant principle of Heaven,
the righteousness of Earth,
and the conduct of the people."'"
Embody Sincerity, Accomplish Benevolence
The Book of Rites states:
"The former kings cultivated ritual to attain righteousness,
and embodied sincerity to attain harmony."
It also states:
"Virtue, the Way, benevolence, and righteousness
cannot be accomplished without ritual."
Adapt to Change, Follow Appropriateness
The Zhuangzi states:
"The ritual principles and laws of the Three Kings and Five Emperors
are like hawthorns, pears, oranges, and pomelos—

change according to the times."
The Book of Rites states:
"Ritual follows appropriateness,

Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:

When Jìn's Shì Gài led troops to invade Qí,
he heard of the Qí Marquis's death and turned back;

Examine Sincerity, Accomplish the Way
The Book of Rites states:
"Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, King Chéng, and the Duke of Zhōu
were selected for this reason.
These six gentlemen
were all meticulous in ritual.
They examined their sincerity,
showing people constancy."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"'Examine' means to accomplish."
"Accomplish the Way" is already seen in the commentary for "accomplish benevolence" above.
Share Heaven's Pneuma, Harmonize with Human Hearts
The Ritual Apocrypha states:

shares the same pneuma as Heaven and Earth,
and accords with the four seasons in sincerity."
The Book of Rites states:
"Ritual
harmonizes with the timeliness of Heaven,

harmonizes with human hearts,

Govern All Officials, Order the Myriad Things
The first part is seen in the commentary for "harmonizing the people";
the second part is seen in the commentary for "harmonizing with human hearts."
Symbolize the Five Phases, Transform with the Four Seasons
The Elder Dai's Book of Rites states:
"Ritual symbolizes the Five Phases,
its meaning lies in the four seasons,
hence it is raised in four aspects:
there is kindness, there is righteousness,
there is moderation, there is flexibility."
The Book of Rites states:
"Therefore, ritual must be rooted in the Great One,
which divides to form Heaven and Earth,
revolves to become yīn and yáng,
transforms to become the four seasons,
and arranges to become ghosts and spirits."
Brotherly Affection, Ruler-Minister Righteousness
The Book of Rites states:
"Without ritual, there is no means to distinguish the affection between men and women, father and son, and brothers,
or the patterns of marriage and degrees of kinship."
It also states:
"The rituals of court audience
serve to clarify the righteousness between ruler and minister;
the rituals of diplomatic visits
serve to make the feudal lords respect one another."
Establish Ruler and Minister, Strengthen Father and Son
The Book of Rites states:
"Ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
father and son, elder and younger brother—
without ritual, these are not fixed."
It also states:
"With ritual and righteousness as the guiding principle,
to rectify ruler and minister, to strengthen father and son, to harmonize brothers, to bring harmony to husband and wife, to establish institutions, and to set up fields and villages."
Distinguish Men and Women, Resolve Suspicion
The Family Sayings of Confucius states:
"Confucius said to Duke Āi of Lǔ:
