or to differentiate the interactions between men and women, father and son.'" "Resolve suspicion" is already seen in the narrative section.
Clarify Right and Wrong, Distinguish Sameness and Difference
Both are seen in the narrative.
Contain Yīn and Yáng, Share with Heaven and Earth
The Book of Han states:
"The aims of the Six Classics converge,
but the application of ritual and music is most urgent.
If one cultivating the self forgets ritual for a moment,
then violence and arrogance enter.
If a ruler governing a state loses ritual for a single day,
then disorder and chaos befall it.
Humans contain the pneuma of Heaven, Earth, yīn, and yáng,
and possess the feelings of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure;
they receive this nature but cannot regulate it."
The Ritual Apocrypha states:
"The movement of ritual shares the same pneuma as Heaven and Earth,
accords with the four seasons in sincerity,
uses yīn and yáng as tallies,
and takes the sun and moon as illumination."
Comprehending Human Sentiments, Following the Heavenly Way
The Book of Rites says:
"Thus, ritual and righteousness
are the great essentials for humanity.
They are the means to cultivate trust and foster harmony,
and to strengthen the bonds of human flesh and skin,
the ties of sinews and bones;
they are the great essentials for nourishing the living and sending off the dead,
and for serving the spirits and gods;
they are the great passage for comprehending the Heavenly Way
and accommodating human sentiments."
The Zuo Zhuan records:
"The Marquis of Qí attacked Cáo,
entering its outer walls,
to punish it for coming to court.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
'Will the Marquis of Qí not escape misfortune?
He himself is without ritual,
yet he punishes those who possess ritual.
Saying, "Why do you perform rituals?"
Ritual is used to follow Heaven;
it is the Way of Heaven.'"
Xún Kuàng of Chǔ, "Rhapsody on Ritual"
There is a great thing,
neither silk nor silk cloth.
Patterns form its fabric,
neither sun nor moon,
yet it illuminates all under Heaven.
The living use it to attain longevity,
the dead use it for burial.
City walls are fortified by it,
the three armies are strengthened by it.
Pure, it leads to kingship;
mixed, it leads to hegemony;
without it, one perishes.
Your servant is ignorant and does not recognize it;
I dare to ask the king about it.
The king said:
"Is this not that which is patterned yet without ornament?
Simple and easy to understand,
yet profoundly principled?
That which the nobleman reveres,
and the petty man does not disrupt?
If nature does not obtain it, one is like a beast;
if nature obtains it, one is fully endowed.
If a commoner upholds it,
he becomes a sage;
if a feudal lord upholds it,
he unifies the four seas.
Utterly clear and concise,
highly accommodating and embodied—
I ask to attribute it to ritual."
Lǐ Délín, "Edict on Revising the Five Rites for Emperor Wén of Suí"
How great is the timely significance of ritual in its application!
Yellow jade discs and dark green bi disks
invoke the spirits of Heaven and Earth;
grains in vessels and sacrificial animals
express reverence in the ancestral temple.
It rectifies the order between father and son, ruler and minister;
it clarifies the rules for marriage and mourning.
Thus, virtue, the Way, benevolence, and righteousness
cannot be accomplished without ritual.
To pacify superiors and transform the people,
nothing is better than ritual.
Edict on Ritual and Music Promulgated During the Zhēnguàn Era
The former kings established ritual,
distinguishing directions and rectifying positions,
structuring the state and organizing the countryside.
They modeled Heaven and Earth to create laws,
communicated with the divine and luminous to implement transformation.
Music arises from within,
ritual is formed from without.
They can shift customs and transform practices;
with bowing and yielding, all under Heaven are transformed.
Is it not only through ritual and music?
Thus, they share the same moderation and harmony,
soundless and formless.
Should one merely adorn the appearance of jade and silk,
or truly revere the performance of bells and drums?
Sacrifices, Part Two
The *Shangshu Dazhuan* says:
“The word ‘sacrifice’ (祭 jì) means ‘to examine’ (察 chá).
To examine means to reach.
It means human affairs reach the spirits.”
The *Erya* says:
“The spring sacrifice is called cí (祠).
Cí means ‘to eat.’
The summer sacrifice is called yuè (礿).
(Pronounced like ‘酌’ zhuó).
New vegetables are suitable for yuè.
The autumn sacrifice is called cháng (嘗).
It involves tasting the new grain.
The winter sacrifice is called zhēng (烝).
Zhēng means
‘to present’ or
‘to advance offerings.’
Sacrificing to Heaven is called liáo chái (燎柴).
After the sacrifice,
a pile of firewood is burned.
Sacrificing to Earth is called yì mái (瘞埋).
After the sacrifice,
it is buried.
Sacrificing to mountains is called guǐ
guǐ
xuán (庪懸).
Either placing (guǐ) or suspending (xuán),
setting it on the mountain.
Sacrificing to rivers is called fú chén (浮沉).
Either floating or sinking,
placing it in the water.
Sacrificing to stars is called bù (布).
Scattering (the offerings) on the ground.
Sacrificing to wind is called zhé (磔).
(Pronounced like ‘張伯’ Zhāng Bó).
Nowadays, the custom is to dismember a dog on the main road;
this is a remnant of that practice.
‘Shì lèi shì mà’ (是類是禡)
is a military sacrifice.
When the army goes on an expedition,
they perform lèi to the Supreme Deity,
and mà at the place of departure.
‘Jì bó jì dǎo’ (既伯既禱)
is a horse sacrifice.”
Bó
is the ancestor of horses.
When about to use horse strength,
one must first sacrifice to their ancestor.
The *Shuōwén* says:
“A sacrifice to remove evil is called fú (祓).
A sacrifice to gather blessings is called guì (禬).
A sacrifice
to report affairs and seek blessings is called dǎo (禱).
A sacrifice on the road is called shāng (禓).
A pure
and sincere offering is called yīn (禋).
A sacrifice to spirits by category is called lèi (禷).
A sacrifice
to the Director of Fate is called bǐ (䃾).
Pronounced like ‘俾利’ bǐ lì.
A sacrifice to the pig ancestor is called lǐ (禮).
A monthly
sacrifice is called zuì (祽).
Pronounced like ‘子內’ zǐ nèi.
The above all come from the *Shuōwén*.
Praying for rain is called yú (雩).
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
‘When the dragon stars appear, perform yú.’
Yú
is a drought sacrifice.
Praying for clear weather is called yǒng (禜).”
According to the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
for disasters of snow, frost, wind, and rain, one performs yǒng.
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“Use yīn sacrifices to worship the August Heaven and Supreme Deity.
Use the shí chái sacrifice for the sun, moon, and stars.
Use the yǒu liáo sacrifice for the Director of the Center, Director of Fate, Master of Wind, and Master of Rain.
Use the blood sacrifice for the altars of soil and grain, the five sacrifices, and the five peaks.
Use sinking and burying for mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes.
Use the pì
(pronounced pǔ bī).
gū sacrifice for the myriad creatures of the four directions.
Use the sì
(pronounced tā de).
offering and guàn
(pronounced gǔ luàn).
libation to feast the former kings.”
The *Lǐjì* says:
“In the first month of spring,
the sacrifice is to the household door,
and the spleen is offered first.
In the first month of summer,
the sacrifice is to the hearth,
and the lungs are offered first.
For the central earth,
the sacrifice is to the central eaves,
and the heart is offered first.
In the first month of autumn,
the sacrifice is to the gate,
and the liver is offered first.
In the first month of winter,
the sacrifice is to the road,
and the kidneys are offered first.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
to the four directions,
to mountains and rivers,
and to the five sacrifices,
yearly.
The feudal lords sacrifice to their regions, to mountains and rivers,
and to the five sacrifices;
yearly.
Great officers sacrifice to the five sacrifices;
yearly.
Officers sacrifice to their ancestors.
Sacrifice to the sun on an altar,
and to the moon in a pit.
The sun in the east,
the moon in the west,
to distinguish the bright and the dark,
to distinguish the inner and the outer.
Sacrifices should not be too frequent,
for frequency leads to weariness,
and weariness leads to disrespect.
Sacrifices should not be too sparse,
for sparseness leads to neglect,
and neglect leads to forgetfulness.
The king establishes seven sacrifices:
the Director of Fate, the Central Eaves, the State Gate, the State Road, the Great Wandering Spirit, the Household Door, and the Hearth.
Feudal lords establish five sacrifices:
the Director of Fate, the Central Eaves, the State Gate, the State Road, and the Public Wandering Spirit.
Great officers establish three sacrifices:
the Clan Wandering Spirit, the Gate, and the Road.
Officers establish two sacrifices:
the Gate and the Road.
Commoners establish one sacrifice.
Either the Household Door
or the Hearth.
When the sage kings instituted sacrifices,

they sacrificed to those whose laws benefited the people, those who died in diligent service, those whose labors stabilized the state, those who could ward off great disasters, and those who could repel great calamities.
The sun, moon, and stars
are what people look up to.
Mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, hills, and mounds
are what people obtain materials from.
Those not of these categories
are not included in the sacrificial canon.”
Category means type.
Presenting reverence / Repaying merit
The *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* says:
“If the palace buildings are not properly arranged,
one cannot sacrifice.
Sacrificing means presenting what is timely,
presenting reverence,
presenting righteousness;
it is not about enjoying flavors.”
Xǔ Shèn’s *Wǔjīng Yìyì* says:
“Dukes and marquises sacrifice to the Hundred Princes.
From ministers and below,
they do not exceed their own clan.
What the ghosts and spirits reach,
if not their own clan, then they succeed to the state’s position.
The Hundred Princes
are rulers of states who first had merit and virtue among the people.
Now in their positions,
they are repaid with sacrifice.”
Red Bull / Black Victim
The *Máo Shī* says:
“Sacrifice with clear wine,
follow with a red bull,
and offer it to the ancestors.”
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“For all yang sacrifices, use red-haired victims;
for all yīn sacrifices, use black-haired victims.”
Zhèng’s commentary:
“Yīn sacrifices are for the northern suburbs and the altars of soil and grain.
Black is yǒu, red is xīng.”
Seven Sacrifices / Five Sacrifices
See above in the narrative.
Yuán Huái’s *Zhènglùn* says:
“There are five great sacrifices of the state:
dì, xiá, jiāo, zǔ, zōng, and bào.
These five are the major nodes of ritual.”
Repaying Virtue / Honoring Grace
Yáng Quán’s *Wùlǐ Lùn* says:
“In ancient times, they honored sacrifice and revered spirits.
Sacrificing in the ancestral temple is to continue providing for them;
sacrificing to Heaven and Earth is to repay their virtue.”
Wáng Chōng’s *Lùnhéng* says:
“The meaning of sacrifice has two aspects:
first, to repay merit;
second, to honor the ancestors.
Repaying merit encourages effort;
honoring the ancestors exalts grace.”
Yùjiǔ (Fragrant Wine) and Lántāng (Orchid Bath)
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"For all libation ceremonies in sacrifices and guest receptions,
blend yùchàng (fragrant wine) to fill the ritual vessels and display them."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Pound the turmeric, boil it, and blend it with chàng wine.
Yù is a plant resembling the orchid."
Liú Yìqìng's Records of the Hidden and Visible says:
"The temple is four zhàng square without enclosing walls,
with a path four chǐ wide along the walls,
flanked by fragrant orchid plants.
Those observing abstinence boil them for bathing,
and then personally perform the sacrifice,
which is called 'bathing in orchid water.'"
Liù Biàn (Six Variations) and Jiǔ Chéng (Nine Completions)
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"With pipes of solitary bamboo,
qín and sè zithers of Yúnhé,
perform the dance of Yúnmén.
On the winter solstice,
played at the circular mound,
if the music undergoes six variations, then all the heavenly deities will descend,
and they can be ritually honored."
The Book of Documents states:
"When the Sháo music of the xiāo pipes reaches nine completions,
phoenixes come to pay homage."
Cháorì (Worshipping the Morning Sun) and Xīyuè (Worshipping the Evening Moon)
The Book of Rites states:
"For worshipping the morning sun and sacrificing to the Five Emperors,
set up the great and small resting enclosures.
Arrange layered mats and layered tables;
it is the same when meeting the feudal lords."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Cháorì means
paying homage to the sun outside the eastern gate in spring."
Liú Xiàng's Biographies of Exemplary Women states:
"At midday, examine and correct human affairs;
at shǎocǎi (dusk), worship the evening moon."
Cáo Dàjiā comments:
"Shǎocǎi refers to
the diminished brilliance (of the sun).
Sacrifice to the evening moon at the autumn equinox,
to welcome the yīn energy."
Lǐdì (Honoring Earth) and Bīnhé (Receiving the River)
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Use jade to make six ritual vessels,
to honor Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
Use a dark blue bì disc to honor Heaven,
use a yellow cóng tube to honor Earth."
The Bamboo Annals states:
"In the first year of Hòu Huāng's accession to the throne,
he received the Hé (Yellow River) with a dark bì disc.
Hunting at the sea,
he caught a great fish."
Cǎitán (Colorful Altar) and Gànxí (Dark Red Mat)
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"Emperor Huán established a temple for Huáng-Lǎo.
In the Zhuólóng Palace of the Northern Palace, an altar was built,
colorful and dazzling."
Wèi Hóng's Old Rituals of Hàn states:
"The emperor proceeds personally,
with all officials following.
All observe abstinence for one hundred days.
For earthly sacrifices, they do not leave;
for sacrificing to Heaven, a purple altar with canopies and curtains.
Emperor Gāozǔ is matched with Heaven,
positioned below the hall facing west,
with dark red canopies and dark red mats."
Yíshè (Appropriate Sacrifice to Shè) and Lèidì (Classifying Sacrifice to the Emperor)
The Book of Rites states:
"When the Son of Heaven is about to embark on an expedition,
he performs the Yí sacrifice at the Shè altar."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Yí is
the name of a sacrifice."
The Book of Documents states:
"Therefore, he performed the Lèi sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
and the Yīn sacrifice to the Six Zōng.
He performed the Wàng sacrifice to the mountains and rivers,
and universally to all the deities."
Sānwàng (Three Wàng Sacrifices) and Liùzōng (Six Zōng)
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"In the thirty-first year of Duke Xī,
four divinations were made for the suburban sacrifice,
but none were favorable.
Thus, the sacrificial animal was released,
but the three Wàng sacrifices were still performed."
The Book of Documents states:
"Perform the Yīn sacrifice to the Six Zōng."
Wáng Sù comments:
"There are six that are honored;
all are offered pure sacrifices.
Bury a shǎoláo (lesser sacrifice) at Tàizhāo,
to sacrifice to the seasons;
near the pits and altars,
to sacrifice to cold and heat.
Wánggōng,
to sacrifice to the sun;
Yèmíng,
to sacrifice to the moon;
Yōuyǒng,
to sacrifice to the stars;
Yúyǒng,
to sacrifice for water and drought.
'Perform the Yīn sacrifice to the Six Zōng'
refers to this."
Shòulí (Receiving Blessings) and Zhìfú (Conveying Blessings)
The Book of Hàn, Biography of Jiǎ Yì, states:
"More than a year later,
Emperor Wén thought of Yì
and summoned him.
When he arrived for an audience,
the emperor was just receiving blessings while seated in the Xuānshì Hall."
Sū Lín comments:
"The main front chamber of Wèiyāng Palace."
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"In charge of the rituals of the capital's sacrifices,
to convey blessings to the state."
Yuánqiū (Circular Mound) and Fāngzé (Square Marsh); Cāngbì (Dark Blue Bì Disc) and Huángcóng (Yellow Cóng Tube)
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"For all music,
with Yuánzhōng as the gōng note,
Huángzhōng as the jué note,
Tàicù as the zhǐ note,
Gūxiǎn as the yǔ note.
On the winter solstice,
played at the circular mound on the earth,
then all the heavenly deities will descend,
and they can be ritually honored.
With Hánzhōng as the gōng note,
Tàicù as the jué note,
Gūxiǎn as the zhǐ note,
Nánlǚ as the yǔ note.
On the summer solstice,
played at the square mound in the marsh,
then all the earthly deities will emerge,
and they can be ritually honored."
Also, the Rites of Zhóu states:
"Use jade to make six ritual vessels,
to honor Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
Use a dark blue bì disc to honor Heaven,
use a yellow cóng tube to honor Earth."
Yǐ Xiǎng Yǐ Sì (To Offer and To Sacrifice) and Shì Lèi Shì Mà (This Classifying and This Mà)
The Máo Poetry states:
"To offer and to sacrifice,
to seek great blessings."
The Dàyǎ states:
"This classifying and this mà,
is the army sacrifice."
Wèi Sūn Gāi's "Rhapsody on the Temple at the Foot of Sāngōng Mountain"
In the western border of Yuánshì County of Zhào State, there are six spirit temples.
I observed one of them,
located on the southern side of Xíng Mountain,
namely the Sāngōng Temple.
Its lofty hall is already steep;
its perilous tower reaches the clouds.
Lattice windows overlook a chasm of ten thousand rèn;
the timber and earth are adorned with the splendor of red patterns.
At that time, I gazed all day long,
and stayed overnight in the eastern wing.
I summoned the local elders
and inquired about the old traditions.
They said the building was first erected seventy years ago;
the three stars shone with divine power,
and indeed sent down sweet rain.
Mountains take form as spirits,
spirits take formlessness as sovereign.
If vapor rises above,
and thunder stirs below,
then public fields are blessed with abundant millet,
and widows benefit from the leftover ears.
This is also why this region makes offerings,
unceasing through the generations.
Thereupon, I took up my brush to compose this rhapsody,
to manifest the reliance on divine spirits,
and to extol the grandeur of the great hall.
Its concluding stanza says:
"Kūn forms the earth's configuration,
Héngyuè emits essence.
Terrifying and rugged, it opens up,
its beauty rising to the great purity.
The three lords assist affairs,
the Rain Master is not idle.
Clouds gather thickly,
moistening all living beings.
Our ancestors, virtuous indeed,
their images and forms are depicted.
Examining the old histories,
the canons and plans are silent."
Jìn Jī Hán's "Rhapsody on the Road Sacrifice"
The practice of the road sacrifice has long been prevalent in custom.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
none fail to employ it.
In the Hàn dynasty, they divined for the day Bǐngwǔ;
the Wèi house selected Dīngwèi.
As for the great Jìn,
they performed the road sacrifice on the Yǒu day of the first month of each season,
each according to their own cyclical movements;
the three dynasties indeed differed.
Although they performed the road sacrifice,
none knew from whence the road sacrifice arose.
The Shuōwén states:
"Praying and invoking the road deity is called the road sacrifice.
Those who have affairs on the road,
whether auspicious or inauspicious, all use the name.
When a gentleman goes on a journey,
they arrange it along the middle of the road;
when the deceased are to be moved,
they call its name in the courtyard.
Some say that over a hundred generations, distant and obstructed,
names all wither and perish.
Grave mounds no longer preserve their inscribed tablets;
wandering souls cannot find lodging in the ancestral temples.
Thus the wise, at the auspicious hour of the year's beginning,
first raise the banners,
waving the colored flags.
They wish to summon the luminous spirits this very night,
hoping the multitude of ancestors will come and rely.
There are two aspects;
looking down, I sigh at the grand spectacle,
and so I describe it in a rhapsody."
Sòng Xiè Zhuāng's "Poem on the Winter Sacrifice in Response to Imperial Command"
Frost and dew congeal the imperial sentiment,
solemn reverence stirs the celestial pull.
The western suburbs extinguish submerged floods,
the eastern sea arises with bright advancement.
Dancing winds waft the dragon banners,
wheel-like clouds float the jade axles.
Purple steps harmonize with pipes and bells,
golden paths unfold in responsive turns.
Now I see the six odes in harmony,
forever hear the nine virtues' moistening.
Observing life, I recognize fortunate abundance,
gazing at my attire, I am ashamed of my meager carriage.
Chén Hóngràng's "Poem on the Spring Night Offering to the Five Peaks"
Night quiet, the jade mats serene,
moon rising, the apricot altar bright.
Incense smoke of a hundred blends exhales,
lamp light of nine subtleties clear.
The Five Peaks move the dragon carriage,
the Ten Isles turn the phoenix pipes.
Eyes envision the numinous beings' demeanor,
heart belongs to the feather garments' lightness.
Orchid dishes present divine offerings,
osmanthus wine conveys distant sincerity.
Joyfully content in myself,
I pour wine, mindful of floating life.
Chén Shūdá's "Poem on the Eight Fast Sacrifices at the Altar of Soil in the Western Garden of the Prefectural City"
Ascending the altar, I prepare the pure sacrifice,
at early dawn, solemnly dividing duties.
Pervading qi, wind and frost accumulate,
ascending light, the sun's hue delays.
Agricultural instruction precedes the eight policies,
warm harmony orders the four seasons.
Praying for the year, I wear the hanging crown,
announcing the silk, I lift the curtain.
Burying in the earth, I honor the remaining libation,
for humans and heaven, there may be provision.
Pepper and orchid complete the clear libation,
the grain vessels clear the fragrant straw.
Dividing the carved meat, I share the sacrificial portion,
filling the courtyard, I descend to receive blessings.
Now relying on knowing ritual propriety,
moreover, I serve in transformed harmony and prosperity.
Liáng Jiāng Yān's "Song Lyrics for the Entrance of the Sacrificial Animals"
The invocator detailed, the scribe prepared,
rituals complete, music presented.
There are animals arrayed,
there are drums suspended.
Rising torches resemble stars,
rushing water akin to lightning.
Suburban torches long prepared,
those sturdy steeds, sleek and black.
To await the break of dawn,
to extend the divine feast.
Also "Song Lyrics for Offering Beans, Hair, and Blood"
Timely reverent, timely sacrificial,
there are objects, there are rules.
We, the exalted sages,
truly embrace bright virtue.
Sacrificial vessels interwoven,
fragrant wine vessels filling four sides.
Millet, the excellent grain,
wine, the profound silence.
Offering connects to the azure deities,
blessings extend to the black-haired masses.
May the spirits descend,
blessing the family, protecting the state.
Also "Song Lyrics for Performing the Arrayed Music"
Yīn revered matching heaven,
Zhōu honored bright sacrifices.
Auspiciousness joins at Fényīn,
dreams align with Tàizhì.
Blue canopies like clouds unfurling,
vermilion halls like rosy clouds rising.
Two luminaries renewed,
five essences announce the beginning.
Thereby to feast them,
great fortune is trodden.
Suburban Mounds, Part Three
The Lǐjì states:
"Sacrificing to the Thearch in the suburbs,
is to fix the position of Heaven."
The Ěryǎ states:
"The round mound, the great altar,
is for sacrificing to Heaven.
The square marsh, the great border,
is for sacrificing to Earth."
The Zhōushū, "Making Luò" chapter, states:
"Establish the mound precinct in the southern suburbs,
to sacrifice to the Supreme God,
with Hòujì as associate."
The Zhōulǐ, "Duties of the Grand Minister of Rites" states:
"Use the yīn sacrifice to sacrifice to the Vast Heaven Supreme God.
Yīn means smoke.
Smoke:
the Zhōu people esteemed scent,
the scent of the smoke
is smelled by the Vast Heaven Supreme God.
On the winter solstice, sacrifice at the round mound,
to the Celestial Thearch Great God.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Vast Heaven,
the Supreme God is the dark heaven."
A dark blue jade disc to ritually honor Heaven.
Zhèng Xuán states:
"Ritually honoring Heaven on the winter solstice,
refers to the Celestial Thearch Great God at the North Pole.
In general, ritually honoring a deity must use its kind;
the disc is round to symbolize Heaven."
A yellow jade cong to ritually honor Earth.
Ritually honor Earth on the summer solstice,
referring to the deity in the Kūnlún Mountains.
The cong is square to symbolize Earth.
Four pointed jade tablets with a base,
to sacrifice to Heaven,
to present to the Supreme God.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"In the center is a disc,
pointed tablets attached on four sides,
all made from one piece of jade.
Thus called four pointed tablets.
Having a base,
means the ends of the pointed tablets extend in four directions.
Some say the four pointed tablets have a base,
meaning the four corners of the pointed tablets.
The Supreme God is the dark heaven."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Ritually honoring Heaven is the suburban sacrifice to Heaven in the Xià calendar.
The Supreme God is the Five Thearchs.
The reason for the suburban sacrifice differing for the Five Thearchs,
speaking of Heaven is to honor and distinguish it supremely."
Two pointed jade tablets with a base,
to sacrifice to Earth,
to present to the four directions.
Two pointed tablets
symbolize the number of Earth, which is two.
Refers to sacrificing to the deity of the Divine Land in the northern suburbs.
The Grand Director of Music plays the Yellow Bell,
sings the Great Lü,
dances the Cloud Gate,
to sacrifice to the heavenly deities.
Refers to the Five Thearchs, sun, moon, and stars.
The king each sacrifices to the Thearch who bestowed his mandate in the southern suburbs in the first month of summer.
Plays the Great Frame,
sings the Responding Bell,
dances the Pool of Harmony,
to sacrifice to the earthly deities."
Sacrifice in the northern suburbs,
refers to the deity of the Divine Land and the Altars of Soil and Grain.
The Lǐjì states:

"The Yǒuyú house performed the dì sacrifice to Huángdì and the suburban sacrifice to Kù, the ancestral sacrifice to Zhuānxū and the temple sacrifice to Yáo; the Xiàhòu house also performed the dì sacrifice to Huángdì and the suburban sacrifice to Gǔn, the ancestral sacrifice to Zhuānxū and the temple sacrifice to Yǔ; the Yīn people performed the dì sacrifice to Kù and the suburban sacrifice to Míng, the ancestral sacrifice to Qì and the temple sacrifice to Tāng; the Zhōu people performed the dì sacrifice to Kù and the suburban sacrifice to Jì,
the ancestral sacrifice to Wénwáng and the temple sacrifice to Wǔwáng."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Dì, suburban, ancestral, and temple sacrifices refer to sacrifices with associate feasting."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"In general, when the hibernating insects awaken, perform the suburban sacrifice."
Yellow Suburb Black Altar
The Book of the Later Hàn states:
"In the second year of the Jiànníng era of Emperor Líng,
they went to welcome the vital breath at the Yellow Suburb,
traveling along the road west of the Luò River bridge.
They encountered a sudden storm,
and the ceremonial carriages in the procession
had their canopies blown off.
All the officials were drenched,
and they returned without reaching the suburban altar.
They ordered the officials to perform the rites
and welcome the vital breath at the Northern Suburb."
! The Book of Hàn states:
"When Gāozǔ entered the passes,
he asked which god the former Qín altar for the Supreme God was used to sacrifice to.
The reply was:
'The Four Emperors;
there are shrines for the White, Yellow, Blue, and Red [Emperors].'
Gāozǔ said:
'I have heard Heaven has Five Emperors,
so why are there only four?'
No one knew the explanation,
so then Gāozǔ said:
'I understand!
They are waiting for me to complete the five.'
He then established a shrine for the Black Emperor,
named the Black Altar."
Vermilion Flames Purple Altar
The Jìn "Suburban Sacrifice Songs" state:
"Prepare the great altar,
to honor the August God.
The vital essence is abundant,
all spirits are guests.
Gather the vermilion flames,
burn fragrant firewood.
Purple smoke rises,
crowning the azure clouds."
They also state:
"Establish the great altar,
to settle Heaven's will.
With thoughtful and wise minds,
divination is followed.
Raise the markers and gather [offerings],
set up the suburban palace.
Field torches are placed,
joyful fires connect.
Passing the first decade,
gather to report at the start.
Adorn the steps and altar,
arrange chambers in the pit."
Lǔ Suburb Yōng Altar
Pronunciation: zhǐ.
The Máo Poetry states:
"August, august is the Sovereign God,
august ancestor Hòujì."
The commentary states:
"Huánghuáng,
means great.
Hòu,
means sovereign,
dì refers to the Celestial God.
The Lǔ suburban sacrifice honors the great, august Sovereign God,
matching him with the beautiful ancestor Hòujì,
their sacrifices follow the rites of the Son of Heaven."
The Book of Hàn states:
"They sacrifice to the Five Emperors at the Yōng Altar,
which is on a mountain.
Looking out in all four directions, one cannot see the four quarters,
hence it is called the Yōng (Enclosed) Altar."
Southern Suburb Northern Altar
The Zhōu Rites state:
"Set up a mound altar in the southern suburbs to sacrifice to the Supreme God,
matching him with Hòujì."
"Northern Altar" see above.
Yellow Jade Dark Sacrificial Animals
The Zhōu Rites:
"Use jade to make six vessels,
to honor Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
Use a dark blue bì to honor Heaven,
use a yellow cóng to honor Earth.
Use a green guī to honor the East, a red zhāng to honor the South, a white hǔ to honor the West, and a black cóng to honor the North."
They also state:
"The Herdsman oversees the herding of the six sacrificial animals,
and multiplies their numbers,
to provide pure sacrificial animals for offerings.
For all yang sacrifices, use red-haired animals with pure coats;
for all yīn sacrifices, use dark-haired animals with pure coats."
Preserve Myriad Years of Life Flourish with a Hundred Blessings
Fù Xuán's "Song for Feasting the Spirits" states:
"Prepare the great border,
bestow fortune upon the August Earth Spirit.
All the gods are moved,
the host of spirits are in array.
Bestow fortune upon Jìn,
and upon all the common people.
Fill the nine regions,
reach the Celestial Court.
Preserve myriad years of life,
extend a hundred million years."
It also states:
"Form the square mound,
revere the nation's treasure.
The wine vessels are already offered,
the meat stands are already enjoyed.
Gather and inspect the jades,
prepare and anoint with gold.
Flourish with a hundred blessings,
established since antiquity.
Grant myriad years of life,
lasting until now."
Later Hàn Dèng Dān's "Rhapsody on the Suburban Sacrifice"
Consulting on changing the era name and the first month,
spreading the new regulations.
Abundant grace overflowing,
containing Táng, pregnant with Yīn.
Upholding the royal standard,
examining the celestial patterns.
Unfurl leisurely ease,
display vast benevolence.
Radiate bright light,
pardon the guilty.
All the dukes, ministers, and administrators,
marquises, earls, and military officers.
The literary forest and splendid ministries,
present their precious tributes.
Barbarian chieftains from Lú and Bā,
come to offer tribute, come as guests.
The jade discs and bi are already presented,
for these ten thousand years.
Solemn, solemn August King,
able to illuminate his virtue.
Responding to portents, treading on fortune,
displaying and spreading his blessings.
Clearly communicating with the illustrious ancestors,
with filial piety, with benevolence.
From Heaven descends peace,
securely stabilizing our people.
Jìn Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the Southern Suburban Sacrifice"
The season is Qīngyáng,
the sun is at the rising quarter.
Our ruler is about to receive the mandate at the spiritual altar,
and changes his steps with jade pendants tinkling.
Ascends the golden carriage,
touches the heavenly grooms.
Raises the six bridle bells,
aligns the eight piebald steeds.
Arrays the five banners under the One Origin,
and shades the sun and moon with the yellow canopy.
Swiftly sends out scout birds for reconnaissance, arranges the leopard tails behind,
martial riders stand alert to clear the way.
Silk-clad guards shine like rippling torches.
Then they proceed to the vast square.
Reach the altar courtyard,
hundreds of officials stand like mountains,
ten thousand chariots gather like clouds.
Summon the invocators and scribes,
present the jade-like sacrificial animals.
Ascend the round mound,
salute the Great Purity.
Honor all the distant peaks,
announce to the August Spirits.
Heaven clarifies its breath,
the sun brightens its essence.
Zhùróng stands solemnly in respectful attendance,
Yánghóu calms and halts in the center.
Then the officers point and warn of the beacon fires,
the flames blaze fiercely, all ablaze.
Honor the imperial ancestors and offer matching sacrifices,
increase the eternal longing of filial thought.
Within the suburban precincts,
outside the bounded regions,
tattooed faces and plant-fiber garments,
loose hair and left-fastened robes.
Swiftly running to the altar,
gathering without prior arrangement.
The feast startles the ghostly regions,
the sound shakes the hills and mounds.
Gazing at the wind from the inverted reflection,
Lónghàn people stand on tiptoe.
Brilliant like stars encircling the celestial bodies,
all like clouds soaring and seas surging.
This is because harmonious ethers connect all around,
the dark net secretly gathers.
The response of spontaneity,
stirred and thus set in motion.
Liang Dynasty, Fù Zhāo, "Poem on Reverent Duty at the Northern Suburbs"
The imperial plan belongs to the vast heavens,
The utmost virtue surpasses the deep abyss.
The reverent gaze follows the rites performed,
All ranks rely on transformation's proclamation.
With proper duty, respectfully bury the sacrifice,
Adorn oneself to serve the solemn purification.
Auspicious airs match the first festival,
Bright winds arrive at the new year.
Zhōu Dynasty, Wáng Bāo, "Poem on Following the Imperial Carriage to the Northern Suburbs"
The emperor reverently performs the bright sacrifice,
Gazing and bowing, he departs east of the river.
The earth's spirit opens the double path,
The camp star emerges from the Purple Palace.
The main street echoes with clear imperial halts,
At the appointed hour, the wind vane rises.
Dense and somber are the Yǔlín cavalry,
Solemn and dignified are the Hǔbēn archers.
Suí Dynasty, Lú Sīdào, "Poem on the Imperial Carriage Departing for the Circular Mound"
At the year's start, selecting the timely day,
The first Xīn day is called heaven's auspiciousness.
At dawn, the palace gates open,
Faintly, the imperial carriage departs.
The imperial carriage leaves the ninefold gates,
Golden-rooted, it drives six dragons.
Banners shift, a thousand chariots move,
Streamers raised, a hundred spirits follow.
Yellow command flags lead with vermilion batons,
Divine drums respond to ornate bells.
Divine songs already continue,
Divine light again shines upon.
In the wind, purple smoke flutters,
Upon the altar, dark jade is buried.
Sòng Dynasty, Yán Yánzhī, "Song Lyrics for the Evening Sacrificial Animal at the Heaven and Earth Suburban Sacrifice"
Reverently awed by the precious mandate,
Solemnly respectful in the imperial sacrifice.
Suddenly receiving widespread bestowal,
Dwelling centrally, expanding the realm.
Fitting the earth, he is called emperor,
Feasting heaven, he acts as sovereign.
The moon's depths come as guests,
The sun's borders offer soil.
Opening the origin, first rectifying,
Rites intersect, music is raised.
The six statutes unite in affairs,
The nine palaces array in order.
There is sacrificial meat in the preparation,
There is purity on the altar stand.
Thus offering the lord's sincerity,
To answer the spirits' blessing.
Suí Dynasty, Yǔ Xìn, "Song Lyrics for the Descent of Spirits at the Square Marsh"
Repaying merit in the yin marsh,
Displaying rites in the dark suburbs.
Flat jades stabilize auspices,
Square tripods ascend to the kitchen.
Tunes from the lone bamboo,
Filtered wine with river grass.
Sound resounds with bells and drums,
Vessels are of pottery and gourds.
Arrayed brilliance, elegant splendor,
Condensed fragrance, lush lichee.
Rivers and marshes flourish with blessings,
Hills and mounds ripple gracefully.
Clouds adorn mountain wine vessels,
Orchids float, sediment settles.
The ritual of the solstice day,
Spirits enjoy this great sacrifice.
Suí Dynasty, Niú Hóng, "Song Lyrics for Suburban Sacrifice to Heaven, the August God"
Initiating the solemn sacrifice,
Thus serving the revered spirits.
From the heights, utmost reverence,
Sweeping the ground, sincere devotion.
The six honored ones follow the light,
The five planets accompany the camp.
Metal and stone harmonize,
Silk and bamboo, clear and mournful.
Our grain offerings are ready,
Our libations are bright.
The primal spirit observes,
A hundred blessings come to fruition.
Liáng Dynasty, Jiǎnwén Emperor, "Ode to the Southern Suburbs"
Solemnly reverent to the bright spirits,
Listening distantly to former footsteps.
Matching heaven's way, honor is supreme,
Welcoming the sun, righteousness is weighty.
Dark wine, pottery and gourds,
Burning firewood, clouds rise high.
Surpassing Shùn, discussing Sháo music,
Encompassing Yáo, praising folded hands.
The suburban palace rests in stillness,
The purple altar newly tranquil.
Silent, the forbidden enclosure,
Shaded, the immortal chambers.
Six armies arrayed across the wilds,
Eight bells shining like the sun.
Hall frames arrayed like stars,
Layered palaces emerge from mist.
Splendid, the virtue's abundance,
Beautiful, the era's prosperity.
Three luminaries increase in radiance,
Seven regulators eternally exalted.
From five directions they gather,
Four brilliances here connect.
Suspended ropes cross bamboo bridges,
Riding deer, chasing the wind.
Having spread bountiful transformation,
Again witnessing auspicious growth.
Golden chariots emerge in the wilds,
Jade dew moistens the steps.
Purple-peeled divine writings,
Flourishing-peace auspicious fungi.
Long-lasting joy, vast and abundant,
Eternally firm, harmonious and bright.
Ancestral Temples, Fourth
The Book of Rites says:
"The Son of Heaven has seven temples:
three on the left (Zhāo) and three on the right (Mù),
together with the temple of the Great Ancestor, making seven.
The feudal lords have five temples:
two on the left (Zhāo) and two on the right (Mù),
together with the temple of the Great Ancestor, making five.
The high ministers have three temples:
one on the left (Zhāo) and one on the right (Mù),
together with the temple of the Great Ancestor, making three.
The shì have one temple.
The common people make offerings in their living quarters.
A temple far removed is called a tiāo.
Beyond the tiāo, an altar (tán) is made.
Beyond the altar, a leveled open space (shàn) is made.
Beyond the leveled open space, they become ghosts."
This all speaks of the gradations in sacrificing to distant ancestors.
From the tiāo and above,
they are all considered destroyed temples.
The Shìmíng says:
"Zōng means 'to honor.'
Miào means 'appearance.'
It is where the form and appearance of the ancestors reside."
The Hànshū Jiùshì says:
"A temple is where the spirit tablets are stored,
arranged according to Zhāo and Mù."
The Shuōwén says:
"The wooden spirit tablet of the ancestral temple is called shí."
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
"It is said that the spirits have nothing to rely on,
so the filial son uses the tablet to continue his heart's connection."
The Analects says:
"The people of Xià used pine,
the people of Yīn used cypress,
the people of Zhōu used chestnut."
Chestnut means 'reverence,'
causing people to be cautious and respectful.
The Wǔjīng Yàoyì says:
"The shape of the wooden spirit tablet is square,
with a hole through the center reaching to the four sides.
For the Son of Heaven, it is one foot two inches long;
for feudal lords, it is one foot long.
Both have the posthumous title inscribed on the back."
Also, Zhì Yú's Juéyí Yàozhù says:
"All spirit tablets of the temple
are stored beneath the western window outside the door.
There is a stone case,
hence the name zōngshí."
The Zhōulǐ says:
"Every five years, there is a dì sacrifice;
every three years, there is a xiá sacrifice."
The Xù Hànshū says:
"Dì means 'to examine carefully.'
It arranges the Zhāo and Mù order,
carefully distinguishing father and son.
Xiá means 'to combine.'
The spirit tablets of the destroyed temples
are combined for a feast at the Great Ancestor's temple."
Dì means 'to scrutinize.'
Dì is held in the fourth month,
xiá in the tenth month.
In the fourth month, the yang energy is above,
the yīn energy is below,
rectifying the principle of noble and base.
In the tenth month, the five grains are ripe,
so flesh and bone gather together to drink wine.
The Juéyí Yàozhù says:
"Dì is held in early summer,
xiá in early autumn.
The two explanations differ."
Therefore, the Hàn Jiùyí says:
"The son is Zhāo,
the grandson is Mù.
Zhāo faces west,
Mù faces east.
Every three years, there is a great xiá sacrifice.
The various emperors, according to Zhāo and Mù, sit in the high temple,
and the spirit tablets of all the destroyed temples are combined for the feast."
The Book of Rites says:
"In all sacrifices at the ancestral temple, the ritual terms are:
For an ox: 'the great unitary warrior';
for a pig: 'the stiff-bristled';
for a suckling pig: 'the plump';
for a sheep: 'the soft-haired';
for a chicken: 'the loud-voiced';
for a dog: 'the soup-offering';
for a pheasant: 'the spread-toed';
for a rabbit: 'the clear-sighted';
for dried meat: 'the governor's offering';
for dried fish: 'the merchant's offering';
for fresh fish: 'the straight offering';
for water: 'the clear cleanser';
for wine: 'the clear libation';
for millet: 'the fragrant blend';
for fine millet: 'the fragrant stalks';
for grain: 'the bright offering';
for rice: 'the fine grains';
for leeks: 'the rich root';
for salt: 'the salty savor';
for jade: 'the fine jade';
for silk: 'the measured silk.'"
Seasonal categories, monthly sacrifices.
Zhāng Fāngxián's Lǔguó Xiānxián Zhuàn says:
"In ancient times, the former kings
had daily sacrifices and monthly offerings,
seasonal categories and yearly sacrifices.
Feudal lords omitted the daily,
high ministers and grandees omitted the monthly,
and common people omitted the seasonal."
The Guóyǔ says:
"Those in the Diàn service area perform sacrifices:
daily sacrifices and monthly offerings
are the instructions of the former kings."
Winter offerings, autumn tastings.
The Máo Shī says:
"'Qián' [means] in late winter offering fish,
in early spring presenting sturgeon.
Abundant are the Qī and Jǔ rivers,
where in the weirs are many fish,
used for offerings and sacrifices,
to bring about great blessings."
The Ěryǎ says:
"Spring sacrifice is called cí;
summer sacrifice is called yuè;
autumn sacrifice is called cháng;
winter sacrifice is called zhēng."
Fragrant blend, fine grains.
The Yílǐ says:
"The first Yú sacrifice uses a soft day.
It is said:
'The mourning son, so-and-so,
dares to use a pure victim, the stiff-bristled, the fragrant blend, and fine offerings.'" "Fine grains" has already appeared in the narrative section.
Jade cup, jade dòu vessel.
The Zhōulǐ says:
"For all guests, when presenting the jade cup, assistance is given."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"This refers to the king's clansmen and the descendants of the two previous dynasties who come for audience.
They act as guests for the king.
The ritual of libation is secondary to the king's, and the guests are treated with ritual.
'Presenting' refers to when the king hosts a feast and presents to the guests."
The Book of Rites says:
"In the sixth month of late summer,
the dì sacrifice is performed for Duke Zhōu in the great temple.
The fragrant wine vessel uses the yellow-eyed;
for libation, the great jade scepter and jade zàn are used;
for offerings, jade dòu vessels and carved guǐ vessels are used;
the cup used is the jade zhǎn."
Summer dì, winter zhēng.
The Book of Rites says:
"Spring sacrifice is called yuè;
summer sacrifice is called dì,
because it is the height of yang.
In ancient times, during the dì sacrifice, rank and robes were bestowed,
following the meaning of yang."
"Winter zhēng" is seen above.
Bì palace, clear temple.
The Máo Shī says:
"The bì palace has its moat."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Bì means 'divine.'
It is where Jiāngyuán, the divine, relied.
Ancient temples were called divine palaces."
It also says:
"'Qīngmiào' sacrifices to King Wén.
After Duke Zhōu completed Luòyì,
he received the feudal lords
and led them in sacrificing to King Wén."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"The clear temple is the palace for sacrificing to those who possess clear and bright virtue.
It refers to sacrificing to King Wén,
whose heavenly virtue was clear and bright.
King Wén embodied this,
so this poem is sung when sacrificing to him."
Spring cí, summer yuè.
The Zhōulǐ says:
"Use the guǐshí sacrifice to honor the former kings;
use the cí to honor the former kings in spring;
use the yuè to honor the former kings in summer;
use the cháng to honor the former kings in autumn;
use the zhēng to honor the former kings in winter."
Dǒng Zhòngshū's Chūnqiū Fánlù says:
"In ancient times, there were four yearly sacrifices,
based on what ripened in the four seasons, to sacrifice to ancestors and parents.
According to ritual,
the summer sacrifice is called yuè."
Zhòu Jīn and Guàn Yù
Wèi Hóng's "Hàn Jiù Yí" states:
"The emperor convened the feudal lords in the temple for the zhòu jīn ceremony,
following the shàngjì ritual, setting up nine attendants to accompany the positions."
The annotation in "Shǐ Jì" says:
"Wine is made on the first day of the first month,
and matures by the eighth month,
called zhòu.
Zhòu means pure.
During Emperor Wǔ's time, zhòu was tasted in the eighth month,
and the feudal lords gathered in the temple,
contributing gold to assist the sacrifices.
This is called assisting gold.
The Zhōu Lǐ states:
'For the ritual of pouring libations with jade,
arrange them to assist the pouring ceremony.'" Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
"Guàn yù refers to guī zàn and zhāng zàn."
Sacrificing to Wǔ and Announcing to Wén
"Máo Shī" says:
"Zhí Jìng,
sacrifices to King Wǔ.
The persevering King Wǔ,
unrivaled in his achievements.
Glorious were Chéng and Kāng,
revered by the Supreme God."
It also says:
"Wéi Tiān Zhī Mìng,
Tàipíng,
announces to King Wén.
The mandate of Heaven,
is solemn and unceasing."
Five Temples and Seven Chambers
"Lǐ Jì" says:
"When there are seven or five temples, none should lack a spirit tablet,
except during the xiá sacrifice to the ancestors,
when there is no tablet."
Fù Chàng's "Jìn Zhū Gōng Zàn" says:
"Wáng Jùn, styled Péngzǔ,
served as Governor of Yōu Province.
After Luòyáng was captured,
he established a temporary imperial court and, because the ancestral temples were burned down,
set up an altar to worship the seven chambers,
along with meritorious officials sharing the sacrifices."
Great Blessing and Pure Blessing
"Máo Shī" says:
"Prayers and sacrifices at the bēng,
the sacrificial affairs are very bright.
The ancestors are revered,
the spirits are enjoyed.
The filial grandson receives blessings,
granting great fortune,
boundless longevity."
It also says:
"Dance with yuè flutes, sheng and drums,
music harmoniously performed.
Offer to the meritorious ancestors,
to complete the hundred rituals.
When the hundred rituals are fulfilled,
there is grandeur and abundance.
Grant you pure blessings,
may your descendants be joyful."
Zhèng Xuán says:
"Chún,
means great.
Gǔ means the spirit representative bestows blessings upon the host."
Triennial Xiá and Quinquennial Dì
"Wǔ Jīng Yì Yì" says:
"Respectfully, according to Shūsūn Tōng, ancestral temples have daily sacrificial rituals,
indicating this was the ancient practice.
A triennial xiá sacrifice,
this is the Zhōu ritual;
a quinquennial dì sacrifice,
is suspected to be the ritual of the former kings."
"Lǐ Jī Mìng Qián" says:
"A triennial xiá,
a quinquennial dì,
visualizing their appearance through their garments.
Three days of purification,
contemplating the will of the relatives,
visualizing what they delighted in,
then entering the temple."
Examining Zhāo-Mù and Discerning Father-Son
Fù Xián's memorial states:
"Earlier scholars explained dì,
dì means to discern.
It is for examining the zhāo-mù order."
"Bái Hǔ Tōng" says:
"When the position is noble and virtue abundant,
its reach extends far,
why is it called dì xiá?
Dì means to discern.
To order the zhāo-mù,
discern father and son,
xiá means to combine."
Manifesting Filial Piety to Communicate with Spirits, Dew Moistens and Frost Descends
"Hàn Shū" says:
"Sacrifices,
are to manifest filial piety in serving ancestors and communicating with the divine."
"Lǐ Jì" says:
"The gentleman harmonizes with the way of Heaven,
spring dì and autumn cháng sacrifices,
when frost and dew have descended.
The gentleman treads upon it,
inevitably feels a sorrowful heart,
not because of the cold.
When spring rain and dew have moistened,
the gentleman treads upon it,
inevitably feels a cautious heart,
as if about to see them."
The Junction of High and Low, The Way of Communicating with Spirits
"Lǐ Jì" says:
"In sacrifices, there are those who distribute to the torch-bearers, cooks, feather-workers, and gatekeepers,
which is the way of benefiting the lowly.
These four types,
are the lowest officials,
while the spirit representative is the most honored.
That the most honored does not forget the lowest with the flavors of the sacrifice,
therefore, when an enlightened ruler is above,
there are none who suffer cold or hunger.
This is called the junction of high and low."
It also says:
"Spreading mats and setting the tǒng vessel,
all are for relying on the spirits.
After announcing prayers in the offering chamber and proceeding to the bēng,
this is the way of communicating with the spirits."
Sòng Dynasty Kǒng Xīn's "Poem on Sacrificing at the Grand Temple"
Girded to attend to royal affairs,
Tying the cap-strings to serve the pure sacrifice.
Solemn within the forbidden gates,
Secluded, cut off from worldly tracks.
Lofty in the high hall,
Layered structures rise like clouds.
At dawn, performing the offering sacrifice,
Reverent and restrained, without respite.
Bowing in the corridors between steps,
Sorrowful, never ceasing.
Liáng Dynasty Zhāng Shuài's "Poem on Fasting Night at the Grand Temple"
Purifying the fast, renouncing splendor,
Silent, the pure temple is still.
Solemnly viewing the sacrificial offerings,
Properly attired, attending the strict inspection.
Sòng Dynasty Yán Jùn's "Invocation for the Seven Temples"
Reverently honoring the bright sacrifice,
Filial piety moves and communicates.
Combined music maintains harmony,
Displaying ritual with grace.
Six dances arrayed solemnly,
Nine transformations reach completion.
The spirits come in thought,
Enjoy this pure devotion.
When the spirits depart,
They pacify our state and home.
Suí Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Grand Temple Morning Libation Song"
Eternal is the divine martial,
Hidden blessings, numinous longevity.
The dragon chart revolution,
The phoenix calendar returns to prosperity.
Merit shifted the former sorrow,
Virtue leapt in mid-sun.
Pure temple, solemn and still,
Fierce tiger stands majestic.
Curved terrace, great hall,
Harmonious sounds of flourishing Táng.
Sacrificial beasts cleansed,
Southernwood blends with fragrance.
Harmonious bells arrive,
Egrets come soaring.
Eternally spread to all states,
Setting an example for all quarters.
Chén Shūdá's "Grand Temple Libation Song"
Clear and bright, the libation poured,
Fragrant wine, only ritual.
Great indeed, filial thought,
Reverent to ancestors and progenitors.
Dragon robe for sacrifice,
Phoenix blade now opened.
Virtue expressed with vermilion strings,
Ascending song on crimson steps.
Mats offer grain sacrifices,
Hall pours sinking ale.
Descending blessings, abundant,
Coming demeanor, multitudinous.
Chǔ Liàng's "Song Lyrics of the Nine Virtues for the Ancestral Temple"
The imperial ancestor was born auspicious,
Shining brightly in the heavens.
Accumulating virtue extends far,
Lush lineage precedes all.
Succeeding heaven and responding to destiny,
Divine might is broadly proclaimed.
Traces began at the Guī River,
Success achieved at Bǎnquán.
The Way's light covers and upholds,
Its sound harmonious as the primal heaven.
Ritual vessels of sacrifice are fully prepared,
Pure animals are used for offerings.
The rites conclude with nine libations,
Music unfolds with four sets of chimes.
Divine blessings bring great fortune,
Far-reaching and everlasting years.
Wáng Càn of the Later Hàn's "Ode to the Grand Temple"
Thinking of the glorious meritorious ancestors,
Their virtue marches with the times.
They first opened the great source,
Bequeathing peace and our norms.
We rest in their achievements,
Following first their Way.
Greatly bright, greatly revered,
Truly timely, O ancestors.
Also
Oh, solemn and pure temple,
Awe-inspiring, bearing auspicious signs.
Multitudes of distinguished men,
Their virtue truly ascends.
Cherishing thoughts, assuming positions,
All hasten within the palace.
No thought is not in harmony,
Forever gazing upon their majesty.
Also
Pacifying the many states,
Harmonizing the four realms.
The nine achievements are complete,
The constant music is in order.
Erect the lofty tooth banners,
Set up the jade discs and feather screens.
Six types of instruments play,
Eight kinds of sounds are raised.
Manifesting great filial piety,
Glorifying the ancestral mothers and fathers.
Recalling martial accomplishments,
Gathering pure blessings.
Wáng Sù's "Ode to the Ancestral Temple"
Bright virtue alone is fragrant,
The August Heaven regards him as son.
Favoring and protecting our Wèi,
Prompting him to rise.
How did he rise?
The common people were then harmonious.
How is he regarded as son?
The mandate rests upon his person.
Oh, how splendid!
He communicates with the divine spirits.
Also
Abundant, abundant sweet dew,
Plentiful, plentiful sweet springs.
Some well up from the earth,
Some descend from the heavens.
Heaven and earth interact in harmony,
All creatures flourish abundantly.
Auspicious signs and fine responses,
Gather like rain.
Repeatedly obtaining bountiful years,
Nourishing our men and women.
The ancestors having been offered to,
Oh, joy and happiness abound.
Altars of Soil and Grain, Fifth
The "Xiàojīng Wěi" says:
"The Shè (Altar of Soil)
is the master of the land.
The land is vast and cannot be fully revered,
so a mound of earth is raised as the Shè,
to repay its merit.
The Jì (Altar of Grain)
is the chief of the five grains.
The grains are numerous and cannot all be sacrificed to,
so the Jì spirit is established for sacrifice."
The "Lǐjì" says:
"Zhù, son of the Lìshānshì,
and Zhōu Qì became the Jì."
When the Lìshānshì possessed the world,
his son was named Zhù,
who could cultivate the hundred grains.
When the Xià declined,
Zhōu Qì succeeded him,
so they were sacrificed to as the Jì spirit.
Lì may also be Liè.
Hòutǔ, son of the Gònggōngshì, became the Shè.
When the Gònggōngshì dominated the Nine Provinces,
his son was named Gōulóng,
who became Hòutǔ.
He could pacify the Nine Provinces,
so he was sacrificed to as the Shè.
The "Shàngshū" says:
"When Tāng had conquered Xià,
he wished to move their Shè,
but could not."
Tāng, succeeding after the abdications of Yáo and Shùn,
obeying heaven and responding to the people,
taking by force but guarding by compliance,
yet felt shame for his virtue.
Therefore, in revolutionizing the mandate and creating institutions,
changing the calendar and altering garments,
he sought to change and establish the Shè and Jì.
Because later generations had none equal to Gōulóng,
he could not do so and thus stopped.
The "Lǐjì" says:
"The king establishes a Shè for all surnames called the Grand Shè;
the king establishes a Shè for himself called the King's Shè;
the feudal lords establish a Shè for the common people called the State Shè;
the feudal lords establish a Shè for themselves called the Marquis's Shè;
for grand masters and below,
forming groups to establish a Shè is called the Established Shè."
The "Hàn Jiù Shì" says:
"The Son of Heaven's Grand Shè
uses a five-colored earth for the altar.
When enfeoffing feudal lords,
take the earth from their designated direction,
wrap it in white thatch and confer it upon them.
Each according to their directional color,
they establish a Shè in their state,
hence it is called conferring the thatched earth."
Showing the Root / Displaying Merit
The "Lǐjì" says:
"The Shè is the way to make the earth divine.
The earth receives from heaven,
therefore heaven is revered and earth is cherished.
Thus people are taught to make beautiful repayments;
families sacrifice to the central roof-god and the state presides over the Shè and Jì,
showing the root."
The "Báihǔ Tōng" says:
"Why does the king have the Shè and Jì?
To seek blessings from heaven and earth and repay their merit.
Why are there trees at the Shè and Jì?
To display merit."
Mounding and Planting / Apportioning Earth
The "Zhōulǐ" says:
"The Fēng official establishes the king's Shè enclosure as the border,
mounds it and plants trees."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Enclosure refers to the altar and its surrounding earthen banks."
The "Zhōushū" says:
"Feudal lords receive their mandate from Zhōu,
and establish a Grand Shè within their state.
Its enclosure: east uses blue earth, south uses red earth, west uses white earth, north uses black earth, the center uses yellow earth.
When establishing feudal lords clearly,
dig and take one side's earth from their direction,
wrap it in white thatch,
and enfeoff them with that earth.
Therefore it is called apportioning earth from the Zhōu house."
Southern Shè / Jì on the Right
The "Shàngshū · Wú Yì Piān" says:
"The Grand Shè uses pine,
the Eastern Shè uses cypress,
the Southern Shè uses catalpa,
the Western Shè uses chestnut,
the Northern Shè uses locust."
The "Zhōulǐ":
"In charge of establishing the spirit positions of the state,
the Shè and Jì are on the right,
the Ancestral Temple is on the left."
Probing for Gold and Obtaining a Sword
The *Soushen Ji* records:
"At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
there was a woman surnamed Yìng,
who gave birth to four sons.
One day, she saw divine light shining upon the village shrine.
She probed the spot
and found gold.
From then on, all her sons became officials and scholars, each gaining a reputation for talent."
The *Lùyì Zhuàn* records:
"Hè Yǔ from Kuàijī once fell ill,
lost consciousness,
and was dead for three days.
Upon reviving, he said that an official had taken him up to heaven to see the celestial court.
Someone led Hè Yǔ into a winding chamber,
where there was a tiered shelf.
On its upper level was a seal,
and within it was a sword.
He was told to take whatever he wished.
Hè Yǔ was too short to reach the upper level,
so he took the sword and left.
At the gate, someone asked what he had obtained.
He replied that he had obtained a sword.
The person said:
'This will only allow you to command the Shègōng (Earth God).'
After Hè Yǔ recovered from his illness,
a ghost indeed came, claiming to be the Shègōng."
Yǔ as Earth God and Abandoning Millet
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Yǔ toiled for the world,
and upon his death, he became the Earth God."
"Abandoning Millet" is discussed in the narrative section.
Yīn Cypress and Hàn Elm
The *Lúnyǔ* states:
"Duke Āi asked Zǎi Wǒ about the Earth God altar.
He replied:
'The Xiàhòu clan used pine,
the Yīn people used cypress,
and the Zhōu people used chestnut,
to make the people tremble with fear.'"
The *Hànshū* states:
"Emperor Gāozǔ issued an edict to establish the Fényú Shè in Fēng,
and in spring, sacrificed to it with sheep and pigs."
Spring Prayers and Autumn Offerings
The *Máo Shī* states:
"The 'Zài Shān'
is about the spring plowing ceremony and prayers to Shèjì (Gods of Earth and Grain)."
It also states:
"The 'Liáng Sì'
is about the autumn offerings to Shèjì.
'With sharp and excellent plows,
we begin work in the southern fields,
sowing all the various grains.'"
Mounding Earth and Planting Trees
The *Shàngshū* states:
"From the sea and Dài to the Huái River is Xúzhōu.
Its tribute is earth,
used for the five-colored soil of the Earth God altar."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"The king mounded five-colored earth to form the Earth God altar.
When establishing feudal lords,
he would cut a portion of the earth from their respective regions and give it to them,
so they could establish their own altars.
The top was covered with yellow earth,
and wrapped with white thatch."

The Zhōu Yì says:

reached the Southern Mountain,
and performed the same ceremonies as at Dài.
In the eighth month, he made a western tour of inspection,
reached the Western Mountain,
and performed the same as before.
In the eleventh month, at the new moon, he made a northern tour of inspection,
reached the Northern Mountain,

using a single bull."

Evaluate balances, align standards.
"Yuè Jué Shū" states:
"Yǔ toured and hunted in Dàyuè,
meeting elders,
collecting poetry and books,
evaluating balances,
and adjusting measures."
"Báihǔ Tōng" states:
"The reason for inspecting and hunting in all seasons,
was to rely on ancestral temples,
thus not exceeding them.
In the middle month of summer,
aligning standards,
finding the middle way."
Sacrifice to the Five Emperors, offer to the Six Lords.
Already seen in the preface.
To be seen in offering to the Three Days.
Prepare the celestial officials, operate the governmental carriage.
Bān Gù's "Hymn of the Eastern Inspection" states:
"Harnessing the Six Dragons,
comparing the Five Chariots.
Aligning the hundred officials,
rehearsing the qualities and simplicity.
Assigning the southern arbiter to manage the calendar,
the sixth day of the middle month.
Preparing the ranks of celestial officials,
with grand honors and attire to inspect the east."
Again, in the "Hymn of the Southern Inspection" states:
"Having sacrificed to ancestors at the western capital,
then attending to the southern court.
At this time, the sage sovereign operates the celestial carriage of officialdom,
erecting flags and banners of the sun and moon."
Cultivate the Five Rites, inquire of the Centuries.
"Shàngshū" states:
"In the second month of the year, inspect the east.
Arriving at Tàizōng,
offering sacrifices,
cultivating the Five Rites with five jades."
Kǒng Ānguó's note says:
"Jade tablets for the five ranks of feudal lords."
"Inquire of the Centuries" is seen in the preface.
Announce teachings, care for the common people.
Eastern Hàn Emperor Zhāng's "Inspection and Comfort Proclamation" states:
"The system of inspection and hunting,
is to announce teachings.
Examine and unify the far and near,
resolving resentment and knots."
Sòng Emperor Xiàowǔ's "Inspection and Relief Proclamation" states:
"Setting foot and seeing with eyes,
truly respects the mandate of Heaven.
Resentment grows deep,
the common people are not yet transformed by it.
From distant obscurity,
finding no place,
thus descending to observe customs,
personally caring for the common people."
Unify the far and near, observe customs.
"Unify the far and near" is seen in the aforementioned "Announce teachings" note.
Sòng Emperor Xiàowǔ's "Inspection and Observation Edict" states:
"I shall unite all colors,
encompass all under Heaven.
At the right time, inspect regions,
observing customs.
Externally consult and examine old practices,
to supplement the concerns of close advisors."
Táng Emperor Tàizōng's "Revisiting Wǔgōng Poem"
Nomadic horse tunes of the north,
startling birds in ancient groves.
How much more now receiving the virtue of spring,
recalling the past stirs deep emotions.
Accumulated goodness enjoys lasting prosperity,
rejoicing in the achievements of martial success.
Clothes hung loose, the world is governed,
with hands folded the lands and books are unified.
The white waters trace old paths,
at Dānlíng visiting the old palace.
Arranged feasts pleased the old elders,
grand banquets gathered at Xīnfēng.
Pausing to comfort the farmers,
turning to consult with the shepherd boy.
Auspicious air surrounds red gates,
propitious clouds scattered in the clear sky.
A solitary islet embraces frost and white,
distant mountains draped in red sunlight.
In this happiness a tune is struck,
briefly to chant the southern wind.
Sòng Fàn Yè's "Lè Yóu Responding to Edict Poem"
The imperial carriage not yet strict,
the literary garden descends in bright presence.
Floating clouds rise from moving canopies,
the morning breeze leads the jade chimes.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Attending the Tour of Fāng Mountain Responding to Edict Poem"
The clear Milky Way by night is bright,
the Fusang tree at dawn is radiant.
Songs arise beneath Cōngyáng,
inspecting feathers morning and evening at the pond.
Striking gold floats on water,
soaring sails over mountain spirits.
Once imbibed in nine heavens' dew,
the amarath knows itself at last.
Northern Qí Yuán Shì's "Accompanying the Imperial Tour to Immortals Poem"
Touring heaven's echoes the immortal call,
spring views stir divine emotions.
Mountain stream combines in its first flow,
mountain flowers bloom early in clusters.
The jade carriage shines in bright scenes,
pearl banners swirl in auspicious winds.
Plains with elevated roads,
fine airs spread far afar.
Zhōu Emperor Míng's "Returning to Old Palace Poem"
The celestial candles adjust autumn airs,
the golden chariot traverses the old palace.
Returning as if passing white waters,
more like entering Xīnfēng.
Autumn pools clear with late chrysanthemums,
cold wells shed sparse paulownia.
Raising cups to invite old elders,
now we hear the song of great winds.
Suí Emperor Yáng's "Return to Capital Poem"
In the Eastern Capital rites and justice arise,
Western Capital chariots and crowns return.
This month is the end of spring,
flowers and willows cling closely.
The cloud carriage clears the racing paths,
the elaborate chariot admires morning sunlight.
Clear percussion and brass play,
glorious banners wave.
The back ranks rise with culture,
the forward drives encourage martial might.
Suí Lǐ Délín's "Accompanying the Imperial Tour Poem"
Great Xià Yáo's remnants of customs,
Fen River traces Han leisurely travels.
Now we follow the dragon carriage,
returning as geese fly in autumn.
The celestial maneuvers clear the chariot paths,
the day's drive follows the magnificent carriage.
Mornings ride the carriage of six energies,
evenings stir the seven-star canopy.
Silent valleys, the birds ponder much,
high winds topple easy autumn pines.
Distant forests barely have color,
remote waters flow without streams.
Splendid capital, the place of beauty,
eyes reaching to the floating clouds.
Only beholding Lìngxiāo pavilion,
how can one see Wàngxiān tower?
Locked gates all sprout fine,
Mandarin duck pools learn sophistication completely.
Awaiting the lord to inscribe the sealing ceremony,
observing the ox-shot on East Mountain.
Again "Returning to Capital Poem"
Supreme benevolence extends literary teachings far,
only the sage declares martial success.
The grand preceptor observes the six principles,
feudal lords inquire of the centuries.
The profound insights seize the opportunity,
training the army across mountains and rivers.
City symbols store rested air,
honored arches drape with flying clouds.
Drums play resonating with thousands,
flags move joined with seven stars.
Steep ridges shields turn the sun,
high peaks horses warm the sky.
Gūshè's gods retire from amusement,
returning from Sāoguān hunt ride.
Awaiting again on East Mountain,
watch the Lord compose the inspection hymn.
Suí Dynasty Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem in Response to the Imperial Edict: Accompanying the Imperial Carriage to Tiānchí"
The supreme sage rules the universe,
His mighty strategy shakes the borderlands.
From the eight directions, he gazes far and wide,
For a thousand miles, banners and flags are drawn.
Driving the giant turtle, he approaches the azure sea,
Reining the divine steed, he treads upon the Jasper Pool.
Winding shores rise with mist and fog,
Deep waves startle whales and dragons.
Also, "Poem: Accompanying the Imperial Carriage to Jìnyáng"
Inspecting the provinces, following ancient records,
Traveling for leisure, aligning with former classics.
The Golden Guards announce the cleared path at dawn,
The Commandants patrol the camps at dusk.
Down steep ridges, swift cavalry descend,
Across remote shores, continuous banners cross.
Stream waters grow colder, murmuring more faintly,
Pine winds from afar blow even clearer.
Just as we behold the emperor's return,
With hairpins and brushes, we ascend Yúntíng.
Suí Dynasty Yú Mào's "Poem Composed in the Imperial Carriage in Response to the Edict: In Harmony with the Imperial Visit to Tàiyuán"
The Táng inspection glorifies imperial rule,
The Xià leisure trip harmonizes with royal demeanor.
Pearled banners display phoenixes with spread wings,
Jade beasts solemnly guard crimson dragons.
Flowing music blends with spring birds,
Intertwining play brushes against flowering branches.
Also, "Poem in Response to the Edict: In Harmony with the Imperial Visit to Jiāngdū"
The imperial tour glorifies the canonical rites,
The auspicious campaign aligns with heavenly will.
Over the watery realm, the imperial carriage soars,
Upon the river's palace, towering ships sail.
Seven elite troops wind through long marshes,
Three-winged fleets span the thoroughfare streams.
Rising early at the break of dawn,
Seeking robes while darkness still lingers.
Clear waves float with morning hues,
Distant woods roll up lingering night mist.
Morning clouds gradually hold the light,
The setting moon slowly wanes its crescent.
Winding ponds echo with songs and pipes,
Far shores gaze upon banners and flags.
As we accompany to behold the Eastern Sovereign,
Ascending to fēng and shàn sacrifices, solemn and reverent.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem in Response to the Command: Harmony on Reaching Shòuchūn"
Shaking mountains with abundant festive music,
The southern tour pursues leisurely travels.
How to conduct the inspection and pacification?
The people's sufferings are truly what is sought.
Patterned cranes adorn light canopies,
Azure dragons decorate cassia boats.
Floating foam encircles sandy islets,
Cold ice floes crowd the rushing currents.
The road points to the Eight Immortals Lodge,
The route passes the Hundred-foot Tower.
Recalling past travels with fondness,
Turning the carriage, we linger awhile.
Rear carriages resound with phoenix flutes,
Front banners reflect colorful tassels.
Dragon-steeds halt the six-horse team,
Flying pavilions ascend with triple rests.
Harmonious tunes of metal and stone play,
Joyful feasting with floating winged cups.
The celestial patterns one can only admire,
How can I mingle among jade and gems?
Shàngguān Yí's "Poem in Response to the Edict: Harmony on Passing the Old Residence"
Stone gates clear in late summer's eve,
Jade carriage rides in early autumn.
Divine banners stir pearl-like rain,
Immortal pipes echo flying streams.
Pèi River's auspicious clouds drift,
Wān suburbs' propitious air floats.
Great winds solidify the Hàn dynasty's foundations,
Gathered mists enter Shùn's jade sphere.
Green parasol trees grace the phoenix estate,
Nurtured orchids adorn the crane boat.
Ceasing warfare, singing of mysterious transformation,
Escorting the imperial carriage, praising the royal journey.
A lost hairpin mistakenly receives bright reward,
Holding the brush, I bear gracious favor.
Eastern Hàn Dynasty Bān Gù's "Eulogy for the Eastern Tour"
Humbly observing the imperial inspection of Mount Dàizōng,
Offering burnt sacrifice to the mountain spirits, gazing upon the mountain officials,
Honoring ancestors in the Bright Hall.
Above, examining Emperor Yáo,
In between, recounting Emperor Shìzōng.
Following and revering Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Rituals and ceremonies fully prepared.
Thus, bright spirits repeatedly respond,
Auspicious signs then descend.
Also, "Eulogy for the Southern Tour"
As the Hàn dynasty receives the mandate anew,
Its lineage leaves eleven generations.
Harmonizing with enduring peace,
Modeling on heavenly principles,
Sacrificing to the High Ancestor,
Illuminating the six hidden realms,
Communicating with spirits and gods.
Having performed the dì sacrifice to ancestors in the Western Capital,
Will again conduct the xiá sacrifice in the Southern Court.
At this time, the Sagely Emperor employs the celestial officials' law-carriage,
Erects banners of the sun and moon.
Eastern Hàn Dynasty Cuī Yīn's "Eulogy for the Eastern Tour"
Behold, the Hàn restoration's third generation,
Oh, how majestic the achievements,
Truly walking that virtuous path.
Continuing the royal mandate,
Inheriting Hàn's meritorious deeds.
Using the earth's measure to model things,
Following heaven's rule to mold and shape.
Thus, examining the Supreme God to seek centrality,
Gathering all stars around the North Star.
Opening the Tàiwēi constellation in the forbidden court,
Summoning Confucian talents for consultation.
At that time, bearing blossoms and fruits,
Summoning you to declare:
'How grand is the Great Hàn,
Already doubly harmonious and brilliantly successive,
Each generation increasing its virtue,
Only this mountain's rites
Long left unperformed,
Are what spirits and men rejoice over,
What all within the seas long for.
Eulogies speak of the Qiáoshān expedition,
Canons record the march to the mountain.
The time to stride through this state,
Is what the people diligently await,
Is it not fitting?'
Then he commands the Grand Coachman,
To tame the six piebalds,
Prepare the road horses,
Admonish the troops.
Thereupon, the imperial carriage mounts the awe-inspiring chariot of celestial spirits,
Drives the symbolic carriage of the Great Unity.
Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices, Part Eight
The Book of Rites states:
"In ancient times, the former kings served Heaven according to its nature,
served Earth according to its nature,
and ascended Mount Tài to report their achievements to Heaven."
Zhōng means accomplishment,
sacrificing to Heaven to report on successful achievements.
The Hétú Zhēn Jì states:
"When a king fēngs Mount Tài,
and shàns at Liángfǔ,
he changes the surname and upholds the standards,
continuing the flourishing and honoring the origins."
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Duke Huán of Qí wished to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
'In ancient times, those who fēnged Mount Tài
and shàned at Liángfǔ
numbered seventy-two families.
Of those I, Yíwú, have recorded,
there are twelve.

Wúhuáishì fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Fúxīshì fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Shénnóngshì fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Yándì fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Huángdì fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Zhuānxū fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Dìkù fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún, Yáo fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún,
Yǔ fēnged Mount Tài,
and shàned at Kuàijī; Tāng fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Yúnyún.
King Chéng of Zhōu fēnged Mount Tài and shàned at Chūshǒu.
All received the Mandate before they could perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
For the ancient fēng and shàn sacrifices,
the millet from Hàoshàng,
and the grain from Běilǐ
were used for the offerings.
From between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
a kind of grass with three ridges
was used for the matting.
From the Eastern Sea came the flatfish,
from the Western Sea came the birds that share wings.
Then there were those that arrived of their own accord without being summoned,
fifteen in number.'" It also states:
"After Qín Shǐhuáng had unified the world
and assumed the imperial throne,
he summoned seventy Confucian scholars and erudites from Qí and Lǔ to the foot of Mount Tài.
They deliberated, saying:
'In ancient times, for the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
they used chariots with rattan wheels,
to avoid damaging the mountain's soil, stones, plants, and trees.'
The First Emperor ascended Mount Tài,
erected a stone to extol his virtue,
making clear his entitlement to the fēng sacrifice.
The fēnged objects were all kept secret,
so later generations could not record them.'
The First Emperor ascended Mount Tài,
encountered wind and rain on the middle slope,
rested under a tree,
and consequently enfeoffed that tree as 'Fifth Rank Grandee.'"
It was a pine tree. It also states:
"Performing the fēng and shàn sacrifices leads to immortality;
Huángdì is an example.
The Confucians wore leather caps,
officials with sashes shot the ox,
and the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài followed the ritual for sacrificing to Tàiyī in the suburbs."
Receiving Heaven Repaying Earth
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continued Book of Hàn states:
"The emperor considered using stone labor difficult,
and also wished to perform the fēng sacrifice by the second month,
so he issued an edict to Liáng Sōng.
He wanted to use the old fēnged stone and empty container,
and merely add another fēnging.
Sōng argued in a memorial,
believing that to receive Heaven's reverence,
it was especially appropriate to make it clear and manifest;
to present the auspicious signs from charts and texts,
it was especially appropriate to make them clearly evident.
Now, using the old fēnging,
and secretly placing the jade tablet under the old stone,
he feared this was not in accordance with the principle of solemnly receiving the Mandate."
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"Heaven holds height as its honor,
Earth holds thickness as its virtue.
Therefore, they increase Mount Tài's height to repay Heaven,
and add to Liángfǔ's thickness to repay Earth."
Descending for Shàn Ascending for Fēng
Xiè Língyùn's "Song of Mount Tài" states:
"Mount Dàizōng, the splendid sacred peak,
towering steeply pierces the cloudy sky.
Ascending for fēng, burying in the lofty altar;
descending for shàn, concealing in Sùrán."
Also, the Báihǔ Tōng states:
"When a king receives the Mandate and rises,
he must ascend to perform the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
to report and repay."
Establishing a Title Recording in Annals
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Fēngshàn Memorial" states:
"His achievements flourished while still in swaddling clothes,
and his honor surpassed that of the two former rulers.
Considering his origins,
he ultimately reached the end.
There have been none with extraordinary merits and unparalleled deeds
that could be preserved until today.
Yet he still trod upon Liángfǔ,
ascended Mount Tài,
established a illustrious title,
and bestowed a revered name."
Yìng Shào's annotation states:
"'Swaddling clothes' refers to King Chéng.
'The two former rulers'
refers to King Wén and King Wǔ."
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continued Book of Hàn states:
"The Hétú Huì Chāng Fú states:
'The great flourishing way of Hàn,
the king of the ninth generation,
shall fēng Mount Tài.
Engrave stone and record in annals,
shàn at Liángfǔ,
then retreat to examine and assess achievements.'"
Increasing Thickness Increasing Height
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"Increase Mount Tài's height to repay Heaven,
add to Liángfǔ's thickness to repay Earth.
To make clear that what is mandated by Heaven,
when achievements are completed and tasks accomplished,
benefits Heaven and Earth.
As if making the high higher,
and the thick thicker,
Heaven shows it is increased in height.
Therefore, Fènggāo County
was established to serve the Eastern Peak,
the place where emperors perform the shàn sacrifice upon dynastic change.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn erected a great altar on the eastern mountain."
Sealing with Gold Engraving Stone
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"Some say the fēng and shàn sacrifices use gold mud and silver cords,
sealed with a gold seal,
meaning that upon achieving success, they perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices to report peace."
The Xiàojīng Gōu Mìng Jué states:
"Fēng at Mount Tài,
examining achievements and offering burnt sacrifices.
Shàn at Liángfǔ,
engraving stone to record the title."
Golden Tablets Stone Container
The Book of Hàn states:
