"In the first year, fourth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
the emperor returned,
ascended and fēnged Mount Tài."
Yìng Shào's annotation states:
"When a king's achievements are complete and order is established,
he reports his success to Heaven.
Engraves stone to record the title,
and there is the sealing with golden tablets, stone boxes, gold mud, and jade containers."
Yìng Shào's Hàn Official Ceremonial states:
"When fēnging and shàning at Mount Tài,
they piled stones at the place where Emperor Wǔ had fēnged,
and raised an altar.
They placed the jade tablet with the written fēng inside this stone,
and then sealed the stone container."
Gold Seal Jade Seal
"Gold seal" see above.
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continued Book of Hàn states:
"In the thirty-second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the emperor approved the memorial of Liáng Sōng and others,
and then sought the precedents from the Yuánfēng era,
to discuss what should be used for the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
The officials memorialized,
that they should engrave one jade tablet one cun two fen square,
and one five cun square."
Three Ridges Six Spikes
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The Son of Heaven alone, with the Palace Attendant and the Chariot Attendant Zǐhóu, ascended Mount Tài.
There was also a fēng sacrifice,
but all matters concerning it were kept secret.
The next day, they descended by the northern path.
On the day Bǐngchén, they performed the shàn sacrifice at the foot of Mount Tài, northeast at Mount Sùrán,
following the ritual for sacrificing to Hòutǔ.
The Son of Heaven personally performed all the obeisances,
wearing yellow robes above and using music throughout.
The grass with three ridges from between the Jiāng and Huái rivers was used as the sacred matting."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Fēngshàn Memorial" states:
"Selecting a single stalk with six spikes for the kitchen.
The annotation states:
'Dǎo means to select.
A single stalk with six spikes
means selecting the fine grain rice in the kitchen,
to supply the sacrifices.'"
Western Jiān and Eastern Dié
In Xiè Zhuāng's "Memorial of the Eight Ministers and Grand Steward, Prince of Jiāngxià, Requesting the Performance of the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices," it says:
"Envoys from the Jiāng and Huái rivers and the Hào region
have their carriages lined up at the Bì Gate;
interpreters for the western Jiān and northern Cǎi tribes
are seen one after another on the roads."
Also, the Shàngshū Zhōnghòu says:
"In ancient times, when the sage kings achieved merit and perfected the Way, auspicious signs appeared;
then they performed the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài.
Now, the flatfish do not come,
the phoenix does not arrive,
the qílín hides away—
it is not yet time to perform the Fēng sacrifice."
Zhèng Xuán says:
"The flatfish
is born from the unusual qi of the east;
its name is dié."
Inspecting the Jade and Sealing with Gold
Sūn Yán's Sòng Shū says:
"Yuán Shū served as a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Tàizǔ, a great northern campaign was launched.
Shū attended the emperor's seat
and calmly said:
'The grand ceremonies of the flourishing kings
have long been abandoned and ruined.
Now is the time to sound the bells at Mount Zhōngyuè,
sweep through Zhào and Wèi,
and inspect the jade at Dàizōng.
The moment has arrived.
I have encountered this once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity
and wish to present a memorial on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
so that our fame may equal that of high antiquity.'
The emperor said:
'Such deeds of great virtue—
how could I be worthy of them?'"
The annotation to the Fēngshàn Yí states:
"Thirty attendants ascend,
and lift the stone cover on the altar.
The Imperial Secretary faces north and kneels;
after the jade tablet is stored,
the attendants cover it again with the stone slab.
The Imperial Secretary seals it with ten stone covers,
also bound with golden cords
and sealed with golden mud,
each side according to its respective color."
Drawing the Divination Slips and Sealing the Covers
Yìng Shào's Fēngsú Tōng says:
"When performing the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
and the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfǔ,
it is said that on Dàizōng there is a golden casket containing jade slips
that reveal the length of a person's lifespan.
Emperor Wǔ drew one that read 'eighteen,'
but he reversed it to read 'eighty.'
Later, his lifespan indeed matched the slip's prediction of longevity."
The Hàn Shū says:
"In the fourth month, on the guǐmǎo day, of the first year of the Yuánfēng era,
the emperor returned and ascended to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài."
Yìng Shào's annotation states:
"When a king achieves merit and brings order to the realm,
he reports his success to Heaven.
Performing the Fēng sacrifice on Dàizōng
assists Heaven in its loftiness.
He engraves stone to record his title,
and there is the sealing of the golden slips, stone casket, golden mud, and jade covers."
Stone Chamber and Heavenly Pass
The Wú Zhì says:
"In the first year of the Tiānxǐ era of Sūn Hào,
there was an empty chamber on the Yángxiàn Mountain in Wúxīng,
and the matters of the Shàn sacrifice were considered a great auspicious sign.
He then sent the concurrent Minister of Works Dǒng Cháo, Zhōu Chǔ, and others to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices for the state,
promulgated an edict to change the era name the following year and grant a general amnesty,
to accord with the stone inscription."
Yìng Shào's Hàn Guān Yí says:
"During the Yuánfēng Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
there was white qi during the day,
and at night, light appeared at the Heavenly Pass.
When the stone gate was opened below,
it was rugged and awe-inspiring."
Sunrise Terrace and Cloudy Palace Towers
Yìng Shào's Hàn Guān Yí says:
"On the southeastern side of Mount Tài,
there is a place called the Sunrise Terrace.
To the north is a stone chamber,
and south of the altar is a basin
containing a jade turtle."
It also says:
"In the thirty-second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the imperial carriage journeyed east on an inspection tour.
On the ninth day of the second month, they arrived at Jìn;
on the nineteenth day, the state rested at a pavilion.
All officials were arrayed in formation,
and on that day, clouds on the mountain formed into palace towers,
which all the common people saw."
Matching Tallies and Displaying Splendor
The Hàn Shū says:
"Gōngsūn Hóng said:
'The Yellow Emperor performed the Fēng sacrifice on the eastern peak, Mount Tài,
and the Shàn sacrifice on the Jiǔ Mountains, matching tallies,
after which he attained immortality.'"
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's Fēngshàn Shū says:
"Thus, drawing upon the strategies of the gentry and scholars,
and capturing the last rays and ultimate brilliance of the sun and moon,
to display splendor and arrange affairs.
Moreover, to properly set forth their meaning
and embellish their writings."
Honored Name and Grand Ceremony
The Fēngshàn Shū says:
"Treading on Liángfǔ,
ascending Mount Tài,
establishing a glorious title,
and bestowing an honored name."
The Hàn Shū, Ní Kuān's Response to Imperial Questions, says:
"Performing the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
and the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfǔ,
revealing the surname and examining auspicious signs—
this is the grand ceremony of emperors and kings."
Qín Rain and Hàn Clouds
The Shǐ Jì says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng erected a stone to extol his merits and virtues,
descended via the northern slope to perform the Shàn sacrifice at Liángfǔ.
While ascending Mount Tài,
he encountered sudden wind and rain on the mountainside
and rested under a tree."
It also says:
"Lǐ Shàojūn said:
'From distant lands, strange beasts, flying birds, and white pheasants were added to the sacrifices,
all arriving at Mount Tài.
At night, there seemed to be light,
and during the day, white clouds rose from the sealed area.'"
Stone Cover and Golden Cords
The annotation to the Fēngshàn Yí states:
"On the altar, a stone slab is placed,
stacked twice,
with steps five feet square
and one foot thick, set in the middle of the altar.
The slab is engraved,
and ten stone covers are placed on it:
two each on the east and west sides,
and two each on the south and north sides.
Above is a stone cover,
like today's lóngzi or yèzi."
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
"Some say the sealing uses golden mud and silver cords;
others say stone mud and golden cords."
Immortal Lǘ and Heavenly Gate
The Hàn Shū says:
"The emperor performed the five-year ceremony and added the Shàn sacrifice at the Stone Lǘ,
located at the southern base of Mount Tài.
Fangshi said it was the Immortal Lǘ."
The Hàn Guān Yí says:
"From the base of Mount Tài, going straight up for seventy lǐ,
one reaches the Heavenly Gate.
It is like peering at a skylight from within a cave."
Engraving Stone and Burying Jade
Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn says:
"It is said that on Mount Tài,
there are over 1,800 inscribed stones,
but only seventy-two can be identified."
Shěn Yuē's Sòng Shū says:
"In the Memorial of Prince Yìgōng of Jiāngxià, it says:
'Carved qi descends upon the palace trees,
and precious dew reveals its flavor in the forbidden forest.
It is fitting to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
and bury jade at Dàizōng.'"
Shooting the Ox and Releasing the Pheasant
The Shǐ Jì says:
"The emperor considered the fangshi's words about the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
but each person's account differed,
and they were not canonical,
making them difficult to implement.
The Son of Heaven descended to Liángfǔ
to perform rituals and sacrifices to the Earth Lord.
On the jǐmǎo day,
he ordered the court scholars to wear leather caps
and, with their sashes fastened, shoot an ox for the ceremony.
He performed the Fēng sacrifice east of Mount Tài,
following the rituals for the Supreme Unity in the suburban sacrifices."
"Releasing the pheasant" has already been mentioned in the annotation for "Hàn clouds."
Square Peaks and Round Altars
Wéi Yào's "Questions and Answers on the Máo Shī" states:
"The poem 'Shí Mài'
is about the inspection tours and sacrifices involving the burning of offerings and gazing at the mountains."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"When the Son of Heaven tours the feudal states,
he performs the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices at the foot of the square peaks."
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Continued Hàn Shū" states:
"In the second month of the thirtieth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the ministers proposed:
'Having been on the throne for thirty years,
it is fitting to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Mount Tài also has its base,
with stones piled in double layers.
Each stone is ten feet long,
one foot thick,
and two feet wide,
all placed on the round altar.'"
Jade Plates, Stone Boxes, Jade Seals, and Stone Clay
All have been mentioned above.
Receiving the Tally and Presenting the Tablet
"The Chūnqiū Hánhánzī" states:
"The means by which the Son of Heaven illuminates and observes,
following the Dipper's pivot,
issuing prohibitions to the world,
upholding the classics and preserving the texts.
Deep contemplation to unite with the spirits,
ensuring long-lasting peace.
The Son of Heaven receives the tally,
and establishes his reign title on a xīn day."
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Continued Hàn Shū" states:
"The imperial carriage ascends the mountain,
arriving at the summit after noon,
and takes position south of the altar.
Facing north,
the Emperor ascends,
the Shàngshū Lìng presents the jade tablet and seal,
and the Emperor personally seals it with a 1.2-inch imperial seal."
Proclaiming Virtuous Edicts and Spreading Glorious Reputations
Zhāng Huá's "Fēng and Shàn Rituals" states:
"The hearts of all within the seas turn to him,
and auspicious signs respond.
The abundance of prepared offerings,
has never been as rich as it is today.
Your Majesty should perform rites at the Central Peak,
conduct the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
and the Shàn sacrifice at Liángfù.
Proclaim virtuous edicts,
clarify your supreme authority.
Enrich blessings and celebrations,
and strengthen the common people."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Fēng and Shàn Memorial" states:
"To expand the ancient six to seven,
spreading it endlessly.
The steles emerge to stir the clear streams,
raising gentle waves.
Spreading glorious reputations,
and elevating abundant achievements."
Spreading Benevolent Influence and Elevating Abundant Achievements
Zhāng Huá's "Fēng and Shàn Rituals" states:
"Since the beginning of humanity,
there have been sovereigns.
The numbers of those who carried out transformation,
cannot be recorded.
Great virtue aligns with the age,
spreading benevolent influence."
"Abundant achievements" are mentioned above.
Lǐ Yìfǔ's "Poem on Envying the Accompaniment to the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
Mount Tiānqí marks a great stronghold,
Rìguān opens a lofty era.
Towering over the Bóxiè Sea,
commanding the Hé and Yí rivers from lofty heights.
Gazing afar, distinguishing the Wú chariots,
ascending high to the Hàn temples.
Establishing the peaks truly makes one great,
the merit of ascent lies here.
The Emperor's plans align with vast destiny,
profound models inspire literary thought.
Reputations spread across the earth's veins,
transformation soars, caressing the celestial axis.
Auspicious registers unveil the precious phoenix,
prophetic charts present the treasure turtle.
Creating the Fēng surpasses ancient Xià,
cultivating the Shàn outshines former Jī.
The eastern queen will soon have an audience,
the western capital leads the six armies.
Stone gates encircle patterned guards,
golden altars reflect embroidered canopies.
Immortal steps overflow with millet and grain,
divine seals shine with auspicious fungi.
Music resounds with Sháo and Huò melodies,
observing rites, embracing both Huá and Yí.
Auspicious air floats over crimson valleys,
glorious light ripples on green banks.
Three beginnings reveal distant blessings,
ten thousand years receive double fortune.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Memorial Urging the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
Great rites share the same rhythm as heaven and earth,
great music shares the same harmony as heaven and earth.
The Six Zōng and Five Emperors,
their sacrificial rites are eternal,
famous mountains and great rivers,
their offerings never cease.
Yet announcing completion at the square peaks,
uniquely differs from ancient precedents,
from court to countryside,
hearts are stirred and thoughts agitated.
I humbly hope you will harness the distinctions of the six breaths,
follow the harmony of the four seasons,
ascend that Dàizōng peak,
and complete this grand ceremony.
Hear the distant echoes of ten thousand years,
continue the ancient traces of a thousand ages.
Zhū Zǐshē's "Memorial Requesting the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
Your servant hears that the great virtue of heaven and earth is called life,
and he who fulfills this life is the paramount ruler.
The great treasure of the sage is called position,
and he who secures this position is the supreme mystery.
How can one not face the altar grounds?
Reverently accord with the lofty heavens,
even though Shùn reached the ancestral temple.
Zhōu transformed the customs of Shāng,
embodying pure virtue through abdication and yielding.
Crossing the turbulent path with shield and spear,
the traces of their steps differ.
The merits of decrease and increase thus vary,
this is truly so!
As for halting at Liángfù,
performing music at the high mound,
increasing the sacrifices to the imperial ancestors,
and presiding over the ritual of shooting the ox.
Examining achievements through sacrificial burning,
continuing the traces of Sháo and Xià,
how could the Way differ?
Cén Wénběn's "Memorial Urging the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
I humbly hope you will comply with the joyful hearts of all states,
and accept the mandate of the three numinous powers.
Prepare the celestial officials for thorough protection,
and magnificent carriages and robes for the inspection tour.
Five carriages aligned in rows,
six dragons reined in pace.
Gaze toward the Tài suburbs and start the journey,
point to Yíng Village as a resting place.
Summon the ministers and scholars,
invite the ritual officials.
Set up the altar grounds,
display the jades and silks.
Sacrifice to the Six Zōng to report to the Supreme Deity,
distribute the five tokens to receive the feudal lords.
Complete the magnificent spectacle for all under heaven,
continue the grand ceremonies of emperors and kings.
So that the mountains acclaim ten thousand years,
and the altar shines with divine light.
Spread abundant blessings endlessly,
and proclaim great glory to future generations.
Gāo Ruòsī's "Memorial Urging the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
I humbly hope you will lift the beads and reflect,
harmonizing all requests with the Emperor's approval.
Open the silk and show compassion,
granting the humble pleas of the people's desires.
Soar with these seal edicts,
stirring those celestial waves.
Summon ten thousand jades to clear the path,
command the eight spirits to halt the carriage.
Lay out Jiāng máo and display Hào shǔ,
adorn with dark bi discs and offer yellow cóng scepters.
Gallop ten thousand years to spread your fame,
reach the nine layers to match the beauties.
Let strung pearls nurture blessings,
opening splendid colors on the golden clay;
touch stones to condense auspiciousness,
sweeping away empty splendor on the stone boxes.
Thus illuminate the prosperous reign,
eternally proclaim the great name.
All living beings,
deeply righteous, leap with joy.
Jítián, Part One
The Shuōwén states:
"The jítián (imperial field) is so called because
the Son of Heaven plows it personally,
as if borrowing the people's labor,
hence it is called 'jí' (register/borrow)."
The Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven plows personally in the southern suburbs,
the feudal lords plow in the eastern suburbs,
in order to provide the sacrificial grains."
The Yuèlìng states:
"The Son of Heaven pushes the plow three times,
the Three Dukes push five times,
the ministers and feudal lords push nine times,
and the commoners finish the entire field."
A note in the Liáng dynasty's "Wǔlǐ‧Jítián Yí" states:
"That field is eight lǐ east of the palace,
extending sixteen lǐ to form one thousand mǔ.
The Son of Heaven uses one set of lěisì (plow),
the Three Dukes use three sets,
the Nine Ministers use nine sets.
A square altar is erected to sacrifice to Xiānnóng (the First Farmer)."
Yìng Shào's Hàn Guān Yí states:
"The Son of Heaven ascends the altar,
after the dukes and ministers finish plowing,
the sèfū (field overseer) sows the seeds.
Generally, the jítián is referred to as the thousand mǔ,
also called the Imperial Field, also called Plowing the Field, also called Eastern Plowing, also called Personal Plowing, also called the Royal Field."
Dark Blue Shaft / Green Turban
Pān Yuè's "Jítián Fù" states:
"The pale green ox is yoked to the light blue crossbar,
the dark blue shaft is attached to the black plow."
Yìng Shào's Hàn Guān Yí states:
"On the day the Son of Heaven plows in the east,
he personally leads the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers,
riding in a green carriage,
driving dark blue horses.
For the dukes and ministers and those below,
their carriages follow the usual protocol."
Green Altar / Ornate Canopy
Pān Yuè's fù states:
"The green altar stands majestic like a mountain,
the emerald canopy spreads out like clouds."
Xú Yuán's fù states:
"Expanding the broad opening of the triple path,
gazing at the distant, long road.
Adding splendor to the canopy not yet startled,
vague, facing the same direction, it has already turned back."
Three Pushes / Thousand Mǔ
The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of spring,
the Son of Heaven personally carries the lěisì (plow),
and personally plows the jítián.
The Son of Heaven pushes three times,
the dukes push five times,
the ministers and feudal lords push nine times."
The Guóyǔ states:
"When King Xuān ascended the throne,
he did not plow the thousand mǔ field."
Guówéngōng admonished him, saying:
"The great affair of man lies in agriculture;
the sacrificial grains for the Supreme Deity
come forth from it;
the multitude of people
are born from it.
Therefore, when the earth's veins begin to stir,
nine days before the proper time."
The Grand Historian informed the Minister of Agriculture, saying:
"When the yang energy is fully steaming,
and the fertile soil begins to move,
then report it to the king.
The king then goes to the fasting palace,
and all officials attend to their duties.
The king plows one furrow,
the ranks follow with three times that,
and the commoners finish the thousand mǔ.
The king did not listen,
and the army was defeated by the Jiāngróng."
A Thousand Pairs / Ten Thousand Reins
Miào Xí's "Jítián Fù" states:
"Command Gōumáng to take charge of the calendar,
instruct Xīzhòng about the farming season.
Following the morning auspices, they set forth,
rejoicing with Tiánzǔ (the Field Ancestor) to the Bīn poems.
Praising the 'Zǎishān' with its thousand pairs,
admiring that from ancient times it has been like this."
Xú Yuán's fù states:
"A thousand carriages proceed hidden like the wind,
ten thousand reins fill the air, turning like mist.
The bright sun shines beautifully over the mulberry fields,
the imperial procession halts and visits the border ridges."
Serve Heaven / Pray to the Soil
The Lǐjì states:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand mǔ field for the jí,
wearing a ceremonial cap with red strings.
Personally holding the plow,
the feudal lords had a hundred mǔ field for the jí.
Wearing a ceremonial cap with blue strings,
personally holding the plow,
to serve Heaven, Earth, the mountains, rivers, soil and grain, and the ancient ancestors,
providing sweet wine, fermented beverages, and sacrificial grains.
From this they are taken,
the utmost in reverence."
The Máo Shī states:
"Zǎishān,
is for the spring jítián and praying to the soil and grain.
Clearing away weeds and trees,
the plowing goes on vigorously.
A thousand pairs weed,
going to the lowlands, going to the paths.
Here come the masters, here come the elders,
here come the younger men, here come the multitude,
here come the strong, here come the helpers."
Teach Provision / Express Reverence
The Lǐjì states:
"Plowing the jí field is how the feudal lords are taught to provide."
The Wǔjīng Yàoyì states:
"The Son of Heaven's jítián is a thousand mǔ,
to provide the sacrificial grains for the Supreme Deity.
When the first month of winter arrives and hibernating insects stir,
after the suburban sacrifice is completed,
he personally leads the dukes, ministers, and senior officials to plow it.
This is to precede the common people and express filial reverence."
Carry the Plow / Hold the Plow
The Lǐjì states:
"Then an auspicious day is chosen,
the Son of Heaven personally carries the lěisì (plow),
placing it on the right side of the carriage,
and the dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials personally plow the jítián.
A note states:
'Yuánchén,
refers to an auspicious day after the suburban sacrifice.
Lěisì,
are farming tools.'" It also says, "In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand mǔ field for the jí,
wearing a ceremonial cap with red strings;
the feudal lords had a hundred mǔ field for the jí,
wearing a ceremonial cap with blue strings.
Personally holding the plow,
to serve Heaven, Earth, the mountains, rivers, and the soil and grain."
Descend the Divine Altar / Cultivate the Imperial Field
Pān Yuè's fù states:
"Our emperor then descends the divine altar,
grasps the paired plow,
his steps marking the field, staining his shoes.
The great reins in hand,
he pushes three times and then stops.
The commoners finish the field,
noble and humble in their ranks,
some five, some nine."
Zhāng Héng's "Dōngjīng Fù" states:
"Riding in a luánlù carriage drawn by dark blue dragons,
with guards between, holding sharp plows.
Personally pushing three times in the Heavenly Field,
cultivating the thousand mǔ of the Imperial Field."
Supply the Ancestral Temple / Serve the Soil and Grain
The Hànshū states:
"Emperor Wén issued an edict saying:
'Agriculture
is the foundation of the empire.
For the jítián,
I personally lead the plowing to supply the sacrificial grains for the ancestral temple.'" The Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven has a thousand mǔ for the jí,
personally holding the plow to serve Heaven, Earth, the mountains, rivers, and the soil and grain."
Jìn Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Plowing"
In the fourth year of the Jìn dynasty,
on the dīngwèi day of the first month,
the emperor personally led the assembled lords
to plow the thousand-acre suburban fields—
a ritual observance.
Thereupon, the field overseer was ordered to clear the capital's outskirts,
the road wardens to sweep the paths,
the border officials to raise the altar's earthen walls,
and the lodging officers to set up the barrier posts.
The azure altar rose majestically like a mountain peak;
the emerald canopies spread like clouds, deep and dark.
The lofty foundation's divine base was firmly laid;
the broad stairways on all four sides were opened.
The fertile fields were rich and lush,
the high grounds level as a whetstone.
The clear Luò River and turbid canals
channeled water, stirring its flow.
Distant paths stretched straight as cords,
nearby lanes like arrows' flight.
Green oxen bore pale yokes,
dark blue shafts attached to black plows;
solemnly arrayed, the teams waited to the left of the hamlet,
awaiting the Son of Heaven's personal tread.
The hundred officials were stationed first,
their positions assigned by duty.
From high to low,
all were obedient servants.
Clad in spring robes of lush green,
they met the rumbling procession of touring carriages.
A gentle breeze arose from light carriage curtains,
fine dust stirred by vermilion wheels.
Standing in ranks, solemnly holding jade tablets,
they gazed upon the imperial carriage with awe and trembling.
Like dew evaporating in the morning sun,
like myriad stars encircling the North Star.
Then the vanguard advanced like fish scales,
the attendant carriages gathered like scales.
The palace gates swung open wide,
three roads abreast for teams of four.
The Chamberlain accompanied the imperial carriage,
the Grand Coachman held the reins.
The empress and consorts presented seeds of early and late crops,
the Minister of Agriculture prepared sowing and planting tools.
The Timekeeper regulated the rhythms of ascent and descent,
the Palace Warden set guards at gates and doors.
The Son of Heaven then mounted the jade carriage,
shaded by the ornate canopy.
Jade pendants chimed and clanged,
silken fabrics rustled softly.
With rumbling and rumbling,
dust swirled to the heavens.
Thus he proceeded to the plowing fields.
Cicada-wing caps gleamed and shimmered,
jade hues solemnly verdant.
Like night-bright jade cut from Jīng mountain's rough stone,
like lush pines clinging to mountain peaks.
Thereupon, our emperor descended the divine altar,
grasped the imperial plow.
Treading the field, staining his shoes,
the great reins in hand.
After three symbolic pushes, he ceased,
and the commoners finished the acre.
Noble and humble in order,
some five pushes, some nine.
I dare compose a eulogy, saying:
"Rejoice in the suburban fields,
gather their thatching grasses;
the great lord arrives,
to plow their soil.
The farmer's three pushes,
all lands revere.
Weed the public fields,
benefit also our private plots.
Our fǔ vessels are full,
our guǐ vessels brimming.
Our granaries rise like hills,
our storehouses like islets.
Remember this, dwell on this,
ever cherish filial thought.
Human effort widespread,
prayer officers correct their words.
Spirits and gods accept the offering,
ease and joy without end.
When one man has blessings,
millions rely on him."
Liáng Wǔdì's "Poem on Imperial Plowing"
At dawn, welcoming the first sunrise,
the pitch-pipes match the Star Bird's season.
A thousand acres of purple fertile soil,
ten thousand acres of pale pond hues.
The solemn carriage waits in rosy dawn,
dew-damp, lingering in gleaming light.
Setting forth while sky still dark,
beating drums, earth not yet quiet.
The azure dragon uncoils, winding,
green prayers lead into the deep.
Dukes and ministers grasp plows and shares,
common folk shoulder hoes and harrows.
One man puts a hundred kings to shame,
three pushes precede a million souls.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on Imperial Plowing"
The classics speak of ancient tales,
observing treasures, composing splendid verses.
How like spring roads stirring,
praying for grain, honoring heaven and man.
The azure dragon pulls jade-axled carriage,
intertwined banners cast curved streamers' shadows.
Leopard-skin canopies catch the early sun,
leopard tails brush wandering mist.
Vast fields, clean rows repeated,
fragrant woods, emerald canopies suspended.
Green altar rises from long furrows,
encampment tents surround straight paths.
Grasping the plow, glorifying imperial rule,
offering tribute, moving royal piety.
Harmony matches metal-stone music,
virtue profound, eulogies composed.
Thus knowing the beauty of personal farming,
also hearing of prosperity and teaching proclaimed.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on Imperial Plowing"
Jade carriage trailing flying mist,
golden coach reflecting green streams.
Rain Master clears distant roads,
Wind Lord calms the far sky.
Divided channels water fertile fields,
churned water circles public lands.
Grass sprouts beyond the green altar,
flowers fly before the dark jade.
Dark jade arrays scepter and disc,
green altar hosts the imperial plowing.
Bending to hoe, then three pushes,
equal measure for all lords.
Orchid field, solemn carriage of fairy herbs,
cassia garden, fragrant jade mats.
Mountain birds harmonize with pipes and strings,
wild beasts join metal and stone.
Cén Wénběn's "Eulogy on Imperial Plowing"
Rightly positioned, reverent in oneself,
embodying the primal, attaining unity.
Gazed upon like clouds,
approached like the sun.
Revering suburban and ancestral temples,
mountains and rivers all ordered.
Teaching prioritizes the Great Way,
learning honors Confucian arts.
Statutes and records preserved,
lessons from Yīn, models from Zhōu Xuān.
Turning carriage to southern fields,
halting procession at eastern hamlet.
Personally plowing imperial fields,
tilling the great land oneself.
Expecting abundant harvests,
ushering in this fruitful year.
Prosperity enriches teaching's resources,
farming is governance's foundation.
Above, diligently sowing and planting,
below, diligently weeding and tending.
Honor and disgrace now clear,
simplicity and purity can return.
When ritual flourishes,
how far is the fēng sacrifice?
Spreading imperial codes,
revering royal measures.
The heir cultivates virtue,
the fortified walls stand firm.
Ministers like Zhōu and Shào,
generals like Xìn and Bù.
Auspices matching Hàn,
blessings equaling Zhōu.
Second: Personal Sericulture
The Lǐjì‧Jìyì states:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords
necessarily had public mulberry groves and silkworm chambers.
Built near rivers, with palaces erected,
walls seven and a half feet high,
thorny walls closed from outside."
The Jìtǒng states:
"The queen sericultures in the northern suburbs,
to supply pure
pronounced zī
garments;
the feudal lords' wives sericulture in the northern suburbs,
to supply ceremonial caps and robes."
The Yuèlìng states:
"In the third month of spring,
the queen and consorts fast and personally gather mulberry leaves,
to encourage sericulture;
in the first month of summer,
sericulture completed,
the queen and consorts present cocoons."
The Liáng dynasty's "Five Rites‧Protocols for the First Sericulturist" states:
"Two days before personal sericulture,
the Grand Invocator, at dawn, sacrifices a grand offering to the First Sericulturist."
Weaving Chamber Mulberry Altar
The *Dōngguàn Hànjì* states:
"Empress Míngdé Mǎ
established a weaving chamber and silkworm chamber within the Zhuólóng Garden,
and frequently visited to observe them."
The *Jìn Yuánkāng Yí* states:
"The empress's mulberry-picking altar is located southwest of the Silkworm Palace."
Silkworm Palace Seal Hall
"Silkworm Palace" see above.
The *Hànshū* states:
"When Empress Dowager Xiàoyuán Wáng became Grand Empress Dowager,
she visited the Seal Hall,
leading the empress and the wives of marquises to pick mulberries."
Northern Suburbs Eastern Park
"Northern Suburbs" see above.
The *Dǒng Bā Yúfú Zhì* states:
"Han empresses picked mulberries in the park of the eastern suburbs."
Light Blue Garments Ornamental Hairpins
The *Dǒng Bā Yúfú Zhì Zhù* states:
"When the Grand Empress Dowager enters the ancestral temple,
she wears dark blue above and black below,
and for silkworm rites, greenish-blue above and light blue below.
Her hairpin is made of tortoiseshell,
one foot long,
with decorative ornaments at the end,
topped with a phoenix."
Distributing Cocoons Equalizing Mulberry
The *Lǐjì* states:
"The empress and consorts personally tend mulberries.
When the silkworm work is completed,
they distribute cocoons and weigh silk,
to provide garments for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices."
It also states:
"The empress and consorts present cocoons,
and then the cocoon tax is collected.
Mulberry is used as the standard,
treating noble and humble, old and young as equal,
to provide garments for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices."
One Branch Three Sprinklings
The *Huánghòu Qīncán Yízhù* states:
"When the empress personally tends mulberries,
she first takes one branch,
holds a basket to receive the mulberry leaves."
The *Zhōu Qiān Gǔjīn Yúfú Záshì* states:
"When silkworms first hatch,
the empress feeds them,
sprinkling water three times and then stopping."
Jìn Mǐn Hóng's "Ode to Personal Silkworm Rearing"
The empress inspects the work to observe diligence,
equalizes abundance and scarcity to levy taxes.
She orders noble ladies to weave fine silk,
supplying the ancient system for ancestral and suburban sacrifices.
Vast grace, beautiful and all-encompassing,
matches the auspicious blessings of spring.
Displaying the wondrous patterns of embroidered insignia,
spreading the brilliant colors of crimson and purple.
Wèi Wéi Dàn's "Eulogy on the Empress's Personal Silkworm Rearing"
Personally plowing the imperial fields,
spreading virtue and issuing decrees.
Praising the first spread of tender mulberries,
contemplating the utmost reverence for suburban and ancestral temples.
Commanding the empress to personally rear silkworms,
having her tend mulberries in the outer fields.
Consulting the timing with Wūxián,
instructing the Grand Diviner to present auspicious signs.
Then, Huáng and Yīng ride as attendants,
Túshān presents the carriage.
Gathering Jiāng and Rén in the rear procession,
carrying Fán and Wèi in the secondary chariots.
Ascending the lofty altar to assume the correct position,
observing auspicious vapors in the morning sun.
Stepping down from the carved imperial carriage,
picking tender branches from the public mulberry trees.
Consorts and concubines solemnly attend to their duties,
each fulfilling their roles and holding baskets.
Providing the six ceremonial robes with their accessories,
displaying filial piety in the seasonal sacrifices.
Magnificent rites flourish within the central court,
divine transformation spreads to the eight directions.
Third: Offering Sacrifice to the Sage
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Whenever a school is first established,
one must first offer sacrifice to the Former Sages and Former Teachers.
When performing the ceremony,
silks must be used.
When the Son of Heaven inspects the school,
at dawn drums are beaten to summon,
in order to alert the multitude.
After the multitude has arrived,
then the Son of Heaven arrives.
He then orders the officials to perform the ceremony,
proceeds to the Eastern Wing,
and offers sacrifice to the Former Elders."
The *Xià Xiǎozhèng* states:
"On the second month, Dīnghài day,
ten thousand enter the school.
Dīnghài is an auspicious day.
'Ten thousand' refers to the shield-and-axe dance,
'enter the school' means the Great Learning,
referring to the present-day Great Lodge
pronounced as
presenting vegetables."
Honoring Teachers Venerating Age
Pān Ní's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"Diligently studying and requesting instruction,
investigating subtleties to comprehend principles.
Honoring teachers and esteeming the Way,
offering sacrifice to the Sage with lofty rites.
Virtue accomplished, teaching order established,
who can say it is not auspicious?"
Yuán Yào's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"The southern school venerates age,
the eastern learning esteems kinship.
Humbling oneself to inquire below,
lowering rites to serve teacher-officials.
Round caps in orderly array,
square collars with respectful demeanor."
Esteeming the Way Revering Confucians
"Esteeming the Way" see above.
Yán Yánzhī's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"The state esteems the position of teachers,
families revere the gate of Confucianism."
Practicing Studies Lecturing on Arts
Yuán Yào's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"When practice of studies is concluded,
the concluding sacrifice then begins.
Sháo music is played in succession,
sheng and yong bells sound alternately.
Thatched roofs and summer halls, serene and harmonious,
pure countenances, earnest and diligent.
Virtue and extravagance both feel ashamed,
displaying sincerity, how could there be shame?"
"Lecturing on Arts" see later in Yán Yánzhī's poem.
Establishing Schools Opening Academies
"Establishing Schools" see above.
Wáng Sēngdá's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"Times peaceful, the Way flows smoothly,
rites complete, music cultivated.
Opening academies to select the talented,
extensive teaching, deep seeking.
Extraordinary people gather like fish scales,
virtuous beauties float like clouds.
Teachers revered, instruction pervasive,
good reverence carries gentleness."
Offering Vegetables Dancing with Shields
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Wearing leather caps and offering vegetables,
shows reverence for the Way."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Vegetables
refer to things like celery and algae."
"Dancing with Shields" see the narrative section.
Solemn Orderly
Wáng Húzhī's "Memorial on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"I respectfully acknowledge following ancient classics,
on this month's auspicious day,
offering sacrifice to the Former Sage,
all officials and people of the land,
following the wind, filled with joy.
Long afflicted with severe illness,
I cannot join the ranks.
Anticipating the sight of solemn, reverent demeanor,
gazing up at the Milky Way,
lying on my pillow, joyful yet sighing."
Also, Fù Xián's "Eulogy on the Crown Prince's Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"Diligent, diligent, the imperial heir,
yearning heart towards Quèlǐ.
Orderly, orderly, the Confucian scholars,
numerous, numerous, the scions of nobles."
Displaying Sacrificial Animals Offering Vegetables
Lǐ Xié's "Poem on Offering Sacrifice to the Sage" states:
"Abundant marshes south of the court,
Mount Tóng north-facing.
The Emperor says to the Master,
display sacrificial animals, present offerings.
The spirits are all drunk and satisfied,
let us speak of the fine feast."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"The Son of Heaven then presents a lamb to open the ice,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
On the first Dīng day, he orders the Music Master to practice dance and offer vegetables,
and the Son of Heaven then leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and grandees to personally go and observe it."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary:
"Music Master,
is the head of music officials.
Ordering the dance
is to accord with the beginning of all things emerging from the earth, to drum and dance.
Before dancing, one must offer sacrifice to the Former Teacher with rites."
Revering the Teacher, Esteeming Seniority
Zhì Yú’s “Ode to the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“Like that flowing spring,
neither overflowing nor stagnant.
Once the lectures are concluded,
the ceremony reveres the teacher with the Shìdiàn.
Raising cups and arranging sacrificial meat,
high and low join in the feast.
Harmoniously they come,
reverently they appear.”
Hé Chéngtiān’s “Ode to the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“In the past, Confucius and Yán Huí,
dreamed of the Zhōu and yearned for the Yú.
Heaven bestowed their excellence,
different eras share the same signs.
Cultivating the classics and lecturing on governance,
probing subtleties and discerning principles.
The Way values honoring one’s work,
humbling the noble and esteeming seniority.”
Honoring the Way, Delighting in Learning
Pān Ní’s “Ode to the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“Focusing on Confucian arts,
devotedly delighting in ancient teachings.
Honoring the Way and yielding to seniority,
humbling the heart to inquire below.
Adorned with golden sounds,
illumined with jade-like luster.
Like a river rising,
like heaven’s motion.”
Hé Chéngtiān’s “Poem on the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“The central yellow shines bright,
beautiful sounds spread afar.
Reverently serving at dawn’s twilight,
practicing rites as day breaks.
What is this daybreak?
Delighting in learning and honoring Confucianism.
Longing for the Western Yōng,
lingering thoughts of the Yí and Zhū rivers.”
Probing the Profound, Discussing the Abstruse
Pān Ní’s “Ode to the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“Then he summoned the high ministers,
then commanded the scholarly officials.
The sage’s countenance solemn,
attendants lecturing respectfully.
Drawing forth fine words,
illuminating the true Way.
Probing the profound and exhausting the abstruse,
reviewing the old to know the new.”
Wēn Qiáo’s “Ode to the Shìdiàn Ceremony” says:
“Expounding on profound meanings,
analyzing to the finest detail.
Presenting words through recitation,
elegant phrases brilliantly displayed.
Pipes and flutes fully played,
harmonious music resounds.”
Minister-Teacher, Noble Scions
Both seen above.
Sòng Yán Yánzhī’s “Attending the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn”
The state esteems the teacher’s position,
families honor Confucian gates.
Receiving the Way and nurturing virtue,
lecturing on arts and establishing words.
The brilliant and clear dawn brightens,
the righteous path dispels this gloom.
Coming to behold the early awakened,
looking back upon later generations.
The Yúxiáng adorned its halls,
the wise plan shines resplendent.
Embracing benevolence, they gather in reverence,
holding wisdom, they come like deer.
Treading to the gate to present books,
stepping forward to offer vessels.
Cleansing the body in profound mystery,
dwelling the mind in the Way’s secrets.
The main hall sets empty mats,
officials select the auspicious day.
The presiding mat holds the teacher’s space,
assistants perform their duties with reverence.
Attendants speak with fitting words,
diligent historians grasp their brushes.
Subtly discerning the auspicious sounds,
the royal records have their account.
Expounding righteousness and inquiring duly,
the great teaching stands firm as a tripod.
Reverently performing the sacrificial rites,
announcing the offering to the sage’s spirit.
The ritual involves observing the ablutions,
music presents songs and sheng pipes.
Qí Wáng Jiǎn’s “Banquet Poem for Attending the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn”
Ritual is the state’s backbone,
righteousness truly the people’s foundation.
The self is cleansed through practice,
the world finds peace through teaching.
Gold smelted becomes a vessel,
water’s course forms ripples.
Approaching fragrance brings aroma,
treading on ice surely brings cold.
Wind stirs the hào-grass palace,
clouds rest on the cān-star lodge.
Ritual surpasses the benevolent Zhōu,
music exceeds the heroic Hàn.
The protective spirits arrive,
prayer officers offer their praises.
After the fragrant wine is finished,
virtue’s fragrance is presented.
Descending from the crown to the upper school,
ascending to feast in the eastern hall.
The Huái minister’s metal is pure,
the feudal guardian’s jade is praised.
Talented men of the time abound,
the state’s noble scions are refined.
Liáng Rèn Fǎng’s “Banquet Poem for Attending the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn on Behalf of the Prince”
Revering the sage is far-reaching,
embracing the Way is profound.
Practicing words moves customs,
resolute action shifts winds.
Advancing with one basket of earth,
enlightening perhaps three layers of ignorance.
Ice indeed forms from water,
gold also lies in smelting.
Only the spirit knows transformation,
in things, words are established.
The Music Master rectifies the Yǎ and Sòng,
all bestowed upon later generations.
Announcing the offering in bright sacrifice,
beholding the Way at the sage’s gate.
Sun and moon never cease,
the teacher’s model is ever honored.
Liáng Shěn Yuē’s “Banquet Poem for Attending the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn”
Honoring learning is ancient,
the Way also far-reaching.
Opening plans to observe mysteries,
establishing gardens to nurture talent.
Deeds lofty as the eastern hall,
righteousness surpassing the Yúntái.
Towering virtuous tutors,
brilliant talented platforms.
Fallen classics must be restored,
neglected sacrifices all offered anew.
Returning phoenixes present cups,
striking metal vessels lay offerings.
Officials debate ceremonies,
functionaries oversee the hanging instruments.
As if spirits follow,
lingering divine gaze wanders.
“Poem for Attending the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn on Behalf of the Prince of Nánjùn”
Righteousness values the teacher’s guidance,
work honors receiving with emptiness.
Following the wind at Xiāngyě,
sweeping with a broom in Xīhé.
Manifesting traces, diminishing light,
lowering sentiments, turning the head.
The Way commands all spirits,
the spirit preserves all existence.
Honoring learning is ancient,
continuing the line, transmitting glory.
Banners and insignia may err,
this Way must not be transgressed.
From hall to inner chamber,
different paths return together.
Vast is the sage’s model,
refined are the Confucian robes.
Jìn Fù Xián’s “Ode to the Crown Prince’s Shìdiàn”
Flourishing imperial heir,
both wise and intelligent.
Spiritually enlightened,
how could he be merely initiated?
Humble in practicing ritual,
nothing is done without reverence.
Thus he prepares fine offerings,
at the state’s Yōng.
Reverently honoring the first teacher,
to repay the sage’s merit.
Diligent imperial heir,
yearning heart for Quèlǐ.
Anticipating this auspicious morn,
divining near the midpoint.
Brilliant carriages and robes,
solemn demeanor and bearing.
Reverently serving the sage’s spirit,
personally receiving the bright sacrifice.
Numerous Confucian scholars,
orderly noble scions.
Clear wine in cups,
not for feasting but for joy.
Rejoicing in the Way’s expansion,
from now it begins.
"Eulogy on the Crown Prince's Sacrifice to Confucius" by Chén Xú Bóyáng of the Liáng Dynasty:
Solemn and dignified is the imperial heir,
lofty and majestic is the deputy sovereign.
His Way honors the ritual vessel,
his Virtue esteems supervision and governance.
In spring he recites, in summer he plays strings,
in winter he writes, in autumn he dances with feathers.
Like the Hàn dynasty summoning scholars to the tent,
like the Zhōu court inquiring of the young attendants.
Soaring and gathering in the halls of ritual,
wandering freely in the mansion of righteousness.
The four seas are without waves,
the three steps are already level.
The heir's carriage arrives,
harmonious bells have sound.
Expanding the teaching, lecturing and practicing,
venerating Confucians, solemnly achieving.
Crimson texts value the Way,
yellow gold is cheaper than bamboo baskets.
The Zhū and Sì rivers flourish the enterprise,
Quèlǐ adds glory.
Green locust trees shade the market,
dark crowns with flying tassels.
Fourth: Court Assemblies
The Book of Rites says:
"When the Son of Heaven has no military affairs,
meeting with the feudal lords is called a court assembly."
Affairs refer to matters of campaigning and conquest.
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"Spring audience is called cháo, summer audience is called zōng, autumn audience is called jìn, winter audience is called yù, occasional meeting is called huì, grand assembly is called tóng."
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"In general, court assemblies
are to rectify the meaning of ranks and titles;
meetings
are to instruct the rules of superior and inferior."
The Mèngzǐ says:
"When feudal lords attend court at the Son of Heaven, it is called:
'Reporting on duties.
One failure to attend court results in demotion of rank,
two failures result in reduction of territory,
three failures result in the six armies being moved against him.'" Zhì Yú's Juéyí Yàozhù says:
"The Hàn system held assemblies in the Jiànshǐ Hall.
The Jìn system held grand assemblies in the Tàijí Hall,
and small assemblies in the Eastern Hall.
For such assemblies, they wore the five seasonal court robes,
and the courtyard was set with metal and stone chimes.
Tiger Guards and banner bearers,
patterned robes with embroidered hems."
The White Tiger Discourse says:
"Whenever a minister sees the ruler, he must have a presentation gift;
the gift is a pledge,
conveying one's own sincere substance."
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"The King holds the zhèn guī;
the guī is decorated with a painted stabilizing mountain.
A Duke holds the huán guī;
double pillars are called huán.
A Marquis holds the xìn guī;
xìn means body,
meaning the guī has a human figure on it.
A Count holds the gōng guī;
gōng also means body.
A Viscount holds the gǔ bì;
gǔ nourishes people,
meaning the bì has a grain pattern.
A Baron holds the pú bì;
pú is used for mats to comfort people,
also meaning the bì has a rush grass pattern.
An isolated senior official holds leather and silk;
a Minister holds a lamb;
a Grand Master holds a goose;
a Scholar holds a pheasant;
a commoner holds a duck;
artisans and merchants hold a chicken."
Also, the White Tiger Discourse says:
"Dukes and Marquises use jade as their gift because
it is not light when dry,
and not heavy when wet.
Grand Masters use a goose as their gift because
it flies in formation,
and stops in rows.
Scholars use a wild pheasant as their gift because
it cannot be lured by food,
nor coerced by force,
and would rather die than be kept in captivity."
Assessing Achievements, Presenting Merits
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"In spring, receive the feudal lords and deliberate on the affairs of the realm."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"When the King sees the feudal lords in spring, he deliberates on whether their affairs are acceptable;
deliberation means assessing achievements."
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xuān year 14:
"Mèng Xiànzǐ said to the Duke:
'Your servant has heard that a small state escapes trouble from a large state
by sending envoys and presenting goods,
thus the courtyard is filled with a hundred displays,
and attending court to present merits.'" Dù Yù's commentary says:
"Presenting the merits of governing the state or of campaigns and conquests to the shepherd."
Pardoning Faults, Removing Evils
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"Zǐchǎn served as minister of Zhèng,
Bó went to Chǔ,
and said:
'Qiáo has heard that when a large state goes to a small state, there are five beauties:

forgiving its crimes and offenses, pardoning its faults and errors, rescuing it from calamity and ruin, rewarding its virtuous punishments, and teaching it where it falls short.'" The Rites of Zhōu says:
"The autumn audience is to remove the evils of the states."
Zhèng's commentary says:
"Evil,
means wickedness."
Deliberating Affairs, Inspecting Merits
"Deliberating affairs" see above.
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"Wěi Qǐjiāng replied to the King of Chǔ:
'For court visits and missions there is the guī,
for offerings and inspections there is the zhāng.
For small matters there is reporting on duties,
for great matters there is inspecting merits.'"
Discussing Ritual, Reporting on Duties
The Zuǒzhuàn:
"Shū Xiàng said:
'The system of the enlightened king
has the feudal lords send annual missions to record their tasks.
Occasional court assemblies
to discuss ritual,
a second court assembly then a meeting to display authority.
A second meeting then an alliance to make clear the bright virtue.
Recording tasks through goodwill,
discussing ritual according to rank,
displaying authority to the multitude,
making bright virtue clear to the spirits.
Since ancient times,
this has never been neglected.'" "Reporting on duties" already seen above.
Displaying Authority, Clarifying Righteousness
"Displaying authority" see above.
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící says:
"Meetings are
for promoting virtue, clarifying righteousness, examining omissions, and handling affairs."
Visiting the Sacred Mountains, Receiving Ministers at Court
The Shàngshū says:
"After the month, then the days,
he visited the Four Sacred Mountains and the multitude of shepherds."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"After,
means completely.
Visit,
means see.
It says Shùn completely, in the middle of the first month, then day by day saw the multitude of shepherds."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" says:
"In ancient times, the Xià sovereign received his multitude of ministers in this land,
and those holding jade and silk were ten thousand states.
Truly it was the lofty assembly of the former kings,
the guiding rule for the four quarters."
Examining Ritual, Rectifying Punishments
The Gǔliángzhuàn says:
"The Marquis of Téng and the Marquis of Xuē came to court.
The Son of Heaven had no affairs,
so the feudal lords attended court to rectify themselves.
They examine ritual and cultivate virtue,
in order to honor the Son of Heaven."
The White Tiger Discourse says:
"When feudal lords send missions to each other,
it is for mutual respect.
Therefore, when feudal lords attend court and send missions,
if the Son of Heaven is without ailment,
laws and regulations will not be changed.
This is to uphold ritual, rectify punishments, unify virtue, and honor the Son of Heaven."
Examining Institutions, Rectifying Ranks and Titles
The Shàngshū says:
"Every six years, the five domains attend court once.
After another six years,
the King then makes a seasonal tour.
He examines the institutions at the Four Sacred Mountains,
the feudal lords each attend court at their respective sacred mountain,
greatly clarifying promotions and demotions."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"Visiting the feudal lords of the four quarters,
each attending court at the foot of their respective sacred mountain,
greatly clarifying the methods for assessing achievements and promoting or demoting."
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"In the summer of the 23rd year of Duke Zhuāng,
the Duke went to Qí to observe the soil sacrifice,
which was contrary to ritual.
Cáo Guì remonstrated, saying:
'Now ritual is what orders the people.
Meetings instruct the rules of superior and inferior,
regulate the measures of wealth and expenditure.
Court assemblies rectify the meaning of ranks and titles,
and lead the order of elders and juniors.'"
To command administrative affairs and to supply tribute duties.
The Zhōu Lǐ, with Zhèng Xuán's annotation, states:
"The feudal lords of the five domains
all send their ministers to visit the Son of Heaven using the rites of a formal visit.
The Son of Heaven receives them according to ritual,
and commands them regarding matters of governance and prohibitions."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Zǐchǎn served as assistant to the Earl of Zhèng when he went to Chǔ.
They lodged but did not build an earthen platform.
He said:
'When a small state goes to a great state, there are five evils:
having its offenses pardoned, having its governance discussed, supplying its tribute duties, following its seasonal commands;
otherwise, increasing its gifts of silk and cloth
to congratulate its good fortune and condole its misfortunes—
all these are calamities for a small state.
Why then build a platform
to proclaim these calamities?'"
To present seasonal offerings and to present precious goods.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn:
"Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn paid a formal visit to Zhōu.
The King instructed the official to inquire about his business.
He replied:
'The officer Qǐ of Jìn is about to present the seasonal offerings to the official in charge of the royal household;
there is no other business.'
The King, hearing this, said:
'The Hán clan will surely flourish in Jìn!
His words do not depart from the old ways.'" The Bái Hǔ Tōng states:
"The formal visit is because ministers and sons wish to know their lord or father is well,
and also should present the precious goods produced by their land to assist in the sacrifices.
Therefore, all are able to perform the rites of formal visits and inquiries."
To instruct superiors and inferiors, and to clarify honor and humility.
"To instruct superiors and inferiors" is seen above.
The Lǐ Jì states:
"Formerly, the Duke of Zhōu received the feudal lords in their positions in the Mingtáng.
The Son of Heaven stood facing south with his back to the screen.
The Mingtáng
is to clarify the honor and humility of the feudal lords."
To discourse on civil virtue and to illuminate ritual propriety.
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící states:
"When the feudal lords hold governance,
honor and humility have their order.
Each comes to court,
to discourse on civil virtue,
to illuminate ritual propriety.
They yield to the laws and institutions of the realm,
and the four quarters receive the standards." The Bái Hǔ Tōng states:
"Court means to see.
Once every five years they come to court,
to prepare civil virtue and illuminate ritual propriety."
Fù Xuán of Jìn's "Rhapsody on the Court Assembly"
I look up to the literary images of the two August Ones,
and chant the imperial virtue in the upper lineage.
I examine the transmitted teachings of Xià Hòu,
and synthesize the canonical institutions of Yīn and Zhōu.
I gather the old ceremonies of Qín and Hàn,
to fix the auspicious gathering at the beginning of the year.
Thus, beforehand they prepare the affairs,
and all officials sincerely command.
The myriad states all present offerings,
each according to their duty.
The reverent capital city,
the lofty Purple Pole.
The Changhe Gate opens,
the Heavenly Gate is wide,
they sit in the main hall of the Supreme Ultimate,
solemn and towering, lofty and steep.
I praise the spacious courtyard's openness and beauty,
and admire the jade steps ascending to the clouds.
The ushers, composed, wait their turn and enter.
Multitudinous and ample,
solemn and practiced.
Taking their positions in layered rows,
they stand facing their mats.
The heralds stand in unison,
the guest rites reach the ninefold [heights].
The many lords yield with virtue,
from beyond the seas they come in unity.
Bundles of silk, abundant and fine,
lambs and wild geese, harmonious and full.
Presenting gifts and holding jade tablets,
the men are solemn in their demeanor.
At this time, the Son of Heaven, in full regalia, rises at dawn,
sits in the martial tent,
leans on the jade table.
Facing directly south, he hears the court,
balancing the scales like the whetstone and arrow.
The many officers and all the nobles,
ascend the steps and present cups.
The imperial grace descends,
auspicious ethers soar upward.
When the rites conclude, the feast begins,
advancing and halting have their pattern.
The six musics play in succession,
stone chimes and pipes clang and ring.
Deep and profound, the drums and bells,
clear and bright, the reed pipes and reeds.
Striking drums, plucking qin and se,
to chant of the former emperors.
Elegant songs harmonize within,
hymns of praise resound abroad.
Emperor Tàizōng's "Poem on Attending Court in the First Month"
The orderly wind opens the season of offerings,
the ash-tube's pitch moves the nascent yang.
All the southern tribes present tribute ranks,
the myriad states court at Wèiyāng.
Though lacking the traces of Shùn and Yǔ,
I joyfully delight in heaven and earth's peace.
Carriages and chariots unite the eight directions,
writings and scripts blend the four quarters.
Resplendent and majestic, caps and canopies,
profuse and orderly, rich robes and insignia.
Feather banners fly on the imperial way,
bells and drums shake the cliff-side corridors.
Dark red silk gleams with rosy-cloud hues,
frosty halberds reflect the morning light.
Morning and night I cherish the ultimate principle,
yet in the end am ashamed to pacify the distant wilds.
Emperor Suí Yáng's "Poem on Receiving Court at the Qiányáng Hall on the Winter Solstice"
The dark winter of the northern path is at its height,
at the southern extreme, the gnomon's shadow and water-clock are long.
Sitting upright, I receive court from the myriad states,
preserving culture, I succeed the hundred kings.
My utmost virtue shames the sun's daily use,
my transforming way shames the era's peace.
The new capital is built at Sōng Peak,
twin watchtowers overlook Luòyáng.
The gnomon's shadow aligns the eight directions,
the roads are even in the four quarters.
The azure sky, frosty blossoms still,
the vermilion courtyard, sunlight bright.
Cap-tassels and pendants, so well-ordered,
bells and drums, how resonant and loud!
Ornamented halberds guard the high hall,
colored pennants divide the long corridors.
The sovereign lacks clear wisdom,
the ministers value only the good.
Boats and oars have their course to follow,
may this kingly transformation flourish hence.
Jiāng Zǒng of Chén's "Poem on Being Assigned the Topic 'Visiting the Emperor at the Chéngmíng Lodge'"
Fog clears at the Rénshòu Hall,
clouds wreathe the Chéngmíng Lodge.
Wheels halt, dark-red canopies drawn,
horses pass, red dust remains.
Scented sable, bowing in embroidered robes,
flowered ribbons, brushing dark steps.
Visiting the emperor, ascending the clear Han,
how different from entering the Purple Void?
Niú Hóng of Suí's "Poem in Response to the Imperial Command on Receiving Court at the Qiányáng Hall on the Winter Solstice"
Reverently I preside over the myriad domains,
the imperial abode commands the eight borders.
Tribute gathers, the finest mao grass,
coming to court, jade tablets and emblems join.
The master of ceremonies, three bows abundant,
the director of rites, nine guests reverent.
Layered balustrades like jade discs,
multiple halls wreathed in ethereal mist.
Xǔ Shànxīn of Suí's "Poem on the Same Topic"
Dense and thick, the guards arrayed on the steps,
ringing and clanging, the tinkling of jade pendants.
The rites exhaust the gathering of the five auspicious tokens,
the music concludes, the nine achievements complete.
Yú Shìnán's "Poem on Early Morning Court"
A myriad households, dawn light breaks,
layered eaves, evening mist withdraws.
Jade flowers halt the night's candles,
golden pot delivers the morning tallies.
Sunlight glows on the blue-lattice hall,
rosy clouds rise from the brocade tower.
Heavy gates open on the main road,
presenting credentials, they usher in kings and lords.
Wèi Zhēng's "Poem in Response to the Imperial Command on Attending Court on New Year's Day"
A hundred spirits attend the Xuānyuán Sovereign,
the myriad states met at Tú Mountain.
How could they compare to today's wise and sagacious,
surpassing the ancients, uniquely brilliant before?
Sound and teaching overflow the four seas,
paying homage like rivers to the sea, parting the hundred streams.
Clanging and vast, jade pendants chime,
glittering and sparkling, golden cicadas gleam.
Fine sunlight shines on carved chariots,
high banners raise emerald mist.
The courtyard's display surpasses the royal assembly,
the grand music rivals that of Heaven's music.
Already I rejoice in the sun of the eastern door,
and again chant the ode of the southern wind.
I wish to offer this glorious celebration,
for ten thousand times ten thousand years hence.
Yán Shīgǔ, "Poem on the Same Theme"
The Seven Regulators begin their jade-armed course,
The Triple Origin's precious calendar is renewed.
Leaning on the screen, he summons all the lords,
With hanging beads, he receives the ninefold guests.
Solemnly arrayed are the herons and egrets,
Grandly assembled, the capped and belted throng.
From the world's edge come interpreters of distant tongues,
From the Western Regions, tribute of wondrous treasures.
Cén Wénběn, "Poem on the Same Theme"
Harmonious times show flourishing fortune,
The upright sun accords with divine tallies.
Virtue combines the rites of the Three Dynasties,
Merit encompasses the maps of the Four Seas.
Crossing deserts, multitudes stand in ranks,
Holding jade tablets, they solemnly advance.
The cleared imperial way resounds with quieted steps,
Music is played, startling the celestial thoroughfare.
Brushing rainbows, the nine banners follow the rule,
The phoenix's ritual, the eight sounds distinct.
Ethereal airs float over the Immortal's Palm,
Warm winds encircle the Emperor's parasol tree.
Celestial patterns illuminate the Seven Regulators,
Imperial grace covers the Nine Regions.
About to join the rite of burying the jade,
I dip my brush at the foot of Mount Dài.
Yáng Shīdào, "Poem on the Same Theme"
Imperial plans encompass the cosmos,
The upright screen belongs to the primal hour.
Ninefold gates adorn the sky's hue,
A thousand portals face the early spring.
Lǐ Bǎiyào, "Poem on the Same Theme"
Transforming reigns illuminate the Tang code,
Receiving Heaven, they follow the Xia calendar.
All spirits guard the imperial precincts,
The Three Luminaries raise streaming banners.
The court is filled with rich rites and music,
The lofty feast honors the capped and belted.
Offering longevity, tallying ten thousand years,
Transforming customs, the ninefold music's harmony.
Zhāng Wéncóng, "Poem on an Early Winter Morning Court with Pan, the State Farm Director"
Napping, I think of the ancients,
Rising early, I gaze at the dawn moon.
Through morning, the palace gates open,
Officials hasten to court audience.
Frosty mists clear the nine thoroughfares,
Rosy light shines on the twin towers.
Ordered are the trappings of culture,
Brilliantly resplendent, fame and clarity issue forth.
Swords at the waist gleam variegated,
Jade pendants chime, pure and far-reaching.
Cén Wénběn, "Ode on the Triple Origin"
The Sheti stars shift their measures,
The first month follows the proper order.
The intercalary remainder concluded,
The offering of the new year just begins.
Then he commands the officers in charge,
Orders the archivists,
To examine the statutes,
And revise the laws and measures.
The rites of the three morning audiences are fully displayed,
The ceremonies for the ninefold guests are all prepared.
Court torches flicker, soaring aloft,
Bright lamps blaze, scattered like stars.
Then comes the first day of the first month,
The season answering to Goumang.
Floating auspicious mists and wafting fine vapors,
They open the Changhe Gate and unveil the Deyang Hall.
The Yu guest shines among the ranks,
The Huhán chieftain stands within the rows.
All officials, grandly assembled; all states, augustly present; gold belts and jade chimes.
Holding gifts and presenting jade tablets,
From within the capital region,
To the outer remote frontiers,
They convey their attentive gaze to the royal assembly,
Presenting tribute to the territorial office.
The master of ceremonies' duties are not neglected,
The heralds' ranks are orderly.
They extend their gaze to the imperial pole,
And also raise their heads to the lofty hall.
Like rivers flowing to the sea,
Like heavy dew drying in the sun.
They raise the toothed banners,
Set out the zhu and yu instruments,
Display the tripods' contents,
And array the wine vessels and stands.
Barriers stand solemn as guards,
Spears and lances bristle, raised in unison.
Five carriages link their axles,
Nine banners wave their streamers.
Feathered canopies lush and luxuriant,
Cloud-like chariots dimly majestic.
They manifest clarity in cultural trappings,
And complete dignity in caps and belts.
Banquets and Feasts, Fifth
The Rites of Zhou states:
"The rituals of banquets and feasts
are for drawing close to guests from the four quarters."
The Han Shi Waizhuan states:
"Not removing one's shoes before taking one's seat is called a formal banquet (lǐ);
going barefoot and sitting up high is called a feast (yàn).
Those who can drink, drink;
those who cannot, stop;
this is called a drinking party (yù).
Closing the gate and not letting guests leave
is called excessive drinking (miǎn)."
The Preface to the Mao Odes states:
"The 'Deer Cry'
is for feasting ministers and honored guests.
The 'Flowering Plum'
is for feasting brothers.
The 'Heavy Dew'
is for the Son of Heaven to feast the feudal lords."
Chanting 'Heavy Dew' and Singing 'Great Wind'
The Zuo Tradition states:
"When Ning Wuzi of Wei came on a friendly mission,
the Duke feasted with him
and chanted for him the 'Heavy Dew'."
The History of the Han states:
"In the twelfth year of Emperor Gaozu,
he attacked Ying Bu.
Returning, he passed through Pei.
He stayed
and set out wine in the Pei Palace,
summoning all his old friends, elders, and younger brothers to assist with the drinking.
He gathered about a hundred and twenty men from within Pei
and taught them to sing.
When the wine was at its height,
the Emperor himself struck the sword and sang:
'A great wind rises, oh! clouds fly and scatter;
My might covers the Four Seas, oh! I return to my hometown;
How can I get brave warriors, oh! to guard the four quarters!'"
Vast Grace and Profuse Kindness
Xún Xù's "Poem on Feasting in Emperor Wu's Hualin Garden" says:
"Gently warm, the spring sun,
The Emperor emerges from Zhen.
Heaven bestows, earth generates,
In response to mid-spring.
Thoughtful and cultured, the sage emperor,
Following the season, upholding benevolence.
Reverently complying with divine principles,
He feasts and entertains his honored guests.
His vast grace spreads universally,
His blessings reach all his ministers."
Qiān Xiù's "Poem on Feasting in the Yaowu Hall" says:
"Bathing in the great flow,
Drinking of the clear fragrance.
About to put down tiny roots,
Forever basking in the morning sun.
Humbly receiving profuse kindness,
May I never be idle or neglectful."
Fragrant Dishes and Sweet Wine
Pān Ní's poem says:
"The sage court appoints the regional lords,
Claws and fangs guarding the northern border.
The crown prince extends sincere affection,
Setting out a feast to send off a distant guest.
Who should attend today's banquet?
None but the court ministers.
Wine is set in the Xuanyou Hall,
Drums are struck by the Lingzhao Pond.
Feathered cups fly with fine wine,
Fragrant dishes prepared with rare delicacies."
Liú Zhēn's poem says:
"In the past I followed the great sovereign,
Ordering the carriages to the southern region.
Passing through that capital of Feng and Pei,
I soared and roamed together with you.
All the guests gathered to sit,
Bright lamps blazing with fiery light.
Clear songs created wondrous sounds,
Myriad dances performed in the central hall.
Golden wine vessels held sweet wine,
Feathered cups passed around without restraint."
Golden Wine Vessels and Jade Cups
"Golden wine vessels" appears above in the note for "sweet wine."
Emperor Wén of Wei's poem says:
"In the clear night I entertain guests,
Bright candles emit lofty light.
Sumptuous dishes spread out like stars arrayed,
Fine wine fills the jade cups."
Ornate Wine Vessels and Feathered Goblets
Fu Xuán's poem says:
"The luan bird gazes at the phoenix,
The moon-charioteer succeeds the bright sun.
A thousand autumns bring this fine gathering,
Ascending to the noble gentleman's chamber.
Ornate vessels hold clear, fine wine,
Rare delicacies overflow in abundance."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's poem says:
"A fine morning opens the season's start,
High towers reach the peak of joy and mirth.
Reaching heaven, brushing against radiant clouds,
Looking down upon the four thoroughfares below.
Feathered goblets float on elephant-shaped vessels,
Precious viands fill the dòu and qū measures."
Bestowing Kindness and Manifesting Virtue
Ruǎn Yǔ's poem says:
"The warm spring stirs harmonious breath,
A worthy lord thereby exalts benevolence.
Bestowing kindness, soothing all creatures,
Extending love to those ever dear.
In the hall above, we entertain each other,
From within and without, seasonal treasures are offered.
The five flavors gather like wind and rain,
Cups and drafts float like clouds."
The Book of Rites says:
"After the libation of return, the musicians ascend to sing,
This is to manifest virtue.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
'Through the meaning of the poems,
They illuminate the virtue of host and guest.'"
Fine Feasts and Joyous Drinking
Wáng Jì's poem "Following Affairs in the Huálín Garden" says:
"Long nets sprinkle scales,
The great kitchen offers wondrous fare.
Things follow the seasons' order,
Feelings are expressed through transformation.
Ultimately gentle yet disciplined,
Reverent at the first mats.
Honored guests are here present,
Seeking blessings for eternal years."
Fu Xuán's "Banquet Poem" says:
"As the day has passed away,
So too have feelings grown deep.
The guests linger with remaining joy,
The host's countenance shows insufficiency.
Let us drink joyously this night,
Warm as jade."
Clarifying Nobility and Baseness, Observing Dignity and Bearing
The Book of Rites says:
"The meaning of the feast rituals for feudal lords,
The sacrificial vessels, animal victims, offerings, and delicacies,
All have distinctions of rank.
This is how nobility and baseness are clarified."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"The Marquis of Wèi feasted Kǔ Chéng Shū,
Nìng Huìzǐ assisted; Chéng Shū was arrogant.
Nìngzǐ said:
'Will Kǔ Chéng Shū's household not perish?
In ancient times, holding a feast
Was to observe dignity and bearing and examine fortune and misfortune.
Now this man is arrogant,
This is the way to incur misfortune.'"
Being Intimate with Guests, Feasting Friends
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"Use the rituals of feasting and banqueting to be intimate with the guests from the four quarters,
When they come for court visits or missions,
The king holds feasting and banqueting rituals to be intimate with them."
The Máo Shī says:
"Cutting Wood,
Is about feasting friends and old acquaintances.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
None have succeeded without relying on friends.
Being intimate with kin leads to harmony,
Not abandoning worthy friends.
Not discarding old acquaintances,
Then the people's virtue returns to厚厚ness."
Bamboo and Wooden Vessels Arrayed, Wine Vessels and Meat Stands Displayed
The Máo Shī says:
"I have seen this gentleman,
The bamboo and wooden vessels are arrayed in order."
Zhāng Huá's poem says:
"When court duties leave leisure,
He summons his assembled ministers.
Officials and carriages gather like clouds,
Wine vessels and meat stands displayed like stars."
Wèi Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on Entertaining Guests"
Thus we feast guests in lofty gathering,
Vermilion curtains brilliant, spread on four sides.
We discern the lavish fare from the central kitchen,
And present the lovely singers of Qí and Zhèng.
Literati display their wondrous discourse,
Flying light brushes to complete compositions.
They speak of the pure customs of times past,
And summarize the principles of sages and worthies.
I delight in the noble principles of the lord,
Gaining fragrance as if from orchids.
Spreading benevolent grace upon humble dwellings,
Surpassing even the Duke of Zhōu forgetting his meal.
Hearing the wind of benevolence, I forget sorrow,
Fine wine clear, dishes sweet."
Jìn Wáng Chén's "Rhapsody on Feasting Honored Guests"
The morning sun shines with radiance,
The weather harmonious and calm.
Ruler and ministers unite in virtue,
Ritual and ceremony greatly illustrious.
We raise feathered goblets in mutual joy,
Connecting with respect and reverence to express sincerity.
Fine viands are prepared with the eight delicacies,
Silk and bamboo present their wondrous sounds.
Music is used for all dances,
Metal instruments achieve harmony.
Zhōng Yí's listening,
The southern wind brings sorrow.
Righteousness moves the noble man,
Filled with emotion, long-lasting thoughts.
I think of my king's measure,
Seeking blessings without deviation.
Only when rites end and praise withdraws,
Is my heart truly bound to the jade steps."
Jìn Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on Receiving Guests"
Receiving guests, summoning visitors,
Gathering my friends and companions.
Lofty discourse, pure feasting,
Expounding principles, studying essence.
Respectful and solemn,
Delighting the heart, indulging feelings."
Suí Xuē Dàohéng's "Rhapsody on Joyous Feasting"
Liáng Xiàowáng, imperial son, imperial grandson,
Relying on favor, receiving grace,
Famed throughout the Western Hàn,
Rituals flourishing in the eastern domain.
He leads graceful, cultured guests,
To sit in the garden of tall, beautiful bamboos.
Water winds and curves around the steps,
A clear, cool breeze enters the pavilion.
I simply gaze intently, looking around,
Then feel melancholy and am moved to speak.
Turning, he said to Méi Chéng:
"I hear the cycles of seasons revolve,
Human life floats like duckweed.
Sages who mend heaven and establish earth
Cannot halt the sun's westward fall;
The strength to channel mountains and settle rivers
Cannot stop the river's eastward flow.
The Hán king's Suānzǎo Terrace
Lies desolate, overgrown, and wild;
The Chǔ state's Yángyún Tower
Is seen only as empty dust.
Thus indeed one can indulge will and heart,
To wander and be at ease.
Exhaust feasting pleasures through the long night,
Blending right and wrong into one."
At that time, frost weighs on courtyard orchids,
Autumn deep, the air cold.
Spanning the long river's gleaming clarity,
Hangs the lone moon, full and round.
Then there are vermilion steps, pale walls,
Mulberry halls, pepper chambers.
Winding and turning,
Shimmering and interweaving, delicate and exquisite.
Enchanting ladies, virtuous beauties,
Jade-like faces among blossoms.
The Weaving Maid descends, stars fall;
Cháng'é comes, the moon empties.
Clear reflections of makeup upon singing fans,
Scattering robe fragrance in the dance breeze.
Cups carved with clouds and thunder,
Wine steeped with cassia, brewed with flowers.
Wiping pearl drops on silken sleeves,
Passing golden cups to fair hands."
Tàizōng Emperor's "Poem on Feasting Assembled Ministers at the Xuánwǔ Gate on a Spring Day"
Fine light opens the auspicious season,
Harmonious breath stirs the fragrant year.
Halting the carriage by Huálín's side,
Holding lofty feast before Bǎiliáng.
Purple court filled with patterned trees,
Vermilion steps linked by dragon robes.
The nine Yí prepare jade mats,
The five Dí array jade feasts.
Entertaining guests, singing "Zhàn Lù",
Vast music plays the "Jūn Tiān".
Full cups float with green ale,
Elegant melodies resonate vermilion strings.
I, ruling over ten thousand states,
Still feel ashamed, governing all eight bounds.
I hope to preserve steadfast integrity,
Humbling myself, urging the search for worthies."
Also, "Poem on Setting Wine at the Feathered Pavilion"
High balconies overlook the green islets,
Soaring eaves rise across the open sky.
Remaining blossoms cluster by the latticed rails,
Scattered willow twigs adorn the carved windows.
Riverside chrysanthemums first show their buds,
Garden pears begin to blush with red.
Worry not that Kūnlún grows dim,
Let us together drain the cup.
Also, "Winter Night, Each in Four Rhymes"
The carved palace quiet, the dragon clepsydra stills,
The splendid tower feasts dukes and marquises.
Pearl curtains stir with candle flames,
Embroidered pillars float in moonlight.
Dust rises as songs begin to sound,
Wind ceases as pipes linger on.
The jade pool hosts many talents,
What more cares at the throne?
An ancient poem says:
Today’s fine feast and gathering,
Such joy is hard to fully tell.
Zithers play with soaring notes,
New melodies wondrously divine.
Hàn Yìng Yáng’s poem
Lofty is the host’s virtue,
A fine gathering draws guests from all sides.
Opening the lodge to welcome the many scholars,
Setting wine in the fresh hall.
Debates resolve pent-up thoughts,
Taking up the brush inspires writings.
Grave and noble are the many gentlemen,
In harmony sharing joy and ease.
Wèi Wéndì’s poem composed in the lecture hall
Today we rejoice in shared pleasure,
Drinking deeply, unaware of drunkenness.
Mournful zithers stir new tunes,
Long flutes exhale clear air.
Also, a poem composed at a feast
In clear night we entertain honored guests,
Bright candles cast lofty light.
