Sumptuous dishes spread like stars arrayed,
Fine wine fills jade cups.
Strings and songs perform new melodies,
Wafting echoes brush vermilion beams.
Lingering notes keep pace with swift rhythms,
Passionate, now stirring and soaring.
Toasts crisscross in profusion,
Elegant dances, how they clang and ring!
Silken tassels fly with the wind,
Long swords rise and fall of themselves.
Wèi Cáo Zhí’s poem
The noble lord honors and loves his guests,
Through the banquet’s end he knows no weariness.
In clear night we roam the Western Garden,
Flying canopies follow one another.
Bright moon clarifies the pure scene,
Constellations arrayed unevenly.
Autumn orchids cover the long slope,
Vermilion blossoms crown the green pond.
Hidden fish leap in clear waves,
Lovely birds sing on high branches.
Divine gusts meet the crimson carriage,
Light chariots shift with the wind.
Liáng Liú Xiàozhuó’s "Poem on Feasting with Attendant-in-ordinary Xú Mǐn"
The great lord pursues feasting joy,
Ten days pass in succession.
Building chambers above Flowery Pond,
Opening windows facing water caltrops and lotus.
Square halls join dense bamboos,
Eaves opposite connect lush boughs.
Light shifts, woods change color,
Wind departs, water leaves ripples.
Though Luòchéng is half veiled,
Loving guests, we await the parting song.
Also, "Poem on Attending a Feast with Liú Gōnggàn, in Response to the Command"
The crown prince feasts in the Western Garden,
Prince Chén returns from audience with the emperor.
Seats arrayed by Flowery Pond’s side,
Elegance and letters fly freely.
A petty minister light as a cicada’s wing,
Striving hard, I wrongly follow in pursuit.
Setting wine to accompany the morning sun,
Lingering, I gaze at evening mist.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú’s "Poem on Attending a Feast at Xuānyóu Hall, in Response to the Command"
The crown prince’s virtue approaches sagehood,
Prince Chén’s talent brushes the heavens.
Returning to feast at Pínglè,
Setting wine facing woods and springs.
Incense smoke mingles with mountain air,
Palace shadows enter the pond’s lotuses.
Lustrous dances shift with the rhythm,
New songs time and again ascend the strings.
Hearing the tunes, ashamed I look back,
Thinking of classics, merely wishing to sleep.
Northern Qí Wèi Shōu’s "Poem on an Autumn Feast Under the Moon"
This evening we gather for a feast,
Moonlight shines on floating dewy blooms.
Messenger stars seem headed toward Shǔ,
Sword-auras have no link to Wú.
Good friendship bonds like metal and stone,
Honored guests comfort with daylilies and thyme.
Why must we be like Yìng and Liú’s kind,
To come again roaming Yèdū?
Northern Qí Yáng Xùn’s "Poem on a Grand Feast of the Nobles"
The palace attendant finishes his report,
The capital governor returns from court.
Opening mats to lead honored guests,
Jade-like delicacies face spring sunlight.
Dust rises from the Golden Guard’s riders,
Fragrance follows the minister’s robes.
Green wine in rhinoceros-horn bowls,
Resounding zithers with precious bridges.
A moment’s shade is truly to be cherished,
A thousand gold is easily spent.
Chén Hòuzhǔ’s "Poem on an Evening Feast at Wénsī Hall"
Evening sun sets with lingering light,
Night garden, emerald canopies fly.
Lotus shadows invade pond waves,
Cloud hues enter mountain doors.
Firefly glimmers cease then rise again,
Dark birds leave then return once more.
Joy peaks, yet drunkenness unspoken,
Cups deep, still regret they’re few.
Also, "Poem on Feasting at Supervisor Lù Shàn’s Residence"
Within the ninefold forbidden gates,
Feasting in spring’s third month.
Clouds clear, mountain trees hide,
Leaves grow, palace locusts dense.
Water green already floats with moss,
Flowers bloom, fruits now forming.
Also, "Poem on Attending a Feast in Suí, in Response to the Edict"
Sun and moon glorify Heaven’s virtue,
Mountains and rivers make the imperial seat majestic.
In this great peace, nothing to repay,
I wish to present a fengshan petition.
Chén Jiāng Zǒng’s "Poem on Attending a Feast at Lóuhú Garden in Autumn, in Response to the Edict"
Green islets welcome the returning imperial carriage,
Jade Pond commands feathered cups.
A thousand gates echo with cloud-like steps,
Four marshes stir with glorious light.
Jade oars on Kūnchí’s waves,
Golden cups spread at Tàiyè Pond.
Red banners shine on isles,
Phoenix canopies circle woods and ponds.
Wilds quiet, heavy shadows vast,
Huái River’s autumn air cool.
Mist clears, towers and gates near,
Sun distant, misty waves long.
Luòyàn feasts surely were like this,
Hàoyǐn banquets could hardly compare.
Decayed and inept, I unworthily receive honor,
With hairpin and tablet I serve in the royal train.
Suí Shěn Jūndào’s "Poem on Attending the Crown Prince’s Feast, in Response to the Command"
The crown prince, overseeing governance in leisure,
Halts his carriage briefly in the forbidden park.
Water low, golden sands shallow,
Clouds high, jade leaves sparse.
Following the kitchen, white-feathered swans,
Chasing angling, purple-scaled fish.
Sated with virtue, truly without end,
Honored to accompany till the feast’s close.
Suí Liú Duānhé’s "Poem on an Early Spring Feast at the Eastern Hall, in Response to the Command"
Wise enjoyment matches spring’s fragrance,
Opening mats facing the painted hall.
Courtyard plums scatter early white,
Eaves willows turn first yellow.
Eight delicacies arrayed on jade stands,
Nine-brew wine brims in golden cups.
Zither notes flow through flying towers,
Song-dust settles among courtesan rows.
Why need the Western Garden’s night,
Vainly to receive bright moonlight?
Yú Shìnán’s "Poem on Attending a Feast, Receiving the Rhyme ‘Qián,’ in Response to the Edict"
Fragrant, the forbidden grove at dusk,
Leisurely, before the cassia boat.
Across the sky, a single bird passes,
Upon the water, a hundred flowers blaze.
Green fields bright with slanting sun,
Blue mountains pale with evening mist.
Unworthily I join the feast’s end,
Holding the brush, like peeking at heaven.
Dù Zhènglún's "Poem on a Banquet at the Northern Gate"
The great lord, in leisure from court duties,
With wise appreciation, delights in woods and springs.
Opening windows overlooking the forbidden park,
Spreading mats on the wilds, fragrant feasts are arrayed.
Uneven songs and pipes drift on the breeze,
Fluttering feather banners hang suspended.
Jade pools flow like sweet wine,
Cloudy pavilions gather not mere mist.
Heavy dew dries under Yáo’s sun,
Warm breezes enter Shùn’s strings.
Great virtue matches the dark creation,
Tiny things bear the potter’s molding.
Wrongly I attend this Jasper Water feast,
And still join the Bǎi Liáng verse.
In vain my name ascends with the moon,
Zōu’s debates record talk of heaven.
Though glad for this radiant dawn,
More I grieve the approaching twilight years.
Still I hope for the rising midday sun,
With cap and gown, reverently I serve.
Xuē Yàozhèng's "Poem on Night Banquet Attendance in Response to Imperial Command"
Heavy gates, bells and water-clocks pass,
Evening opens the Phoenix Palace.
Twin suns amid auspicious haze,
A thousand gates under the bright moon.
Wine feasts float with heavy dew,
Songs chant the flowing wind.
Attendant ministers all drunk and still,
Ever ashamed of such lofty favor.
Wèi Yuánzhōng's "Poem on Banquet Attendance at Yínhuáng Palace in Response to Imperial Command"
Autumn clouds rise over separate halls,
Summer scenes shift at the detached palace.
Cold winds stir jade trees,
Cool air descends to Jasper Pool.
Moat flowers still sprout leaves,
Cliff trees yet put forth branches.
I wish to offer Nánshān’s longevity,
For a thousand autumns ever thus.
Dù Shěnyán's "Poem on Cháng’ān’s Southern Mountains Composed by Imperial Command at a Banquet in the Pénglái Three Halls"
The Northern Dipper hangs by the city’s edge,
Southern Mountains lean before the hall.
Clouds mark golden towers winding,
Treetops hold jade halls suspended.
Half-ridge breathes fine ether,
Mid-peak wreathed in auspicious smoke.
A petty officer holds the offering cup,
Long thus to revere the lofty heavens.
Sū Guī's "Poem on Banquet Attendance at Xìngqìng Pond in Response to Imperial Command"
Golden towers at dawn, night mist withdrawn,
Jasper Pool’s feast gazes on clear streams.
Auspicious phoenixes fly following the imperial carriage,
Lucky fish emerge, sporting, leaping by royal boats.
Curtains align, green trees dense by the mats,
Canopies turn, pale lotus floating shoreward.
As if facing, I secretly compare—a petty minister,
As if crossing, I presumptuously attend the sage lord’s tour.
Liú Xiàn's "Poem Harmonizing with Imperial Visit to Wàngchūn Palace in Spring, in Response to Imperial Command"
Late spring’s spring hues most lovely and bright,
Gardens bloom, imperial feasts arrayed.
Shāng Mountain’s piled emerald rises by the city,
Chǎn River’s floating light joins the tent’s edge.
Orioles hide in tender leaves, singing calls,
Butterflies hinder fragrant thickets, dancing halts.
Joyful seasonal sights now like this,
I wish to attend imperial tours for myriad years.
Mǎ Huáisù's "Poem on Banquet Attendance at Xìngqìng Pond in Response to Imperial Command"
Accumulated waters wind around shell-like walls,
Embracing emptiness, a bright mirror with lingering clarity.
Painted clouds, winding galleries connect crimson curtains,
Reflecting sun, mid-pond outshines colored banners.
Appreciation harmonious, still pipes and flutes are heard together,
Joy prolonged, further seen are magnolia boats light.
No need to seek immortal guests on seas,
Straight to Pénglái here in the imperial capital.
Capping Ceremony, Part Six
The Book of Rites states:
"At twenty, one is capped as an adult."
The "Jīao Tè Shēng" states:
"Capping at the eastern steps,
marks the succession.
Libation at the guest’s position,
adds to one’s accomplishment.
Three caps, each more honorable,
instruct his aspiration.
Capped and given a courtesy name,
respects his personal name."
First added is the black cloth cap,
next the leather cap,
then the ceremonial cap.
The cap more honorable, the aspiration greater.
The "Meaning of the Capping" states:
"Capping is the beginning of rites,
the most important of auspicious events.
For all cappings,
divine the day and choose the guest in the ancestral temple.
Present to the mother,
the mother bows to him;
present to brothers,
brothers bow to him.
Because he is an adult and they perform rites to him.
Thus after capping, attire is complete;
attire complete, then posture correct,
countenance orderly,
speech compliant."
Meaning attire not yet complete,
one cannot seek the three beginnings.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"A ruler’s son at fifteen may father a child,
capped and able to beget,
is according to rite."
Divining at the Gate Capping at the Steps
The Yí Lǐ states:
"For a shì’s capping rite,
divine at the temple gate."
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"Divining,
inquires of the Yì about the day’s auspiciousness.
Capping must divine the day at the temple gate,
emphasizing the gravity of the adult rite."
The Book of Rites, "Meaning of the Capping" states:
"First capping,
is the black cloth cap.
In high antiquity, caps were of cloth;
for solemn occasions, dyed black,
with hanging ties."
Confucius said:
"I have not heard of this;
after capping, discarding it is permissible.
The eldest son is capped at the eastern steps,
to mark the succession."
Cultivating Virtue Respecting the Name
The Yí Lǐ states:
"For a shì’s capping rite,
first addition blessing says: ‘On this fine month, auspicious day,
first add the primary cap.
Cast off your childish aims,
cultivate your adult virtue.
Longevity and fortune be yours,
grant you great blessings.’
Second addition says: ‘On this auspicious month, fine day,
again add your cap.
Revere your dignified demeanor,
refine carefully your virtue.
May your eyebrows last ten thousand years,
forever receive distant blessings.’"
The Book of Rites states:
"Capped and given a courtesy name,
respects his personal name."
Perfecting Virtue Instructing Aspiration
The Yí Lǐ states:
"For a shì’s capping rite,
third addition says: ‘With the year’s correctness,
with the month’s goodness,
all add your cap.
Brothers all present,
to perfect his virtue.
Yellow-haired without bounds,
receive heaven’s blessings.
The junior meets the senior.’"
One Offering Three Additions
The Yí Lǐ states:
"The capped one meets brothers,
brothers bow twice,
the capped one returns the bow.
Meets the assistant,
faces west and bows,
also like this.
Enters to meet aunts and elder sisters,
as meeting the mother,
then changes attire.
In dark formal robe and ceremonial cap,
presents gifts to meet the lady.
Then with gifts meets ministers, great officers, and village elders,
then toasts the guest with a one-offering rite.
The host repays the guest,
with bolts of silk and paired pelts."
"Three additions" see above.
Proper Appearance and Adorning the Face
The "Lǐjì" states:
"What makes humans human
are rituals and righteousness.
The beginning of rituals and righteousness
lies in straightening one's appearance,
adjusting one's countenance,
and harmonizing one's speech.
Thus it is said:
'Putting on a cap marks the beginning of ritual.' " Yìng Hēng wrote in "A Poem for Presenting Caps to Four Princes":
"Auspicious is the righteous month and day,
adorned garments crown the head.
All people beautify their appearance,
few can escape worldly dust and dirt."
Divining Day and Guest Selection
"The Lǐlùn" says:
"Wáng Biāo said that the ritual of capping does not necessarily require a specific day,
it is not strictly tied to the three prime periods.
Also, in the rites,
the summer cap is made with hemp sandals,
and the winter cap with leather sandals,
showing no fixed time is required."
"The Yílǐ" states:
"The ancestral figures complete the announcement,
and the host instructs the guest.
The guest politely declines,
but allows it,
and the host bows twice,
to which the guest returns the bow.
Three days before the event,
the guest is consulted similar to selecting an auspicious day."
Zhèng Xuán's comment says:
"Guest selection,
is to choose who can perform the capping ceremony."
Metal and Stone Rites, Display of Sacrificial Items
"The Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"In the ninth year of Duke Xiāng,
Jìn gathered the feudal lords to attack Zhèng,
and the duke escorted the Marquis of Jìn.
At the riverbank, the Marquis of Jìn entertained the duke,
and inquired about the duke's age.
Jì Wǔzǐ replied:
'In the year of 沙隨 meeting,
our ruler was born.'
The Marquis of Jìn said:
'It has been twelve years,
this is considered a full cycle.
When a star completes a cycle,
a prince at fifteen should have heirs,
when capped, should have children,
this is the rite.
The ruler can be capped now.'
The ministers prepared for the capping ceremony,
Wǔzǐ said:
'The ruler's capping must be conducted with a ritual ban,
with the music of metals and stones,
in the ancestral shrine.
Now, as our ruler is on a journey,
preparations cannot yet be completed.'
Request to borrow from the neighboring states for the ceremony."
"The Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"Mǎ Fáng's son Jù was a regular minor marquis,
in the sixth year, during the first month, he purified the palace,
and the emperor wished to cap Jù,
appointing him as Yellow Gate Cadet overnight.
Under the imperial eaves, sacrificial items were set up,
presiding the capping himself."
Showing Respect, Harmonizing Appearance
As mentioned above.
In the Later Hàn, Yìng Hēng's "A Poem for Presenting Caps to Four Princes"
In the fourth year of Yǒngpíng,
four brothers of his maternal cousin Wáng Jǐng were capped together,
thus he presented them this poem:
"Noble and refined are the four fine brothers,
reaching the age of eighteen.
Auspicious is the righteous month and day,
which crowns the head.
Though without rhinoceros horn cups,
wine is shared in succession for toasts."
In the Later Hàn, Huáng Xiāng's "Ode to the Emperor's Capping"
In the early spring of the third year,
the first ten days of the month of Jiǎnyín.
The emperor prepared to don the black cap,
selecting the auspicious day of Jiǎzǐ.
On that day, honored the Supreme Deity,
and on that occasion, attended to all the gods.
After completing the rites at the ancestral temple,
then returned to the palace.
In formal clothes, he was hosted to a banquet,
with grand chimes striking in the court.
Blessings extended to the barriers and supports,
and sovereigns from distant realms.
All offered toasts from golden vessels,
with jade cups promising longevity."
Sòng Xiàowǔ Dì's "Petition for Prince Jìanpíng's Capping"
Hóng divined a favorable day,
prepared the rites with decorum.
Talents akin to established virtue,
fulfilling the customary precepts.
Also, the "Petition for Prince Guǎnglíng's Capping"
Minister Dǐan's annual rites completed,
selected an auspicious day for the cap.
Concluding the cap ceremony,
in grand attire for the occasion.
Liáng Shèn Yuè's "Capping Blessing Address"
On this auspicious day,
the formal cap is first worn.
Established virtues already embodied,
childlike heart naturally transforms.
Guided thus will be accomplished,
never saying the way is distant.
Nourished by autumn's abundance,
sustained by spring blooms.
Not ashamed to ask others,
hence achieving high repute.
Progeny in thousands,
expanding the family legacy."
Weddings, Chapter Seven
The "Offices of the Grand Minister of Rites" in the *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"Through the marriage and capping ceremonies, men and women are made intimate and complete."
Intimate in their affection,
complete in their nature. The *Book of Rites* states:
"To unite the good of two surnames,
above to serve the ancestral temples,
below to continue the lineage for future generations."
It also states:
"Now the marriage ceremony
is the beginning of ten thousand generations.
Taking a wife from a different surname
is the means to attach distant clans and emphasize distinction."
It also states:
"A man takes a chamber at fifty,
a woman marries at thirty,
this refers to the middle antiquity."
The "Discussion by Shù Xī" states:
"A man may marry at sixteen,
a woman may marry at fourteen."
The "Marriage Ceremony" states:
"The groom enters holding a goose,
bows twice and presents the goose.
The groom goes out,
drives the bride's carriage,
hands her the strap and circles the wheel three times.
They share the sacrificial animal and eat,
join their nuptial cups
and rinse their mouths with wine."
Pronunciation yìn.
It also states:
"When a woman reaches fifteen and is promised in marriage,
she receives the hairpin and the ceremony is performed for her."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"Hūn (marriage)
means performing the rites at dusk, hence it is called hūn;
yīn (matrimony)
means a woman follows her husband, hence it is called yīn."
The *Ěryǎ* states:
"The groom's parents are called yīn,
the bride's parents are called hūn."
Also, the *Shìmíng* states:
"Hūn means completing the rites at dusk;
yīn means the woman's matchmaker.
The three explanations differ and agree with each other."
The *Yílǐ*:
"Marriage has six rites:
Nàcǎi (presenting betrothal gifts).
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"When about to marry,
one must first have a matchmaker convey the words,
then afterward send someone to present the gifts of selection.
A goose is used as the gift,
taking the meaning of the yin and yang coming and going."
Wènmíng (asking the name). Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Asking the name means
divining for the woman to determine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness."
Nàjí (presenting the auspicious divination).
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Divining in the ancestral temple and obtaining an auspicious sign,
then sending someone again to announce it;
the marriage matter is thus settled."
Nàzhēng (presenting the betrothal gifts).
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"For nàzhēng, black and crimson silks are used,
not a goose."
Qǐngqī (requesting the date).
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The yang proposes and the yin harmonizes;
the date should be divined by the husband's family for an auspicious day,
then someone is sent to announce it."
Qīnyíng (personally fetching the bride)."
For nàcǎi, wènmíng, and qǐngqī,
a goose is used in all cases.
The *Fāngyán* states:
"Leaving one's own home is called jià (to marry off)."
The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* states:
"For a woman, marrying is called guī (to return)."
The *Kǎogōng Jì* states:
"The Son of Heaven uses a grain-patterned guī to betroth a woman,
feudal lords use a large zhāng to betroth a woman."
The grain-patterned guī is seven cùn.
Zhèng Xuán states:
"This refers to adding nàzhēng gifts to the bundle of silk."
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Men and women, unless there is a go-between acting,
do not know each other's names."
Zhèng Xuán states:
"Méi (matchmaker) means móu (to plan),
planning to unite different kinds,
causing them to harmonize and complete."
Uniting in goodness / Harmonizing and completing
Both seen above.
Attaching distant clans / Emphasizing distinction
"Attaching distant clans" seen in the narrative.
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Taking a wife,
one prepares wine and food to summon fellow villagers, colleagues, and friends,
in order to emphasize the distinction."
Awaiting the rites / Preparing the objects
The *Máo Shī* states:
"Tightly bound the bundle of firewood,
the Three Stars are in the sky."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"The Three Stars are Shēn,
first appearing in the east in the sky.
Men and women await the rites to be complete,
just as firewood and fodder await human effort to be bound."
The *Liènǚ Zhuàn* states:
"Shēn Nǚ of Shào Nán was promised in marriage,
but the husband's family's rites were not complete.
The woman said:
'The husband's family slights me;
if one object is not prepared,
I will guard my integrity and uphold righteousness,
and will certainly die rather than go.'"
Making intimate and complete / Separating and joining
"Making intimate and complete" seen in the narrative.
The "Offices of the Matchmaker" in the *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"In charge of the separating of the myriad people."
The commentary states:
"Pàn means
half.
Obtaining a mate completes them into husband and wife."
Presenting the bird / Presenting the silk
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"The younger sister of Xú Wúfàn of Zhèng was beautiful.
Gōngsūn Chǔ betrothed her,
and Zǐ Xī sent someone to forcibly present the bird."
Also, Cuī Yīn's "Wedding Text" states:
"Carrying in the fine gifts,
tying the inner girdle and kerchief.
Presenting the bird and offering the goose,
matched with a deer skin."
"Presenting the silk" seen in the narrative.
Tying the kerchief / Applying the girdle
Huángfǔ Mì's "Poem of a Woman's Lament" states:
"The wedding rites are already settled,
the wedding ceremony approaches completion.
Applying the lapel and tying the kerchief,
thrice commanding with earnest instructions."
The *Chūnqiū Gǔliáng Zhuàn* states:
"When a woman marries,
the various mothers apply the girdle and sash.
Admonishing:
'Be careful to follow the words of your parents.'" Xú Miǎo's commentary states:
"Pán means
a waist pouch.
Shēn means
a sash.
The various mothers apply the waist sash,
and also admonish her."
Tying the kerchief / Applying the lapel
The *Máo Shī* states:
"The 'Eastern Hills' poem says:
'Personally tying her kerchief,
the ceremonies are ninety.'" The commentary states:
"Lí is a woman's fragrant tassel for the apron.
When a woman is about to marry,
her mother ties the kerchief and admonishes her."
"Applying the lapel" seen above.
Hundred chariots / Three circles
The *Máo Shī* states:
"This young lady goes to her new home,
a hundred chariots escort her."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"Liǎng means a chariot.
The son of a feudal lord,
marrying to a feudal lord,
is sent off and welcomed by a hundred chariots each."
"Three circles" seen in the narrative.
Driving the wheel / Feeding the horse
"Driving the wheel" seen in the narrative.
The *Máo Shī* states:
"This young lady goes to her new home,
I speak of feeding her horses."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"Zhī zǐ means this young lady,
referring to when a woman marries and goes to her husband."
Sòng Zǐ Qí Jiāng
The Máo Shī, in the "Héng Mén" chapter, states:
"Must one, in taking a wife,
Necessarily have a daughter of Sòng?
Must one, in taking a wife,
Necessarily have a Jiāng of Qí?"
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Why must it be a daughter of a great state to be taken as wife?
One merely seeks her chastity and obedience.
Using this as a metaphor for ministers,
why must they be sages?
One merely seeks their sincerity and filial piety.
Sòng
had the surname Zǐ;
Qí
had the surname Jiāng."
Bidding Farewell to Parents, Distant from Brothers
Dīng Yí's "Fù Fù" says:
"That a woman has her course to follow
Is indeed the constant principle across generations.
Bidding farewell to parents to speak of returning,
She serves the pure dust of her lord." [Note: "Pure dust" is a respectful term for the husband's presence.]
The Máo Shī, "Quán Shuǐ" chapter, states:
"A woman has her course to follow,
Distant from parents and brothers."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"A woman has the way of marriage and departure,
Becoming distant from her kin.
Ritual is based on human sentiment,
Allowing her to return for visits."
Holding Towel and Comb, Preparing for Sweeping and Sprinkling
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The Jìn crown prince Yǔ was a hostage in Qín.
About to flee back,
he said to Lady Yíng:
'Shall I go back with you?'
She replied:
'You are the crown prince of Jìn, yet humiliated in Qín.
Your desire to return
is indeed fitting, is it not?
My humble ruler sent this handmaid to serve, holding towel and comb,
to secure your position.
To follow you back
would be to abandon my ruler's command.
I dare not follow,
nor dare I speak of it.'"
Dù Yù's annotation says:
"Lady Yíng,
the woman given by Qín to marry Yǔ, was Huái Yíng.
'Handmaid'
is a humble term for a woman."
The Lǐ Jì states:
"Presenting a woman to the Son of Heaven is called 'preparing the hundred surnames';
to a feudal lord, 'preparing wine and sauces';
to a high minister, 'preparing sweeping and sprinkling.'"
Zhèng's annotation says:
"Presenting a woman is like sending a woman.
If the groom does not personally fetch her,
then the woman's family sends someone to deliver her.
These are the prescribed words.
'Surname' (xìng) refers to birth."
Sharing the Sacrificial Animal to Eat, Joining the Gourd Cups to Drink
The Lǐ Jì, "Hūn Yì" chapter, says:
"Sharing the sacrificial animal to eat,
joining the gourd cups to drink."
Respectfully noted: Sharing the sacrificial animal means sharing the same animal carcass.
Joining the gourd cups means taking one gourd, cutting it to make two cups for drinking wine.
Yìn
means to drink wine."
Men and Women Correct, Father and Son Intimate
The Máo Shī says:
"Men and women are correct,
marriages are timely."
The Lǐ Jì, "Hūn Yì" chapter, says:
"Marriage rites are what establish the distinction between men and women and set the righteousness between husband and wife.
When men and women are distinguished,
then husband and wife have righteousness.
When husband and wife have righteousness,
then father and son are intimate.
When father and son are intimate,
then ruler and minister are correct.
Therefore it is said: marriage is the foundation of ritual."
Three Days Without Music, Three Nights Without Extinguishing Candles
The Lǐ Jì, "Zēng Zǐ Wèn" chapter, says:
"The family that takes a wife
does not play music for three days,
thinking of continuing the family line.
The family that marries off a daughter
does not extinguish candles for three nights,
thinking of the separation."
Mid-Spring for Completing Marriages, Frost's Descent for Sending Off Daughters
The Zhōu Lǐ, "Méi Shì" office, says:
"In the month of Mid-Spring,
bring together men and women."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
Mid-Spring is when yīn and yáng interact,
to complete marriage rites,
following the timing of heaven.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's discourse says:
"The sage regards men and women, yīn and yáng,
their principles as of the same category.
The way of heaven tends toward autumn and winter when yīn energy congeals,
and toward spring and summer when yīn energy departs.
Therefore it is said:
'When frost descends, send off the daughter;
when ice melts, stop the killing.'"
All Use Autumn and Winter, Must Use Dusk and Dawn
The Shèng Zhèng Lùn says:
"For marriages, the ancients all used autumn and winter."
The Máo Shī says:
"The poplars at the eastern gate,
their leaves are lush."
Máo Cháng's commentary says:
"Men and women missing the season,
do not catch autumn and winter."
The Yí Lǐ, "Hūn Lǐ" chapter, says:
"For all actions, one must use dusk and dawn."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
"Using dawn is for the envoy;
using dusk is for the groom.
Respectfully noted: Sending the envoy to present the dark and light red silks,
the auspicious rite must use the dawn time;
the personal fetching uses the dusk time."
Hàn Dynasty Cài Yōng's "Xié Hé Hūn Fù"
Only the utmost excellence of nature and disposition,
No joy greater than that of husband and wife.
Receiving the creative transformation of essence and spirit,
Truly directed by the divine and luminous.
Affairs profound, subtle, and mysterious,
Indeed the beginning of human relations.
Examining the original source of the remote past,
Observing the guiding principles of yīn and yáng.
Qián and Kūn harmonize their firm and yielding,
Gèn and Duì influence their backs and calves.
"Gé Tán" fears missing the season,
"Biāo Méi" seeks the many gentlemen.
Only in the flourishing age of peace and harmony,
Do men and women attain their proper age.
Marriages are harmonious with no opposition,
Spreading abundant happiness, joyful and flourishing.
The auspicious hour having arrived,
The wedding ceremony is held.
Two families adorned with grandeur,
Dignified ceremonies in proper order.
Honored guests and assembled friends,
Gathering in multitudes like clouds.
Carriages and robes illuminate the road,
Horses prance as if dancing.
Having reached the gate and screen,
Reins are tied, they alight from the carriage.
Matrons, tutors, attendants, and pages,
Goose-footed, stepping in file.
The beautiful woman in rich adornment,
Radiant like spring blossoms.
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Huá's "Shí Gǎn Hūn Fù"
Now the year is at Jǐsì,
Approaching the fourth mid-season.
Those marrying compete to seize the auspicious time,
A splendid, magnificent sight.
Continuing one after another on the road,
The gatherings for weddings
Are not lacking for a single day.
Thus I compose the "Gǎn Hūn Fù", saying:
"Those vulgar taboos of marriage,
Detest the 'ridgepole' being present at this time,
Force the coming year to approach,
Until the stellar cycle has not yet shifted, and so on."
Táng Dynasty Emperor Gāozōng's "Poem on the Emperor's Crown Prince Taking a Consort and Tàipíng Princess's Marriage"
Dragon Tower bright with dawn's light,
Lǔ Lodge opens its morning gates.
Gorgeous sun, rich makeup's shadow,
Low stars shed Wù's radiance.
Jade courtyard floats with auspicious hues,
Silver plaques adorned with lucky signs.
Clouds swirl, flowers wreathe the canopies,
Rosy mists drift, leaves bedeck the flags.
Carved chariots turn on emerald paths,
Stellar carriages return to cinnabar halls.
Pearl pendants chime on morning robes,
Jade discs open like round fans.
Fine headdresses array the splendid feast,
Orchid wine extends the fragrant banquet.
Phoenix music arrays the tiered steps,
Tortoiseshell mats present rare delicacies.
Dancing butterflies, divine incense fresh,
Songs part, scattering plain dust.
Joy condenses among happy noble kin,
Celebration joins the new marriage bond.
Summer's end, fiery breath ceases,
Cool early breeze stirs glorious morn.
Hoping then for all within the six directions' peace,
Together to enjoy ten thousand springs.
Later Hàn Qín Jiā's "Poem on Describing Marriage"
All auspicious signs have gathered,
Two families exchange joy.
Revering this new union,
The six rites are without fault.
Sheep and geese are all prepared,
Jades and silks are abundant.
The gentleman proceeds with the affair,
His dignified demeanor is most composed.
Ah, his appearance!
Solemn are his words.
It also says:
Numerous marriages,
Are the source of fortune and misfortune.
The woman of Wèi brought prosperity to Qí,
Bāo Sì destroyed Zhōu.
Trembling with fear,
Fearing they are not a match.
The spirits open the way to good fortune,
And indeed obtain a fine match.
My beloved,
Receives Heaven's blessings.
Jìn Zhāng Huá's "Poem on Feeling about Marriage"
I ride to visit the eastern town,
The eastern town bustles with activity.
Marriages are held at auspicious times,
Weddings avoid the "ridgepole" days.
Graceful maidens emerge from their chambers,
Lovely are the ladies from noble families.
Pale faces blush with rosy hues,
Beautiful eyes flow with clear brightness.
Splendid are the many relatives gathered,
But to me it seems ordinary.
Like the grass of late spring,
Its glory and bloom will not see the sun again.
Jìn Jī Hán's "Poem on a Married Couple"
I hold the reins of a hundred carriages,
You sing of gathering white southernwood.
I admire your virtuous and kind appearance,
You please the face of your kind mother-in-law.
Cut that double-threaded silk,
Place it on the shared-work silk wadding.
In summer, we fan with wing-to-wing fans,
In winter, we sit on qióngqióng felt.
When hungry, we eat from the same root grains,
When thirsty, we drink from the same stream.
In the morning, we steam a heart-sharing soup,
In the evening, we cook side-by-side flatfish.
We ladle with the joined-nuptial-cup wine,
Receive it with the interlocking-branch tray.
In the morning, we pick same-root gloss ganoderma,
In the evening, we gather twin-spike orchids.
By the balcony, we plant day-lilies,
In the central courtyard, we plant silk trees.
Liáng Hé Xùn's "Poem on Viewing a New Marriage"
In the misty evening, lotus emerges from water,
At rosy dawn, the sun shines on the ridgepole.
How does it compare to the flower-candle night,
When a light fan conceals the rosy makeup?
The groom is radiant,
On the mat, he naturally shines.
What saddens is the high carriage's departure,
Jade pendants sound as they leave the long corridor.
Chén Zhōu Hóngzhèng's "Poem on Viewing a New Bride"
Mòchóu at fifteen years of age,
Comes to be wed into the Zidū family.
The groom's face is like beautiful jade,
The bride's beauty surpasses peach blossoms.
Tearful, she gazes like evening rain,
Smiling, she resembles morning clouds.
Briefly putting aside the light silk fan,
Her beauty is judged beyond compare.
Yáng Shīdào's "Poem on Viewing a Marriage at Early Night"
In Luòchéng, flower-candles stir,
In the relatives' quarters, new moth-eyebrows are painted.
Hiding behind a fan, shyness should be habitual,
Full of emotion, sorrow is already much.
Soft weeping dampens the rouge powder,
A slight glance turns like flowing waves.
Even more laughable is the song of Wūshān,
Vainly telling of much evening rain.
Chǔ Liàng's "Poem on Chanting Flower-Candles"
The orchid path is filled with fragrant breeze,
The plum-wood ridgepole basks in warm slanting sun.
It is said the eastern rider comes,
To seek the southern path carriage.
Dimpled stars approach the night candles,
Brow-moon hides behind light gauze.
Do not say spring is slightly late,
There will surely be flowers that bloom.
Chén Zǐliáng's "Poem on Viewing a New Bride on Qīxī with Carriage Stopped Across the Lane"
Across the lane, the carriage curtain is halted afar,
Not again because of coming late.
Only saying the night is still shallow,
It is not yet time to cross the river.
Zhèng Yì's "Poem on Viewing a New Bride"
At first hairpin age, vying with peach and plum,
New makeup should signal the falling plums.
Seeming to follow morning clouds away,
Yet turning to come with evening rain.
Mixed pendants contain the wind's sound,
Clustered flowers open beyond the fan.
Cháng'é facing this night,
Why need long hesitation?
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem Playfully Presented to Pān Xú at the City Gate Welcoming Two New Brides"
Qín and Jìn are called an old match,
Pān and Yáng have generational kinship.
The three stars have already met,
The four virtues are gentle and bridal.
Cloud light is thin within the hair,
Moon shadow is new upon the fan.
Youthful years and made-up face,
Together make one fragrant spring.
Zhèng Guǐ's "Poem on Viewing Brothers Marrying on the Same Night"
Cherry blossoms open double calyxes,
Lush peach blossoms shine in rainy blooms.
Separate courtyards join in pendant sounds,
Behind fans, adorned beauty is preserved.
Facing the wind, both are like snow,
Reflecting splendor, together like rosy clouds.
Tonight, two goddesses,
Join in one immortal household.
Guō Zhèngyī's "Poem Presented in Harmony on the Crown Prince Taking a Consort and the Princess Descending in Marriage"
The cassia palace first dons the crown,
The orchid side-chamber early ascends with hairpin.
Rites abundant, the prince welcomes in Jìn,
Fragrant reputation descends in marriage to Qí.
Golden turtle opens auspicious knobs,
Precious pheasant ascends immortal branches.
Turning fans bear the night moon,
Raising banners shine upon evening rainbows.
Liú Yīzhī's "Poem on the Same Theme"
Dream of catalpa light on green steps,
Lush peach blossoms fill the purple palace.
Virtue excellent, imperial thoughts far-reaching,
Rites complete, state marriage honored.
Ten thousand households' fame spreads,
Three roads' precious music resounds.
Fragrant wheels send layered scenes,
Colored banners lead immortal rainbows.
Yuán Wànqǐng's "Poem on the Same Theme"
Departing light responds to spring evening,
Imperial descendant descends in autumn season.
Jade pendants harmonize in offering sounds,
Compared to jade, beautifying lush appearance.
Harmonious sounds ascend to phoenix side-chamber,
Intertwined shadows walk on phoenix steps.
Rèn Zhīgǔ's "Poem on the Same Theme"
Imperial descendant ascends green steps,
Royal princess descends from purple abode.
Starlight shifts mixed pendants,
Moonlight offers layered wheels.
Dragon banners flutter at earth's edge,
Phoenix pipes soar to sky's shore.
Pagoda tree shade floats on shallow rapids,
Imperial music fans light dust.
Jìn Pān Yuè's "Response to Zhì Yú's Admonition on New Marriage"
The former kings established rites,
Adapting to the times as proper.
Bowing to follow what is aspired to,
How could it contradict human nature?
A woman has no second return,
A man may have another engagement.
For a woman, beauty truly exists,
For a man, virtue truly exists.
Virtue lies in upholding correctness,
Beauty lies in not being deluded.
Both old and new are broadly embraced,
Righteousness is extended, principle attained.
Yet in matters of nature and emotion,
Truly difficult to settle the heart.
The gentleman over-thinks,
Thus I offer this clear admonition.
Eighth: Death and Mourning
Liú Xī's *Shìmíng* states:
"Death is 'sī' (extinction),
meaning to vanish and dissipate.
For feudal lords, it is called 'hōng' (collapse),
the sound of crumbling;
for senior officials, it is called 'zú' (end),
meaning final conclusion;
for gentlemen, it is called 'bù lù' (no more emolument),
meaning they no longer receive official salary.
Death is also called 'wùgù' (things decayed),
meaning all things rot and decay;
once confirmed dead, it is called 'shī' (corpse),
'shī' means to stretch out,
the bones and joints stretch and loosen,
unable to gather themselves again."
*The Book of Rites* states:
"Alive, he is called father;
dead, he is called 'kǎo' (completed);
'kǎo' means accomplished.
Alive, she is called mother;
dead, she is called 'bǐ' (compared);
'bǐ' means to compare,
meaning compared to the father it is the same.
Dying of old age is called 'zú' (end),
dying young is called:
'bù lù' (no emolument),
dying by enemy hands is called 'bīng' (soldier).
A man should not die in the hands of a woman,
a woman should not die in the hands of a man.
The ruler's wife dies in the main chamber,
senior officials and their principal wives die in their proper chambers.
An untitled wife dies in the lower chamber,
a gentleman's wife dies in her chamber.
Minor officers perform the recall,
those recalling wear court robes.
The ruler uses a dragon robe,
his wife uses a quēdí robe.
Senior officials use black and red,
their titled wives use tǎn yī.
Gentlemen use juébiàn caps,
gentlemen's wives use shuì yī.
In all recall rituals,
men are called by their personal names,
women are called by their courtesy names."
*Chūnqiū Shuōtící* states:
"Objects placed in the mouth are called 'hàn' (mouthful),
imitating food eaten while alive.
The Son of Heaven uses pearls,
feudal lords use jade,
senior officials use jade discs,
gentlemen use cowries."
*The Book of Rites: Sāng Dàjì* states:
"Dressing the corpse is called 'liàn' (encoffining),
minor dressing is inside the room,
major dressing is on the eastern steps.
The ruler uses bamboo mats,
senior officials use rush mats,
gentlemen use reed mats."
*Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"On the bed it is called 'shī' (corpse),
in the coffin it is called 'jiù' (bier).
'Jiù' means final,
no further change."
*Shuōwén* states:
"'Guān' (coffin) means to close,
it can cover the corpse.
Also called 'chèn',
also called 'dú',
a small coffin is called 'huì'."
*The Book of Rites* states:
"The Yǒuyú clan used earthenware coffins,
the Xiàhòu clan used 'jì zhōu' (fired earth enclosure).
'Jì',
pronounced zǐ yì fǎn.
The Yīn people used inner and outer coffins,
the Zhōu people used wall hangings and fans."
*Shìmíng* states:
"Objects sent with the dead are called 'míngqì' (spirit vessels),
vessels for the spirits,
different from those for the living."
*Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"'Fù' means to assist,
'fèng' means to hasten,
used to assist the living and send off the dead,
to remember the end and fulfill final intentions.
Goods and wealth are called 'fù',
carriages and horses are called 'fèng',
objects of enjoyment are called 'zèng',
clothing and coverings are called 'suì'.
Goods and wealth are called 'fù',
also seen in the *Gōngyáng*.
'Zèng' means to match,
'suì' means to bequeath."
*Chūnqiū Shuōtící* states:
"Knowing the living, then give 'fù';
knowing the dead, then give 'fèng'."
Also, the *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* states:
"Horses are called 'fèng',
clothing is called 'suì',
cowries and jade are called 'hàn',
money and wealth are called 'fù'."
The spirit disperses, the form remains.
*Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"Human life
is the gathering of qì;
gathered, there is life;
dispersed, there is death."
Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* states:
"Human death is like the extinguishing of fire.
When a person is ill and dying,
it is no different from a fire about to go out.
When fire goes out, the light vanishes but the candle remains;
when a person dies, the essence perishes but the form remains."
Fate exhausted, things decayed.
*The School Sayings of Confucius* states:
"Duke Āi asked Confucius:
'What is meant by human fate and nature?'
Confucius replied:
'What is divided from the Way is called fate;
what is formed into one is called nature;
transformed by yīn and yáng,
taking shape and emerging is called life;
when transformation ends and fate is exhausted, it is called death.
Thus fate is the beginning of nature,
death is the end of life;
where there is a beginning, there must be an end.'" Liú Xī's *Shìmíng* states:
"All five materials—
glue, lacquer, pottery, metal, leather—
dry and harden before becoming useful.
Since the Hàn dynasty, death has been called 'wùgù' (things decayed),
meaning all things eventually rot and decay."
Qì extinguished, essence exhausted.
Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* states:
"During Wáng Mǎng's time,
when reducing the number of Erudites and disciples of the Five Classics,
one settled old theories by night,
dying beneath the candle,
his concentrated thought unable to bear it,
his pulse ceased and qì was extinguished."
Yáng Quán's *Wùlǐ Lùn* states:
"Humans are born containing qì,
and die when their essence is exhausted.
Death is like 'sī' (extinction),
annihilation.
It is like fire:
when the fuel is exhausted, the fire goes out,
and there is no more light.
Thus after a fire is extinguished,
no remaining flame is left;
after a person dies,
no remaining soul remains."
Inevitable for humans, natural for things.
*Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Fàn Suī advised King Zhāo of Qín:
'Even with the strength of Wū Huò and Rén Bǐ,
or the courage of Mèng Bēn, Qìng Jì, and Xià Yù, they still die.
Death is what humans cannot avoid.'" *The Book of Hàn*:
"Emperor Wén's posthumous edict stated:
'We have heard
that all things under heaven that sprout,
all that live, inevitably die.
Death is the ultimate principle of heaven and earth,
the natural course of things.
Why should it be excessively mourned!'"
Suddenly passed away, silently long asleep.
Fù Xuán's *Four-Character Poem* states:
"Suddenly passed away,
fire extinguished, smoke vanished."
Cáo Zhí's *Skull Poem* states:
"Desolate and silent,
driven along with the Way.
Silently long asleep,
no joy surpasses it."
One coffin of earth, lodged among ten thousand ghosts.
*Huáinánzǐ* states:
"In life, I have a form of seven feet;
in death, I have one coffin of earth."
Also, Lù Jī's *Dirge for Nobles* states:
"Once dwelling in a home of four people,
now lodged among ten thousand ghosts."
Yúfán for encoffining, cowries and jade for the mouth.
*The School Sayings of Confucius* states:
"When Jì Píngzǐ died,
they intended to use the ruler's yúfán jade for his encoffining,
and presented him with pearls and jade.
Confucius heard of this and said:
'Sending off the dead with precious jade
is like exposing a corpse in the central plains,
showing people the path to illicit gain.'" *The Zuǒ Commentary* states:
"When joining Wú to attack Qí,
Chén Zǐháng ordered his men to prepare jade for the mouth."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"Jade in the mouth shows determination to die."
Unharnessing the outer horses to contribute to funeral expenses; using sacrificial robes as burial garments
The Book of Rites - Tan Gong says:
"When Confucius went to Wèi,
he encountered the funeral of his former hostel keeper.
He entered and wept for him mournfully.
Upon exiting,
he had Zǐgòng unharness the outer horses of his carriage and contribute them to the funeral expenses."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Fù means to assist with funeral expenses.
Horses harnessed side-by-side are called cān."
Tan Gong also says:
"In Wèi there was a Grand Historian named
Liǔ Zhuāng,
who was gravely ill."
The lord said:
'If his illness becomes critical,
even if I am in the midst of a sacrifice, you must inform me.'"
The lord bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and pleaded before the ancestral spirit tablet, saying:
'There is a minister named Liǔ Zhuāng.
He is not merely my minister,
but a minister of the altars of soil and grain.'"
Upon hearing of his death,
he requested to go,
and went without removing his sacrificial robes,
then used them as burial garments for him."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Not removing the lord's sacrificial robes to use as burial garments for a minister
shows closeness to the worthy."
Hàn Dynasty Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on a Skull"
Death is rest,
life is toil and labor.
The congealing of winter waters,
how can it compare to the thawing of spring waters?
Honors and rank upon one's person,
are not lighter than a speck of dust or a hair.
What Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu considered shameful,
what Bó Chéng Gāo Táng fled from.
Moreover, I have already transformed,
and roam free with the Dào.
Lí Zhū could not see me,
Zǐyě could not hear me.
Yáo and Shùn could not reward me,
Jié and Zhòu could not punish me.
Tigers and leopards cannot harm me,
swords and halberds cannot wound me.
I flow together with Yīn and Yáng,
I merge my simplicity with the Primordial Qì.
I take Creation as my parents,
I take Heaven and Earth as my bed and mat.
I take thunder and lightning as my drums and fans,
I take the sun and moon as my lamps and candles.
I take the Milky Way as my rivers and pools,
I take the stars as my pearls and jade.
My body joins with Nature,
devoid of emotion, devoid of desire.
Clarify it, it does not become clear;
muddle it, it does not become turbid.
Without walking, I arrive;
without haste, I pursue.
Jìn Dynasty Lǚ Ān's "Rhapsody on a Skull"
Whole skin vanished and gone,
white bones lie scattered.
Four limbs broken and hidden in the grassy thickets,
a lonely soul grieves within the Yellow Springs.
Life then returns to transformation,
light then returns to darkness.
Reaching above and below,
what thing is not thus?
Jìn Dynasty Lù Shìhéng's "Rhapsody on the Great Tomb"
Consider how time is squandered away,
how can the span of human life be measured?
Know that from vigor one reaches old age,
the body from old age reaches extinction.
Gaze upon the deep darkness of the yellow mound,
grieve for the obscured gloom of the underworld springs.
To dash a thousand chariots to pieces is like a single hair,
what value then has wisdom and cleverness?
In vain we make wishes for a moment's reprieve,
pointing to the evening light to swear our oath.
Suddenly, with a breath, vitality is gone,
abruptly, the spirit perishes and the form dies.
Looking upon the myriad things, leaving behind regret,
gathering a hundred thoughts, then passing away forever.
Sòng Dynasty Bào Zhāo's "Rhapsody on Mourning the Departed"
At dawn I climb the southern mountain,
gaze towards that central slope.
Mist envelops the autumn hibiscus,
wind whirls the cold creepers.
Desolate, desolate, wounding the heart,
how grievous it is.
Extinguished like exhausted smoke,
parted like a severed string.
Like a shadow vanishing from the ground,
like a star falling from heaven.
Abandoning a splendid chamber in an enlightened age,
closing the golden door in the underworld springs.
Forever with the mountains and rivers I end myself,
through a thousand ages, remote, never to return.
Longing for a single word from times past,
distant are the multitudes of generations in ancient years.
Later Hàn Dynasty Ruǎn Yǔ's "Poem of Seven Sorrows"
The prime of youth is hard to meet again,
wealth and honor do not return.
The fine time suddenly passes once,
the body becomes earth and ashes.
In the dark darkness, the chamber of the Nine Springs,
the long, long night terrace.
The body exhausted, strength spent,
the essence and soul have nowhere to go.
Fine delicacies are set out but not partaken,
sweet wine fills the cup and goblet.
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Zǎi's "Poem of Seven Sorrows"
How mound upon mound at Běimáng,
four or five lofty tombs are there.
I ask whose graves these are,
all say they are lords of the Hàn dynasty.
Gōng and Wén gaze distantly at each other,
Yuánlíng mound lush and abundant.
In the declining age, rebellion and chaos arose,
bandits and thieves like jackals and tigers.
The ruined earth exceeds a clod,
the side chambers open their dark doors.
The pearl casket parted from the jade-like body,
treasures and jewels seen plundered.
Sòng Dynasty Wú Mài's "Poem on the Brink of Death"
A grieving song enters the pine-lined path,
a cup of wine offered, gazing at the green hills.
Who is not a mound of earth?
Differing only in coming before or after.
Liú Yǔnjì's "Poem on Seeing a Dead Man by the Roadside"
Desolate, merely seeing the sun,
in silent darkness, how can one know the years?
O soul, I cannot ask you,
you must have been upright as a bowstring.
Burial, Part Nine
The Book of Rites says:
"Burial means to conceal,
to conceal means one wishes others not to see it."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"The Son of Heaven is buried after seven months,
when all within the same tracks have arrived;
feudal lords after five months,
when allies have arrived;
great officers after three months,
when colleagues of equal rank have arrived;
gentlemen after more than a month,
when external relatives by marriage have arrived."
The Shì Míng says:
"Burial not according to ritual is called mái (burying),
mái means to let fall into ruin.
Hastening to make it rot and decay, that is all.
Not being buried is called qì (abandonment).
Not obtaining the corpse is called juān (loss),
lost in another territory.
Lowering the coffin into the grave is called biǎn.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn writes it as xiáng,
pronounced bēi liǎn fǎn.
" The Book of Rites says:
"For a lord's burial, a chūn carriage is used,
with four fú ropes and two stone tablets,
guiding the coffin with feather-decked canopies;
for a great officer's burial, a chūn carriage is used,
with two fú ropes and two stone tablets;
guiding the coffin with thatch;
for a gentleman's burial, a carriage is used,
with two fú ropes and no stone tablets."
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
"Zǔ zài means
first loading it in the courtyard,
mounting the axle cart,
taking leave from the ancestral and paternal temples,
therefore it is called zǔ zài."
The Shì Míng says:
"Pulling from the front is called fú,
fú
means to set forth,
to set the carriage in motion to make it go.
Fú is pronounced fú,
the Zhōu Lǐ writes it as fú.
" The Dù Yù Yàojí says:
"For all funeral processions,
the Son of Heaven has six fú ropes,
feudal lords four,
great officers three,
gentlemen two."
Scarlet Bird and Azure Crow
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shí Yí Jì" states:
"Shùn was buried in the fields of Cāngwú,
where there are birds like scarlet sparrows,
coming from Scarlet Island,
expelling multicolored breath,
diffuse like clouds,
named Píngxiāo Sparrow.
They can fly in flocks,
carrying soil to form a mound. "
"Xiàng Zhǒng Shū" says:
"Zhīgōng, son of Qīngwū, calls the mountains thrice connected,
named Umbrella Mountain,
can bury two thousand stones. "
Horse Mane and Dragon Ears
The "Lǐ Jì" states:
"During Confucius’s mourning,
someone came from Yān to observe,
lodging at Zǐxià’s residence.
Zǐxià said:
'This is a sage’s burial, yes?
It is people burying a sage.
What do you come to see?'
In the past, the Master said:
'I have seen burial mounds like halls,
seen them like barriers,
seen them like summer roofs,
seen them like cauldrons. '
I follow the cauldron type,
referring to a mound like a horse’s mane. "
"Xiàng Zhǒng Shū" says:
"Any burial with Dragon Ears,
noble position among the five marquises is assured. "
Golden Waterfowl and Jade Box
"Sān Fǔ Gù Shì" states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng’s burial at Líshān,
creating a mound fifty zhang high,
reaching three springs below,
a seven hundred bu perimeter.
Using moon pearls for sun and moon,
fish fat for lamps,
mercury for the sea,
gold and silver for waterfowl."
"Xī Jīng Zá Jì" states:
"The Han emperor and marquises during funeral processions,
all wore pearl garments and jade boxes,
shaped like armor,
connected with golden threads.
The boxes are carved with dragon, phoenix, turtle, and unicorn motifs,
called dragon-jade boxes at the time. "
Fang Mountain and Luán River
"Shǐ Jì" states:
"In the twentieth year of Lǔ Xiānggōng, Confucius was born,
born after Shūliáng Hé passed,
buried at Fang Mountain,
in Lǔ's eastern fields,
so Confucius questioned the location of his father's grave. "
"Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals" states:
"Long ago, Wang Jìlì was buried at the end of Wō River,
Luán River gnawing at the grave,
revealing the front of the coffin,
King Wén said:
'Ah,
Our predecessor surely wanted one last look at subjects and common people,
Heaven thus made the clear water reveal it. '
Thus the court was opened as a display,
common people all saw it. "
Erecting a Stele and Opening a Corridor
Zhōu Péi’s "Biography of the Worthies of Nányáng" states:
"Zhōu Yàn, styled Shàoqīng,
served as a decision clerk,
adjudged a criminal not deserving death,
prefect Liú Qián wanted to execute him.
Yàn opposed him,
up to nine times,
Qián became furious,
eventually executing him.
Later, the deceased's family submitted a petition,
requesting a review,
Qián saw Yàn in a dream saying:
'The prefect shall be held accountable,
for the day will come when secrets are revealed and he will be judged,
summoned to Cháng'ān,
destined for the silkworm chamber.'
Before reaching there,
Yàn bravely ended his life,
buried discreetly in the royal city,
a stele ensures the commemoration of his burial. "
Xiè Chuò's "Song Shíyílù" states:
"Huán Wēn was buried at the Qīngshān of Gūshú,
the mound leveled without markers,
a tunnel was opened beside the grave,
no stele,
thus obscured the location,
ensuring future generations would not know its whereabouts. "
Jade Coffin and Stone Outer Coffin
Yìng Shào’s "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
"Yè county magistrate Wáng Qiáo,
had a jade coffin displayed in front of the hall.
Qiáo said:
'The Heavenly Emperor summoned me,
to bathe and rest within it,
to be buried east of the city. '" Zhào Yè’s "Wú Yuè Chūnqiū" states:
"King Hélú of Wú’s daughter committed suicide,
Hélú mourned deeply,
she was buried outside the western Cháng Gate.
Dug into the ground to form a pool,
piled earth into a mountain,
beautiful stone for the coffin. "
Fish Lamp and Dragon Box
Both appear as above.
Northern Mang and Southern Ridge
"Xī Jīng Zá Jì" states:
"Āndìng Sōngzhēn,
was skilled in arithmetic.
In Emperor Chéng’s time,
Zhēn once calculated his own life would reach seventy-three years,
he indeed died at that age. "
It also states:
"On the northern slope of Máng,
four zhang west of the lone pine,
digging down seven chi,
I will be buried there.
Upon Zhēn’s death,
following his claim, they excavated,
discovering an ancient empty coffin,
he was buried therein. "
It also states:
"Cáo Chǎng was under Wú Zhāng,
after Zhāng was killed,
none dared to collect and bury him,
Chǎng, claiming to be Zhāng’s disciple,
collected and buried his body.
A monument was erected by Pínglíng people next to Wú Zhāng’s grave,
Zhāng was buried atop Dragon Head Mountain, on the southern ridge. "
Honoring with Carriage and Feathered Canopy
Fù Chàng’s "Jìn Officials’ Rites" states:
"When a Special Advancement official passes,
a ceremonial commander is sent to supervise military funeral matters,
granting special items from the Eastern Garden,
one of each type of five ceremonial garments,
one full set of clothes.
They receive a blue circling red-eared carriage,
forty people for dirges,
a square vehicle,
establishing a seven-lù carriage,
with a marked honor carriage. "
Dīng Fú’s "Han Official Protocols" states:
"When Empress Ling was buried,
she was presented with a vermilion canopy adorned with blue feathers and a four-horse chariot. "
Decorating Carriages and Attaching Banners
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"The carriages have curtain coverings,
black cloth skirts in diverging frames,
plain embroidered silk as roofs on the move. "
Zhèng Xuán states:
"A carriage is adorned as a transport vehicle for the coffin."
It also states:
"During Confucius’s mourning,
Gōngxī Chì marked it as such.
Adorning coffin walls with banners and fringes,
Zhōu customs;
setting up high screens,
Yin customs;
silk ritual banners,
Xià customs. "
Four-Inch Coffin, Five-Inch Outer Coffin
The "Lǐ Jì · Tán Gōng" states:
"Yǒuzǐ said:
'When the Master made provisions in Zhōngdū,
a coffin of four inches,
an outer coffin of five inches,
by this, one understands the desire not to decay swiftly. '"
Vermilion Utensils, Painted Coffin
"Eastern View Han Records · Liang Shāng Biography" states:
"Shāng passed,
awarded a vermilion shòuqì chariot and silver carved yellow jade box. "
"Xiè Chéng’s Latter Han Records" states:
"Emperor Hé posthumously enfeoffed the father of Empress Dowager Lǐng, Liang Sōng, as Marquis of Exalted Parents,
changed the internment,
awarded a painted coffin and jade box shroud from the Eastern Garden."
Halting the Coffin by the Roadside, Ceasing Mourning to Observe the Changes
The Book of Rites states:
"Zēngzǐ asked:
'When the funeral procession reaches the path,
and there is a solar eclipse, does this constitute a change,
and should we not proceed?'
Confucius replied:
'In the past, I followed Lǎo Dān to assist in a funeral in Xiàngdǎng.
When we reached the path, there was a solar eclipse.'
Lǎo Dān said:
'Qiū, halt the coffin on the right side of the road,
cease mourning to observe the changes,
and only after it brightens again, proceed.
This is according to ritual.'"
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Gèng means path;
biàn refers to altered rituals."
Not Reaching the Springs Below, No Odor Reaching Above
Mòzǐ states:
"The ancient sages established the laws of burial:
a paulownia coffin three inches thick,
sufficient to let the body decay;
three layers of burial shrouds,
In the past, Yáo went north to teach the Eight Di tribes,
and died on the way,
buried on the northern side of Gǒng Mountain.
Yǔ went east to teach in Yuè,
and was buried at Kuàijī Mountain,
not reaching the springs below,
with no odor reaching above.
Could it be that the Three Sovereigns lacked resources?
They established this as the method of burial."
Laid Upon Yellow Soil, Buried in Earth
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn states:
"When Zhào Zī was nearing his end,
he told his former officials Zhū Zhī and Xiāo Jiàn:
'Use a simple coffin and light burial goods,
lay me upon yellow soil,
so that I may decay quickly,
and return to the earth.
Do not allow my descendants to change this.'"
Also, the Biographies of Former Worthies of Chǔ states:
"When Hán Jì was dying,
he left instructions:
'Customs tend toward extravagance; replace them with frugality.
Frugality should be moderated by ritual.
If you respectfully heed my words,
dress me in contemporary clothes for burial,
bury me in the earth,
inter me immediately after the grave is dug,
and use earthenware for the burial offerings.'"
Applying Jade Cases, Burying Treasures
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi states:
"Pearls in the mouth and scales of jade
are now commonly used in burials."
The commentary states:
"Pearls in the mouth, objects in the mouth, and scales of jade
refer to applying jade cases to the deceased's body,
like fish scales."
The Discourses of a Recluse states:
"In life, they are not fully cared for,
but in death, lavish funerals are held.
Some use gold-threaded jade cases,
burying treasures, figurines, horses, and carriages,
constructing large tombs,
and planting many pines and cypresses."
Horses Refusing to Move, a Great Bird Walking Slowly
Records of the Investigation of Things states:
"When Hàn's Lord Téng, Xiàhóu Yīng, died,
as the funeral procession reached outside the Eastern Capital Gate,
the four horses refused to move,
pawing the ground and neighing sorrowfully.
They dug under the horses' hooves
and found a stone outer coffin,
with an inscription reading:
'A fine city, lush and dense,
after three thousand years, seeing the white sun.
Alas, Lord Téng dwells in this chamber.'
So they buried him there,
calling it the Horse Tomb."
Huá Qiáo's Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Yáng Zhèn served as Grand Commandant.
The Regular Palace Attendant Fán Fēng was arrogant and unrestrained,
and Yáng Zhèn often admonished him earnestly.
Because of this, they slandered Yáng Zhèn together,
and he was dismissed and sent back to his commandery.
He then drank poison and died.
On the day of his burial, a great bird came,
perched on a tree,
then after a while descended to the ground and walked,
slowly pacing to the front of the coffin, where it stopped and stood,
lowered its head and shed tears.
People gathered to hold it,
but it showed no fear."
Later Hàn Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Tomb"
Thus the hall was erected,
thus its dwelling was arranged.
In winter, it is not cold;
in summer, it is not hot.
Here sacrifices reside,
here spirits dwell.
Jìn Lù Shìhéng's "Rhapsody on Moved by the Mound"
In life, proud of one's traces in the present world;
in death, sharing a dwelling in a single mound.
The form and bones are hidden, sinking below;
the wandering soul floats upward.
Following yīn and yáng, melting and refining,
entrusting to mountains and plains as fields.
Beauty and ugliness blend into one;
who can recognize what they cultivated?
One must transcend the age and gaze afar;
why cling to these trivial displays?
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on Watching the Burial of Wèi Zhēng"
The palace gates gather golden saddles;
the imperial park moves the jade carriage.
The wild outskirts grieve the new parting;
the river bridge is not the old farewell.
A dismal sun shines on sinking peaks;
sorrowful clouds follow the canopy's turn.
Mournful pipes intermittently break;
sad banners suddenly furl and unfurl.
Gazing and gazing, where does emotion end?
Streaming and streaming, tears fall in vain.
No longer the people of former times;
with whom to spend the fragrant spring?
Liáng Hé Xùn's "Poem on a Lonely Tomb by the Roadside"
A lonely tomb by the roadside,
the road built, now already ruined.
Vainly suspecting years accumulated,
not knowing hills and valleys shifted.
How many times autumn leaves yellowed,
together seeing spring streams flow.
Golden silkworms cannot weave;
jade trees never bear buds.
People galloping on the path,
singing and laughing in their extravagance.
Today is not tomorrow;
pitiable, how near this is?
Liáng Yú Qiān's "Poem on Wandering in Cháoshān, Moved by an Ancient Tomb"
Tall woods accompany dawn and dusk;
a lone ridge rests by the river village.
Sparse pines embrace clear waters;
dense bamboos fill the plain.
A desolate tomb changes frozen leaves;
low ridges alter with the years' roots.
Western light, long catalpas fall;
urging you, the cup before the knee.
Chén Yīn Kēng's "Poem on Passing by an Ancient Tomb"
A reclining pine near an ancient tomb;
its age should be deep.
The memorial pillar could hold a candle;
the stele's writing desires gold.
A distant tomb ruined by the road;
a wild tunnel invaded by fields.
Dense wild fog gathers;
dim, the mound's sun sinks.
The hanging sword—where is it now?
Wind in the poplars, empty, sings alone.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem in Response to Yánghóu Seeing Off the Burial of Yuán Jīnzǐ"
Dark springs open the tunnel path;
white sun shines on the fine city.
Once lamenting this road;
a thousand years, how many wounded feelings?
Autumn rain grieves the pine's color;
chill wind swallows the evening sounds.
Returning clouds toward the valley, late;
returning willows against the mountain, light.
Only during the fifteenth night,
the mound's moon temporarily bright.
Suí Yǔ Xìn's "Poem on Seeing Off the Burial of Monk Jiǒng"
Dragon Spring today is sealed;
the stone cave immediately closed.
The jade case destroys the talking staff;
the suspended river falls, the sharp debate.
The incense burner still is cypress;
the yak-tail whisk becomes a pine.
The city gate not ten lǐ away;
mountains winding, already many layers.
Still hearing the incense pavilion's chants;
still listening to the bamboo grove's bell.
Seeing off the guest, wind and dust crowd;
cold outskirts, frost and dew thick.
If the spiritual nature does not perish;
where, then, does the divine principle lie?
Gàn Bǎo's "Sōu Shén Jì" states:
"Wǎngē (dirges) are
the music of the mourning household,
the harmonized voices of those holding the guiding ropes of the hearse.
Dirge lyrics include the two pieces 'Xiè Lù' (Dew on the Onion) and 'Hāo Lǐ' (Mugwort Village).
They originated from Tián Héng's disciples.
When Héng committed suicide,
his disciples, grieving for him, sang these sorrowful songs.
They said a person is like dew on an onion leaf,
easily dried and gone.
It is also said that when a person dies,
their spirit returns to Hāo Lǐ.
Hence there are these two pieces.
The first piece says:
'How easily the morning dew on the onion dries;
tomorrow morning dew will form again,
but once a man dies and leaves, when will he ever return?'
The second piece says:
'Whose land is Hāo Lǐ?
It gathers spirits, wise and foolish alike.
How the ghostly bailiff urges us on!
A man's life allows no slightest hesitation.'
It was not until Lǐ Yānnián that they were separated into two distinct tunes:
'Xiè Lù' to escort princes and nobles,
and 'Hāo Lǐ' to escort officials and commoners,
performed by the pullers singing them."
There are also Long Songs and Short Songs,
speaking of the length of one's lifespan,
which cannot be recklessly sought.
Yú Bìn (Burial Lament) Tián Gē (Field Song)
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states:
"When Wú fought with Qí,
the Qí man Gōngsūn Xià, about to go into battle,
ordered his followers to sing the Yú Bìn."
Dù Yù's commentary says:
"Yú Bìn
is a burial song,
showing a resolve to die."
Qiáo Zhōu's "Fǎ Xùn" states:
"The dirges of today
originated when Emperor Gāozǔ summoned Tián Héng.
Upon reaching Hù Xiāng,
Héng killed himself.
His attendants pulled the hearse to the palace,
but dared not weep aloud.
Therefore they made this song to convey their sorrowful sounds."
Sōng Yún (Pine Clouds) Xiè Lù (Dew on the Onion)
Jiāng Zhìquán's "Dirge for Imperial Concubine Xuān" says:
"The cassia burial garments arrive, dust lies still;
the mats and vessels ultimately remain empty.
Clouds and pines now gather dew;
wind through grass already sounds across the plain."
Wēn Zǐshēng's "Dirge for Prince Qīnghé, the Chancellor of State" says:
"The lofty gate, how could it change its track?
The winding pond still holds lingering ripples.
Who would have thought beneath the blowing tower,
it would turn into the 'Dew on the Onion' song."
Líng Chàng (Bell Chanting) Fú Ōu (Rope Chants)
Tán Dàoluán's "Xù Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"Four or five years before Prince Xī of Wǔlíng was defeated,
he took pleasure in dirges.
He would shake a large bell himself,
making his attendants sing in response."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"The birth of rope chants
necessarily arises from urging on the labor."
Sīmǎ Biāo's commentary says:
"Fú
means pulling the guiding ropes.
'Urging on the labor' means if the effort is slack or slow.
The reason for having chants while pulling the ropes
is because people's efforts are slack, slow, uneven, and not urgently quick."
Liáng Huì (Liáng's Gathering) Yuán Yóu (Yuán's Outing)
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hàn Shū" states:
"Grand General Liáng Shāng, on the third day of the third month, gathered at the Luò River.
After the music and performances reached their peak,
they concluded with the song 'Dew on the Onion',
causing those seated to shed tears."
The "Péi Qǐ Yǔ Lín" states:
"Zhāng Zhàn liked to plant pines before his studio
and raise mynah birds.
Yuán Shānsōng, when going on outings,
liked to have his attendants perform dirges.
People of the time said Zhāng had corpses laid out beneath his roof,
and Yuán conducted funerals on the road."
Wèi Miào Xí's "Dirge Poem"
Alive, I roamed the capital city;
dead, I'm cast away in the wilds.
At dawn I depart from the lofty hall;
by dusk I lodge beneath the Yellow Springs.
The white sun enters Yú Yuān;
the hung chariot rests its team of four.
Though Creation is divine and wise,
how can it preserve me again?
Form and appearance gradually fade and perish;
teeth and hair constantly fall away.
Since ancient times it has been thus for all;
who can escape this fate?
Jìn Lù Jī's "Dirge Poem"
Quiet now within the inner gates,
listen to my 'Dew on the Onion' poem.
Life and death are inevitably different states;
the farewell sacrifice will have its time.
Setting aside the cups between the pillars,
opening the bier to advance the spirit carriage.
The farewell feast, sorrowful, no return;
departing to lodge, no date of coming home.
Another
How towering the layered mounds,
the dark lodge hidden among them.
Vast and boundless to the four extremes,
lofty and high, imitating the azure sky.
Listening sideways to the dark ditch's surge,
lying down to view the sky-well suspended.
How vast and expansive the tomb's night,
the great dusk, how could it dawn again?
Others go and have returning years;
my journey has no year of return.
Once I dwelt in a home of four men;
now I am neighbor to ten thousand ghosts.
Once I was a body of seven feet;
now turned to ash and dust.
Gold and jade I once wore;
now a goose feather, I cannot stir.
Plump flesh feasts the ants;
bones and frame forever vanish, leveled to nothing.
The hall of longevity welcomes goblins;
in emptiness, they host each other.
Ants, why your anger towards me?
Goblins, what kinship have I with you?
Beating my breast, heart pained by bitterness,
a long sigh, none to whom it can be told.
Sòng Táo Qián's "Dirge Poem"
How vast and wild the overgrown grass,
the white poplars too sigh mournfully.
In the harsh frost of the ninth month,
they escort me beyond the distant outskirts.
On all four sides, no human dwells;
high grave mounds stand sheer and steep.
The horse lifts its head and neighs to heaven;
the wind of itself turns bleak and desolate.
Once the dark chamber is closed,
for a thousand dawns it will not open again.
For a thousand dawns it will not open again,
the wise and accomplished can do nothing.
Those who came just now to see me off,
each has also returned to their own home.
Kinsmen may retain some lingering grief;
others have already started singing.
Having died, where shall I go?
Entrusting my body to the same mountain slopes.
Běi Qí Zǔ Xiàozhēng's "Dirge Poem"
In former days I drove a team of four,
paying court to the emperor at Chángyáng Palace.
Banners hung beyond the white clouds,
riders hunted within the red dust.
Now I come towards the Zhāng riverbank,
the plain canopy turns in the mournful wind.
Glory, splendor, song, and laughter—
all ten thousand things become utterly empty.
Suí Lú Sīdào's "Dirge Poem for Prince Péngchéng"
At dawn the palace gates open early,
dimly the spirit carriage sets forth.
Just now seeing the phoenix tower recede,
soon watching the dragon mountain disappear.
Still arrayed are the riders of five camps;
still gathered are the troops from three rivers.
The retinue and guard solemn, not yet returned;
the empty mountains shine with the autumn moon.
Also "Dirge Poem for Princess Cháng of Lèpíng"
The dressing tower faces the imperial way,
the music terrace overlooks the scenic lodge.
Wind enters the early spring morning court;
moonlight fills the cool autumn night.
Before song and laughter could finish,
already I sense life's glory fading.
When by the banks of the Luò River,
in the fields of magic mushrooms, will the dragon team be unharnessed?
Zhū Zǐshē's "Dirge Poem for Empress Wéndé"
The divine capital recedes from the purple road,
white horses yoke the traveling carriage.
Northward goes the road across the bridge,
westward divides the clear Wèi River's flow.
Cold light vanishes into the burial mound;
frosty air enters the pines and catalpas.
Today on the road to the spring terrace,
it is not for a visit to Zhuó Lóng.
Lǐ Bǎiyào "Elegy for Empress Wéndé"
Wandering around the Two-Rites Hall,
sorrowfully gazing at the Jiǔchéng Terrace.
The jade carriage finally bids farewell to the feast,
the jade box remains forever closed.
The wilderness is vast with dark winds accumulating,
the river longs for birds to come.
The cold mountain is silent and the evening is already late,
the imperial burial carries on with remaining sorrow.
Shàngguān Yí "Elegy for the Late Princess of Beǐpíng"
Leaves fall, the garden and pond are vast,
the courtyard empty, wind and dew cold.
The clear sounds of the northern lanes are silent,
the fragrant grasses of the southern rise are withered.
Distant aura still highlights the sword,
floating clouds reflect the cap.
In silence, the qín platform stands late,
autumn shadows fill the well and scrolls.
Also "Elegy for Director Xiè"
Gently secluded, the fine city is remote,
green pines and cypress trees in twilight.
The Lu curtain flutters, about to be rolled up,
the return of the chariot evokes sorrowful glances.
The Chu bell encircles Mount Lú,
the Hu pipes approach the armory.
Regretfully, the suburbs and fields are calm,
smoke rises as returning birds fly past.
Also "Elegy for the Princess of Gāomì"
The Xiāng riverbank hides spiritual traces,
the É Terrace quiet with auspicious sounds.
Phoenix follows the distant flute,
luán descends into the deep mirror.
Frost causes the flowers to fall,
in the wind, the silver candles are breached.
Desolate, the Píngyáng pavilion stands,
the moon cold, the chambers deep.
Also "Elegy for Dowager Consort of King Jiāng"
The yellow crane’s sad song ends,
pepper flowers leave a pure ode.
Dust condenses in the neighboring mirror,
nets gather fish at the harmonious door.
The silver extinguishes, wind candles spent,
pearls faded, the night's wheel is void.
There is another path to South Tomb,
a secluded thicket with sparse leaves.
Luò Bīnwáng "Elegy for the Court Musician"
Whose family land is in Sōng?
Which generation's tomb by the Pine Gate?
A hundred years—thirty thousand days,
one farewell spans thousands of autumns.
The returning sunlight is cold with no shadow,
the distant spring is frozen, no flow.
All things inevitably transform,
where can you hide the tomb?
Liú Yīzhī "Elegy for Emperor Xiàojìng"
Warning against extravagance, the illusionary carriage,
bestowed name records great fame.
Ground leaves turn the Cāngwú wilderness,
the path passes Zǐjù City.
Heavy reflections cover cold hues,
the morning gale breaks the dawn sound.
Once followed the celestial steed afar,
snow and dew sorrowfully give rise to shadows.
Cuī Róng "Elegy for Empress Zétiān"
At night displayed, the empty ban on night,
evening descends on the empty mountain shade.
Sun and moon dim the span of an inch,
heaven and earth suffer—what heart remains?
The purple hall's golden fittings are dark,
the yellow mausoleum's jade throne is deep.
The mirror case never opens again,
the Holy Sovereign's tears soak garments.
Also
the front palace stops court sessions,
the Long Tomb joins in burial and returns.
Mountains and rivers no longer visible,
cultural relics entirely changed.
The shadowy moon obscures the middle road,
the Xuan star falls on the Taiwei.
Only the filial piety of the Son of Heaven remains,
blessing clouds fly over the pines.
Elegant Music First Grade
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"The Son of Heaven observes the customs to create music."
The Shìběn states:
"Kuí created music."
Also, the Lǐjì states:
"Kuí first established music,
to reward the feudal lords."
The Lǐjì states:
"Music,
with its clarity and brightness, resembles heaven;
with its vastness and greatness, resembles earth;
with its beginning and end, resembles the four seasons;
with its circulation, resembles wind and rain."
The Báihǔtōng states:
"Music (yuè) is joy (lè).
The nobleman delights in attaining the Way,
the petty man delights in attaining his desires.
Sound (shēng) is that which sings;
tone (yīn) is that which harmonizes.
The firm and yielding, clear and turbid,
blend and harmonize with each other."
The Hànshū states:
"The five tones are:
gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ.
Shāng means 'to manifest';
when things mature, they can be manifested and measured.
Jué means 'to touch';
things touch the earth and emerge,
bearing pointed horns.
Gōng means 'center';
it dwells in the central position,
spreads to the four directions,
initiates the song and gives birth,
serving as the foundation of the four tones.
Zhǐ means 'blessing';
things are grand and abundantly blessed.
Yǔ means 'dwelling';
things gather and are stored, covered by a dwelling.
In terms of the five phases, jué corresponds to wood,
in the five constants, to benevolence,
in the five affairs, to demeanor.
Shāng corresponds to metal, to righteousness, to speech;
zhǐ corresponds to fire, to ritual, to sight;
yǔ corresponds to water, to wisdom, to hearing;
gōng corresponds to earth, to trustworthiness, to thought.
In terms of ruler, minister, people, affairs, and things,
then gōng is the ruler,
shāng is the minister,
jué is the people,
zhǐ is affairs,
yǔ is things."
The Ěryǎ, "Shì Yuè" states:
"Gōng is called chóng,
shāng is called mǐn,
jué is called jīng,
zhǐ is called dié,
yǔ is called liǔ."
Guō Pú notes:
"These are all alternative names for the five tones,
their meanings are not detailed."
The Wǔjīng Tōngyì states:
"The eight sounds are:
metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, clay, leather, wood.
Metal is bells,
stone is chimes,
silk is strings,
bamboo is pipes,
gourd is shēng,
clay is xūn,
leather is drums,
wood is zhù yǔ."
Zhù,
pronounced chāng lù fǎn,
yǔ pronounced yǔ.
Shìzhì's Jiàng Yuè Lù states:
"Metal includes bells, bó, zhuó, náo;
stone includes chimes;
silk includes qín, sè, kōng, hóu, zhēng, zhù, pípá;
bamboo includes chí, dí, yuè, xiāo, guǎn;
gourd includes shēng, huáng, yú;
clay includes xūn fǒu;
leather includes drums;
wood includes zhù yǔ."
The Guóyǔ states:
