"Metal favors yǔ,
stone favors jué,
bamboo favors shāng,
silk favors gōng,
gourd and clay favor zhǐ.
Lǜ are used to harmonize music,
lǜ are used to balance tones.
Metal and stone set it in motion,
silk and bamboo carry it forward.
Singing chants it,
gourd spreads it,
earthenware supports it,
leather and wood regulate it.
When things attain their constancy, it is called music;
where music gathers is called tone;
tones mutually supporting is called harmony;
the fine and great not exceeding each other is called balance."
The Yuè Wěi states:
"The six lǜ are:
Huángzhōng,
eleventh month;
Dàcù,
first month;
Gūxiǎn,
third month;
Ruíbīn,
fifth month;
Yízé,
seventh month;
Wúyì,
ninth month.
The six lǚ are:
Dàlǚ,
twelfth month;
Jiázhōng,
second month;
Zhònglǚ,
fourth month;
Línzhōng,
sixth month;
Nánlǚ,
eighth month;
Yìngzhōng gǎo,
tenth month.
The yang are lǜ,
the yin are lǚ,
collectively called the twelve monthly lǜ."
Huángdì's music was called Xiánchí,
chí pronounced shī,
the Way was bestowed upon the people,
therefore it was called:
"Xiánchí."
Zhuānxū's was called Wǔjīng,
the Way has roots and stems,
therefore it was called:
"Wǔjīng."
Dìkù's was called Liùyīng,
the Way has essence and splendor,
therefore it was called:
"Liùyīng."
Yáo's was called Dàzhāng,
in Yáo's time, benevolence and righteousness greatly prevailed,
laws and measures were clear and manifest,
therefore it was called:
"Dàzhāng."
Shùn's was called Xiāosháo,
sháo means 'to continue'.
Shùn succeeded Yáo,
following and practicing his Way,
therefore it was called:
"Xiāosháo."
Yǔ's was called Dàxià,
Yǔ succeeded the two emperors,
the Way emphasized great peace,
therefore it was called:
"Dàxià."
The Yīn's was called Dàhuò,
Tāng arose amidst decline,
continuing the Way of the former kings,
therefore it was called:
"Dàhuò."
Huò pronounced hù.
The Zhōu's was called Shuò,
also called Dàwǔ."
Zhōu arose amidst decline,
deliberating upon the Way of Wén and Wǔ,
therefore it was called:
"Shuò."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"Performing grand music always uses bells and drums,
performing the Jiǔ Xià.
Xià are names of musical movements,
like performing wind and percussion music today.
First, Wáng Xià,
performed when the Son of Heaven enters or exits.
Second, Sì Xià,
performed when the sacrificial representative enters or exits,
also performed when the host and guest enter the gate,
performed when entertaining the four directions.
Third, Zhāo Xià,
performed when the sacrificial animal enters or exits.
Fourth, Nà Xià,
performed when entertaining the four directions.
Fifth, Zhāng Xià,
performed when receiving the meritorious.
Sixth, Qí Xià,
performed when great officers sacrifice.
Seventh, Zú Xià,
performed when clansmen attend.
The eighth is called Gài Xià,
played when guests are drunk and leave.
The ninth is called Ào Xià.
Played when the duke enters or exits.
The Son of Heaven uses the music of six dynasties for sacrifices.
The first is called Yún Mén,
the second is called Xián Chí,
the third is called Xiāo Sháo,
the fourth is called Dà Xià,
the fifth is called Dà Huò,
the sixth is called Dà Wǔ.
Shěn Yuē's Sòng Shū says:
"Qín music is called Wǔ Xíng,
changed by Qín Shǐ Huáng.
Hàn music is called Wén Shǐ,
changed by Gāozǔ from Sháo Wǔ.
Wǔ Dé,
created by Gāozǔ.
Dancers hold shields and axes,
symbolizing that the empire's music has used martial means to eliminate chaos.
Ān Shì,
formerly called Fáng Zhōng,
changed by Qín to Shòu Rén,
changed by Xiào Huì to Ān Shì.
Zhāo Róng,
created by Gāozǔ,
derived from Wǔ Dé.
Lǐ Róng,
created by Gāozǔ,
derived from Wén Shǐ and Wǔ Xíng.
Jiā Zhì,
created by Shū Sūn Tōng,
to welcome spirits.
Sì Shí,
created by Wén Dì.
Zhāo Dé,
created by Xiào Wǔ Dì,
offered at Tàizōng's temple.
Shèng Dé,
created by Xiào Xuān,
offered at Tàizōng's temple.
Yún Qiáo, Yù Mìng,
both are Hàn music,
used to sacrifice to heaven and earth.
Bā Yú.
In early Hàn, Bā Yú assisted Hàn with merit,
this dance was created.
Wèi music is called Zhāo Wǔ,
changed from Hàn's Bā Yú.
Zhèng Shì,
changed from Hàn's Ān Shì,
also used as a hymn for spirits.
Yíng Líng,
changed from Hàn's Jiā Zhì.
Wǔ Sòng,
changed from Hàn's Wǔ Dé.
Zhāo Yè,
changed from Qín's Zhāo Róng.
Fèng Xiáng,
changed from Hàn's Yún Xiáng.
Líng Yìng,
changed from Hàn's Yù Mìng.
Dà Sháo,
changed from Hàn's Wén Shǐ.
Dà Wǔ.
Changed from Qín's Wǔ Xíng.
Zhōu Lǐ says:
"The Son of Heaven has palace chimes,
arranged on four sides like a palace.
Feudal lords have xuān chimes,
removing the south side,
leaving three sides,
shaped like a carriage,
also called curved chimes.
Grand masters have pàn chimes,
further removing the north side.
Scholars have tè chimes.
All music performances are called playing,
nine performances complete,
called nine movements.
The end of music is called què,
half of all chimes and stone chimes is called dǔ,
full is called sì.
Half means eight bells and eight stone chimes,
sixteen pieces on one rack.
Observing winds, examining customs
Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Líng Zhōu Jiū said:
'Drums are the carriage of sound,
bells are the vessel of sound,
the Son of Heaven observes winds to create music.'"
Yuè Xié Tú Zhēng says:
"Music listens to its sounds,
harmonizes with tones,
examines with customs,
verifies with categories of things."
Cleansing evil, washing away filth
Wǔ Jīng Tōng Yì says:
"When achievements are made, music is created;
when governance is settled, rites are established,
to prohibit extravagance,
cleanse evil intentions,
and achieve harmony."
Shǐ Jì says:
"All who create music
cause all people to wash away evil filth,
moderate fullness,
to adorn their nature."
Uniting love, establishing harmony
Lǐ Jì says:
"Music is
different forms uniting love."
Sūn Qīngzǐ says:
"Music
examines unity to establish harmony,
follows unity to establish order."
Manifesting virtue, displaying merit
Shěn Yuē's Sòng Shū says:
"Wèi ministers reported:
'Lièzǔ did not establish music and dance,
unable to manifest virtue and display merit.
Songs praise virtue,
dances symbolize events,
in writing,
civil and martial combined as bīn,
holding both civil and martial,
thus sage virtue is made clear.
We respectfully create music called "Zhāng Bīn Wén Wǔ Zhī Wǔ."'"
Wǔ Jīng Tōng Yì says:
"Music
symbolizes virtue and displays merit,
according to the appropriateness of events."
Harmonizing with, interacting in peace
Lǐ Jì says:
"Great music harmonizes with heaven and earth,
great rites align with heaven and earth."
Ruǎn Jí's discourse says:
"Music makes people's spirits peaceful,
prevents declining energy from entering,
heaven and earth interact in peace,
all things gather."
Five sections, four gatherings
Xǔ Shèn's Wǔ Jīng Yì Yì says:
"Music regulates all affairs,
thus having five sections."
Hàn Shū·Lǐ Yuè Zhì says:
"There are Zhèng's four gatherings,
Chǔ's four gatherings."
Sòng Yù's Gāo Táng Fù also says:
"Sound like yú and pipes,
five changes, four gatherings."
Ascending songs, arranging dances
Yí Lǐ says:
"The host ascends to receive the cup,
music ends,
ascends to sing Lù Míng."
Zhāng Héng's Dōng Jīng Fù says:
"Thunder drums rumble,
six changes completed.
Crowned with flowers, holding pheasant feathers,
arranging dances of eight rows."
Honoring virtue, guiding will
Zhōu Yì says:
"Thunder emerges, earth stirs, Yù,
former kings created music to honor virtue,
sincerely offering to God,
to match ancestors."
Wǔ Jīng Xī Yí says:
"Former kings established rites and music,
established rites to regulate affairs,
cultivated music to guide will.
Thus observing their rites and music,
order and chaos are known."
Connecting with spirits, perfecting nature
Shǐ Jì:
"Grand Historian said:
'Music
stirs blood vessels,
connects fluids and spirit,
harmonizing and rectifying the heart.'"
Hàn Shū says:
"Sound music washes away people's evil intentions,
perfects their upright nature,
transforms customs."
Adorning rhythm, forming patterns
Gōngsūn Nízǐ's discourse says:
"Music
examines unity to establish harmony,
Zhèng Dances and Qí Songs
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Southern Capital" states:
"Qí youths sing, and Zhào maidens stand in rows;
Seated, they sing southern songs; rising, they perform Zhèng dances."
Cuī Qí's "Seven Admonitions" states:
"For a moment, the singing pauses and turns;
At times, they chant Qí songs.
Joy reaches its peak, delight is utmost;
Drenched heads warm each other."
Six Movements and Five Descents
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"After six movements, they return to their positions,
To honor the Son of Heaven."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"The six performances symbolize the troops returning and mustering;
Returning to their positions
Means returning to their places and halting."
Wáng Sù comments:
"This symbolizes honoring heaven and earth."
Xǔ Shèn's "Different Interpretations of the Five Classics" states:
"The music of the former kings
Was used to regulate all affairs,
Thus it had five sections.
Slow and fast, beginning and end,
Following the middle pitch, they descend;
After five descents,
No further plucking is allowed."
Yān Pipes and Zhào Zithers
Yuán Ān's "Rhapsody on a Night Banquet" states:
"Strike the Yān pipes,
Tune the Qí reed instruments,
Draw out the gōng and zhǐ notes,
Sing of peace and prosperity."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The King of Qín, while drinking merrily, said:
'I have long heard that the King of Zhào is fond of music;
I ask the King to play the zither.'
A Qín court historian stepped forward
And wrote:
'On such-and-such year and month, the King of Qín met with the King of Zhào at Miǎnchí;
The King of Qín ordered the King of Zhào to play the zither.'" Bào Zhào's "Lyrics of White Ramie" states:
"Qín zithers and Zhào zithers accompany reed pipes and mouth organs."
Qiāng Flutes and Hú Reed Pipes
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén Jiézì states:
"The dí is a seven-hole yuè;
The Qiāng flute has three holes."
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng states:
"Yìng Shào's 'Han Imperial Procession' says:
'Cavalry carry gū.'" The Jìn "Protocols for the First Sericulture" states:
"When the imperial carriage halts, play the small gū;
When it departs, change to the large gū.
Gū is jiā.
Also, the Hú reed pipe;
The Han records mention its melodies,
But do not record their origins."
Five Stems and Six Gems
The "Diagrams and Prognostications on Music" states:
"Emperor Zhuānxū's music is called Five Stems."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"It can establish the roots and stems for the Way of the Five Elements."
The Liezi states:
"During the reign of King Mù of Zhōu, a transformed being came;
King Mù revered him as a deity.
He performed Chéngyún, Liùyíng, Jiǔsháo, and Chénlù to entertain him."
Zhāng Zhàn comments:
"Chéngyún
Is the music of the Yellow Emperor;
Liùyíng,
The music of Emperor Kù;
Jiǔsháo,
The music of Shùn;
Chénlù,
The music of Tāng."
Heavenly Music and Dew Harmony
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào fell ill
And was unconscious for five days.
Biǎn Què said:
'In the past, Duke Mù was like this;
Unconscious for five days,
He awoke on the seventh day,
After two and a half days.'
Jiǎnzǐ awoke
And told his ministers:
'I was at the Emperor's place and very happy;
I roamed with the hundred spirits in the Heavenly Music,
With grand music in nine performances and myriad dances,
Unlike the music of the Three Dynasties;
Its sound moved the heart.'" The "Diagrams and Prognostications on Music" states:
"At the beginning of the year,
Receiving qi from heaven,
Spreading it over the earth,
To bring forth the myriad things in season.
The nodes of the four seasons,
Their movements each have their divisions and sequences,
They must not overstep their constant measures;
This is called the music of Dew Harmony."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"Entering and exiting in season,
As in the monthly ordinances of the twelve months' governance;
Following their entry ensures no disasters or anomalies.
Dew Harmony
Means harmonizing to bring about sweet dew."
Great Xià and Accomplished Zhōu
The "Diagrams and Prognostications on Music" states:
"Yǔ's music is called Great Xià."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"His virtue could magnify all the Xià."
The Annals of Master Yàn states:
"The Grand Master of Qí said:
'The music of Accomplished Zhōu is the Son of Heaven's music;
I dare not perform it.'"
Song Bells and Dance Pipes
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Zhèng bribed the Marquis of Lǔ with two sets of song bells."
Dù Yù comments:
"A set
Is a row."
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The pipe master is in charge of teaching the sons of the state to dance with feathers and blow pipes."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"In the civil dance, some hold feathers and blow pipes;
This is the so-called pipe dance."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Jì Zhá of Wú saw the southern pipe dance."
Move Heaven and Earth, Communicate with Spirits
The Book of Hàn states:
"Music is what the sages use
To move heaven and earth,
Communicate with spirits,
And pacify the myriad people.
Thus, listeners all empty themselves and awe their spirits,
Delighting and receiving its flow.
Thereupon, all within the seas are clothed in its influence,
Its radiance renewed daily,
Without knowing how it is so."
The Book of Rites states:
"Ritual and music operate through yīn and yáng,
Communicating with spirits."
Illuminate Sun and Moon, Influence Mountains and Rivers
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"The Yellow Emperor performed the music of Xiánchí in the wilderness of Dòngtíng,
Playing it with the harmony of yīn and yáng,
Illuminating it with the light of the sun and moon."
The Guóyǔ states:
"Duke Píng of Jìn had composed new music;
Master Kuàng said: 'Music
Influences virtue to broaden it,
And through mountains and rivers to reach it.'"
Jiǎ Kuí comments:
"Music is what communicates the influences of mountains and rivers,
To reach its virtue."
Regulate the Eight Winds, Complete the Myriad Things
The Guóyǔ states:
"Metal is rubbed, stone is struck, silk and wood are plucked, gourds and bamboo are regulated, drums are beaten and played,
To regulate the eight winds."
Jiǎ Kuí comments:
"The eight winds
Are the winds of the eight trigrams."
Ruǎn Jí's "Discourse on Music" states:
"When the sages created music,
They intended to follow the substance of heaven and earth,
And complete the nature of the myriad things."
Heaven and Earth Harmonious, Yīn and Yáng Balanced
The Book of Hàn states:
"As for the myriad things not perishing prematurely,
Heaven and earth are harmonious and auspicious responses arise;
Thus, the Odes say:
'Bells and drums resound,
Stone chimes and pipes ring,
Bringing down abundant blessings.'" The Book of Rites states:
"Music arises from yáng;
Ritual is made from yīn.
When yīn and yáng are balanced, the myriad things attain their place."
Harmonize the States, Transform the People
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Grandly combine music to harmonize the states."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Music is used above to serve the ancestral temples,
And below to transform the common people."
Flowing within, moving outward
The Book of Han says:
"Music is that which
allows the four kinds of flowing to intermingle within and then manifest outward;
this was the method by which the former kings established music."
The Chunqiu Yuanming Bao says:
"Music is that which
fills harmony within,
and moves and manifests outward.
Responding to the time of its manifestation,
they established rites and created music to complete it."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"When harmony fills within,
the villagers and the states all sing of it.
When it moves and manifests outward,
it takes the form of the customs of the four quarters."
Rooted in the heart, reflecting one's nature
The Book of Rites says:
"Music is that from which
sound is born;
its root lies in the human heart,
moved by external things."
The Wujing Tongyi says:
"A king who receives the mandate has six kinds of music;
he must reflect his nature and establish regulations for them,
in order to delight in meeting his ancestors."
Hearing the Sháo music, performing new melodies
The Analects says:
"The Master heard the Sháo music in Qí,
and said:
'I did not imagine that music could reach such heights.'"
Hánzǐ says:
"Duke Líng of Wèi heard a new melody on the Pú River,
and summoned Master Juān to play the se and transcribe it."
The jué note stirs compassion, the gōng note brings magnanimity
Hándān Chuò's Wujing Xiyi says:
"Hearing the jué note, none fail to feel compassion and kindness."
The Han Shi Waizhuan says:
"Tāng composed the Dà Huò;
hearing its gōng note
makes people gentle, good, and magnanimous."
Connecting the eight winds, settling the myriad things
The Huainanzi says:
"Kuí created music,
harmonizing the six pitch standards,
adjusting the five notes,
thereby connecting the eight winds."
Ruǎn Jí's discourse says:
"The former kings' creation of music
was intended to settle the dispositions of the myriad things."
The Way benefits the people, virtue moistens things
The Wujing Tongyi says:
"Why was Huángdì's music called Xiánchí?
Xián means
all,
and to bestow.
In Huángdì's time, the Way was bestowed upon all the people."
The Yuè Yè Tú Zhēng says:
"Huángdì's music is called Xiánchí."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"Xián means
all.
Chí is chosen because it soaks everything without exception;
virtue moistens the myriad things,
therefore it was fixed as the name of the music."
Heaven and earth harmonize, yīn and yáng are in accord
The Lüshi Chunqiu says:
"All music is the harmony of heaven and earth,
the accord of yīn and yáng,
that which brings joy and delight to ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger."
The Shī Jì Lì Shū says:
"Music is not
merely the sound of metal and stone,
the resonance of pipes and strings;
it is the harmony and accord of yīn and yáng."
Offering to the Supreme Deity, summoning Tàiyī
The Zhouyi says:
"Thunder emerges from the earth, stirring joy;
the former kings thereby created music to honor virtue,
richly offering to the Supreme Deity,
to accompany the ancestral spirits."
The Yuè Yè Tú Zhēng says:
"Beat harmonious music in the eastern suburbs,
to summon the soul-spirits,
and bring down the spirit of Tàiyī."
Summoning deities and spirits, offering at the suburban altar and ancestral temple
The Zhouli says:
"The great combined music is used to summon deities and spirits,
to harmonize the states,
to bring accord to the myriad people,
to pacify guests,
to please those from afar,
and to stir animals."
The Book of Han says:
"Music sings of the nine virtues,
recites the six odes;
therefore, when offered at the suburban altar and ancestral temple, the deities and spirits enjoy it."
The shāng note brings decisiveness, the gōng note brings refinement
Hándān Chuò's Wujing Xiyi says:
"Hearing the shāng note, none fail to be decisive and decisive in affairs."
The Wujing Tongyi says:
"Hearing the gōng note, none fail to be refined and harmonious."
Summoning scaled and feathered creatures, stirring wind and clouds
The Zhouli says:
"Of all six kinds of music,
one transformation summons feathered creatures,
three transformations summon scaled creatures."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Transformation means
change.
When the music is complete, it is performed again."
The Xià Zhòngyù Bié Zhuàn says:
"Stirring the southern Chǔ,
blowing the Hú jiā.
Wind and clouds were shaken by it,
stars and planets changed their courses."
The zhǐ note fosters goodness, the shāng note loves righteousness
The Wujing Tongyi says:
"Hearing the zhǐ note, none fail to be good at nurturing and fond of bestowing."
The Han Shi Waizhuan says:
"Hearing the shāng note makes people upright, incorruptible, and fond of righteousness."
Instructing the noble youth, overseeing Chéngjūn
The Shangshu says:
"The Emperor said:
'Kuí,
I command you to oversee music,
and instruct the noble youth.'" Wáng Sù comments:
"The noble youth are the sons of the state."
The Zhouli says:
"The Grand Director of Music oversees the methods of Chéngjūn,
to administer the educational governance of establishing the state,
and to unite the sons and younger brothers of the state."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Jūn means
to adjust.
The music master is in charge of adjusting the sounds;
the Grand Director of Music is in charge of receiving this completed task, which is then called music."
Serving the ancestral temple, pacifying guests
The former is seen in the Shiji, etc.;
the latter is seen in the Zhouli, etc.
Connecting with the divine, harmonizing human principles
The Book of Han says:
"Music is that by which
the sage moves heaven and earth,
and connects with the divine."
The Weizhi says:
"Emperor Wén was on a hunt,
resting midway,
and asked his attending ministers:
'How does the pleasure of hunting compare to the eight sounds?'
Attendant-in-Charge Liú Yè replied:
'Hunting surpasses music.'
Concurrent Attendant-in-Charge Bào Xūn protested, saying:
'Music connects upward with the divine,
downward harmonizes human principles,
honors governance and achieves transformation,
and all states are thereby well-governed.'"
Emptying oneself and awing the spirit, piercing the heart and startling the ear
The Book of Han says:
"Music connects with the divine,
pacifies the common people;
therefore, listeners all empty themselves and awe their spirits."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's Shanglin Fu says:
"Groups of musicians perform in succession,
metal drums rise alternately.
Clanging and booming intermingle,
piercing the heart and startling the ear."
Resonant drumming of the belly, abundant fullness in the ears
The Lüshi Chunqiu says:
"Emperor Zhuānxū commanded Yú Shàn to first initiate the music;
Shàn then lay on his back,
drumming his belly with his tail,
its sound resonant."
The Analects says:
"From the beginning of Master Zhì's performance,
to the finale of the Guānjū,
how abundantly it fills the ears!"
The commentary says:
"The Grand Master of Lǔ, Zhì, recognized the sound of the Guānjū,
and first ordered its finale;
abundantly it fills the ears!
Hearing it, one finds it beautiful."
When achievements are complete, then music is composed; when teaching is revered, rewards are bestowed afterward.
The Book of Rites says:
"When a king's achievements are complete, he composes music;
when governance is settled, he establishes rites.
Those whose achievements are great have their music fully prepared."
The Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall says:
"When peace reigns, then music is composed,
to guard against licentiousness and excess."
The Book of Rites says:
"Thus, when the Son of Heaven creates music,
it is to reward the virtuous among the feudal lords.
When virtue flourishes and teaching is revered,
and the five grains ripen in season,
only then are they rewarded with music."
The music of Zhèng confounds the refined; the music of Qí harms virtue.
The Analects says:
"I detest purple for displacing vermilion;
I detest the music of Zhèng for confounding refined music.
Bāo's commentary says: The music of Zhèng
is the mournful kind of licentious music."
The Book of Rites says:
"The music of Zhèng is fond of excess and confounds the will;
the music of Sòng is like women at feasts and drowns the will;
the music of Wèi is hurried and numerous and troubles the will;
the music of Qí is arrogant and perverse and makes the will proud.
These four kinds are excessive in sensuality and harmful to virtue."
Bells and drums both resound; xūn and chí harmonize in song.
Cáo Zhí's "Seven Exhortations" says:
"Bells and drums both resound,
flutes and pipes sing in unison."
Lù Jī's "Seven Summons" says:
"Metal and stone harmonize and sound together;
xūn and chí join and sing in harmony."
The eight tones harmonize; the five colors do not confuse.
The Book of Documents says:
"The eight tones harmonize,
without encroaching upon their proper order."
The Book of Rites says:
"The five colors form patterns without confusion;
the eight winds follow the pitch-pipes without deviation."
Transform customs and change habits; spread virtue and communicate with the spiritual.
The Classic of Filial Piety says:
"To transform customs and change habits,
nothing is better than music."
Memorials of Wei Dynasty Ministers says:
"Music is that which spreads virtue and communicates with the spiritual."
The Hàozhōng qín; the Kōngsāng sè.
The Songs of Chu says:
"Shatter Bóyá's Hàozhōng."
Wáng Yì's commentary says:
"Hàozhōng
is the name of a qín."
Also, Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Qín" says:
"Duke Huán of Qí had a sounding qín called Hàozhōng."
The Rites of Zhou says:
"The qín and sè of Kōngsāng."
Phoenix songs and simurgh dances; jade pipes and vermilion strings.
Yǔ Chǎn's poem says:
"Xiāo Shǐ blew the sounding pipe;
Prince Wángzǐ sang the phoenix song."
The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says:
"When the simurgh bird hears music and dances,
then the ruler's state is secure."
Yìng Shào's Comprehensive Meaning of Customs says:
"During Emperor Zhāng's reign,
at the shrine of Shùn under the administration of Línglíng, shēng and white jade pipes were obtained."
The Great Commentary on the Book of Documents says:
"The great qín has vermilion strings and reaches Yuè."
Precious sè and patterned qín; red xiāo and purple dí.
The Book of Han says:
"Mǎng Héluó walked and struck the precious sè."
Zhāng Héng's "Imitating the Four Sorrows" poem says:
"The beautiful one left me a lǜqǐ qín."
Also, Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Qín" says:
"Cài Yōng had a qín called Lǜqǐ."
Xiāo Fāngděng's Thirty Kingdoms Chronicles says:
"People of Liángzhōu excavated the tomb of King Liáng, Zhāng Jùn,
and obtained a red jade xiāo and a purple jade dí."
Heavenly pipes, earthly pipes; southern tones, northern tones.
The Zhuangzi says:
"You have heard human pipes but not yet earthly pipes;
you have heard earthly pipes but not yet heavenly pipes."
Guō Xiàng's commentary says:
"Flutes and pipes, varied and uneven,
though ten thousand different, are not dissimilar."
The Lüshi Chunqiu says:
"The woman of Túshān ordered her daughter to go and wait for Yǔ;
the daughter composed a song,
thus began the southern tones.
The two daughters of the Yǒusōng clan waited for the emperor;
they ordered the simurgh to leave two eggs,
which flew north and never returned.
The two daughters composed a song,
thus began the northern tones."
The Yúnhé qín; the shuāngtiáo chí.
The Rites of Zhou says:
"The pipes of gūzhú,
the qín and sè of Yúnhé.
On the winter solstice,
they are performed at the round mound on the earth."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary:
"Yúnhé, Kōngsāng, Lóngmén,
are all mountains."
Guōzi's Account of Penetrating the Hidden says:
"In the second year of the Jiànyuán era,
the emperor raised the Téngguāng Terrace to gaze far in all directions;
on the terrace, he hung a blue jade bell,
suspended a xuánlí stone chime,
blew the shuāngtiáo chí,
and sang the song of clouds coming and going."
Poem by Emperor Táng Tàizōng, "Placing Music on the Three-Storied Pavilion"
The splendid feast shifts with evening's glow,
The purple shāng leads into the night.
Southern Chén, song-dust gathers close,
Divided steps, dance shadows unite.
Sound flows through three places' pipes,
Echo wraps around one layer of strings.
Not like the Qin tower above,
Where playing xiāo vainly seeks transcendence.
Poem by King Liáng, "Viewing Music in Response to an Imperial Command"
Zhào's sè holds a clear tone,
Qín's zhēng concentrates an ethereal sound.
Varied, they array the Nine Xià,
Lingering, they scatter in four directions.
Following the wind, they circle golden beams,
Holding clouds, they reflect in pearl nets.
Alternating performances, not just two or eight,
Complex strings, not merely one or two.
Favored to join the eastern Guo's blowing,
Humbly accompanying the southern wind's appreciation.
Forgetting flavor, I trust in the clangor,
Partaking of harmony, finally bowing and rising.
Light dust already flies and scatters,
Swimming fish also turn and stir.
Grace and radiance truly hard to encounter,
Chanting words, how easily can one let go?
Poem by Suí Hé Tuǒ, "Following Imperial Command to Revise Ancient Music at the Court of Imperial Sacrifices"
Great music leaves behind bells and drums,
Ultimate music values forgetting emotions.
Customs long changed from purity and harmony,
Years deep, ritual teaching arises.
In Xiègǔ, tune the lone pipe,
At Lúnshān, learn the phoenix's cry.
Floating clouds become dance melodies,
White snow serves as song names.
Hearing poetry, the six principles discerned,
Viewing music, the eight winds balanced.
Solemn and majestic, imperial might flows freely,
Deep and continuous, river waters clear.
The music of heaven moves silk and bamboo,
Encompassing the earth, chún and zhēng resound.
Perfect beauty combined with Sháo and Huò,
Awe and virtue altogether Xián and Yīng.
Vast and bright, the fú bell penetrates,
Fluttering and drifting, the pheasant feathers light.
Your servant belongs to a thousand ages,
Fortunate now to join the capped and tasseled.
Walking joyfully bearing the dark jade disk,
At the altar path, hearing the ninefold completion.
Also, "Poem on Viewing Music at the Ministry of Music Section"
The remaining influence of the Eastern Sea is great,
The lingering thoughts of Yáotáng are deep.
How better to view the piān dance,
With drum performances interspersed with chuāng gold.
Clear pipes tune silk and bamboo,
Vermilion strings rhyme the refined qín.
Eight rows display feathered banners,
Six virtues examine understanding of tones.
The ultimate way combines Sháo and Huò,
Filling the courtyard, altogether piān and rèn.
High sky passes the flowing fire,
Setting sun broadens the city's shade.
A hundred spirits harmonize with auspicious blessings,
Ten thousand states look up to the ruler's presence.
Heavenly music is not the city's drums,
And is used to caution the people's hearts.
Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem in Response to the Imperial Edict on Listening to Military Music on a Moonlit Night"
The revolving gate overlooks the ancient battlements,
The patrol path crosses the deep moat.
The moon's chill suggests an autumn night,
The mountain's cold sheds summer frost.
The distant sky clears in the twilight hues,
The pure scene scatters lingering light.
The reed-pipe sounds clamor over Lǒng's waters,
The drum melodies clamor in Yúyáng.
Deep melancholy stirs divine thoughts,
Gazing and listening inspire heavenly compositions.
The heights of Sōng and Dài are ultimately hard to emulate,
Hills and mounds merely strive in vain.
Suí Dynasty Kǒng Déshào's "Poem on Observing the Grand Temple's Performance of New Music"
The great sovereign receives the precious mandate,
Departing in leisure displays success achieved.
The music of heaven, metal and stone resound,
The Dòngtíng's strings and pipes are pure.
The eight tones stir in rich harmony,
The nine transformations blend with rare sounds.
Harmonizing with clouds, leaving wise appreciation,
The fragrant breeze delights the sage's heart.
Splendid achievements outshine Sháo and Huò,
Transforming customs surpasses Xián and Yīng.
Harsh blowing truly has nothing to take,
Leading the dance, clapping for lighthearted life.
Suí Dynasty Biàn Bīn's "Observing the Grand Temple's Performance"
People of old dreamed of the Yellow Emperor,
Still delighting in praising the music of heaven.
How much more now, opening this glorious enterprise,
Creating music to proclaim martial achievements.
The great elegance emerges, returning to principle,
Riding the wind, destroyed yet again suspended.
Central harmony is truly easy to approximate,
But how can Sháo and Xià follow one another?
The sound of the Qiánwéi chime penetrates clearly,
The pipe's tone from Xiègǔ transmits afar.
This petty minister presumptuously purifies his ears,
Long may he serve the strings of the southern breeze.
Suí Dynasty Xǔ Shànxīn's "Poem on Listening at the Grand Temple to the Corrected Classical Music Collated by Cài Zǐyuán of the Chén State"
Wéiyáng established ritual and music,
Order secured, as the former ruler presided.
At Yú's court, observing feathered displays,
The Hàn emperor looked up to struck metal.
Already changed by bells and stones,
They will follow rivers and seas to sink.
The heavy dew abolished, yet order returns,
Inheriting the wind, cut off then sought again.
The dragon-robe patterns leave no old traces,
But Sháo and Xià have lingering sounds.
When the marsh dries, the heroic stems scatter,
People leave behind deep sorrowful thoughts.
Sorrow comes, not lessened by the se,
Tears fall while hearing the qín.
How could it be like Marquis Wén sleeping?
Rather like Wēizǐ's lament, I sing.
Bell performances differ north and south,
The shāng tone varies past and present.
Only Yánzhōu's listening remains,
He should know the sound of a perished state.
Liáng Wǔdì's "Edict Questioning Ministers on Music"
The way of sound and music
Connects with governance.
It is how customs are transformed,
Distinguishing noble and base.
Yet the praise of Sháo and Huò is empty transmission,
The substance of Xián and Yīng leaves no record.
Since Hàn and Wèi,
Decline has grown severe,
Causing the refined and vulgar to mix,
Bells and stones thus erroneous.
Heaven and man lack the discipline of nine transformations,
Court banquets lose the ritual of four suspensions.
Through long passing years,
It will fall to the ground.
I, at dawn, sit in court,
Seeking its essential meaning,
But the old statutes do not survive,
Not yet obtained for correction.
Waking and sleeping, it occupies my thoughts,
Hence my sighs.
You, whose learning is thorough and bright,
May state your views.
Miscellaneous Music, Part Two
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Intricate techniques and licentious sounds,
Clogging the heart and ears,
Cause one to forget harmony and peace,
These are called Zhèng sounds."
Xǔ Shèn's Wǔ Jīng Tōngyì says:
"In the Zhèng state were the Zhēn and Wěi rivers,
Where men and women gathered,
Singing antiphonally, stirring each other.
Now, of the twenty-one poems of the 'Zhèng Odes',
Nineteen speak of women,
Hence Zhèng sounds are licentious."
It also says:
"The music of Zhèng and Wèi
Makes people licentious and dissolute."
Liáng Yuándì's Zuǎnyào says:
"Ancient voluptuous songs included Běilǐ,
Mímǐ,
Jīchǔ, Jiéfēng,
And the Yáng'ē tune.
Also there were variety shows,
Originating in Qín and Hàn,
Such as 'Fish-Dragon Spreading',
Pretending to be beasts in play.
High Rope Phoenix, Ānxī Five Tables,
Both made by Shí Jìlóng,
Seen in the Yèzhōng Jì.
Dūlú Pole-Climbing,
Today's pole scaling,
Seen in the Xījīng Jì.
Ball and Sword,
Ball also called 'bell',
Seen in the Xījīng Jì.
Acrobatic Carts, Mountain Carts, Raising Clouds, Stirring Thunder,
Seen in Lǐ Yóu's "Observatory of Music Rhapsody".
Heel Hanging, Belly Spinning,
Both done on poles,
Seen in Fù Xuán's "Western Capital Rhapsody".
Sword Swallowing, Rope Walking, Fire Spitting,
Seen in the "Western Capital Rhapsody".
Churning Water, Turning Stones, Mist Spitting, Tripod Lifting,
All seen in Lǐ Yóu's "Chánglè Observatory" and Fù Xuán's "Western Capital Rhapsody".
Figure Imitators,
Seen in the Hànshū.
Wéi Zhāo says:
"Today's masks."
Monster Beasts, Treasure-Spitting performances."
All seen in the "Western Capital Rhapsody".
Flowing Zhèng Stirring Chǔ
Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn says:
"An unthatched house
Is not equal to the Ēpáng Palace;
An unhewn rafter
Is not equal to a polished square timber.
Dark wine is not equal to Cāngwú's mellow brew,
Plucking and strumming is not equal to the flowing music of Zhèng."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Promoting the licentious music of Zhèng and Wèi,
Continuing the lingering style of Jīchǔ,
This is why the people of Qí become licentious, dissolute, and sunk in dissipation."
Chǔ Shamans Sòng Dissoluteness
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
"In the decline of Chǔ,
They created shamanic music."
Gāo Yòu's commentary says:
"Male shaman is called xí,
Female shaman is called wū."
The Lǐjì says:
"The music of Sòng pleases women and drowns the will."
Fond of Vulgar Hearing New
The Mèngzǐ says:
"Zhuāng Bào saw the King of Qí and said:
'I am not able to enjoy the music of the former kings,
I merely enjoy the common music of the age!'"
The Lǐjì says:
"Marquis Wén of Wèi asked Zǐxià:
'When I dress formally and listen to ancient music,
I only fear falling asleep;
When I listen to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
I never feel tired.
May I ask why ancient music is like that,
And new music is like this?'"
Eastern Dance Southern Song
Emperor Wén of Wèi's poem says:
"Qí singers begin the eastern dance,
Qín zithers play western tones."
Zhāng Héng's "Southern Capital Rhapsody" says:
"Sitting to southern songs, rising to Zhèng dances,
White cranes fly, silken threads trail."
Beautiful and Subtle Strange and Grand
Liú Shèn's "Lǔ Capital Rhapsody" says:
"Nine-branched dragon candles,
Luxuriant rice, Shòuyáng,
Bestow heavy dew to detain guests,
Summon beautiful, subtle new singers."
Liú Xiàng's Liènǚ Zhuàn says:
"Xià Jié sought beauties from all regions,
Accumulating them in the rear palace.
He made performers, dwarfs, and intimate companions
Lǔ Pavilion, Qín Curtains
The "Gǔliáng Zhuàn" says:
"In the eleventh year of Duke Dìng,
at the meeting at Jiāgǔ,
the people of Qí sent Yōu Shī to dance under the pavilion of the Lǔ lord.
Confucius said:
'Those who laugh at the lord are guilty and should be sentenced to death,
let the Sīmǎ enforce the law.' " Liú Xiàng's "Shuōyuàn" says:
"After Qín Shǐ Huáng had unified the world,
he initiated the labor at Líshān,
sealing the depths of the Three Springs,
and built four hundred palace retreats in Guānzhōng.
All equipped with bells, chimes, curtains, and canopies,
with women entertainers and jesters. "
Song Talents, Dance Styles
The "Hàn Shū" says:
"In mourning, there are rites of weeping and jumping,
in music, there are forms of song and dance.
The righteous complement their sincerity,
the unrighteous prevent their decline."
Biān Ràng's "Zhānghuá Rhapsody" says:
"Dances have no fixed style,
drums have no fixed rhythm.
Following the sound, they respond,
neither long nor short, never faltering."
Zhào's Dance, Yān's Song
Zhāng Huá's "Shàngyǐ Piān" says:
"Exquisite dances arise in Qízhào,
mournful songs emerge from Sānqín."
Wèi Wéndì's "Yān Gē Xíng" says:
"Days of parting are easy, meetings are hard,
the mountains and rivers stretch far and wide.
I yearn for you, yet dare not express it,
sending words through the floating clouds that never return."
Clear Songs, Exquisite Dances
The "Xià Zhòngyù Biézhuàn" says:
"Zhòngyù's cousins, the witches Zhāng Zhōu and Chén Shū,
with charming and alluring beauty,
clear songs and exquisite dances,
appeared like flying immortals."
Eastern Mountain Courtesans, Western Bā Singers
Guōzi says:
"Xiè Gōng kept courtesans at Dongshan."
Jiǎn Wén says:
"Ánshí must come out,
join others in joy,
and cannot but share their worries."
Zhāng Huá's "Qīngbó Piān" says:
"Beauty arose in Qízhào,
alluring singing emerged from the Western Bā.
A single glance caused cities and states to fall,
a thousand gold was no longer of worth."
Dwarf Jesters, Luxurious Music
The "Jiā Yǔ" says:
"Duke Dìng of Lǔ and the Marquis of Qí met at Jiāgǔ,
Confucius acted as minister,
and the jesters and dwarfs of the Qí palace performed before them."
The "Biographies of Exemplary Women" says:
"Xià Jié abandoned rites and propriety,
indulging in women.
He sought beautiful women from all corners,
accumulating them in the latter palace,
creating luxurious music."
Liáng Xiàoyuándì's "Poem Watching Courtesans at Twilight"
"The graceful brows gradually brighten,
Yàn courtesans play in the small hall.
The Hú dance begins in the Qí Pavilion,
bells and chimes emerge along the walkway.
To the rhythm of dragons beating drums,
and back to the phoenix tapping the sheng.
Trees surround the dance mat,
lotus line the courtesans' course.
Dense bamboo leaves cast no shadows,
sparse flowers have a distinct fragrance.
Holding cups while laughing and talking,
this joy and music are endless."
Also "Responding to Lín Poetry of Playful Courtesans"
"As the sun sets in the northern pavilion,
a grand banquet emerges in the southern hall.
Clear songs follow the echoing stream,
dance shadows spring from the pond.
Light flowers scatter the powdered hues,
wind and bamboo blend with string sounds.
Alone think of beneath Yángtái,
hoping to wait for Luòchuān's birth."
Liáng-Zhāomíng Crown Prince's "Lín Poetry of Playful Courtesans"
"The glowing evening light retreats,
relocating the banquet to the front pool.
Springs and reflections coincide,
flowers and faces complement.
Flute sounds like birds chirping,
dancing sleeves describe wind branches.
Revelry knows no drunkenness,
a thousand autumns should be thus."
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Music Ends but Grace Remains Poem"
"The lonely sound of the sheng is sharp and clear,
the dance formation chaotic in motion.
The light shoulders are raised repeatedly,
and long scarves are leisurely changed.
Cloud-like hair adorned with precious flowers,
light makeup tainted with slight sweat.
Officials are both drunk and full,
yet the imperial grace is but half."
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Watching Courtesans with Prince Wǔlíng Poem"
"Yàn courtesans perform exquisite dances,
Zhèng women unleash clear songs.
Shy faces slowly appear,
sending flirtations expressively.
Not unlike stopping a rain walk,
nor less than seeing a water wave.
Imagine you in sorrow as the sun sets,
longing for Lǔ Yáng's spear."
Northern Qí Xiāo Fàng's "Winter Night Viewing Courtesans Poem"
"The beauties grow with the passing year,
together in the dark, unable to sleep.
The silver dragon holds a burning candle,
the golden phoenix rises from the furnace smoke.
Playing the flute starts the melody,
adjusting the zither and tuning strings.
Songs return behind the fan,
dances emerge before the line of courtesans.
From unparalleled eras, hard to reach,
who again counts the immortals?"
Later Liáng Shěn Jūn Yōu's "Awaiting Night Courtesans Poem"
"Through the curtains, the moonlight passes,
as the candles determine the courtesans' position.
Turning, bracelets of jade clink,
stepping with bells of pearls sounding.
A low robe brushes against hair's shadow,
raising a fan to begin a song.
In the box, the music still plays,
the body in the hand responds lightly."
Chén Yīn Kēng Marquis Division's "Empty Residence Courtesans Chant Poem"
"Exquisite people fill the embroidered seats,
with exquisite music moving Kūn strings.
Tall as the Yángtái,
the pool like where Luòpǔ meanders.
Kūn cries behind a singing fan,
flowers fall before a dancing garment.
Emerald willows with the setting sun,
are delicate like late makeup."
Chén Liú Shān Marquis Division's "Empty Residence Courtesans Chant Poem"
"Shijiā's Golden Valley Courtesans,
beautified emerging from the orchid chamber.
Looking at flowers, they fight to smile,
hearing the zither, they can't help but cry.
Singing by the hillside at sunset,
dancing on the front creek of the pool.
Treating people as if they were peach and plum,
no place is left trackless."
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Responding to Watching Courtesans with King Zhào Poem"
"Green pearls like singing fans, thin,
flying swallow like dance garment, long.
The melody follows flowing water,
the flute sound follows the phoenix.
Fine threads bind the chime's frame,
round flowers nail the drum bed.
Suspended, knowing no incorrect tones,
without matters, looks back at Zhōu Láng."
Also "Watching Courtesans Poem"
"Long remembrance of the stone at the sand-wash,
empty memories of shirt rock pounding.
If in Línqiōng there's a convenience,
to explain the understanding of the heart of the zither."
Suí Jiāng Zǒng's "Responding to Watching Courtesans with Prince Héyáng Poem"
"Rising towers invade the azure sky,
the first sun shines on red makeup.
String hearts are glamorous ladies,
the wrong tune moves Zhōu Láng.
Singing together with eyebrow arches,
when dancing stops, fragrance separates briefly.
Beneath the silver lamp, hanging tassels,
do not laugh at the long jade hairpin."
Suí Lú Sīdào's "Night Listening to Neighbor's Courtesans Poem"
"The entertaining building faces three paths,
the blowing stage overlooks nine levels.
The sheng follows mountain cranes,
flutes play water dragons.
Resentful song breaks easily,
exquisite dance postures are hard to find.
Who can temporarily detain guests,
relieve the belt once to follow."
Sui Dynasty, Yú Mào, "Poem on the Court Musicians of Prince Héngyáng's Study Pavilion"
The golden moat lies low by the imperial road,
Jade flutes are playing in the wind.
Gathering kingfisher feathers atop the Tiānjīn Bridge,
Turning phoenix-like on the bird's path.
Before the mirror, the moon seems near,
In the song's place, one feels the dust is empty.
Tonight the Weaving Maiden appears,
Said to be the palace of Wàngxiān.
Sui Dynasty, Xuē Dàohéng, "Poem in Shifting Rhymes on the Performance Grounds, Harmonizing with Attendant Censor Xǔ Shànxīn"
The capital Luòyáng renews the year,
Again belonging to the full moon's wheel.
A jade disc turns alone among the clouds,
A lone mirror hangs suspended in the sky.
All regions gather in assembly,
Every kind of performance comes before.
Facing the thoroughfare, carriages never cease,
Along the road, pavilions connect.
Startled swans emerge from the Luò River,
Soaring cranes descend upon the Yī River plain.
Beauties of stunning quality whirl like wind and snow,
Flute songs harmonize with strings.
Lovely ladies stand solemnly in rows,
Hand in hand they enter the performance grounds.
Robes resemble Hé Píngshū's,
People equal Zhāng Zǐfáng.
High, high the city-dwellers' chignons,
Tall, tall the makeup of those in towers.
Silken skirts fly like peacocks,
Brocade mats hang with mandarin ducks.
Sunlight shines on Bān Jī's fan,
Wind wafts Hán Shòu's fragrance.
All night fish bear lanterns,
Through the night dragons hold candles.
Jesting laughter knows no end,
Singing and chanting follow in succession.
Qiāng flutes chant at Lǒng's peak,
Barbarian dances, Qiūcí tunes.
Masks adorned with gold and silver,
Magnificent robes sway with pearls and jade.
Deep into the night, the play is not yet done,
Finally becoming difficult for people.
Lying down, driving flying jade-bridled horses,
Standing up, riding turning silver saddles.
Leaping swords crisscross,
Swiftly tossing balls again.
Rising and falling, the dance of a hundred beasts,
Waddling and limping, the play of five fowls.
Suānní plays with spotted feet,
Giant elephants droop long trunks.
Green goats kneel then leap,
White horses circle as they ride.
Suddenly glimpse Luófú rising,
In a moment see Yùchāng arrive.
Peak ridges now lofty and steep,
Forest groves also verdant and green.
Elk and deer descend, prance and lean,
Monkeys and apes sometimes crouch and stand on tiptoe.
Golden timekeepers display old markings,
Jade pitch-pipes stir new ash.
Tender shoots of armor droop over roadside willows,
Remnant flowers scatter among garden plums.
Myriad stars gradually grow sparse,
The slanting moon still lingers.
Young nobles still toil at play,
Young masters have not returned.
Together they drink fine jade wine,
Together they tilt parrot cups.
Throughout heaven they meet the sage's day,
The myriad masses rejoice in peace.
Chén Dynasty, Lǐ Yuáncāo, "Poem in Response to Palace Attendant Xiāo on Listening to Courtesans in the Spring Garden"
Light rain disperses fragrant blooms,
The central garden shines with fading sunlight.
Red trees sway the singing fans,
Green pearls float on dancing robes.
Complex strings accompany the wine,
Varied melodies stir thoughts of home.
A sorrowful man on this night,
Ashamed to see the falling blossoms fly.
Chén Dynasty, Zǐliáng, "Poem on Obtaining a Courtesan"
Jīngǔ holds many joyous feasts,
Fine beauties all are fragrant and fair.
Flowing clouds turn upon the mat,
Whirling snow flies within the palm.
Bright moon shines on the singing fan,
Moving clouds meet the dancing robe.
Why must there be peach and plum?
Another kind replaces spring's light.
Hóng Zhígōng, "Poem Harmonizing with Duke Píngliáng on Viewing Prince Zhàojùn's Courtesans"
The small hall displays silk mats,
Marvelous courtesans summoned from Yān and Qín.
Green hues rival painted brows,
Rosy cheeks naturally hold spring.
Joined in dance, all whirl like snow,
Separate in song, together shed dust.
The Qí ensemble cannot be joined,
In vain I wish to ascend the dragon ford.
Shì Fǎxuān, "Poem in Response to Instruction on Viewing Courtesans with Prince Zhàojùn"
Guì Mountain retains the honored guest,
Orchid chamber summons enchanting beauties.
In the city, painting eyebrow tints,
Within the palace, binding slender waists.
Dance sleeves lift before the wind,
Singing voices proud behind the fan.
Zhōu Yú does not look back,
Today the strings and pipes are tuned.
Wáng Jì, "Poem on a Courtesan"
Enchanting lady adorns pure makeup,
Graceful, she emerges from the orchid chamber.
Sunlight shines on her shadow by the window,
Wind blows, filling the road with fragrance.
Earlier, the singing fan was thin,
Today, the dancing robe is long.
She should not let the tune go wrong,
Holding this, she tests Zhōu Yú.
Music of the Four Barbarians, Part Three
"Zhōulǐ ‧ Spring Offices":
"The Dīlóu official is in charge of the music of the four barbarians."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The east is called Mèi,
The south is called Rèn,
The west is called Zhūlí,
The north is called Jìn."
"Lǐjì" states:
"Mèi is the music of the eastern barbarians,
Rèn is the music of the southern barbarians."
Virtue Reaches, Grace Covers
Bān Gù's "Eastern Capital Rhapsody" states:
"The four barbarians perform alternately,
The reach of vast virtue.
Jìn, Zhū, Dōu, Lí,
None fail to gather completely."
"Wǔjīng Tōngyì" states:
"Performing the music of the four barbarians,
Manifests that virtue and grace widely cover the four directions."
Admitted to Lǔ's Temple, Presented at Hàn's Court
"Lǐjì" states:
"Admitting the music of the barbarians and southerners into the Grand Temple,
Broadens Lǔ's influence under heaven."
"Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
"In the first year of Yǒngníng,
The king of the Shàn country of the southwestern barbarians presented music and musicians.
The following year,
At the yuánhuì assembly,
It was performed in the court.
Emperor Ān and his officials watched together,
And greatly marveled at it."
Dītī Performers, Fúlóu Performers
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" states:
"Comedians, dwarfs, Dītī performers."
Guō Pú's commentary states:
"Dītī,
Is the name of western music."
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì" states:
"During King Chéng's time,
South of the southern border was the Fúlóu country.
Some, in the palm of the hand, prepared the music of a hundred beasts,
Twisting and bending between the fingers,
Human forms sometimes several fēn tall,
Divine and strange, suddenly appearing.
The Music Bureau transmitted this performance,
Later generations still learned it."
Covering the Four Directions, Harmonizing the Eight Wilds
See above "Wǔjīng Tōngyì".
Zuǒ Sī's "Wèi Capital Rhapsody" states:
"The sounds managed by the Dīlóu official,
The melodies of Màirèn, Mèi, and Jìn.
To entertain the rulers of the four barbarians,
To harmonize the customs of the eight wilds."
Later Hàn "Poem-Song of Distant Barbarians Admiring Virtue"
Where the barbarians dwell,
The region of the setting sun.
Admiring righteousness, turning toward transformation,
They submit to the enlightened ruler.
The sage's virtue and grace run deep,
Granting people wealth and abundance.
Winter brings much frost and snow,
Summer brings much gentle rain.
Cold and warmth arrive in season,
The tribe's people have plenty.
Traversing danger, undergoing peril,
Not fearing ten thousand lǐ.
Barbarian custom returns to virtue,
Their hearts return to a compassionate mother.
Also, the "Song of Distant Barbarians Cherishing Virtue"
Beyond the wild frontiers,
the land is barren and rocky.
They eat meat and wear furs,
never seeing salt or grain.
Officials and interpreters transmit the customs,
the Great Hàn is peaceful and joyful.
Carrying burdens, they return to benevolence,
forever wishing to be subjects and servants.
Song, Part Four
The Shàngshū says:
"Poetry expresses intent,
song prolongs speech."
Yǒng means
to prolong,
to lengthen the speech.
Cài Yōng's "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" says:
"Song is the sound of music."
The preface to the Máo Shī says:
"Emotion stirs within and takes form in speech.
When speech is insufficient,
one sighs over it.
When sighing is insufficient,
one sings it.
When singing is insufficient,
unconsciously the hands dance it,
and the feet stamp it."
The Shānhǎijīng says:
"Dì Jùn's eight sons
first began to sing."
The Ěryǎ says:
"Sound accompanied by qín and sè is called gē,
singing without accompaniment is called yáo,
also called è."
This means without string or bamboo instruments,
singing alone.
The Hánshī Zhāngjù says:
"Having stanzas and melody is called gē,
without stanzas and melody is called yáo."
Liáng Yuándì's Zuǎnyào says:
"Qí songs are called ōu,
Wú songs are called yú,
Chǔ songs are called yàn,
licentious songs are called wā.

Also there are qīnggē (clear songs), gāogē (high songs), āngē (peaceful songs), huǎngē (slow songs), chánggē (long songs), hàogē (vast songs), yǎgē (elegant songs), hāngē (merry songs), yuàngē (plaintive songs), láogē (labor songs)."
The Hánshī says:
"The hungry sing of food,
the weary sing of their tasks."
Singing upon returning triumphant is called kǎigē (victory songs),
singing with music played in the hall is called dēnggē (ascending songs),
also called shēnggē (rising songs).
Ancient skilled singers include Xián Hēi,
and Dì Kù's singers are seen in the Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
Qín Qīng, Xuē Tán,
Qín Qīng's disciple.
Hán É,
a person of Qí,
these three are seen in the Lièzǐ.
Wáng Bào,
lived by the Qí River, and west of the river they were skilled at ōu.
Mián Jū,
lived in Gāotáng, and the right side of Qí was skilled at singing.
Hù Liáng,
seen in the Huáinánzǐ.
Lǔ person Yú Gōng,
seen in Liú Xiàng's Biélù.
Lǐ Yānnián.
Seen in the Hànshū.
Ancient songs include "Yánglíng", "Báilù", "Cháorì", "Yúlì", "Báishuǐ", "Báiyún", "Jiāngnán", "Yángchūn", "Huáinán", "Jiàbiàn", "Lùshuǐ", "Yáng'ē", "Cǎilíng", "Xiàlǐ Bārén",
all seen in the Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Zhuàn and Liáng Yuándì's Zuǎnyào.
"Bā Què",
songs of Gětiānshì seen in the Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
"Táng Gē",
song of Dì Kù.
"Nánfēng", "Qīngyún",
both songs of Yú Shùn.
"Chénlù".
Song of Tāng, both seen in the Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
Hàn songs include "Dàfēng",
composed by Gāozǔ.
"Zhīfáng", "Báilín", "Zhūyàn", "Jiāomén", "Tiānmǎ", "Fángzhōng",
the above are all from the Jiāojū Gē.
"Shèngtáng", "Cōngyáng",
songs of Wǔdì.
"Hùzǐ",
composed by Wǔdì when observing the breached river,
both seen in the Hànshū.
"Xuányún", "Bùyún".
Songs of Xīwángmǔ,
seen in the Wǔdì Nèizhuàn.
Ancient Yuèfǔ include "Yàngē Xíng", "Yàngē Xíng", "Chánggē Xíng",
composed by Wèi Wǔdì.
"Cháogē Xíng", "Yuàngē Xíng", "Qián Huǎnshēng Gē Xíng", "Zhàogē Xíng", "Jūgē Xíng", "Fànggē Xíng", "Duǎngē Xíng", "Càigē Xíng", "Chéngē Xíng".
Also, according to Gǔjīn Yuèlù,
songs from the end of Jìn onward include "Yínyù Gē", "Yáng Pàn'ér Gē",
in Southern Qí, Yáng Mín's mother entered the palace as a teacher,
children and women called her Yáng Pó'ér,
pó transformed into pàn.
"Fúfēng Gē",
composed by Jìn's Liú Kūn.
"Bǎinián Gē",
in the middle of Jìn's Wáng Dào,
Lù Jī also composed it.
"Báirì Gē",
composed by Sòng's Shěn Yōuzhī,

The song says:
"The white sun sets on the western hills."
"Jiǔqǔ Gē",
composed by Sòng's Hé Chéngtiān.
"Cǎigé Fù Gē",
composed by ancient Yuè people.
"Táoyè Gē",
composed by Jìn's Wáng Xiànzhī.
"Tóngshēng Gē",
composed by Hàn's Zhāng Héng.
"Bìyù Gē",
composed by Jìn's Sūn Chuò.
"Sìshí Gē",
originated from "Zǐyè".
"Zǐyè Gē",
ancient times there was a woman named Zǐyè,
who created this song.
"Shàngshēng Gē",
also named "Cùzhù",
an ancient melody of sorrow and grief.
"Báizhù Gē",
originated in Wú,
composed during Sūn Hào's time.
"Xiāngyáng Báitóngdī Gē", "Qiánxī Gē",
composed by Jìn's Chējì Jiāngjūn Shěn Wán.
"Huānwén Gē",
in the beginning of Jìn Mùdì's reign,
after singing they would call out "huānwén",
hence it became the name.
"Dīng Dūhù Gē",
Sòng Gāozǔ's son-in-law Xú Kuízhī was killed by Lǔ Zhí,
Gāozǔ sent Dūhù Dīng Yǔ to collect and bury him.
Kuízhī's wife called out weeping to the pavilion,
personally inquiring about the funeral arrangements,
each time she asked,
she would sigh and say:
"Dīng Dūhù",
her voice was mournful and poignant,
later people based on her voice expanded it into a song!"
"Tuánshàn Gē",
Jìn's Zhōngshū Lìng Wáng Mǐn liked to hold a white round fan,
his attendant Xiè Fāng sang about it,
hence it became the name.
"Àonǎo Gē".
Jìn's Shí Chóng composed it for Lǜzhū.
Manifesting Virtue, Chanting Merit
The Lǐjì says:
"After the libation, the musicians ascend to sing,
manifesting virtue.
The singers are above,
the gourd and bamboo instruments are below,
valuing the human voice."
Zhāng Zǎi's "Píwǔ Fù" says:
"Thus through song and chant,
one symbolizes virtue;
through stamping of feet,
one expresses emotion fully."
White Qílín, Red Phoenix
The Hànshū says:
"Wǔdì visited Yōng to sacrifice at the Five Altars,
captured a white qílín and composed a song."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"Jiǎ Pèilán said when in the palace,
they often entertained themselves with wind and string instruments, song and dance,
competed in wearing enchanting attire,
to hasten the auspicious times.
On the fifth day of the tenth month,
they would together enter the Língnǚ Temple,
play flutes and strike the zhù,
singing the 'Ascending Clouds' melody.
Then they would link arms and stamp the ground in rhythm,
singing 'The Red Phoenix Has Come'."
Eight Suites Nine Sequences
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
"In ancient times, during the music of Gétiān Shì,
two people held ox tails,
stamped their feet, and sang the eight suites.
The first was called 'Zǎi Rén',
the second 'Xuán Niǎo',
the third 'Suì Cǎo Mù',
the fourth 'Jí Wǔ Gǔ',
the fifth 'Jìng Tiān Cháng',
the sixth 'Dá Dì Gōng',
the seventh 'Zuò Dì Dé',
and the eighth 'Zǒng Qín Shòu Zhī Jí'."
Gāo Yòu's commentary says:
"These are the names of the eight pieces of music."
The Book of Documents states:
"Yǔ said:
'Ah, let the Emperor remember this:
Virtue lies in good governance.
Governance lies in nourishing the people.
Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain must be regulated;
correcting virtue, utilizing resources, and enriching life must be harmonized.
The nine achievements must be ordered,
and the nine orders must be sung.'"
Prolonging Words Deepening Intent
The Book of Documents states:
"Poetry expresses intent,
song prolongs the words,
and pitch-pipes harmonize the sounds."
The General Meaning of the Five Classics states:
"The word for song (gē) means joy (huān),
it deepens the intent and will,
therefore one gives voice and prolongs the words in song."
Containing Zhǐ Emitting Jué
Emperor Wén of Wèi's poem says:
"Sitting together beneath the high pavilion,
entertaining guests with famous performers.
The strings and songs follow the wind, fierce and strong,
emitting yǔ and containing zhǐ and shāng."
Xí Zàochǐ's Records of the Elders of Xiāngyáng states:
"In the past, there was a skilled singer
who sang 'Yánglíng Báilù',
'Cháorì Yúlì',
containing shāng and emitting jué,
with flawless rhythm following the melody."
Numinous Fungus Precious Cauldron
Bān Gù's "Hàn Eulogy: Songs Discussing Merit" states:
"Due to the dew-filled chamber, the numinous fungus grew,
symbolizing the three virtues, an auspicious omen depicted.
Extending lifespan, it illuminated the Northern Capital,
matching the Supreme God, resembling the Tàiwēi constellation,
aligned with the sun and moon, radiating brilliance."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wǔ obtained a precious cauldron beside the shrine of Hòutǔ,
and also, a horse was born in the waters of Wòwā.
He composed the 'Song of the Precious Cauldron and Heavenly Horse'."
Qí's Right Yǐngzhōng
The first reference is found in Mencius.
Sòng Yù's "Response to Questions" states:
"King Xiāng of Chǔ asked Sòng Yù:
'Sir, do you have some failing conduct?
Why do the scholars and commoners speak so ill of you?'
Yù replied:
'There was a guest singing in Yǐngzhōng,
who sang 'Xiàlǐ Bārén'.
Those who joined in the chorus numbered in the tens.
When he sang 'Yángchūn Báixuě',
those in the state who could join in were no more than a few.
The loftier the melody,
the fewer those who can harmonize with it.'"
Remaining Sound Wandering Echo
The Liezi states:
"In the past, Hán É traveled east to Qí.
Running out of provisions,
she passed by Yōngmén,
and sold her singing to borrow food.
Therefore, the people of Yōngmén are skilled singers to this day,
imitating É's remaining sound."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's poem says:
"Strings and songs performed new poems,
wandering echoes brushed the vermilion beams.
Complex sounds rushed to swift rhythms,
passionate and stirring, sometimes激昂."
Shaking Trees Gushing Spring
The Liezi states:
"Qín Qīng restrained himself and sang a mournful song.
The sound shook the forest trees,
the echo halted the passing clouds."
The Jìyì Xuānchéng Records states:
"Twenty lǐ south of Línchéng County is Gài Mountain.
Climbing about a hundred paces, there is the Shūgū Spring.
Common legend says there was a woman of the Shū family,
not yet married,
who was splitting firewood here with her father.
The girl sat down at the spring's location,
and when pulled, she would not move.
They hurriedly informed the family.
By the time they returned,
they only saw a clear, deep spring.
Her mother said:
'My daughter loved music.
If you play stringed music and sing,
the spring will gush forth and flow.'"
Vast Singing Melodious Voice
The Chǔ Cí states:
"Raising the drumstick to strike the drum,
with relaxed, gentle rhythm, singing peacefully.
Presenting yú and sè, singing vast songs,
the spirit dances gracefully in beautiful attire,
fragrance abundant, filling the hall."
The Liezi states:
"In the past, Hán É used a melodious voice,
singing a long song in one melody.
Old and young alike were delighted and clapped."
Leaving the Frontier Ascending Lǒng
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
"Emperor Gāo ordered Lady Qī to sing the song 'Leaving the Frontier, Gazing Homeward'.
Hundreds of attending maidservants all joined her.
The rear palace sang in unison,
the sound entering the clouds."
The Records of Qín Province states:
"In Lǒngxī Commandery is Lǒng Mountain.
On its cliffs, streams pour forth, and in the central ridge, a spring pools,
hence named the Ten-Thousand-Stone Spring.
When the spring overflows,
it spreads and scatters downward.
All ditches and channels are filled.
Therefore, northerners ascending here sing:
'Lǒngtóu flowing water,
scatters and flows in all directions.
Thinking of my journey on duty,
drifting in the vast wilderness.
Climbing high, gazing afar,
tears fall in pairs.'"
Echoing in the Valley Halting Clouds
Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīng Province states:
"In Línhè County's Mǎchéng, there was an old woman skilled in singing.
Her lingering tones echoed in the valley for several days."
Zhāng Huá's Records of Broad Phenomena states:
"Xuē Tán learned singing from Qín Qīng.
Before exhausting Qīng's skill, he bid farewell to return home.
Qīng farewelled him in the suburbs,
then, beating time, sang a mournful song.
The sound shook the forest trees,
the echo halted the passing clouds.
Tán then apologized and begged to return."
Setting Sun Flowing Wind
Shì Zhìjiàng's Ancient and Modern Music Records states:
"The song 'The White Sun Sets Behind the Western Hills'
was composed by Shěn Yōuzhī when he departed from Jīng Province.
Before his defeat,
he longed to return to the capital and composed this song."
Zhāng Xié's "Poem on Continuous Rain":
"The chirping of silk and bamboo instruments playing,
musicians performing wondrous and mysterious tunes.
Mournful songs, vast as the flowing wind,
substantial echoes reverberate the autumn air."
Stone City Golden Gate
Shì Zhìjiàng's Ancient and Modern Music Records states:
"The 'Mòchóu Lè'
also originated from the 'Shíchéng Lè', hence this song.
West of Stone City was a woman named Mòchóu,
skilled in singing ballads.
Moreover, within the harmony of the Shíchéng music was a 'Forgetting Sorrow' melody,
hence this song came to be."
Wéi Zhāo's Comprehensive Historical Records states:
"Zhòu was without virtue.
Bǐgān, knowing that extreme remonstrance would lead to death,
composed the song 'Grooming Horses at the Golden Gate'."
Farewell at Yìshuǐ Gazing at Qínchuān
The Annals of Prince Dān of Yān states:
"Jīng Kē rose to offer a toast,
and sang:
'The wind soughs and sighs, oh, the Yì River is cold.
The brave warrior, once gone, oh, never returns.'" The Xīn Family Records of Sān Qín states:
"At Lǒng and Wèi's Western Pass,
its slope winds nine times.
Above, water pours down in four streams.
A folk song says:
'Lǒngtóu flowing water,
its sound murmurs and sobs.
Gazing from afar at Qínchuān,
liver and guts are severed.'"
Revealing bright teeth and moving crimson lips.
In Fù Yì's "Dance Prose," it is said:
“When the drums beat like a sigh, the clear eyes flutter,
when the sound emerges, bright teeth are unveiled.”
Cáo Zhí's "Seven Inspirations" says:
“Move the crimson lips,
emit a clear sound.”
Beneath the dates vibrant, the blossoms above shimmer.
Pān Yuè’s "Shēng Prose" declares:
“Stop the mournful playing of Zhāng Wén,
and let the fame of Guǎnglíng spread afar.
Chant the tender beauty of the peach grove,
sing of the vibrant dates below.”
Liú Jìngshū's "Garden of Marvels" mentions:
“Niè Bāo of Línchuān,
after being deceased for several years,
suddenly visited Shěn Dàoxí of Nánfēng and sang.
His songs, filled with humor and order,
each time performed delicately among the blossoms above, moving gracefully,
much like a return without hearing of death or resurrection.”
Yáng Shīdào's "Listening to Song and Flute Prose"
Then we open the flying pavilion to the sky,
and gaze upon the carved beams arching as rainbows.
Perform the beautiful tunes of Dōngchéng,
summon the winds of Southern Jīng.
The splendor blooms brilliantly in the morning sun,
long sleeves sweep through the fragrant cluster.
Pace elegantly like a phoenix,
echoes rise like startled swans.
As a minor attendant, humble and trivial,
I partake in the private, joyous banquet.
Hear the celestial tunes at the imperial terrace,
listen to the heavenly sounds in the orchid hall.
Regret the fleeting dusk at Yǎnzī,
lament the difficulty of spreading the palace music.
Holding the long flute brings much shame,
viewing the hole flute incites resentment.
To be only among the common musicians,
proving indeed my unworthy sounds have already been offered.
Xiè Yǎn's "Listening to Song Prose"
At the moment in the Wú Palace in the afternoon sun,
the shadows calm in the bamboo hall.
The clouds begin to fall,
and gentle breezes freshly fan.
The remaining clouds haven’t yet gathered,
and the fading rainbow is still seen.
The jade chariot is already displayed,
and the orchid dishes are now presented.
Ascend the flying pavilion to expand the view,
gaze upon the winding pool while strolling and observing.
Then summon the girl from Zhào,
command the singer from Qí,
to move her jade pendant,
and emerge from the orchid chamber.
Wear the jeweled hairpin and brighten the forehead,
admire the lead flowers adorning the makeup.
Lower the emerald brows and subdue the colors,
glance with undulating eyes and flow with light.
The voice intends to burst but holds the demeanor,
the breath is yet to be regulated but exudes fragrance.
Create continuity with brilliance,
sometimes pause and sway with restraint.
Initially bend the note of the palace, then merge the composition of Zhēng,
finally separate the angle and blend the business.
Conceal the remaining grace with carved fans,
disperse the light dust on the painted beams.
Should the hidden orchids tremble,
fly and stir the land of Chǔ,
bending and stretching with exquisite ease,
casting glances and relaxing a comfortable manner,
thus is their grand assembly.
It’s like the spring birds echoing with transformation,
in their subtle play.
As if the autumn cicada lightly hums and drags the end,
seeming to stop yet connects again,
hesitating to cease but rises anew,
short but unending,
long yet not departing.
Extend and contract in harmony,
relax and possess the substance,
those who listen are swept away from thought and forget their worries,
those who hear feel pleasure and unburden their emotions.
Before the song ends,
the ruler sighs deeply and says:
“Music,
is to connect with the divine,
to moderate desires,
to harmonize heaven and earth,
to regulate customs,
to observe the legacy of past sages,
to discern the light traces of former worthies.
None can govern without it,
and its rise and fall are of utmost importance.”
Thus, the sages take it as a profound warning,
and the gentlemen use it to exhort themselves.
Liáng Xiàoyuán Dì's "Eulogy of Song"
Sweat lightly dampens red powder,
sitting long, the emerald brows knit with worry.
The voice carries into the bells and stone chimes,
the residual notes mingle with the kònghóu.
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Harmonizing Eulogy of Singer Receiving Sunlight"
Unmatched brilliance among the flowers' emerald,
distinct light caresses the powdered surface.
Repeatedly halting the song to fan the air,
sweeping away the dust in the shadow.
Northern Qí Liú Tì's "Clear Song Emission"
Through the fan, one connects to the face slowly,
within the melody, "Spring Eternal" plays.
Long should bewilder the guests seated,
indeed stir the dust of beams.
Chén Zhōuhóngzhèng's "Eulogy of Singer Receiving Sunlight"
Slanting light enters the red fan,
distinctly the clearest view.
Wishing to hold the light on the carved balustrade,
yet making the sound resonate around the beams.
Suí Yǔ Xìn's "Listening to Song"
The harmonics newly taught cease,
the learning at Héyáng commences.
Just allow to hear a single melody,
the residual sound flies for three days.
Dance fifth
Cài Yōng's "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" says:
"Dance is
the expression of music.
It involves bending, stretching, and expanding,
following the regulation of varying lengths and movements."
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"In the beginning of Táotáng,
there was an excess of yin energy stagnating,
and people's qi was obstructed,
so dance was created to lead it out."
"Lǐjì" says:
"For those who manage labor, their dance steps extend far;
for those who manage leisure, their steps are short.
Thus, by observing the dance,
one can know their virtue."
People labor with thin virtue, and few dance.
"Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The Son of Heaven has eight ranks,
sixty-four people.
Feudal lords have six,
forty-eight people.
High officials have four,
thirty-two people.
Gentlemen have two.
Sixteen people.
Dance regulates the eight sounds and moves with the eight winds,
thus it uses eight."
"Zhou Lǐ‧Yuè Shī" says:
"In general, dances include fēi dance, yǔ dance, huáng dance, máo dance, gàn dance, and rén dance."
Fēi is
white silk woven from jade color.
Yǔ is
composed of feathers.
Huáng is
a mix of five-colored feathers like a phoenix's feathers,
used in dance.
The jīng dance uses
the tail of a yak;
gàn dance is
a military dance;
rén dance is
a hand dance;
national altars use fēi,
ancestral temples use yǔ,
the four directions use huáng,
the royal enclosure uses máo,
military affairs use gàn,
celestial bodies use rén.
"Hán Shī" says:
"Wàn,
is a grand dance."
"Erya" says:
"Pó suō,
is dance.
Also, the names of dances through the ages,
include Xiàng Xiāo,
and the dance of Southern Yuè.
King Wén of Zhōu created music.
Martial Virtue,
begins with Wén,
as the dance of the five elements,
Han High Temple dance.
Zhāo Dé dance,
Emperor Wen Temple dance.
Great Virtue dance,
created by Emperor Wu.
Four Seasons dance,
created by Emperor Wen.
Yúnqiáo, Yùmìng dance,
both created by Emperor Guangwu.
Great Military dance,
Emperor Guangwu Temple dance.
Zhāo Wu, Phœnix Flight, Ling Ying, Martial Praise, Martial Beginning, Universal Joy, Jūn Bīn dances,
were all dances of the Wei and Song temples.
Named after regions,
there are Zhōu dance, Zhèng dance, Zhào dance, Bāyú dance, Huáinán dance, Yānyú dance.
Ancient dance tunes include Liquor Dance, Seven Plate Dance,
and Zhāng Héng has the "Seven Plate Dance Ode".
Yíngchén dance, Collection of Feathers dance,
mentioned in Wáng Zǐnián's "Lost Records".
Qiáoxiù dance, Folding Waist dance,
both created by Lady Qī,
mentioned in "Xījīng Zhájì".
"White Talisman Dance",
created during the time of Wú Sūnhào.
Xiànshuǐ dance,
mentioned in Hé Chéngtiān's Compilation.
Cup Plate dance, Gōngmò dance, Sprinkling dance, Brushing dance."
All were popular creations of the early Jin period,
mentioned in Shěn Yuè's "Song Book".
Simulate Merits and Illuminate Virtue
"The Book of the Later Han" says:
"The imperial edict says:
'Songs simulate virtue,
dances simulate merits.
The music and dance of the Guangwu Temple,
is named the Great Military Dance.'" "Shiji" says:
"In the first year of Emperor Jing's reign,
a decree was issued to the Censor.
It states that songs are to manifest virtue,
dances are to illuminate virtue,
and the High Temple first performed the Wénshǐ Five Elements Dance."
Holding Shield,
Wielding Spear
"Shǔjīng" says:
"When the Miao people rebelled,
the Emperor spread cultural virtues,
dancing with shields and feathers on two terraces."
Kǒng Ānguó notes:
"Shields and feathers,
are held by dancers."
"Wǔjīng Tōngyì" says:
"The music of the Eastern Barbarians,
involves spear dancing,
assisting in the growth of seasons;
the music of the Southern Barbarians,
involves feather dancing,
aiding in nurturing the seasons."
Stepping in Rhythm and Responding to Measure
Fù Yì's "Dance Ode" says:
"Stepping in rhythm to the drum,
with spreading intention as wide as the sun.
Roaming in thought without defect,
distant thoughts extend far."
Hào Mò's "Dance Ode" says:
"In sorrow, they cry and leap in rhythm,
in joy, they sing in tune.
Men leap and soar in exuberance,
valiant and solemn;
women move gracefully,
delicate and secluded.
Bending and stretching in accordance with standards,
advancing and retreating in harmony with notes."
Bow and Rise
Cài Yōng's "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" says:
"The expression of music is dance,
involving bowing, rising, unfolding,
following the regulation of varying lengths."
Cuī Yǐn's "Qī Yī" says:
"Flaunting the long sleeves of soaring grain,
dancing with a slender waist in rise and fall.
In profuse intricacy, slightly obscure,
shining brilliantly and then clear again."
Thousand Youths and Eight Ranks
"Hànshū‧Jiàosì lǐ gē" says:
"A thousand youths align dances in eight ranks,
uniting harmoniously with Tāiyī."
Luan's Flight and Dragon's Grace
Biān Ràng's "Zhāng Huá Fù" says:
"Lifting weak supports to wind around,
like green reeds bending.
Suddenly fluttering lightly,
like luans flying in the celestial river."
Fù Xuán's "Què Dōngxī Mén Xíng" says:
"Music and dance in perfect harmony,
moving the body without losing timing.
In retreat like a hidden dragon gracefully,
advancing as a soaring luan in flight."
Extraordinary and Marvelous
Zhāng Zài's "Lín Wǔ Fù" says:
"The Lín dance shines uniquely,
surpassing the rank of all entertainers.
Collecting the legacy of gàn and qǐ,
matching the timing of two and eight."
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Lín Wǔ Fù" says:
"Focusing exquisitely in the music bureau,
covering extraordinary marvels among performers.
Not of the trivial achievements of the ordinary,
but a treasure of the imperial world."
Respond to Sound and Match Rhythm
Fù Yì's "Dance Ode" says:
"Advancing slightly,
like soaring, like walking,
like rising, like bending.
Stirring and responding to the measure,
pointing and glancing to respond to sound."
"Chuci" says:
"Flying swiftly in green canopies,
unfolding poetry, joining in dance.
Resonate with rhythm, match the beat,
the spirits arrive and obscure the sun."
Wáng Yì's notes:
"Indeed again extending poetry and song,
creating elegant music,
joining the harmony of the six pitches,
to match the dance rhythm."
Fèngxiáng Hóngzhù
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Seven Songs" states:
"They wave their long sleeves like a whirlwind swirling,
raise their slender waists like smoke rising.
Now lifting their heads and undulating,
now stamping their feet and standing poised.
In a flurry, turning like dragons and soaring like phoenixes,
suddenly as if toppling, then halting in stillness."
Cáo Zhí's "Seven Expositions" states:
"Leaping and soaring aloft,
coiling and swirling swiftly.
Suddenly you soar like a swan,
then dive like a duck disappearing.
Releasing their light bodies to swiftly advance,
the shadow pursues the form but cannot catch up."
Bōhuí Fēngzhuǎn
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Pipa" states:
"Flying dragons line up to dance,
the women of Zhào stand side by side.
Advancing like startled cranes,
turning like swirling waves."
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"They perform new melodies,
arrange secret dances.
Whirlwinds circle, winds turn,
flowing colors form patterns.
Their long sleeves, graceful and connected,
their long skirts, fluttering and multicolored.
Advancing like soaring dragons,
descending like collapsing clouds."
Yúzī Yìtài
Fù Xuán's "Song of the East and West Gates" states:
"Turning their eyes, flowing with divine light,
leaning and inclining, they possess lingering grace."
Liú Shào's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Zhào" states:
"Then they present the famous entertainers of Zhōngshān,
the courtesans of Xiāngguó.
Dí Dī's wonderful music,
Hándān's talented dances.
Their postures, of unparalleled elegant demeanor,
are truly outstanding and without match."
Běilǐ Xīchéng
Zhāng Huá's "Song of Frivolity" states:
"Běilǐ presents extraordinary dances,
Dàlíng performs famous songs.
The new melodies are exceptionally stirring like Jíchǔ,
the marvelous courtesans surpass Yáng'ē."
Lù Yún's poem states:
"Xīchéng has many elegant dances,
Zǒngzhāng abounds with clear plucking.
Reed pipes sound from crimson lips,
vermilion strings encircle white wrists."
Fēi qīng jū Yū cháng xiù
Zhāng Zǎi's "Rhapsody on the Tàowǔ" states:
"Their hands move without fixed pattern,
their feet do not touch their sashes.
Light skirts fly like simurghs,
fluttering delicately, trailing beyond."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states:
"They swing their long sleeves and dance repeatedly,
fluttering lightly and gracefully, relaxed and joyful."
Lè bīn zhǔ Xié jūn chén
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on Dance" states:
"Moreover, the songs of the Nine Virtues,
the dances of the Nine Sháo,
transform like the soothing south wind,
moisten like timely rain,
shift customs and change habits,
unify and blend Qí and Chǔ.
Used in sacrifice, then gods and spirits come to partake,
used in feasting, then host and guests are joyful.
Compared to this,
which is superior?"
Xiàhóu's "Rhapsody on the Tàowǔ" states:
"In the temple, they move the ancestors,
in the suburbs, they bring down the heavenly spirits.
They draw in harmonious energy between heaven and earth,
and achieve harmony between ruler and minister.
They harmonize ultimate beauty in the ninefold music,
equal the supreme above in wise culture."
Huò chí huò sù Ruò sǒng ruò qīng
Biàn Lán's "Rhapsody on the Xǔchāng Palace" states:
"They perform the Seven Plates in successive movements,
watch their lightness and agility as they flutter lightly,
sometimes slow, sometimes swift,
now here, now spinning."
Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on Dance" states:
"As they advance slightly,
they seem poised, they seem leaning."
Hòu Hàn Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on Dance"
King Xiāng of Chǔ had finished touring Yúnmèng,
and was about to set out wine for a feast.
He said to Sòng Yù:
"I wish to toast my ministers;
how shall we entertain them?"
Yù said:
"I have heard that the stirring Chǔ melodies and Jiéfēng,
the Yáng'ē dances,
are the ultimate spectacle of talented performers,
the most exquisite under heaven.
Ah!
May they be presented?"
The king said:
"Try to compose a rhapsody on them for me."
Yù said:
"Yes, yes.
Then the women of Zhèng advance together,
sixteen girls slowly attend,
their beautiful attire extremely gorgeous,
their gentle grace conveying demeanor.
Their appearance enchanting and alluring,
their rosy faces radiant, displaying splendor.
Their eyebrows, delicate and connected, increasingly curved,
their eyes, flowing glances, with swirling waves.
Pearls and kingfisher feathers glitter and shine,
