And again cause the King of Jīng to chant.
Plaintive, plaintive, the solitary bamboo pipe,
Comes to answer the Yúnhé lute.
Flute, Tenth
The "Fēngsú Tōng" says:
"The flute
was made by Qiū Zhòng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Also, according to Sòng Yù's 'Ode to the Flute':
'Yù lived before the Hàn,
so I fear this account is incorrect.'"
Also, Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Long Flute" states:
"The modern double flute originated from the Qiāng."
The flute,
means to cleanse,
that which cleanses evil filth,
bringing it into elegance and correctness.
It is one chǐ four cùn long,
with seven holes.
The flute's pitch is fixed,
all stringed songs take the flute as standard.
Sources of flute bamboo include:
the bamboo of Yúnmèng,
seen in Wèi Wén's "Letter to Wú Zhì".
the stem from Héngyáng,
seen in Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Flute".
the bamboo from Kē Tíng.
seen in Fú Tāo's "Ode to the Long Flute".
Those skilled in playing the flute in ancient times include:
Mǎ Róng,
seen in Róng's own account.
Yóu Chǔ,
seen in the "Wèi Zhì".
Sòng Huī,
seen in the "Shìshuō":
"Huī
was a disciple of Shí Chóng's Lǜzhū."
Huán Zǐyě and the servant Gù."
seen in the "Yǔlín".
Rare Treasure / Fine Stem
Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Flute" says:
"Fragrant forest, bright stem,
holds a rare treasure;
broad-minded people understand clearly,
delighting in this art."
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Flute" says:
"Whittling a long stem,
three holes, slender and long.
Vast and boundless in flow,
the warrior's tones rise and fall."
Zhāohuá Pipe / Kē Tíng Bamboo
The "Xījīng Zá Jì" says:
"When Emperor Gāozǔ first entered the Xiányáng Palace,
he toured the storehouses,
where gold, jade, and rare treasures
were beyond description.
Among the most astonishing
was a flute two chǐ three cùn long,
with six holes,
inscribed: 'The Pipe of Zhāohuá.'"
Fú Tāo's "Preface to the Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"My colleague Huán Zǐyě possesses an old long flute,
passed down by elders,
said to have been made by Cài Yōng.
Initially, Yōng fled trouble to the region south of the Yangtze,
lodging at the Kē Tíng hostel,
where bamboo was used as rafters.
Yōng looked up and gazed at it, saying:
'Fine bamboo indeed.'
He took it to make a flute,
its extraordinary sound uniquely peerless.
Handed down through generations,
it has survived to this day."
Expressing Resentment / Cleansing Evil
Cài Yōng's "Ode to the Blind Musician" says:
"Heaven, how obscured is this blind man!
His heart, confined and distressed, is stifled and gloomy.
Eyes dark and without sight,
alas, his bosom vexed and sorrowful.
Stroking the long flute to express his resentment,
his breath roars and rumbles, flying forth unrestrained."
"Cleansing evil" already appears in the narrative section.
Conveying Meaning / Delighting the Spirit
Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"It can communicate with spirits and affect things,
portray the spirit and convey meaning,
express sincerity and fulfill intent,
lead in action and initiate affairs."
Fú Tāo's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"Cloud-dwelling birds fold their wings for it,
spring sturgeon leap their scales for it.
From afar, it can communicate with spirits and reach subtleties;
from near, it can depict emotions and delight the spirit."
Stirring and Clear / Pure and Sorrowful
Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"Wandering freely and unrestrained,
vast and expansive, open and boundless—
such is the manner of Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ;
gentle, upright, magnanimous, and resolute—
such is the method of Confucius and Mencius;
stirring, clear, pure, and severe—
such is the integrity of Suí Guāng."
Táo Qián's "Ode to Leisure and Emotion" says:
"Rising, adjusting my belt to await the dawn,
thick frost glistens on the white steps.
Cocks fold their wings, dawn not yet bright,
a distant flute sounds, pure and sorrowful."
Mixed Preludes / Extraordinary Tunes
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" says:
"In the tenth year of the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
the Palace Library Supervisor Xún Xù and Palace Library Director Zhāng Huá ordered Hǎo Yù to play the zither,
while Sòng Tóng blew the flute,
to create mixed preludes in mutual harmony."
Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Flute" says:
"Summon Bó Qí from the cool shade,
pursue Shēnzi to the Jìn city.
For extraordinary tunes and elegant music
are what restrain excess.
Embroidered silks and ceremonial robes
are what ward off the cold."
Portraying the Spirit / Pleasing the Will
"Portraying the spirit" already appears in the annotation above under "conveying meaning."
Fú Tāo's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"In success, it suffices to harmonize virtue and proclaim plans;
in adversity, it suffices to please the will and preserve oneself.
Combining these four virtues, it is called outstanding,
hence renowned among the cultured and treasured as an instrument."
Water Dragon's Cry / Cloud Birds Folding Wings
Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"A dragon cries in water, unseen itself;
cut bamboo and blow it, the sound is similar."
"Cloud birds folding wings" already appears in the annotation above under "delighting the spirit."
Bringing into Elegance and Correctness / Washing Away Grime
"Bringing into elegance and correctness" already appears in the narrative section.
Mǎ Róng's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"It can express sincerity and fulfill intent,
lead in action and initiate affairs,
irrigate and cleanse filth,
bathe and wash away grime."
Leaving Southern Chǔ / Originating from Xīliáng
Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Long Flute" says:
"The eight tones harmoniously blended,
all receive their nature from it.
Goodness upon goodness does not decline,
preserving it for the times.
Cutting off the legacy of Zhèng,
leaving Southern Chǔ.
Beautiful winds, vast and expansive,
flowing freely and flourishing."
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Flute" says:
"Originating from Xīliáng,
flowing vast and boundless."
The "Flute Rhapsody" by Sòng Yù of Chǔ
I once gazed upon the southern slopes of Héng Mountain,
And saw wondrous slender bamboos and unusual trunks,
Sparse-jointed and simple-branched, growing in clusters.
Their location was vast and towering a thousand fathoms,
With sheer streams and lofty mounds,
Rising majestically ten thousand zhang high,
Where paired boulders stood coiled.
The Vermilion River surged to its left,
And the Sweet Spring flowed to its right.
When Master Kuàng was about to play the melodies of "Yángchūn," "Běibǐ," and "White Snow,"
He sought its masculine essence;
When Sòng Yì was to send Jīng Qīng off upon the Yì River,
He obtained its feminine essence.
Then the heavens turned, and the lesser yin arose,
As the white sun declined westward.
He summoned Yán Chūn,
And dispatched Wǔ Zǐ.
They stretched their long necks,
And raised their jade-like hands.
Parting vermilion lips,
They revealed gleaming white teeth.
Ruddy complexions appeared,
And jade-like countenances arose.
They chanted the clear shāng mode,
Pursuing the flowing zhǐ notes.
The "Long Flute Rhapsody" by Mǎ Róng of the Later Hàn
Róng, being widely learned in the classics and elegant writings,
And thoroughly versed in numerology,
Moreover had a natural fondness for music,
Being able to play the qin and blow the flute,
While serving as a Dūyóu.
Having no lingering affairs,
He lay alone in the Píngyáng Wù of Méi County,
Where a traveler from Luòyáng was lodging at an inn,
Playing the flute.
Róng had been away from the capital for over a year,
And upon briefly hearing it, found it deeply mournful yet delightful,
So he composed the "Long Flute Rhapsody."
Its words say:
"Ah, the wondrous growth of the zhōnglóng bamboo,
Upon the northern cliffs of Zhōngnán Mountain.
It leans against the solitary peak of Jiǔchéng,
Overlooking the stone stream ten thousand fathoms deep.
Thus, there are no paths in the secluded intervals,
And human footprints rarely reach.
Gibbons and snub-nosed monkeys chant by day,
While flying squirrels cry by night.
Then banished ministers and exiled sons,
Abandoned wives and parted friends,
Gather downwind,
Collecting their spirits and focusing their ears.
Kuí and Xiāng compared the pitches,
Zǐyě harmonized the modes.
All twelve were fully present,
With Huángzhōng as the foundation.
Observe in detail the rich convergence and complex gathering of melodies and strains,
How abundant they are!
Profuse and resplendent, brilliant and radiant,
Truly delightful!
Waves scattering and broadly extending,
Indeed remarkable!
When the pitches and modes are harmonized,
Mournful sounds also descend.
As the melody ends and the piece concludes,
Remaining strings arise anew.
Intricate fingers repeatedly pluck,
Dense emotions layer upon layer.
Above, it models itself upon the Sháo xiāo and southern yuè,
In the middle, it takes its measure from 'White Snow' and 'Green Waters,'
Below, it adopts the form of 'Yánlù' and 'Bārén.'
At this time, Mián Jū fell silent,
Bó Yá broke his strings.
Páo Bá ceased his bridges,
Shī Xiāng loosened his hangings.
In recent times, double flutes originated from the Qiāng,
The Qiāng people cut bamboo without cease.
A dragon's cry in water, unseen itself,
Cut bamboo and blow it—the sound is similar.
Jīng Fáng Jūnmíng understood tones and pitches,
So based on four holes, he added one more.
The hole added by Jūnmíng came later,
This is called the shāng tone, completing the five notes."
The "Flute Rhapsody" by Chén Fùzài
Pure bamboo, emerald joints,
Braving frost, halting snow.
By river pools, offered as poles,
Cut by the Bā people.
Equipped with the five notes,
Thus set with six holes.
Extraordinary sounds, now restrained, now soaring,
Seem to emerge from Píngyáng.
Melodies congeal in high halls,
Sounds echo deep in inner chambers.
Already following the dance with swirling sleeves,
Also about to accompany songs that circle the beams.
Suddenly, from playing, it turns perilously short,
Then, adjusting the blow, becomes soft and long.
At such a time,
Zhào's sè ceases its songs,
Qí's yú stops its choruses,
Seeing the ivory mats delight the ear,
Hearing the clear flute's vast brightness.
Chén Zhōu Hóngràng's "Poem on the Long Flute Exhaling Clear Air"
The shāng tone transmits from the later hole,
The dragon's chant, stifled, pours forth from the front.
Emotions severed at the Shānyáng lodge,
Breath choked at the Píngyáng hamlet.
Hú horsemen vie to return north,
Especially knowing the bitterness of leaving home.
A traveler's feelings are easily wounded,
Falling tears like interwoven rain.
Chén Hèchè's "Poem on Obtaining the Long Flute Exhaling Clear Air"
Hú frontier invaded by misty fog,
Qiāng flute exhales a clear sound.
Rhyme fitting the Shānyáng melody,
Tone mournful as the Lǒngshàng chant.
Willows broken by the city walls,
Plums blooming in forests beyond the ridges.
Then I know the border-crossing foe,
Fears not the depths of Wǔ Stream.
Suí Yáo Chá's "Poem on Obtaining the Flute"
Composing the tune is a beautiful lady,
Creating the name comes from a skillful craftsman.
Kūn strings at times unmatched,
Phoenix pipes still face each other.
Following songs, its resonance further issues,
Accompanying dances, its sound grows ever brighter.
Winding through cloud-like windows,
Meandering out from embroidered curtains.
Long accompanying within painted halls,
Receiving favor without any yielding.
Liú Xiàosūn's "Poem in Praise of the Flute"
In cool autumn nights, the flute sings,
Flowing breeze, melody of ninefold perfection.
Tune lofty, at times impassioned,
Melody shifting, sometimes desolate and clear.
The traveler harbors parting thoughts,
Neighbors ponder old affections.
Fortunate to have the regard of one who understands the sound,
For a thousand years, there will be extraordinary music.
Sacred, first class
The Book of Documents says:
"Wisdom makes one a sage."
It also says:
"The sage establishes models."
The Book of Changes says:
"Preparing things for their use,
establishing and completing implements to benefit the world,
none is greater than the sage.
One who knows advancement and retreat, survival and perishing, and does not lose his correctness,
is he not the sage?"
The Book of Rites says:
"Great indeed is the Way of the sage,
vast and abundant, it nurtures the myriad things.
Lofty to the heavens,
like heaven and earth, there is nothing it does not support and bear,
nothing it does not cover and shelter.
(Pronunciation note: Tú dào qiē.)
Like the alternating progression of the four seasons,
like the alternating brightness of the sun and moon."
The Family Sayings of Confucius says:
"Formerly, Duke Āi asked:
'What is called a sage?'
Confucius replied:
'What is called a sage is one
whose wisdom penetrates the great Way,
who responds to change without exhaustion,
and who fathoms the nature and disposition of things.'" The Six Secret Teachings says:
"As for the sage,
he brings peace and joy to all the people of the world."
Guǎnzǐ says:
"The sage is like heaven,
impartially covering all;
like earth,
impartially bearing all.
Partiality
brings disorder to the world."
Lǎozǐ says:
"The sage has no constant mind;
he takes the mind of the hundred surnames as his mind.
To the good I am good;
to the not good I am also good."
Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Now Bǔ Liángyǐ
has the talent of a sage but not the Way of a sage.
I have the Way of a sage but not the talent of a sage.
If I teach him, will he indeed become a sage!"
Master Xún says:
"Under heaven there are not two Ways.
The sage is
the sharp instrument of the world."
The Garden of Stories says:
"The sage towards the hundred surnames
is like towards an infant.
He feeds the hungry,
clothes the cold,
nurtures and rears them,
cultivates and grows them,
fearing only that they do not reach greatness."
Receiving the Chart / Added Calculation
The Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào says:
"After four thousand five hundred and sixty years,
the essence returns to the beginning,
grasping the mandate's pivot,
the Hé River Chart arises,
the sage receives and contemplates it."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"'Sage' refers to Yáo.
When heaven grasps the mandate and the person who should arise appears,
the Hé River then issues forth the Chart.
Huángdì and Yáo received it and contemplated it,
in order to receive the calendrical calculations."
The Hé River Chart says:
"Huángdì said:
'For every person born, on the first day,
the Celestial Emperor bestows a calculation of thirty-six thousand,
and bestows upon man twenty cycles.
The sage receives thirty-six thousand seven hundred and twenty months,
while man receives thirty-six thousand.
One cycle governs one year.
The sage has an addition of seven hundred and twenty.'"
Illuminating the Distant / Shining on the Subtle
Shīzǐ says:
"The sage's body is like the sun.
Heaven's sun is a foot in circumference,
yet its light fills heaven and earth.
The sage's body is small,
yet what he illuminates is far."
Yán Yánzhī's Lùn Jiǎn says:
"The sage
with spiritual illumination shines on the subtle,
his principle transcends external achievement."
Emptying the Mind / Rectifying Oneself
Lǎozǐ says:
"The sage empties his mind and fills his belly."
Shīzǐ says:
"The sage centers himself and rectifies himself,
therefore he is called the treasury of heaven and earth."
Joining with Heaven / Matching Earth
The Book of Changes says:
"In ancient times, when the sage created the Changes,
he was mysteriously assisted by the spiritual intelligence and produced the yarrow stalks,
joining with heaven and pairing with earth to establish the numbers."
The Dàdài Lǐjì says:
"Duke Āi asked:
'What is called a sage?
His affairs are great,
matching heaven and earth,
joining with the sun and moon.
Like heaven's governance,
none can fathom it.'"
Matching Tallies / Responding to the Pivot
Hán Shī Wàizhuàn says:
"Shùn was born in Zhūféng,
moved to Fùxià,
and died in Míngtiáo;
he was a man of the Eastern Yí.
King Wén was born in Qízhōu,
and died in Bìyǐng;
he was a man of the Western Yí.
The lands where they lived were separated by great distance,
yet when they attained their will and acted in the Central States,
it was like matching tally halves."
Confucius said:
"Earlier sages and later sages,
their measure is one."
Yīn Kāng's discussion on the Changes says:
"Formerly, Fúxī began by drawing the eight trigrams,
observing the images to respond to the pivot."
Majestic / Vast and Abundant
The Dàdài Lǐjì says:
"Duke Āi asked:
'What is called a sage?'
Confucius replied:
'What is called a sage is one
whose wisdom penetrates the great Way,
who responds to change without exhaustion.
Majestic and pure,
none can follow his path;
this is the sage.'" The Book of Documents says:
"The sage's plans are vast and abundant,
his excellent words are greatly clear."
Acting According to the Time / Dividing with Virtue
Wénzǐ says:
"The sage acts according to the time,
and establishes achievement based on resources.
He guards the clear Way,
restrains the feminine aspect,
follows along and responds to change,
constantly staying behind and not taking the lead."
Zhuāngzǐ says:
"To divide with others by virtue is called sagely;
wisdom like a deep abyss and brightness like the sun and moon is called sagely."
Exhausting Spirit and Knowing Transformation / Exhausting Subtlety and Embodying the Way
Yáo Xìn's Shì Wěi says:
"The sage is lofty beyond reaching,
deep beyond fathoming.
He exhausts spirit and knows transformation;
this is what he receives from heaven."
The Wǔxíng Lùn says:
"The sage exhausts all subtleties,
embodies ultimate appropriateness,
therefore he does not seek to have something to show, yet things naturally draw close to him."
Foreknowledge / Mysterious Illumination
Yáo Xìn's Shì Wěi says:
"The sage alone sees with foreknowledge,
his benevolence is like the spring sun,
his trustworthiness is like shadow and echo."
Yáng Xióng's Wǔjīng Gōushěn says:
"The sage's birth must rely on yīn and yáng.
The principle of yīn and yáng
is what the sage exhausts.
Simply by exhausting the principle of yīn and yáng,
the root of mysterious illumination naturally appears.
This is called not seeking self-knowledge,
yet when principle is exhausted, one naturally knows."
Dual Response / Dual Forgetting
Zǔ Táizhī's Dào Lùn says:
"The great Way proceeds through utmost emptiness and smooth penetration;
the sage responds dually through forgetting and letting go."
Liú Jǐn's discussion says:
"The sage embodies and contains qián and kūn,
therefore he forgets both having and not having."
Not Physiognomized / Without Name
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Táng Jǔ physiognomized Cài Zé and said:
'I have heard that sages cannot be physiognomized;
is it perhaps you, sir?'" Zhuāngzǐ says:
"The ultimate person has no self,
the spiritual person has no achievement,
the sage has no name."
Respond After Being Moved, Act After Speaking
The Zhuangzi says:
"The sage responds only after being moved,
acts only after being compelled,
and rises only when there is no alternative."
The Guanzi says:
"The sage chooses what can be spoken and only then acts.
To steal profit only to later suffer harm,
to steal pleasure only to later have sorrow—
the highest sage does not do such things."
Preparing Things for Use, Perfecting Virtue
The Yijing says:
"Preparing things for use,
establishing and completing implements to benefit the world—
none is greater than the sage."
The Liji says:
"When the sage records affairs,
he considers them with greatness,
cherishes them with reverence,
carries them out with ritual,
cultivates them with filial piety,
begins them with righteousness,
and ends them with benevolence.
Therefore, when the ancients undertook a single task,
the multitude all knew that their virtue was perfect."
Accomplishing Tasks, Creating Things
The Yijing says:
"Now, the Changes—
this is what the sage uses to probe the depths and investigate the subtleties.
Only because of its depth can it penetrate the will of the world;
only because of its subtlety can it accomplish the tasks of the world;
only because of its spirituality can it be swift without haste,
and arrive without going."
The Zhouli says:
"The wise create things;
the skillful transmit them.
The affairs of the hundred crafts
are all the work of sages."
Spiritual Transformation, Heavenly Action
The Wenzi says:
"The sage
unites his virtue with Heaven and Earth,
unites his brightness with the sun and moon,
and is capable of spiritual transformation."
The Zhuangzi says:
"The sage's life is like the action of Heaven;
his death is the transformation of things.
In stillness, he shares virtue with the yin;
in movement, he shares the waves with the yang.
He does not initiate fortune,
nor does he begin misfortune."
Heaven-Endowed, Profoundly Penetrating
The Analects says:
"The Grand Steward asked Zigòng:
'Is your Master a sage?
Why is he so versatile?'
Zigòng replied:
'It is Heaven that endowed him to become a sage,
and also made him versatile.'" The Wenzi says:
"If the sage truly makes his ears and eyes keen and profoundly penetrating,
without being seduced or enamored,
his spirit guarded within,
his physical form not transgressing,
then even observing beyond past generations
and within future affairs
would be insufficient to see."
Pure and Profound, Vast and Boundless
The Da Dai Liji says:
"Duke Āi asked:
'What is called a sage?'
Confucius replied:
'What is called a sage
is solemn, pure, and profound,
such that none can follow him.
This can then be called a sage.'" The Liezi says:
"Confucius said:
'In the West there is a sage.
He does not govern, yet there is no disorder;
he does not speak, yet he is trusted;
he does not transform, yet things proceed of themselves.
Vast and boundless—people cannot name him.'"
Rooted in Heaven and Earth, Aligned with Sun and Moon
The Liji says:
"When the sage establishes models,
he necessarily takes Heaven and Earth as the root,
takes yin and yang as the starting point,
takes the four seasons as the handle,
and takes the sun and stars as the markers."
The Da Dai Liji says:
"Confucius said:
'The sage attends to great affairs,
matching Heaven and Earth,
aligning with the sun and moon,
and mingling with rainbows and clouds.'"
Perfecting the Nine Virtues, Synthesizing the Three Bonds
Kǒng Róng's "Discussion on the Superiority and Inferiority of Sages" says:
"I consider that sages all receive the pure essence of qián and kūn,
inherit the harmonious breath of creation.
They encompass the highest goodness of all conduct,
perfecting the fine beauty of the nine virtues."
Zhì Yú's "In Praise of Confucius" says:
"Zhòngní, the great sage,
encountered a time of darkness and desolation.
The Hé Tú was submerged and obscured,
the phoenix bird hidden away.
Then he set in order ritual and music,
to synthesize the three bonds.
Based on history, he established laws—
this is called the Unrowned King."
Inheriting the Four Seasons, Penetrating All Things
Yáo Xìn's Shì Wěi says:
"What the sage inherits comes from the four seasons,
what he inherits comes from the primal breath."
The Huainanzi says:
"The sage cultivates his Way and methods inwardly,
and does not outwardly adorn himself with benevolence and righteousness.
He does not know the suitability of ears and eyes,
but wanders in the harmony of spirit.
If it is thus,
he horizontally encompasses the six directions,
simultaneously penetrating all things.
This is the wandering of the sage."
Mysteriously Assisting the Divine and Bright, Encompassing Heaven and Earth
The Yijing says:
"The sage created the Changes,
mysteriously assisting the divine and bright,
taking Heaven as three and Earth as two to rely on numbers."
Also, Yáng Xióng's Wǔjīng Gōuchén says:
"Those who know from birth are the highest."
Someone asked:
"Who knows from birth?"
He replied:
"The sage, after the two modes separated,
suspended images arrayed their radiance.
The eight winds were orderly,
the four breaths alternated in control.
Observing the sun and moon, he comprehended the numbers of yin and yang;
roaming freely through the eight nodes,
looking up and down at the dark and yellow.
He encompassed the substance of Heaven and Earth,
exhaustively investigated the mechanism of life.
He looked to Heaven as his teacher,
using it to awaken his own mind.
Therefore it is said he knows from birth—
is this not indeed clear!"
Later Hàn Kǒng Róng's "Discussion on the Superiority and Inferiority of Sages"

Confucius said, "Great indeed was Yáo as a ruler! Only Heaven is great, and only Yáo modeled himself on it." This is the clearest text stating that he covered and surpassed all other sages as the most excellent.
Yáo served as Son of Heaven for over ninety years.
His governance and transformation harmonized with the people's hearts;
the Yǎ and Sòng flowed among the hearing of the multitude.
Therefore, his reputation and virtue became known,
and he was thus called the foremost.
This is what the Yijing means by "the sage remains long in his position, and the world is transformed and accomplished,"
and "after a hundred years, then violence is overcome and killing eliminated,"
and "it must be a generation before benevolence is achieved."
Therefore it is said, "Great indeed was Yáo as a ruler!"
Yáo as a sage
shows that his sageliness is the same as that of other sages,
but he is called a ruler because people saw him as such.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Discourse on Discerning the Sage"
The sage discards emotions and forgets self,
constantly mindful of universally benefiting all.
If he does not ascend to the position of the nine and five,
then his Way cannot be practiced.
It is not that he considers the yellow canopy and jade seal as honorable.
King Wén founded Zhōu but did not complete it;
King Wǔ completed it but did not perfect it.
Although the Duke of Zhōu did not have the fortune of kingship,
he could not fail to bring to completion the achievements of his father and elder brother, the two sages.
If he had not displayed the sagely merit,
established rituals and created music,
then the task of Great Peace would not have been manifest,
and the beauty of the two sages would not have been made clear.
Jìn Huà Tán's "New Discourse"
Now, embodying the Way is sageliness;
wandering in spirit is wisdom.
Embodying the Way, one then entrusts intention beyond physical form;
wandering in spirit, one then exhaustively investigates the beginnings of transformation and change.
Therefore, silent and unmoving,
yet all things are used by me;
solid and mysteriously silent,
yet all mechanisms are operated by me.
Yīn Zhòngkān’s “Discourse on Heaven’s Sagehood”
Heaven is the root and foundation of all things,
profound and silent, speaking not.
The common people live without employing its labor,
and all things flourish without exhausting its toil.
The sage receives Heaven’s illumination,
applies Heaven’s work,
and proclaims its Way.
Zhāng Wéncóng’s “Eulogy for Emperor Tàizōng the Cultured”
Oh, resplendent and divine in valor,
succeeding the times to become a sage.
Below, encompassing the nine regions;
above, aligning the seven regulators.
His achievements unite civil and martial,
his merit surpasses Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ.
What peril did he not overcome?
What calamity did he not dispel?
Men and women alike rejoiced,
their baskets filled with dark and yellow silks.
These offerings arriving
shone brightly for our sovereign.
Our sovereign nurtures and fosters,
sustaining life, embracing creation.
Matching Yáo, ascending the Táng heights;
surpassing Zhōu, residing in Hào.
Gathering and bestowing widely,
clear proof ensures stability.
Sincerely treading this virtue,
he purifies the imperial Way.
The imperial Way reverent and bright,
all under heaven peaceful and harmonious.
The three seasons unharmed,
the hundred grains thus ripen.
Our granaries thus amassed,
like mounds, like hillocks.
Once enriched, then taught,
disputes cease, punishments clear.
Yán Shīgǔ’s “Eulogy on Sage Virtue”
All under heaven cultured and enlightened,
sun and moon steadfastly observed.
The hundred spirits receive their duties,
the three numina harmoniously assist.
The great steps already leveled,
radiance shines resplendent.
Transcending Xuān, striding over Hào,
surpassing Zhōu, outstripping Hàn.
Ten thousand years without bound,
eternally extending distant reckonings.
Later Hàn Zhāng Chāo’s “Eulogy for Master Ní”
Lofty, lofty, Confucius the sage,
praised as preeminent across generations.
His measure matches heaven and earth,
his brightness rivals sun and moon.
Jìn Zhàn Fāngshēng’s “In Praise of Master Kǒng”
Far-reaching, Master Kǒng,
dragon appearing at the ninth second.
Expounding transformation, linking to images,
his Way illuminated the end of Zhōu.
Virtuous Men, Part Two
The Forest of Sayings states:
“Virtuous men
are the nation’s guiding principles,
the people’s hope.
Since ancient times, rulers have relied on them for safety or peril.
Thus the Book of Documents says:
‘Only with a sovereign who is not virtuous can there be no governance;
only with a virtuous man who is not a sovereign can there be no sustenance.’
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu embodied the virtue of a great sage
and diligently attended to spitting out and grasping,
thus all the scholars under heaven vied to return to him.
Had the Duke of Zhōu been arrogant and moreover stingy,
the scholars would surely have soared high and departed far,
and those who arrived would have been few indeed.”
Later Hàn Lǐ Gù’s memorial states:
“Your servant hears that the clear in vital energy become spirits,
the clear among men become virtuous.
Those who cultivate the self regard refining the spirit as treasure;
those who govern the state regard accumulating the virtuous as the Way.”
Huáng Shígōng’s Three Strategies states:
“Harming the virtuous brings calamity to three generations;
obstructing the virtuous brings harm upon oneself;
promoting the virtuous brings blessings flowing to descendants;
envying the virtuous brings an incomplete name.”
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
“Trusting the virtuous and employing them
is the ruler’s wisdom;
discussing the virtuous and yielding to them
is the minister’s loyalty.”
It also states:
“Gaining a thousand lǐ of land
is not as good as gaining one virtuous scholar.”
Another saying states:
“Accumulating a thousand pieces of gold
is not as good as having one virtuous man.”
The Liezi states:
“The difficulty in governing a state
lies in recognizing the virtuous, not in considering oneself virtuous.”
The Analects states:
“When you see a virtuous man, think of equaling him;
when you see one who is not virtuous, examine yourself within.”
Master Xún states:
“The virtuous of antiquity,
in eating, had not enough congee;
in clothing, had incomplete short coarse garments.
Yet they would not advance without propriety,
nor accept without righteousness.”
The Garden of Stories states:
“Those crossing rivers and seas rely on boats;
those reaching distant places rely on carriages;
those aspiring to hegemony and kingship rely on the virtuous.”
Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
“Hàn Emperor Wén established the Garden of Longing for the Virtuous for the crown prince
to attract guests.”
The Zhōu Documents, Yīnfú, states:
“In general, governing a state has three constants:
first, the ruler takes promoting the virtuous as constant;
second, officials take employing the virtuous as constant;
third, scholars take revering the virtuous as constant.
Thus, even a hundred generations hence can be known.”
Following Virtue Delighting in the Way
The Rites of Zhōu states:
“Using virtue to establish ranks makes the people follow virtue.”
The Kǒng Family Masters’ Anthology states:
“In Lǔ there was Gōngyí Qián,
a virtuous man.
He delighted in the Way and cherished antiquity,
serene regarding glory and profit.”
Establishing Offices Setting Ranks
The Book of Documents states:
“Establish offices only with the virtuous,
assign duties only with the capable,
honor virtue and reward merit,
and with folded hands, all under heaven is governed.”
“Setting ranks” appears above.
Matching the Sage Modeling Heaven
Western Liáng’s Martial and Illustrious King’s “Eulogy for Yán Huí the Wise and Enlightened” states:
“Hearing one, penetrating ten,
swifter than divine mechanism.
Employed or set aside, active or withdrawn,
he matched in virtue the sage teacher.”
The Yellow Emperor’s Basic Questions states:
“The virtuous man models himself on heaven and earth,
takes sun and moon as images.”
Jìzǐ’s Profound Insight Línzōng’s Penetrating Illumination
Sūn Zǐjīng’s “In Praise of the Eight Worthies” states:
“Jìzǐ wise and perceptive,
his thoughts refined and subtle.
Profound insight, awakening to the obscure,
touching categories, responding to opportunity.”
Lǐ Yóu’s “Eulogy for Guō Yǒudào, One of the Nine Worthies” states:
“Lofty, lofty, possessing the Way,
heroic aura like morning clouds, brisk and bright;
profound insight, penetrating illumination,
wise mind, elegant and clear.”
Poetry Alludes to the Crane’s Cry Changes Speak of the Wild Goose’s Gradual Advance
The Mao Odes states:
“‘The Crane Cries’
admonishes King Xuān.
The crane in the wild, hearing its cry,
alludes to the virtuous man though dwelling in seclusion,
all people know of him.”
The Changes states:
“Above the mountain is water, Gradual;
the nobleman thereby dwells in virtuous conduct and improves customs.
The wild goose gradually advances onto the land;
its feathers can be used as ornaments, auspicious.”
Master Guǎn Embracing the Uncarved Jade The Chǔ Elder Embracing the Genuine
Lǐ Yóu’s “Eulogy for Master Guǎn the Recluse, One of the Nine Worthies” states:
“Master Guǎn embraced the Way,
nourishing his will, nurturing his spirit.
Embracing the uncarved jade, upholding harmony,
treading trust, relying on benevolence.”
Xiè Wàn’s “Eulogy for the Chǔ Elder, One of the Eight Worthies” states:
“The Chǔ elder submerged in unity,
silently delighting in non-action.
Embracing the genuine within and without,
he gathered and stored his feather ornaments.”
Accumulating Propriety Rich in Righteousness
Rén Gǔ’s “Discourse on the Way and Virtue” states:
“Now the virtuous man
accumulates propriety and righteousness at court,
spreads benevolent winds in the countryside,
making all under heaven joyfully sing and dance for his virtue.”
The Annals of Lü Buwei states:
“Marquis Wén of Wèi passed by Duàngān Mù’s lane and leaned on his carriage rail,
saying:
‘Gānmù is indeed a virtuous man.
Gānmù is rich in righteousness,
while merchants are rich in wealth.’”
State Vessels and Human Exemplars
Wáng Bāo’s “Ode on the Sage Lord Obtaining Worthy Ministers” states:
“The worthy are
the vessels and tools of the state.
When those appointed are worthy, then decisions are simplified and achievements are widespread;
when vessels and tools are sharp, then effort is little and accomplishments are many.”
Bān Mèngjiān’s “Fu on Communicating with the Unseen” states:
“Heaven creates the primal chaos,
establishing life and nature.
To return to the heart and expand the Way,
only the worthy and sagely.
The primal ether moves things,
circulating everywhere without resting.
To preserve oneself and leave behind a name,
is the exemplar of humanity.”
Zǎi Yǔ Soaring Like the Wind, Dài Jiǎo Halting Like Clouds
Wáng Yì’s “Praise of Zǎi Wǒ” states:
“Graceful Zǎi Wǒ,
foremost in speech and words.
His will manifests righteousness, his writings are clear,
his outstanding phrases soar like the wind.”
“Biographies of Former Worthies of Wú: Praise of the Late Assistant Inspector Dài Jiǎo” states:
“Lush and abundant talent,
holding integrity, halting like clouds.
His will sharpens like autumn frost,
pure as ice, clear as jade.”
Gù Chéng Flying Like a Swan, Shǐ Zhòu Standing Like a Phoenix
“Biographies of Former Worthies of Wú: Praise of General Fènwǔ Gù Chéng” states:
“O brilliant Fènwǔ,
resplendent in complete virtue.
At home, he was sure to be heard of;
like a swan flying, he soared high.”
Also, “Praise of Magistrate Shǐ Zhòu of Shàngyú” states:
“O splendid Shàngyú,
golden essence, jade purity.
Standing like a phoenix, poised like a simurgh,
lofty and unshakable.”
Jade Purity and Golden Constancy
Sūn Chuò’s “Praise of Yuán Xiàn” states:
“Yuán Xiàn was profound and silent,
pure as ice, refined as jade.
His will soared beyond the nine heavens,
his person content in humble paths.”
Cháng Jǐng’s “Poem on Ancient Worthies” states:
“Lord Yán embodied deep stillness,
setting his will bright as frost and snow.
His plain integrity surpassed golden constancy,
his pure standard transcended jade clarity.”
Avoiding the Times and Transcending the Mundane
The Analects states:
“The Master said:
‘The worthy avoid the world;
next, they avoid certain places;
next, they avoid certain countenances;
next, they avoid certain words.’” Xú Zhěng’s Yùzhāng “Biographies of Exemplary Men” states:
“Magistrate Shū Shī Yáng, styled Jìrú,
was a man of Yíchūn.
He was grave, tranquil, and serene,
pure and white, transcending the mundane.
He always took yielding in courtesy and putting others before himself as his conduct,
and was called a worthy.”
Presenting Silk and Yielding Clothing
The Outer Commentary to the Book of Songs states:
“Confucius met Qí Chéng Běnzǐ between Tán and Tán;
they tilted their carriage canopies and talked all day.
Greatly pleased,
he turned to Zǐlù and said:
‘Yóu, come here,
take a bolt of silk to present to the gentleman.’
Zǐlù said:
‘I, Yóu, have heard from you, Master,
that for a gentleman to meet another not on the proper way,
or for a woman to marry without a matchmaker,
is not done.’
Confucius said:
‘The Book of Songs says:
“There is a beautiful person,
clear and bright, gentle and fine.
By chance we meet,
fulfilling my wish.”’
Moreover, Qí Chéng Běnzǐ
is a worthy gentleman of the world,
and thus I present this to him.’” Cài Yōng’s “Accounts of the Lute” states:
“Formerly, Sīgézǐ, Chéngwénzǐ, and Shūdānzǐ, three men, were friends.
Hearing that King Chéng of Chǔ favored gentlemen,
they went together to see him.
Among steep cliffs and rugged rocks,
they suddenly encountered a raging storm,
and all took shelter under an empty willow.
Their clothes were thin, their provisions exhausted,
and they reckoned they could not all survive.
The three looked at each other and sighed:
‘Rather than all dying,
would it not be better to give the clothes and provisions to one of us!’
The other two considered Gé to be the worthiest,
and yielded their clothes to him.”
Unfolding Radiance and Concealing Light
Xiè Wàn’s “Ode to Eight Worthies” states:
“Brilliant Qū Yuán,
jade-gleaming, ice-fresh.
He unfurled his brilliance in the kingfisher forest,
unfolded his radiance in the dragon river.”
Lǐ Yóu’s “Ode to Nine Worthies: Chén Tàiqiū” states:
“Virtuous indeed, Tàiqiū,
the very measure of virtue.
He concealed his traces in a humble town,
hid his light within a hundred *li*.”
Flying Simurgh and Soaring Phoenix
Sūn Zǐjīng’s “Praise of Eight Worthies: Guǎn Zhòng” states:
“Master Guǎn bent his bow,
and was an enemy of Huán.
Swiftly he followed Jiǔ,
a mere prisoner in bonds.
Bathed and purified in the western suburbs,
the simurgh flew to Zhān Hill.”
Lǐ Yóu’s “Ode to Nine Worthies: Grand Commandant Huá” states:
“Diligent Jìnghóu,
endowed with fine demeanor.
His noble traces, a phoenix soaring;
his pure dust, a dragon flying.”
Masters of Spirit and Guardians of the State
The School Sayings of Confucius states:
“The worthy man
is the ancestor of a hundred blessings,
the master of the spirits.”
Xú Gàn’s Balanced Discourses states:
“The conduct of a great worthy
does not argue right and wrong or dispute crooked and straight with the vulgar.
Thus, when he achieves his aim, the state becomes harmonious,
the altars of soil and grain become secure.
The myriad people receive his blessings,
and all living things rely on his fortune.”
Discerning Stars and Encompassing the Cosmos
The Yellow Emperor’s Basic Questions states:
“The worthy man
discerns the favorable and unfavorable positions of the stars,
and distinguishes the four seasons.”
Lǐ Yóu’s “Ode to Nine Worthies: Gentleman Jī Zhōngsàn” states:
“Solemn Zhōngsàn,
brilliant, wise, and discerning.
He encompassed the cosmos,
and loftily trod the dark path.”
Diligent and Frugal, Knowing the Manifest and the Subtle
The Book of Documents states:
“The Emperor said:
‘Come, Yǔ,
be diligent in service to the state,
frugal in your household,
not self-satisfied or boastful.
Only thus are you worthy.’” Zhì Yú’s “Praise of Yánzǐ” states:
“Yánzǐ was diligent,
his humane heart never straying.
In conduct, he never repeated a fault;
he knew the manifest and the subtle.”
Beneficent, Kind, Gracious, and Harmonious; Gentle, Good, Respectful, and Frugal
The Zuǒ Commentary states:
“In ancient times, Gāoxīnshì had eight talented sons:
Bófèn, Zhòngkān, Shūxiàn, Jìzhòng, Bówǔ, Zhòngxióng,
Shūbào, Jìlí—loyal, reverent, respectful, virtuous, beneficent, kind, gracious, and harmonious.
The people of the world
called them the Eight Virtuous Ones.”
The Analects states:
“The Master obtained it by being gentle, good, respectful, frugal, and yielding.”
Toiling Body and Hardship, Tempering Integrity and Conduct
The “Musical Movements and Acoustic Patterns” states:
“The Duke of Shào
was a worthy man.
His understanding could not match the sage’s in sharing duties,
so he was constantly trembling with fear.
Thus, he dwelt under a tree to hear cases and make judgments,
toiling his body and enduring hardship.
Only then could he equal the sage.
This is why ‘Zhōunán’ has no praise, but ‘Shàonán’ does.”
The Kong Family Masters’ Anthology states:
“In Lǔ there was a man, Gōngyí Qián,
a worthy.
He tempered his integrity and refined his conduct,
and did not serve the feudal lords.
Duke Mù, through Zǐsī, wished to make him prime minister.”
Waving Away Gold, Declining Jade
Péi Qǐ's "Forest of Sayings" states:
"Guǎn Nìng once had a close friendship with Huá Zǐyú in their youth.
While hoeing vegetables together in the garden,
they saw a piece of gold on the ground.
Guǎn waved his hoe as before,
treating it no differently than tiles or stones.
Huá picked it up and threw it away."
Liú Xiàng's "New Prefaces" states:
"A man of Sòng obtained a piece of jade
and offered it to Minister of Works Zǐ Hǎn.
Zǐ Hǎn did not accept it.
The offerer said:
'The jade craftsman considered it a treasure,
therefore I offer it to you.'
Zǐ Hǎn said:
'You consider jade a treasure;
I consider not being greedy a treasure.
If you give it to me, we both lose our treasures.
It is better that we each keep our own treasure.'
Therefore, the elders of Sòng said:
'It is not that Zǐ Hǎn has no treasure;
what he treasures is different.'"
Emptying Oneself, Forgetting the Mind
"The Separate Biography of Rén Gǔ" states:
"His character was pure and kind,
emptying himself as if inadequate,
reverent and respectful as if in awe.
His cultivation of virtue and practice of righteousness
were all carried out silently and unobtrusively."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"Those who nurture their will forget their form;
those who nurture their form forget profit;
those who attain the Way forget their mind."
Heaven-Granted, Spirit-Assisted
Zhōu Fěi's "Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán" states:
"Huáng Xiàn was pure, tranquil, and comprehended principle,
being sagely, broad, and profound.
He did not boast of his reputation to deceive the times,
nor did he adopt a haughty demeanor to correct customs."
Commentators all said:
"Yánzǐ has been reborn in the Hàn Dynasty!"
Yet his ancestral clan originated from humble origins;
his father was an ox doctor.
He received no proper instruction in his youth,
yet later was able to emerge outstandingly brilliant.
He can truly be called one granted by Heaven."
The "Wénzǐ" states:
"Those who accumulate virtue and the Way
are given by Heaven,
assisted by Earth,
and aided by spirits and ghosts."
Aligned with Sun and Moon, Emulating Heaven and Earth
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"I shall leave this world
and enter the gate of the infinite,
to wander in the fields of the boundless.
I shall share light with the sun and moon,
and be eternal with Heaven and Earth."
Qiáo Zhōu's "Instructions on Models" states:
"Diligence in study to revere wisdom
thus achieves broad accomplishment;
vigorous practice with humble demeanor
thus can exalt virtue.
Therefore, the noble person dwells in humility and expands the Way,
so that his virtue can emulate Heaven and Earth."
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng of Wèi's "Discourse on Yánzǐ"
His mind did not violate benevolence;
his actions held no repeated faults.
Employed, he acted; set aside, he withdrew.
He matched the Sage's covenant.
Hearing and receiving subtle words,
there was none he did not comprehend.
Placed within the "Changes",
to manifest his extraordinary distinction.
His death brought profound grief,
deeming Heaven had bereaved himself.
The reason for such earnest devotion to this extent
is the Sage's commendation of the worthy and wise.
Later Hàn Mí Héng's "Stele for Yánzǐ"
The bearing of profound wisdom
was evident from his earliest nurture.
The talent of supreme brilliance
shone forth in his infancy.
He knew the subtle and knew the manifest;
hearing one, he knew ten.
Zhòngní lacked the achievements of Shùn and Yǔ,
yet the Master embraced the splendor of Yuán and Kǎi.
Jìn Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Eulogy for Zuǒ Qiūmíng"
In an age of chaos, slander prevails;
the Way of the noble person is troubled.
Qiūmíng comprehended the Sage,
and devoted his intent to the "Spring and Autumn".
Subtle words escaped calamity;
deviant conduct did not flow unchecked.
Later Hàn Wáng Càn's "Eulogy for Zhèng Kǎofǔ"
Sincere and earnest, correct father,
responding to virtue, profoundly abundant.
Personally a minister of state,
his clan was of ducal surname.
In years reaching old age,
three generations heard governance.
Who could not be diligent?
He extended kindness and restrained reverence.
Gruel for his mouth,
stooped, he received the command.
His name inscribed on the bronze tripod,
his blessing extended to later sages.
Western Jìn Jī Kāng's "Eulogy for Yuán Xiàn"
Yuán Xiàn savored the Way;
wealth was scant, righteousness abundant.
Dwelling leisurely by a wicker gate,
content in poverty, steadfast in hardship.
Strumming and singing, he found joy himself;
body at ease, mind serene.
When advancing, he responded to Zǐgòng;
far-reaching, he possessed a pure breeze.
Jìn Zhì Yú's "Eulogy for Zuǒ Qiūmíng"
Qiūmíng composed the history
in an age of declining Zhōu.
Interweaving ancient texts,
he sought to broaden fine plans.
Elucidating the kingly canon,
he illuminated and expounded the "Spring and Autumn".
Proclaiming the Sage's intent,
his legacy endures through generations, ever more sublime.
Eastern Jìn Xiè Wàn's "Eulogy for Jī Zhōngsàn of the Seven Worthies"
Far-reaching, O Master,
your outstanding mark, lofty and splendid.
Aspiring to nest-dwellers, cleansing the heart;
emulating Zhuāng, entrusting to outward form.
Thus unrestrained, thus carefree,
transcending these vulgar snares.
Zhōng Qī no longer exists;
to whom shall the entrusted melody be appreciated?
Loyalty, Part Three
The *Han Shi Wai Zhuan* states:
"There are three ways of loyalty:
there is great loyalty,
there is secondary loyalty,
and there is lesser loyalty.
To cover one's lord with the Way and transform him—
that is great loyalty;
to harmonize one's lord with virtue and assist him—
that is secondary loyalty;
to remonstrate against wrong with what is right and incur resentment—
that is lesser loyalty.
The Duke of Zhōu towards King Chéng—
he can be called greatly loyal;
Guǎn Zhòng towards Duke Huán—
he can be called secondarily loyal;
Wǔ Zīxū towards Fūchāi—
he can be called lesserly loyal."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"For a minister to sacrifice his own life, if it benefits his lord, he should do it."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"When Chǔ's Zǐnáng died,
he left words saying Zǐgēng must fortify Yǐng.
Yǐng
was the capital to which Chǔ had moved,
but it had no city walls.
The gentleman said Zǐnáng was loyal:
upon the lord's death, he did not forget to enhance his name;
facing his own death, he did not forget to defend the altars of soil and grain.
Can this be called loyalty?
Loyalty—
it is what people look up to."
It also says:
"Duke Xiàn of Jìn sent Xún Xī to tutor Xī Qí.
He replied:
'Your servant will exhaust the strength of his limbs,
adding to it loyalty and steadfastness.
If it succeeds,
it is due to your lordship's numinous power;
if it does not succeed,
then I will follow it with death.'
The duke said:
'What is called loyalty and steadfastness?'
He replied:
'For the benefit of the ducal house,
knowing of nothing that should not be done—
that is loyalty;
sending off the departed and serving the living,
paired together without suspicion—
that is steadfastness.'" Also, Hú Tū said:
"When a son is able to take office,
his father teaches him loyalty.
Having inscribed his name [on the roster] and presented his gifts [of introduction],
to be of two minds is a crime."
Also: "When Jì Wénzǐ died,
he had no concubines clothed in silk,
no horses fed on grain,
no stored gold or jade,
and no special vessels.
The gentleman therefore knew that Jì Wénzǐ was loyal to the ducal house.
He served as minister to three lords,
yet had no private accumulation.
Can he not be called loyal?"
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Bào Yǒng, styled Jūncháng,
was touring the county
and passed the tomb of Gēngshǐ.
He ordered his carriage to stop and prepared to descend.
His attendant advised him to stop,
but Bào Yǒng said:
'I personally served him facing north as my lord;
how could I bear to have my carriage pass his tomb?
Even if I incur the offense of the Director of Retainers,
I will not avoid it.'
He then descended, wept, and exhausted his grief.
The Emperor heard of this
and asked his ministers:
'For an envoy to act thus,
what do you think?'
Grand Master of the Palace Zhāng Kān replied:
'Benevolence is the ancestor of all conduct;
loyalty is the ancestor of ritual and righteousness.
Benevolence does not abandon the old;
loyalty does not forget the lord.
These are the highest forms of conduct.'
The Emperor was pleased."
The *Shuōyuàn* states:
"Lowering one's body and demeaning one's person,
rising early and retiring late.
Recommending the worthy without slackening,
frequently citing antiquity
to encourage the ruler's intent,
and to secure the state.
One who is like this is a loyal minister."
It also says:
"To go against orders yet benefit the lord is called loyalty."
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"The Emperor, in a great assembly,
pointed to Wáng Cháng and said to the assembled ministers:
'This man led the generals of the Xiàjiāng to assist and support the Hàn house.
His heart is like metal and stone;
he is truly a loyal minister.'
That day he promoted Wáng Cháng to General of Hànzhōng."
Kǒng Dá secured Wèi; Ān Yú stabilized Zhào.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Jìn, because Wèi had rescued Chén,
demanded satisfaction,
sending a man who would not leave,
saying:
'If the guilt has no one to return to,
we will bring our army against you.'
Kǒng Dá said:
'If it benefits the altars of soil and grain,
I beg you use me to satisfy them.'
He then hanged himself and died.
The men of Wèi used this to satisfy Jìn and were spared.
The men of Wèi considered this a meritorious achievement,
and later had his son again take his place."
It also says:
"Zhì Wénzǐ sent word to Zhào Mèng, saying:
'Although the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans were the ones who rebelled,
Dǒng Ānyú was the one who instigated it.
Thus Ānyú plotted the rebellion with them.'
Zhào Mèng was troubled by this.
Ānyú said:
'If I die, Jìn will be at peace and the Zhào clan will be secure.
What use then is life?'
He then hanged himself and died."
Yáng Rén donned armor; Yìng Zhān shouldered spears.
Sīmǎ's *Xù Hànshū* states:
"Yáng Rén, styled Wényì,
was appointed by Emperor Míng to fill a vacancy as a guard at the Northern Palace.
When the Emperor passed away,
the powerful nobles from the various states each vied to enter the palace.
Yáng Rén donned armor and grasped a halberd,
strictly enforcing the gate guard,
so that none dared lightly advance."
The *Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū* states:
"Wáng Dūn was about to rebel.
Emperor Míng asked Yìng Zhān:
'What to do?'
Yìng Zhān said:
'Your Majesty should rouse your majestic might.
Your ministers and others will shoulder spears and follow,
not caring for the disaster of the clan's destruction,
to attack the rebels in accordance with righteousness.'
That very day, Yìng Zhān was made General of the Guard Army,
and they united their hearts to destroy Wáng Dūn."
Zhāng Fēi leveled his spear; Yáo Qī brandished his halberd.
The *Shǔzhì* states:
"The First Ruler fled to Jīngzhōu,
and Lord Cáo pursued him.
The First Ruler abandoned his wife and children and fled,
sending Zhāng Fēi with twenty cavalry to hold the rear.
Fēi held the river and broke the bridge,
glaring and leveling his spear, saying:
'I am Zhāng Yìdé!
Come and decide the battle with me!'
None dared approach."
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Yáo Qī followed Emperor Guāngwǔ to seize territory.
At that time, Wáng Láng's proclamation arrived.
In Jì, troops rose in response to Wáng Láng.
The Emperor hastened his carriage to depart.
The common people gathered to watch,
shouting and filling the road,
blocking the way so it could not be passed.
Yáo Qī rode his horse and brandished his halberd,
glaring and shouting to those on the left and right:
'Make way!'
The crowd all scattered in disarray."
Yáo is pronounced Yáo.
Gěng Gōng extended sincerity; Fù Tóng gave his life.
Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hànshū* states:
"Gěng Gōng defended Shūlè.
Emperor Míng passed away,
relief troops did not arrive,
Chēshī rebelled again,
and together with the Xiōngnú attacked Gěng Gōng.
Gěng Gōng extended sincerity to his soldiers, sharing life and death,
therefore none had two minds."
The *Shǔzhì* states:
"The First Ruler withdrew his army to Yìyáng.
Fù Tóng covered the rear,
resisting and fighting.
His soldiers were all dead.
A Wú general told Tóng to surrender.
Tóng cursed, saying:
'Wú dogs!
How could there be a Hàn general who surrenders!'
He then fought to the death.
His son, Qiān, was appointed Left Palace Attendant.
Later, he served as Guān Yǔ's Area Commander.
In the sixth year of Jǐngyào, he again gave his life in the face of danger.
Commentators praised the generations of loyalty and righteousness in his family."
Jìsūn served as minister of Lǔ; Zhūgě revived the Hàn.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The people of Jìn captured Jì Wénzǐ,
and detained him at Jǔqiū.
Fàn Wénzǐ said to Luán Wǔzǐ:
'Jìsūn in Lǔ
served as minister to three rulers.
His concubines did not wear silk,
his horses did not eat grain.
Can he not be called loyal!'"
The Shǔ Zhì states:
"Zhūgě Liàng submitted a memorial saying:
'Now the south is pacified,
armor and weapons are sufficient.
I wish to exhaust my meager abilities,
to expel the treacherous and wicked.
To revive the Hàn house,
and return to the old capital.
This is how I repay the late emperor and fulfill my duty of loyalty to Your Majesty.'"
Gouging out eyes; Cutting open the heart.
The Shǐjì states:
"The King of Wú granted Zǐxū the Zhǔlòu sword to die with.
Zǐxū looked up to heaven and sighed:
'Gouge out my eyes and place them on the eastern gate of Wú,
so that I may see the Yuè invaders destroy Wú!'
Then he cut his own throat and died."
The Shàngshū states:
"He cut off the shins of those who crossed the river in the morning,
and cut open the heart of the worthy man."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Bǐgān remonstrated loyally.
The tyrant said his heart was different from others',
so he cut it open to examine it."
Upholding the initial command; Yielding precedence afterwards.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"King Píng of Chǔ believed slander,
and sent Fènyáng to kill the crown prince.
The crown prince fled to Sòng.
The king summoned Fènyáng and said:
'The words came from my mouth,
entered your ears.
Who informed Jiàn?'
He replied:
'I informed him.
Your Majesty commanded me to serve Jiàn as I serve you.
I am not talented,
but I cannot be duplicitous.'
Upholding the initial command,
I could not bear the later order,
so I sent him away."
The Hànshū states:
"When Gōngsūn Hóng presented matters to the court,
if there was something unacceptable,
he would not argue openly in court.
He often arranged with Jí Àn to request a private audience.
Àn would speak first,
and Hóng would support him afterwards."
Restoring Chǔ; Returning Zhū.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Initially,
Wǔ Yún and Shēn Bāoxū were friends.
When Wǔ Yún fled,
he said to Bāoxū:
'I will surely overthrow Chǔ.'
Bāoxū said:
'Strive for it.
If you can overthrow it,
I will surely revive it.'
When King Zhāo was in Suí,
Bāoxū went to Qín to beg for troops.
He stood leaning against the courtyard wall and wept,
day and night without ceasing sound,
not a spoonful of drink entering his mouth.
Thus,
the Qín troops marched out."
It also states:
"The army entered Zhū.
The people of Zhū defended themselves at Yì.
Máo Yíhóng of Zhū took bundles of silk and a carriage to seek aid from Wú.
The ruler of Wú attacked Lǔ,
and the ruler of Zhū was returned to his state."
Bósū lamented by day; Xǔ Sù wept at night.
The Zhànguó Cè states:
"When Wú entered Yǐng,
Fénmào Bósū carried dry rations and traveled stealthily.
After ten days he reached the Qín court at dawn.
He stood like a crane without turning.
Lamenting by day, weeping by night,
for seven days he obtained nothing,
not a drop of water or broth entering his mouth.
The King of Qín heard and ran to him,
his cap and sword left behind.
With his left hand he supported his head,
with his right he moistened his mouth.
Thereupon Qín rescued Chǔ,
repelled the Wú army,
and restored the state of Chǔ."
The Xǔ Sù Biézhuàn states:
"Sù served as Palace Attendant to Emperor Mǐn.
The emperor was sent to Píngyáng.
After a short while,
Liú Cōng secretly administered poisoned wine.
The emperor, after eating, felt chest tightness,
and wished to see Sù.
Sù rushed to his side,
but the emperor could no longer speak.
He grasped Sù's hand and shed tears.
Sù sobbed and climbed onto the bed.
The emperor then died in his embrace.
Sù wept and wailed day and night,
his grief moving even creatures of different kinds."
Fortifying Yǐng; Restoring Chén.
"Fortifying Yǐng" appears in the narrative section.
The Jiāyǔ states:
"Confucius read in the history about Chǔ restoring Chén,
and said:
'How worthy was King Zhuāng of Chǔ!'
He valued a single word of trust over a state of a thousand chariots.
Without the loyalty of Shēn Shūshí,
he could not have established this righteousness;
without the worthiness of King Zhuāng,
he could not have accepted this instruction."
Endangering oneself for the state; Offending the ruler's countenance.
The Lǐjì states:
"When Gōngshū Wénzǐ died,
his son Chéng requested a posthumous title from the ruler.
The ruler said:
'In the past, when Wèi faced calamity,
the master endangered his life to protect me.
Is this not steadfast!'"
The Hànshū states:
"Jí Àn, styled Chángrú,
enjoyed bluntly refuting others to their faces,
and could not tolerate people's faults.
When he remonstrated,
he offended the ruler's countenance.
He always admired the conduct of Fù Bó and Yuán Àng."
Bundles of silk; Carrying dry rations.
Both matters already appear in the annotations above.
Braving hardship; Enduring peril.
Xǔ Sù braved hardship to stay by Emperor Mǐn's side.
The bandits all yielded, saying:
"This is a loyal minister of Jìn."
Also, the Bāopǔzǐ states:
"Those who exhaust their lives for the state,
and maintain integrity through peace and peril alike,
are loyal ministers."
Gǒng Shèng pushed away the seal; Hú Gāng hung up his cap.
The Hànshū states:
"When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he sent an envoy bearing the imperial seal and ribbon, galloping on horseback to welcome Gǒng Shèng.
Shèng repeatedly refused and would not accept,
saying:
'I have received great kindness from the Hàn house,
and have no way to repay it.
How could I serve two surnames with this single body!'"
Fàn Yè's Hòu Hànshū states:
"Hú Guǎng's sixth-generation ancestor Gāng
was pure and lofty, with strong principles.
During Emperor Píng's time,
he was recruited by the Grand Marshal.
When Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
he removed his official robes and cap,
hung them at the prefectural gate, and left."
Shí Què destroyed his kin; Yuè Yáng ate his son.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Zhōuyù of Wèi assassinated Duke Huán.
Shí Hòu followed Zhōuyù to Chén.
Shí Què sent a message to Chén, saying:
'These two men
are the ones who assassinated my ruler.
I dare ask you to deal with them.'
The people of Chén captured them and requested instructions from Wèi.
The people of Wèi sent Right Steward Chǒu to oversee the killing of Zhōuyù at Pú.
Shí Què sent his steward Nòu Yángjiān to oversee the killing of Shí Hòu at Chén.
The gentleman said:
'Shí Què
is a pure minister.
He hated Zhōuyù, and Hòu was involved.
He upheld great righteousness by destroying his kin.
This is what is meant by that!'"
The Hánzǐ states:
"Yuè Yáng was a general of Wèi.
Li disregards his clan; Ji does not think of his kin.
The Dongguan Hanji states:
"Wang Lang sent a general to attack Xìndū.
The prominent clan member Mǎ Chǒng opened the city gates to admit them,
capturing Lǐ Zhōng's mother, wife, and children,
and ordering his relatives to summon Zhōng.
At that time, Chǒng's younger brother served under Zhōng as a commandant.
Zhōng summoned him for an audience,
rebuked him for betraying kindness and surrendering the city,
and then struck him dead.
All the generals were astonished and said:
'Your family is in their hands;
why did you kill his brother?'
Zhōng replied:
'If I let the traitor go unpunished,
that would be duplicity.'
The Emperor heard of this and said to Zhōng:
'Now our army is fully prepared;
General, you may return to rescue your mother, wife, and children.'
Zhōng replied:
'Having received Your Excellency's great kindness,
I, Zhōng, am able to devote my life to service;
I truly dare not look inward to my own clan and kin.'" It also states:
"Xìndū had rebelled and was held by Wang Lang.
The King of Xìndū arrested and imprisoned Jì Róng's father, younger brother, wife, and children,
and had them write a letter summoning Róng, saying:
'Those who surrender will be enfeoffed with titles;
those who do not will have their clans exterminated.'
Róng wept and replied:
'One who serves his lord cannot attend to his family.
The reason my kin have been safe in Xìndū until now
is due to the kindness of Lord Liú.
Your lordship's affairs involve contending for the state;
I cannot again think of private matters.'"
Taizong Wen Emperor's "Eulogy for Bǐ Gàn"
The Way was lost, the times were dark;
treachery and villainy were employed together.
With tyrannical rulers and cruel lords,
it was difficult for the upright to dwell.
Though one discerned the signs of survival and ruin,
how could one escape the burden of destruction?
Though one's wisdom encompassed all things,
one could not escape the midst of turmoil and distress.
Thus, when a great edifice is about to collapse,
it cannot be righted by a single timber;
when the Heavenly Way departs,
how can a single worthy preserve it?
Striving without regard for oneself,
preferring death to disloyalty—
those who tread this path of integrity
are rarely found among men.
Therefore, the wind and mist are desolate,
and no trace remains to be sought.
Warm and cool upon the mound,
only an empty name endures.
Though past and present follow different paths,
and the ages are dim and silent,
I follow the ancient precedent.
Thus I confer the posthumous title Grand Preceptor and the posthumous name Zhōngliè Gōng,
with clear wine and a sacrifice of sheep and pigs,
to present this humble offering.
May your wandering spirit, faintly discerned,
illuminate this sincere commendation.
Chén Lǐ Yuáncāo's "Eulogy for Bǐ Gàn" for Emperor Xuān
Since the solitary tyrant ran rampant,
the world crumbled and fell apart.
Observing the cavity and having his heart cut out,
he firmly maintained his sincere integrity.
His loyalty surpassed the bright sun;
his righteousness matched the autumn sky.
Since the age of Fúxī and Huángdì,
he stands alone.
Reading Simǎ Xiāngrú's rhapsodies,
I regret not being his contemporary;
hearing Lǐ Mù's name,
I wish to have him as my general.
Since the Nine Plains produce no more such men,
my regret runs deep through the ages.
I briefly offer this humble sacrifice;
may you, sir, partake of it.
Zhōu Yǔxìn's "In Praise of Yuán Àng Admonishing Emperor Wén"
A thousand chariots on steep tracks,
six reins guiding a perilous journey.
The road winds around pine-covered slopes;
the mountains slant toward Willow City.
At Lóngyuān, the terrain is narrow;
under the Huágài, the wind startles.
The worthy minister grasps the reins—
this can be called loyalty and steadfastness.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's "In Praise of the Entrusted Chapter of The Biographies of Loyal Ministers"
Tàizhēn, heroic and upright,
threw back his sleeves to aid the king.
Bóyóu trod the path of integrity,
perishing in body but his name soaring.
Yíyí Jǐngqiàn,
with his lord lost, he too was lost.
Alas, how noble!
Truly, the state's paragon.
"In Praise of the Remonstrance Chapter of The Biographies of Loyal Ministers"
Zǐzhèng, resolute and firm,
sincerely preserved the altars of soil and grain.
Zhū Yún broke the balustrade,
thus fulfilling his unyielding integrity.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's "Memorial Presenting The Biographies of Loyal Ministers"
Supporting one's father and serving one's lord
is indeed called solemn reverence.
Seeking loyalty from filial piety,
righteousness combines minister and son.
Thus, warming in winter and cooling in summer,
exhaust the rituals of serving one's parents.
Advancing thoughts to promote goodness,
cherish the duty of going forth to serve.
From this we know principle unites lord and parent;
loyalty and filial piety are one body.
Nature and following the path
bring kindness and righteousness to their utmost.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's "Preface to The Biographies of Loyal Ministers"
Now, Heaven and Earth's great virtue is called life;
the sage's great treasure is called position.
Through life, one fulfills filial piety;
through position, one establishes loyalty.
Serving one's lord and serving one's father—
how could the principle of respectful support differ?
Being a minister and being a son—
the path of following is one and the same.
Loyalty is a fine virtue,
truly what I admire and practice.
Now I shall open my cases and set out books,
to thoroughly discuss and examine.
Filial Piety, Part Four
The Ěryǎ says:
"To serve one's parents well is called filial piety."
The Xiàojīng says:
"Filial piety is
the constant law of Heaven,
the righteous principle of Earth,
and the conduct of the people."
The Lǐjì says:
"Zēngzǐ said:
'There are three aspects to the substance of filial piety:
The greatest filial piety is to honor one's parents;
the next is not to bring disgrace upon them;
the lowest is to be able to support them.'
Gōngmíng Yí asked Zēngzǐ:
'Can the Master be considered filial?'
Zēngzǐ said:
'A filial son
anticipates his parents' wishes and fulfills their aspirations,
guiding his parents toward the Way.
I, Shēn, merely provide support;
how can I be considered filial?'"
The Máo Shī says:
"Alas for my parents,
who bore me with toil and hardship.
Without a father, on whom shall I rely?
Without a mother, on whom shall I depend?
When I go out, I am filled with sorrow;
when I return, I have nowhere to go.
O father, you gave me life,
O mother, you nurtured me.
You comforted me, cherished me,
raised me, educated me,
cared for me, looked after me,
and carried me in your arms when I went out and came in.
I wish to repay your kindness,
but it is as vast as the boundless heavens."
The Lúnyǔ says:
"Mèng Yìzǐ asked about filial piety.
The Master said:
'Do not disobey.'
Fán Chí said:
'What does that mean?'
The Master said:
'Serve them with propriety while they are alive;
bury them with propriety when they die;
and sacrifice to them with propriety.'"
The Hán Shī Wàizhuàn says:
"Zēngzǐ said:
'That which, once gone, can never return is one's parents.
Thus, a filial son may wish to support them, but his parents may not wait for him.
Therefore, sacrificing an ox at their grave
is not as good as offering a chicken or a pig while they are still alive.'
When I first became an official,
my salary was no more than a fǔ of grain,
yet I was joyful and happy—
not because I considered it abundant,
but because I was glad to be able to support my parents.
After they passed away,
I once traveled south to Chǔ,
where I obtained a high office.
My hall was nine chǐ high,
and my carriages numbered a hundred,
yet I still faced north and wept—
not because I considered my position lowly,
but because I grieved that I could no longer support my parents.
Therefore, if one's family is poor and one's parents are old,
one should not be selective about office but take any post to serve."
The Xiàozǐ Zhuàn says:
"Lǎo Láizǐ was extremely filial.
He served his two parents,
and even at the age of seventy,
he wore colorful patchwork clothes
and played with young birds by his parents' side."
It also says:
"Wú Tǎnzhī was exceedingly filial by nature.
On the evening of his mother's burial,
he set up nine offerings of food for sacrifice.
Each time he performed a sacrifice,
he wailed in grief until he was breathless.
By the seventh sacrifice,
he vomited blood and died."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
"Those who govern a state must first attend to the root.
Nothing is more fundamental than filial piety.
Filial piety is the fundamental duty of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
and the guiding principle of all affairs.
Hold fast to this one method, and all virtues will follow."
The Lǐjì says:
"Zēngzǐ said:
'The body is
the legacy of one's parents.
To act with the legacy of one's parents—
how dare one not be reverent?
To be disrespectful in one's dwelling is not filial piety;
to serve one's ruler without loyalty is not filial piety;
to hold office without reverence is not filial piety;
to treat friends without trustworthiness is not filial piety;
to lack courage in battle is not filial piety.
If these five are not fulfilled,
disaster will befall one's parents.
How dare one not be reverent?
Filial piety,
when established, fills Heaven and Earth;
when spread, extends across the Four Seas.
To cut down a single tree
or kill a single animal
not in its proper season
is not filial piety.'"
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says:
"When primal energy was in chaos,
filial piety was already within it.
When the Son of Heaven is filial,
celestial dragons bear charts,
earthly tortoises present writings,
calamities are eliminated,
and auspicious clouds wander forth.
When common people are filial,
then marshes and forests flourish,
floating treasures unfold,
marvelous grasses bloom,
and divine fish emerge from the waters."
Ascending the Barren Hill Following the Southern Bank
The Máo Shī says:
"Ascending the Wooded Hill—
a filial son on military service
longs for his parents.
I ascend that barren hill,
gazing toward my mother.
My mother says, 'Alas!
My youngest son is on service,
day and night without rest.
Be careful up there!
May you return and not be abandoned.'"
Shù Guǎngwēi's Bǔwáng Shī says:
"Southern Bank—
filial sons admonish one another to provide support.
I follow that southern bank,
gathering orchids as I go.
My heart yearns for the parental home,
and finds no peace."
Gentle Voice Pleasant Countenance
The Lǐjì says:
"When going to where one's parents are,
one should lower one's voice and speak gently."
It also says:
"A filial son who has deep love
will surely have a harmonious disposition.
One who has a harmonious disposition
will surely have a pleasant countenance.
One who has a pleasant countenance
will surely have a gracious demeanor."
Succeeding in Service Continuing the Aspiration
The Máo Shī says:
"Succeeding King Wǔ—
continuing King Wén.
To love this one man
is to respond as a marquis and follow virtue.
Ever thinking of filial piety,
how illustrious is succeeding in service!"
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Fú means service.
How illustrious were King Wǔ's words about succeeding in the affairs of his ancestors—
referring to attacking Zhòu and stabilizing the world."
The Lǐjì says:
"King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu—were they not perfectly filial!
They excelled in continuing the aspirations of others
and in carrying on the affairs of others."
Granted Lifespan Attaining Longevity
The Hétú says:
"Being filial and obedient to both parents
grants a lifespan of two thousand years.
The Celestial Registrar records such deeds
and grants lifespan as a meritorious achievement."
The Lǐjì says:
"Shùn—was he not greatly filial!
In virtue, he was a sage;
in honor, he was the Son of Heaven.
He possessed all within the Four Seas,
was honored in the ancestral temple,
and his descendants preserved his legacy.
Thus, great virtue must attain its proper position,
must attain its proper emolument,
must attain its proper fame,
and must attain its proper longevity."
Inquiring of the Attendants / Seeking Physicians
The Book of Rites says:
"When King Wén was the Crown Prince,
he visited his father, King Jì, three times a day.
At the first crow of the rooster, he would dress and go to the outer door of the bedchamber,
and ask the attendant on duty among the inner servants:
'How is he today? Is he well?'
The inner servant would reply:
'He is well.'
Then King Wén would be pleased.
When midday came, he would go again,
and it was the same.
When evening came, it was also the same.
If there was any discomfort or irregularity,
then the inner servant would inform King Wén.
King Wén would look worried,
and his steps would become uneven.
Only when King Jì resumed his normal meals
would King Wén then also return to his normal state."
The Apocryphal Treatise on the Classic of Filial Piety: The Support of the Divine Contract says:
"When filial piety and fraternal duty reach their utmost,
they penetrate to the spirits and the brilliant.
When [parents] are ill, [the filial child] expresses his anxiety;
he gazes [with concern] until his forehead is worn and his body emaciated,
seeking physicians to assist in their complete recovery."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"To 'assist'
means to be the wings of one's parents."
Giving Full Joy / Exerting Utmost Strength
The Book of Rites says:
"Zǐlù said:
'How grievous is poverty!
In life, one has nothing with which to support [one's parents];
in death, one has nothing with which to perform the rites.'
Confucius said:
'To give them full joy even while eating bean soup and drinking water—
this may be called filial piety.'" The Analects says:
"Zǐxià said:
'In serving his parents, [a man] can exert his utmost strength;
in serving his ruler, he can devote his life;
in his dealings with friends, his words are trustworthy.
Even if it is said he has not learned,
I would certainly say he has learned.'"
Anticipating Wishes / Observing Countenance
The Book of Rites says:
"Gōngmíng Yí asked Zēngzǐ:
'Can the Master be considered filial?'
Zēngzǐ said:
'What kind of talk is this?
What the gentleman calls filial piety
is to anticipate [parents'] wishes and carry out their intentions,
leading parents to the Way.
I, Shēn, merely provide support;
how can I be considered filial?'" The Records of the Eastern Pavilion says:
"Rǔ Yù, styled Shūyì,
was five years old.
His mother fell ill and could not eat.
Yù would often hold her and weep,
refusing to eat or drink himself.
His mother pitied him,
and forced herself to eat a meal,
deceiving him by saying she was already better.
Yù, observing that his mother's complexion was not normal,
would then again refuse to eat.
His clan relatives all considered him extraordinary,
and therefore gave him the style name Shūyì (Unusual)."
Exerting Strength / Delighting the Heart
The Book of Zhou says:
"Serve parents with loyalty and love,
delighting and revering them;
exert your strength without being rigid,
revering them to put them at ease.
This is loyalty and filial piety."
The Book of Rites says:
"Zēngzǐ said, 'The filial son in nourishing his parents
delights their hearts and does not go against their will,
delights their ears and eyes,
and gives them peaceful rest and food.'"
Fanning the Pillow / Warming the Mat
The Records of the Eastern Pavilion says:
"Huáng Xiāng, styled Wénqiáng.
His father and elder brother were recommended as Filial and Incorrupt.
They had no slaves.
Xiāng personally performed the hard labor,
exerting his heart to provide for them.
His own body had no coverlet or trousers,
yet he provided his parents with the finest flavors.
In summer, he would fan their bed and pillow;
in winter, he would warm their mat."
Yuán Shānsōng's History of the Later Han says:
"Luó Wēi's mother was seventy years old.
When the weather was cold,
he would often use his own body to warm the mat,
and only then let her lie there."
Sincerely Devoted / Diligent and Earnest
The Book of Documents says:
"There is a solitary man below called Yú Shùn.
The Emperor said:
'Yes,
I have heard. What about him?'
The Chief said:
'He is the son of a blind man.
His father is obstinate, his mother is insincere.
His brother Xiàng is arrogant.
Yet he can achieve harmony through filial piety.
He is sincerely devoted to governing,
and does not descend into wickedness.'" The Records of the Eastern Pavilion says:
"When Emperor Zhāng passed away,
Emperor Míng's son was praised for his utmost filial piety,
diligent and earnest at his [father's] knees."
Han Cosmetic Case / Wei Seal
The Records of the Eastern Pavilion says:
"Emperor Míng
was the fourth son of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
born of Empress Yīn.
After ascending the throne,
he constantly thought of and longed for them.
In the first month of the following year,
when he was to visit the Yuánlíng tomb,
he dreamed of the late Emperor and Empress Dowager as joyful as in their lifetime.
At court, leading the hundred officials to the tomb,
he prostrated himself on the imperial couch and looked at the objects in the Empress Dowager's cosmetic case.
Moved, he wept sorrowfully.
He ordered the cosmetics and makeup tools to be replaced.
All those around him wept,
none daring to look up."
The Records of the Three Kingdoms: Book of Wei says:
"In the first year of the Tàihé era of Emperor Míng of Wei,
when first constructing the ancestral temple,
they dug up a seal from the ground,
measuring one inch and nine-tenths square.
Its inscription read:
'The Son of Heaven yearns for and thinks of his kind parent.'
Emperor Míng changed countenance because of it."
Zēng and Mǐn / Xún and Hé
The Analects says:
"How filial was Mǐnzǐ Qiān!
No one finds fault with the words of his parents and brothers about him."
The School Sayings of Confucius says:
"Zēng Shēn, styled Zǐyú,
was devoted to the Way of Filial Piety.
Therefore, Confucius based [his work] on him and composed the Classic of Filial Piety."
Xiāo Guǎngjì's Biographies of Filial Sons says:
"Mǐn Sǔn and Zēng Shēn,
among the disciples,
were most renowned for filial piety.
Those who speak of it today all take Zēng and Mǐn as their basis."
Xún Bózǐ's Family Traditions of the Xún Clan says:
"Xún Yǐ was past the age of sixty,
yet his mother was ninety years old.
He served her with a pleasing countenance, sincerely devoted,
and was known for his filial piety at the time.
During the mourning period, he was haggard,
unrecognizable to his children.
With disheveled hair and wearing the mourning sash,
he received the festival envoy.
Like an infant wailing,
he grieved and mourned, moving those around him."
Fù Xuán, in his writings, praised Xún Xù and Hé Zēng, saying:
"As for King Wén's Way of serving his parents,
who is as compliant and flourishing as Marquis Hé?
And as Marquis Xún?
In ancient times they praised Zēng and Mǐn;
today we have Xún and Hé."
Difficult Countenance / Easy Respect
The Analects says:
"Zǐxià asked about filial piety.
The Master said:
'The difficult part is the countenance.
If there is work to be done, the younger serve the labor;
if there is wine and food, the elders are served first—
can this be considered filial piety?'"
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"This means that having a harmonious and pleasant countenance is difficult.
'Leftover food' is called 'zhuàn'." The Zhuangzi says:
