"To be filial through respect is easy;
to be filial through love is difficult."
Climbing the Mountain and Leaning Against the Door
The *Máo Shī* says:
"Climbing the Mountain"
is about a filial son on military service,
longing for his parents.
I climb that wooded hill,
and gaze toward my father.
My father says, 'Alas!
My son is on service,
day and night without rest.
Take care up there!
May you return and not stay away.'"
Shī Juéshòu's *Biographies of Filial Sons* says:
Zhào Xùn was filial from childhood.
At five or six years old,
whenever he obtained something sweet and delicious,
he never dared to eat it alone,
but would always feed his father first.
When his father went out, he would wait for his return before eating.
If his father was late returning, he would lean against the gate and weep, awaiting him.
After several years, his father passed away.
Xùn, longing and pining, grew thin and haggard,
no different from an adult.
He wailed and wept bitterly.
He lived by his father's grave.
The villagers and clan sighed in admiration,
and his fame spread far and wide.
During the reign of Emperor Ān of Hàn,
he rose to the office of Palace Attendant.
Sucking the Abscess and Tasting the Poison
The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* says:
"Yōng Shū, styled Chángyú,
served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother once suffered from an abscess.
Shū crouched day and night,
never leaving her side,
even to the point of sucking the pus from her abscess."
Zhōu Fěi's *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* says:
"Cài Shùn, styled Jūnzhòng,
possessed a heart of utmost filial piety.
He lost his father young
and served his mother.
Delicious food for the mouth
he dared not taste first.
His mother went to a wedding feast
and, having drunk wine, vomited.
Shùn, fearing she was poisoned,
tasted her vomit.
When his mother developed sores that discharged pus,
he rinsed them with his mouth."
Lù Jì Holds Oranges; Yīn Huī Holds Melons
The *Wú Zhì* says:
"Lù Jì, styled Gōngjì,
was six years old
when he met Yuán Shù in Jiǔjiāng.
Shù brought out some oranges.
Jì hid three in his lapels,
and as he bowed in farewell, they fell to the ground.
Shù said,
'Master Lù, why do you, a guest, hide oranges?'
Jì knelt and replied,
'I wish to take them home for my mother.'
Shù thought him extraordinary."
Xiāo Guǎngjì's *Biographies of Filial Sons* says:
"Yīn Huī was born prudent and sincere.
He lost his father at seven,
wailing in grief until he grew thin and haggard,
and did not engage in playful antics.
When he obtained melons, fruits, or other edible things,
he would hold them in his lapels and present them to his mother,
never eating first."
Bào Yǒng Dismisses His Wife; Guō Dào Buries His Son
The *Dōngguān Hàn Jì* says:
"Bào Yǒng, styled Jūncháng,
was from Shàngdǎng.
In youth he had high aspirations and integrity.
He served his stepmother with utmost filial piety.
His wife once shouted at a dog in his mother's presence,
and Yǒng immediately dismissed her."
Péi Zǐyě's *Sòng Lüè* says:
"Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary Yuán Yú
recommended Guō Dào of Kuàijī,
who served his stepmother with utmost filial piety.
His family was poor when a child was born,
and he worried he could not raise it.
He said to his wife,
'To injure kindness to fulfill filial piety,
I have no regret.'
Thereupon he buried it."
Not Altering and Not Forgetting
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
"When his father is alive, observe his intentions;
when his father is dead, observe his conduct.
If for three years he does not alter his father's way,
he may be called filial."
The *Lǐjì* says:
"The filial piety of former kings
meant their forms were not forgotten by the eyes,
their voices not cut off from the ears,
their hearts' desires and inclinations not forgotten by the heart.
The noble man, while they live, reverently nourishes them;
when they die, reverently offers sacrifice,
thinking to the end of his life not to bring them disgrace."
Chén Jì's Portrait and Dīng Lán's Image
The *Biographies of Former Worthies from Within the Seas* says:
"Chén Shí's son, the former Grand Herald Jì,
styled Yuánfāng,
possessed supreme virtue transcending the common,
with talent and understanding surpassing others.
Devoted and earnest, he served with a pleasant countenance,
never leaving their side.
The Inspector of Yùzhōu, praising his exemplary conduct,
submitted a memorial to the Imperial Secretariat,
and had his portrait displayed in a hundred cities to encourage proper customs."
Sūn Shèng's *Biographies of Recluses* says:
"Dīng Lán
was from Hénèi.
He lost his parents young
and did not have the chance to support them.
So he carved wooden figures,
resembling their forms,
and served them as if they were alive,
paying his morning and evening respects.
Later, the wife of a neighbor, Zhāng Shū, came to borrow something from Lán's wife.
Lán's wife knelt and reported to the wooden figure,
but the wooden figure was displeased
and did not permit the loan.
Shū, drunk and angry, came cursing and reviling the wooden figure,
striking its head with a stick.
When Lán returned,
he saw the wooden figure's expression was unhappy.
He asked his wife,
and she told him everything.
Immediately he seized his sword and killed Zhāng Shū.
The officers arrested Lán.
Lán took leave of the wooden figure to go.
The wooden figure saw Lán
and shed tears for him.
The commandery and county, praising his utmost filial piety
that reached the spirits and gods,
had his portrait painted in the Cloud Terrace."
Dù Xiào Sends Fish; Luó Wēi Presents Fruit
Xiāo Guǎngjì's *Biographies of Filial Sons* says:
"Dù Xiào
was from Bā Commandery.
He lost his father young
and lived with his mother,
renowned for utmost filial piety.
He was on service in Chéngdū.
His mother loved to eat fresh fish.
Xiào, in Shǔ, cut a large bamboo tube,
put two fish inside,
stoppered it with grass,
and prayed,
'My mother must obtain this.'
Then he cast it into the midstream.
His wife went out to draw water
and saw a tube floating sideways, striking the bank.
Finding it strange, she took it and looked:
there were two fish inside.
Smiling, she said,
'This must be sent by my husband.'
She cooked them and presented them.
Those who heard of it sighed in amazement."
Again, Lù Chè's *Biographies of Former Worthies of Guǎngzhōu* says:
"Luó Wēi, styled Dérén,
lost his father at eight
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
Plowing and weeding were his occupation.
He labored diligently, enduring hardship with his body,
to provide support.
The Magistrate summoned him to serve as a minor clerk,
but he did not accept.
Taking his mother, he fled to avoid it,
and lived in seclusion within the boundaries of Zēngchéng County.
The Magistrate then restored his former residence.
Morning and evening he served and attended her,
presenting rare fruits and delicacies
according to the season."
The authorities honored his household, the governor erected a monument at his tomb.
Wèi Shōu’s History of Later Wèi says:
“Yáng Yǐn lost his father at age three,
and was raised by his mother.
His mother passed away at age ninety-three;
Yáng Yǐn was then seventy-five.
He grieved beyond the rites,
and completed the three-year mourning period.
Regretting that he never knew his father,
he resumed wearing the coarsest mourning garments,
vowing to do so for life.
After thirteen years,
his sorrow and longing remained unchanged.
Over three hundred people from his commandery, county, and village submitted a petition praising him.
The authorities memorialized that he should be honored and rewarded,
exempting his entire household from corvée,
and commending his pure filial piety.”
Wáng Lièzhī’s Records of Ānchéng says:
“In the county there was a filial son named Fú Biǎo,
renowned throughout the land for his filial piety.
At age sixteen,
when his mother, née Jiāng, fell ill,
he attended her day and night for several tens of days.
If his mother ate once,
Biǎo ate once;
if his mother did not eat,
Biǎo did not eat either.
Seeing his mother near death,
he wept so bitterly he choked,
and then perished.
Soon after, his mother also died.
In one day, two funerals were held.
They were buried at Sìwàng Gāng.
The governor, Wáng Fǔjūn, erected a pair of honorific pillars
to mark his tomb.”
Wèi Prince Sī of Chén, Cáo Zhí’s “Rhapsody on Cherishing Kin”
I hunt across the plains, driving southward,
and gaze upon my late father’s former encampment.
I tread the ramparts’ usual layout,
recognize where the command banners once halted.
Preserving the offices’ enduring legacy,
my heart seems to glimpse past days.
Turning my steed’s head, I depart forever,
embarking on the long road, seeking the distant.
My feelings cling and look back with care,
my soul in an instant returns ninefold.
Jìn Lù Shìhéng’s “Rhapsody on Longing for Kin”
I grieve the vast expanse of my homeland,
ashamed I cannot maintain the seasonal sacrifices.
Pointing to the southern clouds, I entrust my doubts;
gazing at the homeward wind, I offer my sincerity.
The years swiftly approach their dusk,
the bright stars blaze, about to fade.
The whirling gale sweeps coldly onward,
scattered snowflakes drift down in disarray.
I envy the slender twigs still on the trunk,
mourn the fallen leaves that left the branch.
I preserve the cherished memory of parental care,
moved by the thoughts that stir at dawn.
My elder brother, like fragrant blossoms and lush orchids;
my younger brother, like budding orchids and jade’s glow.
I lament that noble grace comes late to fruition,
grieve that my kind parents departed first.
Jìn Liú Róu’s wife, née Wáng’s “Rhapsody on Cherishing Remembrance”
Far from my kin, dwelling alone,
I remain long bound with sorrow and indignation.
Though I strive by the slightest measure,
never for a moment is there respite.
I recall the joyful service of former days,
attending at their knees, content and at ease.
Gathered with my siblings, composed and calm,
often happy, peaceful, and carefree.
Why is fortune so unfairly adverse,
leaving me alone, cut off by the long road?
Liáng Emperor Wǔ’s “Rhapsody on Filial Longing”
I brood on life’s fleeting passage, sudden as a gap,
lament the river of time that never stops.
Treading frost and dew, I am stricken with grief;
recalling the kindling and grain, tears fall.
Zhòng Yóu longed for dried fish and ever yearned;
Yú Qiū, moved by the wind and tree, grieved long.
Though once I might have given my life,
how could I ever serve both parents?
Jìn Shù Xī’s “Supplementing the Lost Poems,” titled Nán Gāi,
filial sons admonish each other to provide support.
Along those southern banks,
I speak of plucking orchids.
Yearning for the parental home,
my heart finds no peace.
That person there,
should not wander or linger.
Along those southern banks,
the grass grows lush.
That person there,
in expression seeks gentleness.
Yearning for the parental home,
my heart cannot tarry.
Make fragrant your evening meal,
pure your morning delicacies.
There is an otter, an otter,
on the river’s shore.
It rides the waves, dives into the depths,
bites perch, catches carp.
The crying forest birds
are fed by their young.
If nurture is ample but reverence slight,
you resemble only the beasts.
Strive to increase your devotion,
to invite longevity and blessing.
The second piece, titled Bái Huá,
filial sons’ purity and whiteness.
White blossoms, crimson calyxes,
spread over the secluded thicket.
Brilliant, the young man of the house,
as if polished, as if honed.
All morning, thrice he reflects,
never slack in his reverence.
White blossoms, scarlet bases,
on the hill’s corner.
Fresh and bright, the scholar,
dyed yet unchanged.
Exhausting sincerity, offering full respect,
diligent, forgetting toil.
White blossoms, black stems,
on the mound’s curve.
Stately, the unmarried maiden,
without striving, without desire.
Fresh as morning blooms,
none can stain her.
Wèi Wáng Càn’s “Four‑Character Poem on Longing for Kin”
Solemn, august mother,
her virtuous fame resounds.
She aspired to match the former matrons,
her will equaled Jiāng and Sì.
She bore this toil and hardship,
nurturing me, her little son.
I, the little son, was born
into an age without peace.
My stern father toiled in those times,
I followed him on campaign.
Suddenly meeting with misfortune,
deep sorrow gripped me.
Liáng Emperor Yuán’s “Eulogy on Innate Nature” from The Biography of Filial Virtue
They bore me, reared me,
raised me, nurtured me.
They cared for me, looked back to me;
how shall I repay their giving?
The virtue I wish to return
cannot be measured.
A filial piety tiny as a droplet,
a parental kindness vast as rivers and seas.
I lay aside the scroll and sigh,
tears falling in streams.
Jìn Xiàhóu Zhàn’s “Eulogy on Mǐn Zǐqiān”
Devoted Zǐqiān,
embodied centrality and rectitude.
Seeking office, he left his parents;
serving his parents, he showed utmost respect.
Striving in heart, following the traces of the past,
he drew forth words that flow in song.
Chapter Five: Fraternal Love
The Analects states:
"Filial piety and fraternal duty—
are they not the root of benevolence?"
It also says:
"Ah, filial piety—
it is being filial and friendly toward one's brothers."
The Book of Documents, "Jūn Chén" chapter, says:
"Being friendly toward brothers,
one can extend this to governance."
The Erya says:
"Being good to one's brothers is called 'friendship'."
The Book of Songs says:
"When brothers are harmonious,
joy and happiness are deep."
It also says:
"I climb that ridge,
and gaze toward my elder brother.
My brother says:
'Alas,
my youngest brother is on duty,
day and night you must stay together,
be cautious up there!
May you return and not die.'"
Confucius said:
"Brothers should be harmonious and joyful."
The Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán says:
"Chén Shí of Yǐngchuān had a son named Yuánfāng,
and a younger son named Zhòngfāng,
both renowned for their virtue and reputation.
The brothers were filial and supportive,
their household was peaceful and harmonious,
and people throughout the land admired their conduct.
Though all four government offices summoned them,
they did not yield to accept any position.
Once, the brothers visited their fellow commandery resident Xún Shuǎng,
and they feasted together at night.
The Grand Historian reported that virtuous stars had gathered."
The Rites of Zhōu, "Grand Minister of Education" chapter, says:
"The six virtuous behaviors are filial piety, fraternal love, harmony among kin, marital harmony, trustworthiness, and compassion."
The Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"When the ruler is righteous, the ministers are dutiful;
when the father is kind, the son is filial;
when the elder brother is friendly, the younger brother is respectful—
these are called the six harmonies."
Following One's Heart Innate Nature
The Máo Commentary on the Book of Songs says:
"This King Jì,
following his heart, was friendly.
He was friendly to his elder brother,
thus solidifying his blessings."
The Separate Biography of Yǔ Gǔn says:
"When his second elder brother fell ill,
and the epidemic was raging,
Gǔn brought him porridge and broth,
attending to him day and night without rest.
Such fraternal love,
stemmed from his innate nature."
King of Liáng Sharing the Imperial Carriage Qīnghé Sharing a Room
The Book of Hàn says:
"When King Xiào of Liáng came to court,
Emperor Jǐng sent an envoy with a four-horse imperial carriage to welcome him at the palace gate.
Inside, he attended the emperor in the same carriage;
outside, they rode together hunting.
The king's attendants, gentlemen-in-waiting, and ushers
were registered to enter and exit the emperor's palace gates,
no different from Hàn officials."
Zhāng Yíng's Records of Hànnán says:
"Emperor Hé, personal name Zhào,
was the middle son of Emperor Zhāng.
His elder brother Qìng was the crown prince,
but after their mother was slandered and died,
Qìng became the King of Qīnghé.
The emperor was four years old
when he replaced him as crown prince,
yet he remained especially close to Qìng.
Inside, they shared a room;
outside, they rode in the same carriage.
Emperor Zhāng, because of this, pitied Qìng even more,
and his clothing, food, and drink were the same as the emperor's."
Xǔ Jīng Unsheathing His Sword Lǐ Hóng Carving His Seal
Xiè Chéng's Book of the Later Hàn says:
"Xǔ Jīng's nephew had killed someone in revenge,
and the victim's family gathered armed men and came to Xǔ Jīng's house,
intending to kill him.
It happened that Jīng had just returned home on leave from his office,
and he encountered them.
He went out, unsheathed his sword, knelt down, and said:
'The earlier offense was committed without reason,
and the fault lies entirely with me for failing to teach him properly.
My elder brother died early,
and this son is his only heir.
If he is killed,
it would mean the extinction of his line.
I now offer my own life
to atone for this fault.
Even if I die,
it will be as if he is reborn.'
The aggrieved family helped Jīng up and said:
'Assistant Xǔ is known throughout the commandery as a worthy man.
How dare we harm him?'
And so they left."
It also says:
"Lǐ Hóng, courtesy name Fèngxùn,
was benevolent and filial by nature,
and friendly toward his brothers.
His younger brother Yù was insulted and humiliated by someone,
and later Yù secretly gathered allies to take revenge.
He was caught by law enforcement officers
and was to be punished.
At the time, he had no heir.
Hóng was an assistant to the Grand Commandant
and was in the capital.
He grieved that Yù had acted righteously to wipe away shame,
yet their family line would be cut off.
He resolved to take Yù's place.
He carved his seal and returned home,
but fearing that seeing his wife and children
might weaken his resolve,
he went to the northern pavilion of the county
and prepared a statement begging to die in Yù's place.
After sending the statement,
he drank poison and died.
When the county magistrate read the statement,
he was deeply shocked and moved."
Kǒng Róng Contending to Die Lěng Píng Yielding Life
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continuation of the Book of Hàn says:
"Zhāng Jiǎn of Shānyáng
angered the eunuch Hóu Lǎn with his loyalty and integrity.
Lǎn issued a warrant to the commanderies
to arrest Jiǎn.
Jiǎn was an old friend of Kǒng Róng's elder brother Kǒng Bāo,
so he fled to seek refuge.
He arrived when Bāo was out,
and Róng was fifteen or sixteen at the time.
Jiǎn looked down on him for his youth
and did not tell him the situation.
Róng, knowing Jiǎn was an elder,
saw his distressed expression
and said:
'Am I alone incapable of helping you, sir?'
He then took him in and hid him.
Later, a guest leaked the secret,
and officials from the chancellor down secretly came to raid the house.
Jiǎn managed to escape.
Róng and Bāo were immediately arrested and sent to prison.
Róng said:
'I was the one who sheltered and hid him.
I should be punished.'
Bāo said:
'He came to seek me.
The fault lies with me,
not my younger brother.
I should be punished.'
The brothers contended to die for the crime.
The commandery and county could not decide
and submitted the case for review.
An imperial decree ordered Bāo to bear the punishment.
Róng became famous because of this."
Cuī Hóng's Records of Southern Yān says:
"Officials reported that the monk Sengzhi entered Lěng Píng's house in Línzī at night
and violated his widowed sister-in-law, Lady Jì.
Píng and his younger brother Ānguó killed him.
The commandery and county tried the Píng brothers
for murder.
But Píng and Ānguó each claimed to have dealt the fatal blow,
yielding life and contending to die,
their righteousness manifest in the face of crisis."
Pear Blossoms Vitex Leaves
The Book of Songs says:
"The pear blossoms,
so radiant and bright.
Among all people today,
none compare to brothers.
In the face of death's terror,
brothers are deeply concerned."
Zhōu Jǐngshì's Biographies of Filial Sons says:
"In ancient times, there were brothers
who intended to separate.
Going out, they saw three vitex trees sharing a single root,
their leaves joined and shade interwoven.
They sighed and said:
'Even trees delight in togetherness;
how much more should we, who are different?'
They returned and lived in harmony."
Yīn Qìng yields his mansion; Lǐ Mèng yields his garden
Zhāng Yíng's *Records of Hàn Nán* states:
"Yīn Qìng was the Marquis of Tóngyáng.
His younger brothers Yuán and Dān were both court gentlemen.
Qìng, being versed in the *Book of Documents* and cultivating Confucian learning,
yielded his mansion, gardens, fields, slaves, and money,
dividing them all between Yuán and Dān.
Qìng kept only his official seal and ribbon.
His contemporaries praised him."
Chén Shòu's *Biographies of the Venerable Elders of Yì Province* states:
"Lǐ Mèngyuán studied the *Book of Changes* and the *Analects*,
grasping their main principles.
His nature was respectful and compliant.
He lived together with his younger paternal cousin, Jiù.
Jiù suffered from a chronic illness.
Mèngyuán yielded all his fields and gardens,
giving them entirely to Jiù.
He and his wife spun and wove
to support themselves."
Méng is plump; Lǐ is gaunt
The *Records of the Eastern Lodge* states:
"Ní Méng, styled Zǐmíng,
was from Línzī in the state of Qí.
He was benevolent, filial, sincere, and earnest,
not fond of glory and wealth,
and often diligently worked the fields.
He encountered a year of sudden crisis,
when warfare arose everywhere,
and people, starving, ate each other.
He went with his elder brother outside the city to gather vegetables,
and they were captured by the Chìméi bandits,
who wanted to kill and eat them.
He went before the bandits, kowtowed, and said:
'My elder brother is old and frail,
not as plump and strong as Méng.
I wish to take his place.'
The bandits, moved by his righteousness, did not eat them."
It also states:
"Zhào Xiào, styled Chángpíng,
was from Qí in the state of Pèi.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, the world was in chaos,
and people ate each other.
Xiào's younger brother, Lǐ, was captured by starving bandits.
Xiào heard of this
and immediately bound himself and went to the bandits, saying:
'Lǐ has been starving for a long time and is gaunt;
he is not as plump as Xiào.'
The starving bandits were greatly astonished
and released them both."
Shòu carries the banner; Yáo Cháng offers his horse
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Duke Xuān of Wèi had relations with Yí Jiāng,
and she gave birth to Jí Zǐ.
He was entrusted to the Left Prince,
who arranged a marriage for him with a woman from Qí, who was beautiful.
The Duke took her for himself,
and she gave birth to Shòu and Shuò.
Xuān Jiāng and Prince Shuò slandered Jí Zǐ to the Duke,
who sent him to Qí.
He had robbers wait for him at Shēn,
intending to kill him.
Shòu informed him and urged him to flee,
but he refused.
When he set out,
Shòu made him drink wine,
carried his banner and went ahead,
and the robbers killed him."
Cuī Hóng's *Records of the Later Qín* states:
"Yáo Xiāng was fighting Lǐ Lì,
when his horse was hit by a stray arrow and died.
His younger brother, Cháng, dismounted and offered his horse to Xiāng.
Xiāng said:
'How will you save yourself?'
Cháng said:
'If you, elder brother, cross over,
how would this lowly fellow dare harm Cháng?'
Just then, reinforcements arrived,
and they both escaped death."
Ascending the ridge; On the plain
The *Máo Odes* states:
"I ascend that ridge,
and gaze towards my elder brother."
It also states:
"When the wagtail is on the plain,
brothers aid each other in distress."
Lú Yù supports the widowed; Shān Wěi instructs the orphaned
The *Book of Hàn* states:
"Lú Yù, styled Zǐjiā,
was from Zhuō Commandery.
His father, Zhí,
was renowned in his time.
Yù was orphaned at ten.
He encountered turmoil in his home province,
and his two elder brothers died in the calamity.
This was when Yuán Shào and Gōngsūn Zàn were fighting in Yōu and Jì.
A famine occurred,
and he supported his widowed sisters-in-law and orphaned nephews,
being praised for his learning and conduct."
Wèi Shōu's *Book of the Later Wèi* states:
"Shān Wěi's younger brother died young.
Wěi cared for the widow and instructed the orphan.
They lived together for over twenty years,
with deep affection and duty.
He did not accumulate property.
After his death,
his house was sold to fund his burial."
Wáng Shāng yields wealth; Bǔ Shì divides property
The *Book of Hàn* states:
"Wáng Shāng, styled Zǐwēi,
was from Lǐwú in Zhuō Commandery.
Shāng served as a Palace Attendant to the Heir Apparent
and was known for his solemnity, respect, sincerity, and honesty.
When his father died,
Shāng succeeded to the marquisate.
He yielded his wealth, dividing it among his younger brothers from different mothers,
and took nothing for himself."
It also states:
"Bǔ Shì
was from Hénán.
He made his living from farming and herding.
He had a younger brother.
Shì left home,
taking only over a hundred sheep,
and gave the fields, house, and property to his brother.
Shì went into the mountains to herd for over ten years.
His sheep increased to over a thousand.
He bought fields and a house.
But his brother had completely lost his property,
so Shì again divided and gave his to him."
Jiāng Gōng shares a quilt; Lǐ Chōng exchanges clothes
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Sequel to the Book of Hàn* states:
"Jiāng Gōng, styled Bówéi,
was from Guǎngwēi in Péngchéng.
Gōng and his two brothers,
all were renowned for their filial conduct.
Gōng was the eldest.
He shared a quilt to sleep with his two younger brothers, Zhòng and Jì,
and they were very close and affectionate."
Dù Yù's *Records of Rǔnán* states:
"Lǐ Chōng had five brothers.
They were so poor they had not even a *dàn* or *shí* of grain stored.
They went out by exchanging clothes,
and ate only every other day.
His wife secretly said to Chōng:
'We are so poor now.
I have some private wealth.
We could separate and live alone.
With so many people, expenses are extreme.
Don't just impoverish yourselves for nothing.'
Chōng asked to summon the neighbors.
With the household gathered,
he knelt forward and raised a cup,
addressed his mother,
then turned to his wife,
scolded her, and sent her away.
The woman left, weeping as she walked out the door."
Zhào Xiào eats vegetables; Wèi Bà eats coarse grain
The *Records of the Eastern Lodge* states:
"Zhào Xiào, styled Chángpíng,
was from Qí in the state of Pèi.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
the world was newly settled,
and grain was still scarce.
Xiào obtained some grain.
When it was almost cooked,
he told his younger brother Lǐ and his wife to go out.
By the time they returned,
Xiào and his wife had already eaten only vegetables.
When Lǐ and his wife returned,
they said they had already eaten,
so he fed them alone."
Xiè Chéng's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Wèi Bà, styled Qiáoqīng,
was from Jìyīn.
He served as the Grand Administrator of Jùlù.
While administering the commandery,
he never sent clerks back to his hometown,
and his wife and children did not come to the official residence.
He often thought of how hard his elder brother and sister-in-law worked at home,
while he alone enjoyed honor and comfort.
Therefore, he constantly wore coarse clothing and ate coarse grain,
and did not eat the flavor of fish or meat.
His wife personally engaged in sericulture,
his son personally plowed the fields,
and he shared hardships and joys with his brothers,
not allowing himself to be different.
His hometown admired his conduct and was transformed by it."
Chén Yè Sheds Blood, Xú Miáo Holds Pus
Xiè Chéng's *Records of Former Worthies of Kuàijī* states:
"Chén Yè, styled Wénlǐ.
His elder brother perished at sea.
At that time, those who had been with him numbered fifty or sixty;
their flesh had rotted away and they could not be distinguished.
Chén Yè looked up to the August Heaven,
and swore to the Sovereign Earth, saying:
'I have heard that among blood relatives there must be a special connection!'
Thereupon he cut his arm and let the blood flow,
sprinkling it upon the bones.
Immediately, the blood [on his brother's bones] congealed,
while all the rest flowed away."
*Wáng Yǐn's History of the Jìn* states:
"Xú Miáo, styled Shūzhòu,
was from Chúnyú in Gāomì.
He held wealth lightly and valued righteousness,
practicing what is difficult for others.
His elder brother and younger brother died early.
He raised the orphans and widows,
restraining his own food and drink.
For over forty years he lived as a guest with his wife, children, and brothers,
yet the fields, houses, and servants
he yielded to his orphaned nephews.
When his brother died and lay before burial,
there was a festering sore with pus and blood in his mouth.
He took it in his own mouth and removed it.
His conduct in all matters was of this kind."
Sharing Sweet Delicacies, Sharing Clothing and Food
*The Dōngguān Records of the Hàn* states:
"Kǒng Fèn was deeply devoted to his kin.
His younger brother, Qí, was a student in Luòyáng.
Fèn shared his official salary to supply Qí's provisions,
sending him clothes for all seasons,
down to such things as lamp oil and candles.
Whenever he had something delicious to eat,
he would always divide and reduce his portion to send to Qí."
Jiāng Huī's *Records of Chénliú* states:
"Lǐ Quán
was from Píngqiū.
From youth he was intelligent and perceptive,
possessing the highest conduct.
Quán's elder brother was the son of the former wife,
and the stepmother did not love him at all,
yet in matters of clothing and food, she always made him inferior to Quán.
When Quán was just five years old,
he realized his own clothes were better than his brother's.
He immediately took them off and would not wear them,
insisting that only when his brother received the same
would he then wear them.
Thereupon, his mother could no longer show favoritism.
When he grew up,
Quán inwardly obeyed and pleased his mother,
while outwardly serving his elder brother.
Thus, the household was harmonious and amiable,
and was praised by the entire clan."
*The Book of Songs, Minor Odes, "Tang Di" Poem*
The flowers of the cherry tree,
Are they not gorgeously displayed?
Of all the men in the world,
None are like brothers.
In death and mourning,
It is brothers who are most concerned.
When gathered on the plain or mound,
It is brothers who will seek each other out.
The wagtail on the plain,
Brothers hurry to aid in distress.
Though you may have good friends,
They will only heave long sighs.
Jìn Dynasty Lù Shìlóng's "Poem in Reply to Elder Brother Shìhéng"
How far is the end of this long, long road?
Parting is hurried, the sorrow of reunion drawn out.
Bearing thoughts, I long for the journey ahead,
Raising my words as I face the farewell cup.
The southern ford has no ferry to cross,
The northern isle no bridge over the river.
My spirit goes, sharing the feeling of departure,
My body remains, grieving like Shēn and Shāng.
If the paths of the Dipper and Cart diverge,
The Draught Oxen cannot pull the carriage box.
Suí Dynasty Xīn Déyuán's "In Praise of Jiāng Gōng"
Jiāng Gōng was serene and refined,
He and his brothers renounced glory.
Sharing a quilt, they lived in harmony,
Matching in virtue, their reputations equal.
Victorious in battle, yet they withdrew,
Retiring in good grace, they maintained their integrity.
A lone boat sailing straight ahead,
Their traces vanished into the vast blue sea.
Eastern Jìn Dynasty Yǔ Tǒng's "In Praise of Three Orphans"
Fate encountered hardship and peril,
Three orphans stood together.
Like separated birds calling to their young,
By chance they gathered as one.
The grain of virtue now ripened,
Their harmonious voices joined together.
Beginning from those distant forks,
They merged into a single entry.
Zhū Míngzhāng's "In Praise of Minister Wèi"
The *Book of Songs* praises Zhāng Zhòng,
Today we have Zhū Míng.
Sharing wealth, he strengthened friendship,
His clothes did not display his form.
His widowed wife shunned impurity,
The cherry tree added to its glory.
Minister Wèi was aloof and distant,
Yet even the base were moved by his sincerity.
Book Six: Reverence and Respect
*The Analects* states:
"If respect is close to ritual propriety,
it keeps disgrace and insult at a distance."
*The Book of Rites* states:
"Uprightness and freedom from depravity
are the substance of ritual.
Dignity, respect, reverence, and compliance
are the forms of ritual.
Formerly, Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
'How does one respect one's own person?'
He replied:
'When a gentleman errs in speech, others make it a saying;
when he errs in action, others make it a rule.
If a gentleman's speech does not err in wording,
and his actions do not err in rule,
then the common people will be respectful without being ordered.
In this way, one can respect one's own person.
Being able to respect one's own person, one can then bring completion to one's parents.'"
Also, the *Book of Rites, Lesser Rules of Demeanor* states:
"In receiving guests, the host emphasizes respectfulness;
in sacrificial ceremonies, one emphasizes reverence.
The way of reverence and respectfulness
cannot be abandoned."
*The Zuǒ Commentary* states:
"Zhèng Kǎofǔ served Dài, Wǔ, and Xuān,
all three of whom were rulers of Sòng.
With each higher appointment he became more respectful.
Three appointments made him a high minister.
Thus the inscription on his tripod said:
'With the first appointment, I bowed;
with the second, I bent deeper;
with the third, I stooped low.
Stooping is more respectful than bending,
bending is more respectful than bowing.
I walk along the wall,
not daring to walk at ease.
Thus, no one dares to insult me.'"
Being so respectful as this,
others also did not dare to treat him with insolence or disrespect.
*The Analects* states:
"Fán Chí asked about humaneness.
The Master said:
'In private life, be respectful;
in handling affairs, be reverent;
in dealings with others, be loyal.
Even if you go among the barbarians,
these cannot be abandoned.'"
Even though the barbarians lack understanding,
one should still treat them with respect, reverence, loyalty, and trustworthiness.
*The Records of Former Worthies of the State of Lǔ* states:
"In Lǔ there was a respectful scholar
named Fàn.
Having lived to seventy years of age,
his respectfulness increased even more.
In winter he walked in the shade,
in summer he walked in the sun.
During a single meal he would rise three times.
The ruler of Lǔ asked him:
'Your age is very advanced;
why not relax your respectfulness?'
Fàn replied:
'A gentleman loves respectfulness to complete his reputation;
a commoner learns respectfulness to avoid punishment.
Those who praise others are few;
those who malign others are many.
Having lived to seventy years,
I constantly fear the axe and block may be applied to me.
Sī Qí and Zhì Què
The Máo Shī says:
"Sī Qí Tàirén,
the mother of King Wén."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states:
"King Wén's mother,
who constantly thought of being dignified and respectful,
was Tàirén."
The Lǐjì says:
"On the day of the sacrifice, upon entering the chamber,
one must appear reverent as if seeing the deceased in their place;
circling around and exiting the door,
one must appear solemn as if hearing their voice and demeanor.
Exiting the door and listening,
one must appear moved as if hearing their sighs.
Thus, this is the filial piety of the former kings.
Their appearance is not forgotten by the eyes,
their voices do not cease in the ears,
their hearts' desires and cravings are not forgotten in the mind.
Extreme love preserves them,
extreme reverence makes them manifest.
When they are manifest and preserved, not forgotten in the mind,
how can one not be reverent?
A gentleman, while they live, reverently nurtures them;
when they die, reverently offers sacrifices,
thinking to never bring disgrace upon them throughout life."
The Odes Praise Gentleness and Warmth; The Yǎ Speaks of Reverent Care
The Máo Shī says:
"Gentle and warm are the respectful people,
as if perched upon a tree.
Anxious and careful,
as if overlooking a valley."
Again, the Ěryǎ states:
"Solemn and reverently careful,
is to be respectful."
Reverence to Avoid Misfortune; Respect to Preserve One's Position
The Lǐjì states:
"In the ritual of the village drinking ceremony,
the host bows to welcome the guest outside the gate,
enters and makes three bows before reaching the steps,
and yields three times before ascending,
all to express utmost respect and deference.
Washing hands and raising the goblet,
is to express purity.
Bowing upon arrival, bowing for the washing, bowing to receive, bowing to send off, bowing after completion,
all to express reverence,
this is how a gentleman avoids misfortune.
Thus, the sage established this through the Way."
The Xì Cí of the Yì states:
"A gentleman expresses respect to preserve his position."
Adjusting Attire and Removing Headgear
Yú Yù's Huìjī Diǎnlù states:
"Chén Ruì, styled Wén Xiàng,
served as a county clerk.
Ruì was humble, respectful, and deferential,
his conduct was solely reverent and cautious.
When he held the positions of Two Thousand Dan and Nine Ministers,
even when youths and children bowed to him,
he would always adjust his court robes and return the courtesy.
If illness prevented him from returning a bow,
he would pat his forehead in apology."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"The King of Chǔ hunted in Zhōulái,
and encamped at Yǐngwěi.
He sent Dàng Hóu, Pān Zǐ, Sīmǎ Dū, Xiāo Yǐn Wǔ, and Líng Yǐn Xǐ to lead
troops to besiege Xú to intimidate Wú.
The King of Chǔ encamped at Gānxī,
to provide support.
It was snowing,
the king wore a leather cap,
a Qín-style fur coat,
a kingfisher-feather cloak and leopard-skin shoes,
and came out holding a whip.
His attendant, Qífù, followed,
and the Right Yǐn, Zǐ Gé, came in the evening.
When the king saw him,
he removed his cap and cloak and set aside his whip."
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"To show respect to a high minister."
Qú Yuàn Descends at the Gate; Hán Zhuō Hastes to the Altar
Mèng Yí's Tóng Zǎi states:
"During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Qú Bóyù was a person of respect, frugality, and sincere propriety.
When traveling at night,
he would always descend when passing the duke's gate.
Duke Líng once sat with his wife at night,
and a carriage passed the gate without a sound.
The duke said to his wife:
'Do you know whose carriage that is?'
The wife replied:
'It must be Qú Bóyù.'
'How do you know?'
'Bóyù
is one of Wèi's most sincere adherents to propriety.
According to propriety,
one descends at the duke's gate,
and salutes the ruler's horse.
Now the carriage passed the gate without a sound,
meaning he descended at the gate.
If not Bóyù,
who else could travel in darkness without neglecting propriety?'
The duke sent someone to inquire,
and it was indeed him."
Again, Jiāng Wēi's Chénliú Zhì states:
"Hán Zhuō was sincere, steadfast, pure, and firm,
respectful and full of compassion,
broadly learned and well-informed.
He delighted in guiding others toward goodness.
When encountering an altar, he would hasten his steps,
and seeing living creatures, he would not eat their flesh."
Esteeming the Worthy and Respecting the Elderly
The Kǒng Cóngzǐ states:
"Duke Dìng asked:
'What does the Zhōu Shū mean by "employing the employable, revering the reverent, and awing the awe-inspiring"?'
Confucius replied:
'Not losing the Way,
this clarifies it for people.
To be able to employ those who can be employed is to achieve good governance;
to respect those who deserve respect is to esteem the worthy.'"
The Shǐ Jì states:
"Duke Yì of Lǔ's younger brother, Chēng, was solemn and reverent toward the bright spirits,
and respectful in serving the elderly.
In assigning tasks and carrying out punishments,
he would always inquire about inherited instructions and consult past precedents."
Adjusting Headgear and Tucking Robes
Xí Zuòchǐ's Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Zhuàn states:
"Páng Gōng personally tilled the fields.
He and his wife treated each other like guests.
During rest, he would adjust his headgear and sit upright."
Liáng Zuò's Wèi Guótǒng states:
"Shān Tāo, styled Jù Yuán,
possessed great magnanimity from a young age.
Even in his youth,
when elders and clan seniors saw him,
he would sit cross-legged and tuck in his robes."
Zhào Dùn's Feigned Sleep and Máo Róng's Upright Sitting
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Duke Líng of Jìn was unprincely.
Zhào Xuānzǐ repeatedly remonstrated with him.
The duke resented this,
and sent Chú Ní to assassinate him.
Going at dawn,
he found the bedroom door open.
Xuānzǐ, fully dressed for court,
as it was still early,
sat feigning sleep.
Ní retreated and sighed, saying:
'He does not forget reverence and respect;
he is the master of the people.
To assassinate the master of the people is disloyal;
to abandon the ruler's command is untrustworthy.'
Thereupon, he dashed his head against a locust tree and died."
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū states:
"Máo Róng, styled Jì Wěi,
was from Chénliú.
Over forty years old,
he was plowing in the fields.
Once, taking shelter from rain under a tree with his peers,
all the others sat cross-legged facing each other,
but Róng alone sat upright, increasingly respectful.
Guō Línzōng saw this and found him remarkable."
Wèi Wéndì's Yuèfǔ, Duǎn Gē Xíng
Mountains do not disdain height;
waters do not disdain depth.
The Duke of Zhōu spat out his food,
and all under heaven turned their hearts to him.
Wèi Chénsī Wáng's Kōnghóu Yǐn
Setting wine in the high hall,
kinsmen and friends follow my wanderings.
In the central kitchen, a rich feast is prepared;
a lamb is cooked, a fat ox slaughtered.
Long-standing bonds must not be forgotten;
slighting me is especially contrary to righteousness.
The humble virtue of a gentleman,
bowing low—what does he seek?
Sòng Bào Míngyuǎn's Huán Jiùlú Shī
Solemnly attired, joining the cloud-like host,
holding the reins, I tread the final path.
With strict reverence, I tread upon my mulberry and catalpa;
with added respect, I gaze upon my elm and scholar tree.
Intelligence and Acuity, Seventh
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The reason people esteem the swords Gānjiàng and Mòyé
is that they are prized for their ability to cut through things instantly.
The reason people esteem the steed Qíjì
is that it arrives immediately.
If one must wait a long time,
even silkworms can lift stones,
and a nag can travel a great distance.
Therefore, intelligence and quick-wittedness
are the fine qualities of a person."
Liú Shào's Treatise on Human Characters says:
"What the sages and worthies considered beautiful,
nothing is more beautiful than intelligence;
what intelligence considers precious,
nothing is more precious than understanding people.
If one truly possesses the wisdom to understand people,
then all talents can be properly ordered,
and the achievements of various tasks will flourish.
Thus, Yáo was praised for being able to illuminate outstanding virtue,
Shùn achieved merit by promoting the 'Two Eight' [talents],
Tāng gained fame for supporting the worthy of Yǒushēn,
and King Wén established governance by elevating the old man from the banks of the Wèi River.
From this, it can be said:
When a sage governs,
who does not labor their intelligence in seeking out talent,
and then attain ease by employing them?"
The Garden of Stories says:
"In the past, there was Huáng Xiāng, whose courtesy name was Wénqiáng,
a man from Jiāngxià.
He extensively read biographies and records,
and there was no book he did not peruse.
In the capital, he was called 'Peerless under Heaven,
the Child of Jiāngxià, Huáng.'"
The Book of Later Wei says:
"Yuán Shùn of Later Wei, whose courtesy name was Zǐhé,
was the son of Rénchéng Prince Chéng.
At the age of nine,
he studied under Chén Fēng of Lè'ān,
reciting books day and night.
In just fifteen days,
he had mastered them all thoroughly,
which amazed Chén Fēng.
He reported to the Prince:
'I, Fēng, began studying under a teacher at fifteen,
and have continued until my hair turned white.
In all that I have seen and heard,
I have never encountered anyone like him.
Even the Child of Jiāngxià, Huáng,
cannot be called peerless.'
The Prince laughed and said:
'When jade is born in Lántián,
how could it be otherwise?'"
Wáng Tiánzhī's Biographies of Child Prodigies says:
"In recent times, there was Rèn Gǔ of Lè'ān.
At twelve, he began studying under a teacher,
and without needing to ask a second time,
he mastered three classics in one year.
The villagers sang:
'The elder of the Jiǎng clan,
the child of the Rèn clan—
it is said that the Jiǎng family's elders are steadfast in their ways,
while the Rèn family's learning is wise even in youth.'"
The Records of Wei says:
"Wáng Càn was skilled at composing writings.
As soon as he lifted his brush, he completed them,
with no need for revisions.
People often thought he had prepared them in advance."
Knowing Ten from One / Responding to Five
The Analects says:
"Confucius said to Zǐgòng:
'Who is better, you or Huí?'
He replied:
'How dare I compare myself to Huí!
Huí hears one and knows ten.'"
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Chúnyú Kūn met Zōu Jì.
After finishing his speech, he hurried out
and said to his servant:
'With this man, I exchanged subtle words five times,
and he responded to me like an echo following a sound,
which is why the conversation did not last long.'"
Memorizing Silently / Responding Like an Echo
Chén Shòu's Biographies of the Elderly of Yì Province says:
"Zhào Hóng, whose courtesy name was Wēnróu,
when young, read the Book of Documents
and silently memorized its sounds and sentences."
Also, Kǒng Róng's Memorial Recommending Mí Héng states:
"Ānshì [Zhāng Ānshì] memorized silently."
"Responding like an echo" is already mentioned in the note above for "Responding to Five."
Answering About Fruit / Inscribing on Yogurt
Liú Shào's Biographies of Child Prodigies says:
"There was a child of the Yáng family,
a man from Liáng State,
who was very clever at nine.
Kǒng Jūnpíng visited his father,
but his father was not home,
so he called the child out
and set out fruit for him.
Among the fruit were bayberries.
He pointed to them and said to the child:
'This is your family's fruit.'
The child immediately replied:
'I have never heard that the peacock is the family bird of the Master.'"
Liú Yìqìng's Garden of Stories says:
"Someone sent Cáo Cāo a gift.
After finishing it,
he inscribed the character '合' (hé) on the yogurt container to show the crowd.
No one could understand it.
When it reached Yáng Xiū,
Xiū immediately ate it.
Cáo Cāo asked him:
'Everyone else passed it by from afar,
why did you alone eat it?'
Xiū said:
'You, sir, told everyone to take one mouthful,
so why should I doubt it?'"
Reciting a Thousand Words / Composing on a Single Object
Liú Shào's Biographies of Child Prodigies says:
"Xiàhóu Róng, whose courtesy name was Yòuquán,
was a man from Qiáo in Pèi State.
He was clever from a young age,
able to compose writings at seven,
reciting a thousand words of text daily,
and recognizing whatever he saw at a glance."
Zhāng Yǐn's Biographies of Literary Scholars says:
"Zhāng Chún of Wú Commandery
had a fine reputation from a young age.
He once visited General of Agile Cavalry Zhū Jù.
Jù asked him to compose a piece on a single object before sitting down.
Chún responded immediately,
completing it without revising a single word."
Reading Five Lines at Once / Not Missing a Single Character
Xiè Chéng's Book of Later Han says:
"Yìng Fèng read books
five lines at a time."
Wèi Shōu's Book of Later Wei says:
"Zǔ Yíng, whose courtesy name was Yuánzhēn,
was a man from Fànyáng.
At twelve, he became a student of the Central Secretariat.
When Academician Zhāng Tiānlóng lectured on the Book of Documents,
he was selected as the lead lecturer.
All the students gathered.
Yíng had studied late into the night and was weary,
and did not notice it was dawn.
By mistake, he took the Scroll of the Book of Rites of his roommate Lǐ Xiàoyí from Zhào Commandery to the lectern,
placed the Rites text in front of him,
and recited three chapters of the Book of Documents
without missing a single character."
Collating Lost Books / Comparing Missing Characters
The Book of Han says:
"Zhāng Ānshì, whose courtesy name was Zǐrú,
was appointed as a Gentleman Attendant due to his father's position when young.
Because he was skilled in writing,
he served in the Imperial Secretariat.
When the Emperor traveled to Hédōng,
three boxes of books were once lost.
When the Emperor inquired, no one knew their contents,
but only Ānshì recognized them
and recorded everything about them.
Later, when the books were sought and purchased to collate,
not a single character was missing.
The Emperor marveled at his talent
and promoted him to Imperial Secretary."
Xiè Chéng's Book of Later Han says:
"Mí Héng was especially close to Huáng Zǔ's son, Shè.
Héng and Shè read the stele inscription composed by Cài Yōng together.
Shè admired the text
and regretted not having a copy.
Héng said to Shè:
'Although I only read it once,
I still remember the words,
except for two characters that are unclear.'
He then wrote them out.
Shè copied it and compared it,
and found no errors,
except for those two missing characters."
Zhāng Chún of Wú Commandery
had exceptional talent from a young age.
Together with his fellow townsmen Zhāng Yǎn and Zhū Yì, both still youths,
he went to visit General of Agile Cavalry Zhū Jù.
Jù heard of the three's talent and reputation
and wanted to test them.
He said:
"Now that the three worthies have graced this old rustic, my thirst is great.
Please each compose a piece on a single object for me,
and only then may you sit."
Chún said:
"The swift horse is prized for its speed,
the hawk and falcon for their agility.
Why must one ponder deeply?
All can be composed instantly upon seeing."
Jù was greatly pleased.
Yǎn composed a rhapsody on dogs, saying:
When guarding, they have authority;
when hunting, they have captures.
Hánlú and Sòngquè,
their names are recorded in bamboo and silk.
Yì composed a rhapsody on crossbows, saying:
The trunk of the Southern Peak,
the bronze of Zhōngshān.
Responding to the moment, hitting the target,
shooting falcons on high walls.
Wèi dynasty Mí Héng's "Rhapsody on the Parrot, Preface"
At the time, when Crown Prince Shè of Huáng Zǔ was hosting a grand gathering of guests,
someone presented a parrot.
He raised his wine cup before Héng and said:
"Mí the Recluse,
today we have nothing to entertain our guests with.
I consider this bird, having come from afar,
bright, kind, clever, and good,
a precious member among feathered creatures.
I wish you would compose a rhapsody about it,
so that all present may share in the splendid spectacle.
Would that not be good?"
Héng therefore composed the rhapsody,
his brush never pausing,
the text flawless without revision.
Teacher, First
The Book of Rites says:
"In all methods of learning,
revering the teacher is the most difficult.
When the teacher is revered, then the Way is honored;
when the Way is honored, then the people know to respect learning.
Therefore, there are two situations in which a ruler does not treat his subject as a subject:
when he serves as the impersonator of the dead,
then he is not treated as a subject;
when he serves as a teacher,
then he is not treated as a subject.
According to the rites of the Grand Academy,
even when receiving instruction from the Son of Heaven,
he does not face north,
this is how the teacher is honored.
A good learner
makes the teacher at ease yet achieves double the result,
and further attributes it to him;
a poor learner
makes the teacher toil yet achieves half the result,
and further resents him."
The Gǔliáng Commentary says:
"Duke Zhāo of Lǔ said:
'When a child is born,
if it does not escape water and fire,
it is the mother's fault.
When it becomes a youth,
if it does not attend a teacher,
it is the father's fault.'
When attending a teacher,
if learning and inquiry lack proper method,
if the mind and will do not comprehend,
it is the teacher's fault."
Lǎozi says:
"The good person
is the teacher of the not-good person."
Confucius said:
"When three walk together,
among them there must be one who can be my teacher!"
The Shìmíng says:
"In ancient times, a teacher was called Xiānshēng (First Born)."
The Records of Wèi says:
"Xún Yōu, styled Gōngdá.
When Emperor Wén of Wèi was Crown Prince,
the Grand Ancestor (Cáo Cāo) told him:
'Xún Gōngdá is a model teacher for men,
you should treat him with utmost respect and courtesy.'
Yōu once fell ill,
the Crown Prince inquired after his illness,
and alone bowed at the foot of his bed.
Such was the respect and special treatment he received.
A proverb says:
'At three years, choose a teacher.'" Yángzǐ's Fǎyán says:
"Diligence in learning is not as good as diligence in seeking a teacher.
A teacher is
the model and exemplar for people."
Master Xún (Xúnzǐ) says:
"There are four arts of a teacher:
being dignified and inspiring awe—
this qualifies one to be a teacher;
being aged and trustworthy—
this qualifies one to be a teacher;
reciting and explaining without confusion—
this qualifies one to be a teacher;
understanding subtleties and discoursing on them—
this qualifies one to be a teacher."
He also said:
"Gānjiàng, Mòyé, Jùquē, Pìlǘ—
these were fine swords of antiquity,
yet without whetting and grinding they could not be sharp,
without human strength they could not cut.
Huáliú, Qíjì, Xiānlí, Lǜ'ěr—
these were all fine horses of antiquity,
yet they must have the restraint of bit and reins in front,
and the threat of whip and crop behind,
added to the driving of Zàofǔ,
before they could cover a thousand lǐ in a day.
Though a man may have a fine nature and a discerning, wise mind,
he must still seek a worthy teacher to serve,
and choose good friends to befriend.
The teaching of a penetrating teacher
makes disciples feel at ease, joyful, rested, free, reverent, and solemn.
If these six are attained through learning,
then the paths of depravity and perversity are blocked;
if these six are not attained through learning,
then the ruler cannot command his ministers,
the father cannot command his sons,
the teacher cannot command his pupils."
Hánzhàng (Container for Staff) Shùxiū (Bundle of Dried Meat)
The Book of Rites says:
"In all lecture discussions, between mats there is a hánzhàng.
Hán means
to contain.
It contains a staff sufficient for pointing and drawing."
The Analects says:
"For anyone who brings a bundle of dried meat (as tuition),
I have never refused instruction."
Huán Róng Faces East Wáng Xiáng Faces South
The Dōngguān Hànjì says:
"When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he honored Huán Róng with the rites due a teacher.
The Emperor visited the Office of the Grand Chamberlain,
had Huán Róng sit facing east,
set out a table and staff,
and assembled all officials."
Wáng Yǐn's Jìnshū says:
"When the Wèi noble Duke Gāoguìxiāng entered the school,
wishing to honor ancient precedents,
he appointed Wáng Xiáng as the Sānlǎo (Venerable Elder),
and the Palace Attendant Zhèng Xiǎotóng as the Wǔgēng (Vigilant Elder).
Wáng Xiáng faced south with table and staff,
assuming the position of a teacher.
The Emperor faced north to request words of wisdom."
Model and Exemplar Example and Standard
Yáng Xióng's Fǎyán says:
"Diligence in learning is not as good as diligence in seeking a teacher.
A teacher is
the model and exemplar for people."
The Hánshī Wàizhuàn says:
"Wisdom like a spring's source,
conduct that can serve as an example and standard—
such a one is a teacher for people."
Striking the Bell Sounding the Drum
The Book of Rites says:
"One who is good at responding to questions is like striking a bell:
strike it lightly and it sounds lightly,
strike it heavily and it sounds heavily.
Wait for it to resonate fully,
then its sound is exhausted.
One who is poor at answering questions is the opposite."
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
"Dǒng Chūn, styled Jìyáng,
was from Yúyáo in Kuàijī.
In youth he loved learning,
studied under Palace Attendant and Libationer Wáng Jūnzhòng,
receiving instruction in the ancient-script Shàngshū.
Later he went to Jīng Fáng to receive instruction in the Yìjīng.
He exhaustively investigated the sage's intent,
systematically categorized the principles and meanings,
and later moved to establish a refined studio for teaching.
Distant disciples and learners often numbered in the hundreds.
Whenever the students ascended the lecture hall,
the drum was sounded three times.
Holding the classics across their hands,
a hundred men would respectfully pose questions."
The Three [Relations] The Four [Arts]
Cuī Hóng's Hòu Qín Lù says:
"Initially,
when Yáo Hóng was Crown Prince,
he received the classics from the Grand Academy Erudite Chúnyú Qí.
Qí fell ill and was at home.
Hóng considered that a teacher is the model and exemplar for people,
transmitting the teachings of former sages.
Added to the principle of the 'three' [relations—ruler, father, teacher],
this could not be taken lightly.
He personally visited to inquire after his illness,
and bowed at the foot of his bed."
Master Xún says:
"A teacher has four arts,
and transmitting and practicing are not among them."
Virtue in Goodness Superintendent of Accomplishment
The Book of Documents says:
"Virtue has no constant teacher;
one who holds to goodness becomes the teacher."
The Book of Rites says:
"The Director of Music is in charge of the studies;
the father-teacher is in charge of accomplishment.
One man's supreme goodness
brings rectitude to all states—
this refers to the heir apparent."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Sī means
to be in charge."
It also says:
"The Grand Superintendent of Accomplishment discusses and expounds in the Eastern Hall.
All who sit in attendance before the Grand Superintendent of Accomplishment
keep a distance of three mats between them,
so that they may ask questions."
Sitting Behind Curtains Reciting Books Teaching Rites from Behind a Curtain
The Records of the Eastern Lodge of the Han says:
"Zhāng Huàn was sent to the Xiōngnú.
The Xiūtú and the Wūhuán of Shuòfāng rebelled together,
and they set fire to the gate of the General Who Crosses Liáo.
They camped at Chìkēng,
with smoke and fires visible to each other.
The troops were greatly terrified,
each wanting to flee.
Huàn sat calmly behind curtains,
reciting books with his disciples as usual,
and the soldiers gradually calmed down."
Péi Jǐngrén's Records of the Former Qín:
"Fú Jiān visited the Imperial Academy,
and asked the Erudites about the classics.
The Erudite Lú Hú replied:
'For the Rites of Zhōu and the Commentary on the Rites,
there is no teacher.'
The mother of Wěi Chěng, née Sòng,
transmitted her father's learning,
and possessed the pronunciation and meaning of the Rites of Zhōu.
If not for this mother,
there would be no one to teach the later generations.
Thereupon, a lecture hall and study were established for Sòng,
with one hundred and twenty students.
She taught from behind a crimson gauze curtain.
She was enfeoffed with the noble title Xuānwén Jūn,
and was granted ten maidservants."
Methodical Multitudinous
The Analects:
"Yán Huí said:
'The Master is methodical in skillfully guiding people.
He broadens me with culture,
and restrains me with ritual.
I wish to stop but cannot.'"
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Living in Idleness" says:
"The two schools stand side by side,
their twin buildings like one.
On the right, the scions of the state are extended;
on the left, the worthy recluses are admitted.
Multitudinous are the students;
abundant is Confucian learning."
Běihǎi Xīhé
The Book of the Later Hàn says:
"Zhèng Xuán, styled Kāngchéng,
was from Běihǎi.
Xuán loved learning,
studying and reciting day and night,
never tiring of it.
Hundreds and thousands of students sought him out in succession.
The Chancellor of the state, Kǒng Róng, deeply respected Xuán,
and specially established a district called Zhènggōng Xiāng,
and widened his gate, calling it Tōngdé Mén.
Initially, he served Mǎ Róng as teacher.
He questioned him on doubtful points,
then took his leave to return.
Róng sighed and said:
'Now that Zhèng Shēng is leaving,
my Way goes east.'"
The Book of Rites says:
"Zǐxià wept for his son and lost his eyesight.
Zēngzǐ condoled with him, saying:
'You and I served the Master between the Zhū and Sì rivers.
You retired and grew old on the banks of the Xīhé.
You caused the people of Xīhé to compare you to the Master—
this is your first fault.'"
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"This means he did not live up to his teacher."
Building Palaces Constructing Temples
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"Zōuzǐ went to Yān.
King Zhāo held a broom and cleared the way,
requesting to be listed among the disciples and receive instruction.
He built the Jiéshí Palace,
and personally went to serve him as teacher."
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural says:
"Jiè Yǎn
was from an unknown place.
During the time of the First Sovereign of Wú,
he came from the north,
saying he followed his teacher, Báiyáng Gōng, into the Eastern Sea.
Yǎn became known to the Sovereign of Wú,
who detained Yǎn
and built a palace-temple for him.
Within a single day,
he sent people four or five times to inquire after his well-being.
Sometimes Yǎn appeared as a youth of sixteen or seventeen,
sometimes as a man in his prime.
The Sovereign of Wú wished to learn his arts.
Yǎn, because the emperor often had many consorts,
did not teach him for many months."
Skillful Guidance Broad Illustration
The Analects:
"Yán Huí said:
'The Master is methodical in skillfully guiding people.'"
The Book of Rites says:
"The gentleman knows the difficulty and ease of reaching learning,
and knows its good and bad qualities.
Only then can he broadly illustrate;
only after being able to broadly illustrate can he become a teacher."
Southern Outskirts Eastern Mound
The Liezi says:
"Lièzǐ, having taken Húqiūzǐlín as teacher
and befriended Bóhūnmào Rén,
returned to live in the southern outskirts,
with followers numbering in the hundreds."
Wáng Zhìshēn's Records of the Sòng says:
"An edict ordered the recluse Zhōu Jī to establish a school at the Eastern Mound,
where over a hundred people brought their own provisions to receive instruction."
Yànzhēn Sedate and Composed Xuánlǎn Pure and Harmonious
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Yān says:
"Liú Zàn, styled Yànzhēn,
was from Píngyuán.
He was broadly learned in the classics,
a pure Confucian of his time.
Upright and pure, he did not act contrary to ritual.
Mùróng Huī valued his virtue and learning,
and had his heir apparent, Huǎng, serve him as teacher."
Wèi Shōu's Book of the Later Wèi says:
"Liáng Yuè, styled Xuánlǎn,
was from Xīnxīng.
From youth he loved learning,
mastering the classics and commentaries broadly,
leaving nothing uncomprehended.
His nature was pure, harmonious, sincere, and trustworthy;
his words and actions were without fault.
In the early Wèi, he served as Erudite of the Classic of Rites."
Presenting Jade and Silk Bestowing Gold Seal and Purple Ribbon
Jiāng Wēi's Records of Chénliú says:
"Lóu Wàng, styled Cìzǐ,
was from Yōngqiū.
In youth, he studied the Spring and Autumn Annals from the Privy Treasurer Dīng Zǐrán,
and was praised for his moral integrity.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
King Xiào of Zhào heard of his fame
and sent a grandee bearing jade and silk to invite Wàng to be his teacher,
but Wàng did not accept."
Xú Yuán's Book of the Sòng says:
"When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he bestowed upon Yán Yánzhī a gold seal with purple ribbon,
appointing him as Tutor to the Prince of Xiāngdōng."
Jìn Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Living in Idleness"
Teaching has no constant teacher;
the Way is present wherever it is right.
Thus worthy scholars cast aside their seals;
enlightened kings cherish the seal of office.
Instruction is like the wind blowing;
response is like grass bending.
Hàn Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
He commands those who diligently instruct the elders,
the famous Confucian teachers and tutors,
to discuss and discourse on the Six Arts,
examining and harmonizing similarities and differences.
Yìng Qú's "One Hundred and One Poems"
Can sons and younger brothers not be cautious?
Caution lies in selecting teachers and friends.
Teachers and friends must be of good virtue;
then average talent can be advanced and guided.
From the "Preface to the Stele of Guō Yǒudào" by Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn Dynasty:
The gentleman was endowed with heavenly sincerity,
intelligent and wise.
Filial, fraternal, warm, and respectful,
benevolent, sincere, kind, and steadfast.
His integrity and steadfastness were sufficient to manage affairs,
his subtle guidance was sufficient to rectify the times.
Thus he studied and examined the Six Classics,
explored and synthesized charts and weft texts.
He traveled throughout Huáxià,
and gathered at the imperial academy.
Therefore, he rescued the Wén and Wǔ traditions from the brink of collapse,
and preserved subtle teachings from extinction.
At that time, those wearing official caps and tassels,
gentlemen with sashes and pendants,
gazed upon his form and example, clinging like shadows,
listened to his fine reputation and echoed in harmony.
It was like all rivers returning to the great sea,
or scales and shells revering the turtle and dragon.
Thereupon, he lived in seclusion behind a humble gate,
gathering friends and diligently instructing them.
The young and ignorant relied on him,
using him to dispel their obscurities.
The provincial and commandery authorities, hearing of his virtue,
humbled themselves and prepared rituals,
yet none could compel him to come.
The assembled lords admired him,
and thus he was recruited as an assistant in the Minister over the Masses office,
and also recommended as a "Yǒudào" candidate,
but he declined all on grounds of illness,
the documents are not fully recorded here.
From Cài Yōng's "Preface to the Stele of Gentleman Wénfàn, Chén Zhònggōng":
Now, his benevolence, love, gentleness, and warmth,
were sufficient to nurture all living beings;
his breadth, greatness, tolerance, and forbearance,
were sufficient to encompass all directions without limit;
his firmness, resolution, strength, and steadfastness,
were sufficient to awe the violent and rectify the wicked;
his rectification of his person and embodiment of transformation,
were sufficient to mold and shape the hearts of scholars.
The gentleman possessed these four virtues,
therefore his words could be taken as models,
his conduct could bring joy,
his actions could be emulated,
his stillness could be followed.
Thus, the youth of the state,
and later generations from distant regions,
none failed to share admiration and look up to him,
taking him as their model,
following his inclinations and directions,
the harsh and cruel thought of harmony,
disputes and litigations transformed into deference.
Even with a stern ruler and harsh governance,
compelling through punishments and executions,
it was not as swift as the gentleman's subtle guidance.
On Making Friends, Part Two
The "Preface to the Máo Poetry" says:
"Felling Trees,
is about feasting with friends and old acquaintances.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
none have succeeded without the need for friends."

Indirect Remonstrance, Part Three
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"Remonstrance means
to interpose,
to change.
Right and wrong interpose,
to reform and change one's conduct.
Humans possess the five constant virtues,
thus it is known there are five types of remonstrance:
the first is indirect remonstrance,
the second is compliant remonstrance,
the third is observing remonstrance,
the fourth is direct remonstrance,
the fifth is sacrificial remonstrance.
Indirect remonstrance
is wisdom.
Knowing the sprouting of calamity,
seeing what has not yet occurred and indirectly warning of it;
compliant remonstrance
is benevolence,
uttering words humble and compliant,
not opposing the ruler's heart;
observing remonstrance
is propriety.
Observing the ruler's countenance,
if displeased, then withdraw,
if pleased, then advance again,
advancing and retreating according to propriety;
direct remonstrance
is trustworthiness.
To point out
is to substantiate.
Substantiating the matter at hand;
sacrificial remonstrance
is righteousness.
Speaking of the state's harm,
forgetting life for the ruler,
not avoiding loss of life.
Therefore Confucius said:
'There are five types of remonstrance,
I follow the indirect.
Indirect means
when the ruler or father has faults, it is difficult to speak directly.
Either entrust the meaning to odes or rhapsodies to make it appear in words,
or borrow other matters to convey the intent,
hoping for some awakening and turning toward goodness;
remonstrance means
when affairs are improper,
pointing them out and speaking of them.
Above, to the ruler or father,
below, to friends,
discussing without doubt,
there must be benefit.
Therefore Confucius said the ruler has disputing ministers,
the father has disputing sons,
the scholar has disputing friends,
this is what it means.'"
The *Shàngshū* states:
"Every year in the first month of spring,
the herald with his wooden clapper proclaims along the roads,
officials and masters admonish each other,
artisans offer remonstrance through their crafts.
If any are disrespectful,
the state has constant punishments.
Also, as wood follows the marking line to become straight,
so the sovereign follows remonstrance to become sage."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"When parents have faults,
with subdued breath and pleasant countenance,
with gentle voice, remonstrate.
If the remonstrance is not accepted,
rouse respect and filial piety,
and when they are pleased, remonstrate again."
Also, "In serving the ruler, one should wish to remonstrate, not wish to proclaim."
Proclaim means speaking excessively outwardly.
Also, "When parents have faults,
remonstrate but do not oppose."
Confucius said:
"Serving a ruler at a distance and remonstrating
is flattery;
being close and not remonstrating
is parasitical profit."
Gùzǐ said:
"Not remonstrating endangers the ruler,
remonstrating endangers oneself.
Thus the worthy and superior man above dares not endanger the ruler,
below dares not endanger himself.
If after three remonstrances he is not followed, he departs."

"If there is one who can speak fully to his ruler,
and if he is employed, he stays;
if he is not employed, he leaves—
this is called remonstrance."
The *Records of the Three Kingdoms: Book of Wèi* says:
"During the reign of Emperor Míng,
the common people were impoverished and destitute,
yet labor services were at their peak.
Wèi Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
'If not one who would ruin his family for the state
Offending the Countenance and Opposing the Will
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Yáo Qī valued faithfulness and righteousness;
at court, he was concerned for the state and loved his sovereign.
Whenever something did not sit right with him,
he would inevitably offend the sovereign's countenance to remonstrate and argue."
The Records of Wèi states:
"During Emperor Míng's time,
the common people were impoverished and destitute,
yet labor duties were at their peak.
Wèi Jì submitted a memorial saying, 'Compliance with one's countenance is whence affection arises;
opposition to one's will is whence hatred follows.
Therefore, all people comply with the countenance and avoid opposing the will.'" Also, Huán Fàn's Essential Discourses of the Age states:
"To tug at someone's ear
and oppose their will
does not constitute remonstration and argument."
Changing Expression Behind the Screen and Removing the Cap to Kowtow
Cuī Hóng's Former Liáng states:
"Zhāng Jùn feasted with his assembled officials,
discussing the desire for severe punishments and strict regulations.
All present considered it appropriate.
Adjutant Huáng Bīn stepped forward and said,
'Your subject does not see how this can be done.
If the respected and dear ones violate the orders,
then the orders will not be carried out.'
Zhāng Jùn had a stern and fierce nature,
yet he changed his expression behind the screen and said,
'If not for Master Huáng,
I would not have heard of my faults.
This can be called the utmost loyalty.'" Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Whenever something did not sit right with Yáo Qī,
he would inevitably offend the sovereign's countenance to remonstrate and argue.
The Emperor once went out,
and Yáo Qī removed his cap and kowtowed before the carriage, saying,
'The warnings of past and present
are that unexpected changes arise from the unforeseen.
I do not wish Your Majesty to make incognito excursions frequently.'
The Emperor turned his carriage around and returned because of this."
Xiè Yǎn's "Rhapsody on the Emperor's Cultivation of Virtue"
Considering the successive reigns of emperors and kings,
truly their steps and tracks differ in their measures.
None fail to consider that those who often lose gain,
and those who cherish comfort inevitably face peril.
Therefore, trembling with fear,
cautious day by day,
maintaining diligence and frugality,
eschewing extravagance and ease.
Externally, no wild fowl are neglected;
internally, no chambers are left desolate.
Only the worthy are appointed,
only the people are thus cared for.
Then the Three Sovereigns would not suffice to make four,
the Five Emperors would not suffice to make six.
But if one relies on wisdom and boasts of strength,
savage and stubborn,
casting aside the loyal and good,
rewarding the flattering and sycophantic.
Raising lofty towers to reach the heavens,
digging deep pools to sever the earth.
Heavy taxes and burdensome labor,
accumulating treasures and hoarding coins.
Punishing the innocent,
not rewarding the meritorious.
Then Xià Jié could be matched by a second,
Yīn Xīn easily finds his pair.
Hàn Wèi Mèng's "Four-Character Poem Admonishing King Yuán of Chǔ"
State affairs are neglected,
pleasure and wandering are the amusement.
Horses and men roam leisurely,
released and driven about.
What is promoted is not virtue,
what is cherished is not the talented.
Only the parks are expanded,
only flattery is trusted.
Alas, my king,
kinsman of the Hàn.
You have not toiled day and night,
to cultivate a fine reputation.
Wèi Yìng Qú's "One Hundred and One Poems"
Spacious chambers lead to gathering shadows,
high towers attract accumulating sunlight.
How can people of a declining age
be extravagant within palace walls?
Adornment and artifice know no bounds,
timber and earth are clad in crimson light.
Demands and requisitions drain the four seas,
yet elegant intentions remain unsatisfied.
Noble Status, Part Four
The Shuōwén states:
"Guì (noble)
means guī (to return).
It refers to what things return to and look up to.
In the Rǔ and Yǐng regions, they say guì,
sounding like the guī of 'returning to.'"
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Children of noble families,
born in the hands of women,
have never experienced worry or fear in their hearts.
Some, not yet out of swaddling clothes, are granted high official ranks;
barely able to wear robes and caps, they occupy positions of favor and honor,
wielding the authority of life and death.
Holding the power of promotion and demotion,
truly they are to be feared."
The Strategies of the Warring States states:
"Tián Xū was honored by the King of Wèi.
Huìzǐ said:
'Strive hard!
Now, the poplar tree,
planted horizontally, it will grow;
broken and planted, it will also grow.
But if ten people plant it,
and one person uproots it,
then there will be no poplar.
Moreover, with a crowd of ten people,
planting something easily grown,
yet unable to withstand one person—
why is that?
Planting is difficult, removing is easy.
Now, though you have planted yourself with the king, many wish to uproot you.
You are surely in danger!'" The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Lǐ Sī sighed and said:
'I heard Xún Qīng say:
"Things forbid excessive prosperity."
I was once a commoner from Shàngcài;
now, among the ranks of ministers, none stands above me.
This can be called the extreme of wealth and nobility.
When things reach their extreme, they decline.
I do not know where my carriage will rest.'" Xún Bózǐ's Family Biography of the Xún Clan states:
"Only my ancestors,
up to the time of Jìn,
filled the court with eminent men,
their dragon robes resplendent.
Six generations, nine dukes—
is this not magnificent?
Open and extraordinary,
their light illuminated the six directions.
During the restoration,
Chancellor Wáng Gōng sighed and said:
'After Xù, none have matched this glory and favor;
they are the noble family of the realm.'"
Seven Leaves and Five Marquises
Zuǒ Sī's "Poems on History" states:
"Jīn and Zhāng relied on old achievements,
for seven leaves they wore Hàn sable tails."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Chéng enfeoffed his maternal uncles: Tán as Marquis of Píng'ē,

Lì as Marquis of Jiāngyáng,
Gēn as Marquis of Qūyáng,

the world called them the Five Marquises,
their glory and nobility unparalleled in their age."
Jīn and Zhāng, Gěng and Dèng
The Book of Hàn states:
"Among the families of meritorious officials,

were close, honored, and favored,

The Dōngguān Hànjì states:

"The Dèng clan, since the restoration,
for successive leaves were honored and favored,
none could compare."

Sīmǎ Biāo's Book of Hàn states:

Xǔ Shǐ Liáng Dòu

Dangling Three Ribbons Wearing Six Seals
The Book of Han:
"Yáng Pú,

Towers and Pavilions Stretch Continuously Stables and Mansions Face Each Other
Zhāng Fán's Records of the Hàn says:

The Records of the Eastern Lodge says:
