Jìn Zuǒ Sī's "Poems on History"
Crowded within the capital city,
Resplendent are the dwellings of kings and marquises.
Official caps and canopies shade the four roads,
Vermilion carriages vie on the long avenues.
Morning gatherings at the mansions of Jīn and Zhāng,
Evening lodgings at the residences of Xǔ and Shǐ.
To the south, neighbors strike bells and chimes,
To the north, lanes blow sheng and yu pipes.
Ancient Music Bureau Poem
Your household is truly easy to know,
Yet profound and unforgettable.
Gold forms your gate,
White jade forms your hall.
In the hall, wine vessels are arrayed,
Hándān singers are made to perform.
In the central courtyard grows a wondrous tree,
How brilliant are the ornate lanterns!
Two or three brothers you have,
The middle son serves as a court gentleman.
Returning home once every five days,
The road itself shines with light.
Gold adorns the horse's head,
Onlookers fill the roadside.
Qí Bào Zhāo's "In Place of the 'Jīngluò' Poem"
Phoenix towers, twelve layers high,
Four doors, eight elegant windows.
Embroidered corners, golden lotus flowers,
Cassia pillars, jade coiling dragons.
Pearl blinds do not block the dew,
Silk curtains cannot withstand the wind.
Precious curtains worth three hundred thousand,
All for your morning adornment.
Liáng Wú Jūn's "Poem Presented to Zhōu Xīngsì"
Our worthy one in a position of power,
His fame shakes Huáxià.
Vermilion carriage with tortoiseshell ox,
Purple bridle with dappled horse.
Morning flowers dance away with the wind,
Night moon peeps beneath the window.
Thinking you, noble, may easily change friends,
Surely I should be cast aside.
Shào Ān's "Poem Presented to Cài Jūn"
In the past, together in the secluded valley,
You have now moved to the tall tree.
Resplendent and flourishing in blue and purple,
Delving deep into discussions of documents.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem Sent to Yáng Gōng"
The young master flourished in the western capital,
His radiance famed from early on.
Dividing the courtyard to receive wandering scholars,
Emptying the lodge to await timely talents.
From high towers, floating fragrance emerges,
In long corridors, precious bracelets chime.
Faces and flowers, no barrier to smiles,
Singing fans, no obstruction to voices.
Bào Zhāo's "Imitating an Ancient Poem"
A Lǔ guest serves the King of Chǔ,
Carrying gold, clad in red and white.
Having received the master's favor,
And gained the prime minister's regard.
At day's end, leaving court to return,
Carriages and horses fill the roadways.
Clan and faction first to gain glory,
Guests and servants admire from afar.
Wealth and honor are what men desire,
Attaining the Way, what then is there to fear?
Wealth, Part Five
Those who are noble are inevitably wealthy,
but the wealthy are not necessarily noble.
Thus, when scholars desire nobility,
it is actually for the sake of wealth.
However, those who desire wealth
do not do so for the sake of nobility.
From this perspective,
wealth is what people most desire.
Therefore, the *Yìjīng* says:
"To be wealthy is called great achievement."
Confucius said:
"If wealth could be sought,
even as a lowly whip-holding attendant,
I would do it.
If it cannot be sought,
then I follow what I love."
He also said:
"Wealth and nobility are what people desire,
but if obtained not by the proper way,
one should not dwell in them."
Yáng Hǔ said:
"To pursue wealth is to be unrighteous;
to be righteous is not to be wealthy."
The *Family Sayings* records:
"To humble oneself despite wealth and nobility,
who would not associate with such a person?
To respect others despite wealth and nobility,
who would not feel close to such a person?"
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"When using poverty to seek wealth,
farming is not as good as craftsmanship,
craftsmanship is not as good as commerce,
embroidering fine patterns is not as good as leaning against the market gate.
This speaks of the means by which those in humble occupations become wealthy."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals: Zuǒ's Commentary* says:
"When the Qìng clan of Qí perished,
their fief was divided and offered to Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ did not accept it.
Someone asked him:
'Wealth is what people desire;
why do you not accept it?'
He replied:
'Rewards without merit,
wealth without righteousness,
are the medium of calamity.
I do not hate wealth;
I fear losing wealth.'"
The *Garden of Stories* says:
"King Chǔ asked Zhuāng Xīn:
'What is the wealth of a noble man like?'
He replied:
'The wealth of a noble man:
he lends to others but does not trade for profit,
he has surplus food but does not make others serve or labor for it.
His relatives love him,
wrongdoers think well of him,
the unworthy serve him,
all wishing him longevity and happiness, unharmed by misfortune.
This is the wealth of a noble man.'"
Wáng Chōng's *Discourses Weighed in the Balance* states:
"When Yáng Zǐyún composed the *Exemplary Sayings*,
a wealthy merchant from Shǔ offered a hundred thousand in cash,
wishing to be recorded in the book.
Zǐyún did not consent,
saying:
'Wealth without benevolence and righteousness
is like a deer in a pen,
a sheep in a fold.
How can it be recklessly recorded?'"
Huán Kuān's *Discourses on Salt and Iron* says:
"When a man becomes too wealthy, he cannot be employed with official salary."
The *Shàngshū*'s "Five Blessings":
"The second is wealth."
Unofficial Nobility / Cinnabar Mine
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"Wealth is a natural human inclination,
desired by all without learning.
Now, there are those without official rank or salary,
without noble titles or fiefs,
yet who are comparable to such men;
they are called 'unofficial nobility.'"
The *Book of Hàn* says:

her ancestors obtained a cinnabar mine

Counting Gold / Weighing Jade
Xú Guǎng's *Records of Jìn* says:

He calculated his gold and silk,

Wáng Zǐnián's *Records of Omissions* says:

Borrowing Chēzi / Requesting Rúyuàn
Gān Bǎo's *Records of Searching for the Supernatural* says:
"There was a man named Zhōu Chōuzé
who was poor but loved the Way.
One night, he and his wife, exhausted from plowing, fell asleep.

ordering that something be given to them."
The *Registrar's Records* stated:
"This man's physiognomy indicates poverty;
his limit does not exceed this.
Only Zhāng Chēzi is due to be granted ten million.
Since Chēzi is not yet born,
please lend it to him." The Lord of Heaven said, "Good."
Also, the *Records of the Extraordinary* says:
"Ōu Míng of Lúlíng, following merchants, passed by Péngzé Lake.
Each time, he would throw some of what he had on the boat into the lake,
saying it was an offering.
Several years later, passing by again,
he suddenly saw a great road in the lake,
with much dust upon it.
Several officials came on horseback in a carriage to greet Míng,
saying they were sent by Lord Qīnghóng to invite him.
Soon they arrived,
and he saw a mansion with
guards and clerks at the gate.
Míng was very frightened.
An official said:
'Do not be afraid.
Lord Qīnghóng is moved by your repeated offerings,
hence he has invited you.
He will surely give you rich gifts.
Do not accept any of them;
only ask for Rúyuàn.'
When Míng met Lord Qīnghóng,
he requested Rúyuàn,
who was then sent to follow Míng away.
Rúyuàn was a maidservant of Lord Qīnghóng."
When Míng returned home,
whatever he wished for was granted.
After several years, he became very wealthy."
Gold Moat / Coin Well

Accumulating Wealth Like a Mountain / Closing the Gate Forms a Market
Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn* says:

The *Dōngguān Records of Hàn* says:

Qín Zhēn / Wèi Rǎn

The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"The wealth of Marquis Rǎng, Wèi Rǎn,
Copper Mountain and Gold Cavern

and he said:

The Emperor said:

The Dongguan Hanji states:

bestowing gold and silk in great abundance.

indicating their extreme wealth."
Zhuó and Zhèng; Yī and Táo
The Records of the Grand Historian states:

Measuring Cattle and Horses by the Valley; Weighing Pearls and Jade in the Pavilion
The Book of Han states:

Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omissions states:

placing a steelyard upon it

Wine as Water; Beans as Meat
The Book of Han states:

and for your favored minister Dǒng Xián,
bestowing rewards amounting to tens of millions?

all use this to amass wealth.

From Qí Bào Zhāo's "Ode to the River's Clarity"
The officials and people were prosperous and wealthy,
surpassing even the five imperial mausoleum districts in abundance.
The palaces and buildings were grand and magnificent,
towering above mountains and rivers.
From Liáng Liú Xiàobiāo's "Discourse on Broadening the Severance of Friendships"
Wealth equal to that of Táo Zhū and Bái Guǐ;
assets as vast as those of Chéng Zhèng and Luó Shì.
Mountains monopolize copper-rich hills;
homes conceal gold-filled caverns.
Chapter Six: Poverty
Lǚ Chén's Zilin states:
"Jù
means poverty,
emptiness."
Master Xún states:
"Regarding goods, wealth, grain, and rice in a household,
having little is called poverty,
having none at all is called destitution."
The Fangyan states:
"In southern Chǔ, when people are poor,
their clothing is ugly and worn-out.
This is called xūjié.
Jié means familiar and worn-out.
It is also called lǚliè.
Lǚliè
describes the appearance of tattered clothing.
Pronounced 'lóu.'
It is also called lánlǚ."
The Zuo Tradition states:
"Traveling in a firewood cart wearing tattered clothes
refers to poverty."
Yán Yánzhī's Admonitions for the Courtyard states:
"Wealth leads to prosperity,
poverty leads to affliction.
How severe is the affliction of poverty!
Not only does one's appearance become coarse and dark,
but one's spirit and mind may also become dejected and wasted.
Not only will friends distance and abandon you,
but family members will surely reproach and blame you.
If one is not of廉洁 (integrity) and profound discernment,
how can one remain unmoved in one's resolve?
Therefore, to dispel worries and troubles,
nothing is better than cherishing the aspirations of the ancients.
One should identify with the ancients.
When one's insight is deep, worries become shallow;
when one's understanding is far-reaching, troubles become trivial.
In the past, there were those who sang songs with a qin amidst woven thatch—
this is the way of such a principle."
The Book of Songs states:
"I come out of the north gate,
with a heart full of deep sorrow.
Always in distress and poverty,
no one knows my hardship."
It also states:
"Since I came to you,
for three years I have lived in poverty."
The Analects states:
"Poverty and low status
are what people dislike.
If they are not attained through the proper way,
one should not avoid them."
It also states:
"To be poor without resentment is difficult."
The Liezi states:
"Those who seek fame must be廉洁 (incorruptible),
and廉洁 (incorruptibility) leads to poverty."
Six Extremes and Ten Thieves
The Book of Documents, "Six Extremes":
"The first is untimely death,
the second is illness,
the third is sorrow,
the fourth is poverty,
the fifth is wickedness,
the sixth is weakness."
Tàigōng's Six Secret Teachings states:
"King Wǔ asked Tàigōng:
'Are wealth and poverty truly matters of fate?
Or is it due to failure in managing one's livelihood?'
Tàigōng replied:
'Thieves are within one's own household,
due to unwise planning.
The first thief:
sowing and harvesting not in season;
the second thief:
taking a wife who is incapable;
the third thief:
raising too many daughters;
the fourth thief:
neglecting duties for wine;
the fifth thief:
excessive clothing;
the sixth thief:
careless storage of valuables;
the seventh thief:
inconvenient wells and stoves;
the eighth thief:
borrowing at high interest for profit;
the ninth thief:
lighting fires without reason;
the tenth thief:
how can one become wealthy?'"
Empty Shuttles; Bare Walls
The Book of Songs states:
"In the lesser east and greater east,
the shuttles and beams are empty."
The commentary explains:
"This means they have no other goods,
only silk and hemp.
Now, even the shuttles and beams are idle, producing nothing."
The Book of Han states:
"When King Xiào of Liáng passed away,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú returned home to find his family poor,
with nothing but four bare walls standing."
Bramble Gate and Guǐyú Opening
The Book of Rites states:
"A Ru scholar may have a one-mǔ palace,
a room surrounded by walls,
with a bramble gate and a guǐyú opening."
Also, the Zuo Commentary states:
"A bramble gate and a guǐyú opening."
The Fúzǐ states:
Jiāozǐ of Chǔ,
Zhōuzǐ of Lǔ,
and Kuángzǐ of Qí,
lived together on the sunny side of Mount Tài,
residing in a room surrounded by walls.
The bramble gate had no door,
the thatched roof did not provide full shelter,
yet they sang loudly without ceasing."
Worn Robe and Short Hemp Garment
The Analects states:
"Wearing a worn, padded robe."
Huáinánzǐ states:
"In summer, the poor wear hemp garments and rope belts,
eating beans and drinking water,
to endure the summer heat;
in winter, they wear sheepskin robes and short hemp garments that do not cover their bodies, warming themselves by the stove."
Thatched Hut and Thorny Courtyard
Huángfǔ Mì's Biographies of Eminent Scholars states:
"Lǎo Láizǐ
was a man of Chǔ.
He farmed on the sunny side of Méng Mountain,
using reeds for walls,
and weeds for his hut.
A catalpa wood served as his bed,
and mugwort as his mat."
Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Hóng was poor and had no servants;
the fence was broken and collapsing,
with thorns growing thickly in the courtyard."
Ox-Hair Garment and Snail Hut
The Book of Hàn states:
"Wáng Zhāng's family was poor,
and he often slept in an ox-hair garment."
Yú Huàn's Wèi Lüè states:
"Yáng Pèi served as a city governor multiple times,
never concerning himself with personal gain.
Thus, after retiring from office,
his family had no surplus wealth.
He lived in a snail hut,
and his wife and children suffered from cold and hunger."
Eating Once Every Two Days and Sharing Clothes
The Analects states:
"Duānmù Cì arrived with a team of four horses,
to visit Yuán Xiàn.
Xiàn lived among weeds and thorns,
eating only once every two days.
Zǐgòng said:
'How severe is your hardship!'" The Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Lǐ Yuán, styled Dàxùn,
was from Chénliú.
He served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His family was poor,
and the six brothers
shared clothes when going out."
Weedy Eaves and Mulberry Door Pivot
Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Hóng's family was poor;
thorns grew thickly in the courtyard,
and weeds choked the steps and eaves."
Zhuāngzǐ states:
"Yuán Xiàn lived in a room surrounded by walls,
with a mulberry branch as the door pivot and a broken jar as the window."
Dried Minnow and Hung Quail
Zhuāngzǐ states:
"Zhuāng Zhōu's family was poor,
so he went to borrow grain from the Marquis of Jiānhé.
The Marquis said:
'When I collect the taxes from my fief,
I will lend you three hundred gold pieces.'
Zhōu angrily replied:
'Yesterday, as I was coming here,
I saw a minnow in a rut,
who called out to me:
"Do you have a dipper of water to save me?"
'I said:
"Certainly."
I am about to travel to Wú and Yuè,
and I will have the waters of the Western River diverted to meet you.
Will that do?"
The minnow angrily replied:
"That would be no better than looking for me in a dried fish shop."'"
Sūnqīngzǐ states:
"Zǐxià's family was poor,
and his quail-like clothes hung on the wall."
One Gourd and Bare Walls
The Analects states:
"How virtuous is Huí!
With a single basket of food,
and a single gourd of drink."
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Later Yān states:
"Wáng Gāo of Wèijùn was poor,
and had nothing but bare walls."
Thatched House and Weed Hut
The Separate Biography of Lǐ Shào states:
"The gentleman lived in poverty but did not care to manage property.
He owned thirty mǔ of paddy fields
and a thatched house."
Zhāng Héng's "Return to the Fields Rhapsody" states:
"Moved by the admonitions of Lǎozǐ,
I turned my carriage back to my weed hut."
Hardship and Destitution
The Chǔcí states:
"How distressed is the poor scholar,
who has missed his time and whose heart is troubled!"
The Book of Hàn states:
"Lì Yìjī loved to read,
but his family was poor and destitute."
Selling Firewood and Peddling Baskets
The Book of Hàn states:
"Zhū Mǎichén's family was poor,
but he loved to read
and did not manage property.
He often cut firewood
and sold it to buy food."
Hé Fǎshèng's Book of the Jin Restoration states:
"Wáng Měng's family was poor,
and he made a living by peddling baskets."
Jar Window and Mat Door
The Book of Rites states:
"A Ru scholar may have a one-mǔ palace,
a room surrounded by walls,
with a bramble gate and a guǐyú opening,
a weed door and a jar window."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Chén Píng's family was poor,
but he loved to read
and did not engage in livelihood.
He lived in a poor alley,
using a mat as a door,
yet many elders' carriage tracks were at his gate."
Plowing at Night and Laboring by Day
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural states:
"There was a man named Zhōu Chōupēn,
who was poor but devoted to the Way,
and he and his wife plowed at night."
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Later Yān states:
"Wáng Gāo of Wèijùn,
during the famine and chaos at the end of the Qín,
worked as a hired laborer by day with his wife,
and cut grass and fired bricks by night."
Eating Beans and Consuming Goosefoot
The Book of Rites states:
"Zǐlù said:
'How sorrowful is poverty!
In life, one has nothing with which to provide for one's parents.'
The Master said:
'Eating beans and drinking water,
yet bringing them joy to the fullest,
this is what is called filial piety.'" Cuī Hóng's Records of the Later Yān states:
"Wáng Gāo,
during the famine and chaos at the end of the Qín,
lost fifteen family members, including parents and brothers.
When hungry, he ate goosefoot and beans;
when cold, he wore grass garments."
Weed Door and Wormwood Bed
Zhuāngzǐ states:
"Yuán Xiàn lived in a room surrounded by walls,
with a weed door left unclosed."
Huángfǔ Mì's Biographies of Eminent Scholars states:
"Tián Hé was old and his family poor.
He lived in a thatched hut with a wormwood bed,
adhering to the Way and not taking office."
Selling Divinations and Working as a Scribe
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continued Book of Hàn states:
"Fàn Dān
was appointed as Grand Commandant during Emperor Huán's reign.
Dān, considering himself too upright and impatient to follow worldly ways,
wore ragged clothes and sold divinations in the market."
Wèi Shōu's Book of the Later Wèi states:
"Cuī Liàng, styled Jìngrú,
was from Dōngwǔchéng in Qīnghé.
His family was poor,
and he made a living by working as a scribe."
Snow-Worn Shoes, Dusty Rice Pot
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Dōngguō Xiānshēng long awaited an imperial summons at the Gōngchē Office,
impoverished, hungry, and cold.
His worn-out shoes were incomplete.
Walking in the snow,
his shoes had tops but no soles,
so his feet entirely trod upon the ground.
People on the road laughed at him."
Sīmǎ Biāo's Sequel to the Book of the Later Han states:
"Fàn Dān,
during Emperor Huán's reign, was appointed Magistrate of Láiwú,
but did not take up the post.
He encountered the proscription of the partisans.
He then built a thatched hut to live in.
Sometimes his food supply ran out.
The villagers sang of him:
'Dust fills the rice pot of Fàn Shǐyún;
fish breed in the cauldron of Fàn Láiwú.'"
Land for an Awl's Point, Storage of a Dan of Grain
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The Chǔ chancellor Sūnshū Áo knew Yōu Mèng was worthy.
When he fell ill and was near death,
he said to his son:
'After I die,
you will certainly be impoverished.
Go see Yōu Mèng.'
Several years later, he died.
Áo's son indeed became destitute.
Carrying firewood, he met Yōu Mèng
and then visited him, recounting what his father had instructed.
Mèng immediately performed a routine for Áo's son,
persuading the King of Chǔ that Sūnshū Áo had been reborn
and wishing to make him chancellor.
Mèng said:
'I beg to discuss this with my wife.'
After three days, he returned
and said:
'My wife advises to be careful not to become Chancellor of Chǔ.
When Sūnshū Áo was chancellor,
he was utterly loyal.
Upon his death,
his son did not have land enough to stick an awl into.
What is the worth of such a position?'
The king then enfeoffed Áo's son."
Also, the Records of the Three Kingdoms: Book of Wèi states:
"Huà Xīn was always pure and poor.
His salary and gifts he used to relieve his relatives,
so his household had no storage of even a dàn of grain."
Zǐsāng Nearly Ill, Yuán'ān Already Fasting
The Zhuangzi states:
"Zǐyú and Zǐsāng were friends.
There was continuous rain for ten days.
Zǐyú said:
'Zǐsāng must be nearly ill!'
He wrapped up some rice and went to feed him.
Zǐsāng seemed to sing, seemed to laugh,
strummed his qin and said:
'Did my parents wish me to be poor?
Did Heaven and Earth privately impoverish me?
I seek for the one who caused this but cannot find it.'"
The Conduct Records of Former Worthies states:
"Hú Dìng, styled Yuán'ān,
possessed conduct surpassing others.
While observing mourning,
pheasants and hares roamed his courtyard.
The county magistrate sent his Household Registrar to inquire after Dìng.
Dìng had already stopped eating grain."
Shù Xī's "Rhapsody on a Poor Family"
I encounter the adversity of my household,
entangled in the distress of the six extremes.
I lack the abundant virtue of Yuán Xiàn,
but have the deep poverty of this man.
Worried, depressed, vexed, and hard-pressed,
I shall set forth in detail and state my case.
I have a leaky, cramped thatched hut,
unable to shelter me, it gathers dust.
Wishing to be angry and resentful is of no avail,
only adding frustration and solitary indignation.
Covered by the universal canopy of Heaven and Earth,
I hope to lack wealth but possess humaneness.
Hàn-dynasty Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on Expelling Poverty"
You dwell among the six extremes,
cast out to distant wastelands.
Advancing not through virtue,
retreating not accepting flattery.
Long have you been a lingering guest,
what is your intention?
Others all wear embroidered silks,
I, in coarse cloth, am not fully covered.
Others all eat fine rice and millet,
I alone have wild herbs for my meal.
Poor, I have no precious playthings,
with what can I find joy?
I walk on foot, carrying my satchel,
going out or staying in, I change my clothes.
My body performs a hundred labors,
my hands and feet are calloused.
The way of friendship is cut off,
influential officials decline me.
Wherein lies the fault?
It is you who are responsible.
Leaving you, I flee far away,
to the summit of the Kūnlún Mountains.
Yet you follow me again,
flying on high, reaching the heavens.
Leaving you, I climb a mountain,
hiding in caves and grottoes.
Yet you follow me again,
ascending those high ridges.
Leaving you, I enter the sea,
floating on that cypress-wood boat.
Yet you follow me again,
now sinking, now floating.
When I move, you stir;
when I am still, you rest.
Is it that there are no others?
What do you seek from me?
Now you, begone!
Do not linger any longer.
Jìn-dynasty Zuǒ Sī's "Poem on History"
Fluttering, fluttering, the bird in the cage,
raising its wings, it strikes the four corners.
Aloof, aloof, the scholar in the poor lane,
embracing his shadow, he guards his empty hut.
Going out the gate, there is no clear path,
thorns and brambles block the midway.
Plans and strategies cast aside, unaccepted,
lumpish like a fish in a dried-up pond.
Looking outward, not an inch of official salary;
looking inward, not a peck of grain in storage.
Relatives still scorn each other,
friends daily grow more distant.
Sòng-dynasty Táo Qián's "Poem on Impoverished Scholars"
All clans have something to rely on,
the lone cloud alone has nothing to depend on.
Dim, dim, vanishing into emptiness,
when will its remaining glow be seen?
Also, he said:
"Desolate and bleak, the year draws to its close,
clutching my coarse robe, I face the southern eaves.
In the front garden, no remaining beauty;
withered branches fill the northern garden.
Tilting the pot, not a last drop remains;
peering into the stove, no smoke is seen.
Poetry and books pile up beyond my seat,
the white sun departs and does not return."
Also, he said:
"Old Róng Sǒu wore a plain girdle,
happily playing his qin.
Yuán Shēng put on his split shoes,
his clear song resounded with lofty notes.
Gathering his sleeves did not cover his elbows,
wild herb soup was often lacking.
How could he forget to don a light fur robe?
Gaining by improper means is not what he admired."
Also, he said:
"Zhòng Wèi loved his impoverished dwelling,
around his house grew mugwort and artemisia.
Secluded, he cut off social intercourse,
composing poetry, quite skilled indeed.
Aloof, he was content with his vocation,
his joy lay not in poverty or success.
Human affairs are inherently clumsy,
so I may as well long follow my own course."
Sòng-dynasty Yuán Bówén's "Poem Describing Mountain Poverty"
Weary from hired washing in the village lanes,
exhausted from farming and herding by Pines Hill.
Fashioning a lotus-leaf hat by the dewy ravine,
gathering fragrant herbs by the frosty islet.
Startled by white hairs, the years show plain;
skin wasted, worries fill my girdle.
Fortunately, I have a nature for deep seclusion,
the secluded mountains can be my stay.
Liáng-dynasty Wáng Sēngrú's "Poem Lamenting a Beggar"
In youth, vainly pushing the cart;
with white hair, finally filling the ditch.
How can a reed mat suffice?
Beans and pulse cannot provide all.
I know myself, no lover of travel,
begging, yet wishing to hide my shame.
Thank you for your earnest inquiry,
Sòng Xiāo Jǐng's "Poem of the Impoverished Scholar"
The four seasons come and go in turn,
Hardship and toil press with each affair.
In deepest winter, weeping in a threadbare ox-hide blanket,
In the fifth month, a guest clad in fur.
Slowly, the spring day stretches long,
Where can one go to ease the sorrow that comes?
In late autumn, the season for granting clothes,
Yet lotus garments remain unchanged.
Bān Chāo abandoned brush and inkstone,
Lóu Jìng cast off the yoke of the cart.
Though it is said a man's ambition is thus,
It still treads the path of self-promotion.
How virtuous was Master Yán's son,
Drinking water, ever content and joyful.
Jìn Zhāng Wàng's Poem
Desolate ruins, sparse with human traces,
Secluded and remote, the neighborhood gates wide.
The reed fence decays of itself,
The ruined house stands empty and vast.
In the scorching summer, no whole linen cloth,
In the dark winter, no warm coarse garment.
The four limbs suffer from cold and heat,
The six periods weary with hunger and thirst.
Making a living grows ever more haggard and troubled,
When sorrow comes, it cannot be severed.
Jìn Jiāng Yōu's Poem
The wicker gate does not open its door,
The surrounding walls are full of weeds and thorns.
An empty gourd lies overturned beneath the wall,
Dust gathers of itself upon the mat.
Going out, whose son is that?
How utterly exhausted and impoverished!
Liáng Zhū Chāo's "Ode to Poverty"
Every path may be tried,
Only poverty brings no peace.
The window opens to two slices of moon,
Frost-covered feet bear a layer of cold.
Damp mugwort spread on the bed is chill,
Brittle lotus leaves patch clothes with difficulty.
If you say being a guest is easy,
I would draw my sword and play it for you.
Yīng Yuàn's "Miscellaneous Poem"
A poor man speaks to a destitute child:
No coins to grasp in hand.
Plowing all day yields no grain,
So gather kudzu from that northern hill.
Bamboo bowl and gourd ladle ever at ease,
No need for scolding and shouting.
Wèi Wǔ's "Ballad of Common Customs"
In the jar, not a peck stored;
Opening the chest, not a foot of silk.
A friend comes to borrow from me,
I know not how to respond.
Yīng Qú's "Letter to Wéi Zhòngjiāng"
Living in a dwelling as bare as Yuán Xiàn's suspended chime stone,
And encountering the endless rain of the August Heaven,
Firewood and fodder already exhausted,
Grain also depleted and empty.
Advancing, I lack Yánzǐ's unwavering resolve,
Retreating, I lack Yáng Xióng's tranquil composure.
Therefore, I harbor grief,
Truly unbearable.
Also, "Letter to Dǒng Zhònglián"
Grain prices soar and leap,
Begging aid from neighboring households,
Daily obtaining a few pecks,
Yet still having no firewood to cook it.
Mèng Kē trapped between Liáng and Sòng,
Xuānní (Confucius) distressed between Chén and Cài,
Nothing surpasses this.
Going out, I am mocked by servants,
Returning home, I am reproached by wife and children,
Suddenly stirring town-wide indignation.
I no longer know the joy of living in the world.
Parting, Seventh
The "Chǔ Cí" says:
"No sorrow is greater than the sorrow of parting in life."
It also says:
"Desolate and trembling, as if on a distant journey,
Climbing mountains, facing waters, seeing off one who returns."
Jiāng Yān's "Rhapsody on Parting" says:
"That which dims the soul with gloom,
Is nothing but parting!"
"The Family Sayings of Confucius" says:
"When Confucius was leaving Zhōu,
Lǎozǐ saw him off,
Saying:
'I have heard that the wealthy send people off with gifts,
The benevolent send people off with words.'
Though I cannot claim wealth,
I presume the title of the benevolent.
Allow me to send you off with words:
'Those in this world who are clever and deeply perceptive yet near death,
Are fond of criticizing others;
Those who are broadly learned, eloquent, and grand yet endanger themselves,
Are fond of exposing others' faults.'
Confucius said:
'I respectfully receive your instruction.'"
"The Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
"Chén Zūn was sent as envoy to the Xiōngnú,
And took leave of Wáng Dān.
Dān said to Zūn:
'You are going to a remote land,
I have nothing to give you as a gift,
I gift you with not bowing.'
Thereupon he clasped his hands and parted.
Zūn was greatly pleased."
"The Separate Biography of Guǎn Lù" says:
"Zhūgě Yuè bid farewell to Lù,
Admonishing him with two statements:
'You have a fondness for wine,
Though you are temperate and self-restrained,
It cannot be guaranteed.
You must moderate it.
You have the talent of a clear mirror,
Your insights are profound,
But calamity is like oil and fire,
You cannot but be cautious and restrained.
You possess scattered talent, roaming among the clouds and Milky Way,
Do not worry about lacking wealth and honor.'
Lù said: 'Wine must not be taken to the extreme,
Talent must not be fully expended.
I wish to hold wine with propriety,
Hold talent with foolishness,
What troubles could there be?'"
Lodging at Jǐ, Fareast at Mǐ
"The Máo Shī" says:
"We lodged at Jǐ,
Drank the farewell toast at Mǐ."
It also says:
"Shēnbó spoke of departure,
The king gave a farewell feast at Méi."
Floating Clouds, Drizzling Rain
Lǐ Líng's "Poem Presented to Sū Wǔ" says:
"Looking up, I see the floating clouds racing,
Suddenly they pass over one another.
Once separated by wind and waves,
Each is at a corner of the sky."
Sūn Chǔ's "Poem for the Officials of the Western Campaign at the Zhìyáng Post Seeing Off" says:
"Morning wind blows over the forked road,
Drizzling rain falls on autumn grass.
The whole city comes from afar to see me off,
Farewelling me on the thousand-mile road."
Grasping Sleeves, Gathering Reins
Wèi Wéndì's "Poem on Seeing Boat-pulling Soldiers, Brothers Parting" says:
"Leaving my old hometown guests,
Setting off on the ten-thousand-mile road.
Wife and children grasp my sleeves,
Falling tears soak my bosom."
Lù Jī's "Poem on Going to Luòyáng" says:
"Gathering the reins, I ascend the long road,
Sobbing, I bid farewell to close kin.
Ever sighing, I follow the northern shore,
Lingering thoughts knot at the southern ford."
Shēn and Chén, Bowstring and Arrow Notch
Lǐ Líng's "Poem Presented to Sū Wǔ" says:
"Once we were like mandarin ducks,
Now we are like Shēn and Chén stars.
Once we were constantly close,
Now distant as the Hú and Qín."
Lù Jī's "Poem for Gù Yànxiān, Presented to His Wife" says:
"Our forms and shadows parted like Shēn and Shāng stars,
News long cut off, not reaching.
Parting and meeting are hardly constant,
Like that bowstring and arrow notch."
Seeing Off at Southern Bank, Reaching Northern Woods
"The Chǔ Cí" says:
"I join hands and walk in line,
Seeing off the fair one at the southern bank."
Cáo Zhí's "Poem on Parting from a Friend" says:
"The sun hides its light, the sky grows dim,
Passing the distant road, I reach the northern woods."
Northern Lodge, Eastern City
Hàn Wǔdì's "Edict to the Family of Qín Zhuó Zǐhóu" says:
"In springtime, Zǐhóu at the northern lodge,
Parted from his family."
Lù Jī's "Poem Presented to Féng Wénxióng" says:
"The phoenix carriage departs the eastern city,
Seeing you off by the river's bend.
Ascending the tower, I gaze at the towering waves,
How swiftly time passes."
White Clouds and Yellow Crane
The Biography of King Mù states:
"The Son of Heaven feasted with the Queen Mother of the West above the Jasper Pool,
and the Queen Mother sang:
'White clouds are in the sky,
mountains and rivers lie between.'"
Sū Wǔ's "Poem Presented to Lǐ Líng" says:
"The yellow crane, once parted far away,
looks back lingering for a thousand miles.
The northern steed loses its herd,
longing thoughts linger on and on."
Northern Road and Southern Ford
Cáo Biāo's "Poem in Reply to the Prince of Dōng'ē" says:
"The winding path is hard to embrace in heart,
I halt my carriage to bid you farewell.
Mounting the chariot, I take the northern road,
sighing forever as I seek the former tracks."
Lù Yún's "Poem in Reply to My Elder Brother Jī" says:
"Distant is the road, yet it has an end;
how long will the sorrow of parting last?
At the southern ford, the crossing is cut off;
at the northern isle, there is no bridge."
Two Ducks and a Pair of Phoenixes
Sū Wǔ's "Parting Poem for Lǐ Líng" says:
"Two ducks both fly north,
one duck alone soars south.
You shall stay in this lodging,
I shall return to my hometown."
Jī Kāng's "Poem Presented to a Scholar Joining the Army" says:
"A pair of phoenixes hide their radiant light,
folding their wings west of Mount Tài.
A solitary female drifts alone in her wanderings,
lamenting sadly over the pain of separation in life."
Orchid Garden and Peach Lodge
Jī Kāng's "Poem Presented to a Scholar Joining the Army" says:
"Resting my troops in an orchid garden,
feeding my horses on Mount Huà.
The man of Yǐng is gone;
with whom can I fully converse?"
The Jīngzhōu Illustrated Records state:
"Six lǐ south of Xiāngyáng County along the land route is the Peach Forest Lodge,
a place for farewell banquets and seeing off those returning."
Eastern Ford and Western Isle
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Water Classic states:
"East of Shòuchūn County town is the Chánglài Ford,
beside which stands the Cáitáng;
this pavilion is where farewells are made and boats moor."
Dài Kuí's "Rhapsody on Departure" says:
"Carrying a chiming zither beneath the woods,
I adjust the fine fishing line by the long shore.
Turning back to bid farewell across the river,
I see off the graceful one at the western isle."
Four Birds and Three Judas Trees
The Family Sayings of Confucius states:
"When Confucius was in Wèi,
he rose at dawn,
and Yán Huí attended him.
They heard a weeping sound, extremely mournful.
Yán Huí said:
'This weeping is not only mourning the dead,
but also lamenting separation in life.'
Confucius said:
'How do you know this?'
He replied:
'I have heard that birds of Mount Héng
give birth to four chicks.
When their feathers and wings are fully grown,
they are about to part.
They cry mournfully to bid each other farewell.
The sorrowful sound resembles this.'"
Wú Jūn's Sequel to Tales of Qíxié records:
"Tián Zhēn of Jīngzhào
had two younger brothers, making three brothers in total.
They divided the family wealth and lived separately.
In front of the hall was a purple judas tree,
its blossoms exceedingly lush.
They agreed to split it into three parts,
planning to cut it the next day.
Suddenly, overnight, the tree withered and died.
Tián Zhēn saw this
and said in astonishment to his brothers:
'Originally of the same trunk,
when about to be divided it withers.
How much more so for brothers, who share deep affection;
how can they be separated?
This shows that humans are inferior to trees.'
The brothers, moved by this, reunited."
Feeding Horses and Adjusting Oars
Xú Gàn's "Rhapsody on Mournful Parting" says:
"I feed my horse, waiting to cross the river;
my heart, full of regret and sorrow, turns inward in despair.
Profound and dark is the gloom;
layer upon layer, grief increases, wounding the spirit."
Wáng Biāozhī's "Poem on Parting from My Brothers at Fāngshān" says:
"Greasing the carriage, I gather the galloping wheels;
floating the boat, I adjust the flying oars.
The silk dyed black brings mournful sighs;
the forked road stirs sorrowful lament."
By the River and Across the River
Zhào Yè's Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
"When Gōujiàn entered Wú as a vassal,
his ministers escorted him to the bank of the Zhèjiāng River,
where they bid him farewell by the water."
The Annals of the Wú Family states:
"When Wú Qǐ departed,
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi personally saw him off,
crossing west of the river to bid Wú Qǐ farewell."
Flying Swan and Soaring Swan
The Music Bureau's "Song of the Flying Swan" says:
"Thinking of parting from you,
my breath catches, I cannot speak.
Each says, take good care of yourself;
the road is far, returning is hard."
Dù Zhì's "Poem Presented to Guànqiū, Governor of Jīngzhōu" says:
"The swan flies, soaring ten thousand miles,
with one flap it ascends the vast blue sky.
Soaring high, ambition is hard to fulfill;
the parted swan loses all hope."
Clouds Part and Rain Ceases
Zhāng Zǎi's "Poem Expressing My Feelings" says:
"Trekking over mountains and rivers,
traveling a thousand miles to bid farewell.
Yáng Zǐ wept at the fork;
Mòzǐ was moved by the silk.
Clouds part, rain ceases;
ah, how my heart grieves!"
Guō Pú's poem says:
"You are like autumn clouds;
I resemble smoke from the chimney.
High and low, by nature they differ;
once parted, rain ceases under heaven."
Soaring Ducks and Startled Cranes
Sū Wǔ's "Parting Poem for Lǐ Líng" says:
"Two ducks both fly north,
one duck alone soars south.
You shall stay in this lodging,
I shall return to my hometown."
Cáo Zhí's poem says:
"A pair of cranes roam together,
waiting for each other by the Eastern Sea.
The male flies, fleeing north;
the female departs, heading for Southern Xiāng.
Abandoning our joy of necks entwined,
we part, each going a separate way."
Returning Clouds Journey and Startling Wind Scatters
Lǐ Chōng's "Poem Seeing Off Xǔ Cóng" says:
"Coming like a swift wind's joy,
departing like returning clouds on a journey.
Parting and meeting follow nature's constant way;
gathering and scattering—why should they startle?"
Zǎo Tiǎn's "Poem Presented to Shí Chóng" says:
"Gathering like soaring clouds meeting,
suddenly like a startling wind scattering.
Parting brings thoughts of separation;
facing joy only increases repeated sighs."
Departing Carriage and Mooring Oars
Lù Jī's "Poem Presented to Féng Wénxióng" says:
"My carriage departs from the confluence of the turbid Wèi,
driving my horse north of the great river.
Parting and seeking—ancient sorrow;
men of ambition often suffer bitter hearts."
Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on Following Duke Sòng's Gathering at the Jesting Horse Terrace with Minister Kǒng" says:
"The returning guest heads for the seashore,
removing his cap, he bids farewell to the court ranks.
Mooring the oars, he berths at the cassia isle,
pointing at the sun, awaiting the end of music."
Wheel Tracks Converge and Raising the Boat
Fàn Guǎngquán's "Poem on a Farewell Banquet at the Conquest of Barbarians Pavilion for Junior Tutor Wáng" says:
"Hanging up my official cap at the eastern gate's alley,
returning in coarse cloth to the western Táng's feet.
Wheel tracks converge, dust rises on the high road;
farewell offerings hang on the long hillside."
Kǒng Fǎshēng's "Poem on a Farewell at the Conquest of Barbarians Pavilion for Junior Tutor Wáng" says:
"If a man perceives disgrace and peril,
he unties his seal ribbon and raises the returning boat.
Liáng Jiāng Yān's "Rhapsody on Parting"
That which dims the soul and melts the spirit
is nothing but parting.
Consider Qín and Wú, lands severed and distant;
again, Yān and Sòng, a thousand miles apart.
Sometimes when spring moss first sprouts,
or when autumn winds briefly rise.
Thus the traveler's heart is broken,
a hundred feelings, mournful and pained.
The wind soughs with an alien sound,
clouds stretch vast with strange hues.
Boats lie still by the water's edge,
carriages wind slowly by the mountain's side.
Oars idle, not moving forward;
horses whinny coldly, ceaselessly.
Covering golden cups—who will drink?
Laying aside jade zithers, tears soak the carriage rail.
Those who stay lie sorrowful in bed,
dazed as if having lost something.
The sun sinks from the wall, its colors submerged;
the moon climbs the balcony, its light flying forth.
Seeing red orchids receive dew,
gazing at green catalpas touched by frost.
Pacing past vermilion pillars, in vain I close the door;
stroking brocade curtains, empty and chill.
Knowing the lingering steps of a parting dream,
imagining the wandering soul of farewell taking flight.
Ancient Poem
Walking on and on, ever walking on,
From you, sir, parted while alive.
Separated by ten thousand miles and more,
Each at one end of the sky.
The road is hard and long;
How can we know when we'll meet again?
The Hú steeds lean into the north wind,
The Yuè birds nest on southern branches.
Lǐ Líng's "Poem Presented to Sū Wǔ"
Hand in hand we climb the river bridge;
Wanderer, where will you go at dusk?
Pacing by the parting road,
Regretful, unable to speak.
The traveler cannot linger long;
Each speaks of endless longing.
How do we know it is not like sun and moon?
Waxing and waning have their own time.
Strive to uphold bright virtue,
Till white-haired age, let that be our pledge.
Sòng Xiè Língyùn's "Farewell at Fāngshān Poem"
On duty I leave the royal city,
Pointing my course to rest in Ōuyuè.
I cast off the cable with the flowing tide,
Yet, longing for the past, cannot depart.
Rustling, I approach the fading woods;
Bright and clear shines the autumn moon.
A heart full of feeling easily brims over;
Facing things, it is hard to rest.
Sòng Bào Zhàoyuǎn's "Farewell Poem for Attendant Fù"
Light swans play in river pools;
A lone goose alights on an islet.
By chance we met, two drawn together,
Sharing thoughts without end.
Wind and rain favor east and west;
In one corner, suddenly a thousand miles apart.
Recalling the time we roosted together,
Your voice and face fill my heart and ears.
With short wings I cannot soar;
I linger in mist and haze.
Qí Xiè Tiǎo's "Farewell to Fàn Yún at Xīntíng Zhǔ Poem"
Dòngtíng, land where music once spread;
Xiāoxiāng, where imperial princes roamed.
Clouds depart the wilds of Cāngwú,
Waters return to flow in Jiānghàn.
Halting my carriage, I gaze in sorrow;
You cease your oars, hesitating.
Our heart's matters are all finished now;
On the river, only parting sorrow remains.
Qí Wáng Róng's "Night Gathering Poem for Attendant Xiāo's Journey West"
Lingering with my beloved,
Regretting parting at the river bridge.
Collars and sleeves parted three springs;
Rivers and mountains stretch a thousand miles.
An inch of heart knows no far or near,
But borderlands have wind and frost.
Take care, be diligent as the year ends;
Be reverent, guard your radiant countenance.
In the mountains, joy is still absent;
The dùruò blooms in vain its fragrance.
Qí Zhāng Róng's "Parting Poem"
White clouds end upon the mountain;
Clear winds rest beneath the pines.
If you would know the sorrow of parting,
See the bright moon from the lonely terrace.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Farewell to Liú Zhīlín at Xīntíng Poem"
Carriages turn on the Huángshān road;
Boats moor at the White Horse Ford.
Wheels meet as curtains join;
Parting steeds each turn their dust away.
Chángshān rejoiced facing Dài;
Lǒngtóu grieves gazing toward Qín.
Wishing to hold the Hànzhōng strategy,
I return to present it to the campaigner.
Zhōu Wáng Bāo's "Farewell Poem for Attendant Wáng"
Continually I pity the wandering guest,
Sorrowful, regretting leaving the group.
East and west, the palace moat waters;
North and south, Kuàijī's clouds.
The river bridge cuts off both banks;
At the forked road, several paths divide.
Mountains and rivers, distant, unseen;
In my breast and sleeves, your voice from afar is heard.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Poem in Reply to Monk Lín"
A traveler at seventy years of age,
At year's end, journeying far.
Frontier clouds congeal, unresolved;
Lǒng waters freeze, soundless.
Look, sir, how far the sun is;
Consider then the city of Cháng'ān.
Jiāng Zǒng's "Farewell Poem for Yuán of Chāngzhōu"
From the river bridge I gaze toward Lǒngtóu;
Parting hands, the road stretches long.
Years gone startle like lightning;
The day of parting sighs into autumn.
The yellow swan flies far away;
Green hills recede, sorrowful.
Not speaking of clouds and rain dispersed,
It is more like east and west streams flowing apart.
The Most Handsome Man, First
The Family Sayings states:
"The people of fertile soil are beautiful."
The Book of Zhou states:
"A handsome man is called 'pòlǎo'."
The Erya states:
"A handsome scholar is called 'yàn'.
Wǎngwǎng,
huánghuáng,
mùmù—
all mean beautiful."
The Analects states:
"How dignified is Zǐzhāng!"
The commentary says:
"It speaks of Zǐzhāng's magnificent appearance."
The Zuozhuan records:
"Gōngzǐ Bāo was beautiful and dazzling."
The "Dēngtúzǐ Fù" describes Sòng Yù as having a graceful and handsome appearance.
The Book of Han states:
"Zhāng Zǐfáng's appearance was like that of a beautiful woman;
Zhí Bùyí's appearance was exceedingly handsome."
The Records of Wu:
"Sūn Huán's demeanor was upright,
and his mind was intelligent."
The Forest of Sayings states:
"Hé Píngshū had beautiful features and was extremely fair.
Emperor Wén of Wèi suspected he wore powder.
In summer, he gave him hot soup cakes.
After eating them,
he broke into a great sweat,
and wiped himself with his red robe.
His complexion became even more radiant."
"Pān Ānrén was extremely handsome.
Whenever he walked on the road,
groups of old women would throw fruit at him,
often filling his carriage."
The Book of Jin:
"Wáng Méng, styled Zhòngzǔ,
had a beautiful appearance.
He often looked at himself in a mirror
and called his father by his style name, saying:
'Did Wénkāi give birth to such a son!'
Once his hat was torn,
he went to the market to buy a new one.
Groups of old women admired him
and vied to give him hats."
The Book of Han states:
"Zhāng Cāng was plump and white like a gourd.
Dōngfāng Shuò's eyes were like hanging pearls,
his teeth like arranged shells.
Later Hàn's Mǎ Yuán had eyebrows and eyes as if painted."
The Zuozhuan:
"Zǐ Tàishū was handsome, elegant, and cultured."
The Book of Jin:
"Xiè Shàng discussed figures of the central court,
saying Dù Yì had clear skin,
and Wèi Shūbǎo had a clear spirit."
Also, Wáng Róng said:
"Wáng Yǎn's divine bearing was lofty and pure,
like jade trees in a jade forest,
truly a being beyond the mundane world."
Also, Wáng Chéng said to Wáng Yǎn:
"Elder brother, your form resembles the Way, but your divine sharpness is too outstanding."
Also, the Book of Han:
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's carriage and horsemen were dignified and graceful,
leisurely and elegant, very beautiful.
Dū means beautiful.
Jìn's Péi Kǎi's appearance was handsome and spirited;
people of the time called him a jade man."
Riding a goat cart, holding a yak-tail whisk
The Separate Biography of Wèi Jiè states:
"When Jiè was a young boy,
he rode a goat cart in the Luòyáng market.
The entire market exclaimed:
'Whose jade man is this!'
Wáng Yífǔ had beautiful features
and often held a jade-handled yak-tail whisk.
It was the same color as his hand, indistinguishable."
Xiàhóu and Pān, paired jades; nephew and uncle, reflecting pearls
The Guozi states:
"Pān Ānrén
and Xiàhóu Zhàn both had beautiful appearances.
They often walked together,
and people called them 'paired jades'."
The Separate Biography of Wèi Jiè states:
"Wáng Wǔzǐ,
Jiè's maternal uncle,
said to people:
'Yesterday I sat with my nephew.
He shone brightly like a bright pearl beside me,
radiantly illuminating people.'"
Bān Bó exceedingly handsome; Hé Yàn supremely beautiful
The Book of Han states:
"Bān Bó in his youth studied the Book of Songs under Shī Dān.
Grand General Wáng Fèng recommended Bān Bó as suitable to encourage learning.
He was summoned to an audience in the Yànní Hall.
His appearance was exceedingly handsome,
his recitation and speech followed proper method,
and he was appointed Palace Attendant."
The Separate Biography of Hé Yàn states:
"When Yàn was just seven or eight years old,
he was intelligent and divinely perceptive,
his form and appearance supremely beautiful.
When he went out walking,
onlookers filled the road,
all saying he was like a being of the immortals."
Chén Píng, a jade cap; Dǒng Yǎn, selling pearls
The Book of Han states:
"Chén Píng had beautiful features.
The King of Hàn said:
'Though Píng is a man,
he is as beautiful as a jade cap.'" Also states:
"Dǒng Yǎn initially made a living selling pearls with his mother.
When Yǎn was thirteen,
he followed his mother into the household of Princess Píngyáng.
Those around spoke of his loveliness.
The princess raised him
and called him Lord Dǒng."
Obtaining Gé, no regret; peeping at Sòng, not yet consented
The Garden of Marvels states:
"In Yānyáng, Chén Zhōng's daughter was named Fēng.
Her neighbor Gé Bó had a handsome appearance.
Fēng gathered with girls from the village to wind silk.
Jokingly, they said to each other:
'If I could get a husband like Gé Bó,
I would have no regrets.'" Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on Dēngtúzǐ's Fondness for Beauty" states:
"Yù is a man of graceful and handsome appearance,
eloquent in speech,
and by nature fond of beauty.
I wish the King would not let him enter and exit the rear palace."
Sòng Yù said:
"My eastern neighbor's daughter—
add one bit, she would be too tall;
subtract one bit, she would be too short.
Apply powder, she would be too white;
apply rouge, she would too red.
Yet this girl climbed the wall for three years peeping at me,
and I have not yet consented to her."
Dragon's pattern, phoenix's bearing; congealed cream, dotted lacquer
The Separate Biography of Jī Kāng states:
"Kāng was seven feet eight inches tall
and had a fine appearance.
Though his frame was like earth and wood,
and he did not adorn himself,
he had a dragon's pattern and phoenix's bearing—
a natural, heavenly quality."
The Forest of Sayings states:
"Wáng Yòujūn looked at Dù Hóngzhì and said:
'Face like congealed cream,
eyes like dotted lacquer—
this is a man among immortals.'"
Sòng Bāo beautiful and dazzling; Sūn Huán intelligent
See in the narrative section.
Sòng Míng, etc., like jade tablets; Hé Yàn like an immortal
Wáng Zhìshēn's Records of Sòng states:
"Emperor Míng of Sòng, personal name Yù,
had a full and pure appearance,
his substance equal to jade tablets."
"Hé Yàn" matter seen above.
Chén Shěn Jiǒng's "Ballad of the Chang'an Youth"
In Chang'an lived a fine young man,
On a dappled steed with iron-coin markings.
Like the Prince of Chén, his jade bridle adorned,
Like the Queen of Jìn, his golden whip was forged.
His swaying gait swift as a flying swallow,
His sword's edge curved like a lotus petal.
He came and went north of the new market,
Roaming freely by the broad roadside.
By the roadside sat three aged men,
Their faces and temples like withered reeds.
They claimed they were born in the Hàn dynasty,
And in youth had witnessed heroes bold.
The Five Marquises all received daily homage,
The Seven Nobles each boasted of their deeds.
The Jiànzhāng Palace linked the northern gate,
The covered walkways led to southern halls.
The Empress Dowager dwelt in Chánglè Palace,
The Son of Heaven journeyed from Huízhōng.
Jade carriages welcomed the flying swallow,
Gold mountains rewarded Dèng Tōng.
Day after day passed by,
Suddenly they saw the market and court empty.
The Fúsāng tree no longer rose from the sea,
The Kūnlún Mountains toppled eastward.
What time had the youth for questions?
In declining years, fortune met its end.
Children and grandchildren vanished utterly,
No more contact with village and home.
Tears exhausted, eyes grew dim,
Spleen injured, ears turned deaf.
Leaning on his staff, he sought the last elders,
Chanting and singing of the sorrowful old man.
Now by chance I have met this fate,
I dare not seek out the ignorant youth.
Beautiful Women, Part Two
The Máo Shī commentary states:
"A beautiful woman is called yuán."
Hé Chéngtiān's "Compiled Texts" states:
"Fúyú
means beautiful appearance."
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"Xī Shī and Máo Qiáng
are considered beautiful by people.
Fish see them and dive deep,
Birds see them and fly high."
The Zuǒzhuàn records:
"In Zhèng, Xú Wúfàn had a younger sister of great beauty.
Gōngsūn Chǔ and Gōngsūn Hēi competed to betroth her."
Also: "In Sòng, the wife of Kǒngfù Jiā was beautiful.
Sòng Huáfǔ Dū saw her on the road,
Followed her with his eyes and said as she passed:
'Beautiful and radiant!'"
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says:
"The Yān夫人 of Zhūlóu possessed beauty fit for a state."
The Hòu Hàn Shū says:
"Liáng Jì's wife Sūn Shòu was beautifully colored,
Skilled at alluring mannerisms.
She fashioned sorrowful eyebrows,
A weeping makeup,
A 'fallen horse' chignon,
A bending-waist walk,
And a puckered-tooth smile,
Using these to charm and beguile."
Nòng Yù Fēi Qióng
Liú Xiàng's "Biographies of Immortals" states:
"Xiāo Shǐ
lived during the time of Duke Mù of Qín.
He excelled at playing the panpipes,
And could attract peacocks and white cranes.
Duke Mù's daughter Nòng Yù admired him,
And the duke gave her to him as wife.
One morning they flew away following a phoenix."
The "Private Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn":
"The Queen Mother of the West rode in a chariot of purple clouds,
Treading on slippers of dark jade.
She descended from her chariot and ascended the hall,
Called the emperor to sit with her,
And ordered her attendant maid Xǔ Fēi Qióng to play the reed pipes of Yúnhé."
Nán Wēi Xī Zǐ
The Zhànguó Cè says:
"Duke Wén of Jìn obtained Nán Wēi,
And for three days did not hold court.
Then he pushed Nán Wēi away and distanced himself from her,
Saying:
'Later generations will surely have those who lose states because of beauty.'"
Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on the Fan" says:
"Emotions unrestrained are gained outwardly,
The heart joyful and content finds inner peace.
Enhancing the loveliness of the Wú maiden,
Revealing the jade-like countenance of Xī Zǐ."
Chǔ Wá Sòng Yàn
Fú Qián's "General Explications of Common Terms" states:
"In southern Chǔ, a beautiful appearance is called wá."
Yáng Xióng's "Regional Words" says:
"Between Sòng, Wèi, Jìn, and Zhèng,
A beautiful appearance is called yàn."
Jiàng Shù Qīng Qín
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Letter to Fán Qīn" says:
"Among today's exquisite dancers, none are more skillful than Jiàng Shù;
Among pure singers, none are more stirring than Sòng Là."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" says:
"As for those like Qīng Qín and Fú Fēi,
Utterly unique, aloof from the vulgar.
Elegant, graceful, and lovely,
Exquisitely adorned with fine makeup."
Wū Gorge Luò River
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
"West of Dān Mountain lies Wū Mountain,
Where the Heavenly Emperor's daughter dwells.
Sòng Yù said, 'The Heavenly Emperor's youngest daughter is named Yáo Jī.'
The stretch between its head and tail is one hundred sixty lǐ,
Called Wū Gorge,
Named thus after the mountain."
Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on the Luò River Goddess" says:
"Leisurely by the poplar grove,
Gazing over the Luò River.
Looking down, I perceived nothing,
Looking up, I beheld a wondrous sight.
I saw a lovely lady,
By the side of the cliff."
Gāotáng Xiàcài
Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Goddess" says:
"King Xiāng of Chǔ traveled with Sòng Yù to the marsh of Yúnmèng,
And ordered Sòng Yù to compose a rhapsody on the affair of Gāotáng.
That night the king retired,
Dreamt he encountered a goddess,
Whose form was exceedingly beautiful."
Ruǎn Jí's poem:
"The two consorts wandered by the riverbank,
Carefree, soaring with the wind.
Jiāo Fǔ cherished the jade pendants,
Graceful and lovely, fragrant they were.
Their beauty overthrew cities, bewitched Xiàcài,
Lovely faces entwined with heartfelt longing."
Kingfisher-feather Eyebrows Cicada-wing Hairlocks
Lù Jī's "Song of Allure":
"Lovely eyes radiate a jade-like luster,
Moth eyebrows resemble kingfisher feathers.
Fresh skin, how moist it is,
Elegant beauty as if one could feast upon it."
Cuī Bào's "Ancient and Modern Commentary":
"Among the palace ladies of Emperor Wén of Wèi, those he adored most
Included Mò Qióngshù,
Xuē Yèlái,
Chén Shàngyī,
And Chén Qiǎoxiào,
All attending him day and night.
Qióngshù first created the 'cicade hair locks,'
Arranging them so ethereal they resembled cicada wings,
Hence called 'cicade hair locks.'"
Bound-silk Waist Rippling-wave Eyes
Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on Dēngtúzǐ" says:
"My eastern neighbor's daughter,
Her eyebrows like kingfisher plumes,
Her waist like bound silk."
Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on Dance" says:
Sòng Yù's "Gāotáng Rhapsody" with Preface
In the past, the former king
once traveled to Gāotáng.
Weary, he napped by day
and dreamed of a woman,
who said: "I am the daughter of Wūshān.
I am a visitor at Gāotáng.
Hearing that you, my lord, are traveling to Gāotáng,
I wish to offer my pillow and mat."
The king then favored her.
As she departed, she bade farewell, saying:
"I dwell on the sunny side of Wūshān,
on the heights of Gāotáng.
At dawn I become drifting clouds,
at dusk, passing rain.
Morning after morning, dusk after dusk,
beneath the Sunny Terrace."
The king asked:
"When the morning clouds first emerge,
what is their appearance like?" Yù replied:
"When they first emerge,
they are radiant, like pine and catalpa;
as they advance a little,
they are luminous, like a lovely maiden.
Raising sleeves to shade the sun, gazing toward her beloved,
suddenly she changes countenance.
Swiftly, as if driving a team of four horses,
erecting feathered banners.
Chill, like the wind;
desolate, like rain.
When the wind ceases and the rain clears,
the clouds are nowhere to be found.
Gazing from afar on the mountainside,
dark trees flourish in winter.
Brilliant and gleaming,
they dazzle the eyes.
Resplendent like arrayed stars,
their forms cannot be fully described."
Hàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on a Beauty"
To my east neighbor
there is a maiden.
Her dark hair is lush and beautiful,
her moth eyebrows and white teeth.
Her face is splendid, her complexion rich,
her radiance shining bright.
Ever she looks at me with longing,
wishing to detain me to stay together.
She climbs the wall to gaze at me;
three years it has been thus.
I rejected her and did not consent.
In the detached palace, the quiet lodge,
desolate and doubly empty,
the gates are shut by day,
dim as an immortal's abode.
I pushed open her door and entered her hall;
rich and intense was the fragrance,
the embroidered canopy hung high.
A maiden dwelt alone there,
gracefully upon the bed,
a rare flower, elegant and lovely,
pure in quality, radiantly beautiful.
Seeing me, she lingered, about to smile, and said:
"Noble guest, from what state are you a prince?
Is the place you come from not far away?"
Thereupon she set out fine wine
and presented a chiming lute.
I then plucked the strings, playing the tune of "Solitary Orchid" and "White Snow,"
and the maiden sang:
"Alone in my chamber, vast and without support,
thinking of my beloved, my heart is wounded with sorrow.
The beautiful one has come, but oh, how late!
The day already wanes, my lovely color fades.
Dare I entrust myself to you? Long I ponder alone."
Her jade hairpin caught on my cap,
her gauze sleeves brushed my robe."
Wèi Cáo Zhí's "Luòshén Rhapsody"
The charioteer replied:
"I have heard of the goddess of the Hé and Luò rivers,
named Fúfēi.
Could it be her
whom my lord has seen?
What is her appearance like?
I wish to hear of it."
I told him:
"Her form is light as a startled swan,
graceful as a swimming dragon.
Her splendor outshines the autumn chrysanthemum,
her bloom rivals the spring pine.
Dimly, like light clouds veiling the moon;
floating, like swirling wind whirling snow.
Gazing from afar,
she gleams like the sun rising from morning clouds;
approaching to observe,
she glows like a lotus emerging from clear waves.
Her fullness and slenderness are just right,
her height and proportions perfectly balanced.
Her shoulders are as if carved,
her waist as if bound with white silk.
Her neck is long and elegant,
her white teeth revealed.
No perfumed ointment is added,
no powder is applied.
Her cloud-like coiffure towers high,
her long eyebrows delicately arched.
Her red lips are bright without,
her white teeth pure within.
Bright eyes gaze with lovely charm,
dimpled cheeks convey delight.
Her rare beauty is radiant and free,
her demeanor serene, her body composed.
Gentle in emotion, graceful in bearing,
charming in speech.
Her wondrous raiment is unmatched in any age,
her bone structure matches the orb's perfection.
Clad in shimmering silken robes,
she wears jade pendants of yáobì.
Adorned with golden and kingfisher hair ornaments,
strung with bright pearls to illuminate her form.
She treads in patterned traveling shoes,
trailing light skirts of misty gauze.
Faintly, the fragrant aura of secluded orchids;
she lingers in her steps by the mountain's edge.
Then suddenly she moves her body freely,
to roam and play.
Leaning on colored banners to the left,
shaded by cassia flags to the right.
Baring her fair wrist by the divine shore,
she plucks dark lingzhī from the rushing rapids.
My heart delights in her goodness and beauty,
yet my mind is stirred and uneasy.
I compose my gentle expression to calm my will,
upholding ritual restraint to maintain self-control.
Then the Luò River spirit is moved;
she lingers, pacing to and fro.
Divine light parts and joins,
now dark, now bright.
She raises her light form, standing like a crane,
as if about to fly yet not soaring.
Treading on fragrant pepper paths,
walking through sweetgrass thickets, wafting scent.
Singing long to express eternal longing,
her voice mournful and piercing, ever more drawn out.
Lamenting the gourd's lack of a mate,
singing of the Herdboy's solitude.
She lifts her light robe's fine silk,
veiling with long sleeves, she stands waiting.
Swift as a flying duck in body,
floating lightly as a spirit.
Treading lightly over waves with subtle steps,
her silken stockings seem to stir dust.
Her movements lack constant pattern,
now perilous, now secure.'"
And further:
"Crossing the northern islet,
passing the southern ridge.
Winding around the white peaks,
turning toward the clear sun.
Moving her red lips, she slowly speaks,
setting forth the great principles of interaction.
Regretting that the ways of humans and spirits differ,
lamenting that in youth's prime they cannot be matched.
Then turning from low to high ground,
my feet depart but my heart remains.
Leaving behind emotion, I imagine and recall,
gazing back, cherishing sorrow."
Sòng Xiè Língyùn's "Jiāngfēi Rhapsody"
Slender waist and delicate bones,
vermilion robes and white teeth.
Soft gaze, spirited approach,
smooth countenance, fine skin.
The moon emerges, the mountain hides;
the setting sun shines on isles.
Gathering clouds, withdrawing colors,
swirling gusts brush the shores.
Ever my feelings race through dawn and dusk,
how much more this fine encounter left untold.
I cast a bright pearl to present as a gift,
hoping for beauty's grant and soul's union.
Alas, the fair one is distant and remote,
gazing to the sky's edge, speaking bright words.
Fearing the time of unfolding love is not yet due,
I suppress my yearning and pause awhile.
The two beauties of Tiāntāi,
the twin maidens of Gōngtíng.
In blue robes, spirits meet;
in purple garments, forms appear.
Some soar on wings through mist,
some dive and swim across the sea.
Ten thousand miles in an instant,
an inch of shadow unchanged.
Though matters borrow from clouds and things,
Ancient Poem
Green, green, the riverside grass,
Lush, lush, the garden willow.
Full, full, the lady in the tower,
Bright, bright, she stands before the window.
Lovely, lovely her rouged makeup,
Slender, slender she shows her pale hands.
She says she is a courtesan's daughter,
Now married to a wanderer's wife.
The wanderer travels and does not return,
Hard to guard the empty bed alone.
Jìn Dynasty Poem by Ruǎn Jí
The elegant and handsome leisurely noble,
How radiant and splendid his brilliance.
Dark hair at the temples, a ruddy face,
A glance from his eyes shines with light.
The whole city longs for a single look,
He leaves his gaze and comes to pass by.
Wishing to roam through the three spring months,
The morning sun suddenly slips away.
Another Poem
The two consorts roamed by the riverbank,
Carefree, they followed the wind in flight.
Jiāo Fǔ cherished the jade pendants,
Gentle and lovely, with a fragrant air.
Intimate and tender, their joyful love,
For a thousand years, they would not forget.
Enchanting the city, bewildering Xiàcài,
Fair appearance ties the innermost feelings.
Moved and stirred, love and longing arise,
Planting xuāncǎo in the orchid chamber.
Hàn Dynasty "Song of Lǐ Yánnián"
In the north there is a beautiful lady,
Peerless in the world, standing alone.
One glance topples a city's walls,
A second glance topples a kingdom.
How could one not know that toppling city and kingdom,
Such a beauty is hard to find again.
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xuán's Song
There is a lady full of fragrance,
Gracefully she walks in the eastern wing.
Her moth eyebrows like twin kingfisher feathers,
Bright eyes emit a clear light.
Red lips conceal white teeth,
Her fair face like jade tablets.
Her artful smile reveals dimpled cheeks,
Her many charms cannot be fully told.
Her fine demeanor rare in the world,
Is she not the ancient Máo Qiáng?
On her head she wears a golden bùyáo,
In her ears hang bright moon-shaped earrings.
Wèi Dynasty Cáo Zhí's "The Beautiful Lady"
The beautiful lady is enchanting and graceful,
Gathering mulberry leaves at the crossroads.
Soft branches sway gently,
Leaves fall, how they flutter.
Rolling up her sleeves, her pale hands appear,
Her fair wrists adorned with golden bracelets.
On her head, golden sparrow hairpins,
At her waist, green jade pendants.
Bright pearls adorn her jade-like body,
Coral interspersed with mùnán gems.
Her silk garments flutter,
Light skirts swirl with the wind.
Her glance leaves behind radiant splendor,
Her long laughter breathes orchid fragrance.
Travelers halt their carriages,
Resting men forget to eat.
Ancient Yuèfǔ "The Roadside Mulberry"
The sun rises in the southeast corner,
Shining on our Qín family's tower.
The Qín family has a lovely daughter,
She calls herself Luó Fū.
Luó Fū is skilled at gathering mulberry,
She gathers mulberry in the city's southern corner.
Blue silk for her basket's strap,
Cassia branches for her basket's hook.
On her head, a falling-cloud chignon,
In her ears, bright moon pearls.
Pale silk for her lower skirt,
Purple silk for her upper jacket.
Those who see Luó Fū,
Set down their loads and stroke their beards.
Young men who see Luó Fū,
Remove their caps and adjust their turbans.
Plowmen forget their plows,
Hoe men forget their hoes,
Returning home, they grumble and fret.
All because they gazed at Luó Fū.
The governor comes from the south,
His five horses halt, hesitating.
Sòng Dynasty Bào Zhāo's "Hall Song"
Glowing, glowing, ruddy faces flushed,
Busy, busy, like the Weaving Maid's shuttle.
The hall is full of beautiful ladies,
But I face Cháng'é herself.
Zhēng and flutes play and blow,
Singing high, harmonizing well.
Ten thousand songs touch not the heart,
But one song stirs deep emotion.
To know if feelings are deep or shallow,
Listen again to the passing sound.
Ugly People, Third
The "Shì Míng" says:
"Chǒu (ugly),
means foul,
means filthy."
The "Jiā Yǔ" says:
"People from exhausted lands are ugly."
The "Shàng Shū · Hóng Fàn · Six Extremities · Fifth" says:
"È (ugly)."
Kǒng Ānguó says:
"Means ugly and repulsive."
The "Fā Méng Jì" says:
"The ugly man Zōng Miè,
the ugly woman Lí Chūn."
The "Guǎng Yǎ" says:
"Pǐ, suī, méi, pěi, tái, bèi, chuǎi, ?, huī, suī, kē, kuǐ, bèi, chuǎi, ?,
mean ugly."
Pǐ,
pronounced bí reversed;
Suī,
pronounced huǒ yí reversed;
Méi pronounced péi;
Tái pronounced tái;
Bèi,
pronounced pú běi reversed;
Bèi,
pronounced lǎo zhàng reversed;
Suī pronounced jiā;
Kē,
pronounced gǔ lái reversed;
Kuǐ pronounced gǔ;
Qī pronounced qī.
The "Máo Shī" says:
"Not seeing Zǐ Dū,
but meeting a mad jū."
The note says:
"Mad jū,
means a mad and ugly person."
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
"Minister Jiǎ was extremely ugly,
but took a wife who was beautiful.
For three years she did not speak,
he took her to the marsh,
shot a pheasant and caught it,
then his wife began to laugh."
Sūn Qīngzǐ says:
"Duke Líng of Wèi had a minister named Gōngsūn Lǚ,
seven chǐ tall,
his face three chǐ long and three cùn wide,
renowned throughout the world."
The "Shǐ Jì" says:
"Dàntái Mièmíng's appearance was very ugly,
Qín minister Cài Zé had a protruding chin and a broken nose bridge."
The "Jìn Shū":
"Zuǒ Sī was ugly in appearance and stammered in speech."
Hé Chéngtiān's "Zuǎn Wén" says:
"Mó Mǔ,
was an ugly woman."
The "Liè Nǚ Zhuàn" says:
"The orphaned exiled woman of Qí,
her appearance was extremely ugly.
Also, the Qí night-staying woman,
had a large tumor on her neck.
Liáng Hóng's wife Mèng Guāng,
ugly, dark, and fat,
had strength enough to lift a stone mortar."
Short Legs, Pointed Head
Cuī Hóng's "Qián Qín Lù" says:
"Fú Xióng, styled Yuáncái,
during Zhào's Jiànwǔ era was appointed General of the Dragon Steeds.
His appearance was ugly,
with a large head and short legs,
so the army called him 'Big-Headed Dragon Steeds.'"
Liú Mìzhī's "Páng Láng Fù" says:
"His head is bony in the middle and pointed at both ends,
his forehead flat and the back of his head protruding in four places."
Qīnyí and Tuīsǎng
From Zhōu Fěi's "Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán":
"Zhōu Xiè, styled Yànzǔ,
had a sunken chin and a protruding forehead,
and his appearance was extremely ugly.
His mother wanted to abandon him,
but his father said:
'I have heard that among sages and worthies,
their forms are all different from ordinary people.
The one who will raise up our clan must be this child.'
So they raised him."
From "The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi":
"In Chén there was an ugly man named Guō Qià,
with bushy eyebrows and a protruding forehead,
and a complexion as black as lacquer."
Chéng Gōng and Guǎn Lù
From the "Book of the Later Hàn":
"Chéng Gōng's fame spread to the Xiōngnú,
and at that time the Chányú sent an envoy requesting to see him.
Chéng Gōng said:
'The barbarians are dazzled by fame,
they do not recognize reality.
Your servant's form and appearance are ugly,
and should not be shown to distant peoples.'" From the "Records of Wèi":
"Guǎn Lù's facial features were ugly,
and he was fond of wine and food,
lacking dignified bearing."
Sūn Xiù and Áitāi
From the "Book of Jìn":
"Sūn Xiù married the Princess of Hédōng,
but his form was base and short,
beneath even that of servants."
From the "Zhuāngzǐ":
"Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní:
'Is there an ugly man in Wèi?'
He replied:
'There is Áitāi.
Men who associate with him
think of him and cannot leave.
Women plead with their mothers, saying:
"Rather than be someone else's wife,
I would rather be this master's concubine."
Such women number over ten and it does not stop.
This must mean he has something different from others."
I summoned him to observe him,
and indeed his ugliness startled the world.'"
Zǐgāo's Ugly Appearance and Bólún's Base Form
From the "Family Sayings of Confucius":
"Gāo Chái, styled Zǐgāo,
was no taller than six chǐ,
and his form and appearance were very ugly.
As a person he was sincere and filial,
and became well-known among Confucius's disciples,
serving as the magistrate of Chéng."
From Liáng Zuò's "Unified Writings of the Wèi State":
"Liú Líng, styled Bólún,
had an ugly and base form,
and was six chǐ tall.
Yet he indulged his whims and was unrestrained,
carefree and solitary in his contentment,
finding satisfaction in his own time,
often considering the universe to be narrow."
Zhīlí's Hidden Chin and Xià Yǔ's Long Neck
From the "Zhuāngzǐ":
"There was one Zhīlí Shū.
His chin was hidden at his navel,
his shoulders were higher than his neck.
The top of his head pointed to the sky,
his five viscera were positioned above,
and his two thighs were at his ribs."
From the "Shīzǐ":
"Yǔ had a long neck and a beak-like mouth,
and the color of his face was also ugly,
yet the world alone considered him worthy."
Diāojiāo and Mómǔ
From Jiāo Gàn's "Forest of Changes", "Fù zhī Méng" hexagram:
"Diāojiāo took a wife,
with deep-set eyes and a sunken head.
With a bent waist, not charming,
she and her husband opposed each other."
From Hé Chéngtiān's "Compiled Writings":
"Mómǔ
was an ugly woman,
yet the Yellow Emperor loved and favored her."
Dàn's Daughter and Liàng's Wife
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World":
"Wáng Guǎng married Zhūgě Dàn's daughter.
Upon entering the chamber,
they began to exchange words.
Wáng said to his wife:
'Your spirit and demeanor are lowly,
not at all like Gōngxiū.'
The wife said:
'A great husband cannot resemble Yànyún,
yet expects his wife to match the footprints of heroes and outstanding men.'" From Xí Zuòchǐ's "Records of Xiāngyáng":
"Huáng Chéngyàn said to Kǒngmíng:
'You are choosing a wife.
I have an ugly daughter,
with yellow hair and a dark complexion,
but her talent is worthy of matching a gentleman.'
Kǒngmíng agreed.
At the time she was conveyed to him,
people considered it a laughing matter."
The village made a proverb about it:
'Don't act like Kǒngmíng choosing a wife,
ending up with an ugly woman from beyond the river.'"
Upturned Nose and Permanent Tumor
From Liú Xiàng's "Biographies of Exemplary Women":
"There was one Zhōnglí Chūn of Qí,
a woman from Wúyán district in Qí,
the principal queen of King Xuān.
As a person, she was extremely ugly, without equal.
She had a concave head and deep-set eyes,
a long belly and large joints.
An upturned nose and a knotted throat,
a fat neck and sparse hair.
A bent waist and a protruding chest,
skin like lacquer.
Reaching thirty years of age,
she had nowhere to be accepted,
and could not be married off.
Thereupon, brushing off her short coarse garment,
she presented herself to King Xuān.
King Xuān accepted her as his queen."
Also said:
"The woman with the permanent tumor from Qí
was a woman from the eastern outskirts of Qí who gathered mulberry leaves,
the queen of King Mǐn.
She had a large tumor on her neck,
hence she was called 'Permanent Tumor'."
Gūzhú and Hòusòng
From Liú Xiàng's "Biographies of Exemplary Women":
"There was the woman Gūzhú of Qí.
Her appearance was very ugly.
Thrice driven out from her district,
five times driven out from her village,
she passed the age [for marriage] with nowhere to be accepted.
Then she went to King Xiāng's gate and requested an audience.
The king stopped eating and rose with respect.
His attendants said:
'One thrice driven out from her district is disloyal,
five times driven out from her village lacks propriety.
Why is she worthy of honor?'
The king said:
'You do not understand.
When an ox lows and a horse does not respond,
it is because they are different kinds.
This person must have something different.'
So he granted her an audience,
spoke with her, and was pleased with her."
From the "Traditions of the Hán Poetry":
"The King of Qí sent off his daughter with rich gifts,
wishing to marry her to Túmén Dù.
Dù declined on grounds of illness.
His friend urged him, saying:
'Will your descendants just die in a stinking market?
Why decline this?'
Dù replied:
'His daughter is ugly.'
His friend said:
'What do you mean?'
Dù said:
'If my meat is good,
people take it according to the measure and leave,
only regretting there is too little.
If my meat is not good,
even if I add other things to supplement it,
it still will not sell.
Now he sends you off with rich gifts—
it is because his daughter is ugly!'
His friend inquired discreetly,
and the daughter was indeed ugly.
Dù is also written as Tǔ."
Huì Fēi Yǔn Fù
The Hidden Records of Jìn states:
"When Emperor Wǔ was selecting a consort for the crown prince,
deliberations dragged on without resolution.
The Emperor wished to marry the daughter of Wèi Guàn,
while Empress Yáng wished to marry the daughter of Jiǎ Chōng.
The Emperor said:
'The Wèi family's daughter has five points in her favor,
the Jiǎ family's daughter has five points against her.
The Wèi family stock is virtuous and prolific with sons,
upright in bearing, tall, and fair;
the Jiǎ family stock is jealous and bears few sons,
ugly, short, and dark.'"
The Guō Zǐ states:
"Xǔ Yǔn's wife was the younger sister of Ruǎn Dérú,
exceptionally ugly.
After the wedding ceremony concluded,
Xǔ had no intention of ever entering her chambers again.
Huán Fàn advised him, saying:
'The Ruǎn family marrying their ugly daughter to you
must surely have a purpose;
you ought to investigate.'
Xǔ then entered to see her,
and the wife immediately came out, holding the hem of her skirt, awaiting him.
Xǔ said to his wife:
'A wife should possess four virtues;
how many do you have?'
She replied:
'What I, the new bride, lack is only beauty.
But a gentleman should have a hundred conducts;
how many do you possess?'
Xǔ said:
'I possess them all.'
The wife said:
'You favor beauty over virtue;
how can you claim to possess them all?'
Xǔ wore a look of shame,
and thereafter they held each other in high esteem."
Bóxiè Lǒng Lián
The Chǔ Cí states:
"Xī Shī, graceful and beautiful, cannot be seen,
while Mó Mǔ, shuffling and awkward, attends daily."
Again, the Chǔ Cí states:
"Jade tablets and scepters mixed among cooking pots,
Lǒng Lián sharing a palace with Mèng Zōu.
The whole world considers this the constant custom,
thus one is destined for sorrow and hardship, ending in poverty."
Liú Mìzhī's "Ode to Páng Láng"
All you gentlemen seated here,
please lend me your ears.
Listen as I compose this piece,
telling of this affair from Hénán.
The text is extensive and not fully recorded here.
Zhū Yànshí's "Ode to the Black Child"
In the world exists an extraordinary man,
truly he is that dark scholar.
Endowed with this deepest black color,
inside and out he is all alike.
Lying down like a black ox resting,
standing like a black ox poised.
Angry like a mynah bird fighting,
joyful like a cormorant pleased, and so on.
The text is extensive and not fully recorded here.
Liú Sīzhēn's "Ode to the Ugly Wife"
Others all obtain virtuous wives,
why is my fate alone so stingy?
I did not encounter the virtue of Jiāng or Rèn,
but met squarely with an ugly, vile wife.
Her talent meager and frugal,
her appearance worse than Mó Mǔ.
A deer's head, a monkey's face,
a bulging forehead and protruding mouth.
Broken bridge of the nose, pockmarked and tower-like,
two eyes sunken like mortars.
Skin like old mulberry bark,
ears like two hands turned sideways.
Head like a rice-pounding pestle,
hair like a dug-up broom.
Horrible to behold her ugly visage,
unattractive as a door-knocker.
Clumsy and dull at dressing her hair,
carved and painted, yet uglier still.
Rouged cheeks like a dog's licking,
the forehead alone peculiarly thick.
Vermilion lips like trampled blood,
painted eyebrows like a rat's burden.
Powder piled beneath the chin,
not evenly spread on the face.
Neck like a bag of fermented beans,
sleeves like a constantly wiped pot.
Shoes filled as if with mud,
fingernails long and grimy.
Cracked feet could hold chopsticks,
a close look makes one retch.
Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on Dēngtúzǐ's Fondness for Beauty"
Dēngtúzǐ's wife,
with disheveled hair and crumpled ears.
Protruding gums, upturned lips, and sparse teeth,
walking sideways, hunchbacked,
moreover, afflicted with scabies and hemorrhoids.
Yet Dēngtúzǐ is delighted with her.
She has borne him five sons.
Your Majesty, examine this carefully:
who is the one fond of beauty?
Tall People, Fourth
The Zhōu Shū states:
"People of hills and mounds are single-minded and tall."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
