"People of the East are tall."
The Lǐ Dǒu Yí states:
"If the ruler rides earth and becomes king, his people will be tall."
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"Yǔ was nine chi and nine cun tall,
Yīn Tāng was nine chi tall."
The Kǒng Yǎn Tú states:
"Confucius was ten chi tall."
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"Jì Lì's consort gave birth to King Wén, Chāng,
whose body was ten chi tall."
The Wú Yuè Chūnqiū states:
"Wǔ Zǐxū was one zhang tall,
with one chi between his eyebrows."
The Hàn Shū states:
"Hán Wáng Xìn was eight chi and nine cun tall.
Zhāng Cāng was large, tall, fat, and white like a gourd.
Jīn Mìdī was eight chi and two cun tall.
Dōngfāng Shuò was nine chi and three cun tall."
The Hétú Lóng Wén states:
"People of the Lóngbó country are thirty zhang tall.
To the east, one reaches the Dà Qín country,
where people are ten zhang tall.
Another hundred thousand lǐ east is the Tiāo country,
where people are three zhang and five chi tall.
Another hundred thousand lǐ east is the Zhōng Qín country,
where people are one zhang tall.
At the extreme east, south, west, and north of heaven,
there are bronze-headed, iron-browed soldiers,
thirty million zhang tall.
There are also diamond-hard, daring warriors,
thirty million zhang tall.
In the Taiping capital at the center of heaven,
there are capital-armored, ghost-eating, iron-faced soldiers,
thirty million zhang tall."
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shényì Jīng states:
"In the great wilderness of the southwest there is a person
one zhang tall,
with a waist measurement of nine chi.
He treads on tortoises and snakes,
wears a vermilion bird on his head,
leans on a blue dragon with his left hand,
leans on a white tiger with his right hand.
He knows the measures of rivers and seas,
recognizes the quantity of mountain stones.
He understands the speech of all birds and beasts under heaven,
knows the saltiness and bitterness of all grains, plants, and trees.
His name is Shèng (Sage).
Also called Zhé (Wise),
also called Xiān (First),
also called Wúbùdá (All-Penetrating).
Any mortal who sees and bows to him
gains divine wisdom.
Beyond the northwest seas there is a person
two thousand lǐ tall,
with a distance of a thousand lǐ between his two feet,
and a waist measurement of fifteen hundred lǐ.
He only drinks five dǒu of celestial wine daily,
consuming no grains, fish, or meat,
only drinking wine.
He enjoys wandering among mountains and seas,
does not trouble the common people,
does not interfere with the myriad things.
Born together with Heaven and Earth,
his name is Wúlùzhīrén (Man of No Path),
also called Rén (Benevolence),
also called Xìn (Trustworthiness),
also called Shén (Divinity)."
Waist Ten Wéi Footprints Six Chǐ
The Jìn Shū states:
"Yǐn Wěi, styled Jǐngliàng,
had great ambitions from youth,
and did not manage property.
His body was eight chǐ tall,
his waistband measured ten wéi,
he was stalwart and had a vigorous air."
The Shǐ Jì states:
"During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
a giant appeared at Líntáo.
His body was five zhàng tall,
his footprints six chǐ long."
A Giant Appears in Xiāngwǔ, Emerges from Pénglái
The Records of Wèi states:
"In the second year of Xiánxī,
a giant appeared in Xiāngwǔ County,
over two zhàng tall,
with footprints three chǐ and two cùn long.
He had white hair,
and wore a yellow single-layer robe and a yellow headscarf."
The Book of Hàn states:
"During Wáng Mǎng's time,
there was an extraordinary man,
one zhàng tall,
ten wéi in girth,
who called himself 'Jùwúbà'.
He originally came from the coast of Zhāorú, northwest of the Five Cities east of Pénglái.
A light carriage could not carry him,
and three horses could not pull him.
On that very day, a large cart with four horses
was set up with banners to transport him to the palace.
When lying down, he used his thigh as a pillow."
Eyebrows Visible on the Carriage Rail, Bones Filling a Cart
The Gǔliáng Commentary states:
"In the eleventh year of Duke Wén of Lǔ,
Shūsūn Déchén defeated the Dí at Xián.
They were the Tall Dí.
Three brothers,
they greatly harmed the Central States,
and tiles and stones could not harm them.
Shūsūn Déchén
was the best archer.
He shot their eyes,
and their bodies lay across nine mǔ;
he cut off their heads,
and their eyebrows were visible on the carriage rail."
The Discourses of the States states:
"Wú attacked Yuè,
destroyed Kuàijī,
and obtained bones there,
with joints filling a cart.
The ruler of Wú sent someone to ask Zhòngní,
and Zhòngní said:
'In the past, Yǔ assembled his ministers at Mount Kuàijī.
Fángfēngshì arrived late,
and Yǔ executed him.
His bone joints filled a cart;
this was because he was huge.'"
The Tall Dí Were Five Zhàng, Chē Qiānqiū Was Eight Chǐ
The Hongfan Wuxing Commentary to the Book of Documents states:
"The Tall Dí people
were about five zhàng tall."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Chē Qiānqiū's surname was Tián,
and he served as a Gāoqǐn Láng.
When the heir apparent Lì was defeated,
Qiānqiū pleaded the heir apparent's innocence,
and the emperor summoned him for an audience.
Qiānqiū was over eight chǐ tall,
with a very handsome physique and appearance."
Mǎ Téng's Majestic Stature, Zhào Yī's Imposing Build
Yuán Hóng's Annals of Hàn states:
"Chánglè Commandant Mǎ Téng
was eight chǐ tall,
with a massive body,
a majestic and extraordinary face and nose,
and a virtuous and kind nature,
so many people respected him."
The Book of Later Hàn states:
"Zhào Yī, styled Yuánshū,
had an imposing physique and appearance,
and was nine chǐ tall.
He had beautiful beard and eyebrows,
and appeared very majestic.
He relied on his talent and looked down on others,
and was rejected by his local community."
Fishing for Giant Turtles in the Sea, Large Clogs in the River's Flow
The Liezi states:
"In the great abyss, there are five mountains.
The Heavenly Emperor sent giant turtles to carry the five mountains.
In the country of Lóngbó, there was a giant
who hooked six turtles,
gathered and carried them back,
and then burned their bones.
The Emperor was angered
and destroyed the country of Lóngbó."
Zǔ Chōngzhī's Records of the Strange states:
"In the fourth year of Huángshǐ of Fú Jiàn,
a tall man appeared,
five zhàng tall."
He told a man named Zhāng Jìng:
'Now there shall be peace.'
The magistrate of Xīnpíng reported this,
and Jiàn considered it demonic falsehood,
summoning Jìng and imprisoning him.
That month, there was continuous rain,
and the Hé and Wèi Rivers overflowed.
The ford inspector Kòu Dēng, in the middle of the river,
found a large clog,
seven chǐ and three cùn long.
The footprint matched the clog,
with toes over a chǐ long,
and patterns seven cùn deep."
Jùbà Uses His Thigh as a Pillow, Shēn Xiāng Waves the Canopy
"Jùbà" is already mentioned above.
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States states:
"Establishing Left and Right Zhèn Láng and Fúgài Láng,
Shēn Xiāng served as Fúgài Láng,
and was one zhàng and nine chǐ tall."
Ten Zhàng Is the Ultimate Limit, Three Horses Cannot Pull
The Discourses of the States states:
"What is the ultimate limit of human height?"
Zhòngní said:
"The tallest does not exceed ten zhàng;
that is the ultimate limit."
"Three horses" is mentioned in the note for "Emerges from Pénglái."
Línfù a Thousand Lǐ, Zhītí Three Zhàng
Dōngfāng Shuò's Classic of Divine Marvels states:
"In the great wilderness of the southeastern corner, there is Línfù,
a thousand lǐ tall,
with a belly circumference of a hundred fǔ."
Guōzi's Records of the Cavernous Obscure states:
"There are people of the Zhītí country,
three zhàng and two chǐ tall.
They have three hands,
one hand on the chest,
with three fingers on each hand and foot."
Hàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Giant"
In the world there is a giant,
dwelling in the Central Land,
whose abode spans ten thousand lǐ,
yet he cannot linger even briefly.
Grieving the world's constraints and narrowness,
he lightly ascends to journey afar.
Hanging crimson banners of white rainbows,
he wears clouds and mist, floating upward.
Erecting long poles of shimmering brilliance,
he gathers luminous splendor and colorful pennants.
Dangling the Ten Beginnings as tassels,
and trailing comets as streamers.
Waving and pointing with majestic grace,
again swaying elegantly and beckoning.
Grasping comets to make banners,
and draping curved rainbows as silk.
Vast and misty rivers surge and swirl,
as fiery winds billow and clouds float.
Jìn Guō Pú's "Eulogy on the Long-Armed Country"
With arms three zhàng long,
their bodies are like ordinary men's.
What are they,
these long-armed people?
Carrying their lengthy legs,
they fish by the seaside.
Also, "Eulogy on Kuāfù"
Divine Kuāfù,
hard to fathom by reason.
He drained the river and raced the sun,
vanishing in the Dèng Forest.
Touching things and transforming,
responding without constant mind.
Short People, Part Five
The Guóyǔ states:
"The people of Jiāoyáo are three chǐ tall,
the epitome of shortness."
The Fāngyán states:
"Zhūrú,
are short people.
Cǐ,
pronounced zuó qǐ.
Bà,
pronounced pú kǎi.
Mean short."
The "Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn":
"Dōngjùn sent a short person,
seven cùn tall,
named Jùlíng."
The Hànshū states:
"Yán Yánnián was short and vigorous,
agile in handling affairs.
Lóu Hù was short and sharp-witted."
Hé Chéngtiān's "Zuǎnwén" states:
"During the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Zhāng Zhòngshī of Yǐngchuān was two chǐ tall."
The Wèishū states:
"Wáng Càn,
Yuè Jìn were both short in stature."
The "Book of Dream Interpretation" states:
"Dreaming of dwarfs means affairs will not succeed,
undertakings will halt midway and later gain no fame,
laughed at by the common people and looked down upon by others."
The "Shíyí Jì" states:
"On Yuánqiáo Mountain is the country of Tuóyí,
its people are three chǐ tall,
and live ten thousand years.
The people of Guǎngyán country are two chǐ tall."
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Shényì Jīng" states:
"In the northwestern wilderness are little people,
one cùn tall,
wearing red clothes and black hats.
Beyond the Western Sea is the Crane Country,
where both men and women are seven cùn tall."
Zāng Hé Gāo Chái
The Zuǒzhuàn:
"The people of Zhū and Jǔ attacked Zēng,
Zāng Hé went to rescue Zēng,
but was defeated at Hútái.
The people of the state chanted:
'Zāng in his fox-fur robe,
defeated us at Hútái.
Our lord, a mere youth,
employs a dwarf.
Dwarf, dwarf,
defeated us by Zhū.'" The Jiāyǔ states:
"Gāo Chái, styled Zǐgāo,
was no more than six chǐ tall,
and was deeply filial by nature."
Yōu Zhān Cài Yì
The Shǐjì states:
"Yōu Zhān
was a dwarf entertainer of Qín.
When the First Emperor held a banquet,
it rained,
and the shield-bearers on the steps were cold,
Zhān pitied them.
He then shouted loudly:
'You may be tall,
standing in the rain;
I may be short,
but fortunately I rest.'
The First Emperor then had them all replaced."
The Hànshū:
"Cài Yì became Chancellor,
at that time over eighty years old,
short and small with no beard or eyebrows,
resembling an old woman.
He walked hunched over,
often needing two clerks to support him under his arms to walk."
Chǔ Yègōng Qí Yànzǐ
Xúnzǐ states:
"Yègōng Zǐgāo of Chǔ was tiny, short, and thin,
his gait as if his clothes were too heavy for him."
The "Yànzǐ Chūnqiū" states:
"Yànzǐ was short,
and was sent on a mission to Chǔ.
Chǔ made a small gate,
Yànzǐ did not enter,
saying:
'If sent to a dog country, one enters through the dog gate.
Now I am sent to Chǔ,
I should not enter through a dog gate.'"
Cài's Ode to the Bā Horse Guō's Eulogy to the Jìng People
Cài Yōng's "Ode to Short People" states:
"The Bā horse on the peak, the dog under the fence."
Guō Pú's "Eulogy" states:
"Jiāoyáo are extremely tiny,
Jìng people are even smaller,
Jìng pronounced jìng."
Wáng Jìng Dignified and Proper Zhāng Sōng Unrestrained
The Sòngshū states:
"Wáng Jìnghóng's appearance was short and small,
yet he sat and rose with dignity and propriety."
The "Yìbù Zá Jì" states:
"Zhāng Sōng was short in stature,
but unrestrained and lacking in moral integrity."
Lóu Hù Sharp-Witted Yán Yán Agile
Both seen in the narrative above.
Jùlíng Seven Cùn Tuóyí Three Chǐ
Both seen in the narrative above.
Western Sea Fears Cranes Dōngfāng Teases Dwarfs
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Shényì Jīng" states:
"Beyond the Western Sea is the Crane Country,
its people seven cùn tall,
walking as if flying,
a thousand lǐ a day.
No creature dares offend them,
they only fear sea cranes,
for sea cranes swallow them upon encounter.
They live three hundred years,
and do not die inside the crane."
The Hànshū states:
"Dōngfāng Shuò teased the dwarfs, saying:
'The Emperor thinks you people are of no use to the state,
and now wants to kill you all.'
The dwarfs were greatly frightened."
Hàn Cài Yōng's "Ode to Short People"
Dwarfs, short people,
descendants of Jiāoyáo.
Originating from foreign lands,
a different tribe of Róng and Dí.
Abandoning their customs, turning to righteousness,
admiring transformation, striving to follow.
Thus they are in the Central Kingdom,
their forms and appearances categorized.
Named dwarfs,
born resembling their fathers.
Only Yànzǐ,
in Qí, was discerning and brave.
He corrected Jǐng and resisted Cuī,
a blade added, yet unafraid.
The other stunted men,
inferior, hunchbacked, impoverished.
Snarling and spitting angry words,
confronting others.
Ignorant, fond of wine,
liking to demand fines and punishments.
Drunk, they raise their voices,
cursing and railing freely.
People fear and avoid them,
hard to be their companions.
Therefore I compose this ode,
drawing analogies, pairing comparisons.
All capture their image,
truly as described.
Its words say:
"The male Jīng chicken and the duck-like pìtí,
The gǔhú chick and the female quail and wren.
Crowned like the hoopoe, pecking like the woodpecker child,
Observe the short person—their form is like this.
The burrowing locust and the reed jíqū (pronounced zǐ rú),
The pupa in the cocoon, wriggling and squirming.
Pronounced ér xié,
pronounced xū, look at the short person—their form is like this.
The wooden door threshold and the beam's pillar,
The worn chisel head and the broken axe handle.
The drum's bǐngtà and the cobbler's pú,
The removed hammer handle and the garlic-pounding pestle.
Look at the short person—their form is like this."
Guō Pú's "Eulogy to Jiāoyáo"
Jiāoyáo are extremely tiny,
Jìng people are even smaller.
Four limbs just sufficient,
eyebrows and eyes barely discernible.
They are the sixth among slaves.
The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"In ancient systems, there were originally no slaves or maidservants;
even those who committed offenses were sometimes pardoned.
Zāng refers to
those convicted of theft who were confiscated and became government slaves;
huò refers to
fugitives who were captured and became slaves."
The *Shuōwén* states:
"A man who becomes a criminal is called a nú (slave),
a woman who becomes a criminal is called a bì (maidservant)."
The *Fāngyán* states:
"Zāng, yǒng,
(pronounced yǒng)
wǔ, huò,
are all derogatory terms for slaves and maidservants.
In Jīng,
Huái,
the regions of Hǎi, Dài, and Qí,
a male slave is insultingly called zāng,
a female slave is insultingly called huò;
in the northern outskirts of Qí,
and the northern suburbs of Yān,
any man who marries a maidservant is called zāng,
any woman who marries a slave is called huò.
Also, a fugitive male slave is called zāng,
a fugitive female slave is called huò,
all being derogatory terms for slaves and maidservants;
between Qín and Jìn,
a male slave is insultingly called wǔ;
between Yān and Qí,
horse grooms and female servants are all called shēn."
Female servants
are women who perform errands.
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Jì Bù became a branded slave for Zhū Jiā,
Luán Bù was kidnapped and sold as a slave by others,
Wèi Qīng was a slave in a marquis's household."
The *Hànshū* states:
"During Wáng Mǎng's time,
the Xiōngnú invaded and raided,
so he extensively recruited prisoners and private slaves from across the land,
naming them 'Zhūtūxīyǒng' (Boar-Charging Brave Warriors)."
The *Jìnshū* states:
"Lièzōng's mother was originally a maidservant in the weaving workshop,
with a dark complexion,
palace attendants called her Kūnlún.
Tàizōng, through a scheme, favored her,
and she gave birth to Lièzōng.
Also, Péi Xiù's mother was a maidservant;
when Xiù was eighteen,
he had a fine reputation,
but his legal mother was a servant,
and the house was full of guests.
She then ordered Xiù's birth mother to serve food to the guests,
and all the guests, upon seeing her, bowed to her."
Zhōu Xī Jìn Lì
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"There are three hundred xī."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"In ancient times, those implicated in crimes,
men and women confiscated by the state became slaves and maidservants;
those among them with some talent and intelligence were made xī,
which corresponds to the attendant scribes and government maidservants of today."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Fěi Bào
was a lì."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"He was a criminal confiscated by the state to become a slave."
Yí Jiǎ Cì Guāng
The *Shǐjì* states:
"When the various Lǚ clans monopolized power,
Lù Jiǎ said:
'When the world is at peace,
attention focuses on the chancellor;
when the world is in danger,
attention focuses on the general.
If the general and chancellor are harmonious, then the officials will readily submit.'
Thereupon, Chén Píng forged a friendship with the Grand Commandant,
and presented Jiǎ with a hundred slaves and maidservants." The *Hànshū* states:
"The Emperor decreed:
'The Grand Marshal Guāng, loyal and upright in guarding the palace,
has promoted virtue and made clear imperial favor.'
He was rewarded with a total of one hundred and seventy slaves and maidservants."
Zhèng in the Mud Páng under the Stove
Liú Yìqìng's *Shuōyuàn* states:
"All the slaves and maidservants in Zhèng Xuán's household could read.
Xuán once became angry
and had a maidservant dragged into the mud.
Another maidservant came and asked:
'Why are you in the mud?'
She replied:
'I went to make a brief complaint,
but encountered his anger.'" The *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Páng Jiǎn of Hénán encountered turmoil in his youth,
and lost his father.
Later, while digging a well, he obtained over ten million coins.
He sought out an old servant
to oversee the oxen and horses.
During a wedding gathering,
the servant whispered under the stove, 'The mother in the hall
is my wife.'
Jiǎn had this investigated,
and they became husband and wife again as before.
People of the time said:
'Among the various Pángs in the village,
one dug a well and found copper,
another bought a slave and gained a father-in-law.'"
Chén Yúdì Wú Gǔlì
Yìng Shào's *Fēngsútōng* states:
"The Minister of Works Gōngsūn Zhìjié of the state of Chén had an old servant named Yúdì,
who was seventy years old
and skilled in writing and correspondence."
The *Jiāngbiǎozhuàn* states:
"Gǔlì
was a senior slave of Wú."
Spilling Broth and Soiling Clothes Overturning Wine and Accepting the Cane
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Liú Kuān was by nature simple and unassuming.
His wife wanted to test his disposition.
As he was about to attend court,
already fully dressed in his court robes,
she had a maidservant present him with meat broth,
which she then spilled, soiling his court attire.
The maidservant cleaned it up,
but Kuān's expression did not change;
he merely said calmly, 'The broth scalded your hand.'"
Liú Xiàng's *Liènǚzhuàn* states:
"A senior official of the Zhōu court served in Zhōu.
His wife committed adultery with a neighbor.
When the master returned,
fearing he would discover it,
she prepared poison
and ordered a maidservant to serve it to him.
The maidservant said to herself:
'If I serve it, I kill the master;
if I report it, I cause the mistress's death.'
So she pretended to stumble and overturned the wine.
The master, angry, caned her.
The wife, fearing the maidservant would talk,
used another fault as a pretext to have her killed.
The maidservant, facing the cane and about to die, still did not speak.
The master's younger brother heard of this,
directly informed the master,
who then divorced his wife.
He intended to take the maidservant as his wife,
but she declined and committed suicide.
The master then provided a generous dowry and married her off."
Drawing a Sword to Cut the Mat Flat-Headed Servant Carrying Frosty Shoes
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Rén Ān
was a retainer of General Wèi.
He visited the household of Princess Píngyáng.
The host prepared a meal,
and he was seated at the same mat as the mounted slaves to eat.
Ān drew his waist sword, cut the mat, and sat separately."
An ancient poem states:
"On your feet are silk shoes with five patterns,
a flat-headed servant lad carries your frosty shoes."
Shěn Asked About Plowing Liú Made Them Hold the Shuttle
Shěn Yuē's *Sòngshū* states:
"When the enemy occupied Huátái,
Tàizǔ wished to launch a northern expedition,
but Shěn Qìngzhī firmly argued against it.
The Governor of Dānyáng Xú Zhànzhī and the Minister of Personnel Jiāng Zhàn
were both present.
They had Zhànzhī and others challenge Qìngzhī.
He said:
'Governing a state is like managing a household.
For plowing, one should ask the slaves;
for weaving, one should consult the maidservants.
Your Majesty now wishes to attack a state,
yet you consult with these pale-faced scholars.
How can the affair succeed?'
The Emperor laughed heartily."
Liú Mìzhī's *Letter to Heaven* states:
"In the district of Jiànníng,
I finally obtained several years of leisure.
I intended to teach the slaves to plow,
and have the maidservants hold the shuttles."
Dí Qīng Dies in Her Mistress’s Place; Dù’s Tomb Revives a Maidservant
Huángfǔ Mì’s *Later Biographies of Exemplary Women* states:
“In Kuàijī there was a woman named Dí Sù,
a daughter of the Dí family.
She was betrothed but not yet married
when bandits suddenly attacked.
They sought to violate her,
pressing blades to her throat.
Her maidservant was named Qīng.
Qīng begged to take Sù’s place.
The bandits killed Sù,
then tried to assault Qīng.
Qīng said:
‘Earlier I wished to replace Sù,
fearing only that shame and harm would befall her!
Now that Sù is dead,
why should I live?’
The bandits then killed her as well.”
Gān Bǎo’s *In Search of the Supernatural* states:
“When the Jìn dynasty Dù Gǔ’s family conducted a burial,
a maidservant was accidentally shut in and could not get out.
Over ten years later, when the tomb was opened,
the maidservant was still alive.
She said it was as if she had just been sleeping;
after a while she gradually awoke.
When asked,
she herself thought only one or two nights had passed.
Initially buried at fifteen or sixteen,
by the time the tomb was opened and she revived,
she still appeared fifteen or sixteen.
She later married and bore children.”
The Hú Maidservant Skilled in Archery; The Yí Slave Who Hewed Stone
*The Decisive Records of the Three Capital Regions* states:
“Jīn Yī served as commandery accountant,
and remained in Xūdū.
At that time, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi sent his senior clerk Wǔ Bì to lead troops
and guard the Son of Heaven in Xūdū.
Yī was on good terms with Bì.
Bì noticed that Yī had a Hú maidservant skilled in archery,
and Bì often requested her service in his campaigns.”
*The Records of Línyì* states:
“Fàn Wén was originally a slave of a Yí teacher.
With a blade he hewed stone barriers,
as if cutting reeds.
Later he became king of the country.”
“Rhapsody on the Blue-Clad Maidservant” by Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn
Gold is born from sand and gravel;
pearls emerge from muddy clams.
I sigh at such grace and loveliness,
born into lowly station.
Her charming glances, virtuous and fair,
with gleaming teeth and brows like moth antennae.
Her hair arranged crosswise, layered and full,
leaves like drooping sunflowers.
In embroidered sleeves and crimson skirts,
she treads in silken slippers.
With swaying steps, now slow, now brisk,
sitting or rising, she lowers or lifts her head.
Harmonious and cheerful, skilled in laughter,
her vermilion lips stir as she speaks.
Elegant, alluring, martial yet charming,
outstanding and full of grace.
Intelligent, kind, and cautious in heart,
she hastens to tasks as if flying.
In managing the household and cutting cloth,
none can match her pace.
Pure as the *Ospreys* ode,
she does not sink into wickedness or wrong.
Observe her conduct and ways—
rare indeed in this world.
Fit to be a lady of rank,
yet she serves among the maids.
Alas, what fate is yours,
to dwell in such humble state?
In an age lacking a Fán Jī,
Chǔ Zhuāng lacks his Jìn consort.
Moved by ancient Zhèng Jì,
who privately favored Píngyáng.
Thus, while extolling the state,
I pass through your native region.
Though I may find delight and joy,
and pour out my heartfelt feelings,
when cold snow falls thick and fast,
filling courtyard and covering steps,
layered robes and repeated quilts,
tossing and turning, collapsing in rest,
as dawn approaches, nearing daylight,
cockcrow urges one another on,
I prepare the carriage, hasten to depart,
about to leave you, forced to part.
In darkness, in darkness,
thoughts unruly, impossible to dispel.
Zhāng Zǐbìng’s “Satirizing the Rhapsody on the Blue-Clad Maidservant”
What manner of man is this,
enamored of such dazzling beauty?
Eloquent phrases, fine praises,
elegant lines, richly adorned.
The writing may be commendable,
but the intent is base and trivial.
O phoenix, o phoenix,
how your virtue has declined!
Lofty ridges may be adorned—
why must you dwell among thorns?
Sweet springs are fit to drink—
why must you seek muddy filth?
Using a pearl to shoot sparrows,
using a hall’s stream to cut mallows.
A phoenix chick pecking at mice—
how differs it from an owl?
Reviewing past and present,
steps to fortune and disaster:
often they stem from wanton concubines and licentious wives.
Texts warn of the hen that crows;
the *Odes* record the clever woman.
In the decline of the Three Dynasties,
all arose from this.
Jìn captured the Líróng,
and ruined the respectful heir.
Yǒuxià took a Rēng woman,
overturning the clan, ending sacrifices.
Shū Xī took in Shēn;
listening to slander, he became wolf-like.
Mùzǐ privately favored Gēng,
and Shù Niú starved him to death.
Huáng Xiē’s downfall
began with Lǐ Yuán.
Lǔ accepted Qí’s musicians,
and Zhòngní departed.
Duke Wén cherished comfort;
Jiāng reproached his baseness.
Zhōu gradually declined;
King Kāng rose late.
Duke Bì sighed deeply,
pondering deeply the ancient way.
Moved by that *Ospreys* ode,
whose virtue finds no pair.
If only the Duke of Zhōu
had favored it for its grace and virtue,
guarding against the subtle, reproving the gradual,
admonishing ruler and father.
Master Kǒng esteemed it greatly,
placing it at the head of the chapters.
Yàn Yīng, pure in will,
paid no heed to the Jǐng woman.
And then Jùn Bùyí,
when offered Huò’s daughter, did not accept.
Facing honor, he was not misled;
how much less this pretty lad?
Three clans lack order,
bonds are not properly arranged.
Crawling sideways to seek a mate,
moving askew to find a partner.
Marriage without a matchmaker,
the ancestral temple without a master.
The household lacks a proper name;
they rely on wherever they are.
Daughters born become concubines;
sons born become slaves.
At season’s sacrifices,
they address their ancestors:
perhaps in the horse stable,
kitchen, or beside the stove.
Kneeling long facing east,
they exchange cups, intimate with wine.
Inviting all the spirits,
the wicked assume the host’s role.
Much begged for, little given out,
with bronze tiles and iron pillars.
Accumulating silks by the hundred million,
all gather together.
Pretty and charming, hearts joyful,
each in their turn.
The likes of slaves and captives—
truly not worth counting.
Ancient surplus sons-in-law
were still considered dust and grime;
how much more the wise and discerning
who would become a slave’s father?
Liú Yídào’s “Poem on a Dead Slave”
Brief the span of a cinnabar-registered life;
deep the road of return to the Yellow Springs.
Not equal to the trees of Jiānglíng,
for a thousand autumns ever a forest.
Qiáo Zhīzhī’s “Ballad of Lǜzhū”
At the Shí family’s Jīngǔ, new melodies were prized;
Ten hu of bright pearls bought a graceful maiden.
On this day, pitiable—she could only pledge herself;
At this moment, lovely—she won the master’s favor.
Your household’s inner chambers were never hard to enter;
Constantly holding song and dance, she was shown to others.
Arrogant and bold in spirit, beyond all reason;
Proud and overbearing, they forcibly interfered.
Bidding you farewell, leaving,
In the end, she could not bear it;
In vain, covering her face, she grieved over her lead-powder makeup.
A lifelong parting atop the high tower;
A generation’s beauty was spent for you.
Qiáo Dàoyuán’s “Letter to Heaven”
This servant says:
“Gāo’ān,
Both hands are crippled,
Fingers like bamboo tubes,
Fearing wind and hating cold.
The younger one, born in the household,
His name is Ráo.
In his belly, a hard lump,
Large as a rice scoop.
He eats his fill all day,
Yet cannot perform labor.
Accompanying a young boy,
A coarse father, a Wú mother.
Recently, due to the winter festival,
He briefly visited his uncle.
A dog bit his shin,
Flesh fell off like a hand,
Tendons cramped to the bone,
Limping and not healing.
The elder maid, Lái Chéng,
Lost sight in her left eye.
When moving, she falls into the well,
Already dead, then revived.
The next maid, Liáng Xìn,
Has the ailment of Duke Huán’s minister;
Though she walks with wide strides,
She makes no progress at all.
A hidden illness, hard to clarify,
Words cannot fully convey it.
The little maid, Cóng Chéng,
A southern slave,
Her form like a startled roe deer,
Her speech chattering and sharp,
Her voice frightens people.
Only fit to drive chickens,
Unsuited for any other task.
Sent to visit Ā Jī,
Again bitten by a dog,
Collapsed limp as mud.”
Hàn dynasty Wáng Bāo’s “Reprimand to the Bearded Slave”
I observe human beards,
Long and also black,
Soft and supple, well‑ordered.
Luxuriant, like bamboo along a slope,
Lush, like seedlings in spring fields.
Swaying with the wind,
Fluttering with the body.
Then they adorn a full jaw,
Frame moth‑like eyebrows,
Emerge from a fair face,
Present a graceful bearing.
Bound with silk threads,
Moistened with fragrant oils.
Thick and flourishing,
Fine and smooth.
Shaken, they gleam and shine,
Dark as hanging black jade tablets.
Thus, shaking side‑locks, stirring mustaches,
One discourses on Yáo and Shùn;
Ruffling beard, moving whiskers,
One examines good and bad.
Nurturing circular patterns within,
Revealing musical tones without.
Xiàngrú, by this, was elegant;
Zhuānsūn, by this, was majestic.
How can your beard compare?
Both tangled and reddish,
Withered, bald, and sickly,
Weary and toilsome.
Sweat and grime flowing down,
Filthy as mud and dirt,
Coarse, mumbling, tangled and matted,
Day and night keeping company with dust.
No fair face to rely on,
No full jaw to depend on.
Moving, you are troubled by binding and trimming;
Still, you are distressed like a captive.
Ill‑fated as a mustache,
Right upon your jaw,
As a body, it cannot shelter its four limbs;
As a mind, it cannot govern its own frame.
Otter‑like whiskers, gaunt face,
Often like dead ashes.
Truly not equal to the hair‑tails of dogs and sheep,
Nor the fine fur of foxes.
To be your beard—
Is it not indeed hard!
Hàn Wáng Bāo's "The Slave Contract"
Wáng Zǐquán of Shǔjùn,
due to business, arrived at the home of the widow Yáng Huì in Jiānshàng.
There was a slave named Biànliǎo,
whom he asked to go buy wine.
Biànliǎo then took a large staff and went to the top of a grave mound, saying:
"When the gentleman bought Biànliǎo,
he only contracted me to guard the grave;
he did not contract me to buy wine for other men."
Zǐquán was greatly angered and said:
"Does this slave perhaps wish to be sold?"
Huì said:
"The slave's father promised him to someone,
but no one wanted him.
You may draw up a sale contract immediately."
The slave again said:
"If you want me to do it, put everything on the contract.
If it's not on the contract,
Biànliǎo cannot do it."
Zǐquán said:
"Agreed."
The contract text said:
"On the fifteenth day of the first month in the third year of Shénquè,
Wáng Zǐquán, a man from Zīzhōng,
buys from Yáng Huì, a woman of Ānzhìlǐ in Chéngdū, the bearded slave Biànliǎo, who was formerly under her husband's household register,
for a final sale price of fifteen thousand.
The slave shall obey all commands without a word of dissent.
Rise early in the morning and return early.
After eating, wash and clean.
Dwell where you must, pound the mortar,
bind brooms, cut bowls.
Dig wells, dredge ditches,
tie fences, hoe the garden.
Cut paths, block ponds,
carve large yokes from the ground.
Bend bamboo to make handles,
whittle and craft pulleys.
When going out or coming in, you may not ride a horse or ride in a carriage;
sit cross-legged and shout loudly.
Get off the bed and shake your head,
go fishing, cut grass.
Weave reeds, twist hemp for winter use,
draw water, make yogurt.
Help brew ale,
help brew ale.
Glue traps for sparrows, set nets for crows,
weave nets, catch fish,
shoot geese with tethered arrows, shoot wild ducks with pellets,
climb mountains, shoot deer,
enter water, catch turtles.
In the back garden, rear over a hundred geese and ducks,
drive away owls and hawks,
take a whip, herd pigs,
plant ginger, cultivate taro,
raise and nurture piglets and foals.
Remove manure, keep always clean,
feed the horses and oxen.
At the fourth drum, rise and sit,
at midnight, add more fodder.
In the second month, at the spring equinox,
repair dikes, block boundaries.
Trim mulberry trees, strip palm fibers,
plant melons, make sounds.
Yesterday's gourds, separate eggplants, strip palm fibers,
burn tree stumps, clear fields.
Ridge the fields, break up clods,
at midday, weed early.
Sound wèi.
At cockcrow, rise and pound grain,
tend to and manage horses and donkeys.
Also trim three layers,
when there are guests in the house.
Take the pot, go buy wine,
draw water, make porridge.
Sound fǔ.
Wash cups, arrange trays,
in the garden, pull up garlic.
Chop perilla, slice dried meat,
pound meat, make stew.
Taro minced, fish wrapped turtle,
brew tea, finish the meal.
Afterward, cover and store,
close the gate, block the holes.
Feed the pigs, release the dog,
do not quarrel with the neighbors.
The slave shall only eat beans and drink water,
he may not crave wine.
If he wishes to drink fine wine,
he may only moisten his lips and rinse his mouth,
he may not tilt the cup or overturn the dipper.
He may not go out at dawn and return at night,
to socialize and form companions.
Behind the house there are trees,
they should be cut to make boats.
Down to Jiāngzhōu, up to Jiān,
the master, as a government clerk, seeks funds for use.
Push and seek out bad debts, fight and demand,
at Miántíng, buy mats.
Travel to and from Dūluò,
must seek rouge and ointments for the women.
Sell in the small market,
return to the city carrying hemp,
go out to the side, stumble,
lead dogs, sell geese.
In Wǔyáng, buy tea from the Yáng family pond,
carry loads to and from market gatherings,
carefully guard against thieves and pilferers,
when entering the market, do not squat idly or lie down on the side.
Do not use foul language or ugly curses,
daily make knives and bows,
take them into Yìzhōu,
barter for cattle and sheep.
The slave must himself be clever and intelligent,
he may not be foolish or stupid.
Take an axe into the mountains,
cut timber, shape cart shafts.
If remnants, make chopping blocks, wooden clogs, and pig troughs,
burn firewood to make charcoal.
Pound stones, thin the banks,
repair the house, thatch the roof.
Write and carve, replace wooden tablets,
at dusk return,
must bring back two or three bundles of dry firewood.
In the fourth month, you must weed,
in the fifth month, you must harvest,
in the tenth month, gather beans,
pears, persimmons.
When rain falls and there is nothing to do,
weave rushes, plait mats.
Plant peach and plum trees,
pear, persimmon, mulberry, and paper mulberry trees,
one tree every three zhang,
eight chi between rows.
Fruit trees of the same kind together,
arranged vertically and horizontally, properly aligned.
When fruit ripens, gather it,
do not suck or taste it.
When the dog barks, you must rise,
alert and inform the neighbors.
Bar the door, secure the household,
go upstairs and beat the drum.
Carry a shield, drag a spear,
patrol the enclosure three times.
Work diligently and swiftly,
do not wander about idly.
When the slave is old and his strength fails,
plant rushes, weave mats.
When tasks are finished and you wish to rest,
you must pound one dan of grain.
If there is nothing to do at midnight,
wash clothes until they are white.
If there are private collections,
the master provides for guests.
The slave may not have secret affairs,
matters must be reported.
If the slave does not heed instruction,
he shall receive one hundred lashes.
After reading the contract text through to the end,
words exhausted, he gnashed his teeth and pleaded.
Trembling, he kowtowed,
bound his own hands with rope.
Tears fell from his eyes,
snot hung down one chi long.
"It shall be as Gentleman Wáng says,
better to return early to the yellow earth path.
May earthworms bore through my forehead,
had I known it would be like this,
I would have bought wine for Gentleman Wáng,
and not dared to be wicked."
This text has been passed down with many errors;
I hope nothing is omitted."
Shè dì yī
The *Eryǎ* says:
"Shè (赦) means
shě (舍, to release)."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"It means to set aside.
According to the *Yú Shū*, 'For unintentional faults and inadvertent offenses, pardon them.'"
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"The Sīcì official is in charge of the laws of the three pardons."
It also says:
"When the ruler of a state passes through the marketplace, then those condemned to punishment are pardoned."
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
"If there is guilt, one dares not pardon it,
this is correct."
The *Hàn Jiù Yí* states:
"Upon ascending the throne,
changing the reign era,
establishing an empress or crown prince,
pardon all under heaven.
With each pardon,
from those sentenced to death downwards,
including those plotting rebellion and great impiety,
and all those who should not be eligible for pardon,
are all pardoned and cleared.
The order is sent down to the Chancellor and the Imperial Censor,
who again memorialize for approval.
They are separately dispatched, the Chancellor and Imperial Censor riding post-chariots to travel through the commanderies and kingdoms,
releasing prisoners,
and promulgating the edict.
The commanderies and kingdoms each separately dispatch officials with relay station carriages and horses to travel through their subordinate counties,
releasing prisoners."
Also, Xún Yuè's *Hàn Jì Lùn* says:
"Now pardons
are an expedient measure for the times,
not a constant rule.
When the Hàn arose,
inheriting the aftermath of war,
an era of great excesses,
where every household was liable to punishment,
therefore the laws of the Three Articles were established,
supplemented by the order of a great pardon.
To cleanse the foul currents,
and give the people a fresh start,
was due to the circumstances of the time.
Later generations inherited the enterprise,
became accustomed to it and did not reform it,
losing its timeliness.
Therefore Guǎnzǐ said:
'All pardons
bring small benefit but great harm,
therefore over time they cannot overcome their misfortune;
having no pardons
brings small harm but great benefit,
therefore over time they cannot overcome their good fortune.
Pardons are
like dropping the reins of a galloping horse;
having no pardons is
like the lancet and stone for a carbuncle or abscess.'" Also, Wáng Fú's *Qián Fū Lùn* states:
"Sometimes the three luminaries have portents,
the celestial qi indicates a pardon should be granted,
therefore men follow this to bestow virtue."
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"Zhuāng Shēng said to the King of Chǔ:
'A certain star encroaches upon a certain lodge,
it is fitting to repay resentment with virtue.'
The King of Chǔ was about to issue a pardon."
Also, the *Wàng Qì Jīng* says:
"When yellow clouds emanate in all four directions,
it portends a pardon within fifty days."
Also, the *Fēng Jiǎo Shū* states:
"If wind arises on the jiǎyín day of spring,
coming from the shēn direction, it signifies a great pardon,
expected to be fulfilled within sixty days."
Thunder and Rain Bring Release; Letting Be and Forbearance
The *Zhōu Yì* says:
"Thunder and rain bring release;
the nobleman uses this to pardon faults and forgive crimes."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"I have heard of letting be and forbearance towards all under heaven,
I have not heard of governing all under heaven.
'Letting be' means
fearing that all under heaven would become excessive in their innate nature;
'forbearance' means
fearing that all under heaven would alter their inherent virtue.
If all under heaven does not become excessive in their innate nature,
does not alter their inherent virtue,
then is there any governing of all under heaven!"
Lǚ Méng's Illness; Wáng Měng's Sickness
Wéi Zhāo's *Wú Shū* says:
"When Lǚ Méng's illness flared up,
Sūn Quán welcomed him and placed him in the inner palace,
and could not sleep at night.
When there was an improvement during the illness,
he issued a pardon decree."
Cuī Hóng's *Qián Qín Lù* says:
"When Wáng Měng's illness had not yet improved,
Fú Jiān granted a great pardon for those sentenced to death and below."
Clouds Emanate; Wind Comes
"Yellow clouds" emanating in all four directions, see in the narrative section.
The *Fēng Jiǎo Shū* says:
"After the winter solstice, on the dīngsì day,
if there is wind coming from the sì direction,
there will be a great pardon."
Passing Through the Marketplace; Entering the Pass
The *Zhōu Lǐ* says:
"When the ruler of a state passes through the marketplace, then those condemned to punishment are pardoned."
Yuán Shānsōng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
"Jiǎ Biāo traveled to the capital,
Guō Línzōng,
Lǐ Yuánlǐ and others were the leaders of discourse,
their every word and action
was taken as the standard by all under heaven.
When the Partisan Prohibition incident arose,
Jiǎ Biāo said to his comrades:
'If I do not travel west,
the great calamity will not be resolved.'
He then entered the pass,
and devised strategies,
and the Son of Heaven issued a great pardon because of it."
Moving Locks; Singing Branches
Wáng Chōng's *Lùn Héng* says:
"When a pardon decree is about to arrive,
the locks on the prison cells move.
Those within the prison are due to be released,
therefore their responsive influence causes the locks to move."
Yì Fèng's *Fēng Jiǎo Shū* says:
"On the jiǎyín day of spring,
wind blows high, three or four zhàng above the ground.
Branches sing,
coming from the shēn direction.
It signifies a great pardon,
expected within sixty days."
Great Grace; Small Favors
The *Dōng Guān Hàn Jì* says:
"In the first year of Emperor Zhāng's reign,
he pardoned all prisoners under custody in the empire,
those before the bǐngzǐ day of the fourth month,
had their death sentences reduced by one degree and were not to be flogged.
For those ordered to go to Jīnchéng, but the text did not cover fugitives who had not been discovered,
Guō Gōng submitted a sealed memorial saying:
'I humbly consider that the great grace
surely cleanses and pardons all,
those guilty of crimes punishable by death and below
all receive the gift of renewed life,
yet fugitives who are captured
alone do not receive this beneficence.
Your servant believes that those who committed crimes punishable by death before the pardon but were imprisoned after the pardon
could all be spared flogging.
Ordered to go to Jīnchéng,
to preserve human lives,
would benefit the frontier.'
The Emperor approved of it,
and immediately issued an edict pardoning them."
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guózhì* says:
"During the time of Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng,
some said that the Duke was sparing with pardons.
Liàng replied:
'Governing is based on great virtue,
not on small favors.
Therefore Kuāng Héng and Wú Hàn did not wish to grant pardons.
The Late Emperor also said,
"When I moved among Chén Yuánfāng
and Zhèng Kāngchéng,
each time we met,
they exhaustively discussed the ways of order and chaos,
yet never once discussed pardons."
Look at Liú Jǐngshēng and his son,
year after year granting pardons and forgiveness,
what benefit was it to governance?'"
Personally Ploughing; Personally Attending to Governance
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"In the first month of the fourth year of the Tàishǐ era,
the imperial field was first established.
On the dīnghài day,
the Emperor led the assembled officials to personally plough a thousand mǔ,
and granted a great pardon to all under heaven."
The *Wú Zhì* says:
"In the fourth month of the second year of the Tàipíng era of Sūn Liàng,
Liàng attended the main hall,
granted a great pardon to all under heaven,
and began personally attending to governmental affairs."
Eastern Inspection Tour; Southern Suburban Sacrifice
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Xù Hàn Shū* says:
"In the second month of the second year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng,
the Emperor made an eastern inspection tour to Mount Tài.
Reaching Dàizōng,
he performed the chái sacrifice, gazed afar, and ordered the sacrifices to the mountains, rivers, and multitude of spirits,
and granted a great pardon to all under heaven."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"On the xīnyǒu day of the first month of the sixth year of the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì,
the Emperor went to the southern suburb,
and granted a great pardon to all under heaven."
River Blocked, Lake Opened
The Book of Han states:
"In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ, in the fourth month,
he personally visited the breached river,
blocked the river embankment,
composed the 'Gourd Song',
and pardoned the convicts along the route."
Also, the Records of Wú states:
"In the first year of the Tiānxǐ era of Sūn Hào,
Wú Commandery reported
that Línpíng Lake had been choked with weeds since the end of the Hàn dynasty.
Now it had cleared and opened again.
Elders passed down that within a stone box by this lake
was a small stone, greenish-white in color,
four cùn long,
and over two cùn wide.
It was inscribed with the characters for 'emperor'.
Therefore, the era name was changed and a great amnesty was declared."
Silver Seal, Jade Seal
The Records of Wú states:
"In the first year of the Tiāncè era of Sūn Hào,
Wú Commandery reported digging up a silver seal,
one chǐ long,
three fēn wide,
inscribed with characters for the year and month.
Therefore, the era name was changed and a great amnesty was declared."
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Zhào states:
"When Liú Yuānhǎi moved the capital to Píngyáng,
a jade seal was obtained from the Fén River waters.
The inscription read:
'Yǒu xīn bǎo zhī guī Yuānhǎi' (May the newly protected return to Yuānhǎi).
It was likely a seal from the time of Wáng Mǎng.
The presenter had added three characters to it.
Yuānhǎi considered it an auspicious sign for himself,
and declared a great amnesty throughout the land, changing the era name."
Ascending the Terrace, Establishing the Altar
Sīmǎ Biāo's Continuation of the Book of the Later Hàn states:
"In the second year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng, on the Xīnwèi day of the first month,
he performed the ancestral sacrifice to Emperor Guāngwǔ in the Bright Hall.
After the sacrifice,
he ascended the Spiritual Terrace,
gazed upon the clouds and atmospheric phenomena,
and declared a great amnesty throughout the land."
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn states:
"In the twelfth month of the second year of the Xiánxī era,
the Emperor then established an altar
and received the Mandate south of the suburbs.
Proceeding to the front of the Tàijí Hall,
he declared a great amnesty throughout the land."
Divine Light, Fragrant Air
The Book of Han states:
"An edict from the sixth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ said:
'We sacrificed at Shǒu Mountain,
and precious objects emerged from the fields of Kūn,
some transforming into yellow gold.
When sacrificing to the Earth Deity,
divine light shone thrice.
Therefore, pardon those in Fényīn sentenced to death and below.'"
Hé Fǎshèng's Book of the Restoration of Jìn states:
"An edict from the first year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng said:
'The officials followed the statutes and rituals,
reverently performing the suburban sacrifices.
After the burnt offering was made and the spirits enjoyed it,
a fragrant and pure air arose.
Therefore, pardon all under heaven,
so that all may have a chance to reform themselves.'"
Cranes Lingering, Phoenixes Soaring
The Book of Han:
"An edict said:
'We performed the suburban sacrifice and appeared before the Supreme Deity,
and toured the northern border.
Above, We saw a flock of cranes lingering and stopping,
and radiant scenes appearing together.
Therefore, pardon all under heaven.'
Another edict said:
'Auspicious signs appear together,
phoenixes and fenghuang birds soar together.
Therefore, pardon all under heaven.'"
Sweet Dew Descends, Auspicious Star Appears
The Book of Han states:
"An edict from the second month of the second year of the Shénquè era of Emperor Xuān said:
'Recently, phoenixes gathered,
sweet dew descended upon the capital,
and flocks of birds followed them in the tens of thousands.
Therefore, pardon all under heaven.'"
The Records of Shǔ states:
"In the first year of the Jǐngyào era of the Later Sovereign,
an auspicious star appeared.
Therefore, a great amnesty was declared and the era name was changed."
The 'Rhapsody on the Great Amnesty' by Cuī Shí of the Later Hàn
In the second year of the Hàn, in the fourth month, a great amnesty was declared,
washing away evil, discarding filth,
and making a fresh start with all within the seas,
earnestly pondering the path to peace and prosperity.
Shí thereupon composed this rhapsody,
believing that while the Five Emperors had different systems
and the Three Kings different affairs,
their inheriting Heaven and relying on Earth,
and establishing laws and institutions,
was one and the same.
Your Majesty, with Heaven-encompassing greatness,
continuing the traces of former sages,
diligently attends to myriad affairs by day,
and is reverent and vigilant by night.
Yet still pained that punishments have not ceased,
you are about to declare a great amnesty throughout the land,
thereby creating the traces of great peace, and so on."
It also says:
"We shall part the dark clouds,
shine upon the auspicious star,
gather fine grain from the border fields,
collect calendrical plants in the courtyard steps.
We shall stroke the fleshy horn of the qílín,
listen to the harmonious cry of the fènghuáng.
Even the divine transformation of Fúxī,
how could it surpass this great peace?"
Shěn Quánqī's 'Poem on Observing the Amnesty at Tiānmén'
The sage pardons all under heaven,
the dark key moves the round prison gates.
The six jiǎ welcome the yellow ether,
the three primordials bestow purple mud.
The young drummer ascends the western drum,
the rooster of the broad square shakes and leaps.
Song and dance bring forth gold and silk,
vastness covers the distant multitudes.
Also, 'Poem in Reply to Nìng Àizhōu Reporting the Amnesty'
A letter reports the amnesty from the heavens,
the news reaches men from across the sea.
The nine springs open to the white sun,
six wings soar from the azure clouds.
Fate, by chance, receives grace's loan first,
lonely feelings, wronged, remain unresolved.
I pity myself, distinct as the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
who will plead my case to the enlightened lord?
Liáng Shěn Yuē's 'Edict for the Amnesty Following the Southern Suburban Sacrifice'
We rise at dawn and early morning,
pondering these principles of governance.
But Our clarity does not illuminate afar,
and broadening it is not easy.
Looking up, We seek the brilliant achievements of the past,
thinking to bring about peace and prosperity.
Recently, there have been many incidents,
war chariots appearing in successive eras.
Military administration and state ceremonies,
matters and sequences are not uniform.
Punishments and rites are used together,
yet harmony has not been fully achieved.
The feelings of those facing the corner,
We constantly reflect upon with increased sighs.
Now the suburban sacrifice is fully performed,
the hidden and the manifest truly follow.
The grace honors auspicious blessings,
bestowing them upon the myriad people.
Let a great amnesty be declared throughout the land.
The Shuōwén states:
"Shǎng (reward) means
bestowing upon those who have merit.
Cì (bestowal) means
a command,"
as seen in Zhèng Xuán's annotation to the Lǐjì.
It also means favor."
As seen in Hé Yàn's annotation to the Lún Yǔ.
The Shū says:
"For abundant virtue, bestow office;
for abundant merit, bestow reward."
It also says:
"Those who obey commands are rewarded before the ancestral temple;
those who disobey commands are executed before the altar of the soil."
It also says:
"For great merit there is generous reward;
for those who do not follow the way there is public execution."
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn says:
"The ancient rulers of men
encouraged reward and were cautious about punishment,
and were tireless in their compassion for the people.
Rewards were given in spring and summer,
punishments in autumn and winter.
When about to give a reward, they would increase the feasts;
increasing the feasts meant bestowing surplus bounty.
This is how we know they encouraged reward."
The Lǐjì says:
"When the Son of Heaven bestows musical instruments upon the feudal lords,
he uses a zhù (percussion instrument) to present them;
when bestowing musical instruments upon the bó, zǐ, and nán ranks,
he uses a táo (drum) to present them.
'Present' means holding them to convey the command.
Only after a feudal lord is bestowed with bow and arrows may he launch a punitive expedition;
only after being bestowed with the axe of authority may he execute;
only after being bestowed with the guīzàn (jade libation ladle) may he offer fragrant wine."
It also says:
"When the ruler bestows a carriage and horses,
one rides in them to pay respects;
when bestowing clothes,
one wears them to pay respects for the gift.
If the ruler has not given the command,
one does not immediately ride or wear them.
In all bestowals,
the gentleman and the petty man do not receive them on the same day.
This is the principle of reward and bestowal."
Ten Thousand Mǔ of Land / A Thousand Zhōng
The Shǐjì says:
"Lièhóu of Zhào was fond of music.
Three singers from Zhèng
were bestowed with ten thousand mǔ of land."
The Jiāyǔ says:
"Confucius said:
'Since Jìsūn bestowed upon me a thousand zhōng,
my friendships have grown closer.'"
Gold Hook / Jade Jué
The Dōngguān Hànjì says:
"Yáng Cì, having been dismissed from office due to illness and residing at home,
not long after,
was appointed Tàicháng.
An edict bestowed upon him a suit of clothes from the Imperial Wardrobe,
along with the cap, headcloth, sash, jade hú, leather belt, and gold-inlaid hook pendant he himself wore."
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
"Féng Fáng served as Shìzhōng,
and was gradually promoted to Wèiwèi.
He was able to please his contemporaries
and was favored by Emperor Ān.
The emperor visited his residence,
stayed for ten days drinking,
and bestowed upon him a rhinoceros-horn patterned jade-fitted sash pendant knife, a purple-ài sash, and a jade jué."
Purple Sash / Blue Lamb Fur
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
"Féng Fáng was favored by Emperor Ān,
who bestowed upon him a purple-ài sash."
Gě Hóng's Xījīng Zájì says:
"Emperor Chéng was fond of playing cùjū (kickball).
The ministers felt cùjū was too strenuous for the body
and not fitting for one of his exalted status.
The emperor said:
'I enjoy it.
You may select something similar but not strenuous and present it to me.'
Mǎ Hé made a tánqí (a kind of board game) and presented it.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon him a blue lamb fur robe and purple silk shoes,
which he wore for court audiences."
Accumulating Thousands / Tens of Thousands
The Hànshū says:
"Wèi Qīng's elder sister Zǐfū entered the palace and gained the emperor's favor.
Qīng was then serving at Jiànzhāng Palace,
and was not yet well-known.
Emperor Wǔ thereupon summoned Qīng and made him Supervisor of Jiànzhāng and Shìzhōng.
Rewards and bestowals within a few days accumulated to a thousand catties of gold."
The Wèi Zhì says:
"Emperor Míng once dreamed of the empress,
and then ranked the closeness and status of her maternal relatives,
appointing and employing them with varying degrees,
and bestowing rewards amounting to tens of thousands."
Gān's Fields / Sū's Residence
The Shǐjì says:
"Gān Luó requested of Marquis Wén:
'Lend me five chariots,
and allow me to first report to Marquis Wén on behalf of Zhāng Táng.'
The Marquis then spoke of this to the First Emperor.
Sent as envoy to Zhào,
King Xiāng of Zhào welcomed him at the outskirts.
Gān Luó persuaded Zhào to attack Yān,
gaining thirty cities of Shànggǔ,
and letting Qín have eleven of them.
Gān Luó returned and reported to Qín.
He was then enfeoffed and made Shàngqīng,
and furthermore, the fields and residence of Gān Mào were bestowed upon him."
The Hànshū says:
"When Sū Wǔ first returned from the Xiōngnú,
an edict appointed him Diǎn Shǔguó,
with a salary of two thousand dàn.
He was bestowed two million cash,
two qǐng of public fields,
and one residential compound."
Empress's Garments / Emperor's Clothes
The Dōngguān Hànjì says:
"In the third year of the Yǒngpíng era,
the emperor sent a letter to the King of Dōngpíng, Cāng, saying:
'The years and months startle by their swift passage,
the imperial tombs grow gradually distant.
My solitary heart is grieved and sorrowful.
Now I send to you, King, one chest each of the false hairpiece silk and undergarments of the Empress Guāngliè.
You may look upon them from time to time,
to console your thoughts of the soothing breeze and cold spring.'" Cáo Zhí's memorial, citing an edict, said:
"The Emperor inquires of the King of Yōngqiū:
The late emperor often criticized the Hàn emperors
for hoarding clothing and coverlets,
letting them decay in chests and boxes.
His final edict ordered that the clothes and coverlets he wore be bestowed upon the dukes, kings, ministers, officials, and various generals.
Now thirteen kinds are bestowed upon you, King."
Pair of Jade Discs / Thousand Pieces of Gold
The Shǐjì says:
"Yú Qīng was
a traveling persuader.
Treading in straw sandals and carrying a bamboo rain hat,
he persuaded King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
At the first audience, he was bestowed a hundred yì of gold
and a pair of white jade discs.
At the second audience, he was made Shàngqīng of Zhào,
hence he was called Yú Qīng."
The Hànshū says:
"King Xiào of Liáng attracted and hosted heroic men from all quarters.
Gōngsūn Guǐ of Qí had many strange and cunning schemes.
On the day of their first meeting,
the king bestowed upon him a thousand pieces of gold,
and his office reached Zhōngwèi."
Clarifying Virtue / Assessing Merit
The Guǎnzǐ says:
"Clear rewards are not wasteful;
clear punishments are not cruel.
When rewards and punishments are clear,
it is the height of virtue."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Loyal ministers in serving their lord
assess their merit before accepting reward,
not accepting anything improperly;
measure their strength before accepting office,
not coveting rank and salary.
What they are capable of, they accept without declining."
Jade Hú / Gold Casket
"Jade hú" has already been seen in the note for "jade jué."
Zhāng Héng's "Inscription for the Sash Casket Preface" says:
"The Grand Administrator of Nányáng, Bào Dé,
had an edict-bestowed sash and gold casket.
I composed an inscription for it, saying:
'How fine is this casket,
wherein treasure spirits are stored.
Gold tassels and patterned slippers,
their designs daily trustworthy.'"
Gold Knife / Pearl-Studded Sword
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū says:
"The Wǔlíng Wǔxī barbarians caused trouble.
An edict dispatched the Chariot and Cavalry General Féng Gǔn to campaign south.
Gǔn memorialized that Yìng Fèng should be given a set of gold-inlaid knives."
Shěn Yuē's Sòng Shū says:
"Tàizōng, when he was Governor of Xúzhōu,
was bestowed by the Empress Dowager Zhāo with a fire-pearl-decorated lùlu sword."
Receiving the Northern States, Opening Nányáng
The Máo Shī says:
"Its Zhuī and its Mò,
All received the northern states."
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"The Marquis of Hán entered the court of King Xuān,
Who restored him to the old office of his ancestors.
He was granted the Zhuī and Mò,
Receiving the northern states."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"The Marquis of Jìn paid court to the King,
Who gave him the fields of Yángfán, Wēn, Yuán, Cuánmáo,
And thus Jìn first opened Nányáng."
Bó from Rǔnán, Coins from Liáodōng
The Hàn Shū says:
"Emperor Xuān issued an edict:
'Recently, phoenixes gathered in Xīncài,
Thus I bestow one hundred bolts of bó upon the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán.'"
The Dōngguān Hàn Jì says:
"Jì Tóng served as Grand Administrator of Liáodōng for thirty years,
Without storing extra clothes.
Emperor Shìzǔ praised his achievements,
And bestowed one million coins."
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem Bestowed Upon Fáng Xuánlíng by the Civil and Martial Sage Emperor"
The immortal boat on Tàiyè Lake is distant,
In the Western Garden hides a man of great talent.
Before dawn, the war chariots cross,
At cockcrow, the pass opens early.
Also, "Poem Bestowed Upon Xiāo Yǔ"
In fierce wind, the tough grass is known;
In dim daylight, the loyal minister is discerned.
The brave man does not understand righteousness,
The wise man surely cherishes benevolence.
Suí Dynasty Xǔ Shànxīn's "Poem Composed in Response to a Bestowed Poem"
The emperor's way belongs to peace and prosperity,
Astronomical signs are observed in advance.
This life receives nurturing and transformation,
Broadly bestowed, containing much nourishment.
In the Zhèngshǐ era, imperial prestige was revived,
Sitting properly, lingering in fond thoughts.
Evening audience, participating as a close attendant,
Morning grace, lavishly receiving great reward.
Warm trees value silence,
Overcoming hardships, hoping for no error.
Táng Zhōngzōng's "Decree Rewarding Zhāng Rényuàn by the Filial and Harmonious Emperor"
I have heard that generals and commanders achieve merit,
Originally for the sake of the state.
The emperor bestows rewards,
To repay those of outstanding service.
The Commissioner with Discretionary Powers, Grand Commander of the Shuòfāng Circuit, Great General of the Right Garrison Guard Zhāng Rényuàn,
His bearing is upright and elegant,
His demeanor outstanding and heroic.
His strategies are concealed in the jade tent,
His trust placed heavily on the golden altar.
Thus he has repeatedly overseen civil and military affairs,
And served in border garrisons.
As shepherd of Jìmén,
There were no worries of looking east;
Commanding troops at Yúsài,
Just relieved concerns of northern invasion.
Moreover, he personally led the soldiers,
Carrying earth to build the city.
Traversing the crescent moon on the heavenly street,
Splitting long clouds along the earth's veins.
He should be listed for rewards of rivers and mountains,
To honor the glory of belts and whetstones.
He is advanced to the title of Duke of Hánguó,
Bestowed with three hundred rolls of goods,
And one set of clothing.
Also, "Edict Bestowing Clothing and Goods Upon Prince Qiānlǐ of Chéng"
Patrolling the royal guard by day,
Keeping watch over the lofty corridors at night.
Being called claws and teeth,
Truly considered the heart and abdomen.
Great General of the Left Golden Bird Guard, Prince Qiānlǐ of Chéng,
His reputation surpasses the Pèi Xiàn,
His virtue exceeds the Two Nán.
With the high rank of the cornerstone,
Shouldering the heavy responsibility of the Golden Bird.
Detecting treachery without equal,
Pursuing the cunning like a god.
Thus his might shakes a thousand households,
His diligence is proclaimed in the five commands.
Recently, within the guard formation,
There were fraudulent and deceptive persons.
Without a moment's delay,
He swiftly ordered their capture.
The title of capable official,
Has long spread his fragrance.
The name of being fit for duty,
From now on is prominently noted.
He may be bestowed one set of clothing,
Along with one hundred rolls of goods.
Tributes and Offerings, Part Three
The Guǎngyǎ says:
"Gòng,
Is tax,
Is presenting upward."
Zhèng Xuán says:
"Xiàn,
Is offering,
Is delivering,
Is belonging,
Is presenting.
All mean delivering goods to a person,
The meaning of honoring."
The Zhōu Lǐ:
"Presenting the writings of the worthy and capable to the king."
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"Xiàn,
Is offering."
Also says:
"Offering game to sacrifice to the earth god."
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"Xiàn,
Is delivering,
Is belonging."
Also says:
"In ancient times, delivering goods to a person,
Honoring was called xiàn,
Commonly giving was called kuì."
The Máo Shī Jiān says:
"Xiàn,
Is presenting."
According to the Shàng Shū:
"Yǔ distinguished the nine provinces,
According to the land, they made tribute.
Goods that could be specially presented were called gòng,
Those placed in baskets and presented were called fěi.
If not annually tributary,
Requiring an order to bestow before tribute was called xī gòng,
Thus Yǎnzhōu's tribute was lacquer and silk,
Qīngzhōu's tribute was salt and fine hemp cloth, sea products of all kinds, silk and hemp from Dàiquǎn, lead, pine, and strange stones;
Xúzhōu's tribute was the five-colored earth, summer pheasants from Yǔquǎn, solitary tong trees from Yìyáng, floating chime stones from the Sì River, pearls and fish from the Huáiyí;
Yángzhōu's tribute was the three grades of metal, yáokūn and xiǎodàng bamboo, ivory, hides, feathers, and fur, and timber;
Jīngzhōu's tribute was feathers, fur, ivory, hides, the three grades of metal, chūn, gàn, guā, and bǎi trees, whetstones, grindstones, nú stones, and cinnabar, and jùnlù and hù bamboo;
Yùzhōu's tribute was lacquer, hemp, fine hemp cloth, and zhù cloth;
Liángzhōu's tribute was qiú iron, silver,镂, nú stones, chime stones, bears, brown bears, foxes, and woven hides;
Yōngzhōu's tribute was qiúlin and lánggān;
Yǎnzhōu's fěi was woven patterns;
Qīngzhōu's fěi was yǎn silk;
Xúzhōu's fěi was black and white fine silk;
Yángzhōu's fěi was woven cowries;
Jīngzhōu's fěi was black and浅红 silk, jī beads, and silk ribbons;
Yùzhōu's fěi was fine silk floss;
Yángzhōu's xī gòng was packages of oranges and pomelos;
Yùzhōu's xī gòng was chime stone grinders;
Jīngzhōu's presented xī was large tortoiseshells."
The Zhōu Lǐ uses the nine tributes to supply the needs of the state:
First is sacrificial tribute,
Second is consort tribute,
Third is vessel tribute,
Fourth is silk tribute,
Fifth is wealth tribute,
Sixth is goods tribute,
Seventh is clothing tribute,
Eighth is banner tribute,
Ninth is miscellaneous tribute.
Xiàn refers to what is presented beyond the gòng, fěi, and xī gòng."
The Lǐ Jì says:
"When presenting a chariot and horses, hold the reins;
When presenting a horse, hold the bridle.
When presenting a captive, grasp the right sleeve;
When presenting a zither or lute, hold it with the left hand upward.
When presenting a small table, dust it;
When presenting a staff, hold its end.
These are the regulations."
Wán Oxen, Ornamented Horses
The Zhōu Shū says:
"During King Chéng's time,
The western barbarians presented Bǔlú wán oxen.
Wán oxen are small oxen."
Kǒng Cháo notes:
"Bǔlú are the northwestern Róng of Lú,
Now the Lú River is this."
The Dōngguān Hàn Jì says:
"In the twenty-sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
The Southern Chányú sent an envoy presenting two camels,
And ten ornamented horses."
River Tortoise and Sea Shell
The *Book of Documents* says:
"The nine rivers presented the great tortoise as tribute."
Kong Anguo's commentary states:
"A tortoise measuring one foot two inches is called a great tortoise,
it comes from the waters of the nine rivers."
The *Great Commentary to the Book of Documents* says:
"When the Xia dynasty established the five zones of submission,
their influence reached the four seas,
the southern sea offered fish leather, pearls, precious stones, and great shells."
Zheng Xuan's annotation:
"These were the tribute items.
Shells,
in ancient times, were used as currency."
Green Stone Belt and White Jade Ring
The *Wei Lüe* by Yú Huàn says:
"In the third year of the Yángjiā era of the Hàn,
the king of Shūlè country presented a green stone belt from the Western Sea."
Huángfǔ Mì's *Chronicles of Emperors and Kings* says:
"Xīwángmǔ, admiring Shùn's virtue,
came to present a white jade ring and a jué pendant,
along with a map of the expanded territory."
Fire Mouse and Ice Silkworm
The *Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wei* says:
"In the second month of the second year of the Jǐngchū era,
the Western Regions presented fire-washing cloth."
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Classic of Divine Marvels* says:
"Beyond the southern wilderness there is a volcano,
which burns day and night.
In the fire there is a mouse,
weighing a hundred catties,
with fur over two feet long,
fine as silk,
which can be used to make cloth.
It constantly dwells within the fire,
occasionally coming out.
It is white in color,
and if chased and doused with water,
it dies.
Then its fur is collected and spun,
and woven into cloth."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Records of Omissions* says:
"The ice silkworm is ten inches long,
has scales and horns,
and is covered with snow and frost.
Only then does it form a cocoon.
The cocoon is of five colors,
and when woven into brocade,
it does not get wet in water,
nor does it burn in fire.
In the time of Emperor Táng Yáo,
people from the sea presented it,
and it was used for ceremonial robes."
One Section of Sugarcane and Three Boxes of Pears
Dèng Démíng's *Records of Nánkāng* says:
"The soil of Yúdū county is fertile,
particularly suited for sugarcane,
its flavor and color
are unmatched by that from other counties.
One section yields several dozen pieces,
and the commandery presented it to the imperial court."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi once served as Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
and submitted a memorial saying:
'The fine pears of Shānyáng commandery,
respectfully presented: three boxes of sweet pears.'"
Cinnabar and Black Jade
The *Book of Zhou* says:
"During King Chéng's time,
the four barbarians came to present tribute.
The Bólú people, a southwestern tribe,
were the source of cinnabar."
The *Great Commentary to the Book of Documents* says:
"When the Xia dynasty established the five zones of submission,
their influence reached the four seas,
they oversaw the divine tortoises, the dark valleys, and the black jade."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation:
"These were the tribute items."
Silver Pheasant and Red Crane
Gě Hóng's *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* says:
"The king of Mǐnyuè presented to Emperor Gāozǔ one pair each of silver pheasants.
Emperor Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and richly rewarded the envoy."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Records of Omissions* says:
"The country of Túxiū presented green birds and red cranes,
each one male and one female."
Burning Fragrant Grass and Placing Golden Moss
Guō Zǐhéng's *Records of Penetrating the Obscure* says:
"In the first year of the Yuándǐng era,
the Zhāoxiān Gate was erected on the pavilion,
and fragrant grass lamps were lit.
This grass resembles hemp in shape,
and was presented by the Bēnlú country."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Records of Omissions* says:
"During the time of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the country of Zǔlí presented golden moss.
Its color is like coiled gold,
clustering like chicken eggs.
When placed in water,
it spreads over the ripples like fire.
Palace ladies who were favored
were given this golden moss.
Placed on a lacquer tray,
it illuminated the entire room,
and was called 'night moon.'"
Fúyǐ and Quánmí
The *Book of Zhou* says:
"During King Chéng's time,
the Kāng people presented fúyǐ.
Eating its fruit is said to aid in childbirth."
Kǒng Cháo's annotation says:
"The Kāng people are also a branch of the Western Róng.
Eating fragrant grass (fāngyǐ) leads to pregnancy."
Guō Zǐhéng's *Records of Penetrating the Obscure* says:
"In the first year of the Guānghé era,
the Bōzhī country, also called the Bōyì country,
presented divine essence fragrant grass,
also called quánmí,
and also called chūnwú.
One root produces a hundred stems,
the spaces between its branches are like bamboo joints, soft and pliant.
Its bark is like silk,
and can be made into cloth,
the so-called chūnwú cloth.
It is also called fragrant quán,
firm and dense like ice-silk gauze.
Holding one piece,
fills the entire palace with fragrance.
If women wear it,
the fragrance becomes even more intense."
Fragrant Tangerines and Patterned Melons
Yáng Fú's *Records of Strange Things* says:
"The tangerine tree
has white flowers and red fruit.
The peel is fragrant,
and the inside has a delicious taste.
In Jiāozhǐ, there was one tangerine official,
with a salary of three hundred shi,
responsible for the annual tribute of imperial tangerines."
Wáng Yì's *Rhapsody on Lychees* says:
"How great is the sage emperor!
Residing in the central plains.
The eastern wilds present patterned melons with sparse markings,
the southern shores offer splendid tangerines with yellow rinds."
Ancient Yellow Horse and Zíbái Ox
The *Book of Zhou* says:
"During King Chéng's time,
the Quǎnróng presented a patterned horse.
The patterned horse had a red mane and a white body,
eyes like gold,
and was called the 'ancient yellow' steed."
Kǒng Cháo's annotation says:
"The Quǎnróng
are the most distant of the Western Róng."
Also:
"During King Chéng's time,
the Dàxià presented the zíbái ox.
The zíbái ox
is a wild beast,
with the shape of an ox but the teeth of an elephant."
Kǒng Cháo's annotation says:
"Dàxià
is a northwestern Róng tribe."
Joined-Branch Plums and Heart-Shared Pears
Gě Hóng's *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* says:
"When the Shànglín Park was first built,
ministers from distant places each presented exotic fruits,
among them were joined-branch plums."
Also, Duàn Guīlóng's *Records of Liángzhōu* says:
"During Lǚ Guāng's time,
the Governor of Dūnhuáng, Sòng Xīn, presented heart-shared pears."
Jíguāng Fur and Kūnwú Sword
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Records of the Ten Continents* says:
"In the third year of the Tiānhàn era,
the king of the Western Country sent an envoy to present a Jíguāng fur."
The *Liezi* says:
"When King Mù of Zhōu campaigned against the Western Róng,
they presented a Kūnwú sword.
A red blade,
that cuts jade like cutting mud."
Purple Jade Pot and Green Gold Mirror
The *Jiāozhōu Zá Jì* states:
"In the fourth year of Tàikāng,
King Fàn Néng of Línyì presented one purple crystal spittoon
and two green-white crystal spittoons."
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"Mount Tángyè abounds in water jade."
Guō Pú annotates:
"Water jade is crystal."
Guō Zǐ's *Héng Dòngmíng Jì* states:
On the Wàngchán Pavilion there is a green gold mirror,
four feet wide.
During the Yuánguāng era,
the state of Bōzhī presented this green mirror.
It illuminates and reveals chīmèi,
so that all ghosts dare not conceal their forms."
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Edict in Response to Righteous Men of Jīng and Yōng Presenting Goods"
In the early days of the righteous uprising,
each person was eager to exhaust his own resources.
They paid their taxes and emptied their estates,
united in expressing their sincerity.
Now that the words have matured into a uniform principle,
I think of making some recompense.
For those in the three provinces of Xióng, Jīng, and Yǐng who presented goods to aid the army and state,
the authorities shall carefully consider granting exemptions and rewards.
Emperor Zhōngzōng Xiàohé's "Edict Halting the Presentation of Exquisite and Clever Objects"
I concentrate my thoughts on the purple firmament,
and cleanse my mind at the crimson palace gates.
I examine the shallowness and depth of a thousand ages,
and investigate the order and chaos of a hundred kings.
Thatched palaces and pillars of rushes
are truly the pure strategies for reviving a state;
jade mats and pearl garments
are the corrupt practices that endanger a realm.
Since I inherited Heaven's mandate and continued the succession,
bearing the sun and unfolding the charts,
I have hoped to equal the era of the quail's drink,
and wished to tread in the age of the quail's dwelling.
Emperor Wén of Hàn lifting his shoes
has been my concern since youth;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn burning the fur robe
has been my lifelong intent.
Recently, as the imperial tally was newly established
and the precious temple first ascended,
I observed those princes and dukes,
many of whom made presentations.
None failed to sing dragon songs on fine festivals,
or feast on fragrant mornings.
At the time when pepper flowers were offered in praise,
or on the day when chrysanthemum stamens floated in the wine cups,
some carved gold and inlaid jade,
gathering rare treasures from the six directions;
some cut emerald and tailored crimson,
adorning the grass and trees of the three springs.
Those above extended acceptance,
those below pursued acquisition.
The bustle and confusion grew,
pressuring both public and private.
To achieve peace and prosperity,
such harmful practices are not trivial.
Thinking of this,
I deeply find it unacceptable.
It should be rectified and reformed immediately,
and not persist through inertia.
Recommendation and Selection, Part Four
The *Dàdài Lǐjì* states:
"In ancient times, when the feudal lords presented scholars,
one appropriate selection was called 'fond of virtue,'
a second appropriate selection was called 'worthy,'
and a third appropriate selection was called 'having merit.'
Then they were granted the nine bestowals.
If they did not present scholars,
once, their rank was reduced;
twice, their territory was reduced;
three times, both rank and territory were entirely stripped away."
Both rank and territory were completely removed.
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"The reason feudal lords present scholars to the Son of Heaven
is to advance the worthy and encourage goodness.
The reason the Son of Heaven seeks them through invitation
is his desire for righteousness.
In the way of governing a state,
obtaining worthy men brings order,
losing worthy men brings chaos.
Therefore, in the *Yuèlìng*, in the third month of spring, the storehouses are opened,
silks and fabrics are brought out,
circulated throughout the realm,
to encourage the feudal lords
to invite famous scholars
and treat the worthy with courtesy.
There are both those who present and those who are invited,
because when feudal lords present scholars,
the mediocre present themselves,
while those of great virtue present their reputation.
As for those hidden in obscurity,
whom the feudal lords have overlooked,
the Son of Heaven makes them manifest,
and so invites them.
In the *Zhōuguān*,
the duty of the Minor Minister of Education
is that every three years there is a great comparison,
examining their virtuous conduct and mastery of the arts.
Then the worthy and capable are elevated.
The village elders and village grand masters lead their officials and the multitude,
and treat them as guests with courtesy.
The next day,
the village elders and village grand masters, with the group of officials, present the record of the worthy and capable to the king.
The king bows twice and receives it,
deposits it in the Heavenly Storehouse,
and the Inner Scribe keeps a duplicate.
After retiring, they use the village archery ceremony and five matters to inquire of the multitude.
This is called causing people to elevate the worthy,
sending them out to lead them;
causing the people to elevate the capable,
bringing them in to govern them."
The *Hànshū* states:
"Fifty disciples were established for the Erudites,
exempting them from corvée.
In the commanderies, kingdoms, and counties, if there were officials fond of literature,
the two-thousand-bushel officials carefully examined those suitable,
and sent them together with the accountants to the Grand Master of Ceremonies,
where they could receive instruction like the disciples.
After one year, all were examined on their ability to master the year's arts and above,
and were appointed as Literary Officials or Archivists.
Those of high rank
could become Gentlemen of the Palace.
