The Grand Master of Ceremonies recorded and memorialized;
if there were outstanding talents of exceptional grade,
their names were reported.
During Emperor Zhāo's time,
worthy and excellent literary scholars were recommended,
and the number of Erudite disciples was increased to a full hundred.
Also, each year, forty men of the first class were made Gentlemen of the Palace,
thirty men of the second class were made Attendants of the Heir Apparent,
and twenty men of the third class were appointed as Literary Officials or Archivists, as before.
Furthermore, the marquises and officials of two thousand bushels
and the chancellors of the feudal lords were ordered to recommend worthy and excellent, upright and outspoken, remonstrating scholars,
and the provinces were ordered to examine officials and people with outstanding talents and exceptional abilities who could serve as generals or ministers or envoys to distant states.
The commanderies and kingdoms were ordered to recommend those filial and fraternal, with righteous conduct known in their villages,
the three capital regions and the Grand Master of Ceremonies were ordered to recommend the worthy and excellent,
and the commanderies and kingdoms were ordered to recommend those of high rank.
From then on, among the dukes, ministers, grand masters, and officials,
many were cultivated literary scholars.
This is the system of recommendation and selection."
Elevating to Office and Assisting in Governance
The *Shàngshū* states:
"The Emperor said:
'Who will advise on elevating to office those who are timely?'"
The commentary of Kǒng Ānguó states:
"Chóu means who; yōng means to employ.
Who can handle all affairs in accordance with this? He will be elevated and employed."
It also states:
"Shùn said:
'I consult with the Four Peaks.
Is there anyone who can diligently apply himself to glorify the Emperor's affairs,
to be placed in charge of all officers,
to assist in governance and benefit the categories?'"
Recommending the Humble and Promoting in the Purple Court
The *Hánzǐ* states:
Zhào Wǔ recommended forty-six men to his lord,
and when Zhào Wǔ died,
all forty-six men attended as guests.
Such was his lack of private favor.
It also states:
"Zhào Wǔ recommended sixty families of humble scholars and storehouse keepers."
Liú Kūn's "Recommending Rèn Yóu" states:
"I humbly observe that the Assistant Chief Clerk Rèn Yóu
has broad understanding and simple greatness.
His heart is steadfast and firm.
If I can have him respond and promote in the purple court,
he will surely be able to shelter from frost and dew,
increase the glory of the terrace's radiance,
undertake the duty of assisting in governance,
and broaden the principle of urgently seeking the worthy."
Upright and Filially Incorrupt
The *Hànshū* states:
"Emperor Wǔ's edict said:
'The Chancellor, Imperial Counselor, marquises, officials of two thousand bushels, and chancellors of feudal lords
shall recommend worthy, excellent, and upright scholars.'"
Another edict of Emperor Wǔ said:
"Now the edict illuminates the sagely legacy of the former emperor,
ordering the two-thousand-bushel officials to recommend the filially incorrupt.
This is to transform the common people and shift customs."
Presenting a Letter and Casting Away the Official Tablet Chén Shòu’s *Yìbù Qíjiù Zhuàn* says:
“Yán Yǔ, styled Zǐyì,
served as the Gōngcáo in the commandery.
The Inspector recruited him as a Cóngshì,
and the commandery recommended him as a Xiàolián.
He said, ‘A great scholar offers his name;
an inferior scholar offers his person.
To present a letter and offer one’s person
is not the way of a noble scholar.’
He declined the Xiàolián recommendation,
sought a post in the Ministry of Personnel,
and was appointed Magistrate of Wúxī.”
Zhōu Fěi’s *Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn* says:
“Huáng Mù, styled Zǐjìng,
was a man of Ānchéng.
He served as the commandery’s Zhǔbù,
loyal to his superiors and leading his subordinates.
When the court was in order,
the Grand Administrator Jīng Yù recommended Mù as a Xiàolián.
Mù then recommended and yielded to Yīn Zhòngcái.
Yù did not listen,
so Mù, holding his official tablet, went to see Yù and said:
‘As for someone like Zhòngcái,
he is foremost among the six selections.
If I precede him,
it will only give rise to criticism and debate.’
He then cast his tablet inside
and, upon leaving, took to his bed ill.
Yù realized he could not be swayed,
and so followed his wish.”
Benefiting the Guest and Fulfilling the Tribute The *Zhōuyì* says:
“Observing the glory of the state,
it is beneficial to be a guest of the king.”
The *Hànshū* states:
“Cháo Cuò’s policy memorial said:
‘Your humble servant fulfills the tribute.’”
Raised Carriages and Adorned Silk The *Yì Shī* says:
“High and raised are the carriages and chariots,
they summon me with a bow.”
Shīzǐ says:
‘Yáo had a banner for establishing the good.’” The *Hànshū* says: “They summoned Méi Chéng with a comfortable carriage and cattail-lined wheels.”
The *Yì* says:
“Bundles of silk, modest and few,
adorn the hills and gardens.”
Bow and Banner, Cattail and Silk Both are explained in the notes above.
Recommending the Upright and Advancing Unusual Strategies The *Hànshū* says:
“Emperor Wǔ issued an edict to the Chancellor, the Imperial Counselor, the Marquises, the officials of two thousand piculs, and the Chancellors of the feudal states,
to recommend worthy, good, upright, and forthright scholars who offer extreme remonstrance.”
It also says:
“After Wèi Wúzhī recommended Chén Píng,
the King of Hàn made him a Deputy General.

saying he had an affair with his sister-in-law and accepted bribes.
The King of Hàn became suspicious
and reproached Wúzhī.
Wúzhī replied:
‘What I spoke of was his ability;
what Your Majesty asks about is his conduct.
Now, if one had the conduct of Wěishēng or Xiàojǐ,
but was of no benefit to the outcome of victory or defeat,
how would Your Majesty have the leisure to employ him?
Now Chǔ and Hàn confront each other;
I recommended a man of unusual strategies.
I consider that his plans are truly sufficient to benefit the state.
As for an affair with his sister-in-law and accepting bribes,
why should that be cause for suspicion?’”
Presenting to the Heavenly Court and Recommending to the Prime Minister Yú Yù’s *Jìn Shū* says:

served as Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng Commandery.

The *Bié Zhuàn of Zhào Mù* says:

so he supported and urged him with fervent persuasion,

Model for the Hundred Officials and Transforming the Nine Regions Fàn Yè’s *Hòu Hàn Shū* says:
“Chén Zhōng, the Imperial Secretary, submitted a memorial recommending Liú Kǎi, saying:

his advancement and withdrawal followed the proper measure.
The hundred officials look to him as a model,
and all within the seas turn to him with admiration.’” Also, Hé Fǎshèng’s *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
“Huán Wēn submitted a memorial recommending Qiáo Xiù, saying:
‘I have privately heard that Qiáo Xiù of Bāxī,
upholds integrity with steadfastness,
embracing virtue in secluded retirement.
If he were to receive a summons with cattail and silk,

guide and instruct the boisterous populace.
The remote and distant would look up to his influence,
and the nine regions would know transformation.’”
Holding the Brush at the Vermilion Steps and Discussing the Way in the Purple Palace Dù Yù’s *Memorial Recommending Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng* says:
“Consider Sū Zàn, who spreads his conduct in the wilds,
and manifests virtue among the villages,
his heart is open and his intentions straightforward.

and be consulted for upright words,

Lù Yún’s *Writing Recommending Zhāng Zhān* says:
“If he were given a position to speak and advise,
dressed in formal attire at the Grand Academy,
overseeing and compiling the arts and literature,
with his cap-strings hanging at the jade steps,
discussing the Way in the Purple Palace,

Adding Luster to Sun and Moon and Shedding Light Like Rainbow and Nebula Sīmǎ Biāo’s *Xù Hàn Shū* says:
“Chén Fān

Their moral conduct is pure and complete,
and is well-known among the people.

and assisted in illuminating the heavenly work,

adding luster to the sun and moon.’” Kǒng Róng’s *Memorial Recommending Mí Héng* says:
“I humbly observe the retired scholar Mí Héng.
His fine nature is pure and bright,
his outstanding talent is extraordinary.
If he were to leap like a dragon in the heavenly thoroughfare,

A Linked Verse Poem by Liú Gài and Others of the Liáng Dynasty, “Supervising the Examination of Xiùcai at the Yíxián Hall”
The mighty province tests those of exceptional rank,
in the court’s courtyard, one must respond exclusively.
Looking at learning, it is like fletching arrows;
unusual writing is like brocade embroidery.
Liú Gài: Nurturing orchids, they form splendid fields,
their radiance fills carriages, shining like red beads.
Holding office, I detest the official cap and belt;
weary and ill, I decline fame and rank.
Lú Shùnyǐ: To present a memorial, drink the remainder of the row,
the first class honors illuminate past records.
Profound wonders leave no trace behind,
Sūn and Dǒng have left their manner.
Fú Tǐng: The spring breeze holds grace and turns,
lingering light suddenly bright, then dim.
Outstanding talents continue at the central feast,
a multitude of abilities flourish in the imperial age.
Wáng Yíng: Like a swift fishing line affecting shadow and echo,
cutting cattail leaves to enlighten the ignorant and dim.
Since the carved dragon is already revealed,
blue and purple ribbons will soon be worn.
Wáng Yóng: Admirably, like the sound of jade,
and Gāo Càn also like the gathering of orchids.
The wide river is easily pursued,
the Zī water is not hard to match.
Presented scholars bring glory to the ministerial gates,
searching for worthies exhausts the secluded passes.
Skillful discourse, principle without end,
borrowing books, the heart never wearied.
Coming talents, names east and west,
assisting and illuminating, again exiting and entering.
How splendid indeed is the trust in the present,
and as for me, I attend to plow and spade.
**Edict on Seeking Recommendations for Scholars** by Liáng Rénfǎng
Promoting the worthy and bestowing generous rewards,
Concealing the good and meting out clear punishments—
these were the splendid norms of former kings,
and all must follow them.
I have inherited the grand enterprise,
reverently holding the great treasure,
and think of seeking outstanding talents
to assist in achieving harmonious prosperity.
I have listened widely to the nine merits,
and sought talents even among the lowly.
Yet white colts fill the valleys,
and the *chángchǔ* remains uncut.
Therefore, at court I sigh long,
and wait until the sun slants west.
Let it be ordered to broadly consult the ministers and officials,
each recommending those they know.
We shall measure their talents and appoint the capable,
promoting them without regard to precedence.
Thus may we share in the wisdom of discerning the worthy,
fulfilling Our urgent desire for the virtuous.
**Edict on Recommending Scholars** by Suí Jiāngzǒng
Yáo set up the drum for remonstrance,
Yǔ bowed to forthright words.
Seeking the exceptional,
has long been recorded in former texts.
Recommending those who are submerged,
is also heard of in ancient canons.
These are profound principles of governance,
and urgent tasks for emperors and kings.
I, with my limited virtue and ignorance,
reverently bear the grand succession.
Not yet enlightened, I humble myself,
and as the day wanes, my cares increase.
The hundred affairs are often disordered,
and the four ears do not reach far.
I long to hear honest admonition,
gathering both silent and spoken words.
Let all from the Three Dukes down,
each recommend those they know.
Inquire also among the storekeepers,
and extend to the lowly.
If one person has ability,
or a single phrase is usable,
I shall personally hear and consider it,
awaiting such enlightening counsel.
**Memorial Recommending Hú Yuánxiù** by Shěn Yuē
I humbly consider that governing the state and controlling distant regions,
though they require great worthies,
breaking the enemy's vanguard and braving arrows,
also depend on minor uses.
I observe Hú Yuánxiù, the newly appointed Commandant of Qiántáng,
who in early years dashed about,
his will and capability strong and resolute.
In the use of spear and shield,
his spirit overawes a hundred men.
If placed among the six armies,
or set over a single regiment,
he will surely advance to fight fierce enemies,
and repel the strong Hú.
I am truly weak and timid,
and do not understand military matters.
This ignorant and rash, lightly spoken word
fills me with trembling fear.
**Section on Carrying Out Missions**
Wèi Wǔ's Decree on Selection and Appointment states:
"Sending envoys to the four quarters
is something the ancients were careful in choosing.
Thus Confucius said,
'An envoy! An envoy!'
speaking of its difficulty."
According to the *Zhōu Guān*,
the Minor Messenger is in charge of the ritual registers for guests of the state,
to receive envoys from the four quarters.
For all envoys from the four quarters,
great guests are escorted,
minor guests have their gifts received and their words heard.
The Courier is in charge of minor matters of transmission and urgent messages for the state.
For all his missions,
he must carry a banner and tally.
The *Máo Shī* says:
"'Splendid Are the Flowers'
is about the lord sending an envoy.
'Four Steeds'
is about comforting the envoy upon his return."
Also, the *Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"During the Zhōu and Qín dynasties, they often in the eighth month of the year sent light-carriage envoys to collect dialects of different eras,
who upon returning reported them,
and they were permanently stored in the secret chamber."
The *Hàn Jiù Yí* states:
"Envoys bearing the imperial seal-script documents ride in fast relays,
which are post-horses.
Three riders travel day and night, a thousand *lǐ* as the distance."
Also, the *Shuō Yuàn* says:
"When a wise ruler sends a man,
he entrusts him with the task,
but does not restrict him with words.
In the matter of carrying out missions,
the term for it is 'xínglǐ'."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
"The coming and going of envoys."
Dù Yù's commentary:
"'Xínglǐ'
means envoy."
Envoy
The *Lúnyǔ* says:
"The envoy Zǐyǔ polished it."
The commentary says:
"'Envoy'
is the official in charge of missions."
Whenever the state dispatches an envoy on a mission,
going is called 'receiving the command',
returning is called 'reporting back on the command',
also called 'reporting the command'.
Also called 'returning to report'.

Hán Yáng's *Tiānwén Yàojí* says:

then the envoys are loyal and upright."
"Imperial Splendor" see the narrative section.

I hope you will instruct me,
Announcing at the Pass, Transferring Notification

the king of a western country sent an envoy to present tribute.

continuing unabated for a hundred days.

lingering unbroken for months,
signifying that the Middle Kingdom will have a ruler who values the Way.

Jiāng Zǒng of Suí, "Rhapsody on Declining an Envoy Mission"
In the thirty-sixth year of the Great Liáng,
divine achievements flourished as at creation.
Bestowed grace and stored blessings
surpass the bronze vessels of past dynasties;
the grandeur of splendid virtue
shames the modest stones of the Zhōu era.
The moon's cave faces the wind;
the sun's domain gazes upon its favor.
Distant lands knock at the frontier gates;
all tribes bring repeated translations.
Light carriages patrol the routes;
their fame spreads with every step.
Banners and emblems pass by;
deeds surpass the traces of Yǔ.
Raising the utmost beauty of imperial splendor,
galloping with the many affairs of jade-adorned missions.
Some are peerless as from Jiāngxià,
matching the talents of Luòyáng.
Seeking models of virtue in the court,
honoring the finest among the timber.
Drawing upon the three arts of profound learning,
appreciating ornate writings of the four beginnings.
Yet I, simple and lacking ambition,
receive court duties in due order.
Heaven's phoenix rises and unfurls banners,
crossing dragon sands to deliver tribute.
Keen as Jì Zhá discerning songs,
renowned as Shǔguó bearing the mission.
Longing for Sū Zǐ's clapping hands,
recalling Qiānqiū's drawing on the ground.
I wish to encourage myself and drink plain water,
considering my uselessness and reining in the horse.
Alas, lacking strength to repay grace,
I often feel as if placed among thorns.
Suddenly leaving the joyful goodness of Dōngpíng,
again treading the Chéngmíng Hall to wander and rest.
How different from a thousand-mile gallop,
yet how refuse a single coin's unworthiness?
Truly, I have no hope of a wild goose's ascent,
but think of something like a cicada's wing.
Bearing the drenching favor of virtue,
examining my red folly, unadorned.
Ashamed to borrow praise from zither pegs,
spared long service at the onion pole.
On fleeting days of leisure, a moment's respite,
often chanting long, pent-up and tangled.
Unlike metal or stone that can endure,
but like plants and trees, divided and apart.
Advancing in learning, ashamed of mere branches and leaves,
feeble strength, inadequate for the broad road.
Building Bó Xiū's thatched door,
befriending Zhòng Xiàn's mulberry hinge.
Merely delighting in water, not wisdom;
perhaps relying on the valley to play the fool.
Ashamed to feign fame like the Zhōu guest,
rather be a discordant note in Qí's yuè ensemble.
I offer a life of leisure, reclining and gazing,
Northern Qi, Péi Ràngzhī, "Poem on Feasting and Replying to Southern Envoy Xú Líng at the Official Lodge"
Mount Sōng marks the capital city,
Bell Ridge faces the river ford.
Regions differ in customs and soil,
The celestial divisions each have their stars.
You cross the border to plan affairs for your lord,
I seek alliances, mindful of our neighboring ties.
Your talent is praised as bamboo arrows,
My uselessness shames the silk cords of office.
Rows of music, the song-bells resound,
Banners unfurled, jade and silk displayed.
The royal envoy gloriously receives his charge,
To leave a fine reputation, originally without cause.
Hán Xuān was about to visit Chǔ,
Shēn Xū wished to leave Qín.
Just when we hoped to drink north of the river,
Instead I lie ill by the Zhāng waterside.
Ritual wine brims for the triple offering,
The guest feast is rich with the eight delicacies.
A year of plenty, the bronze sparrow chirps,
Weapons stored away, we sit by the golden men.
Clouds come, the carriage canopy rises at dawn,
Sun sets, evening hastens the wheels.
Different states, yet we are like brothers,
Understanding each other, whether old friends or new.
Zhōu, Yǔ Xìn, "Poem on Carrying Orders to Yè"
A great state performs the rites of diplomatic visits,
Kinship and neighborliness are thus strengthened.
Unfurling banners for the plains and lowlands,
Backed by the screen, I report accomplished words.
Westward, braving wind and dew,
Northward pointing, crossing Huányuán Pass.
Meeting in friendship with a noble scion,
Displaying courtesy, I behold the royal grandson.
How to praise the fine trees?
In vain I rejoice, composing of gathering white artemisia.
Four sacrificial animals fill the carved stands,
Three offerings brim the ritual wine vessels.
A subject has no affairs beyond the borders,
When shall I rejoice in these words?
Customs are already different and obstructed,
Mountains and rivers need no further discussion.
No chance to lodge at the southern guesthouse,
In vain I wish to sacrifice at the western gate.
With lingering thoughts, only this parting,
My long-held hope is that we may both survive.
Suí, Yú Máo, "Poem on Receiving Northern Envoys in the South"
Meeting jade, envoys from the Two Xiáo arrive,
Auspicious tallies return from the Three Qín.
Forest cicadas, sparse, about to cease,
River geese, broken off, still fly.
Walls rise high for the guest lodge,
Banners and canopies enter the royal domain.
Together we encourage this fostering of ties,
Just when we should strengthen bonds of hempen and silk garments.
Liáng, Liú Xiàoyí, "Letter to Marquis Yǒngfēng Upon Returning from a Northern Mission"
Feet tread the cold earth,
Body braves the northern wind.
At dusk lodging in traveler's lodges,
At dawn cooking in posting stations.
Drifting and toiling,
I finally reached the land of felt tents.
The mixed tribes deeply transformed,
Greatly admire the Central States.
But felt tents are hard to linger in,
Kumiss is easily tiresome.
The royal schedule has limits,
The time came to reach the Jade Gate.
The Hu slave who shot deer,
Then returned to the country with me.
The Han envoy's staff carved with dragons,
Was still held entering the frontier pass.
Horses bearing alfalfa in their mouths,
Neigh and stand by the old ruins.
Men obtaining grapes,
Return to plant them in their former villages.
Young sons come out to welcome,
Good neighbors offer greetings.
Weary, grasping crab claws,
Hastily covering shrimp bowls.
My ruddy face unchanged,
Somewhat more often drunk on my own.
Spending the whole day thus,
Also to amuse myself.
Borrowed Category Six
Urgent leave, Requested leave, Leave of peace,
Are all names for休假 (leave/休假).
The *Shìmíng* says:
"Urgent (急),
means 'to reach' (及).
It refers to pressing matters that cause one to be reached or to reach [the matter]."
The *Lǐ Fěi Hànshū* says:
"Requested leave (告),
means 'to request' (请).
It means requesting leave for an audience.
Leave of peace (宁),
means 'peace' (安).
Requested leave is called '宁'."
The *Hàn Laws* state:
"For officials of two thousand piculs rank, there is '予告' (granted leave) and '赐告' (bestowed leave).
'予告' is for those in office who have the highest merit,
which by law they ought to receive.
'赐告' is for those who have been ill for three full months and should be dismissed.
The Son of Heaven graciously bestows this leave upon them,
allowing them to take their seal and ribbons, lead their subordinates, and return home to treat their illness.
By the time of Emperor Chéng,
commandery officials of two thousand piculs rank who received '赐告' could not return home;
this began with Féng Yěwáng.
休假 is also called '休沐' (rest and wash)."
The *Hàn Laws* state:
"Officials may have one下沐 (wash) every five days,
meaning rest for washing."
The *Jìn Statutes* state:
"For urgent leave (急假),
one may have five urgent leaves per month.
Within one year,
the limit is sixty days.
For those within a thousand *lǐ*, illness may be extended for twenty days,
and for travel delays and reasons, ninety-five days.
This is the matter.
In documents it is called '归休' (return and rest),
also called '休急', '休澣', '取急', '请急'.
There is also '长假' (long leave) and '併假' (combined leave)."
Bestowed Leave Distributed Rest
"Bestowed Leave" is seen in the narrative.
The *Biography of Wáng Wēi* says:
"Wēi in his youth was a commandery clerk.
Governor Liú Biǎo posted on the gate:
'If anyone can propose beneficial measures for the times,
regardless of whether they are menial servants or lowly, let it be reported.'
Wēi accordingly presented matters,
and was appointed as a provincial clerk,
during the great La festival, rest was distributed."
Shouldering a Load Walking with a Staff
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū* says:
"Xǔ Jīng, styled Zǐzhāng,
lost his father young,
and served his mother filially.
His family was poor, and he served as a clerk,
having no boat or carriage.
On休假,
he would often walk alone, shouldering a load up and down,
his pure integrity praised in his village."
It also says:
"Fàn Dān, styled Shǐyún,
was from Chénliú.
He served as the commandery's merit officer.
Every time he went on休假 up and down,
he would often walk alone with a staff.
His colleagues offered him ox-carts,
but he would not take them."
Zhù Visiting the Sick Wú Paying Respects to Elders
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū* says:
"Zhù Hào, styled Zǐchūn,
had a lofty and ardent will and integrity,
and was sincere in benevolence and righteousness.
When returning home on休假 as an official,
he would first circulate in his village,
condoling with the bereaved and visiting the sick,
and only then return home."
It also says:
"Wú Féng, styled Zǐgāo,
served as a provincial and commandery clerk.
On休假,
he would first comfort and assist those in mourning and filial sons,
next visit the sick, and after finishing,
pay respects and visit the village elders and advanced scholars,
and only then arrive home.
His fame shone far and wide."
The Shuōwén states:
"Wū Péng first created medicine."
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"The Yellow Emperor ordered Qí Bó to taste the flavors of plants and trees,
and to oversee medical treatment and cure diseases.
The books on prescriptions and materia medica of today all originated from this."
The Zhōuguān states:
"The Physician of Diseases is in charge of the illnesses of the myriad people;
in all four seasons there are epidemic diseases.
In spring there is the headache illness,
in summer there is the itchy scabies illness,
in autumn there is the malarial cold illness,
in winter there is the cough and panting illness.
Xiāo means
aching and wasting.
Head illness means
head disease.
Use the five grains and five medicines to nurture their illness;
nurture here means to treat.
Use the five colors, five qi, and five sounds to observe their life or death.
Examine them through the changes of the nine orifices,
and correlate them with the movements of the five viscera.
For all among the people who have diseases,
divide and treat them."
It also says:
"The Physician of Sores is in charge of swellings, ulcers, metal wounds, and broken-bone sores.
For all treatment of sores,
use the five poisons to attack them,
use the five qi to nurture them,
use the five medicines to treat them,
and use the five flavors to regulate them."
The Wùlǐ Lùn states:
"As for physicians,
those without benevolence and love cannot be entrusted,
those without intelligence and clear understanding cannot be appointed,
those without integrity, purity, and goodness cannot be trusted.
Therefore, in ancient times when employing physicians,
they would certainly select those from renowned families.
Their virtue must be capable of benevolence, forgiveness, and broad love;
their wisdom must be capable of clear exposition and subtle comprehension.
They must be able to know the order of heaven, earth, and the spirits,
able to understand the principles of life, fate, fortune, and misfortune,
distinguish the boundaries of deficiency and excess,
and determine the measures of conformity and rebellion.
They assess the severity of the illness,
and measure the amount of the medicinal formula,
penetrating the subtle and reaching the obscure,
not missing even the smallest details.
Only such can be called excellent physicians.
Moreover, the Daoist school values cold,
because plants and trees grow in the cold;
the medical school values warmth,
because the blood vessels flow smoothly with warmth.
If one only knows the general principles,
without comprehending the detailed reasoning,
not knowing that hardness and softness have their degrees of severity,
that seasonal nodes have their varying amounts,
and that progression, regression, fullness, and contraction have their measures and limits,
then a renowned physician who understands the pulses,
seeking them at the cùnkǒu,
can obtain them within the three examinations.
He gauges the seasonal nodes and observes warmth and cold,
correlates pulse theory and matches severity,
and measures medicines and minerals so they all correspond.
This can be called a renowned physician.
There are physicians who are renowned but not good,
and those who are unknown but good.
When a ruler employs physicians,
he must investigate and know them, and then evaluate and select them."
Six Skills Four Schools
Fàn Yè's Hòuhànshū states:
"Guō Yù was
a person from Guǎnghàn.
Initially, there was an old man fishing in the Fú River,
hence called Fú Wēng.
He wrote the Zhēnjīng and Pulse Methods.
His disciple Chéng Gāo sought them for many years,
and the old man then transmitted them to him.
Yù in his youth served Gāo as teacher,
studying the skills of prescription diagnosis and the six subtleties,
and became a Deputy of the Imperial Physicians."
Liú Xīn's Qī Lüè states:
"It discusses the technical arts as comprising four schools:
there is the Medical Classics school, the Prescriptions school, the Bedchamber Arts school, and the Immortals school."
Nine Breaks Ten Perfect
The Chǔcí states:
"One becomes a physician after breaking an arm nine times."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The Chief Physician is in charge of the government orders concerning medicine,
gathers poisonous medicines for medical use,
and at year's end audits the medical affairs.
Ten perfect cures is considered superior,
one failure in ten is next,
four failures in ten is considered inferior."
Feeling the Pulse Attacking the Texture
The Shǐjì states:
"Biǎn Què said to the Zhōngshùzǐ of the Guó crown prince:
'When Yuè Rén practices medicine,
he does not rely solely on feeling the pulse, observing the complexion,
listening to the voice, and inquiring about the form.'" Yuán Zhǔn's Zhèng Lùn states:
"An excellent physician treats disease
by attacking the texture of the skin and muscles."
Master Hand Great Art
Sīmǎ Biāo's Xù Hànshū states:
"When Dōngpíng King Cāng arrived in his kingdom and fell ill,
an edict was issued dispatching the Deputy of the Imperial Physicians to lead master physicians to examine his illness."
Guō Pú's Wūxián Shān Fù Xù states:
"It is said that Wū Xián used great arts to be the physician of Emperor Yáo."
Containing Blood Licking Hemorrhoids
The Hánzǐ states:
"A physician sucks people's sores,
contains people's blood,
not because there is any kinship of flesh and bone,
but because of the benefit involved."
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"The King of Qín had an illness and summoned physicians;
those who licked his hemorrhoids obtained five chariots."
Emerging Snake Fleeing Otter
The Huà Tuó Biézhuàn states:
"The daughter of Hénèi Prefect Liú Xūn suffered from an itchy sore inside her left knee,
and invited Tuó to examine it.
Tuó tied a dog with a rope behind a horse,
then rode the horse pulling the dog.
The dog, exhausted, could not walk,
so he took its severed intestine and pointed it towards the sore.
In a moment, something like a snake emerged from the sore,
three chǐ long."
Also, Liú Jìngshū's Yì Yuàn states:
"At the Xiàmiào in Guǎnglíng,
during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
a woman from the Zhāng family spent the night at dusk under the temple gate.
At night, a creature impersonated her husband and came,
and the woman, bewitched, fell ill.
Hǎilíng's Wáng Zuǎn could treat evil ghosts.
As soon as he inserted a needle,
an otter fled from under the woman's quilt."
Four Difficulties Three Breaks
Fàn Yè's Hòuhànshū states:
"When Guō Yù treated nobles, sometimes he could not cure them.
The Emperor asked the reason,
and he replied:
'There are four difficulties!
Being self-willed and not trusting your servant,
is the first difficulty;
not being careful with one's own body,
is the second difficulty;
the bones and joints not being strong,
is the third difficulty;
loving ease and hating labor,
is the fourth difficulty.'" The Kǒngcóngzǐ states:
"Liáng Qiū Jù encountered viper poison,
and for thirty days did not recover.
All the senior officials of Qí presented methods of attack and treatment.
Jù's disciple said:
'Liáng Qiū has already been treated.
Yet you hastily present prescriptions;
do you want Liáng Qiū to suffer viper harm again?'
Confucius said:
'After breaking an arm three times one becomes a physician.
Liáng Qiū was concerned that there might be others with the same illness asking for prescriptions,
hence the many people spoke of prescriptions.'"
Cleansing Intestines and Washing Viscera Opening the Skull and Arranging the Brain
The Shǐjì states:
"When the Guó crown prince died,
Biǎn Què arrived in the state of Guó.
The Zhōngshùzǐ said:
'He died suddenly from convulsions.'
Biǎn Què said:
'He can still be revived.'
The Shùzǐ said:
'Sir, are you not being deceptive?
Your servant has heard that in high antiquity there was Yú Fū,
who treated illness not using decoctions,
but instead cut the skin and opened the muscles,
cleansed and washed the intestines and stomach,
and rinsed and washed the five viscera.'" Also, the Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Chún Yú opened the skull and arranged the brain."
Piercing the Chest to Insert a Cake Scraping the Bone to Remove Poison
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Wén Zhì stretched tendons
to treat critical conditions.
Zhòng Jǐng pierced the chest
to insert a red cake.
These are but physicians,
yet they were capable of such things."
The Shǔ Zhì states:
"Guān Yǔ was pierced in the arm by a stray arrow,
and whenever it was overcast or rainy it often caused pain.
A physician said:
'The arrowhead is poisoned.
We must cut open the arm and scrape the bone to remove the poison,
then it can be eliminated.'"
Bào Zhāo of the Sòng Dynasty, "Poem on Digging for Solomon's Seal Past Copper Mountain"
Jade-fat is hidden in the central classics,
Water-mushrooms are veiled in inner records.
Precious bait prolongs childhood years,
Life-medicine halts the march of decline.
How much more, storing feelings of ancient times,
Heavy mists conceal their traces.
Goat-horn peaks cleave broken clouds,
Jug-mouth streams flow through narrow stones.
Copper streams by day loom deep and dark,
Dripping stalactite caves weep at night.
Resembling both Wind-Gate stone steps,
And also Heaven-Well's jade walls.
Shuffling, cold leaves scatter,
Gathering, autumn waters pool.
Pine hues follow the wilds deepening,
Moon-dew clings to white grasses.
Vainly guarding thoughts of rivers and seas,
Why value guests from Liáng or Zhèng?
Benevolence and love—in ancient times, no resentment,
Following the Way—what is there to regret today?
Wú Jūn of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Gathering Herbs on Great Cloth Mountain"
I originally dwell north of this mountain,
Following the stream to gather mountain hemp.
Nine stems daily bathed in streamlight,
Three leaves of long-life flowers.
They can cleanse worries and ailments,
Holding them briefly halts the setting sun.
The setting sun cannot be halted,
The passing years indeed remain as before.
How can I obtain Kūnlún Mountain,
With its towering three-pearl trees?
Three-pearl trees begin to sprout,
Crimson leaves ascend vermilion terraces.
Jade pot holds white phoenix lungs,
Golden cauldron cradles azure dragon embryos.
Hán Zhòng and Prince [Jìn],
In which era were there no immortal talents?
If Ānqī should deign to look back,
We shall meet in Pénglái.
Jiāng Yān of the Liáng Dynasty, "Poem on Picking Calamus from the Rocks"
Jade zither long buried in weeds,
Bronze mirror discarded, no longer gazed upon.
Not seen within the empty chamber,
Tangled thoughts of autumn arise.
Strolling slowly along the flowing waves,
Raising oars, floating on spring ripples.
Red cave-mouths stream with mist like silk,
Green waters hold cinnamon's crimson.
Leaning on wine, mood still joyless,
Midday shadows bring sighs.
Whenever sorrows press upon me,
How can ginger-lilies bring relief?
Hoping to gather grass from the rocks,
To halt my fading countenance.
If red carp could be ridden,
Through clouds and mist never to return.
Wáng Wēi of the Sòng Dynasty, "In Praise of Poria"
White poria dwells below,
Spreading luxuriance above.
Its center shaped like fowl,
Its form resembling tortoise-shell divination.
Divine as the Junior Minister,
Preserving and prolonging youth.
Unyielding in final resolve,
Soft red, fit to be worn.
Also, "In Praise of Yǔyúliáng (Limonite)"
Sparse waves soak and permeate,
Merely called common model.
Hidden spirit, secret function,
Divine indeed, without bounds.
Field paths show no favor,
Grains and harvests lack fragrance.
Illustrious virtue, Yǔ's labor,
Truly resides in leftover grain.
Also, "In Praise of Peach Syrup"
Ālù revives the breath,
Hújiāo restrings the cord.
Not equal to peach syrup,
Crossing lands, reaching heaven.
Liquid transforms into jade,
Appearance fixed, attaining immortality.
Men know the scorching sun,
Why not seek shade for years?
Also, "In Praise of Goldthread"
Goldthread's bitter taste,
Left and right interdependent.
Cuts chill, washes away summer heat,
Opens life, lightens the body.
Jīnyún once drove his chariot,
Flying steeds ascended the heavens.
Arriving without traveling,
I have heard of such a man.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of the Liáng Dynasty, "Essay Exhorting Physicians"
Within heaven and earth,
Only humans are most spiritual.
What humans value most,
Is nothing greater than life.
Though length of life has its allotment,
Years and longevity come from heaven,
Yet when cold and heat turn abnormal,
Cravings and desires violate proper measure,
Thus deep cold strikes the head,
Causing ailments differently.
Chopping axes rot the intestines,
Cutting short years in no single way.
To save from this, the essential,
Truly lies in good prescriptions.
There are also poets,
Who sing of Péng Zǔ's longevity and early death.
The state of Qín's praise for Hé and Huǎn,
Jì Liáng's encounter with Master Lú,
Prince of Guó's meeting with Yuè Rén,
And even those who gaze long and become flying immortals,
The wondrous Way of long life,
Still transforms six-and-one with golden elixir,
Alters three-and-seven with silver pills.
Storing the essence of jade characters,
Studying the mysteries of purple texts,
What use is peach resin?
The Northern Dipper does not record its form,
Golden sap is not far,
Bright pearls still shame its price.
Only then can below the gate of practice,
Drumbeats alone be transmitted,
Beside the Yōng sacrifice,
Flute sounds still remain.
The "Zhōu Lǐ" says: Physicians for ailments,
Take charge of the diseases of the myriad people,
Dividing and treating them.
Mid-year, each records their reasons,
Submitting them to the chief physician,
Who knows recovery or non-recovery,
To serve as warning for later methods.
Those who treat illnesses are many,
But most are rash in seeking reward.
Those who harm people are many,
Those who love people are few.
Thus daily handling a hundred prescriptions,
Monthly producing a thousand scrolls,
Never lightening their medicinal properties,
Abandoning them to life or death,
Where then can be obtained
The merit of pure transformation?
And when beloved relatives are afflicted,
Feelings keen for friends,
Illness arises in the vitals,
Ailments emerge like Yúfū's,
Though wishing to exhaust principles and urgency,
Thought finds no outlet,
Why is this so?
Because they never studied fundamentals,
And suddenly find change difficult.
Hemp, deer-pea, and bush-clover
Merely cure headaches;
Wheat-malt, lovage, and cnidium
Temporarily halt "river-fish belly."
Thought does not go beyond its station,
Affairs are confined beneath the carriage shaft,
To seek reversal in Xuándū,
Or spread one's name in green registers,
How can it be achieved?
End of Volume Eight
The Yuán Mìng Bāo states:
"In ancient times, the Sī Guài was in charge of divination."
The Shì Běn states:
"Wū Xián created the art of milfoil divination."
The Lǐ Jì states:
"Tortoise shells are used for divination,
milfoil stalks are used for milfoil divination."
The Bái Hǔ Tōng states:
"There are many dried grasses and withered bones,
why use only milfoil and tortoise shells?
The word for tortoise (guī) implies longevity,
the word for milfoil (shī) implies venerable age."
The Shàng Shū·Hóng Fàn Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn states:
"These are the creatures, plants, and trees that, due to their long life, are able to know good and bad fortune.
The Guī Rén is in charge of the six types of tortoise shells,
each with its own name and characteristics.
The heavenly tortoise is called the líng category,
the earthly tortoise is called the yì category,
the eastern tortoise is called the guǒ category,
the western tortoise is called the léi category,
the southern tortoise is called the liè category,
the northern tortoise is called the ruò category.
The Bǔ Shī is in charge of interpreting the four types of cracks on the opened tortoise shell:
the first is called the fāng crack,
the second is called the gōng crack,
the third is called the yì crack,
the fourth is called the gōng crack."
Kāi means
opening the shell and consulting the cracks for divination.
There are one hundred and twenty basic crack patterns,
speaking of four types of cracks
means dividing them into four categories,
like the three parts of the Yì.
In all divination, observe the height and brightness of the fire,
and use the matter to apply heat to the tortoise shell to produce the cracks.
The Shì Rén is in charge of the three versions of the Yì.
He distinguishes the names of the nine types of milfoil divination:
the first is called the Lián Shān,
the second is called the Guī Cáng,
the third is called the Zhōu Yì;
the names of the nine types of milfoil divination:
the first is called Wū Gēng,
the second is called Wū Xián,
the third is called Wū Shì,
the fourth is called Wū Mù,
the fifth is called Wū Yì,
the sixth is called Wū Bǐ,
the seventh is called Wū Cí,
the eighth is called Wū Cān,
the ninth is called Wū Huán,
used to distinguish good and bad fortune.
Wū should all be read as shì,
a mistake in the character,
gēng means moving the capital city.
Again, the Lǐ Jì states:
"Divination by tortoise shell and milfoil
is what the former sage kings used to make people trust the times and days,
revere ghosts and spirits,
fear laws and decrees,
resolve doubts and suspicions,
and settle indecision.
Therefore, the Zhōu Yì
says: 'To determine the good and bad fortune of the world,
and to accomplish the great endeavors of the world,
nothing is greater than milfoil and tortoise shells.'
The virtue of milfoil is round and spiritual,
the virtue of the hexagrams is square and wise.
Spiritual to know the future,
wise to store the past."
The Hóng Fàn Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn states:
"If one is bothersome, numerous, confused, and disrespectful,
or not precise and solemn,
the spirits will not inform;
or if one observes the hexagrams and examines the cracks,
the divination will not be obtained;
or if the tortoise shell is not spiritual,
the milfoil is not efficacious,
this is the reason for the error,
and the sage cannot rely solely on them.
If both tortoise shell and milfoil divination contradict human wishes,
the spirits and deities will not bless."
Grasping Millet, Holding Gold
The Máo Shī states:
"Pity me, poor and destitute,
facing lawsuits and imprisonment.
Grasping millet to go for divination,
how can I obtain good fortune?"
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"How pitiable!
I, a man of exhausted and scant wealth,
still have matters of lawsuits and disputes,
holding millet to go for divination,
seeking victory or defeat,
how can I obtain good from this?"
The Zhàn Guó Cè states:
"Zōu Jì was the prime minister of Qí,
Tián Jì was the general,
they did not get along.
Zōu Jì told Gōngsūn Hàn,
Hàn sent someone holding ten pieces of gold to divine in the market, saying:
'I am a man of Tián Jì,
I have fought three battles and won three victories,
my fame and power shake the world,
I wish to undertake a great affair,
is it auspicious or not?'
When the diviner came out,
he then ordered the arrest of the diviner and verified his words before the king,
Tián Jì then fled."
Three Types of Cracks, Six Types of Tortoise Shells
The Zhōu Lǐ:
"The Tài Bǔ is in charge of the methods of the three types of cracks."
"Six types of tortoise shells" see the narrative.
Providing the Torch, Raising the Fire
The Zhōu Lǐ:
"The Chuí Shì is in charge of providing the torch and kindling for divination affairs."
Dù Zǐchūn notes:
"Chuí is read like the qiáo in firewood (xīn qiáo),
meaning the wood used to burn and scorch the tortoise shell."
"Raising the fire" see the narrative.
Divine Admonition, Symbolic Revelation
Chén Lín's Dà Huāng Fù states:
"Borrowing tortoise and milfoil divination to determine auspiciousness,
inquiring of divine admonition for good omens."
The Yì states:
"The eight trigrams use symbols to reveal."
Hán Kāngbó notes:
"Using symbols to reveal good and bad fortune to people."
Great Horizontal, Minor Technique
The Shǐ Jì states:
"When Empress Dowager Gāo passed away,
Prime Minister Chén Píng and others sent someone to welcome the King of Dài.
Before the plan was settled,
they divined with a tortoise shell,
the crack pattern said:
'Great horizontal, firm and strong,
I shall become the Heavenly King,
like the glory of the Xià Hòu.'" The Bào Pú Zǐ states:
"Divination is a minor technique,
those who embellish fortune-telling claim it is the wonder of knowing the future."
Tortoise Weary, Milfoil Disrespected
The Máo Shī states:
"My tortoise shell is already weary,
it does not tell me the plan."
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"Divining with milfoil repeatedly and disrespecting the tortoise shell,
the spirit of the tortoise grows weary of it,
and no longer tells the good or bad fortune of the plan.
This means even if the crack is obtained,
the interpretation is not accurate."
The Yì states:
"The first milfoil divination informs,
the second and third times it is disrespected,
if disrespected, it does not inform."
Reverent Divination, Piecemeal Divination
The Shàng Shū states:
"King Wǔ was ill and not at ease,
the two dukes said:
'Let us reverently divine for the king.'" The Guī Cáng states:
"In the past, Hé Bó divined with milfoil about battling with Luò and performed piecemeal divination,
Kūn Wú divined and found it inauspicious."
Kǒng Qiǎo, Yán Xiào
The Jiā Yǔ states:
"Confucius once divined for himself,
and obtained the hexagram Bì,
he looked displeased and uneasy.
Zǐ Zhāng came forward and said:
'Bì is an auspicious hexagram,
why does the Master look displeased?'
Confucius said:
'Fire under the mountain,
Bì,
is not a proper color.'" The Chōng Bō Zhuàn states:
"Confucius sent Zǐ Gòng out, and he had not yet returned.
He told his disciples to divine,
they encountered the hexagram Dǐng,
all said without legs he would not come.
Yán Zǐ covered his mouth and laughed, saying:
'Without legs,
he comes by boat,
Cì will arrive,
in the clear morning.'
Zǐ Gòng indeed arrived in the morning."
Replacing Chén and Capturing Jìn
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Chén Lìgōng gave birth to Jìng Zhòng.
The Zhōu court's Nèishǐ performed a divination by stalks,
obtaining the hexagram Guān changing to Pǐ.
He said:
'This is called "observing the light of the state",
beneficial to be a guest of the king.
Will he not replace Chén and possess the state!'"
It also states:
"The Earl of Qín attacked Jìn.
The diviner Túfǔ performed a divination by stalks, indicating auspiciousness.
They crossed the Yellow River,
and the Jìn marquis's chariot was destroyed.
The earl questioned him,
and he replied:
'This is actually greatly auspicious.
After three defeats, you will certainly capture the ruler of Jìn.'
It indeed turned out as he said."
Modeling on Heaven and Earth, Revering Ghosts and Spirits
The Shǐ Jì states:
"The method of divination models on Heaven and Earth,
and emulates the four seasons."
The Lǐ Jì states:
"Divination by tortoise shell and stalks
is what the former sage kings used to make people trust the timeliness of days,
revere ghosts and spirits,
and fear laws and commands."
Aligning the Small and Great, Distinguishing the Noble and Humble
The Yì states:
"Aligning the small and great lies in the hexagrams."
Hán Kāngbó's commentary states:
"Hexagrams have small and great;
'aligning' means to distinguish."
The Zhōu Lǐ Tú states:
"For Dàfū rank and above,
matters involve both shell and stalk divination;
for Shì, only stalk divination is used.
This is the distinction between noble and humble."
Stalks Short, Tortoise Long; Yang Odd, Yin Even
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Jìn Xiàngōng wished to make Lí Jī his principal wife.
Shell divination was inauspicious,
stalk divination was auspicious.
The duke said:
'Follow the stalks.'
The diviner said:
'Stalks are short, the tortoise is long;
it is better to follow the long.'"
The Yì states:
"Yang hexagrams have many yin lines,
yin hexagrams have many yang lines.
What is the reason for this?
Yang hexagrams are odd, and yin hexagrams are even."
Punishments and Penalties, Ninth
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo states:
"Xíng (punishment) means xíng (to shape)."
The Shuō Wén states:
"Dāo (knife) guarding jǐng (well).
If those who drink enter the well and fall into the stream,
the knife guards it,
cutting off their desires.
Wǎng yán (entangling words) constitutes lì (cursing);
dāo guarding lì constitutes fá (penalty).
Fá means nèi (internal),
falling into harm."
If the well provides drink,
people enjoy it without cease,
then they fall into the stream by themselves.
Therefore, adding dāo is called xíng,
intending to make people fear and thus preserve their lives.
If lì is guarded by dāo,
then they will not act.
Now fá is written with cùn (inch).
Cùn means zhàng chǐ (measurement),
referring to incorporating the standards of the carpenter's line.
Those who used punishments in antiquity
depicted images so that people would not offend.
Generally, for upper punishment: zhěyī (red garments) without trim;
middle punishment: mixed footwear;
lower punishment: mò méng (black head-covering),
worn while residing in the villages, and people felt ashamed by them.
See the Shàngshū Dà Zhuàn.
Therefore, the Báihǔ Tōng states:
"The Five Emperors depicted images;
their garments represented the five punishments.
Those offending against mò (tattooing) covered their heads with cloth;
those offending against yì (nose amputation) wore red garments;
those offending against bìn (kneecapping) had their kneecaps covered with black and marked;
those offending against gōng (castration) wore straw sandals;
those offending against dàpì (death penalty) wore collarless cloth garments."
The Shàngshū states:
"The five punishments have their garments;
this refers to this."
Another version states:
"Using painted kneecaps to represent qíng (tattooing);
grass tassels to represent yì;
wearing straw sandals to represent yuè (foot amputation);
using ài bǐng (artemisia leather) to represent gōng."
Generally, severing a person's limbs
or carving their skin is called xíng.
Painting garments and caps,
differentiating insignia and attire,
is the meaning of lù (humiliation).
See the Shènzǐ.
Later ages had severe punishments, yet people were not deterred.
Therefore, great punishments used jiǎbīng (armor and weapons);
next, fǔyuè (axes and battle-axes);
middle punishments used dāojù (knives and saws);
next, zuānzáo (drills and chisels);
minor punishments used biānpǔ (whips and clubs).
See the Guóyǔ.
Therefore, the Shàngshū·Lǚ Xíng states:
"Only by revering the five punishments
can the three virtues be accomplished.
The five punishments are:
mò (tattooing) penalties, one thousand categories;
yì penalties, one thousand categories;
fèi (foot amputation) penalties, five hundred categories;
gōng penalties, three hundred categories;
dàpì penalties, two hundred categories.
The categories of the five punishments total three thousand."
Also, the Zhōu Guān states:
"The duty of the Dàsīkòu
is to use the five punishments to correct the myriad people."
First, yě xíng (field punishment), promoting achievement and correcting strength;
second, jūn xíng (military punishment), promoting commands and correcting defense;
third, xiāng xíng (village punishment), promoting virtue and correcting filial piety;
fourth, guān xíng (official punishment), promoting ability and correcting duties;
fifth, guó xíng (state punishment), promoting honesty and correcting violence.
Zhèng's commentary:
"Jiū means to investigate differences."
By the time of Qín, Shāng Yāng was employed,
and the law of liánzuò (collective responsibility) was established,
creating the punishment of cānyí (extermination of three generations),
adding ròuxíng (corporal punishment).
For dàpì, there were methods of záodiān (piercing the skull), chōuxié (pulling out ribs), and huòpēng (boiling in cauldrons).
See the Hànshū.
Generally, those with much virtue and little punishment
were the Five Emperors;
those with punishment and virtue half and half
were the Three Kings;
those with much punishment and little virtue
were the Five Hegemons;
those who purely used punishment and perished
were Qín.
See Huàn Fàn's Shì Yào Lùn.
Clarifying Penalties, Applying Punishments
The Yì states:
"Thunder and lightning: Shìkè.
The former kings thereby clarified penalties and promulgated laws."
It also states:
"Thunder and lightning both arrive:
Fēng.
The nobleman thereby adjudicates cases and applies punishments."
Five Accusations, Three Admonitions
The Shàngshū states:
"When both parties are fully present,
the judge hears the five accusations."
The Zhōu Lǐ·Qiū Guān states:
"For all among the people who have wickedness and evil,
three admonitions, then punish."
Adjudicating Cases, Essential Imprisonment
"Adjudicating cases" see note under "applying punishments."
The Shàngshū states:
"For essential imprisonment, ponder and consider
for five or six days up to ten days or a season."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"Yāoqiú (essential imprisonment)
refers to using their essential statements to adjudicate cases."
Heaven's Punishment, State's Penalty
The Shàngshū states:
"Now I only reverently carry out Heaven's punishment."
The Zhōu Lǐ states:
"Five punishments,
the fifth is the state's penalty."
Armor and Weapons, Whips and Goads
The Guóyǔ states:
"Zāng Wénzhòng said to Duke Xī:
'Great punishments use armor and weapons;
next, axes and battle-axes;
middle punishments use knives and saws;
next, drills and chisels;
minor punishments use whips and clubs,
to awe the people.'"
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"The five punishments
are the whips and goads of the Five Emperors."
Six Canons Three Clauses
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The Grand Minister of Education is responsible for establishing the six canons of the state,
to assist the king in governing the feudal lords."
The Book of Hàn states:
"When Gāozǔ first entered the Guānzhōng region,
he established a legal code of three clauses."
Simplified Laws Reduced Punishments
"Simplified Laws" see the annotation under "Three Clauses".
The Continued Book of Hàn states:
"An edict in the second year of the Jiànwǔ reign period stated:
'We shall deliberate with officials of the two-thousand-dàn rank, the various grand masters, erudites, and gentlemen of the palace on reducing punishments.'"
Discarding Ashes Fighting a Fire
Hánzǐ states:
"Under the laws of the Yīn dynasty,
those who discarded ashes in the street were punished.
Zǐgòng asked Zhòngní (Confucius) about the severity of this,
and Zhòngní said:
'Discarding ashes in the street will certainly cause them to blow into people's faces,
which will anger people,
and anger will lead to fights,
fights will lead to the mutual slaughter of the three clans,
therefore, punishing it is justified.'" It also states:
"In Lǔ, a fire broke out in a marshland where firewood was stored.
The north wind was blowing,
driving the flames southward,
and it was feared the capital would be burned.
Duke Āi personally led the people to urge them to fight the fire,
but everyone was chasing wild animals instead, and the fire was not fought.
He then summoned Zhòngní and issued an order:
'Those who do not fight the fire will be considered guilty,
and those who chase wild animals will be punished as if they had entered a forbidden area.'
Before the order had even been fully disseminated,
the fire was already extinguished."
Penal Code Administrative Statutes
The Shàngshū states:
"Judge cases with compassion and reverence,
and clearly consult the penal code."
It also states:
"The Administrative Statutes state:
'Those who act prematurely shall be executed without pardon,
those who fail to act in time shall be executed without pardon.'
Kǒng Ānguó explains:
'The Administrative Statutes
are the statutes for governance from the time of the Xiàhòu clan.'"
Blazing Lightning Accumulated Yin
The Shī Hán Shénwù states:
"Blazing lightning and thunder,
causing unrest and disorder,
this is a response to excessively harsh punishments and governance.
Therefore, the thunder and lightning startle people,
causing the world to be unsettled."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
'Yáng represents virtue,
yīn represents punishment.
Yáng constantly resides in the height of summer,
and is concerned with nurturing, growth, and sustenance;
yīn resides in the depth of winter,
accumulating in empty, unused places.'
From this, it is evident that Heaven favors virtue over punishment."
Red-Clothed Prisoners Vermilion Brush
The Hàn Míngchén Zòushì states:
"Táng Lín said:
'The Qín dynasty established severe punishments, yet bandits filled the mountains,
and red-clothed prisoners lined half the roads.'" The Xiè Chéng Hòuhànshū states:
"Shèng Jí served as Commandant of Justice.
Every year at the winter solstice,
when prisoners were to be sentenced,
his wife would hold a candle at night,
while Jí held a vermilion brush.
Husband and wife facing each other,
they would shed tears while deciding the sentences."
Clear Discernment Overturning Unjust Verdicts
The Book of Hàn states:
"Yú Dìngguó served as Commandant of Justice.
He was discerning and lenient,
and Huáng Bà and others considered him fair and clear-sighted.
Juàn Bùyí served as Governor of the Capital.
Whenever he returned from his rounds with prisoners,
his mother would ask Bùyí:
'Have you overturned any unjust verdicts?
How many people have you saved?'
Bùyí would reply:
'I have overturned many unjust verdicts.'
Only then would his mother be pleased."
Daytime Adjudication Autumn Review
The Book of Hàn states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng relied solely on punishments.
He personally handled documents,
adjudicating cases by day
and managing paperwork by night."
The Book of Hàn states:
"When Yú Dìngguó served as Commandant of Justice,
during the late autumn review of cases,
the emperor would often go to the Xuānshì Hall,
where he would fast and reside while deciding cases,
and the punishments and trials were praised as fair and just."
Planting Locust Trees Thicket of Thorns
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"Plant jujube trees and locust trees,
and hold court beneath them.
The jujube tree has a red heart and thorns,
symbolizing that those who govern should preserve their red (sincere) hearts,
and the thorns represent the facts that prick people.
Their circumstances should lead each to return to the truth.
The locust tree (huái) symbolizes return (guī),
as circumstances are revealed and return to truth."
The Zhōuyì states:
"The top line of the doubled Kǎn hexagram states:
'Bound with cords,
placed in a thicket of thorns,
for three years not attaining release,
ominous.'" Wáng Bì's commentary states:
"The extreme of danger and steepness,
cannot be ascended;
strict laws and severe regulations,
are difficult to violate.
It is fitting to imprison them,
placing them in a place for reflection on their faults."
Yú Shìnán's "Poem on the Theme of Prudent Punishment"
The imperial designs glorify past records,
Supreme virtue manifests a great name.
The Way crowns the beginning of the two principles,
Customs surpass the excellence of the Three Dynasties.
Harmony in music shows transformation's perfection,
Cessation of lawsuits reveals punishments' clarity.
Light penalties are still held in mind,
