Also, the "Edict on Reducing Death Sentences":
I have established a grand enterprise,
illuminating and settling the realm.
Yet the blessings of the main branch
have not yet spread widely to the inner chambers;
the lands of the Teng and Wei
still lack protective screens.
Thinking of the bow-cases,
I cannot forget my concerns.
Enfeoffing two sons to secure a foundation as firm as a rock,
thereby making it even more solid.
Though the celebration originates from myself,
my grace extends broadly to others.
All death sentences may be reduced by one degree,
five-year penal servitude reduced by two degrees,
and sentences of three years or below
shall all be pardoned and released.
Prisoner, Tenth
The *Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"Prisoner (qiú),
means to pursue (qiú).
It means the words are exhausted and the truth obtained,
and they are pursued for punishment due to their crimes.
According to ritual,
criminals are placed in circular earth enclosures.
Therefore, the character for prisoner (囚) is formed by 'mouth' (口) guarding 'person' (人),
this is its image."
The *Shàngshū* states:
"Imprisoning and enslaving upright scholars."
It also says:
"When examining prisoners and pondering their cases,
for five or six days up to ten days,
do not conceal the essential facts about the prisoners."
The *Shī* says:
"Presenting prisoners at the Pàn Palace."
The *Zhōu Guān*:
"The Officer in Charge of Prisoners oversees guarding robbers, bandits, and all prisoners."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Prisoner (qiú),
means to detain (jū),
this is its function."
Lock Moves Dipper Empty
Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* states:
"When an amnesty decree is about to arrive,
then the lock in the prison chamber moves,
and those within the prison are due to be released.
Thus, sensing its response,
causes the lock to move."
The *Hànshū* states:
"There are fifteen stars forming a hook circle;
the handle is called the prison of lowly people.
If the stars within the prison are full, then prisoners are many;
if empty, then they are released."
The *Shī Hán Shénwù* states:
"The Dipper is the celestial prison."
Knock Head on Ground Gaze at Heaven
The *Hànshū*:
"Sīmǎ Qiān, in his letter to Rèn Ān, said:
'At such a time,
upon seeing the jailers, one knocks one's head on the ground;
gazing at the guards, one's heart trembles and breath catches.'" The *Shǐjì*:
"Zhào Gāo interrogated Lǐ Sī,
who was bound and restrained,
confined in prison.
Gazing up at heaven, he sighed, saying:
'Alas, how sorrowful!
An unprincipled ruler—
what plans can be made for him?'"
Summer Leniency Winter Execution
The *Lǐjì* states:
"In mid-summer,
gates and village gates are not closed,
and barriers and markets levy no exactions.
Show leniency to serious prisoners,
and increase their food."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary:
"Leniency (tǐng),
means to relax."
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hànshū* states:
"When Shèng Jí of Kuàijī was Commandant of Justice,
every time the winter solstice arrived,
prisoners sentenced to execution were to be decided.
His wife held a candle at night,
while Jí held the vermilion brush.
Husband and wife facing each other,
they shed tears while deciding their crimes."
Submit to Rack Hasten Shackles
Huá Qiáo's *Hòu Hànshū* states:
"Fàn Pāng, due to the faction affair, was imprisoned in the Yellow Gate Northern Prison.
Pāng, because many fellow prisoners were afflicted with illness,
requested to first submit to the rack,
and thus vied with Yuán Zhōng of the same commandery and others to endure cruel torture."
Yú Huàn's *Wèi Lüè* states:
"Jiǎ Kuí was Registrar to the Chancellor.
The King of Wèi wished to attack Wú.
Kuí remonstrated,
the King grew angry,
and handed him over to the prison officials.
They did not immediately put shackles on him.
Kuí said:
'Hasten to put shackles on me.
The King will suspect that, being in a close position,
I am seeking leniency from you.
He will send someone to investigate.'
The shackles were just fastened
when indeed someone was sent to observe him."
Secured by Three Woods Subject to Five Punishments
The *Hànshū* states:
"Sīmǎ Qiān's letter says:
'Wèi Qí,
a great general,
wore a convict's robe,
secured by the three woods.'" The *Shàngshū* states:
"When both parties are fully present,
the judge hears the five types of statements."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"'Both' refers to the prisoner and the witness;
'present' (zào)
means to arrive.
When both have arrived and are fully present,
then the various prison officials together hear their crimes subject to the five punishments."
Bound by Ropes Confined in Prison
The *Yì* states:
"The top six of Kǎn:
bound with ropes,
placed among thorny thickets.
For three years not attaining
—ominous."
Wáng Bì's commentary states:
"The extreme of danger and steepness,
cannot be ascended;
strict laws and severe regulations,
difficult to violate.
It is fitting they are imprisoned,
placed in a land for reflecting on faults."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Those confined in prison
consider the day long;
those facing execution in the market
consider the day short."
Release Tài Shǐcí Free Fáng Guǎng
The *Wúzhì* states:
"Tài Shǐcí was once captured by the Shānyuè.
Sūn Cè personally untied his bonds,
grasped his hand and said:
'Would you have released me at Shéntāng then?
If you had captured me then,
what would you have done with me?'
Cí said:
'It cannot be measured.'
Cè laughed heartily and said:
'Today's affairs,
I share with you.'" Yú Yù's *Kuàijī Diǎnlù* states:
"Zhōnglí Yì was Magistrate of Tángyì.
A county commoner, Fáng Guǎng, was imprisoned for avenging his father.
His mother fell ill and died.
Guǎng heard of it,
wailed and wept in prison.
Yì felt sorrow and pity for him.
He released Guǎng to see her, saying:
'The crime of not returning,
I, the magistrate, will bear it myself.'
After Guǎng attended the funeral,
he immediately returned to prison on his own."
Reach Winter Rest at La
"Reach Winter" see annotation under "Winter Execution."
The *Chénliú Qíjiù Zhuàn* states:
"Yú Yán was appointed Magistrate of Zīyáng.
Every time the annual seasonal sacrifices and the La festival arrived,
he would release the prisoners to each return home.
The prisoners all felt his kindness,
and returned by the appointed time."
Stone Chamber Golden Rampart
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"The King of Wú confined the King of Yuè, Gōu Jiàn, and Grand Master Fàn Lǐ in a stone chamber.
The King of Wú fell ill.
The King of Yuè said to Grand Steward Pǐ:
'This prisoner-minister requests an audience to inquire after his illness.'
The Grand Steward entered and spoke,
and the King of Wú then received the King of Yuè."
The *Jìn Záshì* states:
"Prince Qí of Jiǒng raised righteous troops,
and imprisoned Prince Zhào of Lún and his five sons in Jīnyōng City."
Inner Palace Eternal Lane
Kǒng Yǎn's *Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ* states:
"Duke Mù of Qín imprisoned his three elder brothers in the inner palace."
The *Hànshū* states:
"When Empress Lü became Empress Dowager,
she then ordered Lady Qī to be imprisoned in the Eternal Lane."
A meteor enters the Pleiades; timely rain falls upon returning to the palace.
Hán Yáng's *Astronomical Compendium* states:
"When a meteor enters the Pleiades,
a noble person will have prisoners bound."
*Records of the Eastern Pavilion* states:
"In the sixth year of the Yongyuan era of Emperor Hé of Hàn, in the seventh month,
the capital suffered drought.
The emperor went to Luòyáng to review the prisoners,
redressed cases of injustice,
and before returning to the palace, timely rain fell."
Bamboo prisoner; Paulownia effigy.
*The Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yàn* states:
"Duke Jǐng planted bamboo
and ordered officials to guard it.
Someone cut the bamboo,
and the duke pursued him with chariots,
captured and imprisoned him.
Master Yàn said:
'A ruler should be generous, kind, and compassionate towards the people.'
The duke then ordered the release of the prisoner who had cut the bamboo."
Wáng Chōng's *Discourses Weighed in the Balance* states:
"When Lǐ Zǐcháng governed,
wishing to understand the circumstances of prisoners,
he used paulownia wood to carve effigies in the shape of prisoners.
He dug pits in the ground as beds
and laid the wooden prisoners within them.
Those whose guilt was just remained unmoving,
while those who were wronged would have their wooden effigies move and emerge on their own."
Suí Dynasty Yú Chuò's "Poem Written While Imprisoned in Wùzhōu"
Though poverty or success may be fated,
fleeing truly brings burden and blame.
Having betrayed grace, I merely stole life;
facing danger, I failed yet to die.
Awaiting judgment is fraught with uncertainty,
laws and prohibitions know no end.
Thick-faced, I shame my friends;
a prisoner's heart feels愧 towards wife and child.
The sage sun first rises in the east,
the passing years press towards the western stream.
Just as I turn from this glorious enlightened age,
forever towards the dark springs below.
Moreover, at this spring season,
the signs of nature startle field and village.
Sunlight dances chaotically on peach-blossom paths,
autumn winds rise along willow-lined trails.
All creatures, moving and still, follow their nature,
alas, I alone sink into disgrace.
Laying down my brush, I will not repeat this tale,
entrusting these feelings to a knowing friend.
Táng Emperor Zhōngzōng's "Edict on Reviewing Prisoners by the Filial and Harmonious Emperor"
Ritual restrains the gentleman,
an established norm since ancient times;
law prohibits the petty man,
a consistent principle throughout history.
Our heart is set on reforming affairs,
our will fixed on punishing transgressions.
Wishing to extend the grace of pardon,
yet fearing to open a path for opportunism.
This is not the way to guide people with rules and models,
nor to bequeath abundance to later generations.
Now that the season of warm harmony is upon us,
we should encourage the work of plowing and sowing.
As the three farming seasons commence their cycle,
we should promote the rules of reverence and care;
with the common people as our heart,
we are moved by thoughts of weeping for the guilty.
To extend our review and leniency,
and once more release those in prison cells,
hoping there will be no injustice of prolonged confinement,
while still demonstrating the warning of minor punishment.
For those prisoners currently confined
within the capital city,
We shall personally conduct a review,
and further order the responsible offices to prepare detailed regulations and report them to Us.
Prison, Eleventh
*Shì Míng* states:
"Prison (yù, 獄)
means 'to accuse' (yù, 也),
it speaks to verifying the true and false in human affairs;
it is also called 'enclosure' (láo, 牢),
meaning the place is solid and secure;
it is also called 'circular earth' (yuán tǔ, 圜土),
meaning walls are built with earth,
their shape being circular;
it is also called 'lingering enclosure' (líng yǔ, 囹圄):
'líng' (囹)
means 'to record' (lǐng, 領);
'yǔ' (圄)
means 'to guard against' (yù, 禦).
It means to record and guard against the prisoners.
According to the *Jí Jiù Zhāng*,
Gāo Yáo created prisons,
and later generations followed this."
*Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"In the Xià dynasty it was called 'tower of sorrow' (yōu tái);
in the Yīn dynasty it was called 'Yǒulǐ';
in the Zhōu dynasty it was called 'líng yǔ' (囹圄), which is this."
*Bówù Zhì* states:
"In the Xià dynasty it was called 'chamber of reflection' (niàn shì);
in the Yīn dynasty it was called 'halt of movement' (dòng zhǐ);
in the Zhōu dynasty it was called 'place of detention' (jī liú):
these are the different names of the Three Dynasties.
Also, 'bì láo' (狴牢)
is another name for prison."
*Family Sayings of Confucius* states:
"When Confucius was Minister of Crime,
there was a father and son who brought suit against each other.
He confined them together in the same cell."
Also, the *Book of Songs* states:
"Fit for the village jail, fit for the state prison."
*Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* states:
"Confinement in the village or district is called 'àn' (犴);
confinement by the court is called 'yù' (獄).
This refers to the matter."
Líng Yǔ (囹圄); Bì Láo (狴牢)
"Líng yǔ" is explained in the narrative section.
*The Book of Hàn* states:
"Those guilty of crimes deserving shackles were all granted 'sòng' confinement."
Yìng Shào's commentary states:
"'Sòng' (頌)
means 'appearance' (róng, 容).
It means they were treated with leniency,
merely kept in the clerks' offices,
and not placed in the prison cells."
Attached to the Dipper's Handle; Resembling the Dipper
*The Book of Hàn* states:
"Fifteen stars form a curved enclosure.
The handle [of the constellation] is called 'the prison of base men'.
If the prison stars are full, then prisoners are many;
if empty, then they are released."
*Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo* states:
"Making prisons round
resembles the Dipper's movement and conjunction."
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
"Making prisons round
resembles the Dipper's movement."
Eastern Market; Northern Bureau
Wèi Hóng's *Hàn Official Ceremonial* states:
"The Eastern Market prison was under the jurisdiction of the Governor of the Capital."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Sequel to the Book of Hàn* states:
"Fàn Pāng, styled Mèngbó,
was imprisoned in the Northern Bureau of the Yellow Gates.
The warden of the Northern Bureau prison said to him:
'All who are imprisoned make offerings to Gāo Yáo.'
Fàn Pāng said:
'Gāo Yáo was a worthy man,
an upright minister of antiquity.
If he knows I am innocent,
he will specially plead my case to the Emperor.
If I am guilty,
what use is making offerings to him?'
The others thereupon stopped."
Lateral Court; Commandery Lodge
*Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Emperor Wǔ reprimanded Lady Gōuyì.
She removed her hairpins and earrings and kowtowed.
The Emperor said:
'Take her away and send her to the Lateral Court prison.'" Wèi Hóng's *Old Ceremonial of Hàn* states:
"The Commandery Lodge prison
adjudicated cases from commanderies and kingdoms throughout the empire reporting their accounts,
and was under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Ceremonies."
Seeing the Mole Cricket, Dreaming of the Ants
Liú Yìqìng's *Yōumíng Lù* says:
"Páng Qǐ, styled Zǐjí, was the governor of Lúlíng during the Jìn dynasty.
His ancestor had been imprisoned due to a legal case,
but he was not guilty.
He saw a mole cricket crawling near him,
and said to it:
'If you have divine power,
and can save me from death,
should you not live?'
He then threw some food to the mole cricket.
It ate it all and left,
but after a while it returned,
its body slightly larger,
which he found strange.
He fed it again,
and within a few days it grew as large as a piglet.
When the verdict came that he was to be executed,
the mole cricket dug a large hole at the base of the prison wall,
and he escaped through this hole.
Later, he received a pardon and survived."
Dōng Wúyí's *Qíxié* says:
"Dǒng Zhāozhī of Dāngyáng County in Wú was crossing the Qiántáng River by boat,
when he saw an ant in the river,
clinging to a short reed,
in desperate straits and near death.
He had a rope tied to the reed and attached to the boat.
When the boat reached the shore,
the ant was saved.
That night, he dreamed of a man in black clothes who came to thank him, saying:
'I am the king of the ants.
If you are ever in dire trouble,
I should be informed first.'
More than ten years passed.
At that time, banditry was rampant in the Jiāngzuǒ region,
and Zhāozhī was recorded as the leader of a robbery,
and imprisoned in Yúyáo.
Zhāozhī thought of the ant king's dream,
that he should be informed in times of crisis:
'But where can I inform him now?'
A fellow prisoner said:
'Just take two or three ants in your palm and pray to them.'
Zhāozhī did as he was told,
and that night he indeed dreamed of the man in black clothes from before, who said:
'Leave quickly,
and enter the Yúháng Mountains.
The world is in chaos,
and a pardon will be issued soon.'
He then awoke to find the ants had gnawed through all his shackles,
and thus he was able to escape from prison.
He crossed the river and fled to the Yúháng Mountains,
where he encountered the pardon and was spared."
Spring Inspection, Autumn Repair
*The Book of Rites* says:
"In the first month of spring,
officials are ordered to inspect the prisons,
remove the shackles,
and halt litigation."
It also says:
"In the first month of autumn,
officials are ordered to revise the laws and regulations,
repair the prisons,
and prepare the shackles."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"The prisons are for detaining and guarding prisoners,
which are the jails of today."
Submitting a Petition, Annotating History
Fàn Yè's *History of the Later Hàn* says:
"The prison officer Shàng Shūláng Zhāng Hóng
submitted a petition praising himself."
Cuī Hóng's *Records of the Later Zhào* says:
"Shí Jìlóng imprisoned the Imperial Secretariat Director Xú Guāng in the imperial prison at Xiāngguó,
where Guāng annotated classics and histories totaling over one hundred thousand characters."
Do Not Delay, Do Not Disturb
*The Book of Changes* says:
"Fire over the mountain
is the hexagram Lǚ.
The nobleman, in light of this, is clear and cautious in punishments and does not delay imprisonment."
*The Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"When Xiāo Hé died,
Cáo Cān was summoned.
Before leaving,
Cān instructed his successor as chancellor:
'Entrust the prisons and markets of Qí to others,
but be careful not to disturb them.'"
Star Prison, Celestial Prison
*The Essential Collection of Astronomy* says:
"When Guànsuǒ is bright,
noblemen are released."
*The Shī Hán Shénwù* says:
"The Dipper is the celestial prison,
presiding over celestial executions."
Round Gate, Level as a Whetstone
*The Rites of Zhōu* says:
"If they have no credentials, they are to be confined within the round earth."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"The round earth
is the prison wall."
Jiāng Yān's *Letter to Prince Jiànpíng* says:
"Violating the common round gate,
holding resentment within the prison door."
Also, Wáng Róng's *Preface to the Qūshuǐ Poems* says:
"Lush grass grows at the round gate."
Wèi Zhǎn's *Memorial on Proverbs* says:
"A proverb says of the Court Prison:
'Level as a whetstone,
with money you live,
without money you die.'
This proverb arose
because life and death depend on the laws and prisons."
Central Capital Offices, Wèiyāng Stable
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Continuation of the History of Hàn* says:
"Emperor Wǔ established the central capital offices prison,
with twenty-six prison heads initially all abolished,
leaving only the Court Prison and Luòyáng with imperial prisons."
Wèi Hóng's *Old Rituals of Hàn* says:
"The Wèiyāng Stable Prison
was in charge of adjudicating cases involving officials of the three bureaus of the grand stable,
under the Grand Coachman and the Imperial Household Grandee."
Harassing the Marquis of Jiàng, Insulting Ānguó
*The Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"When Zhōu Bó was removed as chancellor and returned to his fief,
after more than a year,
whenever the governor or commandant of Hédōng inspected the county,
the Marquis of Jiàng, Bó, fearing execution,
often wore armor
and had his family members hold weapons to meet them.
Later, someone submitted a petition accusing Bó of rebellion,
and he was arrested and tried.
Bó was terrified,
and did not know how to defend himself.
The prison officials gradually harassed and insulted him.
After the Marquis of Jiàng was released,
he said:
'I once commanded a million troops,
yet I never knew how powerful prison officials could be.'"
*The Book of Hàn* says:
"Hán Ānguó was convicted of a crime and imprisoned,
and the prison official Tián Jiǎ insulted him.
Ānguó said:
'Can dead ashes not reignite?'
Tián said:
'If they do, I will drown them.'"
Huáng Bà Receives the Classics, Dù Dǔ Composes a Eulogy
*The Book of Hàn* says:
"Xiàhóu Shèng was imprisoned for opposing Emperor Xuān's proposal to honor Emperor Wǔ's temple,
and the Chancellor's Chief Clerk Huáng Bà was also imprisoned for failing to report the offense.
Both were imprisoned.
Bà wished to study the classics under Shèng,
but Shèng declined, citing their death sentence.
Bà said:
'If one hears the Way in the morning,
one may die content in the evening.'
Shèng admired his words,
and thus taught him.
They remained imprisoned for two more winters,
studying without cease."
Fàn Yè's *History of the Later Hàn* says:
"Dù Dǔ, styled Jìyǎ,
lived as a guest in Měiyáng.
The magistrate sought his company,
but after several requests went unfulfilled,
he grew resentful.
The magistrate became angry,
arrested Dǔ, and sent him to the capital.
At that time, Grand Marshal Wú Hàn died,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ issued an edict:
'Let the scholars compose eulogies for him.'
Dǔ composed a eulogy while in prison.
His composition was the most excellent,
and the emperor praised it,
granting him silk and pardoning him."
Gazing at Heaven, Observing the Ether
*The Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"When Zhào Gāo tried Lǐ Sī,
and Sī was bound and imprisoned,
he gazed at heaven and sighed:
'Alas,
an unprincipled ruler—
what is the use of planning?'"
*The Book of Hàn* says:
"Those who observed the ether said there was an imperial aura in the Cháng'ān prisons."
Wind Over the Marsh, Fire Below the Mountain
*The Book of Changes* says:
"Wind over the marsh
is the hexagram Zhōngfú.
The nobleman, in light of this, deliberates on imprisonment and delays executions."
It also says:
"Fire below the mountain
is the hexagram Bì.
The nobleman, in light of this, clarifies all governmental affairs,
Sui Dynasty, Lǔ Běn, "Poem Written in Prison with Hú Shīdān Before Execution in Húzhōu"
Xi Shūyè's strings have just snapped,
Hán Ān's ashes not yet kindled.
We grieve for each other but cannot meet,
One confined in darkness, the other in the netherworld.
Luò Bīnwáng, "Poem from Prison, Conveying Sentiments to a Close Friend"
In past years, I met a discerning intent,
Admiring talents as precious as Chǔ's timber.
The cave seemed to birth a crimson phoenix,
The arena like a white steed arriving.
Once ensnared by prideful bait,
Thrice sealed, cautious of calamity's seed.
Not speaking of toil's rise and fall,
Suddenly here, at this twisted turn.
The dappled horse's penal codes are stern,
The gray hawk's jailers full of suspicion.
Severed threads are not easily discerned,
Doubtful jade indeed hard to judge.
Measuring plans, ashamed of Zhōu's defenses,
Upright worries stagnate in Xiàtái.
Life's course once shattered,
How many times have I wandered at crossroads?
Into the pit, still wagging my tail,
Lost at the ford, hastily changing course.
Round doors long lie silent,
Sparse nets still vast and wide.
Green plains stir with spring's fragrance,
Yellow sands hasten the traveler's thoughts.
Under an overturned bowl, vainly hoping for sunlight,
The hibernating door not yet startled by thunder.
Frost recedes, yet orchids still wither,
Winds abound, trees repeatedly broken.
The secluded earth, silkworm chambers sealed,
The quiet gate, sparrow nets spread open.
Self-pitying Qín's wrongful pain,
Who pities Chǔ's mournful melody?
Hànyáng's destitute bird guest,
Liángfǔ's reclining dragon talent.
With spirit still charging the Dipper,
No time to chisel through the wall.
Do not speak of Hán Chángrú,
Forever becoming unkindled ashes.
Shěn Quánqī, "Poem of Dark Confinement"
I pity the Zēng family's son,
In the past, there was doubt that made the shuttle drop.
I pity Lord Jī Wén,
Who was not without the owl poem.
Ministers and sons exhaust loyalty and filial piety,
Yet the sovereign is deluded by slander and deceit.
Luxuriant patterns separate bone and flesh,
With hidden resentment, I raise these words.
Another Poem
In ancient times, Gōngyě Cháng,
Though innocent, suffered imprisonment.
The sage descended upon his elder's son,
Since antiquity, praised as uniquely peerless.
I have not a hair's flaw,
With bitter heart embracing ice and snow.
In this era, many are the cultivated talents,
But who can follow the bright path?
Classics, First
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Jīng (classics) means
jìng (path);
diǎn (canon) means
cháng (constant).
This is to say they are like paths that lead everywhere,
and can be constantly used."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"The Five Classics are
the *Yì*, the *Shàngshū*, the *Shī*, the *Lǐ*, and the *Yuè*."
In ancient times, the *Yì*, the *Shū*, the *Shī*, the *Lǐ*, the *Yuè*, and the *Chūnqiū* were considered the Six Classics.
When the books were burned during the Qin dynasty,
the Classic of *Yuè* was lost.
Now, the *Yì*, the *Shī*, the *Shū*, the *Lǐ*, and the *Chūnqiū* are considered the Five Classics.
Furthermore, the *Lǐ* includes the *Zhōulǐ*, the *Yílǐ*, and the *Lǐjì*,
called the Three Rituals.
The *Chūnqiū* has the three commentaries: *Zuǒshì*, *Gōngyáng*, and *Gǔliáng*.
Combined with the *Yì*, *Shū*, and *Shī*,
they are also called the Nine Classics.
Regarding the *Yì*,
according to the *Shìmíng*, it speaks of change and transformation.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
"Fúxī created the Eight Trigrams.
Shénnóng doubled them to form the Sixty-four Hexagrams.
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn extended and elaborated upon them,
dividing them into the Two Changes (*Yì*).
By the time of the Xià people, following Yándì, it was called *Liánshān*.
By the time of the Yīn (Shāng) people, following Huángdì, it was called *Guīcáng*.
King Wén expanded the sixty-four hexagrams and composed the nine and six lines,
calling it the *Zhōu Yì*."
Furthermore, the *Hànshū* states:
"King Wén doubled the six lines of the *Yì*,
composing the upper and lower sections.
Confucius wrote ten pieces such as the *Tuàn*, *Xiàng*, *Xìcí*, *Wényán*, and *Xùguà*.
Therefore it is said, 'The Way of the *Yì* is profound.'
It passed through three sages,
and spanned three ancient eras."
The *Zhōu Yì Zhèngyì* states:
"Fúxī doubled the trigrams,
the Duke of Zhōu composed the line statements.
This account differs from the *Dìwáng Shìjì*.
Furthermore, Confucius composed ten pieces,
also called the *Ten Wings*.
Initially,
Bǔ Shāng wrote a commentary on the *Yì*.
By the Western Hàn, it was transmitted,
and there were those who became masters of it:
Shī Chóu, Mèng Xǐ, Liángqiū Hè, Jīng Fáng, Fèi Zhí, and Gāo Xiāng.
Furthermore, in the Eastern Hàn, Zhèng Xuán,
and in the Wèi, Wáng Bì, both annotated the *Yì*.
The schools of Shī, Mèng, and others,
from the Hàn through the Wèi, were all established,
and their transmission was widespread.
By the Western Jìn,
the schools of Liángqiū, Shī, and Gāo were lost;
the schools of Mèng and Jīng had texts but no masters;
and what Zhèng Xuán and Wáng Bì transmitted was actually the learning of the Fèi school."
Regarding the *Shū*,
according to the *Shìmíng*, it means to record the events of its time.
These are the surviving writings of the ancient emperors and kings,
including the *Sānfén*, *Wǔdiǎn*, *Xùngào*, and *Shìmìng*.
Confucius edited and arranged them,
beginning from Táng and Yú,
down to the Zhōu,
totaling one hundred chapters.
Because they are writings from high antiquity,
they are called the *Shàngshū* (Venerated Documents).
They were all lost when the Qin extinguished learning.
When the Hàn arose,
a man from Jǐnán named Fú Shèng was able to recite twenty-nine chapters from memory.
By the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
when he wished to establish *Shàngshū* studies,
as Fú Shèng was already over ninety years old,
too old to travel,
he then ordered the Court Grand Historian's Archivist Cháo Cuò to go to his home to receive and transmit it.
Fú Shēng produced a *Shàngshū* commentary in forty-one chapters.
Ōuyáng, and the Senior and Junior Xiàhóu transmitted his learning,
each gaining renown.
This is called the New Text *Shàngshū*.
Liú Xiàng's *Wǔxíng Zhuàn*
and Cài Yōng's engraved Stone Classics all used this version.
Later, Prince Gōng of Lǔ demolished Confucius's old residence,
and within a wall discovered the Old Text *Shàngshū* and *Lúnyǔ*,
returning all the writings to the Kǒng family.
Emperor Wǔ then ordered Kǒng Ānguó to collate these texts,
and he produced a commentary and exegesis in fifty-eight chapters.
See the preface and commentaries to the *Shàngshū*.
After Ānguó completed the text,
it later encountered the Hàn witchcraft affair and was not implemented.
During the Wèi-Jìn period,
Zhèng Chōng of Xíngyáng privately obtained it from among the people and transmitted it,
but it alone was not put into practice.
During the Eastern Jìn, Méi Zé of Rǔnán presented it to the throne,
and it was first listed among the official studies.
This then is the Old Text *Shàngshū*.
Regarding the *Shī*,
according to the preface by Bǔ Shāng:
"It is where the aspirations go."
In the past, Confucius edited the *Shī*,
selecting from above the Shāng,
and below from Lǔ,
totaling three hundred and eleven poems.
When the Qin extinguished learning,
six were lost,
leaving three hundred and five extant today.
Initially,
Confucius taught the *Shī* to Bǔ Shāng.
Shāng wrote a preface for it,
and taught it to Zēng Shēn of Lǔ.
Zēng Shēn taught it to Lǐ Kè of Wèi.
Lǐ Kè taught it to Mèng Zhòngzǐ of Lǔ.
Mèng Zhòngzǐ taught it to Gēnmóuzǐ.
Gēnmóuzǐ taught it to Xún Qīng of Zhào.
Xún Qīng taught it to Máo Hēng of Lǔ in the Hàn,
who composed a gloss and commentary,
and taught it to Máo Cháng of Zhào.
People of the time called Hēng the Elder Máo Gōng,
and Cháng the Younger Máo Gōng.
Because these two gentlemen transmitted it,
the *Shī* was therefore named the *Máo Shī*.
See the *Máo Shī Zhèngyì*.
In the Eastern Hàn, Zhèng Xuán,
taking what the Máo glosses did not fully cover or where there were differences,
continued with annotations,
calling them *jiān* (subcommentary).
*Jiān* means
to present or recommend,
meaning to present and complete Máo's ideas.
Regarding the *Lǐ*,
according to the *Shìmíng*, it means *tǐ* (form, embodiment),
meaning it attains the proper form of affairs.
The *Zhōulǐ* and the *Yílǐ*
were both composed and recorded by the Duke of Zhōu.
The so-called 'Three Hundred *Lǐjīng*'
and 'Three Thousand *Wēiyí*' —
the *Lǐjīng* refers to the *Zhōulǐ*,
and the *Wēiyí* refers to the *Yílǐ*.
See the *Sānlǐ Zhèngyì*.
The *Zhōulǐ*:
When the Qin extinguished learning,
it was hidden in mountain caves and house walls,
and therefore was not lost.
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, a certain Mr. Lǐ obtained it
and presented it to Prince Xiàn of Héjiān.
Only the chapter on the *Dōngguān* (Minister of Works) was missing.
They offered a thousand pieces of gold but could not obtain it,
so they used the *Kǎogōng Jì* to supplement it,
and then presented it to be entered into the imperial library.
Scholars of the time considered it incorrect,
and it was not implemented.
When it reached Liú Xīn,
he alone recognized the value of the book,
understanding it contained the traces of how the Duke of Zhōu achieved great peace.
He then first petitioned for it to be established among the official studies.
Later, Zhèng Xuán annotated it.
The *Yílǐ*:
When the Zhōu declined,
during the Warring States period,
the text was also lost.
By the Hàn, what Gāotáng Shēng transmitted was seventeen chapters,
only the *Shìlǐ* (Rites of the Gentleman) remained.
Later generations extrapolated from the *Shìlǐ* to deduce the rites of the Son of Heaven and practiced them.
Later, Mǎ Róng, Zhèng Xuán, and Wáng Sù all produced annotations for it.
The *Lǐjì*:
Originally, it was jointly compiled by disciples of Confucius from what they had heard.
Later, erudite scholars each made additions and deletions.
Zǐsī then composed the *Zhōngyōng*.
Gōngsūn Nízǐ composed the *Zīyī*.
During the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the Erudites composed the *Wángzhì*.
The remaining numerous chapters
all followed this pattern.
By the time of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
Hòu Cāng of Dōnghǎi was skilled in explaining the *Lǐ*.
At the Qūtái Hall, he compiled one hundred and eighty chapters on rites,
called the *Hòushì Qūtái Jì*.
Hòu Cāng transmitted it to Dài Dé of Liángguó and Dé's nephew, Shèng.
They then edited Hòu's records down to eighty-five chapters,
naming it the *Dàdài Lǐ*.
Shèng further edited the *Dàdài Lǐ* down to forty-six chapters,
naming it the *Xiǎodài Lǐ*.
Afterwards,
various scholars added the three chapters *Yuèlìng*, *Míngtáng Wèi*, and *Yuèjì*,
totaling forty-nine chapters.
This is the present *Lǐjì*.
See the *Lǐjì Zhèngyì*.
The *Lǐjì* has annotations by two scholars: Mǎ Róng and Zhèng Xuán.
Mǎ's annotation is now lost,
only Zhèng's annotation circulates in the world.
Regarding the *Chūnqiū*,
according to Dù Yù's preface:
"It is the name for the historical records of Lǔ."
The *Shìmíng* further states:
"It speaks of spring, autumn, winter, and summer,
ending to complete the year.
Mentioning spring and autumn implies winter and summer are known."
In the past, Confucius condensed the history of Lǔ to compose the *Chūnqiū*.
The writing contains praise and blame,
which cannot be seen in the written text.
He orally transmitted it to his disciple Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
Fearing that disciples would each adhere to their own interpretations,
thereby losing the true meaning,
they therefore discussed the Master's words and composed commentaries,
which are now the Zuǒshì Zhuàn.
Initially,
Confucius transmitted the Spring and Autumn Annals to Bǔ Shāng,
and also transmitted it to disciples Gōngyáng Gāo and Gǔliáng Chì,
who each in turn composed commentaries on it,
which are now the two commentaries Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng.
See the Chūnqiū Zhèngyì.
The Zuǒshì Zhuàn has the exegesis of Jiǎ Kuí,
and annotations by Fú Qián and Dù Yù.
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn has the explanatory glosses of Hé Xiū;
the Gǔliáng Zhuàn has the collected explanations of Fàn Nìng.
Also, Confucius explained the Classic of Filial Piety to Zēng Shēn,
and after Confucius passed away,
his various disciples recorded his wise sayings,
calling it the Analects,
which circulated together in the world.
The Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects have annotations by Zhèng Xuán, Hé Yàn, and others.
Eight Trigrams Six Emptinesses
The Zhōu Yì says:
"In the Changes there is the Supreme Ultimate,
which generates the Two Modes.
The Two Modes generate the Four Images,
the Four Images generate the Eight Trigrams.
The Eight Trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune."
It also says:
"The Changes as a book
is constantly shifting,
its transformations do not rest,
it circulates through the six emptinesses."
The commentary says:
"The six emptinesses
are the six positions."
Words as Pivot Dao as Key
The Yì says:
"It speaks of the utmost profundity under heaven and cannot be disordered.
If one's words are good,
then even a thousand li away there will be response to them;
words and actions are the pivot and mechanism of the noble man."
The Yì·Qián Záo Dù says:
"The Changes means
change,
transformation,
and constancy.
It governs these three to complete virtue,
being the key that contains the Dao."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Govern here means to combine;
one word combines these three matters,
to complete the key that contains its virtuous Dao.
Between Qí and Lǔ,
they call the lock of a door or a container for storing objects a key."
Deliberation and Imitation Encompassing and Modeling
The Zhōu Yì says:
"Imitate them and then speak,
deliberate on them and then act,
through imitation and deliberation to complete their transformations."
It also says:
"Encompass and model the transformations of heaven and earth without overstepping."
Wáng Bì's commentary:
"Encompassing and modeling means
to imitate and model heaven and earth and comprehensively encompass their principles."
Mysterious Assistance Manifestation and Application
The Yì·Shuō Guà says:
"In ancient times, when the sages created the Changes,
they mysteriously assisted the spiritual intelligence and produced the yarrow stalks."
It also says:
"They manifested and applied the firm and yielding and produced the lines."
Nine Masters Five Cycles
Liú Xiàng's Bié Lù says:
"The collated Chóu Zhōng Yì Zhuàn,
the Huáinán Jiǔ Shī Dào Xùn,
after removing duplicates, was fixed at twelve chapters.
The King of Huáinán engaged nine men skilled in the Changes,
gathered from them and obtained [their teachings],
titled as the Huáinán Nine Masters Book."
It also says:
"The collated Chóu Zhōng Yì Zhuàn,
the Ancient Five Cycles Book,
after removing duplicates, was fixed at eighteen chapters,
dividing the sixty-four hexagrams,
recording them by day and hour.
From jiǎzǐ to rénzǐ,
altogether five cycles,
therefore called the Five Cycles."
The above concerns the Yì.
Imperial Texts Royal Institutions
The Chūnqiū Shuō Tí Cí says:
"The Shàngshū consists of one hundred and two chapters in total,
arranged in order with detailed accounts.
Shàng means
above,
the surviving texts of the ancient emperors and kings."
Kǒng Ānguó's Shàngshū Xù says:
"Our ancestor Confucius,
discussed the ancient texts and records,
made a cut-off starting from Táng and Yú,
down to the Zhōu.
He lifted their grand outlines,
extracted their essential pivots,
altogether one hundred chapters.
To show rulers the models and norms,
the institutions of emperors and kings,
clear and plain."
Three Schools Hundred Chapters
Liú Xīn's Qī Lüè says:
"Shàngshū
means straightforward words.
Initially, the Óuyáng family's ancestor named it thus,
the Great Xiàhóu and Lesser Xiàhóu again established it in the official academy,
the learning of these three schools
remains particularly detailed today."
Kǒng Ānguó's Shàngshū Xù says:
"Our ancestor Confucius saw the complexity of historical records,
and also feared that readers would not have a uniform understanding,
made a cut-off from Táng and Yú onward,
down to the Zhōu.
He lifted their grand outlines,
extracted their essential pivots,
the texts of canons, counsels, instructions, announcements, oaths, and charges,
altogether one hundred chapters,
in order to expand and magnify the ultimate Dao."
Bestowed by the River Emerged from the Luò
The Xiàojīng Yuán Shén Qì says:
"The Yì excels in change,
the Shū examines the mandate tally bestowed by the River."
Sòng Jūn's commentary says:
"Bestowed by the River means
bestowed by the Hé and Luò rivers to examine the mandate tally."
The Shàngshū says:
"Heaven then conferred upon Yǔ the Great Plan with its nine divisions."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says:
"Heaven assisted Yǔ,
the Luò River produced the writing."
Straightforward Words Evidence of Righteousness
Liú Xīn's Qī Lüè says:
"The Shàngshū
means straightforward words,
transmitted to the present."
It also says:
"The Shī uses [words] to express emotion,
emotion is the tally of sincerity;
the Shū uses [words] for decision and judgment,
judgment is the evidence of righteousness."
The above concerns the Shū.
Five Junctures Six Emotions
The Shī Tuī Dù Zāi says:
"Establish the four beginnings and five junctures to regulate communication,
the juncture between mǎo and yǒu is for reforming governance,
the juncture between wǔ and hài is for changing the mandate.
The spirit is at the heavenly gate,
exiting and entering, listening and observing."
The Chūnqiū Kǒng Yǎn Tú says:
"The Shī contains the five junctures and six emotions."
Sòng Jūn's commentary says:
"The six emotions are the six principles,
namely: fēng, fù, bǐ, xìng, yǎ, sòng."
Gentle and Pure Sincere and Honest
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Warm, kind, pure, and good—
this is the teaching of the Shī."
The Lǐjì says:
"Gentle, soft, sincere, and honest—
this is the teaching of the Shī."
Gathering Subtleties and Gauging the Manifest Connecting Categories and Containing Pattern
The Shī Hán Shén Wù says:
"Gathering subtleties and gauging the manifest,
above connecting to the primordial sovereign,
below ordering the four beginnings,
arraying the five junctures."
Sòng Jūn's commentary says:
"Gathering subtleties and gauging the manifest means
the continuous vine with its melons.
At the beginning of human birth,
gauging its start, it will certainly reach the manifest,
the king possessing all under heaven."
Yán Yánzhī's Tíng Gào says:
"The book of chanting and singing,
takes its connecting categories and containing pattern,
comparing things and gathering phrases,
the Shī is its ancestor."
The above concerns the Shī.
Cultivating the Exterior, Regulating the Interior
The *Book of Han* states:
"Music is used to govern the interior and create harmony;
Rites are used to cultivate the exterior and establish distinctions.
Harmony leads to affection and kinship;
distinctions lead to awe and respect."
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Rites are what regulate the mean."
Receiving Heaven, Serving Earth
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Rites
are what the former kings used to receive the Way of Heaven
and govern human emotions."
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Rites serve Heaven above,
serve Earth below,
honor the ancestors, and revere the ruler and teacher."
Not Following the Law, Formless
The *Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yàn* states:
"Yànzǐ was sent to Lǔ.
Upon returning, he met Zhòngní and said:
'Regarding rites,
one does not hasten in the hall,
and when receiving something while standing, one does not kneel.
Yet you, Master, did the opposite.
Is this in accordance with rites?' Yànzǐ replied:
'When the ruler acts once,
the minister acts twice.
Since the ruler came quickly,
I hastened to return to my position.
The ruler bestowed it from a low position,
so I knelt to receive it humbly.'
Yànzǐ left,
and Zhòngní saw him off.
Returning, he instructed his disciples:
'Rites that do not follow the law—
only Yànzǐ can perform them.'"
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Music without sound,
rites without form,
mourning without garments—
these are called the three formless things."
Powder and Moisture, Tangerines and Pomelos
The *Six Secret Teachings of Tàigōng* states:
"In response to King Wén, it is said: 'Rites
are the powder and moisture of heavenly principle.'"
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The rites, righteousness, laws, and regulations of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
are like hawthorns, pears, tangerines, and pomelos.
Although their flavors are opposite,
they are all pleasing to the mouth."
Consulting Qín Laws, Speaking of Xià Rites
The *Later Book of Han: Discussion of Cáo Bāo* states:
"At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
court regulations lacked written form.
Shūsūn Tōng extensively adopted the classics of rites
and consulted Qín laws.
Although they suited the circumstances and observed the times,
and saved the collapsing system,
the grand institutions of the former kings were largely lacking."
The *Analects* states:
"I can speak of the rites of Xià,
but the state of Qǐ cannot provide sufficient evidence."
The above is on *Rites*.
Examining Portents, Verifying Images
The *Spring and Autumn Grasping Completion Chart* states:
"Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
expounding the relationship between Heaven and humanity,
recording anomalies and examining portents."
The *Spring and Autumn Confucius Chart* states:
"He established the methods of the Five Classics,
applied them to Heaven and Earth,
verified them with charts and images,
compared them with the Three Sovereigns,
and extended them throughout the realm."
Zhōu Laws, Confucian Classics
Dù Yù's *Preface to the Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
"Its general principles and illustrative cases
are all constant institutions for governing the state,
the enduring laws bequeathed by the Duke of Zhōu."
The *Spring and Autumn Confucius Chart* states:
"The *Gōngyáng* fully contains the Confucian classics."
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
"The *Gōngyáng*
refers to Gōngyáng Gāo.
The 'classics' refer to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*."
Four Commentaries, Two Schools
The *Book of Han* states:
"The *Spring and Autumn Annals* criticized and diminished the powerful and authoritative figures of its time,
so the text was concealed and not publicly circulated.
By the late period, oral teachings prevailed,
hence there appeared the commentaries of *Gōngyáng*, *Gǔliáng*, *Zōu*, and *Jiá*.
Among the four schools,
the *Gōngyáng* and *Gǔliáng* were established as official studies."
Liú Xīn's *Seven Summaries* states:
"The two schools of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
sometimes include the four seasons,
and sometimes, with ancient texts lacking events,
do not necessarily include the four seasons."
Concealed Text, Obscured Meaning
The *Book of Han* states:
"The *Spring and Autumn Annals* criticized and diminished the powerful and authoritative figures of its time.
The actual events are all recorded in the commentaries,
so the text was concealed and not publicly circulated
to avoid the difficulties of the time."
Yán Yánzhī's *Court Admonitions* states:
"Among books of praise and blame,
those that employ straightforward language with obscured meaning
to assist in regulating declining rulers—
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is foremost."
Encompassing Three Sages, Recording the Four Regions
The *Spring and Autumn Explanatory Phrases* states:
"The classic text encompasses the standards of the Three Sages."
The *Rites of Zhōu* states:
"Record the affairs of the four regions."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"'Record'
means to chronicle,
such as Lǔ's *Spring and Autumn Annals*, Jìn's *Shèng*,
and Chǔ's *Táowù*."
The above is on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Táng Tàizōng, Emperor of Civil and Martial Sageliness, "Poem on the *Book of Documents*"
Revering literature, I pause in my steps from time to time;
at the Eastern Tower, I halt my carriage again.
I cease dining to ponder the Three Mounds;
I keep the lamp lit to peruse the Five Canons.
With a chilled heart, I witness the forests of meat;
with a startled soul, I observe the depths of indulgence.
Many are the rulers who indulged their passions and grew benighted;
few are the enlightened monarchs who mastered themselves.
Destroying oneself stems from accumulating evils;
achieving fame still comes from amassing good deeds.
Now that I inherit the legacy of a hundred kings,
I tread with caution as the years revolve.
Jìn Fù Xián, "Poem on the *Classic of Filial Piety*"
Establishing oneself and practicing the Way
begins with serving one's parents.
Above and below, there are no resentments;
one is not detested by others.
Filial piety, without beginning or end,
never leaves one's person.
When these three are complete,
one may govern the people.
Serving the ruler with filial piety,
one does not stray from a good name.
Advancing, one thinks of exhausting loyalty;
in righteousness, there is no contention.
Correcting and remedying his faults,
disasters and harms do not arise.
The utmost in filial piety and fraternal duty
penetrates to the divine and luminous.
Also, "Poem on the *Analects*"
Hold fast to the good Way unto death,
ground but not worn thin.
How upright was Shǐ Yú!
He may be called a great minister.
Facing danger, he entrusted his life;
he could devote his person.
Master oneself and return to rites;
excel in learning, then take office.
Wealth and honor lie with Heaven;
practicing benevolence depends on oneself.
Serve the ruler with the Way;
only with death is it finished.
Also, "Poem on the *Máo Odes*"
Do not push the great cart,
lest the dust rise darkly.
With many scholars gathered in dignity,
King Wén found peace.
The enlightened and sincere gentleman
plans the great schemes.
Cultivate his virtue,
and a good end will have a beginning.
Exert yourself in thoughts of withdrawal;
my words are to be heeded.
Thieves' words are exceedingly sweet;
how can they lead to goodness?
Slanderers know no limits;
they have the face to show themselves.
Another, "Poem on the *Book of Changes*"
Humble to cultivate oneself,
Modest yet honored and radiant.
Advancing virtue and refining one's work,
Already possessing established norms.
Splendor and brilliance renewed daily,
Shining upon the four directions.
Petty men are not to be employed,
The way of the noble man prospers.
Another, "Poem on the *Zhouguan*"
The king establishes the state,
Sets up offices and divides duties.
Promoting the worthy and achieving merit,
Selecting from the straightforward and upright.
Eliminating the impure,
Daring not to act contrary.
Conferring ranks according to virtue,
Truly reaching its utmost.
Distinguishing those fit for office,
Reporting to the authorities.
Overseeing prohibitions and warnings,
Administering governance and decrees.
Each fulfills their duties,
To heed the king's commands.
Another, "Poem on the *Zuǒzhuàn*"
The rites of serving one's lord,
Dare I not exhaust sincerity?
Reverently upholding virtue and righteousness,
Establishing customs and reputation.
Manifesting virtue and blocking transgressions,
Not tarnishing one's name.
Dying to benefit the state,
Is considered one's own glory.
This heart does not waver,
Loyal and capable of effort.
Not flattering for gain,
An ancient legacy of integrity.
Severely dismissing the unrighteous,
Preventing them from taking root.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem on the *Book of Rites*"
Jade and silk aid the royal assembly,
Suburban altars harmonize with the sage's sentiment.
Expanding and opening the encircling walls,
The ultimate Way surpasses golden chests.
Firmly rooted in the solid earth,
Far-reaching, soaring to the highest clarity.
Just delighting in the rites of ascent,
Enough to comfort the remaining life.
Xiè Tiǎo of Qí, "Memorial Thanking the Suí Prince for Bestowing the *Zuǒzhuàn*"
Clear and distinct, the finished text,
Recently issued from the inner court.
Kindly encouraging with books in hand,
Compassionately urging study behind curtains.
I, Tiǎo, have not yet seen the mountain of texts,
Long ignorant of river-like classics.
My learning falls short of specialization,
My explanations lack detailed analysis.
Hoping to learn when perplexed,
Polishing feathers to illuminate my ignorant heart,
Keeping bestowed books at home,
Golden chests bequeathing to descendants.
Perusing with divine delight,
Chanting to know profound kindness.
Liú Xiàochuò, "Memorial Thanking for Being Appointed to Serve the Classics in the Eastern Palace"
The crown prince, versed in the four arts, long aware of the three excellences,
Even without study, still returns.
Seeking Confucian elegance broadly,
Responding to matters and examining doubts.
His achievements illuminate the Xià school,
His virtue flourishes in the Zhōu academy.
The feudal lords of Sòng and Lǔ,
Observe the model here.
Participating in grand ceremonies,
None but the nation's finest.
Although I am in charge of classical texts,
Colleagues are not few.
Selected and recommended,
Many are the outstanding talents.
The dragon's light specially bestowed,
Alone I am among the chosen.
If I hear the Way in the morning,
I would still gladly die by evening.
How much more with such heavy grace,
I see life as ever lighter.
Historical Biographies, Part Two
According to the *Shiben Zhu*:
"In the era of Huángdì,
the office of historian was first established.
Cāngjié and Jǔsòng held these positions.
By the time of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
they were divided into left and right positions.
Words were recorded by the Left Historian,
actions were recorded by the Right Historian.
It is said the Left Historian recorded words,
the Right Historian recorded events.
Words are the warp of the *Shàngshū*,
events are the warp of the *Chūnqiū*."
The Zhōu official system had the Grand Historian, Minor Historian, Inner Historian, Outer Historian, and Remonstrance Historian.
These five offices:
The Grand Historian was in charge of establishing the state's six canons, eight laws, and eight regulations,
to oversee the governance of the state;
The Minor Historian was in charge of the state's records, establishing genealogies, distinguishing the zhāo-mù order;
if there were affairs, he would announce the king's taboos;
The Inner Historian was in charge of the king's eight instruments of control,
writing the king's commands and keeping duplicates;
The Outer Historian was in charge of writing external commands,
in charge of the records of the four quarters, in charge of the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, in charge of disseminating book titles to the four quarters;
The Remonstrance Historian was in charge of governance orders for the states, cities, and myriad people,
to assist the Prime Minister,
in charge of drafting documents."
The *Qǔlǐ* says:
"The historian carries his brush,
the officer carries his words.
The Xià had Grand Historian Zhōng,
the Yīn had Grand Historian Zhì,
the Zhōu had Grand Historian Yì, Grand Historian Dān, Grand Historian Shūfú, Historian Zhòu, Historian Sū, Historian Zhào."
Confucius said:
"Zhōu Rén
was a good historian of antiquity.
Lǎozǐ was the Zhōu Archivist,
and also the Pillar Historian,
which were his duties."
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
"In Jìn, Zhào Chuān assassinated Lord Líng.
Grand Historian Dǒng Hú wrote:
'Zhào Dùn assassinated his lord.'
Dùn said:

Qín burned the ancient classics,

second, small seal script,
created by Lǐ Sī, Zhào Gāo, and Hú Mǔ Jìng during the reign of the First Emperor;

used for tally passes;

sixth, signboard script,
used for gate inscriptions;
seventh, shū script,
inscribed on spears and halberds;
eighth, clerical script,

used for official documents in government offices,
and adopted by the Hàn dynasty.

"Bāo Xián, styled Zǐliáng,
was well-versed in the *Lǔ Odes* and the *Lúnyǔ*.
He settled in Dōnghǎi,
and established a refined lodge to lecture and teach."
Lecturing in the Marshes Holding Classics by the Field Banks
Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"Yáng Lún was proficient in the Old Text *Shàngshū*.
He did not accept summons from the commanderies and prefectures,
but lectured and taught in the great marshes,
and his disciples numbered over a thousand."
It also says:
"Sūn Qī in his youth was a student,
proficient in the *Jīngshì Changes* and the Old Text *Shàngshū*.
His family was very poor,
and he herded pigs in the marshes.
Scholars would all hold their classics by the banks of the fields to pursue him."
Liáng Rén Fǎng's *Poem Urging Officials to Pursue Learning*
Evening candles press upon the western elms,
The setting [sun] warns of the southern fields.
I say, I was originally indolent and lax,
In my declining years, elms and willows have accumulated.
Entering this realm, I thirst for teacher-ministers,
Facing governance, I revere beneficial friends.
Late meals, yet I wish to hold the classics crosswise,
All day long, I think of holding the broom.
Though I delight in distinguishing orchid from mugwort,
Of what use is clearing away wormwood and weeds?
Chén Zhōu Hóngzhèng's *Poem on Rising Early in the Academy to Listen to Lectures*
At dawn, I join the lower seats,
Leisurely, I step out of the layered gates.
In the north hall, the moon has slightly faded,
On the southern branches, magpies already fly.
Early frost hangs mistily,
First fog rises densely.
Though the strict watchman's clappers have ceased,
The tall gates are still shut.
Already grieving the year's course is swift,
Again sighing that my heart's matters are thwarted.
All my life I loved mountains and seas,
In former days, I especially prized subtlety.
I have not yet understood how to lightly leave my person behind,
I should only return after failing the examinations.
Suí Yǔ Xìn's *Poem Matching Hé Yìtóng's 'Concluding a Lecture and Expressing My Feelings'*
Having no name, I then lecture on the Way,
When stirred, I surely discuss subtleties.
I yield the seat of ritual to Anjīng,
And set right my vocation, arranging Confucian robes.
I seem to have found the joy of wandering freely,
Able to join in abandoning the lecture and returning.
At the Stone Canal, people briefly rest,
At Huáyīn market, it is temporarily sparse.
Autumn clouds lower the evening air,
Short shadows slant with lingering light.
Fireflies push through tangled grass to emerge,
Wild geese abandon broken reeds to fly.
There is another path at Pínglíng,
Desolate, a traveler's temples grow thin.
Truly I rejoice, cherishing modest inquiry,
Meeting you, sir, to discuss entering the subtle.
Emperor Yuándì of Liáng's "Stele Inscription on the Crown Prince's Lecture"
The Crown Prince accumulates thunder to plant virtue,
doubles brightness to serve as the two luminaries,
his achievements surpass those of the feudal lords,
his Way is loftier than that of the heir apparent.
The palace walls rise layer upon layer,
high mountains are gazed upon with reverence,
the gates of Chénghuá
resemble even more the gate of Tōngdé,
the gardens of Bówàng
instead resemble the market of Huáyīn.
The household stewards and numerous sons
all enter the four disciplines,
the horse-washers and rear chariots
are all versed in the six arts.
Turning the golden carriage, he descends to the Pìyōng Academy;
with jade-like countenance, he passes through the Huái Market.
Examining his suspended mirror in the high hall,
the wine vessel at the crossroads awaits to be filled,
looking back and suddenly forward,
broad in learning and restrained in ritual.
He will cause the palace of the eldest son in the easternmost reaches
not to be inscribed solely on silver plaques.
The preface of the Crown Prince of Nánpí
how could it merely excel with golden steles?
Chén Jiāngzǒng's "Stele Inscription on the Crown Prince's Lecture at the Imperial Academy"
Our Great Chén's rule over the world,
is like water spreading its long waves,
like the Jade Star tracing its eternal course.
Chónghuá gave birth to wisdom,
rising from the wilderness of the great foothills;
Jìngzhòng inherited the enterprise,
flourishing indeed as the omen of the crying phoenix.
Moreover, with vast talent as rich as the sea,
unrestrained thoughts pouring like a spring,
holding the brush and setting it to paper,
he stirs the songs and ballads of the eight directions;
single phrases and fragments of speech
harmonize with the rhythm of the five tones.
Clouds fly and winds rise,
pursuing and surpassing the verses of the Hàn Emperor;
with lofty views and splendid pools,
he far surpasses the poems of the Wèi Emperor.
Thus, he further establishes the library of collected books,
opening the path for offerings and contributions.
Curtained tents hold fragmented remnants,
family walls preserve lost and scattered works.
Secret classics from the Purple Terrace,
rare texts in green cases,
moth-eaten books from Yǔlíng,
scattered bamboo slips from Sōng Mountain,
what is held by the outer historians,
what is managed by the broad inner chambers,
all are adorned with lead and wooden tablets,
engraved on light yellow silk,
this is the cultivation of literary education.
Literature, Part Five
Regarding literature,
Confucius said:
"How resplendent are its literary patterns!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Our Master's literary patterns,
we can hear of them."
See the *Analects*.
For poetry expresses intent,
songs prolong speech,
see the *Shàngshū*.
What is recited without singing is called *fù*.
In ancient times, one who could compose *fù* upon ascending heights,
offer sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
make oaths for armies,
write eulogies for mourning rites,
inscribe inscriptions on vessels,
could then become a senior official!
After the Three Dynasties,
literary compositions gradually increased,
moreover, proclamations and edicts were announced to the states,
dispatches and manifestos were presented to the armies,
memorials and petitions to express feelings and reasons,
admonitions and warnings to correct errors and evils,
praises and eulogies to beautify descriptions,
stele inscriptions to illuminate merits and virtues,
posthumous titles and memorials to commend words and deeds,
laments and condolences to mourn the fallen,
reports and petitions to communicate sentiments from below,
notes and memorials to present to the ancestral temple with respect,
discourses and deliberations to balance principles,
refutations and critiques to examine discrepancies,
this is a general outline.
Spirit as Master, Form as Foundation
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎnlùn* says:
"In literature, spirit is the master;
the purity or turbidity of spirit has its substance,
it cannot be forced by effort to achieve."
Zhì Yú's *Wénzhāng Liúbié Lùn* says:
"Contemporary *fù* take the depiction of forms as the foundation,
and the correction of meaning as an aid."
Càn's Equal, Huá's Literary Excellence
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎnlùn* says:
"Wáng Càn excels in lyrical *fù*,
Xú Gàn often possesses untrammeled spirit,
yet Càn is his equal."
*Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū* says:
"Ruǎn Jí saw Zhāng Huá's *'Jiāoliáo Fù'*,
and considered him a talent fit to assist a king;
Chénggōng Suǐ also praised Huá's literary excellence and superior meaning."
Embellishment, Criticism
*Analects* says:
"In preparing a diplomatic dispatch,
Bì Chén drafted it,
Shìshū deliberated on it,
the diplomatic officer Zǐyǔ polished it,
and Dōnglǐ Zǐchǎn embellished it."
Cáo Zhí's *Letter to Yáng Xiū* says:
"Liú Jìxù's talent cannot reach that of the authors,
yet he criticizes literary works,
picking out their strengths and weaknesses."
Rules of Diction, Words and Phrases
Lù Shìhéng's *Wénfù* says:
"The universal rules of diction and literary principles,
I indeed hold them in my heart and adhere to them."
Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* says:
"When learning becomes familiar through practice,
one can infer categories and produce literature;
literature sprouts from external cultivation,
it is not necessarily that true talent matches the literature.
Moreover, shallow ideas in flowery words,
without the depth of roots and stems,
fail to see the greater substance."
Reed Pipes, Drumming and Blowing
*Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"The Five Classics are the reed pipes,
the Three Ancient Texts are the gold and jade."
Liú Yìqìng's *Shìshuō* says:
"Sūn Xìnggōng's *Sāndū* and *Èrjīng*,
are the drumming and blowing of the Five Classics."
Carving Dragons, Drawing Tigers
*Shǐjì* says:
"Diāolóng Shì, Tántiān Yǎn—the writings of Zōu Yǎn,
are adorned like dragon patterns,
hence called 'carving dragons.'"
Cáo Zhí's *Letter to Yáng Xiū* says:
"Kǒng Zhāng's talent
is not skilled in lyrical *fù*,
yet he often claims to be of the same style as Sīmǎ Chángqīng,
like drawing a tiger that ends up looking like a dog."
Swimming Fish Emerge from the Abyss, Flying Hares Cross Mountains
Lù Shìhéng's *Wénfù* says:
"Thus, profound words are restrained,
like a swimming fish biting a hook emerging from the depths of a deep abyss."
Chén Lín's *Reply to the Letter of the Prince of Dōng'ē* says:
"Clear diction and marvelous phrases,
blazing brilliantly, illuminating the scenery,
are like flying hares and shooting stars,
crossing mountains and leaping over seas,
which even dragon-steeds cannot catch up to.
How could plodding horses hope to match their pace?"
Compare the Four Disciplines, Like the Five Colors
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎnlùn* says:
"Literature fundamentally shares the same origin but differs in its branches;
memorials and deliberations should be elegant,
letters and discourses should be reasoned,
inscriptions and eulogies value substance,
poetry and *fù* desire beauty,
these four disciplines are different,
so those skilled in them are specialized."
Lù Shìhéng's *Wénfù* says:
"As a thing, it is manifold in appearance;
as a form, it undergoes frequent changes;
in conveying ideas, it values ingenuity;
in employing language, it prizes refinement.
As for the alternation of sounds,
it is like the five colors enhancing each other."
Weak Style, Vigorous Diction
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Letter to Wú Zhì* says:
"Zhòngxuān alone excels in lyrical *fù*,
but it is a pity his style is weak,
insufficient to elevate his writing.
As for what he excels in,
the ancients could not far surpass him."
Fù Xuán's *Preface to Linked Pearls* says:
"Bān Gù's metaphors are beautiful, his diction vigorous,
his writing broad and magnificent,
most truly capturing the style."
Carving Jade, Engraving Ice
Yáng Xióng's *Model Sayings* states:
"Someone said: 'Fine jade is not carved;
beautiful words are not adorned.'
What does this mean?"
The reply:
"'If jade is not carved,
fányú jade cannot be made into vessels;
if words are not adorned,
the canons and counsels cannot become classics.'"
Huán Kuān's *Discourses on Salt and Iron* states:
"To lack the substance within yet learn its ornamentation from without
is like drawing on grease or engraving ice—
wasting time and effort."
Cinnabar and Azure, Silk Gauze
Yáng Xióng's *Model Sayings* states:
"Someone asked: 'Was Qū Yuán wise?'
The reply:
"'Like jade, like crystal,
he then transformed into cinnabar and azure.'"
Lǐ Guǐ's commentary states:
"The wise understand Heaven's mandate;
like jade, like crystal,
they are polished yet not worn thin.
Now Qū Yuán, exiled,
stirred by emotion, then transformed;
though possessing literary talent,
it is merely the argument of cinnabar and azure!"
Lǐ Chōng's *Discourses on the Literary Forest* states:
"Pān Ānrén's writing
is like the feathers of soaring birds,
the silk gauze of garments."
Manifesting Hàn, Narrating Yīn
Yáng Xióng's *Critique of the Qin and Eulogy of the New* states:
"In the past, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú composed a piece on the fēng and shàn sacrifices
to manifest the excellence of the Hàn house."
Chéng Xiǎo's *Letter to Fù Xuán* states:
"Duke Wén sang of Zhōu,
Master Kǒng narrated Yīn;
their fame resounds for a thousand years,
their achievements are passed to later generations."
Holding the Snake Pearl, Galloping the Steed's Hooves
Cáo Zhí's *Letter to Yáng Xiū* states:
"At that time,
every person claimed to hold the pearl of the divine snake,
every household claimed to embrace the jade of Jīngshān."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Canon of Literature* states:
"These seven masters
left no learning untouched,
borrowed no expressions from others.
All galloped their thoroughbreds for a thousand *lǐ*,
raising their hooves in unison to race together."
Chángqīng's Warm Elegance, Gōnggàn's Sublime Excellence
*Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
"Méi Gāo's literary compositions were swift and agile,
Chángqīng's creations were slow and deliberate;
both attained the finest reputation of their time,
yet Chángqīng's works were warm and elegant from start to finish."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Letter to Wú Zhì* states:
"Gōnggàn possessed an untrammeled spirit,
but it was not yet forceful.
The finest of his five-character poems
are sublimely excellent, surpassing his contemporaries."
Wáng's Rhapsodies, Ruǎn's Prose; Kǒng's Letters, Lù's Discourses
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Canon of Literature* states:
"Wáng Càn excelled at poetic rhapsodies;
Chén Lín and Ruǎn Yǔ's memorials, petitions, and letters
are outstanding in the present day."
Lǐ Chōng's *Discourses on the Literary Forest* states:
"Someone asked:
"How can one call it literature?"
The reply:
"Kǒng Wénjǔ's letters,
Lù Shìhéng's discourses—
these can be called accomplished literature."
Jìn Dynasty Lù Jī's *Rhapsody on Literature*
Whenever I observe the works of talented scholars,
I privately feel I have grasped their devoted intent.
Their deployment of language and choice of words
are indeed highly varied.
Beauty and ugliness, good and bad—
can they be spoken of?
Whenever I compose literature myself,
I especially perceive its true nature.
I constantly worry that ideas do not match the objects,
that writing fails to capture the ideas.
It is not that understanding is difficult,
but that execution is difficult.
Therefore, I compose this rhapsody on literature
to describe the magnificent diction of past scholars,
and thereby discuss the origins of the merits and flaws in literary composition.
Standing in the central realm, I gaze into the profound;
nourishing my emotions and will with the ancient canons.
Following the four seasons, I sigh at the passing of time;
observing the myriad things, my thoughts grow profuse.
I grieve for fallen leaves in the stark autumn;
I delight in tender branches in the fragrant spring.
My heart, awe-stricken, embraces frost;
my will, soaring, approaches the clouds.
I chant of the splendid achievements of worldly virtue;
I recite the pure fragrance of ancestors.
I wander through the forest and treasury of literary works;
I admire the refined elegance of beautiful diction.
Moved, I lay aside the scroll and take up the brush,
to express it roughly in this writing.
At the beginning,
all vision is withdrawn, all hearing turned inward;
immersed in thought, probing widely.
The spirit gallops to the eight extremes;
the mind roams ten thousand fathoms high.
When the conception arrives,
emotions, like dawn light, grow increasingly vivid;
objects, clear and distinct, come forth in turn.
I pour out the essence of all writings;
I rinse with the fragrant richness of the Six Arts.
I gather the omitted texts of a hundred generations;
I collect the lost rhymes of a thousand years.
I discard morning blossoms already opened;
I unfold evening blooms not yet stirred.
I observe past and present in an instant;
I touch the four seas in a blink.
Then I select meanings and arrange them by section;
I examine words and assign them their places.
Those bearing light all rise up;
those harboring sound must be plucked.
Sometimes I follow the branch to shake the leaves;
sometimes I trace the wave to seek the source.
Sometimes I proceed from the hidden to the manifest;
sometimes I seek the easy and obtain the difficult.
Sometimes, like a tiger's transformation, beasts are subdued;
sometimes, like a dragon's appearance, birds scatter.
Sometimes it is settled and easy to apply;
sometimes it is jagged and uneasy.
I exhaust my clear mind in concentrated thought;
I refine myriad considerations into words.
I encompass heaven and earth within form;
I crush the myriad things at the brush's tip.
Ah, this endeavor is truly delightful,
and surely revered by sages and worthies.
I tax emptiness to demand substance;
I knock on silence to seek sound.
I contain vast distances within a foot of silk;
I pour out torrential abundance from an inch of heart.
Words, expanded, grow ever broader;
thoughts, probed, grow ever deeper.
I sow fragrant blossoms, richly scented;
I send forth green branches, lush and dense.
Brilliant, like wind flying and whirlwinds rising;
lush, like clouds arising in the literary forest.
Thus, those who dazzle the eye prize extravagance;
those who satisfy the heart value aptness.
Those who exhaust words have no constraint;
those who discourse broadly seek only openness.
Poetry follows emotion and is ornate and delicate;
rhapsody embodies objects and is clear and bright.
Stone inscriptions display ornamentation to complement substance;
elegies are lingering and sorrowful.
Inscriptions are broad yet concise, warm and smooth;
admonitions are rhythmic and pause, pure and vigorous.
Eulogies are leisurely and richly ornate;
discourses are subtle and precise, clear and fluent.
Memorials are level, penetrating, refined, and elegant;
persuasions are dazzling and artfully deceptive.
Though distinctions lie herein,
one must also prohibit depravity and restrain excess.
The essentials are that words convey and principles are upheld;
thus, prolixity is not to be adopted.
Chén Jiāngzǒng's *Poem: Composing Three Rhapsodies in One Day, in Response to the Prince's Command*
The Crown Prince's discerning appreciation is vigorous;
in the clear night, we roam the northern garden.
With brush in hand, I complete three rhapsodies;
passing the cup, we face the ninth autumn.
Flying words, patterned silk's splendor;
falling on paper, waves and billows flow.
Dense trees echo with cold cicadas' sound;
dark eaves hold the mournful cries of sparrows.
Green banks brighten the layered halls;
blue hills shine on the nearby tower.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, "Letter in Reply to Zhāng Zuǎn Thanking Him for Presenting His Collection"
You have loved literary compositions since youth,
and now it has been twenty-five years.
I have privately considered this matter:
the sun, moon, and three celestial bodies,
the fire-dragon and the axe-head emblem,
are still manifested in celestial phenomena;
they are made clear in human affairs.
How much more should literary expression not cease,
and songs and odes not be discontinued!
If one does not become a stalwart man,
Yáng Xióng indeed used petty words to undermine the Way;
if one is not called a gentleman,
Cáo Zhí also used clever disputation to damage discourse.
Judging them by the standards of punishment,
their crimes would be unpardonable.
As for when spring light falls in the courtyard,
and the breeze turns the huì orchids.
When autumn rain clears at dawn,
and the first leaves fall from the eaves' wú-trees.
When floating clouds arise over the wilds,
and the bright moon enters the tower.
Sometimes summoning relatives and guests,
suddenly setting the stately carriage in motion.
Jade cups repeatedly filled,
parrots suddenly toppled.
In those past years at the three frontiers,
I lingered for four long years.
Barbarian mists joined the sky,
campaign banners brushed the sun.
At times hearing the watchtower flute,
distantly listening to the frontier reed-pipe.
Sometimes homesickness is desolate,
sometimes heroic spirit surges with indignation.
Therefore, I pondered and wrote short pieces,
patching together mediocre notes,
expressing what met the eye and wrote the heart,
composing according to events.
Liáng Shěn Yuē, "Letter to Fàn Shùzēng Discussing the Rhapsody of Prince Jìnglíng"
Now, to drift vaguely upon the vast currents,
is to not recognize the shores;
to present bells and stones in a jumble,
is to fail to distinguish the gōng and shāng notes.
Though one may recite them over and over,
compile and separate, the characters vanish,
ultimately there is no way to respond adequately to your sagely intent,
or slightly express my modest strengths.
Liáng Jiāng Yān, "Preface to Miscellaneous Style Poems"
Now, the songs of Chǔ and the airs of Hàn,
were already not of one bone;
the creations of Wèi and the works of Jìn,
certainly also represent two styles.
It is like indigo and vermilion forming colors,
the variations of intermingling are endless;
gōng and jué notes making music,
the graceful and charming forms are limitless.
Thus, how could moth-eyebrows have the same appearance,
yet all stir the soul?
How could fragrant grasses share the same scent,
yet all please the spirit?
Is this not so?
As for the various worthies of the age,
each is stuck in their own delusions,
none fail to praise the sweet and then reject the pungent.
They love the red and then disparage the plain,
how can this be called broad illumination of all methods,
or the forbearance, far-reaching vision, and universal love spoken of?
However, the rise of the five-character line,
was surely not a change from antiquity.
But west of the pass and at Yèxià,
styles were already rarely the same.
North of the river and south of the river,
methods were quite different.
Therefore, the distinctions between dark and yellow, warp and weft,
the differences between gold sinking and jade floating,
I believe each possesses its own beauty and combines excellence.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn, "Preface to the Collected Works of the Duke of Zhào"
I have heard that when Píngyáng struck the stones,
the valleys thereby harmonized;
when Dàxià blew the bamboo pipes,
wind and clouds were moved by it.
Compared to that which contains and expresses innate sensibility,
modulates and regulates the force of words,
subtly transforms the springtime sun,
and reflects the light of the white sun,
how can they be spoken of in the same breath?
The Pillar of State, the Duke of Zhào,
when he speaks, it forms discourse;
when he takes up the brush, it becomes a composition.
Unrestrained manner flows forth unrestrainedly.
New sentiments surge upward,
wind and rain vie in flight,
fish and dragons each transform.
Compared to jade tablets and discs,
the assembly at Túshān had ten thousand layers;
likened to clouds and mist,
the cliffs of Chìchéng are a thousand fathoms high.
His writing partakes of the celestial phenomena;
it immediately enters the books of the Office of Astronomy.
His rhymes touch upon silk and paulownia;
they all belong to the observatory of the Director of Music.
Speaking of its grandeur,
then it is like the roc rising halfway to heaven;
speaking of its delicacy,
then it is like the wren's nest on a mosquito's eyelash.
How could it merely be like bears and brown bears ascending in the morning?
The layered city embraces the sun and moon's radiance,
its light and blaze fly by night,
the Southern Dipper touches the aura of flood-dragons.
In former times, Qū Píng and Sòng Yù,
began with profound sorrow and lament;
Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng,
were born in an age of separation.
Since the end of the Jiàn'ān era of Wèi,
and the Tàikāng era of Jìn onward,
carving insects and engraving seals,
the style changed three times.
Everyone claimed to hold the pearl of the spiritual snake,
and embrace the jade of Jīng Mountain.
The Duke selects and blends from the Elegant and the Odes,
harmonizes and tunes the pitch-pipes.
If the words were discordant with the key points,
then the Qūtái Academy would not consider them;
if the sounds stopped at simple strumming,
then the National Academy would not select them.
Thus he became the pillar and beam of the literary garden,
the crown and leader of the forest of letters.
The Great Elegant supports the wheel,
the Lesser Mountain bears the canopy.
Brush, Part Six
The Shì Míng says:
"Brush (bǐ),
means to relate (shù),
it means to relate affairs and speak of them."
According to the Bówù Zhì:
"Méng Tián invented the brush."
Also according to the Shàngshū Zhōnghòu:
"A dark turtle emerged bearing a chart,
the Duke of Zhōu took up a brush and wrote it down in timely script."
The Qǔ Lǐ says:
"The historian carries the brush,
the officer carries the words."
This shows that before the Qín dynasty, brushes already existed.
Probably the various states did not have a name for it,
but Qín alone obtained the name,
and Méng Tián further modified it, adding and subtracting."
Therefore, the Shuō Wén says:
"In Chǔ it is called yù,
in Wú it is called bùlǜ;
in Yān it is called fú,
in Qín it is called bǐ, which is correct."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"According to Hàn regulations,
the Son of Heaven's brush,
has its base (fū) inlaid with precious stones.
(Pronunciation: fū.)
The hairs are all from autumn hares,
made by the official craftsman Lù Hù.
Also, the case is made of assorted treasures,
set with jade discs and kingfisher feathers,
each worth a hundred pieces of gold."
The Hàn Shū says:
"The Imperial Secretary, the Attendant Gentleman, the Chancellor, and the Gentleman,
are monthly supplied with one pair of large-tube brushes."
Fù Xuán says:
"By the end of the Hàn, a brush case,
was carved from gold,
adorned with Hé's jade,
inlaid with Suí pearls,
and patterned with kingfisher feathers.
The brush, if not with a rhinoceros-horn shaft,
must have an elephant-tusk tube,
a rich fox's core,
and autumn hare's hairs!"
Such were the affairs.
Ornamental Rhinoceros Horn and Kingfisher Feathers
The Fù Zǐ says:
"By the end of the Hàn, brushes,
if not with a rhinoceros-horn shaft,
must have an elephant-tusk tube."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"According to Hàn regulations,
the Son of Heaven's brush,
has a case made of assorted treasures,
set with jade discs and kingfisher feathers,
each worth a hundred pieces of gold."
Wú Lǜ Zhào Háo
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
"The brush is used for writing.
In Chǔ it is called yù,
in Wú it is called bùlǜ.
In Yān it is called fú,
in Qín it is called bǐ."
Wáng Xīzhī's Bǐ Jīng states:
"In Hàn times, the various commanderies presented rabbit-hair brushes.
They came from Hóngdū,
but only the hairs from Zhào state were suitable for use.
People of the time all said rabbit hairs have no inherent superiority or inferiority;
it is the tube and hand that have skill or clumsiness."
Xiě Tú Shū Dú
The Shàngshū·Zhōnghòu states:
"A dark turtle emerged bearing a chart on its back.
The Duke of Zhōu took up a brush and wrote it down in timely script."
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū states:
"Dìwǔ Yǒng was appointed as the Supervising Army Censor to oversee Yōuzhōu.
Cài Yōng and other famous talents and scholars from across the land all gathered,
holding a farewell feast at the Pínglè Hall.
Gāo Biāo, seeing Yǒng off, was present at the banquet.
He then took up a brush and wrote on a tablet."
Dāngmiàn Míng Xīn
Cài Yōng wrote in a letter:
"To the Attendant-in-Waiting in charge of affairs,
we may never meet again.
