Only these brush-written letters
can serve as a face-to-face meeting."
Fù Xuán's "Brush Inscription" states:
"Brilliant is the red tube,
gentle and soft the light brush-tip.
Upright in color is the dark ink,
inscribing the heart and writing down words."
Bǎo Fū Jīn Xiá
The Xījīng Zá Jì states:
"According to Hàn regulations,
the Son of Heaven's brush
had its base adorned with inlaid jewels,
and the hairs were all from autumn rabbits."
Fùzǐ states:
"By the end of the Hàn, a brush case
was carved from gold
and adorned with Héshì jade."
Jiā Diǎn Yì Zì
The Wú Zuò Guó Tǒng states:
"The ruler of Wú, Sūn Quán,
once dreamed of bowing northward to the Celestial Emperor.
Suddenly he saw a person using a brush to place a dot on his forehead.
He raised the matter and asked the recluse scholar Xióng Xún about it.
Xún said:
'This is auspicious.
Your Highness is sure to become a sovereign (zhǔ).
The king (wáng) is the head of men,
the forehead is the top of the king.
Adding a dot atop "king" (wáng)
forms the image of the character "sovereign" (zhǔ).'"
The Wú Zhì states:
"Zhūgě Kè's father, Zhūgě Jǐn,
had a long face resembling a donkey.
Sūn Quán held a grand assembly.
He had someone lead a donkey in,
with a long label attached to its face
that read 'Zhūgě Zǐyú' (Jǐn's courtesy name).
Kè knelt and said:
'I beg for a brush to add two characters.'
He was then given a brush.
Kè added below it: '...'s donkey.' The entire assembly burst into laughter."
Chán Xǐ Lòu Guǎn
Fù Xuán's "Brush Rhapsody" states:
"Thus, master craftsmen exhausted their skill,
famous artisans displayed their art.
They wrapped it with plain hemp fibers
and coated it with dark lacquer."
Wáng Xīzhī's Bǐ Jīng states:
"Someone once presented me with a bamboo tube lacquered in deep green and an engraved tube.
I have kept them for many years.
These too are lovely to admire and handle.
Must one necessarily have gold, jewels, carving, and polishing
for it to be considered a treasure?"
Xiàng Guǎn Bǎo Xiá
Wáng Xīzhī's Bǐ Jīng states:
"In the past, some used colored glaze or ivory for brush tubes.
They were indeed beautifully adorned.
However, a brush must be light and convenient;
if heavy, it becomes clumsy."
The Xījīng Zá Jì states:
"According to Hàn regulations,
the Son of Heaven's brush
had its base adorned with inlaid jewels,
and the hairs were all from autumn rabbits.
The official craftsman Lù Hù made them.
He used assorted jewels to make the case,
and set jade discs within it."
Bān Tóu Yán Zhì
The Dōngguān Hàn Jì states:
"Bān Chāo's family was poor.
He threw down his brush and sighed:
'A true man should emulate Fù Jièzǐ
and Zhāng Qiān, achieving merit in foreign lands and being enfeoffed as a marquis.
How can I long toil with brush and inkstone!'"
Yú Huàn's Wèi Lüè states:
"Yán Fēi was the governor of Hédōng.
He instructed people delivering rent carts
to bring along two bundles of firewood
for use in cold weather,
to warm brushes and inkstones."
Zhì Tóng Guǎn Zhuì Cuì Xiá
Fù Xuán's "Eagle and Hare Rhapsody" states:
"The hare said to the eagle:
'You harm living things,
yet benefit the world.
Fine hairs are selected for binding,
and red tubes are fashioned to hold them.'"
Fùzǐ states:
"By the end of the Hàn, a brush case
was adorned with Suí pearls
and ornamented with kingfisher feathers."
Lì Xiàn Chénggōng Diāo Jīn Shì Bì
Cài Yōng's "Brush Rhapsody" states:
"In ancient times, Cāng Jié initiated the enterprise.
With ink and brush came their function,
and writing and tallies arose!
As for the creation of the supreme sages,
nothing precedes the brush in establishing laws.
Examining in detail its origins,
investigating thoroughly its accomplishments,
it is resplendent and brilliant,
unsurpassable!"
Fùzǐ states:
"By the end of the Hàn, a brush case
was carved from gold
and adorned with Héshì jade."
Hòu Hàn Cài Yōng "Brush Rhapsody"
Consider the source of these writing hairs:
They come from the cunning hare in late winter.
Its nature is keen and fierce,
its body swift and fleet of foot.
Carve patterned bamboo to make the tube,
add lacquered silk threads for binding.
Its shape is rounded and straight,
dyed with dark ink to fix its color.
It paints the yīn and yáng of heaven and earth,
praises the great achievements of Fúxī.
It exhausts the virtuous deeds of the Five Emperors,
proclaims the vast and grand canonical texts.
It records the meritorious campaigns of the Three Kings,
and manifests the audiences of the eight hundred lords.
It transmits the Six Classics and connects the Hundred Schools,
establishing the royal standard and ordering the constant norms.
It synthesizes human affairs from obscurity,
assisting the dark and mysterious with bright spirits.
Its analogies and metaphors are many,
no application fails to harmonize.
Hard above and soft below,
this is the position of heaven and earth.
The new replacing the old,
this is the sequence of the four seasons.
Round, harmonious, upright, and straight,
these are the ultimate standards of compass and square.
Dark tip and yellow tube,
these are the colors of heaven and earth."
Jìn Fù Xuán "Brush Rhapsody"
Select the fine hairs of the extraordinary hare,
gather the superior plumes from precious pelts.
Rinse them with clear water,
perfume them with secluded orchids.
Fine bamboo of emerald hue,
red tube containing cinnabar.
Thus, master craftsmen exhaust their skill,
excellent artisans display their art.
Wrap it with plain hemp fibers,
coat it with dark lacquer.
Richness and restraint achieve balance,
neither ornate nor plain.
Then, dip it in the pure soot of fragrant pine,
write patterned images onto white silk.
Movement responds to the hand and follows the heart,
radiant light flows and stars are scattered."
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì "Poem on a Brush Rest"
Splendor manifests in the jade case,
beauty praised as a pearl net.
Nothing compares to the wonder of this device,
carved and adorned with myriad forms.
Reaching upward, it writes holding flowers,
stretching sideways, it learns from the immortal's palm.
Liáng Dynasty Xú Chī's "Ode to the Brush Poem"
Originally emerging from the spiritual mountain,
Its name is passed down due to the auspicious grass.
The fine tip receives accumulated moisture,
The delicate substance disperses fragrant mist.
Straightly writing flying thistle documents,
Horizontally bearing fallen catkin scrolls.
Once grasped in the hand, it becomes weighty,
How could one recall Zhòng Shēng's sacrifice?
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pú's "Brush Eulogy"
In ancient times, knots were tied in ropes,
Replaced by written contracts.
It weaves through heaven and earth,
Intertwines all arts.
Used daily without awareness,
Its merit covers ten thousand generations.
Later Hàn Dynasty Lǐ Yóu's "Brush Inscription"
The brush's strong will,
Distinguishes all affairs.
Though the seven techniques are numerous,
They can still be explained.
Words from the mouth cannot be chosen,
Four horses cannot overtake the tongue.
The brush's errors,
Faults and blame cannot be erased.
Jìn Dynasty Wáng Yǐn's "Brush Inscription"
How can making a brush,
Require only rabbit hair?
Hard to adjust and not easily worn,
There is also deer hair.
Liáng Dynasty Yǔ Jiānwú's "Thanks for the Gift of a Bronze Inkstone and Brush Rest"
Grinding ink on green stone,
Already treading Kǒngzǐ's altar;
The tube inserted into a bronze dragon,
Still laughs at Wáng Shēng's jade.
Western Region barbarians,
Lying on woven golden mats;
Wandering immortal boys,
Hidden behind lotus-patterned screens;
All come forth from Liáng Garden,
To bestow upon this narrow room.
Paper, Seventh
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Paper,
Is like a whetstone,
Meaning it is smooth like a whetstone.
In ancient times, silk was used,
Cut according to the length of the writing,
Tailored to the matter,
Called banner paper.
Thus its character includes silk,
The poor did not have it,
Some used cattails to write on,
As Lù Wēnshū cutting cattails shows.
Until the Yuánxīng era of Emperor Hé of the Later Hàn Dynasty,
The Regular Attendant Cài Lún,
Shredded old cloth, pounded, and made paper,
Thus its character includes cloth."
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" states:
"The Yellow Gate Attendant Cài Lún oversaw the Imperial Workshop in making paper,
Which is called Cài Hóu paper.
Also, the Wèi person Héjiān Zhāng Yī presented the 'Ancient and Modern Character Explanations,'
Its cloth radical section says,
Paper is now written with the cloth radical,
Thus its character includes cloth."
Seen in the "Hànjì" and "Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū."
Another says:
"Lún pounded old fishing nets to make paper,
Called net paper.
Later people used raw cloth to make paper,
Silk threads like hemp,
Called hemp paper.
Using tree bark to make paper,
Called bark paper."
Seen in the "Dǒng Bā Jì" and "Bówùzhì."
Like Stone, Square Floss
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Paper,
Is like a whetstone,
Smooth like a whetstone."
Fú Qián's "Tōngsúwén" says:
"Square floss is white paper."
Wrapping the Core, Patching the Quilt
Wáng Xīzhī's "Brush Classic" says:
"After selecting the hairs, wrap the root of the core with hemp paper,
Then take the upper hairs and thinly spread them,
So the core is not visible,
Then secure it."
The "Xiè Chéng Hòuhànshū" says:
"Yáng Xù, styled Shūzǔ,
Was the Governor of Nányáng.
He led with purity,
Only sleeping under a single cloth quilt,
When worn,
Patched it with barbarian paper."
Serving as Slips, Replacing Bamboo Strips
Fù Xián's "Ode to Paper" says:
"Having created contracts to replace ropes,
And making paper to serve as slips.
Like frugality adapting to circumstances,
Only change is suitable.
Unfurl it and it stretches,
Release it and it curls."
Huán Xuán's "False Affairs" says:
"In ancient times, there was no paper,
So bamboo strips were used,
Not out of reverence.
Now all who use bamboo strips,
Replace them with yellow paper."
Yellow Documents, White Petitions
The "Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū" says:
"Liú Biàn was a fourth-rank clerk,
The inspector pushed a cart of yellow paper,
Ordering Biàn to copy documents.
Biàn told the inspector:
'Liú Biàn is not someone who copies yellow paper for others.'
The inspector demoted Biàn two grades for his offense,
Assigning him as a Clerk in the Imperial Secretariat."
Cuī Hóng's "Qiányān Lù":
"In the third year of Mùróng Jùn's reign,
General Guǎngyì, Duke of Mínshān, presented a memorial on yellow paper.
Jùn said:
'My title is no different from before,
Why should this be done?
From now on, only white paper should be used for petitions.'"
Pounding Nets, Holding Flowers
Zhāng Huá's "Bówùzhì" says:
"During the Hàn Dynasty under Emperor Huán,
A man from Guìyáng, Cài Lún,
First pounded old fishing nets to make paper."
Sūn Fàng's "Western Temple Inscription" says:
"The Western Temple in Chángshā,
Had its multi-story structure collapsing,
Plans were made to rebuild it.
That day, an imperial prince held paper flowers and planted them in the ground,
The temple's east and west sides were over ten zhàng apart,
Thus a pagoda was built,
Exactly where the flowers were."
Fragmentary Lines, Divided Sentences
Gān Bǎo's memorial says:
"I previously wished to compile records of ancient and modern strange and unusual events,
Gathering scattered and lost materials,
To unify them.
Extensively inquiring among those who know,
Fragmentary lines on scraps of paper,
Each matter different."
Zhāng Hàn's poem preface says:
"At the end of the Yǒngkāng era,
Suffering from illness and weakness,
Old friends often visited.
Often in quiet moments, I composed a poem,
Dividing sentences and changing paper,
Each with separate readings."
Imperial Workshop, Secret Repository
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
"The 'Cài Lún Biography' states:
'Lún oversaw the Imperial Workshop in making paper.'"
Yú Yù's memorial says:
"The Secret Repository has over thirty thousand pieces of cloth paper."
Light Blue and Red, Green and Red
The "Dōnggōng Jiùshì" says:
"When the Crown Prince is first appointed,
He is given one hundred pieces each of light blue and red paper."
Huán Xuán's "False Affairs" says:
"An edict orders the Price Stabilization Office to make green, red, light blue, and peach blossom paper,
Make it extremely fine,
Order it to be done quickly."
Rattan Corner, Peach Blossom
Fàn Nìng's instruction says:
"Local paper cannot be used for official documents,
All must use rattan corner paper."
Huán Xuán's "False Affairs" says:
"An edict orders the Price Stabilization Office to make green, red, light blue, and peach blossom paper,
Make it extremely fine,
Order it to be done quickly."
Assistant's Box, Right Army's Storehouse
Wèi Wǔ's order says:
"From now on, all assistants, attendants, and deputies,
Shall each month on the first day present gains and losses,
Written on paper and sealed in boxes.
The office shall provide one paper box each at court."
Péi Qǐ's "Lùnlín" says:
"Wáng Yòujūn was the Magistrate of Kuàijī,
Xiè Gōng requested paper from him.
The storehouse had only ninety thousand pieces,
All were given to him.
Huán Xuānwǔ said:
The Legacy of Cài Lún; The Remaining Paper of the Táng Era
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" states:
"About a hundred paces from Zǎoyáng County is the residence of Cài Lún,
which remains largely intact.
Beside it is a pond,
named Càizi Pond.
Lún,
a man of the Hàn Emperor Shùn's time,
first used fishing nets to make paper.
The people of the county still mostly know how to make paper today,
which is indeed Lún's legacy."
"Xiānxián Xíngzhuàng" states:
"Yán Dǔ studied the 'Zuǒzhuàn' from Táng Xījì.
He wished to copy it but had no paper,
so Jì gave him some leftover paper.
Dǔ thought the paper was unsuitable for writing,
so he borrowed the original to recite it."
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xián's "Ode to Paper"
Indeed, the world has substance and ornament,
thus principles have decrease and increase.
Therefore, rites change with the times,
and implements evolve with affairs.
Having created tallies to replace knotted cords,
paper was then made to replace bamboo slips.
As for this thing,
its beauty is precious,
modest and square, it has its rules.
Its substance pure, its nature genuine,
containing patterns, holding elegance.
Truly fond of this culture,
taking what is fine from others,
to make it new for oneself.
Unrolled, it lies flat;
released, it curls.
It can bend, it can stretch;
it can be hidden, it can be revealed.
Liáng Dynasty Jiāng Hóng's "Poem on Red Paper for Fù Jiànkāng"
Miscellaneous colors are hardly remarkable,
only red is uniquely suitable.
Glistening like a lotus blooming,
light and bright like a rosy cloud parting.
Carved substance rolled with fragrant paste,
cut flowers receiving a hundred harmonies.
If not encountered by a refined person,
how could it enter a seat of elegance?
Later Liáng Emperor Xuān's "Poem on Paper"
Gleaming white like frost and snow,
square and straight like arranged chess pieces.
To express feelings and record events,
how could it be like the time of fishing nets?
Suí Dynasty Xuē Dàohéng's "Poem on Moss Paper"
In the past, responding to spring colors,
it drew clear water, floating on pure streams.
Now, receiving the jade brush,
it spreads characters, changing silver hooks.
Jìn Dynasty Yú Yù's "Memorial Requesting Paper from the Imperial Archives"
In the Imperial Archives, there are over thirty thousand pieces of cloth paper,
unsuitable for writing imperial documents,
and thus not allocated for use.
I humbly request four hundred pieces,
to be given to the historiographical clerks,
for writing the Daily Records.
Liáng Dynasty Liú Xiàowēi's "Letter of Thanks for Bestowed Official Paper"
Your servant and Xiè Gǔ
are both ashamed of our foundational sagacity.
Your servant's scaling ladders
truly feel inferior to Lǔ Bān's skill;
Gǔ's city walls and fortifications
lacked a defender like Qínzǐ.
Attacking the weak and insulting the fallen,
our labor was very slight.
To record merit and bestow rewards,
the favor is excessively deep.
Though again, the Yè palace's phoenix-carried paper,
the Hàn dynasty's fishing-net paper,
the Píngzhǔn Bureau's peach blossom paper,
the Palace's paper mulberry paper—
truly, we are ashamed before this smoothness,
and thank you for this fresh luster.
Inkstone, Part Eight
"Shìmíng" states:
"An inkstone (yàn),
is for grinding (yán),
it can grind ink to make it moist and smooth."
"Cóngzhēng Jì" states:
"In the Confucius Temple of the State of Lǔ,
there is one stone inkstone,
likely an object from the Master's lifetime."
"Hànshū" states:
"When Emperor Xuān was in humble circumstances,
he often studied sharing the same inkstone and mat with Zhāng Péngzǔ."
"Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Wáng Chōng placed brushes and inkstones
by each door, window, wall, and pillar in his room,
and wrote the eighty-five chapters of 'Lùnhéng'." Wèi Wǔ's "Memorial on Various Objects" states:
"Among the imperial objects are pure silver three-banded round inkstones,
one large and one small."
"Jìnshū" states:
"Emperor Wǔ and Liú Hóng were the same age,
and studied sharing the same inkstone in their youth."
"Dōnggōng Gùshì" states:
"When the Jìn Crown Prince first received his appointment,
he was given one lacquered inkstone
and one hundred ivory pieces.
Records mention a lacquered writing inkstone;
this is the event."
Jìn Silver; Kǒng Stone
Xiāo Fāngděng's "Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū" states:
"In the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
Liú Cōng invited the Emperor to a banquet.
The Emperor said to him:
'When you were Prince of Yùzhāng,
I, along with Wáng Wǔzǐ, visited you.
You gave me a zhè wood bow and a silver inkstone.
Do you remember?'
Cōng replied:
'How dare I forget?
I only regret that I did not recognize the imperial countenance sooner that day.'" Wǔ Jízhī's "Cóngzhēng Jì" states:
"Before the Master's bed, there is one stone inkstone,
made very simple and ancient.
Likely an object from the Master's lifetime."
Stream Source; Stone Cave
"Yǒngjiā Jùn Jì" states:
"The Inkstone Stream has one source,
with many stone inkstones within."
Liú Chéngzhī's Sòng Dynasty "Yǒngchū Shānchuān Jīngǔ Jì" states:
"The Xīngpíng stone cave
is over two hundred zhàng deep.
The stone is blue-green,
suitable for making inkstones."
Silver Band; Golden Pool
Wèi Wǔ's "Memorial on Various Objects" states:
"Among the thirty kinds of imperial objects,
there is one pure silver three-banded inkstone.
Pure silver three-banded round inkstones,
one large and one small."
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Inkstone" states:
"Following square and round to determine its form,
forging metal and iron to make its pool.
Wood is valued for its softness,
stone is prized for its moist firmness.
Adding the adhesive strength of colored lacquer,
it holds the virtue of profundity, pure and mysterious."
Imperial Mat; Placed on Pillars
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Eulogy" states:
"Its three feet hooked like the Xià tripod,
resembling the stars and constellations supporting each other.
Providing endless secret uses,
serving the ease of the imperial mat."
"Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Wáng Chōng placed brushes and inkstones
by each door, window, wall, and pillar in his room and wrote the 'Lùnhéng'."
Square and Round; Patterned and Scattered
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Praise" states:
"Some thin, some thick,
some round, some square.
Patterned colors, scattered hues,
soaking and dyeing the tips of brushes.
Dotting ink for writing characters,
illuminating classics and documents."
Generating Writing; Containing Profundity
Fán Qīn's "Inkstone Praise" states:
"Looking upon this inkstone,
it generates writing.
Since the time of the ancient Huángdì,
it has been passed down endlessly."
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Inkstone" states:
"Wood is valued for its softness,
stone is prized for its moist firmness.
Adding the adhesive strength of colored lacquer,
it contains the profound virtue of purity and mystery."
Seized by the Inspector; Borrowed from the Prefect
"Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hànshū" states:
"Yáng Bān was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Zhào Kǎi falsely accused him, and a prison cart was sent to summon him,
seizing his brush and inkstone."
"Liú Dàoshì Zhuàn" states:
"Liú Gēn, styled Jūn'ān,
could summon ghosts.
Prefect Zhāng said to him:
'I hear you can make people see ghosts.
Make them appear visibly,
or else you will be punished.'
Gēn said:
'Lend me the brush and inkstone before you, Prefect.'
He then wrote a memorial and tapped the table with it.
In a moment,
five hundred ghosts bound the Prefect's deceased parents and brought them forth."
Writings endure forever; slander and evil cannot stain them.
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Inkstone" says:
"Since writing was created,
inkstones and ink have been arrayed.
Writings endure forever,
recording achievements and merits."
The "Inkstone Record from the Tàigōng's Golden Coffer" says:
"Graphite and ink combine to produce blackness;
evil hearts and slanderous words
cannot stain its purity."
The Wèi Empress frequently used them; the Jìn Emperor shared one in youth.
Wáng Chén's "History of Wèi" says:
"Empress Zhēn loved writing from the age of nine,
often using her brothers' brushes and inkstones.
They said to her:
'You should practice women's work, yet you study writing—
do you intend to become a female scholar?'
The Empress replied:
'Ancient virtuous women all studied the successes and failures of former ages
to serve as warnings for themselves.
If one does not know writing,
how can one learn of them?'"
Emperor Yuán of Liáng's "Biographies of Loyal Ministers" says:
"Liú Hóng
was from the state of Pèi.
Hóng resided in Luòyáng,
and was the same age as Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
sharing an inkstone for writing in their youth."
Fù Xuán of Jìn's "Rhapsody on the Inkstone":
Gather the hidden simplicity of the northern mountains,
select the most suitable among all materials.
Determine its form according to square and round,
forge metal and iron to form its pool.
Establish the division of upper and lower,
matching the cosmic model of the two realms.
Wood is valued for its softness,
stone prized for its moist firmness.
Add the adhesive strength of colored lacquer,
embodying the pure mystery of gentle virtue.
Yáng Shīdào's "Poem on the Inkstone":
The round pool resembles jade-like water;
light brushes are dyed with misty splendor.
Though the general seeks to secure distant lands,
if cast aside, it should not be far neglected.
Fán Qīn of Wèi's "Ode to the Inkstone":
With the marvelous craftsmanship of Bān and Chuí,
gaze upon wondrous forms from distant lands.
Examine the divine auspices of mountains and rivers,
recognize the jade-like beauty within.
Bind it with cords of compass and square,
borrowing the legacy of Biàn's model.
Imitate the primal creation of chaos,
emulate Xīhé's corner of the sun.
Hook three legs like the Xià dynasty tripod,
symbolize the mutual support of stars and constellations.
Serve endless secret uses,
grace the desk and mat with ease.
Fán Qīn of Wèi's "In Praise of the Inkstone":
Square as the image of earth,
round like the constancy of heaven.
Patterned colors scatter hues,
soaking and dyeing the tips of brushes.
Dotting ink for characters and texts,
illuminating bright statutes and records.
It gives without claiming virtue,
bestows kindness without bounds.
Soaked in sweet fluids,
it absorbs flowing light.
Wáng Càn of Wèi's "Inscription on the Inkstone":
At the dawn of writing,
replacing knotted cords.
People discern official principles,
and numerous achievements arise.
In the latter days of the age,
ornamentation flows to excess.
Writing fails to guide conduct,
texts do not express the heart fully.
Simplicity is diluted and scattered,
customs collapse and sink.
Ink moves and brushes dye,
honor and disgrace depend on this.
Reflect on this, dwell on this,
abide only in correctness.
Ink, Part Nine
The "Explaining Names" says:
"Ink (mò)
means 'obscure' (huì),
indicating it resembles things dark and black."
The "Continued Hàn History" states:
"The Keeper of the Palace is in charge of the imperial brushes and ink."
The "Hàn History" says:
"The Imperial Secretary, his deputies, assistants, and gentlemen
are monthly bestowed one large inkstick from Yùmí and one small inkstick."
The "Wèi Official Ceremonial" states:
"When the Imperial Secretary selects
and tests gentlemen who are former Filial and Incorrupt candidates capable in documents,
one day before the test,
they are summoned to assemble in the main hall,
and provided with brushes and ink to submit responses."
The "Records of the Eastern Palace" states:
"When the Crown Prince is first appointed,
he is given four pellets of fragrant ink—
this is the practice."
Spraying paper; dotting silk.
Gě Hóng's "Biographies of Immortals" says:
"Bān Mèng,
no one knows from where,
would chew ink and spray it,
forming characters all over the paper,
each with its own meaning."
Wáng Chōng's "Discourses Weighed" says:
"Critics neither know whence repeated harms arise,
nor that those suffering such harms act virtuously and purely.
Using mud to daub a lump,
using ink to dot silk—
who can perceive it?
The clear attracts dust,
the white gathers grime.
The stain of the blue fly
often lies on plain silk."
Two spirals; nine sons.
Lù Yún's "Letter to My Elder Brother" says:
"One day I ascended the Three Terraces.
Lord Cáo had stored hundreds of thousands of catties of graphite,
saying it could be burned and then reused.
But it is not so.
Have you, brother, seen it?
Now I send two spirals."
The "Zhèng Family Wedding Greetings and Eulogies" says:
"The ink of nine sons,
stored within pine soot.
Its nature is inherently enduring;
may descendants plan its borders."
Spitting fish; painting the palm.
Gě Hóng's "Biographies of Immortals" says:
"Gě Xuán saw a large fish for sale
and said to the seller:
'May I trouble this fish to go to the River Earl?'
The fish owner said:
'The fish is already dead.'
Xuán said:
'Do not worry.'
He then wrote a cinnabar message on paper placed in its mouth
and cast it into the water.
After a while, the fish revived,
leaped onto the bank,
spat out an inked message,
green as a leaf, and departed."
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Gleanings" says:
"Zhāng Yí
and Sū Qín shared the same ambition.
They took turns cutting their hair to support each other,
or hired out their labor to copy books.
When they encountered texts of the sages on their travels
with no means to record them,
they would paint the characters with ink on their palms and thighs.
Returning at night,
they would split bamboo strips to write them down."
Bestowed by Gě Gōng; presented to Yǔ Liàng.
Gě Gōng's "Letter to the Chancellor of Liáng" says:
"You further bestowed fine ink,
which a humble scholar like myself does not possess.
Even crushing my bones
and shattering my liver and gall
would be insufficient to repay this kindness."
Xiāo Fāngděng's "Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States" says:
"Wáng Yǐn began compiling his 'History of Jìn,'
totaling eighty-eight scrolls.
His family was poor and lacked paper,
so he could not complete his ambition.
He then traveled south,
presenting himself to Táo Kǎn in Jīng Province.
Again, in Jiāng Province, he presented himself to Yǔ Liàng,
and only then obtained paper and ink,
finally completing the book."
Cutting firewood to buy; praying at the stone shrine.
Hé Fǎshèng's "History of the Restoration" says:
"Gě Hóng loved learning
and often cut firewood to sell for buying paper and ink."
Gān Bǎo's "Records of the Search for the Supernatural" says:
"West of Yì Province is a shrine
that calls itself Huáng Shígōng.
Initially, those praying bring one hundred sheets of paper, one pair of brushes, and one pellet of ink.
First, a sound is heard from the stone chamber,
then fortunes are told,
Heaven Rains Ink, Pine Soot
The *Collection of Portents and Auspices* says:
"When heaven rains ink,
the ruler and ministers are without virtue, and slanderers advance."
Cáo Zhí's "Yuefu Poem" says:
"Ink comes from the soot of green pines,
Brushes come from the hairs of cunning hares.
The ancients were inspired by bird tracks,
Thus writing was created and judgments made."
Presenting to Husband, Bestowed by Decree
The *Collection on Women* says:
"*The Letter from the Wife of the Crown Prince of Jí to Her Husband* says:
'And I present to you ten snails of writing ink.'"
Cài Zhì's *Han Officialdom* says:
"The Imperial Secretaries, their deputies, assistants, and gentlemen
are each month bestowed one large inkstick and
one small inkstick from Yúmí."
Zhùyáng Mountain, Huáihuà Moat
Shèng Hóngzhī's *Records of Jīngzhōu* says:
"In Zhùyáng County there is an Ink Mountain,
whose rocks are all like ink."
Gù Wēi's *Records of Guǎngzhōu* says:
"In Huáihuà Commandery, a moat was dug
and much graphite was obtained,
fine and suitable for writing books.
Dài Yánzhī's *Record of a Western Campaign* says:
'Fifty *li* north of Graphite Mountain,
the mountain has much graphite that can be used for writing.'"
Supplied for Seasonal Occasions, Blended with Cinnabar and Musk
The *Dōngguān Records of the Hàn* says:
"When Empress Héxī Dèng ascended the throne,
she completely prohibited all tribute offerings from the myriad states,
only allowing the seasonal supply of paper and ink."
Wéi Zhòngjiāng's *Ink Recipe* says:
"The method for blending ink:
Take one *liang* of true cinnabar,
and half a *liang* of musk.
Both are pounded finely.
Afterwards, combine them all in an iron mortar
and pound thirty thousand times with the pestle.
More pounding is better,
but it must not be done beyond the second or ninth month."
Hàn Dynasty Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Inkstone"
Since writing was invented,
the inkstone and ink have been arrayed.
Soot and stone adhere to the brush,
flowing and extending.
Banners and Flags, First
The *Explaining Names* says:
"*Jīng* (banner)
means essence (*jīng*),
speaking of having essential light.
*Qí* (flag)
means to expect (*qī*),
speaking of expecting together with the masses below."
According to the *Lièzǐ*:
"The Yellow Emperor battled the Flame Emperor,
using eagles, hawks, and kites as banners and flags,
which was likely the beginning of banners and flags."
The *Offices of Zhōu* says:
"The Director of Standards oversees the objects of the nine flags,
each name having its category,
to await state affairs.
The sun and moon are the *cháng*,
intertwined dragons are the *qí*.
Plain silk is the *zhān*,
variegated silk is the *wù*.
Bears and tigers are the *qí*,
birds and falcons are the *yú*,
turtles and snakes are the *zhào*.
Whole feathers are the *suì*,
split feathers are the *jīng*.
The dragon banner has nine streamers,
symbolizing the Great Fire star;
the bird banner has seven streamers,
symbolizing the Quail Fire star;
the bear flag has six streamers,
symbolizing the Punishment star;
the turtle-snake banner has four streamers,
symbolizing the Encampment star;
the bow banner with crooked arrows
symbolizes the Bow star."
The *Explaining Names* says:
"The names of the nine flags:
The sun and moon are the *cháng*.
Painting the sun and moon on its end,
it is erected by the Son of Heaven,
speaking of constant brightness.
Intertwined dragons are the *qí*.
*Qí*
means to lean on.
Painting two dragons leaning on each other,
made entirely of a single red color,
without patterned colors,
it is erected by the feudal lords.
Plain silk is the *zhān*.
*Zhān*
means reverence (*zhàn*),
reverently respecting oneself alone.
Erected by the Three Solitaries,
symbolizing having no affairs.
Bears and tigers are the *qí*.
*Qí*
means to expect (*qī*).
Speaking of expecting together with the masses below.
Erected by army generals,
symbolizing their ferocity like bears and tigers.
Birds and falcons are the *yú*.
*Yú*
means praise (*yù*).
Erected by army officers,
if they hasten urgently to affairs,
then there will be praise.
Variegated silk is the *wù*,
also called *pèi*,
with assorted colors attached to its edges like a swallow's tail.
Erected by commanders,
symbolizing the mixture of things.
Turtle banners are the *zhào*.
*Zhào*
means omen (*zhào*).
The turtle knows the auspicious or inauspicious omens of *qì*,
erected at the rear,
to observe and assess the form and omens of appropriate matters.
Whole feathers are the *suì*.
*Suì*
means a smooth and sleek appearance.
Split feathers are the *jīng*,
attached to the top of the flagpole with yak tails."
Also, the *Guǎngyǎ* says:
"The Son of Heaven's banner is nine *ren* high,
feudal lords' are seven *ren*,
high officials' are five *ren*,
and officers' are three *ren*.
The *Rites: Hán Wénjiā* says:
'The Son of Heaven's flag is nine *ren*,
with twelve streamers trailing to the ground;
feudal lords' are seven *ren*,
with nine streamers level with the chariot's crossboard;
ministers and high officials' are five *ren*,
with seven streamers level with the chariot's side-rails;
officers' are three *ren*,
with five streamers level with the head.
Also, the *yá* flag
is erected by the general.'"
The *Yellow Emperor's Military Decisions* says:
"When there is an attack or campaign,
make a five-colored *yá* pennant.
The green *yá* flag leads east,
the red *yá* flag leads south,
the white *yá* flag leads west,
the black *yá* flag leads north,
the yellow *yá* flag leads to the center.
This is its meaning."
Summoning the Gamekeeper, Alerting the Masses
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
"Duke Jǐng of Qí summoned the gamekeeper with a banner,
but he did not come,
so he was about to kill him."
The *Book of Rites* says:
"If there is water ahead, then raise the green banner."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"To raise (*zǎi*)
means what is called lifting at the head of the banner,
that which is used to alert the masses."
Raising Leather, Split Feathers
Zhèng's Record, Wáng Zàn asks:
"Lifting at the head of the banner,
should it all be done with leather?
Is that exhaustive?"
Zhèng replies:
"All together, leather is placed at the head,
but it is not exhaustive."
The *Rites of Zhōu* says:
"Split feathers make a banner."
Raising Green, Esteeming Black
"Raising green" is already seen above.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* says:
"When Qín unified the world,
taking the beginning of the Water Virtue,
all yak-tail staffs and flags esteemed black."
Wing Star Bright, Birds Gather
The *Astronomical Essential Collection* says:
"If the Wing star is bright,
banners and flags are used."
The *Zhào Clan's Military Treatise* says:
"If birds gather on the general's banner,
the general's rank and emolument increase."
Setting up Gates and Establishing Roads
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The official in charge of encampments erects curtained palaces and sets up banner gates."
The commentary notes:
"Banners are raised to mark the gates."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wén's edict said:
'At court, there is the banner for presenting good counsel.'" Yìng Shào's commentary states:
"Yáo established the five thoroughfares,
to encourage people to present good counsel."
At Jùn and Along the River
The Máo Shī states:
"Lonely stands the banner on its pole,
in the city of Jùn."
The Book of Later Wèi states:
"Tàizǔ advanced his army to the river,
lining the banks with banners for over a thousand lǐ."
Nine Names and Five Methods
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The Sīcháng is in charge of the nine types of banners and their names."
The Hé Tú states:
"Fēng Hòu said:
'I inform you of the Emperor's five banners.'
The eastern method: the Azure Dragon is called a Qí;
the southern method: the Red Bird is called a Shǔ;
the western method: the White Tiger is called a Diǎn;
the northern method: the Black Serpent is called a Qí;
the central method: the Yellow Dragon is called a Cháng."
Nine Rèn and Six Liú
Both are seen above.
Kingfisher Phoenix and Black Serpent
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Lǐ Sī's memorial said:
'Now Your Majesty erects banners of kingfisher and phoenix,
and sets up drums of divine alligator.'" "Black Serpent" is already seen above.
Modeling on Birds and Resembling Rainbows
"Modeling on Birds" is already seen in the commentary for "Five Methods."
Wáng Chén's "Rhapsody on a Farewell Banquet" states:
"Dragging the long banner of Zhāoyáo,
like a winding rainbow hanging from the sky."
Auspicious Light and Victorious Aura
Hǎo Méng's divination states:
"If there is light upon the banners,
the sovereign will have great joy,
and extended years and increased longevity."
The Huángdì Chūjūn Jué states:
"On the day the yá banner is first erected,
auspicious energy comes in response.
Banners and pennants pointing toward the enemy,
this is called an imposing array,
a righteous and orderly banner,
a sign of great victory."
Setting Yellow and Esteeming Red
Zhōu Qiān's Miscellaneous Records of Carriages and Attire states:
"Emperor Yuán of Jìn first instituted the banner of five oxen,
placing the azure on the left,
and the yellow in the center."
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"The Lord of Pei offered sacrifices to Huángdì and Chīyóu in the Pei courtyard,
and all his banners and flags esteemed the color red."
Raising Azure and Hanging Red
Military Orders state:
"Upon hearing the sound of thunder drums,
raise the white pennant and silk banner,
all large and small vessels shall advance to battle,
those who do not advance shall be beheaded.
Upon hearing the sound of metal,
raise the azure banner,
all vessels shall halt,
those who do not halt shall be beheaded."
Wáng Sūnzi states:
"Jié and Zhòu, one was banished to Náncháo,
the other's head was hung on a red banner.
This is for no other reason
than their failure to regulate wealth and their tyranny against the people."
Five Oxen and Four Beasts
"Five Oxen" is already seen in the commentary above.
The Book of Rites states:
"In front marches the Vermilion Bird, behind is the Dark Warrior,
to the left is the Azure Dragon, to the right is the White Tiger,
with Zhāoyáo above,
urgently strengthening their fury."
The commentary notes:
"Using these four beasts for military formations,
imitates Heaven.
Painting the Zhāoyáo star on banners and flags,
to rouse and intensify the army's fierce wrath."
Startling the Army and Pointing at the Enemy
The Shī Tuīduò Zāi states:
"The ruler issues commands to transform the world,
thunder rises and startles the hibernating insects.
Observing banners and drums,
moving the three armies,
startling to behold them advance,
their movement and transformation reveal the disposition of Heaven."
The Huángdì Chūjūn Jué states:
"On the day the yá banner is first erected,
joyful energy comes in response.
Banners and pennants pointing toward the enemy,
or coming with the wind,
this is a sign of great victory."
Bestowing the Yellow Bird and Modeling on the Azure Dragon
Mòzǐ states:
"A red bird descended holding a document in its beak,
saying:
'Command Zhōu Wénwáng to attack Yīn,
Heaven bestows upon King Wǔ the banner of the yellow bird.'" "Modeling on the Azure Dragon" is already seen in the commentary above.
Wú Hú Zōng's "Rhapsody on the Great Yá Banner"
In the eighth year of Huángchū,
a yellow dragon appeared.
Sūn Quán assumed the imperial title,
and changed the era name in response to the auspicious sign.
He created a great yellow dragon yá banner,
constantly kept within the army,
advancing and retreating according to its direction,
and commanded Zōng to compose a rhapsody.
It says:
"The Wolf and Bow stars manifest their images,
truly embodying the essence of warfare.
The sage observes the models,
emulating and planning accordingly.
First creating instruments and tools,
then seeking their completion.
The four numinous creatures now deployed,
the yellow dragon positioned in the center.
Adorning it with the sun and moon according to Zhōu regulation,
it is truly called the Tàicháng.
Majestic and uniquely standing,
the gaze of the six armies rests upon it."
Later Hàn Téng Fǔ's "Prayer for the Yá Banner"
Reverently presenting the grand sacrifice,
purely offering to the distant numen.
The responsibility of pushing the chariot wheel,
is truly to punish those who do not submit to court.
The Way of Heaven assists the compliant,
upright, honest, clear, and bright.
Sòng Zhèng Xiān's "Prayer for the Yá Banner"
Purifying the sacrificial animals beforehand,
presenting this reverent offering.
Since the lofty yá banner has been erected,
the righteous blade's edge grows sharper.
Humans and spirits share the same principle,
the three realms are in mutual accord.
May this numinous mirror,
surely perceive and discern.
Distinguishing rebellion from obedience,
loyalty and filial piety manifest integrity.
Cause the vicious and ugly to be annihilated in time,
sovereign serene, ministers joyful.
Deploying troops on the southern plains,
triumphantly returning to the western marches.
The sacred vessels gain added luster,
the four borders forever peaceful.
Chén Zǐ'áng's "Oath at the Military Banner Ceremony"
For the ancient kings raised armies
to punish the guilty.
When treacherous usurpers seize power,
and barbarian tribes show no reverence,
they must be executed in the marketplace or court,
and slaughtered across the open plains.
Our Imperial House nurtures all states,
cherishes and pacifies the myriad barbarians.
Auspicious clouds touch the constellations,
white jade rings arrive as tribute—
this has endured for many years.
Now the savage Jié of the Qìdān
dare disrupt Heaven's constant order;
they swarm like hornets on Wán Mountain,
devour the Liáo frontier like wild boars.
Indulging in poison as if it were feasting,
they act as baleful stars of strife.
Heaven detests their savagery,
so the state must launch a punitive campaign.
The Emperor commands me
to solemnly execute the royal punishment.
Now the great army is assembled,
the auspicious hour aligns.
The yak-tail banners are raised first,
feathered pennants form the front ranks.
The barbarians tremble at our might,
the officers and soldiers heed the oath.
We await Heaven's mandate,
to eradicate calamity for the people.
O ye spirits,
smite these vile foes!
Summon Tàiyī,
gather Léigōng,
assist the White Tiger,
mount the Azure Dragon.
Let stars stream from comet tails,
ice melt across the northern borders.
May blades remain unstained by blood,
and barbarians and Huáxià unite as one,
to manifest the virtue of our Son of Heaven.
Truly this shall be the spirits' achievement.
Is it not that uprightness can illuminate all,
leaving no great enemy unchecked,
lest the spirits be shamed?
Second of the Sword
The *Shìmíng* says:
"Jiàn (sword),
means jiǎn (to restrain),
it is that by which one guards against and restrains extraordinary events."
According to the *Guǎnzǐ*:
"In ancient times, from the Gětiānlú Mountains,
metal was extracted and emerged.
Chīyóu received it and fashioned it,
making it into swords and armor;
this was the beginning of the sword."
The *Zhōuguān* states:
"The Yǔtáo clan made swords.
The là (blade body) was two and a half cùn wide.
Là refers to the two edges.
Pronunciation liè.
The two cóng (flats along the spine) are half of that.
The sword spine is ground on both sides towards the edge.
Using the width of the là as the circumference of the jīng (hilt/tang).
Its length is double that.
Jīng refers to the part of the sword held by the person, upwards from there.
Center its jīng,
and set its hòu (pommel?).
This means from the center it slightly increases in size.
The shēn (blade) length is five times the jīng length,
weight nine lüè,
pronunciation lüè.
This is called the upper specification,
worn by the upper gentlemen;
shēn length four times the jīng length,
weight seven lüè,
called the middle specification,
worn by the middle gentlemen;
shēn length three times the jīng length,
weight five lüè,
called the lower specification,
worn by the lower gentlemen.
Later, Chǔ had Lóngquán,
Qín had Tài'ē, Gōngshì.
Wú had Gānjiàng, Mòyé, Zhǔlòu.
Yuè had Chúngōu, Zhànlú, Háocáo, Yúcháng, Jùquē, and other swords.
The *Yuèjuéshū* says:
"The King of Chǔ summoned Fēnghúzi,
ordered him to go to Wú and Yuè,
to see Ōuyězi.
Gānjiàng had him make three iron swords:
one called Lóngquán,
two called Tài'ē,
three called Gōngshì.
The King of Chǔ asked him:
'What are Lóngquán, Tài'ē, and Gōngshì?'
Fēnghúzi replied:
'Lóngquán's appearance is like ascending a high mountain,
overlooking a deep abyss;
Tài'ē is lofty and majestic,
like the waves of flowing water;
Gōngshì's pattern rises from the grain,
and stops at the spine,
like pearls that cannot be bent,
the pattern like a flowing, unbroken stream.
Jìn and Zhèng heard of these three swords,
sought them but could not obtain them,
so they raised an army and besieged the city of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ, holding the Tài'ē sword, ascended the city wall and brandished it,
the soldiers became confused,
blood flowed for a thousand lǐ,
and the heads of the men of Jìn and Zhèng all turned white.'"
The *Wúyuè Chūnqiū* says:
"Gānjiàng
was a man of Wú.
He and Ōuyězi studied under the same master.
Hélǘ had him make two swords:
one called Gānjiàng,
two called Mòyé.
Mòyé
was the name of Gānjiàng's wife.
When Gānjiàng was making the swords,
the essence of the metal and iron would not flow.
Gānjiàng and his wife then cut off their hair and clipped their fingernails,
and threw them into the furnace.
Then the metal and iron became moist and they succeeded in completing the swords.
The yang one was called Gānjiàng and had a tortoise-shell pattern,
the yīn one was called Mòyé and had a flowing grain.
Gānjiàng concealed the yang one and brought out the yīn one,
presenting it to Hélǘ."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"The King of Wú granted Zǐxū the Zhǔlòu sword to die with."
The *Wúyuè Chūnqiū* also says:
"King Yǔncháng of Yuè engaged Ōuyězi to make five famous swords:
one called Chúngōu,
two called Zhànlú,
three called Háocáo,
four called Yúcháng,
five called Jùquē.
A Qín visitor, Xuē Zhú, was skilled at appraising swords.
The King of Yuè took Háocáo, Jùquē, Yúcháng and others to show him.
Xuē Zhú said of them all:
'These are not precious swords.'
He took Chúngōu to show Xuē.
Zhú said:
'Brilliant like the splendor of the bending sun;
deep and serene like lotuses first born on the lake.
Observing its pattern is like watching the march of the arrayed stars;
observing its light is like water overflowing a pond.
This is Chúngōu.'
He took Zhànlú to show him.
Xuē Zhú said:
'Excellent!
It holds the flower of metal and iron,
and emits the essence of silver and tin.
It harbors pneuma and entrusts numinous power,
possessing the spirit of wandering forth.
Wearing this sword can repel the enemy and attack foes.
If a ruler has rebellious designs, it will leave him for another state.'
Yǔncháng then presented Zhànlú to Wú.
The Wú prince Guāng assassinated King Liáo of Wú,
and Zhànlú left for Chǔ."
In Hàn, there was the sword with which Gāozǔ cut the serpent.
See the *Hànshū*.
In Wèi, there were the three swords of Emperor Wén: Fēi, Jǐngliúcǎi, and Huáfēng.
See the *Diǎnlùn*.
In Wú, there were the six swords: Báihóng, Zǐdiàn, Bìxié, Liúxīng, Qīngmíng, and Bǎilǐ.
See Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù*.
All could sever horses and oxen on land,
strike wild geese in the water,
and when facing the enemy, cut through armor and shields.
The *Zhànguócè* says:
"The swords of Hán's soldiers
all came from Míngshān, Tángxī,
Mòyáng, Yuǎnféng;
Lóngquán, Tài'ē,
all sever horses and oxen on land;
strike wild geese in the water,
and when facing the enemy, cut through armor and shields!"
These are the famous vessels of the world.
See the *Lièzǐ*.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven was capped and
girded with a sword at twenty;
the feudal lords were capped and
girded with a sword at thirty;
the grand masters were capped and
girded with a sword at forty;
menial servants were not capped.
Commoners could gird a sword when they had official duties,
but could not when they had no duties.
See the *Jiǎzǐ*.
According to ritual propriety,
the sword is worn on the left,
symbolizing the Azure Dragon.
The knife is worn on the right,
symbolizing the White Tiger.
See the *Chūnqiū Fánlù*.
According to old regulations,
a Duke of the highest rank, with the Nine Commands, could wear his sword and tread upon the palace hall.
The heir apparent's ritual status was equal to that of all the lords,
so he should be able to wear his sword and ascend the hall.
Some say that in the Hàn and Wèi, the heir apparent's regulations did not include removing the sword,
from which we know that wearing the sword and treading the hall had been practiced for a long time.
According to Hàn ceremonial,
all ministers wore swords,
but removed them upon reaching the palace steps.
In the Jìn dynasty, they began to be replaced with wooden ones,
the noble ones still having jade pommels,
the humble ones using clam shell.
Gold, silver, and tortoiseshell were used for carved decoration.
See Zhōu Qiān's *Yúfú Záshì*.
Generally, the sword's mouth is called xín.
See Lǚ Jìng's *Yùnjí*.
The nose is called wèi.
See the *Zìlín*.
The scabbard is called shì.
See the *Fāngyán*.
The case is called yī.
See the *Shuōwén*,
also called ráo, pronunciation rào.
Iron Essence, Metal Tip
The *Yuè Jué Shū* states:
"The King of Chǔ summoned Fēng Húzǐ and asked him:
'I hear the King of Wú has Gānjiàng,
and Yuè has Ōuyě.
May I request these two men to make iron swords?'
Fēng Húzǐ said:
'Excellent.'
Thereupon, he sent him to Wú to see Gānjiàng,
and to Yuè to see Ōuyězǐ,
and had them make iron swords.
Ōuyě and Gānjiàng excavated Cí Mountain,
drained its streams,
and obtained its iron essence,
forging two swords."
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"Gānjiàng
was a man of Wú.
He studied under the same master as Ōuyě,
and both made swords.
Yuè had previously come to present three swords.
Hélǘ obtained them and treasured them,
so he ordered Gānjiàng to forge two swords.
Gānjiàng said:
'In the past, when my master was smelting.'
The tips of the metal and iron would not melt.
Husband and wife both entered the smelting furnace."
Adorned with Shark, Carved with Clam
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"Shark skin has pearl-like patterns and is tough;
it can be used to adorn the edges of swords."
The *Zhōu Qiān Yúfú Záshì* states:
"The sword has existed for a long time.
Later, only court attire included wearing a sword.
In the Jìn dynasty, it was replaced with wood.
The noble ones adorned the pommel with jade,
the lowly ones carved it with clam shell."
See the narrative section.
Tortoise Pattern, Dragon Motif
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"Wú sent Gānjiàng to forge two swords.
The male was called Gānjiàng,
and it bore tortoise patterns and dragon motifs."
Cáo Pī's *Wèi Dū Fù* states:
"As for swords, there are those of flowing color, a treasure,
and those of plain substance, a gem.
At times like a rainbow gathering, waves reflecting,
or like tortoise patterns and dragon motifs.
Wearing them can awe the hundred barbarians;
pointing and commanding can clear away chaos and disturbance."
Bùguāng, Fēijǐng
Cáo Zhí's *Qī Qǐ* states:
"The Bùguāng sword,
its splendor and ornamentation are rich and intricate."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎn Lùn* states:
"Selecting this fine metal,
I commanded the state's master craftsman.
Refine and smelt it,
until it has been folded a hundred times.
Rinse it with the clear Zhāng River;
its light resembles a shooting star.
Its name is Fēijǐng."
Qí Metal, Chǔ Iron
The *Guóyǔ* states:
"Duke Huán asked:
'The state of Qí lacks armor and weapons.
What should be done about it?'
Guǎnzǐ said:
'For minor crimes, impose fines of metal.
Distinguish and pardon, inquire into crimes.
Use the fine metal collected to cast swords and halberds,
and test them on dogs and horses.'" The *Shǐjì* states:
"King Zhāo of Qín sighed at court, saying:
'I hear that if Chǔ's iron swords are sharp, then its warriors are brave.'"
Jade Pommel, Pearl-edged
Zhāng Chǎng's *Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì* states:
"The Crown Prince's ceremonial ornaments included a sword with a jade pommel."
The commentary to the *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"Shark skin has pearl-like patterns and is tough;
it can be used to adorn the edges of swords."
Rhinoceros-hilted, Fish-patterned
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎn Lùn* states:
"I am fond of fencing.
I commanded the state's master craftsman
to make a treasured weapon.
Adorn it with patterned jade,
and fit it with a rhinoceros horn hilt."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"When Chúngōu and Yúcháng swords were first cast in the mold,
strikes could not break them,
thrusts could not pierce them.
But after being whetted and polished,
they could cut through water and sever dragon boats."
Commentary:
"The Yúcháng's pattern winds and twists like fish intestines."
Bestowed upon Féng, Rewarded to Wèi
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Féng Yì was sent west to attack the Red Eyebrows in Guānzhōng.
The Emperor personally bestowed upon Féng Yì from Hénán a seven-foot imperial sword with jade and shell decoration."
Zhāng Yíng's *Hàn Nán Jì* states:
"Wèi Yìng,
courtesy name Yǐnbó,
was a man of Rènchéng.
He was proficient in the Lǔ School of the *Shījīng*,
and Emperor Zhāng esteemed him.
He was frequently summoned for audience and debated difficult points before the Emperor,
and was specially rewarded with swords, jade pendants, and clothing."
Pìlǘ, Jùquè
Master Xún (Xúnzǐ) states:
"Gānjiàng, Mòyé, and Pìlǘ
were all fine swords of antiquity."
"Jùquè" is mentioned above.
Inlaid with Jīng Jade, Holding Yuè Metal
Cáo Zhí's *Qī Qǐ* states:
"The Bùguāng sword,
its splendor and ornamentation are rich and intricate.
It is set with pearls from the Black Dragon,
and inlaid with jade from Jīng Mountain."
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"A Qín visitor, Xuē Zhú, was skilled at appraising swords.
The King of Chǔ took out the Zhànlú sword to show him.
Zhú said:
'Excellent!
It holds the essence of metal and iron,
and emits the quintessence of silver and tin.'" Already mentioned above.
Observing Heaven, Divining the Aura
Zhào Yè's *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"Wú sent Gānjiàng to forge two swords.
One was called Gānjiàng,
the second was called Mòyé.
Mòyé
was the name of Gānjiàng's wife.
When Gānjiàng forged the swords,
he gathered the essence of five mountains,
combined the excellence of six metals,
observed heaven and awaited earth,
so that yīn and yáng shone together."
Léi Cìzōng's *Yùzhāng Jì* states:
"Before Wú perished,
a constant purple aura was seen between the Ox and Dipper constellations.
Diviners believed it signified the rise of Wú,
but only Zhāng Huá thought otherwise.
After Wú was pacified,
this aura grew even brighter.
Huá said:
'This is the aura of a precious sword.'"
Commanding Cities, Striking in Markets
"Commanding cities" is already mentioned in the narrative.
As for "striking in markets",
the *Wèi Liáozǐ* states:
"If one bandit, grasping a sword, strikes in the market,
ten thousand people will all avoid him.
Your servant believes it is not that this one man alone is brave,
but that the ten thousand people in the market are all unworthy."
Bellows Blowing, Furnace Astonished
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* states:
"Gānjiàng said:
'In the past, when my master was smelting.'
The tips of the metal and iron would not melt.
Husband and wife then cut off their hair and clipped their fingernails,
and threw them into the furnace.
They had two hundred youths blow the bellows to strengthen the charcoal,
and only then did the metal and iron become molten."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Diǎn Lùn* states:
"I am fond of fencing,
skilled at using the short to overcome the long.
Selecting this fine metal,
I commanded the state's master craftsman.
Refine and smelt it,
until it has been folded a hundred times.
When it was first completed,
its five colors astonished the furnace,
and the great bellows blew of their own accord."
Relocating the Site, Piercing the Heavens
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The knives of Zhèng,
the axes of Sòng,
the scrapers of Lǔ,
and the swords of Wú and Yuè—
if moved from their place of origin, they cannot be made excellent,
for it is the local climate that makes them so."
Léi Cìzōng's Records of Yùzhāng states:
"Before Wú fell,
a constant purple aura was seen between the constellations Dǒu and Niú.
Zhāng Huá heard that Léi Kǒngzhāng was profoundly skilled in astrological portents,
so he invited him to stay overnight.
Dismissing others, he asked Kǒngzhāng:
'Only between Dǒu and Niú is there an unusual aura;
it is the essence of a treasure
piercing up to the heavens!'
Kǒngzhāng explained in detail,
and so he was appointed magistrate of Fēngchéng County,
where two swords were unearthed."
Fallen Bamboo, Belted Locust
Zhào Yè's Spring and Autumn Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
"King Yǔncháng of Yuè commissioned Ōu Yězǐ to forge five swords,
three large and two small.
The third was named Háocáo.
A Qín visitor, Xuē Zhú, was skilled at appraising swords.
The king took Háocáo to show him.
Xuē Zhú said:
'This is truly not a treasure sword.
Now Háocáo has five colors,
but they are dull and lack luster.
Its radiance has already perished,
its spirit is lost.
This sword, if not disgraced by failing to cut,
will fall into the drinking vessel!'
The king said:
'I placed the sword atop a bamboo hut;
it fell as I passed by,
cutting the neck of a golden beast.
The blade drank its moisture,
and I considered it sharp.'"
The Biographies of Former Worthies by Zhōu Fěi states:
"Xǔ Jiā served as a minor clerk under the county merit officer Yí,
often holding a sword to attend the merit officer.
On the first day of the month at morning court,
he also carried a torch.
Jiā then indignantly sighed:
'A man serving as a clerk
cannot avoid menial tasks.'
With that, he threw the torch to the ground,
belted his sword to a locust tree,
and hurried out the government gate."
Liáng Wú Jūn's "Ode to a Treasure Sword"
I have a treasure sword,
born from the Kūnwú Stream.
Reflecting people like reflecting water,
cutting jade like cutting mud.
Its blade's edge, frosty and severe;
on its scabbard, winds bleak and drear.
I send word to young master Zhāng:
When will you come to take it along?
Cuī Róng's "Ode to a Sword"
A treasure sword emerges from Kūnwú,
tortoise and dragon flank the pearl of hue.
Five essences first present their art;
ten households vie to praise its part.
From its scabbard, aura strikes Dǒu and Niú;
its mountain form twists like a pulley true.
To know what under heaven is most prized,
take this and ask Fēng Hú, the wise.
Lǐ Qiáo's "Treasure Sword Piece"
Wú mountains open,
Yuè streams run dry,
three metals smelted to a treasure's edge on high;
quenched in green waters,
mirrored in red clouds,
five colors shimmer, light in misty shrouds.
On its back inscribed, words for ten thousand years;
on its front dotted, the seven stars appear.
Tortoise shell varied, white rainbow hue;
pulley twisting, golden adornments true.
Startling rhinoceros, cut through—how sharp, how right?
Fine horses driven in herds—none can match its might.
Wind and frost severe, on scabbard clear;
essence and aura afar, between stars appear.
Avoiding disaster, dawn pierces Jìn emperor's abode;
fleeing calamity, night enters Chǔ king's road.
Once matched with a great immortal, mate,
tiger's roar, dragon's cry soar to heaven's gate.
Dōnghuáng elevates to Zǐwēi's seat;
Xīwáng wears it down to Chìchéng's fields' beat.
Long peace has stilled spear and shield affairs;
by fortune, it fills civil and martial prepares.
Warding dark disasters, fit for kings;
adding life, extending years, behind heaven's springs.
Guō Yuánzhèn's "Ancient Sword Song"
Have you not seen Kūnwú's iron smelt flying fiery smoke,
red light and purple aura both strikingly evoke?
Skilled artisans forge and temper year on year,
cast a treasure sword named 'Dragon Spring' clear.
Dragon Spring's color like frost and snow;
skilled artisans sigh in wonder at its marvelous glow.
In a glassy case, lotus flowers bloom;
inlaid gold rings reflect the bright moon's gloom.
Just when the world knows no dust of war,
luckily it guards a gentleman's core.
Its gleam darkly gleams, green serpent's hue;
its patterns piece by piece, green tortoise scales true.
Not only does it bond with roving knights,
but also has drawn close to heroes' heights.
Why speak of midway being cast aside,
drifting fallen by an ancient prison's side?
Though buried again, of no employ,
still each night its aura can pierce the sky.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Memorial Thanking for the Bestowal of Fāngzhū Swords, Etc."
Just opened from jade cases,
carved wonders dazzle the eyes.
First unveiling the ivory fastenings,
beautiful adornments array in ties.
Already matching cinnabar clouds' glow,
suddenly rivalling azure clouds' show.
Its body's pattern inherently prized;
the vessel's use alone is aptly sized.
Cold and warmth both splendid bear,
left and right reflect each other's share.
Jìn Péi Jǐngshēng's "Inscription on a Patterned Sword"
A vessel is known by its sharpness shown,
its substance praised by the name made known.
A fine sword stands upright and bright,
embodying culture, marshalling might.
On land it severs dark rhinoceros horn;
in water it slices light feathers borne.
Nine merits thus its image hold;
seven virtues are its support bold.
Jìn Zhāng Xié's "Inscription on the Tài'ē Sword"
The sword Tài'ē,
each age enhances its beauty's play.
Tempered with clear waves,
honed on Yuè's whetstone saves.
Like jade thus gleaming,
as a shadow in water streaming.
Without motion, solemnity it brings;
all lands follow its guiding strings.
Swords, Part Three
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Dāo (刀)
means dào (到, to arrive).
It is used for chopping and striking,
reaching its target and then striking it.
Its tip is called the fēng (锋),
meaning it is as sharp and poisonous as a bee's sting.
Its base is called the huán (环),
as its shape resembles a ring."
Another source says:
"Huángdì (黄帝) collected metal from Shǒushān (首山),
and first cast it into a dāo."
See Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòng Míng Jì*.
Through the ages, there have been the Wú dāo, Chì dāo, Róng dāo, Luán dāo.
The *Guīcáng* says:
"Using the great auxiliary Wú dāo,
Yǔ (禹) was thus brought forth."
The *Shàngshū* says:
"The red dāo and great instructions,
the great bi disc and wǎn yǎn jades,
were placed in the western chamber."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"The precious dāo, the red dāo,
is a type of xiāo (削, scraper/knife)."
The *Máo Shī* says:
"He holds his luán dāo."
The commentary says:
"The dāo has luán (bells)."
The *Máo Shī* also says:
"With what did he adorn it?
With jade and yáo stone,
the scabbard ornament and the róng dāo."
The commentary states:
"Zhōu (舟)
means to wear/belt.
Róng dāo indicates there are military affairs."
Zhèng dāo,
see the *Zhōulǐ*.
Mèng Láo,
The *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* says:
"Mèng Láo
is a precious dāo of Lǔ (鲁)."
Xīróng sharp dāo,
see the *Kǒng Cóngzǐ*.
The King of Qín obtained it,
and it cut jade as if cutting wood.
Kūnwú jade-cutting dāo,
see the *Shízhōu Jì*.
During the time of King Mù of Zhōu,
it was presented by the Western Hú,
and it cut jade as if cutting mud.
Míng Hóng dāo,
see Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòng Míng Jì*.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn bestowed it upon Dōngfāng Shuò.
Bǎi Bì precious dāo,
The *Diǎnlùn* says:
"The Wèi Crown Prince Cáo Pī forged the Bǎi Bì precious dāo.
The first was called Língbǎo,
the second Hánzhāng,
the third Sùzhì.
He also made the Lùmò dāo,
also named the Lónglín dāo."
The three dāo: Bǎiliàn, Qīngdú, Lòuyǐng.
See Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù*,
the dāo of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
The ancients cast dāo
on the bǐngwǔ day of the fifth month,
taking pure fire essence,
to harmonize with its numerical principle.
See Yú Xǐ's *Zhìlín*.
Also, Ruǎn Shī's making of dāo
received methods from the spirit of metal essence.
On the gēngxīn day of the seventh month,
he saw the metal god at the gate of the smelting workshop,
and bowed twice to the west.
The metal god taught him the proper balance of water and fire,
the refinement of the five essences,
the use of yīn and yáng phases,
and the harmonization of hardness and softness.
In three years, he made one thousand seven hundred and seventy dāo.
These dāo had flat backs and double-edged blades,
square mouths and broad heads.
They could cut the finest thread without severing it,
and chop hard, solid objects without any change or damage.
See Yáng Quán's *Wùlǐ Lùn*.
The so-called hundred-refined sharp weapon,
to ward off inauspiciousness,
and subdue evildoers,
refers to this.
See Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's *Nèijiè Lìng*.
Wú dāo Zhōu bǎo
"Wú dāo" has already been mentioned in the narrative.
The *Bówùzhì* says:
"Chì dāo
is a precious vessel of Zhōu."
Tuōguāng Lòuyǐng
The *Lóngyú Hétú* says:

"Lòuyǐng" has already been mentioned in the narrative.
Slaughtering oxen Beheading tigers

and his dāo could still shave hair."
Hé Yàn's *Inscription for the Tiger-Beheading Dāo* says:
"Using this to create this vessel,
chī-tigers are beheaded."
Copper-mouthed Gold-headed

Xiè Shàng's *Letter to General Yáng Zhēngnán* says:

Gathering metal Cutting jade
Both are seen in the narrative.
Zhuān Zhū holding it Líng Tǒng dancing with it
The *Lièshì Zhuàn* says:

placed it inside a fish's belly,
and used it to stab King Liáo."
The *Wú Shū* says:
"Líng Tǒng resented Gān Níng for killing his father.
Níng always guarded against Tǒng,
and did not meet with him.
At a gathering at Lǚ Méng's place,
when the wine was flowing freely,
Tǒng then performed a dāo dance.
Níng rose and said:

White Tiger image Golden Horse form
The *Chūnqiū Fánlù* says:
"The dāo is on the right,
it is the image of the White Tiger."
Lǐ Yóu's *Inscription for the Golden Horse Book Dāo* says:
"The skillful smelter refines the hard steel,
the golden horse entrusts its form."
General bestows upon Gù Inspector gives to Xiáng
Bān Gù's *Letter to Dòu Xiàn* says:
"This month, the Palace Attendant, by order, bestowed upon Gù a handled dāo,
saying:
'This is what the Grand General wore when he was young.
Now he bestows it upon Gù.'
I ponder this great kindness,
both joyful and ashamed." The *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Initially,
Wèi's Xúzhōu Inspector Rénchéng Lǚ Qián,
had a waist dāo.
A craftsman examined it,
believing that only one of the Three Dukes could wear this dāo."
Qián said to his *Biéjià Wáng Xiáng*:
"If it is not the right person,
the dāo might cause harm.

Shī Wàng wielding the dāo Páo Dīng moving the blade
The *Chǔcí* says:
"How did Chāng recognize Shī Wàng in the market?
He raised his voice wielding the dāo, and then the ruler was pleased."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Páo Dīng dissected an ox for Lord Wénhuì.
Dīng said:
'Now, my dāo has been used for nineteen years!
It has dissected several thousand oxen,
yet the blade is as if newly ground on the whetstone.
Those joints have spaces.
And the blade's edge has no thickness.
Using what has no thickness to enter where there is space,
how ample and roomy, there must be plenty of space for the blade to move!
Therefore, after nineteen years,
the blade's edge is like new.'"
Quenched in clear streams Honed on Yuè whetstones
Lǐ Yóu's *Inscription for the Golden Horse Book Dāo* says:
"Quenched in clear streams,
honed on Yuè whetstones."
On land, it slices rhinoceros and wild oxen In water, it severs whales and giant rays
Wáng Càn's *Dāo Inscription* says:
"On land, it slices rhinoceros and wild oxen,
in water, it severs whales and giant rays."
Ode to the Precious Sword by Cáo Zhí, Prince of Chén of Wèi
During the Jiàn'ān era,
the King of Wèi commanded his officials to forge five precious swords,
marked with dragons, bears, birds, and sparrows.
The Crown Prince obtained one,
and I, along with my brother the Marquis of Ráoyáng, each received one.
There was the enlightened sovereign of the Great Hàn,
whose thoughts reached the profound and touched the mysterious,
spreading literary elegance to achieve broad influence,
and promoting military preparedness to ward off calamity.
Then they were whetted with stones from the five directions,
and polished with the soil of Central Yellow.
They measured the round sun to fix the rings,
and gave form to divine concepts through craftsmanship.
On land, they cleave rhinoceros hide;
in water, they sever dragon boats.
Lightly striking, swiftly cutting,
the blade does not slow the flow.
They surpass the Jùquē of Southern Yuè,
and excel the Tài'ē of Western Chǔ.
Truly, they are wielded by the Perfected One,
seeking Heaven's favor and bearing its charge.
Memorial of Thanks for the Bestowed Shànshèng Sword by Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng
The icy blade holds brilliance,
carved jade displays ornamentation.
Its name matches its pure substance,
its spirit is hailed as Tuōguāng.
When the five treasures were first completed,
Cáo Pī first received one;
now the Shànshèng is newly forged,
and your foolish servant is wholly favored by its grace.
Bestowing Hán Fēi's writings
would not suffice for comparison;
granting the Bóshān brush
is lighter still than this.
Inscription on the Cuò Adorned Sword by Lǐ Yóu of Later Hàn
Wearing it with adornment,
restrains martial display and elevates culture.
Is it merely for beauty's sake?
It is to caution one's own person.
Inscription on the Lùmò Sword by Emperor Wén of Wèi
O resplendent fine blade,
tempered truly in its season.
Compared to a qilin's horn,
nothing surpasses this.
May it never meet misfortune,
preserved for all ages.
Inscription on the Precious Sword by Cáo Zhí, Prince of Chén of Wèi
This precious sword is forged,
both ground and whetted.
Not for崇尚武力,
but to guard my person.
It does not strike the qilin's horn,
nor trample the luán's talons.
Inscription on the Wénshēn Sword by Zhāng Xié of Jìn
The precious sword, once completed,
exhausts principle and captures utmost subtlety.
Intricate patterns swirl like waves,
flowing light shines like lightning.
Bows, Fourth
The Shì Míng says:
"A bow (gōng),
is like the vault (qióng);
when drawn, it arches high."
According to the Shì Běn:
"Huī first made the bow."
Sòng Zhōng notes:
"Huī
was a minister of the Yellow Emperor."
Also, Master Xún says:
"Chuí made the bow."
The Mòzǐ says:
"Yì made the bow."
These three accounts differ.
The Yì Jīng speaks of bending wood to make the bow,
and sharpening wood to make arrows.
The bow and arrow's
utility to awe the world
is derived from the Kuí hexagram.
The Zhōu Guān states:
"The Director of Bows and Arrows oversees the methods of the six bows, four crossbows, and eight arrows,
distinguishing their names and types,
and managing their storage,
as well as their distribution.
The six bows are: the king's bow, the arc bow, the jiā bow, the yǔ bow, the táng bow, and the great bow.
In mid-spring, bows and crossbows are presented;
in mid-autumn, quivers of arrows are presented.
When distributing them,
the king's bow and arc bow are given to those who shoot at armor, leather, or wooden targets;
the jiā bow
and yǔ bow
are given to those who shoot at targets of hide, birds, or beasts;
the táng bow and great bow
are given to students of archery, envoys, and those being rewarded."
Also, the bow-maker crafts the bow,
selecting the six materials strictly in their proper seasons.
Once the six materials are gathered,
the skilled artisan harmonizes them.
The core wood (gàn)
is for long range;
the horn (jiǎo)
is for speed.
The sinew (jīn)
is for penetration;
the glue (jiāo)
is for cohesion;
the silk (sī)
is for strength;
the lacquer (qī)
is to withstand frost and dew.
In making a bow,
the core wood is split in winter,
and the horn is soaked in spring.
Sinew is prepared in summer,
and the three materials are joined in autumn.
For the Son of Heaven's bow,
nine joined form a circle;
for a feudal lord's bow,
seven joined form a circle;
for a minister's bow,
five joined form a circle;
for a scholar's bow,
three joined form a circle."
Also, Master Xún says:
"The Son of Heaven has a carved bow,
feudal lords have vermilion bows,
ministers have black bows."
The Sān Lǐ Tú states:
"Vermilion bows
are used by the Son of Heaven;
travel bows (lǚ gōng)
are used by ministers and below."
The Ěr Yǎ says:
"A bow with binding is called mǐ,
now an horn bow.
One adorned with metal is called xiǎn;
with clam shell, yáo;
with jade, guī."
Using metal, clam, or jade to adorn the two ends of the bow
gives rise to these names based on their categories.
The Shì Míng also says:
"The end of the bow is called xiāo,
meaning xiāo
is the tip.
It is also called mǐ,
made of bone,
smooth and sleek.
The center is called fǔ.
(Pronounced fú zhǔ fǎn.)
Fǔ
means to hold (fǔ).
It is where one grips.
Between the xiāo and fǔ is called yuān.
Yuān
means curved (wǎn).
Wǎn
means bent."
Also, the Shuō Wén says:
"Diāo,
(dīng kūn fǎn.)
is a painted bow;
Xuān,
(xū quán fǎn.)
is an horn bow;
hú,
is a wooden bow;
juān,
is a curved bow;
Shāo,
(shū zhāo fǎn.)
is a bow that is convenient and swift;
jué

Although the official armor was public property,
