The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"The feudal lords met at Xiāng,
then attacked Bīyáng.
Dí Hǔmí set up the wheel of a large chariot
and covered it with armor to use as a shield."
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Armor"
The application of armor and helmets
is to ward off sharp points and arrows.
Valuing its sturdiness and hardness,
sometimes rhinoceros or wild buffalo hide is used.
Internally, it preserves the body;
externally, it does no harm.
It resembles a benevolent person,
whose way is vast and great.
Those who love virtue find peace;
those who love war face peril.
Relying solely on wisdom and depending on force
is not the way of a gentleman.
Cáo Zhí of Wèi's "Memorial on the Armor Bestowed by the Late Emperor"
The Late Emperor bestowed upon your servant armor:
one suit of Black Radiance, one suit of Bright Radiance,
and one suit of double-sided armor.
Now, in an age of rising peace,
with no affairs of war,
I beg that it all be handed over to the Armory Section for management.
Yǔ Yì of Jìn's "Letter on Armor to Mùróng Huàng"
Dèng Bǎichuān previously sent this one suit of double-sided rhinoceros-hide armor.
Although it cannot be considered exquisite,
it is still an unusual object,
so I am sending it to you.
Section Seven: Saddles
The Shuōwén states:
"A saddle is
the tack and gear for a horse."
The Yántiělùn states:
"In ancient times, there were only rope bridles, leather shoes, and hide pads.
Later generations used leather saddles and iron bits without ornamentation.
Later still, there came to be carved-path saddles."
The Sānfǔ Juélù states:
"Liáng Jì gave a carved-path saddle to Gōngsūn Fèn as a gift."
Purple Velvet High-Bridge Saddles:
Officials of Wèi each had one set of purple velvet high-bridge saddles.
Some were adorned with gold, silver, or kingfisher feathers.
The Yǒngchāng Jì states:
"Emperor Wén of Qín had gold and silver saddles
adorned with kingfisher feathers."
There were also mud-guards and sweat-guards,
also called yǎn-hàn.
Tasseled tails and jade ornaments were also used as adornments on saddles.
The Shìshuō states:
"Wáng Wǔzǐ once rode a horse
fitted with a linked-dryland mud-guard.
There was water ahead,
and the horse refused to cross.
Wáng said,
'This must be because it values the mud-guard.'
He had someone remove it,
and the horse then crossed."
Officials each had one set of woven mud-guards.
The Yántiělùn states:
"Now, the wealthy have embroidered felt sweat-guards and tassels,
♀ (Note: The character is pronounced gū biàn fǎn.)
♂ Officials of Wèi each had one set of red velvet jade ornaments and stone tasseled tails."
Fú Qián's Tōngsúwén states:
"All bridle ornaments are called jade ornaments."
Carved-Path – Golden Ridge
"Carved-path" is mentioned in the narrative.
The Sānfǔ Juélù states:
"Gōngsūn Fèn of Pínglíng was known throughout the capital for his wealth.
Liáng Jì, knowing Fèn was frugal and stingy,
gave him a carved-path saddle as a gift,
then proceeded to borrow fifty million from him.
Suspended Pillar Illuminating People
The Records of the Wei states:
"The Grand Ancestor's saddle,
stored in the warehouse, was gnawed by mice.
The warehouse clerk feared death.
Dèng'āi Wáng Chōng pierced a single-layered robe with a knife to make it look as if gnawed by mice,
and falsely wore a worried expression.
The Grand Ancestor asked him about it.
Chōng said:
'Common belief holds that if mice gnaw one's clothes,
it is inauspicious for the owner.'
The Grand Ancestor said:
'This is nonsense!'
Soon after, the warehouse clerk reported the gnawed saddle.
The Grand Ancestor laughed and said:
'My son's robe was at his side and was gnawed,
how much more a saddle suspended on a pillar?'"The ancient Music Bureau poem "Army Campaign Poem" by Zuǒ Yánnián states:
"How joyful is army life,
driving forth astride a pair of piebalds.
Saddle and steed shine white upon the men,
the dragon-steed moves of its own accord."
Purple Velvet Kingfisher Feather
Both have been seen above.
Bestowed upon Huán Welcoming Lǔ
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"In the first year of the Yǒngyuán era,
he went west to pay respects at the imperial tombs.
Huán Yù concurrently held the post of Commandant of the Feathered Forest Guard.
The Emperor bestowed upon him two horses along with saddles, bridles, and protective sweat-cloths."
Also, the Records of Wú states:
"When Lord Cáo was defeated and fled,
Lǔ Sù was the first to return.
Sūn Quán held a grand feast for all the generals.
As Sù was about to enter the pavilion to pay his respects,
Quán showed him courtesy
and said to him:
'Zǐjìng, you should dismount and remove your saddle to welcome him;
this would be sufficient to show your intent.'"
Bestowed upon Zhào Sent to Sūn
Sīmǎ Biāo's History of the Hàn states:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ summoned Zhào Xǐ,
had him presented and bestowed upon him a saddled horse,
and appointed him to await orders at the Public Carriage Office."
Also, "sent to Gōngsūn Fèn" has been seen above.
Colored Glaze Rose Quartz
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital states:
"During Emperor Wǔ's time,
the country of Shéndú presented a white-light colored glaze saddle,
which in a dark room illuminated an area of ten zhàng."
Also, "Emperor Wǔ obtained the Heavenly Horse of Èrshī,
and had a saddle made of rose quartz stone."
Hanging in the Long Woods Ascending the High Mountain
Xiè Huìlián's poem states:
"Hang the saddle by the side of the long woods,
water the horse at the bend of the distant river."
Liú Kūn's "Song of Fúfēng" states:
"Tether the horse beneath the tall pine,
mount the saddle atop the high mountain peak."
Cáo Zhí of Wèi, "Memorial Presenting a Silver Saddle":
In the era of the late Martial Emperor,
this silver saddle set was decreed.
Initially, I dared not ride it;
respectfully, I present it.
Liú Yìgōng of Sòng, "Letter of Thanks for the Golden Beam Saddle":
Bestowed upon your servant a golden beam bridge saddle for imperial use,
its craftsmanship exquisite and ingenious,
fitting for the dragon-steeds.
Your sagely benevolence reaches down to me,
graciously bestowing this radiant gift.
Lǐ Yóu of the Later Hàn, "Inscription on the Saddle":
Galloping and chasing in haste,
leaping and vaulting, covering the ground.
Though one may be skilled and accustomed,
there will also be stumbles and falls.
When the well rope frays at the jug,
nothing escapes ruin.
Reins, Eighth
The Explanation of Names states:
"Reins (pèi) are for guiding (fú),
meaning to pull, lead, guide, and control the horse.
The ornaments of the reins
include the bit, headstall, cheekpieces, halter, bridle, and noseband,
each fulfilling its function.
The bit (xián),
is what is in the mouth.
The headstall (lè),
is a network (luò),
a network over the head to lead it. Cheekpieces (biāo)
enclose (bāo),
enclosing the sides of the mouth.
The halter (jī),
restrains (jiǎn),
that which holds and controls it. The bridle (jiāng)
is a boundary (jiāng),
tying it so it cannot go beyond the boundary limit.
The bridle is also called a dì,
thus the Expanded Cāng Dictionary says dì
means horse bridle.
The noseband (kòng),
carries the meaning of control."
The Common Language says:
"That which controls the horse is called a noseband (kòng).
The reins in relation to the horse
are like a ruler using officials to govern the people."
Thus the Family Sayings states:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven took the Inner Historian as his left and right hands,
used virtue and law as the bit and headstall,
and the hundred officials as the reins.
One who is skilled at driving horses
adjusts the bit and headstall,
aligns the reins and whip,
balances the horse's strength,
and harmonizes the horse's heart.
Thus, without a sound from the mouth, the horse responds;
without raising reins or whip, it covers a thousand lǐ.
One who is skilled at governing people
unifies their virtue and law,
rectifies their hundred officials,
balances and equalizes human strength,
harmonizes and pacifies human hearts.
Thus, commands are not repeated yet people obey;
punishments are not used yet all under heaven is ordered."
Commanding a Halt Crossing the Boundary Sacrifice
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The Pot-Carrier Official holds the reins to command a halt."
Minister Zhèng's commentary states:
"Suspend the reins at the place where a halt should be made.
Also, the Grand Charioteer is in charge of driving the jade carriage for sacrifices.
When it comes to crossing the boundary sacrifice (bá),
the King personally drives from the left.
The Charioteer descends and prays,
then ascends and receives the reins;
after crossing the boundary sacrifice, he then drives forth."
As If Moistened Luxuriant
The Máo Odes states:
"My horses are young steeds,
the six reins are as if moistened."
It also states:
"My horses are white-maned blacks,
the six reins are luxuriant."
In Hand Correcting the Body
The Máo Odes states:
"The team of four stallions is very robust,
the six reins are in hand."
The Family Sayings states:
"One who is skilled at driving horses corrects his body to gather the reins."
A Thousand Chariots Halted A Hundred Horses Aligned
Bān Gù's "Eulogy on the Eastern Inspection Tour" states:
"The imperial carriage stirred with solemnity,
all the lords held their breath.
Ten thousand riders aligned their bits,
a thousand chariots halted their reins."
Emperor Míng of Wèi's "How Good It Is" states:
"A hundred horses aligned their reins,
driven by Zàofǔ."
The Ruler's Governance The Minister's Emolument
The Family Sayings states:
"Mǐnzǐ Qiān was governor of Fèi,
and asked Confucius about governance.
Confucius said:
'The ruler is the man,
the officials are the reins,
punishments are the whip.
The governance of a ruler
consists merely of holding the reins and whip!'"The Huáinánzǐ states:
"Authority and measurement
are the ruler's carriage.
Ranks and emoluments
are the minister's bit and reins."
Commands Control Subordinates Rites Regulate the People
The Kǒng Family Masters' Anthology states:
"The Master said:
'Now, government orders
are the ruler's bit and reins,
used to control subordinates.'"It also states:
"When Confucius went to Wèi,
General Wénzǐ of Wèi asked him:
'Now, if regulating them with punishments still does not prevail,
how can rites regulate them?'
Confucius said:
'Regulating people with rites
is comparable to using reins in driving.'"
The galloping horse discards the reins, mounting the carriage and taking hold of them.
The *Guanzi* says:
"All amnesties
bring small benefits but great harm,
thus over time they cannot withstand their calamity.
Therefore, amnesties are
like discarding the reins of a galloping horse.
Not granting amnesties is
like the grinding stone for carbuncles and abscesses."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says: "When Wáng Liáng or Zàofǔ were charioteers,
upon mounting the carriage and taking hold of the reins,
the horses became orderly and well-aligned."
Carrying the pot suspended, the Grand Servant holds them.
"Carrying the pot suspended" has already been seen in the commentary on the Ling Shě.
The *Bǎiguān Chūnqiū* says:
"For the Grand Procession,
the Dukes and Ministers lead the way,
the Grand Servant holds the reins,
and the Great General accompanies in the carriage.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ of the Eastern Hàn performed the suburban sacrifices in Dōngjīng,
for the Procession of Law, the Governor of Hénán led the way,
the Commandant of Imperial Carriages held the reins,
and the Palace Attendant served as the accompanying rider."
Obtaining it in the hand, responding to it in the heart.
The *Lièzǐ* says:
"All charioteers obtain it from the bit,
respond to it with the reins,
obtain it in the hand,
and respond to it in the heart."
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Reins":
The reins are controlled in the hand,
urgency and relaxation must be timely.
Rewards and punishments are in the heart,
harmony and balance are what is considered.
Horses know a good charioteer,
they advance and cover the road.
People know good governance,
orders are carried out and prohibitions are observed.
Whip, Ninth
Whip, switch, and cane,
are all names for horse goads.
What the *Shuōwén* calls 'driving whips',
in ancient times were made of leather,
used to flog criminals,
and also to drive horses,
hence their character is composed with '革' (leather).
The *Shū* says:
"The whip serves as official punishment,"
this was applied to the people.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Holding the whip and bow in the left hand."
It also says:
"Although the whip is long,
it does not reach the horse's belly,"
this was applied to horses.
Later, bamboo replaced leather,
hence the two characters for switch and cane,
are also both composed with '竹' (bamboo),
likely because the meaning of driving, switching, and caning gave rise to the names.
The *Hànshū*:
"Lóu Jìng said:
'King Tài of Zhōu, because of the Dí invasion,
leaned on his horse cane and left to dwell in Qí.'" The *Lǐjì* says:
"Those presenting carriages and horses hold the switch and the mounting cord.
When the ruler's carriage is about to be harnessed,
then the servant holds the switch and stands before the horses,"
this is the matter.
Chǔ command, Qín ballad.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"King Líng of Chǔ sent troops to surround Xú to intimidate Wú,
the King of Chǔ stationed at Gānxī,
to provide support.
It snowed,
the king wore a leather cap,
a Qín fur coat,
a kingfisher-feather cloak and leopard-skin shoes,
and came out holding a whip."
Dù Yù's commentary says:
"Holding the whip to issue commands."
Cuī Hóng's *Fú Qín Lù* says:
"During Fú Jiān's time,
in Guānzhōng there was a ballad:
'Long-sheathed horse whip strikes the left thigh,
when Tàisuì moves south, one should avoid the enemy.'"
Lǐ's inscription, Cáo's rhapsody.
Lǐ Yóu composed the "Inscription on Horse Whip and Cane,"
fully recorded later.
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Rhapsody on Facing the Wō River" says:
"In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
following the Emperor to pay respects at the tombs,
then rode horses to tour and view the eastern stronghold,
following the Wō River.
Stopped the horse and wrote with the whip,
composing the 'Rhapsody on Facing the Wō River.'"
Holding iron, burying bronze.
Xiāo Fāngděng's *Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū* says:
"Wáng Dūn plotted to harm Wáng Chéng,
but Chéng had twenty followers,
holding iron horse whips as guards."
Wú Kuài's *Fēndì Jì* says:
"Liù Shān is where
Gōu Jiàn cast bronze on this mountain.
If the bronze did not melt, he buried it,
and canes grew above.
Gōu Jiàn sent an envoy to take them and plant them from Nánshè,
adorned them as horse canes,
and presented them to Wú."
Holding the whip, throwing the switch.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says:
"Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn said to the King of Chǔ:
'In the left hand I hold whip and bow,
in the right I carry quiver and bow-case,
to engage with you, my lord.'" The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says:
"Yáng Hǔ was about to kill Jì Sūn at Pǔ,
and had Lín Nán drive for him.
Upon reaching Mèngqú,
Lín Nán threw down the switch,
and had Yáng Yuè get down to retrieve the switch."
Qí people, counting horses.
The *Kǒngcóngzǐ* says:
"Punishment is to regulate the people,
compared to charioteering,
it is the whip and switch."
The *Hànshū* says:
"Shí Qìng, as Grand Servant, was driving out,
the Emperor asked how many horses were in the carriage.
Qìng used the switch to count the horses,
raised his hand and said:
'Six horses.'"
Horse cane, camel whip.
"Horse cane" has already been seen in the narrative.
The *Wèi Bǎiguān Míng* says:
"Two camel horse whips."
Propping on the ground, pointing at the sky.
The *Yì Yuàn* says:
"Once a man was riding a horse through the mountains,
and from afar saw two old men
playing chūpú facing each other,
so he approached them.
He propped himself on the ground with his switch to watch them,
thinking it was only a short while.
Looking at his horse whip,
it had already rotted away."
The *Sòngshū* says:
"When the righteous uprising began,
Huán Xuán was defeated in battle.
As he was about to flee,
Hú Fān grabbed Xuán's horse bridle and said:
'Now the Imperial Forest archers
still number eight hundred;
if we abandon this and return,
can we regain it?'
Xuán merely pointed at the sky with his horse whip."
Qí punishment, dream interpretation.
"Qí punishment" has already been provided in the commentary on "Qí people."
The *Mèngshū* says:
"Interpreting a dream where one obtains a whip or switch
means one will have an errand."
Yuè bronze, Jìn gold.
"Yuè bronze" see commentary on "burying bronze."
The *Shìshuō* says:
"Wáng Dūn was in Gūshú,
Emperor Míng of Jìn went out to observe,
Dūn noticed and pursued the Emperor.
The Emperor gave a gold horse whip to an old woman guest,
the pursuers asked the old woman.
The old woman said:
'He left long ago!'"
Adorned with coral, fitted with ivory.
The *Liángzhōu Jì* says:
"In the second year of Xiánníng,
when Zhāng Jùn's tomb was opened,
a whip was obtained,
adorned with coral."
Zhāng Huá's "Poem on the Frivolous" says:
"Transverse hairpin carved from tortoiseshell,
long whip fitted with ivory."
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Horse Cane"
The charioteer's cane and switch,
demonstrate authority and anger.
The defeat at Dōngyě,
was due to excessive supervision and blame.
Hunting, Tenth
The Book of Changes says:
"When Fúxī ruled the world,
he knotted cords to make nets,
for hunting and fishing,
which likely derived from the principle of Lí.
This was its beginning."
The Báihǔ Tōng says:
"Why do kings and feudal lords engage in hunting?
To rid the fields of pests,
above to supply the ancestral temples,
and below to assemble and select the masses of officers."
Therefore, the Ěryǎ says:
"The spring hunt is called sōu,
the summer hunt is called miáo,
the autumn hunt is called xiǎn,
and the winter hunt is called shòu."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"Sōu means to search out,
taking those unfit for service.
Miáo is to rid the crops of pests,
xiǎn is to follow the killing qi,
shòu is to obtain game,
taking it without discrimination—
this is the meaning of ridding the fields of pests."
Furthermore, the Book of Rites says:
"In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven and feudal lords had no pressing affairs,
they hunted three times a year.
First, for dried meat offerings,
second, for guests,
third, to fill the ruler's kitchen.
Having no affairs and not hunting was called disrespectful;
hunting not in accordance with ritual was called wasting Heaven's creatures.
The Son of Heaven did not surround completely,
feudal lords did not surprise whole herds.
When the Son of Heaven killed, the great banner was lowered;
when feudal lords killed, the small banner was lowered.
When high ministers killed, the auxiliary chariots stopped;
when auxiliary chariots stopped, the common people hunted.
When otters sacrifice fish,
then the foresters enter the marshes and weirs.
When jackals sacrifice beasts,
then hunting begins.
When turtledoves transform into hawks,
then nets and snares are set.
When plants and trees wither and fall,
then they enter the mountain forests.
Before insects hibernate,
they did not use fire to hunt,
did not take fawns or eggs.
They did not kill the pregnant,
did not slaughter the young,
did not overturn nests."
It also says:
"In the last month of winter,
the Son of Heaven teaches hunting to practice the five weapons."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation says:
"The rituals of hunting
teach people methods of warfare—
this is the meaning of supplying the ancestral temples above and assembling and selecting below."
Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng Zhāngjù says:
"Liè (hunt)
means jié (swift),
meaning to take swiftly.
Hunting is also called shòu,
shòu means pursuing beasts."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Book of Songs mentions hunting
as capturing beasts.
It is also called tián.
Tián
means field.
Thus, the Ěryǎ's meaning of ridding the fields of pests
is another name for hunting.
Discussing Military Affairs / Practicing Warfare
Bān Gù's "Eastern Capital Rhapsody" says:
"As for following the seasons to search and hunt,
selecting chariots and troops to discuss military affairs,
they must be governed by royal regulations,
taught with the Fēng and Yǎ."
The Book of Rites says:
"In the last month of autumn,
the Son of Heaven teaches through hunting,
to practice the five weapons."
The annotation states:
"The five weapons refer to the five arms:
bow, arrow, shū, spear, and dagger-axe."
Three Drives / One Side
The Book of Changes says:
"The king uses three drives,
losing the game in front."
Huángfǔ Mì's Dìwáng Shìjì says:
"Chéng Tāng went out
and saw a netter praying.
Tāng asked him:
'What are you praying for?'
The netter said:
'Those from the heavens above,
those emerging from the earth,
those coming from the four directions—
all enter my net.'
Tāng heard and said:
'Alas!
That is exhaustive!
If not Jié, who could do this?'
He then ordered three sides removed,
leaving only one side."
Capturing Game / Grand Hunt
The Máo Shī says:
"Hunting chariots are yoked,
four stallions stout and strong.
To the east lies Fǔ's grasslands,
we drive to conduct the hunt.
This lord goes to the miáo hunt,
selecting troops with loud cries.
Banners raised, ox-tails set,
they capture game at Áo."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Rhapsody on the Military Hunt" says:
"Gāozōng campaigned against Guǐfāng,
Huángdì had affairs at Bǎnquán.
Angered by treacherous preparations for violence,
indignant at Wú barbarians' lack of submission.
To train troops through military discussion,
thus grandly hunting in the field gaps."
Four Divisions / Two Foresters
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park" says:
"Leather-covered carriages in front, guides and wanderers behind,
Sūn Shū holding the reins,
Duke Wèi as attendant,
retinue followers moving crosswise,
emerging from among the four divisions."
Yìng Chàng's "Rhapsody on the Military Hunt" says:
"Then he ordered the officials,
to patrol the land all around.
Two foresters clear the wilds,
three attendants mark the game."
Arouse the Troops / Drill the Ranks
Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on Chángyáng" says:
"In peace, do not neglect danger;
in safety, do not forget peril.
Thus, in times of plenty, send out troops,
array chariots, arouse the troops.
Muster forces at Wǔzuò,
train horses at Chángyáng.
Test strength on cunning beasts,
examine martial skill on swift game."
Wáng Càn's "Rhapsody on the Military Hunt" says:
"Follow the ancient way to roam at leisure,
clearly encouraging aid to farms and gardens;
use spare days in slack seasons,
display miáo hunts and drill the ranks."
Jìn Drum / Forester's Flag
Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng Zhāngjù says:
"In the last month of autumn,
the Son of Heaven teaches through hunting,
to practice the five weapons,
and promulgate horse administration.
When going out,
they follow the season to take game;
in the ritual,
the general holds the jìn drum,
the division leader holds the tí drum,
the brigade leader holds the qíng drum,
to teach sitting, rising, advancing, retreating, slow and fast rhythms."
The Rites of Zhōu says:
"The mountain forester administers the laws and orders of mountains and forests.
If there is a grand field hunt,
he clears the wilds of the mountain fields and at the hunt's end,
plants the forester's flag in the center,
gathers the game and marks the ears."
Eastern Ford / Southern Park
Emperor Wén of Wèi's poem says:
"Covered carriage in Yè's palace,
military hunt at Eastern Bridge Ford.
Layered nets form dense meshes,
hunting nets float like clouds."
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Feather Hunt" says:
"Then the imperial carriage lingers,
delays and moves at ease,
raises the Heavenly Ford at Yīluò,
gazes afar, gathering at the Southern Park.
Greatly commanding the hunters,
competing in pursuit, driving far,
light chariots swift as gales,
feathered riders galloping like lightning."
Huáng Cén and Zǐ Mò
Yìng Chàng’s “Rhapsody on the Imperial Hunt” states:
“Then he ordered the officials,
to patrol the land and search all around.
Two marshals cleared the fields,
three overseers marked the game.
To the north they reached the great plain,
to the south they crossed Huáng Cén.”
Wáng Càn’s “Rhapsody on the Hunt” states:
“Crossing Zhāng Pǔ to form a horizontal battle line,
leaning on Zǐ Mò to march together.
Setting up layered encirclements on the western foothills,
arraying swift steeds on the eastern outskirts.”
Jīn Jiāo and Shí Shì
Zhāng Xié’s “Seven Summonses” states:
“In the white autumn season,
the moon has already bestowed garments.
Heaven congeals, earth closes,
winds sharpen and frost flies.
He will use the season to carry out slaughter,
facing Jīn Jiāo to drill the troops.”
The Yuè Jué Shū states:
“Lè Yě is
Yuè’s hunting ground.
It was greatly enjoyed, hence called Lè Yě.
On its mountain is a stone chamber,
where Gōu Jiàn rested and planned.”
Boasting to Chǔ and Flaunting to the Hú
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú’s “Rhapsody on the Imperial Park” states: “The King of Chǔ sent Zǐxū to Qí,
and the King of Qí mobilized all his chariots and cavalry,
to go hunting with the envoy.
After the hunt,
Zǐxū went to boast to Master Wūyǒu,
with Master Wúshì also present.”
Yáng Xióng’s “Preface to the Rhapsody on Chángyáng” states: “The next year, the Emperor planned to greatly flaunt to the Hú people the abundance of game,

From Bāo Xié in the west,
to Hóngnóng in the east,
and driving south to Hànzhōng.
They spread nets and snares,
to catch bears, brown bears, porcupines,

The Emperor, moved by Heaven’s majesty’s stern severity,
thought of Tàihào’s observation of hunting.
He marked the forests and foothills, cleared thickets and marshes,
cut brambles and catalpas, leveled brushwood and stumps.
Then the phoenix presented the calendar,
the Grand Coachman prepared the carriage.
Chīyóu led the vanguard,
the Rain Master cleared the road.
Mountain spirits guarded the formation,
myriad deities cleared the way.
Xīhé held the reins,
reining in to journey west.
The emerald canopy lush and splendid,
the simurgh bells tinkling clear.
Valleys and streams grew pale and still,
hills and mounds shook and swayed.
Then the imperial carriage lingered,
delaying, leisurely.
Raising the Heavenly Ford at Yī Luò,
far gathering in the southern park.
Greatly summoning the hunters,
they vied to chase and drive long.
Light chariots swift and fierce,

Mist converging, clouds gathering,
waves flowing, rain pouring.
Horses trampled elk and deer,
wheels crushed foxes and hares.
Bows not drawn in vain,
arrows not shot idly.
Birds startled into nets and snares,

Wèi Wáng Càn’s “Rhapsody on the Feathered Hunt”
The Lord then rode a light carriage,
drove a team of four blacks,
grasped a shooting star,
carried the Fán Ruò bow.
Selecting followers, commanding officers,
all exerted themselves fully.
Banners and flags like swirling clouds,
blades and edges like a forest交错.
Gleaming, spitting fire,
illuminating the wilds, obscuring the marshes.
Mountains and rivers thus shook and swayed,
grass and trees thereby broke and fell.
Birds and beasts trembled in terror,
souls forgotten, breath seized.
Lifting heads, they met nets,
shifting feet, they encountered blows.
Hearts pierced, stomachs torn,
brains burst, cheeks shattered.
Hawks and hounds vied in pursuit,
swift and swirling.
The fallen like rain,
the stiff like islets.

Táng Tàizōng’s “Poem on the Civil and Martial Sage Emperor Going Hunting”
The King of Chǔ at Yúnmèng Marsh,
the Hàn Emperor at Chángyáng Palace.
How could they compare to using farming leisure,
reviewing martial prowess beyond Huán Sōng?
Three drives arrayed sharp troops,
seven elite ranks displayed heroic talent.
Cold wilds, frosty air white,
plains burning, fires red.
Carved spears, summer-quiver arrows,
feathered riders, green-sunken bows.
Terrified beasts hid in deep ravines,
startled birds scattered from emerald skies.
Long mists dimmed the setting sun,
shrubs shook in the stern wind.
This is called relieving the people’s suffering,

Also, “Poem on the Winter Hunt”
Fierce, fierce, the cold wind rises,
dismal, dismal, flying clouds float.
Frost thick like the vast marsh,
ice solid congealing clear streams.
Golden saddles mostly from Shàngyuàn,
jade bridles galloping over flat fields.
Banners and flags converge from four views,
nets and snares sought on one side.
Chǔ hunters vied to strike down rhinoceroses,
Qín archers contended, deer distressed.
Beasts and snakes fled into dense trees,
birds and ducks rose from Lèzhōu.
Riders reined in, plain’s dust stilled,
spears turned back, ridge’s sun gathered.
My heart is not for leisure at Luò Ruì,
my thoughts lie in roaming Wèi Bīn.
Wild game excess is not my joy,
holding the reins brings yet more worry.
Zhōu Wáng Bāo, "Poem on Viewing the Hunt with Attendant Zhāng"
Returning from the winter hunt in Shànglín,
Back from practicing archery in the fields.
Again ascending Xuānqū Tower,
Once more hunting in Huángshān's enclosure.
In harsh winter, mulberry and cudrania wither,
Amid cold frost, horses and riders grow stout.
Leashed hounds follow rabbits' rise,
High falcons press pheasants in flight.
Alas, the distant guest arrives,
Weary from toiling at border garments.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn, "Poem on Joining Zhūgě Lǎn's Military Hunt"
Grasping weapons, displaying martial valor,
Unleashing the hunt, startling the capital's borders.
Swift riders gallop a thousand miles,
High nets rise in a hundred layers.
Leaping deer fall to horses' hooves,
Starving flying squirrels drop to sword points.
Cloud roots connect to burning fires,
Bird paths cut off fowl tracks.
Gathering heroes from all four seas,
Thus to train in military arts.
Hàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, "Letter Advising Against Hunting"
Your servant hears that among creatures of the same kind, some possess extraordinary abilities;
thus for strength, Wū Huò is praised,
for swiftness, Qìng Jì is spoken of,
for courage, Bēn Yù is expected.
Your servant foolishly believes that if this is true for humans,
it must also be so for beasts.
Now Your Majesty delights in traversing perilous terrain,
grappling with fierce beasts.
Should you suddenly encounter a beast of exceptional prowess,
startled in an untenable place,
and it assails the pure dust of Your Majesty's retinue carriages—
the chariot unable to turn its axles,
the men with no time to employ their skills—
even if you had the abilities of Wū Huò or Péng Méng, they would be of no use,
and dry wood and rotten stumps
would all become hazards.
This is like having Hú and Yuè rise beneath your chariot wheels,
and Qiāng and Yí pressing against your carriage shafts—
is it not perilous indeed!
Even if all is perfectly safe and without mishap,
still, this is not what the Son of Heaven should approach.
Moreover, one clears the road before proceeding,
and only gallops after reaching the middle path.
Yet even then, accidents from broken bits or axles may occur;
how much more when treading through lush grass
or racing over hillocks and ruins?
With the pleasure of pursuing game ahead,
and no mind within for unforeseen changes,
the potential for harm
is not difficult to imagine!
To treat lightly the weight of the myriad chariots,
not considering it security and joy,
but to venture onto paths with one chance in ten thousand of danger for amusement—
your servant privately believes this is not what Your Majesty should choose.
For the clear-sighted foresee what has not yet sprouted,
and the wise avoid danger before it exists.
Disaster often lies hidden in obscurity and subtlety,
and erupts from what people overlook.
Thus the common saying goes:
"A household with accumulated wealth of a thousand gold,
does not sit under the eaves."
These words, though small,
can illustrate greater truths.
Your servant hopes Your Majesty will take heed and graciously consider this!
Hunting, Part Eleven
The *Shuōwén* states:
"Yú (fishing)
means catching fish."
According to the *Shīzǐ*,
in the age of Suìrén,
the world had much water,
so he taught people to fish.
Later, Yáo sent those living near water to fish,
and Shùn also fished at Léizé,
likely because they followed and refined this method.
The *Wénzǐ* states:
"Yáo sent those by the water to fish,
and those in the mountains to gather wood.
The task suits the tool,
the tool suits the person."
The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states:
"Shùn fished within Léizé."
Fishing as an activity
includes angling, nets, quán, gū, liǔ, chāo,
(pronounced cè jiāo fǎn).
zhào, cén,
(pronounced qián).
zēng, gǒu, lǐ, liáng, yǎn, bēi,
(pronounced lì zhī fǎn).
and xiān, among others.
Each is used differently,
but catching fish is the same result.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The angler is still,
the netter lifts;
their methods differ,
but catching fish is the same."
Angling
refers to using a single cocoon filament for the line,
a fine needle for the hook,
a slender bamboo rod for the pole,
and split grains for bait.
It can draw a cart-filling fish from a hundred-ren deep river,
within turbulent currents.
The line does not break,
the pole does not bend,
because it yields to the water's force.
The above describes Zhān Hé's angling,
seen in the *Lièzǐ*.
Some use cassia as bait,
forge a hook of yellow gold,
inlaid with silver and jade,
and suspend a kingfisher-feathered line.
The above describes a Lǔ person's angling,
seen in the *Quēzǐ*.
Nets
are made by knotting ropes.
As the *Yì* says, "He knotted ropes to make nets,
for hunting and fishing,
likely taking this from the Lí hexagram."
A quán
is made of bamboo;
see the *Guǎngyǎ*.
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"What is called gōu dá is referred to as bì, that's it."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"A quán is used to catch fish;
once you have the fish, you forget the quán."
Gū
is a large net.
See the *Ěryǎ*.
The *Shī* says:
"He casts the net, huò huò,
the zhān and wěi fish leap, bō bō."
A liǔ
is a curved weir.
See the *Guǎngyǎ*.
The *Shī* says:
"Fish caught in the liǔ are cháng and shā,
that's it.
A chāo
is made with brushwood."
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"Chāo is called shàn,
(pronounced suǒ jiàn fǎn).
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"Chāo is today's brushwood net."
A zhào
is woven from fine bamboo."
The *Ěryǎ*:
"Zhuó is called zhào."
Zhuó,
(pronounced zǔ jiào fǎn).
A cén
is made by accumulating firewood in water,
The *Ěryǎ*:
"Bái sēn is called cén, that's it."
A zēng
involves setting up four wooden posts in the water and stretching a net,
pulled up and down by a windlass.
See the *Fēngsú Tōng*.
The *Shuōwén* states:

Also, the *Chǔcí* says:

A gǒu
is made from bent bamboo.
See the *Shuōwén*.
The *Shī* says:

A lǐ

The *Guǎngyǎ* states:

a liáng
is a wooden barrier across water to catch fish."
See Zhèng Xuán's annotation to the *Lǐjì*.
The *Shī* says:

do not open my gǒu."
Yǎn
is a net for cí fish;
bēi
is for catching shrimp.
See the *Guǎngyǎ*.
is for catching crabs;
xiān

See Hé Chéngtiān's *Zuǎnwén*, which states:

These are all tools and implements for fishing,
these are recent creations,
hence not recorded by the poets of old.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The sage uses the Way and Virtue as his pole and line,
benevolence and righteousness as his hook and bait.
Casting these into the world,
what among the myriad things is not his?
Stretch heaven and earth to form his cage,
use the rivers and seas as his great net,
then how could there be any loss of fish or birds?
Thus, an arrow is not as good as a corded arrow,
a corded arrow is not as good as a net,
a net is not as good as the formless image,
this is also the meaning of fishing and angling."

Xiǎo Gān Jīng Ěr
Both seen in the narrative.
Sitting Among Rushes, Leaning Against Willows

White Dragon, Purple Cowrie

Biàn Stream, Fú River

Jìn Pān Ní's "Rhapsody on Fishing"
I lift my will to the floating clouds,
delight my body in a thatched hut.
Seeking the distant traces by the Wèi's banks,
I wander and fish to amuse myself.
Left hand grasping a long bamboo,
right hand releasing the flying line.
Golden hooks attached to the rod,
sweet baits hanging fragrant.
Shoals of fry surge forth,
swimming scales gather across.
Touching the bait, they are captured;
meeting the hook, they are seized.
Long lines flutter profusely,
light rod moves with practiced ease.
Clouds drift, gusts race,
light flashes, electricity enters.
Before the nimble creatures can be startled to flee,
dozens have already been caught.
Moreover, the freshness of roasting,
the flavor of simmering.
A hundred dishes, a thousand variations,
unique fragrances, different aromas.
Following the heart's desire,
too many to record.
Then I order the cook
to slice this hidden carp.
Lightning cuts, stars flow,
radiance scatters, strands unravel.
Following the wind, leaving the blade,
continuously piling like snow.
Garlic from the western tribes,
ginger from the southern barbarians.
Sour and salty harmoniously blended,
balanced and combined with skill.
Harmonizing spirit, calming body,
easy to ponder, hard to forget."
Chén Yīnkēng's "Poem on Watching Fishing"
Clear river calms its evening waves,
fishing companions pull light boats.
Silk lines hang, splashing distant water;
bait sinks, secretly connecting the flow.
Song voices now break, now continue;
oar shadows suddenly float across.
A word for those who rinse their hat-strings:
the blue waves in the end detain the wanderer."
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Song of the Fishing Rod"
My dwelling built by the Long River's side,
angling by the broad stream's shore.
Bamboo rod horizontal like kingfisher feathers,
cassia marrow cast like yellow gold.
As men approach, waterbirds vanish;
as oars cross, shore flowers sink.
Lotus sways, fish are seen nearing;
line runs out, the pool feels deep.
The Wèi's waters must in the end be divined;
the blue waves I merely chant of in vain.
Vainly sighing as the fragrant bait sinks,
alone I see the presence of a greedy heart."
Suí Lǐ Jùrén's "Song of the Fishing Rod"
Murmuring, facing river and sea;
vast and gleaming, belonging to the waves.
I spare not the golden bait,
rejoicing only in the kingfisher-bamboo rod.
Slanted line controls the swift current,
steady oar descends the flying rapids.
Deep pool, wind comes easily;
level stream, mist disperses hard.
A word for the court and market's guests:
Lùò Bīnwáng of the Táng Dynasty, "Response to an Imperial Edict on the Fishing Rock"
I was traveling during the third summer-heat period
and arrived at Qīlǐ Tān.
This place is the river mouth of Xīn'ān.
Here lies Yán Zǐlíng's fishing rock.
The clear pool is extremely pure,
transparent to the bottom,
where schools of fish can often be seen distinctly, as if walking on water.
Among the boatmen was a fisherman
who tried taking a hook and casting it.
Some fish swam by without paying it any heed,
while others took the bait but then stopped and spat it out.
He lifted the rod and pulled it up,
and thus caught one.
When it first emerged,
it thrashed its tail and raised its fins,
as if relying on its strength to free itself.
As it weakened slightly,
it then flapped its gills and foamed at the mouth,
as if bending its body to plead for mercy.
Alas!
Its fate was controlled by man,
and its way was exhausted by me!
I wished to call out to Féng Zǐ from my lower seat,
but how could I cry out to Zhuāng Zhōu in the middle of the road?
I then prayed for it, saying:
"When a fierce beast fights,
it is trapped in a cage or pit;
when a raptor strives,
it is confined in a cage or pen;
when a plain turtle is moistened,
it is caught with disheveled hair at the gate;
when a white dragon shows its divinity,
its scales are caught in a net.
Why not hide in the mud and dwell in a burrow?
Why then swallow the hook?"
Thereupon, I released it into the river,
allowing it to fulfill its natural course of life."
At that time, a fellow traveler turned and questioned me:
"When a supreme person deals with things,
he considers the traces before acting,
conceals his intentions before moving,
never changes his purpose from beginning to end,
and neither regret nor resentment arises in his heart.
Yet you, sir, sank the line into the river,
brought the fish onto land,
cooking it could serve to practice governance,
offering it could aid the kitchen.
Earlier you sought it—
what was your aim?
Now you release it—
what is your desire?"
I smiled and replied:
"The sage is not rigidly attached to things,
the wise man must adapt to the times.
To know the subtle is called divine,
to embrace life is called the Way.
Yǐn Yǐ,
a sage,
was imprisoned by Xià;
Kǒng Qiū,
a worthy,
was threatened in Kuāng.
With the endowment of wisdom,
they still suffered the calamity of hidden sorrows;
how much more so for the scaled and feathered tribes?
Can they avoid the burden of hooks and arrows?
Thus, earlier I had intent,
fearing I might not obtain it;
now I have no intent,
having obtained it, I seek no more.
Seeking and releasing—
are they not both beautiful?
Cooking and offering—
are they not both harmful?
Moreover, to relieve hunger, half a bean can fill the stomach;
in governance, a single word can uplift the state.
Why must one rely on a small fish to illustrate the rule of three wonders,
or cut short a great life to satisfy a single meal?
To capture without killing—
can this not be called benevolent?
To obtain without consuming—
can this not be called upright?
Furthermore, those who hold a fishing rod as their task
follow the legacy of Tàigōng.
His form sat upon the rock of Pánxī,
his omen responded to the jade tablet of Zīshuǐ.
In this manner,
was he fishing in the river?
Or was he fishing for the state?
Only then does one understand that among the ancients skilled in fishing,
was it not Tàigōng alone?
And even more marvelous than this—
was it not King Wén alone?
King Wén made the six directions his hook,
suspended the four borders as bait.
He presented it in the pure temple,
cast it into the great river.
With one pull, he obtained Tàigōng;
with a second lift, he elevated Shàngfù.
From this perspective,
those who squat at Kuàijī and sink their hooks
are but followers of the fish market;
those who lean on the vast sea and bear turtles
are but the affairs of fishermen.
These are the practices of the petty,
how could they understand what the great man fishes for?"
The Way, First
The "Língbǎo Zhēnyī Zìrán Jīng Jué" states:
"The Great Way
cannot be forcibly named.
Forced to name it, it is called 'Great';
forced to term it, it is called 'Way.'"
The "Suíshū Jīngjí Zhì" states:
"It is the profundity of the myriad things,
the ultimate subtlety of the sage."
The "Tàixuán Zhēnyī Běnjì Jīng" states:
"Without ancestor or superior,
yet uniquely able to be the beginning of the myriad things,
thus named Yuánshǐ.
Operating the Way, all is supremely honored,
and eternally abides in the Two Purities,
emerging above the heavens,
thus called Tiānzūn."
The "Běnxíng Jīng" states:
"The Way says: Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn,
due to my meritorious deeds of causation,
bestowed upon me the title of Tàishàng Dàojūn."
The Gāoshàng "Lǎozǐ Nèi Zhuàn" states:
"Tàishàng Lǎojūn's surname is Lǐ,
given name Ěr,
courtesy name Bóyáng.
His mother once saw the essence of the sun descend,
like a shooting star flying into her mouth,
and thus conceived.
After seventy-two years, she gave birth.
Often, five-colored clouds encircled his form,
and beasts of the five elements guarded his hall.
Under a plum tree by the Wō River in the state of Chén,
he was born from a cut in the left armpit."
It also states:
"Crane-haired, dragon-visaged,
broad forehead, long ears.
Large eyes, sparse teeth,
square mouth, thick lips.
His forehead had three lines reaching the hairline,
sun-cornered, moon-suspended.
His nose had pure bone with twin pillars,
his ears stood tall with three gates.
His crown bore sunlight,
his body nourished white blood.
His face congealed like gold,
his tongue woven with brocade patterns.
His form was twelve feet tall,
his teeth numbered forty-eight.
He received the divine charts, precious chapters, and methods of transformation from Yuánjūn,
as well as the arts of reverting cinnabar, subduing fire, water-mercury
(hú zǒng fǎn)
and liquefying gold,
seventy-two chapters in total."
The "Hòu Wèi Shì Lǎo Zhì" states:
"Its teaching
removes evil burdens,
cleanses the mind and spirit,
accumulates deeds and merits,
gathers virtue and increases goodness.
Then there are those who ascend to heaven in broad daylight,
living eternally in the world.
Moreover, the Three Primes, Nine Palaces, one hundred twenty officials, and all various deities
are all under its governance."
Ancestor of Qì, Preceding the Emperor
The "Xuánmiào Nèipiān Jīng" states:
"The origin of the primordial Way begins with the primordial head,
ancestor of the myriad qì."
"Lǎozǐ" states:
"The Way is empty, yet when used,
it blunts its sharpness,
untangles its knots,
harmonizes its light,
unites with its dust.
Profound! It seems to exist,
I do not know whose child it is,
it appears prior to the Emperor."
Wáng Bì's commentary states:
"The Emperor
is the Heavenly Emperor."
Lending Three, Giving Birth to One
The Mingwei Jing says:
"The Way of Heaven is good at lending,
lending with three qi.
The upper qi is called shǐ,
its color is pure blue;
the middle qi is called yuán,
its color is pure white;
the lower qi is called hài,
its color is pure yellow."
The Lǎozǐ says:
"The Way gives birth to one."
Sūn Dēng's commentary says:
"The wondrous one resides within the great void,
mysterious transformations rely on the function of the ultimate Way,
therefore, according to its origin, it is called giving birth."
Touched by a Star, Dreaming of the Sun
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"Lǎozǐ's mother was touched by a great shooting star and became pregnant."
The Hòushèng Jiǔxuán Dàojūn Lièjì Jīng says:
"The mother of the Hòushèng Lord,
first dreamed of dark clouds,
with the sun and moon entwined around her form,
then was touched and conceived."
Surname Lǐ, Style Name Zhī
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"Lǎozǐ was born into the Lǐ family,
thus taking Lǐ as his surname."
The Shàngqīng Sāntiān Jūn Lièjì Jīng says:
"The Shàngqīng Perfected One's surname is Huán,
style name Zhī,
he was a person from the time of Zhōnghuáng."
Entrusted to Hóng's Womb, Born from Lǐ's Armpit
The Běnxíng Jīng says:
"The Supreme Lord of the Way,
entrusted himself to the womb of the Hóng clan,
concentrating his spirit in the mansion of the jade fetus."
The Dàodé Jīng Xùjué says:
"During the Zhōu dynasty, he again entrusted his spirit to Mother Lǐ,
and was born from her left armpit.
He was born with white hair,
and was called Lǎozǐ."
Xuánnǚ Swallows Qi, Holy Mother Dreams of Clouds
The Xuánmiào Nèipiān Jīng says:
"The three qi,
after 810,000 trillion years,
transformed and gave birth to the Mysterious and Wondrous Jade Maiden.
Again, after another 810,000 trillion years,
the three qi transformed,
into five colors, dark and yellow,
the Wondrous Jade Maiden then swallowed them through her mouth.
After 810,000 trillion [years],
he transformed and was born from the left armpit of the Mysterious and Wondrous Jade Maiden.
He was born with white hair,
therefore he was called Lǎozǐ."
"Holy Mother Dreams of Clouds" see the note under "Dreaming of the Sun."
Combining Qi to Form a Name, Pointing to a Tree for a Surname
The Guīshān Yuánlù Jīng says:
"The High Jade Emperor, the Supreme Imperial Lord, and the Nine Heavens Jade Perfected,
all take the virtue of emptiness as their style names,
and combine the two qi to form their names."
The Xuánmiào Nèipiān Jīng says:
"Lǎojūn was born entrusted to Mother Lǐ,
Mother Lǐ had no husband,
Lǎojūn pointed to a plum tree and said:
'This shall be my surname.'"
Holding Ten, Treading Five, Double Pillars, Three Gates
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"According to the Zhū Tāo Yù Zhá and the Jīn Xiāo Nèijīng,
both say Lǎozǐ's feet tread three and five,
his hands hold ten patterns,
his nose bones are double pillars,
his ears have three gates."
Green Intestines, Red Marrow, Blue Kidneys, Green Liver
The Lièjì Jīng says:
"If the Sānyuán Palace has jade tablets, green intestines, and red marrow."
It also says:
"In the Xuándū Dāntái, there are those with imperial golden characters,
then they have green livers with purple veins,
blue kidneys with patterned silk."
Green Sinews, Purple Brain, Holding the Sun, Wearing Stars
The Dàojūn Lièjì Jīng says:
"If there are mysterious registers and jade records in the Dipper,
then naturally there are green sinews,
if the Sānyuán Palace has jade tablets, green-purple brain, brocade tongue."
Seventy-Two Colors, Thirty-Two Lights
The Guīshān Yuánlù Jīng says:
"From the High Void Sovereign's head, bearing a circular light,
with seventy-two colors."
It also says:
"The Tàiwēi Celestial Emperor Lord,
his body produces thirty-two colored precious lights."
The Shànghuáng Yùdì Jūn Then Chanted the Hidden Book of Yùqīng
Upper radiance emits morning glow,
golden firmament lush with purple purity.
Three essences shine on jade fans,
the nine mysteries ascend to summon spirits.
Hands plucking flowers from green woods,
turning to cover the Tàiyuán Court.
Resting and feasting in the green chamber,
flying steps penetrate the Jade Capital.
Carrying the Zhūjǐng Jade,
long mists confuse the empty camp.
Mysterious return, self-governing and preserving,
why complain about having no life?
Eastern Jìn Zhàn Fāngshēng's Poem "Various People Together Discussing Lǎozǐ"
My life is fortunate to be concentrated and clear,
waves of wisdom fiercely contend and knot.
Flowing and drifting, losing the true lineage,
thus following the track of weak loss.
Though wishing to return to the old homeland,
buried and obscured, the way back is cut off.
Cleansing away what is not the mysterious wind,
how can the dusty heart rest?
Great indeed, the five thousand words resound,
specially set for the loss of the Way.
Reflecting it truly like a water mirror,
all dust and filth become clear and transparent.
Eastern Jìn Sūn Chuò's "In Praise of Lǎozǐ"
Lǐ Lǎo does nothing,
yet there is nothing he does not do.
The Way is one with Yáo and Confucius,
his traces are also numinous and extraordinary.
Blocking the passes, mirroring within,
darkening the spirit, cutting off the shores.
Eternally merging with the primordial qi,
in harmony with the two modes for long.
Later Northern Zhōu Yǔwén Yòu's "Preface to the Actual Blossoms of the Daoist Teaching"
The undifferentiated primordial embryo,
born before heaven and earth.
Mysterious and wondrous, natural and spontaneous,
existing beyond the opening of creation.
The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way,
thus explained through golden registers.
Superior virtue is not conscious of virtue,
entrusted to the Jade Capital to expound.
High, it cannot be measured,
deep, it cannot be fathomed,
closing it, it illuminates the three lights,
spreading it, it extends through the six directions.
Vast and great,
in grasping it, one exhausts its profound depths.
Indistinct and hazy,
how can one fully explore its images and things?
The precepts of the ten good deeds,
the codes of the four poles,
the sounds of golden slips and jade characters,
the meanings of jade boxes and silver inscriptions.
The inner teaching of ascending to the mysterious,
the superior purity of the numinous treasure.
The chapters of the five elders' red writings,
the records of the seven sages' purple texts.
Therefore, they shine among the seal scripts,
illuminate those diagrams and records,
mysterious scriptures and hidden texts,
can be spoken of.
As for encompassing heaven and earth,
nurturing and cultivating the cosmos,
nothing is too great,
nothing is too small.
Following it, one cannot see its back,
welcoming it, one cannot see its front.
Circulating through the six voids,
subtle and faint, the three qi.
The supreme great Way,
wanders above the empty void;
the Brahma-form Celestial Worthy,
appears in the Lónghàn kalpa.
On the day of Dīng-Mǎo,
paying respects to the green youth of Dōnghuá;
when the hour reaches Gēng-Yín,
reverently at Táishān in silent stillness.
Hàn history also records that the Way has thirty-seven schools,
ninety-three chapters,
this only briefly outlines the ancestral paths,
not delving into the profound mysteries.
How can one detail the differences of the golden elixir,
or comprehend the wonders of the stone casket?
Those who see it are still confused,
those who hear it hesitate.
Without the teachings of the Celestial Worthy,
lacking the words of the great sage,
how could one ingest the four-petal elixir,
rarely recognize the five-colored brilliance.
Petty and trivial,
why not each speak their part?
Immortals, Second
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Those who grow old yet do not die are called immortals (xiān).
Xiān
means 'to migrate' (qiān),
to migrate into the mountains.
Therefore, the character is formed with 'person' beside 'mountain'."
Wèi Bóyáng's *Zhōuyì Cāntóngqì* states:
"Only the sages and worthies of old,
embraced the Mysterious and held fast to the True.
Their bodies ingested the Nine Cauldrons,
their transformations merged and became one.
The 'Nine Cauldrons' refer to the essence of cinnabar.
Containing the essence and nurturing the spirit,
they penetrated the virtue of the Three Primes.
Heaven, Earth, and Man.
Their vital fluids and skin texture,
their sinews and bones became firm.
All evils were repelled and expelled,
the upright qi constantly remained.
Accumulating over a long time,
they transformed their form and became immortals."
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu —
these three spirit mountains,
where various immortals and the elixir of immortality are found.
Their palaces and towers are made of gold and silver.
Before reaching them,
from afar they appear like clouds;
but upon arrival,
the three mountains instead lie beneath the water.
When one wishes to reach them, the wind pulls the boat away,
and ultimately none can arrive."
Cuī Xuán's *Shān Làixiāng Jì* states:
"Lǎozǐ was the teacher of the thirteen sages;
cultivating one's nature to attain immortality,
each had their own method.
In all, there are thirty-six methods:
some use the Five Phases and Six Jiǎ arrays,
some ingest substances to strengthen bones and sinews.
Some [use] deep alleys and great rocky gates,
some through breathing see the dāntián.
Some through flowing principles return to the divine elixir,
some through inhalation and exhalation roam Tiānshān.
Some through Yuányáng grow nine parts,
some through tranquility and non-attention preserve the five sense organs.
Some through purity and stillness soar on high clouds,
some through the Three Luminaries establish the Dipper's return.
Some through Three and Five ultimately return again,
some through sound and net dwell by the seashore.
Some through the Three Yellows reside in the pò and hún souls,
some through Tàiyī's movement achieve balance.
Some use the Six Jiǎ to command the Six Dīng,
some through sacrificial offerings summon ghosts and spirits.
Some through blowing and warming sink into deep springs,
some through the Gate of Life secure the spiritual root.
Some by riding Xuánjī obtain the Jade Spring,
some through focused guarding ascend to heaven.
Some through Chaos preserve our years,
some through grasping know the Blocked Gate.
Some use Tàiyī to support the heroic aura,
some through Emptiness and Non-being sever the essence-spirit.
Some through the Huángtíng ride the boy servant,
some through supporting Heaven's virtue become divine immortals.
Some through the Jade Balance pillar ascend to heaven,
some through the Six Jiǎ wander the Mysterious Gate.
Some through guiding and stretching bend and extend,
some through solitude remain in the human world.
Some through medicinal stones ascend soaring clouds,
some through the Nine Paths attain the Red Spring.
Some in the three hairs of the Juéyīn region,
some through abandoning desires merely preserve the spirit."
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
"Those who seek immortality
must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, obedience, benevolence, and trustworthiness as their foundation.
If one does not cultivate virtue but only pursues arts and techniques,
one will ultimately not attain longevity.
For those who commit major evil deeds, the Director of Fate deducts a jì (twelve years),
for minor faults, a suàn (one hundred days).
According to the severity of the offense,
the amount deducted varies."
Guìfù Máojūn
The *Péishì Guǎngzhōu Jì* states:
"Guìfù
often ate cassia leaves.
People recognized his divinity and revered him.
One morning, he bid farewell to his village,
and drifted ethereally into the clouds."
Gě Hóng's *Shénxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Máojūn returned after completing his study of the Dao,
saying of himself, 'I have received a divine appointment,
on such-and-such a date I shall take up my post.'
When the time came, he ascended a feathered carriage and departed."
Chìsōng Huángshí
Liú Xiàng's *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Chìsōngzǐ
was the Rain Master during Shénnóng's time.
He ingested the Water Jade Powder,
and taught Shénnóng to ingest it.
He entered fire and burned himself.
He ascended to the Kūnlún Mountains,
often staying in the Queen Mother of the West's stone chamber,
rising and falling with the wind.
Yándì's youngest daughter pursued him,
and also attained immortality and went with him."
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Huángshí Jūn
cultivated Péngzǔ's arts.
He was several hundred years old,
yet still had a youthful appearance.
He also studied terrestrial immortality (dìxiān),
not seeking to ascend on clouds."
Jīnmǔ Yùfēi
The *Kōngdòng Língzhāng Jīng* states:
"The Purple Tenuity illuminates the Seven Terraces,
the Soaring Tree flourishes with jade-colored mists.
The multitude of sages gather in the gemstone palace,
the Golden Mother commands a clear song."
The *Língbǎo Chìshū Jīng* states:
"Yuánshǐ issued the command,
Tàizhēn prepared the brush,
the Jade Consort dusted the mat.
They cast gold to make the tablets,
and engraved the texts on jade chapters."
Shāntú Yuánkè
Liú Xiàng's *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Shāntú was a person from Lǒngxī.
A horse trampled him, breaking his leg.
A Daoist in the mountains taught him to ingest rehmannia, angelica, qiānghuó, and scrophularia. After ingesting them for a year,
his illness was cured and his body became light.
He pursued the Daoist to ask him,
who said of himself:
'I am an envoy of the Five Peaks.
If you can follow me,
you will not die.'
Shāntú followed him for over sixty years,
then returned to observe mourning for his mother.
He departed again,
and none knew where he went."
It also says:
"Yuánkè
was a person from Jìyáng.
He grew five-colored fragrant herbs,
for ten years,
and ingested their fruit.
A five-colored moth alighted on the tips of the fragrant herbs;
Yuánkè collected and nurtured it.
It produced mulberry leaves.
During the silkworm season,
a woman came at night,
claiming to be Yuánkè's wife.
She explained the silkworm's condition,
and Yuánkè went with her.
The silkworm cocoons were as large as basins.
After reeling the silk, they both departed,
and none knew where they went."
Mùgōng Táozhèng
Liú Xiàng's *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Chìsōngzǐ Yú
was a person from Huángdì's time.
He did not eat the five grains,
but ate the flowers of a hundred herbs.
By Yáo's time he was a carpenter,
able to rise and fall with the wind and rain."
It also says:
"Níng Fēngzǐ
was Huángdì's Director of Pottery (Táozhèng).
Someone visited him,
and tended the fire for him.
He could produce five-colored smoke,
and accumulated fire to burn himself,
then rose and fell with the smoke."
Lóngshī Yúlì
Liú Xiàng's *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Shīmén could command fire,
and ate peach and plum blossoms.
He was the Dragon Master for Xià's King Kǒngjiǎ.
Kǒngjiǎ killed him and buried him in the wilderness,
but one morning, wind and rain came to welcome him."
It also says:
"Chìxūzǐ
was a person from Fēng.
It is said he was the Overseer of Fish (Yúlì) during Duke Mù of Qín's time.
He ate pine nuts, asparagus root, and stone fat.
His lost teeth grew anew,
his fallen hair grew back.
Later he left and stayed at Wūshān for over seventy years,
and none knew where he ultimately went."
Eastern Jin Dynasty, Guō Pú’s “Poem on Wandering Immortals”
The Sun Valley spews forth divine radiance,
The Fusāng trees stand dense, a thousand fathoms high.
Vermilion clouds rise over the eastern mountains,
How dazzling and bright is the morning sun!
Whirling winds flow through the winding lattice,
From the secluded chamber, an extraordinary sound emerges.
Serenely, my heart holds eternal thoughts,
Alone, I gaze afar in distant musings.
Looking up, I long to spread cloud-like wings,
Stretching my neck, I raise a jade-white hand.
Whistling proudly, I cast off the world’s snares,
Indulging my passions, I wander alone.
Though the bright Way seems obscure,
Within it lies wondrous imagery.
To emulate the sages, one should strive in virtue,
To envy fish, one should first weave the net.
Another poem says:
Gathering herbs, I roam the famous mountains,
Hoping to rescue my declining years.
Breathing in the jade-nourishing essence,
Mysterious energy fills my breast.
Ascending as an immortal, I stroke the dragon team,
Swiftly driving, I ride upon the galloping thunder.
Fresh robes chase the lightning’s gleam,
Cloud-canopies follow the swirling winds.
With my hand I tug Xīhé’s reins,
With my foot I tread, and the Gate of Heaven opens.
The Eastern Sea seems but a hoof-print puddle,
Mount Kūnlún a mere anthill.
In the vast, boundless, dim expanse,
Looking down, one cannot but feel sorrow.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng’s “Poem on Wandering Immortals”
Water blossoms probe the spirit’s depths,
The sun’s essence fathoms divine mysteries.
Having heard the secrets of the highest immortals,
I keep the cinnabar, yet hesitate to take it.
Concealing my name, I wander as a historian,
Hiding my traces, I dwell in an official’s post.
Winding are the days at Phoenix Terrace,
Clear are the affairs of Cypress Hall.
Xiāo Shǐ lingers briefly,
Awaiting me to mount the dragon carriage.
Liáng Shěn Yuē’s “Poem in Response to Prince Jìnglíng’s ‘Wandering Immortals’”
At dawn I halt at the Gate of Heaven Palace,
By dusk I feast at the Pure Capital’s towers.
Soaring canopies embrace the shooting stars,
Lowered bridles avoid the traveling moon.
The Nine Peaks follow in confusion,
Rainbow banners suddenly rise and vanish.
The Blue Bird departs yet returns,
High halls where clouds never cease.
Kudzu flowers still hold lingering light,
I linger here, drying my hair.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn’s “Poem in Harmony with Prince Zhào’s ‘Wandering Immortals’”
Hiding in mountains, still gathering herbs,
Having the Way, one finds a master to follow.
Jīngzhào’s Chén Ānshì,
Chéngdū’s Lǐ Yìqī.
From the Jade Capital comes the crane lore,
From Tàiyī, the flying turtle is received.
White stones scent fresh taro,
Blue clay yields fine ripe mushrooms.
Mountain spirits meet a mirror’s reflection,
Woodcutters encounter a game of Go.
Stone patterns like scattered brocade,
Vine tendrils like tangled silk.
Where is Pénglái?
The Hàn empress wishes to worship from afar.
“Pacing the Void Lyrics”
Eastern Brightness, nine mushroom canopies,
Northern Torch, five cloud carriages.
Fluttering into inverted reflections,
Emerging and vanishing amid mist and clouds.
Spring springs flow down jade gutters,
Blue birds head toward Golden Splendor.
The Hàn emperor gazes at peach pits,
The Qí marquis asks about jujube blossoms.
Shàngyuán should send wine,
Coming and going to Cài Jīng’s home.
Another lyric
The northern pavilion overlooks the Mystic Water,
The southern palace sits atop crimson clouds.
Dragon mud seals jade tablets,
Celestial fire refines true texts.
Shàngyuán’s wind and rain scatter,
Mid-heaven’s songs and pipes divide.
An empty carriage ascends a thousand fathoms,
Ethereal fragrance is heard for ten thousand miles.
Sòng Dynasty Xiè Língyùn’s “Eulogy for Prince Zǐ Jìn”
A fine nature is not without beauty,
Yet hard to sustain for a hundred years.
The heir’s palace is not without honor,
But how can it compare to ascending cloud-heaven?
Prince Zǐ loved purity and stillness,
For the mortal realm is truly clamorous.
He hoped to see Fúqiū Gōng,
And with you soar and flutter together.
Also “Eulogy for an Old Man and Five Youths Beneath a Cliff”
A man gathering herbs on Héng Mountain,
Lost his way, his provisions exhausted.
Resting beneath a cliff, he sat down,
And saw them speaking face to face.
One old man, four or five youths,
Immortals or recluses, indistinguishable.
Their writings are not of worldly teaching,
These men must be sages and worthies.
Taoist Priests, Third
The “Tàixiāo Lángshū Scripture” says:
“One who practices the Great Way
Is called a Taoist priest.
What is a ‘priest’?
It is principle,
It is affairs.
Body and mind follow principle,
Only the Way is followed.
Following the Way makes one a priest,
Hence called a Taoist priest.”
The “Lóuguān Original Record” says:
“King Mù of Zhōu esteemed divine immortals,
So, through Master Yǐn, established Lóuguān,
Summoning reclusive and eremitic persons,
And appointing them as Taoist priests.”
It also says:
“When King Píng moved east to Luòyì,
He again appointed seven Taoist priests.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng, Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Appointed thirty-seven persons.
Emperor Huì of Jìn ordained forty-nine persons,
Granting three hundred households.
Later, Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Wèi established altars across the nine provinces,
And ordained thirty-five more persons.
Emperor Wén visited Yōng,
Paid respects to Master Chén Chì,
And appointed fifty Taoist priests.”
The “Sāndòng Taoist Code” says:
“There are five kinds of Taoist priests:
First, celestial truth Taoist priests,
Such as Gāoxuán Huángrén and his kind;
The “Qūhuò Treatise” says:
“Yùhuázi, Guǎngchéngzi, Zǐfǔ Xiānshēng, Zhōnghuáng Zhēnrén, Héshàng Zhàngrén are also such.”
Second, divine immortal Taoist priests,
Such as Dù Chōng, Yǐn Guǐ;
The “Qūhuò Treatise” says:
“Chìsōngzi, Guǐgǔzi, Liú Shūqīng, Yuè Zǐcháng, Ānqī Xiānshēng, Wáng Fāngpíng, Lǚ Nǚshēng are also such.”
Third, mountain-dwelling Taoist priests,
Such as Xǔ Yóu, Cháo Fù;
The “Qūhuò Treatise” says:
“Wáng Ní, Shàn Juǎn, Dōngyuán Gōng, Yònglǐ Xiānshēng are also such.”
Fourth, renunciant Taoist priests,
Such as Sòng Lún, Péng Chén;
The “Qūhuò Treatise” says:
“Dù Chōng, Péng Zōng, Wáng Tàn, Fēng Jūndá, Wáng Zǐnián, Chén Bǎochì, Lǐ Shùnxīng are also such.”
Fifth, householder Taoist priests,
Such as Huáng Qióng,
Jiǎn Kēng and their kind.”
Master Lù says:
“All Taoist priests
Take the Way and Virtue as father,
Take divine illumination as mother,
Take purity and stillness as teacher,
Take great harmony as friend.
Three hundred great precepts
To avert disasters yet unmanifest.
Two thousand dignified observances
To foster blessings of spontaneity.”
Plain Tallies Red Luminary
The “Supreme Cinnabar Slips and Ink Registers Scripture” says:
“If one receives the Dharma rank,
Up to the titles of Zhēnyī and Tàiyī plain tallies,
One may be appointed to the position of Xiānshēng.”
The “Numinous Treasure Five Refinements Scripture” says:
“In the past, during the Red Luminary era, Taoist priest Zhèng Rén’ān,
His merit and virtue not yet fulfilled,
Died at the slope of Chángsāng, north of Róng.
Xuánhé Xiānshēng, using the Five Refinements Life-Corpse Talisman here,
Caused him to rise lushly,
Becoming the Highest Palace’s Southern Emperor Lǎojūn.”
Enlightened Master, Without Friends
The Taiping Jing says:
"An enlightened master teaches ten disciples,
these ten teach a hundred,
the hundred teach a thousand,
the thousand teach ten thousand."
The Zhengao says:
"The oral instruction of Lǐ Shàojūn states:
'When a Daoist leaves the world,
he does not serve kings or lords,
this is to be without a ruler.
Solitary and independent,
this is to be without friends.'"
Jìqiū, Guǐgǔ
The Liexian Zhuan says:
"As for Jìqiū Gōng,
he was a Daoist at Mount Tài.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn made an eastern inspection tour,
he then donned a ceremonial cap,
wore yellow robes,
and holding a qin, came to welcome the Emperor, saying:
'Do not ascend,
you will certainly injure your finger.'
The Emperor ascended,
his left finger broke,
and he established a shrine for Jìqiū Gōng."
"Guǐgǔ" matter is seen in the narrative section.
Shànrěn, Jùqū
The Lingbao Wulian Jing says:
"In the past, in the land of Shànrěn, there was a Daoist,
surname Xiàn,
style Xìnrán,
master Wúcháng."
The Zhengao says:
"During the time of King Xiào of Qín,
the Daoist Zhōu Dàbīn
went to plant five kinds of fruit at the foot of Mount Jùqū."
Xuánhuáng, Qīngchì
The Dongzhen Yinyuan Yuchen Jinhua Yujing says:
"Vermilion characters, phoenix one,
bright light shines upon the pavilion.
The upper seat is xuánhuáng,
the middle sequence is heavenly truth."
Laozi's Lide Jing says:
"Daoists have upper, middle, and lower ranks,
those deeply versed in the Dao are many, named upper seat."
The Guishan Yuanlu Jing says:
"The August Sovereign, Master of Myriad Beginnings,
in the autumn three months, transforms his form into three-colored lights: qīng, chì, and purple."
Sānjǐng, Èrhuī
The Taishang Basu Zhenjing says:
"All who follow the Three Luminaries,
are called disciples of the Three Luminaries.
Having guided three persons, entrusted to master and friends, and having received transmission,
they may be called masters of the Three Luminaries method."
The Shangqing Zichen Jun Jing says:
"The Upper August Master, Zǐchén Jūn,
is the descendant of the Two Radiances,
coalescing the essence of the Jade Dawn."
Guìrén, Jǐhù
The Dongyuan Jing says:
"Daoist guìrén all come from heaven."
"Jǐhù" matter is seen in the narrative section.
Dōngyuán Gōng, Xīmén Huì
The Hanshu says:
"Dōngyuán Gōng, Qǐlǐ Jì, Xiàhuáng Gōng, Yònglǐ Xiānshēng,
are the Four Hoary Ones."
See narrative section.
The Hanshu says:
"The Daoist Xīmén Huì,
knew that Wáng Mǎng would soon end,
and the Liú family would again become Son of Heaven."
Wèi Zhīgǔ, "Poem on Not Finding Mr. Lǐ at Xuanyuan Guan"
Where is the feathered guest now?
Vainly I seek between the Yī and Luò rivers.
Suddenly I hear he has returned to Kǔ County,
Again I imagine him entering Hánguān Pass.
Not yet a thousand-year parting,
He should still return in seven days.
Immortals cannot be seen,
Lonely, I return to Péng Mountain.
Guan, Fourth
The Taishang Jueyi Jing says:
"Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn was at Xiéchéníng Guān."
The Zhutian Neiyin Jing says:
"The Supreme One observes the bestowal of sins and blessings,
opens the gates of life and death.
Jiǔlíng Guān governs the great cycles of heaven and earth,
Dònglíng Shàngguān governs and serves the Imperial Lord.
Zǐyáng Guān governs clouds and wind,
Běilíng Guān opens the eight writings within the void.
Tōngyáng Guān governs those who have attained deliverance,
Dàlíng Guān governs those who have attained deliverance and ascended as immortals, becoming Tàihé Zhenren."
Yǐn Guǐ's Louguan Xianshi Zhuan says:
"King Mù of Zhōu asked Dù Chōng,
'A spiritual dwelling for resting in mystery,
should be cultivated as a guān.'"
The Daoxue Zhuan says:
"At the southern cave of Máo Mountain,
there is Chóngyuán Guān.
The Daoist Zhāng Yǔnzhī,
in front of the guān, on separate land, built Jīnlíng Guān;
the female Daoist Wáng Dàolián,
entering Lóng Mountain, herself built a guān complex,
named Xuányào Guān;
Zhāng Yuánshǐ again built Xuánmíng Guān at the southern cave of Máo Mountain."
Yùxū, Jīndòng
The Waiguo Fangpin Jing says:
"In the north there is Yuánzhōu,
its land three thousand li square,
without color, form, or shadow,
only possessing the Yùxū Zǐguǎn."
The Dongxuan Jing says:
"Jīndòng Sùxū Guǎn,
is where Jīnmǔ Tàisù Sānyuán Jūn resides."
Zǐguǎn, Dānshì
The Yuhuang Xuansheng Ji says:
"Wandering dragons crisscross above the Zǐguǎn."
The Taidong Wujing Zhujue says:
"As for the Dānshì,
it is the hall of the vermilion fire heavenly chamber."
Cóngxiāo, Míngxiá
The Dongxuan Wuxing Jing says:
"Zhōnghuáng Lǎojūn said:
'Since you know the body's storehouse,
you should also know the home of heaven, earth, and parents.
The five cities and twelve towers,
their true secrets lie within the Cóngxiāo Guān.'"
The Sanyuan Jing says:
"Yuánshǐ Tiānwáng, at the Míngxiá Guǎn,
beneath the great dawn cloud gate,
taught and bestowed upon the three heavens' jade youth."
Sānyīn, Jiǔlíng
The Zhengao says:
"Ancient outstanding people changed their appearance at the Sānyīn Guǎn,
and had childlike faces at the nine-refined corpse."
"Jiǔlíng" matter is seen in the narrative section.
Xīhuá, Běilíng
The Qusu Jueci Jing says:
"The exalted Jade Emperor's verse says:
'Eyes immediately upon the Xīhuá Guǎn,
mind united with the Vast Cold Palace.'"
"Běilíng" matter is seen in the narrative section.
Chén Yīnkēng, "Poem on Visiting the Shixing Daoguan"
Purple terrace, high without limit,
Green stream, a thousand fathoms deep.
By the altar, I meet a medicine ladle,
Within the cave, I peruse immortal books.
In the courtyard, a crane dances, riding the scriptures,
In the pond, fish swim, controlled by reins.
Gradually dusk, the allium leaves close,
Approaching twilight, the hibiscus flowers sparse.
Vainly let the axe handle rot,
I myself cannot ascend the void.
Later Zhōu Emperor Wǔ, "Edict Establishing the Tongdao Guan"
Imperial Edict:
"The ultimate Dao is vast and profound,
perfectly formed, without boundaries.
Its substance encompasses emptiness and existence,
its principle reaches the utmost mystery and profundity.
But since the forked paths have divided,
the flowing sources have grown ever more distant.
Purity has departed, simplicity scattered,
form and breath thus hang suspended.
Hence, three Mohist schools and eight Confucianists,
vermilion and purple compete with each other.
Nine schools of thought and seven summaries,
different doctrines vie for supremacy."
The *Buddhabhūmi Śāstra* states:
"Buddha means
awakening.
Awakening to all modes of wisdom,
and further able to awaken sentient beings,
like waking from sleep or dream,
therefore named Buddha."
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha,
descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into the womb in the palace of King Śuddhodana in Kapilavastu in the Western Regions,
and was born from the right side of Queen Māyā.
At that time there were many auspicious signs,
and he could speak upon birth."
The *Běnxiàng Jīng* states:
"At age nineteen,
he left the city, renounced household life, and studied the path,
diligently practicing with vigor,
and after six years of meditation attained enlightenment.
He possessed the thirty-two marks
and eighty excellent characteristics."
The *Buddhabhūmi Śāstra* states:
"His clan was Śākya,
his title was Muni Buddha."
The *History of the Northern Wei, Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism* states:
"In general, the teachings say that
all living beings,
due to their actions, possess a consciousness-spirit that does not perish through the three periods of time.
All good and evil deeds,
must receive retribution.
Gradually accumulating superior karma,
refining away coarseness and baseness,
through countless forms,
cleansing and tempering the spirit,
one ultimately attains the unborn and realizes the Buddha Way.
The stages of mind-cultivation within this,
the levels are not uniform,
all proceed from shallow to deep.
Relying on the subtle to become manifest,
it lies in accumulating benevolence and compliance,
eliminating desires and cravings,
practicing emptiness and stillness to achieve pervasive illumination."
"At the beginning of cultivating the mind,
one relies on the Three Refugees: Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
There are also the Five Precepts:
abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants.
Their general meaning is the same as benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness."
The *History of the Suí Dynasty, Treatise on Classics and Books* states:
"Śākyamuni, during his lifetime, taught for forty-nine years,
even gods, dragons, humans, and ghosts came to hear the Dharma,
and many disciples attained the path and realized the fruits.
Later, between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara,
on the fifteenth day of the second month, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Translated, it means extinction and liberation,
also described as eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
His disciple Kāśyapa, together with others, compiled and recorded his teachings,
into twelve divisions.
Emperor Míng of the Later Hàn,
dreamed at night of a golden man flying in the palace courtyard,
and asked his court about it.
Fú Yì answered that it was the Buddha.
The emperor sent envoys to India,
who obtained Buddhist scriptures and an image of Śākyamuni.
From then on, the Buddha Dharma spread throughout China."
Detached from Characteristics / Severed Speech
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata arises and abides in various states,
namely the characteristics of liberation, detachment, and extinction,
ultimately returning to emptiness."
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:
"The Dharma has no name,
because speech is severed."
Chamber of Compassion / Gate of Wisdom
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"With compassion as the chamber,
gentleness and patient endurance."
The *Wéidù Jīng* states:
"With universal wisdom as the gate,
and the Dharma as the chamber."
Dragon's Pace / Simurgh's Voice
The *Buddhanāma Sūtra* states:
"Dragon Pace Buddha."
The *New Sūtra* states:
"Simurgh Voice Buddha."
Golden Vehicle / Jewel Treasury
The *Buddhanāma Sūtra* states:
"Golden Vehicle Buddha."
It also says:
"Jewel Foot Buddha,
Jewel Treasury Buddha."
Dew Mountain / Golden Sea
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Nectar Mountain,
the Buddha extols its merit."
The *Virtue Sūtra* states:
"Flame Light Realm Golden Sea Tathāgata."
Jewel Isle / Golden Realm
The *Buddhanāma Sūtra* states:
"Homage to Jewel Isle Buddha."
It also says:
"Golden Color Realm Buddha."
Sun Moon Lamp / Sandalwood Sea
The *Ten Directions Buddhanāma Sūtra* states:
"Thirty Trillion Sun Moon Lamp Bright Buddha."
The *Contemplation of the Buddha Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"Five Hundred Sandalwood Sea Buddha."
Jewel Armpit / Golden Arm
The *Contemplation of the Buddha Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"Between the marks under the Buddha's armpits hang five jewels,
like maṇi pearls,
reaching up to the Buddha's armpits."
The *Daśabhūmika Śāstra* states:
"The Buddha's arms are long, passing the knees,
like golden pillars."
Character Hair / Wheel Teeth
The *Daśabhūmika Śāstra* states:
"The Buddha's hair is the color of black bees, within which are the characters 'virtue' and 'peace'."
The *Saṅgharakṣa Sūtra* states:
"On the Tathāgata's teeth is the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel."
Seven Full / Eight Level
The *Daśabhūmika Śāstra* states:
"The Buddha's body has seven places full,
namely the two hands, two shoulders, two feet, and the neck."
The *Buddhabhūmi Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha's body is level and full in eight places, inside and out,
the three peaks, abdomen, and navel are even and of uniform excellent color."
Golden Essence Hair / Jewel Fire Eyebrows
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"Because the Buddha does not impose evil upon beings,
he attained the mark of hair the color of golden essence."
The *Mālā Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha's eyebrows resemble jewel fire."
Lapis Lazuli Throat / Coral Tongue
The *Samādhi Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha's throat is like a lapis lazuli tube."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra* states:
"The Buddha's tongue mark is the color of coral."
Pearl-Lustrous Hair / Golden Flower Face
The *Vimaladattā Sūtra* states:
The Venerable Ānanda praised in verse:
'Between the brows grows a white hair,
its beautiful luster like a true pearl.'" The *Xiūdào Jīng* states:
"The Buddha's face shines like a golden flower."
Prince of Qí, Wáng Róng's "Poem on Scolding the Four Great Gates"
Swift are the hundred years,
continuous these six senses.
Appearing and disappearing in dim confusion,
arising and dwelling in clinging habits.
Multitudinous are my desires,
busily you provide.
Not to virtue, it is said:
"Return,
only calamity gathers thus.
Greedy people corrupt their kind,
insatiable, they bring it on themselves.
Bright cycles offer no hope,
why weep in the dark void?"
Also, "Poem on the Evil Gates for Householders, Men and Women"
On the grindstone, it wears;
jade, though born hard.
Where one dwells must shift,
how can one be called worthy?
Ice melts in spring days,
orchids wither in autumn years.
Heaven teaches such kinds,
and habits shift with feeling.
Fate tallies with three windows,
life entwined with ten bonds.
Here then one settles to stay,
worry and fear just extend.
Also, "Poem on the Great Gate of Shame"
