The orchid chamber changes its rush-heart mind,
the banner cliff transforms its yī-grass.
Vermilion and azure must fade,
silk and plain cloth not always bright.
The crooked axle can be straightened with the line,
the strange wood is then carved with pattern.
One basketful may form a mountain,
a hundred lǐ, weary on the midway road.
Honoring the Hàn makes one a king's minister,
the great Chǔ speaks of preserving the source.
Strive! Virtue is not alone,
the ultimate words are not fabricated.
Also, the poem "Gate of Diligence":
Even the two mountains north of Yù can be moved,
And the isle in the river can also be made.
Utmost sincerity reaches beneath frost and dust,
The force of will can part metal and stone.
With a son joining palms, a fine name is established;
The king of the time cuts his hair, and fine repute hangs down.
In the past, diligence of heart had little decline or fall;
Why not strive diligently to escape sorrow and peril?
Victory banners and Dharma drums are raised and struck;
Wise masters and the assembly of the Way rush in throngs.
Living beings and selflessness are solemnly arrayed;
Ignorance and selfhood—who can perceive them?
Also, the poem "Gate of Dedication":
Vast are the nine lands, each with different forms;
Tumultuous are the four kinds of birth, not of one sentiment.
Driving chariots and urging horses, they sacrifice to worldly pursuits;
Trading writings and selling righteousness, they flaunt empty fame.
The three Mò schools dispute, unable to agree;
The seven Rú schools are depressed, never unified.
Auspicious and inauspicious taboos, along with numerology and arts,
Grasping and relinquishing, parting and joining—truly they run rampant.
Morning sun and evening moon—what after all is gained?
Plunging off cliffs and throwing themselves into fire—vainly they throw away life.
Alas, you who have lost the Way, turn back your carriage;
Follow that flowing water speeding toward the Eastern Sea.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Praise of the Thousand Buddhas":
The Way has that which accords and fits,
Principle has no twofold return.
Quiescent illumination is the same;
Form and appearance are both negated.
A thousand awakenings correspond and respond,
Successively striking the hidden mechanism.
The seven venerables are far distant;
With gratitude I recall their earlier departure.
What has passed is already extinguished,
The future has no image.
Not a single instant halts;
Three thoughts arise together.
Not permanent, not abiding,
Not now, not past.
Though the Bhadrakalpa is remote,
Cultivating it is like an echo.
Dwelling in forests, relying on trees,
Turning from rooms, leaving homes.
Buddhas before, Buddhas after,
Their traces are like turning wheels.
Some roam in Firmness,
Some rest in shade of the Nāgakeśara.
Able to reach this essential point,
They may be likened to the Ganges' sands.
Gathered, gathered, the host of sages,
All share this wondrous ultimate.
Earlier and later, varying in sequence,
Each follows his vow-power.
Secret traces broadly spread the Way;
When the number ends, then they ascend.
Vowing to witness the coming age,
Eternally transmitting the excellent awareness.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Inscription on an Image of Śākyamuni Buddha":
Accumulated wisdom becomes clarity,
Accumulated causes become karma.
How was the Able One moved?
About to roar the wondrous Dharma.
Halting light, he ascended to heaven,
Descended to be born from the right flank.
First he went out the four gates,
Finally transcended the nine kalpas.
Far-seeking for spiritual nature,
Vastly pursuing the dark chariot-track.
Though the Way has a gate,
Its trace leaves no mark.
Object and self both relinquished,
Mind and activity alike extinguished.
Once gone, the later mind—
Can the hundred negations ever be exhausted?
Thus relying on principle's awakening,
Awakening expressed through words.
Words do not spread themselves;
What brings them forth is the body.
When something comes, there must be response,
Like clay on the potter's wheel.
Responding to me with form,
Yet I am dim and blind.
Guarding compassion in the great night,
How to pull out this suffering?
Looking up, I seek the honored spirit;
The Dharma-words are uttered.
Without the exemplary form,
Dimly, whom would one see?
Bodhisattva, Part Six
The *Sūtra of Crossing the World* says:
"The bodhisattva wears a Dharma crown and headcloth,
and the seal and ribbon of the Way."
The *Sūtra on Contemplating the Two Bodhisattvas Medicine King and Medicine Superior* says:
"Medicine King and Medicine Superior
are twelve hundred yojanas in height.
In accordance with sentient beings,
they appear either eighteen zhang tall,
or eight chi tall,
and are purple-gold in color."
The *Sūtra of Ākāśagarbha* says:
"Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's body is immeasurable and boundless,
of a hundred thousand colors,
and fifty kinds of light.
Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva's body is twenty yojanas tall;
on his head is a wish-fulfilling pearl of purple-gold color,
boundless."
The *Sūtra of Upholding the Dharma Gate* says:
"Bodhisattva Superior to Enemies stands in empty space,
covering the world with flowing, glazed clouds.
He rains golden-colored flowers,
sinking-water incense,
red pearl canopies, dark-blue lapis lazuli canopies, and coral canopies."
The *Great Collection Sūtra* says:
"Bodhisattva Amoghavajra, by the power of samādhi,
makes the ground level and even,
like the palm of a hand.
There are eight avenues of tāla trees,
interwoven and spread out.

Among them are golden tāla trees with silver leaves and flowers, silver trees with lapis lazuli leaves and flowers, crystal trees with agate leaves and flowers, agate trees with conch-shell leaves and flowers, conch-shell trees with pearl leaves and flowers, and red pearl trees with golden leaves and flowers."
The *Sūtra of Vigor Transcendence* says:
"The bodhisattva was a fish king.
When fishermen caught a school of fish with a net,
he planted his head upside-down in the mud,
raised the rope with his tail and held it,
so that the many fish could live."
The *Collection of Six Pāramitā Sūtras* says:
"The bodhisattva was a parrot king
with a following of three thousand.
Two parrots had strength surpassing the rest;
they held a bamboo pole in their beaks
to serve as a carriage.
The king gathered upon it,
flying and alighting to play."
The *Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom* says:
"The bodhisattva was a kalaviṅka bird,
friends with an elephant and a monkey,
dwelling together under a pippala tree.
They asked each other:
'We do not know who should be the eldest.'
The elephant said:
'I remember seeing this tree when it was below my belly;
now it is this big.
I should be the eldest.'
The monkey said:
'I once squatted on the ground and reached the tree's top with my hand;
I should be the eldest.'
The bird said:
'I ate the fruit of this tree in the pippala grove;
the seed passed out with my droppings,
and the tree grew.
Thus reasoning,
I should be the greatest.'
The elephant then said:
'The one born earlier, the senior,
should be honored and provided for.'
Immediately the elephant carried the monkey on its back,
the bird perched on the monkey,
and they traveled around."
The *Sūtra of the Nine-Colored Deer* says:
"The bodhisattva was a deer
with fur of nine colors
and horns like white snow."
The *Sūtra of Saṅgharakṣa* says:
"The bodhisattva stood practicing;
a bird nested on his head.
Fearing the eggs would fall,
and before the birds could fly,
he never left."
Dream Pillow Flying Bowl
The *Uruvilvā Sūtra* says:
"Once there was a youth
who cultivated awakening in the world,
transformed into female form,
and was born into a elder's family.
His mother dreamed of a lapis lazuli pillow with a jeweled canopy;
the bodhisattva said:
'The child you carry is Bodhisattva Empty Brightness.'"
The *Sūtra of Universal Arising Samādhi* says:
"The bodhisattva's alms bowl
flew through the air and came naturally."
Pigeon King Lion
The *Great Collection of Pāramitā Sūtras* says:
"The bodhisattva was a pigeon king."
The *Uruvilvā Sūtra* says:
"There is Bodhisattva Lion-Eye King."
Sun City Star Kalpa
The *Sūtra of Creating Heaven and Earth* says:
"In the land of Jìhélóu, the people had no light of sun or moon;
Bodhisattva Precious Light went to create the sun city."
The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"It is the Star Constellation Kalpa."
Hand Flower Mind Earth
The *Xu Kong Zang Jing* states:
"From the hands of the Bodhisattva Bǎoshǒu, countless flowers, fragrances, and jeweled necklaces emerge."
The *Sì Bùdé Jīng* states:
"A bodhisattva's mind is equal to the earth."
Three Vows Four Pledges
The *Púsà Nèi Jiè Jīng* states:
"A bodhisattva should uphold the three vows."
The *Jiāyè Jīng* states:
"A bodhisattva has four kinds of definitive pledges."
Eight Directions Seven Grades
The *Bǎonǚ Jīng* states:
"The bodhisattva Shèlìfó is without affliction in the eight directions."
The *Yàn Lóu Tàn Jīng* states:
"There are seven grades of bodhisattvas."
Heavenly Sons Hold the Tree Emperor Shakra Listens to Sutras
The *Pǔ Yào Jīng* states:
"When the bodhisattva attained the Way,
he entered the water to bathe.
Eighty thousand heavenly sons,
each holding a tree branch,
the bodhisattva grasped a branch and emerged."
It also states:
"When the bodhisattva descended into his mother's womb,
the heavenly emperor, Shakra, and Brahmā
all came to listen to the sutras."
Eastern Jìn Dynasty, Shì Huìyuǎn's "In Praise of the Bodhisattva Tánwújié"
Diligent, the great master,
the Way profound, numbers exhausted.
Like that great chasm,
all streams are drawn in.
The shore needs no ferry,
the path does not turn its carriage.
Three currents open their source,
herein they merge and vanish.
Sòng Dynasty, Fù Liàng's "In Praise of the Bodhisattva Wénshūshīlì"
In the past, the Dragon Seed,
now, the Child of Truth.
Transforming through practice, roaming the world,
none know his ford.
Gathering with the assembly leader,
he investigates the subtle, exhausting the spirit.
He elucidates the profound and obscure,
guiding and reaching gods and men.
Also, "In Praise of the Bodhisattva Mílè"
In time, there is no equal queen,
in the Way, no second authority.
The dragon lies hidden in Tuṣita,
holding the reins, awaiting the time.
Dim is the long night,
cherishing and longing in thought.
Longing for the joyful bright dawn,
fixing thought on the spiritual time.
Monks, Part Seven
The *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* states:
"Four rivers enter the sea,
they lose their river names.
Four castes become śramaṇas,
all are called Shì clan.
The *Zūnshèng Jīng* calls them Bhikṣus,
the various sutras call them Bhikkhus."
The *Hàn Míngdì Nèi Zhuàn* states:
"Móténg and Zhú Fǎlán
were the first monks in the land of Hàn."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Sēng Hán
was the first monk in the land of Wú."
The *Cháng Āhán Jīng* states:
"A śramaṇa's robe and bowl follow his person,
like a flying bird."
The *Sìshí'èr Zhāng Jīng* states:
"A monk walking the path is like an ox carrying a deep mud,
exhausted, not daring to look left or right."
The *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* states:
"Śramaṇas all use grass mats for beds."
The *Sìfēn Lǜ* states:
"Śramaṇas teach laypeople using worldly methods."
The *Zhèngfǎ Niàn Jīng* states:
"A śramaṇa must not approach any bird-catchers,
frivolous debaters, or non-Buddhist practitioners."
The *Āhán Jīng* also states:
"Do not keep elephant troops, horse troops, chariot troops, or infantry."
Six Dharmas Five Gates
The *Chéngshí Lùn* states:
"As it is said, a bhikkhu who perfects the six dharmas
can blow apart the Snowy Mountains with the wind from his mouth."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Sēng Dū attained the essentials of the meditation dharma,
and thus refined the five gates."
Jūlín Píngshū
The *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* states:
"Nourishing the holy assembly,
not losing dignity and decorum,
this is the bhikkhu Āruò Jūlín."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Lúshān hermit Liú Yímín met Sēng Zhào."
The *Bōrě Wúzhì Lùn* states:
"Unexpectedly, in this very age,
there is again a Píngshū."
Lírì Mítiān
The *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* states:
"Sitting in meditation, entering samādhi,
the mind free from error and confusion,
this is the bhikkhu Lírì."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Xí Zàochǐ once visited Dào'ān and said:
'Throughout the four seas, Xí Zàochǐ.'
He replied:
'Under the vast heaven, Shì Dào'ān.'"
Péngqí Yīngjùn
The *Zēngyī Āhán Jīng* states:
"Eloquent in speech and debate without obstruction,
and also able to compose verses.
Reciting and praising the virtue of the Tathāgata,
this is called the bhikkhu Péngqíshě."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Zhī Dùn often kept a hawk.
People asked him why?
He replied:
'I admire its divine prowess.'"
Pine and Cypress Parasol Tree
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Yáo Xìng asked Minister Yáo Sōng,
'What is Sēng Ruì like?'
He replied:
'Truly the pine and cypress of Yè and Wèi.'" It also states:
"Huì Shào was about to immolate himself in the eastern stone chamber.
At his end, he said to his fellow students:
'Where I burn my body, a parasol tree shall grow.'
Three days later, it indeed grew there."
Three Grades Four Paths
The *Wúwéi Jīng* states:
"There are three kinds of śramaṇas:
those who sit in meditation are the highest grade,
those who recite sutras are the middle grade,
those who assist the assembly are the lowest grade."
The *Qǐng Sēng Fútián Jīng* states:
"There are four kinds of holy monks:
those of the fruit of the path, bodhisattva monks, Buddha's response monks, and holy response monks."
City of Flowers Bēidù's Bowl
The *Fǎzàng Zhuàn* states:
"The bhikkhu Mǎmíng,
in the City of Flowers,
attained the Way simultaneously with five hundred princes."
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"When Zhū Língqī returned from an envoy to Gāolì,
he encountered a storm and drifted to an island.
He saw a temple with a stone figure.
Língqī sincerely repented,
and it became a real person.
Thereupon, he gave a bowl to Bēidù.
Dù obtained the bowl,
went straight into the clouds,
then returned to receive it,
saying:
'I have not seen this bowl
for four thousand years.'"
Immortal Star Chanting for Dragon Rain
The *Gāosēng Zhuàn* states:
"Dàokāi came from the west,
traveling seven hundred lǐ a day."
The Grand Astrologer reported to Shí Hǔ:
"An immortal star has appeared,
a noble person will enter the land."
It also states:
"Shā Gōng,
during Fú Jiān's time, there was a drought.
He chanted, and a dragon descended into his bowl,
and heaven immediately sent heavy rain."
Suí Dynasty, Jiāng Zǒng's "Poem Inscribed on Master Kǎi's Mountain Hut at the Guǎngguǒ Temple in Jīngxīng"
Resting the boat, awaiting the fragrant peak,
sad at parting in the cold woods.
Bamboos near, their branches intertwined and tangled,
mountains long, the remote path deep.
Lightly flying, entering the shadow of meditation,
the setting sun casts sparse shade.
Not seeing the form that casts itself into the clouds,
only the heart that broke the cassia branch remains.
Poem "Climbing White Horse Mountain's Humíng Temple" by Kǒng Déshào of Suí
Famous peaks mark scenic wonders,
Perilous summits stretch far, winding and dense.
Forming images, establishing the encircling pole,
Great strength reveals the grand design.
Layered terraces rise like the Vulture Peak,
Lofty halls draw near the sun-crow.
Briefly sharing a journey to Lángyuàn,
Again akin to entering an immortal capital.
Three forms open jade-green inscriptions,
Ten thousand doors reveal golden fittings.
Focusing the mind, exhausting former rites,
Seeking the Way, grasping central emptiness.
Gazing afar to the ends of the earth's axis,
Long looking reaches the corners of heaven.
White clouds rise from beams and pillars,
Crimson clouds reflect on brackets and rafters.
Dewy flowers seem like rinsed brocade,
Spring moon resembles sunken pearls.
Today, guests of the Peach Blossom Spring,
Look at each other, losing the return path.
Edict of Emperor Wǔchéng of Northern Qí "Converting the Sāntái Palace into Dàxīng Shèng Temple"
Wishing to extend the importance of diligent cultivation,
Thinking of returning to the path of joyful giving.
Flesh and skin are not spared,
How much less a city-state as treasure.
Hoping to aid all under heaven,
Reaching the ultimate perfection,
The Sāntái Palace may be made the Dàxīng Shèng Temple.
This place reaches the height of architectural grandeur,
Exhausts the beauty of vermilion and white.
Strange marvels abound in its carvings,
Brilliance differs from painted colors.
May it cause spiritual minds to stir and resonate,
Divine beings to gather and converge.
True enlightenment is serene,
Where there is feeling, there is sure connection.
Transforming into a pure land,
Broadly gathering virtuous multitudes.
Minds like crystal,
The Dharma-wheel ever turning.
Spreading sweet dew throughout the great chiliocosm,
Shining the lamp of compassion across vast kalpas.
Edict on Building Temples by Emperor Míng of Later Zhōu
The decree states:
"Filial piety moves spirits,
Gazing at heaven, boundless.
None fail to spread gold to build Jetavana,
Flow silver to form treasure halls.
Thus we know the Deer Park is attainable,
The Crane Grove not far.
Daring to follow the odes and hymns,
Relying on solemnity.
Wishing to make merit equal heaven and earth,
Raising songs in no time.
The Grand Preceptor, Duke of Jìn, oversees and establishes,
Ascending hills and ridges,
Building temples and constructing."
Edict of Táng Zhēnguàn Era on Establishing Temples at Battle Sites
The Suí dynasty lost the Way,
The nine regions seethed.
We personally commanded the main army,
Bringing this clear punishment.
Vowing to shepherd, ascending heights,
Never a year of peace.
There were fierce dogs,
Caught in this boiling net.
Biting beards in righteous indignation,
Ending holding their tallies.
Each following their duty,
All have praiseworthy deeds.
Days gone, months passed,
The flowing river now distant.
Though even Xiàng Jǐ defied fate,
Mounds and trees mark his grave,
Bào Xìn gave his life,
Vermilion and white shown in the celestial chart,
Still we fear beneath the nine springs,
They may yet suffer cauldrons and boilers,
Within the eight difficulties,
Forever bound by ice and fire,
Deeply pained in heart,
Forgetting rest and sleep.
Therefore, to plant fields of blessing for them,
To aid their ethereal souls,
At all places where battles occurred since raising righteousness,
For righteous warriors and fierce foes who fell in battle,
Each shall have a temple built,
To invite excellent companions.
Hoping the Dharma-drum's vibrations,
Transform blazing fires into blue lotuses.
Where pure chants are heard,
Change the sea of suffering into sweet dew.
The responsible offices shall fully assess the locations,
And establish temple names,
Assign monastic followers,
And repair monastery buildings,
Prepare detailed regulations and report,
To fulfill Our compassionate and sorrowful intent.
Furthermore, order Yú Shìnán, Lǐ Bǎiyào, Chǔ Suìliáng, Yán Shīgǔ, Cén Wénběn, Xǔ Jìngzōng, Zhū Zǐshē, etc., to compose stele inscriptions,
To record these meritorious deeds.
Capital Cities, First
Celestial Treasury Imperial Domain
The Book of Han states:
"Liú Jìng advised the emperor to establish the capital in Guānzhōng.
The emperor was doubtful.
The ministers on his left and right were all men from east of the mountains,
and most urged him to establish the capital in Luòyáng,
saying:
'To the east lies Chénggāo,
to the west lie Xiáo and Miǎn.
With the Yellow River at its back and facing Luò,
its defenses are also sufficient to rely upon.'
Zhāng Liáng said:
'Although Luòyáng has these defenses,
its territory is small,
extending no more than several hundred lǐ.
The land is poor,
and it is exposed to enemies on all four sides.
This is not a state suited for military use.
As for Guānzhōng,
to the left are Xiáo and Hán,
to the right are Lǒng and Shǔ,
with fertile plains stretching a thousand lǐ.
To the south lies the abundance of Bā-Shǔ,
to the north lie the benefits of the Hú pastures.
It is defended by barriers on three sides,
using only the eastern side to control the feudal lords.
This is what is called a thousand-lǐ wall of metal,
a state of the Celestial Treasury.'"
Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"The flowers and fruits it produces
are the finest of the Nine Provinces;
the defensive barriers it possesses
make it the most secure region under heaven.
Therefore, its influence spreads across the six directions,
and it has thrice become the Imperial Domain."
Girded by Jīng Pierced by Wèi
Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"The Western Capital of Hàn
lies within Yōngzhōu.
Its name is Cháng'ān,
girded by the great rivers of the Hóng, Jīng, and Wèi."
The Charts of the Three Capital Regions states:
"Qín Shǐhuáng unified all under heaven
and made Xiányáng his capital.
The Wèi River pierced through the capital,
to mirror the Heavenly River;
a bridge spanned it from south to north,
to emulate the Herd-boy star."
Building Fēng Establishing Luò
The Book of Songs states:
"King Wén received the Mandate,
and achieved these military merits.
Having attacked Chóng,
he built his city at Fēng."
The Book of Han states:
"In ancient times, the Duke of Zhōu established the city of Luòyì,
considering it to be at the center of the earth.
The feudal lords formed a protective screen on all four sides,
therefore the capital was established there."
Three Bó Two Zhōu
Huángfǔ Mì's Records of Emperors and Kings states:
"The Yīn had three Bó.
In Liáng State,
one Bó was in Hénán.
Gǔshú was the Southern Bó,
which was the capital of Tāng.
Méng was the Northern Bó,
also called Jǐng Bó,
the place where Tāng held his covenant.
Yǎnshī was the Western Bó,
to which Pángēng moved."
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"During the time of King Nǎn, Eastern and Western Zhōu divided their territory,
and King Nǎn moved his capital to Western Zhōu."
Thousand Lǐ Four Xiàn
The Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall states:
"What is meant by 'capital'?
It is the name for a settlement of a thousand lǐ.
It models the diameter of the sun and moon, which is a thousand lǐ."
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"Four xiàn make a dū,
to manage the affairs of the land."
Dwelling at Tái Moving to Yōng
The Anecdotes of the Three Capital Regions states:
"Hòu Jì of Zhōu dwelt at Tái,
Gōng Liú moved to Bīn,
and Dǎnfǔ moved to the southern side of Qí Mountain."
The Charts of the Three Capital Regions states:
"Qín Dé Gōng moved from Qiān to Yōng."
Modeling the Sun Mirroring the Heavenly River
"Modeling the Sun" is explained in the note for "Thousand Lǐ".
"Mirroring the Heavenly River" is explained in the note for "Pierced by Wèi".
Second Move Five Moves
The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi states:
"One move creates a settlement,
a second move creates a capital,
a third move creates a state."
The Book of Documents states:
"Pángēng moved five times,
and was about to move to Bó Yīn."
Jiàn and Chán Hé and Luò
The Book of Documents states:
"We then divined east of the Jiàn River
and west of the Chán River,
and only at Luò was the omen favorable."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states:
"Xiáo and Hán possess the abode of emperors and kings,
Hé and Luò form the neighborhood of rulers."
Pouring from a High Eave Setting the Tripod
The Book of Han states:
"Qínzhōng
is a state of strategic advantage.
Its terrain is convenient,
so that to attack the feudal lords from there
is like pouring water from the high eave of a roof."
The Records of Emperors and Kings states:
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
established Luòyì and set the tripod there.
The present Dǐngzhōng Observatory north of the Luò River southwest of Luòyáng is this place."
Yī and Luò Xiáo and Hán
Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Luò" states:
"Following the plans and sites of successive dynasties,
relying on the natural defenses of the terrain.
Diverting the great flow from Kūnlún,
occupying the twin rivers of Yī and Luò."
The Book of Han states:
"Zhāng Liáng said:
'As for Guānzhōng, to the left are Xiáo and Hán,
to the right are Lǒng and Shǔ.'"
Unifying the Four Directions Encompassing the Six Directions
The Essential Meanings of the Five Classics states:
"When a true king receives the Mandate,
founding a state and establishing a capital,
he must place the capital in the central region.
This is to gather the harmony of heaven and earth,
to occupy the correct position of yīn and yáng,
to uniformly govern the four directions,
and to control the myriad states from the center."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states:
"As for the capital of Shǔ,
it is where water and land converge,
encompassing the six directions and serving as a crossroads."
Where Winds and Rains Meet Gathering Heaven and Earth
Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital" states:
"In ancient times, when the former kings established their capitals,
they surveyed all the remote corners,
leaving no land unexamined.
They measured the shadows with the gnomon,
finding neither shortening nor lengthening.
They gathered where the winds and rains met,
and only then established the royal city."
"Gathering Heaven and Earth" is already explained in the note for "Unifying the Four Directions".
Holding Chénggāo Occupying Hángǔ
Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on Luòyáng" states:
"Holding the steep defenses of Chénggāo,
supported by the lofty mountains of the Two Xiáo."
Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"To the left, it occupies the defenses of Hángǔ and the Two Xiáo."
Pinnacle of the Four Directions Center of the Eight Extremities
The Book of Songs states:
"The city of Shāng is majestic,
the pinnacle of the four directions."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"The city of Shāng
is the capital."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wèi" states:
“Western Capital Rhapsody” by Bān Gù of the Later Hàn
The Western Capital of Hàn
lies in Yōngzhōu,
and is called Cháng'ān.
To the left, it holds the barriers of Hángǔ and the two Xiáo passes;
marked by the mountains of Tàihuà and Zhōngnán.
To the right, it borders the perils of Bāoxié and Lǒngshǒu;
girded by the great rivers of Hóng Hé, Jīng, and Wèi.
Its blossoms and fruits
are the richest soil of the Nine Provinces;
its defensive strongholds
are the profound region of the world.
Therefore, its influence spreads across the six directions,
thrice becoming the imperial domain.
Zhōu rose like a dragon here,
Qín glared like a tiger here,
until the Great Hàn received the Mandate and made it its capital.
Looking up, it comprehended the essence of the Eastern Well constellation;
looking down, it harmonized with the numinous signs of the Hé Diagram.
Fèngchūn proposed the plan,
Liúhóu elaborated it to completion.
Heaven and humanity responded in unison,
to manifest the imperial brilliance.
Thus, with fond regard, He gazed westward,
and truly established the capital here.
“Luò Capital Rhapsody” by Fù Yì of the Later Hàn
At the convergence of Hàn's celestial fortune,
Shìzǔ received the Mandate and quelled the chaos.
Embodying the sage资质 of divine martiality,
he grasped the covenant and sanction of heaven and humanity.
He brandished lightning banners across the four wilds,
wiping away the remnants of calamity from the cosmos.
He received the imperial title at Gāoyì,
and built the walls and palaces of this capital.
Following the plans and omens of past dynasties,
it still relies on the natural strength of perilous passes.
Cloaked by the great flow from Kūnlún,
it rests upon the twin rivers of Yī and Luò.
Holding the rocky barriers of Chénggāo,
supported by the lofty mountains of the two Xiáo.
Dǐzhù churns the waves, linked behind;
Sāntú and Tàishì converge before.
Secured by the high peak of Sōnggāo,
soaring steeply to the heavens.
“Southern Capital Rhapsody” by Zhāng Héng of the Later Hàn
Oh, illustrious and joyful capital,
both beautiful and prosperous.
South of the secondary capital,
it lies on the sunny side of the Hàn River.
Carved from the fertile lands of Zhōu and Chǔ,
it straddles Jīng and Yù as its borders.
Its terrain is high, dry, open, and spacious,
so richly abundant it is hard to detail.
Now, as for its geographical features:
Wǔguān blocks its west,
Tóngbǎi marks its east.
The flowing Cānglàng forms its moat,
the broad Fāngchéng serves as its wall.
Tānggǔ gushes behind it,
Jìshuǐ washes its breast.
Pushing rapids and drawing swift currents,
it connects through three directions.
“Shǔ Capital Rhapsody” by Zuǒ Sī of Jìn
Now, the Shǔ Capital
had its foundations laid in ancient times,
and its state was founded in the middle antiquity.
It opens Língguān as its gate,
envelops Yùlěi as its dwelling.
Girded by the twin flows of the two Jiāng rivers,
it rests against the layered barriers of Éméi.
Where water and land converge,
it combines and intersects all within the six directions.
Also, “Wèi Capital Rhapsody”
The land of Wèi
corresponds to the constellations Bì and Mǎo,
its people descendants of Yú and Xià.
The mulberry and catalpa of former kings,
the lingering dust of successive sages.
Examining its position among the four recesses,
it is the center of the eight cords;
measuring its cold and heat,
frost and dew are evenly distributed here.
“Yáng Capital Rhapsody” by Yǔ Chǎn of Jìn
Leaning against Zhōngyán to build its dwellings,
facing the sunny pool to open the river.
Precipitous are the cliffs of Fāngshān,
towering stands the numinous peak of Báishí.
Converging the deep ravines of Qīngxī,
resting upon layered walls a hundred spans wide.
Spanning the flying bridge of the Vermilion Bird,
opening to the distant thoroughfare of nine directions.
Poem “On the Theme: How Splendid the Famous Capital” by Chén Kǒnghuàn
Jīngluò is truly a famous capital,
its beauty rivals Pénglái and Húliang.
Nine-colored carvings of tortoiseshell,
hundred blessings ascend the pepper-scented paths.
Gold trappings adorn the swift steeds,
lotus designs decorate the well-pulleys.
All say the ceremonial robes are magnificent,
fully surpassing the Commander of the Imperial Guards.
Poem “In Harmony: Returning to the Capital” by Xǔ Shànxīn of Suí
Double brilliance elucidates the imperial chart,
grand audience receives the coming deliverance.
Divining at Luò establishes the new city,
following Qín returns to the old capital.
Thunder-alerts guard the three celestial bodies,
stars arrayed, the seven elite troops drive forth.
Following the wind, phoenix plumes break,
glistening in the sun, fish-whiskers trail.
Laws and regulations exhaust rites and music,
carriages and retinue fully equipped in attire.
The imperial carriage returns to Fēnghào,
the imperial procession passes through Fényú.
Slowly, the years and seasons change,
gradually, the seasonal sights fade.
Remaining flowers shine on jade plum trees,
slender leaves trim圭-shaped parasol trees.
Morning and evening, ten thousand states gather,
like seas meeting, a hundred rivers pour in.
My humble life encounters the great creation,
suddenly, glory and decay are transformed.
Poem “On the Theme: Wú Capital” by Yú Shìnán
Dividing the wilds, it connects to Huái and Sì,
its stellar path corresponds to Dǒu and Niú.
Jade tablets display grand charts,
yellow banners float with auspicious air.
Divided three ways, it opened hegemon's enterprise,
for ten thousand *lǐ* it settled the Divine Land.
High terraces overlook the lush gardens,
flying pavilions span the clear streams.
River waves like a plain canopy,
sea mists resemble pearl towers.
Wú songs have their own joy,
still like traveling within a mirror.
Poem “On the Theme: Shǔ Capital” by Chǔ Liàng
Constellations shine upon Chējǐng,
their rays span Liáng and Mín.
Submerged rhinos face the river banks,
four-horse chariots enter the city gates.
Heroic plans leave many traces of hegemony,
through the ages, selected famous ministers.
Rows of riders, official caps and tassels abundant,
containing elegance, poetic rhapsodies renewed.
Having found the path of the immortal raft,
no need to seek out Yán Zūn.
Poem “On the Theme: Wèi Capital” by Lǐ Bǎiyào
The fiery fortune's essence fades,
the pure capital's precious mandate opens.
The imperial capital prospers in three directions,
ten thousand states come to the royal court.
Xuánwǔ Gate opens the distant steps,
golden phoenixes ascend the layered towers.
Suddenly, immortal boys present elixirs,
often, cups are tilted to avoid the summer heat.
Southern lodges summon extraordinary scholars,
western gardens attract the finest talents.
Yet we still regret for Liú Gōnggàn,
weary and ill by the clear Zhāng River's bend.
Poem “Gazing Back at Jīngluò from Returning Běimáng” by Zhèng Yì
Climbing the slope of Běimáng on foot,
lingering, I gaze for a while.
Yuǎnluò flourishes as the imperial seat,
its scale exhausts grandeur and strength.
Three rivers divide to set up peril,
two Xiáo provide great defenses.
Flying towers amid purple mists,
layered terraces above azure clouds.
Green locust trees flank the imperial way,
stretching long, broad, and vast.
Left and right, many mansions and residences,
unevenly housing generals and ministers.
At dawn, returning from audience with the emperor,
carriages and horses pursue and visit each other.
Clerks and followers each of different streams,
cultural objects display distinct forms.
Dust and clamor darken the rising sky,
flutes and pipes follow the wind, wafting.
But I, solitary and upright,
throughout my life, alone have sunk into obscurity.
In the secluded mountains, there are cassia groves,
why sit here in melancholy?
Emperor Gāozōng of Táng's "Edict on the Celestial Sovereign Establishing the Eastern Capital"
We have heard that treading upon Mount Huà and consolidating virtue,
the strategic advantage of one against a hundred is likened to pouring water from a high roof.
Divining at Luòyáng and returning to benevolence,
the seven-hundred-year reign is revered as the establishment of the tripods.
Thus, controlling fertile lands within the heavenly storehouse,
opening the imperial domain along the banks of the Wèi River,
embracing rich soil within the royal city,
and spreading green palaces upon the river isles.
The layout of markets and court,
adorn the imperial region's nine thoroughfares;
the crimson and purple plains,
stretch across the divine highlands for a thousand lǐ.
The splendor of the two capitals,
has existed since ancient times.
This capital, at the heart of the cosmos,
facilitates tribute and taxes from the four directions;
connecting wind and rain,
it equalizes the homage of all states.
The regulations of Qūfù are still diligently followed,
the land measured by the gnomon remains resplendent.
How can the homeland where the emperor resides
alone be called a capital among the four passes?
The city where the king's residence lies
should not be established as a state only within the three rivers.
It is appropriate to change the Luòyáng Palace into the Eastern Capital.
The beams above and the eaves below,
their toils of the past are difficult to surpass;
the broad halls and lofty towers,
our name now changes that of old.
Following this established precedent,
we manifest the imperial abode.
City Walls, Second
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"Inside is the inner wall,
outside is the outer wall."
The Shìmíng explains:
"Chéng (city wall),
means 'to contain,'
as it contains and receives the capital;
guō (outer wall),
means 'to expand,'
as it expands and lies outside the city wall."
The Fēngsútōng states:
"Guō is also called fú,
fú also means 'great.'"
According to the Huáinánzǐ,
Gǔn built the city wall.
The Wúyuèchūnqiū states:
"Gǔn built the inner wall to protect the ruler,
and constructed the outer wall to guard the people.
This is the beginning of city walls."
The Wǔjīng Yìyì states:
"The Son of Heaven's city wall is nine rèn high,
that of dukes and marquises is seven rèn,
that of earls is five rèn,
that of viscounts and barons is three rèn."
Also, the commentary to the Gōngyáng Zhuàn states:
"The Son of Heaven's city wall is a thousand zhì long,
seven zhì high;
that of dukes and marquises is a hundred zhì long,
five zhì high;
that of viscounts and barons is fifty zhì long,
three zhì high."
The Báihǔtōng states:
"The Son of Heaven's is called a lofty wall,
meaning it is high and grand;
that of the feudal lords is called a barrier wall,
meaning they dare not act on their own authority,
but defend for the Son of Heaven.
According to the Yuèlìng,
every year in the first month of autumn,
the city walls are repaired;
in the mid-autumn month,
the city walls are built."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Calculate the length in zhàng,
estimate the height and lowliness.
Measure the thickness,
and fathom the depth of the moats.
Consider the earth and the terrain,
discuss the distance and proximity.
Estimate the duration of the project,
calculate the labor and manpower.
Consider the materials to be used,
record the provisions to command the labor.
This is the principle of building city walls."
The Shìmíng also states:
"The parapet on the city wall is called pìnì,
meaning to watch vigilantly from the openings for any unusual activity."
It is also said:
"Pí,
means to assist in the height of the wall."
It is also said:
"Nǚqiáng (battlement),
means it is low and small,
compared to the wall,
like a woman to a man."
What the Shuōwén calls dié
is also the battlement.
Crescent Moon, Long Clouds
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"From Dùnyáng County to Miǎnkǒu,
north of the water is the Quèyuè (Crescent Moon) City,
one lǐ to the west is the Mǎqí City.
Its circumference is five lǐ,
and its height is one zhàng."
Bào Zhào's "Rhapsody on the Ruined City" states:
"Jagged like a broken bank,
towering like long clouds."
Empress, Lady
Lì Dàoyuán's commentary to the Shuǐjīng states:
"The waters of the Lǔyáng Pass
pass southwest of Mount Héngshān,
and flow west of the Huánghòu (Empress) City.
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Emperor Guāngwǔ dispatched Palace Attendant Fù Jùn, bearing credentials, to welcome Empress Guāngliè at Wèiyáng.
Jùn mobilized over three hundred soldiers
to guard the empress along the road back to the capital.
Since they rested at this location,
the city thus obtained its name."
The Hànshū states:
"The Xiōngnú sent the Right Commandant to intercept the Hàn army at Fūyángjūshān.
General Èrshī dispatched two thousand cavalry from the dependent states' Hú tribes to engage them.
The enemy troops were defeated and scattered,
and the Hàn army pursued them north in victory,
reaching Fàn Fūrén (Lady Fàn) City."
Xī'ān, Nánwǔ
Cuī Hóng's Běiliáng Lù states:
"Jǔqú Méngxùn and others
recommended Duàn Yè as Governor of Liángzhōu,
and Yè built Xī'ān City."
Dǒng Lǎn's Wúdì Jì states:
"On an island in the sea, King Héliǘ of Wú, bearing a grudge against Yuè, waged war and built a city,
named Nánwǔ City,
to defend against Yuè.
Later, the First Sovereign of Wú also
repaired and strengthened it to prepare against Wèi."
Overlooking the River, Treading on Mount Huà
The Jīngzhōu Tújì states:
"Northwest of Yúfù County is Chìjiǎ City,
connected to Báidì City in the southeast,
and facing the great river to the west."
Jiǎ Yì's "Discourse on the Faults of Qín" states:
"The First Emperor of Qín, raising the remaining might of six generations,
wielded a long whip to rule the world,
treading on Mount Huà as his wall,
and using the Yellow River as his moat."
Purple Earth, Golden
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù states:
"The Great Wall built by Qín
had earth that was all purple,
and the Hàn fortresses were the same,
hence it is called the Purple Frontier."
Shěn Yuē's Sòngshū states:
"The Dí chieftain Yáng Nándāng invaded Hànzhōng,
and the Administrator of Wèixīng, Xuē Jiàn, occupied Huángjīn (Golden) City."
Thousand Lǐ, Nine Layers
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shízhōu Jì states:
"On the Kūnlún Mountains, there is a city of accumulated gold called Tiānyōng City,
with a face spanning a thousand lǐ."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"On the Kūnlún Mountains, there is a layered city of nine tiers,
its height being eleven thousand one hundred and ten lǐ."
Xuāntù, Báilù
The Hànshū states:
"In the sixth year of the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
a certain commandery and kingdom relocated and built the Xuāntù City in Liáodōng."
Wáng Xīnzhī's Shǐxīng Jì states:
"Hányá has three cities:
Báishā City, Mǎ'ān City, and Báilù City.
South of the city is Báilù Ridge."
Thousand Zhàng, Nine Rèn
The Jīngzhōu Tújì states:
"Báidì City faces the great river to the west,
is two hundred zhàng high in the southeast,
and a thousand zhàng high in the northwest."
Xǔ Shèn's Wǔjīng Yìyì states:
"The Son of Heaven's city wall is nine rèn high."
Heavenly Precipice Center of the Earth
The "Jīngzhōu Tújì" says:
"South of Yílíng County, across the river,
there is the old city of Lù Kàng.
Its circumference is ten lǐ,
three hundred and forty paces.
It uses the mountains as its walls,
with sheer cliffs on all sides like a heavenly precipice."
The "Zhōushū" says:
The Duke of Zhōu said:
'I fear that the Zhōu house will not endure and become the pillar of all under heaven.'
So he built a great capital in the center of the land,
erecting a city wall six hundred and twenty zhàng square."
The "Zhōulǐ" says:
"On the day of the summer solstice at dawn,
if the gnomon's shadow measures one foot five inches,
it is called the center of the earth,
where heaven and earth converge.
Where the four directions meet and intersect,
there a royal state should be established."
Lowering Fish Roaming Deer
Yuán Shānsōng's "Yídū Jì" says:
"Sixty lǐ east of Lángshān County, there is a mountain
named Xiàyú Chéng (Lower Fish City).
It has sheer cliffs on all sides,
with only two paths leading up,
both perilously steep.
The mountain top has a circumference of about twenty lǐ,
with forests, ponds, and water.
People farmed on the mountain.
In the past, during the Yǒngjiā chaos,
the local people climbed here to escape the bandits.
They held it for a full year.
When their food ran out,
they caught fish from the pond and threw them down to the bandits
to show they were not destitute.
The bandits then retreated and dispersed,
hence it was named Xiàyú Chéng (Lower Fish City)."
Wáng Xīnzhī's "Shǐxīng Jì" says:
"In Hányá, there is a Báilù Chéng (White Deer City).
During the Xiánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man named Zhāng Fáng served as magistrate for ten years,
and his governance was very benevolent.
Herds of white deer roamed about.
He caught one and presented it,
so it was named after this."
Securing the State Outer Wall of a City
Zhào Yè's "Wú Yuè Chūnqiū" says:
"Yáo heeded the words of the Four Peaks
and employed Gǔn to regulate the waters.
Gǔn said:
'The Emperor faces heavenly disasters,
and his people are not at peace.'
So he built inner and outer city walls,
to secure the state."
Wáng Sù's memorial says:
"A city having an outer wall
is like bones having skin.
If the inner and outer are different,
then the protective barrier is incomplete.
If skin and bones are separated,
then the whole body is not intact."
Yán's Fields Liào's Burial
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Confucius said to Yán Huí:
'Your family is poor and your dwelling humble;
why not take office?'
Yán Huí replied:
'I do not wish to take office.
I have fifty mǔ of fields outside the outer wall,
enough to provide congee,
enough to provide silk and hemp.
Playing the qín is enough for my own joy;
I do not wish to take office.'"
The "Hòuhànshū" says:
"There was a man named Liào Fú in Rǔnán
who devoted his will to a humble gate.
He was buried north of the outer wall upon his death,
and was called 'Mr. North of the Outer Wall.'"
Wèi Wéndì's "Rhapsody on Ascending the City Wall"
In the first month of spring,
the year just begins.
The gentle breeze starts to blow freely,
so mild and pleasant.
I ride my carriage eastward,
ascending that city corner.
Leisurely gazing into the distance,
I find joy and delight.
The plain is broad and open,
fields in the middle cleared.
Fine wheat covers the ridges,
lining the roads and thoroughfares.
Flowing stems and scattered leaves,
stand leaning, supporting each other.
Water ripples as it flows long,
fish swim abundantly eastward.
The wind, fluttering, has arrived,
the sun, dimmed, shifts westward.
I gaze at the old lodge and speak of returning,
forever carefree and doing nothing."
Sòng Bàozhāo's "Rhapsody on the Ruined City"
Towering like a broken bank,
soaring like long clouds.
They used magnetite to ward off assaults,
daubed red clay to create flying patterns.
Observing how firmly the foundations and gates were secured,
to pass on for ten thousand sacrifices under one ruler.
It lasted through three dynasties,
over five hundred years,
yet finally split like a melon, divided like beans.
As for the white poplars, they fell early.
The frontier grasses withered beforehand,
sharp, biting frosty air.
Rustling, howling wind's might,
lonely tumbleweeds stir by themselves,
startled sand sits and flies.
The moats have already been leveled,
the lofty corners have already crumbled.
Looking straight for a thousand lǐ,
one sees only rising yellow dust.
As for those carved gates and embroidered curtains,
the foundations of singing towers and dancing pavilions.
Jade pools and jade trees,
hunting forests and fishing isle lodges,
the sounds of Wú, Cài, Qí, and Qín,
the amusements of fish, dragons, birds, and horses,
all have vanished like scent extinguished, ashes gone,
smoke settled, echoes ceased.
The lovely beauties of the eastern capital,
the fair ladies of the southern land,
orchid hearts and silk-like purity,
jade faces and crimson lips.
Their souls buried in dark earth,
their bones abandoned in barren dust.
Do they recall the joyful pleasures of sharing the imperial carriage,
the bitter toils of the detached palaces?
The song says:
"Border winds rise, ah! cold on the city walls,
well paths vanish, ah! mounds and graves ruined.
A thousand ages, ah! ten thousand generations,
all end together, ah! what more to say?"
Liáng Wú Jūn's "Rhapsody on Wú City"
Ancient trees and desolate mist,
for several hundred, a thousand years.
They say it was built by the King of Wú,
relocated by the King of Yuè.
To the east, remnant water where swords were cast,
to the west, an old mound where cranes danced.
Encircling the vast estate of Jùqū,
girdling the distant mountains of Gūsū.
I, your servant, am filled with stored resentment,
a thousand sorrows, a hundred million regrets.
Moreover, brambles and thorns are bleak and dense,
thickets of vines spread everywhere.
The pavilion's parasol tree, a hundred chǐ tall,
all grow branches from the ground.
The stairs' bamboos, ten thousand stalks,
some reach the tips without leaves.
No spring lotuses or summer hibiscus are seen,
only autumn cicadas and winter butterflies are heard.
Tree demons run at dawn,
mountain ghosts startle at night.
I did not know within the Nine Provinces and Four Seas,
there still existed such a Wú city."
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on Returning to the City from Dùn"
The Hànzhǔ waters first turn green,
the Jiāngnán grasses again turn yellow.
Sunshine warms the hearts of cattails,
breezes carry the fragrance of plum blossoms.
The expedition boat moors by the scalding moat,
the returning rider rests at the golden dry moat.
Dancing halls, robes always folded,
singing terraces, strings not yet strung.
Holding this, I go forth unhindered,
who thinks of guarding an empty bed?"
Liáng Wáng Yún's "Poem Harmonizing with the Marquis of Xīnyú on Patrolling the City"
The Chānghé Gate dims, already dusk,
the Gōuchén Palace deep, nearing twilight.
Roosting crows clamor on the city walls,
evening sparrows pass through the woods.
Garrison guards patrol and watch from time to time,
gathering authority, they stride in peace.
The elevated walkway leads to Wénchāng,
the palace guards connect to the armory.
The bronze crow greets the early wind,
the golden palm catches the morning dew.
The ornamental screen divides the dawn light,
the parapet gives rise to autumn mist.
Entrusted with the lofty duty of defending the city,
I idly think of the rhapsody of Líng Jūn.
As for me, just now ill and exempted,
I preserve tranquility in my hills and gardens.
Later Wei dynasty Wēn Zǐshēng's "Poem on Accompanying the Imperial Carriage to Jīnyōng City"
This city is truly magnificent and fair,
Its soaring ridgepoles naturally stand side by side.
Dense and vast, they embrace the traveling winds,
Lofty and towering, they conceal the flowing light.
The imperial moat connects to the clear Luò River,
The royal thoroughfare leads to the crimson screen.
Deep and tranquil, the water forms patterns,
Uneven and varied, the trees cast interwoven shadows.
The Chángmén Gate has long been closed,
How silent is the detached palace!
Fine grasses edge the jade steps,
High branches shade the well with its paulownia.
Faintly, the evening islets grow dark,
Soughing, the dusk wind turns cold.
The divine procession raises emerald banners,
Heaven oversees, maintaining solemn vigilance.
I, your servant, follow from the lower ranks,
Encountering favor, I truly am most fortunate.
Though the broad road is already peaceful,
With my feeble strength, how shall I gallop?
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem on Climbing an Ancient City on an Autumn Evening"
The sun sets, the journey ahead is long,
Melancholy, I approach the ancient city.
On crumbling walls, cold sparrows gather,
On desolate battlements, evening birds startle.
Over the dense and somber thickets,
A distant, solitary wisp of smoke rises.
The glow of sunset shines with lingering radiance,
The misty air clarifies the evening's clarity.
The autumn wind turns, shaking leaves loose,
This feeling—how can it be pacified?
Later Hàn dynasty Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Capital City"
Heaven's hazards are not to be climbed,
Earth's hazards are hills and mounds.
The emperor and kings establish hazards,
Receiving them from Heaven and Earth.
Palaces, Part Three
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Gōng (palace)
means qióng (vaulted).
It refers to the roof appearing above the walls,
Lofty and vaulted."
The *Zhōuyì* states:
"In high antiquity, people dwelt in caves and lived in the wilds.
Later, sages replaced these with palaces and houses.
With beams above and eaves below,
To shelter from wind and rain.
This was probably taken from the Dà Zhuàng hexagram;
This was its beginning."
Also, the *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"The Yellow Emperor created palaces and houses
To ward off cold and warmth."
The *Shìběn* states:
"Yǔ created palaces and houses."
The two accounts differ.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor had the Hé Palace.
See the *Guǎnzǐ*.
Yáo had the Èr Palace.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
"Yáo met Shùn
In the Èr Palace."
The Huī Palace.
See the *Xiàng'ér Jīng*.
Tāng had the Biāo Palace.
See the *Mòzǐ*;
It was the palace where Tāng received the Mandate.
The Zhōu had the Hāo Palace.
The *Dàdài Lǐ* states:
"The Zhōu's virtue and favor were harmonious and pervasive,
The mugwort grew lush and tall,
And was used as palace pillars,
Thus named the Hāo (Mugwort) Palace."
The Zhèng Palace, the Chūn Palace.
See the *Jìnián*;
These were the chambers where King Mù resided.
The Qín had the Qínián Palace, Xìn Palace, and Liángshān Palace.
See the *Shǐjì*;
All were resided in by the First Emperor.

The Hàn had the Chánglè Palace, Wèiyāng Palace, Pèi Palace, Línguāng Palace, Gānquán Palace, Lóngquán Palace, Shǒushān Palace, Jiāomén Palace, Míngguāng Palace, Wǔzuò Palace, Wànsuì Palace, Chíyáng Palace, Pútáo Palace, Zhú Palace, Shòu Palace, Jiànzhāng Palace, Huángshān Palace, Tàiyī Palace, Sīzǐ Palace.
See the *Hànshū*.
Palaces like Chánglè
Were either in the capital
Or in outer commanderies.
Some were where the king resided,
Others were sites for sacrificial worship.
Some were established for specific reasons.
Yèguāng Palace, Tánglí Palace, Fúlì Palace.
See the *Sānfǔ Huángtú*.
Guì Palace.
See the *Sānfǔ Gùshì*.
Dǐnghú Palace, Yíchūn Palace, Gǔkǒu Palace, Wàngxiān Palace, Tōngtiān Palace.
See the *Hàn Wǔ Gùshì*.
The Later Hàn had the Nán Palace, Běi Palace, Hútáo Palace.
See the *Dōngguān Hànjì*.
The Wèi had the Yè Palace.
See the *Wèilüè*.
The Wú had the Tàichū Palace, Zhāomíng Palace.
See the *Wúzhì*.
These various palaces
Were all made by casting metal and combining earth,
To signify nobility.
See the *Lǐjì*.
It is also like how in astronomy there is the Zǐ Palace,
Wénchāng and the Five Palaces.
See the *Shǐjì*, "Tiānguān Shū".
And how among immortals there are palaces of gold, jade, and lapis lazuli.
See the *Shízhōu Jì*.
However, since ancient times, 'palace' and 'house' were the same.
From the Hàn onward, the term was elevated to be used for the emperor's title,
And those below consequently avoided using it.
See the *Fēngsú Tōng*.
The *Lǐjì* states:
"For officers of the 'mìng' rank and above,
Father and son each have separate gōng (quarters)."
It also states:
"A scholar may have a gōng (dwelling) of one mǔ,
A room surrounded by walls on four sides."
This shows that shì and commoners both used the term gōng.
Zǐwēi Xuánwǔ
The *Yuèyè Túzhēng* states:
"Among the celestial officials is the Zǐwēi Palace,
The Northern Pole, Tiānyī, Tàiyī, Gōuchén, and the Rear Palace."
The *Shǐjì*, "Tiānguān Shū" states:
"The Northern Palace is Xuánwǔ; Xū, Wēi; Wēi is the Covering Star."
Chánglè Wèiyāng
The *Hàn Wǔ Gùshì* states:
"The Jiànzhāng and Chánglè Palaces
Were all connected by covered passageways for imperial carriages.
With suspended beams and flying galleries,
One did not need to use regular paths."
The *Hànshū* states:
"In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ, upon reaching Cháng'ān,
Xiāo Hé built the Wèiyāng Palace."
Liù Xīng Wǔ Huáng
The *Chūnqiū Wényào Gōu* states:
"The Dipper bears the basket of six stars,
Called the Wénchāng Palace,
Which are the six repositories."
The *Shǐjì*, "Tiānguān Shū" states:
"Xiánchí is the Wǔ Huáng."
Bùgāo Wàngyuǎn
The *Sānfǔ Huángtú* states:
"Jīngzhào had the Bùgāo Palace."
It also states:
"Cháng'ān had the Wàngyuǎn Palace."
Wàngxiān Jílíng
Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòngmíng Jì* states:
"In the third year of the Yuánfēng era, the Wàngxiān Palace was built."
The *Xīyuè Jì* states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn inspected the Five Sacred Peaks,
With abundant and complete sacrificial offerings.
Therefore, he established a palace at their base,
Called the Jílíng Palace."
Yàohuá Yǎngdé
The *Xījīng Zájì* states:
"Liáng Xiàowáng built the Yàohuá Palace."
Also, King Zhào Rúyì's palace
Was called the Yǎngdé Palace."
Xuán Bèi Zhāng Qí
Yán Zhù's *Xiàng'ér Jīng* states:
"Yáo hung a shell-decorated carriage at the Wū Palace."
The *Hànshū* states:
"Emperor Wǔ established the Shòu Palace,
And displayed feathered banners to honor the Divine Lord."
Yōufáng Zhāotái
The *Hétú* states:
"Yáoguāng pierced the moon,
Inspiring an old woman in a secluded chamber,
Who gave birth to the Black Emperor."
The *Sānfǔ Huángtú* states:
"Cháng'ān had the Zhāotái Palace."
Sàsuō Xiāoyáo
The *Hàn Gōnggé Míng* states:
"Cháng'ān had the Sàsuō Palace."
The *Gāolǘ Yànzhì* states:
"Mùróng Xī built the Xiāoyáo Palace."
Hāo Zhù Tánglí
Both are mentioned in the narrative section.
Sì Bǎo Wǔ Zuò
The *Xījīng Zájì* states:
"Emperor Wǔ had a Seven-Treasures bed, a mixed-treasures table, a toilet-treasures screen, and a row-of-treasures canopy,
Set up in the Guì Palace.
People of the time called it the Sì Bǎo (Four Treasures) Palace."
The *Hànshū* states:
"In the second year of the Hòuyuán era of Emperor Wǔ,
He visited the Wǔzuò Palace in Zhōuzhì."
Zhāng Yàn's commentary states:
"There were wǔzuò trees,
Hence the palace was named after them."
Escape Summer Yíchūn
The Yuè Jué Shū states:
"Now the prefectural residence has a rear hall building constructed by Chūnshēn Jūn,
which served as the Escape Summer Palace."
The Hàn Gōng Gé Míng states:
"Cháng'ān had the Yíchūn Palace."
Pray for Years, Prolong Life Increase City, Cultivate Pool
The Hàn Gōng Gé Míng states:
"Cháng'ān had the Qínián Palace,
and the Yánshòu Palace."
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states:
"The Qīlǐ Palace, the Zēngchéng Palace,
the Zēngchéng Palace was located within the walls of the Gānquán Palace.
Cháng'ān had the Xiūchí Palace."
Hàn Liú Xīn's "Gānquán Palace Rhapsody"
Surpassing the subterranean chambers of the shady realm,
Passing through the autumn city of Yánggǔ.
Circling the heavenly gate where phoenixes soar,
Treading upon Huángdì's bright courtyard.
Crowning the high mountains to make a dwelling,
Riding upon Kūnlún to make a palace.
Following the old sites of Xuānyuán,
Residing within the vastness of the North Star.
Turning away from Gònggōng's dark capital,
Facing Yándì's Zhùróng.
Along the stone gate's celestial ladder,
Cassia and trees intermingle to form rows.
Fragrant scents waft lingeringly.
Kingfishers and peacocks fly and soar,
Phoenixes alight and gather to roost.
Sweet wine springs forth in the central courtyard,
Stirring the clear streams that ripple and flow;
Yellow dragons swim and writhe,
Divine turtles sink into jade mud.
Detached palaces and viewing towers,
Connect and adjoin, linked together.
Clouds rise like waves surging,
Stars spread out filling the mountains.
High peaks and steep barriers,
Overlooking vast expanses.
Deep forests, cattails and reeds,
Gushing water and clear springs.
Lotus flowers and buds,
Water caltrops, water chestnuts, duckweed, and artemisia.
Camphor trees and assorted woods,
Nannu, pine, oak, and cork oak.
Privet and Indian laurel,
Peach, plum, jujube, and Chinese hackberry.
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì's "Poem on the Newly Completed Ānlè Palace"
Gazing afar amidst the clouds and mist,
Carved rafters reflect crimson red.
Pearl blinds admit the morning sun,
Golden splendor brushes the night wind.
If you wish to know where song and music reside,
Come and visit the Ānlè Palace.
Zhōu Míngdì's "Poem on Passing the Old Palace"
Jade candles harmonize the autumn air,
The golden carriage traverses the old palace.
Still as if crossing the Báishuǐ River,
Even more like entering Xīnfēng.
Autumn pools soak the late chrysanthemums,
Cold wells shed sparse paulownia leaves.
Raising a cup to toast the elders of old,
Now I hear the song of the great wind.
Chén Yīn Kēng's "Poem on the Newly Completed Cháng'ān Palace"
The new palace is truly magnificent,
Viewing its towers amidst the clouds.
Far and high, soaring kites look up,
In continuous flight, congratulatory sparrows come.
Layered railings lodge the cold mist,
Cinnabar wells see summer lotuses bloom.
Paved stones don new brocade,
Beam flowers paint early plum blossoms.
If you wish to know the prosperity of Ānlè,
Song and music mingle with the dust.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Eulogy on the Old Palace of Dāntú"
The sagely ancestor, divine and outstanding,
With Yáo's traces and Hàn's valor.
Mountains steep, ambitions grand,
Heaven displays martial prowess.
Fallen destiny now ascends,
Hegemonic strategy about to gallop.
The clear Wèi runs with beacon fires,
The turbid Hé offers warnings.
Relying on steep Jiànguān,
Depending on deep Guìlǐng.
Classic statutes abandoned in ruins,
Rites and music sunk in rivers.
Rescuing the collapsing structure,
Pulling the drowning from perilous waves.
Exhausting things to call them auspicious,
Reaching spirits to entrust harmony.
Mysterious essence shields the sun,
Cinnabar feathers nest in Ē.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription for the Yǒng'ān Palace"
The joyful yellow hall,
Follows the mean and harmony.
The old dwelling cherishes its roots,
New fruits delight in spring.
Observation platforms gather the Way,
Causing the stars to be overseen.
Abundant deeds, broad virtue,
To harmonize with heaven and man.
Ten thousand blessings come to aid,
Joyful entertainment, everlasting delight.
Palace Halls, Fourth
The Cāngjié Piān states:
"A diàn (殿),
is a large táng (堂 hall).
Before the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
its name is not recorded."
According to the Shǐjì, "Basic Annals of Qín Shǐ Huáng,"
it first says:
"Constructed the front hall,
above which ten thousand people could sit,
below which a flagpole fifty zhàng high could be erected."
The Hànshū records halls such as Gānquán, Hándé, Fènghuáng, Míngguāng, Gāomén, Qílín, Báihǔ, and Jīnhuá.
Gānquán and those following are all names of halls.
Hàn palaces also had halls such as Dàxià, Chángqiū, Zhūniǎo, Yùtáng, Fēiyún, Zhāoyáng, Yuānluán, Tóngmǎ, Xiāo Hé, Cáo Cān, and Hán Xìn.
The Hòu Hànshū records halls such as Déyáng, Wēnmíng,
located in Hándān.
Yáng'ān, and Huáguāng.
The Luòyáng Gōngdiàn Bù records
Wèi halls such as Tàijí, Jiǔlóng, Fúróng, Jiǔhuá, and Chéngguāng.
The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū records
the Jǐngfú Hall,
located in Xǔchāng.
the Tīng Hall
located in Yè.
and other halls.
The Jìn Gōng Gé Míng records
halls such as Língpǔ, Bǎizǐ, Yúquán, and Qīngmíng.

Hall names through the ages,
some continued, some changed,
only Wèi's Tàijí.
From Jìn onwards,
the main hall was always named this.
Zhì Yú's Juéyí Yào annotation states:

with left cè (墄 stepped side) and right píng (平 ramp side).
The interlocking bricks are arranged alternately,
the successive cè form the steps.
In the ceremony of the Nine Bestowals,
the 'nà bì' (receiving the staircase) to ascend,
means receiving this bì to enter the hall."

The "Rhapsody on the Clear Summer Hall" by Hé Shàngzhī of the Sòng dynasty
displays continuous rainbow beams,
arranges carved ornate rafters.
Latticed doors with kingfisher coins,
clear verandas with vermilion steps.
As for the deep chambers and winding rooms,
profound and secluded.
At first they seem easy to follow,
but in the end are difficult to fully grasp.
A slight movement stirs a breeze,
treading on peppered paths releases fragrance.
Every encounter becomes a feast,
a brief visit feels like many days.
Leaning against steep rocks behind,
facing deep valleys ahead.
From start to end, serene and somber,
stirring the clear, drawing the turbid.
Gushing springs wash the steps and thresholds,
distant winds arise between the pillars.
Though summer is intense, it is not scorching,
the air, just clear, nurtures all.
Sad cranes cry at dusk,
mournful gibbons wail at dawn.
Língzhī mushrooms cover the cliffs,
immortal flowers blanket the ponds.
The poem "Attending a Banquet at Yáoquán Hall" by Jiāng Zǒng of the Suí dynasty
The waterside pavilion leads to Yìyì Hall,
the stone path connects to the grand hall.
Wildflowers, unplucked, unrecognized,
traveler's bamboo, naturally unaligned.
Sparrows startle, as if about to take flight,
cicadas clamor, seeming to hold coolness.
How can one speak of the golden hall's side,
where I hasten to offer a jade pond's cup?
Also, the poem "Attending a Banquet at Línfāng Hall"
The water clock paces back and forth on its own,
the imperial hall presents feathered cups.
The bridge lies flat, as if the water has receded,
distant rocks appear, as mountains open up.
Before the woods, twilight's colors grow still,
near the flowers, fragrance draws near.
At Xīzī, grieving as dusk is caressed,
in this pavilion, I presumptuously roam as a companion.
The "Inscription for Déyáng Hall" by Lǐ Yóu of the Later Hàn dynasty
The imperial heavens hang their images,
to show the emperors and kings.
Beside the Zǐwēi constellation,
grand and vast, its radiance spreads.
The Great Hàn embodies heaven,
continuing with Déyáng.
Lofty, grand, tall, and splendid,
embracing and receiving all directions.
Within, it consolidates court tributes,
without, it displays distant frontiers.
The "Inscription for Tàijí Hall" by Xú Líng of the Chén dynasty
Now, the purple canopy and yellow banners,
the royal aura of Yángdū endures long;
like a tiger crouching, a dragon coiling,
the physical form of Jīnlíng is firm and steadfast.
The heavenly abode is bright and elevated,
the great resting place is dignified and solemn.
High, it corresponds to the Duānmén gate,
looking up, it models the Yíngshì constellation.
It returns to those with virtue,
like that Hé Tú diagram.
Transmitting our splendid brightness,
its meaning matches the Shāng dynasty's tripods.
As for Tàijí Hall,
it models the Dǐ and Kàng constellations.
The position of the king is revered,
with level ground on the left, steps on the right;
the hall of the Son of Heaven is noble,
yet in the past, it faced ashes and embers.
Many years have passed,
the world's way is prosperous and peaceful,
it is fitting to restore its splendor.
Supervising Army Officer Zōu Zǐdù reported,
saying that on this day, suddenly a great catalpa pillar,
came drifting and moored at the rear islet's shore.
Lofty and at ease,
like the immortal raft on the Hàn River;
swaying on the waves,
resembling the new court's dragon pagoda.
Solitary and towering from the spiritual mountain,
truly manifesting heaven's gift.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng received the sage mandate,
planning to repair and restore.
Eastern barbarians spied on the river,
western barbarians violated the imperial path.
Just as it was settled in the center,
armies were urgently raised.
Measuring it by the sun,
disasters and mishaps repeatedly occurred.
Thus it is known that where the Qín people halted,
the Hàn founder indeed made his palace;
the auspicious aura of Wú's capital,
was where Emperor Yuán made his dwelling.
A thousand brackets, resplendent and magnificent,
ten thousand architraves, towering and steep.
Planting green water caltrops stirs gentle breezes,
unfolding red lotuses tames the flowing fire.
Gazing afar from Gānquán,
one sees the main hall's lofty grandeur;
looking distantly from Hángǔ,
one admires the imperial residence's exquisite beauty.
Truly, it can align with the three lights and show the cosmos,
gather ten thousand states and receive homage from the feudal lords.
Thus, I was commanded, humble subject,
to compose this inscription, saying:
"The Yōngzhì altars face each other,
uneven, never-ending.
Looking back from Yǎnshī,
towering, the Déyáng Hall.
Reaching high to touch Tàiyī,
gazing straight upon Yáoguāng.
Lofty, the spiritual pillar,
resplendent, the flowing patterns.
How beautiful the palace chambers,
how fine this auspicious day.
The imperial screen hangs its tassels,
at court, the clear path is guarded.
Music complete with Sháo and Xià,
rituals blending refinement and substance.
The imperial procession is without clamor,
the royal banners are thus serene.
Solemn are the ministers and officers,
harmonious are the assistants and aides.
The Hàn seated with carved screens,
the Zhōu people with balustrades and lattices.
The city corners bear inscriptions,
the hall and offices all have mottos.
How much more the imperial resting place,
should proclaim the state's classics.
May the flowing models and instructions,
forever stand in the heavenly court."
Pavilions, Part Five
The *Shuōwén* states:
"A lóu (樓) is
a multi-storied building."
Furthermore, the *Shìmíng* states:
"It refers to the numerous, orderly arranged windows, doors, and various apertures for shooting arrows."
According to the *Hànshū*,
during the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
a fāngshì (方士) said that the Yellow Emperor built five cities and twelve towers,
to await divine beings.
Also, Gōngyù Dài from Jǐnán presented a diagram of the Yellow Emperor's Bright Hall,
in which there was a hall
with no walls on any of its four sides,
roofed with thatch and allowing water to flow through,
with a circular palace wall forming a covered walkway.
Above it was a tower,
entered from the southwest.
This was likely the beginning of towers.
Later, Wèi had the Lìqiáo, and Yuè had the Fēiyì.
Hàn had the Jǐnghán,
all being names of towers.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Marquis Wǔ of Wèi said to Xú Wúguǐ:
'I have long wished to see you, sir!
I desire to love the people and act righteously;
can I then cease warfare?'
Xú Wúguǐ replied:
'You cannot.
Loving the people is the beginning of harming them;
acting righteously and ceasing warfare
is the root of creating warfare.
If you proceed from this,
you will likely not succeed.
Generally, achieving beauty creates the vessel for ugliness.
Although you act with benevolence and righteousness,
it will nearly be hypocrisy.
Form inevitably creates form;
completion inevitably has its replacement;
change inevitably leads to external conflict.'
You also must certainly not array your splendid crane formations between the Lìqiáo towers."
A commentary notes:
"Lìqiáo
is the name of a watchtower."
The *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* says:
"Gōujiàn erected the Fēiyì Tower."
The *Hànshū* states:
"Emperor Wǔ erected the Jǐnghán Tower,
which was fifty zhàng high."
The Yǔlín Pavilion Tower,
is seen in the *Hànshū*.
Mǎ Bóqiān Tower, Zhēnnǚ Tower.
Seen in the *Hàn Gōng Gé Míng*,
located in Cháng'ān.
Wèi had the Báimén Tower.
Located in Xiàpī.
The *Wèi Zhì* says:
"When Lǚ Bù was defeated,
he then ascended the Báimén Tower.
The siege was pressing,
Lǚ Bù descended and surrendered,
and thus he was captured alive."
Wú had the Báiquè Tower.
Seen in the *Wú Jì*.
Jìn had the Sìxīng Tower, Yífèng Tower, Xiángfèng Tower.
Seen in the *Jìn Gōng Gé Míng*.
The *Yōumíng Lù* states:
"On the five-story tower of the Fèngyáng Gate in Yèchéng,
two golden phoenixes were placed.
When Shí Jìlóng's power was about to decline,
one flew into the Zhāng River."
The *Shùyì Jì* says:
"On the river is the Huánghè Tower."
Táo Jìzhí's *Jīngdū Jì* says:
"The Sòng Huálín Garden built the Jǐngyún Tower."
The *Qí Shū* states:
"A bell was placed on the Jǐngyáng Tower,
to have the palace ladies hear the bell and rise early to adorn themselves."
Moreover, towers are where [immortals] dwell.
The *Shǐjì* states:
"Immortals are fond of dwelling in towers,
setting out provisions to await divine beings."
The *Mòzǐ* states:
"On city walls, every thirty bù, a sitting watchtower is placed,
projecting four chǐ beyond the parapet.
Every hundred bù, a wooden tower,
the front of the tower being nine chǐ [wide];
every two hundred bù, a standing tower,
set back two zhàng five chǐ from the city wall."
Also, the *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The origins of disorder
all lie in excess and indulgence.
Erecting great frameworks,
raising palaces and halls,
with connecting towers and plank walkways.
Chicken roosts and Jǐnghán structures,
pillars, beams, and brackets,
mutually supporting each other.
Ornate wooden decorations—
this is indulgence in wood.
Construction through successive dynasties
has varied."
Jǐnghán, Lìqiáo
are both mentioned in the narrative.
Pánlóng, Yífèng
Bào Zhāo's "Jīng Luò Piān" says:

with four doors and eight elegant windows.
Carved rafters with golden lotus flowers,

The *Jìn Gōng Gé Míng* says:
"The Zǒngzhāng Observatory has one Yífèng Tower,
on the observatory for broad views,

Five xún, One hundred chǐ
Sūn Chǔ's "Dēng Lóu Fù" says:

Observing vapors, Awaiting spirits
Xiāo Fāngděng's *Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū* says:

Half the city, Projecting beyond the parapet
Huánzǐ's *Xīn Lùn* says:

were ridiculed by their subordinates.

and resided in half the city.
From this, it was known that his generals and ministers were not the equals of Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn."
"Projecting beyond the parapet" is seen in the *Mòzǐ*,
already detailed in the narrative.
Overlooking the rainbow, Soaring phoenix
Zhāng Héng's "Xījīng Fù" says:
"The Shénmíng Tower rises majestically alone,

Beams poised on floating pillars,
layered brackets linked to bear the load.
Overlooking the long mane of the curving rainbow,
observing where the Cloud Master relies."
The *Jìn Gōng Gé Míng* says:
"The Zǒngzhāng Observatory has a Xiángfèng Tower."
Reaching the clouds, Roosting clouds
The *Shìshuō* says:
"The Língyún Tower's buildings were extremely精巧,
first weighing all the timber materials to balance them,
so that lightness and heaviness were appropriate,
and only then constructing it.
Thus, there was not the slightest error,
and they bore each other's weight in succession.
Although the tower was lofty and steep,
it constantly swayed with the wind,
yet never collapsed.
Emperor Míng of Wèi ascended the tower,
fearing its precarious state,
and had it propped up with large timbers.
The tower then immediately collapsed.
Commentators said it was because the balance of lightness and heaviness was disrupted."
Shèng Hóngzhī's *Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
"Over a hundred bù west of the city,
there is a Qīxiá Tower.
Established by Línchuān Prince Kāng of the Sòng."
Five stories, One hundred zhàng
The *Yōumíng Lù* says:
"The five-story tower of the Fèngyáng Gate in Yèchéng."
Guōzǐ says:
"After Zhōngjūn Yīn was dismissed from office,
he resented Jiǎnwén, saying:
'The superior man ascends a hundred-zhàng-high tower,
only to have the ladder taken away.'"
Jìn Sūn Chǔ's "Rhapsody on Ascending the Tower"
There is the city wall of a hundred zhi,
Topped by a storied tower of five xun.
Following the enlightened king to ascend and roam,
I pass a leisurely day to delight my heart.
Cooing turtledoves preen their feathers among mulberry and elm,
Wandering ducks rinse their wings in the white waves.
Shepherd boys chant and whistle along the paths,
Boatmen beat their oars and raise songs.
Hundreds of officials gather like clouds,
Following to sit upon the splendid terrace.
Fine dishes fill the platters,
Choice wine overflows the cups.
They discuss the Three Mounds and Five Canons,
Expounding the judgments of sages and wise men.
Liáng Jiǎnwén's "Poem in Response to Ascending the Běigù Tower"
Chōnglíng, land of auspicious aura,
Jìshuǐ, palace of the phoenix.
How much more this Xú region,
Its rivers and peaks surpass Zhōulǐ.
The emperor's heart loves to tour and gaze,
His roaming ascent rivals that to Kōngtóng.
Let us drive the path-clearing heralds,
Spare the lad of Xiāngyě his toil.
Misty cliffs unveil the early sun,
Clear skies halt the evening rainbow.
Departing sails enter the clouds,
Distant stars emerge from the sea.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Ascending the Xuánchàng Tower"
Precipitous peaks join the northern hills,
A round tripod rises from the southern ridge.
Within stands a wind-riding pavilion,
Looking back upon the river's shade.
Cliff dangers ever shift and change,
Rapids calm, alternating shallow and deep.
Water flows originally from three branches,
The terrace high overlooks all four directions.
Above are guests parted from the crowd,
Each harboring a longing to return.
Setting sunlight glows on the long shore,
Brilliant rays illuminate the midstream.
Clouds birth darkness on ridge fragments,
Sun descends, half-shading the stream.
Truly lovely, yet not my land,
Why not withdraw the official's pin?
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Poem on Ascending the Yángyún Tower"
I ascend the Yáng Terrace,
No dreamer of Gāotáng's tryst.
Turning my head to gaze toward Cháng'ān,
A thousand lǐ, I cherish three worthy friends.
Reflecting, I am ashamed to have entered Chǔ,
Special favor equal to Shēn and Bó.
Western floods have receded,
Zhāoqiū frost and dew accumulate.
Lóngmén cannot be seen,
In vain I admire frost-defying cypress.
Sòng Bào Zhāo's "Inscription on the Língyān Tower"
Overlooking the river, railings arrayed,
Gazing at the view, extending the steps.
Accumulating pure wind along the path,
Embracing radiant hues in misty trails.
Looking down upon Huái and the sea,
Bending the gaze toward Jīng and Wú.
My king erected this structure,
With artistic thought, a divine abode.
May it last ten thousand springs,
Nurtured by numinous support.
Section Six: Terraces
The "Shìmíng" states:
"Tái (terrace),
means chí (to hold).
It says building earth solid and high,
Enables it to sustain itself."
According to the "Shānhǎi Jīng," there is the Xuānyuán Terrace.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"On the mountain of the Queen Mother of the West,
There is the Xuānyuán Terrace.
Archers dare not face westward,
Fearing the Xuānyuán Terrace."
Emperor Yáo's Terrace, Emperor Shùn's Terrace.
Located northeast of the Kūnlún Mountains.
Later, Xià had the Xuán Terrace and Jūn Terrace.
The "Guīcáng" says:
"Xiàhòu Qǐ divined and offered sacrifices to spirits at the ruins of Jìn,
And built the Xuán Terrace."
It also says:
"Offered sacrifices to spirits at Dàlíng and ascended the Jūn Terrace."
Yīn had the Lù Terrace.
The "Shàngshū" says:
"Distributed the wealth of the Lù Terrace."
The "Shǐjì" says:
"Zhòu increased taxes to fill the Lù Terrace."
And the Nándān Terrace.
The "Jìn Shù Xī Jí Zhǒng Shū Chāo" states:
"King Wǔ of Zhōu personally captured Shòu at the Nándān Terrace."
Zhōu had the Líng Terrace.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"King Wén built the Líng Terrace."
And the Chóngbì Terrace.
Seen in the "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn."
Qín had the Zhāng Terrace.
Seen in the "Shǐjì."
The Fènghuáng Terrace.
Seen in the "Lièxiān Zhuàn."
The Wànghǎi Terrace.
Seen in the "Qídì Jì."
And the Lángyá Terrace.
The "Shǐjì" states:
"The First Emperor built the Lángyá Terrace,

Hàn had the Bóliáng Terrace, Jiàn Terrace.
Built by Emperor Wǔ.
The Shénmíng Terrace, Bāfēng Terrace, Sīzǐ Terrace.
All seen in the "Hànshū."
Later Hàn had the Yún Terrace.
Seen in the "Dōngguān Hànjì."
Wèi had the Tóngquè Terrace, Jīn Terrace, Bīngjǐng Terrace, Língyún Terrace, Nánxún Terrace, Jiǔhuá Terrace.
Seen in the "Wèizhì."
Wú had the Diào Terrace.
Seen in the "Wúzhì."
Jìn had the Chóngtiān Terrace and Zhīshì Terrace.

This is a brief overview.
Also, the "Wǔjīng Yìyì" states:
"The Son of Heaven has three terraces.
The Líng Terrace to observe celestial phenomena,
The Shí Terrace to observe the four seasons and transformations,
The Yòu Terrace to observe birds, beasts, fish, and turtles.
Feudal lords are lower,
They may not observe celestial phenomena,
So they have no Líng Terrace.
They only have the Shí Terrace
And the Yòu Terrace."
Five Rèn, Nine Layers
The "Shuōyuàn" states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ built a terrace five rèn high."
The "Lǎozǐ" states:
"A terrace of nine layers
Begins with accumulated earth."
Observing Heaven, Gazing at the Moon
Liú Xiàng's "Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn" states:
"The Son of Heaven's is called the Líng Terrace,
Feudal lords' is called the Shí Terrace,
Used to observe changes in celestial phenomena."
Guō Zǐhéng's "Dòngmíng Jì" states:
"Emperor Wǔ ascended the southern end of the Wàngyuè Terrace,
Three ducks flew in a flock,
And soon descended to the terrace.
The emperor was pleased with them.
By evening,
The ducks roosted at the terrace's end."
Observing the Sun, Measuring Stars
Zhào Yè's "Wúyuè Chūnqiū" states:
"Fàn Lí built a roaming terrace on Guàishān,
Using it as a Líng Terrace,
To gaze upward at celestial phenomena,
Observing changes and anomalies of the sun and moon."
The "Báihǔ Tōng" states:
"The Son of Heaven establishes the Líng Terrace
To examine the relationship between heaven and man,
Observe the convergence of yīn and yáng,
And measure the verification of stellar movements."
Ten Tiers, Nine Layers
The "Chǔcí" states:
"A jade terrace of ten tiers,
Who could reach its limit?"
The "Shīzǐ" states:
"A jade terrace of nine layers,
Yet Yáo lived in a thatched hut."
Bǎiqǐn and Páojū
The Hánzǐ states:
"Duke Jǐng and Yànzǐ traveled to Shàohǎi,
ascending the terrace of Bǎiqǐn.
Gazing upon his state,
he said:
'How magnificent and grand, is it not?'"
The Guóyǔ states:
"King Líng of Chǔ built the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and ascended it with Wǔ Jǔ.
He said:
'Is the terrace not beautiful?'
Wǔ Jǔ replied:
'Our former lord King Zhuāng built the Páojū Terrace.
Its height did not exceed what was needed to observe the state's vital energy,
its size was no greater than required to accommodate ritual vessels for banquets.
The people were not deprived of their seasonal labors,
and officials did not alter the court's regular affairs.
Now you have built this terrace,
exhausting the people's strength and resources,
taking several years to complete it,
yet no feudal lords have come.
If you consider this beautiful,
Chǔ is surely in peril!'"
Jiǎ Kuí's annotation states:
"Páojū
is the name of a high terrace."
Yáo's Inspection and Xià's Feast
Wáng Sháozhī's Shǐxīng Jì states:
"In Hánkuāng County there is Yáo Mountain.
Yáo inspected the regions and reached this place,
establishing a traveling terrace there."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Xià Qǐ held a feast at the Jūntái."
Recording Rites and Storing Books
The Hànshū·Yìwénzhì states:

Admiring Xǔ and Cherishing Qīng

Xǔ Yóu, ashamed to hear of Yáo's offer to abdicate to him, climbed this mountain.
