Cáo Zhí of Wèi, Prince Sī of Chén's "Rhapsody on Ascending the Terrace"
Following our enlightened lord in leisurely travel,
I briefly ascend the terrace to delight my spirit.
I see the celestial storehouse widely opened,
and behold the works of sagely virtue.
High halls are built, towering and steep;
paired towers float in the great clarity.
I erect a splendid observatory that reaches the sky,
connecting flying galleries to the western city.
Facing the long flow of the Zhāng River,
I gaze upon the lush growth of myriad fruits.
I look up to the gentle harmony of the spring breeze,
and listen to the mournful cries of a hundred birds.
Heaven's work is already established with awe,
and our family's wish is doubly fulfilled.
Spreading benevolent transformation throughout the cosmos,
we offer utmost reverence in the capital above.
Though Huán and Wén achieved greatness,
how could they compare to our sagely brilliance?
Splendid and beautiful indeed,
your gracious favor extends afar.
Assisting the royal house,
you pacify those four quarters.
Equal to heaven and earth in measure,
matching the sun and moon in radiant light."
Lián Jiānwéndì's "Poem on the Zither Terrace"
Through overgrown steps I tread the ancient path,
again imagining the zither's music played in wanderings.
Sound and visage ceased ten thousand springs ago,
yet a lofty name remains through a thousand years.
Slender branches grow from ancient trees;
old rocks withstand the new stream's flow.
From ancient times, sighs pass back and forth;
the flowing river never ceases its course."
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Poem on Passing the Ruined Terrace of Jiànchāng"
In Lǔ's land I view the abandoned hall;
in Hán's city I recall the terrace of old.
Zhòngxuān's plains and marshes are full;
Zǐjiàn's mournful wind arrives.
Summer lotuses still grow inverted;
autumn windows remain leftward open.
Painted clouds still drip with rain;
inscribed stones already sprout moss.
When you joyfully gaze to the four directions,
know that I recall the Seven Sorrows."
Chén Zǔsūn's "Poem on Ascending the Palace Named Ascending Terrace"
Alone, I harbor thoughts of longing,
Casually opening the Phoenix Terrace.
Lotus spreads fragrance upward,
The bright moon's light just arrives.
Departing cranes scatter with the clouds,
Flying blossoms return like snow.
Longing for friends in the bamboo grove,
Before the window, night after night, I listen.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Cloud Terrace"
The former dwelling of the Zhōu clan,
Only the Hàn inherited and followed.
Lofty terrace, towering and steep,
Above, it obstructs the azure clouds.
Displayed for a hundred million years,
To lead by old regulations.
People cultivate their conduct,
And the state prospers.
Hall, Seventh
The *Shìmíng* says:
"Hall,
means grand and bright in appearance."
According to the *Lǐjì*:
"The Son of Heaven's hall is nine chǐ high,
feudal lords' seven chǐ,
high officials' five chǐ,
scholars' three chǐ."
The *Shàngshū Dàzhuàn* states:
"The Son of Heaven's hall is nine zhì high,
dukes and marquises seven zhì,
viscounts and barons five zhì."
One zhì is three zhàng long.
Halls of successive dynasties,
the *Lùnhéng* says:
"Mòzǐ claimed Yáo and Shùn's halls were three chǐ high."
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* says:
"King Wǔ entered Yīn and ascended the hall,
saw beautiful jade,
and said:
'Whose jade is this?'
Someone said it was the feudal lords' jade,
so the king took it and returned it to them.
All under heaven heard of this and said:
'The king is incorruptible with wealth.'"
The *Hànwǔ Gùshì*:
"There was a Jade Hall,
twelve zhàng above the ground."
The *Hànshū* says:
"Emperor Chéng was born in the Jiǎ Guàn's painted hall."
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* says:
"When Emperor Guāngwǔ was born, there was red light,
and the hall was as bright as day."
The *Xù Hànshū* says:
"Emperor Líng built the Ten-Thousand-Gold Hall in the Western Garden,
and the Wèi ministers' memorials mention the Jiǎn Wú Hall."
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* mentions the Wèi Máo Hall,
seen in Lì Shàncháng's *Shuǐjīng Zhù*.
The *Jìn Gōngquē Míng* lists the Yáomǔ Hall, Yǒngguāng Hall, and Chángshòu Hall.
Seen in the *Jìn Gōnggé Míng*.
In commanderies and kingdoms,
north of Lǔ City was Confucius's Learning Hall.
Seen in the *Guó Dūchéng Jì*.
Shǔ had Wén Wēng's Lecture Hall.
Seen in the *Huáyáng Guózhì*.
Běihǎi had Zhèng Xuán's Confucian Scholars' Lecture Hall.
Seen in Zhèng Xuán's *Biézhuàn*.
Yǒngkāng County had the Jìnyún Hall.
Where the Yellow Emperor refined elixirs.
Fèiběi had the Jīnǔ Hall.
Built by Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
all the above seen in the *Sòng Yǒngchū Shānchuān Gǔjīn Jì*.
Mount Kūnlún had the Guāngbì Hall.
Where the Queen Mother of the West resided,
seen in the *Shízhōu Jì*.
This is a brief overview.
Also, Zhì Yú's *Juéyí Yào* commentary says:
"In the palace hall,
only the Son of Heaven occupies a bed,
all others sit on mats.
In front are set mats and small tables.
The Son of Heaven's palace hall
is nine mats wide east to west,
seven mats long north to south,
hence it is said: measure halls by mats,
measure rooms by small tables.
According to ritual,
in the hall, steps follow closely,
below the hall, steps are spread out."
Wǔ
means footprint,
seen in the *Lǐjì*.
One says:
"The hall is as distant as a hundred lǐ,
below the hall as distant as a thousand lǐ,
the gate courtyard as distant as ten thousand lǐ."
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
"Now, a walker in one day
conveys news from a hundred lǐ.
If there is an affair in the hall,
and the ruler does not hear of it for a month,
a walker in ten days
conveys news from a thousand lǐ:
if there is an affair in the hall,
and the ruler does not hear of it for ten months,
a walker in a hundred days
conveys news from ten thousand lǐ;
if there is an affair at the gate courtyard,
and the ruler does not hear of it for a year,
this is called being distant by ten thousand lǐ."

Fertile and Lofty Land

Xiāo’s Dwelling and Yàn’s Divination
The *Hànshū* states:
“When Xiāo Hé served as Chancellor of State,
he purchased fields and residences,
always choosing remote alleys and secluded places.
He did not build walls or elaborate houses for his home.
He said:
‘If my descendants are virtuous,
they will emulate my frugality;
if they are not virtuous,
these will not be seized by powerful families.’”
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
“Duke Jǐng of Qí wanted to change Yànzǐ’s residence.
While Yànzǐ was away in Jìn,
the duke rebuilt his house,
and it was completed by the time he returned.
After paying his respects,
he had it demolished and restored to its original neighborhood dwellings,
allowing the former residents to return.
He said:
‘The proverb says:
“It is not the house one should divine about,
but the neighbors.
You, my neighbors, have already divined about this!
To go against divination is inauspicious.
A gentleman does not act contrary to propriety,
nor does a petty person act against what is auspicious.”’
In the end, he restored it to its original state.”

Kǒng’s Zither and Hé’s Gold
“Kǒng’s zither” is mentioned in the narrative.
Gān Bǎo’s *Sōushénjì* states:
“The Zhāng family of Wèijùn was extremely wealthy,
but suddenly grew old and their wealth dissipated.
They sold their house to Chéng Yìng,
but Yìng’s entire family fell ill.
They then sold it to Hé Wén.
Wén first took a large knife alone
and entered the northern hall at dusk, hiding on a beam.
During the first watch,
a figure over ten feet tall,
wearing a tall hat and a red headscarf,
called out:
‘Slender Waist!’
Slender Waist responded:
‘Why is there a human scent?’
He replied there was none,
and the figure left.
Wén then called out to Slender Waist,
asking:
‘Who was that in red clothes and hat earlier?’
He replied:
‘It is Gold,
hidden under the western wall of the house.’
He asked Wén:
‘Who are you?’
Wén replied:
‘I am the Pestle,
now under the stove.’
Wén dug and found three hundred catties of gold,
burned the pestle,
and from then on became immensely wealthy.”

Also, “In the Hàn dynasty, when Xuē Bāo and his brothers decided to divide their property,

Táng Tàizōng’s “Poem on Passing by My Old Residence”
At Xīnfēng, the emerald carriage halted,
At Qiáoyì, the sounding reed pipes ceased.
The garden overgrown, a path now broken,
The terrace ancient, half its steps askew.
The former pond, its old waters dried,
The trees of yesteryear now bloom anew.
Once I left this place behind,
The four seas became my home.
Suí Jiāng Zǒng’s “Poem on Returning Home at Year’s End”
Melancholy thoughts of springs and stones arise,
I drive my carriage forth from towers high.
Bamboo shoots in spring, a playful sight,
Plum blossoms after snow, a startling delight.
The verdant hills are fine to face,
Yellow scrolls I open from time to time.
Long ropes cannot bind the sun in place,
A cup of turbid wine I pour and climb.
Also, “Poem on Returning South to Seek My Thatched Market Residence”
In youthful years, I left Gǒngluò behind,
White-haired now, I enter Huányuán’s gate.
Riding spring’s breath, I tread my homeland’s ground,
Strolling slowly, plucking fragrant herbs I find.
The ruined path grieves for old friends now gone,
The ravaged woods recall the wise of yore.
Seeing the well, the paulownia still known,
Viewing the willow, the gate I recognize once more.
Fallen flowers, hard to gather all in sight,
Birds’ cries in stillness easily break the quiet.
No one comes to share my silent plight,
Nowhere to speak of warmth or chill’s disquiet.
A hundred years, alone I stand this way,
Heart’s sorrow—what more is there to say?
Suí Yuán Xínggōng’s “Poem on Passing by an Old Residence”
The ruined city after countless battles fought,
A desolate town, its four neighbors now connected.
The general’s halberd already broken,
The foot soldier’s path grows more restricted.
On the flute tower, mountain birds now call,
In the song hall, wild insects clamor loud.
Deep grass obscures the winding trails,
Dried waters leave the winding ponds empty.
In the woods, the bright moon fills the space,
Here and there, the spring breeze gently blows.
Only a ruined well remains in place,
Still flanked by two paulownia trees in rows.
Táng Yáng Shīdào’s “Poem on Returning to My Mountain Residence”
In late spring, I return to the old ridge,
Lingering, I savor the passage of years.
Fragrant grasses, no path to be seen,
Empty mountains, flowers falling in showers.
Dangling vines sweep the secluded stones,
Lying willows hinder the floating rafts.
Birds disperse, the thatched eaves grow still,
Clouds part, the streamside door tilts askew.
Still this path by the spring remains,
As are the mists and glows of yesteryear.
Memorial of Gratitude for the Imperial Grant of a Residence by Emperor Yuán of Liáng
I humbly consider that when the Hàn dynasty granted a residence to Wǔ Lún,
it truly signified a pure and upright official.
When the Wèi dynasty favored Wèi Zhēn,
it was to honor his mediocrity and integrity.
None compare to the Lingguāng Palace, magnificent and resplendent,
or the Suīyáng residence, bright and elevated.
To the north, it connects with the city walls and towers,
resembling the residence of Marquis Zhēn.
Gazing east toward the markets and streets,
it brings glory deeper than the gate of Yùzhāng.
In the past, when Lángwàng was not yet pacified,
the champion general declined a residence.
While the Mǎchí Pond still lay as a barrier,
the Yōngqiū prince yielded his mansion.
I am ashamed that my distant aspirations fall short of Huò Qùbìng and Cáo Cāo,
yet I only understand that the sovereign's command must not be disobeyed.
Reflecting again on my mediocrity and simplicity,
even nine deaths would not suffice as recompense.
Inscription for the Residence of Zhūgě Wǔhóu by Xí Zàochǐ of Jìn
When a great man takes action,
he revives this declining ethos.
Carving simplicity into elegant brilliance,
the owl's perch is made abundant.
His righteousness served as a model for all people,
his Way harmonized with the times.
From ancient times he settled here,
where the dragon coiled.
He personally plowed the western fields,
and forever whistled on the eastern peaks.
His traces retreated into the central woods,
his spirit concentrated atop the cliffs.
None could fathom his profundity,
who could gauge this joy?
O magnificent and grand master craftsman,
gracefully soaring in the morning sun.
He overturned cliffs to search for treasure,
his lofty net reaching the ninefold heavens.
Auspicious clouds gathered,
and the imperial carriage summoned him thrice.
Storehouse Treasury, Section Nine
The *Shì Míng* states:
"A storehouse (kù)
is a lodging.
A lodging means
it is where things are kept."
Also, the *Shuō Wén* states:
"A storehouse (kù)
is where war chariots are stored."
Treasury (tǎng),
pronounced tái dǎng fǎn.
It is where gold and cloth are stored.
Therefore, the name for storing
is called a storehouse treasury.
"Treasury storage" is seen in the *Hàn Shū*.
Generally, to secure the state and govern the people,
and to control the distant from the near,
one must first fill it.
Seen in the *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū*.
Therefore, heaven has stars of the celestial storehouse treasury.
The *Chūnqiū Wén Yào Gōu* states:
"The multitude of stars south of Zhěn are called the Celestial Storehouse."
Also, Hán Yáng's *Tiānwén Yào Jí* states:
"The Celestial Accumulation
is the Son of Heaven's treasury."
The king examines the capacity of the five storehouses.
The *Lǐ Jì* states:
"In the third month of spring,
examine the capacity of the five storehouses."
The first is the chariot storehouse,
the second is the weapons storehouse,
the third is the sacrificial vessels storehouse,
the fourth is the musical instruments storehouse,
the fifth is the banquet vessels storehouse.
Seen in Cài Yōng's *Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù*.
It is said that when Tāng and Wǔ defeated Jié and Zhòu,
and there was no trouble within the seas,
they built five storehouses to store the five weapons.
Seen in the *Shāng Jūn Shū*.
Then, Lǔ's Zǐ Shèn ascended the storehouse of the Dàtíngshì clan to gaze out.
Seen in the *Zuǒ Zhuàn*.
Dù Yù's annotation:
"Dàtíngshì is the name of an ancient state,
located within the walls of Lǔ,
where a storehouse was built at that place."
In the seventh year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Xiāo Hé established the eastern tower, front hall, and armory.
Seen in the *Hàn Shū*.
Also, when Gēngshǐ arrived at Cháng'ān,
the imperial treasury storage and armory
all remained undisturbed as before.
Seen in the *Dōng Guān Hàn Jì*.
These are the five storehouses.
Some say the king stores among all under heaven,
the feudal lords store among the common people,
the farmers store in their granaries,
and the merchants store in their chests and boxes.
Seen in the *Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*.
Zhōng Huì's *Chú Ráo Lùn* states:
"A state being called wealthy
lies in enriching the people.
It does not solely mean that the treasury is full
and the granaries are solid.
Moreover, if the treasury is full
and the granaries are solid,
it is not bestowed by heaven above,
but all taken from the people.
Then the people are impoverished and the state is empty."
Precious Terrace and Pearl Treasury
The *Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn* states:
"When the terrace where Duke Píng of Jìn stored his treasures burned,
they fought the fire for three days and three nights before extinguishing it.
Prince Yàn congratulated him, saying:
'I have heard that the king stores among all under heaven,
the feudal lords store among the common people,
the farmers store in their granaries,
and the merchants store in their chests and boxes.
Now the common people store outside,
yet taxes and levies never cease!
In the past, Jié and Zhòu were cruel and oppressive,
and were executed by all under heaven.
Now the August Heaven sends down calamity upon the storage terrace—
this is your good fortune.'"
Hán Yáng's *Tiānwén Yào Jí* states:
"The five stars of Lízhū are north of the Xūnǚ constellation;
Lízhū is the treasury."
Banquet Vessels and Forbidden Weapons
Cài Yōng's *Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù* states:
"Examining the capacity of the five storehouses
means examining how much is to be used."
The five storehouses:
the fifth is the banquet vessels storehouse,
already seen in the narrative.
The *Xiè Chéng Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"During the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
the armory building collapsed on its own.
The Director of the Capital Region Xǔ Bīng submitted a memorial, saying:
'The armory is where forbidden weapons are kept;
it is a state prohibition,
and the disaster is profound.'"
Celestial Pond and Imperial Treasury
The *Chūnqiū Wén Yào Gōu* states:
"Xiánchí is called the Celestial Pond,
the carriage lodging of the Five Emperors."
Sòng Jūn's annotation states:
"Lodging
means storehouse.
It is the treasury for the carriages of the Five Emperors."
"Imperial treasury" already seen in the narrative.
Gathering Armor and Storing Gold
Jiāo Gòng's *Yì Lín* states:
"The armory, the military treasury,
is where armor and weapons gather.
It is neither a city nor a village,
and cannot be dwelled in."
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuō Wén* states:
"The treasury is where gold and cloth are stored."
Fish Gathering on the Roof and Dragons Appearing in the Well
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
"During the Jiāpíng era,
two fish gathered on the roof of the armory."
The *Jìn Shū* states:
"In the fifth year of Tàikāng,
two dragons appeared in the well of the armory."
Inscription for the Armory by Lǐ Yóu of Later Hàn
Claws and teeth that seize and bite,
the foremost in sharpness and reach.
Venomous stings and piercing thorns,
preserved in spears and arrows.
The sage manifested symbols,
and the five weapons were arrayed.
Inscription for the Armory by Zhì Yú of Jìn
To have wealth without righteousness
is the calamity of a household.
Do not cherish mere dirt and dust,
The *Shiming* states:
"Mén (door),
means mēn (to feel),
signifying that from the outside it is something people feel and touch."
Furthermore, the *Shuowen* states:
"The character 'mén' consists of two 'hù' (door leaves),
it is pictographic.
Chānghé,
is the gate of heaven."
The *Shuowen* states:
"People of Chǔ call a gate chānghé."
The constellation Jiǎo is also the gate of heaven,
as seen in Hán Yáng's *Tiānwén Yàojí*.
Gāomén, Kùmén, Zhìmén, Yìngmén, Lùmén,
are the gates of the Son of Heaven.
Zhèng Xuán's annotation on the *Lǐjì* states:
"The Son of Heaven has five gates:
Gāo, Zhì, Kù, Yìng, Lù.
Lǔ had Kù, Zhì, and Lù,
thus feudal lords had three gates."
One says the main gate of the king is called Yìngmén,
the outer gate is called Gāomén,
as seen in the *Ěryǎ* and Máo Cháng's annotation on the *Shījīng*.
From within to the forbidden palace area is the Diànmén (palace gate),
going out to the main road is the Yèmén (side gate).
See Yìng Shào's annotation on the *Hànshū*.
Yè (掖),
means it is at the side (yè) of the Sīmǎ Gate.
When the king travels,
a Chēgōng Yuánmén (carriage palace gate with shafts) is set up,
a Wéigōng Jīngmén (curtained palace with pennant gate),
if there is no palace, then a Rénmén (human gate) is provided.
See Zhèng Xuán's annotation on the *Zhōuguān* which states:
"Arranging carriages as a fence,
then raising the carriage shafts to mark the gate;
spreading curtains to make a palace,
then erecting pennants to mark the gate;
deploying guards all around,
then stationing tall men to mark the gate."
The Sīmén official is in charge of receiving the keys and locks,
to open and close the gates of the state.
See the *Zhōuguān*.
Hàn,
is the inner gate within the outer wall of the city;
see the *Fēngsútōng*.
Hàn,
means hàn (to guard).
It means serving as a protective screen for people to guard against hardship.
Yán,
is the gate within a neighborhood;
Huì,
is the outer gate of a market.
See the *Shuowen*.
Cháng'ān had Xuānpíngmén, Wànqiūmén, Héngmén; the Eastern Capital had Xuāndémén, Lǐchéngmén, Qīngqǐmén, Zhāngyìmén, Rénshòumén, Shòuchéngmén.
See *Hàn Gōngdiàn Míng*.
Also had Zhāngchéngmén, Zhíchéngmén, Luòchéngmén.
See *Sānfǔ Huángtú*.

Luòyáng had Shàngxīmén, Guǎngyángmén, Jīnmén, Xiǎoyuànmén, Kāiyángmén, Zhōngdōngmén, Shàngdōngmén, Sīmǎmén, Běiquēmén, Xuánwǔmén, Nányèmén, Běiyèmén, Dōngyèmén, Xīyèmén, Zhǐchēmén, Nánduānmén, Jīnmén, Jiǔlóngmén, Báihǔmén, Chūnxīngmén, Qīngsuǒmén, Jīnshāngmén, Yúnlóngmén, Shénwǔmén, Yíqiūmén.
See *Luòyáng Gùgōng Jì*.
Also had Dàxiàmén, Chángchūnmén, Zhūmíngmén, Qīngyángmén.
See *Jìn Gōnggé Míng*.
Having double gates and striking the night watchman's clapper,
to await violent intruders,
is probably derived from the hexagram Yù.
See the *Zhōuyì*.
It also says Gèn represents gates and towers.
When officials and scholars enter or leave the ruler's gate,
they pass to the right of the threshold stone,
and do not step on the threshold.
Whenever entering with a guest,
at each gate yield to the guest.
When the guest reaches the chamber door,
then the host requests to enter to prepare the mat,
the host enters the gate and goes right,
the guest enters the gate and goes left.
See the *Lǐjì*.
Gate names include Zhèngmén (main gate), Chóngmén (double gate), Tōngmén (passage gate), Héngmén (crossbar gate), Bìmén (wall gate), Jìnmén (forbidden gate).
The *Máoshī* says:
"Beneath the crossbar gate,
one can linger and rest."
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"King Wén of Zhōu made a jade gate,
meaning it was adorned with jade."
The *Hànshū* says:
"South of the Tàiyè Pond there was a wall gate."
"Forbidden gate" has already been mentioned above.
Zhuólóng Fēitù
Yuán Hóng's *Hàn Jì* states:
"In the second year of the Jiànchū era,
the officials, following the old statutes,
requested to enfeoff the maternal uncles.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
'Previously, passing over the Zhuólóng Gate,
I saw the carriages of the external families like flowing water and horses like dragons,
I did not reprimand or get angry at them.
I merely cut off their annual allowances,
hoping they would know to silently desist.'" *Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Fēitù Gate."
Qīngqǐ Huángjīn
*Hàn Gōngdiàn Míng*:
"Cháng'ān had a Qīngqǐ Gate."
A musical song says:
"Yellow gold is your gate,
white jade is your hall."
Hánzhāng Jiànlǐ
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Hánzhāng Gate."
It also says:
"There was a Jiànlǐ Gate."
Tónglóng Jīnmǎ
The *Hànshū* says:
"Emperor Chéng, when crown prince, was cautious,
initially residing in the Guì Palace.
The Emperor urgently summoned him,
the crown prince exited the Lónglóu Gate,
not daring to cross the imperial roadway."
Zhāng Yàn's annotation states:
"On the gate tower there was a bronze dragon."
Zhāng Yíng's *Hàn Nán Jì* states:
"Mǎ Yuán memorialized saying:
'During Emperor Wǔ's time,
a man skilled at judging horses,
cast and made a method of bronze horses and presented it.
An edict ordered the horse to be set up outside the Lǔbān Gate,
then it was renamed the Jīnmǎ Gate.'"
Tīngzhèng Dēngxián
Liú Chéngzhī's *Sòng Yǒngchū Shānchuān Gǔjīn Jì* states:
"Before Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's Tīngzhèng Hall,
there was a Tīngzhèng Gate."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's *Huái Fù Xù* states:
"Wáng Càn was on duty at the Dēngxián Gate."
Xīshǔ Dōngyáng
The *Huáinánzǐ*:
"From the earthen mountain in the northeast,
called the Cāng Gate:
the southeast is called the Bōmǔ Mountain,
called the Yáng Gate;
the south is called the Nánjí Mountain,
called the Xīshǔ Gate."
*Jìn Gōngquè Míng* states:
"The east gate of Luòyáng city was called the Dōngyáng Gate."
Guǎngdé Mínglǐ
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Guǎngdé Gate."
It also says:
"There was a Míngdé Gate."
Tóngmǎ Shíniú
The *Shǐjì* says:
"The Jīnmǎ Gate,
had a bronze horse beside the gate building,
hence it was called the Jīnmǎ Gate."
Cháng Qú's *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
"King Xiào of Qín appointed Lǐ Bīng as governor of Shǔ,
Bīng made five stone rhinoceroses,
to suppress the water spirits.
One was at the Shìqiáo Gate,
now called the Shíniú Gate."
Qīngmíng Chānghé
Lì Yuán's annotation on the *Shuǐjīng* states:
"Xiányáng was originally a detached palace,
the second gate from the north end on the east side,
was originally named the Qīngmíng Gate."
It also says:
"Chānghé,
was Hàn's Western Upper Gate."
Dìngdǐng Wàngzhōng
*Gǔjīn Dìmíng* states:
"Hénán had a Dìngdǐng Gate."
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng*:
"Luòyáng had a Wàngzhōng Gate."
Rénshòu Shénxiān
*Hàn Gōngdiàn Míng* states:
"Cháng'ān had a Rénshòu Gate."
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Shénxiān Gate."
Hándé Chéngmíng
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Hándé Gate."
*Jìn Gōnggé Míng* states:
"Luòyáng city had a Chéngmíng Gate."
Nánduān Běiyè
Both are seen in the narrative.
Jìngfǎ Chónglǐ
*Luòyáng Gùgōng Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Jìngfǎ Gate."
*Jìn Gōnggé Míng* states:
"Luòyáng had a Chónglǐ Gate."
Quèfēi and Huìfú
The "Names of the Old Palaces in Luòyáng" states:
"Luòyáng had a Quèfēi Gate."
It also says:
"There was a Huìfú Gate."
Xīyǔ and Ángchē
Hé Shàngzhī memorialized, saying:
"The king has nine banners.
When feathered plumes are arranged to form a gate,
it is called a jīngmén (banner gate).
Similarly, using chariots to form a gate is called a yuánmén (chariot shaft gate)."
The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"The official in charge of lodgings
manages the lodging places for the king's assemblies and meetings.
He sets up double rows of bìhù (palisades),
and establishes a chariot encampment with a yuánmén."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"This refers to when the king travels and encamps,
using chariots as a fence.
Then the chariot shafts are raised to mark the gate."
Shòu Guǎnjiàn and Xiū Héshàn
The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"The Gatekeeper
is in charge of receiving the keys and locks to open and close the city gates."
The "Lǐ Jì" says:
"In the second month of spring,
repair the doors and leaves."
Jiànchūn and Yíqiū
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Shuǐ Jīng" says:
"The Gǔshuǐ flows east under the stone bridge of the Jiànchūn Gate,
which is the Shàngdōng Gate.
It is also called the Shàngshēng Gate.
In the Jìn dynasty, there was a Jiànyáng Gate."
The "Names of the Old Palaces in Luòyáng" says:
"Luòyáng had a Yíqiū Gate."
Yúnlóng Fènghǔ and Wànchūn Qiānqiū
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Shuǐ Jīng" says:
"The Shénshòu Gate
faces east towards the Yúnlóng Fènghǔ Gate.
On the horizontal beams,
cloud dragons and wind tigers are all carved."
The "Record of Luòyáng Palaces and Buildings" says:
"Luòyáng had Wànchūn Gate and Qiānqiū Gate."
Chén Hé Xū's "Poem: Awaiting Edict at the Jīnmǎ Gate"
Under the Hàn's unified rule,
all states gather in tribute.
Flying tassels brush the morning mist,
light carriages follow the morning breeze.
The locust-lined road reflects green ribbons,
sunlight adorns golden sable caps.
At this moment serving as an expectant official,
who would still think of fishing and woodcutting?
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Gate Inscriptions"
The establishment of gates
marks the meeting point of dwellings.
They admit the good and ward off evil,
sound the watch to prevent harm.
Also "Inscription for the Zhōngdōng Gate"
Zhōngdōng occupies the middle,
its month corresponds to mǎo.
The oriole sings,
the hawk conceals its claws.
Remove the shackles,
do not pursue lawsuits.
Also "Inscription for the Kāiyáng Gate"
Kāiyáng is in the first month,
its position and month are sì.
Clear and bright marks the season,
the sun rises higher.
Also "Inscription for the Jīnchéng Gate"
The name has its fixed position,
its month is wèi.
Warm winds gather heat,
birds of prey practice their skills.
Also "Inscription for the Yōngchéng Gate"
Yōng Gate occupies the center,
its position and month are yǒu.
Blind winds bring cold and turbidity,
wild geese return to the mountains.
Also "Inscription for the Xiàchéng Gate"
Xià Gate corresponds to the first month,
its position and month are hài.
Yīn and yang do not communicate,
the rainbow hides its colors.
Welcome winter at the northern altar,
follow where the yin resides.
Also "Inscription for the Gǔchéng Gate"
Gǔ Gate is north-central,
its position corresponds to zǐ.
The Great Yin governs punishment,
killing and warfare begin here.
Later Wèi Wēn Zǐshēng's "Prayer for the Raising of the Beam at the Chānghé Gate"
The king establishes the state,
matching the Tàiwēi constellation.
The great lord issues the command,
the high gates open their leaves.
An auspicious day is chosen,
divination shows no violation.
The carved beam is raised,
the elegant wings now soar.
Eight dragons distant and deep,
nine layers lofty and grand.
Residing in the palace, receiving blessings,
facing the sun, draped in robes.
The sovereign has cause for celebration,
all within the four seas turn to him.
Walls, Part Eleven
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"A wall is called yōng."
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"Yōng, yuán,
are walls."
The "Shìmíng" says:
"A wall (qiáng),
is a barrier (zhàng),
that which is used to shield oneself;
a yuán,
is support (yuán),
that which people rely on for defense and protection;
a yōng,
is containment (róng),
that which is used to conceal and hide one's form."
According to the "Huáinánzǐ":
"Shùn built houses, erected walls, and thatched roofs,
causing people to know to leave caves and cliffs,
each having their own homes.
This was the beginning."
The "Shàngshū Dàzhuàn" says:
"The Son of Heaven has a grand wall (bēn yōng),
the feudal lords have a sparse wall (shū zhù)."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Bēn
means great,
meaning the great wall is straight and upright.
Shū
means diminished.
Zhù is also a wall,
meaning it diminishes at the top and bottom,
and is not straight and upright."
The "Xīnxù" says:
"The walls of feudal lords have black and white plaster,
but not the colors of cinnabar and azurite."
Also the "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"There are walls to conceal what is unsightly."
The "Shényì Jīng" says:
"Beyond the northwestern border, on Dàxià Mountain there is a palace
with walls made of gold;
beyond the southern border, on Wǎngmíng Mountain there is a palace
with walls made of red stone;
beyond the southwestern border, on Lǎoshòu Mountain there is a palace
with walls made of yellow copper;
beyond the southeastern border, on Huìqīng Mountain there is a palace
with walls made of blue stone;
beyond the western border, on Xīmíng Mountain there is a palace
with walls made of white stone."
The "Nánzhōu Yìwù Zhì" says:
"In the country of Dàqín (Roman Empire),
they use glass for walls."
These are examples of such things.
The "Shìmíng" also says:
"A wall (bì),
is to ward off (pì),
meaning it wards off wind and cold."
The "Hànshū":
"Lǔ Gōngwàng Yú damaged Confucius's old house,
and within the wall found ancient classical texts."
Also, "Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's family in Chéngdū
had only four bare walls."
Also, "Consort Zhào Jiéyú resided in the Zhāoyáng Palace hall,
the wall bands were often inlaid with golden rings."
The "Hòu Hàn Jì":
"Lángyé King Jīng was fond of palaces and buildings,
renovated halls and pavilions,
and decorated wall bands with gold and silver."
The "Hàn Guān Diǎnzhí":
"Within the Hàn imperial court, all walls were coated with foreign powder,
and painted with ancient martyrs."
These are examples of such things.
As for the names of walls,
there are carved walls;
see the "Shàngshū".
High walls, encircling walls, long lofty walls; as for walls, there are plastered walls, red walls;
see the "Chǔ Cí".
White walls;
see Cáo Zhí's memorial.
Jade-like walls;
see Zhāng Xié's "Seven Commands".
Silver walls.
See the "Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn".
A Thousand Ren; Nine Zhang
Jiāo Gàn's *Forest of Changes* states:
"A wall a thousand ren high,
misfortune does not enter the gate."
Mèng Ào's *Record of a Northern Campaign* states:
"Southwest of the lightning-avoidance chamber in Yè City's stone ditch,
north of it is the Huálín Wall,
nine zhang high,
one li in circumference."
Carved Characters; Stored Books
Gě Hóng's *Biographies of Immortals* states:
"Bái Hé,
a man from Liáodōng,
studied under Lord Wáng.
Lord Wáng told him:
'I am going to Yíngzhōu for a while,
you stay in this stone chamber,
look intently at the north wall,
after a long time you should see writing on the wall,
read it and you will attain it.'
Hé looked for three years,
then saw on the wall the *Tàiqīng Scripture* carved by the ancients,
recited it and became an immortal."
Kǒng Ānguó's *Preface to the Book of Documents* states:
"Duke Gòng of Lǔ was fond of building palaces,
he demolished Confucius's old residence,
to expand his own dwelling,
and within the house walls obtained the books of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu stored by his ancestors."
Reaching the Shoulder; Obscuring the Eyes
*The Analects* states:
"The wall of Cì reaches only to the shoulder."
Jiāo Gàn's *Forest of Changes* states:
"Yù's Kǎn,
the wall is high, obscuring the eyes."
Cinnabar and Azure; Purple and Plain
Liú Xiàng's *New Prefaces* states:
"The walls of the feudal lords have the colors of dark and whitewash,
not the hues of cinnabar and azure."
Cài Zhì's *Duties of Hàn Officials* states:
"Within the ministries, all walls are coated with lead powder,
bounded with purple and plain,
depicting ancient martyrs."
Yáo's Image; Yǔ's Writing
*Family Sayings* states:
"Confucius observed the walls of the four gates,
there were images of Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu,
each with depictions of good and evil,
warnings of rise and fall."
*Record of Héng Mountain* states:
"East of Gānquán there is a stone cliff,
the writing carved by Yǔ is here."
Blue Stone; Yellow Gold
See Dōngfāng Shuò's *Classic of Divine Marvels* and the *Book of Hàn*,
both are mentioned in the narrative.
Adorned with Embroidered Axe Pattern; Decorated with Silver
*Book of Hàn* states:
"Jiǎ Yì said:
'Embroidered axe patterns,
were the garments of ancient Son of Heaven.
Now wealthy merchants and great traders,
when hosting grand gatherings to summon guests,

"Lángyé King Jīngdū Jǔ,
fond of palaces,
the wall bands of his halls and pavilions,
were all decorated with gold and silver."
Already mentioned in the narrative.
Drawing Light; Hanging Edicts
*Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
"Kuāng Héng studied diligently but had no candle,
the neighbor's house was not accessible,
so Héng bored a hole through the wall to draw in its light,
and read by reflecting the book against it."
Cuī Shí's *Correct Discourses* states:
"Those now in charge of provinces and commanderies,
disobey the imperial edicts themselves,
acting willfully in their comings and goings.
Thus the local saying goes:
'Provincial and commandery edicts,
are like thunderclaps.
Once the edict is received,
it's just hung on the wall.'"
Painting Martyrs; Carving Loyal Ministers
"Painting martyrs" see *Duties of Hàn Officials*,
already detailed in the narrative.
Dài Yánzhī's *Record of a Western Campaign* states:
"Before Lǔ Gōng's tomb at Jiāoshì Mountain,
there is a stone shrine.
All four walls are of blue stone,
with raised reliefs of loyal ministers, filial sons, and chaste women,
beside each image are carved stone inscriptions recording the stele texts."
Sòng Zhīwèn's *Poem on the Cranes Painted on the Ministry Wall*
On the whitewashed wall, immortal cranes are painted,
Their proud bearing holds much true spirit.
Fluttering, they ultimately do not depart,
Surely it is because they cherish the grace of favor.
Liáng Shěn Yuē's *Memorial Impeaching Censor Kǒng Tuó for His Insolent Inscription on the Ministry Wall*
Respectfully submitted: The court attendant and censor-in-waiting, your subject Kǒng Tuó,
is obscure and unknown from the seas,
yet mistakenly ranked among the splendid ministries.
Acting in temporary posts, coming and going,
is the common duty of officials.
Moreover, the lowly position of Dōnggāo,
does not rely on abundant resources,
a temporary labor of ten days,
how can it be called base or humiliating?
Yet he brazenly uttered these vile words,
inscribing them within the forbidden ministry,
comparing things and linking categories,
in a manner wholly inappropriate.
To dismiss him to the ranks of the commoners,
truly accords with the court's laws.
We, your subjects, have deliberated,
and request that based on the present matter, Tuó be removed from his official post,
and he be immediately detained.
Chapter Twelve: Parks and Enclosures
*General Meanings of Customs* states:
"Yuàn (park),
means yùn (to accumulate),
referring to where firewood and kindling are accumulated."
*Shuōwén* states:
"A yuàn that has a garden is called a yòu (enclosure),
yòu also means 'to have'."
*The Annals of Lü Buwei* states:
"When the former kings made parks, enclosures, gardens, and ponds,
it was sufficient for viewing and for physical exertion,
not because they were fond of frugality by nature."
Thus, Zhōu had the Líng Yòu.
*The Book of Songs* states:
"The king was in the Líng Yòu."
Máo Cháng's commentary states:
"A yòu is for rearing birds and beasts.
The Son of Heaven's is one hundred li,
the feudal lords' forty li."
Guó Yóu.
*The Rites of Zhōu* states:
"The Yòu Rén oversees the prohibitions on the beasts of the Guó Yóu."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The small parks and pleasure grounds at the imperial detached palaces of the state."
Hàn had Shànglín, Lèyóu, Bówàng, Huángshān;
Later Hàn had Hóngdé, Bìguī, Língkūn, Guǎngchéng, and various other parks.
See the *Book of Hàn*, the *Book of Later Hàn*, and the *Later Hàn Annals*.
Jìn had Pínglè, Lùzǐ, Sāngzǐ, and various other parks.
All were in Luòyáng,
see *Names of Jìn Palaces* and the *Register of the Twelve Districts of Hénán*.
Some say enclosures have woods and ponds,
to ward off disasters,
the rest are all grain-producing land.
See the *Discourses of the States*.
When it declined,
galloping and hunting for pleasure,
robbed people of their time,
and exhausted their strength.
See the *Huáinánzǐ*.
Thus, Dōngfāng Shuò in the *Book of Hàn* said:
"Striving for the vastness of parks and enclosures,
showing no concern for the farming seasons,
is not the way to strengthen the state and enrich the people,
this is what is meant."
Their names for parks:
include Tiānyuàn, Jìnyuàn, Shàngyuàn;
for enclosures: Jūnyòu, Língyòu, Shàngyòu.
Huángshān; Báishuǐ
*Book of Hàn* states:
"Huò Yún, when due at court audience,
often claimed illness and went out privately.
With many followers and guests,
he set out hunts in the Huángshān Park."
Táo Jìzhí's *Record of the Capital Region* states:
"Fùzhōu Mountain is about twenty li in circumference,
it has a forest named the Báishuǐ Park."
Taking Beasts; Sporting with Foxes
Wèi Hóng's *Old Rituals of Hàn* states:
"The Shànglín Park is three hundred li in breadth and length,
it has a director, assistant directors, and left, right, and central commandants.
One hundred and fifty pavilions and parks,
within the park a hundred kinds of beasts are reared,
deer and river deer are used for sacrificial offerings and entertaining guests.
The Son of Heaven hunts with bow and arrow in the park in autumn and winter,
taking countless birds and beasts."
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's *Seven Summonses* states:
"In the park, sport with the nine-tailed fox,
in the enclosure, perch the three-legged crow."
Following the Plains, Spanning the Valleys
Bān Gù's "Eastern Capital Rhapsody" says:
"Following the plains and wilds, they made parks;
Conforming to flowing springs, they formed ponds.
They grew duckweed and algae to harbor fish in the depths,
And enriched the rushes and grasses to nurture beasts."
Zhāng Héng's "Western Capital Rhapsody" says:
"The Shanglin Imperial Park,
Spanned valleys and covered hills.
To the east it reached Dǐnghú,
Diagonally bordering Xìliǔ."
Gānquán, Shànglín
The "Sanfu Huangtu" says:
"Within the Gānquán Park,
The Xiānrén Observatory was built,
Running along the mountain valleys.
Reaching Yúnyáng,
It was 381 lǐ long,
Entering Yòufūfēng.
In total, it encompassed 540 lǐ in circumference."
Wèi Hóng's "Hàn Jiù Yí" states:
"The Shànglín Park
Was 300 lǐ in breadth and length,
Containing seventy detached palaces,
Each capable of accommodating a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen."
Hóngdé, Guǎngchéng
The "Dōngguān Hàn Jì" says:
"In the first year of the Yánxī era of Emperor Huán,
The Hóngdé Park was established."
Xuē Yíng's "Hòu Hàn Jì" says:
"In the fifth year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng,
A grand hunt was held at the Guǎngchéng Park."
Gāowàng, Hànpíng
The "Hòu Hàn Shū" says:
"In the sixth year of the Yǒngchū era,
An edict ordered Yuèxī to establish three parks: Chánglì, Gāowàng, and Shǐchāng.
It also ordered Yìzhōu to establish the Wànsuì Park,
And Qiánwéi to establish the Hànpíng Park."
Sīxián, Bówàng
The "Xījīng Zájì" says:
"Emperor Wén established the Sīxián Park for the Crown Prince,
To attract guests."
The "Hàn Shū" says:
"When Crown Prince Lì reached capping age,
A Bówàng Park was established for him at his palace,
To enable him to receive guests."
Sāngzǐ, Guìlín
The "Hénèi Shí'èr Jìng Bù" says:
"West of Luòyáng city was the Sāngzǐ Park."
Táo Jìzhí's "Jīng Bāng Jì" says:
"North of Jiànkāng County,
Was the Guìlín Park of the Hàn dynasty."
Raising Beasts, Shooting Swans
The "Shuōwén" says:
"A park with a garden is called a 'yòu';
Another explanation is that a place for raising birds and beasts is called a 'yòu'."
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
"Duke Xiàn of Wèi shot swans in the park."
Monthly Sacrifice, Autumn Construction
The "Dà Dài Lǐ" says:
"In the first month, sacrifice is made at the Leek Park.
The Leek Park
Is the hedge of the garden."
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
"In the autumn of the eighteenth year of Duke Chéng, the Deer Park was built;
It is recorded because it was an untimely act."
Liáng Dynasty Jì Shǎoyú, "Poem on Roaming the Jiànxīng Park"
Dānlíng embraces the heavenly capital,
Zǐquán continues to Shànglín.
Jade terraces reach a hundred feet high,
Silver trees rise a thousand xún.
Water flows with the shadows of caps and canopies,
The wind carries the sound of songs and flutes.
Hesitating, I pity the picking of kingfisher feathers,
Looking back as I walk, I regret the lost hairpin.
As the sun sets, the courtyard light shifts,
The square carriage curtain repeatedly moves the shade.
I wish to say the joy is not yet at its peak,
Not to speak of loving gold."
Chén Dynasty Shì Hóngyǎn, "Poem on Roaming an Old Park"
Lóngtián remains in the old park,
Fén water forms lingering ripples.
Gazing with melancholy hurts the roaming eye,
Bitterness and sorrow fill my thoughts.
Cold mist saddens the tall trees,
Condensed dew transforms the light vines.
Marsh mallows still bear water chestnuts,
Pond bamboos still invade the lotuses.
The autumn wind merely hastens itself,
No longer is there the song of white clouds."
Lú Cángyòng, "Poem in Response to 'Roaming the Park on Lìchūn'"
The imperial carriage halts at the city gate for a heavenly excursion,
The light lingers in the upper park, renewed late.
Jade terraces half enter the Huángshān road,
Jade railings border the dark Bà ford.
Plum fragrance awaits to fall before the song,
Orchid scent first returns with the wine of spring.
Fortunate to be counted in the jade terrace offering longevity,
I wish to accompany the thousand acres at the farmers' hour."
Shěn Quánqī, "Poem in Response to 'Roaming the Park on Lìchūn'"
The eastern suburbs briefly turn the welcoming spring procession,
The upper park first circulates the celebratory cups.
Wind shoots at fox ice, breaking a thousand shards,
Vital force strikes the fish-key, opening the nine passes.
Searching in the woods for grass, one then knows the lichee,
In the hall vying for flowers, all are plum blossoms.
Songs and flutes, bearing grace, return late on the road,
As roosting crows descend halfway, the phoenix city arrives."
Chapter Thirteen: Gardens and Plots
The "Shuōwén" says:
"A 'yuán' (garden)
Is for planting fruit trees;
A 'pǔ' (plot)
Is for planting vegetables."
According to the "Tiānwén Yàojí":
"The Gourd Star is the Son of Heaven's fruit garden;
Also, the Celestial Garden governs fruits, vegetables, and stored provisions."
The "Shǐ Jì" mentions the Liáng Garden, Qī Garden, and the Chǔ Orange and Pomelo Garden.
The "Sān Qín Jì":
"The Hàn had fruit gardens."
The "Sān Qín Jì" states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's fruit garden had large chestnuts."
The "Wèi Zhì" mentions the Fānglín Garden and the Tóng Garden.
Fānglín was later altered to avoid the taboo of the young emperor's name,
Hence it was called the Huálín Garden.
The "Jìn Gōng Gé Míng" lists the Língzhī Garden and the Pútáo Garden.
These all take their names from the plants, trees, and fruits.
There are also the Xuán Garden,
See the "Zhuāngzǐ".
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" mentions the Xuán Garden.
The Shū Garden,
See the "Huáinánzǐ".
The Melon Plot,
See the "Suǒ Yǔ".
The Reed Plot, Flower Plot, and Bamboo Plot,
See the "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù".
The Táng Plot,
See the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū".
Although these are established based on plants and trees,
They are also named according to circumstances.
Língzhī, Xiān Huì
"Língzhī" has already been described in the narrative section.
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì" says:
"On the third level of the Kūnlún Mountains,
Below are fields of língzhī and plots of huì orchids,
Each spanning tens of thousands of qǐng,
Where groups of immortals plant and weed."
Pútáo, Mùxu
The "Jìn Gōng Gé Míng" says:
"The Luòyáng Palace had the Qióngpǔ Garden and the Língzhī Shící Garden;
Yè had the Míng Hú Garden and the Pútáo Garden."
Guō Zhòngchǎn's "Qiúchí Jì" says:
"East of the city was the Mùxu Garden."
Zhuólóng, Míng Hú
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hàn Shū" says:
"The Zhuólóng Garden was located at the northwest corner of Luòyáng."
The "Jìn Gōng Gé Míng" says:
"Yè had the Míng Hú Garden."
Palanquin on Foot, Flying Canopies
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Xiàoliè Fù" says:
"Ascending the main hall to hear governance,
Managing the discipline of all offices.
Wandering leisurely in the rear courtyard,
Resting in the quiet chambers.
Walking the palanquin in the Western Garden,
Sitting idly in the Jade Hall."
Cáo Zhí's poem says:
"The noble lord respectfully loves his guests,
At the banquet's end, he knows no weariness.
In the clear night, we roam the Western Garden,
Flying canopies pursuing one another."
Planting Peaches, Nurturing Fruits
The "Máo Shī" says:
"In the garden are planted peach trees,
Their fruit is for food."
The "Zhōu Guān‧Jiǔ Zhí":
"The second is gardens and plots,
Nurturing fruit trees."
Requesting Good Fields and Lending to the Poor
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Wáng Jiǎn, serving as a general of Qín,
when about to campaign against Chǔ,
requested a great many fine fields, houses, gardens, and ponds."
The Records of the Eastern Watchtower of Hàn states:
"In the first year of the Xiàohé reign period,
an edict was issued to the officials,
that the detached palaces, gardens, and ponds in the capital
should all be lent to poor people."
Holding a Hoe and Finding a Seal
The Book of Hàn:
"Sūn Bǎo served as the Governor of the Capital District.
He appointed Hóu Wén as the Eastern District Inspector.
Dù Jùjì of Bàlíng secluded himself behind closed doors, not interacting with the world,
holding a hoe to tend his own garden,
not daring to break the law."
The Annals of Later Hàn states:
"During the reign of Emperor Huán,
Dài Yì of the Pèi Kingdom,
while hoeing his garden, found a gold seal."
Fǎ Zhēn Not Glancing at the Garden and Fàn Dān Hired Himself Out
The Book of Later Hàn states:
"Fǎ Zhēn secluded himself in the great marshes,
discussing and lecturing on arts and techniques,
for years without glancing at gardens or orchards."
The Traditions of the Elderly of Chénliú states:
"Fàn Dān's learning mastered the Three Classics,
yet he often hired himself out to water gardens."
Also, "Dǒng Zhòngshū of the Former Hàn lowered his curtains to study,
for three years without glancing at gardens or orchards."
Beginning to Dwell in Xiāngyì and Surplus Profit in Shānyáng
The Records of Chénliú states:
"Yuán Yǔ
was a man of Xiāngyì.
Yǔ first dwelt in a garden,
hence the world called him Lord of the Garden.
Xiàng Xiù and Lǚ Ān watered gardens in Shānyáng,
collecting the surplus profit,
to supply the expenses for wine and food."
The Hànyīn Old Man Carrying a Jar and Zhuāng Zhōu Serving as an Official
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"An old man of Hànyīn carried a jar to draw from a well,
fetching water to irrigate his garden.
Zǐgòng taught him to use a well-sweep,
but the old man disliked its use of mechanics,
and would not listen."
Also, "Zhuāng Zhōu once served as the official of the lacquer garden in Méngyi."
Liáng Jiāng Yān's "Rhapsody on the Rabbit Garden of the Prince of Liáng"
Some who value antiquity and disparage the present,
I say:
"Why is it so?"
If there are no understanding ears, then so be it!
I shall merely compose in the ancient rhapsody style,
to rival Méi Shū's composition:
"Golden ponds stretch far and wide,
green bamboo clothes the slopes.
Winding and verdant,
seeming near, yet again distant.
Waterfowl, geese and ducks,
cormorants, wild geese.
Flying up to Héngyáng,
roosting down in Miǎn and Hàn.
In tens and fives,
suddenly gathering, then scattering again.
Thereupon the retinue of the grandee,
returning in season,
spring sun just dawning,
vermilion blossoms not yet dry."
Sòng Xiè Língyùn's "Poem on Returning to the Old Garden"
Floating boat on thousand-ren chasms,
grasping reins on ten-thousand-xún peaks.
Rushing foam no peril enough,
stone beds hardly counted hardship.
My master reveals true feelings,
reaching into his bosom to bestow fine verses.
Liáng Yuándì's "Poem on Wandering in the Rear Garden"
Late spring holds much fine air,
slanting light falls as the sun sets high.
Sunshine on the pond, hues shallow,
clouds returning, mountain views dense.
Entering the woods, lost on winding paths,
crossing islets, separated by perilous peaks.
Also, "Poem on the Evening Scene Wandering in the Rear Garden"
From the high carriage, let me gaze afar,
bright scenery enters the river bridge.
Waves horizontal, mountain crossing shadows,
rain ceased, leaves gleam with light.
Sun shifts, flower colors change,
wind scatters, water patterns lengthen.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú's "Poem on Following the Crown Prince Out to Xuánpǔ"
Spring light rises from the splendid watchtower,
stepping lightly, ascending the hilltop.
Pavilion shadows overlook flying canopies,
oriole songs enter the panpipes.
Water returns, climbing old islets,
trees grow tall, joining the former bridge.
Green lotuses bear patterned leaves,
red vines climb with slender sprouts.
Wishing to follow, ashamed of my plain prose,
how can it compare to jasper and jade?
Jìn Pān Ní's "Ode to the Rear Garden"
Vast and obscure in antiquity,
remote and bound by knotted cords.
Great simplicity not yet dispersed,
mysterious transformation moist and congealed.
Fúxī and Huángdì followed in steps,
the Three Dynasties succeeded one another.
The Five Virtues changed kingship,
refinement and substance rose in turn.
Heaven's mandate is not constant,
it aids the humble and assists the faithful.
Then it turned its gaze to our emperor,
gloriously possessing the great Jìn.
Meeting the time, receiving the throne,
heaven and man are in accord.
Harmonious qi fills the four directions,
gracious moisture spreads all around.
Spirits and deities announce auspicious signs,
the four numinous creatures offer their substance.
Wandering dragons ascend the clouds,
phoenixes in proper form shade the sun.
Sweet dew flows at dawn,
sweet springs gush and overflow.
Huáxià now at peace,
the eight wildernesses quiet and still.
People also have a saying,
how shall I find rest?
So he summoned his ministers and officers,
to follow the emperor on his excursion.
Long mats spread afar,
broad canopies all around.
Fine dishes, fragrant indeed,
sweet wine, gentle in thought.
Lofty, towering peaks,
billowing, dark currents.
Soaring birds beat their wings,
swimming fish float along.
Brilliant, enlightened Son of Heaven,
grave and solemn, the many officials.
Literary men, gathered in throngs,
martial men, mighty and grand.
Lecturing and discussing in Huálín,
practicing archery in the rear garden.
Dignified demeanor already complete,
bows and arrows thus at ease.
Sincere and respectful, modest virtue,
majestic and solemn, the sage's countenance.
Bestowed with feasts and drink,
instructed with words of counsel.
Millet and grain already harvested,
goods and wealth already abundant.
Benevolent winds silently flow,
imperial transformation increasingly exalted.
Conscripts lay aside their armor,
warriors cease their warfare.
Distant barbarians admire the kindness,
remote Yuè peoples gaze upon the influence.
Let there be no negligence or disrespect,
consider the end from the beginning.
Let there be no complacency or ease,
in fullness, think of emptiness.
Chapter Fourteen: Roads and Paths
The Shìmíng states:
"Dào (道) means to tread;
lù (路) means to be exposed.
It refers to what people tread upon and is thus exposed and seen."
According to the Ěryǎ, a single thoroughfare is called a dàolù (道路, road).
Two thoroughfares meeting is called qípáng (歧旁),
meaning a branching path that diverges to the side.
Three thoroughfares meeting is called jùpáng (劇旁),
because many paths branch off to the sides, hence it is called 'jù' (intense).
Four thoroughfares meeting is called qú (衢).
Five thoroughfares meeting is called kāng (康).
Six thoroughfares meeting is called zhuāng (莊).
Kāng means joy.
Zhuāng means flourishing.
It refers to the intersection being joyful and flourishing.
Seven thoroughfares meeting is called jùcān (劇驂).
A team of horses has four.
Here there are seven,
comparing it to an intensely crowded team of horses.
Eight thoroughfares meeting is called chóngqī (崇期).
Chóng means many.
Many roads meet and converge here.
Nine thoroughfares meeting is called kuí (逵).
Kuí is also called kuí (馗).
It is said to resemble a tortoise's shell,
hence it is called kuí (馗),
as seen in the Shuōwén.
The path within a temple compound is called táng (唐).
The Shìmíng also says:
"The road beneath a city wall is called háo (豪).
Háo means to soar.
It refers to the place within the capital where one soars and drives chariots.
A path used for walking is called xī (蹊)."
Xī means to wait.
It is said that for swift hunting it is used separately,
thus one returns and waits on the main road.
Furthermore, the Guǎngyǎ states:
"Yì (墿), guǐ (軌), gèng (堩), jiē (街), jìng (徑), huán (闤), huì (闠), gāng (阬), háng (阬), gān (阬) all mean dào (道, road)."
Yì is pronounced yì.
Gèng is pronounced gèng.
Gāng is pronounced gāng.
Háng is pronounced háng.
Gān is pronounced gān.
Also, "zhěn (畛), tú (涂), chén (陳), qiān (阡), mò (陌), shù (術) are also different names for roads."
The Zhōuguān states:
"Above the ditches there are zhěn."
The Shìmíng states:
"Tú (涂) means to cross.
It refers to that by which one can pass through."
The Tángtú states:
"Chén (陳) refers to the place where host and guest meet and are arrayed."
The Fēngsútōng states:
"North-south [roads] are called qiān,
east-west [roads] are called mò."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"When Zǐchǎn was minister of Zhèng,
peach and plum trees hung over the shù (roads)."
In ancient times, when the Yellow Emperor was Son of Heaven,
the craftsmen built the capital.
Within the capital were nine north-south and nine east-west roads.
The main roads were nine tracks wide,
the ring roads were seven tracks wide,
and the country roads were five tracks wide.
The Héfāngshì was in charge of reaching all the roads under heaven,
extending to the four borders.
Whenever boats, carts, or vehicles on the roads became entangled,
they were ordered and set moving.
Whenever those with tallies or those of rank arrived,
then they cleared the way and prohibited those in the wilds from crossing transversely or taking shortcuts.
See the Zhōuguān.
Also, the Lǐjì states:
"On the roads,
men keep to the right,
women keep to the left,
and vehicles proceed down the center."
These are matters concerning roads.
The Wǔjīng Yàoyì states:
"Those about to depart perform a zǔdào ceremony.
It is also called sìxíng,
meaning to sacrifice to the god of the road to pray for safety."
Jùcān (Intensely Crowded Team) and Fāngguǐ (Parallel Tracks)
"Jùcān" has already been explained in the narrative.
Zuǒ Sī's "Shǔdū Fù" states:
"Opening the nine pairs of thoroughfare gates,
planning the broad roads for parallel tracks."
Guībèi (Tortoise Shell) and Yángcháng (Sheep Gut)
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
"Kuí (馗) is a nine-way thoroughfare.
It resembles a tortoise's shell,
hence it is called kuí."
Wèi Wǔdì's "Kǔhán Xíng" states:
"The Yángcháng slope winds and twists,
causing the cart wheels to break."
Wáng Zhìshēn's Sòng Jì states:
"The Dí person Yáng Nándāng
dwelt on Chóuchí Mountain.
It was twenty lǐ high,
with a winding sheep-gut path,
thirty-six turns."
Bādá (Eight Thoroughfares) and Jiǔwěi (Nine East-West Roads)
The Ěryǎ states:
"Eight thoroughfares meeting is called chóngqī."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"When the craftsmen built the capital,
there were nine north-south and nine east-west roads,
the main roads being nine tracks wide."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Within the capital means inside the city walls.
Both the north-south and east-west roads
could accommodate nine tracks.
Track refers to the width of a rut."
Lùxī (Deer Path) and Mǎjì (Horse Tracks)
The Zhōuyì states:
"Gèn represents jìnglù (small paths)."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"Paths in the fields are called jìnglù.
Gèn represents them because
it takes after the paths of deer and hares in the mountains."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the Shuǐjīng states:
"South of Jìnchāng Commandery and at the Mǎtígǔ in Guǎngwǔ,
on a large rock there are horse tracks,
as if naturally formed by treading in mud.
Therefore, the local custom calls it the Tiānmǎ Jìng (Heavenly Horse Path)."
Jiǔmò (Nine Lanes) and Sìqú (Four-Way Intersection)
The Hàn Gōngdiàn Shū states:
"Within Cháng'ān there were nine mò (lanes)."
Hé Fǎshèng's Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"In the second year of the Shēngpíng era of Emperor Mù,
an edict stated:
'The Cìfēi Commander Wáng Ráo suddenly presented me with poison to ward off evil.
This is an inauspicious object;
how could it be rashly presented?'
Thereupon, he immediately had Ráo whipped two hundred times,
ordered Diànzhōng Sūn Yún to supervise,
and had it burned at a four-way intersection."
Yíng Zhōng (Welcoming the Bell) and Xùn Duó (Proclaiming with the Wooden Clapper)
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"There was a state called Fēngyóu in Zhōngshān.
Zhì Bó wanted to attack it but had no way.
He cast a large bell,
two cart-widths square, to give to them.
The lord of Fēngyóu
cut away the banks and filled the streams to welcome the bell.
[Zhì Bó] then attacked,
and Fēngyóu was thus destroyed."
The Shū states:
"Every year in the first month of spring,
the qiúrén proclaims with a wooden clapper on the roads."
Jiāohuì (Intersection) and Duōqí (Many Forks)
The Ěryǎ states:
"Five thoroughfares meeting is called kāng."
Sūn Yán's commentary states:
"Kāng means joy.
It is the joyful intersection of roads."
The Lièzǐ states:
"A neighbor of Yángzǐ lost a sheep.
He led his family and asked Yángzǐ's servant boy to chase it.
Yángzǐ said,
'Losing one sheep, why so many pursuers?'
They replied,
'There are many forked roads.'
When they returned,
he asked if they had caught the sheep.
They said,
'No.
Among the many forked roads,
there were further forks.
We did not know where it went,
so we returned.'
Yángzǐ said,
'The great road loses sheep because of its many forks;
scholars lose their lives because of their many methods.'"
Hidden Gold Piled Stones
The Book of Han states:
"Jiǎ Shān said:
'The Qín dynasty extended eastward to the farthest reaches of Yān and Qí,
and southward to the utmost limits of Wú and Yuè.
The imperial roads were fifty paces wide.
They were paved with golden hammers,
and planted with green pines,
making the galloping roads so magnificent
that they reached this extent.'"
The annotation says:
"Hidden means to construct."
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"Wáng Bà served as the Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ.
He repaired the Fēihú Road to Píngchéng,
piling stones and spreading earth
for over three hundred lǐ."
Three Avenues Nine Tracks
Bān Gù's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"Opening up the broad roads of three avenues,
establishing the twelve thoroughfare gates."
"Nine tracks" is seen in the narrative.
Bamboo Fences Planted Locust Trees
Huán Jì's Records of Wú states:
"In the second year of the Tiānjì era,
the Commandant of the Guards, Cén Hūn, submitted a memorial to repair the hundred offices.
From the palace gate to the Vermilion Bird Bridge,
government offices were built lining both sides of the road.
Moreover, broad roads were opened,
causing men and women to walk separately.
High walls were built along both sides of the road,
covered with tiles,
or bamboo fences were made."
Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Qín states:
"After Fú Jiān conquered Yān and Zhào,
from Cháng'ān to the various provinces,
he planted locust and willow trees lining both sides of the roads.
There was one pavilion every twenty lǐ,
and one lodge every forty lǐ.
Travelers obtained supplies along the route,
and merchants and artisans conducted trade on the roads."
Establishing Border Stations Arranging Pavilions
The Discourses of the States states:
"The Zhōu system had it that:
'Trees were arranged to mark the roads,
and border stations were established to guard the roads.'"
This refers to setting up officials as inspectors.
The Records of the Eastern Lodge states:
"Wèi Sà served as the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
He cut through mountains to open roads,
and arranged pavilions and established post stations."
Slaying the Serpent Burning the Poison
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Hàn Gāozǔ, as a village head, was escorting laborers to Líshān.
At night, passing through a marsh,
there was a serpent blocking the road.
Gāozǔ drew his sword and slew the serpent,
cutting it in two,
and the path opened for several lǐ."
"Burning the poison" is mentioned in the annotation for "four thoroughfares."
Wrapping Horses' Hooves Overturning Wheels
Rèn Yù's Records of Yìzhōu states:
"The river bends along the Zuǒdān Road,
according to the map, located north of Yīnpíng County,
west of Chéngdū.
The road is extremely perilous,
where Dèng Ài wrapped his horses' hooves and suspended his chariots."
Pān Ní's "Rhapsody on Treacherous Roads" states:
"The road is deep and the land narrow,
the slopes steep and the tracks long.
Wheels and carriages overturn,
men and horses collapse and stiffen."
Cassia Roads and Orchid Paths Seven Lanes and Nine Byways
Liú Yìgōng's poem states:
"The flying stream bounds the cassia road,
the deep forest covers the orchid path."
Cáo Zhí's poem states:
"East and west, traversing seven lanes,
north and south, crossing nine byways."
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Poem on the Road While on Duty to Zhūfāng"
Parting from the dampness, I leave the imperial capital,
ascending and packing to serve the imperial majesty.
The vast wilderness connects to the azure sea,
the linked suburbs trace back to the Hé region.
Sunlight shines on the Green Hill Island,
dust rises from the land of Hándān.
The river shifts, the forest banks grow faint,
the cliffs deep, the misty peaks layered.
The harsh year withers the grass on the stone steps,
the noon cold scatters the trees on the ridges.
Tangled and lush, the evening whirlwind rolls,
stumbling and faltering, the evening clouds lie low.
My lofty aspirations are not easily followed,
my banner-bearing body truly hard to govern.
Do I admire the phoenix tree of Zī Palace?
Just now, I decline the bamboo of the Rabbit Garden.
What words can express this constrained heart?
My lost tracks may yet be recovered."
Suí Sūn Wànshòu's "Poem on Returning Eastward on the Road"
Neither official studies nor governance achieved,
my heart of return naturally unsettled.
My hometown still a thousand lǐ away,
in the mountain forests, gibbons cry at night.
People grieve, the cloud colors turn bleak,
the traveler's mind accustomed to the wind's sound.
Though my constrained sorrows have many threads,
all are but one wounding sentiment."
Táng Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Poem Expressing My Feelings on the Journey"
Bó Jiāo exiled north of the frontier,
Tíng Bó sent to Liáodōng.
Why am I, then, a traveler,
alone guarding within Yúntái?
The road is long, already dusk falls,
times peaceful, yet this path reaches its end.
Uprooting my heart, I mourn the shore grass,
half-dead, I fall like the cliff-side paulownia.
My eyes follow the geese of Héngyáng,
my feelings wounded by the riverside maples.
Fortune, ah, truly lies hidden,
now, indeed, hard to attain.
A true man has his own aspirations,
why grieve that office is not just?"
Chén Xú Líng's "Stele Inscription for the Dānyáng to Shàngyōng Road"
The later king bestowed virtue,
upon the myriad common people.
Lofty writings mirror the constellations,
wondrous meanings commune with the divine.
Achievements surpassing the transfer to Xià,
merits exceeding the entry into Qín.
The time is that of Great Accumulation,
the hexagram reaching that of Fellowship.
Benevolent rain just drips,
the meditative branch alone springs.
The emperor's virtue is profound,
the imperial grace exceedingly deep.
Observing Yǔ's traces,
we see Yáo's heart."
Markets Fifteenth
The Fēngsú Tōng states:
"Market (市 shì)
means 'to rely upon' (恃 shì).
It means that after exchange and trade, people depart,
relying upon it to avoid scarcity."
According to the Zhōu Yì‧Xì Cí:
"Shénnóng Shì established markets at midday,
attracting the people of the world.
He gathered the goods of the world,
people exchanged and then departed,
each obtaining what they needed,
this was probably derived from the hexagram Shì Hé."
Shì Hé,
is the name of a hexagram.
It speaks of establishing methods to bring things together.
Another version says:
Zhùróng created the market,
as seen in the Shì Běn.
Sòng Zhōng's commentary says:
"Zhùróng,
was a minister of Zhuānxū,
and served as the Fire Official for Gāoxīn Shì."
The Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo states:
"Shénnóng created the market.
When the Gāoyáng Shì declined,
the market officials did not maintain it,
so Zhùróng restored the market."
The Zhōu Lǐ says that after establishing a state, a market is set up,
its stations are arranged,
its order is established,
its shops are regulated,
its goods and wealth are displayed,
and measures are issued.
When establishing a state, the court must face the front and the market be at the back.
The king establishes the court,
the queen establishes the market,
an image of yīn and yáng complementing each other.
The Sī Shì oversees the governance, education, administration, and punishments of the market,
its measures and prohibitions,
using stations and order to divide the land and organize the market,
using arranged shops to distinguish goods and stabilize the market,
using administrative orders to prohibit wasteful goods and equalize the market,
using merchants to increase wealth and circulate currency.
The Grand Market,
is held at midday,
with the hundred clans as the main participants;
the Morning Market,
is held in the morning,
with merchants as the main participants;
the Evening Market,
is held in the evening,
with peddlers as the main participants.
Again, the Fēngsú Tōng states:
"Market is also called 'market well' (市井 shìjǐng),
meaning that when people go to the market to sell something,
they should wash it at the well,
make it fragrant and clean,
and then go to the market."
Another explanation says:
"In ancient times, twenty mǔ made one jǐng (well-field unit),
and markets were established around wells,
hence the term."
Also, market lanes are called huán,
market gates are called huì,
and lanes are called hóng.
Seen in Yán Yánzhī's Zuǎn Yào.
Empty spaces within the market are called chán,
seen in Zhèng Zhòng's commentary on the Zhōu Lǐ.
Another says it refers to market dwellings.
Market towers are called flag pavilions (旗亭 qítíng).
Zhāng Héng's "Xī Jīng Fù" says:
"Flag pavilions stretch for five lǐ."
Xuē Zōng's commentary says:
"Market towers have pavilions erected on top."
As for market names,
there are Nine Markets, Four Markets, Three Markets.
The Sān Fǔ Jiù Shì says:
"Cháng'ān had nine markets."
The Dānyáng Jì says:
"The capital had four markets."
The Luòyáng Jì says:
"Luòyáng had three markets."
One version says the Zhōu Lǐ states:
"If markets are held morning and evening,
then there are three markets."
Square Market,
seen in the Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú.
Gold Market,
the Luòyáng Jì says:
"The Gold Market was within the great city."
Garden Market, Fighting Arena Market,
the Dānyáng Jì says:
"The garden city market was called Yuànlíng,
and at Yuànlíng there was a Fighting Arena Market."
Capital Market,
the Liè Xiān Zhuàn says:
"Xuán Sú sold medicine at the capital market."
Capital Market.
Seen in Wáng Sù's "Jǐngfú Diàn Fù".
Establish Stations / Open the Grounds
"Establish Stations" is seen in the narrative.
Bān Gù's "Xī Dū Fù" says:
"The nine markets opened their grounds,
goods were arrayed and lanes divided."
Yīn Palace / Qí Palace
Tàigōng's Liù Tāo says:
"King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
and captured two ladies.
He asked them:
'As the Yīn state was about to perish,
were there any portents?'
They said:
'The Yīn ruler delighted in building palaces,
the largest of his palaces had nine markets.'" The Zhànguó Cè says:
"As the Qí state was about to perish,
were there any portents?"
One of them said:
"Duke Huán of Qí had seven markets in his palace."
Crane Dance / Wolf Enters
Zhào Yè's Wú Yuè Chūnqiū says:
"King Hé Lǘ of Wú had a daughter,
who resented the king for eating steamed fish before her,
and so committed suicide.
Hé Lǘ grieved for her,
and buried her west of the state outside the Chāng Gate.
He then had white cranes dance in the Wú market,
ordering ten thousand people to follow and watch."
Liú Xiàng's Hóng Fàn Zhuàn says:
"In the fourth year of King Huì of Qín,
a wolf entered the market of Xiányáng.
In the sixth year of King Zhāo,
a wolf again entered the market of Xiányáng."
Read Books / Wash Utensils
Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū says:
"Wáng Chōng, styled Zhòngrèn,
was from Kuàijī.
His family was poor and had no books,
so he often wandered the market shops of Luòyáng,
reading the books for sale.
He could memorize them after a single glance,
and thus became broadly learned in the many classics."
The Hàn Shū says:
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú went with Wén Jūn to Línqióng,
sold all their carriages and horses to buy wine,
and had Wén Jūn tend the wine shop counter.
Xiàngrú personally worked alongside the hired laborers,
washing utensils in the market."
Hundred Goods / Myriad Merchants
The Guǎn Zǐ says:
"The market
is the standard for goods,
therefore when the hundred goods are cheap, the hundred profits are obtained."
Already seen in the narrative.
Zuǒ Sī's "Shǔ Dū Fù" says:
"Adjacent to Shǎochéng,
connecting to its west.
Where marketplaces converge,
a river of myriad merchants.
Rows of lanes a hundred layers deep,
shops arrayed in thousands vast."
Transmit Jade / Suspend Gold
The Shǐ Jì says:
"Jade caskets come from Kūnshān,
bright moon pearls come from the four seas,
transmitted and sold in the market.
When sages obtain them,
they consider them great treasures."
It also says:
"Lǚ Bùwéi, as Chancellor,
gathered scholars of various arts,
had them write down what they knew,
and compiled the Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
He displayed it at the gate of the Xiányáng market,
suspended a thousand pieces of gold above it,
stating that anyone who could add a single character
would be given the thousand gold.
At the time, no one was able to."
Play Chí / Strike Zhù
The Shǐ Jì says:
"Wǔ Zǐxū fled Zhāoguān,
traveling by night and hiding by day.
When he reached Língshuǐ,
having no means to feed himself,
he played the chí to beg for food in the Wú market,
and later became a hegemon with Hé Lǘ of Wú."
It also says:
"When Jīng Kē reached Yān,
he loved and befriended a skilled player of the zhù.
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù,
and Kē sang along in the market,
enjoying themselves together.
After a while they wept together,
as if no one else was around."
Cloud-like Canopies, Stars-like Abundance
Wáng Yì's "Luòyáng Rhapsody" states:
"Three markets were first established,
Shops opened and boundaries set.
Rows of stalls stretch like clouds,
Tall buildings rise in layers."
Zuǒ Sī's "Shǔ Capital Rhapsody" states:
"Adjoining the Lesser City,
Connecting to its west,
Where markets and shops converge,
A river of ten thousand merchants.
Hundredfold rows of lanes,
Thousands upon thousands of shops arrayed.
Goods and wealth piled like mountains,
Fine silks abundant as stars."
Méi Fú and Hán Kāng
The Book of Hàn states:
"When Wáng Mǎng brought chaos to governance,
Méi Fú one morning abandoned his wife and children and left for Jiǔjiāng.
To this day, legends say he became an immortal.
Later, some saw Méi Fú in Kuàijī,
Having changed his name and become a gatekeeper at the Wú market."
Fàn Yè's Book of the Later Hàn states:
"Hán Kāngbó,
Courtesy name Bóxiū,
Was a man of Bàlíng, Jīngzhào.
He often gathered herbs on famous mountains,
And sold medicine at the Cháng'ān market,
Never haggling over prices."
Passing by Shops and Leaning at the Gate
Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Wú Capital Rhapsody" states:
"Light carriages rein in to pass through the lanes,
Towered ships hoist sails to glide past the shops."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Embroidering fine patterns is not as good as leaning by the market gate,
This saying refers to the means of the poor engaged in petty trades."
Jīng's Drinking and Niè's Butchering
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"After Jīng Kē arrived in Yān,
He drank in the Yān market."
Already seen in the annotation for "Playing the Zhù."
It also states:
"Niè Zhèng,
Was a man of Zhǐ.
Having killed a man and fleeing from enemies,
He went with his mother and elder sister to Qí,
And made butchering his livelihood.
Lowering his aspirations and humbling himself,
He lived among the market commoners."
Bīn Pavilion and Hú Village
Huán Tán's New Discourses states:
"The Bīn Pavilion district of Fúfēng,
Is said to be where the Great King originally dwelled.
Its people have a gathering,
Saying:
'If we do not hold night markets together,
As if not keeping to the appointed time,
Then there will be great disasters.'" The Yuèjué states:
"The Wú market,
Was built by Lord Chūnshēn,
Located in Hú Village."
Jìzhǔ's Divination and Jūnpíng's Augury
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ practiced divination at the eastern market of Cháng'ān."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Yán Jūnpíng practiced divination and augury in the Chéngdū market.
He considered divination a lowly trade,
Yet one that could benefit the masses.
If there were wicked, improper, or unjust matters,
He would speak of them according to the milfoil and tortoise shells."
Xìnlíng's Visit and Yíliáo's Seclusion
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"In Wèi there was a recluse named Hóu Yíng,
Aged seventy,
His family was poor,
And he served as a gatekeeper at the Dàliáng city gate.
Lord Xìnlíng of Wèi, the Lord of Xìnlíng, held a grand banquet for guests.
The lord, with his carriage and retinue,
Vacated the left seat and personally went to welcome him.
Master Hóu said to the lord:
'I have a friend among the butchers in the market,
I wish to trouble your carriage and retinue to visit him.'" The Biographies of Former Worthies of the Chǔ State states:
"Xióng Yíliáo,
Was a man of Chǔ.
He lived in seclusion south of the market,
And did not yield to the times."
Jìn Chéng Bóyángpíng's "Rhapsody on the Joyful Market"
The market's rise,
Began with Emperor Yán's creation.
Gathering goods and wealth for utility,
No other labor compares.
Thus, a thousand lanes are arrayed,
Hundreds of clans dwell within,
Streets and avenues face each other,
Connected beams and adjoining houses.
Then, eyes speak and brows flicker,
Noses twitch and mouths move.
Wisdom is discussed within inches,
Profit is sought down to the slightest fraction.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānyú's "Poem on Watching the Market Close"
The flag pavilion overlooks the imperial road,
The wandering gaze briefly turns the carriage.
It is not following dancing cranes,
But pondering dried fish.
Through the tortoise, one knows Jìzhǔ,
By the wine, one sees Xiàngrú.
At midday, people already gather,
By dusk, they still do not disperse.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on the Market Full at Noon"
Cloudy towers give rise to brocade-like clouds,
The flag pavilion bright under the beautiful sun.
Dust flies on the roads of the three markets,
Canopies enter the ninefold city.
Bamboo-leaf wine fills the cup,
Peach blossoms adorn light ribbons.
Only the struggle for fame and profit is seen,
Who knows the sentiment of great seclusion?
Jìn Wáng Biāozhī's "Edict on Regulating the Market"
The ancients shared the market and court,
Did they not consider that where the masses gather,
One must surely eliminate misconduct?
Recently inspecting the Shānyīn market,
Much is found not according to law.
Some shops are in disarray.
Some merchants evade taxes,
Falsely using the names of the powerful,
Monopolizing the profits of trade,
Oppressing the weak and humble.
They seize control of crucial locations.
Subordinate cities, indulging in leniency,
Also act in this manner.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Response to the Edict on Moving the Market"
In the past, the great Confucian Zhāng Kǎi,
Still moved the Hóngnóng market.
The skilled calligrapher Yí Guān,
Still attracted guests to the wine shop.
Moreover, one whose virtue encompasses Xún Zhōu,
Whose reputation surpasses Liáng Chǔ.
Scholars who admire the wind and cherish righteousness,
Raise sleeves to form curtains;
Those who lie before chariots or cling to carriages,
Shoulder to shoulder, follow one another.
Thus, the place where Wáng Chōng read books,
Is moved far to the desolate outskirts;
The place where Shí Bāo sold iron,
Is instead moved to the river's edge.
The sage's virtue is humble,
Unsettled by noise and crowding,
Wishing to have the flute-playing and crane-dancing,
Return to the old market grounds.
Let the fortune-tellers and mutton butchers,
Please depart from the new market gate.
Yet those who trade goods delight in staying,
The multitude of Bīn and Qí are hard to disperse.
Jìn Chéng Gōngsuí's "Admonition for the Market Chief"
Trading to have what is lacked,
The market and court have their places.
People rely on them for resources,
Goods are arranged accordingly.
After trading, they withdraw,
Each obtaining what they need.
When Cáo Shēn served as Chancellor of Qí,
He governed with purity and righteousness.
Evil could not be disturbed,
Entrustments had their place.
I, the market official in charge of shops,
Dare to inform those in charge.
Water Clock, First
The Liang Dynasty's *Classic of Water Clocks* states:
"The creation of water clocks
likely originated in the time of Xuānyuán,
and was used throughout the Xià and Shāng dynasties."
The *Zhōu Guān* says:
"The Clepsydra Officer guards them with fire and water,
dividing the day and night.
In winter,
he heats water in a tripod cauldron until it boils,
and then pours it (to prevent freezing)."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"In winter, water freezes,
so he heats water to boiling and pours it,
meaning he pours it on the clepsydra."
The Liang Dynasty's *Classic of Water Clocks* states:
"At the winter solstice,
the daytime clepsydra measures forty-five marks.
After the winter solstice, the days lengthen;
every nine days, one mark is added,
until the summer solstice,
when the daytime clepsydra measures sixty-five marks.
After the summer solstice, the days shorten;
every nine days, one mark is subtracted."
Perhaps this was a method inherited from the Qín,
applied in the Hàn dynasty.
Hándān's *Wǔjīng Zhéyí* states:
"According to the Hàn system,
also, three days before the winter solstice during the day,
and three days after the winter solstice,
the daytime clepsydra measures forty-five marks,
and the nighttime fifty-five marks.
Three days before the summer solstice during the day,
and three days after the summer solstice,
the daytime clepsydra measures sixty-five marks,
and the nighttime thirty-five marks."
The *Yuánjiā Qǐjū Zhù* states:
"Using sunrise and sunset to determine day and night,
at the winter solstice, daytime is forty marks,
and at the summer solstice, nighttime should also be forty marks;
at the summer solstice, daytime is sixty marks,
and at the winter solstice, nighttime should also be sixty marks.
At the spring and autumn equinoxes,
day and night are each fifty marks.
