Now, the nighttime limit is reduced.
Before sunrise, after sunset, and during the twilight periods,
two and a half marks each are added to the daytime.
Thus, at the summer solstice, daytime is sixty-five marks,
at the winter solstice, daytime is forty-five marks,
and at the equinoxes, daytime is fifty-five marks."
Zhāng Héng's *System of the Water-Powered Armillary Sphere* states:
"Using bronze to make vessels,
stacked in two tiers with a difference in height.
Filled with clear water,
each has an opening at the bottom.
A jade dragon spouts water into two pots,
the right for night,
the left for day."
Yīn Kuí's *Water Clock Method* states:
"The apparatus has three tiers,
all circular with a diameter of one foot,
standing at different heights on a water chariot with a dripping mechanism,
with a golden dragon's mouth spouting water.
It turns and pours into the dripping mechanism's warp and weft,
with a cast golden timekeeper on the lid,
complete with robes and cap,
holding an arrow with both hands."
Lǐ Lán's *Water Clock Method* states:
"Using bronze to make a siphon,
to draw water from the vessel,
and spout it from a silver dragon's mouth."
Counterweight Vessel and Balancing Channel
Lǐ Lán's *Water Clock Method* states:
"Store water in a vessel,
use bronze to make a siphon,
shaped like a curved hook,
to draw water from the vessel.
Spout it from a silver dragon's mouth into a counterweight vessel.
One shēng of leaking water,
weighs one jīn on the scale,
corresponding to one mark of time."
Yīn Kuí's *Water Clock Method* states:
"The leaking water is all spouted from a golden dragon's mouth at the bottom of the vessel,
turned and poured into the dripping mechanism's warp and weft,
flowing into the balancing channel below."
Flowing Pearls and Arrow Holder
Lǐ Lán's *Water Clock Method* states:
"Using a jade pot and jade tube with flowing pearls for a horse-borne traveling clepsydra.
Flowing pearls
is another name for mercury."
Zhāng Héng's *System of the Water-Powered Armillary Sphere* states:
"Holding the arrow with the left hand,
pointing to the marks with the right hand,
to distinguish the early and late hours of the day."
Timekeeper and Mark Registrar
Yīn Kuí's *Water Clock Method* states:
"From noon to midnight,
is also fifty marks.
There is a lid on the pot's mouth,
inside which a celestial float carries the arrow out through the lid.
A cast golden timekeeper is on the lid."
Huán Tán's *New Discourses* states:
"When I served as a court gentleman,
I was in charge of the clepsydra.
Dryness, dampness, cold, and warmth cause variations in measurement,
hence there is dusk, dawn, day, and night,
cross-referenced with gnomon shadows."
Bronze Scribe and Golden Attendant
The *Jìn Qǐjū Zhù* states:
"In the twelfth year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era,
the officials reported that the crown prince's palace was newly established,
but lacked a water clock.
After consulting the bronze water clock of the Yǒng'ān Palace,
a Clepsydra Scribe was appointed."
Zhāng Héng's *System of the Water-Powered Armillary Sphere* states:
"A cast golden bronze immortal stands by the left pot,
and a golden attendant stands by the right pot."
Star Scribe and Golden Attendant
The *Tiānwén Yàojí* states:
"The Female Scribe star is northwest of the Pillar,
the Female Scribe turns the clepsydra, marking movement and stillness."
"Golden Attendant" is explained in the note for "Golden Attendant."
Three Drums and One Bell
Wèi Hóng's *Old Ceremonials of Hàn* states:
"At the beginning of summer and autumn, daytime is sixty-two marks.
At the summer solstice, daytime is sixty-five marks.
When the nighttime clepsydra lacks five marks,
five drums are beaten;
when it lacks three marks,
three drums are beaten."
Lì Shàncháng's *Commentary on the Water Classic* states:
"The east gate of Luòyáng's Jīnyōng City,
called the Hánchūn Gate,
has a retreat gate to the north.
On the western side of the city wall, observation towers are placed every fifty paces,
with a bell placed in a lookout hut,
to harmonize with the clepsydra drums."
Nine Days and Five Watches
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Continued Book of Hàn* states:
"Huò Róng memorialized, saying
the water clock's rate changes by one grade every nine days,
not corresponding with the heavens,
unlike the Xià calendar which matches the gnomon shadows.
The clepsydra's forty-eight arrows,
with gnomon shadows as marks,
have little discrepancy."
Wèi Hóng's *Old Ceremonials of Hàn* states:
"The five watches: First Watch, Second Watch, Third Watch, Fourth Watch, Fifth Watch."
Lù Jī's (Lù Shìhéng) *Rhapsody on the Water Clock*
The inch-long tube, bowed down, attests to the sincerity of yīn and yáng;
The foot-long gnomon, raised up, anticipates the cycles of the sun and moon.
The dark bird suspended, and the eight winds respond according to their nature;
The jade sighting-tube established, and heaven and earth cannot deceive.
Having exhausted the spiritual and fully transformed,
Also setting the clepsydra to examine the hours,
Then lifting the golden pot to the southern net,
Hiding dark waters to the northern restraint.
Imitating the full and diminished tones of tuned bells,
Revealing the low and high as steps.
Spurting the hanging spring to shoot afar,
Striding the flying path to gather remotely.
The hidden yīn creature receives the waves,
Swallowing the constant flow as if ladling.
Therefore, its coming resembles divine creation,
Its going is like ghostly illusion.
Mouth receiving, chest spewing,
Water without stagnant gullet.
Form finer than a solitary silkworm's thread,
Passing like a chariot of heaven's lightning.
In harmony with the four seasons to achieve the utmost,
Pointing to dusk and dawn without end.
Its structure is simple,
Yet its performance is sincere;
Its borrowed materials are coarse,
Yet its application is refined.
The accumulated water does not exceed one bell,
The guided flow does not exceed one bamboo strip.
Yet those who use heaven rely on its sensitivity,
Those who divide earth depend on its evenness.
Subtle listeners borrow its acuity,
True observers avail themselves of its clarity.
Truly a marvelous technique for probing the profound,
Though without spirit, it is as if numinous.
Brocade Canopies and Silk Curtains
The *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"When Confucius returned to Wèi,
he saw the lady inside a brocade canopy.
Confucius bowed facing north with his head to the ground,
and the lady bowed twice from within the canopy."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Shí Yí Jì* states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn used coral for his bed,
and purple brocade for his canopy."
It also states: "Emperor Wǔ enjoyed traveling incognito.
At the pleasure palaces beside the ponds,
he used lacquered pillars
and spread curtains of black silk.
The vessels, clothing, and imperial carriages
all favored the color black."
Planning Strategies and Compiling Calendars
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"In the first month of the sixth year of Hàn,
when meritorious officials were enfeoffed,
Zhāng Liáng had never achieved any military merit in battle.
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
'Formulating strategies within the command tent,
and securing victory a thousand *lǐ* away—
this is Zǐfáng's (Zhāng Liáng's) achievement.'"
Liú Xīn's *Letter to Yáng Zǐyún* states:
"Xiāo Hé created the laws,
Zhāng Cāng compiled the calendar;
both were completed within the curtains of the tent
and presented at the king's gate."
Weaving Fine Threads and Displaying Ornate Silks
Liú Xiàng's *Shuō Yuàn* states:
"Yànzǐ reported to Duke Jǐng of Qí:
'Moreover, gather bushels and pecks, however small,
to fill the granaries;
weave together fine, sparse threads
to form canopies and curtains.'"
Gě Hóng's *Shénxiān Zhuàn* states:
"The Eight Lords of Huáinán came to the gate of Huáinán King Ān.
All had white hair and beards.
The king wished for them to be younger,
so the eight lords all transformed into youths of fifteen or sixteen.
The gate officer reported this to Ān.
Hearing this, he did not even put on his shoes
but immediately went out to welcome them.
He ascended the Terrace of Immortal Longing,
displayed curtains of ornate silk,
and set out mats of ivory."
Ránmíng Recites and Yánnián Rests
The *Dōng Guān Hàn Jì* states:
"Zhāng Huàn,
styled Ránmíng,
was sent to the Xiōngnú.
The Xiūchú and the Wūhuán of Shuòfāng rebelled together.
They burned the gate of the General Who Crosses Liáo,
deployed encampments across the barren land,
with beacon fires visible to each other.
The troops were greatly terrified,
each wanting to flee.
Huàn sat calmly within the tent,
reciting texts with his disciples,
composed as ever.
The soldiers gradually calmed down."
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"Liú Yánnián, King of Jiāngdū, served as a general.
He was skilled at pacifying and commanding his troops.
For resting and sleeping, he used only cloth curtains."
Wáng Róng of Southern Qí's "Poem on the Curtain"
Fortunate to be adorned with pearls,
Enveloping your pillars, layer upon layer.
When the moon shines, it does not refuse to be rolled up;
When the wind comes, it always lifts lightly.
Often gathering the scent of the golden censer,
At times halting the sound of the jade zither.
I only wish to set out a jar of wine,
With orchid lamps shining through the night.
Screen, Third
The *Shì Míng* states:
"A screen (píngfēng)
is to block the wind (zhàng fēng).
The yǐ is placed behind,
for one to lean upon."
The *Lǐ Jì* states:
"The Son of Heaven stands facing the yǐ."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The yǐ
is a screen."
It also states:
"The Son of Heaven stands with his back to the yǐ,
facing south."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"'With his back to the yǐ' means
a screen with an axe pattern is placed between the door and window."
The *Zhōu Guān* states:
"The official in charge of arrangements sets up the imperial dais (huáng dǐ)."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The dǐ
is the rear panel.
The screen's dǐ
is dyed with feathers resembling phoenixes as decoration."
Xiè Chéng's *Hòu Hàn Shū* states:
"When Zhèng Hóng was Grand Commandant,
he recommended Dì Wǔ Lún for Minister of Works.
Lún's rank was lower.
During the New Year's audience each year,
Hóng would humbly bow.
The emperor inquired and learned the reason,
so he ordered a mica screen to be placed
to separate them."
This then became a precedent.
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
"After Tàizǔ pacified Liǔchéng,
he distributed the captured vessels.
There was a plain screen,
which he gave to Máo Jiè, saying:
'You possess the demeanor of the ancients,
so I bestow upon you the attire of the ancients.'"
The *Qí Shū* states:
"In Xiāngyáng, tomb robbers opened an ancient grave
and obtained a jade screen."
Wú Jūn's *Qí Chūnqiū* states:
"Yídū King Liú Kēng,
at age ten,
was discussing past words and deeds with Jí Jǐngyào.
An attendant accidentally knocked over a screen made of nánmu burl wood, which fell on his back.
His expression did not change,
and he continued speaking without pause."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Shí Yí Jì* states:
"Dǒng Yǎn set up a purple glass screen."
The *Xī Jīng Zá Jì* states:
"Guǎngchuān King Liú Qùjí opened the tomb of King Āi of Wèi
and found a stone screen."
It also states: "The painted wooden screen in the Zhāoyáng Hall
was like spider silk threads."
Green-Dyed and White Characters
The *Sòng Yuánjiā Qǐjū Zhù* states:
"In the sixteenth year,
Censor-in-Chief Liú Zhēn memorialized:
'It is rumored that the former Governor of Guǎngchuān, Wéi Lǎng,
while in Guǎngzhōu, had made twenty-three silver-coated lacquer screens
and one green-dyed screen.
I request that Wéi Lǎng be held accountable based on this matter and stripped of his former official position.'"
Wáng Yǎn's *Sòng Chūnqiū* states:
"Emperor Míng had many taboos and prohibitions.
The banned and avoided items numbered in the dozens or hundreds.
He also disliked the character 'white.'
On screens inscribed with famous texts from antiquity,
if there was the character 'white,'
he would have it changed,
replacing it with black, yellow, red, or purple
as appropriate."
Mica and Fire-Arranged
The *Xī Jīng Zá Jì* states:
"When Zhào Fēiyàn became empress,
her younger sister presented her with a mica screen, a 'returning wind' mat, and a seven-flower fan."
The *Shí Yí Jì* states:
"Dǒng Yǎn once rested in the Room of Prolonged Clarity.
Above was set a fire-arranged screen,
arrayed with candles of divine hemp."
Two Sets for Taking a Consort and Four Panels for Virtuous Women
The *Jìn Dōnggōng Jiù Shì* states:
"When the crown prince takes a consort,
there are two sets of four-panel screens for dressing the hair,
and fourteen panels of brocade-ground screens,
with bronze ring fasteners."
Liú Xiàng's *Qī Lüè Bié Lù* states:
"Your subject Xiàng, together with the Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate, Xīn, collated the *Liè Nǚ Zhuàn*.
We grouped similar types together into seven chapters,
to illustrate the effects of fortune, misfortune, glory, and disgrace,
and the distinctions between right and wrong, gain and loss.
These were painted onto four panels of a screen."
Sūn Liàng's Carved Auspicious Signs and Shí Jílóng's Painted Immortals
Cuī Bào's *Gǔ Jīn Zhù* states:
"Sūn Liàng made a glass screen,
carved with one hundred and twenty kinds of auspicious response images."
Lù Huì's *Yèzhōng Jì* states:
"Shí Jílóng made a screen with gold-inlaid folding joints,
covered with white silk.
It was painted with righteous men, immortals, birds, and beasts."
"Rhapsody on the Screen" by Liú Ān of the Hàn Dynasty
This screen alone,
Comes from a deep valley.
Its roots are deep, its branches lush,
It is called a lofty tree.
Solitary by nature, humble and weak,
It fears the strong clans of metal.
Uprooted and moved to different soil,
It lies prostrate in the ditch.
Drifting and in peril,
With no safe place to set foot.
Longing to be among the weeds,
Where the woods have scrub oaks.
Yet often without chance,
Grieving in sorrow and bitterness.
Heaven enlightens my heart,
I encounter a modest salary.
The court gentleman repairs and arranges it,
Gathering and collecting the discarded plain wood.
The master craftsman works on it,
Carving, engraving, cutting, and hewing.
Though the surface is cracked and peeling,
Its heart is truly steadfast and sincere.
Equal to transformed vessels and objects,
It shelters and shades the honored house.
Placed to the left and right,
Near the lord’s head and feet.
Relying on being completed and saved,
Its grace is vast and profound.
What kindness bestowed, what fortune met,
Sharing favor and receiving moistening grace.
Had it not met a benevolent person,
It would forever remain withered wood.
"Rhapsody on the Screen" by Qián Shèng of the Hàn Dynasty
The screen encircles completely,
Shielding my lord and king.
Layered blossoms and accumulated embroidery,
Piled jades and connected scepters.
Linked with patterned brocade,
Reflected in flowing yellow.
Painted with ancient heroes,
Majestic and lofty.
The feudal lords find it fitting,
Longevity without end.
"Screen Poem" by Xiāo Què of the Suí Dynasty
The Qín emperor approached Jiéshí,
The Hàn emperor visited the bright court.
Not merely for repeated tours and pleasures,
But truly out of love for long life.
Reading records, he knew the locations of provinces,
Viewing maps, he saw the shapes of mountains.
At dawn recognizing the aura of immortals,
At night discerning the Shǎowēi star.
Ingesting silver, he had secret arts,
Steaming cinnabar, he transmitted ancient scriptures.
The wind shakes the hundred-shadowed trees,
Flowers fall in the Ten-Thousand-Spring Pavilion.
The flying stream appears whiter up close,
The clustered bamboos seem greener from afar.
Carefree, preserving clarity and ease,
Thereby maintaining joy in nature and disposition.
Zhōu Yǔxìn's Chant on "Screen Poem"
The high tower spans a thousand xún,
The layered eaves align a hundred chǐ.
Clouds pass, three parts nearer,
Flowers fly, twice as low.
Playing the flute near white cranes,
Mirror-gazing, dancing like a pheasant.
Why laboriously worry about dusk?
The night crow has not yet cried.
Another Poem
From Sānwēi emerge phoenix wings,
Across Jiǔbǎn pass dragon scales.
The road is high, trees within the mountains,
Clouds are low, people on horseback.
Echoing cliffs, the sound of spring water drips,
Deep valleys, birds sing of spring.
Halting the horse to come and ask,
Surely knowing there is one surnamed Qín.
Inscription by Lǐ Yóu
When stored away, it lies hidden and secluded,
When used, it is set up and displayed.
Standing, it must be upright and straight,
Placed, it must be square and proper.
Blocking wind and evil influences,
Resisting fog and dew.
Serving above, shielding below,
Never losing its constancy.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Memorial Thanking for the Bestowal of a Green Lǜ Chess Piece Screen"
Your subject Gāng memorializes:
The imperial edict was conveyed by Wáng Fúhuì, who announced the imperial decree,
Bestowing upon me a green lǜ chess piece screen of twenty panels.
It exhibits the skill of Bān and Mǎ,
Combined with the thoughtfulness of Cáo and Shǐ.
Equal to the green jade of Tiāntāi,
Mingled with the fine names of water blossoms.
It makes the mica window
Ashamed of its beauty.
The琉璃扇
Feels inferior in its reflections.
Looking up, I receive your sacred kindness,
Gracefully bestowed, reaching down to me.
Joy follows the coming of grace,
My ears hear like a phoenix dancing.
Words are exhausted in gratitude,
Further resembling the three seals.
Unable to bear the sincerity of engraved gratitude,
I respectfully present this memorial to express thanks for your notice,
Respectfully submitted.
Curtains, Fourth
The Shìmíng says:
"Lián means lián (modesty),
To screen and conceal oneself is modesty and shame."
The Guǎngyǎ says:
"Chān,
Pronunciation bì yī fǎn,
Below pronounced dān.
Means lián."
Yáng Xióng's Fāngyán says:
"Between Sòng, Wèi, Chén, Chǔ, Jiāng, and Huái,
Bó is called qū,
Or called qū.
West of the pass it is called bó,
In Nánchǔ it is called péng bó."
The Shuōwén says:
"The shape that receives objects curvedly."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"The mausoleums and resting halls of the Hàn,
All use bamboo for curtains,
With water patterns and images of dragons and phoenixes."
The Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì says:
"Curtains and screens all have green cloth borders and trims."
Xiè Chuò's Sòng Shíyí says:
"Dài Míngbǎo enjoyed favor across dynasties,
His family accumulated a thousand in gold,
His eldest son was arrogant and dissolute.
He made a five-colored bead curtain,
Which Míngbǎo could not forbid."
The Sūnqīngzǐ says:
"A modest room with reed curtains and straw mats,
Can nourish the body."
Divine House with White Pearls, Numinous Pavilion with Kingfisher Feathers
The Hànwǔ Gùshì says:
"The emperor built a divine house,
Using white pearls for curtains and screens,
Secured with tortoiseshell,
And ivory for the slats."
The Dòngmíng Jì says:
"In the twentieth year of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
He built the Zhāolíng Pavilion,
With kingfisher feathers and fine hairs for curtains."
Zhāoyáng's Pearl Curtain, Míngguāng's Jade Screen
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"The Zhāoyáng Hall wove pearls into curtains,
When the wind arrived, they chimed,
Like gold, jade, pearls, and gems."
The Sānqín Jì says:
"The Míngguāng Palace is west of the Jiàntái,
Using gold, jade, pearls, and gems for screens."
Táng Tàizōng's "Poem on Curtains by the Civil and Military Emperor"
Unevenly hanging over jade windows,
Unfurling and reflecting in the orchid palace.
Pearl light sways the pale moon,
Bamboo shadows disturb the clear breeze.
Colors scatter on silver hooks,
Patterns slant within cassia doors.
Only when mingled with silks and satins,
Together they charm the rooms and lattices.
Southern Qí Yú Yán's "Chant on Curtains Poem"
When the dark porch meets the bright moon,
The purple hall on an autumn wind day.
Vaguely, the light of Confucian brilliance,
Dimly reflecting on faces and forms.
Clear dew hangs along the eaves,
Spider silk densely across the door.
Lifting it open, who will join me to face it?
Closing it to darkness, alone as if lost.
Suí Lú Sīdào's "Poem on Pearl Curtains"
The mirror-like curtain, bright about to gather,
Shining on the railing, colors nearing dawn.
Pitiable, sparse then dense,
Faintly reflecting the person by the window.
Floating clarity carries distant breezes,
Containing light, stirring fine dust.
Falling flowers brushed away time and again,
Awaiting the spring on the jade steps.
Beds, Fifth
The *Shìmíng* states:
"Chuáng (bed)
means zhuāng (to load),
that which is used to load oneself."
Yáng Xióng's *Fāngyán* states:
"Between Qí and Lǔ it is called zé,
meaning the bed boards.
Between Chén and Chǔ it is sometimes called zǐ,
its frame, between Běi Yàn and Cháoxiǎn, is called shù.
West of the Hánguān Pass,
between Qín and Jìn it is called gàng.
In Nán Chǔ's Zhào,
between Dōng Qí and Hǎi Dài it is called zǐ.
Pronounced shēn.
Its upper board,
north of Wèi,
between Zhào and Wèi is called dié."
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Xī is called chuáng,
a bathing bed is called zhāo."
Pronounced sháo.
The *Shuōwén* states:
"Chuáng,
is that which gives comfort to the body;
zé,
is the crosspiece of a bed;
zǐ,
is the bed mat;
gàng,
is the front wood of the bed."
Fú Qián's *Tōngsú Wén* states:
"A bed three chi five cun is called a tàbǎn,
a single-seater is called chèng,
eight chi is called chuáng."
The *Tiānwén Jí* states:
"Outside the Zǐgōng Gate there are six stars of the Tiānchuáng constellation."
The *Zhànguó Cè* states:
"Lord Mèngcháng traveled to five states.
When he reached Chǔ,
they presented him with an ivory bed."
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
"Emperor Wǔ had a qībǎo bed made,
which was placed in the Guìgōng Palace."
The *Jìn Dōnggōng Jiù Shì* states:
"When the Crown Prince took a consort,
there were plain cypress beds with bracket feet, eight-plank beds, and lacquered beds."
The *Yèzhōng Jì* states:
"Shí Jìlóng's imperial bed
was three zhàng square.
There was a revolving bed
for shooting birds and beasts."
The *Shénxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Wèi Shūqīng entered Huàshān Mountain,
above which dense purple clouds gathered,
and there was a white jade bed."
The *Shāngzǐ* states:
"If the ruler resides upon a kuāng bed,
then all under heaven will be greatly ordered."
The *Yān Shū* states:
"Gōngsūn Fèng lived in seclusion at Chānglí Jiǔchéng,
sleeping on an earthen bed."
The *Sòng Shū* states:
"Emperor Gāozǔ once suffered from bodily heat.
Someone presented a stone bed,
but he smashed it,
disliking the toil of the people."
Coral Tortoiseshell
The *Hàn Wǔdì Nèi Zhuàn* states:
"Emperor Wǔ received from the Queen Mother of the West the twelve matters of the true forms of the Liùjiǎ Língfēi.
The Emperor stored them in a golden table,
sealed them in a white jade case.
He used coral for the bed,
purple brocade for the curtains,
and placed them upon the Bóliáng Terrace."
The *Xījīng Zá Jì* states:
"Hán Yān used tortoiseshell for a bed."
Ivory Qí Horn
"Ivory" has already been described in the narrative.
The *Yìwù Zhì* states:
"The qíláng resembles a deer in shape,
but its horns point forward.
When entering the forest, its horns get caught,
so it always stays in flat, shallow grass.
If chased into the forest, it can be caught.
Its hide can be used to make shoes and socks,
its horns are squarely set with four points.
Southerners therefore use them to make squatting beds."
Six Stars Seven Treasures
"Six Stars" has already been described in the narrative.
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
"Hán Wǔ,
style name Dàowēi,
was appointed General of the Dragon Soaring.
The Governor of Yǐngzhōu once presented a seven-treasure bed and an ivory mat."
Sitting Through Lying Sunken
Huángfǔ Mì's *Gāoshì Zhuàn* states:
"Guǎn Níng,
style name Yòu'ān.
From crossing the sea until his return,
he always sat on a single wooden couch.
After more than fifty years,
the places on the couch where his knees rested were all worn through."
Liú Xiàng's *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states: "Xiū Yánggōng was on Huàyīn Mountain.
In a stone chamber there was a suspended stone couch,
the top of which was completely worn and sunken."
Goddess's Gold Immortal's Stone
The *Mǎ Míngshēng Bié Zhuàn* states:
"Míngshēng followed the goddess into a chamber,
and lay upon a golden bed with a jade table."
Lì Shàncháng's *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states:
"The Yí River
passes south of a stone chamber on the right.
A villager named Luò Dū, when young, came to the side of this chamber to gather honey,
and saw an immortal sitting on a stone bed."
Poem on a Bed by Emperor Xuān of Later Liáng
Carved from Héngshān's white jade,
Supported by the Hàn palace's coral.
Crouching knees, stretching out from long sitting,
Repeatedly shifting for comfort's sake.
Poem on the Húchuáng in Response to Command by Liáng's Yǔ Jiānwú
Its fame spread from foreign lands,
Its use entered the central capital.
Feet askew, yet form upright,
Pattern slanted, yet body level.
Facing distant guests in the hall,
Commanding the start of a campaign.
How does it compare to beneath the Zī lodge,
Lingering in service to glorious brightness?
Inscription on a Bed by Lǐ Yóu
Where the body finds comfort,
Is where one rests and sleeps in harmony and joy.
Vigilant and reverent at night,
Exalting virtue, distancing from wickedness.
Mat, Part Six
The *Shìmíng* says:
“A mat (xí),
means to release (shì),
for it can be rolled up and released.”
The *Shuōwén* says:
“A yán,
is a bamboo mat.”
The *Sānlǐ Tú* says:
“A scholar’s cattail yán,
is seven chǐ long,
three chǐ three cùn wide,
and has no border (chún).”
The *Zhōulǐ* says:
“The Royal Treasury is in charge of the king’s rènxí,
the rènxí and diànxí.
The Supervisor of Mats and Couches is in charge of the names and types of the five kinds of couches and five kinds of mats.
For all grand court audiences and audiences with feudal lords,
a guānxí with a fēn border is laid,
over it a zǎoxí with a painted border is added,
and over that a cìxí with a fǔ border is added.
When feudal lords perform sacrifices,
they use a cattail yán with an embroidered border.”
Fēn,
means white embroidery.
Chún,
means a border.
Cì,
means a mat made of animal hide.
Zǎoxí,
are made by shaving cattail shoots and weaving them with five colors,
like today’s héhuān mats;
‘painted’ refers to cloud patterns.
Cìxí, or peach-branch mats,
have patterns arranged in rows.
The *Hánzǐ* says:
“Xià Yǔ used rushes for his mattress and mat.”
The *Shàngshū* says:
“When King Chéng was about to pass away,
facing south in the window alcove,
a double layer of mièxí with fǔ borders was spread;
Kǒng Ānguó’s commentary:
“Miè,
is peach-branch bamboo.”
Facing east in the western wall alcove,
a double layer of dǐxí with zhuì borders was spread;
dǐ,
means cattail flower.
Facing west in the eastern wall alcove,
a double layer of fēngxí with painted borders was spread;
fēng,
means guān.
Facing south in the western side chamber,
a double layer of sǔnxí with black fēn borders was spread.”
Sǔn,
means cattail bamboo.
The *Hànshū*:
“Emperor Wén used guān and cattail for mats.”
The *Dà Wèi Zhūzhōu Jì* says:
“In Jùlù,
the Guǎng’ē Marsh has many reeds.
Fine imperial mats are produced there,
which often contain mica.”
The *Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì* says:
“The Crown Prince had a single-seat dragon-whisker mat, a red leather mat, a patterned mat, and a scripture mat.”
The *Shǐjì* says:
“In ancient times, for the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
mats of zū jiē were used.”
The *Hàn Jiùyí* says:
“For sacrifices to Heaven,
a purple altar with dark blue mats and six-color patterned silk mats;
for sacrifices to the mountains,
white jiān grass mats.”
Five Fragrances Six Colors
The *Yèzhōng Jì* says:
“Shí Jìlóng made mats,
wrapping five fragrances in gold,
mixing them with five-colored threads, and weaving them with cattail skin.
He bordered them with brocade of six colors;
these mats were used for sacrifices to Heaven.”
Already described in the narrative.
Máo Jiā Shī Ài
Zhōu Fěi’s *Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn* says:
“Zhèng Jìng used máo jiā for mats,
often staying in the shade of willow trees.”
Huángfǔ Mì’s *Gāoshì Zhuàn* says:
“After Lǎo Láizǐ’s parents passed away,
he lived in seclusion on the southern side of Méng Mountain.
He used a wolfberry wood bed,
and shī ài grass for mats.”
Green Cattail White Guān
The *Shíyí Jì* says:
“During the time of King Mù of Zhōu,
when the Queen Mother of the West came,
green cattail mats were spread,
with yellow guān grass cushions.”
The *Sòng Yuánjiā Qǐjū Zhù* says:
“Censor-in-Chief Liú Zhēn memorialized:
‘It is rumored that Guǎngzhōu Governor Wéi Lǎng,
in the prefectural department, had 322 new white guān mats made.
I request that Wéi Lǎng be stripped of his former official position based on this incident.’”
Returning Wind Half Moon
See the section on screens in the ‘Shì Duì’.
The *Shíyí Jì* says:
“The chéng grass is five chǐ tall,
its leaves are dark blue,
its stems are like gold,
and its shape resembles a half-moon.”
It is also said:
“Half-moon grass,
has no flowers or fruit,
its texture is soft and gentle,
and it can be used to make cloth and mats.”
Féng’s Inscription Zhāng’s Rhapsody
Féng Yǎn’s *Xí Qián Yòu Míng* says:
“Cultivate your appearance,
adorn your clothing.
Embellish it with words,
fill it with virtue.
The inscription on the right rear says:
‘Second only to cap and sash,
composed and constant in demeanor.
The splendor of dignified bearing,
is the flower of virtue alone.’” Zhāng Yǐn’s *Wénshì Zhuàn* says:
“Zhāng Chún, Zhāng Yǎn, and Zhū Yì were all young when
they went to visit General of Agile Cavalry Zhū Jù.
Zhū Jù, hearing of the three men’s talent and fame,
wanted to test them,
and said:
‘I want you to compose a rhapsody on an object.’
Zhāng Chún then composed a rhapsody on the mat, saying:
‘Mats are set out in winter,
bamboo mats are spread in summer,
bowing and yielding before sitting,
this is fitting for a gentleman.’”
Fǔ Embroidered Border Scale and Phoenix Decoration
“Fǔ embroidered border” is already described in the narrative.
The *Shíyí Jì* says:
“King Zhāo of Yān set out scale-patterned mats,
scattering quán wú incense.
Scale-patterned means
the mats were adorned with assorted treasures to form patterns of clouds, mist, unicorns, and phoenixes.”
Dài Gained Fifty Yīn Had Eight or Nine Layers
Xiè Chéng’s *Hòu Hànshū* says:
“Dài Píng,
courtesy name Cìzhòng.
He was recommended for the míngjīng examination in Rǔnán Commandery,
summoned as an Erudite,
and appointed Gentleman of the Palace.
During the New Year’s court congratulations,
the emperor ordered the assembled ministers to discuss the classics and histories,
taking turns to question and challenge each other.
If someone’s interpretation was not thorough,
his mat was taken away
and given to the one with the thorough interpretation.
Dài Píng accumulated fifty mats.”
The *Yīnshì Jiāzhuàn* says:
“Yīn Liàng served as Erudite and Lecturer Grand Master.
When Confucian scholars debated, the winner was awarded a mat.
Yīn Liàng sat upon eight or nine layers of mats.
The emperor said:
‘Should not learning be like this!’”
Southern Qí Xiè Tiǎo’s Poem
Born in the land of tides,
the setting sun shines unevenly.
The islet is covered with dù ruò,
the secluded isle overgrown with jiāng lí.
Meeting you, I gather them in time,
at the jade seat, offering a golden cup.
I only wish for silken robes to brush it,
never letting plain dust cover it.
Liáng Liǔ Yùn’s Poem
Shining on the sunlit islet’s edge,
swaying by the side of the green pool in the breeze.
Though lacking the silk of a solitary cocoon,
fortunate to have the color of a blue robe.
Silken sleeves bear little light dust,
ivory beds bear many beautiful adornments.
I hope you drink on orchid-scented nights,
with fair companions resting at times.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu’s Inscription
Spread mats to receive guests,
scholars, whether foolish or wise.
Whatever is available at the time,
why must it be qiān zhūn?
Chén Zhōu Hóngzhèng's "Poem on the Bamboo Fan with a Patterned Bamboo Frame"
Qi silk and Chǔ bamboo,
Have always been far apart in nature.
To express the sorrow of the Xiāng River maiden,
It should also carry the lament of Bān Jī.
Sòng Xiè Huìlián's "In Praise of the White Feather Fan"
Only this white feather,
Embodies such purity.
Cool as the clear breeze,
Plain as ice and snow.
Its form is precious,
Thus it brings delight.
Waving it in sleeves and lapels,
To ward off the summer heat.
Wáng Xiànzhī's "Song of the Peach Leaf Round Fan"
A round fan painted with seven treasures,
Shining bright as the moonlight.
To dispel the heat for my beloved,
Remember each other, never forget.
Liú Zhēn's Wife's "Ode to the Five-Season Painted Fan"
The fiery sovereign's flying chariot,
Draws the radiance along the crimson path.
Ruíbīn responds to the pitch pipes,
Melting essence harmonizes with the dawn.
The five symbols take their positions,
All things are thus arrayed.
Duì descends with the white beast,
Zhèn ascends with the blue dragon.
Sun and moon cast clear light,
Immortal youths come in attendance.
Resting upward on emerald cliffs,
Reflecting downward in orchid ponds.
Mysterious branches lush and dense,
Flowers and trees uneven and varied.
Like the longevity of mountains,
Like the grace of pine trees.
Eternal bestowal of agelessness,
Moving with the passage of time.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Memorial of Thanks for a Bestowed Fan"
Your subject Gāng respectfully submits:
The edict messenger, Rào Sēngmíng, conveyed the imperial decree,
Bestowing upon me one large fine silk fan painted with willow and cicada mountain patterns.
Its patterned bamboo strips finely split,
Its fragrance emanating from sea sandalwood.
Solemn and clear breeze,
Makes even the ivory mat seem unworthy;
Gently scattering colors,
Makes the summer room feel frosty.
The dew-drinking green cicada,
Responds to the lingering scenes of the three summer periods;
Flocks of yellow sparrows,
Bring the southern winds of the sixth month.
Shading the sun, casting coolness,
Its fragrant splendor puts my own to shame;
Its floating coolness dispels the heat,
The tip of the duckweed feels ashamed of its breeze.
The sage's ingenuity in creation;
Bestowed upon this lowly and shallow one,
The kindness of the royal house in bestowing fine objects.
Hereby graciously bestowed,
I receive it with heartfelt gratitude,
And bow with increased joy and excitement.
Respectfully submitting this memorial to express my thanks,
Respectfully submitted.
Part Eight: Incense Burners
Lú Chén's "Sacrificial Methods" states:
"Incense burners,
For seasonal sacrifices,
Are placed beside the seats."
Xú Yuán's "Family Rituals" states:
"For wedding processions,

"Hàn Official Duties" states:

They keep clothes clean,
Hold incense burners,
Burn incense,

"Records of the Eastern Palace of Jìn" states:
"When the crown prince first receives his appointment,

"Records of Yèzhōng" states:

Xí Zuòchǐ's "Records of Xiāngyáng" states:

While on duty at the palace,
He once went to the toilet,

Silver-coated Gold-carved
"Records of the Eastern Palace of Jìn" states:
"In the twenty-second year of Tàiyuán,
When the crown prince married Lady Wáng,
There were two silver-coated Bóshān incense burners with connected trays of three shēng capacity."
"Gold-carved" is mentioned in the narrative.
Four Surroundings Nine Layers
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" states:
"There was a skilled craftsman in Cháng'ān named Dīng Huàn,
Who made a reclining mat incense burner.
Also called an 'under-quilt incense burner,'

Liáng Zhāomíng Crown Prince's "Rhapsody on the Bronze Bóshān Incense Burner"
Like the marvel of the Xià tripod,
Resembling the bizarre descriptions in the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."
Crafting one vessel with many qualities,
Truly this object is extravagant.
At that time, the Frost Goddess governed the cold,
Red light obscured the scenery.
The round sun rose over the eastern peak,
The crimson orb hid behind the western ridge.
Green curtains already lowered,
Orchid-scented oil lamps not yet extinguished.
Kindling pine and cypress fires,
Burning orchid and musk fragrances.
Glowing brightly within,
Fragrance wafting outward.
Like auspicious clouds displaying colors,
Like the star of virtue spreading light.
The Qí lady gazes with joyful eyes,
The Yān maiden smiles skillfully with arched brows.
Duke Liú heard of it and bestowed it,
The Yuè girl was captivated and left her fragrance.
Truly, its name is fine and its vessel beautiful,
Forever to be enjoyed and admired in the splendid hall.
Chén Fùzài's "Rhapsody on the Bóshān Incense Burner"
The vessel resembles the southern mountains,
Its fragrance transmitted from western lands.
Dīng Huàn skillfully cast it,
Combining craftsmanship with carving.
Musk fire buried in cinnabar,
Orchid smoke obscuring darkness.
Structured like perilous peaks,
Interlaced with various trees.
Cold nights contain warmth,
Clear evenings emit mist.
Its making is ingenious,
Uniquely praised as precious and fine.
The atmosphere is dense and misty,
Perpetually like spring.
Following the wind, it surpasses a thousand brews of wine,
Scattering fragrance like a great beauty.
Ancient Poem "Poem on the Incense Burner"
All four seats, be not noisy,
I wish you to hear a song's words.
Let me speak of the bronze burner vessel,
Towering like the southern mountains.
Its upper branches resemble pine and cypress,
Its lower roots are based on a bronze tray.
Carved patterns of various kinds,
Intricately connected by Lílóu.
Who could make this vessel?
Gōngshū and Lǔ Bān.
Vermilion flames burn within it,
Blue smoke drifts among them.
Following the wind into your embrace,
All four seats cannot but rejoice.
Fragrant breezes cannot long remain,
Only leaving the orchid grass to wither.
Southern Qi Dynasty Liú Huì's "Ode to the Boshan Incense Burner"
Uneven and luxuriant, splendid and beautiful,
Layered and dense, charming in their profusion.
They obscure a thousand kinds of trees,
Appearing and disappearing among myriad mountain ranges.
Above is engraved the Prince of Qín,
Riding a crane amidst purple mist.
Below is carved the posture of a coiled dragon,
Raising its head, half holding a lotus in its mouth.
Beside it flows the lovely Yī River,
With mushroom-shaped canopies emerging from the cliffs.
There are also Hàn dynasty wandering maidens,
Gathering feathers, playing with lingering beauty.
How mixed and blended are the glorious colors,
The intricate embroideries shine even more brightly together.
Embroidered deer sometimes leap or recline,
The sparse woods are deep and lush.
Concealing blossoms, they never fully bloom,
Holding fragrance, unwilling to burn.
Wind stirs the trees by the jade steps,
Dew moistens the lotus in the winding pond.
Cold insects fly in the night chamber,
Autumn clouds vanish in the dawn sky.
Liang Dynasty Shěn Yuē's "Matching Liú Huì, Governor of Yōngzhōu's 'Ode to the Boshan Incense Burner'"Casting in metal truly sets the standard,
Expressing thoughts must rely on skilled craftsmen.
Condensing fragrance awaits the crimson flame,
First smelting the copper from Shǒu Mountain.
Its magnificent form is indeed rugged and lofty,
Its leaning posture truly exquisite and intricate.
Peaks and ridges confront each other,
Cliffs and caves extend endlessly.
Chìsōngzi wanders upon it,
Gathering his feet, riding light swans.
Dragons coil beneath it,
Lifting their heads, gazing at the layered heavens.
The mountain sides have many wondrous trees,
Some solitary, some in clusters.
Among the cliffs are elusive maidens,
Their sleeves hanging as if holding the wind.
Like pheasants in flight, never ceasing,
Like tigers glaring, brimming with remaining vigor.
Climbing the mountain raises heavy screens,
Left and right, silk and tong trees are drawn.
A hundred harmonies exhale in the clear night,
Orchid smoke fills all four sides.
Like that lofty morning air,
Touching stone, encircling Huà and Sōng mountains.
Mirrors, Section Nine
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"Jiàn is called a mirror."
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Mirror,
means reflection,
it has light and reflection."
The "Hánzǐ" says:
"The people of old had eyes too short to see themselves,
so they used mirrors to view their faces.
Wisdom too short to know themselves,
so they used the Dào to rectify themselves.
A mirror bears no guilt for revealing flaws,
the Dào bears no blame for illuminating faults.
Eyes losing the mirror have no means to adjust beard and eyebrows,
the self losing the Dào has no means to know confusion."
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"The lord of ten thousand chariots,
people flatter him greatly.
Yet having nothing to mirror himself,
his ruin and demise are not far off.
Who then can serve as a mirror?
Is it not only the scholars?
A mirror illuminating oneself has minor merit,
a scholar illuminating oneself has great merit."
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"When someone points out his flaw, he resents the person;
when a mirror reveals his ugliness, he praises the mirror."
The "Shēnzǐ" says:
"How could one not know that a mirror, set with precision and non-action,
naturally contains both beauty and ugliness!"
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"The mind of the ultimate person is like a mirror,
neither sending nor welcoming,
responding without storing,
thus prevailing over things without worry or injury."
The "Huáinánzǐ" also says:
"Thus, if a palace attendant obtains a halberd,
he uses it to cut mallows;
if a blind man obtains a mirror,
he uses it to cover a cup.
One cannot give a mirror to a blind man,
nor point out flaws to a chaotic ruler."
The "Shàngshū Dì Mìng Qī" says:
"Jié lost the jade mirror,
and used his beast of devouring."
The jade mirror symbolizes the clear and bright Dào,
the devouring beast symbolizes tyranny.
The "Shàngshū Kǎo Líng Yào" says:
"Qín lost the golden mirror,
fish eyes entered as pearls."
The golden mirror symbolizes the bright Dào.
The First Emperor,
son of Lǚ Bùwéi,
speaks of chaos replacing truth.
The "Wénzǐ" says:
"Now a mirror does not set forms,
therefore it can have forms."
The "Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì" says:
"When the Crown Prince takes a consort,
there is a large dressing mirror, one chi eight cun.
A small silver-flowered mirror, one chi two cun,
both with clothing fasteners included.
A lacquer case contains three silver-flowered gold-leaf mirrors,
with silver dragon-head lotus-shaped fastener locks included."
Gold-inlaid, Silver-flowered
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's "Memorial Listing Thirty Kinds of Miscellaneous Utensils",
includes one gold-inlaid iron mirror, one chi two cun, and one nine cun.
"Silver-flowered small mirror" see the narrative.
Nine Cun, Three Chi
The "Liú Zhèn Biézhuàn" says:
"Using a nine cun bright mirror to illuminate the face and look at it,
he said:
'Today I recognize my own form,
I shall make sure not to forget.
In this way, my spirit does not scatter,
illness and affliction cannot enter.'"
The "Yèzhōng Jì" says:
"The mirrors in Shí Jìlóng's Three Terraces and inner palace,
some have a diameter of two or three chi,
some are one chi five cun."
Hundred-refined, Four-regulating
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Dǐyí" says:
"A mirror refined a hundred times,
can count beard and eyebrow hairs,
yet a recluse scholar does not see Tài Mountain."
The "Bàopǔzǐ" says:
"Using a bright mirror nine cun to reflect oneself,
with concentrated thought and focus,
after seven days one sees spirits,
and immortals know affairs a thousand li away.
Bright mirrors are used, sometimes one,
sometimes two,
called four-regulating mirrors."
Seeing Deer, Reflecting Dogs
The "Bàopǔzǐ" says:
"In the past, Zhāng Gàiyǒng and Ǒu Háochéng, two men,
concentrated their thoughts in a stone chamber on Yúntái Mountain in Shǔ.
Suddenly four men appeared,
in yellow silk single-layered robes and coarse cloth headscarves,
came before them,
and said:
'How toilsome, Daoist masters!
Laboring in seclusion.'
Thereupon the two men looked at themselves in the mirror,
and they were deer."
The "Xù Sōushén Jì" says:
"At the foot of Línlǜ Mountain there was a lodge,
whenever people passed by and stayed overnight,
some would fall ill and die.
At that time, there was a man named Zhì Bóyí,
who stayed there,
lit a bright candle and sat.
In the middle of the night, suddenly over ten people came,
and played dice games together.
Bóyí secretly used a mirror to reflect them,
and they were a pack of dogs."
Responding to Speech, Copying Form
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì" says:
"During King Mù's time,
the Jùqú state presented a fire-qi mirror,
when people spoke, the mirror would respond with sound."
Lù Jī's "Letter to Younger Brother Yún" says:
"Before the Rénshòu Hall,
there is a large square bronze mirror,
over five chi tall,
three chi two cun wide.
Placed dimly in the courtyard,
facing it copies human forms."
Gold-leaf, Jade Glory
"Gold-leaf mirror" see the narrative.
The Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò says:
"The glory of jade,
the essence of stone,
exterior like sunlight,
interior like myriad stars.
When two people see each other and know each other's feelings,
The Radiance of Pearls, the Color of Stone
The "Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì" states:
"When divine spirits overflow with abundance,
the use of all treasures brings forth pearl mirrors."
Sòng Jūn comments:
"Large pearls possess radiance and can serve as mirrors."
The "Shíyí Jì" states:
"During the time of King Mù of Zhōu,
there was a mirror resembling stone.
This stone was white like the moon,
and when it illuminated a face, it appeared like snow,
thus it was called the moon mirror."
Dark Tin Powder, Golden Cord
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
"When a bright mirror is first cast, its form is dim and unclear.
But after applying dark tin powder to it,
and polishing it with white felt,
then beard, eyebrows, and hair
can be clearly discerned."
Xiāo Fāngděng's "Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū" states:
"When Mùróng Chuí attacked Yè,
Fú Pī sent his cousin to request aid,
and presented Xiè Xuán with a bronze mirror
and a golden, intricately woven cord,
using them as tokens of trust."
Rénshòu Hall, Xiányáng Palace
"Rénshòu Hall" is mentioned in the annotation for "depicting form."
The "Xījīng Zájì" states:
"When Emperor Gāozǔ first entered the Xiányáng Palace,
there was a square mirror,
measuring four feet nine inches in width,
bright on both sides.
When a person came to look into it, they appeared upside down.
If one covered their chest and approached,
their intestines, stomach, and five viscera
were clearly visible without obstruction."
There is Guidance and Grace, No Concealment or Grasping
Fúzǐ states:
"The Way of the ultimate person is like a mirror:
it has clarity and illumination,
it has guidance and grace."
Jiǎ Yìzǐ states:
"The mirror stands as a standard, residing
without concealment or grasping.
Beauty and ugliness inevitably arrive,
each finding its proper place."
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xián's "Mirror Rhapsody"
Following the yin position in the western region,
gathering the firm essence of autumn metal.
Invoking Zhùróng to express reverence,
commanding Ōu Yě to undertake its crafting.
Basking in the radiant light of the sun and moon,
modeling its image after the shining spirit.
Without partiality towards beauty or ugliness,
yet all forms are necessarily detailed.
Similar to the faithful records of a good historian,
it reveals according to good and evil.
Graceful and virtuous ladies,
lofty and dignified consorts.
Grieving over the fading of spring's splendor,
fearing the decline of jade-like beauty.
Gazing at clear brows to mirror themselves,
vying in lofty elegance to shine upon each other.
If then cloud-like hair is disheveled on the head,
and crimson brows fade in color.
Should this vessel be lacking,
who could then adorn their appearance?
Together with the mute and blind in darkness,
nearing a face yet failing to recognize it.
The noble person knows appearance cannot be left unadorned,
thus introspects and admonishes oneself.
Having seen the past and considered the future,
then feels reverence in the hidden depths.
Observing the bright clarity awaiting polish,
one thereby cleanses the heart.
Seeing a flaw in the sun's reflection,
one seeks instruction from Confucian gentry.
Thus, how could there be neglect of one's countenance,
or licentiousness in one's thoughts?
Liáng Dynasty Liú Huǎn's "Rhapsody on Looking into a Mirror"
Night's tallies are exhausted,
dawn's bell is about to cease.
Light comes from outside the window,
shadows vanish before the curtain.
The King of Jīng wishes to rise,
attendant concubines should return.
Curtains drawn in the front chamber,
inner gates unbarred.
Opening the screen, easily folded,
rolling up the blinds, spread out.
Scratching the head, adjusting the coiffure,
hairpins entwining the locks.
Approaching water by the steps,
light reflecting in the basin.
Surprised that last night's powder is still blended,
smiling at the disarray of remaining makeup.
Wishing to open the case and adorn anew, then by the window fetch the mirror.
Its stand, originally from the Wēn clan of the royal palace,
with an inscription on the back: "May it benefit descendants."
Four sides, swirling winds like flowing water,
balustrades encircling like a city gate.
Distinctly clear as if unobstructed,
before the reflection, even more lovely.
Recently, rouge is not needed for complexion,
even now, fine brows still trace with dark pigment.
Suí Dynasty Kǒng Fàn's "Poem Harmonizing with the Sovereign's Mirror Poem"
On days the Tiger Guard sorrowfully rises,
the dragon mirror beholds the face.
Favor unrequited, gratitude unpaid,
vainly sighing, hair like silk.
Suí Dynasty Lǐ Jùrén's "Poem on a Mirror"
The Wèi palace knew its original name,
the Qín tower recognized its former appellation.
The phoenix emerges from its stand,
the dragon comes to life within its case.
Without waves, the water chestnut moves of itself,
without night, the moon is ever bright.
Not only does it reflect lovely beauties,
it also repels mountain spirits.
Zhōu Dynasty Yǔ Xìn's "Poem on a Mirror"
Opening the jade case, a mirror within,
lightly brushing dust with fine ash.
Its light like a sheet of water,
its reflection shows people on both sides.
The moon rises without a cassia tree,
flowers bloom not following spring.
Try hanging it on Huáinán bamboo,
capable of seeing the four neighbors.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwén Emperor's "Poem on a Mirror"
Always by one's side, down to the smallest measure,
who says looking in a mirror is rare?
Like ice yet showing no water,
like a fan ever holding light.
Fully opening the tortoiseshell case,
and rolling up the woven garment.
If it fell into Xiàngrú's hand,
one might suspect Zhào's jade disk returned.
Later Hàn Dynasty Lǐ Yóu's "Mirror Inscription"
Cast bronze to make a mirror,
to tidy and adorn the countenance.
Cultivate your ritual robes,
correct your cap and attire.

there was one pure silver mirror stand with triple bands,
and four pure silver mirror stands for the seven noble ladies and princesses."
The "Jìn Eastern Palace Old Affairs" states:
"When the Crown Prince took a consort,
among the items used was one fine tortoiseshell mirror stand."

Tortoiseshell is mentioned in the narrative.

"A fine coral mirror shines with radiant light."
Southern Qí Dynasty Xiè Tiǎo's "Poem on a Mirror Stand"
Exquisite like vermilion pillars,
towering like dark gate towers.
Facing the phoenix over clear water,
dangling dragons holding the bright moon.
Reflecting powder, brushing rouge makeup,
arranging flowers, combing cloud-like hair.
Jade-like beauty seen only by oneself,
often fearing your affection may cease.
Chén Shūdá's "Poem on an Empty Mirror Stand upon Entering the Palace"
Now its adornment abandoned,
decaying by the roadside.
Cháng'é and the bright moon,
together descend past the frontier mountains.
Boats, Eleventh
Western Jìn Zǎo Jù's "Ode to the Boat"
How deep and vast are the rivers and seas,
Alas, boundless and stretching far and wide.
Those are blocked off and unseen,
These, from here, remain unheard.
Though the same earth bears all,
Truly different eras and divided ways.
Praise the sage king's divine transformation,
Reason penetrates the subtle and reaches the obscure.
Lament the people's separation and obstruction,
Pity the king's teachings not reaching all.
Established vessels to be used,
Thus, following celestial signs, boats were made.
To cross the surging waves' untrodden tracks,
To traverse great rivers' dark currents.
No water too deep to cross,
No road too broad not to take.
Carrying heavy, solid, stagnant matter,
Though it sinks and floats in turn.
Drifting Yān's cauldron to Wúkuài,
Turning metal and stone in the vast waves.
Against the boundless, rolling expanse,
Not halting progress nor ceasing to advance.
Ascending Yánghóu's swift shores,
Like a phoenix soaring and a dragon...
Though the journey floods the sky and sweeps fiercely,
Long holding joy without worry.
Riding the current, it departs,
Meeting resistance, it stops.
Receiving command like an echo,
Only moving with the times.
Not shunning toil nor hating motion,
Not seeking ease nor self-contentment.
Not greedy for wealth to seek merit,
Not sparing strength nor desiring lightness.
Abundance and frugality follow its substance,
What it bears matches its original form.
Though not riding, it often floats,
Though facing peril, it remains upright.
Wandering through twists and turns,
Moving together with the times.
Broadly carrying, well bestowing,
The heart harbors no schemes.
Encompassing all things,
Enduring disgrace, embracing glory.
Only what the traveler desires to carry,
Mixing noble and base within one gate.
Embracing the universal through virtue,
Widely receiving, comparable to heaven and earth.
Moved by such broad utility,
Truly, the way of humanity resides herein.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem: Snow Reflecting the Night Boat"
Yellow clouds obscure the bird's path,
White snow falls on the duck-prowed boat.
Dividing sand reflects on icy shores,
Shining cranes gather on cold streams.
Mast winds blow shadows down,
Silken cables mingle with floating blossoms.
If the boat's beam were cassia wood,
It would seem like moonlight shining on autumn.
Liáng Wáng Yún's "Poem on a Light and Swift Boat"
My lord adorns the light and swift,
Swaying and rocking, surpassing flying clouds.
Rippling waves shimmer with ibis colors,
Flowing waters gleam with dragon patterns.
Like lightning's flash, already brilliant and fleeting,
Like a bird's flight, again surpassing the flock.
In an instant, covering a thousand miles,
Yet lingering at this forked road's parting.
Liáng Yuándì's "Poem on Boat Names"
Floating clouds fly at the sky's edge,
Three-winged boats chase each other.
By the pond, white swans dance,
Deep in the woods, blue sparrows return.
Pine streams reflect shooting star trails,
Cassia windows slant with moonlight's glow.
Thinking of this, emotionless to the extreme,
In the high tower, tears stain my robe.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Boats and Oars"
The benefit of boats and oars,
Is like that of carriages and horses.
Carrying heavy loads over long distances,
To aid all under heaven.
Observing wind and waves,
Exploring rivers and wilds to the fullest.
Acting with care and caution, in the end, nothing is impossible.
Wáng Shūyuán's "Praise of the Boat"
Reaching far, bearing heavy loads,
Each according to its means.
On land, one drives chariots,
On water, only boats are used.
With weak oars and light sculls,
They aid crossing and fulfill needs.
Remembering those fishermen,
Rowing and singing clear songs.
Xiè Língyùn's "Praise While Serving on a Boat Excursion"
Rowing painted ibis boats, wandering among orchids,
Ponds and islets recede, rocks stand uneven.
Sun hidden by clouds, moon shines on woods,
Wind distant and cool, water ripples in waves.
Volume Twelve: Carriages
Qiáo Zhōu's "Ancient History Examination" states:
"Huángdì made the carriage,
In Shàohào's time, oxen were added,
In Yǔ's time, Xī Zhòng drove horses."
The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"The jade carriage,
With yáng trappings and tasseled bridle.
Twelve layers of ornamentation,
Erects the tàicháng banner with twelve streamers for sacrifices.
Jade on the horse is called lù.
Yáng,
pronounced yáng,
is a metal plate on the horse's forehead,
carved from metal,
known as engraved yáng.
Fán,
pronounced pán,
refers to the horse's broad belt today.
These fán and yīng are all five-colored,
adorned with colorful woolen fabric.
Twelve layers of ornamentation,
each layer,
is a complete set.
The tàicháng is among the nine banners, painted with sun and moon.
The gold carriage, with hooked fán and yīng,
nine layers of ornamentation,
erects the dàqí banner for receiving guests,
and for enfeoffing those of the same surname;
The ivory carriage, with vermilion fán and yīng,
seven layers of ornamentation,
erects the dàchì banner for court audiences,
and for enfeoffing those of different surnames;
The leather carriage,
with dragon-reined corded yīng,
five layers of ornamentation,
erects the dàbái banner for military campaigns,
and for enfeoffing the four guards;
The wooden carriage, with front fán and crane yīng,
erects the dàhuī banner for hunting,
and for enfeoffing feudal states."
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shū" states:
"Hàn system,
the imperial golden-rooted comfort carriage,
standing carriage,
wheels all vermilion patterned,
black hubs with two linchpins,
flying linchpin covers.
With gold foil entwined dragon carriage, leaning armrests,
spiritual patterns painted on the wheel guards.
Patterned beasts crouch on the yoke rail,
dragon heads hold the yoke.
Simurghs and sparrows stand on the crossbar,
spiritual patterns painted on the shafts.
Kingfisher feather canopy with yellow lining,
known as the yellow canopy.
Golden flowers adorn the wheel spokes,
ends erect pennant banners,
with twelve streamers.
Painted with sun, moon, and rising dragons,
drawn by six black horses,
plus yak tail,
large as a dipper,
placed on the left side horse's yoke,
known as the left dào.
The five-colored standing carriage,
five-colored comfort carriage,
are all similar.
The grand empress dowager, empress dowager, and empress's ritual carriage,
ride double pheasant feather canopy golden-rooted carriages.
Added blue crossbar trappings,
blue curtained interior,
cloud and spirit patterns painted on the shafts,
gold-coated with five colors.
Crown prince and princes all have comfort carriages,
vermilion patterned wheels,
leaning beast and crouching deer yoke rails,
pennant banners with nine streamers,
painted with descending dragons.
Imperial grandsons ride green carriages."
Wandering Ring and Auxiliary Linchpin
The "Máo Shī" states:
"Wandering rings and flank straps,
hidden traces and glossy connections."
Liú Xī's "Shì Míng" states:
"The wandering ring is on the back of the central horse,
outside the flank horses.
Reins pass through it,
wandering, moving forward and back without fixed position."
Cài Yōng's "Dú Duàn" states:
"Imperial carriages,
all have auxiliary linchpins,
applying linchpins on the outside,
then additionally setting linchpins."
Zhōu Yú Yīn Lù
The Zhōu Lǐ states:
"The Yǒuyú clan esteemed pottery,
the Xiàhòu clan esteemed craftsmanship,
the Yīn esteemed carpentry,
the Zhōu esteemed carriages."
"Yīn lù" appears in the Lúnyǔ.
Zhū Lán Zǐ Gài
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hàn Shū Yúfú Zhì" says:
"As for the minor envoy carriage,
its orchid carriage has vermilion red hubs,
a white canopy with red curtains.
It is accompanied by forty outriders,
and is used by those who pursue arrests, investigate cases, or have official orders to apprehend."
Wèi Shōu's Hòu Wèi Shū says:
"The comfort carriage,
has a purple canopy with vermilion lining,
identical to that of dukes and marquises.
For viscounts and barons, it has a black canopy with blue lining."
Bù Yú Wò Niǎn
Zhāng Chǎng's Jìn Dōnggōng Jiùshì says:
"The crown prince has one walking carriage."
The Yèzhōng Jì says:
"When Shí Jìlóng's empress went out to Sōng,
she rode in a lù niǎn.
Sometimes it was a vermilion-lacquered reclining carriage,
using mica in place of gauze.
Looking out from within or without in all four directions,
everything was completely transparent."
Qīng Niú Bái Lù
The Guān Lìng Nèi Zhuàn says:
"Yǐn Xǐ once climbed a tower and looked out in all four directions.
He saw purple qi reaching from the eastern extreme westward,
and joyfully said:
'A sage should be passing through the capital.'
He indeed saw Lǎojūn arriving in a carriage drawn by a black ox."
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"Shěn Yì studied the Way in Shǔzhōng,
and traveled together with his wife.
On the road they encountered a carriage drawn by a white deer."
Yī Qì Liù Cái
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"Among vessels, the carriage is the one that gathers the most craftsmen."
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Xù Hàn Shū Yúfú Zhì" says:
"Xī Zhòng served as Chēzhèng (Director of Chariots),
preparing materials according to the season,
all six materials being of excellent quality."
Zhū Lún Tóng Jué
Huà Hé's "Guā Mǎ Fù" says:
"Saddles of felt and stitched fur,
pearl-adorned wheels with jade-like radiance."
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén says:
"Jué,
refers to the curved bronze hook on the chariot's side rail.
Pronounced gōng zhuó fǎn."
Pí Xuān Gé Lù
The Hàn Guān Jiě Gǔ says:
"The Grand Coachman's stables and carriage repository,
contain leather-canopied and phoenix-flagged carriages.
Hú Guǎng said:
'Horses have stables,
carriages have repositories.
Pí xuān,
refers to a canopy made of tiger skin.'" The Zhōu Lǐ, annotated by Zhèng Xuán, says:
"Gé lù,
is a carriage pulled by leather and lacquered."
Fǎ Yīnyáng Xiàng Rìyuè
Lǐ Yóu's "Xiǎo Chē Míng" says:
"The round canopy symbolizes heaven,
the square carriage base symbolizes earth.
The wheels follow the principles of yīn and yáng,
in motion they do not separate."
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"The wheel has thirty spokes,
symbolizing the sun and moon."
Huángjīn Chē Bìyù Niǎn
The Wú Zhì says:
"During the Chūpíng era,
a children's rhyme said:
'Golden carriage,
with patterned, variegated ear,
at the Héchāng gate,
an emperor will emerge.'"
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì says:
"King Mù of Zhōu drove a carriage of gold and jade,
from morning till night,
traversing the entire cosmos."
Sān Cùn Xiá Sì Chǐ Zhōu
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"That which enables a carriage to travel a thousand lǐ,
lies in its crucial three-inch linchpin."
The Zhōu Lǐ:
"Regarding the measurement of the carriage pole,
for state horses, the pole's depth is four chǐ, seven cùn.
For field horses, the pole's depth is four chǐ."
Sān Yún Niǎn Qī Xiāng Chē
The Zhēnrén Wáng Jūn Nèi Zhuàn says:
"Divine beings ride in carriages of three clouds."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi, in his "Letter to Yáng Biāo," said:
"Now I present to you two painted-wheel carriages with four-view open canopies and seven fragrances."
Lún Chóng Yá Yuán Liǎng Wěi
Dǒng Bā's "Yúfú Zhì" says:
"The imperial golden-root carriage has five vehicles,
their wheels all have vermilion patterns,
double linchpins and double hubs."
Zhāng Yī's Pī Cāng says:
"The light carriage's shaft has two ends."
Dàimào Xiāng Zhūyú Wǎng
Zhōu Qiān's Yúfú Záshì says:
"For the five lù carriages,
behind the two side compartments,
all use kingfisher feathers."
A note says:
"Kūn,
is the name of a large bird,
its feathers are connected, fine, and sharp,
