Shí Chóng's "Nú Quàn" says:
"When making a carriage,
one should take the spokes from large, fine white locust wood,
and the felloes from cornelian cherry."
Gélóng (Wicker Basket) Hégài (Lotus Canopy)
Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shū" states:
"Gāozǔ (Emperor Gaozu of Liu Song) was pure, frugal, and had few desires.
At the head of his bed was an earthen screen,
and on the wall hung a gélóng (wicker lantern)."
"Hégài (Lotus Canopy)" is explained in the annotation for "Fèngnǎo (Phoenix Brain)."
Bǎizhī (Hundred Branches) Jiǔguāng (Nine Lights)
Fù Xuán's "Cháohuì Fù" states:
"The splendid lanterns are like trees of fire,
blazing with the brilliance of a hundred branches."
"Hàn Wǔdì Nèizhuàn" states:
"The Queen Mother of the West sent an envoy to tell the Emperor:
'On the seventh day of the seventh month,
I shall come for a brief visit.'
On that day, the Emperor swept and cleaned the palace,
and lit the jiǔguāng (nine lights) lanterns."
Yuánzhī (Salamander Fat) Fènggāo (Phoenix Grease)
Both are mentioned in the narrative.
Héngmǎn (Constantly Full) Chángshēng (Eternally Lit)
Both are mentioned earlier.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Dēng Fù" (Rhapsody on Lamps)
As the nine dragons approach dusk,
and three cups of wine are set aside.
The jade hook is half-raised,
the weak trees are fully lowered.
The window hides brightness within the whitewashed wall,
the willow adds darkness to the orchid chamber.
Kingfisher-feathered pearl quilts,
tasseled feather curtains.
Unfolding the folding screen,
covering the lotus-patterned traveling screen.
Rolling up the clothes on the bed of the Queen of Qín,
sending the pillow to the terrace of Jīng.
Then there are a hundred branches on the same tree,
four illuminations connecting the trays.
Fragrance added by burning honey,
scent mingled with burning orchids.
The embers last through the long night,
the light blue in the cold night.
Elegant splendor shimmering,
yuánzhī (salamander fat) shining brightly.
Moving scales and armor on the whale fish,
flames gleaming on the calling crane.
When moths flutter, shattered flowers fall chaotically;
when the wind rises, meteors drift down finely.
Moreover, in the deep night at Shànglán,
with clear wine from Zhōngshān.
The consort of Chǔ retains guests,
Hán É blends her voice.
Low songs keeping rhythm,
wandering strings ceasing their sound.
Gleaming red embers,
blazing crimson glory.
Suddenly, jiǔguāng (nine lights) connect in colorful splendor,
or twin blossoms shine together brightly.
Send word to Sū Jìzǐ,
he should understand the lingering glow's sentiment.
Liáng Jiāng Yān's "Dēng Fù" (Rhapsody on Lamps)
Huáinán Wáng,
truly resplendent.
Summoned the colorful maidens,
fed them cinnabar,
to learn the phoenix's cry.
Purple clouds vanished,
the white sun sank.
Hung bright lamps,
dispersed the dark shadows.
Turning to the scholar of Xiǎoshān, he said:
"Can this be rhapsodized?"
Then, strumming the sè, he spoke:
"As for the lamps of the great king:
Copper blossoms, golden stands,
intricate forms, carved shapes.
Jade-green as cloud vapor,
jade-white as immortal spirits.
Double streams, hundred branches,
gorgeous curtains filling the hall.
Illuminating brocade-ground patterned mats,
reflecting off embroidered pillars and singing zhēngs.
Indulging the vastness of divine cultivation,
why doubt and seek eternal peace?
This is the boastful extravagance of feudal lords,
which recluses do not pursue.
As for the lamps of common people:
Not silver, not pearls,
no ornament, no embellishment.
The heart does not value luxury,
the vessel aims for simplicity.
Thus, dew chills the curtains,
wind knots the gauze.
Fireflies already draw near the cassia,
moths wish to leave the orchids.
Autumn nights feel like years,
autumn sentiments like threads.
Resentful of this embrace,
saddened by this autumn season.
Inevitably, sitting by the lamp sighing,
wishing to speak but forgetting words.
As for when frost seals garden oranges,
ice cracks pond sedges.
Clouds and snow boundless,
rivers and seas just turning dark.
Winter grease already congealed,
winter arrows not yet measured.
Melancholy connects the winter heart,
solitary and desolate the winter dusk."
Again, red lamps hang bright,
only for your sake.
Suí Jiāng Zǒng's "Sānshàn Diàn Yè Wàng Shāndēng Shī" (Poem: Gazing at Mountain Lanterns from Sānshàn Hall at Night)
A hundred flowers seem to bloom at night,
illumination all around as if containing spring.
Brightly they appear alongside stars,
gracefully facing the moon, ever new.
Gathering pearls, not from Hépǔ;
giving jade pendants, different from the riverbank.
If on the road to Fúsāng,
one could say they rival the sun's wheel.
Liáng Fàn Jìng's Wife, Shěn Shì's "Yǒng Dēng Shī" (Poem: Chanting on a Lamp)
The splendid feast day already dusk,
the silken curtains, the moon not yet returned.
Blossoming, scattering crane colors,
containing light, emerging from nine subtleties.
The breezy veranda stirs crimson flames,
the waterside pavilion, pale clear radiance.
Not pitying the light moths circling,
only fearing the dawn flies will fly.
Liáng Jì Shàoyú's "Yǒng Cán Dēng Shī" (Poem: Chanting on a Dying Lamp)
The dying lamp still not extinguished,
about to expire, yet raising its glow.
Only one or two flames remain,
just enough to loosen the silk robe.
Nán Qí Xiè Tiǎo's "Yǒng Dēng Shī" (Poem: Chanting on a Lamp)
Emerald green sprouts from the slanting stream,
treasures stored within the Dàngshān peaks.
Drawing stems like immortal palms,
holding light akin to the candle dragon.
Flying moths circle again and again,
light blossoms four or five layers deep.
Alone facing a lovesick night,
emptily shining on seamless clothes.
Hòu Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Jīnyáng Dēng Míng" (Inscription on the Golden Ram Lamp)
Wise men strive in their tasks,
only fearing the day insufficient.
The golden ram carries the light,
creating brightness to continue.
Fù Xuán's "Dēng Míng" (Inscription on a Lamp)
Gleaming splendid lamp,
containing moisture, shining with spirit.
Plain grease flows liquid,
dark wick stands tall.
Dānshuǐ (Cinnabar River) radiates brilliance,
flying radiance in the orchid pavilion.
Zhú (Candles) Part Fourteen
"Zhōu Lǐ" states:
"For all major state affairs,
the Sīhuǐ official supplies bēn zhú (hemp candles),
which are hemp candles.
Another says large candles.
For sacrifices, míng zhú (bright candles) are supplied."
Using a suì (fire-making tool) to obtain míng huǒ (bright fire) from the sun.
"Yí Lǐ" states:
"At banquets, then the shùzǐ (sons of concubines) hold candles on the eastern steps,
the Sīgōng official holds candles on the western steps.
The Diànrén holds large candles in the courtyard,
the Hūnrén makes candles outside the gate.
Whenever candles arrive,
rise."
Distinguishing day and night.
"Lǐ Jì" states:
"The candle should not show its bá."
Bá means
the base.
It is considered improper if the candle is left until completely burnt out,
as if too much ember causes weariness.
Lù Shìhéng's "Máoshī Cǎomù Shū" states:
"Wooden knotweed pounded makes candles,
bright as sesame candles."
"Hòu Wèi Shū" states:
"When Shìzǔ campaigned south,
Liú Yìgōng presented là zhú (wax candles)."
"Shì Shuō" states:
"Shí Jìlún used là zhú (wax candles) for cooking."
Shining on the Wall Reflecting on Books
The *Strategies of the Warring States* states:
"Gān Mào left Qín and went to Qí.
As he passed through the pass, he met Sū Jìzǐ,
who said:
'Among the women working at night on the river, there was one whose family was poor and had no candle.
The other women working at night together wanted to dismiss her.'
The one without a candle said:
'Because I have no candle,
I always arrive first,
sweep the room alone and lay out the mats.
Why begrudge the light shining on the eastern wall?'"
The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* states:
"Kuāng Héng studied diligently but had no candle.
His neighbor had candlelight,
so he bored a hole in the wall to let the light through,
and read by reflecting the light onto his book."
Cutting Off Cap Tassels Laying Out Mats
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Strategies* states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ feasted his ministers with wine.
When dusk fell and the candles went out,
someone tugged at the robe of a beauty.
The beauty grasped and broke off the tassel of his cap.
She reported this to the king.
The king said:
'When people are drunk, they lose propriety.
Why should we wish to display a woman's chastity and humiliate a gentleman?'
He then ordered:
'Let all ministers cut off their cap tassels,
and only then light the candles.'"
Liú Xiàng's *Biographies of Exemplary Women* states:
"There was a woman named Xú Wú from Qí,
a poor woman from the eastern seacoast.
She once joined with her neighbor Lǐ Wú to share candlelight for spinning at night.
Lǐ Wú said:
'Xú Wú's share of candles often falls short.
Please do not spin at night.'
Xú Wú said:
'Because I am poor,
I always rise early and arrive first,
and retire to bed last.
I sprinkle, sweep, and lay out the mats
to await those who come.
Now, adding one more person
does not make the candle shine brighter;
removing one person
does not make it dimmer.
Why begrudge the leftover light on the eastern wall?'"
Increasing Brightness Sitting in Darkness
Wáng Fú's *Discourses of a Recluse* states:
"The light of a candle placed in a corner
illuminates a dark room.
The front candle shines fully,
and the rear candle increases the brightness.
The two depend on each other
to create great light."
Xiè Chéng's *Later Book of Hàn* states:
"Bā Zhī served as Governor of Yángzhōu.
He would sit with guests in darkness,
not lighting the official candles."
Beauty Wearing a Candle Flying Insects Flocking
The *Terrestrial Mirror Chart* states:
"If you see a beauty wearing a candle and walking,
there is jade at the place from which she emerges."
The *Master Who Embraces Simplicity* states:
"When a bright candle is raised at night,
flying insects flock to it in swarms."
King Wǔ Raising at Dawn Shào Wēng Displaying at Night
Wáng Chōng's *Discourses Weighed in the Balance* states:
"When King Wǔ attacked Shāng,
his troops reached Mùyě.
At dawn, he raised grease candles
to temporarily conceal his unpreparedness."
The *Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn* states:
"When the favored Lady Lǐ died,
the Emperor greatly missed and mourned her.
A man from Qí named Shào Wēng claimed he could summon her spirit.
So at night, he displayed bright candles,
and the Emperor stayed in another tent.
From afar, he saw Lady Lǐ,
but could not approach to look at her."
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng's "Rhapsody on Facing the Candle"
In the mica window, patterned felt is joined;
Inside the dogwood curtain, a brocade mat is spread.
Do not take the night-shining pearls yet,
Nor need you light the golden ram lantern.
The waning moon at the third watch has not yet risen;
At midnight, the stars in vain cling to the sky.
So hang the twin-hearted bright candle,
Place it on the carved golden beautiful tray.
A sleeping dragon coils beside it,
A pair of phoenixes rest inverted.
Turn away from evil and take the upright path,
Push open the lattice window and fear its width.
Green torches hold emerald,
Red candles contain cinnabar.
Leopard fat suits the fire,
Ox tallow endures the cold.
Bronze lotuses embrace stems and twine around branches,
Golden lotuses intertwine and jointly exhale lotus blooms.
Observe the shining brilliance of the horizontal rays,
See the stumbling of the honey-like tears.
Gradually feel the flowing pearls run,
Look closely—many are the crimson flowers.
Deep into the night, the colors are lovely;
The flame stirs as the wind passes.
Late at night, only the tongs are troublesome;
In cold weather, fear not the moths.
Calamus wine is passed—the banquet is about to end;
The jade-green dancer finishes—her silk robe is thin.
Shadows stretch across the long pillow,
Mist rises toward the fruit plate.
Reflected light returns within the golden screen,
Affectionately, the two gaze at each other.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Rhapsody on Facing the Candle"
At Lóngshā and Yàn Fortress, armor should feel the cold;
On Tiānshān, the moon sets—the traveler's clothes are thin.
Before the lamp, mending clothes seems dim;
Under the moon, threading a needle feels most difficult.
Pick the lampwick, hold the cassia candle,
Return it to the lampstand, place it on the candle tray.
Cast phoenixes holding lotuses in their beaks,
Painted dragons sleeping side by side.
The embers high—doubt they've been trimmed many times;
The wick damp—temporarily hard to relight.
The bronze lotus holds the tearful wax,
The iron tongs are stained with floating smoke.
I knew well that snowlight could reflect on paper,
But marvel again that the lampwick now yields coins.
The lotus curtain, cold stand, window brushed by dawn;
The bamboo cage, perfumed fire, fragrance fills the floss.
Beside it hangs a fine trickle,
Above it circle flying moths.
The light clear, cold enters;
The flame dim, wind passes.
The man of Chǔ's cap tassels all fell off;
The lord of Yān's letters often went astray.
The night wind blows,
The fragrance follows,
In the garden of tulips,
The pool of lotuses.
Qín Shǐhuáng warding off evil is not worth mentioning;
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's foreign incense—what is so marvelous?
The evening stars vanish,
The fragrant grasses rest.
Still holding it to shine on the night excursion,
How could it be less than the moon over the Western Garden?
Wáng Yún of Liáng's "Poem on Candles"
Holding the candle, I lead the fine occasion;
Flowing shadows pass over the single curtain.
Faintly discern the embroidered quilt;
Dimly see the moth eyebrows.
The reed torch's brightness is not precious;
The charred embers—how could they be doubted?
What I fear is that affection may change,
Shining on you as you seek to reverse the chess game.
Liú Xiàochuò of Liáng's "Poem on the Candle Illuminating Chess"
The strings and pipes at Nánpí have ceased;
After the chess game, guests are still detained.
Under the sun, the room grows dark;
The splendid candle summons the fair one.
Side light fully illuminates the board;
Reflected flowers half conceal the figure.
Do not decline though slender hands grow weary,
Lest shame make night turn to dawn.
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng's "Poem on Candles"
The flame, hearing the wind, stirs and moves;
The flower blooms without waiting for spring.
It suppresses a thousand lines of tears,
Not because it misses someone.
Another poem says:
Nine dragons coil—the flame stirs;
Shining all around—flowers follow its light.
Liú Xiàoyí's "Memorial of Gratitude for the Bestowal of Patterned Silk and Candles upon My Daughter's Departure from the Palace"
Xiàoyí respectfully addresses Your Majesty's attendants:
Yuán Wénchéng conveyed the imperial decree,
informing me that Your Majesty, aware of my private arrangements for sending off [my daughter],
graciously bestowed twenty bolts of patterned silk
and twenty sticks of candles.
My family has always been poor and humble,
and many matters are difficult and lacking.
Golden-threaded chambers like those of Huán,
were never something I could aspire to.
Even the dowry prepared by Mèng Jī,
would still seem inadequate.
Yet this exceptional favor has specially descended upon me,
bringing both precious and splendid gifts.
Fashioned into fine garments,
their double beauty would be hard to match.
Held alight without ceasing,
they could last for three nights.
My rank and status are lowly and insignificant,
and such matters are far removed from glorious bestowals.
This descent of compassionate generosity,
truly reveals [Your Majesty's] heartfelt concern.
I, a petty man of humble station,
how could I ever repay this, never forgetting it?
And so forth.
Smoke, Part Fifteen
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"On the winter solstice,
when the jiǎzǐ [cycle] receives command and wood governs affairs,
fire-smoke is green for seventy-two days;
when the wùzǐ [cycle] receives command and earth governs affairs,
fire-smoke is yellow for seventy-two days;
when the gēngzǐ [cycle] receives command and metal governs affairs,
fire-smoke is white for seventy-two days;
when the bǐngzǐ [cycle] receives command and fire governs affairs,
fire-smoke is red for seventy-two days;
when the rénzǐ [cycle] receives command and water governs affairs,
fire-smoke is black for seventy-two days."
The Lièxiān Zhuàn states:
"In ancient times, a divine being visited Níng Fēngrén,
and tended the fire for him.
He could produce smoke of five colors.
He taught [Níng Fēngrén] to pile up firewood and burn himself,
ascending and descending with the smoke."
Fēngrén
was the Director of Pottery during the time of the Yellow Emperor.
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The official in charge of frogs oversees the removal of frogs and toads,
by burning male chrysanthemums.
If the ashes are sprinkled on them, they die;
if the smoke is spread over them, they revive.
Thus all water creatures become silent."
The Jìn Shū states:
"When Fú Jiān was about to face disorder,
in Guānzhōng, earth burned without fire,
and great smoke arose,
covering an area of several tens of lǐ,
and did not dissipate for over a month.
Later, he was destroyed by Mùróng Chōng."
The Hòu Wèi Shū states:
"When Mùróng Chāo was about to perish,
during the firewood sacrifice at the southern suburbs,
flames rose but smoke did not emerge.
The Director of the Spiritual Terrace, Zhāng Guāng, told people:
'When the fire is strong but the smoke perishes,
will the state not perish?'"
The Shíyí Jì states:
"Duke Wén of Jìn set fire to the forest seeking Jiè Zǐtuī.
A white crow circled the smoke and cawed,
sometimes alighting beside Jiè Zǐtuī.
The fire could not burn him.
The people of Jìn praised this,
and built a terrace,
calling it 'Terrace of Longing Smoke.'"
It also states:
"West of Yuánqiáo Mountain is a Star Pool,
from which emerges rotten stone,
often floating on the water.
Red in color and hollow in substance,
resembling a lung.
When burned,
its fragrance can be smelled for several hundred lǐ.
Its smoke rises to the heavens,
forming fragrant clouds,
and when the clouds spread everywhere, they become fragrant rain."
Fire Contains [Smoke]; Water Extinguishes [It]
Yán Yánzhī's "Linked Pearls" states:
"Fire contains smoke, yet smoke hinders fire;
cassia harbors borers, yet borers damage the cassia.
However, when fire prevails, the smoke perishes;
when borers grow strong, the cassia breaks."
The Hàn Shū states:
"During the reign of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
there was a children's rhyme that said:
'Well water overflows,
extinguishing hearth smoke,
flooding the Jade Hall,
flowing through the Golden Gate.'"
Cawing at the Hearth; Removing Frogs
Both are seen in the narrative section.
Reaching the Heavens; Connecting with the Clouds
Shěn Yuē's Sòng Shū states:
"Huán Xuán sent Huán Qiān to garrison Dōnglíngkǒu,
and Biàn Fànzhī to garrison west of Fùzhōu Mountain.
Emperor Gāozǔ personally led his troops in a charge against them.
The northeast wind was strong,
so he ordered fires to be set.
Smoke billowed to the heavens,
and Qiān's and the other armies
collapsed instantly."
Liú Xiàng's "Inscription on the Incense Burner" states:
"Within are orchid and musk,
vermilion fire and blue smoke.
Luxuriantly spreading in all directions,
upward connecting with the azure clouds."
Five Colors; From All Sides
The "Biography of Xǔ Mài" states:
"Mài's childhood name was Yìng.
He possessed the art of the Way.
Yán Qìng of Gāopíng came to Yìng to receive instruction.
Just as Qìng was leaving,
Yìng burned incense,
and five-colored smoke emerged.
Yìng also departed,
and none knew where he went."
Pān Ní's "Rhapsody on Fire" states:
"Dark smoke gathers from all sides,
clouds steam and mists collect."
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng's "Poem on Smoke"
Floating in the air, covering varied shadows,
enveloping trees, dense with flowering vines.
Suddenly like sunset clouds emerging,
somewhat akin to ascending the clouds of Wū.
Reflecting light, flying a hundred rèn high,
scattered by the wind into nine layers.
Wishing to hold its kingfisher color,
at times emerging from the whale-oil lamp.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on Smoke Crossing the Narrow River Village"
Thatch and orchids line both banks,
wild fires illuminate the midstream.
The village chief harbors night shadows,
the narrow river is crossed by floating smoke.
Gathering light darkens the birds' perches,
dividing fire illuminates the fishing boats.
The mountain man does not cook with cassia,
fortunate to share the burning of firewood blossoms.
Qiáo Zhōu's *Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo* states:
"In ancient times, people ate hair and drank blood.
Suìrén first created fire by drilling wood,
and people began to roast and grill."
*Yuán Mìng Bāo* states:
"The word 'fire' (huǒ) signifies compliance and following,
hence its character formation.
The character is formed by the components 'person' (rén) and 'scatter' (sàn)."
*Shuō Wén* states:
"Hàn,
means steaming fire;
Wēi,
means fire in a basin;
Biāo,
means flying fire;
Jiǒng Yuè,
means the light of fire."
*Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"Fire caused by humans is called 'fire',
fire from heaven is called 'disaster'."
*Chūnqiū Fánlù* states:
"If a ruler is deluded by slander and evil,
alienating kin within,
and estranging loyal ministers without.
The blame extends to fire, resulting in great drought,
and there will certainly be fire disasters."
*Chūnqiū Qiántán Bā* states:
"If fire emerges from a well,
a worthy scholar will rise from among the people."
Fire symbolizes the worthy;
when the worthy are suppressed and stagnant,
the symbol emerges from a well.
*Zhōu Yì* states:
"Fire in the sky,
is the hexagram *Dà Yǒu*.
The nobleman uses it to suppress evil and promote good,
complying with heaven's excellent mandate."
Again, *Chūnqiū Fánlù* states:
"If fire does not flame upward,
there will be much lightning in autumn,
due to the ruler's lack of clear vision."
*Guó Yǔ* states:
"If fire burns the ritual vessels,
descendants will be doubtful,
due to the ruler's disregard for the five constants."
Constants,
mean norms.
*Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"Fire is the yang of the south,
its radiance is brightness.
The sage faces it to govern,
taking its symbol."
Transformed Sparrow Floating Crow
Yú Huàn's *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"The Earl of Qín went out hunting,
reaching Xiányáng,
a great bird descended floating,
transforming into a white sparrow.
It held a green cinnabar document in its beak,
and alighted on the ducal carriage."
*Shǐ Jì* states:
"When King Wǔ had crossed the river,
fire descended from above and then again from below,
reaching the king's roof,
flowing into a bird,
its color red."
Outward Illumination Inward Darkness
Zhàn Fāngshēng's discourse states:
"Common talkers believe
that fire illuminates outwardly but lacks the ability to contain shadows,
and reflects inwardly but lacks the power to distinguish light and dark."
Zhāng Yǐn's *Wénshì Zhuàn* states:
"The Lí fire resides darkly within,
therefore it can be reflected upon."
Burning Orchids Burning Mulberry
*Bàopǔzǐ* states:
"Fearing the loss of fire on Wūshān,
worried that orchids and mugwort would be burned together."
*Huáinánzǐ* states:
"In summer, burn mulberry for fire drill fire,
in winter, burn pine for fire drill fire."
Ascending the Repository Constructing a Shrine
*Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng all had fires,
Zǐ Shèn ascended the repository of Dàtíngshì to observe them."
*Hàn Shū*:
"Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng gathered in a shrine,
at night constructed a fire and imitated a fox's cry,
shouting:
'Great Chǔ rises,
Chén Shèng is king.'"
Bundling Hemp Moving Firewood
*Hàn Shū* states:
"Kuǎi Tōng said:
'In my village, there was a woman
who was on good terms with several elder women.
One night, meat was lost,
her mother-in-law thought the woman had stolen it,
and sent her away.'
A village elder woman then bundled hemp and went to borrow fire from the house that lost the meat,
saying:
'Last night, dogs got the meat,
fought and killed each other,
I need fire to bury them.'" Huán Tán's *Xīn Lùn* biography states:
"It is said that Chún Yú Kūn went to a neighbor's house,
saw their chimney was straight,
and firewood was piled beside it,
and told them:
'This invites fire disaster.'
He immediately made the chimney curved and moved the firewood far away."
Glowing Halberds Fire-born Spears
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū* states:
"In the first year of Yǒngxīng of Jìn Emperor Huì,
Chéngdū Wáng attacked Chángshā.
Every night, the blades of spears and halberds had flames,
like hanging candles."
*Hàn Shū* states:
"In the home of Chēshī's later king Gū Jù,
fire sprouted from the tip of a spear.
His wife Bàizī Zōu said to Gū Jù:
'Fire sprouting from a spear tip,
this is the aura of war.'"
Covering Windows Sealing Cracks
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
"Zǔ Yíng loved to study,
continuing day into night.
His parents feared he would become ill,
and forbade him.
Later, he lit a fire to read,
using clothes and quilts to cover the windows,
fearing others would notice."
*Hánzǐ* states:
"An elder is cautious about fire,
sealing its cracks;
Bái Guī walks the dikes,
blocking their holes.
Therefore, the elder has no fire calamity,
Bái Guī has no flood disaster."
Linking Chickens Tethering Oxen
Hé Fǎshèng's *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Yīn Hào went on a northern expedition,
Jiāng Yóu served as his chief clerk.
Yóu took several hundred chickens,
tying their feet with long ropes,
and all were attached with fire.
He drove them out all at once,
they flew over the moat,
gathered on the Qiāng camp,
and the fires all ignited."
*Shǐ Jì* states:
"Qí Jié attacked Jímò,
Tián Dān took a thousand oxen,
bound spears to their horns,
tethered fire to their tails,
and drove them out through the city walls.
Warriors followed behind the oxen,
the fire illuminated,
and whatever they touched died."
Pearls Warding Lotus Repelling
*Guó Yǔ* states:
"Chǔ's Wángsūn Yǔ visited Jìn,
and said to Zhào Jiǎnzǐ:
'Pearls are sufficient to ward off fire disasters, therefore they are treasured.'" Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū* states:
"The palace halls have round springs and square wells combined with lotus flowers,
to repel fire omens."
Flickering Fierce
*Shàng Shū* states:
"Do not be like fire just beginning to flicker,
its burning place,
the order is not to extinguish it."
*Shī* states:
"Like a fierce fire,
then none dare to stop me."
In Mud On Water
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
"During Zhāng Tiānxī's time,
there was fire burning in mud."
*Zhōu Yì* states:
"Fire over water,
is the hexagram *Wèi Jì*."
Línqióng Well Shénqiū Cave
Liú Jìngshū's *Yì Yuàn* states:
"Línqióng has a fire well."
*Kuò Dì Tú* states:
"Shénqiū has a fire cave,
its light illuminates a thousand *lǐ*."
Extending to the Northern Tower, Leaping Over the Eastern Neighbor
Fàn Yè's *History of the Later Hàn* states:
"During Emperor Zhāng's reign,
the mansion of the Prince of Xīnpíng caught fire,
which spread to the northern tower and rear hall."
Cuī Hóng's *Records of the Former Zhào* states:
"When Liú Yīn's great-grandmother's coffin was awaiting burial,
the western neighbor's house caught fire,
and the wind was fierce.
Liú Yīn and his wife kowtowed and prayed,
and the fire then leaped over and burned the eastern neighbor's house instead."
Prairie Fire, Flames Rising
The *Shū* says:
"Like a fire spreading across the prairie,
one cannot approach it."
The *Shū* also says:
"Of the Five Phases,
the second is fire,
and fire is characterized by flames rising."
Transforming into a Sparrow, Flowing Down as a Crow
Yú Huàn's *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"Tàibó went out hunting,
reaching Xiányáng,
when a great bird flowed down
and transformed into a white sparrow.
It held a green cinnabar document in its beak
and alighted upon the ducal carriage."
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"After King Wǔ had crossed the river,
fire descended from above,
reaching the king's roof,
and flowed down in the form of crows."
Drilling for Fire, Producing Clouds
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
"The Yellow Emperor drilled wood to produce fire,
in order to cook meat and fish."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Refining earth produces wood,
refining wood produces fire,
refining fire produces clouds,
refining clouds produces water,
refining water produces earth."
Refining Wood, Melting Metal
"Refining wood" see above.
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"When fire blazes, water extinguishes it;
when metal is hard, fire melts it."
Summer Burning, Winter Dryness
The *Lǐ* states:
"In late summer, fire is brought out
for burning (fields)."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"In summer, yang energy overcomes yin energy to form water.
Water prevails,
therefore the summer solstice is damp;
fire prevails,
therefore the winter solstice is dry."
Recording Things, Naming Officials
The *Shàngshū Dà Zhuàn* states:
"Suìhuáng used fire to record things."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"Tánzǐ used fire to record (the seasons),
therefore he was the Fire Master and named things with fire."
Nìng Fēng, È Bó
The *Lièxiān Zhuàn* states:
"Nìng Fēngzǐ
was the Pottery Overseer for the Yellow Emperor.
He controlled fire
and could create five-colored smoke."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"The Fire Regulator È Bó of the Táotáng clan
dwelt in Shāngqiū
and used fire to mark the seasons."
Dry Bamboo, Old Locust
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"Dry bamboo contains fire,
but without drilling, it will not ignite."
It also states:
"An old locust tree can produce fire;
long-accumulated blood becomes phosphorescence—
people find this unremarkable."
Glowing Terrace, Burning Stone
The *Jùnguó Zhì* states:
"At the remote volcanic mountain in Liánhún Prefecture,
there is a fire well
so deep its bottom cannot be seen.
Fiery vapor rises upward,
like faint lightning.
If one ignites grass with it, smoke and fire erupt;
it is called the Glowing Terrace."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Shíyí Jì* states:
"People from Wǎnqú
crossed the Black River and arrived,
addressing Qín Shǐhuáng:
'In our country, we polish burning stones at night
to substitute for sunlight.
This stone comes from Rán Mountain,
where the soil and rocks all shine with their own light.'
When drilled or struck, fire emerges;
a piece as large as a chestnut can illuminate an entire room."
Moving Firewood, Burning Reeds
The *Hànshū* states:
"Initially,
the Huò clan was extravagant,
and Xú Fú of Màolíng said this was excessive.
He submitted three memorials,
but they were always dismissed.
Later, the Huò clan was executed and exterminated,
and those who had reported them were all enfeoffed.
Someone then submitted a memorial on behalf of Xú Fú, saying:
'A guest visited a host
and saw the host's chimney
with firewood piled beside it.'
The guest said:
'You should bend the chimney
and move the firewood far away,
otherwise there will be a fire disaster.'
The host did not heed this.
Soon his house caught fire,
and the neighbors together rescued him,
fortunately extinguishing it.
Thereupon, he slaughtered an ox, set out wine,
and thanked his neighbors.
Those who were scorched and injured were given seats of honor,
but he did not reward the one who had advised bending the chimney.
Someone said to the host:
'If you had listened to the guest's words earlier,
you would not have spent on ox and wine,
and ultimately would have had no fire disaster.
Now, when discussing merit and inviting guests,
you forget the kindness of the one who advised bending the chimney and moving the firewood,
while treating those with burnt heads and scorched foreheads as honored guests?'
The host realized his error and invited that guest.'
Emperor Xuān summoned Xú Fú and appointed him as a Gentleman."
The *Wú Zhì* states:
"Yáo Guāng possessed fire arts.
Sūn Quán piled several dozen bundles of reeds
and had Yáo Guāng sit atop them,
then set a fierce fire to burn them.
When the reeds were consumed,
he sat upright in the ashes,
holding a scroll of a book."
Covering the Window, Sealing the Cracks
The *History of the Later Wèi* states:
"Zǔ Yíng loved to study,
continuing day into night.
His parents feared he would become ill,
so forbade him.
Later, he lit a fire to read by,
using his clothes to cover the window."
The *Hánfēizǐ* states:
"A prudent man guards against fire by sealing the cracks."
Guǎng Tree, Fúyù Bird
The *Nányuè Zhì* states:
"In Guǎngzhōu, there is a great tree
that can ward off fire."
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"On Fúyù Mountain,
there is a bird named Yù.
It resembles a kingfisher but has a red beak,
and it can guard against fire."
Zhùróng, Huílù
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"The south
corresponds to fire.
Its emperor is Zhùróng,
and his assistant is Zhūhú."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states:
"Zǐchǎn performed an exorcism against fire for Yuánpǔ Huílù."
Kūnlún Mountains, Cauldrons and Boilers
The *Shū* says:
"When fire blazes on the Kūnlún Mountains,
jade and stone are both consumed."
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"The Cook oversees the provision of cauldrons and boilers,
supplying the measures of water and fire."
In the Mud, Upon the Water
Wèi Shōu's *History of the Later Wèi* states:
"During Tiānxī's time,
fire burned in the mud."
The *Zhōu Yì* states:
"Fire above water
Línqióng Well and Shénqiū Cave
Liú Jìngshū’s Yì Yuàn states:
"In Línqióng there is a fire well,
measuring five feet across,
and two or three zhàng deep."
Kuò Dì Tú states:
"Shénqiū has a fire cave,
its light illuminates a thousand lǐ."
Western Jìn Pān Ní’s "Rhapsody on Fire"
Its form arises from no sign,
its sound issues from no semblance.
Seeking it, one cannot find its root;
listening, one cannot hear its echo.
When it comes, none see its trace;
when it departs, none know its going.
It resembles the Great Way not yet departed,
and the primal breath vast and boundless.
Thus it can broadly nourish all living things,
sustain and nurture the myriad kinds.
Abundant yet not violent,
bestowing yet not wasteful.
Its transformations have no fixed direction,
its uses are never exhausted.
Drilling wood to create fire,
it molds and fashions all forms.
It harmonizes the five flavors,
transforms rank and raw smells.
Wine brewing and cooking,
by this are achieved.
And when it burns the wilds and sweeps the plains,
blazing flames radiant and fierce.
Forest trees are snapped and torn,
sand grains are scorched and melted.
Soaring light cuts off the view,
clouds scatter, rainbows spread.
Then the rushing wind stirs and rouses,
fiery light dashes and flees.
Dark smoke closes in from all sides,
clouds steam, mists gather.
Mountains and hills thereby collapse and crumble,
rivers and marshes thereby surge and boil.
Departing as if driven by wind,
swift as lightning fading away.
Desolate the vast sky,
the wilds left with not a remnant.
No lowland is not turned to ash,
no open field is not laid waste.
Once the thickets and weeds are cleared,
the nine wilds become quiet and pure.
It purges withered branches in the bitter autumn,
awaiting the coming spring to renew life.
Its raising voice and unleashing wrath
are the might of thunder and lightning;
its bright illumination and far-reaching discernment
are the radiance of sun and moon;
its molding and shaping of all things
is the work of creation’s design;
its aiding and nurturing of all living beings
is the grace of heaven and earth.
Therefore the highest sages modeled fire to establish rites,
Zhèng Qiáo relied on its fierceness to set governance.
Its function and effect concern past and present,
its merit and achievement are manifest among the hundred clans.

I praise the fire virtue as noble.
It contains the numinous brilliance of the great sun,
embodies the pure and firm upright breath.
The former sages gazed upward in contemplation,
penetrating the divine and awakening to the numinous.
They exhausted the divine and completed the numbers,
investigated the subtleties to reach utmost essence.

its sound issues from no semblance.

Then Dí Yá oversees the feast,

Harmonious soups and fine fermented drinks,

Boiling giant turtles and cooking alligators,

Grinding and tempering arms and armor,

Dài Kuí’s "Rhapsody on Fire"
Fire relies on fuel to transmit its flame,
humans rely on breath to enjoy their years.
If fuel and breath can be exhausted,
how can flame and years eternally extend?
Jìn Chéng Gōngsuí’s "Admonition on Fire"
My household suffered a fire,
the buildings were completely burned,
utensils and belongings utterly gone.
So I went to the four neighbors,
to compose an admonition on fire,
saying:
"The classics and texts became ashes,
the chapters and writings became charcoal."
Zhū Xuán’s "On the Dim Fire Not Being Hot"
Master Zhū was traveling between the Hé and Luò rivers,
about to lodge at an inn,
when he encountered a fire at the inn,
and there was an old innkeeper.
The master lifted his robes and descended from the carriage,
circled around and peered inside,
and saw him panting and already dead.
The master said:
"Alas!
Fire’s flourishing of things,
has reached such a point!"
His disciple Kǒng Kūn stepped forward and said:
"Strange indeed is the master’s talk!
As for fire’s heat,
among physical forms it burns and consumes,
on skin and flesh it scorches and destroys,
why speak of it flourishing things?"
Crown, First Rank
Liú Xī's *Shìmíng* states:
"The guān (crown)
means 'to pass through,'
it is that which passes through and contains the hair."
Dǒng Bā's *Hàn Yúfú Zhì* states:
"In high antiquity, people dwelled in caves and lived in the wilds,
wearing fur and covering themselves with hides.
Later generations of sages changed this.
Seeing that birds and beasts had the forms of crests, horns, manes, and beards,
they then made guān, miǎn, yīng, and ruí."
*Chūnqiū Fánlù* states:
"The guān being on the head
is the image of Xuánwǔ.
Xuánwǔ
is the most stern and awe-inspiring in appearance.
Its image is on the right,
yet the cap, conversely, is placed on the head;
this is the ultimate in martiality, yet it is not used."
*Sānlǐ Tú* states:
"The guān of the Great Antiquity,
made of cloth, was dyed black when neatened;
later it was taken as a guān,
this is the beginning of the guān.
The present military guān is its surviving image."
*Chūnqiū Héchénɡ Tú* states:
"The Celestial August Great Emperor
is the North Star.
Embracing the origin and holding the yang,
he releases essence and emits light.
Residing in the Purple Palace,
he controls and governs the four directions.
His guān has five colors."
It also states:
"The Yellow Emperor wears a guān with yellow patterns,
the White Emperor wears a guān with white patterns,
the Black Emperor wears a guān with black patterns."
*Lǐjì* states:
"Wearing a yellow guān to sacrifice
gives rest to the field laborers."
*Jiāyǔ* states:
"A senior official pleading for punishment
uses a white guān with yak-tail tassels."
*Lǐjì* states:
"A black guān with vermillion silk tassels
is the guān of the Son of Heaven;
a black cloth guān with hempen ruí
is the guān of the feudal lords;
a black guān with cinnabar silk tassels
is the fasting guān of the feudal lords;
a black guān with dark green silk tassels
is the fasting guān of the shì;
a plain white guān with a black band
is the guān of the descendants;
hanging ruí five inches long
is the guān of the idle wanderers;
a black guān with a plain white band
is the attire of those not ranked.
For the dwelling guān, the band is attached;
from the Son of Heaven down to the commoners,
the ruí is only added when there is an affair."
*Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Zhèng Zǐzāng was fond of collecting snipe-feather guān."
*Huáinánzǐ* states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ was fond of the xiè (mythical beast) guān."
Gōngsūn Qūzǐ states:
"Qū Dào wore a mò guān."
*Zhànguócè* states:
"King Kāng of Sòng made a headless guān to show his bravery."
*Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"Sòng Xíng
and Yǐn Wén made Huàshān guān to express themselves."
*Hànwǔ Nèizhuàn* states:
"Lady Shàngyuán wore a Nine-Clouds Night-Light guān,
and the Queen Mother of the West wore a Tàizhēn Morning-Infant guān."
Quèdí (Ward Off Foes) Jìnxián (Promote Worthies)
*Sānlǐ Tú* states:
"The Quèdí guān
is four inches wide in front,
four inches long overall,
and three inches high in the back.
Guards wear it."
*Yúfú Zhì* states:
"The Jìnxián guān
is the ancient black cloth guān.
It is the attire of Confucian scholars.
It is seven inches high in front,
three inches in the back,
and eight inches long.
Dukes and marquises have three crossbeams,
those below the fully two-thousand-dan rank down to Erudites have two crossbeams,
and those below Erudites down to minor clerks have one crossbeam."
Xièzhì (Mythical Beast) Jùnyí (Bird Name)
*Hàn Guānyí* states:
"The xièzhì beast by nature gores the unjust,
therefore those who uphold the law use the shape of its horn for their guān."
*Shǐjì* states:
"During Gāozǔ's time,
there was Jí Rú;
during Xiàohuì's time,
there was Hóng Rú.
They were charming, flattering, and highly favored,
sleeping and rising with the emperor.
Therefore, during Emperor Huì's time, the gentlemen of the palace
all wore jùnyí guān,
shell-decorated belts,
applied powder and rouge,
comparing themselves to the likes of Hóng and Jí."
Chánchì (Cicada Wing) Quèwěi (Maggie Tail)
*Hànshū* states:
"Zhāng Chǎng's younger brother Wǔ was Chancellor of Liáng.
He said:
'To control a cunning horse, one benefits from bit and whip,
and should use the 'posterior pillar cicada-pattern' to strongly rein it in.'" Rúchún's annotation states:
"Huì
means cicada.
The guān is as fine as a cicada's wing;
this is the present guān of the Imperial Censor."
It also states:
"When Gāozǔ was a village head,
he then made a guān from bamboo bark."
Yìng Shào's annotation states:
"He used the bark of newly sprouted bamboo to make a guān;
this is the present magpie-tail guān."
Tiězhù (Iron Pillar) Jīnyán (Golden Forehead)
*Hàn Guānyí* states:
"The Attendant Censor
is an office from the Zhōu dynasty.
He served as the Historian Under the Pillar,
wearing the legal guān.
It is also called 'posterior pillar,'
with iron used for the pillar."
Xú Yuán's *Shìwèn* states:
"The Tōngtiān guān
is made with a golden broad-mountain cicada,
called the 'golden forehead.'"
Quèfēi (Ward Off Wrong) Jiāoràng (Mutual Deference)
*Sānlǐ Tú* states:
"The Quèfēi guān
is worn by the palace attendants and historians,
it is three inches high."
*Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Mǎ Yuán had an old acquaintance with Gōngsūn Shù.
Yuán went from Jì into Shǔ.
Shù was very pleased to see him,
and went with him into the ancestral temple,
ordering him to wear the Jiāoràng guān,
and stand at the position of old friendship."
Wǔcǎi (Five Colors) Sìchóng (Four Layers)
*Sānlǐ Tú* states:
"The Wǔcǎi Fāngshān guān
is made with each using its colored gauze for the guān.
When the Son of Heaven sacrifices in the temple,
with eight rows of dancers,
the performers of the Five Elements dance wear it."
*Yúfú Zhì* states:
"The Shùshì guān
has five colors.
The upper garment is dark blue, the lower garment black, with a round front;
its construction is uneven,
meandering in four layers.
King Wǔlíng of Zhào was fond of wearing it,
but it is not used nowadays."
Xiàshōu (Xià Headgear) Yīnxǔ (Yīn Headgear)
*Lǐ Wángzhì* states:
"The people of Xià wear the shōu for sacrifice,
and informal clothes for caring for the aged.
The people of Yīn wear the xǔ for sacrifice,
and plain white clothes for caring for the aged."
Shuāngruí (Double Tassels) Dānxǐ (Single Silk Cap)
*Máoshī* states:
"Five pairs of hempen sandals,
the guān's ruí come to a double stop."
*Hànshū*:
"Jiāng Chōng was summoned for an audience with the emperor.
He wore a plain gauze unlined robe,
and a dānxǐ bùyáo guān."
Jīndāng (Golden Earpiece) Zhūtiàn (Pearl Earplug)
*Yúfú Zhì* states:
"The military guān,
also called the military biàn great guān,
is worn by all military officials.
Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants add a golden dāng,
with an attached cicada as pattern,
and sable tail as ornament."
Cuī Hóng's *Qiányān Lù* states:
"Mùróng Jùn instituted the píngshàng guān,
and bestowed it upon all below the Commandant of Justice.
For the Directors of the Palace Library,
pearl tiàn were separately applied."
Warm Marten, Vigorous Pheasant
The *Hàn Guān Yí* states:
"The Shìzhōng wears a golden cicada and left marten.
Gold is chosen for its firmness and strength,
unconsumed even after a hundred smeltings.
The cicada is chosen for its dwelling on high and pure diet,
its mouth located beneath its armpits.
The marten is internally vigorous and externally warm."
It also states:
"The Hǔbēn cap is adorned with two pheasant tails.
The pheasant
is the most vigorous and resolute among birds of prey."
Wrapped Shield, Overturned Cup
The *Yúfú Záshì* states:
"When Chǔ and Hàn met at Hóngmén,
Xiàng Jí plotted to endanger Gāozǔ.
Fán Kuài heard of this
and grew anxious.
He then tore his garment to wrap a shield,
wore it as a crown,
and pushed his way into the feather-adorned camp."
"Overturned Cup" appears in the narrative on the biàn.
Summoning Yú, Bestowing upon Yuè
"Summoning Yú" appears in the parallel couplet on "banners."
The *Chūnqiū Shì Ē* states:
"Hé Xiū said:
'Bestowing a crown upon the Yuè people,
they will never consider it a favor.'"
Kingfisher Tassels, Crimson Strings
The *Liáng Shū* states:
"The Son of Heaven wears the Yuǎnyóu crown,
adorned with a golden cicada and kingfisher tassel strings."
"Crimson Strings" appears in the narrative.
Dove Brushing, Crow Gathering
Xiāo Fāngděng's *Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū* states:
"In the first year of Yǒngkāng of Jìn, during the grand assembly in the first month,
a dove entered the martial tent at the imperial seat
and brushed against the crown of Sīkōng Zhāng Huá."
Fú Hóu's *Gǔjīn Zhù* states:
"When Lǔ Shēn was hoeing melons,
a three-legged crow came and gathered upon his crown."
Wèi Qí's "Ode on the Crown"
Exquisite and fine strings,
light as cicada wings.
Honored as the primal adornment,
esteemed as the head's attire.
The nobleman is reverent and cautious,
self-strengthening without error.
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Crowns and Headcloths"
The crown is the primal attire,
the headcloth is the head's garment.
The nobleman is reverent and cautious,
self-strengthening without error.
Fù Xuán's "Inscription on the Crown"
When dwelling on high, do not forget danger;
when above, do not forget reverence.
Fear brings safety,
reverence brings uprightness.
Biàn, Part Two
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"Biàn means to grasp,
holding the hair."
The *Shìmíng* states:
"The biàn is like two hands joined together in a clasp
(pronounced fèn).
At that time,
if made of jué leather,
it is called a jué biàn;
if made of deerskin,
it is called a pí biàn;
if made of mèi leather,
it is called a wéi biàn."
Dǒng Bā's *Yúfú Zhì* states:
"The jué biàn,
also called miǎn.
It is eight cùn wide,
twelve cùn long,
shaped like a jué vessel.
Small in front, large in the back.
Its top resembles the color of a jué vessel's head,
with a gather holding the hairpin,
which is what is called the Xià's shōu and Yīn's xǔ
(pronounced xū yǔ fǎn).
It is worn by dancers of the Yúnqiáo dance
during sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the Five Suburbs, and the Bright Hall."
The *Sānlǐ Tú* states:
"The jué biàn
is the attire of scholars assisting the ruler in sacrifices.
It is worn for sacrifices in the ancestral temple
and lacks hanging beads.
The wéi biàn
is the military attire of kings and feudal lords."
The *Yúfú Zhì* states:
"The pí biàn shares the same design as the wěimào,
seven cùn long,
four cùn high.
Its shape is like an overturned cup,
tall and broad in front,
low and sharp in the back.
This is what is called the Xià's wúzhuī
and the Yīn's zhāngfǔ.
During the Grand Archery Ceremony at the Pìyōng,
dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and great officers performing the rites wear the wěimào,
while those handling affairs wear the pí biàn
and dress in coarse hemp garments."
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"The Biànshī is in charge of the king's pí biàn,
adorned with five-colored jade qí,
and an ivory dǐ with a jade hairpin."
Qí is the same as qí,
meaning to tie.
It refers to five-colored jade threaded and tied in the seams.
The *Wèi Tái Fǎng Yì* states:
"Five-colored jade
refers to a single piece of jade with five colors.
The dǐ
is made of ivory and encircles the base of the biàn,
like the biàn dǐ made by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi.
Generally, it has a hairpin but no strings."
Cáo Bāo said:
"The Son of Heaven's biàn is adorned with white jade."
The *Zuǒzhuàn* states:
"Chǔ's Zǐ Yù made himself a qióng biàn."
The *Yèzhōng Jì* states:
"Shí Jìlóng had several dozen palace maids
all dressed in black gōu garments,
with heads adorned in divine biàn.
Like today's ritual of first wearing a crown,
the Queen Mother of the West wears the Jiāodài Língfēi ribbon,
and Lady Shàngyuán wears the Fèngwén Línhuá ribbon."
Kylin Leather, Ivory Base
The *Hànshū* states:
"When Wáng Mǎng first presented new music at the Bright Hall and Grand Temple,
the assembled ministers wore biàn made of kylin leather."
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"The Biànshī is in charge of the king's pí biàn,
with an ivory dǐ and jade hairpin."
Patterned Like a Qí, Adorned Like a Deer
The *Máoshī* states:
"The virtuous gentleman
wears a biàn patterned like a qí."
Máo Cháng's annotation states:
"Qí
means pattern."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"In ancient times, simplicity prevailed,
and deerskin was worn first,
chosen for its patterns."
Placed on the Head, Gathering the Hair
The *Gǔliáng Zhuàn* states:
"Though the biàn crown may be old,
it must be placed on the head.
Though the Zhōu house may decline,
it must come before the feudal lords."
The *Máoshī* states:
"The refined gentleman
has earplugs of beautiful stone,
and his biàn gathers like stars."
The annotation states:
"The biàn is used to gather the hair."
Announcing the New Moon, Attending Court
The *Jiāyǔ* states:
"Feudal lords wear pí biàn
to announce the new moon at the Grand Temple."
The *Zhōulǐ* states:
"When attending court, they wear pí biàn attire."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states:
"This refers to attending to affairs of the outer court."
Seal, Part Three
Liú Xī's *Shìmíng* states:
"A seal,
is a token of trust,
used to seal objects as proof.
It is also said to mean 'to rely on,'
as sealed objects are entrusted accordingly."
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuōwén* states:
"It is the token of trust held by those in power."
Wèi Hóng's *Hàn Jiù Yí* states:
"The seals of feudal lords and kings
are made of gold with a camel knob,
and the inscription reads 'xǐ';
for marquises,
the gold seal has a turtle knob,
and the inscription reads 'yìn';
for chancellors and generals,
the gold seal has a turtle knob,
and the inscription reads 'zhāng';
for officials with a salary of two thousand shí,
the silver seal has a turtle knob,
and the inscription reads 'zhāng';
for officials with salaries of one thousand shí, six hundred shí, and four hundred shí,
the bronze seal has a nose knob,
and the inscription reads 'yìn'."
*Xù Hànshū·Lǐyí Zhì* states:
"Seals and imperial seals,
for kings, are made of jade with silver inlay patterns.
For noblewomen and elder princesses, they are made of bronze with inlay."
Hé Fǎshèng's *Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Kǒng Yú passed by Yútíng,
releasing a turtle into the stream,
and the turtle looked back to the left as it swam midstream.
Later, for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yútíng,
and when the marquis seal was cast,
the turtle on it looked back to the left.
Even after recasting, it remained the same.
The seal artisan reported this to Kǒng Yú,
who then understood,
and took it to wear."
*Sōushén Jì* states:
"When Zhāng Hào was the chancellor of Liáng,
just after a rain,
a bird resembling a mountain magpie
flew close to the ground.
He ordered someone to catch it,
and it turned into a stone.
Zhāng Hào ordered it to be broken open,
and inside was a gold seal,
with the inscription:
'Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety.'
Zhāng Hào presented it,
and it was stored in the palace.
Later, the court counselor Fán Héngyí from Rǔnán submitted a memorial:
'In the times of Yáo and Shùn, such an official position existed,
and now a seal has descended from heaven,
so it should be reinstated.'"
Casting a Turtle Providing Horses
"Casting a turtle" is mentioned in the narrative.
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
"Emperor Gāo decreed:
'For military alerts, provide sparrow seals,
and for relay tallies, provide horse seals next.'"
Gold Turtle Jade Dragon
"Gold turtle" is mentioned in the narrative.
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèi Shū* states:
"In the first year of the Yǒngmíng era of Emperor Gāozǔ,
a person from Shànggǔ Commandery presented a jade seal,
with a dragon pattern on it."
Zhǒnglóng Catching a Magpie
Quān Chēng's *Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn* states:
"Bāwú County
is a mixed area of Sòng, Chén, and Chǔ,
formerly the Zhǒnglóng Township of Nínglíng in the State of Liáng.
Now its capital's seal inscription reads 'Zhǒnglóng'."
"Catching a magpie" is mentioned in the narrative.
Holding a Hook Carving a Date
*Mèng Shū* states:
"The seal hook represents what a son receives as emolument.
Dreaming of a seal hook means one will have a son.
Holding or swallowing a seal hook
indicates a pregnant woman.
If the hook emerges from the abdomen, it signifies breastfeeding.
Losing the seal means harm to the child,
or miscarriage while pregnant.
If a wife has a child,
holding it in the mouth
means the child will be within the household."
*Huáng Jūn Zhì Shǐ Hǔ Bào Fǎ* states:
"A Daoist priest should carve a seal from the heart of a date tree,
four cùn square."
Jìn Fù Xuán's "Inscription on Seals"
In ancient times, the former kings,
modeled on heaven, established rules.
Thus, seals were created,
to serve as tokens of trust for all states.
Taking inspiration from celestial measures,
they were inscribed and carved.
Refined and meticulous,
upright and virtuous in nature.
With the foundation established, the Way arises,
returning to profound silence.
The highest rulers tied knots,
and below, there was no disorder or wickedness.
Hòu Hàn Hú Bóshǐ's "Inscription on Sealed Robes"
The illustrious sovereign above,
bestows robes as symbols of command.
Wearing red ribbons and holding gold,
they shine and adorn.
Spreading their benevolence far and wide,
pacifying and comforting the four states.
Promoting kindness, grace, and harmony,
gentle and virtuous as the standard.
Maintaining constancy in their hearts,
they receive abundant blessings.
Ascending to positions and enjoying longevity,
with descendants numbering in the thousands.
Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Seals"
With red ribbons on the robe,
without a seal, it lacks clarity.
Tallies, passes, and tokens,
without a seal, cannot function.
With turtle knobs or ox-nose shapes,
you serve as the standard.
Sashes, Fourth
The *Hàn Guān Yí* states:
"A sash (shòu)
is that which receives and bears.
It serves to distinguish noble from base,
and manifest those who possess virtue."
Lǚ Chēn's *Zì Lín* states:
"A sash (shòu)
is a ribbon (fú)."
Dǒng Bā's *Yú Fú Zhì* states:
"During the Warring States period, the ribbon pendants were removed,
leaving only the silk cord (suì),
which was used as a marker of rank.
The Qin then connected colored braids to the cord,
making the marker of rank bright and clear.
These were then interwoven to form the sash,
hence it was called 'shòu' (to connect/receive).
The imperial carriage uses a yellow-red sash of five colors,
with yellow, red, light blue, and dark blue, pure yellow as the guī (standard color),
measuring 2 zhang 9 chi in length,
with 500 'heads' (shǒu, a unit of fineness);
the Grand Empress Dowager, Empress Dowager, and Empress are all the same.
Also, the *Hàn Guān Yí* states:
"The imperial sash has a yellow ground with bone (pattern?), white feather, and blue-crimson border.
Five colors,
400 heads,
2 zhang 3 chi in length."
Feudal kings have a red sash of four colors,
red, yellow, light blue, dark blue, pure red as the guī,
2 zhang 8 chi in length,
300 heads;
princesses, high-ranking noble ladies (dà guìrén),
and feudal lords are all the same.
Also, the *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
"Four colors,
crimson ground with bone (pattern?), white feather, and blue, yellow, red colors,
2 zhang 1 chi,
206 heads.
Marquises,
crimson ground, dark blue, light blue, three colors,
120 heads,
2 zhang 8 chi in length."
Noblemen of various states and the Chancellor have a green sash of three colors,
green, purple, dark blue, pure green as the guī,
2 zhang 1 chi in length,
240 heads;
Dukes, Marquises, and Generals have a purple sash of two colors,
purple, white, pure purple as the guī,
1 zhang 7 chi in length,
180 heads;
Princesses and enfieffed lords are the same.
Also, the *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
"The Chancellor, Imperial Secretary, and the Xiongnu (Chanyu?) are also the same."
The Nine Ministers and officials with rank of fully 2000 shi,
one source says a blue-green *guā* sash
*Guā* is a purplish-blue color,
*guā* pronounced like *guā* (melon).
Officials of 2000 shi rank,
have a blue sash of three colors,
blue, white, red, pure blue as the guī,
1 zhang 7 chi in length,
120 heads;
also, the *Hàn Guān Yí*:
"The sash has a blue ground with feather (pattern?),
peach-blossom light blue,
1 zhang 8 chi in length."
From the blue sash and above,
the *yì* (cord connecting sash to seal) is always 3 chi 2 cun long,
of the same colors as the sash but with half the number of heads.
The *yì*
is the ancient pendant cord (pèi suì).
The pendant cord received and connected (to the sash?),
hence called *yì*.
Above the purple sash,
between the *yì* and the sash,
one may attach jade rings or penannular jades (*jué*).
Officials of 1000 shi and 600 shi have a black sash of three colors,
blue, red, dark blue, pure blue as the guī,
1 zhang 6 chi in length,
80 heads;
also, the *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
"Ink (black) sash, white feather, blue ground, crimson, two colors,
1 zhang 7 chi in length."
Officials of 400 (shi),
Assistant Magistrates (chéng wèi).
Officials of 300 (shi),
Chiefs of districts (zhǎng xiàng).
Officials of 200 and 100 shi,
all have a yellow sash of one color,
pure yellow as the guī,
1 zhang 5 chi in length,
60 heads."
Also, the *Hàn Guān Yí* says:
"Yellow sash with border, 80 heads,
1 zhang 7 chi in length."
The *Jìn Lìng* states:
"The Crown Prince, his consort, and the various Kings,
have black and vermilion sashes;
Commandery Princesses,
vermilion sashes;
Commandery Marquises,
blue and vermilion sashes."
The *Yú Fú Zhì* also says:
"From the black sash and below,
the *yì* cord is 3 chi long,
of the same colors as the sash but with half the number of heads.
Officials of 100 shi have a blue-dark blue sash of one color,
twisted and intricately woven guī,
1 zhang 2 chi in length.
Generally, first single strands are spun into one silk thread,
four threads make one *fú*,
five *fú* make one 'head' (shǒu),
five 'heads' make one pattern unit (wén),
the pure color of the pattern unit forms one guī.
More 'heads' means finer threads,
fewer means coarser threads,
all are 1 chi 6 cun wide."
The *Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn* states:
"The Queen Mother of the West bestowed a girdle with a Lingfēi sash,
and the Lady of the Primordial Supreme wore a phoenix-patterned Línhuá sash."
Peach Blossom Lì Grass
The sash for 2000 shi officials is peach-blossom light blue,
fully described in the narrative notes.
The *Hàn Shū* states:
"Feudal Kings,
first established by Emperor Gāozǔ,
had gold seals and *lì* (green) sashes."
Rú Chún's commentary says:
"*Lì*
means green."
Jìn Zhuó says:
"*Lì*
is the name of a plant.
It comes from Píngchāng County in Lángyé,
resembles mugwort,
can be used to dye green,
and thus became the name of the sash.
*Lì* is pronounced *lì*."
Five Colors Four Colors
The *Xī Jīng Zá Jì* states:
"When Zhào Fēiyàn became Empress,
her younger sister presented her with a five-colored patterned sash."
"Four colors" is mentioned in the narrative.
White Mugwort Blue-Green *Guā*
Jiāo Gòng's *Yì Lín* states:
"For officials of 2000 shi rank,
it is the white mugwort sash."
The *Shǐ Jì* states:
"Emperor Wǔ summoned Master Dōngguō,
and appointed him Commandery Commandant.
The master had long waited for an audience at the Gōngchē office,
walking in the snow,
his shoes had tops but no soles.
When he was appointed to the 2000 shi rank,
he wore the blue-green *guā* sash."
Black-Vermilion Blue-Purple
"Black-vermilion" is mentioned in the narrative.
The *Jìn Yǒng'ān Qǐjū Zhù* states:
"In the fourth year of Tàikāng,
the officials reported,
the state of Shànshàn sent its son Yuányīng to serve at court,
and Yīng was appointed Cavalry Commandant.
He was granted the temporary seal of Marquis Guīyì,
and one set each of blue and purple sashes."
Red Ground Crimson Border
The *Hàn Míngchén Zòu* states:
"The Grand Minister of Works Zhū Yóu memorialized:
'The Assistant of the Chariot Office has a dark yellow sash,
but the edict says the imperial sash has five colors,
why is there so much yellow?'
It should be changed to use red silk for the ground."
"Crimson border" is seen in the narrative.
Sash Case Inscription by Zhāng Héng of the Later Hàn
Bào Dé, Governor of Nányáng,
had a sash case bestowed by imperial edict upon his late father,
passed down through generations and used.
At that time, Dé refurbished the case,
and Héng, then serving as Dé's Registrar,
composed an inscription, saying:
"Splendid is this case,
wherein treasures are stored.
Cap tassels, girdle ribbons, and shoes,
their patterns daily attest (to rank).
The Sovereign used it to bestow upon me,
making me a servant of the Emperor.
Wearing these mandated robes,
with phoenix-sealed ribbons of mugwort-dyed silk.
Heaven blesses bright virtue,
greatly rewarding the blessed and benevolent.
May its glory shine on his descendants,
may sons and grandsons embody the divine.
The vessel itself is old,
but its contents are ever new.
Like the affairs of the Duke of Zhōu,
the seven streams have their neighbors."
The Later Han Dynasty's Hú Guǎng's "Inscription for the Official Seal Case"
How splendid is this seal case,
A model among all vessels.
It is bestowed upon the gentleman minister,
To bear this seal and ribbon.
Bestowed by imperial command,
To commend his fine virtue.
Prepared for self-cultivation,
Used for self-admonishment.
Loyal, respectful, reverent, and virtuous,
Few fail to take him as a model.
Without regret or stinginess,
Gods and men bring him blessings.
Hu Fifth
Hu,
is the hand tablet.
The Shìmíng states:
"Hu,
means sudden.
When the ruler has instructions or when one has a report to make,
it is written on it,
to guard against forgetting suddenly."
The Yúfú Záshì states:
"When pointing and gesturing before the ruler,
or receiving commands before the ruler,
write on the hu.
The hu is used for everything."
Everything,
means all.
The Lǐjì states:
"The Son of Heaven uses jade,
feudal lords use ivory,
high officials use bamboo decorated with fish whiskers.
Scholars may use bamboo with an ivory base."
Decoration means adornment;
high officials adorn bamboo to make hu,
not daring to use pure objects on par with the ruler.
The Dàdài Lǐ states:
"The Son of Heaven uses tǐng,
tǐng,
means upright and square, facing all under heaven.
Feudal lords use shū,
shū,
curved in front and straight in back,
inferior to the Son of Heaven.
Shū is pronounced shū.
High officials use hu."
Curved in front and curved in back,
showing deference in all matters.
The Sānlǐ Tú states:
"Scholars' hu are adorned with ivory,
high officials are adorned with fish whiskers."
Shark's whiskers.
The Yúfú Záshì also states:
"In ancient times, both noble and humble held guī tablets,
to record the ruler's government orders.
When there were matters,
they would tuck them into their waist belts.
Since the Five Dynasties,
only the eight senior ministers and the shàngshū who hold hu,
attach a white brush to the head of the hand tablet,
wrapped in a purple pouch.
The other princes, dukes, ministers, and scholars,
merely hold hand tablets,
the tablet primarily signifies respect.
Not holding hu,
indicates they are not record-keeping officials."
Fish Whiskers Ivory
Both are mentioned in the narrative.
Recording Goodness Writing Responses
Zhōu Qiān's Yúfú Záshì states:
"Yìng Zhòngyuǎn said:
'In the past, Jīng Kē pursued the King of Qín,
afterwards, the court attendants carried daggers to guard the palace gates,
to prepare for unexpected events.
From then on, all attending officials carried swords and daggers.'" Hàn Gāozǔ abandoned military affairs and promoted culture,
and first instituted the use of hand tablets to replace them.
Therefore, Zhòng Chángzǐ said:
"Hu are used to record the ruler's instructions and orders,
to record good deeds and criticize faults,
today's hand tablets imitate this."
The Lǐjì states:
"When going to the ruler's place,
the historian presents the ivory hu,
to record thoughts and responses to commands."
Smooth Grain Gleaming in Hand
The Xiāng Shǒubǎn Jīng states:
"It should have smooth and straight grain,
from top to bottom straight as a bowstring,
and must not have grain that breaks off at the edges."
Liú Yìgōng's memorial states:
"The sage emperor's grace is generous and weighty,
bestowing upon me a splendid tassel and jade hu,
a precious cap adorning my head.
A precious tablet gleaming in my hand,
unsuitable for someone as frail and shallow as I,
to wear and receive."
With Mèng Qí Striking Qián Fèng
Guō Zǐhéng's Dòngmíng Jì states:
"Mèng Qí,
was a reclusive man of the Zhōu from Qīng Rǔ.
He was about seven hundred years old,
and spoke of early Zhōu events as if they were before his eyes.
Qí once attended the Duke of Zhōu ascending the altar,
Qí used his hand to stroke King Chéng's foot,
and the Duke of Zhōu gave him a jade hu."
The Jìn Jì states:
"Wáng Dūn appointed Wēn Qiáo as Governor of Dānyáng,
Qiáo inwardly wished to leave Dūn but outwardly feigned reluctance.
Qián Fèng sensed this,
but did not speak.
Qiáo knew he would slander him,
so during a public gathering at Dūn's residence,
he forced wine on Fèng,
who refused to drink,
and Qiáo struck Fèng with his hand tablet."
Wáng Shēngzhī's "Hu Eulogy"
Prudence is the essence of virtue,
only goodness uses it gloriously.
Revere superiors and honor the worthy,
nobility does not exceed the norm.
Thus this vessel is made,
prepared against forgetfulness.
Apply ritual according to the occasion,
ascent and descent have their rules.
Pèi Sixth
Lǚ (Footwear) Seventh
The Shìběn states:
"Yú Zé made straw sandals and shoes."
The Shìmíng states:
"Lǚ (footwear),
is lǐ (ritual/propriety),
adorning the feet to serve as ritual.
It is also called lǚ,
meaning 'to restrain',
that which restrains the feet.
People of Qí call straw sandals 'fèi bùjiè',
meaning they are cheap and easy to obtain,
each should keep their own,
and not borrow from others."
The Shuōwén states:
"Sǎ,
are children's shoes."
Also, dī,
are straw sandals.
The Jiǎzǐ states:
"The Son of Heaven wears black square-toed shoes,
feudal lords wear plain white square-toed shoes,
and high officials wear plain white round-toed shoes."
The Jìn decree on footwear states:
"Footwear for soldiers and artisans of various trades,
colors must not exceed green, blue, and white.
Footwear for male and female servants,
color must not exceed pure blue.
In ancient times, those selling paintings wore one white shoe and one black shoe."
The Yántiělùn states:
"In ancient times, commoners wore coarse straw sandals and grass shoes,
now the wealthy wear leather boots and silk shoes."
Treading Frost / Walking in Snow
The Máo Shī states:
"East and west, great and small,
their looms are empty.
Tightly woven hemp sandals,
can tread upon the frost."
The Shǐjì states:
"Dōngguō Xiānshēng awaited an audience at the Gōngchē bureau,
impoverished, hungry, and cold,
his clothes worn and incomplete.
Walking in the snow,
his shoes had tops but no soles,
his feet entirely touching the ground,
people on the road laughed at him."
Nourishing the Body / Adorning the Feet
The Sūnqīngzǐ states:
"Coarse silk shoes,
can nourish the body."
"Adorning the feet" is discussed in the narrative section.
Kneeling to Move / Sitting to Retrieve
The Lǐjì states:
"When facing an elder while wearing shoes,
kneel to move the shoes,
and bend down to put them on."
It also states:
"When a gentleman drinks wine,
after three cups he withdraws,
then sits to retrieve his shoes,
and discreetly puts them on before leaving."
Adorned with Cinnabar Leopard / Adorned with Vermilion Clam
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"King Mù built the Chūnxiāo Palace,
and the Queen Mother of the West came,
wearing shoes adorned with cinnabar leopard patterns."
Liú Zhēn's Lǔ Dū Fù states:
"Delicate silk shoes,
resplendent and fresh.
Embellished with patterned fastenings,
adorned with vermilion clams."
Zhòngzǐ Weaves / Xiàofǔ Repairs
Huángfǔ Mì's Gāoshì Zhuàn states: "Chén Zhòng,
courtesy name Zǐzhōng,
was from Qí.
He went to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ wished to make him chancellor.
His wife said:
'You weave sandals for a living,
tranquil and without ambition,
joy lies within this!'
He then declined the envoy."
The Lièxiān Zhuàn states:
"Xiàofǔ,
from Jìzhōu,
repaired shoes in the market of Qūzhōu.
For decades,
it was remarkable that he did not age."
Duke Wén Loses / King Zhāo Breaks
The Hánzǐ states:
"Duke Wén of Jìn battled the people of Chǔ,
reaching Fènghuáng Ridge.
His shoe strap came loose and fell off,
so he tied it himself."
The Jiǎyìzǐ states:
"Long ago, King Zhāo of Chǔ battled the people of Wú.
The Chǔ army fled, and his shoe broke,
losing it.
After walking thirty paces,
he turned back to retrieve it.
His attendants asked:
'Why spare a single broken shoe?'
The King said:
'Although Chǔ is poor,
how could I begrudge a single broken shoe?'
He thought of leaving together with it and not returning without it."
Later Liáng Emperor Xuān's "Ode to Shoes Poem"
A pair appearing, echoing sounds proclaimed,
Flying together, at times displaying wonder.
In humble places, even more exquisite,
Constantly secure, why grieve their fall?
Fù Xuán's "Inscription on Shoes"
Be warned!
Remember to tread the upright path without wickedness.
Uprightness is the road to fortune,
Wickedness is the omen of misfortune.
Later Hàn Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on Patterned Shoes"
Thus were these shoes made,
Patterned yet martial in substance.
Truly manifesting wisdom,
Humble to govern the self.
Treading this embankment path,
Cutting off that dust of the world.
Fur Garments, Eighth
The Shuōwén states:
"Fur garments
are clothing made from animal hides."
The Báihǔ Tōng states:
"They assist women's work by providing warmth.
In ancient times, black robes were worn with lamb fur, and
yellow robes with fox fur.
Although there were many birds and beasts,
only fox and lamb were chosen,
because they are light and warm.
The fox, because it dies with its head toward its burrow,
symbolizes that the nobleman does not forget his origins.
The lamb, because it kneels to suckle,
symbolizes humility and obedience."
The Lǐjì states:
"In the first month of winter,
the Son of Heaven begins wearing fur garments."
The Zhōuguān states:
"The Fur Officer makes the grand fur garment,
to provide the attire for the king's sacrifices to Heaven;
this is lamb fur.
In mid-autumn, fine fur garments are presented,
and then feathered creatures are distributed.
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"These are fur garments with axe-pattern embroidery.
'Distributing feathered creatures'
means giving flying birds to the various officials."
In late autumn, service fur garments are presented,
to be kept for distribution as rewards."
These include items like blue fox fur and fawn fur.
Since doves transform into hawks at this time,
rewards are given during this season.
The Wǔjīng Yàoyì states:
"The feudal lords wear fur garments with axe-patterns when vowing before the hunt,
which combine lamb and fox fur to create the axe pattern."
The Lǐjì states:
"A white fox fur robe
is worn with an embroidered silk undergarment.
A nobleman wears a blue fox fur robe, with leopard-skin cuffs and a black silk undergarment;
a fawn fur robe, with blue wolfhound-skin cuffs and a pale yellow undergarment;
'wolfhound'
refers to a northern dog.
'Pale yellow'
is a bluish-yellow color.
A lamb fur robe with leopard-skin trim
is worn with a black undergarment;
a fox fur robe is worn with a yellow undergarment.
An embroidered silk robe with a fox fur robe
is the attire of feudal lords.
Dog and sheep fur robes are not worn with undergarments,
as commoners have no ornamental attire.
Wearing an undergarment with a fur robe
is to display beauty."
The Wǔjīng Yàoyì states:
"In ancient times, fur was worn underneath,
covered with a silk garment,
over which the court robe was added.
During an audience,
one would open the court robe to reveal the fur lining.
The covering garment is called the undergarment.
'Undergarment' implies exposure,
a term meaning it can be seen,
thus used to display beauty and present elegance as an ornament.
Adding the court robe over it is called 'donning'.
Opening it is called 'wearing the undergarment'.
The grand fur garment is not covered,
returning to simplicity to emphasize its plain nature."
The Máo Shī states:
"The nobleman wears a fox fur robe,
the boatman wears a bear fur robe."
The Jìn Lìng states:
"White-spotted deer fur, roaming hairs,
white fox fur,
yellow sable collar,
spotted white sable,
and Hùnzǐ Qúsōu fur garments are all prohibited items."
Fox Armpit Fur Pheasant Head
Wáng Bāo's Sìzǐ Lùn states:
"A fur robe worth a thousand pieces of gold
is not made from a single fox's armpit fur."
The Jìn Xiánníng Qǐjū Zhù states:
"Grand Marshal Chéng Jù presented one pheasant-head fur robe.
An imperial edict stated:
'This fur robe is not ordinary clothing;
it wastes resources and effort.
It should be burned in front of the palace hall.'"
Black Sable Blue Phoenix
The Zhànguó Cè states:
"Sū Qín persuaded Lǐ Duì,
and Duì gave Qín a black sable fur robe
and a hundred yì of gold."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"King Zhāo of Zhōu made two fur robes from blue phoenix feathers,
one called 'Warm Substance',
the other 'Comforting Flesh',
often used to ward off the cold."
Plain Brocade Purple Silk
The Lǐjì, commented by Zhèng Xuán, states:
"If the lord wears a white fox fur robe,
he covers it with a plain brocade garment,
so that it can be worn as an undergarment."
The Xījīng Zá Jì states:
"Qìng Ān, at fifteen,
served as an attendant to Emperor Chéng,
excelling at playing the qin.
Empress Zhào favored him,
informed the emperor,
and he was allowed to enter the inner palace.
Extremely favored,
he often wore a purple silk fur robe
and lived with the empress."
Swan-feather Cloak Phoenix Feather
Liú Yìqìng's Shìshuō states:
"Xiè Wàn went with Ān to visit Jiǎnwén,
wearing a white silk turban and a swan-feather cloak to meet him,
and they conversed together."
"Phoenix feather" is mentioned in the note for "Blue Phoenix."
Leopard-fur Apron Lamb-skin Sleeves
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"King Wǔ issued an extravagant decree stating:
'Only those wearing leopard-fur aprons and leopard fur robes
may enter the temple,
hence leopard skin costs a hundred pieces of gold.'
Among the families of meritorious officials,
some possessed fur robes worth a thousand zhōng but could not obtain a single leopard skin."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Qí placed the Wèi lord in Lái,
and Yòuzǎi Gǔ followed him but later escaped back.
The people of Wèi intended to kill him.
Gǔ pleaded:
'I was not pleased from the start!
I am like a fox fur robe with lamb-skin sleeves.'
Thus, he was pardoned."
Dù Yù comments:
"'Fox fur robe with lamb-skin sleeves'
means the whole body is mostly good,
with only a small part bad.
It metaphorically means that although he followed the escape,
his crime was minor."
Sùshuāng Fox and Raccoon Dog
The Xījīng Zá Jì states:
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and Zhuō Wénjūn returned to Chéngdū,
living in poverty and distress.
He took his sùshuāng fur robe to the market to trade for wine,
to enjoy with Wénjūn."
The Lún Yǔ states:
"Black robes with lamb fur,
white robes with fawn fur,
yellow robes with fox fur.
Informal fur robes are long,
with the right sleeve short.
There must be a sleeping robe,
one and a half times the body's length.
Thick fox or raccoon dog fur is used at home."
Blue Wolfhound Black Fox
"Blue wolfhound" is mentioned in the narrative.
The Huángdì Chūjūn Jué states:
"Huángdì battled Chīyóu
but had not yet prevailed.
The Queen Mother of the West sent someone wearing a black fox fur robe
to deliver a talisman to him."
Three Ornaments Thousand Yì
Guō Pú's Máo Shī Shíyí states:
"How splendid the lamb fur robe,
how bright the three ornaments!"
The Máo Shī Zhù states:
"Three ornaments
refer to three virtues.
'Ornaments' means that in ancient times, fur robes were decorated with white silk ornaments,
as in the earlier line 'five tassels of white silk.'"
The Mòzǐ states:
"The waters of the rivers are not from a single source;
a fur robe worth a thousand yì is not from a single white fox."
Dark Splendor Green Cloud
"Dark splendor" is detailed in the following memorial by Xiè Zhuāng.
Sòng Yù's Fēng Fù states:
"The master's daughter,
shaded by the sun's splendor,
wore a green cloud fur robe."
Blue Fox White Howler Monkey
"Blue fox" is mentioned in the narrative.
The Wèi Zhì states:
"The people of Fúyú wear fur robes of fox, raccoon dog, white howler monkey, and black sable."
The Shuōwén states:
"Wine,
is 'jiù' (to approach).
It is that by which one approaches the goodness or evil in human nature.
Another interpretation says it is 'zào' (to create),
the source from which good and ill fortune are created."
The Shìmíng states:
"Wine,
is 'yǒu'.
Brewed from rice and yeast,
it matures and its flavor becomes excellent.
It is also said to be 'cù' (urging),
for whether capable or not, all are strongly urged and compelled to drink it."
The Hànshū states:
"Wine is
heaven's beautiful bounty,
that by which emperors and kings nourish the world, perform sacrifices to pray for blessings, support the weak and nurture the sick; it is the gathering of a hundred blessings."
The Jiǔjīng states:
"The foul drink from the hollow mulberry tree,
fermented with millet and wheat,
to become mellow wine,
marks the beginning of wine;
black plum and nǚqū,
Hú bǎn fǎn.
Sweet rú
and milk
ninefold infused,
clarified into a hundred varieties,
marks the culmination of wine."
The Shuōwén states:
"Tú,
tú
is wine starter;
lǐ,
is wine that ripens overnight;
láo,
is wine with sediment;
zhòu,
is triple-fermented wine;
lí,
is thin wine;
xǔ,
is fine wine."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Yílǐ states:
"Lǐ,
is rice wine."
The Shìběn states:
"Yí Dí first created láo wine,
transforming the five flavors.
Shào Kāng made shú wine."
The Chūnqiūwěi states:
"Generally, when making wine from millet,
yang must rely on yin to be able to act.
Therefore, wheat is used to ferment millet into wine."
Wheat is yin.
The yeast is steeped first,
then the millet is added later,
hence it is said yang influences all rely on yin.
They combine and ferment,
which is its action.
All things involve the mutual influence of yin and yang,
not only in making wine.
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The Master of Wine oversees the regulations concerning wine,
allocates materials for wine-making according to established methods,
and distinguishes the names of the five 'qí'.
The first is called 'fàn qí',
the second 'lǐ qí',
the third 'àng qí',
the fourth 'tí qí',
the fifth 'chén qí'.
They are made according to regulated stages,
hence the name 'qí' (regulated).
'Fàn' means
when finished, the dregs float and drift about,
like the Yíchéng láo wine of today.
'Lǐ' is like 'tǐ' (body),
when finished, the juice and dregs remain together,
like the sweet wine of today;
'Àng' is like 'wèng' (jar),
when finished, its color is deep and rich,
like the Cuó white wine of today;
'Tí' is when finished it is reddish,
like the Ruòxià wine of today;
'Chén' is when finished the dregs sink,
like the Wèi wine made today.
He distinguishes the substances of the three wines:
the first is 'shì jiǔ' (occasion wine),
the second 'xī jiǔ' (aged wine),
the third 'qīng jiǔ' (clear wine)."
Shì jiǔ,
is like the yì wine of today.
Xī jiǔ is long-aged wine,
the old yì of today.
Qīng jiǔ,
is that which is brewed in winter and matures in summer today.
The Hánshī states:
"Regarding the rituals of drinking:
not removing one's shoes and proceeding in order is called 'lǐ' (ritual);
going barefoot and taking one's seat,
is called 'yàn' (feast);
those who can drink, drink;
those who cannot, stop,
this is called 'yù' (moderate drinking);
uniform in demeanor,
