equalizing the many and the few,
is called 'chén' (indulgence);
shutting the door and not going out,
is called 'miǎn' (drunken excess).
Therefore, a gentleman may feast,
may drink moderately,
but may not indulge,
and may not succumb to excess."
The Lǐjì states:
"Raising pigs and making wine
are not intended to create calamity.
Yet lawsuits increase,
showing that the spread of wine leads to calamity.
Therefore, the former kings established rituals for wine:
in the ritual of a single offering,
host and guest bow a hundred times,
so one may drink all day without becoming drunk.
This is how the former kings prepared against the calamity of wine."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The Píng Officer is in charge of regulating wine."
He causes people to use wine in moderation.
The Kǒngcóngzǐ states:
"Formerly, Lord Píngyuán was drinking with Zǐgāo
and pressed wine upon Zǐgāo,
saying:
'There is an old proverb: Yáo and Shùn drank a thousand zhōng,
Confucius a hundred gū.
Zǐlù, though hesitant,
still drank a hundred kē.
The sages and worthies of old
were all capable of drinking.
Why do you, sir, decline?'
Zǐgāo said:
'From what I have heard,
sages and worthies surpassed others through virtue and the Way,
I have not heard they did so through drinking!'
Lord Píngyuán said:
'If it is as you say, sir,
then how did this saying arise?'
Zǐgāo said:
'It arose from those fond of wine,
as words to encourage and urge others on,
not because it was truly so.'"
Xuánbì Piǎoqīng
The Lièxiānzhuàn states:
"Master Ānqī met with a goddess at Yuánqiū,
and drank deeply of the fragrant Xuánbì wine."
Cáo Zhí's rhapsody states:
"The Piǎoqīng of Cāngwú."
Yíchūn Zànxià
The Wúlù states:
"Yíchūn county in Ānchéng produces fine wine."
The Fēngtǔjì states:
"As for wine, the five píng of Zànxià are renowned during the Ruíbīn month."
Wǎnyè Qióngsū
The Shíyíjì states:
"The Queen Mother of the West offered King Mù the Wǎnyè clear wine."
The Nányuè Fūrén Zhuàn states:
"The Lady set out Qióngsū green wine for Prince Wángzǐ Qiáo."
Liáng Market Ruǎn's Kitchen
The Lièxiānzhuàn states:
"The Wine Guest
was a guest at a wine shop in the Liáng market.
He made wine that was always excellent,
earning ten thousand cash a day.
He offended someone and was driven away,
and the host's wine then turned sour and spoiled.
Ruǎn Jí heard that the Infantry Commandant's kitchen had much fine wine
and its brewer was skilled,
so he requested to be appointed Commandant."
Cutting Rushes Cutting Cassia
The commentary to the Wànbìshù states:
"Cut rushes steeped in wine will thicken it."
The Chǔcí states: "Set out cassia wine and pepper broth."
The commentary states:
"Cut cassia and put it in the wine."
Basket of Láo Àng Qí
The Huángshígōng Jì states:
"In ancient times, a fine general
was presented with a basket of láo wine.
He cast it into the river,
and ordered his officers and men to drink from the flowing stream."
"Àng qí" see the narrative section.
Língshuǐ Chéngxiāng
The Wúlù states:
"East of Xiāng there is Língshuǐ wine,
which is famous."
The Jīngzhōu Jì states:
"In Chéngxiāng of Guìyáng commandery there is an official in charge of wine."
Qīngtián Xuánchàng
The Gǔjīn Zhù states:
"In the state of Wūsūn, there is a green field pit,
which, when filled with water, acquires the taste of wine,
very rich and fine,
like good wine.
When it is drunk dry, one can refill it with water,
and as soon as it is emptied, it becomes wine again.
But it cannot be kept for long;
if kept too long, it turns bitter and undrinkable.
It is called Qīngtián wine."
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Xuánchàng was cast aside without shame,
while thin wine is lavishly poured in the hills and gardens."
Drinking Pèi Hān
The Shī states:
"The king is in Hào,
joyously drinking wine."
The Shǐjì states:
"When Hàn Gāozǔ passed through Pèi,
he set out wine,
and when he was merry,
he struck the zhù and sang."
Huānbó Bàishǒu
The Yìlín states:
"Wine is the 'joy-bringer',
dispelling sorrow and bringing pleasure."
The Chén Shòu Yìbù Zhuàn states:
"The wife of Yángzǐ Jù
was the daughter of Liú Yìgōng.
Her courtesy name was Gōngpú.
She was chaste, diligent, and well-versed in ritual,
and had four sons and two daughters.
After Jù died,
she taught and upheld the rules of the inner chamber,
and all her actions followed the proper norms.
Her eldest son, Yuáncóng, once went out drinking
and returned home.
His mother refused to see him
for ten days.
Only after he apologized through his younger brothers
did she reprimand him, saying:
'Drinking without excess
is in accordance with ritual.
But you have indulged to the point of ruin,
becoming negligent and disrespectful.
You have initiated the path to ruin yourself;
how can you lead your younger brothers?'"
Lifting the Sì Holding the Claws
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"When Jìn's Zhào Mèng, Shūsūn Bào, and the Cáo minister entered Zhèng,
the Earl of Zhèng feasted them all together. Mùshū, Zǐpí, and the Cáo minister rose and bowed,
lifting the sì-cup and saying:
'Our small state relies on you;
we know we can avoid calamity!'" Hè Fǎshèng's Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"Bì Zhuó often said to others:
'With a wine cup in my right hand
and a crab claw in my left,
floating and paddling in a pool of wine—
that would be enough to fulfill a lifetime.'"
Not Excessive Having Abundance
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Wine completes the rites;
it should not be followed by excess."
The Máo Shī states:
"Chopping wood hu-hu,
straining wine, there is abundance."
The annotation says:
"Using a basket, it is said:
'Straining, abundance,
means excellence.'"
Military Law Rules of Drinking
The Shǐjì states:
"Empress Gāo established the various Lǚ as kings.
The kings monopolized power and acted arbitrarily.
Zhūxūhóu Liú Zhāng entered to attend a banquet hosted by Empress Gāo.
Empress Gāo ordered Zhāng to be the overseer of wine.
Zhāng said:
'I am a descendant of military men;
I request to enforce military law during the drinking.'
Empress Gāo said:
'Very well.' When the drinking reached its height,
one of the Lǚ fled from drinking.
Zhāng pursued him, drew his sword, and beheaded him.
He then returned and reported:
'There was one who fled from drinking;
I have respectfully enforced military law and executed him.'" Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn states:
"Wèi Wénhóu was drinking with his ministers
and appointed Gōngchéng Bùrén as the overseer of the drinking rules.
He said:
'Whoever does not finish his drink shall be fined a large cup.'
When Wénhóu did not finish his drink,
Bùrén raised the large cup and fined the lord."
The "Lí Wine Rhapsody" by Zhāng Zài of the Western Jìn Dynasty
Only the creations of sages and worthies
are valued for leaving lasting achievements.
Praising Kāng Dí's foresight,
they also responded to heaven and followed human nature.
Modeling the wine banner after celestial signs,
they made sweet wine to nourish the spirit.
Though both wise and foolish share this fondness,
it seems the great transformation treats all equally.
Nothing remains unchanged,
yet wine alone grows newer with age.
It endures through prosperity and decline without abandonment,
remaining precious across a hundred generations.
Thus, when Zhōngshān opens in winter,
and mellow vintage is released in autumn;
when Cháng'ān offers spring tribute,
and Lèlàng sets out summer offerings;
with floating foam spreading like duckweed,
and fragrance intensely rich;
spreading exceptional beauty in this sage era,
truly pleasing to both humans and gods.
Never before had such precious wine
emerged from Xiāngdōng.
Not yet renowned in the imperial capital,
it lay hidden in the land of Wú.
In the past, it met with heaven and earth's adversity,
but now encounters the opening of the six directions.
Spreading exceptional beauty in this sage age,
proclaiming the ultimate flavor for universal harmony.
Not merely by exhausting the principles of its making,
but truly blessed by the essence of springs and soil.
Thus, this wine
possesses unparalleled merit.
With the three processes properly regulated,
the five fermentations must be balanced.
Brewing begins in autumn,
and completion is announced in spring.
Rich in flavor, harmonious and nourishing,
pure in color, clear and mellow.
It soothes the spirit and mind,
guides the breath and nurtures the body.
It dispels sorrow and dissolves worries,
suits one's nature and follows one's feelings.
Those who speak of it praise its fine intent;
those who taste it abandon affairs and forget glory.
Thus, gathering like-minded friends,
we roam and wander.
Honored guests gather like clouds,
seated in a square around.
Setting golden goblets by the southern pillars,
pouring floating cups that swirl in the stream.
Preparing fresh delicacies in elegant array,
presenting seasonal dishes, rare and fine.
Rituals and propriety in order,
toasts are offered and returned.
Faces slightly flushed,
overflowing thoughts, joyful and serene.
Virtuous words, gentle and calm,
expanding this noble way.
All attain their wishes and are satisfied,
desiring to dwell content in a single hill.
Thus, when joy and harmony are complete,
the sun declines in the western sky.
The host chants "Zhàn Lù",
the guests sing "Lí Jū".
The servants prepare the carriage,
to return to their abodes.
Then leaning on the carriage rail, turning the wheels,
driving light steeds on the broad road.
Returning to the humble gate to conceal one's traces,
perusing the classics of former sages.
Moved by Xià Yǔ's caution against subtle dangers,
enlightened by Yí Dì's alienation.
Reflecting on past events as a warning,
all faults arise from wine alone.
Lamenting Qín Mù's drunkenness,
slaying good men and discarding worthies.
Praising Wèi Wǔ's ability to repent,
recording the repeated dancing at the first feast.
Observing success and failure in ancient times,
to pass on to the future in this piece.
Zōu Yáng’s “Rhapsody on Wine”
The clear becomes wine,
The turbid becomes sweet ale.
The clear is sagely and bright,
The turbid is dull and foolish.
All are made from the wheat of Qūjīqiū,
Brewed from the rice of wild fields.
Flowing light, shimmering and bright,
Sweet and rich, thick and dense.
Once the ale and sweet wine are ready,
The green porcelain jars are opened.
Scooping and straining,
Filtering and settling.
Common folk take joy in it,
Gentlemen use it in rites.
As for its varieties:
Shāluò green Líng wine,
Wūchéng Ruòxià,
The clear wine of Lord Qí.
Guānzhōng white and light,
Qīngzhǔ rich and mellow.
Condensed ale, strong aged wine,
One awakening after a thousand days.
Yáng Xióng’s “Rhapsody on Wine”
The leather wine-sack, glib and smooth,
Its belly large as a pot.
All day it holds wine,
People again come to buy.
Often used as a vessel of state,
Recorded among the imperial carriages.
Judging from this,
What fault has wine?
Liú Xiàoyí’s “Memorial Thanking the Prince of Jìn’ān for Bestowing Yìchéng Wine”
Xiàoyí respectfully states:
“Having received your instruction,
You bestowed upon me four vessels of Yìchéng wine.
As the year ends, all is bleak,
In the shadows, all is grim.
These two truths
Converge at this moment.
Even the minor official’s monkey fights
Could not bring a smile.
The grandee’s pheasant shooting
Was not enough to lighten my face.
Suddenly, I encountered jars pouring forth peppery fragrance,
Pots opening with jade-like liquor.
Hàn dynasty flagons could not compare,
Yīn dynasty cups never met its like.
Fāng Píng, drunk, fled to become an immortal.
Xī Hé, indulging, neglected his duties.
Relying on this extraordinary gift,
I shall indulge in private drinking.
Before I have glimpsed the shame of the empty vessel,
I have already seen my cap pushed high.
Pricking my ears to seek sound,
I hear no thunderclap.
Clearing my mind to gaze intently,
How could I perceive the mountain’s height?
Curing illness, dispelling sorrow—
This has already been proven.
Leaving behind glory, disregarding lowliness—
In this matter, there is no deceit.
In the midst of intoxication,
I still know to inscribe my gratitude.
I cannot fully express it.”
Dài Kuí of the Eastern Jìn’s “In Praise of Wine”
I gathered with Wáng Yuánlín at the Lùlì Pavilion,
Facing the cup, plucking the zither,
Savoring the essence between these two things,
Thus we jointly composed this praise:
“The rise of mellow wine
Does not contradict principle.
The ancients, once exhilarated,
Opened to the utmost joy.
When a guest rides upon it,
He topples like a collapsing mountain.
His eyes cut off from all movement,
His ears shut to swift thunder.
All distinctions vanish into darkness,
Only emptiness remains in the heart.”
Yǔ Chǎn’s “Admonition Against Wine”
Divine intelligence and wisdom
Are what make humans spiritual;
Likes, dislikes, emotions, and desires
Are what make humans alive.
Intelligence operates through constant nature,
Desires find peace in spontaneity.
Thus I know that exhausting intelligence harms nature,
And indulging desires loses authenticity.
Thereupon, I smash the golden flagon,
Shatter the jade bowl,
Break the rhinoceros-horn cup,
And discard the goblet and ladle.
Liú Tán’s “Admonition on Wine”
Thus the great enterprise was established,
Called Kāng, called Dí.
Wine was made at the altar of the soil,
And presented to the enlightened ruler.
Looking up, they sacrificed to the vast heaven;
Looking down, they offered to the earth spirit.
The numinous deities enjoyed the prayers,
And the roles of host and guest were distinguished.
Tasting wine completes the rites,
Thus the constant moral order is arranged.
This is the use of wine.
Liú Bólún of the Jìn’s “Ode to the Virtue of Wine”
There was a Great Man, a Master,
Who considered heaven and earth as a single morning.
Ten thousand ages as a brief moment,
The sun and moon as his windows,
The eight directions as his courtyard and roads.
He walked without leaving wheel tracks,
Dwelt without house or hut.
With the sky as his canopy, the earth as his mat,
He followed his whims wherever they led.
When stopping, he grasped goblets and cups;
When moving, he carried flasks and pots.
Only wine was his pursuit,
What did he know of the rest?
There were noble young lords,
Officials and retired scholars,
Who heard of my reputation,
And debated my conduct.
They rolled up their sleeves, raised their collars,
Glared with angry eyes, gnashed their teeth.
They expounded on ritual and law,
Right and wrong swarmed like bees.
The Master, at this moment, was just holding a jar to catch the dregs,
Sipping from his cup, swishing the ale.
His beard bristling, he sat with legs sprawled,
Pillowed on yeast, cushioned on lees.
Without thought, without worry,
His joy was boundless.
Suddenly, he was drunk;
Dimly, he awoke.
Looking down upon the myriad things,
All bustling like duckweed on the river.
The two proud men attending beside him
Were like the gourd and the caterpillar.
End of Chapter Twelve
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu states:
"Millet undergoes five transformations:
first, transformed by yang energy, it sprouts and becomes seedlings;
then it flowers and becomes grain;
after three transformations, it becomes what is called millet;
after four transformations, it is pounded in a mortar, and the husked rice emerges from its shell;
after five transformations, it is steamed into cooked rice that can be eaten."
The Zhou Shu states:
"Huángdì first steamed grain to make cooked rice."
The Liji states:
"The steward is in charge of the king's food and drink.
Food
refers to cooked rice;
drink
refers to wine and beverages.
For food, six grains are used:
rice, millet, broomcorn millet, fine millet, wheat, and wild rice.
Millet, broomcorn millet, rice, and fine millet,
yellow fine millet, xǔ and zhuō."
Xǔ is pronounced xǔ,
meaning harvested when ripe.
Zhuō is pronounced zǔ jiǎo fǎn,
meaning harvested when unripe.
The Lüshi Chunqiu states:
"Among the finest cooked rice are
the grain of Xuánshān,
the millet of Bùzhōu,
the jì of Yángshān,
and the jù of Nánhǎi."
Kàn Zé's Jiǔ Zhāng states:
"Millet rice costs fifty,
coarse rice costs seventy,
husked rice costs fifty,
refined rice costs forty-eight,
imperial rice costs forty-two."
The Fēngtǔ Jì states:
"For refined polished rice,
take seven or eight out of ten parts,
and rinse it until it turns green.
Steam it into cooked rice,
and its color becomes purplish-black.
Cook and eat it with east-flowing water, and wash with it to ward off misfortune."
Wáng Lièzhī's Ānchéng Jì states:
"In Máo Tíng of Ānchéng Commandery,
thirty lǐ from Wǎngtóng Tíng,
the fields of the two tíng are fertile.
Their rice is fragrant,
and the cooked rice is like congealed fat."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"In all matters of food, observe the spring season."
Cooked rice should be warm, balanced, and harmoniously blended.
The Sòng Dōnggōng Yí Jì states:
"Two attendants are in charge of announcing the serving of the regular meals for the courtiers."
The Lǐjì states:
"Do not grab rice with your hands,
do not spill rice,
do not fan rice."
Wèi Hóng's Hàn Jiù Yí states:
"During fasting, two food attendants rotate the trays,
presenting thirty-six types of meat
and nine-grain rice."
The Qiánfū Lùn states:
"Eating fine millet and meat
may please the eyes,
but it is not as edible to the mouth as coarse millet and steamed goosefoot."
The Hánzǐ states:
"When Sūnshū Áo served as prime minister,
he ate coarse rice and vegetable soup."
The Yànzǐ Chūnqiū states:
"When Yànzǐ served as chancellor of Qí,
he ate unhusked millet rice."
Zōng Gōng's Xiàozǐ Zhuàn states:
"Chén Yí, a man from Wú, served as a commandery clerk.
His mother enjoyed eating the scorched rice from the bottom of the pot.
While Chén Yí was on duty,
he always carried a bag,
and whenever he cooked,
he would take the scorched rice to give to his mother."
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shényì Jì states:
"In the east, there was a man named Huáng Fù,
who ate ghosts as his food
and drank mist as his beverage."
Cuī Hóng's Qián Qín Lù states:
"Fú Jiān appointed Qǐhuó Xià Mò as Left Garrison Captain,
the Hú man Hù Mónà as Right Garrison Captain,
and the eunuch Shēn Xiāng as Canopy Attendant.
Mò and the others were eighteen chǐ tall
and were all strong and skilled archers.
The three men each ate
one dàn of rice
and thirty jīn of meat per meal."
Fragrant Wild Rice and Extraordinary Rice
Cáo Zhí's Qī Qǐ states:
"Fragrant wild rice and refined husked rice,
frost-stored and dew-nourished mallows."
Lù Jī's Qī Zhēng states:
"Divine fields yield extraordinary rice,
ears of fine grain.
They contain moisture and emit fragrance,
with pure tips and jade-sharp edges."
Refined Rice and Moist Richness
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"The grand broth is not fully prepared,
and the millet food is not refined."
Dù Yù's annotation states:
"It is not refined rice."
Fù Xùn's Qī Huì states:
"Fragrant jīng rice in early winter,
rich fine millet in late autumn.
Carved wild rice seeds,
red shellfish and eastern wall plants.
Moist and fine, smooth,
flowing with richness and fragrance."
Unhusked Millet and Polished Jīng Rice
The Hànshū states:
"When Gōngsūn Hóng became chancellor and was enfeoffed as a marquis,
he ate a single meat dish with unhusked millet rice."
Yú Huàn's Wèi Lüè states:
"Tàizǔ teased Wáng Lǎng, saying:
'I cannot emulate your past practice in Kuàijī of polishing jīng rice for cooked rice.'
Lǎng replied:
'It is truly difficult to be appropriate.
Someone like me should not polish rice,
but you, my lord, today could polish rice yet do not.'"
Full Vessels and Supplementary Tripods
The Máo Shī states:
"There are full vessels of cooked food,
and curved thornwood ladles."
Máo Cháng's annotation states:
"Méng
describes the appearance of a full vessel.
Sūn
means cooked food."
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Feasts have fine goods,
meals have supplementary tripods—
this is the height of ritual."
The Millet of Dàliáng and the Millet of Bùzhōu
Zhāng Xié's Qī Mìng states:
"The millet of Dàliáng,
the rice of Qióngshān.
Táng Jì sowed its roots,
and the Divine Farmer tasted its blossoms."
For "the millet of Bùzhōu," see the narrative section.
Western Lǚ and Eastern Wall
Wáng Càn's Qī Shì states:
"Western Lǚ's fine millet,
Yùsù's pure white rice.
Guāzhōu's red yeast rice,
mixed in equal parts.
Soft, smooth, rich, and moist,
melting in the mouth."
For "Eastern Wall," see the annotation under "Moist Richness."
The Jù of Nánhǎi and the Wild Rice of Dōnghú
For "the jù of Nánhǎi," see the narrative section.
Xú Gàn's Qī Yù states:
"The jīng rice of the southern lands,
the wild rice of Dōnghú."
Chapter Thirteen: Congee
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"Zhōu (粥) is mízhān (糜饘)."
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Mí (糜) is boiling rice until it becomes soft and mushy;
zhōu (粥) is the watery part floating on top of the mí,
hence it is called zhōu."
The "Zhōushū" says:
"The Yellow Emperor first cooked grain to make zhōu."
The "Fēngtǔ Jì" says:
"When the sun is due south on the winter solstice,
and the Yellow Bell pitchpipe marks the growing daylight,
on this day, when things begin to sprout and stir,
they make zhānzhōu (饘粥) to nourish the young.
It is customary to use red beans to make mí,
to symbolize the color."
The "Tiānwén Yàojí" says:
"The Jade Well constellation governs the zhōu kitchen."
Guō Yìgōng's "Guǎngzhì" says:
"The red millet from Liáodōng
was used by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi for the imperial zhōu."
The "Nányuè Zhì" says:
"In Lúlíng city, there is a well,
half green and half yellow.
The yellow water is sweet and smooth, suitable for making zhōu;
its color is like gold,
resembling ash water,
and it is very fragrant."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The inscription on the tripod reads:
'With this I make zhān,
with this I make zhōu,
to feed my mouth.'"
The "Shuōwén" says:
"In Zhōu it is called zhān,
in Sòng and Wèi it is called jiān (餰)."
Yáng Xióng's "Fāngyán" says:
"Within Chǔ and Chǔ,
when invited to eat wheat, it is called fēi (餥)."
Pronounced fúwèi fǎn.
The "Yèzhōng Jì" says:
"The custom in Bīngzhōu is that,
one hundred days after the winter solstice,
they commemorate Jiè Zǐtuī by cutting off fire,
eating cold food for three days,
and making dry zhōu.
In the central plains, this is considered the Cold Food Festival."
The "Liángzhōu Yìwù Zhì" says:
"Gāochāng is a remote land,
different from Huáxià.
In cold weather, they drink cold water;
in hot weather, they sip luóshé."
The local people call zhōu [luóshé].
Throwing the Cup / Supplying the Sack
The "Biézhuàn of Guō Línzōng" says:
"Línzōng once stayed at the school in Chénguó.
He saw a youth named Wèi Dégōng seeking to stay near his room,
to provide cleaning services.
Once when Línzōng was unwell,
he ordered zhōu to be made at midnight.
After one sip,
he angrily scolded him, saying:
'Making zhōu for an elder,
yet it has sand and is inedible.'
He threw the cup to the ground.
Dégōng made it again and presented it;
after three scoldings,
Dégōng's expression never changed."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The people of Jìn captured the Marquis of Wèi
and placed him in a deep chamber.
Nìngzǐ Zhí supplied him with sack zhān."
Dù's annotation:
"Zhān is mízhōu."
Crumbled Yeast / Chopping Ice
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" says:
"In the fourth year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng era,
when the capital's grain was exhausted,
they crumbled yeast to make zhōu
to feed the emperor."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's "Kǔhán Xíng" says:
"Traveling on and on, the day grows distant;
men and horses are hungry together.
Carrying sacks to gather firewood,
chopping ice to make mí."
Cooking Grain / Floating Fat
"Cooking Grain" is mentioned in the narrative.
The "Qíxié Jì" says:
"Zhāng Chéng of Wú County rose at night
and suddenly saw a woman
standing at the south corner of his house.
Raising her hand, she beckoned to Chéng, saying:
'This place is your family's silkworm room;
I am the local deity.
On the fifteenth day of the first month next year,
you should make white zhōu
and float fat on top.'
Afterward, they had great silkworm harvests every year.
Nowadays, making gāomí (膏糜) imitates this."
The Liú Family Uncovers the Pot / The Yǐn Family's Array of Tripods
The "Xù Sōushén Jì" says:
"Liú Chígǒu of Lè'ān had a home in Xiàkǒu.
Suddenly, a ghost came to the Liú household,
fond of stealing food.
Liú then went to another house to boil gěgé (治葛),
took two shēng of the juice,
secretly brought it home.
Toward evening, the whole family made zhōu,
leaving one bowl uneaten,
then poured the gěgé juice into it and placed it on a tile,
covering it with a pot.
After everyone was settled,
they heard the ghost coming from outside,
uncovering the pot and eating the mí.
After a short while,
it vomited on the roof,
and from then on, it ceased."
The "Lùyì Zhuàn" says:
"During the Zhōu dynasty, the Yǐn family was noble and prosperous;
for five generations, they did not eat separately.
Several thousand people suffered famine,
so they arrayed tripods to make zhōu.
Listening to it,
the sound could be heard for tens of lǐ."
Meat, Fourteenth
The "Shuōwén" says:
"Yáo (肴) is assorted meat;
yān (腌) is pickled meat;
fán (膰) is cooked meat for the ancestral temple."
The "Gǔliáng" says:
"Shèn (脤) is sacrificial meat placed on the altar.
Raw is called shèn,
cooked is called fán,
which is likely community meat."
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Meat is said to be 'tuō (脫)'."
This means stripping its skin.
Yáng Xióng's "Fāngyán" says:
"Between Cháoxiǎn and Lièshuǐ,
all sun-dried meat and the five internal organs of cattle and sheep are called bó (膊)."
The "Jiāyǔ" says:
"Those who eat meat are brave and fierce."
The "Lǐjì" says:
"Tender meat is bitten off with the teeth;
dried meat is not bitten off with the teeth."
It also says:
"Pound it and roast it,
remove its membrane,
pronounced zhǎn.
Weave reeds,
lay beef on them,
sprinkle powdered cinnamon and ginger on top,
and salt it.
Dry it and eat it.
If you want tender meat,
soak it and fry it with hǎi (醢).
If you want dried meat,
pound it and eat it."
Yú Huàn's "Diǎnlüè" says:
"For the great triennial sacrifice in the ancestral temple,
each tàiláo (太牢) is divided,
the left portion offered to the Supreme Deity,
the right portion offered to the Supreme Empress.
The leftover meat piled on the altar amounts to several thousand jīn,
called the 'sole altar'."
Yìyì (鶂鶂) / Xīngxing (猩猩)
Wáng Chōng's "Lùnhéng" says:
"Zhòngzǐ's elder brother had a salary of ten thousand zhōng,
but Zhòngzǐ considered his brother's salary unrighteous and would not eat from it;
he considered his brother's house unrighteous and would not live in it.
Avoiding his brother and leaving his mother,
he lived in Yúlíng.
One day upon returning,
someone had given his brother a live goose.
He said:
'What use is this yìyì thing?'
Another day, his mother killed this goose and gave it to him to eat.
His brother came in from outside and said:
'This is the meat of that yìyì thing.'
Zhòngzǐ, ashamed to go against his earlier words,
immediately spat it out."
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"Among delicious meats,
are the lips of the xīngxing."
Crow Carrying, Rat Stealing
The Book of Han says:
"Kunmo, king of Wūsūn, his father Nándōumí,
was of a small state.
The Dàyuèzhī killed him and seized his land.
He was left in the wilds,
placed among the grass,
and from afar, beasts were seen suckling him.
Moreover, a crow carried meat and flew beside him.
Considering this divine,
they took him to the Xiōngnú."
It also says:
"Zhāng Tāng's father was the assistant magistrate of Cháng'ān.
When he went out,
Tāng was left guarding the house.
A rat stole some meat.
Upon returning, his father angrily caned Tāng.
Tāng dug up the rat and the leftover meat,
indicted the rat,
drafted a legal document,
conducted an interrogation and pronounced judgment,
and took both the rat and the meat.
He completed the case
and executed the rat by dismemberment in the courtyard."
Placing Poison, Holding Rushes
The Discourses of the States says:
"Lí Jī, on the ruler's order, commanded Shēnshēng, saying:
'The ruler has dreamed of Qí Jiāng;
you must quickly offer sacrifices to her.'
Shēnshēng performed the sacrifice at Qūwò
and sent the sacrificial meat to Jiàng.
While the duke was hunting, Lí Jī placed poison in the wine
and aconite in the meat."
Jiǎ Kuí's commentary says:
"Jǐn
is aconite."
Zāng Róngxù's Book of Jin says:
"When Zhào Gāo was chancellor,
he called a deer a horse
and held rushes, calling them meat."
Bear's Paw, Chicken's Toe
The Zuo Tradition says:
"Duke Líng of Jìn ordered his cook to stew a bear's paw.
It was not done,
so he killed him.
He placed him in a basket
and carried him through the court."
It also says:
"Chǔ crown prince Shāngchén surrounded King Chéng with palace guards
and requested to eat a cooked bear's paw before dying,
but the king did not listen."
Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"A good learner is like the king of Qí eating chicken:
he must eat several thousand of their toes before being satisfied."
Yīn's Park, Xià's Mountain
Gōngsūn Nízǐ says:
"King Zhòu of Yīn made a park of meat."
The Chronicles of Emperors and Kings says:
"King Jié of Xià made mountains of meat and forests of dried meat."
Placed on the Stand, Put in a Sack
The Zuo Tradition says:
"The duke was about to go to Táng to watch the fish.
Zāng Xībó said:
'If the flesh of birds and beasts
is not placed on the sacrificial stand,
then the duke does not shoot them.
This is the ancient rule.'"
It also says:
"Zhào Xuānzǐ hunted at Shǒushān
and rested beneath a mulberry tree.
He saw Língzhé starving
and gave him food.
Língzhé left half,
saying:
'I have been away serving as an official for three years;
I do not know if my mother is still alive.'
He asked to save it for her.
Xuānzǐ had him finish it
and gave him a basket of food and meat,
placing it in a sack to give to him."
Chewing at the Butcher's, Fair Distribution in the Village
Huán Tán's New Discourses says:
"Hearing of the pleasures of Cháng'ān,
one goes out the gate and laughs toward the west.
Knowing the delicious taste of meat,
one chews in front of the butcher's door."
The Book of Han says:
"Chén Píng distributed the meat for the village sacrifice very fairly.
The village elders said:
'How well the young master Chén acts as steward!'
Píng said:
'If I could steward the world,
it would be just like this meat.'"
Elephant Trunk, Swallow's Rump
Zhāng Xié's "Seven Summonses" says:
"The paw of a sealed bear,
the toe of a honking fowl.
Swallow's thigh and gorilla's lip,
yak tail and elephant trunk."
Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"Among delicious meats,
the rump of the swift swallow,
the shank of the Mídàng."
Dragon's Liver, Swallow's Thigh
Fù Xuán's "Seven Admonitions" says:
"Roasting the fetus of the phoenix,
slicing the liver of the flying dragon."
"Swallow's thigh" is mentioned in the note on elephant trunk.
Ox Spleen, Pig Liver
Liú Jìngshū's Garden of Marvels says:
"A man in Shānyīn often ate beef.
His left spleen then made ox-like noises.
Whenever he exerted himself, it worsened;
only when he ate did it stop."
The Dongguan Han Records say:
"Mǐn Zhòngshū lived as a guest in Ānyì.
Old, ill, and poor,
he could not afford meat,
so he bought one slice of pig liver each day."
Wúsǔn, Zhuīfù
The Classic of Divine Marvels says:
"In the south, there is a beast
named Wúsǔn.
Its meat can only be made into fermented fish paste."
Also, the Record of Ten Continents says:
"Beneath the bronze pillar of Kūnlún,
there is a round chamber.
Its walls are ten feet square.
Upon it is a bird
named Xī.
Its left wing covers Dōngwánggōng;
its right wing covers Xīwángmǔ.
Its meat is like vinegar;
immortals find it sweet.
Zhuīfù
shares the breath of heaven.
Those who are not immortals eat it,
and its meat is bitter like brine.
The Shìmíng states:
"Gēng (broth),
means wāng (abundant liquid),
its juices are abundant and clear."
The Shuōwén states:
"Gēng,
is the harmony of the five flavors,
it is boiled pork broth."
The Guǎngyǎ states:
"Gēng is called qì."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"On the sacrificial stand, the dàgēng comes first."
Dàgēng,
is meat broth.
The Lǐjì states:
"Dried meat broth, chicken broth, broken rice, dog broth, rabbit broth,
are seasoned with rice grains and not with polygonum."
Tú,
is rice.
All broths,
are blended with the harmony of the five flavors,
and the rice grain seasoning,
then polygonum is not used.
Miào Xí's Jìyí states:
"For summer sacrifices, the harmonized broth is garnished with mallow;
for autumn sacrifices, the harmonized broth is garnished with scallions;
for winter sacrifices, the harmonized broth is garnished with chives."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The cooking official, for sacrificial ceremonies,
provides the dàgēng and xínggēng;
it is the same for guests."
The Lǐjì states:
"Dàgēng is not seasoned."
Liú Zhēn's Máoshī Yìwèn states:
"Xínggēng,
has vegetables, salt, and fermented beans in it,
the vegetables are for their appearance to be edible,
hence it is named xíng."
The Lǐjì also states:
"Broth and food,
from the feudal lords down,
to the common people,
have no distinctions.
A gentleman does not have two kinds of broth and sliced meat;
on the zǐ and mǎo days, millet food and vegetable broth are eaten.
Whenever seated to the right of others,
one does not gulp broth.
This is also to avoid appearing hasty.
One does not season the broth.
That is adjusting the flavor.
If a guest seasons the broth,
the host apologizes for not being able to cook well."
The Shǐjì states:
"When Yáo possessed the world,
his food was coarse grains,
and his broth was made of wild greens."
Liú Xiàng's Xīnxù states:
"When King Zhòu ruled the world,
he killed the cook because the bear broth was not fully cooked."
Plum Su, Chive Garnish
Lù Jī's Máoshī Cǎomù Shū states:
"Méi (plum),
is a type of apricot.
Its fruit is red and sour,
and cannot be eaten raw.
Boiled and sun-dried, it becomes sū,
which can be added to broths and stews."
"Chive garnish" is seen in the narrative.
Dipping in the Cauldron, Blowing on Pickles
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
"Zǐgōng's index finger moved,
he said to Zǐjiā:
'I will surely eat something unusual.'
When they entered and saw Duke Líng,
the cook was about to butcher a soft-shelled turtle.
Zǐgōng looked at him and laughed, saying:
'Indeed.'
When the turtle broth was served to the officials,
Duke Líng summoned Zǐgōng but did not give him any.
Zǐgōng was angry,
dipped his finger in the cauldron,
tasted it, and left."
The Chǔcí states:
"One burned by broth blows on pickles."
Wáng Yì's annotation states:
"It means a person who has been scalded by drinking broth,
and is wary in his heart,
upon seeing pickles,
fears them and blows on them."
Cooking Monkey, Serving Pheasant
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"In Chǔ, someone cooked a monkey,
and invited his neighbor,
the neighbor thought it was dog broth and found it delicious.
Later, hearing it was monkey,
he crouched on the ground and vomited up all he had eaten;
this is one who does not know flavor."
The Chǔcí states:
"Péng Kēng served pheasant broth, how did the emperor enjoy it?"
Wáng Yì's annotation states:
"Péng Kēng,
is Péng Zǔ,
fond of harmonizing flavors,
skilled in preparing pheasant broth to serve Emperor Yáo."
Zǐqī Flees to Chǔ, Yáng Zhēn Enters Zhèng
The Zhànguócè states:
"The Lord of Zhōngshān feasted his officials,
Sīmǎ Zǐqī was present,
the mutton broth was not served to all,
Zǐqī angrily fled to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ attacked Zhōngshān,
the Lord of Zhōngshān fled,
saying:
'My lord lost his state over a cup of mutton broth.'" Liú Xiàng's Shuōyuàn states:
"Zhèng attacked Sòng,
Sòng was about to do battle,
Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed the soldiers,
his charioteer Yáng Zhēn was not given any.
When battle commenced,
he said:
'Yesterday the mutton broth was your affair,
today's matter is my affair.'
He drove Huà Yuán into Zhèng,
and the Sòng army was defeated."
Zhāng Hàn's "Dòugēng Fù"
In the fine autumn, excellent beans,
hang from branches, pods stand firm.
They are cut, they are harvested,
filling baskets, overflowing boxes.
Fragrant, gleaming, harmoniously blended,
relieving hunger, answering urgency.
Dried Meat, Section Sixteen
The Shìmíng states:
"Fǔ (dried meat),
means bó (to bind),
dried and bound together."
It also states:
"Xiū (dried meat strips),
means xiūsuō (shrunken),
dried and shrunken."
The Shuōwén states:
"Fǔ,
is dried meat;
xiū,
is fǔ;
bó,
pronounced bǔ mò fǎn.
Thin fǔ is dried on the roof;
wàn,
is bone fǔ;
qú,
is fǔ strips."
The Zhōulǐ states:
"The là official is in charge of dried meat,
all matters concerning the fǔ, là, hū, and pàn of hunted animals.
Things are dissected, spread out, and dried,
this is called dried meat.
Thinly sliced, it is called fǔ;
pounded and seasoned with ginger and cinnamon, it is called jiā.
Xiū and là are small things that are dried.
For sacrifices,
they provide bean fǔ, offered fǔ, hū
hū.
pàn."
Lú Chén's Jìfǎ:
"For spring sacrifices, use fǔ;
for summer, use pì
píng bī fǎn.
fǔ."
The Yílǐ states:
"For the local drinking ceremony,
the host stands east of the western steps,
and offers fǔ.
When setting out on a journey, performing the zǔ ceremony,
the bá sacrifice is performed with fǔ.
For the capping ceremony of a gentleman,
the guest faces east and offers fǔ."
The Lǐjì also states:
"A woman's gift is fǔ and xiū.
For a great man's banquet ritual,
if there is fǔ, there is no kuài (minced meat);
if there is kuài, there is no fǔ."
The Gǔliáng states:
"Bundles of dried meat strips,
are not carried across borders,
for the most honored one, there is no duplication."
Zhuó Clan, Là Official
The Hànshū states:
"The Zhuó clan, by selling fǔ, had a train of riders;
Zhāng Lǐ, by being a horse doctor, struck bells."
"Là official" is seen in the narrative.
Recovering Without Diminishing
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shényì Jīng* says:
"In the northwest wilderness, there is leftover wine and recovering dried meat.
Its flavor is like that of a river deer.
Eat one piece,
and another piece reappears."
Gě Hóng's *Shénxiān Zhuàn* says:
"Zuǒ Cí visited Liú Biǎo and requested to reward the army.
There was one vessel of wine,
and one plate of dried meat.
A hundred people in succession ladled wine to give to the soldiers,
each person receiving three cups of wine,
and one piece of dried meat.
Ten thousand men were all served,
yet the wine vessel remained as before,
and the dried meat also did not diminish."
Four Strips Two Curved Pieces
*The Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says:
"When Duke Zhāo of Lǔ fled the state,
the Marquis of Qí sent Gāozi to present a basket of food and four strips of dried meat, bowing with his head to the ground and receiving it with the lapel of his garment."
Hé Xiù's commentary says:
"Bent in the middle is called qú,
straight is called tǐng."
*The Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"Zhào Xuānzi was about to go to Jiàng,
and saw a starving man under a shady mulberry tree.
Xuānzi gave him two curved pieces of dried meat.
The man bowed and received them but did not dare eat them.
Asked the reason,
he said:
'Your servant has a mother,
and will take these to give to her.'
Xuānzi further bestowed upon him two bundles of dried meat,
and then he departed."
Immortal Unicorn Ice Rat
Gě Hóng's *Shénxiān Zhuàn* says:
"Wáng Fāngpíng arrived at Cài Jīng's home,
and together with Má Gū prepared a feast.
They tore dried meat and ate it,
like finely roasted badger,
and said it was unicorn dried meat."
Dōngfāng Shuò's *Shényì Jīng* says:
"In the north, there is layered ice for ten thousand lǐ,
a hundred zhàng thick.
There is a shrew mouse under the ice,
that eats the grass and water beneath the ice.
Its flesh weighs ten thousand jīn,
and can be used to make dried meat."
Jade Branches Golden Arrow
*The Chǔcí* says:
"Snap jade branches to make delicacies."
Wáng Yì's commentary says:
"Delicacies,
refer to dried meat."
*The Zhōuyì* says:
"Biting on dried meat,
one obtains a golden arrow."
Wáng Sù's commentary says:
"The four lines are pure yīn trigrams,
the image of bones.
Bones are within the image of dried meat.
The image of metal,
is that with which one hunts wild fowl to eat them,
yet instead one obtains a golden arrow.
The noble man, when encountering flavor, must consider its poison;
when encountering profit, must prepare for its difficulty."
Yáo's Fan Shāng's Forest
Wáng Chōng's *Lùnhéng* says:
"In Yáo's kitchen, dried meat grew by itself,
in the shape of a fan,
shaking and producing coolness."
*The Liùtāo* says: "Shāng used dried meat to make a forest."
Straight Spine Whole Trunk Left Curved Right Tip
Dù Yù's *Shū Fù* says:
"Dried meat is straight-spined and whole-trunked,
coarse deer and fat elk."
*The Lǐjì* says:
"When placing dried meat strips,
the curved piece is on the left, the tip on the right."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Bent in the middle is called qú."
Táng Chén Zǐ'áng's "Chénwěi Fù"
Vast is heaven, ah!
And myriad are the things.
Life's transformations, ah!
Are like tangled threads.
Some, with spirits fond of uprightness,
find heaven silent and still;
some, with the Way abhorring tyranny,
find heaven vast and obscure.
This wondrous beast of immortal realms,
what fault did it bear to meet calamity?
It dwelt first in mountain marshes' depths,
fed in lands of lush grass.
Harmed none for its own gain,
sought no profit, lived in harmony.
Why, emotionless, submit to change,
yet feel grief that will not fade?
Caught at last in nets, compelled,
given to butcher, suffered wound.
Not for this tail's usefulness,
was it slain within this hall.
To grace your carved stand as delicacy,
placed among your golden plate's treasures.
It shares the host's joyful feast,
facing fine mats and precious lutes.
Though truly fair this moment is,
can joy compare with days long past?
A guest, moved, sighed and said:
"Fate cannot be known,
spirits hard to fathom.
Fortune, misfortune, regret, distress,
have never had an end.
Consider heaven's Way in use:
none more divine than dragon.
Yet slaughtered, made to paste,
it knew not its own doom.
Among a king's auspicious signs,
none wiser than the qílín.
Harmed in wilderness,
it knew not its own benevolence.
Since spirit cannot know itself,
nor sage his own mind,
how much less those who dwell in woods and valleys,
the mountain deer and wild elk?
The ancients had a saying:
heaven and earth's heart,
holds within no cunning.
Follow it, and all is smooth;
act against, and meet early death.
Surely all things share one nature;
what need for forced emotion?"
Thus it is said:
"Heaven's divine intelligence,
moves along with things.
It does not act before them,
but follows as they stir.
Therefore, the perfect man has no self,
the sage has no knowledge.
If you wish to keep whole and shun harm,
simply be vast and follow this."
Cakes, Seventeenth
*The Shìmíng* says:
"Bǐng (cake),
means bìng (to combine),
kneading wheat flour to make it combine.
Húbǐng (barbarian cake),
means using húmá (sesame) on it."
*The Shuōwén* says:
"Bǐng,
is miàncí (flour cake)."
Yáng Xióng's *Fāngyán* says:
"Cake is called tuō,
or called zhāng,
or called hún."
Xú Chàng's *Jìjì* says:
"In the fifth month, wheat ripens; offer the new harvest,
begin rinsing and making white cakes."
Cuī Shí's *Sìmín Yuèlìng* says:
"At the beginning of autumn, do not eat boiled cakes or water-kneaded cakes."
Cuī Hóng's *Qiánzhào Lù* says:
"Shí Jìlóng avoided the word hú (barbarian),
and changed húbǐng to mábǐng (sesame cake)."
Lactation Mántóu
Fàn Wāng's *Cízhì* says:
"In summer, offer lactation cake stew;
in early autumn, offer sparrow delicacies;
in early winter, offer and sacrifice water-drawn noodles."
Lú Chén's *Jìfǎ* says:
"For spring sacrifice, use mántóu, tángbǐng, suǐbǐng, láowán.
Summer, autumn, and winter are the same.
For summer sacrifice, additionally use rǔbǐng (milk cake);
for winter sacrifice, use huánbǐng (ring cake)."
Leavened Water-drawn
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's *Qí Shū* says:
"In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng, first month,
an edict stated:
'For the four-season sacrifices at the Grand Temple,
offer Xuān Emperor leavened cakes.'" It also says:
"Hé Jì served as Left Director of the Secretariat of the Minister Over the Masses.
The Grand Ancestor was Commander of the Guards.
He and Hé Jì associated,
and often held joyful feasts.
The Emperor was fond of water-drawn noodles.
Hé Jì had the women personally prepare and serve them to the Emperor."
Cross Pattern One Basket
The "Wáng Yǐn Jìn Shū" states:
"Hé Zēng was noble and wealthy for generations;
he would not eat steamed buns unless they had a cross pattern on top."
The "Dōng Guān Hàn Jì" states:
Emperor Guāngwǔ asked Dì Wǔ Lún:
"I heard that when you served as a market clerk,
someone gave your mother a basket of buns.
Knowing they came from outside,
you seized them.
Your mother then took the buns out of her mouth."
Lún replied:
"This truly did not happen;
it is because people think I am foolish and ignorant
that they spread such words."
Bóyè Hài Day
Xún Shì's "Sì Shí Liè Zhuàn Chuán" states:
"For spring sacrifices, there are mántóu buns;
for summer sacrifices, bóyè replaces mántóu,
and those who cannot make them use white ring-shaped buns."
The "Zá Wǔ Xíng Shū" states:
"Eating buns on the Hài day of the tenth month
ensures one remains free from illness."
Presenting to Hú Gōng Giving to Wáng Yuè
Gě Hóng's "Shén Xiān Zhuàn" states:
"Hú Gōng
came from afar to sell medicine
and often hung a gourd on his seat.
Every day after entering,
he would jump into the gourd.
The market clerk Fèi Chángfáng saw this from upstairs
and knew he was no ordinary man.
He personally cleaned for him
and also offered buns.
Hú Gōng told Chángfáng to jump into the gourd with him,
where they saw towers and pavilions in five colors,
layered gates and corridors,
and dozens of attendants."
Xiè Chuò's "Sòng Shí Yí Jì" states:
"Lángyá's Wáng Yuè
cultivated integrity from a young age,
was upright and disciplined,
and served as an official in the Ministry of Personnel.
When colleagues from neighboring departments gathered,
they gave Yuè a bowl of buns,
but he firmly declined,
saying:
'The cost is indeed small,
but since youth, I have never wished to accept others' favors.'"
Liú Zǐyáng Knows Salt Hé Píngshū Suspects Powder
Huángfǔ Mì's "Xuán Yàn Chūn Qiū" states:
"Wèi Lún, as a court attendant, met in the capital
and visited me, discussing flavors.
Lún mentioned that the late Wèi attendant Liú Zǐyáng, when eating buns,
could discern the salt's origin, a pinnacle of taste.
I said:
'In the past, Shī Kuàng recognized firewood from worn-out wood,
and Yì Yá distinguished between the Zī and Miǎn rivers.
Is Zǐyáng's skill perhaps lesser?'
Lún replied:
'Jìn's Shī Kuàng and Yì Yá
were masters of antiquity.
Wèi's Zǐyáng
is a master of today.
Why doubt him!'"
Qián Qǐ's "Yǔ Lín" states:
"Hé Píngshū was exceptionally handsome,
with an extremely pale face,
leading Emperor Wèi Wéndì to suspect he wore powder.
Later, in the height of summer,
he summoned him
and gave him hot buns.
After eating them,
he sweated
and wiped himself with his red robe,
his complexion becoming even more radiant,
convincing the emperor."
Shù Xī's "Bǐng Fù"
In the early days of spring,
when yin and yang intersect,
the cold has dissipated,
and warmth is not yet heat.
For feasts at this time,
mántóu buns are fitting.
When summer's heat returns,
and pure yang spreads freely,
wearing light silk and drinking cold water
brings coolness with the shade.
For buns at this time,
nothing compares to bóyè.
When the autumn wind grows fierce
and the Great Fire star moves west,
birds and beasts shed their fur,
and trees lose their leaves.
While dishes are still warm,
qǐsōu buns can be served.
In the deep cold of winter,
at morning gatherings,
with noses frozen by mucus
and frost forming outside the mouth,
to satisfy hunger and ward off shivers,
soup buns are supreme.
Yet each has its season,
suited to its time.
If their order is mistaken,
they cannot achieve perfection.
What can span winter and summer,
used all year round,
fitting every season,
and always appropriate?
Only láowán buns!
Then, finely sifted flour,
like flying snowflakes.
Sticky and elastic,
moist and glossy.
For meat, lamb shoulder and pork ribs,
half fat, half lean.
Chopped like snake heads,
scattered like pearls and gravel.
Ginger shoots and scallion roots,
finely sliced and minced.
Cinnamon ground to powder,
pepper and orchid sprinkled.
Mixed with salt and fermented beans,
stirred into a cohesive blend.
Then, with roaring flames and boiling broth,
fierce steam rises.
Shaking sleeves and robes,
kneading and pounding.
Dough slips through fingertips,
hands intertwine and cross.
In a flurry of motion,
like stars scattering, hail falling.
No meat escapes the steamer,
no dough spills from the buns.
Delicate and thin,
crisp yet unbroken.
Soft as spring silk,
white as autumn cloth.
Aroma wafting abundantly,
fragrance spreading far and wide.
Passersby drool downwind,
servants chew empty-mouthed, glancing sideways.
Those holding utensils lick their lips,
attendants standing by swallow dryly.
Yǔ Chǎn's "È Bǐng Fù Xù"
Fàn Zǐcháng
once visited me overnight.
He made chicken stew buns
and served them widely,
but the sentiment felt hollow.
The wondrous flavor lacked substance,
so I wrote this "È Bǐng Fù" to express it.
As for Dǒng Lú, famed in splendid markets,
and Hé Jūn, peerless in skill among common stalls;
noblemen marvel at trailing threads,
Shù Zǐ praises softness like spring silk.
Color must be like frost blossoms, snow-white,
meat like brocade vying with clouds, tender and fair.
Gold First
The Eryǎ says:
"Gold is called dàng,
the finest kind is called liú,
ingot gold is called bǎn,
and that of utmost luster is called xiǎn.
Among the treasures of the southwest,
are the metal and stones of Huàshān."
Dàng is pronounced dàng.
Liú,
pronounced with the initial l and final iu,
is precisely purple-ground gold.
Xiǎn,
has the most luster.
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén says:
"Metal has five colors,
with yellow gold being the foremost.
Long buried, it does not decay;
repeatedly smelted, it does not lose weight.
It is the element of the west."
The Zhōuyì says:
"Qián represents metal."
The Shàngshū says:
"Metal is said to follow and transform."
The Zhōuyì Cāntóngqì says:
"Yellow earth
is the father of metal;
flowing pearls
are the mother of water."
The Hòuhànshū says:
"Yìzhōu is where gold and silver are produced."
The Huáyáng Guózhi says:
"In Guǎnghàn, the Fú River has gold and silver mines."
The Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū says:
"Póyáng Lè'ān produces gold.
Digging over ten zhàng into the earth,
and sifting through the sand,
what is obtained is as large as beans
or as small as millet grains.
South of Xiànglín in Nánjùn, there were four states,
all claiming to be Hàn people,
who offered gold as tribute and paid taxes."
The Hòuwèishū says:
"Zhīdòu state produces gold and silver,
and Hé Gōu Qiāng state produces gold and pearls."
The Qíshū says:
"The golden chariot
appears when the king is supremely filial.
The golden man
swims in the rear pond when the king possesses abundant virtue.
Línyì has a golden mountain,
whose liquid flows into the bay."
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"Róng Chénggōng ingested the three yellows and attained immortality,
namely realgar, orpiment, and gold."
The Hànwǔ Nèizhuàn says:
"The Queen Mother of the West possesses the nine elixirs, golden liquid, and golden syrup."
The Línyì Jì says:
"The finest gold is purple-ground gold,
also called Yángmài gold."
The Mèngzǐ says:
"Double gold
is fine gold."
"Jade discs, after five hundred years, produce yellow mercury,
after five hundred years, produce gold,
and after a thousand years, gold becomes a yellow dragon.
Jade discs
are stone.
The central number is five,
hence they transform every five hundred years.
Hòng is pronounced hú gòng fǎn.
Hòng
is gold and mercury.
Qín considered one yì as one unit of gold, weighing one jīn,
while Hàn considered one jīn as one unit of gold."
Purple Light Red Aura
The Jìn Yǒnghé Qǐjū Zhù says:
"Lù Yǒng, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, submitted a memorial stating
that north of Gǔchéng,
he saw a purple-red light by the water's edge
and obtained a piece of gold,
shaped like the teeth of a seal."
The Dìjìng Tú says:
"The aura of gold is red-yellow;
when it amounts to over ten million jīn,
its light is as large as a mirror or plate.
When the gold aura is great,
it is red above and blue below."
Mountains Ringing Rooms Illuminated
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì says:
"During the time of Shàohào,
gold rang in the mountains,
and silver surged from the earth.
Some resembled turtles or snakes,
others suddenly took the forms of humans or ghosts."
Cuī Hóng's Hòuyàn Lù says:
"Dǒng Tǒng addressed Mùróng Chuí, saying:
'I have heard that Your Majesty possesses six marvels,
the first of which
was a golden light illuminating the room.'"
Bestowed upon Guō Inviting Zhuāng
Zōng Gōng's Xiàozǐ Zhuàn says:
"Guō Jù
was from Wēn in Hénèi.
When his wife bore a son,
he deliberated:
'Raising a child will prevent me from working
and hinder my ability to provide for my parents;
I should kill and bury him.'
As his spade entered the ground,
he found a cauldron of gold,
with an iron document on top stating:
'A cauldron of gold
is bestowed upon the filial son Guō Jù.'" The Hánshī Wàizhuàn says:
"King Xiāng of Chǔ sent an envoy
carrying a thousand jīn of gold to invite Zhuāngzǐ,
intending to make him chancellor.
Zhuāngzǐ firmly declined and did not accept."
Illuminating Demons Hitting Frogs
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì says:
"On Fāngzhàng Mountain, there is a pond
with mud that is golden in color and pungent in taste.
Using this mud to make vessels
can produce cinnabar,
and after a hundred smeltings, it can become gold.
The gold is bluish in color
and illuminates ghosts and demons,
just as it illuminates a face, leaving them unable to hide their forms."
The Yāndānzǐ says:
"The Crown Prince and Jīng Kē were at the Eastern Palace,
observing by the pond.
Kē picked up a tile and threw it at a frog.
The Crown Prince offered a golden pellet,
and Kē used it to hit the frog.
When offered more,
Kē said:
'It is not that I value the Crown Prince's gold,
but my arm is simply sore.'"
Sealed Document Sealed Seal
The Shàngshū says: "King Wǔ fell ill,
and the Duke of Zhōu made a golden-bound coffer."
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary states:
"It was a document of prayer for life,
stored in a cabinet
and sealed with gold,
so that no one would open it."
The Chūnqiū Yùndǒu Shū says:
"When Shùn was the Son of Heaven,
he toured eastward
and observed a five-colored yellow dragon.
It carried a chart on its back and placed it before Shùn.
The chart was encased in a box of yellow jade,
tied with a golden cord,
and sealed at both ends.
The inscription read:
'Gold
is the Yellow Emperor's tally and seal.'"
Probing the Dove Transforming Magpie
Liú Yìqìng's Yōumíng Lù says:
"In Cháng'ān, there was a man named Zhāng
who was alone in his room during the day.
A dove flew in on its own
and perched on the bed opposite.
Zhāng disliked this,
opened his robe, and prayed:
'Dove,
have you come to bring me misfortune?
If you perch on the ceiling, it will be my blessing?
Enter my bosom.'
The dove fluttered and flew into his bosom.
When he reached in to feel it,
he could not find it,
but instead obtained a golden belt hook,
which he treasured.
From then on,
his descendants flourished."
It also says:
"Zhāng Hào of Chángshān was Chancellor of Liáng.
After a fresh rain,
a bird resembling a mountain magpie
flew down and fell to the ground.
People rushed to seize it,
and it transformed into a round stone.
Hào broke it open with a hammer
and obtained a golden seal,
inscribed:
'Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety.'"
Pearl, Third
The "Yì Kūn Líng Tú" states:
"When virtue reaches its utmost excellence,
the five stars align like a string of pearls."
The "Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí" states:
"When governance is fair,
and virtue reaches the deep springs,
then rivers and seas produce bright pearls."
Fán Wényuān's "Qī Jīng Yì" states:
"The pearl mother:
a large pearl is in the center,
surrounded by smaller pearls."
The "Ěr Yǎ" states:
"Among the beautiful things of the west,
Mount Huòshān abounds with pearls and jade."
The "Hòu Hàn Shū" states:
"Pearls are the yin essence within clams;
dìlì refers to the color of bright pearls;
jī refers to pearls that are not round.
Fúyú produces pearls
as large as sour jujubes."
Cháng Qú's "Huáyáng Guó Zhì" states:
"Guǎngyáng County's mountains produce green pearls.
In Bónán County of Yǒngchāng Commandery, there is a luminous pearl cave
that produces luminous pearls.
Pearls include yellow, white, green, and blue-green pearls."
The "Hòu Wèi Shū" states:
"The Hé Gōu Qiāng state produces gold pearls."
Fú Wújì's "Gǔ Jīn Zhù" states:
"In the first year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng,
bright pearls appeared in Guàntáo,
as large as plums,
radiant and shining.
In the third year,
bright pearls emerged from the seabed of Yùzhāng,
as large as chicken eggs,
measuring four inches and eight fen in circumference.
In the fifth year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé,
a surrendered person from Yùlín obtained a large pearl,
measuring five inches and seven fen in circumference."
The "Shān Hǎi Jīng" states:
"The Three Pearl Trees grow on the Chìshuǐ River.
Their form is like that of cypress trees,
with leaves all made of pearls."
Xú Zhōng's "Nánfāng Cǎo Wù Zhuàng" states:
"Pearl diving is usually done in the third month,
with sacrifices of five animals offered in prayer.
If the sacrificial rites are flawed,
the wind will stir the sea waters.
Sometimes large fish are near the clams.
White clam pearls, three and a half cùn long,
are found in the Zhànghǎi Sea.
Those one and a half cùn with luminous color,
and a small side shaped like an overturned cauldron, are first grade;
these are dāng pearls, of three grades total.
Those one and three fen cùn with luminous color,
but not perfectly round, are second grade;
these are huá pearls, of three grades total."
Guō Yìgōng's "Guǎng Zhì" states:
"There are pearls called night-luminous pearls;
there are perfectly round pearls
that, when placed on the ground, do not stop rolling all day.
There are stone pearls,
made by casting stone,
also called morning pearls."
Night-Luminous Bright Moon
Yú Huàn's "Wèi Lüè" states:
"The Dàqín state produces bright pearls, night-luminous pearls, and truly white pearls."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "Nányuè Zhì" states:
"In the sea, there are large pearls, bright moon pearls, and crystal pearls."
Illuminating Golden Towers Returning to Jade Terraces
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Shén Yì Jīng" states:
"In the northwest wilderness,
there are two golden towers,
one hundred zhàng apart.
There is a bright moon pearl,
two chǐ in diameter,
illuminating a thousand lǐ."
Tàigōng's "Liù Tāo" states:
"When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he released those detained by King Zhòu,
pardoning their crimes,
and returned the pearls of the Jade Terrace."
Spitting into Marshes Hiding in Rivers
The "Chūnqiū Bǎo Qián Tú" states:
"Spitting pearls into the marsh,
who would not hold them in their mouth?"
Sòng Jūn's annotation states:
"When pearls appear in the wild marshes,
who would not take and hold them as treasures?"
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"Cultivating one's Way is called preparedness;
not letting external things挫 one's will is called completeness.
The noble person, understanding this,
conceals their affairs within,
and flows freely, passing through all things.
If so,
they hide gold in the mountains,
and hide pearls in the rivers."
Stringing Stars Illuminating the Moon
The "Shàngshū Kǎo Líng Yào" states:
"On the jiǎzǐ winter solstice,
the sun, moon, and five planets all rise from牵牛,
the sun and moon like strung pearls."
Guō Zǐhéng's "Dòng Míng Jì" states:
"The Emperor built the Gānquán Wind-Watching Tower.
On the tower, a white pearl was obtained,
like a flower branch.
The Emperor used it to adorn the canopy of the Jiǔhuá,
gazing at it as if it illuminated the moon."
Phoenix Holding Dragon Spitting
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shí Yí Jì" states:
"Huángdì's son, named Qīngyáng,
was called Shàohào,
also named Zhì.
He had the auspicious sign of white clouds,
and was titled the White Emperor.
A phoenix brought a bright pearl to the courtyard in its beak.
Shàohào then picked up the pearl and kept it close,
using its light to illuminate and clothe the world."
The "Shàngshū Kǎo Líng Yào" states:
"Mǎo jīn emerges from the Zhěn constellation,
grasping fate with a profound tally.
Chì is used to conceal,
the dragon spits pearls."
Zhèng Kāngchéng's annotation states:
"Cáng means secret;
zhū means treasure.
It is a metaphor for the Way.
The Chì Hàn will use the secret Way of Heaven."
Nine Grades Six Marvels
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "Nányuè Zhì" states:
"Pearls have nine grades.
Those larger than five fen up to one cùn eight or nine fen are the large grade,
having luster,
with one side slightly flat,
resembling an overturned cauldron,
are called dāng pearls.
Next to dāng pearls are zǒu pearls.
Next to zǒu pearls are huá pearls.
Next to huá pearls are lěiluǒ pearls.
Next to lěiluǒ pearls are guānyǔ pearls.
Next to guānyǔ pearls are shuì pearls.
Next to shuì pearls are cōngfú pearls."
The "Mòzǐ" states:
"The Héshì jade disc,
the night-luminous pearl,
three thorns and six marvels—
these are what the feudal lords call fine treasures."
Laughing at Dancing Cranes Holding the Spirit Snake
Sūn Róuzhī's "Ruì Yìng Tú" states:
"When Jìn Pínggōng played the qín,
two pairs of black cranes descended,
holding bright pearls in their beaks and dancing in the courtyard.
One crane lost its pearl,
searched for it and then fled.
Shī Kuàng covered his mouth and laughed."
Cáo Zhí's "Letter to Yáng Dézǔ" states:
"Wěicháng is renowned in Qīngtǔ;
Gōnggàn displays literary brilliance in the coastal regions;
Déliǎn rose to prominence in Northern Wèi;
you, sir, look down from the capital.
At this time,
everyone considers themselves to hold the pearl of the spirit snake,
each household claims to embrace the jade of Jīngshān."
Gleaming Jade Clams Hidden in Golden Sand
Guō Pú's "Jiāng Fù" states: "Jade clams bask in the sun, their pearls gleaming;
stone clams raise their flowers in time with the seasons."
Cáo Zhí's "Yuǎn Yóu Piān" states:
"Night-luminous pearls,
hidden beneath golden sand.
Who sends them to be gathered?
The Hàn women, the Xiāng River goddesses."
From Huángzhī, Lost at Chìshuǐ
The *Record of Línyì* states:
"On Huángzhī Island, the households are prosperous and numerous,
abounding in bright pearls and various treasures."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"The Yellow Emperor was traveling north of the Chìshuǐ River,
and ascended the heights of Kūnlún to gaze southward.
Upon returning,
he lost his Mysterious Pearl in the Chìshuǐ River.
He sent Wisdom to search for it, but it could not be found.
He sent Lí Zhū to search for it, but it could not be found.
He sent Yángài (or Kòngdàn) to search for it, but it could not be found either.
Then he sent Xiàngwǎng, who found it.
The Yellow Emperor said:
'How strange!
Could it be that Xiàngwǎng was the one who could find it?'"
Measuring an Inch, Diameter a Foot
The *Hánshī Wàizhuàn* states:
"A fine jade measuring a foot in length,
even buried under ten rèn of earth,
cannot conceal its radiance;
a fine pearl measuring an inch in diameter,
even submerged under a hundred rèn of water,
cannot conceal its brilliance."
Wáng Zǐnián's *Shíyí Jì* states:
"During the time of King Zhāo of Yān,
there was a black bird with a white head
that gathered at the king's dwelling.
It held in its beak a Pearl of Penetrating Light,
round and one foot in diameter.
This pearl was as black as lacquer,
yet when hung within a chamber,
no spirit could conceal its essence."
Illuminating Carriages, Enchanting Rivers
The *Shǐjì* states:
"The King of Wèi and King Wēi of Qí met for a hunt in the suburbs.
The King of Wèi asked:
'Although my state is small,
I still possess ten pearls, each an inch in diameter,
that can illuminate twelve carriages front and back.
How can a state of ten thousand chariots have no treasures!'" Lù Jī's *Wénfù* states:
"When stones contain jade, the mountain glows;
when waters hold pearls, the rivers enchant."
Three Colors, Seven Hues
Shěn Yuē's *Sòngshū* states:
"Emperor Wén ordered the Grand Astrologer Qián Lèzhī to construct a small armillary sphere,
arranging the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
Inside and outside, white pearls along with blue and yellow pearls of three colors were used to represent the three celestial images,
with the sun, moon, and five planets all positioned along the ecliptic."
The *Xījīng Zájì* states:
"The sword with which Gāozǔ slew the white serpent
was adorned with pearls of seven hues and jade of nine splendors,
and encased in a box inlaid with variegated five-colored glass.
Even when the sword was kept indoors,
its radiance still shone outward."
One Casket, Worth a Thousand Gold
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
"Duke Huán asked Guǎnzǐ:
'In the past, the Zhōu held all under heaven,
the feudal lords submitted as guests,
and their teachings spread throughout the realm. Yet they were usurped by their subordinates—why so many times?'
Guǎnzǐ replied:
'The ruler apportioned lands for tribute,
and when they gathered at the market court, the flow was uniform:
one casket of gold,
one casket of pearls from Jiāngyáng.
This is called making the few seem many,
and the narrow seem broad.'" The *Zhuāngzǐ* states:
"By the river, there was a poor family
that relied on weaving reeds for sustenance.
Their son dove into the river
and obtained a pearl worth a thousand gold."
White Blossom, Patterned Mirror
Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòngmíng Jì* states:
"The Emperor built the Gānquán Observing Wind Tower,
and atop it obtained a white pearl,
resembling a blossoming branch."
The *Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì* states:
"When spirits and numina flourish,
and all treasures are employed,
then the Pearl Mother becomes a patterned mirror."
Sòng Jūn's commentary states:
"When one attains in serving the spirits and luminaries,
then the patterned pearl has a radiance that can serve as a mirror."
Gathering from Turbid Waters, Sinking in Dānquán
The *Bàopǔzǐ* states:
"Those who recognize treasures will surely gather bright pearls from turbid waters;
those who appreciate fragrance will surely pick fragrant orchids from foul marshes."
Rén Gǔ's *Dàolùn* states:
"The pearl of Dānquán
sinks into the yellow mud;
the treasure of Fányú
lies hidden within distant stones."
Adorning a Cassia Casket, Inlaying a Golden Tray
The *Hánzǐ* states:
"A man of Chǔ was selling his pearl in Zhèng.
He made a casket of magnolia wood for it,
perfumed it with cassia and pepper,
adorned it with pearls and jade,
and inlaid it with rose-gem."
Wèi Shōu's *Hòu Wèishū* states:
"In the autumn of the second year of Hépíng under Emperor Wǔ,
an edict ordered the Central Imperial Workshop to make twelve golden trays,
inlaid with rose-gem, pearls, and jade."
Liáng Wú Jūn's "Rhapsody on Shattered Pearls"
The precious moon is born thence,
crossing shores, following streams.
It displays the beauty of Wèi,
and claims the worthiness of Chǔ.
Already gracing mats, it approaches splendor,
and adorning shoes, it ascends to loveliness.
How could it bear favor to meet the times?
Alone, wearing purity, it soars to heaven.
Yínghuái stirs with lightning,
Gānhǎi quakes with thunder.
The bright pearl is shattered,
in the river's bend.
Gazing at the round flow, it loses its turn,
seeing the broken water, it forgets to return.
It declines the auspicious adornments of the Lí Palace,
and powders the divine embryo of the numinous clam.
As if someone's voice is faint and obscure,
the fragrant emblems break, the bright pearls shatter.
Bright pearls shatter—grief, how to declare?
The pearl's form—no longer whole.
Caressing the variegated jade pendant,
lamenting the dimly lit golden feast.
How can it illuminate carriages or serve as a jade candle?
Only yellow dust and cold mist remain.
Let me sing a song:
"The ford of the Jade River is already soaked,
the grass of secluded orchids also unfolds.
Again I hear of the solitary shine of珩璧,
but do not see the bright pearl in the palm.
It is finished!
If the azure clouds can be esteemed,
I shall dwell together with the shattered pearls."
Jìn Jiāng Tǒng's "Inscription on True Pearls"
Continuing these shady reflections,
connected to the sundial of the great sun.
Praising that golden birth,
pure sound made manifest.
Jìn Guō Pú's "Eulogy on the Clam"
All things transform and molt,
their principle knows no bounds.
The metamorphosis of sparrow into pheasant,
holding pearls, embracing璫.
With the moon waxing and waning,
its breath aligns with dark and full.
Jade, Part Four
The Book of Changes says:
"Qian represents metal,
and jade."
The Luoshu says:
"If the king does not hoard gold and jade,
then purple jade appears in the deep mountains.
If clothing and adornments do not exceed sacrificial garments,
then jade blossoms emerge."
The Da Dai Li says:
"When jade is in the mountain, the trees become moist."
The Ruiying Tu says:
"The jade urn
is a response of the sage.
It fills itself without drawing water;
if the king's eating and drinking are moderate,
it appears."
The Book of Rites says:
"The gentleman compares virtue to jade:
warm, smooth, and lustrous—
this is benevolence;
dense and firm—
this is wisdom;
dense
means fine.
Firm
means solid in appearance.
Dense
is pronounced as zhǐ rěn fǎn.
Fine is pronounced as zhì yīn zhì.
Sharp but not cutting—
this is righteousness;
cutting
means injuring.
Hanging as if falling—
this is propriety;
when struck, its sound is clear and far-reaching, long and lingering,
ending abruptly—
this is music;
far-reaching
means resounding.
Abrupt
means the appearance of stopping,
pronounced as qū yīn qū.
Flaws do not conceal beauty,
beauty does not conceal flaws—
this is loyalty;
flaws
are blemishes in jade;
beauty
refers to the fine parts within.
Its brilliance radiates all around—
this is trustworthiness;
brilliance is read as fú,
radiance is read like the sheen of bamboo arrows, yún.
Floating sheen
refers to the color and luster of jade.
Color and luster radiating all around,
without any obscurity,
resembles trustworthiness.
Its aura like a white rainbow—
this is heaven;
its spirit manifested in mountains and rivers—
this is earth;
gui and zhang jades presented directly—
this is virtue;
what all under heaven value—
this is the Way."
The Book of Songs says:
"Thinking of the gentleman,
warm as jade.
Thus the gentleman values it."
The Li Han Wen Jia says:
"When jade and stone are properly placed, then Venus remains constantly bright."
The Li Ji Ming Zheng says:
"When the king obtains the rites and regulations,
then in the valleys there is white jade."
The Yi Lun Yu says:
"Ten pieces of jade are called a qū;
working jade is called zhuó,
also called diāo.
Two pieces of jade are called jué;
five jué make a qū.
Diāo
means working uncut jade.
Jué is pronounced jué.
Cuō,
jade color fresh and white;
yíng,
jade color;
yīng,
jade radiance;
qióng,
red jade;
xuán, jǐn, yú,
fine jade;
wǔ.
Three-colored jade.
Líng, qiāng, chēng, huáng,
huáng.
The sound of jade;
jade pendants;
tiàn,
earplugs;
zǎo,
jade adorned with water plants."
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"Jué,
two pieces of jade joined together.
Jué is pronounced jué.
Chāng chōng,
jade worn in the ears by barbarians.
On Jìyì Mountain and Lùtái Mountain,
there is much white jade;
Yúcì Mountain has much Yīngyuán jade.
From Tàimào Mountain, the Yùshuǐ River flows,
containing much patterned jade.
On Mì Mountain,
the Dānshuǐ River flows,
containing much jade paste.
Its source bubbles and boils,
and the Yellow Emperor ate it.
Where the jade paste emerges,
the five colors become clear,
the five flavors become fragrant.
Jǐnyú jade is firm, solid, and luminous,
the five colors emerge,
harmonizing softness and hardness.
Heaven, earth, and spirits
eat and feast on it.
The gentleman wears it
to ward off inauspiciousness.
From Lóngshǒu Mountain,
the Ruòshuǐ River flows,
containing much fine jade;
from Fànggāo Mountain,
the Míngshuǐ River flows,
containing much dark green jade.
Píngqiū lies east of Sānsāng,
where there is leftover jade."
The Records of the Ten Continents says:
"Yíngzhōu has jade paste like wine,
called jade wine.
Drinking a few sheng causes intoxication,
enabling one to live long."
The Jingzhao Records says:
"Lántián produces fine jade like indigo,
hence called Lántián."
The Materia Medica says:
"Jade
tastes sweet,
grows like white-haired elder,
consuming it prolongs life."
Warding Off Magpies Perching Crows
Huán Kuān's Discourses on Salt and Iron says:
"Beside Kūnlún Mountain,
uncut jade is used to ward off crows and magpies."
Liú Zhēn's "Ode to Pure Contemplation" says:
"Tying the Fúsāng of Dōng'ē,
connecting to the candle dragon of the western thunder.
Ascending the green and rugged mountain,
treading the path of lín and mín.
Jade trees with emerald leaves,
above perch golden crows."
Divine Treasure Imperial Omen
Cài Yōng's "Qin Cao" says:
"Biàn Hé
was a rustic of Chǔ,
often dwelling in the mountains farming.
He obtained an uncut jade
and presented it to King Huái.
The king considered it deceitful and disrespectful,
cut off his feet,
and Hé composed a song:
'Flowing Yí River,
passing through Jīng Mountain;
essence and energy gather densely,
valleys towering high;
within lies a divine treasure,
brilliantly bright.
Digging the mountain to gather jade,
difficult the task.'"
The Li Han Wen Jia says:
"Dragon horses, gold, and jade
Adorning the Staff with a Dove, Named the Swallow Hairpin
The *Xu Hanshu* states:
"The Three Elders and Five Seniors hold jade staffs."
It also says:
"In the mid-autumn month,
the commanderies and circuits all conduct inspections and compare people.
Those who have just reached seventy years of age
are granted a jade staff.
For those eighty or ninety,
the rites include additional gifts.
The jade staff is nine feet long,
with its tip adorned with a dove.
The dove is
a bird that does not choke,
wishing that the elderly do not choke."
Guō Zǐhéng's *Dòng Míng Jì* states:
"In the first year of Yuándǐng,
the Zhāolíng Pavilion was built.
There was a divine maiden
who left a jade hairpin for the Emperor.
The Emperor gave it to Zhào Jiéyú.
By the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
the palace ladies still saw this hairpin.
They conspired to smash it.
When they looked clearly at the hairpin case,
they only saw a white swallow soaring straight to the sky.
Afterwards, palace ladies often made jade hairpins,
hence naming them jade swallow hairpins,
which are said to be auspicious."
Six Ritual Jades, Three Thorns
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"Using jade to make the six ritual jades,
to rank the states.
The King holds the zhèn guī,
the Dukes hold the huán guī,
the Marquises hold the xìn guī,
the Earls hold the gōng guī,
the Viscounts hold the gǔ bì,
the Barons hold the pú bì."
The *Mòzǐ* states:
"The Héshì jade disc,
the luminous pearl,
three thorns and six rarities.
These are the fine treasures of the feudal lords."
Chuíjí, Fúyún
Zhāng Yī's *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Zhāohuá, báihéng,
xuánhuáng, hébì,
fányú, chuíjí,
are all jade."
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
'May I ask why the gentleman values jade and disdains mǐn stone?'
He replied:
'Flaws do not obscure the beauty,
beauty does not conceal the flaws,
this is loyalty;
its luster radiates outward,
this is faithfulness.'"
Jīngqiú, Lǔ's Treasure
Liú Kūn's poem says:
"In my hand is a dark jade disc,
which comes from the jade of Jīngshān."
The *Yì Lúnyǔ* states:
"Fányú
is the precious jade of Lǔ."
Confucius said:
'How beautiful is fányú!
Viewed from afar,
it is resplendent;
viewed up close,
it is serene.
One excels in texture,
the other excels in trustworthiness.'"
White Rainbow, Blue Aura
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
'May I ask why the gentleman values jade and disdains mǐn stone?'
Confucius said:
'Jade is something
the gentleman compares to virtue.
Warm, smooth, and lustrous,
this is benevolence;
its aura is like a white rainbow,
this is heaven.'"
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Xu Hanshu* states:
"During Emperor Huán's time,
at night, a blue aura appeared beneath the wall of the Guānglù official's quarters.
Looking at it,
they found a jade hook and jué.
The hook was seven cun and two fēn long,
the jué was five cun and four fēn,
one each,
both intricately carved."
Qiónghuā, Yáoruǐ
The *Máo Shī* states:
"Adorn it with qiónghuá, oh!"
Liú Zhēn's *Qīnglǜ Fù* states:
"Inlaid with splendid jade to roof the house,
paired with realgar to form the steps.
Profusely adorned with yáoruǐ,
mixed with jade dust."
Five Virtues, Three Colors
The *Wǔjīng Tōngyì* states:
"Jade possesses five virtues:
warm, smooth, and lustrous,
resembling wisdom;
sharp yet harmless,
resembling benevolence;
firm yet unyielding,
resembling righteousness;
flaws within
must show without,
resembling faithfulness;
hanging as if falling,
resembling propriety."
The *Yì Lúnyǔ* states:
"Jade is like brightness,
three-colored jade."
Chāngchéng Ruǐ, Chángzhōu Yīng
The *Hàn Wǔ Nèizhuàn* states:
"Queen Mother of the West said:
'Chāngchéng jade ruǐ, Yèshān fire jade.
Also, Chángzhōu, also named Qīngqiū,
has immortal herbs and divine medicines,
sweet juices and jade essence,
there is nothing it does not possess.'"
Seeing Purple Light, Floating Blue Aura
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Shū* states:
"Purple jade:
if the king does not hoard gold and jade,
then its light appears in the deep mountains."
The *Dìjìng Tú* states:
"Jade
is the essence of stone.
When within stone,
if the mountain rocks are moist and water seeps nearby.
Where it resides,
the aura is clear and floats,
the aura is bluish-white with circular light revolving,
and the ground there is constantly moist."
Jìn Fù Xián's *Yù Fù*
All things derive life,
jade receives its essence.
Embodies the firmness of heaven,
matches the purity of heaven.
Thus treasured and esteemed since ancient times,
its precious use is limitless.
How could it merely be compared to a gentleman?
It is the standard for royal measure.
Its beauty is such as this.
When its light lay hidden in the Jīng wilderness,
the uncut jade yet unworked.
The multitude saw it as mere stone,
only known by Biànzǐ.
Abandoned and neglected for a thousand years,
suddenly in one morning, it was recognized.
Becoming the great treasure of the state,
offered to the spirits in bright sacrifice.
How could mere worth of connected cities suffice to speak of it?
I rejoice in encountering a true knower."
Money, Fifth
The Rites of Zhōu states:
"The Spring Office has four senior officers,
eight middle officers,
and sixteen junior officers."
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Spring (quán) is sometimes written as coin (qián)."
The Discourses of the States states:
"In the twenty-first year of King Jǐng of Zhōu,
he intended to cast large coins,
to relieve and save the people,
and thus there were mother coins circulating with authority over the child coins."
The mother is heavy,
twice as heavy,
hence it is called the mother;
the child is light,
half as light,
hence it is called the child.
The Book of Hàn states:
"Regarding the use of currency, gold, coins, cloth, and quán,
before the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
the details are not recorded.
The Zhōu established the circular system of the nine treasuries.
The circle (yuán) is the coin.
When Qín unified the realm,
currency was in three grades,
with gold as the highest currency.
Copper coins had the same substance as Zhōu coins,
inscribed 'bàn liǎng',
and weighed as inscribed.
In the second year of Empress Gāo of Hàn,
the eight-zhū coin was issued,
and in the sixth year, the five-zhū coin was issued.
Yìng Shào says:
"Qín made coins,
with the same substance as Zhōu coins,
inscribed 'bàn liǎng',
which were eight zhū."
The Hàn considered them too heavy,
and instead cast pod coins,
which are the elm pod coins among the people today.
People worried they were too light,
so the eight-zhū coin was reissued.
The five-zhū coin
is what Yìng Shào called the pod coin.
In the fifth year of Emperor Wén,
the ban on private coin casting was lifted,
and the four-zhū coin was created.
Yìng Shào says:
"The four-zhū coin inscription
was also called 'bàn liǎng'."
In the first year of the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ,
the three-zhū coin was issued.
In the fifth year,
the three-zhū coin was abolished,
and the bàn liǎng coin was issued.
At that time, many people in the commanderies and kingdoms cast coins,
so the ministers requested that the capital cast official red-edged coins.
The edge (zè)
was made of red copper as a rim.
One was worth five,
and for official taxes, non-red-edged coins were not accepted,
