and the commanderies and kingdoms were forbidden from casting coins.
Only the Three Offices of Shànglín were ordered to cast coins,
and throughout the realm, only official coins could circulate.
When Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
he changed the Hàn system,
creating large coins,
with a diameter of 1.2 inches,
weighing twelve zhū,
inscribed 'large coin fifty wén'.
He also created tally knives and inlaid knives,
with rings like large coins,
and bodies shaped like knives,
two inches long,
inscribed 'tally knife' and 'inlaid knife'.
Inlaid with gold,
the inscription read 'one knife worth fifty',
circulating together with the five-zhū coin, making four types in total.
When Mǎng assumed the throne,
he abolished the inlaid knives, tally knives, and five-zhū coins,
and instead created gold, silver, turtle shell, cowrie, coin, and cloth types,
named 'treasure currency'.
Small coins, next at seven fen, three zhū,
were called 'gōng coin ten'.
Next at eight fen, five zhū,
were called 'yòu coin twenty'.
Next at nine fen, seven zhū,
were called 'zhōng coin thirty'.
Next at one inch, nine zhū,
were called 'zhuàng coin forty'.
Together with the previous large coin fifty,
these were the six types of coin currency."
The Records of Wèi states:
"In the third year of the Huángchū era,
due to high grain prices, the five-zhū coin was abolished."
The Chronicles of Huáyáng states:
"Gōngsūn Shù abolished copper coins,
and established iron coins,
so the people could not conduct trade."
The Book of Sòng states:
"In the seventh year of Yuánjiā,
the Six-One Coin Office cast four-zhū coins."
The Sòng Summary states:
"During the Tàishǐ era,
private casting was permitted, and coins became greatly debased.
A string of coins was three inches long,
called 'goose-eye coins'.
Even smaller ones were called 'thread-ring coins',
strung with thread,
they would not sink in water.
The market no longer counted them,
a hundred thousand would not fill a handful.
A dǒu of rice cost ten thousand,
and other goods were similarly priced,
so by this time, goose-eye and thread-ring coins were banned,
while the rest remained in general use."
Shark-pattern Goose-eye
Guō Zǐhéng's Records of the Vast and Obscure states:
"The Emperor ascended the Moon-Watching Terrace,
and three green ducks transformed into three small boys,
all wearing green damask-patterned jackets,
together holding three large coins with shark patterns,
which they placed before the Emperor's table.
Their bodies were still but their shadows moved,
so they were named 'light-shadow coins'."
Péi Zǐyě's Sòng Summary states:
"Shěn Qìngzhī proposed allowing private casting, and coins became greatly debased,
a string of coins was three inches long,
called 'goose-eye coins'."
Redeeming crimes Buying office
The Book of Hàn states:
"Princess Lónglǜ was ill,
so she used a thousand jīn of gold,
and ten million coins,
to preemptively redeem one death sentence for her son Zhāopíng Jūn,
and Emperor Wǔ permitted it."
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Nine Provinces states:
"Emperor Líng sold offices,
and the Commandant of Justice Cuī Liè paid five million coins
to buy the office of Minister over the Masses.
On the day Liè was appointed,
the Son of Heaven stood at the balcony,
looked at his attendants and said:
'I regret not holding out a little,
it could have reached ten million.'"
Qīngfú Báizhuàn
Gān Bǎo's In Search of the Supernatural states:
"In the south, there is an insect,
shaped like a cicada but larger,
its eggs attached to grass leaves like silkworm seeds.
If you take the eggs home,
the mother will fly to them.
Kill the mother and smear its blood on the eggs,
and smear the eggs on the mother,
use them on coins for market trade,
and they will quickly return on their own.
The Huáinánzǐ technique uses them to return coins,
and they are called qīngfú."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Emperor Wǔ changed the coins,
creating white gold from silver and tin,
considering that for heaven nothing is better than the dragon,
for earth nothing is better than the horse,
for humans nothing is better than the turtle.
Thus there were three grades of metal,
the first weighing eight liǎng,
circular,
inscribed with a dragon,
named 'báizhuàn'."
Selecting one Throwing three
Huá Qiáo's Later Book of Hàn states:
"Liú Chǒng, styled Zǔróng,
was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
His governance was not burdensome or harsh,
and he was summoned to be the Minister of Works.
In Shānyīn, there were five or six old men,
each bringing a hundred coins to send off Chǒng, saying:
'We rustics have never known the commandery court,
but since Your Excellency came,
dogs do not bark at night,
and people do not see officials.
Now we hear you are to leave us,
so we have come on our own to respectfully see you off.'
Chǒng selected one large coin from each and accepted it."
Zhào Qí's Decisions and Records of the Three Capital Regions states:
"Xiàng Zhòngshān, a pure man of Ānlíng,
when watering his horse at the Wèi River,
would always throw three coins into the water before leaving."
White Metal, Red Edge
The Book of Han states:
"Emperor Wu changed the currency,
creating white metal from silver and tin."
It also says:
"During Emperor Wu's time, the coins from the commanderies and kingdoms were often lightweight,
so the high ministers requested that the capital mint official 'red edge' coins."
Rú Chún's annotation says:
"They used red copper to make the rim."
Body Corresponds to Heaven, Square Hole Models Earth
The "Discourse on the God of Money" by Qímǔ Shì states:
"Gold is the father,
silver is the mother,
lead is the eldest son,
tin is the principal wife.
Their nature is firm and strong,
requiring fire from beginning to end.
Its round body corresponds to heaven,
its square hole models earth."
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jin states:
"During Emperor Hui's time, there was a 'Discourse on the God of Money' which said:
'The form of money
has the image of heaven and earth.
Its accumulation is like mountains,
its flow is like rivers.'"
Several Jars, One Bag
Wáng Sháozhī's "Records of Shǐxīng" states:
"On the eastern bank of Láokǒu,
there is a square stone.
Over a hundred rèn high,
its shape resembles a terrace."
A note says:
"Elders pass down a tale about this stone:
long ago, three men cut wood to build a bridge,
and played atop the stone.
They saw several jars of coins,
and together took half a jar back."
Zhào Yī's poem says:
"Worried, I lean against the north hall,
facing the tomb, I stand by the gate.
Though filled with knowledge of letters and history,
it's worth less than a single bag of coins."
Three Offices Mint, Nine Treasuries System
The Book of Han states:
"The commanderies and kingdoms were forbidden from minting coins,
it was exclusively ordered that the Three Offices of Shànglín mint them,
and it was decreed that coins not minted by the Three Offices could not circulate in the realm."
It also says:
"The Grand Duke established the Nine Treasuries Circular System for the Zhōu."
Lǔ Bāo of Jin's "Discourse on the God of Money":
The form of money,
has the image of heaven and earth.
Its accumulation is like mountains,
its flow is like rivers.
Its movement and stillness have their time,
its use and storage have their measure.
Convenient for marketplaces,
one need not worry about loss or damage.
Hard to decay, it symbolizes longevity,
never exhausted, it symbolizes the Way.
Thus it can endure long,
a divine treasure for the world.
Dear as an elder brother,
its style name is Square Hole.
Lose it and you are poor and weak,
gain it and you are rich and prosperous.
Without wings it flies,
without feet it runs.
It loosens stern, severe countenances,
opens mouths that are hard to make smile.
Those with much money stand in front,
those with little money stay behind,
and so on."
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Memorial on Coins"
How could I expect, in my poverty and illness, standing with empty walls,
to be graciously favored with such exceptional gifts?
Named after elm seeds,
yet not thrown onto the Drinking Horse Bridge.
Valued as round coinage,
would I dare discard it in the field where chickens are cursed?
Briefly transferred from the Zhōu treasury,
just passed through Hàn minting.
First descending to the princely gates,
suddenly illuminating my humble chamber.
Green duck-shaped coins presented as tribute,
they laugh at Yífǔ's refusal to speak of them;
red-edged coins with dangling strings,
they esteem Héjiān's ability to count them.
Brocade, Part Six
Liú Xī's "Explaining Names" states:
"Jǐn (brocade)
is like jīn (gold).
Its creation requires great labor,
its price is like gold,
hence the character is formed from 'silk' and 'gold'."
The "Records of Dānyáng" state:
"Successive dynasties still lacked brocade,
yet Chéngdū alone was praised for its excellence.
Thus during the Three Kingdoms period,
Wèi purchased it from Shǔ,
and Wú also obtained supplies from Western Shǔ,
only by this time did they begin to have it."
The "Records of Yìzhōu" state:
"The Brocade City is south of Yìzhōu, east of Zuóqiáo, on the south bank of the flowing river,
it was the site of the old Brocade Palace of Shǔ times.
The area is called Brocade Lane,
the city walls still remain."
The "Records of Yèzhōng" state:

"Brocades include: Great Ascending Heights, Small Ascending Heights, Great Bright Light, Small Bright Light, Great Bó Mountain, Small Bó Mountain, Great Cornelian Cherry, Small Cornelian Cherry, Great Intertwined Dragons, Small Intertwined Dragons, Grape Pattern Brocade, Spotted Pattern Brocade, Phoenix and Vermilion Bird Brocade, Tāo Pattern Brocade, Peach Pit Pattern Brocade.
Some are blue damask,
some white damask,
some yellow damask,
some green damask,
some purple damask,
some Shǔ damask.
The craftsmanship involves hundreds of variations,
impossible to name them all."
Dragon Pattern, Vermilion Bird
The Records of Wèi state:
"During the Jǐngchū era,
the Queen of Wō was granted five bolts of crimson-ground dragon pattern brocade."
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng" states:
"The Imperial Repository contains phoenix brocade and vermilion bird brocade."
Spotted Pattern, Green Ground
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng" states:
"Brocade and gauze were woven in the Zhōngshàng Workshops,
the three offices each had several hundred people,
producing spotted pattern brocade."
The "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" state:
"When Emperor Wu obtained the Heavenly Horses of Èrshī,
he used rose quartz for saddles and bridles,
inlaid with gold and silver,
and used green-ground five-color brocade for the horse trappings."
Brocade-Wrapped Pole, Brocade-Tied Hair
The Ěryǎ states:
"Plain brocade wraps the flagpole."
Guō Pú's annotation says:
"It means using white-ground brocade to sheath the flag's pole."
The Book of Rites states:
"For a youth's attire,
he wears black cloth garments edged with brocade.
A brocade sash,
and also a brocade cord to tie the hair."
Mooring Boats, Pulling Carts
Wéi Zhāo's Book of Wú states:
"Whenever Gān Níng moored his dwelling,
he often used silk brocade to tie up his boat,
and when leaving, would cut and discard it to show his manner."
Shēyú's "Extended Biographies of Jiāngbiǎo" states:
"Lù Xùn attacked Liú Bèi at Yílíng,
Bèi abandoned his ships and fled on foot.
He burned leather armor to block the road and had his soldiers use brocade to pull carts,
fleeing into Báidì."
Resembling Clouds and Rosy Mists, Like Lamps and Candles
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Gleanings" states:
"People from the Zhī country came from time to time to present tribute,
offering 'battlement brocade'.
Its patterns resembled clouds and rosy mists,
overlaid with sun and moon,
like the towers and battlements of a city wall."
It also says:
People from the Zhī country came from time to time to present tribute,
offering 'arrayed brocade',
its patterns resembled arrays of lamps and candles."
Simurgh Pattern, Tiger Pattern
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Gleanings" states:
"King Líng of Zhōu raised the Kūnzhāo Terrace,
to feast his assembled ministers.
He displayed simurgh-pattern brocade,
its patterns like soaring simurghs."
The "Hàn Official Ceremonial" states:
"The Leader of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household Rapid as Tigers is an ancient office.
They wear a single robe of plain gauze,
and tiger-pattern brocade trousers.
The other Gentlemen-of-the-Household are the same."
Bright and Smooth
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng" states:
"Shí Jìlóng in winter used a tent with cooked brocade and tassels,
with pure gold dragon heads at its four corners,
holding five-colored tassels,
or sometimes yellow silk gauze.
Bóshān patterned brocade or sometimes purple silk gauze,
and large and small bright brocade."
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Omissions" states:
"On Yuánqiáo Mountain,
named Huánqiū.
To the east there is cloud stone,
five hundred lǐ wide,
with silkworms seven cùn long,
black in color,
having horns and scales.
They are covered with frost and snow,
and then make cocoons,
one chǐ long,
multicolored in hue.
Woven into patterned brocade,
it does not get wet in water,
its substance light, soft, and smooth."
Flying Swan and Patterned Bird
Guō Zǐhéng's "Records of the Mysterious and Hidden from Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Various States" states:
"In the first year of Yuándǐng,
the Zhāoxiānlíng Pavilion was built west of Gānquán Palace.
Curtains were woven from kingfisher feathers and unicorn hair,
there was running dragon brocade,
and there was flying swan brocade."
"Records of Strange Things" states:
"The brocade bird,
its patterns are like cinnabar-ground brocade,
with interlaced colorful designs.
Common people, seeing its resemblance to brocade,
thus call it the brocade bird."
The Seven-Character Palindromic Poem Woven in Brocade by Sū Shì, Wife of Dòu Tāo, Governor of Qínzhōu Under Former Qín Fú Jiān
Benevolent and wise, cherishing virtue, sage Yú and Táng,
True and marvelous, displaying splendor, doubly glorious chapters.
Ministers worthy, only sages match heroic sovereigns,
Companions separated, drifting adrift on Jiāng and Xiāng.
Rivers and streams block, distinct from mountain ridges,
People and scholars feel desolate, lamenting the long road.
Humble self, pitying my own state in secluded chamber,
Lowly as a woman, possessing both softness and strength.
Beloved ones, whom do I think of, whom do I yearn for?
Pure and chaste in will, equal to ice and frost.
New and old perhaps differ vastly, facing a wall,
Spring sun warm and lush, orchids wither fragrantly.
Qín clear, flowing Chǔ, stirring strings and shāng,
Playing melodies, emitting sounds, sorrowful and heart-wrenching.
Harmonious tones, chanting thoughts, only empty hall,
Heart worried, increasing longing, harboring grief and sorrow.
Embroidery, Seventh
"The Rites of Zhōu" states:
"Having all five colors is called embroidery,
this refers to what is used for embroidering garments."
"Explaining Names" states:
"Embroidery (xiù),
means to adorn (xiū),
patterns adorned."
"The Book of Documents" states:
"I wish to observe the images of the ancients,
sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
mountains, dragons, pheasants, and painted designs.
Temple vessels, water plants, fire, rice grains, axes, and bow-shaped patterns, embroidered on fine silk."
"The Book of Rites" states:
"In the mid-autumn month,
order the officials that patterned embroidery should be constant,
must follow its former ways.
That which is used in interactions with the spirits
cannot be the same as that used for comfort and pleasure.
Therefore, there is the beauty of axe and bow patterns and patterned embroidery,
the esteem for coarse cloth,
returning to the beginnings of women's work."
"Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo" states:
"The Weaving Maid (Zhīnǚ) is spoken of as a divine maiden,
completing garments and establishing norms,
thus Qí was able to produce patterned embroidery,
in response to the way of heaven."
Women's work affairs, Qí was able to make divine under heaven,
thus hanging it to clothe people obtains this energy.
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"Merchants may not wear brocade, embroidery, damask, fine silk, crepe, coarse silk, ramie cloth, or felt.
Emperor Jǐng's edict stated:
'Brocade, embroidery, and patterned ribbons
harm women's work.'
It also said:
'Axe and bow patterns
are the garments of ancient Son of Heaven.
Now rich men and great merchants,
at fine gatherings summoning guests,
use them to cover walls.'"
"Records of the Eastern Palace of Jìn" states:
"When the crown prince takes a consort,
there is one crimson cup-patterned silk embroidered width coverlet."
"Master Xún" states:
"The Son of Heaven,
his position is most weighty,
revered without superior.
His garments and coverings have the five colors mixed and interwoven,
colors emphasize patterned embroidery,
additionally adorned with pearls and jade."
"Fàn Zǐ Jìrán" states:
"In ancient times, common people in old age only then wore silk,
the rest wore only hemp and kudzu,
thus called 'cloth-clad.'
Now the rich wear damask embroidery, gauze, and fine silk,
plain silk gauze and ice brocade.
Fine-patterned embroidery comes from Qí,
top price twenty thousand per bolt,
medium ten thousand, low five thousand."
Connected Mist and Covering the Ground
"Records of the Mysterious and Hidden from Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Separate States" states:
"In the first year of Yuándǐng, the Xiānlíng Pavilion was built,
curtains woven from kingfisher feathers and unicorn hair.
There was connected mist embroidery,
and running dragon brocade."
"Qiántán Bā" states:
"If the Son of Heaven's patterned embroidery covers the ground,
the earth will surely tremble,
and the lineage will be cut off without heir."
Adding Five Colors and Forming Six Ritual Gifts
Wáng Chōng's "Discourses Weighed in the Balance" states:
"Before embroidery is stitched,
before brocade is woven,
how do silk and plain cloth differ?
Add the skill of the five colors,
apply the ornament of needle and thread,
then patterns and designs dazzle brilliantly.
Scholars having literary compositions
is like silk and cloth having the work of the five colors."
"The Rites of Zhōu" states:
"Combine the six ritual gifts: guī jade with horses, zhāng jade with skins, bì jade with silk, cóng jade with brocade, hǔ jade with embroidery, huáng jade with bow patterns.
These six things
are used to harmonize the goodwill of the feudal lords."
Clothing Horses and Ornamented Dragons
"Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a beloved horse,
clothed it with patterned embroidery,
placed it beneath a splendid house.
Made a bed of dew for it,
fed it with dates and dried meat."
Guō Zǐhéng's "Records of the Mysterious and Hidden from Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Separate States" states:
"Gānquán Palace had rosy light embroidery,
and had ornamented dragon embroidery."
Liáng Zhāng Shuài's "Rhapsody on Embroidery"
Seeking the wondrous skill of creation,
indeed adorning transformation through the hundred crafts.
None comes before axe-patterned embroidery,
since Emperor Yú observing customs.
Mingling water plants, fire, and rice grains,
luxuriant mountains, dragons, and pheasants.
As for observing its stitching and joining,
and its imitation and reliance.
Turtles and dragons form patterns,
immortals and spirits become images.
Gathering the five colors to exhaust thought,
drawing on gauze and fine silk to inspire conception.
Possessing the forms of all things,
exhausting the shapes of myriad transformations.
Already rich in splendor and dense in color,
also densely luminous and sparsely bright.
Like spring marshes raising blossoms,
resembling autumn Milky Way containing stars.
Already interspersed with red and bordered with purple,
also showing black and wrapped in white.
Interspersing green bamboo and fragrant herbs,
mingling green pines and fragrant trees.
As for the maidens of Hándān,
the young men of Wǎn and Luò.

"Luxuriant are the millet sprouts,
the rainy weather enriches them.
Long and far my journey south,
Shào Bó toils for them."
The Erya says:
"Zhìzhì
means to reap."
Liú Xī's Explanation of Names says:
"Zhìzhì
is the sound of cutting millet and broomcorn millet."
Moving the East Gate Southern Tribes Present
The Han Feizi says:
"Wú Qǐ wanted to attack a small Qín outpost.
He placed one dàn of red millet outside the gate.
He ordered that anyone who could move this to outside the west gate
would be rewarded with superior fields and houses.
People competed to move it.
Then he issued an order, saying:
'Tomorrow we attack Qín.
Those who can be first to ascend
will be appointed as senior officers,
and rewarded with superior fields and houses.'
Thereupon they attacked it,
and took it in one morning."
Shěn Yuē's Book of Sòng says:
"In the time of the Yellow Emperor,
southern tribesmen riding white deer came to present jùchàng."
The Erya says:
"Jù
is black millet."
Offered in the Ancestral Temple Sacrificed to Sī Hán
Notes on Ancient and Modern Matters says:
"In the first year of the Yuánxīng era of Emperor Hé,
black millet plants with double grains grew in Rènchéng.
Three dǒu and eight shēng of grain were obtained,
and offered in the ancestral temple."
The Zuozhuan says:
"Shēn Fēng replied to Jì Wǔzǐ, saying:
'When they store ice,
they use a black male and jù millet
to sacrifice to Sī Hán.'"
Dù Yù's commentary says:
"Black male means a black sacrificial animal,
jù millet is black millet.
Sī Hán
is the dark, obscure spirit of the north.
Therefore, all things used are black.
Since the activity is conducted outdoors,
they sacrifice to that spirit."
Granaries Full Pò Zàng
The Mao Odes says:
"Our millet is abundant,
our broomcorn millet is lush.
Our granaries are already full,
our open stores are by the hundred million."
Guō Yìgōng's Extensive Records says:
"Pò zàng
is jì (broomcorn millet)."
Ripens in Fourth Month Leader of the Five Grains
Guō Yìgōng's Extensive Records says:
"Bī mài jì ripens in the fourth month."
Xǔ Shèn's Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters says:
"Jì (broomcorn millet)
is the leader of the five grains."
Jade-like Paste and Gem-like Grains
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is Qióngzhī millet.
It is said that its substance is white like jade,
soft and smooth like paste,
and eating it ensures a full lifespan without illness."
It also says:
"On Yuánqiáo Mountain, also named Huánqiū,
there is a square lake a thousand li wide.
Many large cranes dwell there,
standing ten feet tall.
They fly in flocks along the lake's edge,
gathering Bùzhōu millet in their beaks and carrying it to the top of Huánqiū.
The millet grows in ears,
fifty feet high,
and its grains are gleaming like jade."
Dragon Branches and Phoenix Crown
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is Lóngzhī millet.
It is said that its branches twist and curve like swimming dragons,
and eating it makes one an excellent runner."
It also says:
"There is Fèngguān millet,
resembling a phoenix's crown.
Those who eat it gain great strength."
A Thousand Stalks and Five Transformations
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is Yúnqú millet.
It grows in clusters,
with leaves resembling lotus leaves.
Eating it improves one's complexion.
The millet stalks are mostly red with some yellow,
all twenty feet long,
with a thousand stalks growing together in clusters."
Chūnqiū Shuōtící states:
"Millet undergoes five transformations:
first, transformed by yang, it sprouts as seedlings;
second, it flowers and becomes grain stalks;
third transformation yields what is called millet;
fourth, entering the mortar, the husked rice emerges from its shell;
fifth, steamed into cooked rice, it becomes edible."
Large Grains and Long Branches
Yáng Quán's Wùlǐ Lùn states:
"All seeds have strength or weakness,
and soil has hardness or softness.
Strong seeds suit the soil,
producing tall stalks with sparse grains,
long ears and large kernels."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is Yàozhī millet.
It is said that its branches are long and pliant,
swaying without wind,
and eating it grants longevity."
Fragrant Stalks and Salt-drill
Lǐjì states:
"In the rites for sacrificing at the ancestral temple,
liáng millet is called xiāngqí."
Guō Yìgōng's Guǎngzhì states:
"Yánzuàn liáng has grains like louse eggs.
Emperor Wén of Wèi used it to make congee."
And so on.
Long Stalks and Large Eyes
Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"Beans that obtain the right season
have long stalks and short pods.
Their pods grow in clusters of fourteen,
with many branches and numerous nodes,
competing in leaves and abundant in fruit."
Chūnqiū Zuǒzhùqī states:
"The spirit of beans is Língzhào,
seven feet tall,
with large eyes,
and in tune with the seasons."
Purple Flowers and Green Color
Guō Yìgōng's Guǎngzhì states:
"Jù beans,
seedlings resemble small beans.
They have purple flowers,
and can be made into flour.
They grow in Zhūtí."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there are Qīnglí beans.
They bend their leaves upon seeing the sun.
Those who eat them do not hunger for years.
The bean stalks are all as thick as a finger and green,
with a single stalk spreading luxuriantly over several acres."
♀End of beans♂
Purple Color and Red Lettuce
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is purple-fruited hemp,
with grains like millet
and purple color.
Pressed into oil,
the juice is like clear water.
Eating it enables one to see ghosts and spirits."
It also says:
"There is Dàoyè hemp,
resembling inverted lettuce,
reddish-purple in color.
Also called Hóngbīng hemp,
it is said to bear fruit only when icy cold."
Boosts Energy and Flying Brightness
Běncǎo Jīng states:
"Hemp seeds taste sweet and are non-toxic.
They mainly replenish the center and boost energy,
making people plump and healthy."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"There is Fēimíng hemp,
with black leaves
and fruit like jade.
When wind blows, it scatters like dust,
also called Míngchén hemp."
Red Ice and Purple Grains
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"At the farthest east of the eastern realm,
there is Dàoyè hemp,
red in color.
Also called Hóngbīng hemp,
eating it makes one's complexion fair and clear."
It also says:
"There is purple-fruited hemp,
with grains like millet."
♀End of hemp♂
One Stalk and Nine Ears
Jìn Qǐjū Zhù states:
"In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
auspicious wheat appeared in Fúfēng Commandery,
with two ears on a single stalk.
All were inclined and had branches,
yielding three times the usual grain."
Cuī Hóng's Qiánliáng Lù states:
"In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
auspicious wheat with nine ears on a single stalk
grew in Gūzāng."
Three Leaves and Two Forks
Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"On the mountains in early summer,
all grains grow three leaves and then yield barley."
Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"When Zhāng Kān was Governor of Yúyáng,
he encouraged people to plow and sow,
leading to great prosperity.
The people sang:
'Mulberry trees without clinging branches,
wheat ears forking in twos.'"♀End of wheat♂
Jìn Dynasty Zhāng Hàn's "Ode to Bean Soup"
Then comes the fine beans of early autumn,
with hanging branches and upright pods.
They are cut and harvested,
filling baskets and chests.
Fragrant, gleaming, harmoniously blended,
relieving ailments and meeting urgent needs.
Sipping a cup in season,
one swallows and sighs thrice.
Living in a humble town,
I face many hardships.
Though plagued by empty stores,
my joy never ceases.
Recalling bygone days,
I sip bean soup seeking peace.
Jìn Dynasty Zhàn Fāngshēng's "In Praise of Sunshoots"
Lush and lovely fine shoots,
tall and slender by the steps.
Tender leaves flourishing thickly,
round thorns sparsely planted.
Flowing moisture enriches the roots,
gentle dew washes their color.
The Eryǎ states:
"Chrysanthemum,
is Zhìqiáng."
Zhōu Chù's Fēngtǔ Jì says:
"Rìjīng,
Zhìqiáng,
are all alternative names for the flower and stem of the chrysanthemum.
It grows by the water's edge,
its blossoms are resplendent.
When the frost descends,
only this plant flourishes luxuriantly.
The ninth month corresponds to the pitch-tube Wúshè,
customarily, on the Double Ninth Festival, seasonal plants are used."
The Míngshān Jì says:
"The Taoist priest Zhū Rúzǐ ingested chrysanthemum plants,
and ascended to heaven riding on clouds."
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Rìjīng, Gēngshēng, Zhōuyíng,
are all one chrysanthemum.
But the root, stem, flower, and fruit have different names;
some are ineffective,
because they are not the true chrysanthemum."
It also says:
"Chrysanthemum flowers resemble Yì flowers,
they are distinguished simply by their sweetness and bitterness.
Chrysanthemum is sweet while Yì is bitter,
hence the saying 'bitter as Yì'."
Yìng Shào's Fēngsútōng says:
"In Lì County of Nányáng, there is a Sweet Valley,
with sweet and delicious water.
It is said that on its mountains grow large chrysanthemums,
water flows down from the mountains,
obtaining their nourishing essence.
In the valley, there are over thirty households,
who no longer need to dig wells.
They all drink this water,
the eldest live to 120 or 130,
the middle-aged to over a hundred,
the youngest to seventy or eighty.
They are called 'great longevity',
because chrysanthemums lighten the body, boost energy,
and make people strong and robust."
The Běncǎo Jīng says:
"Chrysanthemums include Jīn jú, Bái jú, Huáng jú.
Chrysanthemum flower is also called Jiéhuā,
also Chuángōng,
also Yánnián,
also Báihuā,
also Rìjīng,
also Gēngshēng."
It also says:
"Yīnwēi is also called Zhūyíng,
also Nǚhuā.
There are two kinds of chrysanthemum:
one with purple stems,
fragrant and sweet-tasting,
its leaves can be made into soup,
this is the true chrysanthemum.
Another with green stems and large,
smelling like mugwort,
bitter and inedible,
is called Yì.
This is not the true chrysanthemum."
White Blossoms, Yellow Stamens
The Wúshì Běncǎo says:
"Chrysanthemum blossom is also called Báihuā."
Lú Chén's "Chrysanthemum Rhapsody" says:
"Jade-green leaves spread like clouds,
yellow stamens scattered like stars.
Glistening bright and splendid,
lush and graceful, elegant and beautiful."
Green Stems, Purple Stalks
Zhōng Huì's "Chrysanthemum Blossom Rhapsody" says:
"Green stems, red tips."
Jī Hán's "Chrysanthemum Flower Inscription" says:
"Resplendent red chrysanthemums,
flourish even more in late autumn.
Whirling petals, round and elegant,
jade-green leaves, purple stalks.
Numerous immortal disciples,
eat their fallen blossoms."
Kneading Jade Blossoms, Gleaming Golden Flowers
Zhōng Huì's "Chrysanthemum Flower Rhapsody" says:
"Plucked with slender hands,
caught with light kerchiefs.
Kneaded like jade blossoms,
placed between crimson lips.
Those who ingest it live long,
those who eat it commune with spirits."
Zuǒ Jiǔpín's "Chrysanthemum Eulogy" says:
"Splendid, beautiful essence,
imbued with ethereal harmony.
In spring, lush jade-green leaves,
in autumn, gleaming golden flowers."
Phoenixes Gather, Stars Scatter, Clouds Spread
Pān Ní's "Autumn Chrysanthemum Rhapsody" says:
"Fragrance reaches the distant depths,
light illuminates marsh and plain.
Summoning immortals, invoking spirits,
phoenixes dance, simurghs prance.
Flying stems, scattered leaves,
intertwining, one after another.
Roaming maidens gaze upon their glory and smile artfully,
yuānchú birds gather from afar and sing sweetly."
Lú Chén's "Chrysanthemum Rhapsody" says:
"How extraordinary is this plant,
undergoing seasonal change yet unharmed.
Surpassing the cold-hardiness of pines and cypresses,
excelling the winter fragrance of magic mushrooms.
Jade-green leaves spread like clouds,
yellow stamens scattered like stars."
Wèi Zhōng Huì's "Chrysanthemum Flower Rhapsody"
How marvelous the autumn chrysanthemum,
alone flourishing amidst congealing frost.
Rising luxuriantly in late spring,
displaying grandeur in autumn's metal.
Spreading vines, lush and dense,
covering slopes, cloaking ridges.
Pale stems, green leaves,
green stalks, red tips.
Fragrant fruits abundant,
gleaming splendor, radiant.
Gentle breezes stir,
shining, casting light.
Then, in the first month of late autumn,
the ninth day's number aligns.
Wine set in splendid halls,
grand gatherings to delight the heart.
All plants wither and fade,
fragrant chrysanthemums just begin to bloom.
Profuse blossoms, dazzling bright,
some yellow, some green.
Then there are Máoqiáng, Xīshī,
Jīng ladies, Qín princesses.
Lovely forms, enchanting beauty,
a single glance topples cities.
Raising slender, fair hands,
snow-white wrists revealed.
Looking up, stroking cloud-like hair,
looking down, playing with fragrant blooms."
Jìn Pān Ní's "Autumn Chrysanthemum Rhapsody"
Hanging brilliant colors surpassing lotus,
wafting fragrance excelling orchid groves.
Roaming maidens gaze upon their glory and smile artfully,
yuānchú birds gather from afar and sing sweetly.
If perfected beings pick its fruit,
Queen Mother receives its blossoms.
Some fill emptiness to nurture nature,
some enhance beauty to display charm.
Already prolonging life for lasting longevity,
also dispelling illness and curing ailments."
Táng Tàizōng Wén Huángdì's "Poem on the Remaining Chrysanthemum"
Stairside orchids congeal dawn frost,
bank chrysanthemums reflect morning light.
Dew thick, late smiles dry,
wind strong, faint remnant fragrance.
Slender leaves lose light green,
round flowers scatter broken yellow.
Still bearing this year's hue,
again forming next year's fragrance."
Sòng Bào Zhāo's "Reply to Xiūshàngrén's Chrysanthemum Poem"
Wine from wild field rice,
chrysanthemums from high ridge grass.
Flavor and appearance, what marvel again,
able to make you enthralled.
Jade bowls merely bring shame,
for you, ashamed this autumn.
Golden lids cover ivory plates,
how to resolve heart's solitary sorrow?"
Chén Shūdá's "Chrysanthemum Poem"
Amidst frost, open purple bases,
under dew, emit golden blossoms.
Only let them meet picking,
how refuse alone late blooming?"
Lotus, Thirteenth
Forgetting Sorrow, Dispelling Melancholy
Shù Xī's "Fāméng Shuō" states:
"Xuāncǎo can make one forget sorrow."
Zhāng Huá's "Bówùzhì" states:
"The 'Shénnóng Jīng' says:
'Medicinal herbs nurture one's nature,
meaning héhuān dispels anger,
and xuāncǎo makes one forget sorrow.'"
Wáng Lǎng's "Letter to the Crown Prince of Wèi":
"Not neglecting your gracious letter,
it serves to comfort and refresh.
Reading it brings joy and laughter,
quenching thirst and hunger.
Even if xuāncǎo makes one forget sorrow,
and gāosū relieves fatigue,
nothing surpasses this."
Liáng Dynasty Xú Miǎn's "Rhapsody on the Xuāncǎo Flower"
Observing the poets' analogies and inspirations,
they entrust plants to compose verses.
Only the renowned xuāncǎo,
planted to forget sorrow.
Thus, in quiet melancholy,
the courtyard is serene and tranquil.
Tall trees cast their shade,
orchid fragrance blends with their shadows.
Admiring the clusters of competing blossoms,
delighting in the roots vying for prominence.
Some bloom red, others scatter purple,
all flourishing in early spring.
Truly, this flower stands alone in beauty,
casting golden hues in the fiery season.
It shines with colors to dispel ailments,
and carries fragrance evenly.
It does not rely on the héhuān tree,
nor await the bamboo shoots of new branches.
Like lotus in the lingering heat,
and cicadas in the early autumn dew.
Its leaves hang on four sides,
its calyx has six petals.
Also called yínán,
adding this name brings auspiciousness.
Elegant but not gaudy,
refined but not plain.
It unfurls and curls with the dimming and brightening,
flourishing and withering with wind and frost.
Laughing at dùhéng and jiēchē,
how can other plants compare?
Suí Dynasty Yáng Xiūzhī's "Poem on Xuāncǎo"
Blossoming in the depths of secluded streams,
scattering colors over winding halls.
Gentle and moist with clear dew,
subtly serene with benevolent breezes.
Each morning embracing beautiful scenes,
each night facing splendid ponds.
Suí Dynasty Wèi Yànshēn's "Poem on Xuāncǎo Before the Steps"
Green grass brimming with fragrance,
lush and vibrant before the hall.
Hearts adorned with buds about to bloom,
leaves already long by the railing.
Clouds pass without casting shadows,
winds bring sudden fragrance.
Given the name 'forget sorrow',
yet my sorrows remain unforgotten.
Duckweed, Fifteenth
"Ěryǎ" states:
"Píng,
is duckweed.
Guō Pú says:
'In Jiāngdōng, it is called zǎo.'
The larger ones are pín."
Zhōu Chù's "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
"Píngpín,
is another name for water celery."
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
"Among delicious vegetables,
is the pín of Kūnlún."
"Lǐjì" states:
"In the third month of spring,
duckweed begins to grow."
"Huáinánzǐ" states:
"Duckweed takes root in water,
trees take root in soil."
"Huáinán Wàn Bì Shù" states:
"Old blood transforms into duckweed."
The essence of gathered blood reaches the underworld.
"Běncǎo" states:
"Water duckweed,
also called water blossom,
pungent and cold in taste.
Treats sudden fever and body itch,
reduces water qi,
darkens beard and hair.
Long-term consumption lightens the body,
grows in Léizé."
Floating Rootless on Water, Crossing the River to Obtain Fruit
Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén" states:
"Píng,
is duckweed,
rootless,
floating on water to grow."
"Jiāyǔ" states:
"The King of Chǔ crossed the river and obtained a duckweed fruit,
as large as a dou,
red as the sun.
Cutting it open and eating it, sweet as honey."
Growing in Marshes, Dwelling in Clear Ponds
"Běncǎo Jīng" states:
"Water duckweed, also called water blossom,
pungent and cold in taste.
Grows on pond and marsh waters,
treats sudden fever and body itch.
Reduces water qi,
overcomes wine."
Hé Yàn's poem states:
"The tumbleweed loses its root,
drifting and floating with the wind.
Vast are the paths of the four seas,
endless, how can they be filled?
I wish to be a duckweed plant,
lodging in a clear pond.
Let me rejoice in today,
what comes after, I do not know."
Green in Color, White in Blossom
"Fàn Zǐ Jìrán" states:
"Water duckweed comes from Sānfǔ,
the green-colored ones are good."
"Wú Shì Běncǎo" states:
"Water duckweed, also called water lián,
grows on pond and marsh waters.
Leaves round and small,
one stem, one leaf,
roots enter the water.
Blossoms white in May,
gathered in March,
dried in the sun."
Used in Sacrifices, Offered to Kings and Lords
"Máo Shī" states:
"Gathering pín,
the wife of a senior official, able to follow the rules,
can then honor ancestors,
and participate in sacrifices."
"Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Vegetables like pín, fán, yùn, and zǎo,
can be offered to kings and lords."
Western Jìn Dynasty Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Rhapsody on Duckweed"
Strolling along the long canal, gazing afar,
viewing the tiny grass following the waves.
Scattered and floating, clear and lush,
solitary, born in the divine pond.
Relying on fine roots to nourish itself,
it drifts freely upon the water's surface.
Spreading round leaves to stretch its form,
emitting emerald hues tinged with pale blue.
Sheltering the splendid scales of slender fish,
shading the clear waters of orchid ponds.
Serenely flowing with the current,
gracefully following the wind.
Sometimes clinging thinly to the bank's edge,
or lingering in the rushing currents.
Rising and falling without constancy,
drifting back and forth endlessly.
Looking up to the bright sun,
leaning down upon the green water.
Restless in stillness,
moving without fixed path.
Calm when the flow rests,
stirred when waves disturb.
Light and prone to drift,
unstable and easily swayed.
Like a lone minister standing apart,
following wherever exclusion leads.
Within, single-minded in serving the court,
without, resolved to shun factions.
Duckweed, out of water, withers and dies,
a scholar, without support, meets wrongful fate.
Seeing this grass, filled with emotion,
I know the straight path is hard to abandon.
Southern Qí Dynasty Liú Huì's "Poem on Duckweed"
Pitiful pond duckweed,
misty purple and green.
Cleverly opening and closing with the waves,
following the water's rise and fall.
Tiny roots unattached,
slender leaves, what need for stems?
Drifting, hard to predict,
lingering, as if with feeling.
Yǔ Jiānyú's "Poem on the Pond Duckweed"
The wind flips it, now green, now purple;
Waves rise, at times sparse, at times dense.
Originally I lamented its lack of roots,
Yet was surprised it could bear fruit.
Moss, Part Sixteen
Zhōu Chù's *Fēngtǔ Jì* says:
"Shífà
is water moss.
It is bluish-green in color,
and grows on rocks."
*Ěryǎ* says:
"Tán
is stone clothing."
Guō Pú says:
"It is water moss,
also called shífà."
Also, *Guǎngyǎ* says:
"Shífà
is stone clothing."
*Shuōwén* says:
"Tái
is water clothing."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's *Nányuè Zhì* says:
"Seaweed is also called hǎitái,
or hǎiluó,
growing on rocks in the sea."
*Guǎngzhì* says:
"In empty rooms where no one walks, moss grows,
sometimes green, sometimes purple.
It is also called yuánxiǎn,
or lǜqián."
Shífà (Stone Hair) Water Clothing
*Ěryǎ* says:
"Tán
is stone clothing."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"It is water moss,
also called shífà,
eaten by people in Jiāngdōng."
Zhāng Yī's *Guǎngyǎ* says:
"Shífà
is stone clothing."
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuōwén* says:
"Tái
is water clothing."
Covering the Steps Growing in the Pavilion
Wáng Zhìshēn's *Sòng Jì* says:
"Wáng Wēi,
courtesy name Jǐngxuán,
was the younger brother of Grand Guardian Wáng Hóng.
Minister of Personnel Jiāng Zhàn admired his talent and ability,
and recommended him for the position of Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
Wáng Wēi pleaded serious illness and declined the appointment,
and subsequently sent a letter to Jiāng Zhàn severing ties.
For over ten years,
he did not step beyond his threshold.
He dwelled in a humble, confined room,
where moss and grass covered the steps."
Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Moon" says:
"When Prince Sī of Chén first lost Yīng Yáng and Liú Zhēn,
he was deeply grieved and had much idle time.
Green moss grew in the pavilion,
fragrant dust settled on the terrace.
Silently, sorrow filled his heart,
unhappy even at midnight."
Liáng Dynasty Jiāng Yān's "Rhapsody on Green Moss"
I carved a chamber into the mountain cliff,
and there was green moss there.
Moved by what I saw,
I composed this piece.
Ah, the clinging green moss—
it has no color or form to compare it to.
It must dwell in seclusion and stillness,
seeming imbued with a deep, hidden sorrow.
Thus, where it resides on rocks,
pines and junipers cast intertwined shade.
Spring rain perpetually pours,
looking down across the stream.
Gazing up at the crumbling cliff,
one grieves at the perilous hollows.
Only the flowing water rushes by,
yet it can twist and bend, growing upward,
and mottled, spreading below.
Exceptional men value its steadfast essence,
Daoist priests delight in its reclusive charm.
Chewing pine resin to elevate their thoughts,
holding alchemical scriptures in eternal reverence.
If it is in the water,
then it mirrors the belts of lakes and marshes,
encircling ponds and woods like brocade.
The lovely hues of spring ponds,
the pleasant songs of sunlit birds.
The green suburbs have not faded beneath the white sun's shine,
the road stretches a thousand miles where the green grass is deep.
Thus it grows in the water, swaying and drifting,
emerging from the waves, soaking and spreading.
Borrowing green twigs, it gathers emerald,
lending yellow blossoms, it unfolds gold.
The traveler from Liáng,
though his horse is weary, cannot bear to leave.
The maiden of the Tùyuán Garden,
though her silkworms hunger, cannot restrain herself.
How desolate it is—
moss accumulating like tangled nets.
Gazing at the distant, indistinct green moss,
one grieves for a hundred generations, how much regret!
Therefore, what it evokes
is sorrow born of feeling,
emotion stirred by lament.
The soul's thoughts are severed,
the spirit's reflections linger.
Observing that magnolia and camphorwood,
straightened by the marking line, meet untimely death.
And as for the climbing fig and lovage,
they are cherished for their fragrance and displayed.
How perfect is the green moss, useless,
who can know how much or how little it is?
Liáng Dynasty Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Green Moss"
Already misty-green on the steps,
floating on water, again spreading endlessly.
Tiny roots as if about to break,
fine filaments seemingly reconnecting.
The long wind hides the slender grass,
the deep hall engulfs the patterned moss.
Twining lushly, with none to offer it,
luxuriant and flourishing, merely pitiable.
Plum, Part One
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuōwén* says:
"Lǐ
is a fruit.
The character combines 'tree' with the phonetic 'child.'
Shù
is the ancient form of lǐ."
*Ěryǎ* says:
"Xiū is a plum without fruit.
Guō Pú's annotation says:
'Also called Zhàolǐ.'
Zuòjiēlǜlǐ
is the present-day màishúlǐ.
Bóchìlǐ; peaches and plums have ugly pits.
For jujubes and plums, one says 'dì' to remove the stem."

"For fruits like peaches and plums, one removes the stem by 'dì'-ing.

Boiling plum bark in water

Green Substance, Blue Skin

Its abundant splendor overflows outward.
Its jade-green substance transforms to vermilion,
Its form matures with the turning seasons."

Gathered from Spring Mountains, Sunk in Cold Water

Lúshān White, Fánglíng Pale Blue
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Accounts of the Strange" states:
"During the time of Yuán Běnchū,
a spirit appeared east of the river,
named Lord Dùsuǒ.
People together built a temple for him.
A woman of the Sū family in Yǎnzhōu fell ill,
and went to pray.
She saw a man
wearing a plain white single-layered robe,
with a tall hat resembling a fish's head.
He said to Lord Dùsuǒ:
'Long ago on Lúshān we shared white plums together.
Not long ago? It has already been three thousand years.
How easily the sun and moon pass!
It makes one feel regretful.'
After he left,
Lord Dùsuǒ said:
'That was the Lord of the Southern Sea.'" Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Plum" states:
"Then there are the Huángjiàn plums from Héyí,
The pale blue plums from Fánglíng.
One tree bears three colors,
Different flavors, distinct names."
Northern Mountains, Southern Commanderies

Dark Spring, Cold Water
Yǔ Xuán's "Ode to the Silent Well" states:

Dark Cloud, Green Jade

Autumn Fruit, Winter Blossoms

Sinking Vermilion, Floating Color

"Floating colors, dappled and variegated,
the red ones are like cinnabar."
Sweet and Fresh, Transparently Clear
"Records of the Two Capitals" states:
"In the Jiāqìng ward of the Eastern Capital there is a plum tree,

"Cài Yán of Wǔyuán, from the □ mountain, said:

Western Jìn Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Plum"
Planting the famous fruit of the Central Plains,
its deep roots set in fragrant gardens.
Admiring the rows of trees, lush and dense,
praising the slender branches, graceful and supple.
Then the long boughs spread in all directions,
dense leaves cast layered shade.
The evening light turns its glow,
casting shade beside the orchid grove.
Then comes the rustling morning breeze,
drifting, falling blossoms.
Its essence is hidden within, solidly formed,
its abundant splendor overflows outward.
Its jade-green substance transforms to vermilion,
its form matures with the turning seasons.
A clear Jué note sounds, and a subtle sourness arises;
a great Gōng note stirs, and harmonious sweetness is born.
Once fully ripened and mature,
its five colors have distinct patterns.
By kind and category divided,
some are vermilion, some are yellow.
Sweet and sour in perfect measure,
their beauty surpasses the honeycomb.
Floating colors, dappled and variegated,
the red ones are like cinnabar.
Entering the mouth, juices flow freely,
their exquisite flavor is hard to trace.
Seeing them gladdens the heart,
tasting them calms the spirit.
Then there are the Huángjiàn plums from Héyí,
the pale blue plums from Fánglíng.
One tree bears three colors,
different flavors, distinct names.
These were unseen by ancient generations,
yet all ascend to be served in purple chambers.
They satisfy the palates of ten thousand states,
and fill the offerings to the spirits and gods.
In the past, I wondered at the ancients receiving gifts,
and repaying them with precious jade.
But savoring this flavor's marvelous excellence,
I then know such repayment is too light.
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Plum"
Then there are the Huángjiàn plums from Héyí □□,
the pale blue plums from Fánglíng.
One tree bears three colors,
different flavors, distinct names.
Its essence is hidden within, solidly formed,
its abundant splendor overflows outward.
Its jade-green substance not yet transformed,
its form matures with the turning seasons.
By kind and category divided,
some are vermilion, some are yellow.
Sweet and sour in perfect measure,
their beauty surpasses the honeycomb.
Táng Dynasty Emperor Tàizōng's "Poem on Obtaining the Theme 'Plum'"
The Jade Balance flows through the cassia orchard,
a well-trodden path can truly be sought.
Orioles sing beyond the dense foliage,
butterflies play amid the fragile blossoms' hearts.
Beautiful scenes glow with morning's colors,
light mists disperse the evening shade.
Briefly gazing by the radiant columns' side,
then looking afar to the numinous mountain woods.
Also, "Poem on Picking a Plum"
Its coiled roots are planted on the isle in the sea,
its interlocking boughs stretch across, leaning on the sky.
Unfurling blossoms, their light illuminates the four seas;
curling leaves, their shade covers the three rivers.
Liáng Dynasty Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Chanting the Màilǐ Plum"
Green jade crowns the Western Sea,
blue stones fill the outer regions.
Transformed into fruit within the central garden,
beneath it forms a road and thoroughfare.
Being first is truly worthy of esteem,
yet for its smallness, it is hard to surpass.
Its color rivals the pale blue of Fánglíng,
its flavor steals the glory of the cold-water vermilion.
Plucking it, wishing to present it,
for the imperial table, I yet hesitate.
Liáng Dynasty Wáng Yún's "Poem in Reply to Yuán, the Golden Purple Official, Who Sent Vermilion Plums"
Plum blossoms in spring display their hues,
bearing fruit below, they form a well-trodden path.
Pān Yuè chanted of the Golden Valley,
the Wèi Empress sank them in the cold stream.
Meeting your gift of enchanting beauty,
I move it for enjoyment into my lofty chamber.
Ashamed I have no jade to give in return,
I merely use it to adorn my secluded dwelling.
《Ancient Songs and Poems》
A peach tree grows by the dew-laden well,
A plum tree grows beside the peach.
Insects gnaw at the peach tree’s roots,
The plum tree stiffens in its stead.
Trees of the same kind wound each other,
Flesh and blood too may be forgotten.
Liang Dynasty Shěn Yuē’s “Ode to the Plum”
A green jade crown in the Western Sea,
Blue stones fill the transformed realm.
Transformed into a treasure of the Middle Kingdom,
Beneath it, roads and paths form.
Its hue moistens like Fánglíng’s pale silk,
Its flavor surpasses the vermilion of cold water.
Suí Dynasty Jiāng Zǒng’s “Ode to the Plum”
The fine tree grows early,
Spring winds scatter its blossoms.
Only where a path is trodden,
How many are those who adjust their caps?
Ever known by the side of the dew-laden well,
Again neighboring the lush peach tree.
Nài, Second

like stored treasures.”

Set in the Mystic Chamber, Cast into the Clear Stream

Mystic Clouds, Sweet Dew

in the depth of winter at midnight,
four perfected beings descended,

Liáng Dynasty Xiè Zhèn’s Matching Poem on Nài Blossoms with Xiāo the Imperial Academy Scholar
Both glorious at the festival’s start,
alone outstanding in late high autumn.
Spitting green, they transform the fading garden,
unfurling red, they sway in the falling park.
Not following fantastical transformations to grow,
how could they rely on warmed pipes to flourish?
Fortunate to be plucked like jade blossoms,
for you, I send them afar.
Liáng Dynasty Chǔ Yún’s “Ode to the Nài”
Chéngdū prizes plain quality,
Jiǔquán praises white beauty.
Red and purple outshine summer’s splendor,
fragrance overwhelms spring orchids.
Shining in the sun, renewing their fragrance,
in the grove, late stems sprout.
Who planted these three trees?
In the end, they rival the eight cassias.
Not yielding to those in Yuánqiū,
pure and bright at the splendid court’s edge.
Liáng Dynasty Chǔ Yān’s “Nài Poem”
Chéngdū prizes plain quality,
Jiǔquán praises white beauty.
Red and purple outshine summer’s splendor,
fragrance overwhelms spring orchids.
Say, who values these three trees?
In the end, they rival the eight cassias.
Wèi Dynasty Cáo Zhí’s “Memorial of Thanks for Bestowed Nài”
This evening, the palace tiger warrior proclaimed the decree,
bestowing upon us, your subjects, a box of winter nài.
Since nài ripen in summer,
yet now they grow in winter,
things are treasured for being out of season,
favor is profound for surpassing taste,
this is not what we, your subjects, should bear.
We received a reply, the decree to Zhí and others stated:
“The mountain nài came from Liángzhōu,
the journey was long.
Moreover, coming east, the weather turned warm,
hence the nài changed color and are not fine.”

The Diǎnshù states:
"The peach is

Luxuriant Blossoms, Sweet Fruit

the son of the Marquis of Qí."

Suitable for Five Fertile Soils, Already Stolen Three Times
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"In five fertile soils,
the tree suitable is the peach."
The Hànwǔ Gùshì states:
"The Eastern Commandery presented a short person;
the Emperor called for Dōngfāng Shuò.
When Shuò arrived,
the short person pointed at Shuò and said to the Emperor:
'Queen Mother plants peaches,
which bear fruit once every three thousand years.
This man is no good;
he has already stolen them three times.'
Later, the Western Queen Mother descended,
brought out seven peaches,
ate two herself,
and gave five to the Emperor.
The Emperor kept the pits in front of him;
the Queen Mother said:
'What are these for?'
The Emperor said:
'I wish to plant them.'
The Queen Mother laughed and said:
'This peach bears fruit once every three thousand years;
it cannot be planted in the mortal world.'"
Purple Veins, Green Color
The Xījīng Zájì states:
"When the Shànglín Park was developed,
ministers from distant regions each presented famous fruits,

"When the Shànglín Park was developed,
ministers from distant regions presented famous fruits,
including the Xiānghétáo."

Wǔlíng Source, Luòyáng Road
Táo Qián's "Táoyuán Jì" states:
"During the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man from Wǔlíng was fishing
and followed a stream,
forgetting the distance of the road.
Suddenly, he came upon a forest of flowers,
with fragrant blossoms lining both banks, fresh and beautiful,
and falling petals swirling everywhere.
At the end of the forest, he found a mountain,
with a small opening.
At first, it was extremely narrow,
but after walking four or five steps,
it suddenly opened up to a bright and spacious view.
Villages and houses were connected,
and the sounds of chickens and dogs could be heard.
The clothing of the men and women
was entirely like that of outsiders.
Seeing the fisherman, they were surprised
and prepared wine and food for him.
They said their ancestors had fled the troubles of the Qín dynasty,
leading their wives and children to this place,
and thus became isolated from the outside world.
They asked what era it was now,
unaware of the Hàn dynasty,
let alone the Wèi or Jìn.
After leaving,
he reported to the prefect,
who sent people to follow him and search for the place,
but they became lost and could not find it again."
Sòng Zǐhóu's "Dǒng Jiāoráo Shī" states:

The spring wind rises from north to south,
Cloud Terrace, Dew Well
The Biographies of Immortals states:
"Zhāng Líng ascended Cloud Terrace Mountain's sheer cliffs with his disciples.
On the mountain was a peach tree,
as thick as an arm.
An ancient song lyric says:
'The peach grows by the dew well.'"
Fertile Soil, Huá Lín Garden
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"In soil of the fifth fertility,

The Records of Jìn Palaces and Pavilions states:
"In the Huá Lín Garden, there were seven hundred and thirty peach trees."
Red Calyx, Purple Blossoms
An ancient poem says:

"Cinnabar [blossoms] hold up the dew,

Observing the Season, Foretelling the Year
Cuī Shí's Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People states:
"On the third day of the third month, when peach blossoms are abundant,
farmers observe the season and plant."
The Discourses on Salt and Iron states:
"When peach and plum trees bear much fruit,
the coming year will be bountiful."
Spring Blossoms, Summer Fruit
Jiāo's Forest of Changes states:
"The peach puts forth spring blossoms,

Hán's Outer Commentary states:
"Plant peach and plum in spring,
reap their fruit in summer."
Three Thefts, Half a Bite
The Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
"The Eastern Commandery presented a short man.
The Emperor summoned Dōngfāng Shuò.
The short man pointed at Shuò and said:
'The Queen Mother's eastern garden peach
bears fruit once every three thousand years.
This fellow has already stolen it three times.'"
The Hánzǐ states:
"Long ago, Mí Zǐxiá was favored by the Lord of Wèi.
While strolling in the fruit garden,
he ate a peach and found it sweet.
He gave half to his lord to eat.
The lord said:
'How loyal! He forgot his own mouth and gave it to me.'"
The Queen Mother Descends, Guān Yǐn Travels
The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn states:
"The Queen Mother of the West descended to the Emperor's palace on the seventh day of the seventh month.
She ordered her maids to fetch peaches.
Shortly, they presented seven on a jade tray.
The Queen Mother gave five to the Emperor
and ate two herself."
The Biography of Gatekeeper Yǐn Xǐ states:
"He followed Lǎozǐ on a westward journey,
visited the Most True Queen Mother,
and together they ate green peaches."
"Ode to the Peach" by Fù Xuán of the Western Jìn Dynasty
Behold the precious fruit of the eastern garden,
imbued with the numinous harmony of yīn and yáng.
With pliant roots, trees stand in rows,
adorn the long fields, splendid and arrayed.
Ripening first in summer,
first offered in the temple halls.
When autumn treads upon the Xīn month,
its flavor grows yet longer.
There is also the winter peach,
cold as ice and frost.
It harmonizes the spirit and pleases the mind,
gratifying the mouth as one desires.
Its blossoms ascend to grace the inner court,
adorning the fair faces of beauties.
Its fruit fills the void and cures hunger,
truly, its merits are hard to fathom.
I praise the oxen rested in this grove,
rejoice in the peace of all nations.
Gazing at the sea islands with deep feeling,
I long for the numinous mountain of Dùsuǒ.
Why does this tree alone flourish so?
Its branches and twigs, profuse and graceful.
Roots like coiling dragons, clouds entwined,
spreading ten thousand lǐ, twisting and winding.
It wards off the evil demons of a hundred ghosts,
stations Shén Shū to oversee wickedness.
Repels the malign and aids the upright,
how can mere beauty and glory suffice to tell?
"Ode to the Peach" by Fù Xuán of the Jìn Dynasty
Behold the precious fruit of the eastern garden,
imbued with the numinous harmony of yīn and yáng.
With pliant roots, trees stand in rows,
adorn a hundred acres, splendid and arrayed.
Ripening first in summer,
and offered in the temple halls.

It releases the spirit and pleases the mind,
gratifying the mouth as one desires.

adorning the fair faces of beauties.
Its fruit fills the void and cures hunger,
truly, its merits are hard to fathom.
I praise the oxen loosed in this grove,
rejoice in the peace of all nations.
Gazing at the sea islands with deep feeling,
I long for the numinous mountain of Dùsuò.
Why does this tree alone flourish so?
Its branches and twigs, graceful and fair.
Roots like coiling dragons, clouds entwined,
spreading a thousand lǐ, twisting and winding.
It wards off the evil demons of a hundred ghosts,

"Ode to the Garden Peach" by Wǔ Jízhī of the Sòng Dynasty
Alas, the wondrous fruit of the Queen Mother,
peerless in blossom and fruit, both abundant.
Ripened by summer's blazing sun,
yet also matures through winter's cold.
A marvel of rare growth, hard to propagate,
late to wither, early to bear.
Shénnóng and Huángdì savored its taste,
the Hàn Emperor marveled at its rarity.
In the grove, it turned back the plowing ox;
by the house, it bore the god who shares evil.
Jǐng's courage perished from insufficiency,
increasing guilt through sweet division.
Though wordless, a path forms beneath it;
it filled the dishes for the Lord of Wèi.
The season's order begins anew,
the Zhōunán repeats its verses.
Selection for offerings has its rules,
only the finest for medicinal blends.
In Lǔ, supporting the coffin repented of the thorn;
in Chǔ, offering the orphan served the king.
"Ode to the Fading Peach" by Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn
Lofty, elegant peaks,
exhale cassia's glory, pine's vigor.
Alone, the radiant peach tree, dazzling bright,
lightly lifts its splendor from the cold traces.
Then ten thousand trees form brocade,
ten groves take wing.
Moss patterns stirred by wind,
flowers ignite the tree's hue.
Emanating the free spirit of Qín's source,
wafting the flowing fragrance of Hàn's ribbons.
Like orchid lamps burning through the night,
like a bright mirror at morning toilette.
Traces completed, roaming free,
radiance brilliant, dazzling the mud.
Amid Zhēndìng's pears for eating,
mingled with Fánglíng's pale green plums.
Its fragrance hard to cease,
its brilliance without peer.
Unfurling like dawn's light about to rise,
scattering like lightning's glow about to adorn.
Then wind sheds the new branches,
frost flies from the old leaves.
The enchanting boy delights in dangling his hook,
the lovely concubine of toppled cities laments.
Táng Tàizōng Emperor's "Poem on the Peach"
In the forbidden park, spring's radiance fair,
the flower-lined path, adorned with splendid trees.
Adorning branches, hues both deep and light,
glistening dew-drops, scattered, varied light.
Facing the sun, they share a thousand smiles;
greeting the breeze, together waft one scent.
How is it by the immortal ridge's side,
alone it blooms, its distant fragrance veiled?
Suí Dynasty Xiāo Què's "Poem in Response on Lóngmén Peach Blossoms"
Long heard of the dew well's opening,
now see them planted at Lóngmén.
Few trees tell it's not the frontier pass;
tall blossoms differ from Shàoyuán.
Judging the season, they should not yet bloom,
so wish their shade returned to the gallery.
Just speak of being plucked and done,
still better than chasing the whirling wind.
Kǒng Shào'ān's "Poem on the Radiant Peach in Response to Imperial Command"
Leaves still gather, touching their own shade;
flying fragrance seeks to fill the air.
Unheeded, the remaining petals fall,
tumbling to sink within the dew well.
Poem on Peach Blossoms by Emperor Tàizōng Wénwǔ Shèng Huángdì
In the forbidden garden, spring’s radiance is splendid;
Along the flower-lined path, splendid trees decline.
Adorning branches, shades both deep and light;
Dew-drops sparkle with uneven gleam.
Facing the sun, they share a thousand smiles;
Welcoming the breeze, together emit one fragrance.
How is it that by the side of immortal peaks,
Alone they stand out, concealing distant light?
Poem on Early Peach Blossoms by Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì
Early peach blossoms, lovely in fresh hues,
Shine upon the earth, emitting their fragrance.
Among the branches, purple swallows linger;
Within the flowers, a light scent arises.
Falling petals enter the dew-filled well;
Intertwining branches brush the splendid hall.
If reflected against the willows before the window,
One might suspect a rouge-and-powder adornment.
Poem on Peach Blossoms by the Pond by Liáng Rènfǎng
Already declined from the garden of the Western King,
Again gathered are the branches of Suíshān.
By chance meeting the affection of admirers,
They perch by the side, following the pond.
The blossoms open, brilliantly red;
The fruits mature in summer, abundant and lush.

Ah, the cherry as a tree,
before all fruits, it bears splendor.
Already lush, spring arrives;
suddenly luxuriant, winter welcomes.

hanging like a sturdy vessel, late to mature.

emerald colors reflect the long river.

Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, "Poem in Response to Prince Nánpíng Kāng's Gift of Red Cherries"
Reflections flow upside-down amidst emerald clusters,
Dew-drops bead the crimson fruit held aloft.
Flowers flourish, butterflies vie in flight,
Branches dense, birds lose sight of each other.
Already lovely as the golden hairpin melon,
Still fair as the jade plate's tangerine.
How could it differ from plums like pellets?
I do not envy duckweed resembling the sun.
May they grow forever by the platform, drooping,
Long companion to the dense cloud-like cassia.
Vainly I offer this tribute of sweetness,
In the end, ashamed to wield the brush.

"In Shí Hǔ's garden, there was a Western Queen Mother jujube tree,
with leaves in both winter and summer,
and flowers blooming in the ninth month."
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Jujube"
There is a fine tree from Pénglái,
planted in the fertile soil of the Divine Land.
It raises its sturdy stems to pierce the void,
its deep roots spreading and growing.
To the north, shaded by mountain passes,
to the south, facing the three rivers.
Some are spread across Yān and Zhào,
some are abundant in Hédōng.
Then, its lush branches gather from all sides,
rich, luxuriant, and dense.
Luxuriant are its white blossoms,
abundant are its vermilion fruits.
Crisp as scattered snow,
sweet as honey held in the mouth.
The crisp ones are best fresh,
treasures of the summer.
The firm ones are best dried,
offered as delicacies to gods and men.
There is a jujube as large as a melon,
from the seashore.
It preserves life and boosts vitality,
consuming it is like attaining divinity.
Chén Hòuzhǔ's "Rhapsody on the Jujube"
In the fragrant garden, trunks stand in rows,
dense branches, a lush network.
Few stamens remain on the stems,
leaves dark, branches many.
There is also a wondrous tree,
its branches swaying in the wind.
Deep at night, shadows come,
but none compare to its red-hearted, beautiful fruit.
Crimson substance, fine branches,
double thorns share the shade,
branches and calyxes alike are precious.
Presented on golden plates with ice water,
offered on jade trays with deep cups.
This joy in the heart is unending,
dreams of it stir the gut again and again.
Jìn Dynasty Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Jujube"
White blossoms abundant,
vermilion fruits very plump.
Color like frost and snow,
sweet as honey held in the mouth.
Later Qín Dynasty Zhào Zhěng's "Poem on the Jujube"
In the northern garden, there is a tree,
its leaves spread, casting heavy shade.
Outside, though many thorns,
inside, it truly holds a red heart.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on the Jujube"
Floating splendor rivals the beauty of Qí's waters,
dangling colors, strange indeed in Zhèng's capital.
White, profuse blossoms, lush and dense,
purple fruits marked abundantly.
Wind sways the sheep-horn tree,
sun shines on chicken-heart branches.
Gǔchéng surpasses rock honey,
Péngyuè displays immortal grace.
Already heard of Ānyì's excellence,
eternally flourishing by Yùmén's edge.
Later Qín Dynasty Zhào Zhěng's "Poem on the Jujube"
In the northern garden, there is a tree,
its leaves spread, casting layered shade.
Outside, though many jujube thorns,
inside, it truly holds a red heart.
Liáng Dynasty Jiǎnwén's "Poem on the Jujube"
Floating splendor rivals the beauty of Qí's waters,
dangling colors, strange indeed in Zhèng's capital.
Sunlit, profuse blossoms, lush and dense,
purple characters marked abundantly.
Wind sways the sheep-horn tree,
sun shines on chicken-heart branches.
Gǔchéng surpasses rock honey,
Péngyuè displays immortal grace.
Already heard (collation note: "heard" is suspected to be the correct character instead of "閨")
of Ānyì's beauty,
eternally flourishing by Yùmén's edge.
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pǔ's "In Praise of the Jujube"
Establishing the state, distinguishing directions,
outside the court, nine thorn trees.
According to material, determining significance,
red heart, upright and honest.
Numerous are the ministers and officers,
illuminating this imperial duty.
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pǔ's "In Praise of the Jujube"
Establishing the state, distinguishing directions,
outside the court, nine thorn trees.
According to material, determining significance,
red heart, upright and honest.
Numerous are the ministers and officers,
illuminating this imperial duty.
Chestnut, Number Six
The Máo Shī says:
"On the slope, there is lacquer,
in the lowland, there are chestnuts."
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"Chestnuts are found in all five regions,
but Zhōu, Qín, Wú, and Yáng are especially abundant.
Only the chestnuts of Yúyáng and Fànyáng
are sweet, delicious, and long-lasting in flavor,
other regions cannot compare.
In the Wōhán state, superior chestnuts are as large as chicken eggs,
but also short in flavor and not tasty.
In Guìyáng, there are chestnuts that grow in clusters,
as large as a shuttle."
The Zhōu Guān says:
"Among the offerings in the bamboo baskets for the feast are chestnuts."
The Hàn Shū says:
"In Yān and Qín, a thousand chestnut trees
make one the equal of a marquis with a thousand households."
The Xī Jīng Zá Jì says:
"The Shànglín Garden had Hóu chestnuts, Guī chestnuts, Kuí chestnuts, Zhēn chestnuts, and Yìyáng chestnuts."
The Xīn Shì Sān Qín Jì says:
"In Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's fruit garden,
fifteen large chestnuts made one dǒu."
Women's Gifts, Basket Offerings
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Women's gifts do not exceed hazelnuts, chestnuts, jujubes, and dried meat."
The Zhōu Lǐ says:
"Among the offerings in the bamboo baskets for the feast are chestnuts."
From Nán'ān they emerge, from the northern shores they are presented.
Wáng Bāo's "The Servant's Contract" states:
"In Nán'ān, gather chestnuts and pick tangerines."
A note says:
"Nán'ān,
a county name,
produces excellent chestnuts and tangerines."
Wáng Yì's "Litchi Rhapsody" states:
"The western envoy presented grapes from the Kūnlún Mountains,
the northern state of Yān offered the giant chestnuts from the northern shores."
One tree in Huálín, a thousand trees in Yān.
"The Names of Jìn Palaces and Pavilions" states:
"In the Huálín Garden, there is one chestnut tree,
and six marquis chestnut trees."
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"In Yān and Qín, a thousand chestnut trees
make a man equal to a marquis with a thousand households."
The Qín king's park, the Hàn emperor's orchard.
"Hán Fēizǐ" states:
"When Qín suffered famine,
Marquis Yìng said to the king:
'The fruits in the five parks,
vegetables, acorns, dates, and chestnuts,
are enough to keep people alive.
I request they be distributed to them.'"
"Records of the Three Qín" states:
"In Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's fruit orchard,
fifteen large chestnuts made one dǒu."
At the foot of Huà Mountain, by the bend of the Rǔ River.
"Records of Huà Mountain" states:
"At the foot of the western mountain, there is a chestnut forest.
Since its cultivation,
it has grown lush and abundant."
Lì Yuán's commentary on the "Water Classic" states:
"In the bend of Rǔnán,
there is an area of several qǐng,
above which is Chestnut Mountain.
Its flavor does not equal the fruit of Nán'ān.
Yān annually tributes four hundred shí,
to fill the imperial storehouse.
The water islet is called Chestnut Isle."
Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn's "Lament for the Former Chestnut Tree Rhapsody"
A fine tree from distant lands, oh,
stands before the hall of the sacred temple.
It spans the two gates for passage, oh,
lining the steps on either side.
Unfazed by frost and snow, it never withers, oh,
flourishing in spring and summer.
Following its nature, it sprouts joints, oh,
sprouting green shoots and verdant blossoms.
Its form is graceful and luxuriant, oh,
like brilliant green jade.
Chén Lù's "Chestnut Rhapsody"
In all seasons, they flourish abundantly,
among the myriad fruits, darkly fragrant.
Green plums are fragrant in spring,
red peaches are sweet in summer.
How fragile are the many kinds,
only this substance lasts long.
Outwardly thorny like trifoliate orange and thorns,
inwardly pure, surpassing ice and frost.
Brought from Nán'ān for their clarity,
arrayed at Yùsù, hanging in clusters.
For offerings, jujubes and hazelnuts stand together,
added to baskets, water caltrops and foxnuts accompany.
On golden plates, their beautiful colors,
on jade stands, their fresh luster.
The Zhōu people used them for solemn reverence,
the grand officials praised them at Bǎiliáng.
Liáng Lù Bīn's "Poem on Chestnuts in Mixed Meter"
Valued as treasure in the Hàn dynasty,
the tree esteemed in prosperous Zhōu.
Blossoms first bud in crimson summer,
fruits fall in plain autumn.
Placed on jade plates,
mixed with pepper and rice.
Arranged on ivory mats,
blended with rare delicacies.
Pear, Number Seven
"Shuōwén Jiézì" states:
"Pear,
a fruit.
From the wood radical, with 'lì' indicating sound."
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"North of the Huái, south of the Róng, between the Hé and Jǐ rivers, a thousand pear trees
make a man equal to a marquis with a thousand households."
The Jìn Statutes state:
"For officials in charge of guarding pear trees,
one clerk is appointed."
"Yǐn Xǐ's Inner Biography" states:
"Lǎozi traveled west,
visited the Queen Mother of the West,
and together they ate purple pears."
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Inner Biography" states:
"Among the fruits of the Supreme Elder,
there is the Mystic Light Pear."
"Xīn's Records of the Three Qín" states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's orchard,
also called Fánchuān,
and also called Yùsù.
There are large pears as big as a five-shēng vase.
When they fall to the ground, they break.
Their owners use cloth sacks to catch them.
They are called Hánxiāo Pears."
Hé Yàn's "Discourse on the Nine Provinces" states:
"Ānpíng has good dates,
Zhēndìng has good pears."
"Guǎngzhì" states:
"Zhānggōng's Summer Pear from Běimáng in Luòyáng
is the only tree of its kind in the realm.
There are pears from Chángshān, Zhēndìng, Shānyáng, Jùyě; pears from Suīyáng in the state of Liáng; pears from Línzī in Qí commandery; Gǎo pears from Jùlù; Tíng pears from Shàngdǎng,
small and sweet.
Jiàngǔ pears from Xīnfēng; pears west of the pass are mostly for imperial use.
Guǎngdū pears weigh six jīn,
several people share one to eat.
Also, the imperial pears of Zhēndìng
are as big as a fist,
sweet as honey,
crisp as ice,
and can relieve vexation and satiety."
Pronunciation: quǎn, fǎn.
Zhēndìng, Guǎngdū.
Emperor Wén of Wèi's edict states:
"Zhēndìng pears are as big as a fist,
sweet as honey."
Guō Yìgōng's "Guǎngzhì" states:
"Guǎngdū pears weigh six jīn,
several people share one to eat."
Língguān, Yùsù.
Xiè Tiǎo's "Thanks for Pears" states:
"Their flavor comes from the shade of Língguān,
their essence resides by the banks of the Jade Ford."
"Xīn's Records of the Three Qín" states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's orchard, named Fánchuān,
also called Yùsù,
has large pears as big as a five-shēng vase.
When they fall to the ground, they break.
They are called Hánxiāo Pears."
Dàgǔ, Jùyě.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Life of Leisure" states:
"Zhānggōng's pears from Dàgǔ,
Marquis Liáng's black persimmons."
Guō Yìgōng's "Guǎngzhì" states:
"There are pears from Chángshān and Zhēndìng,
and pears from Shānyáng and Jùyě."
Grown in Xuánpǔ, planted in Qīngtián.
Wáng Zàn's "Pear Eulogy" states:
"In the tenth year of Tàikāng,
the western branch of a pear tree
joined with the central branch,
growing in the Xuánpǔ Garden.
The crown prince ordered his attendants to compose a eulogy."
"Records of Yǒngjiā" states:
"The households of Qīngtián village grow many pear trees.
There is one pear tree
called the official pear.
It measures one wéi and five cùn in circumference,
and is consistently offered as tribute, named the imperial pear."
Sweet and fragrant, moist and glossy.
"Hán Fēizǐ" states:
"Those who plant hawthorns, pears, tangerines, and pomelos
find them sweet to eat,
fragrant to smell."
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states:
"Purple pears, moist and glossy;
hazelnuts and chestnuts, bursting from their shells."
Liáng Shěn Yuē's "Poem on Pears Composed by Imperial Command"
From Dàgǔ they come, already heavy,
the road from Mín Mountain is also difficult.
Not meant to be broken,
only to enter the jade plate.
Liáng Liú Xiàochuò's "Poem on Pear Blossoms Composed by Command at a Banquet"
Yùlěi praises their moist gloss,
Jīngǔ chants their fragrant beauty.
How can they compare to beneath the dragon tower,
where plain leaves reflect on splendid doors?
Amidst rain, they seem like falling sleet,
with the wind, they flutter like butterflies.
Do I not pity their drifting fall?
I wish they would enter the ninefold gates.
Later Liáng Emperor Xuān's "Poem on Large Pears"
Dàgǔ has long been praised,
the southern wilds are truly rich in treasures.
Green leaves already hold dew,
purple fruits again contain moisture.
Sweetness, Number Eight
Zhōu Chù's *Fēngtǔ Jì* says:
"Gān,
a type of citrus,
is exceptionally sweet and delicious in flavor.
There are yellow ones,
and there are red ones,
which are called húgān."
Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù* says:
"Gān fruits shaped like pomegranates
are also called húgān."
*Guǎngzhì* says:
"There are huánggān,
with a single pit.
There is the Chéngdū píngdì gān,
as large as a shēng,
with a bluish-yellow color.
Qiánwéi Nán'ān County produces huánggān."
*Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
"The old gān orchard north of the river in Yídū Commandery
is named Yídū gān."
*Xiāngyáng Jì* says:
"Lǐ Shūpíng, on his deathbed,
instructed his son, saying:
'On Lóngyáng Isle there are a thousand wooden slaves (citrus trees),
and when the gān and jú ripen,
you will obtain several thousand bolts of silk annually.'"
*Shényì Jīng* says:
"East of the borderlands there is Jiànchūn Mountain,
□□ where there are many beautiful gān trees."
*Fēngtǔ Jì* says:
"Gān and jú types,
their flavors sweet and delicious,
are exceptional.
There are yellow ones,
and there are red ones.
The red ones are called húgān."
*Guǎngzhì* says:
"There are twenty-one varieties of gān,
including the Chéngdū píngyè gān,
as large as a shēng,
with a bluish color."
Lú Chén's *Jìfǎ* says:
"Use gān for winter sacrifices."
Flat Calyx, Round Fruit
Guō Yìgōng's *Guǎngzhì* says:
"The Chéngdū píngdì gān,
is as large as a shēng,
with a bluish-yellow color."
Hú Jì's *Gān Fù* says:
"The three autumns alternate their course,
the first cold treads upon frost.
The hú shape already appears,
the round fruit shines brightly."
Parting the Yellow Husk, Hanging the Red Fruit
Pān Yuè's *Shēng Fù* says:

tip the pale porcelain to pour the líng."
Liú Zhào's *Gān Shù Fù* says:

hung with red fruit."
Revived in Xīpíng, Eaten Together at Dōngwàng
Fàn Nìng's memorial says:
"In Xīpíng Village under the jurisdiction of Nánchāng County Magistrate Xiè Liè, there was a gān tree.
After withering and dying for a year,
it revived this year.
Its branches and leaves are luxuriant,
and now it bears many fruits."
*Shùyì Jì* says:
"South of Nánkāng Commandery is Dōngwàng Mountain.
A man entered the mountain.
On the mountaintop was an orchard,
where all kinds of fruit trees were planted,
their rows neat and orderly,
as if by human hands.
Gānzi were just ripe,
three people ate together,
until full.
He pocketed two,
wanting to show people as proof.
A voice from the air said:
'Quickly release the two gān.'
Then you may leave."
Like Water Chestnut Flowers, Rivaling the Píngshí
Hú Jì's *Huánggān Fù* says:
"Illuminating the plains and lowlands,
casting shade upon the wild groves.
Red and yellow blaze in the morning glow,
fleeting shadows meet the parting light.
Like water chestnut flowers embroidering a patterned well,
resembling the Candle Dragon holding a golden earring."
Xiè Huìlián's *Gān Fù* says:
"Rivaling the píngshí by the riverbanks,
surpassing the jade fruit of Kūnlún Mountain."
Surpassing Jade Fruit, Like a Golden Earring
Both see the annotations above.
A Thousand Trees, Ten Specimens
*Xiāngyáng Jì* says:
"Lǐ Héng planted a thousand gān trees on Wǔlíng's Lóngyáng Isle."
*Jīngkǒu Jì* says:

Zhījiāng
*Jīngzhōu Jì* says:
"Zhījiāng has famous gān."
Transformed into a Kite, Encountered a Viper
*Yì Yuàn* says:
