If you eat the fruit on the spot,
you may take as much as you like.
But if you try to take some away,
you will immediately encounter a large viper."
Yellow Husk, Jade Nectar
Pān Yuè's *Fù* says:
"Part the yellow husk to offer the gān,
tip the pale □ to pour the líng."
Liú Xiàoyí's petition says:
"Peel off that golden skin,
swallow this jade nectar.
Sweeter than the píngshí,
cooler than an ice scepter.
Instantly dispels vexation and hunger,
immediately removes intoxication."
Liú Jǐn's *Gān Shù Fù*
Oh, the profound creation's continuous flow,
arrays all forms in their destined encounters.
I admire the lush beauty of plants and grasses,
yet reserve the highest praise for the gān tree.
Born as a parasite in southern Chǔ,
spreading eastward for ten thousand lǐ.
Its roots bathed in cold springs,
its elegant branches raised to catch the dew.
Dense leaves form a spreading shade,
cleansing fine dust to reveal pure whiteness.
Facing the clear air at dawn,
gentle breezes flow at dusk.
Though its blossoms may fly in garden ponds,
it shares the steadfast spirit of the cliff pine.
Through changing seasons it grows more true,
enduring cold and heat with constant virtue.
Sòng Xiè Huìlián's *Gān Fù*
I praise the beautiful tree in the cold garden,
admiring this uniquely virtuous fragrance.
Its substance is luxuriant and embraces the wind,
its nature is upright and withstands the frost.
Its color likened to the evening glow,
its roundness matched to the morning sun.
Rivaling the píngshí by the riverbanks,
surpassing the jade fruit of Kūnlún Mountain.
I offer it to you, my lord, in the Xiāng region,
for your enjoyment in the hall's corner.
Washed by rain and braving frost,
may its fragrance spread unendingly.
Jìn Hú Jì's *Huáng*
Collation note: It seems there is a missing character after "Huáng".
*Fù*
This wondrous fruit of Jiāngnán,
draws upon heaven and earth's true yang.
Born in a marvelous land of a distant region,
planted in the faraway home of the Vermilion Bird.
Located south of the Hàn,
all on the yin side of the Jiāng.
To the left harmonizes with orchid shores,
to the right connects with cassia groves.
Girdled by clear streams of rushing water,
facing the high peaks of lofty mountains.
The three autumns alternate their course,
the first cold treads upon frost.
Illuminating the plains and lowlands,
casting shade upon the wild groves.
Like water chestnut flowers embroidering a patterned well,
the Candle Dragon driving his golden earring.
Sòng Xiè Huìlián's *Gān Fù*
I praise the beautiful ice in the cold garden,
admiring this uniquely true fragrance.
Its luxuriant foliage embraces the wind,
its nature is upright and withstands the frost.
Its color likened to the evening glow,
its roundness matched to the morning sun.
Pure as the píngshí by the riverbanks,
surpassing the jade blossoms of Kūnlún Mountain.
Liang Dynasty, Xú Líng's "Ode to the Sweet Orange"
Vermilion fruits stand tall in Jīngnán,
Their precious quality excels in beauty.
In the Shanglin Garden, mingled with fine trees,
By the river pool, interspersed with tall bamboos.
Ten thousand households rival the fief of a lord,
A thousand trees rise in the state of Jīng.
Green leaves spread lushly,
White blossoms fragrant and abundant.
When presented, they grace the banquet's joy,
Truly they thrive under clouds and rain.
Liang Dynasty, Xú Líng's "Ode to the Mandarin Orange"
Vermilion fruits stand tall in Jīngnán,
Their precious quality excels in beauty.
In the Shanglin Garden, mingled with fine trees,
By the riverbank, interspersed with slender bamboos.
Ten thousand households are enfeoffed,
Annotation: It seems there is a missing character after "enfeoffed."
A thousand trees rise in the state of Jīng.
Green leaves spread lushly,
White blossoms fragrant and splendid.
Liang Dynasty, Yǔ Jiānwú's "Thanks for the Gift of Mandarin Oranges"
Their fame spreads across the land,
From afar, the clan of Wǔlíng's deep waters thrives, their spirit flourishing,
Far away, the Jiànchūn Ridge opens.
Wáng Yì composed a rhapsody,
Pairing them with lychees.
Zhāng Héng crafted verses,
Linking them with rock honey.
Enough to make the duckweed fruit seem not sweet,
And grapes still less flavorful.
Jìn Dynasty, Wáng Shēngzhī's "In Praise of Sweet Oranges"
Integrity is tested in peril,
Constancy is valued in conduct.
Two trees preserve their glory,
Through four seasons, equally capable.
In substance, they are beautiful,
In flavor, they are grand.
Distinctly divided in the southern region,
In the north, they become trifoliate oranges.
Zōng Bǐng's "Ode"
Resplendent, fine fruits,
Luminous as bright stars.
Their color like southern gold,
Their form like the pearls of Suíhóu.
Orange, Section Nine
The "Tribute of Yǔ" says:
"Between the Huái River and the sea lies Yángzhōu,
Its tribute includes packages of oranges and pomelos."
Kǒng Ānguó says:
"Small ones are called oranges,
Large ones are called pomelos."
The "Zhōu Documents" say:
"In autumn, eat hawthorns, pears, oranges, and pomelos."
The "Zhōu Rites" say:
"Oranges crossing north of the Huái become trifoliate oranges,

The "Chūnqiū Yùndǒu Shū" says:
"The Xuán star scatters to become oranges."
The "Hànshū" says:
"In Jiānglíng, a thousand orange trees

Zhāng Bó's "Wú Lù" says:
"In Jiàn'ān Commandery, there are orange trees.

"Lú oranges ripen in summer.

White Flowers, Vermilion Fruits
Lǐ Yóu's "Seven Laments" says:
"The soil of Liáng is lush and beautiful,
Where Lú oranges grow.
White flowers and green leaves,
Spreading luxuriantly, flourishing in winter."
Cáo Zhí's "Orange Rhapsody" says:
"Vermilion fruits do not wither,

Green Leaves, Golden Garment
The Chǔ Cí's "Ode to the Orange" says:
"A splendid tree of the sovereign's land,
The orange comes to serve.
Receiving its mandate, it does not move,
Born in the southern state.
Deep-rooted and hard to transplant,
It strengthens its resolve.
Green leaves and white flowers,
Abundant and praiseworthy."
Lǐ Yóu's "Seven Laments" says:
"Golden garment, white within,
Patterned texture, full inside.
Its flavor is extraordinary,
Its delight endless."
Carrying Three, Tossing Two
The "Wúzhì" says:
"Lù Jì was six years old
When he met Yuán Shù in Jiǔjiāng.
Oranges were brought out,
Lù Jì carried three away.
Bowing in farewell, they fell to the ground.
Lù Jì said:
'I wish to take them home for my mother.'
Shù was greatly amazed by him."
Táo Qián's "Sōushén Hòujì" says:
"In the eastern wilds of Kuàijī, there was a woman
Surnamed Wú,
Named Wàng.
On the road, she suddenly saw a noble figure
Sitting solemnly upright—
It was the image of Marquis Jiǎng.
She tossed two oranges to him,
And he appeared repeatedly.
Thus, affection grew between them."
Jiànchūn Mountain, Déyáng Hall
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Shényì Jì" says:
"Beyond the eastern borders lies Jiànchūn Mountain,
Where many oranges and pomelos grow."
Lǐ Yóu's "Déyáng Hall Rhapsody" says:
"Oranges, pomelos, and cherries,
A hundred fruits grow in clusters."
Wèi Dynasty, Cáo Zhí's "Orange Rhapsody"
Sown across ten thousand lǐ, planted afar,
Arrayed in the gardens of the Bronze Sparrow Terrace.
Turning away from the warm air of the river isles,
Dwelling in the harsh purity of the dark north.
The land changed, the soil different,
Thus it lost its life.
There, it does not wither;
Here, it withers first.
Vermilion fruits do not wither,
How then can they have white flowers?
Lamenting the unevenness of cold and heat,
Sighing at the eternal separation of flower and fruit.
Raising leaves to face the southern breeze,
Hoping the warm air may be embraced.
Swaying branches rustle with flowing sound,
Awaiting southern birds to come and perch.
Where spiritual virtue moves,
Nothing is too small not to harmonize.
The divine is subtle yet easily stirred,
Trusting the Way of Heaven is not false.
Once rooted, yet without a trunk,
Surely it bears leaves but no flowers.
Gradually transforming darkly without change,
It does not display virtue to the state and family.
Stroking slender branches with a sigh,
Mourning how hard plants are to transform.
Liang Dynasty, Fàn Yún's "Garden Orange Poem"
Fragrant branches bear cold emerald,
Garden fruits turn frosty vermilion.
Transplanted roots from Chǔzhōu,
Come to shade the broad courtyard corner.
Liang Dynasty, Shěn Yuē's "Garden Orange Poem"
Green leaves thrive with dew,
Vermilion buds await frost's moisture.
If only they enter the jade plate,
Their golden garment is not what I cherish.
Zhōu Dynasty, Lǐ Yuáncāo's "Miscellaneous Ode to the Orange Tree in the Garden"
A fine tree from the shade of Wū Mountain,
Divided roots transplanted to Shànglín.
White flowers like sleet and snow,
Vermilion fruits like hanging gold.
Shadows spread over the crimson ground,
Fragrance flies across the jade peaks.
Inherently possessing a quality to withstand winter,
Able to keep a heart through the year's cold.
Wáng Shūzhī's "In Praise of Sweet Oranges"
Integrity is tested in peril,
Constancy is valued in conduct.
One tree preserves its glory,
Through four seasons, equally capable.
In substance, it is beautiful,
In flavor, it is grand.
Distinctly divided in the southern region,
In the north, they become trifoliate oranges.
Plum, Tenth
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"Plum
belongs to the apricot category.
Its tree and leaves are both like the apricot's, only darker."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"In the early Hàn dynasty,
when the Shànglín Park was being cultivated,
the various ministers each presented famous fruits.
There were Hóuméi, Zhūméi, Zǐhuāméi, Tóngxīnméi, Zǐdìméi, and Lìyǒuméi."
The Yìwù Zhì says:
"The yángméi (bayberry/red myrica) resembles a pellet,
ripening in the fifth month."
The Guǎngzhōu Jì says:
"On the summit of Lúshān there is a lake,
several qǐng in breadth.
There are yángméi and mountain peaches.
One can only eat one's fill of them there,
and cannot take them away."
The Guǎngzhì says:
"In Shǔ, the plum is called lǎo,
as large as a wild goose egg.
Both méi and lǎo can be used to make oil.
Huángméi (yellow plum)
is made from ripe lǎo."
Lǎo is pronounced lǎo.
The Máo Shī says:
"The plums are falling,
their fruits are now seven.
On the mountains are fine grasses,
and also chestnuts and plums."
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"Plum
belongs to the apricot category.
Its tree and leaves are both like the apricot's, only darker."
The Dàdài Lǐ says:
"In the fifth month of the Xiǎozhēng calendar of summer,
plums are boiled to be used as sacrificial bean offerings."
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
"On Língshān, among its trees are many plums."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"In the Shànglín Park there are Zhūméi, Tóngxīnméi, Zǐdàiméi, Yān□méi, Lìzhīméi, and Zǐhuāméi."
Purple Calyx, White Blossoms
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"When cultivating the Shànglín Park,
the various ministers each presented famous fruits.
There were Zǐdìméi and Yānzhīméi."
Liú Yìqìng's poem "Yóu Tuó Hú Shī" says:
"The warm scene turns harmonious and mild,
plants and trees daily grow more lush.
Plum blossoms cover the trees in white,
peach and apricot trees display their glorious splendor."
One Branch, Three Fruits
Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn says:
"The Yuè envoy Zhū Fā, holding a single branch of plum, presented it to the King of Liáng.
A minister of the King of Liáng named Hánzǐ,
looking at those around him, said:
'How could there be a case of presenting a single branch of plum to the ruler of a state with established institutions?'" The Máo Shī says:
"The plums are falling,
their fruits are now three."
Brightens the Eyes, Fragrances the Mouth
The Wúshì Běncǎo says:
"Plum kernels brighten the eyes,
boost qì, and prevent hunger."
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"Plums dried in the sun become là (dried plums).
In soups, stews, and minced dishes,
they can also be held in the mouth to fragrance it."
Dried Là on Yúnshān, Flourishing Splendor by the Luò's Shore
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
"On Yúnshān,
its fruits are dry là."
Guō Pú's annotation says:
"Là
means dried plums."
Pān Yuè's "Xiánjū Fù" says:
"Retiring to live in leisure,
by the shore of the Luò."
It also says:
"Plums, apricots, yù, and dì, and such kinds,
with their flourishing, gorgeous, and ornate adornment.
Their blossoms and fruits shine resplendently,
beyond what words can fully describe."
Harmonizing Broth, Quenching Thirst
The Shàngshū says:
"If you make harmonious broth,
you are the salt and the plum."
The Shì Shuō says:
"When Wèi Wǔdì was on a march and got lost,
the entire army was thirsty.
The Emperor commanded:
'Ahead there is a large plum grove,
abundant with fruit, sweet and sour, which can quench thirst.'"
Jade-like Cassia, Red Jade
Suí dynasty poet Jiāng Zǒng's poem says:
"Fill golden cups, urge the jade-like cassia wine,
beneath the falling plum trees, fitting for song and dance."
Zhōu dynasty poet Yǔ Xìn's poem says:
"Lovely to break off for honored guests,
on a golden plate, offer red jade."
Falling White Silk, Hanging Ice
Liáng dynasty poet's poem says:
"Fluttering light, dancing together with snow,
falling white silk mingles with the icy pond."
Zhōu dynasty poet Yǔ Xìn's poem says:
"The tree's merit: hanging ice falls,
the branch high, outstretched hands feel the cold."
Breaking Off Blossoms, Picking Buds
Lù Kǎi's poem "To Fàn Yè, Presenting a Plum Branch" (Note: The character "yú" in the original seems likely to be "méi").
♂The poem says:
"Breaking off a blossom, I meet a courier,
to send to the man at Lǒngtóu.
South of the river, I have nothing,
so I'll just present a branch of spring."
Suí dynasty poet Jiāng Zǒng's "Luò Méi Shī" says:
"The peach and plum, the beautiful woman, wish to reflect each other,
picking buds, pulling blossoms, they come laughing together."
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Méihuā Fù"
In the palace of layered walls,
within the spiritual park.
Marvelous trees of ten thousand kinds,
common plants of a thousand clusters.
Light divided, shadows mingled,
branches abundant, trunks connecting.
The cold sundial changes its mark,
winter ashes shift in the tube.
All are withered and sere,
color faded, broken by wind.
The year turns, breath renews,
shaking weeds, stirring dust.
The plum blossom is especially early,
uniquely able to recognize spring.
Some, receiving the sun, display gold,
suddenly, mixed with snow, don silver.
They exhale beauty in forests shining on all sides,
unfold glory on roads with five forks.
Now like jade strung together and pearls scattered apart,
and also like ice suspended and hail spread about.
Leaves tender, emerging yet unformed,
branches sprouting hearts, inserted into the old.
Fluttering, half-falling, flying through the air,
fragrance following the wind, traveling far.
Hanging with delicate, drifting gossamer,
mingling with thick, misty morning fog.
Vying with the falling powder from the tower,
vying with the woven plain silk from the loom.
Then, the beautiful ladies in deep chambers,
appearance gentle, heart refined.
They pity the early flowers, startled by the season,
marvel that spring's light dispels the cold.
Lined garments just becoming thin,
gauze sleeves first becoming single.
They break off these fragrant blossoms,
lift these light sleeves.
Some insert them in their hair and ask others,
some give broken branches to each other.
They regret the great emptiness before their hair coils,
dislike the golden hairpins turning old.
Gazing at their shadows on the vermilion steps,
they play with these delicate charms.
Spring windows opened wide,
silk curtains rolled up on four sides.
The spring wind blows the plum, fearing they will all fall,
your humble handmaid, for this, knits her moth-eyebrows.
Holding the flower's color to compare,
constantly worried, fearing to miss the time.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng: "Rhapsody on Plum Blossoms"
Plum blossoms emerge especially early,
Uniquely able to sense spring.
Some, bathed in sunlight, unfold like gold;
Others, touched by snow, don silver.
Petals half-fallen drift through the air,
Their fragrance carried far by the wind.
They catch on endless drifting gossamer threads,
And veil in dense morning mist.
They vie with powder fallen from tower railings,
Outshine the weave upon the loom.
Now blooming bright beside the cliffs,
Now holding buds above the pond.
They cast their hues toward jade steps,
Brush gauze windows with their boughs.
Seven-character verse expresses the Bǎiliáng ode;
Three circulations transmit Wèi Wǔ's marvel.
Then, in deep chambers, lovely ladies,
With gentle looks and joyful hearts,
Pity the early flowers startled by the season,
Marvel that spring's light dispels the cold.
Gazing at their shadows on vermilion stairs,
They toy with these delicate charms.
The spring wind blows the plums, I fear they'll all fall;
Your humble handmaid frowns her moth-eyebrows for this.
Holding flowers to compare their hues,
Constant sorrow fears missing their time.
Chén Xuān: "Rhapsody on Eating Plums"
Cáo Cāo, without a forest, halted thirst;
Fàn Chí, of Jìn, believed and tasted first.
Bestowed a famed fruit of the time,
He cherished the pit and grew solemn.
Once they sang of the sour jujube terrace,
Now they praise the plum's fine sour taste.
Eyes share Cáo Mán's sight of the form,
Unlike Wéi Dàn hearing the thunder.
Throat choked, he thinks of soul-staff;
Depressed near death, he seeks immortal's cup.
Not pitching arrows for Heaven's laughter,
But like the prince's guest, he chuckles.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng: "Poem on Seeking Plum Blossoms in the Snow"
Utterly surprised plum blossoms are late,
All vie to peek amid the snow.
Lower branches, low, can be seen;
High places, distant, hard to know.
All shy, regret bared wrists,
Yield, saying waists are frail.
Surely must still cut colored silk,
Learn to make two or three branches.
Liáng Hé Xùn: "Poem on Early Plum Blossoms"
In the Tù Garden, marking nature's sequence,
Most startling in time are plum blossoms.
Bearing frost, they bloom by the road;
Reflecting snow, they brave the cold to open.
Branches stretch before the Quèyuè Pavilion,
Flowers surround the Língfēng Terrace.
Morning sprinkles tears at Chángmén Palace,
Evening halts the cup at Línqióng.
They should know they'll fall early,
So they chase the start of spring here.
Liáng Wáng Yún: "Matching Vice Censor-in-Chief Kǒng's Poem on Plum Blossoms in the Snow"
Spring waters not yet stirred,
Garden trees already know first.
Flashing light, they dance with snow;
Falling white, they blend with icy ponds.
This spring they vie to bloom in season,
Still branches from years past.
Only my long, haggard face,
Facing the mirror, cannot bear to look.
Liáng Yǔ Jiānwú: "Poem with Vice Director Xiāo on Picking Plum Blossoms"
Window plums begin to bloom at dawn,
Courtyard snow melts as evening falls.
Snapping flowers, pull the short tree;
From dense thickets, enter slender twigs.
Hanging ice drips on jade hands,
Thorns held within brush spring waists.
A distant road, in the end, hard to send;
Fragrance merely lingers on itself.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn: "Poem on Plum Blossoms"
In normal years, mid-twelfth month,
Already feel plum blossoms fade.
Don't believe spring is late this year;
All come to look amid the snow.
Trees shake, hanging ice falls;
Branches high, reaching hands grow cold.
Had I known I'd seek and not find,
Truly regret wearing thin clothes.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng: "Poem on Seeking Plum Blossoms in the Snow"
Utterly surprised plum blossoms are late,
All vie to peek amid the snow.
Lower branches, low, can be seen;
High places, distant, hard to know.
Surely must still cut colored silk,
Learn to make two or three branches.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng: "Poem on Plum Blossoms"
Plums hold early spring trees,
Still face the delayed sunlight.
People harbor memories of years past;
Flowers bloom on last year's branches.
Liáng Bào Quán's Poem
Pitiful, beneath the steps they flutter,
Drifting waves chase the wind, circling back.
Passing blinds, brushing silken curtains;
Winding round windows, falling on dressing tables.
Suddenly gone with slender hands,
Then returned, pinned in hair.
Traveler's heart often sees this;
Sorrowful brows furrow, how can they open?
Liáng Hé Xùn: "Early Plum Blossoms Poem"
In the Tù Garden, marking nature's sequence,
Startling in time are plum blossoms.
Bearing frost, they bloom in the dew;
Reflecting snow, they brave the cold to open.
Branches stretch before the Quèyuè Pavilion,
Flowers spread from the Língfēng Terrace.
Knowing they should fall early like jade,
They chase to the Shànglín Garden.
Jiānwú's Poem
Window plums begin to bloom at dawn,
Courtyard snow melts as evening falls.
Snapping flowers, pull the distant tree;
From dense thickets, enter slender twigs.
Hanging ice drips on jade hands,
Thorns held within brush spring waists.
A distant road, in the end, hard to send to the south;
Fragrance merely fades on its own.
Chén Yīn: "Poem on Appreciating Snowy Plums"
Spring nears, cold though shifts;
Plums unfold, snow still drifts.
Following wind, together they fall;
Shining sun, not both melt away.
Leaves open, following foot's shadow;
Flowers abundant, aid heavy boughs.
Now coming, gradually different from yesterday;
Toward evening, clearly better than dawn.
Had I known I'd seek and not find,
Truly regret wearing thin clothes.
Pomegranate, Part Eleven
The "Pì Cāng" says:
"Pomegranate,
is of the apple family."
The "Bówù Zhì" says:
"Zhāng Qiān returned from his mission to the Western Regions,
and obtained pomegranates, walnuts, and grapes."
Miào Xí's "Sacrificial Rites" says:
"In autumn, offer fruits such as pears, dates, apples, and pomegranates."
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" says:
"During the reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Línyuán in Wǔlíng presented pomegranates,
with six fruits on one stem."
The "Yèzhōng Jì" says:
"In Shí Hǔ's garden were pomegranates,
their fruits as large as bowls,
and their taste not sour."
Zhōu Jǐngshì's "Lúshān Jì" says:
"On the summit of Xiānglú Peak is a large flat rock,
capable of seating several hundred people.
Mountain pomegranates grow hanging there.
In mid-third month they bloom;
their color resembles pomegranate but is lighter,
red blossoms with purple calyxes,
brilliant and lovely."
Red Stamens, Purple Calyx
Xiàhóu Zhàn's "Rhapsody on Pomegranates" says:
"Green calyxes join on green stems,
Red buds emerge from red stamens.
Vividly holding pistils,
Resplendently scattering pearls."
Zhōu Jǐngshì's "Lúshān Jì" says:
"Mountain pomegranates have red blossoms with purple calyxes,
brilliant and lovely."
Six Fruits, Thousand Chambers
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" says:
"Línyuán in Wǔlíng presented pomegranates,
with six fruits on one stem."
Pān Ní's "Rhapsody on Pomegranates" says:
"A thousand chambers share one stem,
Ten seeds alike as one.
Colorful and abundant,
Their light hangs down, their substance shines."
Lù Jī of the Western Jìn Dynasty, "Rhapsody on Melons"
How excellent is the virtue of the melon,
Surpassing all other fruits, none can match its worth.
Abundant in the harmony of pure blessings,
It spreads its flourishing growth across the fields.
Turning away from the fragrant spring as it first bears fruit,
It extends itself as the red summer draws near.
Its long vines stretch forth luxuriantly,
Its elegant form advances in unbroken continuity.
It sends out long tendrils toward Guǎngwǔ,
Brilliantly connecting like mist, linking like clouds.
Moved by the fine season, it hastens its joints,
Bathed in gracious dew, it grows ever fresher.
As for their profuse spread, interwoven and mixed,
Lush and graceful, swaying gently.
Reaching from there to here,
They pass by one another in turn.
Basking in the bright sun, they glisten and shine,
Fanned by the gentle breeze, rippling like waves.
There are creeping vines that extend far and wide,
Resembling the pepper plant in their great numbers.
Golden tendrils sprout from elegant tips,
Jade-like fruits form on supple branches.
Sheltered by emerald shadows, they nurture themselves,
Adorning long stems, scattered like stars.
Now, as for their varieties and kinds,
There are guālóu, dìngtáo.
Huángpián, báibó,
Jīnwén, mìtǒng.
Xiǎoqīng, dàbān,
Xuángàn, sùwǎn,
Líshǒu, hǔfán.
Dōnglíng comes from the Qín valley,
Guìsuǐ arises from the Wū Mountains.
Five colors compare to images,
Different shapes, unusual forms.
Some have plain exteriors yet reveal beauty within,
Some have kind hearts but homely faces.
Some display patterns embracing green,
Some are clad in white yet harbor crimson.
Their fragrance, whether strong or subtle, is equally present,
Their bodies, whether long or short, are invariably round.
Fù Xuán of Jìn, "Rhapsody on Melons"
Prepare the soil and sow the seeds below,
Broadcast them with proper method.
Responding to fate and awaiting the season,
They break the husk and slowly emerge.
Thus day by day and month by month they progress,
Once the mother plant forms, it coils and spreads.
Then come the dense leaves, lush and abundant,
Intertwining with the winding, long stems.
They display a pure hue of jade-green,
Golden blossoms gleam with bright clarity.
Nurtured by human effort,
Cultivated by the six breaths.
Yellow surpassing golden silk,
Green rivaling contained emerald.
Though the líshǒu is sweet and delicious,
It cannot match the wondrous grandeur of Dōnglíng.
Long have there been mìtǒng,
And qīng guālóu.
Fine flavors overflow the mouth,
Fresh kinds have few peers.
In the moment of a single bite,
One may shake one's head up to three times.
Select the finest from fragrant gardens,
Repeatedly choose their treasures.
Cleave them with a Wú knife,
Present them on a vermilion plate.
Split and opened down the middle,
Though divided, they seem whole.
Their substance combines three flavors,
Their aroma rivals fragrant orchids.
They grow sweeter when chilled,
Gladdening the spirit, refreshing and dispelling cares.
Fine flesh, dense inner part,
Much pulp, few segments.
Rich essence, uniquely superb,
Eating them, one never tires.
Pine, Part Thirteen
The Shuōwén says:
"Sōng,
a tree.
From the radical mù (木), with gōng (公) indicating sound.
In ancient script, róng (榕),
from the radical mù (木), with róng (容) indicating sound."
The Shàngshū says:
"Qīngzhōu
tributes silk and hemp from the Dài valleys,
lead, pine, and strange stones."
Guō's Xuánzhōng Jì says:
"Pine resin sinks into the earth,
after a thousand years becomes poria cocos."
Liú Xiàng's Shénxiān Zhuàn says:
"Yǔ Wòquán loved to eat pine nuts,
could fly through the air,
swift as a galloping horse.
He offered pine seeds to Yáo,
but Yáo could not ingest them.
Sōng means 'bestowal,'
those who in that time ingested them
all lived to three hundred years."
The Sōngshān Jì says:
"Sōnggāo Mountain has great pine trees,
some a hundred years old,
some a thousand.
Their essence transforms into green oxen,
or into crouching turtles;
gathering and eating their fruit grants longevity."
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Among pine trees three thousand years old,
their bark contains accumulated resin,
shaped like a dragon,
called 'flying node fungus.'"
Also, the Yùcè Jì says:
"A thousand-year-old pine tree,
its sides spread out,
its topmost twigs do not grow tall.
Gazing at it from afar,
it looks like a prostrate canopy,
and within it are creatures.
Some like green oxen,
some like green dogs,
some like humans,
all living ten thousand years."
The Wángyìzǐ says:
"Among trees are the fúsāng, pine, and cypress,
all receiving the purest pneuma,
different from other kinds."
The Guǎngzhì says:
"Seeds of an old pine a thousand years old,
yellow-white in color,
taste like chestnuts,
edible."
The Běncǎo says:
"Pine resin comes from Lǒngxī;
the kind like glue is good.
Pine resin is also called pine fat,
bitter and warm in flavor;
long-term consumption lightens the body and prolongs life."
Perching Phoenixes Tethered Horses
Xiè Chéng's Hòuhànshū says:
"Fāng Chǔ, styled Shèngmíng,
was from Dānyáng.
Appointed as a Langzhōng,
he encountered his mother's mourning,
abandoned his post to perform the rites.
Carrying earth, he built a burial mound,
planted over a thousand pines, cypresses, and rare trees.
Phoenixes perched upon them,
white rabbits roamed below."
Liú Kūn's "Fúfēng Poem" says:
"Tethered the horse beneath the tall pine,
rested the saddle atop the high peak.
Fierce, fierce, the mournful wind arises,
cold, cold, the mountain stream flows."
Chowrie Dragon Shape
Zhōu Jǐngshì's Lúshān Jì says:
"North of the Shímén cliff
is the pine forest,
with several hundred pine trees,
all large enough to embrace,
nearly twenty zhàng tall.
They cluster together on the sheer cliff,
facing south over the Shímén stream.
Looking up from within the stream,
they appear distinct, like paired chowries.
From Xúnyáng looking toward the gathering,
they are clearly visible."
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"In the bark of pine trees is resin,
shaped like a dragon."
Prostrate Canopy Flying Node
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"The Yùcè Jì says:
'A thousand-year-old pine is like a prostrate canopy.'"
Also says:
"In the bark of pine trees is accumulated resin,
called 'flying node fungus.'"
Pure Blossoms Elegant Leaves
Yǔ Sùzhī's "Pine Eulogy" says:
"Flowing moisture, flying sap,
settled essence, deeply congealed.
Pure blossoms hold fragrance,
reaching up to brush the white snow."
Zuǒ Jiūpín's "Rhapsody on Pine and Cypress" says:
"Spread the slender stems, lush and dense,
display the elegant leaves, verdant and green."
"Rhapsody on Pine and Cypress" by Zuǒ Jiǔpín of the Western Jìn Dynasty
How wondrous the lushness of this tree,
Rooted upon the steep, towering peak.
Cloaked by the winding, dark-hued stream,
Facing the clear water's pure white waves.
Its tall trunk rises straight and slender,
Gathering fragrant, verdant leaves and blossoms.
Spreading its delicate stems in dense profusion,
Displaying elegant leaves of lush green.
Arrayed with emerald fruits, abundant and full,
Their subtle fragrance lingers, ever sweet.
In rich, luxuriant growth, yet gracefully parted,
Its aura is solemn, pure, and cool.
Answering the long wind, its branches sing,
Like the lingering notes of silk and bamboo strings.
Endowed with nature's steadfast strength,
It endures harsh winter without withering.
Though hoarfrost congeals, its stem stands firm,
Nearing spring's youth, it blooms in splendor.
Like a nobleman adapting to the seasons,
Or a true man upholding integrity.
Chìsōng wandered beneath it and attained the Way,
Wén Bīn ate its fruit and gained long life.
Poets sing of its lush glory,
Matching the Southern Mountain in eternal peace.
"Poem on the Courtyard Cypress" by Wèi Shōu of the Northern Qí Dynasty
The ancient pine resembles a tilted canopy,
The new cypress mimics a censer peak.
Defying the cold, its emerald hue remains unyielding,
Greeting the warmth, its green grows even richer.
Chewing its leaves lightens the heavy body,
Tasting its fruit transforms the aged visage.
It shall make the musk deer of the central terrace,
Leave the mountain yet still follow.
Chapter Fifteen: Scholar Tree
The Chūnqiū Shuōtící states:
"The scholar tree
is the essence of the Void Star."
The Yuánmìngbāo states:
"To plant a scholar tree and hold court beneath it
is because 'scholar' (huái) means 'to return' (guī),
where sentiment is seen returning to substance."
The Ěryǎ states:
"The leaves of the guardian scholar tree
close by day and open by night.
The scholar tree has large, dark leaves."
Guō Pú comments:
"The guardian scholar tree
closes its leaves by day and spreads them open at night."
Sūn Yán states:
"'Close' means to fold together,
'open' means to spread out."
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"An old scholar tree may produce fire,
long-stagnant blood becomes will-o'-the-wisp.
People find it unremarkable."
When blood-essence lies upon the ground,
exposed for a hundred days,
it becomes will-o'-the-wisp.
The Guǎngzhì states:
"Scholar tree wood comes in several kinds: green, yellow, white, and black."

"The scholar tree

If one gathers its seeds on the tenth day of the tenth month and consumes them,

Intertwined Branches, One Heart; A Thousand Acres at the Tips
Zhì Yú's "Eulogy on Intertwined Branches" states:
"Within the precincts of the Eastern Palace's Zhèngdé Hall,

Two trunks, one heart,
to multiply the root and base."
Fù Xuǎn's "Rhapsody on the Scholar Tree" states:
"Leaf upon leaf, luxuriant and well-spaced,

Pine and ivy cling as parasites,
densely connecting to the outermost tips.
Stretching across a thousand acres,
lush, dense, and shadowy."
Closed by Day, Open by Night; Rabbit Eyes and Mouse Ears
The Ěryǎ states:
"The leaves of the guardian scholar tree

Guō Pú comments:
"The guardian scholar tree closes its leaves by day and spreads them open at night.
East of the River there is a scholar tree

commonly named 'Join-at-Dusk,'

The principle is the same."
Sūn Yán comments:
"'Close' means to fold together,
'open' means to spread out."
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"When the scholar tree grows,
by the fifth day of late spring it has 'rabbit eyes,'

"Rhapsody on the Scholar Tree" by Cáo Zhí of the Wèi Dynasty
I admire the splendid beauty of this fine tree,
Beloved and prized by the supreme sovereign.
Leaning against the ornate halls of Wénchāng Palace,
It stands tall and dense before the main gate.
I gaze upon its vermilion rafters shaking their twigs,
Rooted firmly by the patterned steps.
Spreading a deep, broad shade to cover all,
Like an enlightened ruler bestowing grace.
"Rhapsody on the Scholar Tree" by Wáng Càn of the Wèi Dynasty
This wondrous tree in the central hall,
Endowed with nature's fine qualities.
Raised from the fields and planted here,
It casts glorious light upon the courtyard steps.
Since its foundation lies in palace and ministry,
Its roots are planted deep and vast.
Birds wish to roost and fold their wings here,
Men look to its shelter and open their robes.
"Rhapsody on the Scholar Tree" by Zhì Yú of the Jìn Dynasty
Now observe its flourishing form,
Examine where it dwells.
Full and luxuriant, thick with foliage,
Lush, dense, and well-spaced.
It delights the paired orioles that flit about,
And pleases the solitary osprey, king of hawks.
In spring, birds that teach farming perch here,
In summer, crows that feed their parents rest.
"Rhapsody on the Scholar Tree" by Wáng Jì of the Jìn Dynasty
When the dragon ascends the southern path,
And fire gathers at high noon,
This tree expands its lush verdure,
Creating coolness in the silent heat.
Its branches stir, summoning the wind,
Its leaves shake, bringing forth the cool.
Its brightness surpasses the eight portals,
Its deep shade exceeds the nine chambers.
"Poem on the Scholar Tree" by Fán Qīn of the Wèi Dynasty
The fine tree puts forth emerald leaves,
Arrayed beside the twin palace gates.
Graceful, they sway with the wind,
Their soft hues scattering in dazzling array.
Chapter Sixteen: Paulownia
The Shī Yì Shū states:

Abundant,
describes a flourishing appearance.

róng,

Specially grown at Yìyáng, flourishing beside Dòngtíng.

Green peaks sprout trunks, dark streams take root.

Cuī Qí's Qī Juān states:

Phoenix soars, simurgh gathers.
Fù Xián's Wútóng Fù states:
"Halting the noble's dragon carriage,

Gazing upon the abundant flowers and fruits,

Liú Yìgōng's Huálín Sì Ruì Tóngshù Gānlù Zàn states:

Three trees, one leaf.

"In the Huálín Garden, three trees of green and white tóng."

Solitary growth, half-dead.
"Solitary growth" reference seen in the note for "green peaks sprout trunks."

"The tóng of Lóngmén,

In winter, whipped by fierce winds, sleet, and flying snow,
in summer, stirred by thunderclaps and lightning bolts."
Stops the yuānchú, awaits the luánzhuó.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"The yuānchú sets off from the South Sea and flies to the North Sea,
it will not perch except on the wútóng,
it will not eat except on bamboo seeds."
Sīmǎ Biāo's poem "To Shān Jùyuán" states:
"Placing myself in solitude and peril,

its leaning branches await the luánzhuó."
Wútóng Fù by Xiāo Zǐliáng of Southern Qí
Planting yītóng in the vast garden,
lamenting how swiftly it becomes a forest.
Relying on layered pillars to burst into beauty,
facing the flat terrace to form shade.
Then sprouting leaves at dew's beginning,
also bearing fruit as stars sink.
Raising slender twigs to adorn the scenery,
containing clear breeze to scatter sound.
Eliciting elegant chants from distant past,
flowing pure appreciation in the present.
Surely only after phoenix and simurgh gather,
how could swallows and sparrows approach?
Not only by the side of Chǔ palaces,
nor solely on the peaks of Yì Shān.
Far beyond the reach of common weeds,
forever paired with the immortal qín in the Way.
Tóngshù Fù by Liú Yìgōng
This numinous timber of the wútóng,
luxuriant in sparse woods, outstanding in beauty.
Dark roots penetrate through to hidden springs,
dense leaves hang lush, increasing in abundance.
Erecting tall trunks,
shading the morning sun.
Summoning flying simurghs,
calling phoenixes.
Sweet mists sprinkle moisture on its stems,
clear breezes flow gently through its branches.
Red clouds blaze gloriously above it,
white waters soak and moisten its banks.
Poem on Wútóng from Visiting the Eastern Hall by Xiè Tiǎo of Southern Qí
Lonely tóng outside the north window,
tall branches over a hundred zhàng high.
Leaves growing so graceful,
leaves falling even more spreading.
Without flowers, again without fruit,
with what to gift the parting dweller?
Cut into guī and zhāng tablets,
enough to command the Cānxū constellation.
Poem on the Lonely Tóng by Shěn Yuē of Liáng
When the Lóngmén tóng reaches a hundred chǐ,
parting clouds, standing alone in youth.
Dividing roots to shade the jade pool,
waiting for the tall simurgh to gather.
Jointly Composed Rhyming Poem on the Courtyard Tóng by Wú Jūn of Liáng
Lóngmén has a marvelous jiǎ tree,
calling itself a wútóng branch.
Flowers radiant, fruits遮掩映,
fine leaves able to spread apart.
Not descending for the Zhōu king's sons,
vainly awaiting the shift of years and seasons.
Sudden harsh winds fiercely intertwine,
thus causing none to know it.
Poem on the Tóng by Wèi Yànshēn of Suí
Not seeking to be cut for making a sè,
what use in carving into a guī tablet?
Wishing to be placed in the splendid courtyard,
branches spread, awaiting the phoenix to perch.
Willow, seventeenth.

yí
pronounced 'shí tí fǎn'.

Flowing Silk, Flying Catkins

Ninefold, Ten Arm-Spans

Red Leaves, Green Twigs
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīnzhù states:
"The bulrush willow grows by the water,

Chén Lín's "Liǔ Fù" says:

Dragon Scales, Phoenix Wings

Liú Yìqìng's Shìshuō says:
"Duke Huán campaigned to Jīnchéng,
saw the willows he planted when in Lángyé,

Lush Thoroughfares, Shading Clear Pools

Later Hàn Wáng Càn's "Liǔ Fù"
Beholding this tree's lush abundance,
so graceful and slender,
branches spreading wide and extending far,
stems dense and soaring high.
Human emotions stirred by old things,
the heart melancholy, increasing cares.
Walking, letting the eyes roam and gaze afar,
seeing the former site of city walls and ramparts.
Awakening to the words of non-birth,
truly pondering hardship and harboring fear.
Praising the sweet pear tree not being felled,
fearing to dare burden this tree.
If keeping distance and withdrawing from it,
how could the carriage be slow and not frequent?
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Liǔ Fù"
O, magnificent tree of the Central Kingdom,
your rare beauty is truly precious.
Receiving the generous bestowal of divine spirits,
you exist in accordance with Creation.
The four seasons advance in succession,
leaving winter and entering spring.
When other plants have not yet stirred,
you first sprout and lead the season.
As abundant virtue shifts and moves southward,
the Star Bird aligns and governs the division.
Responding to the prosperous time, you flourish and multiply,
raising your emerald leaves, pure green.
Tall trunks arching, pointing like rainbows,
soft branches supple, trailing like sashes.
Above, spreading and luxuriantly scattered,
below, interlocking like dragon scales.
Then, as the glorious sun reaches Chúnshǒu,
the auspicious wind fans, increasing warmth.
Abundant shade spreads wide and covers all,
your person kind and affable, never weary.
Teams of four horses gaze and tilt their canopies,
travelers look up and turn their regard.
Upholding utmost virtue without boasting,
how could you scorn the lowly and choose the base?
Harboring vital essence and spirit, you live attached,
preserving your fine form, ample and full.
Even a foot-long cutting can be planted and grow,
truly enduring and steadfast, worthy of praise.

with a pheasant's head and a snake's body.
It had not yet fully transformed.
This is also an instance of bamboo turning into a snake and the snake turning into a pheasant."
Dài Kǎizhī's "Treatise on Bamboo" states:
"Chicken neck bamboo
resembles bamboo but is finer."
Lush and Dense, Elegant and Graceful
Wáng Biāozhī's "Rhapsody on Mǐnzhōng" states:
"As for bamboo, there are light-yellow sheaths and white shoots,
vermilion culms and green tubes.
They cluster densely on the hills and mounds,
spreading luxuriantly across the plains and marshes."
Méi Chéng's "Rhapsody on the Rabbit Garden of the King of Liáng" states:
"Tall bamboos, elegant and graceful, flank the pond's waters."
Transforming Snake, Flying Magpie
The "transforming snake" matter is seen in the note under "Pheasant Head."
"Mòzǐ" states:
"Gōngshūzǐ carved bamboo and wood to make a magpie.
When the magpie was completed, it flew,
not descending for three days.
He considered himself ingenious."
Leaf as Sandal, Bark as Cap
Dài Kǎizhī's "Treatise on Bamboo" states:
"Mèi bamboo,
in the region between the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers, is called gān.
It is over a foot in size,
with leaves as large as sandals,
which can be used to thatch boats."
"The Book of Hàn" states:
"When Gāozǔ was a village head,
he made a cap from bamboo shoot bark."
Yìng Shào's commentary states:
"He used the bark of newly sprouted bamboo to make a cap,
which is the present-day magpie-tail cap."
Vermilion Writing, Green Slips
"Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Zhì Bó led Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào.
Xiāngzǐ fled to Jìnyáng.
Yuán Guò arrived later
and at Wángzé saw three men.
They were visible from the waist up,
but not from the waist down.
They gave Yuán Guò two sections of bamboo,
entreating him, saying:
'Take this for me and give it to Zhào Wúxù.'
Yuán Guò reported to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ fasted for three days,
then personally split the bamboo.
Inside was vermilion writing that said:
'I am the celestial official Yáng Hóu of Mount Huòtài.'"
Yìng Shào's "Comprehensive Meaning of Customs" states:
"After killing the green, it can be written on and copied.
Respectfully, according to Liú Xiàng's 'Separate Records':
Killing the green means simply using green bamboo slips to write on.'"
Ten Fathoms, Hundred Feet
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "Records of the Southern Yue" states:
"Sòngchāng County has thorny bamboo,
ten fathoms long,
as large as a jar.
Even the shorter ones are sixty to seventy feet.
It forms dense bamboo thickets with thin leaves.
Below are hook-like thorns,
some at the ends of the branches like sharp needles."
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Classic of Divine Wonders" states:
"In the southern wilderness,
there is pèi bamboo.
It is a hundred zhang long,
with a circumference of two zhang, five or six feet.
Its wall is eight or nine inches thick,
and it can be used to make boats."
Shading Deep Valleys, Sweeping Round Pools
Cáo Pí's "Rhapsody on the Xiāng Region" states:
"Its bamboos include yúndāng and báiwū,
solid-hearted and deep-blue clans.
They flourish along dark islets,
their kindred dense in winding corners.
Lush and verdant on hillocks,
they shade and reach into deep valleys."
Zhèng Jìzhī's "Records of Dōngyáng" states:
"Mount Kūn is ten lǐ from Mount Wúchéng.
Its peaks and ridges are lofty and steep,
often rising elegantly above the clouds."
The elders transmit a tale:
"On the ridge is a round pool,
with both fish and turtles.
Beside the pool grows extremely large bamboo.
When the wind comes, it bends and sweeps the ground,
always clean as if swept by human hands."
Rhapsody on Tall Bamboo by Jiǎnwén Emperor of Liáng
There are graceful and lush young bamboos,
growing in clusters by the river.
The beauty of yùrùn and táozhī bamboos,
the names of yúcháng and yúnmǔ bamboos.
Sunlight shines, flowers sway;
wind stirs, branches lightly dance.
Prince Chén rejoices in the past;
the small hall stands with its axis.
Now bidding farewell to an old friend,
I also compose a rhapsody on tall bamboo.
Admiring the guest's unique excellence,
I look upon myself and feel ashamed.
Rhapsody on Cliffside Shoots by Gù Yěwáng of Chén
The Odes sing of the Qí River's waters;
the "Lí Sāo" praises the riverbanks.
The cliff pities the stone-sweeping bamboo;
the spirit values the altar-sweeping bamboo.
It has welcomed the singing phoenix,
and also frolicked with the soaring simurgh.
It enters the moonlit night of fan-painted walls,
reflected in the turbulent rapids of Yuán and Lǐ.
It carries the crisp clarity of the autumn wind,
mingled with the jade-like elegance of lush bamboo.
It accompanies joyous feasts on autumn nights,
equal in steadfast virtue to the winter's cold.
Rhapsody on Língqiū Bamboo by Jiāng Yān of Liáng
I climb the rugged green cliffs,
enter the resplendent vermilion palace.
I gaze upon the winding curves of the Qǔjiāng River,
look toward the verdant green of the southern mountains.
Spring blossoms flourish richly on the stone banks;
summer hues glow red on the sandy shores.
Far-reaching, they connect to purple forests and secret wilds;
nearby, they encircle jade gardens and forbidden borders.
Here, green bamboos surround the peaks,
emerald groves stretch across the ridges.
Their dark-green hues are varied,
their deep-blue shadows dazzling.
Above, serene and leisurely they remain;
below, gentle and tranquil they stand.
Veiled in the crimson aura of rosy clouds,
shaded by the white light of the bright sun.
Thus, neither flower nor medicinal herb,
neither fragrant nor richly scented.
Yet precious, surpassing divine herbs;
treasured, exceeding sacred trees.
Flanking the pond waters, elegant and graceful;
encircling the garden pond, tall and upright.
Unaffected by frost, they do not wither;
in midsummer's heat, they grow more solemn.
Often renowned throughout Huá and the Róng tribes,
they excel uniquely on water and land.
Moreover, there are the Morning Cloud Lodge,
the Walking Rain Palace,
windows lofty and tinged with green,
doors hesitating, overlooking the void.
Ornate lattices open wide, holding back the sun;
vermilion curtains drawn, retaining the breeze.
Covered by the deep lushness of jùnlù bamboo,
intertwined with the misty density of xiǎodàng bamboo.
Some grow to the left of the zhīquè palace,
some are planted east of the lùhán palace.
These are all places where golden carriages come and go,
where jade chariots circulate and pass through.
“Rhapsody on Bamboo Flowers” by Xiāo Dàhuán of the Suí Dynasty
Alas, the clarity of spring’s hues,
Reflects the sunlit stream, pure and limpid.
Flowers twine round trees, vying in laughter;
Birds fill the wilds, all singing together.
On crumbling banks, duckweed merges;
Along slanting paths, grasses twine.
Warm branches are thick with catkins,
And silken threads lie across the heated paths.
Roaming bees gather to carry pollen,
Sporting butterflies flit, adorned with petals.
The cuckoo is about to cry, as the fragrant herbs rest;
Wild geese begin to depart, as reeds sprout.
There are also lush, embroidered bamboos,
Graceful and slender, with green stems.
Their pale branches bear the dew,
And their light-yellow sheaths welcome the wind.
Following the Hàn calendar’s seasons,
The moonlit cassia stands amid the grove.
At times, their shadows ripple in the pleasure pond,
Their fame lingers in the auspicious palace.
They learn to be the responding dragon in Gé River’s waters,
And host the phoenix in the square paulownia.
The Seven Worthies of Luòyáng,
The two maidens by the Xiāng River’s banks.
They tilt their emerald canopies, hesitating,
And drift in lotus boats, at ease.
Unrestrained, they pride themselves;
Charming, they laugh and speak.
Caressing tender shoots, they seem to weep;
Gazing at steadfast bamboo, they order wine to be poured.
“Poem on Bamboo” by Emperor Táng Tàizōng, the Literary Emperor
Upright branches screen the winding steps,
Jade-green leaves bear the cold frost.
Sweeping the window, they part the dragon’s shadow;
Facing the pond, they await the phoenix’s flight.
“Poem on Bamboo” by Emperor Liáng Xiàoyuán
From Xiègǔ, new pipes are drawn,
In Qí Garden, joints are renewed.
Becoming a dragon, they return to Gé River;
As horses, they head toward Bīngzhōu.
Kē Pavilion overlooks the sheer ravine,
Táozhī bamboos flank the slender stream.
Their crowns mimic the lotus’s form,
Their flowers invite the majestic phoenix to roam.
If the King of Qióng were to present them,
Zhāng Qiān should be enfeoffed as a marquis.
“Ode to Bamboo” by Liú Xiàoxiān of the Liáng Dynasty
Bamboo grows in the desolate wilds,
Brushing the clouds, rising a hundred xún high.
No one values its lofty integrity,
In vain, it embraces its steadfast heart.
Ashamed to be stained by the Xiāng consorts’ tears,
Too humble to enter the palace’s zither.
Who can fashion a long flute?
Then it shall produce a dragon’s roar.
“Ode to Bamboo” by Xiāo Fàng of the Northern Qí
Branches swaying in the wind grow delicate,
Shadows guarding against dew grow denser.
Having welcomed the phoenix from Dānxuè,
They also become the dragon of Gé Slope.
“Poem on Bamboo at a Banquet” by Yīn Kēng of the Chén Dynasty
A cluster of bamboo flanking the pond,
Verdant and unafraid of the cold.
Its leaves brew Yíchéng wine,
Its skin is cut for Xuē County hats.
The Xiāng River dyes parting tears,
Héng Ridge brushes immortal altars.
To see its lush, splendid hues,
One should come to the Rabbit Garden.
“Poem on the Emerald Bamboo in the Mountains” by Zhāng Zhèngjiàn of the Chén Dynasty
Tall bamboo hangs over the cliffs,
The wind here differs from that by the pond.
In layered ravines, high integrity hides;
In dense groves, sturdy branches conceal themselves. Clouds form, but the dragon has not yet ascended;
Flowers fall, as the phoenix prepares to move.
Do not speak of dwelling in Xiègǔ Valley,
Líng Lún no longer plays his flute.
“Poem on Bamboo Flanking the Pond” by Hè Xiū of the Chén Dynasty
Green bamboo shadows lie uneven,
Graceful, they curve along the pond.
Meeting autumn, their leaves do not fall;
Enduring winter, their color does not fade.
The wind brings melody to the evening path,
Gathering phoenixes stir the spring branches.
What delights the recluse of high virtue,
Is not waiting for Líng Lún’s flute.
“Poem on Bamboo by the Pond” by Yú Shìnán of the Táng Dynasty
Jade-green, brushing the clouds in substance,
Dangling splendor reflects in the clear pond.
Waves ripple with wind-blown shadows,
Flowing, swaying branches guard against dew.
Dragon scales shimmer in Xiègǔ Valley,
Phoenix wings brush the continuous ripples.
To know its nature that defies winter,
Only the year’s cold can tell.
Lion, First
According to Shuōwén, it says:
“Xiāo,
is the lion.”
Xiāo is pronounced with the fanqiè hū jiāo.
Ěryǎ says:
“Suānní is like a zhàn māo,
it eats tigers and leopards.”
Guō Pú notes:
“That is the lion.
Suān is pronounced suān,
ní is pronounced ní,
zhàn is pronounced with the fanqiè shì jiān.”
Hànshū·Xīyù Zhuàn says:
“There is a lion resembling a tiger,
pure yellow,
with tail-tip hair as large as a dǒu.”
Sīmǎ Biāo’s Xù Hànshū:
“In the first year of the Héping era,
the Ānxī Kingdom sent an envoy to present a lion and fúzhī,
shaped like a qílín but without horns.”
Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn says:
“Suānní can run five hundred lǐ a day.”
Shízhōu Jì says:
“Jùkū Zhōu is located in the western sea at the shēn-wèi position,
each side measuring three thousand lǐ,
connecting to Kūnlún to the north by twenty-six lǐ.
There are lions, bìxié, záochǐ, tiānlù, and beasts with long teeth, bronze heads, and iron foreheads.”
Subduing the Fox Attacking the Elephant
Zhāng Huá’s Bówùzhì says:
“Cáo Cāo campaigned against Mòdú,
passed through Báiláng Shān,
encountered a lion,
ordered men to fight it,
causing many casualties.
Then a creature emerged from the forest,
like a fox,
and leaped onto the yoke of the imperial carriage.
As the lion approached,
it jumped onto the lion’s head,
and the lion submitted, not daring to rise.
Thus, they killed it.
Upon returning with the lion,
before reaching forty lǐ,
all chickens and dogs ceased crowing and barking.”
Sòng Bǐng’s “Preface to the Painting of a Lion Attacking an Elephant” says:
“Liáng Bóyù recounted from the monk Shì Sēngjí:
‘Once, traveling from Tiānzhú,
heading toward Dàqín,
suddenly heard from dozens of lǐ away a roaring, earth-shaking clamor,
startling heaven and terrifying earth.
Shortly after,
saw all beasts fleeing in haste,
stampeding until their tracks vanished,
and four giant elephants arrived suddenly.
They used their trunks to scoop mud, coating themselves several chǐ thick,
and repeatedly snorted while standing at the corners.
Suddenly, three lions attacked the elephants,
blood flowing like a gushing spring,
giant trees and grass flattened.’ ”
Eating Leopards Resembling the Qílín
Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn says:
“Suānní can run five hundred lǐ a day.”
Guō Pú notes:
“That is the lion,
it eats tigers and leopards.”
Sīmǎ Biāo’s Xù Hànshū says:
“The Tiáozhī Kingdom produces lions and rhinoceroses.
In the first year of the Zhānghé era of Emperor Zhāng,
the Ānxī Kingdom sent an envoy to present a lion and fúzhī,
shaped like a qílín but only without horns.”
Sparse Fur Like a Zhàn Tail Large as a Dǒu
Ěryǎ says:
“Suānní is like a zhàn māo,
it eats tigers and leopards,
with sparse fur.”
Hànshū·Xīyù Zhuàn says:
“The Wūyì Kingdom has lions,
resembling tigers,
pure yellow,
with tail-tip hair as large as a dǒu.”
Chéng Jìngzé's Dream and the Defeat of the Línyì Army
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's "History of the Qí" states:
"Wáng Jìngzé's mother was a witch.
Jìngzé was born with a purple birthmark,
and she said to others:
'This child has the physiognomy of drums and horns.'
When Jìngzé grew older,
he had nipples several inches long under each armpit,
and he dreamed of riding a five-colored lion."
Later, he attained the positions of Grand Commandant and Duke of Xúnyáng."
Shěn Yuē's "History of the Sòng" states:
"Zōng Què accompanied Tán Hézhī on the campaign against Línyì.
They crossed seas and traversed mountains,
finally entering Xiàngpǔ.
The King of Línyì, Fàn Yángmài, brought his entire nation to resist them,
blocking the waterways to prevent their crossing.
He armored his elephants fully,
forming an endless line before and behind.
Què, knowing that foreign lands had lions,
whose majesty subdued all beasts,
had their likeness fashioned,
to confront the elephants.
The elephants indeed panicked and fled,
throwing the enemy ranks into chaos.
Què then, along with the cavalry commander Mǎ Tōng, fiercely crossed the channel directly,
and the infantry followed,
joining in a spirited attack.
Yángmài fled in disarray,
his forces scattering all at once,
and thus they conquered Línyì."
Yú Shìnán's "Rhapsody on the Lion"
Only when the August King governs the age,
does he receive Heaven's mandate and model himself on its greatness.
He spreads the ultimate Way throughout the realm,
and extends benevolent influence beyond the seas.
He connects with phoenix nests through script and carriage tracks,
and adorns dragon courts with caps and sashes.
Barbarian tongues are silenced in the foreign quarters,
and local treasures are presented at the royal assembly.
From the remote corners of the earth,
and the distant lands beyond the peaks,
comes a divine beast from the far-off regions,
arriving through repeated translation to be presented.
As for its form,
its sinews and bones are intertwined,
a posture and build most extraordinary.
Broad-chested with a long tail,
strong bristles and soft down.
Hooked claws and saw-like teeth,
concealing sharpness and storing ferocity.
Ears laid back, paws coiled,
awaiting an opening, borrowing momentum.
And when it bristles its mane and licks its lips,
it comes and goes with sudden swiftness.
Eyes glaring like lightning,
voice roaring like thunder.
It pulls apart tigers, devours pí beasts,
splits rhinoceroses, divides elephants.
It crushes suí sì beasts between jaw and palate,
and subdues the Bā snake within its grasp.
Where it treads, forests and foothills are destroyed;
where it roars, rivers and lakes are shaken.
It tames its fierce spirit with a devoted heart,
and thus, moved by virtue, cleaves to benevolence.
Joining the hundred beasts in guided dance,
it comes, tamed, among the six domestic animals.
This shows creatures lack fixed nature,
but follow transformation as if by spirit.
Like scales and feathers changing substance in the Huái Sea,
or metal and tin becoming vessels on the potter's wheel.
At this time,
the myriad people gaze with joy,
all officials sigh in praise.
They delight in the far-reaching spread of sound and teaching,
and belong to this brilliance at its dawn.
I, your servant, recording with brush, am honored by fortune,
to have set eyes upon this wondrous spectacle.
In accord with civil virtue, it presents an auspicious sign,
and thus I compile this in the Eastern Library."
Elephant, Part Two
"The Ěryǎ" says:
"Among the fine things of the south,
are the rhinoceroses and elephants of Liáng Mountain."
"The Shuōwén" says:
"The elephant has a long nose and tusks.
It is a great beast of Nányuè,
giving birth once every three years.
The elephant's body has four legs and is large."
"The Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū" says:
"The scattered light of the pivot becomes the elephant."
"The Records of Dàyuān" says:
"The people of Shéndú country ride elephants into battle."
"The Wú Lù Dìlǐzhì" says:
"Páng County in Jiǔzhēn Commandery has many elephants.
They live in the mountains,
and are abundant within the commandery and in Rìnán."
"The Praise of the Jìn Dukes" says:
"During the Jìn, Nányuè presented a tame elephant.
It was kept in a marshy meadow,
and a carriage was made for it.
Several dozen musicians from the Yellow Gate
had the Yuè people ride it.
At every grand assembly on the first morning of the year,
it would enter to fill the courtyard.
When the Emperor traveled, the elephant carriage would lead the way,
to test the bridges.
Later, the elephant struck and killed a man with its trunk.
The officials prayed over it and then killed the elephant.
It hung its trunk and wept,
blood flowing on the ground, not daring to move.
Afterwards, the court deliberated and decided elephants were of no practical use,
and sent them all back to Yuè."
Wàn Zhèn's "Nánzhōu Yìwùzhì" says:
"Common legend says the elephant's tusks shed yearly,
and it still cherishes them.
It digs the earth and hides them.
If a person wants to take them,
they must make false tusks and secretly go to exchange them.
If the elephant realizes, it will not hide them in the old place.
The trunk serves the mouth,
looking at the head, it seems like a tail."
"The Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"Among delicious meats,
is the tender meat of the hairy elephant."
Gāo Yòu says:
"The meat of the hairy elephant is delicious."
Zhāng Huá's "Bówùzhì" says:
"In the Southern Sea were four elephants,
each with a mate.
When one female died,
for over a hundred days,
the male covered himself with mud,
and alone refrained from drinking wine or eating meat.
When the local official asked the reason,
he shed tears as if in mourning."
Hiding Tusks and Employing the Trunk
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "Nányuèzhì" says:
"Elephant tusks are over ten feet long.
When they shed their tusks, they hide them deeply.
If one carves wood to replace them, one can obtain them.
Otherwise,
even if one exhausts the owner,
one must obtain them to stop."
Wàn Zhèn's "Nánzhōu Yìwùzhì" says:
"The elephant as a beast
has a most peculiar form.
Its body is several times that of an ox.
Its eyes are no larger than a pig's.
The trunk serves the mouth,
looking at the head, it seems like a tail.
Docile and obedient to instruction,
it kneels upon hearing words.
Its plain tusks are jade-white,
praised in records and texts.
It bears heavy loads over great distances,
walking like a moving hill."
Weeping for its Young and Mourning its Mate
Jiǎngzǐ's "Wànjī Lùn" says:
"When Zhuāng Zhōu's wife died, he sang and said:
'Those who comprehend life and fate,
proceed from the lowly to the noble.
They do not grieve over death and life.
Zhōu cannot be discussed.
Now, when an elephant sees its calf's skin,
it weeps regardless of distance.
How could Zhōu bear it!'" Zhāng Huá's "Bówùzhì" says:
"Long ago in the Southern Sea were four elephants.
When one female died,
the male appeared as if in mourning."
Burning Body and Torch Tail
"The Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"The elephant has tusks that cause its body to be burned."
It also says:
"Wú attacked Chǔ.
Zhēn Yǐngù was in the same boat as the King.
The King had him drive torch-bearing elephants to charge the Wú army."
Dù Yù says:
"They tied torches to the elephants' tails and set them ablaze,
to startle the Wú army,
and repel them."
War in Tiānzhú and Plowing in Cāngwú
Fàn Yè's "History of the Later Hàn" says:
"The state of Dōnglí had its capital at Zhìqí City,
over three thousand lǐ southeast of Tiānzhú.
It was a large state.
Both men and women were eight chǐ tall,
but timid and weak.
They rode elephants and camels to travel to neighboring states.
When there was an invasion,
they rode elephants to fight."
Huángfǔ Mì's "Dìwáng Shìjì" says:
"Shùn was buried beneath Cāngwú.
There, a herd of elephants often plowed for him."
Its body is several times larger than an ox's, yet its eyes are no bigger than a pig's.
Wàn Zhèn's "Treatise on Strange Things of the Southern Regions" states:
"The elephant's body is several times larger than an ox's,
but its eyes are not as large as a pig's.
Its trunk is six or seven chǐ long,
as thick as an arm.
All the food it eats
is taken with it."
Guō Pú's "Illustrated Eulogy to the Classic of Mountains and Seas" states:
"Its eyes are no bigger than a pig's."
The Finest Things of the South, the Essence of Yáoguāng
"The Eryǎ" states:
"Among the finest things of the south,
are the rhinoceroses and elephants of Liáng Shān."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals: Pivotal Mechanism of Revolutions" states:
"The essence of Yáoguāng
scatters to transform into elephants.
If the tong trees of the Jiāng and Huái rivers
are felled without restraint,
then Yáoguāng will not shine brightly."
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pú's "Illustrated Eulogy to the Classic of Mountains and Seas"
The elephant is truly massive,
its body huge, its appearance strange.
Its flesh equals ten oxen,
its eyes no bigger than a pig's.
Looking at its head is like looking at its tail,
its movement like a hill shifting.
The Qílín, Part Three
"The Eryǎ" states:
"The qílín
has the body of a jūn, an ox's tail, and one horn."
"Shuōwén" states:
"The qílín
is a benevolent beast."
"The Spring and Autumn Annals: Preserving the Qian Diagram" states:
"The Year Star scatters to become the qílín."
"The Book of Documents: Median Prognostication" states:
"During the time of Huángdì,
qílín were in the imperial park."
"Máoshī Yìshū" states:
"The qílín
has horse-like hooves.
Yellow in color with round hooves,
the tip of its horn is fleshy.
Its sound matches the huángzhōng pitch.
It appears when the ruler is supremely benevolent."
"The Dàdài Lǐ" states:
"There are three hundred sixty furred creatures,
and the qílín is their leader."
"The Book of Rites" states:
"The qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon
are called the Four Numinous Creatures.
If the qílín is kept as a domestic animal,
then beasts will not bolt."
Pronounced hū jué fǎn.
Cài Yōng's "Monthly Ordinances" states:
"Among the Five Beasts of the Celestial Palace,
are the great horn, Xuānyuán, and the trust of the qílín.
All qílín
are born from fire,
and roam in earth.
Therefore, cultivate its mother,
to bring forth its child;
it is the essence of the Five Phases.
When vision is clear and rites are cultivated, then the qílín arrives."
"The Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"In the spring of the fourteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
a hunt in the west captured a qílín.
Chú Shāng, the charioteer of the Shūsūn clan, captured it.
Considering it inauspicious,
he gave it to the gamekeeper.
Zhòngní observed it
and said:
'It is a qílín,'
and only then took it." "The Spring and Autumn Annals: Responsive Essence Talisman" states:
"The qílín has one horn,
signifying that all within the seas share one ruler.
If the ruler does not cut open wombs
or break open eggs,
then it appears in the suburbs."
"Huáinánzǐ" states:
"When qílín fight, the sun and moon are eclipsed."
"Guǎngyǎ" states:
"The qílín
embodies benevolence and upholds righteousness.
Its walking steps are in accordance with the compass,
its turns and returns in accordance with the square.
It roams only choosing suitable land,
soars only to settled places.
It does not tread on living insects,
nor break living grass.
It does not live in groups,
nor travel in flocks.
It does not fall into traps,
nor become ensnared in nets."
Hé Fǎshèng's "Record of Auspicious Signs":
"The qílín is the leader of furred creatures,
a benevolent beast.
The male is called qí,
the female is called lín.
The male's cry is called 'roaming sage,'
the female's cry is called 'returning prosperity.'
Its summer cry is called 'supporting the young,'
its autumn cry is called 'nourishing peace.'"
Wood Essence, Benevolent Beast
"The Spring and Autumn Annals: Confucius's Expanded Diagrams" states:
"When the Cāng declines,
the qílín does not flourish.
The qílín
is the essence of wood."
Sòng Jūn states:
"The qílín, as wood essence, generates water,
therefore it is called yīn.
Wood qi favors earth.
Earth is yellow, wood is green,
therefore the qílín's color is bluish-yellow.
'Not flourishing' means being seen restrained."
Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén" states:
"The qílín
is a benevolent beast.
It has the body of a jūn, an ox's tail, and a fleshy horn.
Qí follows the radical lù (deer) with qí as its phonetic.
Lín
is the female qí.
It follows the radical lù (deer) with lín as its phonetic."
Wolf's Head, Ox's Tail
Hé Fǎshèng's "Record of Auspicious Signs of the Jin Restoration":
"The qílín has the body of a jūn, an ox's tail,
a wolf's head, one horn,
and is yellow with horse-like hooves."
One Horn, Five Hooves
"The Spring and Autumn Annals: Responsive Essence Talisman" states:
"The qílín has one horn,
signifying that all within the seas share one ruler.
If the ruler does not cut open wombs or break open eggs, then it appears in the suburbs."
"The Book of Han" states:
"Zhōng Jūn accompanied the Emperor on an excursion to Yōng,
where a white qílín was captured.
It had one horn and five hooves.
Also obtained was a tree,
with branches growing sideways,
which then joined back together.
The Emperor found this strange.
Zhōng Jūn replied:
'Wild beasts joining horns
signifies sharing the same root.
Many branches attaching inwardly
shows there is nothing external.
Such responses as these
likely foretell those who will undo their braided hair, discard their left-fastening garments, don caps and sashes, and wrap themselves in robes and gowns,
thereby receiving the ultimate transformation!'"
Driving six flying steeds, spitting three scrolls
The "Chūnqiū Mìng Lì Xù" states:
"The Luòshū Zhāi Wáng Pì says:
'After the Cìmín people perished, the Six Sovereigns emerged,
Heaven and Earth decreed the changes to sequence and sever.'"
Sòng Jūn said:
"The perishing of the Cìmín people marks the end of the era when people first dwelled in caves.
The Six Sovereigns,
these are the ones counted among the people below.
Chénfàng had a large head and four breasts,
and was called 'Huáng Cì Qū Dì Bó'.
Chénfàng
is the name of Cì Qū.
Dì Bó
is a place name.
Driving six flying qílín,
following the sun and moon.
Flying
refers to the qílín beast having wings and the ability to fly.
Following the sun and moon
means following their courses.
He ruled for two hundred and fifty years."
The "Xiàojīng Gǔ Qì" states:
"Kǒngzǐ dreamed at night that in the region of Fēngpèi, red smoke and vapor arose.
Yán Huí and Zǐ Xià accompanied him to observe it.
Driving a carriage to the northwest of Chǔ, at the temple of the Fàn clan,
they saw a grass-gathering boy beating a qílín,
injuring its front left leg.
He bundled firewood and covered it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Child, come here,
what is your surname?'
The boy said:
'My surname is Chìsōng,
my courtesy name is Shíqiáo,
and my given name is Shòujì.'
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Have you perhaps seen something?'
'What I saw was a beast,
like a musk deer with a sheep's head,
with horns on its head,
and flesh squares at their tips.
It fled westward because of this.'
Kǒngzǐ uncovered the firewood to look at the qílín beneath,
Kǒngzǐ hurried forward,
the qílín covered its ears,
and spat out three scrolls of writing.
Kǒngzǐ carefully read them."
From the "Sōushén Jì".
The domesticated four numinous creatures, the essence of the five elements
The "Lǐjì" states:
"The qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon are called the four numinous creatures.
If the qílín is domesticated, then beasts will not flee."
Cài Yōng's "Yuèlìng Zhāngjù" states:
"Among the five celestial beasts,
there is the faith of the Great Horn, Xuānyuán, and the qílín.
All qílín are born from fire,
and roam in earth.
Thus, cultivating their mother brings forth their child,
this is the essence of the five elements.
When vision is clear and rituals are cultivated, the qílín arrives."
The "Qílín Ode" by Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn Dynasty
Oh, magnificent Great Horn,
descending to give birth to the numinous beast.
Vision clear, rituals cultivated,
the qílín comes in trust.
The Spring and Autumn Annals have already recorded it,
and you have come to announce its completion.
Commoner Shǐ Zǐchú,
captured it in the western hunt.
The "Qílín Ode" by Xuē Zǒng of Wú
Sublime indeed, qílín,
the chief among beasts.
When governance is peaceful, you appear in the light,
otherwise, you retract your feet.
Virtue is used to guard the body,
not displaying fangs or horns.
In awe during the time of Táng,
Emperor Yáo preserved blessings.
Entrusting your form to Great Wú,
to illuminate distant fortune.
Heaven blesses the sage emperor,
who enjoys these myriad states.
The "Qílín Ode" by Wǔzhāo King of Xīliáng
With a single horn and round hooves,
walking in accordance with rules.
Roaming, it must choose its ground,
soaring before settling.
It does not enter traps,
nor is it caught in nets.
Its virtue is such that none are not kingly,
for it, the leg was broken.
Horses, Part Four
According to the "Chūnqiū Shuōtící" it says:
"The essence of earth becomes the horse,
born in the twelfth month,
responding to yin and aligning with yang to combine their functions.
Thus humans harness horses,
bearing heavy loads and reaching distant places to benefit all under heaven.
The moon's course is swift, therefore horses are good at running."
The "Zhōuguān" says:
"Horses over eight chǐ are called lóng (dragons),
over seven chǐ are called lái,
over six chǐ are called horses."
It also says:
"For all studs,
they occupy one in four.
Three mares to one stud.
In spring, sacrifice to the Horse Ancestor and restrain the foals;
the Horse Ancestor
is the celestial team of four;
restraining the foals
means not letting them approach their mothers.
In summer, sacrifice to Xiānmù,
distribute horses and castrate the studs;
Xiānmù
refers to the first horse breeders,
then they are called studs.
In autumn, sacrifice to the Horse Shè;
the Horse Shè
is the first horse rider.
The Shìběn says:
"Xiàngtǔ created riding horses."
In winter, sacrifice to Mǎbù."
Mǎbù
is the spirit that brings disasters to horses.
For all grand sacrifices, court audiences, and assemblies,
horses are selected by color and distributed,
decorated ceremonial horses are led with whips in hand,
and the rearing of second silkworms is prohibited.
Yuán
means again.
In astronomy, the constellation Chén corresponds to the horse,
the silkworm is the essence of the dragon,
when the moon aligns with Huǒ, the silkworm eggs are bathed,
thus silkworms and horses share the same vital energy.
Nothing can excel in two aspects,
prohibiting second silkworms
is to avoid harming horses.
The "Lǐjì" says:
"Officials and scholars,
when descending at the duke's gate,
salute the carriage horses.
Riding a carriage horse must be in court attire,
walking a carriage horse must be in the middle of the road.
Trampling the fodder of a carriage horse is punishable,
if a carriage horse dies,
it is buried with a curtain."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"All horses go out at midday,
and come in at midday."
Zhōng
refers to the spring and autumn equinoxes.
They are released at the spring equinox,
and brought in at the autumn equinox.
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Táotú horses,
in the northern sea there is a beast shaped like a horse,
named táotú,
green in color.
Wild horses,
like horses but smaller.
Extremely powerful;
róng,
white above the knees only zhù;
zhù,
refers to the two hind knees being white,
zhù pronounced as zhù.
All four cannon bones white;
zēng,
zēng.

shǒu,
commonly called tàxuě horses.
Both front feet white;
xí,
xī.

qú,
qú.

qǐ,
left white;
jǐ,

left white;
zhù,
liú horses with white belly;
yuán,
lí horses with white haunches;
yù,

White rump;
yàn,

yàn,

Tail white;
láng,
láng.
Dí sǎng,
white forehead,
white reaching the nose;
xuán,
sù,
nose bridge.
Face and forehead all white only máng.
Pronounced mò jiāng fǎn.
Sǎng,
means forehead.
Whorled hair on the chest suitable for riding,
whorled hair under the belly like teats,
is a thousand-lǐ horse.
Behind the elbow jiǎn yáng.
On the flank fú fāng,
gàn, xié.
On the back què guǎng,
pronounced jué,
these are all locations of whorled hair.
Inverted hair jū yǎn.

Male called zhì,

Female called shè.

grass horse.
Blue-white mixed hair;
zhuī,
yellow-white mixed hair;
pī,
pronounced pī,
today's peach blossom horse.
Dark white mixed hair;
yīn,
today's reddish-white horse.
White horse with black mane;
luò,

quán,
quán.
Black muzzle.
guā
light yellow color.

jiàn
xián.
