yú,
for ancestral temple sacrifices, uniformity of hair,
purity is valued.
For military affairs, uniformity of strength,
strength is valued.
For hunting, uniformity of speed,
swiftness is valued.
Horses eight chǐ tall are called róng."
Hé Chéngtiān's "Zuǎnwén" says:
"A horse at one year is called zhù,
zhù.
At two years is called jū,
at eight years is called bā.
bā.
lì huì fǎn.
Refers to horse color.
fǎng,
fáng.
Horse with bent shin;
wén,
wén.
Horse with yellow eyes.
zhōng,
zhōng gāo fǎn.
Horse's gait."
The "Hànshū" says:
"In the second year of Yuánshòu,
horses were born in the Yúwú River.
North of Shuòfāng.
In the fourth year of Yuándǐng,
horses were born in the Wòwā River."
Among wild horses there are extraordinary ones,
drinking from the river,
local people captured them with fodder.
Presenting the horses,
they were considered divine and extraordinary,
hence it is said they emerged from the water.
It also says:
"The Dàyuān state has over seventy separate towns,
with many fine horses.
The horses sweat blood,
said to be descendants of celestial horses."
In the land of Dàyuān, on the Qiáo Mountains, there are horses,
but they cannot be obtained.
Therefore, they take five-colored mares and place them beneath the mountains,
and when they mate and give birth to foals,
all of them sweat blood,
and the people of the land call them the sons of heavenly horses.
The "Hànshū Yīnyì" says:
"Yǎoniǎo refers to
a divine horse,
with a red beak and a black body."
The "Wèi Zhì" says:
"The land of Huì produces guǒxià horses,
which were presented as tribute during the Hàn dynasty,
standing three chǐ tall."
Yú Huàn's "Diǎnlüè" says:
"The divine horse is
the essence of the river.
The Dài horse is
the essence of yīn."
Cháng Qú's "Huáyáng Guózhì" says:
"In Huìwú County, there is the Yuánmǎ River.
The yuánmǎ could travel a thousand lǐ in a day,
and died in Shǔ.
Today, the Yuánmǎ Tomb is that very spot.
The county has a Yuánmǎ Shrine.
When commoners graze their animals at the foot of the mountains,
sometimes a fine foal is born,
which is a son of the yuánmǎ."
It also says:
"Four divine horses
emerged from the Diānchí River."
The "Sòngshū" says:
"In the fifth year of the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Tǔyùhún Shíyín sent an envoy to present dancing horses."
The "Xījīng Zájì" says:
"When Emperor Wén returned from Dài,
he had nine fine horses,
all of them the finest in the land.
One was named Fúyún,
one was named Chìdiàn,
one was named Juéqún,
one was named Yìbiāo,
one was named Zǐyàn,
one was named Lǜlí Cōng,
one was named Lóngzǐ,
one was named Lín Jū,
one was named Juéchén,
and they were called the Nine Excellences."
The "Fúruì Tú" says:
"When noble men are valued and horses are despised,
then white horses with red manes gather,
and they appear when the worthy and virtuous are employed."
It also says:
"When carriages and horses are regulated, they appear.
Ténghuáng refers to
a divine horse.
Its color is yellow,
also called Chénghuáng,
also known as Fēihuáng,
sometimes written as Gǔhuáng,
sometimes called Cuìhuáng,
also named Zǐhuáng.
Its appearance resembles a fox,
with two horns on its back.
It comes from the land of the Báimín,
and riding it can grant a lifespan of three thousand years."
The Yellow Emperor rode it.
The "Xiàngmǎ Jīng" says:
"Bólè said:
'The horse's head is like a king and should be square,
the eyes are like a chancellor and should be bright,
the spine is like a general and should be strong,
the belly is like a city wall and should be expansive,
the four legs are like officials and should be long.
The eyes should be set high and deep,
the nostrils should be large.
On the nose, there should be a pattern like the character "wáng" or "huǒ,"
and the inside of the mouth should be red.
The knee bones should be round and prominent,
the ears should be close together and upright,
small and thick.
In the method of judging horses,
first eliminate the three types of weak horses and the five types of inferior horses,
then judge the rest.
A large head with a small neck is the first weakness,
a weak spine with a large belly is the second weakness,
a small neck with large hooves is the third weakness.
As for the five inferior types:
a large head with drooping ears is the first inferiority,
a long neck that does not bend is the second inferiority,
short upper body and long lower body is the third inferiority,
large thighs with short ribs is the fourth inferiority,
shallow hips with thin thighs is the fifth inferiority.'"
Qīnglóng Báitù
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"Yī Yǐn advised Tāng, saying:
'The Son of Heaven cannot attain the ultimate flavor,
so he must have the likes of Qīnglóng
and the mounts of Yífēng.'" Gāo Yòu's annotation says:
"These are all names of horses,
swift as the passing wind."
Cuī Bào's "Gǔjīn Zhù" says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng had seven famous horses:
Zhuīfēng, Báitù, Nièjǐng, Zhuīdiàn, Fēihé, Tóngjué, and Chénfú."
Rúlóng Sìlù
The "Hòuhànshū" says:
"When Empress Mǎ passed by the Zhuólóng Gate,
she saw her maternal family inquiring about her well-being,
with carriages like flowing water and horses like dragons."
The "Hánzǐ" says:
"Wèi Sìjūn said:
'A horse that resembles a deer is worth a thousand gold,
yet there are horses worth a thousand gold but no deer worth a single gold.
Why is that?
It is because horses are useful to people,
while deer are not useful to people.'"
Pēnyù Liúzhū
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
"The Son of Heaven traveled east to Huángzé,
and stayed overnight at Qūluò.
He said:
'In the pools of Huáng,
the horses spurt sand,
and the royal people are majestic;
in the marshes of Huáng,
the horses spurt jade,
and the royal people enjoy longevity and abundance.'" Fù Xuán's "Chéngyú Mǎ Fù" says:
"They spray foam like mist,
and their flowing sweat is like pearls."
Qiānlǐ Jiǔyì
The "Hànshū" says:
"During Emperor Wén's time,
someone presented a thousand-lǐ horse.
The emperor issued an edict, saying:
'With the luán banners ahead
and the accompanying carriages behind,
an auspicious journey covers fifty lǐ a day.
If I ride a thousand-lǐ horse,
where would I go alone?'
Thus, he returned the horse."
The "Xījīng Zájì" says:
"When Emperor Wén returned from Dài,
he had nine fine horses,
which were called the Nine Dragons."
Zhūyì Gǎoshēn
Huáng Zhānglóng's "Mǎ Fù" says:
"The place where the dragon-horse emerges
is in the distant realm of Tàiméng.
It shares the deep abyss of Yúyuān,
reaching the limits where heavenly light shines.
Born on the shores of rivers and seas,
adorned with patterned markings and crimson wings.
Endowed with the pure transformation of divine energy,
it is nurtured and praised in Dàyuān."
The "Zhōushū" says:
"The 'Wáng Huì' chapter states:
'People ride Chénghuáng;
Chénghuáng resembles a fox,
and it has five fleshy horns.
The patterned horses of the Quǎnróng
have red manes and white bodies,
eyes like yellow gold,
and are called the mounts of Gǔhuáng.'"
Héjīng Kūnxiàng
Yú Huàn's "Diǎnlüè" says:
"The divine horse is
the essence of the river."
The "Zhōuyì" says:
"Kun is fundamentally prosperous,
beneficial for the steadfastness of the mare."
Wáng Bì's "Wényán" commentary says:
"The dragon is used to describe Qián,
the horse is used to clarify Kūn,
selecting symbols according to the meaning of the matter."
Qiáolù Bēndì
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Chewing grass and drinking water,
kicking up their heels and dwelling freely,
this is the true nature of horses."
The "Hànshū" says:
"Some horses kick and gallop, yet they can travel a thousand lǐ;
some scholars bear the burden of vulgar customs, yet they can achieve merit and fame."
Bēnxiāo Zhuīdiàn
Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì" says:
"When King Mù of Zhōu ascended the throne,
he toured the world,
driving eight dragon-steeds,
named Juédì, Fānyǔ, Bēnxiāo, Yuèyǐng, Yúhuī, Chāoguāng, Téngwù, and Xiéyì."
Cuī Bào's "Gǔjīn Zhù" says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng had seven famous horses:
Zhuīfēng, Báitù, Nièjǐng, Zhuīdiàn, Fēihé, Tóngjué, and Chénfú."
Red and Piebald, Green and Black
The Mao Odes states:
"Fat and large are the stallions,
In the wilds of the distant borders.
Of those fat and large,
Some are white-legged and yellow;
Some are pure black and bay;
Some are dappled and piebald;
Some are red and green;
Some are spotted and black-maned."
Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Zàofǔ, skilled in charioteering, found favor with King Mù of Zhōu,
and obtained a team of black-maned steeds, gentle blacks, red horses, and green-eared ones.
He toured the west on an inspection,
and was so delighted that he forgot to return."
Unicorn Form, Chicken Eyes
Zhāng Jùn's Illustrations and Eulogies of the Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
"On Dūn Mountain there is a beast,
named Gǔ,
with the form of a unicorn and a single horn."
The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents states:
"Sànyíshēng went to the Quǎnróng tribe and obtained fine horses,
those with gray bodies, red manes, and chicken eyes,
taking ninety-six of them.
He displayed them in Zhòu's court,
and when Zhòu came out and saw them,
he turned back to look and said:
'Who is this man?'
Sànyíshēng then hurried forward and said:
'I am an envoy from Chāng, a minister of the western borderlands.'"
Green Steeds, Fine Steeds
The Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò states:
"Fine steeds and green-eared ones,
flying hares and green horses,
are the world's excellent horses.
But if used to catch mice in the deep palace,
they are not as good as a lame cat."
Master Xún states:
"Red horses, piebald horses, fine steeds, and green-eared ones,
slender steeds and green-eared ones,
were the excellent horses of antiquity."
White Horse Rhapsody by Liú Yìgōng of Sòng
Only the sovereign has creation,
Only the spirits hold secrets.
Splendid aura, refined essence,
Profound love, pure excellence.
The eight directions bow in homage at court,
The nine wilds gather their robes to present tribute.
Elephant chariots display virtue to serve the carriage,
Dragon horses dwell in benevolence to receive the reins.
Thus Zhōu praised surpassing wheels,
Hàn had heavenly steeds.
Their form stems from the heavenly axis,
Their life derives from the watery position.
This red-white is outstanding,
Transcending the age, called a fine steed.
As for its appearance,
Erect body, light feet,
High forehead, gleaming eyes.
Fierce spirit, powerful voice,
Long strides, clear vision.
Presented in the western park,
Its virtue proclaimed in the eastern capital.
Its worth overwhelms all Xià,
The spectacle exhausts the capital city.
Adorned with shimmering golden ornaments,
Raising tinkling jade bells.
Releasing singing arrows at the hanging moon,
Galloping across long tracks in distant fields.
Deploying four armored steeds to show goodwill,
Gleaming two spears with double tassels.
Surpassing old stables without peer,
Examining past speed to compare fame.
Red-White Horse Rhapsody by Yán Yánzhī of Sòng
In the twenty-second year of Sòng,
Glorious achievements shine through successive reigns.
Martial valor is solemnly displayed,
Civil instruction reaches harmonious perfection.
The peace of the three steps can be ascended,
The path of a rising king is already joined.
Seeking the kingdom's beauty in old histories,
Examining regional records in past documents.
In ancient times, when the Yellow Emperor ascended the throne,
Flying Yellow served in the stables.
When the later Táng received the mandate,
Red markings awaited the sun.
Hàn's way prospered and heavenly steeds displayed talent,
Wèi's virtue flourished and marsh horses offered their substance.
This marvelous steed of surpassing excellence,
From former ages occasionally appears.
Together glorified in auspicious records,
Thus to honor and guard divine majesty,
To support and protect the imperial procession.
Therefore, essence and radiance harmonize in attendance,
Spiritual creatures all find their place.
When the enlightened mandate first established its foundation,
All nine regions submitted in obedience.
Some braved dangers to receive the calendar,
Others came from afar to present tribute.
Merely observe its attached sinews and erected bones,
Drooping mane and planted hair.
Double pupils like paired mirrors,
Two cheeks harmonizing with the moon.
Extraordinary form, peaks emerging,
Unique appearance, elegance radiating.
Leaping beyond, leaving dust tracks behind,
Galloping swiftly, vanishing from sight.
Yet indulgence in hunting excursions,
Serves as a mirror to former kings.
Recklessness above others,
Brings regret from righteous principles.
The Son of Heaven then halts his carriage, reconsiders,
Rests his troops, unpacks baggage.
Reflects on Wǔ and Mù,
Models himself on Wén and Guāng,
Relieves the people's suffering,
Cultivates the state's statutes.
Guards against the boar's ruin of charioteering,
Promotes the flying bird's perch on the yoke.
Thus reverently follows what is often neglected,
Vigilantly prepares against the unforeseen.
Carriages have the safety of double wheels,
Horses lack the waywardness of straying.
Placed in the depths of the Zhuólóng stable,
Entrusted with the rank of red millet.
Care and nurture know benevolence,
Following to old age, meeting its end.
Adding worn curtains,
Receiving the fallen form.
Heavenly affection complete,
Imperial grace fulfilled.
Dancing Horse Rhapsody by Xiè Zhuāng of Sòng
The Son of Heaven orders the three lights,
Governs all realms.
Draws from the Cloud Classic's lasting statutes,
Shapes by the River Chart's inherited measures.
Thus virtue and grace shine above to heaven and seep below to springs,
Auspicious signs of good fortune all belong,
Glorious and cherished responses surely follow.
The moon's shadow presents auspicious signs,
The heavenly axis manifests its aura.
Bestowing scenes upon Ēpáng,
Receiving inspiration from heavenly steeds.
Treading the plains and outskirts, following the light,
Leaping flowing springs, swimming in substance.
Leaving the water cave, heading southward,
Departing Lúntái, arriving eastward.
Ascending the Bì Gate, returning with tribute,
Covering the Zhī courtyard, presenting reins.
And when nurtured in peace at the fine steed's enclosure,
Advanced to harness at the dragon's pool.
Shining grandly in the state's stables,
Adorning two steeds in the imperial stables.
Surpassing Yì Field, crossing green lands,
Outrunning Lán Pond, trampling Purple Swallows.
The five kings dim their gaze,
The Sūn clan is bewildered by its mystery.
The Eastern Gate could not depict it,
The Western River could not transmit it.
Already fed with millet to balance its nature,
Also adorned with pendants to honor its tracks.
Nourishing heroic spirit in patterned silks,
Storing galloping form in candlelight.
Holding the sharp shadow of soaring clouds,
Restraining the fleeting feet of chasing lightning.
Now layered and cast in crimson silk,
Also linked in pattern with red piebalds.
Observe its twin jades matching the model,
Three seals fitting the chart.
Dark bones full,
Swallow chamber empty.
Yang principle contends,
Hidden strategies wind.
Sweat flies red,
Foam flows like pearls.
As for the "Sìxià" already rising,
The "Cǎiqí" already presented.
First pacing, dragon-like bowing,
Finally sleek, phoenix-like gazing.
Meeting the "Tiáolù" with flying bells,
Rising "Chéngyún" with startling arrows.
Depicting the Qín fields' dust-filled distance,
Shaping the Wú Gate's trailing silk.
Exhausting the Yú court's prancing steps,
Exploring the wilds' buried wheels.
Tang Emperor Taizong Wenhuangdi, "Ode to a Horse Drinking Water"
Its mane-bones drink from the long stream,
As rushing currents sprinkle its bridle-tassels.
Fine ripples gather where it snorts and sprays,
Tangled waterweeds entwine around its hooves.
The water's gleam slants upon the saddle,
The horse's shadow lies across the flowing stream.
It seems to turn within a heavenly pool,
Where surging waves give birth to dragon-steeds.
Chén Shěnjǐong, "Poem on a Frontier Horse's Longing to Return"
In deep autumn the frontier horse grows stout,
Facing the border, it deeply yearns for home.
Bridle to bridle, they cross the Sea of Reeds,
Tongues tied, they descend to Jīnwēi.
Already they have broken the fish-scale formation,
And are about to crush the crane-wing encirclement.
They long ever more for the road through tall catalpas,
Golden saddles turned toward the setting sun.
Yáng Shīdào, "Ode to a Horse Drinking Water, Composed by Imperial Command"
At dawn he reins in the dragon-steed,
Playing with its shadow, they emerge from the flowering grove.
Pacing gracefully along the spring ravine,
In swift succession they cross the green stream.
Moss-stained currents dye the silk bridle,
Clear waters mirror the carved hairpin.
Once mounted for a drive to the Jasper Pool,
How could one recall the shadow of the Long Wall?
Yáng Shīdào, "Ode to a Horse"
A precious horse, rare and wondrous, departs from Wèiyāng,
Its carved saddle gleams with purple-gold adornment.
On newly sprouted spring grass it gallops in the Upper Park,
As autumn winds begin to stir, it frolics at Chángyáng.
Its jade bridle-bells repeatedly pass beside Zhāngtái,
With delicate steps it treads past Zhuólóng.
In vain have Han generals year after year ridden forth,
For Wǎnchéng now presents its famed king in tribute.

Four ears, eight legs

with its tail coiled around its horns,

Suppressing with white, riding blue
Guō Pú's "Forest of Mysteries" says:
"Fāng Shūbǎo of Yìxīng contracted typhoid fever and was near death.
He asked Guō Pú to divine for him,
and the result was inauspicious.
He was told to seek a white ox to suppress the illness,
but could not find one.
Only Yáng Zǐxuán had a white ox,
but he refused to lend it.
Guō Pú managed to obtain it for him,
and that very day, a large white ox came from the west,
and went straight to Fāng Shūbǎo.
He was startled,
and his illness was immediately cured."
"The Biography of the Pass Official" says:
"In the first year of Wújí of the Zhōu dynasty,
Lǎozǐ was crossing the pass.
The pass official Yǐn Xǐ first instructed the gatekeeper:
'If there is an old man coming from the east,
riding a blue ox pulling a simple cart,
do not let him pass through the gate.'
That day, they indeed saw an old man riding a blue ox cart requesting to cross the pass.
The gatekeeper went in to report,
and Yǐn Xǐ said:
'Yes,
the Way has now arrived!
I have seen the sage!'
He immediately took his official seal and went out to welcome him,
performing the rites of a disciple."
Eastern barbarians divine with bones, Xīhé raises cows
Yáng Fāng's "Uncovering the Depths of the Five Classics" says:
"The people of the eastern barbarians
use ox bones to divine matters,
revealing good or bad fortune,
and they are never wrong.
Oxen are not creatures endowed with wisdom,
yet their bones have such efficacy."
"The Kǒng Cóngzǐ" says:
"Yī Dùn,
a poor scholar of Lǔ,
hearing of Lord Zhū's wealth,
went to ask him about the method.
He was told:
'If you wish to become rich quickly,
raise five cows,
and then go to Xīhé,
and raise large numbers of cattle and sheep south of Yīshì.
Within ten years,
your offspring will number in the tens of thousands,
and your wealth will rival that of princes and dukes.'"
Sòng Kǒng Nìngzǐ's "Ode to the Yak"
This creature is born,
dwelling in remote and rugged places.
It hides in the vast wilderness of Mínyú,
and drinks from the clear streams of Yōngzhǔ.
It gallops with unmatched strides,
its adorned head mingling with the young sheep.
Its long, thick hair is lush,
its fierce nature hesitant and cautious.
Surpassing the lamb's fat like grease,
matching the ephemeral mayfly's elegance.
It serves as a symbol in rites and music,
and also as an asset in military campaigns.
It upholds the excellence of feudal lords,
and brings order to the barbarian frontiers.
Tributary gifts come to court in ranks,
surpassing even the lands of Yìnjǔ.
And so on.
Liǔ Gùyán's "Poem on a Dead Ox"
One morning leaving the purple carriage canopy,
a thousand miles parting from the Yellow River.
Facing its harness, one can only weep,
knocking its horns, how can one hear its song?

Yuán Shū's "Collection of Humorous Writings: The Nine Bestowals for the Lord of Lúshān"
When the three armies march overland,
And grain transport is arduous.
Strategists halt their calculations,
And warriors sigh in lament.
Then you bray from Shàngdǎng,
Responding fervently to the call.
Traversing rugged terrain for a thousand miles,
Carrying sacks to deliver meals.
Thus achieving great merit,
Unfading through the ages,
This is indeed your achievement.
Your voice rises with the times,
Never silent day or night.
Above, it matches the celestial signs,
Below, it accords with the water clock.
Responding to the watch with long brays,
Not a hair's breadth off.
Though the clepsydra is famed,
It cannot compare to your virtue.
This again is your wisdom.
When heaven and earth are dark,
And the three luminaries obscured.
You still remember the heavenly hours,
And do not cease your voice.
This again is your clarity.
Green-backed and crimson-bodied,
With long cheeks and a broad forehead.
Its long tail hangs behind,
And its huge ears stand erect.
This again is your form.
When the fine wheat is ripe,
Truly fine flour is needed.
Turning the millstone round the axle,
Swift as spinning lightning.
Benefiting our multitudes,
Offered to gods and spirits.
This again is your ability.
You have the merit of aiding armies,
And are further endowed with many abilities.
Therefore, we dispatch the Grand Master of the Palace, Lǘqiū Luó, to bestow upon you the titles of Grand Herald of the Bridle and Reins, General of the Spotted Hoof, and Marquis of Gōngtíng.
With Lújiāng in Yángzhōu, Lúlíng in Jiāngzhōu, Tónglú in the State of Wú, and Zhūlú in Hépǔ.
We enfeoff you as the Duke of Lúshān.
Zāng Dàoyán's "Lament for a Donkey"
Now, auspicious signs correspond to feelings,
And noble conduct is manifested in deeds.
Thus, in selecting talent and assigning posts,
One must seek the exceptional.
In examining ability and verifying utility,
One also considers reputation and reality.
If names are determined by appearance,
Then designations are marked accordingly.
As for voice, appearance, rank, and title,
They are bestowed based on these.
There was an extraordinary being,
A galloper from the western regions,
Robust and upright in physique,
Endowed with a calm and elegant nature,
Wise, perceptive, broad, and detailed.
Its high voice carried far and wide,
Truly a famous colt of the donkey clan.

They would stage camel fights,

Knows Water Sources, Detects Water Veins

The quicksand stretches over a thousand lǐ,

Sometimes there are hidden water flows,
Which people cannot detect.
They all ride camels.
Camels can detect water veins.
When they encounter such a spot, they halt and refuse to move,
Stamping the ground with their feet.
People dig at the spot where they stamp,

Fills Outer Stables, Flanks Zhōngyáng Gate
"Records of the Grand Historian: Sū Qín's Biography" states:

Will surely fill your rear palace.
And the fine camels and excellent horses of Yān and Dài
Will surely fill your outer stables.'" Lù Huì's "Yèzhōng Jì" states:

One zhàng in length,
One zhàng in height,
With feet like oxen.
Their tails are two chǐ long,
And their backs resemble horse saddles.
They stand outside the Zhōngyáng Gate,
Facing each other along the road."
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pú's "Shānhǎi Jīng Illustration Camel Eulogy"
The camel is a wondrous beast,
Bearing a fleshy saddle.
Swiftly traversing the quicksand,
Displaying merit in the remotest lands.
Secretly knowing water sources,
Its wisdom is evident.

Earth Monster Mountain Spirit
The Guóyǔ states:
"Huánzi dug a well

'From what Qiū (I) have heard,
it is a sheep.
The monsters of wood and stone are Kuí and Wǎngliǎng,
the monsters of water are dragons and Wǎngxiàng,
the monster of earth is called Fényáng.'"
The Zhōuyì Biānmóu Lèi states:
"Tàishān lost its golden rooster,
Xīyuè lost its jade sheep."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The golden rooster and jade sheep
are the spirits of the two mountains."
Soft Hair Ram's Head
The Lǐjì states:
"In all sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
a sheep is called 'soft hair'."
The Shī states:
"The ewe has a large head,
three stars are in the eaves gutter."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"A female sheep is called zāng.
Bēn
means large."
Scolding Stones Eating Pearls
Gě Hóng's Shénxiān Zhuàn states:
"Huáng Chūpíng
was from Dānxī.
At age fifteen,
he was herding sheep
when a Daoist priest took him to Jīnhuá Mountain.
His elder brother, Chūqǐ,
searched for Chūpíng
for many years without finding him.
Seeing a Daoist priest in the market,
he followed him to seek his brother.
After they met and spoke,
he asked where the sheep were.
Píng said:
'The sheep are near the east side of the mountain.'
His brother went to look
and saw only white stones.
Píng said:
'Sheep, rise up, rise up!'
Then all the white stones rose up,
becoming tens of thousands of sheep."
Liú Yìqìng's Yōumíng Lù states:
"In Luòxià there was a ravine cave.
A wife wanted to kill her husband
and pushed him down.
After a long time he reached the bottom
and found a cave.
Palaces and halls were adorned with gold and jewels,
brighter than the three lights (sun, moon, stars).
The people were three zhàng tall,
and there were nine such places.
When he finally said he was hungry,
a tall man pointed to a sheep under a tree
and told him to kneel and stroke the sheep's beard.
At first he got one pearl,
which the tall man took.
The next time he also got one.
Later he was told to eat it,
which cured his hunger.
He asked the names of the nine places,
requesting to stay and not leave.
The reply was:
Red Fur, White Blood
The "Xu Yi Ji" says:
"Yú Liàng of Wúxīng,
in the eighth year of the Yǒngmíng era, was appointed as a clerk in the Protectorate Army office.
While in his usual sleeping place, he heard the sound of a sheep.
Suspicious it was a supernatural creature,
he secretly peeked through the door,
and saw a sheep beneath his bed.
It was about two feet tall,
its fur color like cinnabar,
filling the room with a brilliant light."
The "Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn" says:
"The Quǎnróng feasted King Mù at the slope of Léishǒu,
and presented four fine horses.
The Son of Heaven sent Kǒng Yá to receive them,
saying:
'On the plains of Léi River,
there are black oxen with white horns,
and there are black sheep with white blood.'"
Five Rams, Six Flying
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"When Bǎilǐ Xī was yet unrecognized,
after Guó perished,
Xī herded oxen in Qín,
and was sold for the price of five ram skins.
Gōngsūn Zhī obtained him and presented him to Duke Mù,
who employed him.
His plans were never inappropriate,
his actions always successful."
The "Chūnqiū Mìng Lì Xù" says:
"There was a man with a yellow head and large belly,
who emerged to govern Tiānqí.
After three hundred and four years, he was succeeded by a spirit,
who was called the August Spirit.
He emerged from Huái,
driving six flying sheep.
He governed for three hundred years,
with five generations spanning fifteen hundred years."
Weighs Ten Jīn, Three Feet Tall
Guō Yìgōng's "Guǎng Zhì" says:
"The large-tailed sheep,
has fine fur and thin skin.
Its tail is broad on the sides,
weighing nearly ten jīn,
and comes from Kāngjū."
The "Chūnqiū Shuō Tí Cí" says:
"The sheep (yáng),
signifies 'detailed' (xiáng),
meaning to change through detail.
Combining three elements gives life,
to nourish the scholars.
Therefore, the sheep is three feet tall."
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pú's "Shānhǎi Jīng Tú Qián Yáng Zàn"
The sheep of the Yuèzhī,
their kind roam the wilds.
They stand six feet tall,
their tails also like those of horses.
How to verify this?
The matter is seen in the Ěryǎ.
Pig, Ninth
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Shǐ,
means pig.
East of the river, it is called xī.
Wèi fén,
wèi,
pronounced yáng chuí fǎn.
Commonly called a small castrated pig a wèi zǐ.
Yāo tún.
The last born,
commonly called yāo tún.
Zòu zhě wēn.
Pronounced wēn,
now called wēn zhū.
Short head,
skin texture wrinkled and puckered.
A pig gives birth to three zōng,
zōng.
Two shī, one tè,
where it sleeps in the trough,
all four hooves are white.
Gāi,
its tracks deep,
extremely strong.
È,
pronounced è,
a pig five feet tall.
Female bā; a pig five feet tall is è."
A large pig is è,
now in Yúyáng, large pigs are called è.
Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén" says:
"Hù,
pronounced xǔ bǔ fǎn.
A small piglet;
xī,
a piglet three months old;
zōng,
pronounced zǐ gōng fǎn.
A piglet six months old,
or said to be one year old called zōng.
Bā,
a female pig;
fén,
castrated.
Pig jiān,
pronounced gōng yán fǎn.
A three-year-old pig;
jiā,
a robust pig;
wèi,
castrated;
yì,
yì.
Commonly named pig yì;
yì,
pronounced yú lì fǎn.
A pig's breath.
Huàn,
raising pigs by penning them with grain."
Hé Chéngtiān's "Zuǎn Wén" says:
"In Liángzhōu, shǐ is called zhū,
pronounced zhī yú fǎn.
In Hénán, it is called zhì,
in Wú-Chǔ, it is called xī.
Pronounced huǒ qǐ fǎn.
In Yúyáng, zhū is called è,
in Qí-Xú, a small pig is called zǔ.
Pronounced shì zhǔ fǎn.
Mì,
mì.
A white pig with a black head.
Wēn,
a pig with coarse hair."
The "Lǐjì" says:
"In all sacrificial rites,
the pig is called 'stiff-bristled' (gāng liè)."
The "Chūnqiū Shuō Tí Cí" says:
"The Dipper Star scatters its essence at times to become the pig,
born in the fourth month,
in accordance with heavenly principle."
Cuī Bào's "Gǔjīn Zhù" says:
"The pig is also called 'cānjūn' (adjutant)."
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"The zhì pig,
large ones have meat up to a thousand jīn.
The háo zhū (porcupine),
shaped like a piglet with white hair,
the hairs large like hairpins with black tips."
Guō Pú says:
"Zhì,
is a pig.
It has coarse bristles along its flanks,
several feet long,
and can shoot objects with the bristles on its neck."
Stiff Bristles, Clustered Awls
The "Lǐjì" says:
"In all sacrificial rites,
the pig is called 'stiff-bristled',
the piglet is called 'plump and fat'."
Guō Pú's "Shānhǎi Jīng Tú Háo Zhì Zàn" says:
"The clan of the stiff-bristled,
is named the bristly boar.
Its hairs are like clustered awls,
within them are propelled arrows."
White Head, Green Hooves
The "Dōngguān Hànjì" says:
"Zhū Fú wrote to Péng Chǒng,
reproaching him, saying:
'Bótōng boasts of himself,
thinking his merit surpasses all under heaven.
In the past, in Liáodōng, there was a pig,
born with a white head.
Deeming it unusual, they presented it.
Upon reaching Hédōng,
they saw all the pigs there were white,
and returned ashamed.
If your merit
were discussed in the imperial court,
it would be like the Liáodōng pig.'"
The "Yǎngshēng Yào Jí" says:
"Pigs with white hooves and green claws should not be eaten."
Chángyuán Marsh Mùlán Bridge
The *Dōngguān Hànjì* states:
"Wú Yòu lost his father at the age of twenty,
and lived alone.
His household had not even a peck of grain,
yet he would not accept relief or gifts.
He often herded pigs in Chángyuán Marsh."
Xí Zàochǐ's *Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Zhuàn* states:
"The Mùlán Bridge
is what is now called the Zhūlán Bridge.
Liú Héjì, because this bridge was near reeds
and had cordate houttuynia,
raised many pigs east of the bridge.
The Xiāngyáng Prefect, Prefect Pí, said:
'This creates such a pig-dung stench,
it should be renamed Zhūlán Bridge!
Do not call it Mùlán Bridge anymore.'
At first it was said in jest,
but the common people then changed its name."
Lord of Lǔ Ford Great Orchid King
The *Fúzǐ* states:
"A man from Shuò presented a great pig to King Zhāo of Yān,
and the cook prepared it as food.
After the pig died,
it appeared in a dream to the Yān Chancellor, saying:
'The Creator burdened me with the form of a pig,
feeding me on human filth.
Now, relying on Your Excellency's spiritual power, I have transformed
and have finally become the Lord of the Lǔ Ford.'"
Yuán Shū's *Páixié Jí: Dàlán Wáng Jiǔxī Wén*
In the tenth year of Dàhài,
the first day of the ninth month being yǐhài,
on the thirteenth day, dīnghài,
the Earl of Běiyān sent an envoy, the mighty boar Háoxī,
to confer the patent upon the Great Orchid King, saying:
"We consider that you, my lord, received the deep essence of the Great Yin,
manifesting your form among dark substances,
with a body plump and vast.
You grew without a care, roaming at leisure,
sustained by the nurture of the ruler.
Though without noble rank, you had your station—
this is your purity, my lord.
In former times, you were enfeoffed in the state of Yīn-Shāng,
and were called the Swine Clan.
Your glory flourished in that age,
your name passed down for a thousand generations—
this is your beauty, my lord.
White hoofs were celebrated in the odes of Zhōu,
crossing waves answered to portentous signs.
Songs and chants linger on people's lips,
resounding through a thousand years—
this is your virtue, my lord.
When you, my lord, roamed the wilds with others,
you alone were the mighty one.
Looking upon the herd of hundreds,
from west to east they went.
Bending to snort foam created mist,
raising your bristles aloft generated wind.
Against fierce poison you would surely bite,
when facing foes you would surely attack.
Charging far ahead, driving straight in,
no formation kept its front intact—
this is your courage, my lord."
Dogs, Tenth
The *Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu* states:
"Dogs are born after three months,
as yang is governed by the number three,
therefore dogs are each three chǐ tall."
The *Ěryǎ* states:
"When a dog gives birth to three pups,
they are called zōng.
Two shī and one qí,
are called qí.
Those not yet fully furred,
are called gǒu.
Extremely strong,
is called zhào.
Zhào.
Máng,
dog,
a dog four chǐ tall is called áo."
The *Shuōwén* states:
"Jiǎo,
a dog with much hair;
Xiē,
pronounced xū yè fǎn.
A dog with a short snout.
Yín,
pronounced hú zhǎn fǎn.
A dog that barks incessantly;
Áo,
a dog whose heart can be commanded.
Zhuī,
pronounced yán jiā fǎn.
A robust dog;
Dí,
a red dog."
Lǚ Chēn's *Zìlín* states:
"Lú,
a fine dog of Hán;
Què,
què.
A fine dog of Sòng;
Yàn,
pronounced wǔ jiàn fǎn.
A dog that chases tigers."
Hé Chéngtiān's *Zuǎnwén* states:
"A guard dog is called fén,
pronounced fú běn fǎn.
In Lǒngxī, a dog is called yóu.
Yǒu.
Nóng,
pronounced nǎi róng fǎn.
Níng,
pronounced nǎi gēng fǎn.
All are dogs with much hair.
Yào,
pronounced nǎi jiào fǎn.
Zhì,
pronounced jū lì fǎn.
Diāo,
diāo.
A dog with a curled tail."
The *Zhōuguān* states:
"A dog with red thighs is restless and has a strong odor."
The *Zhōushū* states:
"The qúsōu dog,
is a dew dog.
It can fly,
and eats tigers and leopards."
The *Guǎngyǎ* states:
"Yīnyú, Jìn'áo, Chǔ Rúhuáng, Hán Lú, Sòng Què,
are all types of dogs."
The *Guǎngzhì* states:
"Dogs have names like 'suspended hoof' and 'tail'."
The *Shānhǎijīng* states:
"On Yīnshān there is a beast,
its shape like a wildcat.
With a white head,
its name is Tiāngǒu."
It also states:
"The táo dog is like a dog,
blue in color,
it eats people starting from the head."
It also states:
"On Jīnménzhīshān there is a red dog,
named Tiāngǒu.
When it descends, there will be warfare."
The *Zá Wǔxíng Shū* states:
"A white dog with tiger stripes,
keeping it can bring ten thousand dàn;
a black dog with white ears,
keeping it brings wealth and honor;
a black dog with white feet,
benefits descendants;
a white dog with a yellow head,
brings great fortune to the household;
a yellow dog with a white tail,
generations will have officials;
a yellow dog with white feet,
benefits people."
The *Hànshū*:
"Emperor Gāozǔ said:
'Do you gentlemen understand hunting?
The one who chases the beasts for others,
is the dog;
the one who points out the tracks and shows the beast,
is the man.'" The *Shǐjì* states:
"Zhí's dog barks at Yáo.
It is not that Yáo is unkind,
but it barks because he is not its master."
The *Xījīng Zájì* states:
"Lǐ Tíng, a youth of Màolíng,
loved racing fine dogs to chase beasts,
or using hawks and sparrowhawks to catch hares,
all given fine names.
Dogs had names like Xiūháo, Líjiàn, Báiwàng, Qīngcáo."
The *Hòu Hànshū* states:
"Emperor Gāoxīnshì had a dog named Pánhù,
its markings were five-colored.
At that time, the Quǎnrōng troops were strong,
so he offered a reward: whoever could obtain the head of the Quǎnrōng general Wú,
would be given his youngest daughter.
Pánhù obtained it,
so the youngest daughter followed Pánhù up the southern mountains,
gave birth to twelve boys and girls,
who married among themselves,
and later flourished."
Gān Bǎo's *Sōushénjì* states:
"Pánhù,
originally an old woman in Emperor Gāoxīnshì's palace.
She had an ear ailment,
a doctor probed to treat it,
and something as big as a cocoon came out.
It was placed in a gourd dipper,
and covered with a plate,
after a while it transformed into a dog.
Its markings were five-colored,
hence named Pánhù."
The *Zá Wǔxíng Shū* states:
"A white dog with tiger stripes,
the Lord of the Southern Dipper: keeping it can bring ten thousand dàn.
A black dog with white ears,
is the Great King's dog,
keeping it,
brings wealth and honor;
a black dog with white front feet,
benefits descendants;
a white dog with a yellow head,
brings great fortune to the household;
a yellow dog with a white tail,
generations will have officials;
a yellow dog with white front feet,
benefits people."
Metal Domestic Animal, Dipper Essence
Yìng Shào's *Fēngsútōng* states:
"Killing a dog and dismembering it for exorcism,
the dog is a metal domestic animal.
Exorcism,
means to ward off,
to suppress metal so it does no harm."
The *Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu* states:
"Seven times nine is sixty-three,
yang energy penetrates,
therefore the Dipper moves,
and dogs are born after three months."
Sòng Jūn's annotation states:
"The dog,
is born from the essence of the Dipper."
Black Dragon, Green Zhān
Táo Qián's *Sōushénjì* states:
"Zhāng Rán of Guàijī Jùzhāng,
kept a very swift dog,
named Black Dragon."
Zhōu Chǔ's *Fēngtǔjì* states:
"Dogs include Green Zhān, White Sparrow,
Flying Dragon, Tiger Cub.
Docile, swift, alert,
hard to befriend but easy to command."
Erect Ears, Focused Spirit
Jiǎ Dàizōng's *Dàgǒu Fù* states:
"Erecting ears to listen attentively."
The *Sōushénjì* states:
"Zhāng Rán had a young wife,
who had an affair with a slave.
They plotted to murder Rán,
and prepared a meal to eat together,
the slave drew a knife and leaned against the door.
Rán had a dog named Black Dragon,
its spirit focused, licking its lips and watching the slave,
Rán also sensed it,
and shouted loudly:
'Black Dragon!'
The dog responded by wounding the slave.
The slave fell to the ground,
and [Rán] then took the knife and killed him."
Yellow Chin, Red Pupil
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
"Xiǎn,
a black dog with a yellow chin."
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Coursing Hound" says:
"Turning its gaze, light flows,
vermilion glows, red pupils."
Long Ears, Short Snout
The Báizé Tú states:
"A black dog with a white head,
long ears and curled tail,
is a dragon."
The Cài Shì Qīng Lùn states:
"The rabbit that gazes afar,
the pig with white hooves,
the dog with a short snout,
the horse with a long head.
These beasts,
still show their nature through their form and posture;
how much more so the appearance of a gentleman,
surely it is not without external signs?"
Lǚ Áo, Zhōu Dog
The Shàngshū states:
"The Western Lǚ presented áo."
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn states:
"Duke Líng had a Zhōu dog,
called an áo."
Bell Hooves, Saw Teeth
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Coursing Hound" says:
"Stretching joints, taut sinews,
leopard ears, dragon form.
Hooves like knotted bells,
body formed of five fish."
Zhōu Chù's Fēngtǔ Jì states:
"Dogs include the Qīng Zhān, Bái Què,
Fēilóng, Hǔzǐ, Xiē Xiāo, Wǔ Yú,
wolf teeth, saw teeth."
Sòng Nào, Hán Lú
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"In the village lane, dogs fought.
It was a Sòng man's mediocre dog.
His family named it Nào.
Chasing the dog but not catching it,
he stopped and gazed after it,
thinking himself at fault."
The Zhànguó Cè states:
"Qí wished to attack Wèi.
Chúnyú Kūn said to the King of Qí:
'Hán Lú
is the mightiest hound in the world;
Dōngguō Qūn
is the craftiest hare within the seas.
Hán Lú chased Dōngguō Qūn,
three times around the mountain,
five leaps over the peaks.
The hare exhausted itself ahead, the dog tired itself behind,
each died where it was.'"
White Head, White Teeth
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"On Yīn Mountain there is a beast,
its shape like a wildcat.
White head,
its name is Tiāngǒu."
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Coursing Hound" says:
"Feet suspend hooked claws,
mouth holds white teeth.
Head resembles a soaring chī-dragon,
tail like a leaping snake."
Delivering Letters, Carrying an Egg
The Shùyì Jì states:
"Lù Jī's home was in Wú.
He said to his dog:
'My family has absolutely no letters.'
He tied a bamboo tube to the dog's neck.
The dog swiftly ran towards Wú.
His family wrote a reply,
placed it inside the bamboo tube,
and it galloped back to Luò."
Guō Yuánshēng's Shùzhēng Jì states:
"A palace woman of ancient Xú State
conceived and gave birth to an egg,
which she abandoned by the water's edge.
There was a dog named Hòu Cāng,
who carried it back.
Soon it became a person,
and thus became the heir of Xú."
Duì Hexagram, Dǒu Constellation Essence
The Yì states:
"Duì represents the dog."
Sòng Jūn said:
"The dog
is born from the Dǒu constellation."
Lú Líng, Lǚ Áo
The Máo Shī, "Guó Fēng," states:
"The Lú bell tinkles,
that man is handsome and kind.
The Lú with double rings,
that man is handsome and strong."
The Shàngshū states:
"The Western Lǚ presented áo,
the Grand Guardian then composed the 'Lǚ Áo'."
Qīng Qiāo, Huáng Cāng
The Xījīng Zájì states:
"Yáng Wànnián's hunting dog was named Qīng Qiāo,
worth a hundred gold pieces."
The Chén Shū states:
"After Zhāng Biāo was defeated,
he left with his wife, Lady Yáng.
Only the dog he raised, Huáng Cāng, was before and behind them,
never leaving."
Wū Lóng, Chì Hǔ
The Sōushén Jì states:
"A man of Kuàijī, Zhāng Rán, kept a very swift dog,
named Wū Lóng."
The Sānguó Diǎnlüè states:
"Qí Gāo Wěi considered the Fúsī dog to be Chì Hǔ."
Bark at a Shape, See the Head
The Qiánfū Lùn states:
"One dog barks at a shape,
a hundred dogs bark at the sound."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"When hungry horses fill the stable,
they are quiet, not seeing fodder;
when hungry dogs fill the palace,
they are quiet, not seeing the head.
Seeing the head and the fodder,
then their movement cannot be stopped."
Suspended Hoof, Huge Mouth
The Shuōwén states:
"Quǎn,
is the dog that has suspended hooves."
It also states:
"Jiǎo,
is a young dog.
The Xiōngnú have jiǎo dogs,
with huge mouths and black bodies."
Chase a Deer, Seize a Hare
The Shǐjì states:
"A dog chasing a deer does not look back at a hare."
Fàn Suī advised King Zhāo of Qín:
'For Qín to govern the feudal lords,
is like unleashing Hán Lú to seize a lame hare.'"
Yínyín, Ái'ái
The Chǔ Cí states:
"Fierce dogs yínyín, barking to meet me;
passes and bridges closed, impassable."
The Guǎnzǐ states:
"When Guǎn Zhòng was about to die,
he said to Duke Huán:
'There is a dog barking ái'ái,
morning and evening,
wanting to bite my thigh, yet I do not die.
You must remove it.'
He meant Yì Yá and Shù Diāo would certainly cause rebellion.'"
Huáng Ěr, Bái Cāng
The Shùyì Jì states:
"Lù Jī in his youth enjoyed hunting.
In Wú,
a powerful guest presented a swift dog,
named Huáng Ěr.
Jī later served in Luò.
Jokingly he said to the dog:
'My family has absolutely no letters.
Can you gallop there?'
The dog wagged its tail and made sounds in response.
Jī wrote a letter,
placed it in a bamboo tube,
and tied it to the dog's neck.
The dog swiftly ran towards Wú.
His family wrote a reply, placed it inside the bamboo tube,
and it galloped back to Luò."
Guō Yuánshēng's Shùzhēng Jì states:
"A palace woman of ancient Xú State conceived and gave birth to an egg,
which she abandoned by the water's edge.
There was a dog named Bái Cāng,
who carried it back.
Soon it became a person,
and thus became the heir of Xú."
Traveling a hundred lǐ, three chǐ tall
The Biography of King Mù states:
"The Son of Heaven's dogs travel a hundred lǐ,
capturing tigers and leopards."
Guǒ Bān's "Colloquialisms of Wèi and Jìn" says:
"In the seventh year of Tàikāng,
beneath the suburban altar to Heaven,
there was a white dog,
three chǐ tall,
its fur bright and lustrous.
It constantly lay still,
but upon seeing people, it would depart."
Wèi dynasty Jiǎ Dàizōng's "Rhapsody on the Great Dog"
I was born amidst the flourishing governance of the great Wèi,
yet encountered a royal road not yet opened.
Advancing, I could not achieve merit to amend faults;
retreating, I could not wield the strategies to defend the state.
The Emperor asked, "Who shall advise?"
I was expelled to the northern wilderness.
Crossing that western frontier,
a great dog was captured.
Its head,
cannot be fully described;
its bone structure,
cannot be clearly distinguished and explained.
Majestic and imposing,
a fierce and powerful appearance.
Proudly standing eight or nine chǐ tall,
its form like an arrowhead,
its features as if carved.
Fur surpassing purple brilliance,
double eyebrows like white jade discs.
At times stretching and shaking vigorously,
like a winged dragon leaping and darting.
Claws akin to blades and spears,
teeth like interlocking halberds.
Hearing the clamor of forest beasts,
it suddenly breaks chains and crushes stones.
Against the wind it howls long,
seeking wild birds.
Nose sniffing faint scents,
eyes discerning light tracks.
Glaring and bursting with rage,
swiftly shaking and bristling.
As if the celestial beam snapped,
the earthly pillar split,
dragging down a white elephant, breaking its back,
biting and pulling the six-hued beast, snapping its spine.
Pushing aside bears and brown bears, shattering their chests,
seizing beast heads, severing their arteries.
Where claws strike, like swords slicing,
where teeth wound, like spear thrusts.
Seeing it in the moment before death,
blood springs forth like arrows shooting.
Thus driving the great herd of deer,
into the steep narrows of a deep valley.
Those fleeing die first,
those advancing are struck,
none left before,
not a single one behind.
Yet in its subdued state,
it reveres its master and recognizes people.
By day, no peeping intruders;
by night, no treacherous guests.
Hearing through a hundred lǐ,
barking fiercely through the night.
If barbarians disturb Xià,
and warriors differ in conduct.
Light coffins singly gathered,
men and horses gagged.
The fierce fire first perceives,
the sound just shatters.
Ears pricked, listening sideways, then Héng Shān trembles;
facing south and growling, then Huò Shān crumbles.
Eyes glaring straight ahead, then layered hills collapse;
roaring and charging forth, then heavy gates burst open.
Not merely beneficial for my hunting,
but indeed able to secure the state and guard the four borders.
In the past, a man of Sòng had the fame of Què;
Hán state treasured its great Lú.
Mímíng roused it against the giant áo;
Pánhù received it from the barbarian capital.
Famed dogs through a hundred generations,
dare any other dog compare?
Surpassing the swift-trotting xiēxiāo,
how could the Lú Lìng be worth recording?
Western Jìn Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Coursing Hound"
Indeed, none is as light and swift as the hawk,
none as fierce and agile as the tiger.
Only the fine hound, by its innate nature,
combines the vigor and prowess of these two paragons.
Responding to the radiant light of Heaven and humanity,
conforming to celestial patterns and dwelling nearby.
Relying on the harmonious energy of water and wood,
tempering metallic essence to aid itself.
Gathering black-beaked creatures in the autumn quarter,
residing within the primal substance's inner abode.
Truly, Hán Lú could not withstand it,
how could the Jìn áo hope to resist?
Then it crossed Lú Spring,
traversed flowing sands.
Passed beyond the three lights,
spanned the great river.
Rare in generations, it came as tribute,
becoming a treasure for the imperial house.
Its bone structure remarkably unusual,
its appearance admirable.
Feet dangling hooked claws,
mouth holding pure white teeth.
Head resembling a soaring chī dragon,
tail like a coiling snake.
Long neck, broad flanks,
wide in front, tapered behind.
Full skull, close-set ears,
long bifurcation, relaxed mouth.
Extending joints, taut sinews,
leopard ears, dragon form.
Hooves like fastened bells,
five-fish body perfected.
Momentum as if scaling azure clouds,
eyes like stars in a spring.
Turning its gaze, light flows,
vermilion glow, crimson essence.
Shaking Rú Huáng and awing Sòng Què,
surpassing ancient marvels and spreading fame.
Thus seeking faint tracks,
treading leftover traces.
Form swift as leaping waves,
momentum like a startled dragon.
Outdistancing the morning crow's light swiftness,
halting fierce beasts' fleeing paths.
Drifting like shooting stars, scenes connecting,
passing through profound darkness and soaring up.
Scaling ridges, crossing gullies,
traversing mountains, leaping valleys.
On plains, none escape;
in forests, no deer hide.
Gazing at zhǐ marshes, frolicking and roaming,
strolling on lán banks, galloping freely.
Then delighting the will in parks and enclosures,
wandering carefree on the middle road.
Focusing on lush grasses awaiting tracks,
pursuing the crafty hare of the eastern outskirts.
Already vast and expansive,
displaying wondrous sight along the long road.
Both swift and unmatched before,
yet leisurely and measured.
Joy reaching its peak, emotions released,
speedy feet not yet wearied.
Restraining martial ferocity to submit to the net,
obeying commands and turning back.
Attributing merit and beauty to the leash-holder,
unlike Pánhù's unforeseen end.
Grateful for nurturing and cherishing virtue,
wishing to be employed in later hunts.
Hearing the carriage's jingling bells,
the swift xiēxiāo lingers, pacing to and fro.
Deer, Eleventh
The Erya says:
"Deer:
the male is called jiā,
the female is called yōu,
their young are called mí,
the exceptionally strong ones,
are called jiān."
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says:
"Yáoguāng scatters and becomes deer.
If the Jiāng and Huái rivers are not sacrificed to, then Yáoguāng does not shine brightly,
and pigs give birth to deer."
The Hengbo Zhuan says:
"A deer's antlers fall off by themselves after three years."
The Shiji says:
"In ancient times, leather currency was used,
and feudal lords employed it for diplomatic gifts and offerings.
They used a square foot of white deer skin,
edged with painted patterns as currency,
valued at four hundred thousand.
When kings, marquises, and feudal lords attended court audiences, presented offerings, or conducted diplomatic missions,
they were required to use this currency,
presenting it along with jade discs,
before they could proceed."
The Han Xi Yi Zhuan says:
"In Yúnnán County, there is a divine deer with two heads,
which feeds on poisonous plants."
The Baopuzi says:
"Deer live for a thousand years;
after reaching five hundred years, their fur turns white."
The Ruiying Tu says:
"When a ruler inherits the laws and institutions of the former sages,
without any loss or omission,
then white deer appear."
The Erya says:
"Jīng,
is a large páo,
(pronounced bó jiāo fǎn).
It has an ox's tail and a single horn.
Jī,
is a large jūn,
with hairy fur and dog-like feet."
Máo,
refers to long, hairy tails.
The Shuowen says:
"Jī is sometimes written as jǐ,
or sometimes as jīng."
Four White Deer Drawing a Carriage Six Flying Deer
The Yuejue Shu says:
"King Gōujiàn of Yuè possessed a treasured sword.
Xuē Zhú said:
'This is Jùquē,
not a treasured sword.'
The king said:
'Indeed.
When Jùquē was first completed,
I was sitting on the dew altar,
when in the palace, four white deer drawing a carriage passed by,
startling the galloping chariot.'"
The Chunqiu Liming Xu says:
"The divine carriage is drawn by six flying deer,
transforming over three hundred years."
Three-Horned Seven Stars
Fu Hou's Gujin Zhu says:
"In the ninth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
a three-horned deer appeared in Jiānglíng."
Liú Jìngshū's Yiyuan says:
"Péng Zēng of Lè'ān, Póyáng, shot a deer,
and between its antlers was a Daoist seven-star talisman,
which also contained the name, hometown, and dates of his ancestor.
Thereupon, he gave up hunting."
Seeking Companions Bleating Fawn
The Chuci says:
"Flying birds call to their flock,
and deer bleat seeking their companions.
Strike the gōng note and the gōng responds;
pluck the jué note and the jué resonates."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's Short Song says:
"The roaming deer bleat softly,
carrying grass in their mouths, the fawns cry.
Graceful flying birds,
nest with their young tucked under their wings."
Yellow-Clad Purple-Patterned
Liú Yìqìng's Youming Lu says:
"Xiè Kūn of Chénjùn
once stayed overnight in a pavilion
that had a history of causing deaths.
Late in the fourth watch,
a yellow-clad figure called Yòuyú to open the door,
then extended an arm through the window.
Xiè Kūn grasped the wrist
and pulled with all his might,
causing the arm to detach, and the figure fled.
The next day, upon inspection,
it turned out to be a deer's leg.
Following the trail of blood, he captured the deer."
Táo Qián's Soushen Houji says:
"A man named Lái from Huáinán
was planting beans in his field
when he suddenly saw two women
of exceptional beauty,
wearing purple-patterned jackets and green skirts.
Though it was raining, their clothes remained dry.
On his wall hung a bronze mirror,
and in the mirror, he saw two deer.
He struck them with a knife and captured them,
making dried meat from them."
Qí's Pursuit Róng's Hindrance
The Han Shi Waizhuan says:
"Duke Jǐng of Qí pursued a white deer to Mǔqiū,
where he met a border official who said:
'May our lord live long,
devalue gold and jade,
and treasure the common people.'
The duke said:
'Well said.'"
The Zuozhuan says:
"It is like hunting a deer:
the people of Jìn seize it by the horns,
while the various Róng tribes pull it by the legs."
Awarded a Hundred Jin of Gold Lives a Thousand Years
The Guanzi says:
"Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
'Chǔ is a powerful state.
If we raise an army to attack it,
I fear our strength may be insufficient.
What should we do?'
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
'My lord, offer a high price to buy their deer,
and immediately build a city spanning a hundred lǐ.
Send people with twenty million coins
to purchase live deer from the people of Chǔ.'
The people of Chǔ abandoned their farming to hunt deer.
Guǎn Zhòng then informed the merchants of Chǔ:
'For delivering live deer,
you will be awarded a hundred jīn of gold;
for ten deliveries, a thousand jīn of gold.'"
The Baopuzi says:
"Deer live for a thousand years;
after reaching five hundred years, their fur turns white."
Lǎozǐ Riding a Deer Queen Mother's Messenger
Cuī Xuánshān's Laixiang Ji Li Mu Bei says:
"Lǎozǐ descended riding a white deer and entrusted himself to Mother Lǐ."
Sūn Róuzhī's Ruiying Tu says:
"During the time of the Yellow Emperor,
the Queen Mother of the West sent a messenger riding a white deer
to present a white jade ring as an auspicious token,
symbolizing the metal element of the west."
Yú Shìnán's Ode to the White Deer
Only the splendid achievements of the imperial king
manifest the auspicious signs of the emperor's virtue.
There is an auspicious beast from the metal element of the west,
which reveals its luminous form in the famous capital.
It is both tame and harmonious in the suburban fields,
and also leaps and rests in the mountain corners.
Its plain fur displays colors,
its frosty hairs correspond to the diagrams.
It feasts with honored guests in elegant poetry,
and accompanies immortal travelers on the celestial road.
Thus, it can establish beautiful auspicious signs
and spread its fame through the canons and plans.
Wú Xuē Zǒng's Eulogy to the White Deer
Gleaming white deer,
with a gentle and tame physique.
Its substance is bright and shining,
like swan geese or frost.
Rabbit, Chapter Twelve
The Erya says:
"A rabbit's young is called fù,
(pronounced fū wàn fǎn).
Its tracks are called háng;
the exceptionally strong ones are called xīn."
The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says:
"Yùhéng scatters and becomes rabbits."
The Liji says:
"In the rites of sacrificing at the ancestral temple,
the rabbit is called 'bright-eyed.'"
Fu Hou's Gujin Zhu says:
"In the first year of the Jiànpíng era,
a white rabbit was captured in Shānyáng,
with eyes as red as cinnabar."
The Shanhaijing says:
"On Dàchí Mountain, there is a beast like a rabbit
with a rat's head.
It uses its back to fly,
and is named the flying rabbit.
It flies away using the hair on its back."
Wáng Chōng's Lunheng says:
"A female rabbit becomes pregnant by licking the male's fur,
and when giving birth,
the young emerge from its mouth."
The Ruiying Tu says:
"The red rabbit is an auspicious beast;
Red Eyes Flying on Back
Fú Hóu's *Notes on Past and Present* states:
"In the first year of the Jiànpíng era of Emperor Chéng,
a white rabbit was obtained in Shānyáng,
its eyes were red like cinnabar."
*The Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"On Tiānchí Mountain there is a beast like a rabbit,
with a rat's head.
It flies using its back,
named the flying rabbit.
It flies using the hair on its back."
Obtaining Kneecaps Presenting Shoulder
Yìng Shào's *Comprehensive Meaning of Customs* states:
"Rabbit kneecaps:
common custom says that during the Là and Zhēng festivals when offering sacrifices to ancestors and eating,
whoever obtains rabbit kneecaps,
calls them 'fortune'.
They are rewarded with cold wine,
and the fortunate one brings people good luck."
*Dōngguān Records of the Hàn* states:
"When Wáng Láng was pursuing him,
he galloped from east of Jì southeast to Nángōng.
Féng Yì presented wheat porridge and rabbit shoulder,
and thus they crossed the Hūtuó River."
Disturbing the Chamber Circling the Mountain
Fàn Yè's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Cài Yōng was by nature sincerely filial.
When his mother died,
he built a hut beside the tomb mound.
There was a rabbit that tamely disturbed his chamber."
*Strategies of the Warring States* states:
"Qí wanted to attack Wèi.
Chúnyú Kūn said to the King of Qí:
'Hán Lú
is the mightiest hound in the world;
Dōngguō Qūn
is the craftiest rabbit within the seas.
Hán Lú chased Dōngguō Qūn,
they circled the mountain three times,
leapt over the mountain five times.
The rabbit was exhausted ahead,
the hound was worn out behind.
An old farmer saw them,
and without the toil and fatigue, he seized their achievement.'"
Pounding Medicine Mixing Elixir
Fù Xuán's *Song Lyrics* state:
"The rabbit pounding medicine in the moon—how can that suffice to speak of?
The divine crow sporting among the clouds—how can that suffice to speak of?"
*Bàopǔzǐ* states:
"The method for the Hé'ān Elixir:
mix rabbit blood with cinnabar and honey,
steam it for one hundred days.
Take two pills the size of wútóng seeds.
After one hundred days,
two divine maidens will come to attend,
and you can command them."
Leisurely Nimble
*The Máo Poetry* states:
"'Rabbit, Leisurely',
lamenting Zhōu.
There is a rabbit, leisurely,
a pheasant caught in the net."
It also states:
"Nimble is the crafty rabbit,
meeting a hound it is caught.
Coming and going are the circulating words,
the heart keeps count of them."
Dancing at Hào Roaming the Tomb
*The Bamboo Annals* states:
"In the third year of King Xuān,
there was a rabbit dancing at Hào."
Xiè Chéng's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Fāng Chǔ, styled Shèngmíng,
lost his father young,
and served his mother filially.
When his mother died,
he carried earth to form a tomb mound,
planting a thousand rare trees.
Luan birds perched upon them,
white rabbits roamed below."
Shooting Heads Carving Fur
Fàn Yè's *Book of the Later Hàn* states:
"Liú Kūn,
during Wáng Mǎng's time,
taught disciples,
constantly over five hundred people.
Every spring and autumn during the sacrificial feast and archery ceremony,
he always prepared and arranged the classical rituals.
Using plain wood and gourd leaves for sacrificial vessels,
mulberry bows and mugwort arrows,
to shoot at rabbit heads.
Each month when performing the rites,
the county magistrate would lead his officials to observe."
Zhāng Fán's *Records of the Hàn* states:
"Liáng Jì established a rabbit park in Hénán,
issued moving directives to the localities,
transferring and breeding live rabbits.
He carved their fur as a mark.
Anyone who violated this faced punishment up to death."
Eastern Jìn Wáng Yì's "Rhapsody on the Rabbit"
states: August is the great Jìn,
our ancestors' glory shines again.
Firm is the thick earth as our foundation,
vast are the heavenly cords as our guiding principle.
We shall soon don court robes to cross the Jiāng,
spreading proclamations to ten thousand states.
Return the imperial coffin to the old burial ground,
and serve the sagely emperor in Luòyáng.
Establish the distant fortune of the restoration,
and match the Two Forms in length.
Thus in antiquity, those with virtue received auspicious signs and enjoyed eternal peace,
those without virtue could not bear them and they became disasters.
Red crows descended upon King Wén of Zhōu,
and he still proclaimed, 'How excellent!'
Mulberry and grain grew in the Yīn court,
but King Zhòngzōng restrained himself to achieve benevolence.
Pheasants alighted on the tripod's ears,
and King Wǔdīng blamed himself to teach purity.
Fox, Thirteenth
*Shuōwén Jiězì* states:
"Fox,
a demonic beast,
ridden by ghosts.
It has three virtues:
its color is harmonious and balanced,
small in front, large behind,
when dying, its head faces the mound.
From the radical 'dog', with 'melon' sound."
*Ěryǎ* states:
"Raccoon dog, fox, badger, and raccoon dog,
are a category.
Their feet are padded,
their tracks are called 'niǔ'."
Niǔ,
pronounced zhǐ tóu fǎn.
*Báihǔ Tōng* states:
"When a fox dies, its head faces the mound,
not forgetting its origin,
showing it does not forget danger.
When virtue reaches birds and beasts,
then the nine-tailed fox appears; nine
signifies matching obtains its proper place,
offspring multiply and flourish.
As for the tail,
posterity shall be prosperous."
*Chūnqiū Qiántán Bā* states:
"When the white fox arrives,
the people benefit;
if it does not arrive, those below become arrogant and willful."
*The Classic of Mountains and Seas* states:
"On Wǔdū Mountain,
the Black Water emerges.
Upon it are dark foxes with bushy tails."
Guō's *Records from the Mysterious Mean* states:
"A thousand-year-old fox becomes a licentious woman,
a hundred-year-old fox becomes a beautiful woman."
*The Daoist's Record of Famous Mountains* states:
"The fox
is a licentious woman of ancient times.
Her name was Zǐ.
Zǐ transformed into a fox,
therefore many such monsters call themselves Ā Zǐ."
*Bàopǔzǐ, Jade Tablet Records* states:
"Foxes, raccoon dogs, and wolves all live eight hundred years.
Upon reaching three hundred years,
they temporarily transform into human form."
*Poetry Meaning Inquiry* states:
"The category of fox
includes raccoon dog, badger, and raccoon.
The young of the raccoon dog is called huán.
The huán's shape differs from the raccoon dog category;
common people all call it huán.
Pronounced hú xuǎn fǎn.
The young of the raccoon dog resembles the raccoon."
*Ěryǎ* states:
"The young of the raccoon dog is huán.
The female is called 'máo',
pronounced cái zhài fǎn.
Nowadays, Jiāngdōng calls the raccoon dog 'máo'.
The young of the badger is huān."
Badger,
is also called 'tún'.
Another name is huān.
It also states:
"The young of the raccoon is 'huān'."
Nowadays, some call the raccoon 'húlí' (fox-raccoon).
Fear of Dogs Head Towards the Hill
Liú Jìngshū's "Yì Yuàn" states:
"Hú Dàoqià claimed to be from Guǎnglíng,
and was fond of music and medical arts.
His body had a pungent odor,
so he often used fine incense to mask it,
but he particularly feared fierce dogs.
Knowing the day of his death,
he warned his disciples:
'Once my breath ceases, bury me immediately,
do not let dogs see my corpse.'
He died in Shānyáng,
and after encoffining, the coffin felt empty.
Upon opening it to look,
the corpse was nowhere to be seen.
People at the time all said he was a fox."
"The Book of Rites" states:
"The ancients had a saying:
'When a fox dies, its head faces the hill,
this is benevolence.'" "The White Tiger Discussions" states:
"When a fox dies, its head faces the hill,
not forgetting its origin."
Holding Fire Listening to Ice
"The Biography of Guǎn Lù" states:
"At night, two small creatures like beasts,
holding fire in their hands,
blew on it with their mouths.
A scholar raised a knife and cut them at the waist,
looking at them, they were foxes.
From then on, there were no fire disasters."
Guō Yuánshēng's "Shù Zhēng Jì" states:
"When the north wind is strong,
and the river ice begins to form,
it is necessary for foxes to walk on it.
It is said this creature is good at listening;
it listens for no sound of water under the ice,
and then crosses the river."
Possessing Three Virtues Leading All Beasts
Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén" states:
"The fox,
is a demonic beast,
ridden by ghosts.
It possesses three virtues:
its color is harmonious and balanced,
small in front and large in back,
and when it dies, its head faces the hill."
"The Strategies of the Warring States" states:
King Xuān of Chǔ asked his ministers:
'I hear the people of the north fear Zhāo Xīxù,
is this truly so?'
Jiāng Yǐ replied:
'A tiger sought all beasts to eat them,
and caught a fox.'
The fox said:
'The Heavenly Emperor commanded me to lead all beasts,
now if you eat me,
you would be defying the Heavenly Emperor's command.
If you do not believe me,
I will walk ahead of you,
you follow behind me,
and see if any beast dares not flee upon seeing me?'
The tiger thought it reasonable,
and so went with it.
All beasts fled upon seeing them."
Responding to Xià Yǔ Auspicious for Zhōu Wén
Zhào Yè's "Wú Yuè Chūnqiū" states:
"Yǔ was thirty and still unmarried.
Traveling to Túshān,
he feared the time was late and he would have no heir,
saying:
'My marriage,
must have a sign!'
Then a nine-tailed white fox came before Yǔ.
Yǔ said:
'White,
is the color of my garments.
Nine tails,
are the proof.'
Then the people of Túshān sang:
'Graceful white fox,
nine tails lush and full.
Establishing household and family,
our capital shall prosper.'
Thereupon he married the woman of Túshān."
Guō Pú's "Shānhǎijīng Tú Zàn" states:
"An auspicious sign for Zhōu Wén."
Jìn Dynasty Guō Pú's "Shānhǎijīng Tú Jiǔ Hú Zàn"
The wondrous beast of Qīngqiū,
the nine-tailed fox.
Appears when the Way soars,
emerges bearing a book in its mouth.
An auspicious sign for Zhōu Wén,
marking divine tallies.
Rat, Fourteenth
"Shuōwén" states:
"Shǔ (rat),
is the general name for burrowing creatures.
Pictographic.
All characters related to shǔ derive from it."
"Ěryǎ" states:
"Fén shǔ (mole rat),
travels underground.
Yǎn shǔ (hamster),
stores food in its cheek pouches.
Xī shǔ (tiny rat),
has a poisonous bite.
Sī shǔ (sī rat)
pronounced 'sī' above.
Yòu shǔ (weasel),
today's weasel resembles a diāo (marten),
reddish-yellow in color,
with a large tail,
and eats mice.
In Jiāngdōng it is called shēng.
Qú shǔ (shrew),
pronounced 'qú'.
A small jīngqú (shrew).
Shí shǔ (large field rat),
shaped large like a rat,
head like a rabbit,
tail has fur.
Greenish-yellow in color,
likes to eat millet and beans in the fields.
In Guānzhōng it is called qú shǔ.
Bào wén tíng shǔ (leopard-patterned tíng rat),
pronounced 'tíng'.
Patterned like a leopard.
Jú shǔ (jú rat),
pronounced 'gú mì fǎn'.
Resembles a rat but is bluish-black,
lives in trees.
Wú shǔ yí yóu (flying squirrel)."
Shaped like a small fox,
resembles a bat,
with fleshy wings.
Flies and nurses its young,
also called 'flying birth',
its call sounds like a human voice.
"Shuōwén" states:
"The fén shǔ (mole rat),
is transformed by the bóláo (shrike);
shǔ (rat),
is what commands mice."
Shù Xī's "Fā Méng Jì" states:
"The Western Regions have cloth from fire rats,
the Eastern Sea has wood that does not turn to ash."
Yú Huàn's "Wèi Lüè" states:
"The country of Dàqín has poison-warding rats."
Liú Jìngshū's "Yì Yuàn" states:
"The Western Regions have a kingdom of rat kings,
where large rats are as big as dogs,
medium ones like rabbits,
and small ones like ordinary rats.
Their heads are all white.
If merchants passing through their kingdom
do not first pray and make offerings,
they will gnaw on people's clothes."
"Shānhǎijīng" states:
"On Dānxūn Mountain,
there is a beast.
Its shape is like a rat,
but with a rabbit's head and deer's ears.
It flies using its tail,
named the ěr shǔ (ear rat).
It can ward off all poisons."
"Zhèng Shì's Xuán Zhōng Jì" states:
"A hundred-year-old rat
transforms into a bat."
"Jìn Tàikāng Dì Jì" states:
"Niǎoshǔ Mountain is in Shǒuyáng County, Lǒngxī.
The rats' tails are short like domestic rats.
Their burrows go three or four chǐ deep,
with rats inside
and birds outside."
Dèng Démíng's "Nánkāng Jì" states:
"In the stone chamber of Nánkāng's Yīng Mountain,
there is a golden rat,
sometimes seen among a hundred strange phenomena."
"Zhān Shū" states:
"If a rat gnaws on a person's collar,
good fortune will arrive,
auspicious."
"Běncǎo" states:
"Yǎn shǔ (mole rat),
in the world also called yǐn shǔ (hidden rat).
Shaped like a rat but without a tail,
black with a long nose."
"Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"When a mole rat drinks from the river,
it drinks no more than fills its belly."
Eating Fire, Drinking Spring Water
The Erya says:
"The flying squirrel is called yíyóu."
Guō Pú notes:
"It resembles a small fox,
eats smoke and fire.
It can descend from heights,
but cannot ascend from below."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nányuè Zhì:
"The bamboo rat resembles a mole rat,
often burrowing in the ground,
drinking spring water and gnawing bamboo."
Carrying Embers, Gnawing Saddles
Shì Fǎxiǎn's Fóyóu Běnjì says:
"At the Jetavana Monastery,
incense was burned and lamps kept lit,
day and night without cease.
A mouse carried an ember and burned the banners and canopies,
eventually reducing the entire monastery to ashes."
The Wèi Zhì says:
"Dèng'āi Wáng Cáo Chōng,
styled Cāngshū.
At that time, military and state affairs were numerous,
and punishments were severe.
The Grand Ancestor's saddle was in the storehouse,
and was gnawed by a rat.
When reported to the Grand Ancestor,
he laughed and said:
'Even my son's clothes beside him were gnawed,
let alone a saddle hanging on a pillar?'"
Jade Stars, Golden Chambers
The Chūnqiū Yùndòu Shū says:
"The Jade Balance Star scattered and became rats."
Dèng Démíng's Nánkāng Jì says:
"In Nánkāng, there is a stone chamber in the mountains,
called the Golden Hall,
golden inside.
Golden rats are occasionally seen there."
White Tail, Gray Fur
Guō Pú's Dònglín says:
"In Xuānchéng Commandery, there is a hidden rat,
as large as an ox,
shaped like a rat,
with feet like an elephant.
Each foot has three nails,
all resembling donkey hooves.
Its body is red,
with white on its chest and the base of its tail."
The Yìwù Zhì says:
"The mother rat
has a head and feet like a rat.
Its fur is gray, its mouth sharp,
as large as a water buffalo,
yet it fears dogs.
When there are external disasters in the paddy fields,
they originate from rats."
Stealing Meat, Holding Pearls
The Shǐjì says:
"Zhāng Tāng,
a man of Dùlíng,
his father was the Assistant Magistrate of Cháng'ān.
While Zhāng Tāng was guarding the house,
upon returning, he found that rats had stolen meat.
His father angrily whipped him.
Zhāng Tāng dug into the rat burrow,
found the rat and the remaining meat,
and prosecuted the rat, subjecting it to interrogation."
Liú Jìngshū's Yìyuàn says:
"During the Jǐngpíng era,
there was a great flood in Dōngyáng.
Cài Xǐfū of Yǒngkāng took refuge at Nánlǒng.
At night, a large rat
came floating on the water.
It crouched at the corner of Xǐfū's servant's bed.
The servant took pity and did not harm it,
often giving it food.
After the floodwaters receded,
Xǐfū was able to return to his former residence.
The rat, using its front paws, held up a blue silk-wrapped paper,
containing about three catties of pearls,
and placed it before the servant's bed,
chirping as if wanting to speak."
Having Skin, Lacking Bones
The Máo Shī says:
"Observing the Rat,
criticizing lack of propriety.
Observing the rat, it has skin;
but a person without dignity.
A person without dignity,
why not die?"
Gān Bǎo's Sōushén Jì says:
"During the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
in Kuàijī Commandery, crabs and crabs all transformed into rats,
which devoured rice in great quantities,
causing disaster.
Those newly formed had flesh but no bones."
White Belly, Gray Back
The Guǎngzhì says:
"The white gibbon rat,
has a long tail and white belly.
Skilled at climbing,
slightly different from ordinary rats."
Guō Pú says:
"It resembles a small fox,
like a bat,
with fleshy feet and a short tail,
purple fur on its head and flanks.
Gray patterns on its back,
yellow below its belly,
with a mottled white snout and neck."
Long Claws, Short Tail
The Erya says:
"The flying squirrel is called yíyóu."
Guō Pú notes:
"It resembles a small fox,
with short feet and long claws."
The Guǎngzhì says:
"The mole rat has deep-set eyes and a short tail."
Eating Birds, Destroying Oxen
The Erya says:
"The yǎn rat."
Guō Pú notes:
"In Jiāngdōng, what is called the yǎn rat
resembles a rat.
Large and eats birds,
found in trees."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's Letter to Wáng Lǎng says:
"Though bedbugs are small,
they disturb peaceful sleep.
Though the xī rat is tiny,
it can still destroy a sacrificial ox."
Flying Tail, Soaring Back
The Shānhǎi Jīng says:
"On Dānxūn Mountain,
there is a beast.
Its shape resembles a rat,
with a rabbit's head and elk's ears.
Its cry is like a barking dog,
it flies using its tail,
and is named the ear rat."
Guō Pú's Shānhǎi Jīng Tú Fēishǔ Zàn says:
"Some soar with their tails,
some ascend with their whiskers.
Flying, crying, beating their wings,
suddenly soaring on their backs.
Truly without fixed abode,
only by divine power are they borne."
Ten Thousand Catties of Flesh, Three Hundred Years of Life
Dōngfāng Shuò's Shényì Jì says:
"In the north, at the glacial ravines,
rats emerge from beneath the ice.
Their appearance resembles rats,
with flesh weighing ten thousand catties."
The Bàopǔzǐ·Yùcè Jì states:
"Rats live three hundred years;
when full-aged, they turn white.
They are adept at using humans for divination,
and are named Zhòng.
They can know the auspicious and inauspicious events of a year and matters a thousand miles away."
Seen at the Eastern Palace, Captured in the Northern Garden
The Jìn Qǐjū Zhù says:
"In the fifth month of the first year of Yuánkāng,
a white rat was once seen at the Eastern Palace."
The Hòu Wèi Shū says:
"In the spring of the third year of Yǒngxīng,
a white rat was captured in the Northern Garden,
and soon died.
Upon dissection,
all three offspring in its belly were white."
The "Ode to the Destructive Rat" by Lú Yuánmíng of the Later Wèi Dynasty
They tread on solid ground and push through emptiness,
Nesting in dwellings and inhabiting burrows.
They only drink and devour in the mountains and marshes,
All lurking and hiding in the forests and thickets.
Thus, ancestral temples have their places,
Lush grasses have their distinct locations,
How much more so for these tiny creatures.
They stray from their groups and seek different companions,
Violating order as they advance.
In terms of sentiment, they are hard to approve.
As recorded in the Ěryǎ,
Their kinds are many and varied, but examining their appearance and nature,
They are all not worthy of esteem.
Some dwell in the wild, separated by the Yīn Mountains,
Some share burrows, neighboring Bōzhǒng.
Some drink from rivers to fill their bellies,
Some inhale smoke and roam among towering forests.
Yet those discussed today
Emerge from holes in people's walls.
Alas, among all things,
They are the most contemptible.
Their fur and bones are unfit for amusement or admiration,
Their fat and flesh are not served on sacrificial vessels or meals.
Thus, Huáinán, in his lightheartedness,
Vomited his intestines, never to be recovered.
Dōng'ē, constrained by his body,
Merely claimed immortality and was reprimanded.
As for their appearance,
They are wretched and miserable, sighing and moaning,
With eyes darting and glancing.
Their whiskers resemble half-drooping ears of wheat,
Their eyes are like split bean pods,
Their ears akin to newly grown pagoda tree leaves,
Their tails like the dregs of leftover wine.
Then there are the old ones,
Emaciated, scabby, and mangy,
Full of cunning schemes,
Unmatched among the multitude.
They rely on the community, wary of the vessels,
Skillfully understanding self-preservation.
Deeply hidden and tightly concealed,
Cleverly able to seek and find.
Some descend by following ropes,
Some are thrown high from the ground.
They climb onto looms and cabinets,
Shake doors and move curtains.
Anxious all morning,
Noisy all evening.
Therefore, the poet composed verses,
Truly calling them massive.
They steal the precious vessels of Tāng,
Overturn the fragrant oils of Liú Kūn.
They damage the slanted collars of embroidered robes,
Destroy layered silk garments.
Cáo Shū thus offered admonitions,
Zhāng Tāng was demoted because of them.
There are also reclusive scholars,
Weary wandering guests.
They cut off celebrations and condolences to nurture true simplicity,
Dismiss attendants to seek poetry and the Yì.
Courtyards are solemn and clean,
Rooms are empty and silent.
Then the rats seize the opportunity,
Scampering east and west.
Some stroke their whiskers on the bed,
Some poke their foreheads out the door,
Their appearance quite relaxed and leisurely,
Their demeanor without fear or caution.
They also lead their companions,
Joyful and spirited.
They overturn boxes and cases,
Trample over cushions and mats.
Together they insult and scorn,
Utterly without propriety or restraint.
Alas, the vastness of heaven and earth,
Produces these things—what benefit do they bring?
Monkey, Fifteenth
The "Máoshī Cǎochóng Jīng" says:
"Náo
is the míhóu (macaque).
People of Chǔ call it mùhóu (macaque),
the old ones are called chán
(pronounced in xián).
hú.
Chánhú are swift and agile,
their cries are jiào jiào and sorrowful."
The "Bàopǔzǐ‧Yùcè Jì" says:
"In the mountains, on shēn days, they are called the ruler's monkeys,
monkeys live eight hundred years."
The "Fánlù" says:
"Yuán resembles the monkey,
large and black.
Long forearms,
lifespan eight hundred years.
They enjoy guiding their qì."
The "Zhōu Suǒshì Xiàozǐ Zhuàn" says:
"Yuán,
belongs to the lodging category.
Some are yellow-black with connected arms,
light nests, skilled at climbing.
Able to spin in empty wheels,
fond of singing.
If the female is captured by humans,
she will not live alone thereafter."
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Lèi hóu resembles the monkey,
people of the South Sea call it lèi hóu.
Jué resembles a dog,
it is the mǔhóu (female monkey).
Color bluish-black,
holds people,
fond of looking around.
Juéfù is good at looking back,
fèifèi resembles humans.
Disheveled hair, runs swiftly,
eats humans.
Wēiyí has a long spine and is ní,
ní (pronounced shǎo lì).
Wèi has an upturned nose and long tail."
Wèi resembles the míhóu but larger,
bluish-black.
Tail several feet long,
resembles an otter,
tail tip forked,
nose exposed and upturned.
When it rains, it hangs itself from a tree,
using its tail to plug its nose.
Also says:
"Nà
(pronounced nǚ huá).
No forefeet.
Jū,
belongs to the jué category.
(pronounced jié yú).
Resembles a leopard but shape like a míhóu,
very hairy, vigorous and swift.
Its head can lift stones to throw at people."
Also says:
"Méng sòng resembles a monkey but smaller,
purplish-black.
Can be kept to catch rats,
better than cats."
The "Shuōwén" says:
(pronounced huǒ mù).
Resembles a dog.
Yellow above the waist,
black below the waist.
Eats mǔhóu."
The "Wú Lù‧Dìlǐ Zhì" says:
"Guǒrán,
belongs to the yuán-nà category.
Color greenish-red with patterns,
lives in trees."
The "Shuōwén" says:
(pronounced yú).
The "Yùpiān" pronounces it fú fèi.
Human body, reversed heels,
when laughing, its upper lip covers its eyes.
Also called xiāo yáng,
resembles a jǐ,
skilled at climbing trees."
Liú Xīn's "Guǎngzhōu Jì" says:
"Fēng mǔ resembles yuán but has no tail,
upon seeing people, seems ashamed.
Bends its neck and knocks its head,
if killed, when wind blows, it revives."
The "Kuòdìtú" says:
"Xīngxing,
human face, pig body,
knows people's names."
Holding the Beam, Climbing Trees
