Yuán Shū's "Páixié Jí‧Chángshān Wáng Jiǔ Mìng Wén" says:
"When it comes to planning for oneself but losing one's place,
tethered and bridled among humans.
Tamed by reins, subdued by restraints,
led only by whim.
Climbs pillars to roam,
holds beams to sleep.
Gathers leftovers,
indulges the mouth as it pleases."
The "Máoshī" says:
"Do not teach the náo to climb trees."
Máo Cháng's annotation says:
"Náo,
belongs to the yuán category."
Sūn Yán's annotation of the "Ěryǎ" says:
"Náo,
is the mǔhóu."
Red Lips, Red Feet
Fù Xuán's "Ode to the Ape" says:
"Adorned with a red turban,
Stockinged with crimson cloth.
They paint its face,
Redden its lips,
Raise its brows and furrow its forehead,
As if sorrowful or angry."
The "Jiāngshèng Geographical Records" say:
"On Shè Mountain there are mountain apes,
With red feet,
Sometimes seen.
When deep winter snow accumulates,
There is always a line of footprints."
Riding an Ox, Subdued by Rats
Guō Bān's "Anecdotes of the Wei and Jin" says:
"Sīmǎ Xuānwáng appointed Zhōu Tài as the governor of Xīnchéng.
Zhōng Yù said to Tài:
'You, having just doffed your commoner's clothes, ascend to the ministerial office;
A beggar riding a small carriage—
How swift is that?'
Tài replied:
'You, the son of a wise lord,
Possessing literary talent from youth,
Thus hold a minor official post.
A macaque riding a clay ox—
How slow is that?'
All the guests were pleased and convinced."
Wáng Chōng's "Discourses Weighed in the Balance" says:
"The strength of mosquitoes and horseflies
Is not equal to that of oxen and horses.
That oxen and horses are troubled by mosquitoes and horseflies
Is a matter of circumstance.
A deer's antlers are sufficient to gore a dog;
A monkey's hands and feet are sufficient to grapple with a rat.
Yet the deer is subdued by the dog,
And the monkey is subdued by the rat,
Because their claws are not sharp enough."
Insect Nature, Beastly Body
"Qiáozi's Admonitions on Law" says:
"That which makes humans noble
Is their ritual propriety.
A human without ritual—
Is he not like a macaque?
Though bearing human semblance, his nature is that of an insect."
Ruǎn Jí's "Ode to the Macaque" says:
"Its body bears many resemblances yet is not of the same kind;
Its appearance is aberrant and impure.
Outwardly perceptive and clever yet without measure—
Thus a human face upon a beastly body."
Hòu Hàn Wáng Yánshòu's "Ode to the Monkey"
Probing the creation and transformation of Heaven and Earth,
Truly divine and marvelous, extraordinary and strange.
The Way, profound and subtle, mysterious and wondrous,
Indeed, there is nothing it does not accomplish.
There is the cunning creature, the monkey,
Ugly in form and base in demeanor.
Its facial features resemble an old man,
Its torso seems like a small child.
Eyes glaring fiercely.
(Note: wǔ liú fǎn.)
Dazzling (hū pàn fǎn.)
Xù,
Gaze sharp and piercing.
Eyelashes fluttering (hū yuè fǎn.)
Dim (hū mí fǎn.)
Protruding (niǎo jué fǎn.)
High-set eyes and curved forehead,
Agile.
Glancing swiftly (hū jiǔ fǎn.)
And glancing askance (huī lí.)
Nose sniffing (xǔ jiě fǎn.)
Snoring (xǔ hòu fǎn.)
To sniff and inhale (xǔ jiā fǎn.)
(xǔ jiā fǎn.)
Ears twitching and perking up to listen.
Mouth knowing.
Holding in the mouth (hū tiǎn fǎn.)
Flabby (dān) and (zé xián fǎn.)
Gnashing (zōu.)
Lips (chún) (zhì fǎn.)
Smacking (ér shè fǎn.)
And (pǐ bēi fǎn.)
(yán bēi fǎn.)
Teeth jagged and protruding (yǎn) (xiàn.)
Yǎn,
Chewing (niè) (rǎn.)
And mumbling (ér yè fǎn.)
Wriggling.
Storing food in both cheeks,
Gradually transferring it to the stomach and spleen.
Crouched like a rabbit, sitting like a dog,
Voice chattering and gibbering.
Sometimes hiccuping (gé gé) and,
Again chirping (dī dí xiù huǒ lì fǎn.)
As if crying.
Posture fawning and obsequious (hū diàn fǎn.)
And foolish (zǒng gàn.)
(Pronunciation: gòng.)
Gaping and staring, wide-eyed and dazed.
Dull (tāi.)
Glancing askance (yuàn.)
Staring blankly (zǐ gōng fǎn.)
And searching.
Glancing swiftly (shì.)
Swift (xī.)
Soft (ruǎn.)
(ér yuǎn fǎn.)
Timid and fearful.
Zī.
Born in the deep mountains' lush forests,
Dwelling among steep cliffs and perilous peaks.
Nature swift and suspicious, quick,
Manner erupting and unrestrained.
Climbing hundred-ren tall trees,
Scaling slender, swaying long branches.
Back to desolate, steep ravines,
Facing unfathomable, dark streams.
Following twisting boughs and twigs,
Sometimes grasping rotten wood to climb perilously.
As if about to fall yet catching hold again,
A tangled, chaotic display of weakness and strength.
Sometimes leaping in groups (tǔ diào fǎn.)
Swift as lightning,
Sometimes hanging like melons or dangling like gourds.
Above, reaching with hands to grab and snatch,
Below, planting feet to climb and stand.
Reaching to clutch wildly,
Then retracting arms and darting like lightning.
At times desolate and bleak,
Suddenly gazing sidelong, leisurely and calm.
Sometimes trampling and kicking (jué.)
To tread and roam,
Again chattering and clustering together.
Leaning on steep heights to arrange
Rafters (chuán.)
(Chì yuán fǎn.)
Treading perilous perches to leap and dance.
Suddenly surging forth, light and swift,
Truly difficult to capture in detailed description.
Sharing joys and sorrows with humankind,
Fond of eating dregs and drinking lees.
So, setting wine by its side,
They compete to drink (huǒ yuán fǎn.)
And gallop.
Dazed (xù huǒ shǔ fǎn.)
Bewildered and intoxicated (hóu huǒ hóu fǎn.)
To the point of confusion and drunkenness,
Drowsy and asleep, unaware.
Temporarily seizing its mane (zǐ gōng fǎn.)
(huǒ jié fǎn.)
To bind it,
Then adorning it with tassels to tether and bridle.
Returning to lock and tie it in the courtyard stable,
Onlookers gasp and forget their weariness.
Chén Xiāo Quán's "Poem: Night Apes Crying"
The cassia moon's shadow just appears,
Apes' cries drift far on the wind.
Beyond the cliff, they call to companions still,
Over the deep pool, their echoes ring empty.
Vines hang as if to fetch a drink,
Branches creak as if avoiding a bow.
Especially those three cries that bring tears,
Soaking robes, never ceasing.
Phoenix, Part One
The Kǒng Yǎn Tú states:
"The phoenix is
the essence of fire."
The Máo Shī Cǎochóng Jīng states:
"The male is called fèng,
the female is called huáng.
Their chicks are called yuèzhuó,
or are called fènghuáng.
Another name is yuèzhuó,
another name is yǎn."
The Máo Shī Shū states:
"The phoenix will not perch except on the paulownia tree,
and will not eat except on bamboo seeds."
The Lúnyǔ Zhāi Shuāi Shèng states:
"The phoenix has six resemblances and nine treasures.
The six resemblances are:
first, its head resembles heaven;
second, its eyes resemble the sun;
third, its back resembles the moon;
fourth, its wings resemble the wind;
fifth, its feet resemble the earth;
sixth, its tail resembles the weft stars.
The nine treasures are:
first, its beak contains fate;
second, its heart conforms to measure;
third, its ears hear comprehensively;
fourth, its tongue can bend and stretch;
fifth, its colors are radiant;
sixth, its crest is like the compass of Zhōu;
seventh, its spurs are sharp hooks;
eighth, its sound is stirring and lofty;
ninth, its belly bears the pattern of a door.
Its call while walking is called guīxī;
its call while resting is called tífú;
its call at night is called shànzāi;
its call at dawn is called hèshì;
its call while flying is called lángdū.
Only the Yellow [Emperor] knows me;
holding bamboo seeds he comes.
Therefore, the Master wished to dwell among the Nine Yi,
to follow the phoenix in play."
Sòng Jūn said:
"'Weft'
refers to the five planets.
'Measure',
refers to the foot.
'Zhōu' should be 'cǎi',
meaning vermilion color.
'Door',
is that through which one enters and exits,
responding to the peace and harmony of the world.
'Yellow',
refers to the yellow center that connects with principle.
When the phoenix encounters chaos, it dwells in concealment among the Nine Yi."
Xǔ Shèn's Shuōwén states:
"The phoenix,
is a divine bird.
Tiān Lǎo said the phoenix's form:
in front like a qilin, behind like a deer,
with a snake's neck and a fish's tail.
Dragon patterns on a turtle's back,
a swallow's jaw and a chicken's beak,
fully displaying the five colors.
It emerges from the land of the nobleman in the east,
soaring beyond the four regions.
It passes over Kūnlún,
drinks at Dǐzhù,
bathes its feathers in the Ruòshuǐ,
and rests at night in the Dān Palace.
Its appearance signifies great peace and tranquility in the world.
The character is composed of the radical 'bird' with 'fán' indicating its sound.
When the phoenix flies, flocks of birds follow it in the tens of thousands."
Huángfǔ Mì's Dìwáng Shìjì states:
"The Yellow Emperor fasted and purified himself in the central palace,
and sat by the Xuánhù River on the Luò.
Then a great bird appeared,
with a chicken's head and a swallow's beak,
a turtle's neck and a dragon's form,
qilin's wings and a fish's tail,
its shape resembling a crane.
Its body was complete with the five colors,
three patterns forming characters:
the character on its head read 'shùndé' (obedient virtue),
the character on its back read 'xìnyì' (trust and righteousness),
the character on its breast read 'rénzhì' (benevolence and wisdom).
It did not eat living insects,
nor tread upon living grass.
Sometimes it rested in the emperor's eastern garden,
sometimes it nested in the corner-tower pavilion.
When it ate and drank,
it would inevitably sing and dance of its own accord,
its sound like panpipes and reed organs."
The Hànshū states:
"In the third year of the Yuánshǐ era,
phoenixes gathered in the Eastern Sea,
and envoys were sent to offer sacrifices at that place.
During Emperor Xuān's time,
phoenixes, divine sparrows, and sweet dew descended and gathered in the capital,
and a general amnesty was granted throughout the land.
Phoenixes gathered in the Shànglín Park,
and so the Phoenix Hall was built,
in response to the auspicious omens."
The Rènzǐ states:
"The phoenix is the beauty among feathered creatures,
the qilin is the finest among furred creatures,
the turtle and dragon are the chiefs among shelled creatures,
and pián and nán are the most excellent among all timbers.
These are the noble things among creatures."
Holding the Chart / Presenting the Seal
The Chūnqiū Hécéng Tú states:
"The Yellow Emperor sat by the Xuánhù River on the Luò,
viewing with Dà Sīmǎ Róng Guāng and others.
A phoenix, holding a chart in its beak, placed it before the emperor.
The emperor bowed twice and received the chart."
Sòng Jūn's annotation:
"Xuánhù
is the name of a stone chamber."
It also states:
"Yáo sat in a boat,
viewing with Tàiwèi Shùn.
A phoenix, carrying a chart on its back, presented it to Yáo.
The chart was in a casket made of red jade,
three chǐ long,
eight cùn wide.
With a yellow jade fastener,
a white jade cord,
sealing both ends.
Its inscription read the five characters: 'Tiān Chìdì Fú Xǐ' (Heaven Red Emperor's Talisman Seal)."
Dānxué (Cinnabar Cave) / Zǐtíng (Purple Court)
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"On Dānxué Mountain,
there is a bird named the phoenix.
This bird sings and dances of its own accord.
Its appearance signifies great peace and tranquility in the world."
Cài Yōng's Qín Cāo states:
"During the time of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the world was transformed,
and phoenixes came to dance in the court.
King Chéng then took up the qín and sang:
'The phoenix soars, oh, in the purple court;
What virtue have I, oh, to move the spirits?'"
Six Virtues / Five Resemblances
Huán Xuán's Fènghuáng Fù states:
"Among feathered creatures, uniquely extraordinary,
only the luán and huáng are called paragons.
Distant realms they transcend to perch,
basking in the morning sun at the Cinnabar Cave.
Possessing six virtues to form their pattern,
their brilliant plumage shines with luxuriant splendor."
The Hán Shī Wàizhuàn states:
"Only the phoenix can exhaustively investigate the myriad things,
and penetrate heaven and earth.
Therefore, if one obtains two of the phoenix's resemblances,
then the phoenix will pass by;
if one obtains three of the phoenix's resemblances,
then the phoenix will gather there;
if one obtains four of the phoenix's resemblances,
then in spring and autumn it will descend and approach;
if one obtains five of the phoenix's resemblances,
then the phoenix will dwell there for life.
The Yellow Emperor said:
'Ah! Truly so!
How dare I compare myself to it?'"
Ten Offspring / Five Chicks
Jiāo Gòng's Yì Lín states:
"The phoenix has ten offspring,
sharing the same nest and mother,
joyful in protecting each other."
It also states:
"The phoenix gave birth to five chicks,
raised in the southern suburb.
The nobleman is healthy and peaceful,
his person glorious, happy, and joyful."
Nesting in the Pavilion / Perching on the Paulownia
The Shàngshū‧Zhōnghòu states:
"When Yáo had been governing for seventy years,
a phoenix alighted in his court.
Bó Yǔ bowed and said:
'During the time of the Yellow Emperor Xuānyuán, phoenixes nested in the corner-tower pavilion.'" The Shī Yìshū states:
"The phoenix is named yuèzhuó.
It will not perch except on the paulownia tree,
and will not eat except on bamboo seeds.
Various texts say the yuèzhuó is a type of phoenix,
but this differs from the above."
Wind-like Wings / Cloud-like Bearing
The Lúnyǔ Zhāi Shuāi Shèng states:
"The phoenix has six resemblances,
the fourth is its wings resemble the wind."
Jìn Táo Qián's poem "Reading the Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
"The divine phoenix strokes its cloud-like bearing,
the sacred luán lets fall its jade-like tones.
Though not treasures of this world, they win the heart of the Queen Mother of the West."
Golden beak, vermilion crest
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng" states:
"When Shí Jìlóng's empress was at the viewing tower,
an imperial edict written on five-colored paper
was placed in the phoenix's mouth.
Once the phoenix held the edict,
attendants released several hundred zhang of crimson rope,
and as the pulley turned,
the phoenix descended.
The phoenix was made of wood,
painted in five colors with lacquer,
its beak and feet all adorned with gold."
Jìn-dynasty Gù Kǎizhī's "Rhapsody on the Phoenix" states:
"Its vermilion crest blazes with twin plumes."
Yang essence, numinous substance
"The Pheasant Cap Master" states:
"The phoenix is the bird of the Quail Fire constellation,
the essence of yang.
If virtue can summon it,
its essence arrives in full."
Gù Kǎizhī's "Rhapsody on the Phoenix" states:
"Its numinous substance soars aloft."
Perching on the emperor's parasol tree, gathering in the king's valley
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn" states:
"The Yellow Emperor then donned yellow robes,
fastened a yellow sash,
and wore a yellow crown.
He fasted in the central palace,
and the phoenix arrived, obscuring the sun.
The Yellow Emperor descended to the eastern steps,
facing west, bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
saying, 'August Heaven bestows blessings,
I dare not refuse this mandate.'
The phoenix then alighted in the emperor's eastern garden,
perched on the emperor's parasol tree,
ate the emperor's bamboo fruit,
and never departed for the rest of its life."
Jiāo Gòng's "Forest of Changes" states:
"The divine bird of five colors,
the phoenix is king.
It gathers in the king's valley,
enabling the lord to find his place."
Five-colored feathers, thousand-gold plumage
"Dōngguān Hàn Jì" states:
"In the seventeenth year of the Jiànwǔ era,
a phoenix arrived,
standing eight or nine chǐ tall,
with five-colored feathers.
It gathered in Yǐngchuān,
flocks of birds following it,
covering several qǐng of land,
and remained for seventeen days before departing."
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Gleaned Fragments" states:
"King Zhāo of Zhōu used blue phoenix feathers to make two fur coats,
one called 'warm substance,'
the other called 'mild flesh,'
often used to ward off cold.
By the end of King Lì's reign,
these items were still treasured.
When King Lì was exiled to Zhì,
people obtained and prized them.
Those guilty of crimes punishable by death
could redeem themselves with blue phoenix feathers to avoid execution,
a single feather being valued at a thousand gold."
Táng Tàizōng Wén Huángdì's "Rhapsody on the Phoenix"
There was a majestic phoenix
that rested its wings facing the morning sun.
It roamed through purple mists at dawn,
and drank dark frost at dusk.
Riding the long wind to lift its pinions,
it soared to the heavenly paths and flew far.
When it flew west, the misty atmosphere dimmed;
when it flew east, the sun and moon cast radiant light.
It transformed into a peng in the northern regions,
and instructed flocks of birds in the southern wilds.
It descended only when chaos plagued the world,
and revealed itself in times of enlightened rule.
Fortunately, it relied on noble men,
to lean on and be supported.
Drawing upon these winds and clouds,
it washed away the dust and grime.
Parting the obscuring shade beneath the leaves,
it emitted radiant splendor among the branches.
Its immortal wings, once bent, stretched out again;
its divine voice, once silenced, rose once more.
Gazing upon the eight extremes, it soared aloft;
approaching the nine heavens, it stood tall.
It sought to broaden virtue among all birds,
not to seek glory for itself alone.
Thus it lingered, moved by virtue,
looked back with admiration, cherishing the worthy.
Relying on the wise, disasters dispersed;
entrusting itself to the talented, blessings extended.
Gratitude for kindness grew ever stronger,
the will to repay merit just beginning to unfold.
Not because knowing is hard and action easy,
but thinking of leaving a legacy to complete what came before.
May the flow of blessings from virtue and worthiness
continue for ten thousand generations, fragrantly transmitted.
Jìn-dynasty Fù Xián's "Rhapsody on the Phoenix"
I gaze upward at the celestial patterns, beholding them fully,
observing the divine images in the great clarity.
Ah, the birth and nurturing of this majestic phoenix,
imbued with the pure essence of the vermilion element.
Thus it embodies all wonders,
and possesses the virtue of the five numinous creatures.
It loathes the filth and turmoil of worldly dust,
and fears the ease with which the vulgar net ensnares.
Its heart is vast and far-reaching,
its intent drifting, embarking on distant journeys.
Soaring through the vast expanse, it rises lightly,
ascending beyond the clear empyrean, transcending form.
Then, when the dragon ascends to the ninth and fifth positions,
the time is one of great brightness.
Expanding the prosperous right path,
harmonious and peaceful.
Moved by sagely transformation, it comes in response,
praising the Sháo music in its nine movements.
Adapting to the times, it advances or withdraws,
truly, its comings and goings follow principle.
How could it court harm for its beauty?
Surely it is honored for its virtue.
For a thousand years, none have seen it,
yet suddenly it flutters into the court.
When the responding dragon arrives,
may there be resonance with this sincerity.
Yet noble men overlook this,
so I compose this piece on a humble creature to express my feelings.
Though its ornate beauty may be admired,
I lament the grand aspirations it embodies.
Daring to sharpen my dullness on this final trace,
I am but rubble beside jade and jasper.
Later Hàn Liú Zhēn's "Phoenix Poem"
The phoenix gathers on the southern peak,
lingering by the roots of solitary bamboo.
In its heart, it never wearies,
spreading its wings, soaring through purple mists.
Is it not often toilsome?
Ashamed to flock with sparrows.
When will it come in response?
Only when a sage and enlightened ruler appears.
Chén-dynasty Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's Poem on Obtaining the Theme: The Majestic Phoenix Perches on the Parasol Tree
From beneath the cinnabar mountain, the majestic phoenix
comes to gather in the emperor's parasol tree.
About to dance, spring blossoms fall;
about to fly, autumn leaves lie bare.
Its reflection shines in the waters of Lóngmén;
its voice enters the wind of Dòngtíng.
There is another song of parting,
yet again harmonized with silk and paulownia.
Crane, Number Two
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"Cranes are as large as geese,
measuring three chǐ in length,
with greenish-black legs,
standing over three chǐ tall.
They have red cheeks and red eyes,
and a beak four cùn long.
Most are pure white,
but some are bluish-gray.
Those that are bluish-gray
are what people today call 'red-cheeked.'
They often cry at midnight;
their call is high and clear,
audible for eight or nine lǐ,
and only when they are old does their voice become lower.
Nowadays, people in Wú and scholar-official families all raise them in their gardens.
They also cry when the roosters crow."
The Fán Lù says:
"Cranes know midnight;
the crane
is a water bird.
At midnight, the water's energy is at its peak;
sensing this vital breath,
they become even more joyful and cry out.
The reason cranes live so long
is that there is no breath of death within them."
The Xiàng Hè Jīng says:
"The crane
is a yang bird,
yet it moves through yin.
It relies on metal energy and depends on fire essence to nurture itself.
The number of metal is nine,
the number of fire is seven;
thus, after seven years it undergoes a minor transformation,
after sixteen years a major transformation,
after one hundred and sixty years transformations cease,
and after one thousand six hundred years its form becomes fixed.
Its body values purity,
hence its color is white.
Its cry reaches the heavens,
hence its head is red.
It feeds in water,
hence its beak is long.
It soars forward, hence its hind toes are short;
it perches on land, hence its legs are tall and its tail sparse;
it glides among clouds, hence its feathers are abundant and its flesh sparse.
It has a large throat to expel the old,
and a long neck to draw in the new;
thus its lifespan is great and immeasurable.
The reason its body lacks the two colors green and yellow
is that the energies of wood and earth are nurtured internally,
and thus are not manifested externally.
Therefore, when moving it must rely on islets and banks,
and when resting it does not gather in wooded groves.
It is truly the patriarch among feathered creatures,
the qílín of the immortals.
The superior markings of a crane are:
a slender head and vermilion crown,
protruding eyes and dark pupils,
a high nose and short beak.
䯓
Pronunciation: gù jiě fǎn.
Cheeks 𩨛
Pronunciation: dé zhái fǎn.
Ears,
a long neck and compact body.
Swallow breast, phoenix wings, sparrow feathers, tortoise back, turtle belly,
soaring forward and drooping behind,
tall shanks and thick joints,
broad thighs and slender toes—
these are the complete set of superior markings.
When it cries, it is heard in the heavens;
when it flies, it soars a thousand lǐ in one ascent.
In its second year, the crane sheds its down feathers
and changes its black spots.
In its third year, it begins to brood.
After another seven years, its flight feathers are fully formed;
after another seven years, it flies brushing against the Milky Way;
after another seven years, it dances in rhythm;
after another seven years, its cries throughout the twelve hours of day and night accord with musical pitch.
After another one hundred and sixty years, it ceases to eat living creatures;
again its large feathers fall out,
downy feathers grow,
becoming snow-white or pure black,
unsoiled by mud or water.
After another one hundred and sixty years, male and female gaze at each other,
and without their pupils moving, conception occurs.
After one thousand six hundred years, it drinks but does not eat,
and flocks together with luán and phoenixes.
When a sage is on the throne,
it soars with the phoenix over the suburbs."
Yang Bird Immortal Fowl
The Huáinán Bā Gōng Xiàng Hè Jīng says:
"The crane
is a yang bird,
yet it moves through yin."
Bào Zhāo's "Wǔ Hè Fù" says:
"Magnificent, the immortal fowl transformed from an embryo."
Golden Robe Jade Feathers
The Xījīng Zá Jì says:
"In the first year of the Shǐyuán era,
a yellow crane descended upon the Tàiyè Pond.
The Emperor composed a song, saying:
'The yellow crane flies, descending upon Jiànzhāng,
its feathers rustling, its steps stately.
Gold for its robe, chrysanthemums for its skirt—
reflecting on my shallow virtue,
I am ashamed before your auspicious sign.'"
Bào Zhāo's "Wǔ Hè Fù" says:
"Shaking its jade feathers, it approaches the rosy clouds."
Soaring Over Zǐgài Nurtured in Qīngtián
Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì says:
"Mount Héng has three exceedingly beautiful peaks;
one is called Zǐgài.
When the sky is clear and bright,
a pair of white cranes
always circle and soar above it,
their clear cries ringing out."
The Yǒngjiā Jùn Jì says:
"There is a Zhūmù Stream,
nine lǐ from Qīngtián.
In this place lives a pair of white cranes
that bear offspring every year.
When the young grow up, they leave;
only the parent pair remains.
They are exquisitely white and lovely,
and many say they are nurtured by immortals."
Entering the Canopy Riding in a Carriage
Lǐ Zūn's Tàiyuán Zhēnrén Máo Jūn Zhuàn says:
"When a devotee of the Way enters the temple,
they may see a white crane enter the canopy.
White cranes
are all emissaries of the Ninefold Cyclically Transformed Elixir."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
"Duke Yì of Wèi was fond of cranes;
some cranes rode in carriages."
Drinking from the Jasper Pool Soaring Over the Golden Grotto
Bào Zhāo's "Wǔ Hè Fù" says:
"In morning they play in the fields of magic mushrooms,
at dusk they drink from the Jasper Pool."
Lǐ Zūn's Tàiyuán Zhēnrén Máo Jūn Nèi Zhuàn says:
"Máo Yíng stayed at Mount Jùqū
and told his two younger brothers:
'I must leave to assume an official post,
and will not be able to visit frequently.'
The elders sang:
'Mount Máo connects to the golden grotto,
the rivers and lakes lie downstream.
Three deities ride white cranes,
each dwelling on a mountain peak.
Good rain irrigates the rice paddies,
the dry fields also become abundant.
Wives and children are safe in the hall,
leaving me without a care.
The white crane soars over the golden grotto—
when will it come to wander again?'"
White Feathers Dark Pupils
Wáng Shàozhī's Shénjìng Jì says:
"Over a hundred lǐ south of Xíngyáng Commandery,
there is Lán Rock.
A pair of cranes is often there,
their white feathers gleaming brightly,
flying together and perching side by side from dawn till dusk.
Legend says that long ago a husband and wife both secluded themselves here;
after several hundred years,
they transformed into these cranes."
The Huáinán Bā Gōng Xiàng Hè Jīng says:
"The superior markings of a crane
are protruding eyes and dark pupils."
Red Cheeks Vermilion Crown
The Shī Yì Shū says:
"The crane's form is like a large goose,
with red cheeks and red eyes."
The Xiàng Hè Jīng says:
"The superior markings of a crane
are a slender head and vermilion crown,
a long neck and compact body."
Tortoise Back Phoenix Wings
The Huáinán Bā Gōng Xiàng Hè Jīng says:
"The superior markings of a crane
are sparrow feathers and tortoise back."
It also says:
They drink the waters of the Róngxī and peck at the duckweed of the Tài Lake.
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Omissions" states:
"During the reign of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
the state of Túxiū presented a green phoenix and a red crane,
each one male and one female.
They were fed with the grain of Tángāo,
and given the waters of the Róngxī to drink."
Hé Yàn's poem says:
"A pair of cranes fly wing to wing,
soaring in play through the vast clear sky.
Ever fearing to be caught in nets,
worries and perils come together in a single morning.
How could they compare to gathering at Tài Lake,
following the current to peck at floating duckweed?"
Cáo Zhí of Wèi, "Rhapsody on the White Crane":
Alas, the pristine bird of pure white beauty,
imbued with wondrous aura, auspicious and kind.
Nestled deep in secluded woods it dwells in seclusion,
shaded by the lingering light of layered shadows.
Its solitary nest perched on a slender branch,
it fears the rushing wind it cannot withstand.
Lacking the carefree spirit of the sand-pear tree,
it rejoices that its six pinions remain unharmed.
By chance encounter, a stroke of fortune,
it gains the chance to fly wing-to-wing with the luan-phoenix.
Sharing feather and robe, kin in spirit,
Painful that this fine meeting is cut short,
meeting stern disaster and encountering calamity.
Together they sigh deeply, filled with dread,
suppressing their sobs, unable to raise their voices.
Bào Zhào of Sòng, "Rhapsody on the Dancing Crane":
Scattered through obscure classics, tested against creatures,
the wondrous immortal bird transformed from an embryo.
Endowed with a floating, expansive, elegant substance,
embracing a clear, far-reaching, luminous heart.
Pointing toward Pénglú, it turns its pinions,
gazing at Kūnlàng, it lifts its voice.
Circling the realm of the sun, it wheels in flight,
exhausting the Milky Way, soaring high in search.
Treading divine regions, already far it journeys,
accumulating numinous sacrifices, now growing many.
Eyes hold cinnabar, shining like stars,
crown congeals purple, misty splendor.
It draws its rounded throat in slender grace,
pauses its long toes in grand beauty.
Layered frost-feathers play with shadows,
shaking jade plumage, it approaches the clouds.
At dawn it plays in the fields of magic mushrooms,
at dusk it drinks from the Jade Pool.
Weary of rivers and seas, it roams the marshes,
ensnared by cloud-nets, it finds itself captive.
Leaving the silent solitude of the imperial realm,
returning to the noisy lowliness of the human world.
The year grows steep and daunting, sorrowful at dusk,
the heart desolate and mournful, grieving at parting.
And so on.
Jiǎnwén Emperor of Liáng, "Poem on Obtaining the Dancing Crane":
Coming from afar, from the fields of magic mushrooms,
flying across, the deep waters of Wǔxī.
Swiftly stirring, it rests by the market of Wú,
with uneven pace, it follows the Jìn lute.
Strange sounds carry across distant streams,
beating wings brush through flowered woods.
If you wish to know beyond material things,
at Yīluò there are clear waters.
Wú Jūn of Liáng, "Poem Chanting the Crane":
Originally one who rode in a carriage,
now a bird beneath your steps.
Humbled, yet with many fine features,
its clear cry holds wondrous tones.
Yīn Kēng of Chén, "Poem Chanting the Crane":
By the pond, often dancing alone,
facing its shadow, sometimes calling in solitude.
Suddenly moving with steps of the courtyard,
at times turning into the sound of the lute.
Kǒng Déshào of Chén, "Poem on Obtaining the Huátíng Crane":
The Huátíng crane that lost its mate,
its favor of riding in a carriage thus ended.
Over the three mountains, piercing bitter mist,
across a thousand miles, stirring mournful winds.
Its heart fearful as the white dew descends,
its voice severed amidst colored strings.
What words for this creature's transformation,
turning again like Liáodōng.
Chicken, Part Three
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící" states:
"The chicken represents accumulated yang,
an image of the southern direction.
Fire is the essence of yang,
things blaze upward,
thus when yang emerges, the chicken crows,
responding through kindred resonance.
The word for chicken (jī) means 'auspicious' (jiā),
auspicious and rising, it sets the time for people,
nothing more precious."
It excels at setting the schedule for people's rest and early rising.
"Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū" states:
"The Jade Balance Star scatters to become chickens.
If one distances oneself from the Yǎ and Sòng,
and promotes actors and entertainers,
then roosters will have five legs."
"Ěryǎ" states:
"Large chickens are called Shǔ.
The young of Shǔ are called Yú.
Chickens not yet fully grown are called Liàn.
Exceptionally strong ones,
are called Fèn.
A chicken three chǐ tall is called Kūn.
Perching on a stake is called Jié.
Nesting in a hole dug in a wall is called Shí."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"Shǔ
refers to the present-day Shǔ chicken.
Yú
is the name for chicken offspring.
Nowadays, in Jiāngdōng, young chickens are called Liàn.
Kūn
is an ancient name for chicken."
"Yì Lín" states:
"Xùn represents the chicken.
The chicken crows marking the seasons,
the household is joyful and carefree."
"Shàngshū" states:
"When a hen crows at dawn,
it is a sign the household will decline."
"Hánshī Wàizhuàn" states:
"Tián Ráo said to Duke Āi of Lǔ:
'Now the chicken,
with a crown upon its head,
represents civility;
with spurs on its feet for combat,
represents martial prowess;
daring to fight when an enemy is before it,
represents courage;
informing each other when food is seen,
represents benevolence;
keeping watch at night without missing the time,
represents trustworthiness.
Although possessing these five virtues,
you still daily boil and eat them.
Why is that?'
Because they come from too near at hand."
"Zhōu Guān" states:
"Artisans and merchants present chickens."
This takes from their acting on time.
"Lǐjì" states:
"In the rites of sacrificing at the ancestral temple,
the chicken is called Hànyīn."
"Fēngsútōng" states:
"Calling chickens is called 'zhū zhū.'
Common saying:
'Tradition says chickens were originally transformed from an old man named Zhū,
so now calling chickens is all "zhū zhū."'"
Cuī Bào's "Gǔjīn Zhù" states:
"The chicken is also named 'candle-night.'"
"Guǎngzhì" states:
"Chickens include breeds with bearded cheeks, five toes, golden shanks, and reversed wings.
Large ones are Shǔ,
small ones are Jīng.
White chickens with golden shanks are beautiful.
Long-tailed chickens,
with tails slender and long,
over five chǐ in length,
come from the Eastern Yi state of Hánguó.
Jiǔzhēn Commandery produces long-crowing chickens."
"Lóngyú Hétú" states:
"A black chicken with a white head,
eating it will make one ill.
Chickens with six toes also kill people,
chickens with four spurs also kill people,
chickens with five colors also kill people."
"Báizétú" states:
"Chickens with four spurs and double wings
are dragons.
Killing them will cause death by thunder."
"Lún Mùshū" states:
"Raise a white chicken,
make it recognize its master's voice and form.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
and the ninth day of the ninth month,
use a five-colored ribbon five cùn long as you wish,
tie it around the chicken's neck,
and take the chicken to a famous mountain.
Release the chicken on the mountain,
lift your head and chant:
'You must remember to crow at dawn,
the chicken's heart will open with understanding.'"
"Běncǎo" states:
Jade Earrings and Golden Spurs
Xí Gǔ's "Rhapsody on the Long-Crowing Rooster" says:
"A vermilion comb and jade earrings,
both crimson and plain are applied."
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"The roosters of Jì and Hòu fought.
The Jì clan put mustard on their rooster,
and the Hòu clan made golden spurs for theirs.
Píngzǐ was enraged,
so he increased his palace at the expense of the Hòu clan
and moreover reprimanded them.
Therefore, Hòu Zhāobó also resented Píngzǐ."
Mustard Feathers and Blossom Comb
The Zuǒzhuàn says:
"The roosters of Jì and Hòu fought.
The Jì clan put mustard on their rooster."
Dù Yù's commentary states:
"They pounded mustard seeds and sprinkled them on its feathers."
Some say:
"They mixed glue and sand and sprinkled it to make a 'mustard rooster.'"
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nányuèzhì says:
"The rooster's comb opens in four parts like a lotus blossom,
and its crowing is clear and penetrating."
Turquoise Comb and Black Feathers
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's "In Praise of the Long-Crowing Rooster" says:
"Its turquoise comb is resplendent and lush,
its jasper spurs are beautifully arrayed.
It distinguishes dusk from nightfall,
greets the dawn and startles the morning."
Fù Xiūyì's "Rhapsody on Fighting Cocks" says:
"Black feathers, dark and gleaming."
Golden Legs and Iron Spurs
Guō Yìgōng's Guǎngzhì says:
"There is a breed of rooster with golden legs and reversed wings."
The Wúshí Wàiguózhuàn says:
"Fàn Xún of Fúnán
used iron to make artificial spurs for fighting cocks,
and gambled for money with his generals."
Able to Speak and Skilled at Fighting
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyíjì says:
"The country of Hántú is seventy thousand lǐ from the royal capital.
The people are skilled at taming birds and beasts;
their chickens and dogs are all made able to speak."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"During Emperor Chéng's reign,
Jiāozhǐ and Yuèxī presented a long-crowing rooster.
They immediately tested it against the water clock,
and not a moment was off.
Its long crowing did not cease for the duration of a meal,
and it had long spurs and was skilled at fighting."
Turquoise Radiance and Crimson Light
Fù Xiūyì's "Rhapsody on Fighting Cocks" says:
"Turquoise radiance, lush and flowing with azure."
Cáo Zhí's "Poem on Fighting Cocks" says:
"Fierce eyes emit a crimson light."
Double-Headed and Four-Winged
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyíjì says:
"In the second year of Tàichū,
the Yuèzhī presented a double-headed chicken,
with four feet and one tail.
When it crowed, both heads crowed together."
Wèi Shōu's Hòu Wèishū says:
"In the summer of the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
a clerk, Shǐ Yuánxiǎn, presented a chicken with four feet and four wings."
The Wèishū says:
"Cuī Guāng, styled Chángrén,
was from Qīnghé, Hédōng.
In the summer of the first year of Zhèngshǐ,
a clerk, Shǐ Yuánxiǎn,
presented a chicken with four feet and four wings.
An edict ordered the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhào Yōng to ask Cuī Guāng about it.
Cuī Guāng submitted a memorial stating:
'Numerous wings and feet
are also an image of subordinates inciting one another.
It is a chick and not yet grown,
its legs are weak and rather small;
this also means its power is still slight,
and it is easy to control.'
Emperor Wǔ read it and was pleased.
A few days later, Xiǎn, Hào, and others were all executed for their crimes.
Thereafter, the respect for Cuī Guāng increased even more."
Flying Beyond the Seas and Crowing in the Clouds
Guō Zǐhéng's Dòngmíngjì says:
"There is a far-flying chicken.
At dusk it returns to rely on people,
at dawn it flies far to the four seas,
going in the morning and returning in the evening."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nányuèzhì says:
"In Wēipíng there is a great cave.
When heavy clouds darken the sky,
a rooster crows within the clouds."
Slender Tail and Long Pinions
The Wèizhì says:
"Mǎhánguó produces slender-tailed chickens."
Liú Zhēn's "Poem on Fighting Cocks" says:
"Long pinions startle the rising wind,
strong quills are fully spread."
Catching Dew and Announcing Dawn
The Jiāngbiǎozhuàn says:
"Nánjùn presented a long-crowing, dew-catching rooster."
The Xījīng Zájì says:
"During Emperor Chéng's reign,
Yuèxī presented a dawn-announcing rooster.
They immediately tested it against the water clock,
and not a moment was off."
Táodū and Golden Cave
The Yuánzhōngjì says:
"On Táodū Mountain there is a great tree called Táodū.
Its branches are three thousand lǐ apart.
Upon it is a heavenly rooster.
When the sun rises and shines upon the tree,
the heavenly rooster crows,
and all the roosters under heaven crow."
The Shùyìjì says:
"By the river in Yúdū County there is a stone chamber.
Often a divine rooster, colored like gold,
emerges from the cave, spreads its wings, and crows long.
Seeing people, it flies back in.
It is called the Golden Cave."
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on Fighting Cocks"
Black feathers, dark and gleaming,
white down, sharp and radiant.
Faint red mingled with pale yellow,
turquoise radiance, lush and flowing with azure.
Five colors interwoven into patterns,
substance luminous, beautiful, and full.
Viewed from the front as if leaning back,
viewed from the side as if tilting.
Eyes shaped like compass-drawn circles,
beak as if carved and polished.
High breast, steeply poised,
both wings level and even.
Leaping body, tense form,
fierce stance bursting forth.
Claws like tempered steel,
eyes like shooting stars.
Raising wings with the wind,
stroking pinions, crowing long.
Fierce will, unrestrained,
power soaring to the heavenly court.
Sometimes pacing hesitantly,
sometimes stepping lightly, at ease.
Sometimes scratching the ground, looking up and down,
sometimes stroking wings, not yet raised.
Sometimes glancing back like a wolf, glaring like an owl,
sometimes soaring like a simurgh, dancing like a phoenix.
Sometimes feigning retreat to lure the foe,
sometimes meeting death against a strong opponent.
Then in chaotic tumult,
like thunder clashing, lightning striking.
Striving, straining bodies to clash,
vying like falcons fierce, like eagles glaring.
Those gaining advantage soar to the ninth heaven;
those losing footing sink to the ninth earth.
Merely observing their battle,
then no spur strikes in vain,
no wing flaps without purpose.
Intent like a hungry eagle,
stance like a swift tiger.
Xí Gǔ's "Rhapsody on the Long-Crowing Rooster"
I praise the fine beauty of the crowing rooster,
its wisdom profound as a spirit, entering the obscure.
It discerns the turning of the celestial mechanism,
determines with utmost precision dusk and dawn.
Responding to spring at approaching daybreak,
suddenly standing like a crane, pausing like a phoenix.
Then it beats its wings to herald the hour,
and so stretches its neck to crow long.
As for its original form and appearance,
and the details of its feathery adornment:
vermilion comb and jade earrings,
both crimson and plain are applied.
Resplendent and magnificent,
five colors shimmering.
Exceptional posture, overflowing brilliance,
radiant hues, gloriously arrayed.
Dignified and luxuriant,
fluttering, swaying in the wind.
Fanning its six pinions to increase its glow,
spreading its downy feathers to hang down.
Its paired spurs rise steeply,
its long tail trails gracefully.
Jìn Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on Fighting Cocks"
Viewed from the front, it seems to lean back;
Viewed from the side, it appears to tilt.
Its eyes are shaped like compass-drawn circles,
Its beak as if carved sharp.
Its high breast stands steep and lofty,
Its pair of wings lie perfectly even.
It leaps and stretches its body,
An angry momentum bursts forth.
Its claws are like tempered steel,
Its eyes like shooting stars.
It raises its wings to catch the wind,
Strokes its pinions and lets out a long cry.
Its fierce spirit runs wild and free,
Its force threatens to overwhelm the celestial court.
Sometimes it paces hesitantly, lingering,
Sometimes it treads lightly, at ease.
Sometimes it scratches the ground, looking up and down,
Sometimes it strokes its wings, not yet raised.
Sometimes it glances back like a wolf or stares like an owl,
Sometimes it soars like an eagle or rises like a swan.
Sometimes it feigns turning its back to lure the foe,
Sometimes it meets its end against a strong opponent.
Those who gain the upper hand dominate the highest heavens;
Those who lose their footing sink to the deepest earth.
Xí Gǔ's "Rhapsody on the Long-Crowing Cock"
I praise the fine beauty of the crowing cock,
Whose wisdom reaches the divine and enters the obscure.
It discerns the turning points of the celestial mechanism,
Determining with utmost precision dusk and dawn.
Responding to the verdant sun as dawn approaches,
Suddenly it stands like a crane and pauses like a phoenix.
Then it beats its wings to herald the hour,
And so extends its neck in a long crow.
As for its original form and appearance,
And the detailed elegance of its plumage:
Vermilion crest and jade ear-pendants,
Red and white both applied.
Resplendent and magnificent in profusion,
Colors shimmer and flow.
Its exceptional posture brims with gorgeousness,
Its brilliant hues radiate in splendor.
It fans its six pinions to increase their glow,
Spreads its downy feathers hanging low.
Wèi Cáo Zhí's "Poem on Fighting Cocks"
All the heroes are at their peak of might,
Their twin plumes naturally fly aloft.
They wave their feathers, stirring the clear breeze,
Their fierce eyes emit a crimson light.
I wish to be aided by wildcat ointment,
To always command this arena.
Later Zhōu Wáng Bāo's "Poem on Watching Fighting Cocks"
With mincing steps they begin to stride across,
Their spirit and will seeking to overpower.
Jealousy of the foe makes golden glints arise,
Suspicion within the flock brings mustard powder to life.
Entering the arena, they seem to issue a challenge;
Driving back the retreat, they resemble pursuing troops.
Who would know that beneath Hángǔ Pass,
With people gone, the city gate stands open alone.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Poem on Fighting Cocks"
Joy and pleasure truly know no end,
In the eastern suburbs spring is fit for outings.
A hundred flowers are not of one hue,
New fields hold many different streams.
Dragon tails stretch across the Milky Way,
Chariot boxes head toward the garrison tower.
Jade crests first alert the enemy,
Mustard-smeared feathers suddenly suspect companions.
Ten days of arrogance already full,
Nine victories, their force ever strong.
If by chance Tián Ráo were to see this,
He would surely be able to persuade the Marquis of Lǔ.
Chén Chǔ Jiè's "Poem on Fighting Cocks on the Eastern Suburb Road"
Spring suburban companions for cockfighting,
Facing the enemy, they meet each other.
Deceiving the flock, they push through sleeves to emerge,
Bearing courage, they startle toward the arena.
Brocade-like feathers invade, spurs scattered,
Mustard-smeared feathers mingle with rising dust.
Just like after a battle concluded,
Upright integrity entrusted to a former crow.
Liáng Jiǎnwéndì's "Piece on Fighting Cocks"
Jade crests first startle the enemy,
Mustard-smeared feathers suddenly suspect companions.
Ten days of arrogance already full,
Nine victories, their force ever strong.
If by chance Tián Ráo were to see this,
He would surely be able to persuade the Marquis of Lǔ.
Liáng Liú Xiàowēi's "Piece on the Crowing Cock"
A red cock displays its kingfisher feathers,
Envying the foe, it gains sole command of the arena.
Within its wings it holds mustard powder,
Beyond its spurs gleam golden rays.
I wish to be granted the Huáinán elixir,
To make it soar among the clouds once.
Zhōu Yǔ Xìn's "Poem on Fighting Cocks"
Open the casement, gaze toward Píngzǐ,
Gallop the horse, look for Chénwáng.
Wildcat ointment smokes to vex the fighting foe,
Mustard powder dirties the springtime arena.
Unfurling wings, lotus blossoms stir;
Suspecting the flock, brocade breasts expand.
Chén Xú Líng's "Poem on Fighting Cocks"
Jìzǐ merely sought amusement,
Chénwáng wished to display his talent.
Flowery crests already balanced strength,
Golden claws again startled the decoy.
Fighting phoenixes shame brocade robes,
Paired simurghs disgrace the mirror stand.
If Chéncāng proves trustworthy,
Seek the treasure cock to come.
Chén Zhōu Hóngzhèng's "Poem on an Old, Defeated Fighting Cock"
In youth and prime, it crushed mighty foes,
With sidelong glances breeding suspicion and jealousy.
Once following the years and months of decline,
Ruined and decayed, its feathers shed swiftly.
Leisurely watching spring light fill the scene,
In the eastern suburbs, the grass color differs.
No longer the strength to crow first,
Only the empty intent to command the arena remains.
Eagle, Fourth
The "Yì Tōng Guà Yàn" says:
"The eagle is
a bird of prey that kills."
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"On the day of the Waking of Insects,
the eagle transforms into a turtledove.
On the day of the End of Heat,
the eagle then sacrifices birds."
The "Dà Dài Lǐ" says:
"In the first month, the eagle becomes a turtledove.
The eagle
represents its time of killing;
the turtledove
represents not its time of killing.
It is good at changing and turning to benevolence,
therefore we speak of it in full.
The turtledove becoming an eagle turns to not being benevolent,
therefore we do not exhaust our words on it."
The "Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo" says:
"Yáoguāng scatters to become eagles.
On the day of the Beginning of Autumn, eagles and sparrowhawks strike."
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"The eagle
is the shuāngjiū."
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"The white jué
is an eagle."
The "Guǎngzhì" says:
"An eagle at one year is called 'huáng',
at two years 'fǔ',
at three years 'qīng'."
Subduing the Fledgling Roc Chasing Birds and Sparrows
The "Kǒngshì Zhì" says:
"King Wén of Chǔ loved hunting.
All the swift hounds and famous eagles under heaven gathered there.
Someone presented an eagle,
saying it was not the equal of the king's eagles.
Soon, within the clouds there was a creature,
hovering and soaring, drifting and floating,
vividly white, its form indistinguishable.
The eagle then raised its wings and ascended,
straight as a flying bolt of lightning.
In a moment, feathers fell like snow,
blood showered like rain.
After a long while,
a great bird
fell to the ground dead.
Measuring its two wings,
they spanned several tens of lǐ.
The edges of its beak were yellow.
None among the crowd could identify it.
A gentleman of broad learning said:
'This is a fledgling of the great roc.
It had just begun to fly,
therefore it was subdued by the eagle.'
Thereupon he richly rewarded the presenter."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"Zǐchǎn first got to know Ránmíng.
He asked him about governing.
He replied:
'Regard the people as your children.
When you see the unrighteous, punish them,
like eagles and sparrowhawks chasing birds and sparrows.'"
Spring Transformation, Autumn Cry
The Book of Rites says:
"In the second month of spring,
the eagles begin to learn.
In the first month of autumn,
the eagles sacrifice birds,
and begin to carry out executions."
Emperor Wén of Wèi, in his "Reply to Fán Qīn's Letter," says:
"Thus, the autumn wind shakes the branches,
the spring eagle cries in autumn,
this can be said to be a sound harmonizing with bells and stones,
a spirit responding to wind and pitch pipes."
Fierce Spirit, Majestic Form
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Eagle" says:
"It contains the fierce spirit of the fiery Li trigram,
and receives the pure essence of metal's strength.
Alone it perches in the woods and wilds,
then soars and circles in the celestial court."
It also says:
"Its beak is sharp as a Wú halberd,
its eyes resemble bright stars.
Its majestic form is peerless through the ages,
its untamed spirit flows forth freely."
Ashamed of Sparrows, Intercepting Swans
Fù Xuán's "Song of Long Melancholy" says:
"The gray eagle sharpens its claws and wings,
ashamed to flock with swallows and sparrows.
Success or failure lies with the falconer,
do not let the bird of prey worry."
Sūn Chǔ's "Rhapsody on the Eagle" says:
"There is a handsome bird of metal's strength,
born among the rugged cliffs of Jǐngxíng.
It captures cunning hares on the plains,
and intercepts swans and phoenixes by the river islets."
Perching in Lush Trees, Striking the Central Plains
Jiāo Gòng's Forest of Changes says:
"The eagle perches in lush trees,
awaiting the sparrows coming and going."
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Eagle" says:
"Though it roams freely in spacious halls,
it longs to strike fiercely across the central plains."
Green Talons, White Feathers; Ornate Jesses, Golden Rings
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on Shǔ Capital" says:
"As for eagles, they are like shooting stars brightening the sky,
like darting lightning flashing light.
With green talons and white feathers,
they are like drifting snow and heavy frost."
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Eagle" says:
"It strives to spread its wings but cannot rise,
strokes its wings but has nowhere to soar.
Adorned with colorful ornate jesses,
fastened with jade-adorned golden rings."
Suí Dynasty Wèi Yànshēn's "Rhapsody on the Eagle"
Only this bird's transformation and nurturing,
truly originates from Zhōng Mountain.
It borrows the fierce spirit of the Metal phase,
and possesses the fiery essence of the Fire virtue.
How numerous are the schemes of the hunter,
deploying horizontal nets to ensnare and bind it.
Attaching light threads to both cheeks,
tying long leather straps to both feet.
Its flight does not follow its innate nature,
its food does not satisfy its desires.
Its swift wings are thus temporarily furled,
its ambitious heart is thereby self-confined.
As for its appearance, it is not of one kind,
its features are many and varied.
Its talons should be heavy and cross-shaped,
its tail is prized when resembling a Hélú jar.
Standing like a planted tree,
gazing like a melancholy barbarian.
Its beak is like a sharp sword,
its legs are like thorny branches.
Some are white like scattered blossoms,
red like drops of blood.
Large patterns like brocade,
fine spots like tie-dye.
Eyes like bright pearls,
feathers like frost and snow.
Body heavy as metal,
claws hard as iron.
Some also have a flat, knife-cut crown,
a head round as an egg.
Broad breast, long neck,
thick sinews, short shanks.
Thick wings, strong feathers,
wide thighs, soft flesh.
Seeking practical use,
these are all exceptional companions.
Some resemble quail heads,
some resemble owl heads.
Red eyes, yellow feet,
slender bones, small elbows.
Lazy yet easily startled,
cunning and hard to lure.
Cannot be called to perch,
flies but cannot outrun.
Such as these,
better not to have them.
As for those that eat swiftly and digest quickly,
this is their nature.
A neck like a hare's, standing like a monkey,
this indicates no illness.
The vent should not be large,
the crop dislikes being soft.
The leash should not be too thin,
the back should not pant.
Those born in caves prefer to crouch,
those nesting on water often stand.
Long double shanks mean slow to rise,
short six wing feathers mean swift flight.
Plumage changes repeatedly,
its color is not constant.
Born in Yín, mature in Yǒu,
all are called 'huáng.'
Two weeks old, they become 'bǎo,'
a thousand days old, they become 'cāng.'
Though said to soar in the void,
their nature differs from other birds.
Females have large bodies,
males have small forms.
Meeting dogs, they startle and suspect,
encountering humans, they become tame and gentle.
Raised from chicks, they have few ailments,
caught wild, they are more cunning.
Observing them is easy,
training them is truly difficult.
The perch must be high and distant,
the mews must be splendid and spacious.
Ginger is used to generate heat,
wine is used to dispel cold.
The glove must be warm,
the meat must not be stale or dry.
Approach them to foster familiarity,
keep them calm to make them settled.
By day, never leave your hand,
by night, let them sleep by fire.
Slightly increase their feathers,
slightly decrease their meat.
Muscles lean, intestines thin,
heart harmonious, nature tamed.
Thoughts cut off from the clouds,
ambition set on the chase.
Suí Dynasty Emperor Yáng's "Poem on the Eagle"
Migrating northward, intending for Héng,
suddenly fell into the fowler's net.
Already bound by ornate jesses,
still presented to the nobleman.
Green talons are truly peerless,
white feathers are indeed hard to match.
Deep eyes manifest this name,
broad breast is considered beautiful.
Startled beasts have no time to flee,
suspicious birds have no leisure to rise.
Though honored upon the glove,
no longer has the will to soar among the clouds.
Volume Five: The Crow
The Shuōwén states:
"The crow,
is a filial bird."
The Chūnqiū Yùndǒushū states:
"Flying with feathered wings is yang,
and yang qi is benevolent,
hence the crow feeds its parents in return."
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo states:
"Within the sun there is a three-legged crow,
the essence of yang, its warmth and moisture."
Warmth and moisture,
are words for gentle growth.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
"When virtue reaches birds and beasts,
then white crows descend."
The Dōngguān Hànjì states:
"In the third year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng,
in Dàijùn Gāoliǔ, a crow gave birth to offspring.
It had three legs,
was as large as a chicken,
red in color,
with horns on its head,
over an inch long."
Zhāng Bó's Wúlù states:
"In Péngzé, there are crows that catch pellets;
travelers throw pellet-like rice at them,
and whether high or low, they never miss."
The Sòng Qǐjūzhù states:
"In the thirteenth year of Yuánjiā,
the commoner Tán Hé of Yángxiàn County presented a white crow,
its pure white body gleaming,
as if shining like jade.
Consulting auspicious charts,
it was truly an auspicious sign."
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīnzhù states:
"The crow is also called a raptor bird."
The Tōngsúwén states:
"A white-headed crow is called a xiá."
Pronounced zhì bā fǎn.
The Shīyìwèn states:
"There are the pī crow,
pī pronounced pǐ.
the yǎ crow,
which is the Chǔ crow."
The Ěryǎ states:
"The yùsī and pījū."
These are Chǔ crows.
It also states:
"The yǎ crow is small and vocal,
with a white belly."
It also states:
"Crows and magpies are similar,
their feet retract."
They retract their feet under their belly when flying.
It also states:
"There are the yàn crow, shān crow, yán crow, yàn bái dòu crow, and zhú shān crow."
The zhú resembles a crow but is smaller,
with a red beak, nests in holes,
and is found in the west.
Solar Bird Yang Bird
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The crow,
is the sound of exhaling.
Taking its assistance to qi,
hence it is called 'wūhū.'
The crow is the bird within the sun,
thus it is depicted as such."
Zhāng Héng's Língxiàn states:
"The sun is the ancestor of yang essence,
accumulated to form the crow.
The crow has three toes,
which is the number of yang."
Holding Umbrellas Gathering on Crowns
Liú Yìqìng's Shìshuō states:
"When Xú Gànmù was young,
he once dreamed of a crow descending from the sky,
holding a long-handled umbrella and planting it in his courtyard.
The crow then flew back up to the sky and brought down another umbrella,
planting three umbrellas in total.
The crow then cawed loudly,
made an ominous sound, and left.
Later, Xú indeed fell ill,
and met an unfortunate end."
Fú Hóu's Gǔjīnzhù states:
"Zēng Shēn was hoeing melons,
when a three-legged crow gathered on his hat."
Returning to Fly Feeding in Return
The Máo Shī states:
"Those yùsī with their caps,
return flying in orderly rows."
The Qiáozi Fǎxùn states:
"Filial piety,
is the foundation of conduct.
Those who neglect the foundation and seek the trivial,
have never been seen to attain it.
Even if they do attain it,
the noble person does not value it.
Even crows feed their parents in return,
how much more should humans, who lack filial hearts?"
Nesting at the Door Painting on Walls
Cháng Qú's Huáyáng Guózhì states:
"In Dào County, the filial son Wú Shùn,
cared for his mother,
and a red crow nested at his door."
The Fēngsútōng states:
"According to the Míngdì Qǐjūzhù:
'While touring east to Tàishān,
upon reaching Xíngyáng,
a crow flew and cried over the imperial carriage.'
The imperial guard Wáng Jí shot it,
and composed a verse:
'Crow, crow, cawing,
I draw my bow and shoot its left flank.
May Your Majesty live ten thousand years,
and I become a two-thousand-bushel official.'
The emperor rewarded him with two million coins,
and ordered the pavilion walls to be painted with crows."
Red Essence White Body
Xuē Zǒng's Chìwū Sòng states:
"Magnificent red crow,
essence of the sun.
Vermilion feathers, red essence,
rarely born across generations."
Also, his Báiwū Sòng states:
"Brilliant white crow,
pure body like plain silk.
Paying respects at the ancestral temple,
it comes to watch over."
Transforming into Fish Holding a Magpie
The Nányuè Jì states:
"The cuttlefish,
often floats on the water.
Crows see it and think it is dead,
so they peck at it,
but it then wraps around and captures the crow,
hence it is called the crow-thief fish.
Now, some say crows transform into it."
The Wúlì states:
"When the King of Wú established a spirit shrine,
he built a temple outside the Cānglóng Gate.
At that time, crows nested on the Zhūquè Gate.
There were also two crows,
holding a magpie and placing it before the spirit seat.
Some obtained a divine text,
explaining the intention to change the era name,
so they changed Chìwū to Tàiyuán."
Eight Offspring Nine Chicks
An ancient Yuèfǔ song says:
"The crow gave birth to eight or nine offspring,
perching calmly on the Qín family's osmanthus tree.
Once, my Qín family had a prodigal son,
who used Suīyáng's combined pellets."
Sīmǎ Biāo's Xù Hànshū states:
"During Emperor Huán's time,
a children's rhyme said:
'Crows on the city wall,
tails all askew,
one year they give birth to nine chicks.
Fathers become officials,
sons become conscripts,
one conscript dies,
a hundred carriages come.'"
Liáng Xú Miǎn's "Rhapsody on the Magpie"
Observing the many kinds among feathered creatures,
Indeed, large and small, they fly in flocks.
Now like clouds, they ascend and spread;
They also perch on eyelashes and forget to return.
Thus, there is this bird,
With six pinions fully equipped.
In life, it does not hide in silence;
In substance, it has black and white.
It does not shun coolness for warmth,
But traverses the four seasons, dashing about.
Emerging from Kūn Mountain, it touches jade;
Entering Zhào Nán, it inspires rhapsodies.
Its knowledge foretells the coming;
Its nest knows the wind.
Compared to a determined scholar,
When the time arises, it becomes heroic.
Meeting dense foliage, it soars and gathers;
Riding clear breezes, it goes east and west.
Bearing auspicious brightness, it attains its nature,
Roaming parks and gardens to end its days.
Wèi Shōu's "Poem on Watching a Magpie on a Willow"
Turning from the year, its heart can discern;
Ascending spring, its nest forms itself.
Standing withered, it follows the rain's clearing;
Leaning on branches, it awaits the bright moon.
I suspect it emerged from a carved cage;
Surely, it was startled by touching jade.
With gentle chirping, it brushes the supple twigs;
Turning back, it shakes its light feathers.
Why alone does Lí Lóu's intent
Go unheard by those beside?
Liáng Xiāo Jì's "Poem Chanting the Magpie"
Wishing to avoid the slippery new branches,
It returns to fly to its old nest.
This morning, hearing its voice brings joy;
A letter from home is sure to return.
Suí Wèi Yànshēn's "Chanting Playfully on a Magpie Nest in a Garden Tree"
Fearing jade, its heart is often alarmed;
Filling the river, its strength is already spent.
At night, it flies still circling the tree;
At dawn, it sings and faces the wind.
Knowing the future, it does not boast of itself;
Recognizing the years, it does not speak of merit.
Sooner or later, the time should arrive,
When lightly it rises, soaring through the void.
Wild Goose, Seventh
The "Ěryǎ" says:
"Wild ducks and wild geese are similar;
Their feet are webbed."
Guō Pú says:
"The membrane between their toes is connected like a web.
Pronounced 'bǔ.'"
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"Hé,
pronounced hé,
also pronounced jiā.
É, cāng hé, are wild geese."
Yáng Xióng's "Fāngyán" says:
"Wild goose,
east of the pass is called hé é,
south of Chǔ is called é,
or called cāng hé."
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"On the day of White Dew, the wild goose arrives.
If the wild goose does not come,
distant people will rebel.
On the day of Lesser Cold, the wild goose heads north.
If the wild goose does not head north,
the people will not cherish their return."
The "Yílǐ" says:
"A great officer holds a wild goose,
taking it as a sign of awaiting the season to act.
In wedding rituals, when the proposal is sent down,
the betrothal gifts are presented with a wild goose."
The "Lǐjì" says:
"In the first month of spring, the wild goose arrives.
In the last month of autumn, the wild goose comes as a guest.
In the last month of winter, the wild goose heads north."
The "Chūnqiū Fánlù" says:
"Among all ceremonial gifts,
a great officer uses a wild goose.
The wild goose has its kind,
with the elder above the others,
necessarily having order.
The wild goose flies in ranks,
thus it is used as a ceremonial gift."
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"Wild Goose Gate Mountain,
wild geese emerge from within it,
north of Gāoliǔ."
The "Liángzhōu Jì" says:
"Within the boundaries of Liángzhōu County lies Wild Goose Barrier Mountain.
Tradition says this mountain has a large pond,
where wild geese roost and gather,
hence it is named Wild Goose Barrier."
The "Shísānzhōu Jì" says:
"In Shàngyú County, there are wild geese
that work the people's fields.
In spring, they pull out weed roots with their beaks;
in autumn, they peck away the filth.
Therefore, the county officials forbid the people from harming these birds wantonly;
violators are punished without pardon."
Gather at Dark Pass Shot in Shànglín
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Rising from the northern border of the cold gate,
gathering at the dark pass to dwell in peace.
Guests on the shady banks of the Ruò River,
there are the isolated isles of the desert."
The "Shǐjì" says:
"Sū Wǔ was among the Xiōngnú.
Emperor Zhāo sent an envoy to negotiate peace.
Sū Wǔ then secretly met the Hàn envoy at night,
instructing the envoy to tell the Chányú:
'The Son of Heaven shot a wild goose in Shànglín Forest;
he obtained a wild goose,
its foot tied with a silk letter,
saying Sū Wǔ and others are at a certain marsh.'
The envoy spoke as instructed,
and the Chányú was greatly astonished,
then sent Sū Wǔ back."
Pass Yúnmèng Cross Barrier Gate
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Galloping to the southern corner of Wū Mountain,
hastening to the distant borders of Péngzé.
Passing Yúnmèng to roam in delight,
casting into Jiāng and Xiāng to rest midway."
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" says:
"Wild Goose Barrier connects north to Wènyáng Commandery of Liángzhōu.
Between them lie east-west ridges,
reaching the sky without end.
Clouds fly, winds soar;
gazing at the cliffs, wings turn back.
Only one place is low;
when northern wild geese reach the barrier,
they adjust their pinions to cross,
hence named Wild Goose Barrier.
It is the same as Wild Goose Gate."
Play in Dark Islets Bathe in Clear Springs
Yáng Hù's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Pushing through cloudy ruins, soaring up and down,
sifting weak waves, leisurely drifting.
Advancing fiercely into the great clarity,
retreating to play in dark islets."
Chéng Gōngsuí's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Above, waving pinions in the crimson sky;
below, washing feet in clear springs.
Traversing the farthest reaches of heaven and earth,
delighting in the pure warmth of harmonious breath."
Join Feathers Brush Wings
Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose Fleeing the Arrow" says:
"Joining feathers and pinions to go north and south."
Yáng Hù's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Floating like a drifting boat on river waves,
colored like fallen snow on mountain recesses.
Harmoniously, sorrowfully calling among the clouds,
riding the wind, approaching emptiness, sharpening clarity and harmony.
Faintly, glimpsed as if entering clear dust,
supporting the sun, brushing wings, scattering radiant nets."
Turn from Youthful Spring Soar in Dark Moon
Sūn Chǔ's "Rhapsody on the Wild Goose" says:
"Welcoming plain autumn to travel south,
turning from youthful spring to rest north.
Ascending long rivers to cry out,
surmounting great waves to beat wings."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"Sun birds then soar,
in the dark moon.
Thousands of kinds, myriad voices,
clamor among themselves."
Xiāo Guǎngjì notes:
"Sun birds,
are of the wild goose kind."
Emerge from Gāoliǔ Pass Jǐng Mountain
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"Wild Goose Gate Mountain,
wild geese emerge from within it,
north of Gāoliǔ."
The "Jīngzhōu Tújì" says:
"Northwest of Jù County, within Pínglǐ,
lies Wild Goose Floating Mountain.
This is the Jǐng Mountain mentioned in the Shānhǎi Jīng,
from which the Jù River flows.
Over thirty lǐ high,
with long cliffs stretching far,
towering trunks piercing the sky.
Wild geese flying south and returning north
pass all over it;
the locals thus changed the mountain's name."
Cáo Zhì of Wèi, "Rhapsody on the Snared Wild Goose"
I pity the lone goose, so solitary and unique,
My heart is sorrowful, wounded within.
Seeking its kind, so rare and exceptional,
It bears the auspicious blessings of heaven above.
Embracing the pure qi of balanced harmony,
It journeys forth with the turning of the four seasons.
Fleeing the deep winter to the southern reaches,
Avoiding the blazing summer in the northern lands.
White dew chills and drifts on the air,
The autumn wind rises from the western Shang.
Moved by the seasonal cycle's return,
It borrows the paths of Wei to soar aloft.
Joining wings with others, north and south,
Its spirit carefree, eternally content.
But then I see the Fan clan release their mechanism,
Loosing fine silk cords that pierce the clouds.
My frail body's light wings are ensnared,
Suddenly I fall, broken, parted from the flock.
My traveling companions startle and cry as they flee,
In vain I crane my neck—none hear my call.
Chén Hòuzhǔ, "Rhapsody on Geese Passing the Night Pavilion"
Gazing at the mountain pillars in spring,
Warm stones give birth to moss.
Clouds shift with the bamboo's sway,
The moon shares the water's brightness.
Briefly wandering the evening path,
I listen to the passing cries of frosty geese.
Their passing cries already mournful and sharp,
Still bearing the tones of frontier passes.
Riding the wind, the leading flock speeds ahead,
Shrouded in darkness, the rear group startles.
Long has the silk borne words now faded,
Reeds bundled, the broken carrying-pole light.
Their flight, mingled with cries, sometimes chaotic,
Their cries, mingled with flight, sometimes scattered.
Already settled is the sorrow of the empty chamber,
Yet lengthening still is the sigh from the singing tower.
The empty chamber, the singing tower—originally silent,
How much more this cold night, lifting the pearl curtain?
Heart sad, I play the pipe, the tune unfinished,
Hands stroking the strings,
I strum a while.
Strumming the pipe,
And setting forth a song,
Only turns sorrowful feelings more abundant.
Táng Tàizōng Huángdì, "Poem on an Early Goose Emerging from Clouds, Singing"
Early autumn, jade-like dew clear,
An early goose emerges from the void, calling.
Beyond the clouds, its shadow flits chaotically at times,
Carried by the wind, its cry seems suddenly muffled.
Liú Xiàochuò of Liáng, "Poem on the First Returning Geese"
Dòngtíng's spring waters green,
The traveling geese return from Héngyáng.
Wheeling high then dipping low,
They wish to fly toward the Dragon Gate.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Chén, "Poem on Geese, Composed in Cháng'ān"
To the south, I long for Dòngtíng's waters,
To the north, I think of the Yànmén Pass.
Both grain and millet are worthy of longing,
They fly away, then fly back again.
Wáng Zhòu of Suí, "Poem on Geese, Presented upon Seeing Off Attendant Zhōu to Garrison the Southern Frontier"
Traveling geese bid farewell to Héngyáng,
The sky cold, the pass road long.
Their journey broken by the arrow's path,
Their voices hoarse from braving the frost.
Caught by the snare, none pity them,
Able to cry out, they only wound themselves.
How better to be companions, floating freely,
Preening feathers, sporting in the square pond.
Yǔ Xìn of Zhōu, "Poem on a Lone Flying Goose on an Autumn Night"
The lost flock's cold goose—its cry pitiable,
At midnight, flying alone by the moon's side.
Helplessly, the human heart again holds memories,
Tonight, with it, I shall lie sleepless.
Yú Shìnán, "Poem on Autumn Geese"
At dusk, the frosty wind grows urgent,
Wings and feathers find it hard to bear.
Yet, bearing the intent to deliver letters,
In linked flight they enter Shànglín Park.
Parrots, Part Eight
The *Shuōwén* says:
"Yīngwǔ (parrot)
is a bird that can speak.
The character yīng (鸎) derives from the phonetic 'yīng' (嬰) with the bird radical.
The character wǔ (䳇) derives from the phonetic 'mǔ' (母) with the bird radical."
Liú Ài's *Chronicles of the Hàn Emperors* says:
"In the first year of the Xīngpíng era (194 CE),
the barbarians of Yìzhōu presented three yīngwǔ.
An edict stated:
'Previously, Yìzhōu presented three yīngwǔ,
which consumed three *sheng* of hemp seeds each night.
Now grain prices are soaring high.
These birds bring no benefit, only loss.
They may be handed over to General Ānxī Yáng Dìngyīn,
to be returned to their native land.'"
The *Shānhǎi Jīng* says:
"On Huángshān and Shùlìzhīshān, there is a bird.
Its form resembles an owl,
with a red beak and a human-like tongue.
It can speak.
Its name is yīngwǔ."
Guō Pú states:
"The yīngwǔ's tongue resembles a child's tongue.
There are some with five colors.
There are also pure white and pure red ones."
The *Guǎngzhōu Jì* says:
"Gēndù produces five-colored yīngwǔ.
I have seen the white ones,
as large as a hen."
The *Nánfāng Yìwù Zhì* says:
"Yīngwǔ (parrots) come in three kinds.
The green ones are as large as a wūjiù (Chinese tallow tree bird).
One kind is white, as large as a chīxiāo (owl).
One kind is five-colored.
Those larger than the green ones are found throughout Jiāozhōu and Bānán.
The five-colored ones come from Dùbózhōu.
Generally, birds have four toes:
three pointing forward,
one pointing back.
This bird has two toes pointing back."
Pale Yellow Wings, Kingfisher-Green Collar
Cáo Pī's "Rhapsody on the Parrot" says:
"In form, it gazes like a pheasant, looks around like a crane;
it stands like a simurgh, rests like a goose.
Its vermilion beak holds a glow,
its pale yellow plumage shines on its wings."
Mí Héng's "Rhapsody on the Parrot" says:
"Feet of dark reddish-blue, beak of cinnabar red,
green clothes, kingfisher-green collar."
Cinnabar Feet, Purple Plumage
Fù Xuán's "Rhapsody on the Parrot" says:
"It soars like a phoenix, stands like a simurgh;
its substance is splendid, its kingfisher-green glory.
Suspended crimson divides at its cinnabar feet,
graceful vermilion beak glimmers brightly."
Sūn Chàng's *Yìwù Zhì* says:
"The yīngwǔ (parrot),
its plumage is sometimes dark green,
sometimes purple-red.
Its beak is curved like an owl's, its eyes deep-set.
It walks like a dove or sparrow, yet can imitate human speech.
Therefore, it is seen as particularly precious."
Chooses Its Grove, Pecks at Blossoms
Mí Héng's "Rhapsody on the Parrot" says:
"In flight, it does not alight recklessly;
when soaring, it must choose its grove."
Guō Pú's "Eulogy for the Illustrations of the *Shānhǎi Jīng*" says:
"The yīngwǔ, the intelligent bird,
perches in groves, pecks at blossoms.
Its four toes divide the middle;
when walking, it uses its beak."
Like a Hen, Resembles an Owl
The *Wú Shí Wàiguó Zhuàn* says:
"East of Fúnán is the Zhànghǎi (Swollen Sea),
which sometimes produces five-colored yīngwǔ.
I have seen the white ones,
as large as a hen."
The *Nánfāng Yìwù Zhì* says:
"Yīngwǔ (parrots) come in three kinds.
One kind is large and white, like a chīxiāo (owl)."
Through Dreams Worrying About the Worthy, Moved by Spirit to Extinguish Fire
Zhōu Xuān's "Book of Dreams" says:
"The parrot represents the dwelling of the deceased.
To dream of a parrot
means worrying about the deceased.
If it is in the hall,
it means worrying about the eminent and worthy."
Liú Yìqìng's "Records of Manifestations" says:
"A parrot flew and settled on another mountain,
where the birds and beasts of the mountain all loved and respected each other.
The parrot thought to itself,
'Although this is joyful, it cannot last long,'
and then left.
Several months later,
a fire broke out on the mountain.
Seeing it from afar,
the parrot dipped its feathers in water
and flew to sprinkle it over the fire.
A heavenly deity said:
'Although you have the will,
how can it be enough?'
The parrot replied:
'I know I cannot save it,
but I once lived as a guest on this mountain.
The birds and beasts there acted with goodness,
all like brothers.
I cannot bear to see it!'
The heavenly deity was moved and praised it,
and immediately extinguished the fire."
"Rhapsody on the Parrot" by Mí Héng of the Later Hàn
This bird from the Western Regions,
displays a wondrous, natural grace.
Its body bears the exquisite essence of metal,
and contains the bright radiance of fire's virtue.
Clever by nature and able to speak,
its mind is astute and knows opportunity.
Thus it plays and roams on lofty peaks,
and perches in deep, secluded places.
It never flies to gather recklessly,
and when soaring, always chooses its woods.
With dark blue feet and a crimson beak,
green feathers and an emerald collar.
Its brilliant, beautiful appearance,
and clear, lovely voice.
Though of the same feathery kin,
its wisdom and heart are truly distinct.
Matched with the phoenix in beauty,
how can common birds compare in virtue?
"Rhapsody on the Parrot" by Cáo Zhí of Wèi
Praising the fine bird of the Central Land,
transcending its kind with a special name.
Moved by warm yang, it spreads its wings,
retreating to great yin to take form.
Meeting the traveler's strict net,
its six pinions are broken, leaving nothing.
Its body entangled in heavy bonds,
the lone female cries and returns alone.
How could I cherish my own body?
I pity the fledglings not yet able to fly.
To divide my flesh to moisten the cauldron,
what hope dare I have for complete salvation?
Receiving the profound virtue of nurture,
I serve the master's glorious light.
I lament my lightness against such heavy favor,
fearing the fine grace may falter.
Often restraining my heart with fear,
though at peace, I feel as if in peril.
Forever crying sadly to repay virtue,
hoping never to tire till the end.
"Rhapsody on the White Parrot" by Yán Yánzhī of Sòng
I, holding office at Chóngxián,
witnessed a divine marvel.
There was a white parrot,
clad in white, treading in black,
gentle in nature, eloquent in speech.
From distant lands beyond nine translations,
it became a treasure in the celestial court.
Together with many scholars,
admiring its wonder, I thought to compose a rhapsody.
Its words are:
"Endowed with form in the pure realm,
continuing the line of the cold gate.
In appearance, treading black yet clad in purity,
in nature, nurtured and also gentle.
Regretting the phoenix's lack of discernment,
pitying the morning oriole's vain clamor."
"Rhapsody on the Red Parrot" by Xiè Zhuāng of Sòng
Its wise nature harmonizes with brightness,
its heavenly instinct naturally understands.
It discerns the nation's speech within the central realm,
and reaches distant sounds in far-off lands.
And when clouds shift and rosy clouds stand still,
when sleet falls and snow flutters,
resplendent and gradual like pheasant feathers,
graceful and at ease like swan flight.
Leaping through woods, flying over peaks,
brilliant like lightning overflowing smoky gates.
Gathering in fields, perching in gardens,
radiant like peach blossoms adorning jade gardens.
As for when the air is pure and isles clear,
mist descends and cliffs sink.
The moon draws light on green waters,
clouds trace shadows on azure woods.
Lǐ Yìfǔ's "Poem on the Parrot"
Dragged by the line, leaving the vast sea,
touching the net, departing layered peaks.
With folded wings within the carved cage,
thoughts extend to the edge of colored clouds.
Longing for companions, morning cries keen,
separated from the flock, night shadows cold.
Able to speak is especially precious,
mutually aiding, I recall Cháng'ān.
Dragon, Ninth
The "Shuōwén" says:
"The dragon,
chief of scaled creatures,
can be hidden or bright,
can be small or large,
can be long or short.
At the spring equinox, it ascends to heaven;
at the autumn equinox, it enters the river."
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"Those with scales are called jiāo dragons;
those with wings are called yìng dragons;
those with horns are called qiú dragons;
those without horns are called chī dragons."
The "Fāngyán" says:
"A dragon not yet ascended to heaven is called a pán dragon."
The "Hétú" says:
"Yellow gold after a thousand years gives birth to a yellow dragon;
green gold after a thousand years gives birth to a green dragon;
red and white gold after a thousand years each give birth to dragons."
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
"In ancient times, dragons were kept,
so there were the Huànlóng clan and the Yùlóng clan in the state.
Huàn
means to rear.
Long ago, there was Liào Shū'ān.
Liào
is an ancient state name.
Shū'ān
was its ruler's name.
He had a descendant named Dǒng Fù,
who truly loved dragons greatly.
He could seek out their desires to feed them,
and many dragons returned to him.
Thus he tamed and reared dragons
to serve Emperor Shùn,
and Shùn bestowed upon him the surname Dǒng."
The "Yuánmìng Bāo" says:
"The dragon means to sprout,
the yang within yin.
Thus it is said when the dragon rises, clouds flourish."
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"The yìng dragon dwells at the southern extreme.
It slew Chīyóu and Kuāfù,
and could not return above.
Thus the yìng dragon remained on earth.
