Therefore, there are frequent droughts below.
When drought occurs, making the form of an yìng dragon,
then great rain is obtained."
The qi responds to what is felt.
The "Kuòdìtú" says:
"The mountain of the dragon pool is high on four sides.
In its midst is a pool,
seven hundred lǐ square,
where groups of dragons dwell.
There are many five-flower trees,
which the dragons eat.
It is forty-five thousand lǐ from Kuàijī."
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"The jiāo dragon lies hidden in rivers,
but its eggs are split on hills.
The male calls from the wind above,
the female calls from the wind below.
As for transformation,
it is the utmost of form and essence.
People do not see the dragon flying and rising to heights
without wind and rain supporting it."
The "Bàopǔzǐ" says:
"There are natural dragons,
and dragons transformed from snakes and caterpillars."
It also says:
"In the mountains, on chén days, what is called the rain master
is the dragon."
The "Ruìyìngtú" says:
"The yellow dragon says:
'The essence of divine spirits,
the chief of the four dragons.
When the king does not drain ponds to fish,
and virtue reaches the deep abyss,
then it responds to the qi and swims in ponds and marshes.'"
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"A rotten melon transforms into a fish—
such is the transformation of things."
The Lièzǐ says:
"North of Zhōngfà there is the Míng Sea,
where fish are a thousand lǐ wide,
their bodies matching that size."
The Guǎngzhì says:
"The small fish of Wǔyáng,
as large as needles,
are said to number a thousand to a jīn,
and the people of Shǔ make them into paste."
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù says:
"Large carp are called zhān,
and large zhān are called wěi.
White fish:
the males are called pī.
Fish roe tends to gather and float on the water's surface,
and is called duckweed."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Zhān Gōng's fishing
caught a carp a thousand years old."
Táo Hóngjǐng's Běncǎo says:
"The carp is foremost among fish,
its form is lovely,
and it can also undergo divine transformations.
It can even fly over mountains and lakes,
which is why Qín Gāo rode upon one.
Also, carp zhǎ [fermented fish]
should not be combined with small bean leaves,
as eating them harms people
and also triggers various sores.
The lǐ fish,
also called tóng,
pronounced chú méng fǎn.
Its flavor is sweet,
non-toxic,
and it primarily dispels water qi,
facial swelling, and the five types of hemorrhoids.
The shàn fish,
flavor sweet,
very warm and non-toxic,
is said to be transformed from celery roots."
It also says:
"It is transformed from human hair,
and making it into a stew to eat is very nourishing.
The bào fish,
flavor pungent,
non-toxic,
primarily expels atrophy, limpness, wrist fractures, and stagnant blood.
The fù
pú jiǎo fǎn.
fish
treats green blindness and seminal loss.
The mán
mò yú fǎn.
lí
lì xī fǎn.
fish,
flavor sweet,
shape similar to the shàn,
can climb trees and eat vine flowers,
and is taken to make dried meat for eating."
The Guǎngzhōu Jì says:
"The fáng fish,
broad, plump, and sweet,
is among the finest of fish.
Jīngní are a hundred zhàng long,
and their size matches that.
Females are called ní,
males are called jīng.
Their eyes are the bright moon pearls,
which are not seen after death.
They have eyes,
and when they spout waves, they obscure the sun and clouds."
The Ěryǎ says:
"Lǐ—
now called red carp.
Zhān—
now called huángyú in Jiāngdōng.
Yǎn—
now the yǎn-foreheaded white fish.
Nián.
Also called tí.
Pī,
large hù,
small ones are called zhào.
Hù resembles nián but larger,
color white,
or the large ones of yí are called hù.
Shéng,
small fish.
Unformed fish roe.
The xiè fish,
large ní are called xiè,
resembles nián,
has four legs,
and its cry resembles a child's."
The Nányuè Zhì says:
"Zhān,
xún
zǐ lín fǎn.
type.
Long nose, soft bones,
several zhàng long, and its bones are edible,
resembles huáng but longer.
The jù fish,
has something like iron saws on its left and right sides.
resembles shíshǒu,
or is said to be the male shíshǒu.
The zhí fish,
plump and delicious with plenty to spare,
is highly valued by the locals.
In Wèi Wǔ's time, four people ate zhí.
The zhān fish is as large as a five-dǒu lián,
a zhàng long,
mouth under the chin,
often comes up the river in the third month,
and is often caught at Mèngjīn.
Yellow and plump,
only used to make zhǎ,
and also found in the Huái River."
The Máo Shī Yìshū says:
"The wěi fish comes from the sea,
in the third month it comes up from the river.
Now at the cave in the mountain belly on the north cliff east of Gǒng County's Luò crossing.
Old accounts say the north cave connects with rivers and lakes,
and zhān and wěi come from the north cave
into the river.
Wěi resembles zhān but is bluish-black in color,
with a small, pointed head,
like an iron helmet,
mouth under the chin,
large ones seven or eight chǐ,
and people in Yìzhōu call it wěi.
Cháng,
large ones are called wáng wěi,
small ones are called shū wěi,
also called xún,
flesh color white.
Now people in Dōnglái and Liáodōng call it wèi fish,
or call it the spirit fish,
because a Lèlàng commandant drowned in the sea
and transformed into this fish.
Xù resembles fáng but has a large head,
an unpleasing fish,
hence the saying:
'Buying fish and getting xù
is worse than eating vegetables.'
In Xúzhōu it is called lián.
Lǐ rán fǎn.
The shā
shā.
fish,
blows sand,
resembles jì fish but narrower and smaller,
often opens its mouth to blow sand,
also called chóngchún yuè.
The shā cháng
cháng.
fish,
also called yánghé,
yellow cheeks, bones straight,
a large and powerful huáng fish.
The yú lí fish,
has patterned markings on its back,
pure blue on its belly,
now used to decorate bow cases and step patterns.
When the sea tide is about to come or rain is about to fall,
its hairs all stand up;
when the tide recedes and the sky clears,
the hairs lie down.
It often knows the sea tide from a thousand lǐ away."
The Shānhǎijīng says:
"The guì
jué wèi fǎn.
fish,
large mouth and fine scales,
with patterned colors.
The yáo
yǔ zhāo fǎn.
fish,
shape like a carp,
fish body with bird wings,
blue patterns,
white head and red beak.
Often swims from the Western Sea to the Eastern Sea,
flies at night,
its sound like a luán bird,
and its appearance brings great harvests.
The héluó fish,
one head and ten bodies,
its sound like a barking dog,
eating it cures abscesses.
The qí
yì.
fish,
large body and head,
sound like an infant."
Eating it cures madness.
Zhuān
Pronounced as "shì liàn fǎn".
The pearl turtle,
resembles lungs but has eyes,
has six legs.
There is the pearl fish,
shaped like a crucian carp,
with bristles like a pig,
its cry resembles that of a suckling pig,
and its appearance heralds drought across the land.
The bó fish,
shaped like a sturgeon but with one eye,
its cry sounds like retching,
like the sound of a person vomiting.
Its appearance heralds rebellion across the land.
The tí fish, with red eyes and red fins,
is fatal if eaten.
Líng
Pronounced as "líng".
fish,
has spines on both its back and belly,
like triangular water caltrops."
The Wú Lù states:
"The cuò fish,
also written as 䱜.
After the fish spawn,
the fry go out to seek food in the morning,
and by evening all return into their mother's belly."
The Shuǐ Jīng states:
"The sea qiū
Pronounced as "qiě yóu fǎn".
fish,
is several thousand lǐ long,
dwells in burrows on the seafloor.
When it enters its burrow, the seawater becomes the tide;
when it emerges, the tide recedes.
Its comings and goings are rhythmic,
hence the tides occur on schedule."
The Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The shark,
its skin can be used to adorn knives.
When its young are startled, they retreat into their mother's belly."
The Wú Dì Zhì states:
"The yellow croaker,
by autumn transforms into a crowned duck,
and the crowned duck's head still contains a stone."
The Nán Yuè Jì states:
"The cuttlefish,
also called 'the petty clerk of River Earl Hé Bó',
often floats on the water surface.
When crows see it and think it is dead,
they go to peck at it,
whereupon it seizes the crow by coiling around it,
hence it is called the 'crow thief'.
Now, the 'pǐ wū huà zhī' celestial ox fish,
is three zhàng in length and width,
with eyes as large as peck measures,
its mouth located on its flank,
exposing teeth without lips.
It has two fleshy horns like arms,
two wings six chǐ long,
and a tail five chǐ long.
The flatfish,
cannot swim unless paired,
in Jiāngdōng it is called 'wáng yú'.
Long ago, King Yuè was preparing sliced fish,
he had cut it open but not yet sliced it,
when it fell into the water,
and transformed into this fish."
The Línhǎi Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The flatfish,
resembles a fish split left and right.
In Nányuè it is called 'bǎn yú'. The mermaid,
resembles a human,
is three chǐ long,
and is inedible."
Zhāng Huá's Bówù Zhì states:
"The ox fish,
has eyes like an ox,
and a shape like a calf.
When its skin is peeled and hung up,
the hair stands up when the tide comes in,
and lies down when the tide goes out."
Also, the Nánfāng Cǎo Wù Zhuàng states:
"The water zhū fish,
resembles a pig in shape."
Also, the Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The deer fish,
has two horns on its head like a deer."
Has wings, no scales.
Liú Xiàng's Liè Xiān Zhuàn states:
"Zǐ Mò,
was a man from Shūxiāng.
He was skilled at entering the water to catch fish.
Once he caught a red carp,
and, admiring its color,
placed it in a pond,
and regularly fed it with rice and grain.
After a year it grew over a zhàng long,
then grew horns,
and had wings."
The Hé Tú states:
"Huángdì was traveling on the Luò River,
and saw a carp three zhàng long,
with a blue body and no scales,
and red patterns forming characters."
A thousand jīn, seven lǐ.
The Dà Wèi Zhū Zhōu Jì states:
"At Xiǎopíngjīn there is a cave,
from which carp come and go.
The larger ones weigh a thousand jīn,
are blue in color,
and have skin like shark skin."
Shěn Yíng's Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Yì Wù Zhì states:
"Carp are a hundred paces long;
folklore speaks of a seven-lǐ sturgeon fish."
Like a shark, resembles a dragon.
The Dà Wèi Zhū Zhōu Jì states:
"Every year in mid-third month,
sturgeon emerge from caves.
They enter the river,
weighing a thousand jīn,
blue in color,
with skin like a shark,
the skin has pearl-like patterns,
and the mouth is under the jaw."
The Máo Shī Yì Shū states:
"The sturgeon's body resembles a dragon,
with a pointed head,
and mouth under the jaw.
Its back and underside have armor,
the larger ones weigh over a thousand jīn."
The northern sea's kūn, the southern sea's whale.
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"In the northern sea there is a fish,
its name is Kūn.
Its size is such that no one knows how many thousand lǐ it spans."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shí Yí Jì states:
"The Black River,
is at the North Pole.
Its water is thick, black, and stagnant,
and earth-clouds arise from it.
There is a black kūn fish,
a thousand chǐ long, like a whale.
It often flies to the southern sea,
but sometimes drifts and loses its way,
dying on the shores of the southern sea.
Its flesh and bones all dissolve,
only its gall remains, hard as stone,
and it is a superior immortal medicine."
Like a beast, like a snake.
Shān Qiānzhī's Nán Xúzhōu Jì states:
"The líng fish,
resembles a carp with four feet."
The Wú Dū Fù states:
"The so-called líng fish resembles a beast."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nán Yuè Zhì states:
"The líng fish,
is a carp.
Its shape is like a snake with four feet,
its belly girth five or six cùn,
its head resembles a lizard,
and its scales are like armor."
The Yì Wù Zhì calls it línglǐ.
Black body, green eyes.
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nán Yuè Zhì states:
"The black cuò fish,
is entirely black,
and two zhàng long."
The Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Jì states:
"The cuò fish has deer-like patterns and green eyes."
Tiger-shaped, shrimp-tailed.
Shěn Yíng's Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The tiger cuò,
is five zhàng long,
with yellow and black spots.
Its ears, eyes, teeth, and fangs somewhat resemble a tiger's form.
Only it lacks fur,
and sometimes transforms to become a tiger."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Nán Yuè Zhì states:
"The shrimp cuò is five zhàng long,
with a tail like a shrimp."
White belly, spotted patterns.
Shěn Yíng's Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Yì Wù Zhì states:
"The cuò fish,
has a pure white underside,
and is five chǐ long."
It also says:
"The tiger cuò is three chǐ long,
with yellow spotted patterns."
Saw-like Teeth, Frosty Fangs
Wàn Zhèn's *Nánzhōu Yìwù Zhì* states:
"The crocodile's teeth form a net-like array;
they sever like knives and saws.
It dwells in water,
feeding primarily on fish."
Yǔ Chǎn's *Wúdū Fù* states:
"Crocodile scales, frosty fangs."
Pearl Patterns, Poisonous Tail
Liú Xīnqī's *Jiāozhōu Jì* states:
"The shark emerges from Hépǔ;
it is three chǐ in length,
with armor on its back,
adorned with pearl-like patterns.
Its toughness can be used to decorate knife edges,
and it can also be used to file objects."
*Shānhǎi Jīng* states:
"Mount Yān,
from which the Zhāng River flows,
abounds with sharks."
The annotation states:
"The shark has pearl-like patterns,
a green tail,
and is poisonous.
Its skin can be used to decorate knife and sword edges."
Spring Arrival, Autumn Transformation
*Línhǎi Yìwù Zhì* states:
"The large yellow croaker;
the smaller ones are called 'jūshuǐ',
the next size is called 'chūnlái',
a distinct variety of large yellow croaker.
There is also the 'shítóu',
seven to eight cùn long,
similar to the large yellow croaker."
Zhāng Bó's *Wú Lù* states:
"Lóu County has large yellow croaker,
which transform into wild ducks by autumn."
Side-by-Side Standing, Paired Swimming
*Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Jì* states:
"The flatfish stands side-by-side,
moving together with bodies joined,
it is the flounder."
Sūn Chuò's *Wàng Hǎi Fù* states:
"The wángyú plays alone,
while the flounder swims in pairs."
Resembling an Otter, Like an Ox
Yáng Fú's *Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Jì* states:
"The fish-ox resembles an otter,
as large as a calf,
with bluish-yellow fur,
its fur resembling felt.
It knows the ebb and flow of the tide."
"Rhapsody on Observing Fish" by Xījìn Zhì Yú
Observing the scaled clan in the sparkling pond,
gazing at the feathered flocks by the rapid's edge.
There are carp from the Wèi springs,
and catfish from the Zhuó slopes.
Splashing and leaping,
submerging in waves, heading afar.
Gathering in the bends of the winding shore,
chasing in the depths of the gentle waters.
Clustering like spokes converging,
some leaping, some sinking.
Flickering and darting swiftly,
dazzling the eyes, startling the heart.
Merely gazing to the utmost yet gaining nothing,
I envy the tender delicacy of fresh dishes.
Then six pillars rise together,
constructed crosswise into a net.
Weaving reeds into rafts,
stirring wood to agitate the waves.
Rushing and turning, pressing close,
the current unable to form ripples.
Fish, not yet alarmed, lose their course,
suddenly meeting waves in the swift rapids.
Truly, the terrain's advantage prevails,
ensuring advance without return.
Stewed catfish and sliced carp,
also various delicacies.
Dishes and fruits arrayed together,
both delicious and tender.
Floating cups along the open channel,
toasting over the plain waves.
competing in quick-wittedness on the swift stream.
Once joyful and unwearied,
I wish to continue through day and night.
Alone by the river, filled with emotion,
moved by the passing of things, unwilling to part.
Only seeking to establish a lasting name,
I long for the setting sun's fading light.
Fearing lingering may corrupt virtue,
I cease my joy and order the carriage.
At this time,
embracing profound seclusion,
I await wine and food.
Feasting in comfort and ease,
joyful feelings not yet peaked.
Words of chosen inspiration,
rectifying excess with straightness.
Pleased yet not fully content,
none fail to sigh.
Liáng Zhāng Lǜ's "Poem on Leaping Fish in Response to Imperial Command"
Furling scales, hidden in dense algae,
lifting heads to receive clear ripples.
Why roam the vast seas?
Rather leap in the Tiānquán Pond.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on Fish Leaping, Water Flowers Blooming"
Rippling hues of peach blossom waters,
gazing at the brocade-washing stream.
Leaping at the shore, pearls seem to emerge;
by the pond, they float like mirrors.
Riding waves, catching falling petals,
touching bait, avoiding sunken hooks.
Just swimming beyond lotus leaves,
how could they enter King Wǔ's boat?
Suí Ruǎn Zhuó's "Poem on Fish Swimming Under Lotus"
Spring hues reflect on clear ponds,
swimming and diving, following along.
Not yet on the path to Lóngmén,
they play by the lotus pond.
Touching waves, lotus fragrance stirs;
riding currents, leaf shadows part.
Forgetting each other, they find their own joy—
how could Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ understand?
Suí Cén Dé Rùn's "Poem on Fish"
Sword-shadows merge with invading waves,
pearl-gleams, water-fresh, anew.
East of the lotus, one may play at will—
what need to ascend Lóngjīn?
Turtles, Eleventh
The Luò Shū states:
"The spiritual turtle,
with its dark patterns and five colors,
is the essence of divine spirits.
Its raised back emulates heaven,
its flat underside emulates earth.
It can perceive survival and demise,
illuminate fortune and misfortune.
When the ruler is impartial and without faction,
and venerates the elderly, then it appears."
The Hóng Fàn Wǔ Xíng states:
"The turtle signifies longevity;
after a thousand years it becomes numinous—
this is a beast that knows fortune and misfortune."
The Zhōu Guān states:
"The turtle officer is in charge of the six types of turtles,
each with its own name and characteristic.
The heavenly turtle is called the 'spiritual kind',
the earthly turtle is called the 'unraveling kind',
the eastern turtle is called the 'fruitful kind',
the western turtle is called the 'thunder kind',
the southern turtle is called the 'hunting kind',
the northern turtle is called the 'compliant kind'.
Each is distinguished by its directional color and its body.
'Kind' indicates they are not uniform.
Colors refer to: heavenly turtle black,
earthly turtle yellow,
eastern turtle blue-green,
western turtle white,
southern turtle red,
northern turtle black.
Generally, turtles are captured in autumn,
and processed in spring.
Each according to its type
is placed in the turtle chamber;
the six turtles each have separate chambers.
In early spring, the turtles are anointed with blood,
and sacrifices are offered to the ancestors of divination."
The Dà Dài Lǐ states:
"Of the three hundred sixty armored creatures,
the divine turtle is the chief."
The Yì Lǐ states:
"The Son of Heaven's turtle is one foot two inches,
the feudal lords' eight inches,
the senior officials' six inches,
the scholars and commoners' four inches.
The turtle is
the elder among the yīn creatures.
A turtle of three thousand years
ascends to roam upon the curled-ear plant.
The elder knows first,
thus the noble man, when undertaking affairs, must consult it."
The Lǐ Tǒng states:
"The image of the divine turtle:
its upper roundness emulates heaven,
its lower squareness emulates earth.
On its back is a disc emulating hills and mountains;
dark patterns interweave
to form the constellations.
Five lights shine brightly,
dark brocade patterns circulate,
responding in turn to the four seasons,
length one foot two inches.
It illuminates fortune and misfortune,
speechless yet trustworthy."
The Yùn Dǒu Shū states:
"The Yáoguāng star scattered and became turtles."
The Ěr Yǎ states:
"Turtles with three feet are called bēn turtles.
Those with heads lowered are called líng,
those with heads raised are called xiè.
Those with the front shell covering are called guǒ,
those with the rear shell covering are called liè.
Those leaning left are called bù lèi,
those leaning right are called bù ruò.
First is the divine turtle,
second is the spiritual turtle,
third is the shè turtle—a small turtle
with a belly shell that folds,
able to open and close by itself.
Fourth is the treasure turtle,
fifth is the patterned turtle,
sixth is the divination turtle,
often hidden beneath clumps of yarrow.
Seventh is the mountain turtle,
eighth is the marsh turtle,
ninth is the water turtle,
tenth is the fire turtle."
The Shǐ Jì states:
"Master Chǔ said:
'Those who can obtain a famous turtle,
wealth and goods will come to them,
their households will surely become greatly wealthy, up to tens of millions.
First is the Northern Dipper turtle,
second is the Southern Stars turtle,
third is the Five Planets turtle,
fourth is the Eight Winds turtle,
fifth is the Twenty-Eight Mansions turtle,
sixth is the Sun and Moon turtle,
seventh is the Jade turtle,
eighth is the Nine Provinces turtle:
in all, eight names.'
These turtle diagrams each have writing on the underside of the belly;
the writing says:
'Such-and-such's turtle.
It need not be a full foot two inches;
obtaining seven or eight inches is already precious.'" It also states:
"Above there is dense yarrow,
below there is a divine turtle.
Where yarrow grows with a hundred stems,
below it there is often a turtle guarding it,
and above it there are blue clouds covering it.
An old man in the south used a turtle to prop his bed leg.
After twenty years,
the old man died.
When the bed was moved,
the turtle was still alive,
not dead.
The turtle can circulate qì and conduct breathing exercises."
The Sòng Lüè states:
"The commandery of Wú presented a six-eyed turtle."
The Nán Qí Shū states:
"In the Yǒngmíng era,
Táng Qián presented one green-haired divine turtle."
The Xuán Zhōng Jì states:
"Of the great creatures in the southeast is the giant áo,
which carries the Pénglái Mountain on its back,
circumference a thousand lǐ.
The giant áo
is a giant turtle.
Also, a thousand-year-old turtle
can speak with humans."
The Nán Yuè Zhì states:
"Turtle shell,
also called 'divine house',
comes from the Southern Sea,
born in ponds and marshes.
In Wú and Yuè it is called yuán zhù.
The divine turtle is as large as a fist and colored like gold;
its upper shell on both sides is like saw teeth.
Its claws are extremely sharp,
and it can climb large trees
to catch chirping cicadas;
it is extremely delicious to eat.
It is not suitable for divination
due to its small size.
The Fúlíng giant turtle
has patterns like hawksbill turtle;
commonly called the spiritual turtle."
The Bào Pú Zǐ states:
"A thousand-year-old turtle
possesses all five colors;
the two bones on its forehead protrude like horns.
It floats upon lotus leaves,
or stays beneath clumps of yarrow,
above which there are sometimes white clouds.
Coiled snakes, turtles, and snakes
when hibernating feed on qì.
In summer they eat freely yet become very thin,
in winter they hibernate in burrows and become very fat."
The Bó Wù Zhì states:
"Generally, turtles and tuó crocodiles have no males;
they conceive through communion with snakes.
Turtles and tuó crocodiles are all oviparous."
Cuī Bào's Gǔ Jīn Zhù states:
"The turtle is named 'Dark-Robed Superintendent'."
The Guǎng Zhì states:
"Zī
(pronounced zī wéi fǎn).
Yí
(pronounced yí jiā fǎn).
Shape like a turtle,
comes from Jiāozhōu.
Mountain turtles live on mountains eating grass,
over a foot long."
The Liǔ Shì Guī Jīng states:
"A turtle of one thousand two hundred years
can divine the beginning and end of heaven and earth.
How to say this?
Three thousand and forty-two divinations rely on the shell of a thousand-year-old turtle of heaven and earth.
Black turtles have five colors;
use them according to the season."
Emulating Heaven, Resembling Earth
The Lǐ Tǒng states:
"The image of the divine turtle:
its upper roundness emulates heaven,
its lower squareness emulates earth.
On its back is a disc emulating hills and mountains;
dark patterns interweave
to form the constellations."
The Luò Shū states:
"The spiritual turtle:
its raised back emulates heaven,
its flat underside resembles earth."
Ten Péng Four Grades
The Book of Changes says:
"Or one may benefit from a turtle worth ten péng."
Wáng Bì's commentary states:
"The turtle is an object for resolving doubts.
To obtain benefit and acquire a turtle worth ten péng
means receiving the utmost assistance from both Heaven and humanity."
The Book of Hàn says:
"The yuánguī (great turtle) has a jù shape,
measuring one chi and two cun in length,
valued at one thousand one hundred and sixty coins,
constituting ten péng of chǐ bèi.
The gōngguī (duke's turtle), nine cun or larger,
valued at five hundred coins,
constitutes ten péng of zhuàng bèi;
the hóuguī (marquis's turtle), seven cun or larger,
valued at three hundred coins,
constitutes ten péng of gōng bèi;
the zǐguī (viscount's turtle), five cun or larger,
valued at one hundred coins,
constitutes one péng of xiǎo bèi.
These are the four grades of treasure."
Black Robe Embroidered Skirt
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"King Yuán of Sòng asked the Erudite Wèi Píng:
'Last night, in my dream, I saw a gentleman
wearing black and embroidered garments,
riding in a light carriage.'
He said:
'I am an envoy of the Jiāng River to the Hé River,
but Yù Qiě captured me and I cannot leave.
My body is in distress,
with no one to tell my plight.
As you, King, possess virtue and righteousness,
I have come to inform you.
What creature am I?'
Wèi Píng then rose, holding his divination board,
and replied:
'In the past, on a rénzǐ day when the lodge was at Qiānniú,
the envoy should have been wearing black garments and riding in a covered carriage.
His name is 'turtle'.
Could Your Majesty send someone to inquire and seek him?'
The King said:
'Excellent!'"
Sūn Huì's "Rhapsody on the Turtle's Words" says:
"There was a gentleman in dark robes,
wearing black and embroidered clothes.
He rode in a light carriage, swift and lofty,
driving through clouds and mist, soaring high.
Wind and rain surged for him like lightning,
the five colors blazing and resplendent."
Chìlíng Báiruò
Liǔ Lóng's Classic of Turtles says:
"Turtles have five colors,
used according to the season.
The qīnglíng turtle
is suitable for use in spring,
facing east while seated to the west;
the chìlíng turtle
is suitable for use in summer,
facing south while seated to the north."
The Mòzǐ says:
"In ancient times, the Xiàhòu clan sent Fēilián to smelt metal at Chēn Mountain
to cast tripods at Kūnwú,
and had Wēng Nányǐ scorch the shell of a báiruò turtle."
Nesting on Lotuses Ascending Trees
The Records of the Grand Historian:
"Master Chǔ said:
'In the beautiful forests south of the Jiāng,
turtles dwell there,
often nesting upon fragrant lotus leaves.
On the left side of its shell is inscribed:
"Jiǎzǐ and Chóngguāng.
He who obtains me, a commoner, shall become a ruler;
he who possesses land and governs rightly,
a feudal lord who obtains me shall become an emperor."'"
Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omissions says:
"On the fifth level of the Kūnlún Mountains,
there is a divine turtle,
one chi and nine cun in length.
It has four wings,
and after ten thousand years, it ascends trees to dwell,
and can also speak."
Vermilion Characters Black Patterns
The "Zhōnghòu" chapter of the Book of Documents says:
"Yáo cast jade discs into the Luò River,
and a black turtle emerged bearing a writing on its back,
with vermilion characters in red lines,
and stopped at the altar.
Again, jade discs were cast into the Hé River,
and a black turtle emerged,
with red lines forming an inscription."
The Lǐ Tǒng says:
"The image of the divine turtle
has a carapace above,
modeled after hills and mountains,
with black patterns interwoven,
forming the array of constellations."
Spring Scorching Winter Consecration
The Illustrations of the Three Ritual Classics says:
"For the turtle shell,
in spring, scorch the rear left;
in summer, scorch the front left;
in autumn, scorch the front right;
in winter, scorch the rear right."
Cài Yōng's "Explanations on the Monthly Ordinances" says:
"In the first month of winter,
order the Grand Diviner to consecrate the turtle shells and stalks.
Sacrifice to the turtle shells and stalks with animals,
smearing them with the blood of the sacrifice,
which is called 'consecrating the turtle'.
'Consecration' refers to
the turtle shells used for divination.
The 'stalks' refer to
the yarrow stalks used for milfoil divination."
Traveling on Land Dwelling in the Abyss
Jiāo Gòng's Forest of Changes says:
"The turtle, weary of rivers and seas,
travels on land without cease,
bringing upon itself desiccation and withering,
losing its metropolitan abode."
Lǐ Yóng's "Rhapsody on the Turtle" says:
"Its substance corresponds to the Lí trigram's image,
its position is fixed, dwelling in the Kǎn trigram.
I despise those gluttonous jaws,
yet expend my numinous tally.
Floating on the Luò River,
I see the weft texts.
Penetrating secret profundities,
comprehending mysterious emptiness."
Propping the Bed Hanging in the Chamber
The Records of the Grand Historian says:
"An old man in the south used a turtle to prop the legs of his bed
for over twenty years."
It also says:
"Take a turtle and place it in the northwest corner of a room,
hang it up before entering a deep, vast forest,
and you will not become lost."
Supervisory Courier Divine Envoy
The Notes on Ancient and Modern Matters says:
"The turtle is named 'Black-robed Supervisory Courier',
'Divine Envoy',
referring to the divine turtle."
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the River" says:
"responding to Jiāofǔ's loss of his pendant,
pitying the divine envoy entangled in nets."
Brocade Patterns Golden Color
The Lǐ Tǒng says:
"The image of the divine turtle
is like black brocade patterns in motion,
changing in response to the four seasons."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Records of Nányuè says:
"When the divine turtle appears,
it is as large as a fist and colored like gold."
Nourishing Qì Containing Spirit
Guō Pú's "Eulogy on the Turtle in the Illustrations to the Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"Water circles three directions,
hidden sources bubbling and boiling.
Here the numinous turtle dwells,
wagging its tail, nourishing its qì.
Master Zhuāng was moved by this,
waving his fishing rod, disdaining the noble."
Shěn Huáiyuǎn's Records of Nányuè says:
"The divine turtle emerges from the river waters.
The Lújiāng commandery often presents live turtles to the Grand Diviner,
for they darkly contain spiritual knowledge,
Looking Left, Turning Right
The Zāng Róngxù Jìn Shū states:
"Kǒng Yú,
courtesy name Jìngkāng,
was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
In his youth, he once obtained a turtle
and released it into a stream.
As the turtle reached midstream, it looked back left several times.
Later, when casting his marquis seal,
the turtle on the seal faced left.
Recasting it still resulted in the same.
The seal artisan reported this,
and Kǒng Yú, realizing its significance,
took it to wear."
The Xù Sōushén Jì states:
"Huáng Zhě of Póyáng
entered the mountains to gather jīngyáng plants
and lost his way.
After several days,
he suddenly saw a large turtle.
Huáng Zhě then chanted to it,
saying:
'You are a spiritual creature,
and I am lost, not knowing the way.
Now I shall ride on your back,
and wherever your head faces shall be the path.'
The turtle immediately turned right,
and Huáng Zhě followed it.
After about ten lǐ,
he reached a stream,
which was used by traveling merchants for boats."
Three Legs, Four Wings
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
"South of Dàruò Mountain,
Kuáng Water emerges
and flows into the Yī River.
There are many three-legged turtles."
Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì states:
"On the fifth layer of Kūnlún,
there are divine turtles with four wings."
Pure Green, Emerald Hairs
The Shàngshū·Zhōnghòu states:
"When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent for seven years,
he established rituals and music.
King Chéng looked towards Luò,
sank a jade disc,
and after the ceremony concluded,
the king withdrew.
There was a dark turtle with pure green and a bluish glow,
its back shell inscribed with writing.
It ascended to the altar,
and crimson patterns formed characters,
which the Duke of Zhōu transcribed."
Xú Zhànzhī's Cuì Guī Biǎo states:
"A man from Jùróng County
captured a turtle.
Its body was covered in emerald hairs,
and it soared through clouds and flew in flocks."
Dà Méng, Yuán Xù
The Huáinánzǐ states:
"The Zhōu people's simple jade tablets
originate from ancient stones;
the divine turtle Dà Méng
emerges from gullies and ravines."
Liú Jìngshū's Yì Yuàn states:
"During the Wú period,
a man entered the mountains
and saw a large turtle.
He carried it back,
intending to present it to the King of Wú.
At night, he stayed in Yuè Village,
tying his boat beneath a mulberry tree.
In the middle of the night,
the tree suddenly called out to the turtle:
'Yuán Xù, how did you end up here?'
The turtle replied:
'I traveled without choosing an auspicious day,
and now I am about to be cooked.
Even so,
even if all the firewood from the southern mountains were used,
it could not boil me.'"
Cáo Zhí of Wèi's "Shén Guī Fù"
Turtles are said to live a thousand years.
Once, someone gave me a turtle,
but it died after a few days,
its flesh completely withered away,
leaving only its shell.
Moved by this, I composed a rhapsody,
saying:
"I praise the virtuous establishment of the Four Numinous Creatures,
each dwelling hidden in one direction.
The Azure Dragon coils atop the eastern peak,
the White Tiger roars on the western ridge.
The Dark Warrior gathers at the northern gate,
the Vermilion Bird perches in the southern lands.
They follow benevolent winds to wax and wane,
responding to sagely times before taking flight.
Alas, the divine turtle, this wondrous creature,
embodies the natural essence of heaven and earth.
Below, it levels with the earth as its model;
above, it curves like the vaulted sky as its law.
It follows yīn and yáng in its breath,
hiding its brilliance in deep springs.
It feeds on floating dust to nourish its qì,
drinks inexhaustible morning dew.
Its graceful steps rise and fall with ease,
at times turning like a luán, gazing like a crane.
Suddenly, millennia pass without concern,
circling boundlessly within the primal essence.
Moved by the white spirit's soaring flight,
yet ultimately not spared from Yù Qiě.
Though treasured in ancestral temples,
it suffers the grave fate of being carved and stripped.
Wishing to lament to the Supreme Deity,
it would feel ashamed before swimming fish.
Fearing peril in sinking mud,
it seeks fragrant lotuses to nest and dwell.
Content in dark clouds, loving tranquility,
it does not soar wildly or change its ways.
In ancient times, Yán Zhōu upheld integrity,
invoking this spirit as a parable.
Alas, fortune's path is fraught with hardship;
by the riverbank, it was encountered and captured.
Returned to cage and pen, confined in seclusion,
it met a benevolent man of sincere virtue.
By day, gazing and watching until dusk,
by night, comforted until dawn.
Meeting calamitous disaster, it fell,
its life cut short, never to revive.
Heaven's way is obscure, not yet clear;
divine spirits are hidden, hard to illuminate.
Huáng Shì vanished in empty marshes,
Sōng and Qiáo transformed into stumps.
Snakes shed scales on level shores,
dragons molt bones in deep valleys.
Clearly, all things undergo change;
I suspect this spirit merely shed its shell."
Běi Qí Zhào Rúzōng's "Yǒng Guī Shī"
Having spirit, it can entrust dreams;
without intent, it understands self-preservation.
Unable to lie beneath the yarrow,
it stubbornly roams atop lotuses.
Bearing the chart is not its hope;
propping the bed is but an empty stay.
If granted to drag its tail once,
it would surely turn its head time and again.
Jìn Guō Pú's "Ěryǎ Guī Zàn"
Heaven-born divine creature,
the turtle of ten pairs.
Some roam in fire,
some roam among yarrow.
Though said to differ in kind,
their forms share one return.
Diligently applied for use,
exhausting numbers, fulfilling subtleties.
Cicada, Twelfth
The Erya says:
"Tiáo,
diào.
Láng
liáng.
Tiáo, tángtiáo, zhá,
zhá.
Qīngqīng, jié, máotiáo, mián,
mí jiān fǎn.
Mǎtiáo, ní, hántiáo."
Sūn Yán says:
"Láng,
possesses all five colors.
Tiáo,
is the small green cicada within the palace.
Miányǎn has a green mouth,
is a small cicada."
Guō Pú's annotation states:
"Tiáoláng is commonly called húchán,
in Jiāngnán it is called tánglì,
resembling a cicada but smaller,
with patterns,
in Jiāngdōng, jié is called máo.
Jié resembles a cicada but is small and green,
also called mǎchán,
the largest among cicadas.
Ní,
is hánjiāng,
resembling a cicada but smaller,
green and red."
Yáng Xióng's Fāngyán says:
"Shéjué,
shé pronounced xī.
Jué pronounced jué.
In Qí it is called xīlù,
in Chǔ it is called línggū,
pronounced líng.
In Qín it is called shéjué.
East of the pass it is called diāoliáo,
the first character pronounced diāo,
the second pronounced liáo.
Or it is called tíliáo,
the first character pronounced tí.
Or it is called tíngmù.
Tíng.
In Western Chǔ and Qín it is commonly named,
in Jiāngdōng it is called tíliáo.
In Chǔ it is called tiáo,
between Sòng and Wèi it is called tángtiáo,
now húchán.
Between Chén and Zhèng it is called lángtiáo,
between Qín and Jìn it is called chán,
between Hǎi and Dài it is called jì.
Jì.
The large ones are called láo,
or called miánmǎ,
the small ones are called màizhá.
Zá.
Those with patterns are called qīngqīng,
the female is called zǔ.
Pronounced zǔ yī fǎn.
Large and black ones are called zhàn,
zhàn.
Black and red ones are called nítiáo.
Láo is called máotiáo,
yīng is called hántiáo.
Hántiáo,
is àntiáo."
These various cicada names,
all come from the Erya,
but many are contradictory or erroneous,
and cannot be relied upon in detail.
Yīng pronounced yīng.
The Shuōwén says:
"Chán,
makes sound with its wings."
The Lǐjì says:
"In the mid-summer month, cicadas begin to sing,
in the first month of autumn, cold cicadas sing."
Xú Guǎng's Chēfú Zázhù says:
"Attendant officials add diāochán,
taking its purity, drinking dew and not eating."
Wáng Chōng's Lùnhéng says:
"Qícáo transforms into fùyù,
fùyù turns into chán,
growing two wings,
unlike qícáo."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Cicadas have no mouth but sing,
and die after thirty days.
Chán, míng, húchán, diāoliáo, máochán,
in total five kinds."
The Máo Shī says:
"Alas, you Yīn-Shāng,
like tiáo, like táng."
Tiáo,
is chán;
táng,
is yǎn.
The Erya says:
"Lángtiáo,
possesses all five colors.
Tángtiáo,
commonly called húchán.
Yīng, máotiáo,
resembles a cicada but is small and green.
Mián, mǎtiáo,
the largest among cicadas.
Ní, hántiáo."
Is hánjiāng,
small, green, and red.
The Lǐjì·Yuèlìng says:
"In the mid-summer month, tiáo begin to sing,
in the last month of autumn, cold cicadas sing."
The Tángōng:
"Fàn has a crown and chán has ruí."
The Zhōushū says:
"Five days after the summer solstice,
tiáo begin to sing.
If they do not sing,
noble ministers become dissolute;
on the day of the beginning of autumn,
cold cicadas sing.
If they do not sing,
ministers do not strive diligently."
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì says:
"Cicadas have no strength,
therefore they do not eat."
The Fāngyán says:
"Chán,
in Chǔ is called tiáo,
between Sòng and Wèi it is called tángtiáo,
between Chén and Zhèng it is called lángtiáo,
between Qín and Jìn it is called chán,
between Hǎi and Dài it is called jì,
or called miánmǎ.
The small ones are called língzhé,
those with patterns are called qīngqīng.
The female is called pǐ,
large and black ones are called jiàn,
black and red ones are called ní."
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Cicadas drink but do not eat,
and molt after thirty days."
It also says:
"Cicadas have no mouth but sing,
a natural phenomenon."
The Fēngtǔjì says:
"In the seventh month, huìgū sing in the morning,
hánjiāng sing in the evening."
Drinking dew Listening to the wind
Xú Guǎng's Chēfú Zázhù says:
"Attendant officials add diāochán,
taking its drinking dew and not eating."
Fù Xuán's Chán Fù says:
"Listening to the autumn wind and singing in harmony."
Chirping in the courtyard Flying over water
The Dǒng Zhòngshū Dáwèn says:
"Niú Hēng asked Dǒng Zhòngshū:
'Cicadas are named Qínǚ,
why?'
He replied:
'In the past, the queen of the King of Qí,
resented the king and died,
her corpse transformed into a cicada,
ascended a courtyard tree and chirped mournfully.
The king regretted it,
hence called Qínǚ.'" The Wénzǐ says:
"Flying birds return to their homeland,
rabbits run back to their burrows.
Foxes die with their heads toward the hill,
hánjiāng fly over water.
Each depends on where it was born,
Ní, hántiáo."
Guō Pú's annotation of the Erya says:
"Ní,
is hánjiāng."
Chǔ Chǔjiè's "Ode to the Cicada in the Wind"
The autumn wind arrives in the courtyard,
And on the tall willows, cicadas sing.
Sometimes a lone chant briefly breaks,
Then a chaotic chorus suddenly links again.
Hanging dark tassels, their hissing settles;
Avoiding the yellow sparrow, their voices shift.
For the sorrowful, it is easy to startle—
Listening quietly stirs wounded feelings.
Hearing cicadas, one never tires;
Again, the wind arises between them.
In the end, they do not compare trees to loneliness,
But instead drink dew, shining in glory.
Wèi Prince Chén, Cáo Zhí's "Ode to the Cicada"
Only the cicada is pure and clean,
Hiding its kind in the great shade.
In the blazing sun of midsummer,
It begins to wander in fragrant woods.
Within, it holds harmony and does not eat,
With all things, it has no demands.
Perched on high branches, it lifts its head,
Rinsing with the clear flow of morning dew.
Hidden in the dense leaves of tender mulberry,
It delights in quiet dwelling to escape the heat.
Bitterly, the yellow sparrow brings harm;
It fears the mantis’s strong axe.
There is a fluttering, cunning boy,
Who applies a subtle stickiness and entangles me.
He delivers my body to the cook,
Returning to fiery coals to be roasted.
Autumn frost falls thickly by night,
The summer wind fiercely passes the courtyard.
The air, grievous and oppressive, weakens my frame;
My feet clutch the wood but lose the stem.
Chanting hoarsely, it ends in ruin;
Appearing withered, it loses its form.
Jìn Fù Xián's "Ode to Sticking a Cicada"
The cherry tree gives much shade,
And its fruit ripens early.
There was a cicada singing there,
So I ordered it caught with sticky paste.
Reflecting later, while the cicada delighted in this tree,
It did not know the sticky trap was coming.
Just as humans delight in wealth and honor,
And do not anticipate disaster’s approach.
There is a precious tree with fine fruit,
Lush and broadly covering my courtyard.
In the glaring height of summer,
Alone, solemn and self-purifying.
So I gazed and looked all around,
And saw a singing cicada on a slender branch.
Sheltered by emerald leaves, it chants long,
Truly its joy lies here.
If one delights in what pleases,
One never knows the sticky trap is coming.
It is not that your fate is especially thin,
But you seek comfort and forget danger.
Alas, those who long indulge in favor,
Let this sight serve as self-admonishment.
Jìn Lù Shìlóng's "Ode to the Cicada"
In the past, people praised the chicken for having five virtues,
And writers composed odes to it.
As for the cold cicada,
Its talents match those beauties,
Yet no one has thought of it,
And none have described it thus.
Now, having tassels on its head,
Is its pattern;
Containing breath and drinking dew,
Is its purity;
Not consuming millet or grain,
Is its integrity;
Dwelling without building nests,
Is its frugality;
Responding to the season and keeping constancy,
Is its trustworthiness;
Adding a crown and headdress,
Takes its appearance.
The gentleman takes up its conduct,
Can serve his lord,
Can establish himself—
Is it not the insect of highest virtue?
Ah, the cold cicada, sensing the cycle,
Greets the fine season and then journeys.
It holds the harmonious breath of the two realms,
Receives the pure spirit of primal heaven.
Its body, genuine and refined in fine substance,
Ejects mournful sounds, delicate and clear.
In form, lovely as the summer cicada;
In voice, beautiful as the musical scales.
Fluttering like flying flames stirred by startling wind,
Ethereal like light clouds adorning the great sun.
Then it shakes its long tassels to show its head,
Spreads light wings for swift flight.
Scoops the falling dew of morning blossoms,
Holds misty warmth for evening meal.
Gazes north to the woods where phoenixes fly,
Gathers on dense trees where dragons coil.
As for when the year draws to its close,
The heavens turn cold.
Sensing the cycle, its sad voice
Makes poor scholars hold sorrow.
Some sing of my long journey,
Some chant of that one without robes.
Yuán Sī sighed in his thatched hut,
The lonely bamboo chanted at Shǒuyáng.
It does not wear grass to defile itself,
Nor toils its body to build a nest.
Its will is higher than the cuckoo,
Its integrity subtler than the owl.
It clings to a dry branch to dwell forever,
Leans on tall woods’ winding twigs.
Then it is adorned with a dark crown,
Enhanced as head ornament.
Reflecting patterned creatures on vermilion robes,
It manifests fragrance and bright virtue.
Sòng Yán Yánzhī's "Ode to the Cold Cicada"
At first, desolate and gathered in chant,
Finally, graceful and alone, it draws out.
The Yuè traveler intones a song crossing the Zhāng;
The Dài horse yearns for the faith of heading to Yān.
It does not borrow tassels from a Fàn crown,
Nor carves its body for human rank.
It breaks on the clear gale and sinks down,
Clusters on high trees, then drifts and falls.
Táng Tàizōng Wén Huángdì's "Poem on the Weak Willow and Autumn Cicada"
Scattered shadows on jade steps, the willow;
Holding emerald, it hides a singing cicada.
Tiny form concealed among leaves,
Chaotic chorus born before the wind.
Liáng Chǔ Yún's "Poem on Chanting the Cicada"
Avoiding sparrows among tall branches,
Flying in empty, ornate hall curves.
In cold skies, its chirps often grow hoarse;
As dusk falls, its sounds grow ever faster.
Dense chants as if about to end,
Long notes still linking one to another.
Drinking dew does not show purity;
Light body knows contentment easily.
Liáng Xiāo Zǐfàn's "Poem on Hearing Cicadas in the Back Hall"
Trying to follow the faint breeze far,
Casually with summer leaves’ profusion.
Lightly flying to avoid Chǔ sparrows,
Drinking dew, it enters Wú gardens.
Flowing notes wind through clustered beans;
Remaining echoes cut through high galleries.
May I ask the border-town traveler—
Wounded feelings, how can they be spoken?
Later Liáng Shěn Jūnyōu's "Poem with Lù Tíngwèi on the Early Startled Cicada"
As dusk falls, wild winds arise;
Wood cicadas await the season to sing.
Gazing at branches, I guess several spots;
Searching the air, I fix on a few sounds.
In secluded places, chanting never ceases;
Leaves stir, clamor startles the flock.
Only the magistrate of Héyáng
Especially dislikes the autumn wings’ lightness.
Chén Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on the Sparse Cold Tree and Evening Cicada"
Cold cicadas clamor in the poplars and willows;
Northern blasts assail the parasol trees.
Leaves distant, flying hard to stay;
Branches broken, shadows all empty.
Sounds sparse after drinking dew,
Chants cut off as snapped strings.
Still, due to the shaking, falling place,
Loneliness exhausts the autumn wind.
Also, "Poem on the Autumn Cicada Scorching the Willow, in Response to Prince Héngyáng's Command"
Autumn geese sketch the distant sky;
Garden willows gather startled cicadas.
Competing in clamor on long branches,
Striving to fly before falling leaves.
Wind high, they know their chirps are urgent;
Near trees, one feels the sounds connect.
Long willows drain their scorching cries—
How could they know Cài Yōng’s strings?
Chén Liú Shān's "Poem on Chanting the Cicada"
Its voice flows in the Shànglín Park;
Its shadow enters the attendant’s cap.
If it can drink dark heaven’s dew,
Why refuse the tall willow’s cold?
Yú Shìnán's "Poem on the Autumn Cicada"
Dangling tassels, it drinks clear dew;
Flowing notes emerge from sparse parasol trees.
Perched high, its voice naturally carries far—
Not because it borrows the autumn wind.
Lǐ Bǎiyào's "Ode to the Cicada"
With a pure heart, it drinks dew on its own,
Its mournful cry suddenly chants in the wind.
Before it ascends beside the ornate cap,
It startles first amidst the shaded leaves.
Suí Dynasty Yán Zhītuī's "Poem on Listening to the Singing Cicada"
Listen to the autumn cicada,
The autumn cicada grieves,
Not in just one place.
Slender willows, high-flying at dusk,
Tall poplars, bright moon at dawn.
Chaotic, they raise autumn sounds,
Uneven, they disturb a person's thoughts.
A lone chant is like a turning flute,
A chorus of noise mimics tuning pipes.
Suddenly drifting, lingering sounds,
Often containing broken, severed notes.
Hanging in shade, it finds its own joy,
Drinking dew, it alone is pure.
Short tassels—what is there to prize?
Thin wings—not ashamed of being light.
Hidden under the mantis, particularly hard to see,
On the jadeite pole's tip, extremely easy to startle.
Appearance and demeanor originally from the Guìlín Garden,
With no affairs, lingering in the Nándǒu City.
Within the city, the emperor's domain,
Jīn, Zhāng, Xǔ, and Shǐ.
Power and influence hot as boiling water,
Ardor and spirit clamorous through the city.
Sword glints like shooting stars falling,
Horse colors like floating clouds rising.
Tripods and stands display dragon and phoenix,
Metal and stone harmonize gōng and zhǐ.
Within the passes, full of Jì Xīn's heart,
West of the passes, abundant with Confucius.
How could one use the state-founding ministers of Duke Yú?
Who loves the traveling persuaders of King Hán?
Rosy cheeks, once like spring flowers,
White temples, in a moment, turn to autumn splendor.
The heart and guts have their own limits,
How can they bear to be made a turning wheel cart?
Liáng Dynasty Emperor Jiǎnwén's "Poem on Listening to the Early Cicada"
Grass-drinking, inscribed with first calls,
Cicada thoughts, after flowers fall.
Suddenly drinks the dew of Sānwēi,
At times shades under the five-officer willow.
Zhuāng's painting, the western roc's wings,
Wèi's rhapsody, fitting the cicada's head.
The cassia tree allows one to linger,
Do not say the mountain stay is long.
Liáng Dynasty Chǔ Yún's "Poem on the Cicada"
Avoiding sparrows among fragrant branches,
Flying in the empty, ornate hall's corners.
Cold sky, its chirps frequently hoarse,
Sunset, its sounds grow more urgent.
Dense chants as if about to end,
Long tones still continue one after another.
Drinking dew is not for pure robes,
Light body easily knows contentment.
Liáng Dynasty Fàn Yún's "Ode to the Early Cicada"
Sound follows the spring stream, faint,
Should be as light as autumn dust.
Auspicious tassels dip celestial fluid,
Flying yellow receives the clear dew.
Chén Dynasty Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Poem on the Sparse Cicada in Cold Trees at Dusk"
Cold cicadas clamor in the willow trees,
Northern blasts assail the paulownia.
On leaves, flying hard to stay,
Branches broken, shadows together empty.
Sound sparse after drinking dew,
Song cut off within broken strings.
Still because of the withering place,
Desolate, exhausted by autumn wind.
Also
Autumn geese sketch the distant sky,
Garden willows gather startled cicadas.
Finally clamor within long branches,
Struggle to fly before dense trees.
Wind high, knows the chirping urgent,
Trees near, feel the sounds connected.
Long fields, the cries flow to exhaustion,
How would they recognize Cài Yōng's strings?
Chén Dynasty Liú Shān's "Ode to the Cicada"
Sound flows to the Shànglín Garden,
Shadow enters the guardian minister's cap.
Gaining drink of dark heaven's dew,
Why refuse the tall willow's cold?
Suí Dynasty Wáng Yóulǐ's "Poem on the Cicada Singing in the Tall Willow"
Garden willows chant coolness long,
Chirping cicadas respond to season, startled.
Dew below, tassels constantly damp,
Wind high, wings turn lighter.
Leaves sparse, flying more distant,
Autumn sounds ring clear on their own.
Why speak of hiding among branches?
Thus entering Cài's zither sounds.
Suí Dynasty Jiāng Zǒng's "Ode to the Cicada"
White dew, cool breezes blow,
Vermilion brightness, setting sun shifts.
Singing branches clamor in forest willows,
Flowing sounds pervade terraces and pools.
Yú Shìnán's "Ode to the Cicada"
Dangling tassels drink the clear breeze,
Flowing sound emerges from sparse paulownia.
Residing high, its voice travels far naturally,
Not by relying on the autumn wind.
Butterfly, Thirteenth
Cuī Bào's "Annotations on Past and Present" states:
"Jiádié (butterfly),
also called yě'é (wild moth),
also called fēngdié (wind butterfly).
In Jiāngdōng, it is called tàmù.
It is the one with white color and green back.
There are those as large as a bat,
either black,
or with green spots,
named fèngzǐ,
also called fèngchē,
also called guǐchē.
They live among orange trees south of the Yangtze."
"Sōushénjì" states:
"Rotten reeds become crickets,
wheat becomes butterflies."
"Lièzǐ" states:
"Língxì (plantain) getting damp soil becomes wūzú,
this is containment and mutual generation.
Its leaves become butterflies."
"Lièzǐ" states:
"The root of wūzú becomes qícáo (grub),
its leaves become butterflies."
Cuī Bào's "Annotations on Past and Present" states:
"Jiádié, also called yě'é,
also called fēngdié.
Eastern people call it tàmò.
It is the one with white color and green back.
There are those as large as a bat,
either black,
or with red spots,
named fèngzǐ.
Also called fèngchē,
also called guǐchē.
They live in citrus orchards south of the Yangtze."
"Continued Annotations on Past and Present" states:
"Turtles and soft-shelled turtles have no males,
bees and butterflies have no females."
Entering Dreams, Sporting in the Garden
"Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"Once, Zhuāng Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
a fluttering butterfly indeed,
perfectly content in its own way,
unaware of being Zhōu.
Suddenly he awoke,
and there he was, solidly Zhōu.
He did not know whether Zhōu had dreamed he was a butterfly,
or the butterfly was dreaming it was Zhōu!"
Ancient Yuèfǔ song lyrics "Jiádiéxíng":
"Butterfly wanders, butterfly frolics, sporting in the eastern garden,
how could it suddenly meet the March nurturing swallow,
which seized it among the alfalfa."
Transforming Silkworm, Molting
"Hàn Shílù" states:
"Right Gate Guard General-in-Chief Xǔ Qiān said:
'I received orders to go to Fù Prefecture.
Reaching Dàicūn in Fùpíng County,
there were [silkworms] covering several li.
One evening, it was said they all transformed into butterflies and flew away.'"
"Lǐngbiǎo Lùyì" states:
"On the leaves of hèzǐcǎo, in spring twin insects are born,
eating all its leaves.
Yuè women collect them in their dressing cases,
raising them like silkworms,
picking the leaves to feed them.
When the insects age and stop eating,
they molt into butterflies.
The butterflies are reddish-yellow.
Women collect and wear them,
Zhuāng Zhōu Dreams; Children Chase Butterflies
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Once, Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
a fluttering butterfly indeed,
and did not know he was Zhōu.
When Zhōu awoke,
he was startled to find himself Zhōu.
He did not know whether Zhōu had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly was dreaming of being Zhōu.
Between Zhōu and the butterfly,
there must certainly be a distinction.
This is called the transformation of things."
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"Children with their hair in tufts abandon a thousand pieces of gold to chase butterflies;
the Yuè people discard the eight delicacies and find snakes and turtles sweet."
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, "Ode to a Butterfly"
Evening mist rises in the empty garden,
Carefree and alone, I have not yet returned.
Emergent plumes hide in the tall willows,
Red lotuses brush against water's gown.
Once more these butterflies follow the wind,
In pairs they fly upon the flowers.
I send word to those who know my heart,
May our shared resolve never be broken.
Liú Xiàochuò of Liáng, "Ode to a Plain Butterfly"
Following bees, it circles the green huì orchids,
Avoiding sparrows, it hides among the blue ferns.
Reflecting the sun, it suddenly vies to rise,
Riding the wind, it briefly returns together.
Appearing and disappearing, seen among the flowers,
Unevenly, it flies at the edges of leaves.
Fortunate fragrant blossoms, do not fade,
This fine tree wishes to rely on you.
Xú Fǎng of Liáng, "Poem on a Butterfly Alighting on Grass, in Response to a Command"
In the autumn garden, the flowers have all fallen,
The fragrant chrysanthemums come back in number.
Who would have known it was not a dream creation,
Upon waking from sleep, it still constantly flies.
Ancient Music Bureau, "Song of the □ Butterfly"
Butterfly wanders, butterfly roams in my eastern garden,
Alas, it has not yet returned?
In the third month, the swallows nurture their young,
Playing together among the alfalfa.
Ancient Poem
The butterfly flies high in the morning,
By evening it rests among the mulberry trees.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, "Ode to a Butterfly"
Evening mist drifts in the empty garden,
Carefree and alone, I have not yet returned.
Emergent plumes hide in the tall willows,
Red lotuses brush against water's gown.
Once more these butterflies follow the wind,
In pairs they fly upon the flowers.
I send word to those who know my heart,
May our shared resolve never be broken.
Xú Fǎng of Liáng, "Poem on a Butterfly Alighting on Grass"
In the autumn garden, the flowers have all fallen,
The fragrant chrysanthemums have not yet returned in number.
Who would have known it was not a dream creation,
Upon waking from sleep, it still constantly flies.
Firefly, Fourteenth

is also called 'illuminator'."
The *Guǎngyǎ* says:

is the phosphorescence of the firefly."
The *Lǐjì* says:

rotten grass turns into fireflies."
The *Dàdàilǐ‧Xià Xiǎozhèng* says:
"The red bird presents the white bird.
The red bird,
refers to the dānliáng.
The white bird,
refers to the mosquito.
The reason they are called 'birds',
is to emphasize their being nurtured.
All creatures with wings are called birds.
'Presents' means
to offer,
but not to eat completely."

Bird Presents; Repels Horse
The *Dàdàilǐ* says:
"The red bird presents the white bird."
The *Huáinán Wànbì Shù* says:
"Fireflies repel horses."
The annotation says:
"Take fireflies, wrap them in sheepskin,
and place them in the earth.
Horses see them and neigh,
retreating, not daring to proceed."
Transforms Grass; Flowing Gold
The *Yì Tōng Guà Yàn* says:

Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Fireflies" says:

like red blossoms illuminating petals.
Fluttering and flickering,
like flowing gold within sand."
Jǐngtiān; Huīyè
Both seen in the narrative.
Night Illuminator; Nightly Traveler
The *Běncǎo* says:

"Nightly traveler" see above.
Flowing Gold; Bears Fire
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Fireflies" says:

A tradition says:
"The firefly bears fire on its face, yet is cold."
Lights Books; Repels Horse
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Chē Yìn's family was poor and had no oil.
He gathered fireflies in a silk bag
to illuminate his nighttime reading."
The *Huáinánzǐ Wàn Shù* says:

wrap them in sheepskin,

Horses see them and neigh,

Rotten Grass Transforms; Damp Ground Produces
The *Géwù Lùn* says:
"Fireflies are transformed from the roots of rotten grass and rotten bamboo.
Initially, they are not yet like insects,
but already have light beneath their bellies.
After several days, they change and can fly."
It also says:
"Fireflies are born in shady, damp ground,
around the time of the Great Heat,
obtaining the qi of the great fire and transforming into this illuminating creature."
Fù Xián of the Western Jìn, “Rhapsody on Fireflies”
Hidden in the empty hall, so silent and still,
My thoughts wander far, finding no peace.
Through the long night, wakeful and alert,
Quiet sorrow brings many wounds.
I lament how this light vanishes like smoke,
Born near decaying grass, transformed into life.
Moved by the poet’s distant thoughts,
I gaze upon the flickering glow in the front courtyard.
Not despising its humble form,
It seeks to add radiance to the great pure heavens.
Though it cannot supplement the sun and moon,
It hopes to illuminate its own lowly shape.
When the morning sun hides its light,
It must journey through the dark of night.
Advancing, it does not rival heaven’s brightness;
Retreating into obscurity, it still shines.
Truly it resembles the worthy minister,
Who, though distant and excluded, offers utmost loyalty.
Thus from a small thing, great principles are drawn—
This is what the writer celebrates.
Borrowing its light to make you bright,
It may yet exemplify loyalty and steadfastness.
Pān Yuè of the Western Jìn, “Rhapsody on Fireflies”
Soaring in the dark mystery of the great yīn,
Holding nocturnal radiance, it roams in purity.
Gleaming like a flying bolt of lightning vanishing at night,
Twinkling like a shifting star flowing through clouds.
Moving, it gathers the sun’s brilliance,
Blazing like a Suí pearl.
Sparkling, shimmering,
Like cinnabar blossoms illuminating petals.
Fluttering, glimmering,
Like flowing gold upon sand.
Now flying, now alighting,
Its light and color are truly splendid.
No sound, no scent,
Its bright shadow stretches afar.
It sips morning dew in the open wilds,
Sheltered beneath a single hanging leaf.
It has no desires toward the myriad things,
How could it fear or heed the snares?
And when the night is doubly dark,
With wind, rain, and deepening gloom,
All things bewildered and confused,
Alone it flutters on its journey.
Its wondrous form shines bright,
In darkness, it grows more glorious.
Like the wise and virtuous in their time,
When the age is benighted, their Way shines clear.
Like orchid fragrance in seclusion,
Surpassing all scents, growing ever sweeter.
Drifting with yīn and yáng,
It does not strive for food or drink.
Asked why the katydid knows no fear,
It aspires to the purity of Yí and Huì.
Admiring the exquisite beauty of this tiny insect,
I take up my colored brush to compose an inscription.
Xiāo Hé of the Liáng, “Matching the Rhapsody on Fireflies”
I open a book to amuse myself,
Delighting in night-flying grass-fireflies.
Now by the railing they gleam and turn,
Or near the window they spread their light.
Suddenly soaring, then briefly hidden,
At times climbing the sky, shining brighter.
Bamboo casts shadows past the window,
Orchids send fragrance on the breeze.
At this moment, leisurely joy is strong,
The fine night lingers on.
Gazing at Cháng’é’s clear radiance,
Watching the flickering crowds at play.
Like fire flying over dry sand,
Like stars flowing in the clear Milky Way.
Entering the dark night, their light pure,
Leaving bright lamps, their color dim.
Sometimes by the pond they cast rippling reflections,
Floating together with the constellations.
Noticing the night-watch tallies nearly spent,
I see their faint glow gradually fade.
Then as the slanting moon sinks west,
Shining alone on thatch and pillars,
I watch the dawn river low in the Han,
Hear the distant sound of awaiting tide.
See the fading stars lose their color,
Observe morning birds on their early flight.
I grieve that Fúsāng spews forth its light,
Obscuring this tiny form, leaving it dim.
To express what my heart has not fully said,
I take up my brush to write my feelings.
Pān Yuè of the Jìn, “Rhapsody on Fireflies”
Praising the essence of the flickering glow,
Transcendent and unique among its kind.
The Eastern Hills feel it and sigh deeply,
The traveler sighs, remembering Xià.
Soaring in the dark mystery of the great yīn,
Holding nocturnal radiance, it roams in purity.
Gleaming like a flying flame in nightly wanderings,
Bright as a shifting star flowing through clouds.
Moving, it gathers swift brilliance,
Blazing like falling pearls.
Sparkling, shimmering,
Like fine cinnabar illuminating petals.
Fluttering, glimmering,
Like flowing gold upon sand.
Drinking deep dew in the open wilds,
Sheltered beneath a single hanging leaf.
It has no desires toward the myriad things,
How could it fear or heed the snares?
Fù Xián of the Jìn, “Rhapsody on Fireflies”
I once dwelt alone,
Unable to sleep at night,
And saw fireflies.
Moved by the sight,
I took one to light myself,
And composed this rhapsody.
The words say:
“Hidden in the empty hall, so silent,
My thoughts wander far, finding no peace.
Through the long night, wakeful and alert,
Quiet sorrow brings many wounds.
I lament how this light vanishes like smoke,
Born near decaying grass, transformed into life.
Moved by the poet’s distant thoughts,
I gaze upon the flickering glow in the front courtyard.
Not despising its humble form,
It seeks to add radiance… though it cannot supplement the sun and moon.
It hopes to illuminate its own lowly shape,
When the morning sun… it must journey through the dark of night.
Advancing, it does not rival heaven’s brightness;

Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, “Poem on Fireflies”
Once paired with autumn grass,
Now light as the evening breeze.
Soaring skyward like falling stars,
Brushing trees as if blossoms bloom.
Screens seem lit by divine fire,
Curtains gleam like night pearls bright.
If you gather their radiant light,
I would not fear this body’s lightness.
Jì Shàoyú of Liáng, “Poem on Fireflies Flying in Moonlight”
From afar, sometimes veiled by curtains,
Approaching slantwise as if fearing the window.
Toward moonlight, their glow fades away,
By the pond, their shadows double.
Shěn Xuán of Liáng, “Poem on Fireflies”
Fireflies transform from rotting grass,
Their flickering light not constant.
Rain falls but does not dim their glow,
Sunrise, yet they steal its shine.
Alighting on trees like shooting stars,
Gathering on grass like lingering flames.
From afar, they seem to burn,
But grasped, they only gleam.
Yáng Jìn of Chén, “Poem on Autumn Fireflies Illuminating Book Wrappers”
Autumn window, the last glow gone,
Into darkness, early fireflies come.
Suddenly gathering, sharing one hue,
Ever-bright, never falling ash.
Flying shadows scatter like gold dust,
By the curtain, pale book-wrappers open.
Holding light that never fades,
Under night moon, idly they linger.
Yú Shìnán, “Poem on Fireflies”
Fleeting, tiny flowing light,
Fluttering on delicate, weak wings.
Fearful none may know them,
Alone in darkness, they shine.
Lǐ Bǎiyào, “Poem on Fireflies”
Inside, pitying the dim lamp,
Outside, fearing the bright moon.
Not shunning dew’s damp touch,
Only for night’s journey they strive.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng, “Poem on Fireflies”
Once paired with autumn grass,
Now light as the evening breeze.
Soaring skyward like falling stars,
Brushing trees as if blossoms bloom.
Screens seem lit by divine fire,
Curtains gleam like night pearls bright.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng, “Poem on Fireflies”
Alighting on skin, strangely not hot,
Gathering on grass, wondrously smokeless.
Arrayed beneath lamps, they seem dim,
Turning in rain, they appear to burn.
Chén Yángjìn's "Poem on Autumn Fireflies Illuminating Book Wrappers"
Autumn window's lingering light fades away,
Into darkness early fireflies make their way.
Suddenly gathering, sharing the same hue,
Constantly glowing, how could they turn to ash anew?
Flying shadows scatter like golden dust,
Circling curtains, book wrappers open in trust.
Holding brightness, never ceasing to shine,
Under the night moon, idly they intertwine.
Jìn Guō Pú's "In Praise of Fireflies"
Glimmering, they journey through the night,
Tiny insects, delicate and slight.
Born from decaying grass they rise,
Like scattered sparks before our eyes.
